Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 1–2 (part 1 of 2):

Surat Al 'Imran. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ ﴿Allah—there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾ ﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3] ﴿before, as guidance for mankind, and He sent down the Criterion. Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah will have a severe punishment, and Allah is Mighty, Owner of Retribution﴾ [Al 'Imran: 4] ﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in the heaven is hidden from Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 5] ﴿He is the One who forms you in the wombs however He wills. There is no god but Him, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [Al 'Imran: 6] ﴿He is the One who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are precise (muhkamat)—they are the foundation of the Book—and others that are ambiguous (mutashabihat). As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous in it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation. But none knows its interpretation except Allah. And those firmly grounded in knowledge say, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord." And none will be reminded except the people of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7] ﴿"Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us from Yourself mercy. Indeed, You are the Bestower﴾ [Al 'Imran: 8] ﴿"Our Lord, indeed You will gather the people for a Day about which there is no doubt. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 9] ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve—their wealth and their children will not avail them against Allah at all, and they are the fuel of the Fire﴾ [Al 'Imran: 10] ﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh and those before them, who denied Our signs; so Allah seized them for their sins. And Allah is severe in punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 11]

(al-Tawrat): It is a Hebrew noun. The grammarians have labored over its derivation and its morphological pattern, although the grammarians have established that non-Arabic names do not admit derivation and are not measured (by Arabic patterns), meaning Arabic derivation.

As for the derivation of (al-Tawrat), there are two opinions. The first is that it comes from wara al-zand yari, when it strikes and fire appears from it, so the Torah is a light from error. This derivation is the view of the majority. Abu Fayd Muwarraj al-Sadusi held that it is derived from warra (to conceal, to allude), as it is reported that he, when he wanted to travel, would make allusion to something else, because most of the Torah is allusion (tawriya).

As for its pattern, al-Khalil, Sibawayh and the rest of the Basrans held that its pattern is fawʿala, and the taʾ is a substitute for a waw, as it was substituted in tuwlij; so its origin is "wawrat" and its pattern is wawalaja, because both come from warra and from walaja; so it is like hawqala. Al-Farra' held that its pattern is tafʿila, like tawsiya, then the kasra of the ʿayn was changed to a fatha and the yaʾ to an alif, as they said in nasiya and jariya: nasah and jarah.

Al-Zajjaj said: it seems he permits in tawsiya "tawsah," and this is not heard. Some Kufans held that its pattern is tafʿala, with a fatha on the ʿayn, from warraytu bika zanadi (I kindled my fire with you). The imala (inclination) of al-Tawrat is permissible, and it has been read so, as will come, God willing.

(al-Injil): It is also a Hebrew noun, and it should not admit derivation, and it is not measured. They have said its pattern is ifʿil, like ijfil, and it is derived from al-najl, which is the water that seeps from the earth. Al-Khalil said: the earth became najal (moist), and there is najal in it, when water comes out of it. Al-Najl also means offspring and progeny, as said by al-Khalil and others; and najalahu abuhu means his father fathered him. Abu al-Qasim al-Zajjaji related in his Nawadir that the word najl is applied to a child, and that the term is among the words with two opposite meanings. Al-Najl also means throwing something. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Injil is taken from al-najl, which is the origin; this inclines toward what al-Zajjaji related.

Abu al-Fath said: it is from najala, when its offspring appears, or from the emergence of water from the earth; so it is extracted either from the Preserved Tablet or from the Torah. It was also said: it is derived from al-tanajul, which is mutual contention, named so because people contend about it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-Tawrat and al-Injil are two non-Arabic names; their derivation from warya and najl has been strained, and their patterns, mutafʿala and ifʿil, are valid only after they are considered Arabic. End of quote. His words are correct, except that in his statement "mutafʿala" there is a lapse: he did not mention the Basran view that its pattern is fawʿala, and he did not point out, regarding tafʿila, whether its ʿayn is kasra or fatha. It was also said: it is derived from najala al-ʿayn (the eye's tears), as if it widened what was restricted in the Torah.

Al-Intiqam: it is an ifti'al from al-niqma, which is punishment and victory. It was also said: it is punishing for a sin with intensity. It is said: naqama and naqiha, when he disapproved; and intaqama, he punished.

Sawwara: he made for it a form. It was said: it is an intensive form from "sara yusawwiru," when he inclined and turned to a state; and since depiction is inclining to a state and establishing it within, its form came as an intensive. Al-sura is the appearance in which a thing is by composition. Al-Marwazi said: depiction is the initiation of a likeness without anyone having preceded it with its like.

Al-Zaygh: inclination. From it: the sun declined (and the eyes swerved). Al-Raghib said: al-zaygh is inclination away from uprightness toward one of the two sides; zagha, zala and similar are close in meaning, but zagha is used only for what goes from truth to falsehood.

Al-Ta'wil: a verbal noun of awwala, and its meaning is the end of a thing and its outcome, as said by al-Raghib. Others said: ta'wil is the return and the reference. He said:
"I refer the ruling to its proper course; my judgment is not by unjust desire."

Al-Rusukh: firmness. He said:
"Indeed my love for Layla has taken root in the heart; her days refused that it should change."

Al-Hibah: a voluntary gift. One says: wahaba yahibu hibatan. Its origin is that the present tense comes as yafʿilu with a kasra on the ʿayn, and therefore the waw was dropped since it fell between a yaʾ and a kasra. But since the ʿayn is a throat letter, it was given a fatha with consideration of the implied kasra, as in wada'a yada'u. However, this one was given a fatha because its last radical is a throat letter. Originally they are yuwhibu and yuwdi'u. And wahaba may mean "made," in which case it takes two objects. The Arabs say: wahabani Allah fidaka, that is, "may Allah make me your ransom." In this sense it is not conjugated, so with this meaning only the past tense is used.

Ladun: an adverb, and it is rarely separated from "min" (from), as Ibn Jinni said. Its meaning is the starting point of a limit in time or place, or other non-spatial things. It is indeclinable according to most Arabs, and its inflection is a Qaysi dialect feature. This is when it has a fatha on the lam, a damma on the dal, and the nun follows. Those who make it indeclinable say that because it resembles particles in having one fixed usage and not admitting being the subject of a predication, unlike ʿinda and ladayya, which do not have one fixed usage, for they can denote starting point and other things, and are used as adjuncts and as core elements. Adjuncts are common, and among core elements is "And with Him are the keys of the unseen" [al-An'am: 59] and "And with Us is a Book that speaks with truth" [al-Mu'minun: 62]. Some explained the reason for indeclinability by saying: its reason is that it indicates adjacency to a thing and is specific to it, unlike ʿinda, which is not specific to adjacency; so in it there is a meaning not indicated by the adverb, but rather of the kind indicated by a particle. It is as if it implicitly contains the particle that should have been set to indicate proximity. Similar are thumma and hunaa, because they were made indeclinable when they came to contain the meaning of the particle that should have been set to indicate reference. Those who inflect it, namely Qays, do so by analogy with ʿinda, because its position is suitable for ʿinda. There are nine dialects other than the first: ladun, ladnun, ladinun, ludnun, ladini, lad and lud, ludu and lat, by changing the dal to a taʾ. It is frequently prefixed to a singular noun, and rarely to a clause. An example of its prefixing to a verbal clause is the poet's words:
"A felled one of women whom he pleased and who pleased him, since youth grew until his locks of hair became black-grey."

And another said:
"We have clung, since you asked us, to your agreement, so let there be no inclination among you toward dissension."

An example of its prefixing to a nominal clause is the poet's words:
"He recalls his luxury since you were young, until you became one with two white temples like the eagle."

It also came prefixed to "an" (that) with a verb. He said:
"And would that ladun did not cut off 'an' and 'layta' (would that), the kinship of a near relative and the right of a Muslim."

The rulings of ladun are numerous and are discussed in the science of grammar.

Al-Ighna': repelling and benefiting. One says: so-and-so has great wealth, that is, he repels and benefits. Al-Da'b: habit. Da'aba 'ala kadha: he persisted in it and was constant. Zuhayr said:
"I will surely set out at dawn, then I will surely keep at it until night, unless a child delays me."

Al-Dhanb: the tail; because punishment follows it, and from it comes dhanb and dhunub, because it follows what pulls.

(p-373) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ ﴿Allah—there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾ This surah, Surat Al 'Imran, is also called al-Zahra' (the Radiant), al-Aman (the Security), al-Kanz (the Treasure), al-Mu'ina (the Helper), al-Mujadila (the Disputing), Surat al-Istighfar (the Surah of Seeking Forgiveness), and Taybah (the Good). It is Medinan. Its verses number sixty. The occasion of its revelation, as mentioned by the majority: "A delegation of Christians of Najran came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; they were sixty riders, among them fourteen of their nobles, three of whom their affairs depended upon: their commander al-Aqib Abd al-Masih, the owner of their caravan al-Sayyid al-Ayham, and their scholar Abu Harithah ibn Alqamah, of the Banu Bakr ibn Wa'il." He mentioned their dignity and fine bearing (p-374) and appearance. They remained in Medina for days, disputing with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about Jesus. At times they claimed he was Allah, at times the son of God, and at times the third of three; while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned to them attributes of the Creator, the Exalted, and their negation regarding Jesus, and they agreed with him on that. Then they refused except denial. Then they said: "O Muhammad, do you not claim that he is the Word of Allah and a spirit from Him?" He said: "Yes." They said: "That is enough for us." So Allah revealed concerning them the beginning of this surah, up to about eighty-odd verses of it, until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invited them to mubahala."

Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning the Jews who hated Jesus, who slandered his mother, and who denied what Allah sent down to him of the Gospel.

The connection of this surah with what precedes it is clear. When He mentioned at the end of al-Baqarah, "You are our Protector, so give us victory over the disbelieving people" [al-Baqarah: 286], it was fitting to mention Allah's victory over the disbelievers, since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ debated them and refuted them with radiant proofs and decisive arguments. Then He recounted their circumstances, refuted their beliefs, mentioned His own exaltation above what they say, and the origin of the creation of Mary and her son Jesus, and so on through what He refuted against them. And since the opening of the last verse of al-Baqarah is, "The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord" [al-Baqarah: 285], this implies belief in Allah and in the Books; so it was fitting to mention the attributes of Allah, what was sent down to His Messenger, and what was sent down to others, may Allah's blessings be upon them.

The seven readers recited "Alif, Lam, Mim, Allah" with a fatha on the mim and without the hamzat al-wasl. Abu Bakr, in some of his transmissions from Asim, read with a sukun on the mim and with a hamza (qat'), and al-Farra' mentioned this reading from Asim. This reading is also reported from al-Hasan, Amr ibn Ubayd, al-Rawasi, al-A'mash, al-Burjumi and Ibn al-Qa'qa', who stopped on the mim just as they stopped on the alif and lam, which is the proper way, and then began after it, as you say: "wahid, ithnan" (one, two).

Abu Hayyan: Abu Hayyah read with a kasra on the mim, which Ibn 'Atiyyah attributed to al-Rawasi, and al-Zamakhshari attributed to Amr ibn Ubayd, saying: he imagined movement because of the meeting of two sukuns, but it is not acceptable. He means this reading. He said, and others said: that is poor, because the ya' prevents it, and the correct reading is the fatha, the reading of most people. Al-Akhfash said: "Alif, Lam, Mim Allah" with a kasra on the mim is permissible because of the meeting of two sukuns. Al-Zajjaj said: this is an error, and the Arabs do not say it because it is heavy.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on 3:1–2 (part 2 of 2):

Scholars differ about the vowel on the *mim* (the *fatha*). Sibawayh held that it was given a vowel because two quiescent letters met (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*, the meeting of two unvocalized consonants), just as they vocalized in *min Allah* ("from Allah"). The *hamzat al-wasl* (the connecting *alif*) drops in continuous speech, as it drops in *min al-rajul* ("from the man"). The *fatha* was preferred over the *kasra* because of the *ya'*, as in their saying *ayna* and *kayfa*, and because the *kasra* would have been added before the *ya'*, so the heaviness disappeared.

Al-Farra' held that the vowel is a *haraka naql* (a transferred vowel) from the *hamzat al-wasl*, because the letters of the alphabet are pronounced with a pause (*yunwa bi-ha al-waqf*), and what follows them is pronounced as a fresh start (*yunwa bi-ma ba'dahā al-isti'naf*). So the *hamza* is treated as if it were still present, as in the hemistichs of verse:

*latasma'unna washikan fi diyarikum * * * Allahu akbaru ya tharat 'Uthmana*

("You will certainly hear soon in your abodes: Allah is greatest! O avengers of Uthman!")

This view is weakened by the scholars' consensus that the *alif* of the definite article is dropped in continuous speech, and what drops does not receive a transferred vowel. This was stated by Abu 'Ali.

Al-Zamakhshari chose al-Farra's view, that the *fatha* on the *mim* is the vowel of the *hamza* after the *hamza* was dropped for lightness. He raised questions and answered them. He said: "If you ask, how can its vowel be placed on the letter before it when it is a *hamzat al-wasl* that does not appear in continuous speech, so its vowel should not appear either, since the vowel's appearance is like its own appearance? I say: this is not continuous speech, because the *mim* is treated as pause and quiescence, and the *hamza* is treated as present. It was dropped for lightness, and its vowel was placed on the preceding quiescent letter to indicate it. A parallel is their saying *wahid ithnan* ("one, two"), with the vowel of the *hamza* placed on the *dal*."

This question and answer are not sound. He claimed that the *mim*, when vowelled, is pronounced as a pause, and that this is not continuous speech but a pause. This contradicts what the Arabs and the grammarians agree upon: one never pauses on a vowelled letter at all, whether its vowel is an *i'rabi* (inflectional), *bina'i* (fixed), *naqli* (transferred), for *iltiqa' al-sakinayn*, for quotation (*hikaya*), or for imitation (*ittiba'*). Thus in *qad aflaha*, if the *hamza* is dropped and its vowel moved to the *dal* of *qad*, you may not pause on the *dal* with a *fatha*. It must be quiescent, by agreement.

As for his statement, "a parallel is their saying *wahid ithnan*, with the vowel of the *hamza* placed on the *dal*": Sibawayh mentioned that they give the last *wahid* a *ishmam* (a partial rounding) because it is fixed (*li-tamakkunihi*). He did not report the *kasra* as a dialect form. If the *kasra* is correct, then *wahid* is not pronounced as a pause, as al-Zamakhshari claimed, nor is its vowel a transferred vowel from the *hamzat al-wasl*. Rather, it is joined to *ithnan*, so two quiescent letters meet, the *dal* of *wahid* and the *tha'* of *ithnayn*. The *dal* is given a *kasra* because of their meeting, and the *hamza* is dropped because it does not appear in continuous speech.

As for the evidence that al-Farra' cited, their saying *thalathatun arba'atun* with the *hamza* placed on the *ha'*: there is no proof in it, because the *hamza* of *arba'a* is a *hamzat qat'* (a full *hamza*) in continuous speech, following what precedes it and beginning the word. This is not like the *hamzat al-wasl* of *min Allah*. Also, their saying *thalathatun arba'atun* with transfer does not involve a pause on *thalatha*. If one paused on it, it would not accept a vowel. Rather, it was kept as a *ha'* in continuous speech, considering what it had become in some state, not because it is a pause.

Then al-Zamakhshari raised a second question: "If you ask, why not claim that it was vowelled because two quiescent letters met?" I say: because the meeting of two quiescent letters does not concern us in pausal position. This is like your saying *hadha Ibrahimu*, *wa-Dawudu*, *wa-Ishaqu*. If the meeting of two quiescent letters in pausal position required vowelling, the two *mim*s of *alif-lam-mim* would have been vowelled because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, and the other quiescent letter would have been awaited."

This question and answer are: the question is sound, and the answer is sound. But the one who said that the vowel was because two quiescent letters met does not imagine that he meant the meeting of the *ya'* and the *mim* in *alif-lam-mim* in pausal position. Rather, he meant the two quiescent letters that are the final *mim* and the *lam* of the article, like the meeting of the *nun* of *min* and the *lam* of *al-rajul* when you say *min al-rajul*.

Then al-Zamakhshari raised a third question: "If you ask: they only failed to vowel for the meeting of two quiescent letters in *mim* because they wished to pause, and they could pronounce two quiescent letters. But when a third quiescent letter comes, vowelling is necessary, so they vowelled." I say: the proof that the vowel is not for the meeting with a quiescent letter is that they could have said *wahid ithnan* with the *dal* quiescent and the *hamza* dropped, joining two quiescent letters, as they said *asyam* and *madyaq*. When they vowelled the *dal*, it was known that its vowel is only the vowel of the dropped *hamza*, and not for the meeting of two quiescent letters.

This question and answer are: "If you ask, why did they not vowel for the meeting of two quiescent letters?" by "the two quiescent letters" he means the *ya'* and the *mim* in *mim*. Then the justification comes with his words: "because they wished to pause and could pronounce two quiescent letters," meaning the *ya'* and the *mim*. Then he said: "If a third quiescent letter comes," meaning the *lam* of the article, "vowelling is necessary," meaning on the *mim*. So they vowelled, meaning the *mim*, because it met a quiescent letter, the *lam* of the article. If they had not vowelled, three quiescent letters would have been gathered, and this is impossible. This is the explanation of the question.

As for al-Zamakhshari's answer to his question, it does not fit. He argued that the vowel is not for meeting a quiescent letter by the possibility of gathering two quiescent letters in their saying *wahid ithnan*, by quiescing the *dal* while the *tha'* is quiescent and the *hamza* drops. But they rejected this possibility in favour of moving the *hamza*'s vowel to the *dal*. This is obstinacy against what is perceived, since this is not possible at all, nor is it within human ability to join in speech the quiescence of the *dal*, the quiescence of the *tha'*, and the dropping of the *hamza*.

As for his statement, "they gathered two quiescent letters," this cannot be gathered, as we have said. As for his statement, "as they said *asyam* and *madyaq*," this is possible, as it is in *rad* and *dall*, because this involves the meeting of two quiescent letters within the limits set for them in grammar, so it can be pronounced. It is not like *wahid ithnan*, because the first quiescent letter is not a letter of weakness (*harf 'illa*), nor is the *tha'* in an assimilated (*mudgham*) letter, so the two cannot be gathered.

As for his statement, "when they vowelled the *dal*, it was known that its vowel is only the vowel of the dropped *hamza* and not for the meeting of two quiescent letters," it is built on the premise that gathering two quiescent letters in *wahid ithnan* is possible. The vowel for the meeting of two quiescent letters is only where they cannot both be present in pronunciation. He claimed that the vowel of the *dal* is the vowel of the dropped *hamza* for the meeting of two quiescent letters. We have already mentioned that this is not possible. If the *kasra* on the *dal* is correct, as this man reported, then its vowel is for the meeting of two quiescent letters and not by transfer.

Al-Farra's view, and al-Zamakhshari's choice of it, has been rejected by the statement: the vowel on the *mim* cannot be the vowel of the *hamza* placed on it, because of the corruption and contradiction in that. The quiescence of the final *mim* is on the intention of pausing on it, while placing the vowel of the *hamza* on it is on the intention of continuous speech. The intention of continuous speech requires dropping the *hamza*, while the intention of pausing on what precedes it requires its presence and separation. This is contradictory. This is a sound refutation.

What has been established from these words is that when the Arabs enumerate names ending in quiescence, both in continuous speech and in pause, if the last quiescent one meets another quiescent letter, it is vowelled because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. So this vowel in the *mim* of *alif-lam-mim Allah* is the vowel of the meeting of two quiescent letters.

The discussion of *alif-lam-mim* (2:1) has preceded in the beginning of al-Baqarah, and the disagreement of people over it is widespread, such that nothing can be established from it to rely on in its interpretation or the interpretation of similar disconnected letters (*al-huruf al-muqatta'a*).

The discussion of *Allahu la ilaha illa Huwa al-Hayyu al-Qayyum* has preceded in the verse *wa-ilahukum ilahun wahid la ilaha* (2:163) and at the beginning of the Verse of the Throne (2:255), so there is no need to repeat it here.

Ibn 'Atiyya reported from al-Qadi al-Jurjani that, regarding the composition (*nazm*), he held that the best view here is that *alif-lam-mim* refers to the letters of the alphabet, as if he were saying: "These letters are your Book," or something similar.

The statement *Allahu la ilaha illa Huwa al-Hayyu al-Qayyum nazzala 'alaykal-kitab* indicates, by what its meaning implies, what has been omitted from it, which is a predicate about the letters. He said: such omission in its composition is like His statement: *afaman sharaha Allahu sadrahu lil-Islami fa-huwa 'ala nurin min rabbihi* (39:22), where the response is omitted, indicated by His statement *fa-wailun lil-qasiyati qulubuhum min dhikri Allah* (39:22). Its estimate is: "like one whose heart is hardened." From this is the poet's saying:

*fala tadfinuni inna dafni muharramun * * * 'alaykum wa-lakin khamiri Umma 'Amir*

("Do not bury me, for my burial is forbidden to you, but leave me to she who is called *Khamiri Umm 'Amir*" [i.e., the fox]).

That is: "but leave me to her who is called *Khamiri Umm 'Amir*."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: this view is good, that the predicate of *Allah* be that *nazzala* (He sent down), so that the sentence connects to this meaning that al-Jurjani mentioned. But there is a point of consideration in it, because its likeness is not correct in resemblance to the meaning he went towards. What he said about the verse is possible, but the more eloquent arrangement of the verse is that *alif-lam-mim* not be joined in meaning to what follows it, and that *Allahu la ilaha illa Huwa al-Hayyu al-Qayyum* be a new, independent sentence, definitely, a sentence refuting the Christians of Najran who came as a delegation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), argued with him about 'Isa son of Maryam, and said: "He is Allah." End of his words.

Ibn Kaysan said: the position of *alif-lam-mim* is in the accusative, and the estimate is: "Recite *alif-lam-mim*," and "upon you *alif-lam-mim*." It may also be in the nominative, meaning "this is *alif-lam-mim*" and "that is *alif-lam-mim*." It was mentioned from al-Jurjani's statement that it may be a subject (*mubtada'*), with its predicate omitted, meaning: "These letters are your Book."

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and 'Alqama ibn Qays read *al-Qayyam*. Kharija said that in the codex of 'Abd Allah it is *al-Qayyim*, and this was also reported from 'Alqama.

*Allah* is in the nominative as a subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is *la ilaha illa Huwa*. *Nazzala 'alaykal-kitab* (3:3) is a predicate after a predicate. It is also possible that *nazzala* is the predicate, and *la ilaha illa Huwa* is a parenthetical sentence (*jumlat i'tiraD*). The detailed discussion of the *i'rab* of *la ilaha illa Huwa al-Hayyu al-Qayyum* has preceded in the Verse of the Throne, so there is no need to repeat it here.

Al-Razi said: the opening of this sūrah is wondrous, because when they disputed, it was as if it were said: either you dispute about knowledge of Allah, or about prophethood. If it is the first, then it is false, because the rational proofs show that He is *Hayy Qayyum* (Ever-Living, Sustainer), and the Ever-Living, Sustainer is impossible to have a child. If it is the second, then it is false, because the path by which you know that Allah Most High sent down the Torah and the Gospel is the very same path that stands here, and that is the miracle (*mu'jiza*).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 1–2 (part 1 of 2):

Surat Al 'Imran. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ ﴿Allah—there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾ ﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [Al 'Imran: 3] ﴿before, as guidance for mankind, and He sent down the Criterion. Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah will have a severe punishment, and Allah is Mighty, Owner of Retribution﴾ [Al 'Imran: 4] ﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in the heaven is hidden from Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 5] ﴿He is the One who forms you in the wombs however He wills. There is no god but Him, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [Al 'Imran: 6] ﴿He is the One who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are precise (muhkamat)—they are the foundation of the Book—and others that are ambiguous (mutashabihat). As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous in it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation. But none knows its interpretation except Allah. And those firmly grounded in knowledge say, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord." And none will be reminded except the people of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7] ﴿"Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us from Yourself mercy. Indeed, You are the Bestower﴾ [Al 'Imran: 8] ﴿"Our Lord, indeed You will gather the people for a Day about which there is no doubt. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 9] ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve—their wealth and their children will not avail them against Allah at all, and they are the fuel of the Fire﴾ [Al 'Imran: 10] ﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh and those before them, who denied Our signs; so Allah seized them for their sins. And Allah is severe in punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 11]

(al-Tawrat): It is a Hebrew noun. The grammarians have labored over its derivation and its morphological pattern, although the grammarians have established that non-Arabic names do not admit derivation and are not measured (by Arabic patterns), meaning Arabic derivation.

As for the derivation of (al-Tawrat), there are two opinions. The first is that it comes from wara al-zand yari, when it strikes and fire appears from it, so the Torah is a light from error. This derivation is the view of the majority. Abu Fayd Muwarraj al-Sadusi held that it is derived from warra (to conceal, to allude), as it is reported that he, when he wanted to travel, would make allusion to something else, because most of the Torah is allusion (tawriya).

As for its pattern, al-Khalil, Sibawayh and the rest of the Basrans held that its pattern is fawʿala, and the taʾ is a substitute for a waw, as it was substituted in tuwlij; so its origin is "wawrat" and its pattern is wawalaja, because both come from warra and from walaja; so it is like hawqala. Al-Farra' held that its pattern is tafʿila, like tawsiya, then the kasra of the ʿayn was changed to a fatha and the yaʾ to an alif, as they said in nasiya and jariya: nasah and jarah.

Al-Zajjaj said: it seems he permits in tawsiya "tawsah," and this is not heard. Some Kufans held that its pattern is tafʿala, with a fatha on the ʿayn, from warraytu bika zanadi (I kindled my fire with you). The imala (inclination) of al-Tawrat is permissible, and it has been read so, as will come, God willing.

(al-Injil): It is also a Hebrew noun, and it should not admit derivation, and it is not measured. They have said its pattern is ifʿil, like ijfil, and it is derived from al-najl, which is the water that seeps from the earth. Al-Khalil said: the earth became najal (moist), and there is najal in it, when water comes out of it. Al-Najl also means offspring and progeny, as said by al-Khalil and others; and najalahu abuhu means his father fathered him. Abu al-Qasim al-Zajjaji related in his Nawadir that the word najl is applied to a child, and that the term is among the words with two opposite meanings. Al-Najl also means throwing something. Al-Zajjaj said: al-Injil is taken from al-najl, which is the origin; this inclines toward what al-Zajjaji related.

Abu al-Fath said: it is from najala, when its offspring appears, or from the emergence of water from the earth; so it is extracted either from the Preserved Tablet or from the Torah. It was also said: it is derived from al-tanajul, which is mutual contention, named so because people contend about it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: al-Tawrat and al-Injil are two non-Arabic names; their derivation from warya and najl has been strained, and their patterns, mutafʿala and ifʿil, are valid only after they are considered Arabic. End of quote. His words are correct, except that in his statement "mutafʿala" there is a lapse: he did not mention the Basran view that its pattern is fawʿala, and he did not point out, regarding tafʿila, whether its ʿayn is kasra or fatha. It was also said: it is derived from najala al-ʿayn (the eye's tears), as if it widened what was restricted in the Torah.

Al-Intiqam: it is an ifti'al from al-niqma, which is punishment and victory. It was also said: it is punishing for a sin with intensity. It is said: naqama and naqiha, when he disapproved; and intaqama, he punished.

Sawwara: he made for it a form. It was said: it is an intensive form from "sara yusawwiru," when he inclined and turned to a state; and since depiction is inclining to a state and establishing it within, its form came as an intensive. Al-sura is the appearance in which a thing is by composition. Al-Marwazi said: depiction is the initiation of a likeness without anyone having preceded it with its like.

Al-Zaygh: inclination. From it: the sun declined (and the eyes swerved). Al-Raghib said: al-zaygh is inclination away from uprightness toward one of the two sides; zagha, zala and similar are close in meaning, but zagha is used only for what goes from truth to falsehood.

Al-Ta'wil: a verbal noun of awwala, and its meaning is the end of a thing and its outcome, as said by al-Raghib. Others said: ta'wil is the return and the reference. He said:
"I refer the ruling to its proper course; my judgment is not by unjust desire."

Al-Rusukh: firmness. He said:
"Indeed my love for Layla has taken root in the heart; her days refused that it should change."

Al-Hibah: a voluntary gift. One says: wahaba yahibu hibatan. Its origin is that the present tense comes as yafʿilu with a kasra on the ʿayn, and therefore the waw was dropped since it fell between a yaʾ and a kasra. But since the ʿayn is a throat letter, it was given a fatha with consideration of the implied kasra, as in wada'a yada'u. However, this one was given a fatha because its last radical is a throat letter. Originally they are yuwhibu and yuwdi'u. And wahaba may mean "made," in which case it takes two objects. The Arabs say: wahabani Allah fidaka, that is, "may Allah make me your ransom." In this sense it is not conjugated, so with this meaning only the past tense is used.

Ladun: an adverb, and it is rarely separated from "min" (from), as Ibn Jinni said. Its meaning is the starting point of a limit in time or place, or other non-spatial things. It is indeclinable according to most Arabs, and its inflection is a Qaysi dialect feature. This is when it has a fatha on the lam, a damma on the dal, and the nun follows. Those who make it indeclinable say that because it resembles particles in having one fixed usage and not admitting being the subject of a predication, unlike ʿinda and ladayya, which do not have one fixed usage, for they can denote starting point and other things, and are used as adjuncts and as core elements. Adjuncts are common, and among core elements is "And with Him are the keys of the unseen" [al-An'am: 59] and "And with Us is a Book that speaks with truth" [al-Mu'minun: 62]. Some explained the reason for indeclinability by saying: its reason is that it indicates adjacency to a thing and is specific to it, unlike ʿinda, which is not specific to adjacency; so in it there is a meaning not indicated by the adverb, but rather of the kind indicated by a particle. It is as if it implicitly contains the particle that should have been set to indicate proximity. Similar are thumma and hunaa, because they were made indeclinable when they came to contain the meaning of the particle that should have been set to indicate reference. Those who inflect it, namely Qays, do so by analogy with ʿinda, because its position is suitable for ʿinda. There are nine dialects other than the first: ladun, ladnun, ladinun, ludnun, ladini, lad and lud, ludu and lat, by changing the dal to a taʾ. It is frequently prefixed to a singular noun, and rarely to a clause. An example of its prefixing to a verbal clause is the poet's words:
"A felled one of women whom he pleased and who pleased him, since youth grew until his locks of hair became black-grey."

And another said:
"We have clung, since you asked us, to your agreement, so let there be no inclination among you toward dissension."

An example of its prefixing to a nominal clause is the poet's words:
"He recalls his luxury since you were young, until you became one with two white temples like the eagle."

It also came prefixed to "an" (that) with a verb. He said:
"And would that ladun did not cut off 'an' and 'layta' (would that), the kinship of a near relative and the right of a Muslim."

The rulings of ladun are numerous and are discussed in the science of grammar.

Al-Ighna': repelling and benefiting. One says: so-and-so has great wealth, that is, he repels and benefits. Al-Da'b: habit. Da'aba 'ala kadha: he persisted in it and was constant. Zuhayr said:
"I will surely set out at dawn, then I will surely keep at it until night, unless a child delays me."

Al-Dhanb: the tail; because punishment follows it, and from it comes dhanb and dhunub, because it follows what pulls.

(p-373) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ ﴿Allah—there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting.﴾ This surah, Surat Al 'Imran, is also called al-Zahra' (the Radiant), al-Aman (the Security), al-Kanz (the Treasure), al-Mu'ina (the Helper), al-Mujadila (the Disputing), Surat al-Istighfar (the Surah of Seeking Forgiveness), and Taybah (the Good). It is Medinan. Its verses number sixty. The occasion of its revelation, as mentioned by the majority: "A delegation of Christians of Najran came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; they were sixty riders, among them fourteen of their nobles, three of whom their affairs depended upon: their commander al-Aqib Abd al-Masih, the owner of their caravan al-Sayyid al-Ayham, and their scholar Abu Harithah ibn Alqamah, of the Banu Bakr ibn Wa'il." He mentioned their dignity and fine bearing (p-374) and appearance. They remained in Medina for days, disputing with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about Jesus. At times they claimed he was Allah, at times the son of God, and at times the third of three; while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned to them attributes of the Creator, the Exalted, and their negation regarding Jesus, and they agreed with him on that. Then they refused except denial. Then they said: "O Muhammad, do you not claim that he is the Word of Allah and a spirit from Him?" He said: "Yes." They said: "That is enough for us." So Allah revealed concerning them the beginning of this surah, up to about eighty-odd verses of it, until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invited them to mubahala."

Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning the Jews who hated Jesus, who slandered his mother, and who denied what Allah sent down to him of the Gospel.

The connection of this surah with what precedes it is clear. When He mentioned at the end of al-Baqarah, "You are our Protector, so give us victory over the disbelieving people" [al-Baqarah: 286], it was fitting to mention Allah's victory over the disbelievers, since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ debated them and refuted them with radiant proofs and decisive arguments. Then He recounted their circumstances, refuted their beliefs, mentioned His own exaltation above what they say, and the origin of the creation of Mary and her son Jesus, and so on through what He refuted against them. And since the opening of the last verse of al-Baqarah is, "The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord" [al-Baqarah: 285], this implies belief in Allah and in the Books; so it was fitting to mention the attributes of Allah, what was sent down to His Messenger, and what was sent down to others, may Allah's blessings be upon them.

The seven readers recited "Alif, Lam, Mim, Allah" with a fatha on the mim and without the hamzat al-wasl. Abu Bakr, in some of his transmissions from Asim, read with a sukun on the mim and with a hamza (qat'), and al-Farra' mentioned this reading from Asim. This reading is also reported from al-Hasan, Amr ibn Ubayd, al-Rawasi, al-A'mash, al-Burjumi and Ibn al-Qa'qa', who stopped on the mim just as they stopped on the alif and lam, which is the proper way, and then began after it, as you say: "wahid, ithnan" (one, two).

Abu Hayyan: Abu Hayyah read with a kasra on the mim, which Ibn 'Atiyyah attributed to al-Rawasi, and al-Zamakhshari attributed to Amr ibn Ubayd, saying: he imagined movement because of the meeting of two sukuns, but it is not acceptable. He means this reading. He said, and others said: that is poor, because the ya' prevents it, and the correct reading is the fatha, the reading of most people. Al-Akhfash said: "Alif, Lam, Mim Allah" with a kasra on the mim is permissible because of the meeting of two sukuns. Al-Zajjaj said: this is an error, and the Arabs do not say it because it is heavy.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on 3:1–2 (part 2 of 2):

Scholars differ about the vowel on the *mim* (the *fatha*). Sibawayh held that it was given a vowel because two quiescent letters met (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*, the meeting of two unvocalized consonants), just as they vocalized in *min Allah* ("from Allah"). The *hamzat al-wasl* (the connecting *alif*) drops in continuous speech, as it drops in *min al-rajul* ("from the man"). The *fatha* was preferred over the *kasra* because of the *ya'*, as in their saying *ayna* and *kayfa*, and because the *kasra* would have been added before the *ya'*, so the heaviness disappeared.

Al-Farra' held that the vowel is a *haraka naql* (a transferred vowel) from the *hamzat al-wasl*, because the letters of the alphabet are pronounced with a pause (*yunwa bi-ha al-waqf*), and what follows them is pronounced as a fresh start (*yunwa bi-ma ba'dahā al-isti'naf*). So the *hamza* is treated as if it were still present, as in the hemistichs of verse:

*latasma'unna washikan fi diyarikum * * * Allahu akbaru ya tharat 'Uthmana*

("You will certainly hear soon in your abodes: Allah is greatest! O avengers of Uthman!")

This view is weakened by the scholars' consensus that the *alif* of the definite article is dropped in continuous speech, and what drops does not receive a transferred vowel. This was stated by Abu 'Ali.

Al-Zamakhshari chose al-Farra's view, that the *fatha* on the *mim* is the vowel of the *hamza* after the *hamza* was dropped for lightness. He raised questions and answered them. He said: "If you ask, how can its vowel be placed on the letter before it when it is a *hamzat al-wasl* that does not appear in continuous speech, so its vowel should not appear either, since the vowel's appearance is like its own appearance? I say: this is not continuous speech, because the *mim* is treated as pause and quiescence, and the *hamza* is treated as present. It was dropped for lightness, and its vowel was placed on the preceding quiescent letter to indicate it. A parallel is their saying *wahid ithnan* ("one, two"), with the vowel of the *hamza* placed on the *dal*."

This question and answer are not sound. He claimed that the *mim*, when vowelled, is pronounced as a pause, and that this is not continuous speech but a pause. This contradicts what the Arabs and the grammarians agree upon: one never pauses on a vowelled letter at all, whether its vowel is an *i'rabi* (inflectional), *bina'i* (fixed), *naqli* (transferred), for *iltiqa' al-sakinayn*, for quotation (*hikaya*), or for imitation (*ittiba'*). Thus in *qad aflaha*, if the *hamza* is dropped and its vowel moved to the *dal* of *qad*, you may not pause on the *dal* with a *fatha*. It must be quiescent, by agreement.

As for his statement, "a parallel is their saying *wahid ithnan*, with the vowel of the *hamza* placed on the *dal*": Sibawayh mentioned that they give the last *wahid* a *ishmam* (a partial rounding) because it is fixed (*li-tamakkunihi*). He did not report the *kasra* as a dialect form. If the *kasra* is correct, then *wahid* is not pronounced as a pause, as al-Zamakhshari claimed, nor is its vowel a transferred vowel from the *hamzat al-wasl*. Rather, it is joined to *ithnan*, so two quiescent letters meet, the *dal* of *wahid* and the *tha'* of *ithnayn*. The *dal* is given a *kasra* because of their meeting, and the *hamza* is dropped because it does not appear in continuous speech.

As for the evidence that al-Farra' cited, their saying *thalathatun arba'atun* with the *hamza* placed on the *ha'*: there is no proof in it, because the *hamza* of *arba'a* is a *hamzat qat'* (a full *hamza*) in continuous speech, following what precedes it and beginning the word. This is not like the *hamzat al-wasl* of *min Allah*. Also, their saying *thalathatun arba'atun* with transfer does not involve a pause on *thalatha*. If one paused on it, it would not accept a vowel. Rather, it was kept as a *ha'* in continuous speech, considering what it had become in some state, not because it is a pause.

Then al-Zamakhshari raised a second question: "If you ask, why not claim that it was vowelled because two quiescent letters met?" I say: because the meeting of two quiescent letters does not concern us in pausal position. This is like your saying *hadha Ibrahimu*, *wa-Dawudu*, *wa-Ishaqu*. If the meeting of two quiescent letters in pausal position required vowelling, the two *mim*s of *alif-lam-mim* would have been vowelled because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, and the other quiescent letter would have been awaited."

This question and answer are: the question is sound, and the answer is sound. But the one who said that the vowel was because two quiescent letters met does not imagine that he meant the meeting of the *ya'* and the *mim* in *alif-lam-mim* in pausal position. Rather, he meant the two quiescent letters that are the final *mim* and the *lam* of the article, like the meeting of the *nun* of *min* and the *lam* of *al-rajul* when you say *min al-rajul*.

Then al-Zamakhshari raised a third question: "If you ask: they only failed to vowel for the meeting of two quiescent letters in *mim* because they wished to pause, and they could pronounce two quiescent letters. But when a third quiescent letter comes, vowelling is necessary, so they vowelled." I say: the proof that the vowel is not for the meeting with a quiescent letter is that they could have said *wahid ithnan* with the *dal* quiescent and the *hamza* dropped, joining two quiescent letters, as they said *asyam* and *madyaq*. When they vowelled the *dal*, it was known that its vowel is only the vowel of the dropped *hamza*, and not for the meeting of two quiescent letters.

This question and answer are: "If you ask, why did they not vowel for the meeting of two quiescent letters?" by "the two quiescent letters" he means the *ya'* and the *mim* in *mim*. Then the justification comes with his words: "because they wished to pause and could pronounce two quiescent letters," meaning the *ya'* and the *mim*. Then he said: "If a third quiescent letter comes," meaning the *lam* of the article, "vowelling is necessary," meaning on the *mim*. So they vowelled, meaning the *mim*, because it met a quiescent letter, the *lam* of the article. If they had not vowelled, three quiescent letters would have been gathered, and this is impossible. This is the explanation of the question.

As for al-Zamakhshari's answer to his question, it does not fit. He argued that the vowel is not for meeting a quiescent letter by the possibility of gathering two quiescent letters in their saying *wahid ithnan*, by quiescing the *dal* while the *tha'* is quiescent and the *hamza* drops. But they rejected this possibility in favour of moving the *hamza*'s vowel to the *dal*. This is obstinacy against what is perceived, since this is not possible at all, nor is it within human ability to join in speech the quiescence of the *dal*, the quiescence of the *tha'*, and the dropping of the *hamza*.

As for his statement, "they gathered two quiescent letters," this cannot be gathered, as we have said. As for his statement, "as they said *asyam* and *madyaq*," this is possible, as it is in *rad* and *dall*, because this involves the meeting of two quiescent letters within the limits set for them in grammar, so it can be pronounced. It is not like *wahid ithnan*, because the first quiescent letter is not a letter of weakness (*harf 'illa*), nor is the *tha'* in an assimilated (*mudgham*) letter, so the two cannot be gathered.

As for his statement, "when they vowelled the *dal*, it was known that its vowel is only the vowel of the dropped *hamza* and not for the meeting of two quiescent letters," it is built on the premise that gathering two quiescent letters in *wahid ithnan* is possible. The vowel for the meeting of two quiescent letters is only where they cannot both be present in pronunciation. He claimed that the vowel of the *dal* is the vowel of the dropped *hamza* for the meeting of two quiescent letters. We have already mentioned that this is not possible. If the *kasra* on the *dal* is correct, as this man reported, then its vowel is for the meeting of two quiescent letters and not by transfer.

Al-Farra's view, and al-Zamakhshari's choice of it, has been rejected by the statement: the vowel on the *mim* cannot be the vowel of the *hamza* placed on it, because of the corruption and contradiction in that. The quiescence of the final *mim* is on the intention of pausing on it, while placing the vowel of the *hamza* on it is on the intention of continuous speech. The intention of continuous speech requires dropping the *hamza*, while the intention of pausing on what precedes it requires its presence and separation. This is contradictory. This is a sound refutation.

What has been established from these words is that when the Arabs enumerate names ending in quiescence, both in continuous speech and in pause, if the last quiescent one meets another quiescent letter, it is vowelled because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. So this vowel in the *mim* of *alif-lam-mim Allah* is the vowel of the meeting of two quiescent letters.

The discussion of *alif-lam-mim* (2:1) has preceded in the beginning of al-Baqarah, and the disagreement of people over it is widespread, such that nothing can be established from it to rely on in its interpretation or the interpretation of similar disconnected letters (*al-huruf al-muqatta'a*).

The discussion of *Allahu la ilaha illa Huwa al-Hayyu al-Qayyum* has preceded in the verse *wa-ilahukum ilahun wahid la ilaha* (2:163) and at the beginning of the Verse of the Throne (2:255), so there is no need to repeat it here.

Ibn 'Atiyya reported from al-Qadi al-Jurjani that, regarding the composition (*nazm*), he held that the best view here is that *alif-lam-mim* refers to the letters of the alphabet, as if he were saying: "These letters are your Book," or something similar.

The statement *Allahu la ilaha illa Huwa al-Hayyu al-Qayyum nazzala 'alaykal-kitab* indicates, by what its meaning implies, what has been omitted from it, which is a predicate about the letters. He said: such omission in its composition is like His statement: *afaman sharaha Allahu sadrahu lil-Islami fa-huwa 'ala nurin min rabbihi* (39:22), where the response is omitted, indicated by His statement *fa-wailun lil-qasiyati qulubuhum min dhikri Allah* (39:22). Its estimate is: "like one whose heart is hardened." From this is the poet's saying:

*fala tadfinuni inna dafni muharramun * * * 'alaykum wa-lakin khamiri Umma 'Amir*

("Do not bury me, for my burial is forbidden to you, but leave me to she who is called *Khamiri Umm 'Amir*" [i.e., the fox]).

That is: "but leave me to her who is called *Khamiri Umm 'Amir*."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: this view is good, that the predicate of *Allah* be that *nazzala* (He sent down), so that the sentence connects to this meaning that al-Jurjani mentioned. But there is a point of consideration in it, because its likeness is not correct in resemblance to the meaning he went towards. What he said about the verse is possible, but the more eloquent arrangement of the verse is that *alif-lam-mim* not be joined in meaning to what follows it, and that *Allahu la ilaha illa Huwa al-Hayyu al-Qayyum* be a new, independent sentence, definitely, a sentence refuting the Christians of Najran who came as a delegation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), argued with him about 'Isa son of Maryam, and said: "He is Allah." End of his words.

Ibn Kaysan said: the position of *alif-lam-mim* is in the accusative, and the estimate is: "Recite *alif-lam-mim*," and "upon you *alif-lam-mim*." It may also be in the nominative, meaning "this is *alif-lam-mim*" and "that is *alif-lam-mim*." It was mentioned from al-Jurjani's statement that it may be a subject (*mubtada'*), with its predicate omitted, meaning: "These letters are your Book."

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and 'Alqama ibn Qays read *al-Qayyam*. Kharija said that in the codex of 'Abd Allah it is *al-Qayyim*, and this was also reported from 'Alqama.

*Allah* is in the nominative as a subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is *la ilaha illa Huwa*. *Nazzala 'alaykal-kitab* (3:3) is a predicate after a predicate. It is also possible that *nazzala* is the predicate, and *la ilaha illa Huwa* is a parenthetical sentence (*jumlat i'tiraD*). The detailed discussion of the *i'rab* of *la ilaha illa Huwa al-Hayyu al-Qayyum* has preceded in the Verse of the Throne, so there is no need to repeat it here.

Al-Razi said: the opening of this sūrah is wondrous, because when they disputed, it was as if it were said: either you dispute about knowledge of Allah, or about prophethood. If it is the first, then it is false, because the rational proofs show that He is *Hayy Qayyum* (Ever-Living, Sustainer), and the Ever-Living, Sustainer is impossible to have a child. If it is the second, then it is false, because the path by which you know that Allah Most High sent down the Torah and the Gospel is the very same path that stands here, and that is the miracle (*mu'jiza*).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 3–4:**

﴿He has sent down to you the Book with truth﴾. Here "the Book" (al-Kitab) means the Qur'an, by the consensus of the exegetes. It is repeated frequently, and what is meant is the Qur'an, which became a proper name by dominance (bi-l-ghalaba). The majority of readers read *nazzala* with doubling (tashdid) and *al-Kitab* in the accusative. Al-Nakha'i, al-A'mash, and Ibn Abi Abla read *nazala* without doubling and *al-Kitabu* in the nominative. With this reading the verse admits of two possibilities. The first is that it is a new sentence (munqati'a). The second is that it is connected to what precedes it, meaning: "the Book was sent down to you from Him." Here He mentioned the one to whom it was sent down, which is His saying *"to you" (alayka)*, and He did not mention the one to whom the Torah was sent down, nor the one to whom the Gospel was sent down. This singles him out and honours him by mention. He used the address form because of the intimacy (mu'anasa) found in direct address. He used the particle *ʿalā* because of its sense of elevation, as if the Book enveloped him and covered him (ﷺ). The meaning of "with truth" (bi-l-haqq) is "with justice." This was said by Ibn Abbas, and it has two senses. The first: justice regarding what He made obligatory for you, namely bearing the burdens of prophethood. The second: justice regarding what He singled you out with, namely the honour of prophethood.

It was also said: "with truthfulness regarding what was disputed," said by Muhammad ibn Jarir. It was said: "with truthfulness regarding what it contains of reports about the earlier generations." It was said: "with truthfulness regarding what it contains of the promise of reward for obedience and the threat of punishment for disobedience." It was said: the meaning of "with truth" is "with clear proofs and decisive demonstrations."

The *bāʾ* (with) may indicate causation (sababiyya), i.e., "because of the establishment of the truth." It may also indicate circumstance (hal), i.e., "while being true," as in the example: "Zayd went out with his weapon," meaning "armed."

It was also said that the implied term is "before you," so the omitted element is the pronoun of the Messenger. The apparent sense is that it is a qualifier for the Torah and the Gospel, and it was not made dual because it is a verbal noun (masdar). It was said: it is a qualifier for the Gospel alone, and it was omitted from the Torah, and this saying that is for the Gospel indicates it. ﴿And He sent down the Criterion﴾. It was said: "the Criterion" is every matter that distinguished between truth and falsehood, in what came before and what occurred after. Thus the flood of Noah enters this interpretation, and the parting of the sea for the drowning of Pharaoh, and the day of Badr, and all of God's other acts which separate truth from falsehood. It was said: "the Criterion" is the victory. Al-Razi said: the preferred view is that what is meant by "the Criterion" here is the miracles which God joined to the sending down of these books. This is because when they claimed that these were sent down from God, they needed to establish their claim by miracles, and the miracles were the Criterion, because they distinguish between the claim of the truthful and the liar. So when He mentioned that He had sent them down, He sent down with them what is the Criterion. Ibn Jarir said: by sending down the Qur'an He sent down the decisive judgment between truth and falsehood concerning what the factions and the adherents of the religions disagreed about. It was said: "the Criterion" here means the rulings which God clarified so that by them truth could be distinguished from falsehood.

"The Criterion" is originally a verbal noun, and these interpretations indicate that it is meant as an active participle, i.e., "the one who distinguishes," and it is permissible that it be meant as a passive participle, i.e., "that which is distinguished," as God Most High said: ﴿And a Qur'an We have divided, that you might recite it to the people over a duration﴾ [al-Isra: 106].

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God will have a severe punishment﴾. "Those who disbelieve" is general, and it includes those whose cause the verses were revealed for, namely the Christians of the delegation of Najran. Al-Naqqash said: it refers to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Ka'b ibn Asad, the Banu Akhtab, and others.

﴿And God is Almighty, Owner of Retribution﴾. That is, unassailable (mumtani') or dominant, who is not overcome, or one who is victorious, possessing punishment. It has been said earlier that describing with *dhu* is more emphatic than describing with *sahib* (companion), and for that reason the word *sahib* does not occur among the attributes of God. He indicated by "Almighty" the complete power, which is one of the attributes of the essence, and He indicated by "Owner of retribution" that He is the doer of punishment, which is one of the attributes of action. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Owner of retribution" means He has a severe retribution, such that no one else can match it in retribution. End of quote. The phrase "Owner of retribution" does not indicate this attribute by its wording alone; rather this is known from outside the wording.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 5–6 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah.﴾ ﴿It is He who shapes you in the wombs however He wills.﴾ (شَيْءٌ, shay'un, "thing") is an indefinite noun in a negative context, so it is general. It indicates complete knowledge of both universals and particulars. He expressed the whole world by "earth and heaven," since these are the greatest things we witness. Shaping in whatever forms He wills indicates complete power. Through knowledge and power the meaning of al-qayyumiyyah (the Self-Subsisting Sustainer) is fulfilled, for He is the one who maintains the affairs and necessities of creation. This also refutes the Christians, whose argument for ascribing divinity to Jesus was that he informed people of the unseen, which relates to knowledge, and that he brought the dead to life, which relates to power. The verse thus alerts that the God is the one who knows all things, so nothing is hidden from Him. It does not follow that because Jesus knew some unseen matters he must be God. It is known necessarily that Jesus did not know all knowable things. The verse also alerts that God is the one with complete power, so nothing is beyond Him. It does not follow that because Jesus was able to give life in some instances he must be God. It is known necessarily that Jesus was not able to form and give life to images by his own power. Rather, his informing about some unseen matters, and his creating and giving life to some forms, happened only by Allah's informing him through revelation and empowering him to do so. All of this was in the manner of a miracle that Allah brought about and similar ones through the hands of His messengers. In mentioning shaping in the womb there is also a refutation of those who claim that Jesus is God, since it is known necessarily that he was shaped in the womb.

It has been said: in His words ﴿nothing is hidden from Him﴾ there is a warning against opposing Him, secretly and openly, and a threat of recompense. It has also been said that the meaning is: nothing of what they say about the matter of Jesus, peace be upon him. Al-Zamakhshari said: He is aware of the disbelief of the disbeliever and the faith of the believer, and He will recompense them for it. Al-Maturidi said: Nothing is hidden from Him of the matters that are hidden from creation, so how could your deeds, which are apparent to you, be hidden from Him? All of these are particularizations, but the wording is general, so all of this falls within it. Al-Raghib said: ﴿nothing is hidden from Him﴾ is more eloquent in origin than (yaʿlamu, "He knows"), although the use of both words in this sense conveys one meaning.

Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr and al-Rabi' said: His words ﴿It is He who shapes you﴾ are a refutation of the naturalists (ahl al-tabi'ah), who make nature an acting, independent agent. (كَيْفَ يَشاءُ, kayfa yashā', "however He wills"). Al-Maturidi said: In this there is the nullification of the view of those who make the opinion of the qa'if (the physiognomist who determines lineage by resemblance) a proof in claims of descent, because He made knowledge of shaping in the wombs His own. How then could the qa'if know that He shaped the child from his water when there is resemblance in the forms? End of quote. The better view is that these sentences are independent: the first is an informing about His complete knowledge, the second about His complete power and will, and the third about His exclusive divinity. It is also possible that it is a predicate of (inna, "indeed").

Al-Raghib said: Here (yuṣawwirukum, "He shapes you") is in the present form, while elsewhere (faṣawwarakum, "then He shaped you") is in the past form, because there is no consideration of times in His acts. Words are used for this only to indicate times according to the languages. Also, (faṣawwarakum) relates to the mode of decree, and God's act is in the status of what has already been completed. (yuṣawwirukum) is according to what appears to us moment by moment. End of quote.

Tawus read (tasawwarakum), meaning: He shaped you for Himself and for His worship, like your saying: "I made property (athlah), i.e., I made it a root (aṣl), and I made it an athlah for myself (ta'assaltuhu) when you establish it for yourself." The form tafa''ala can also come with the meaning of fa''ala, as in tawalla meaning wallā ("he turned away").

The meaning of ﴿however He wills﴾ is: in regard to length and shortness, color, maleness and femaleness, and other differences. In His words ﴿however He wills﴾ there is an indication that this occurs with a cause and without a cause, because it depends solely on His will.

(كَيْفَ, kayfa, "how") here is conditional (li-l-jazā'), but it does not put the verb in the jussive. The object of (yashā', "wills") is omitted because the meaning is understood. The estimate is: however He wills to shape you. Compare His words ﴿He spends however He wills﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:64), i.e., however He wills to spend. (كَيْفَ) is in the accusative governed by (yashā'). The meaning is: in whatever state He wills to shape you, He shapes you. Its accusative status is as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). The omission of the verb of the conditional is because what precedes it indicates it, as in the saying: "You are a wrongdoer if you do (such and such)." The estimate is: "You are a wrongdoer; if you do it, then you are a wrongdoer." This clause has no place in grammatical analysis (i'rab), although it is related in meaning to what precedes it, and its relation is like the relation of "if you do" in your saying: "You are a wrongdoer."

The breaking down of this speech and its grammatical analysis according to what we have mentioned cannot be understood except after practice in i'rab and the mastery of the subtleties of grammar.

Some said: ﴿however He wills﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial phrase, governed by (yuṣawwirukum, "He shapes you"). The meaning of the circumstance is: He shapes you in the wombs while being able to shape you, possessing that. It has been said: the estimate in this state is: He shapes you according to His will, i.e., desiring, so it is a circumstance of the subject of the name of Allah. Abu al-Baqa' mentioned this, and permitted that it be a circumstance of the object, i.e., He shapes you transformed according to His will.

Al-Hawfi said: It is possible that the clause is in the position of a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: He shapes you in the wombs as the shaping of will, and as He wills.

﴿There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ He repeated this sentence that indicates the negation of divinity from anyone other than Him, and its restriction to Him, as an emphasis of what precedes it from His words ﴿There is no god but He﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:255 / Ali Imran 3:2), and as a refutation of the one who claimed divinity for Jesus. It is fitting that it comes after the two preceding attributes of knowledge and power, since whoever possesses these two attributes is the one characterized by divinity and no other. Then He mentioned the attribute of might (al-'izzah), which indicates the absence of a counterpart, and wisdom (al-hikmah), which necessitates the shaping of things with perfect precision.

﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are definite, they are the foundation of the Book, and others that are unspecific.﴾ (Ali 'Imran 3:7) The connection of this to what precedes it is that: when He mentioned the proportioning of the structure and its shaping into beautiful forms, which is a corporeal matter, He digressed to knowledge, which is a spiritual matter. The delegation of Najran had raised among their doubts His words ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:171). So He clarified that the Qur'an, in part, has definite wording (muḥkam), protected from ambiguity, and in part, is unspecific (mutashābih), which is what admits several meanings.

We will mention the statements of the exegetes concerning the muḥkam and the mutashābih. The description of the Qur'an as having definite verses means that it is complete, its wording is most eloquent, and its meaning is most sound. No speech equals it in these two qualities. Its description as mutashābih is in His words ﴿a Book whose parts resemble one another﴾ (al-Zumar 39:23), meaning that some of it resembles others in kind and in confirmation. Here, however, mutashābih is that which admits of several meanings, and the mind is unable to distinguish between them, as in ﴿Indeed, the cows have become confused to us﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:70), and ﴿they were given it in resemblance﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:25), meaning: of differing tastes but similar appearance. From this comes the phrase "the two matters became confused" (ishtabaha al-amrān), when they are not distinguished from each other. Those who perform tricks are called "the people of confusions" (ashab al-shubah).

You may say: a word that is coined for a meaning that does not admit of anything other than it is a text (naṣṣ). Or it admits of two possibilities, one of which is preponderant over the other; then in relation to the preponderant it is apparent (ẓāhir), and in relation to the less preponderant it is interpreted (mu'awwal). Or it admits of possibilities without preponderance; then it is shared (mushtarak) in relation to both, and ambiguous (mujmal) in relation to each one of them. The common element between the text and the apparent is the muḥkam, and the common element between the ambiguous and the interpreted is the mutashābih, because lack of understanding occurs in both categories.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah, al-Rabi', and al-Dahhak said: The muḥkam is the abrogating (nāsikh), and the mutashābih is the abrogated (mansūkh). Mujahid and Ikrimah said: The muḥkam is that which Allah has made clear as lawful and unlawful, so its meanings are not confused. The mutashābih is that whose meanings are confused. Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, and al-Shafi'i said: The muḥkam is that which admits of only one aspect, and the mutashābih is that which admits of several aspects of interpretation. Ibn Zayd said: The muḥkam is that whose wording is not repeated, and the mutashābih is that whose wording is repeated. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Ibn Dhi'ab, and what is implied by the statement of al-Sha'bi, al-Thawri and others said: The muḥkam is that whose interpretation the scholars understand, and the mutashābih is that which Allah has kept knowledge of to Himself, such as the establishment of the Hour, the rising of the sun from its west, and the coming of Jesus.

Abu 'Uthman said: The muḥkam is al-Fatihah. Muhammad ibn al-Fadl said: It is Surat al-Ikhlas, since it contains only tawhid. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: The muḥkamat are those that have no alteration (taṣrīf) and no distortion (taḥrīf). Muqatil said: The muḥkamat are five hundred verses, because they expand their meanings, so they were the mother of branches, from which analogies were made and from which others were generated, like a mother from which offspring come. For this reason He called them "the Mother of the Book." The mutashābih are the stories and the parables.

Yahya ibn Ya'mur said: The muḥkam are the obligatory duties (farā'id), and the promise and the threat (al-wa'd wa al-wa'īd). The mutashābih are the stories and the parables. It has been said: the muḥkam is that which stands by itself and does not need inference, and the mutashābih is that whose meanings of rulings are not understood by reason, such as the numbers of the prayers, and the specification of fasting to the month of Ramadan rather than Sha'ban. It has been said: the muḥkam is the stories that are established in one wording, and the mutashābih is that whose wording varies, such as His words ﴿then suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:20), ﴿then suddenly it was a manifest serpent﴾ (al-A'raf 7:107), ﴿We said: "Load (it)"﴾ (Hud 11:40), and ﴿"Embark"﴾ (al-Mu'minun 23:27).

Abu Fakhitah said: The muḥkamat are the openings of the surahs, from which the surahs are derived, like (Alif Lam Mim) and (Alif Lam Mim Ra'). It has been said: the mutashābih are the openings of the surahs, the reverse of the first. It has been said: the muḥkamat are those in Surat al-An'am up to the end of the three verses, and the mutashābihat are (Alif Lam Mim) and (Alif Lam Mim Ra'), and what was confusing to the Jews of these and similar letters, when they heard (Alif Lam Mim) and said: by the abjad reckoning this is seventy-one, so it is the end of the term of this community. Then when they heard (Alif Lam Ra') and others, they were confused. Or it is what was confusing to the Christians from His words ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:171). It has been said: the mutashābihāt are what there is no way to know, such as the description of the face, the two hands, the hand, and the istiwa' (settling/establishment). It has been said: the muḥkam is what Allah commanded in every Book He sent down, such as His words ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite..."﴾ (al-An'am 6:151) and the verses following, and ﴿Your Lord has decreed...﴾ (al-Isra' 17:23) and the verses following. Everything other than the muḥkam is mutashābih. (p-382)

Most jurists said: The muḥkamat are those made definite by clarity, so when the listener hears them, he does not need to interpret them, because they are apparent and clear. The mutashābihat are what differ from that. Ibn Abi Najih said: The muḥkam is that which contains the lawful and the unlawful. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: The mutashābih is that which has several aspects and about which scholars differ, like the two verses concerning the pregnant woman whose husband has died. 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas say she observes the longer of the two terms; 'Umar, Zayd, and Ibn Mas'ud say it is the delivery of the child. Their disagreement concerns abrogation. Likewise there is disagreement concerning bequest to an heir, whether it has been abrogated or not. Likewise, the apparent conflict of two verses, as to which of them is to be given precedence when abrogation is not known, such as ﴿and lawful to you is what lies beyond that﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:24), which implies the combining of relatives by ownership of the right hand, and ﴿and that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:23), which prohibits that. Does the second prohibit this?

The meaning of "the Mother of the Book" (umm al-kitāb) is the majority of the Book, since the muḥkam among the verses of Allah is abundant and has been detailed. Yahya ibn Ya'mur said: This is like how Mecca is called "the Mother of the Cities" (umm al-qurā), Marw is called "the Mother of Khurasan," and the head is called "the Mother of the Head" (umm al-ra's) for the gathering place of the faculties, since it is the most vital place.

Ibn Zayd said: "jimā' al-Kitāb" (the main body of the Book). He did not say "ummahāt" (mothers, plural), because he treated the muhkamāt as one thing and the totality of the mutashābihāt as another, and one of them is the "umm" (origin) of the other. A parallel is ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50], where He did not say "two."

It is possible that (hunna) means each one of them, like ﴿flog them eighty lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 4], meaning each one of them. It has been said that it is also possible that the singular was used in place of the plural, as in ﴿and over their hearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7].

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Umm al-Kitāb" means the origin (asl) of the Book, to which the mutashābihāt are referred back and by which they are interpreted. Examples: ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ [al-An'am: 103], ﴿looking at their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 23], ﴿He does not command indecency﴾ [al-A'raf: 28], ﴿We commanded its affluent ones﴾ [al-Isra': 16]. End of quotation.

This is according to his Mu'tazili doctrine that Allah is not seen: he made the muhkam "No vision perceives Him," and the mutashābih "looking at their Lord." Ahl al-Sunnah reverse this, or distinguish between perception (idrak) and seeing (ru'yah). Among the muhkam is mentioned ﴿Your Lord was not forgetful﴾ [Maryam: 64] and ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52]; and among its mutashābih is ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67]. The apparent meaning of forgetting (nisyan) is the opposite of knowledge, and its less preponderant meaning is abandonment (tark).

The adherents of the schools differ regarding the muhkam and the mutashābih: whatever agrees with their school is muhkam for them, and whatever contradicts it is mutashābih. So ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29] is muhkam according to the Mu'tazilah, and ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30] is mutashābih; others are the reverse.

Turning a word from its preponderant meaning to its less preponderant meaning requires a separate (munfasil) proof. If the proof is verbal (lafzi), it is not complete except when a conflict occurs, and there is no preference in turning to one over the reverse. There is also no certainty in a verbal proof, whether it is a text (nass) or apparent (zahir), because it depends on speculative (zanni) matters, and that is not permissible in fundamental matters (al-masa'il al-usuliyyah). Therefore, moving to the less preponderant meaning does not occur through a decisive rational indication. When it is known that a word is diverted from its apparent meaning, there is no need to specify the intended meaning, because that would be preferring one metaphor (majaz) over another metaphor, and one interpretation (ta'wil) over another.

Among the heretics (mulahidah) is one who attacked the Qur'an for containing the mutashābih and said: They claim that the obligations of creation are tied to this Qur'an until the Day of Resurrection, yet we see every owner of a doctrine holding to it according to his doctrine. The determinist (Jabri) holds to verses of compulsion: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾ [al-An'am: 25] and ﴿and in their ears deafness﴾ [al-An'am: 25]. The Qadari says: this is the doctrine of the disbelievers, mentioned in a context of blaming them, in His saying ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are in coverings from that to which you invite us, and in our ears is deafness"﴾ [Fussilat: 5], and in another place ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are uncircumcised"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88].

Those who affirm the vision (of Allah) hold to His saying ﴿looking at their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 23], and the others hold to His saying ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ [al-An'am: 103]. Those who affirm a direction (jihah) hold to His saying ﴿they fear their Lord above them﴾ [al-Nahl: 50] and His saying ﴿the Most Merciful, established above the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], and the others hold to His saying ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. So how is it fitting that the muhkam should be referred back to the less preponderant, in this manner? Thus ends the words of Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, and some of it has been summarized.

The scholars have mentioned benefits in the coming of the mutashābih, and the best of them is what al-Zamakhshari mentioned. He said: If you say, "Why was not the whole Qur'an muhkam?" I say: If all of it were muhkam, people would cling to it because of the ease of its meaning, and they would turn away from what requires investigation, reflection, and inquiry through reasoning and argument. Had they done so, they would have abandoned the path by which the knowledge of Allah and His Oneness is reached only through it. Also, there is the trial and distinguishing in the mutashābih between one who is steadfast upon the truth and one who wavers regarding it. And there is the benefit of the scholars competing and exerting their minds in extracting its meanings and referring them back to the muhkam, which contains great benefits, abundant sciences, and attaining high ranks with Allah. Moreover, the believer, who holds that there is no contradiction or discrepancy in the speech of Allah, when he sees in it what conflicts in its apparent sense, is concerned to seek what reconciles it and makes it run on one course. So he reflects and reviews his own understanding and that of others, and Allah grants him success, and the agreement of the mutashābih with the muhkam becomes clear to him. He then increases in tranquility toward his belief and in strength in mastering it. Thus ends the words of al-Zamakhshari, and it is a composition of what people have said about the benefit of the coming of the mutashābih in the Qur'an.
