When He, exalted, mentioned at the beginning of the surah ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting. He has sent down upon you the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 2], He mentioned here the manner of the Book, and used the relative pronoun (alladhi), since its relative clause refers back to the previous revelation (tanzil) and to something known in it. His saying ﴿He it is who has sent down upon you the Book; in it are verses that are muhkam...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7] to its end is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning that He left it in these two aspects, muhkam and mutashābih. The word (ayat) is in the nominative, functioning as the subject of the prepositional phrase (min-hu), since it has been relied upon; it is also permissible for it to be nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), and the sentence is then circumstantial. It is also possible that the sentence is a new independent sentence. The description of the verses as muhkam is true in that each verse is muhkam. As for His saying ﴿and others are mutashabihat﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7], ukhar is an adjective of a deleted noun, ayat. The description by similarity (tashabuh) is not valid for the singular of ukhar: if you said wa-ukhra mutashabihah, it would not be valid except in the sense that some of it resembles other parts of it. The intended meaning here is not this sense, because the resemblance intended here occurs only between two or more things. So this description is valid with the plural, since each of its units resembles the rest, though this does not apply to a single unit. It is like ﴿two men who fight﴾ [al-Qasas: 15], though one does not say rajul yaqtatil ("a man who fights"). The discussion of ukhar has already been covered in His saying ﴿then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], so there is no need to repeat it here.

Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned that al-Mahdawi confused the matter of ukhar and spoiled the words of Sibawayh, so he paused at that part of al-Mahdawi's speech.

﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]: they are the Christians of Najran, because they confronted the Qur'an regarding the matter of Jesus, as said by al-Rabi'. Or they are the Jews, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi, because they asked that this verse of the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) be retained. Deviation (zaygh) here is their obstinacy.

Al-Tabari said: This is the most likely, and he mentioned the dialogue of Huyayy ibn Akhtab and his companions with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during the period of his mission, and their extracting the calculation of the time from the openings of the surahs, and their moving from one number to another, until they said: "It has confused us; we do not know whether to take the many or the few? And we do not believe in this." So Allah, exalted, sent down ﴿He it is who has sent down upon you the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7], the verse.

Ibn Mas'ud and a group of the Companions, Mujahid, Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, and others interpreted deviation as the inclination away from guidance.

Qatadah said: They are those who deny the resurrection, for it says at its end ﴿and none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7], and that is nothing but the Day of Resurrection, for He concealed it from all creation. Qatadah also said: They are the Harurites (al-Haruriyyah), who are the Kharijites (al-Khawarij), and whoever interprets a verse not in its proper place. He also said: If the Harurites are not the Sabā'iyyah Kharijites, then I do not know who they are. Ibn Jurayj said: They are the hypocrites. It has been said: They are all the innovators (al-mubtadi'ah).

The apparent wording is general regarding those who deviate from the truth. Every group among those mentioned has deviated from the truth, so the wording includes them, even if it was revealed concerning a specific cause, because the lesson is in the generality of the wording.

﴿so they follow that of it which is mutashabih﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]. Al-Qurtubi said: Those who follow the mutashābih are either seekers of doubt, contradiction, and repetition; or seekers of the apparent meanings of the mutashābih, such as the anthropomorphists (al-mujassimah), who affirmed that He is a body and a form, with a face, an eye, a hand, a side, a leg, and a finger; or seekers of presenting an interpretation and clarification through direct observation. For example, a man asked Ibn 'Abbas about things that seemed to conflict in the Qur'an, such as ﴿and they will not ask one another﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 101], ﴿and they approached one another, questioning﴾ [al-Saffat: 27], ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ [al-Nisa': 42], and ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23], and the like. Ibn 'Abbas answered him with what removed the contradiction from him. Or they are those who follow it and ask about it with a question meant to trap, as happened with Usaybigh and 'Umar, when 'Umar struck his head until blood ran down over his face. Thus ends his words, summarized.

﴿seeking discord and seeking its interpretation﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]: He gave two causes for their following the mutashābih. The first is seeking discord (al-fitnah). Al-Suddi, Rabi', Muqatil, and Ibn Qutaybah said: it is disbelief (kufr). Mujahid said: doubts and confusion (al-shubuhat wa-al-labs). Al-Zajjaj said: corrupting relations among people (ifsad dhat al-bayn). It was said: the doubts with which they argued against the delegation of Najran.

The second cause is seeking the interpretation (ta'wil). Ibn 'Abbas said: they sought knowledge of the duration of the Prophet's (ﷺ) mission. It was said: ta'wil means tafsir (explanation), as in ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not have patience﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. Ibn 'Abbas also said: they sought the outcome of the affair of the believers, the final destiny of their Book, religion, and law, and the awaited end. Al-Zajjaj said: they sought the interpretation of their resurrection and revival. So Allah, exalted, informed that the interpretation of that and its time is ﴿the Day they see what they were promised﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], namely the resurrection and the punishment; ﴿those who had forgotten it will say﴾ [al-A'raf: 53], meaning those who had neglected it; ﴿the messengers of our Lord had certainly come﴾ [al-A'raf: 53], meaning: we have now seen the interpretation of what the messengers had told us. Al-Suddi said: they wanted to know the outcomes of the Qur'an, which is its interpretation, namely when some of it would be abrogated (yunsakh, naskh). It was said: seeking its ta'wil is seeking the reality of its true nature and the depth of its meanings.

Al-Razi said words summarized as follows: the meaning of ta'wil here is that for which there is no evidence in the Book, such as "When is the Hour?" and the measures of reward and punishment for each responsible person.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Those in whose hearts is deviation﴾ are the people of innovations (ahl al-bida'), so they follow the mutashābih, clinging to the mutashābih which admits what the innovator inclines to, that which does not match the muhkam, and admits what matches it from the saying of the people of truth. "Seeking discord" means seeking to tempt people away from their religion and mislead them, and "seeking its interpretation" means seeking to interpret it in the manner they desire. Thus ends his words, and it is a good statement.

(p. 383)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 5–6 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah.﴾ ﴿It is He who shapes you in the wombs however He wills.﴾ (شَيْءٌ, shay'un, "thing") is an indefinite noun in a negative context, so it is general. It indicates complete knowledge of both universals and particulars. He expressed the whole world by "earth and heaven," since these are the greatest things we witness. Shaping in whatever forms He wills indicates complete power. Through knowledge and power the meaning of al-qayyumiyyah (the Self-Subsisting Sustainer) is fulfilled, for He is the one who maintains the affairs and necessities of creation. This also refutes the Christians, whose argument for ascribing divinity to Jesus was that he informed people of the unseen, which relates to knowledge, and that he brought the dead to life, which relates to power. The verse thus alerts that the God is the one who knows all things, so nothing is hidden from Him. It does not follow that because Jesus knew some unseen matters he must be God. It is known necessarily that Jesus did not know all knowable things. The verse also alerts that God is the one with complete power, so nothing is beyond Him. It does not follow that because Jesus was able to give life in some instances he must be God. It is known necessarily that Jesus was not able to form and give life to images by his own power. Rather, his informing about some unseen matters, and his creating and giving life to some forms, happened only by Allah's informing him through revelation and empowering him to do so. All of this was in the manner of a miracle that Allah brought about and similar ones through the hands of His messengers. In mentioning shaping in the womb there is also a refutation of those who claim that Jesus is God, since it is known necessarily that he was shaped in the womb.

It has been said: in His words ﴿nothing is hidden from Him﴾ there is a warning against opposing Him, secretly and openly, and a threat of recompense. It has also been said that the meaning is: nothing of what they say about the matter of Jesus, peace be upon him. Al-Zamakhshari said: He is aware of the disbelief of the disbeliever and the faith of the believer, and He will recompense them for it. Al-Maturidi said: Nothing is hidden from Him of the matters that are hidden from creation, so how could your deeds, which are apparent to you, be hidden from Him? All of these are particularizations, but the wording is general, so all of this falls within it. Al-Raghib said: ﴿nothing is hidden from Him﴾ is more eloquent in origin than (yaʿlamu, "He knows"), although the use of both words in this sense conveys one meaning.

Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr and al-Rabi' said: His words ﴿It is He who shapes you﴾ are a refutation of the naturalists (ahl al-tabi'ah), who make nature an acting, independent agent. (كَيْفَ يَشاءُ, kayfa yashā', "however He wills"). Al-Maturidi said: In this there is the nullification of the view of those who make the opinion of the qa'if (the physiognomist who determines lineage by resemblance) a proof in claims of descent, because He made knowledge of shaping in the wombs His own. How then could the qa'if know that He shaped the child from his water when there is resemblance in the forms? End of quote. The better view is that these sentences are independent: the first is an informing about His complete knowledge, the second about His complete power and will, and the third about His exclusive divinity. It is also possible that it is a predicate of (inna, "indeed").

Al-Raghib said: Here (yuṣawwirukum, "He shapes you") is in the present form, while elsewhere (faṣawwarakum, "then He shaped you") is in the past form, because there is no consideration of times in His acts. Words are used for this only to indicate times according to the languages. Also, (faṣawwarakum) relates to the mode of decree, and God's act is in the status of what has already been completed. (yuṣawwirukum) is according to what appears to us moment by moment. End of quote.

Tawus read (tasawwarakum), meaning: He shaped you for Himself and for His worship, like your saying: "I made property (athlah), i.e., I made it a root (aṣl), and I made it an athlah for myself (ta'assaltuhu) when you establish it for yourself." The form tafa''ala can also come with the meaning of fa''ala, as in tawalla meaning wallā ("he turned away").

The meaning of ﴿however He wills﴾ is: in regard to length and shortness, color, maleness and femaleness, and other differences. In His words ﴿however He wills﴾ there is an indication that this occurs with a cause and without a cause, because it depends solely on His will.

(كَيْفَ, kayfa, "how") here is conditional (li-l-jazā'), but it does not put the verb in the jussive. The object of (yashā', "wills") is omitted because the meaning is understood. The estimate is: however He wills to shape you. Compare His words ﴿He spends however He wills﴾ (al-Ma'idah 5:64), i.e., however He wills to spend. (كَيْفَ) is in the accusative governed by (yashā'). The meaning is: in whatever state He wills to shape you, He shapes you. Its accusative status is as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). The omission of the verb of the conditional is because what precedes it indicates it, as in the saying: "You are a wrongdoer if you do (such and such)." The estimate is: "You are a wrongdoer; if you do it, then you are a wrongdoer." This clause has no place in grammatical analysis (i'rab), although it is related in meaning to what precedes it, and its relation is like the relation of "if you do" in your saying: "You are a wrongdoer."

The breaking down of this speech and its grammatical analysis according to what we have mentioned cannot be understood except after practice in i'rab and the mastery of the subtleties of grammar.

Some said: ﴿however He wills﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial phrase, governed by (yuṣawwirukum, "He shapes you"). The meaning of the circumstance is: He shapes you in the wombs while being able to shape you, possessing that. It has been said: the estimate in this state is: He shapes you according to His will, i.e., desiring, so it is a circumstance of the subject of the name of Allah. Abu al-Baqa' mentioned this, and permitted that it be a circumstance of the object, i.e., He shapes you transformed according to His will.

Al-Hawfi said: It is possible that the clause is in the position of a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: He shapes you in the wombs as the shaping of will, and as He wills.

﴿There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ He repeated this sentence that indicates the negation of divinity from anyone other than Him, and its restriction to Him, as an emphasis of what precedes it from His words ﴿There is no god but He﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:255 / Ali Imran 3:2), and as a refutation of the one who claimed divinity for Jesus. It is fitting that it comes after the two preceding attributes of knowledge and power, since whoever possesses these two attributes is the one characterized by divinity and no other. Then He mentioned the attribute of might (al-'izzah), which indicates the absence of a counterpart, and wisdom (al-hikmah), which necessitates the shaping of things with perfect precision.

﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are definite, they are the foundation of the Book, and others that are unspecific.﴾ (Ali 'Imran 3:7) The connection of this to what precedes it is that: when He mentioned the proportioning of the structure and its shaping into beautiful forms, which is a corporeal matter, He digressed to knowledge, which is a spiritual matter. The delegation of Najran had raised among their doubts His words ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:171). So He clarified that the Qur'an, in part, has definite wording (muḥkam), protected from ambiguity, and in part, is unspecific (mutashābih), which is what admits several meanings.

We will mention the statements of the exegetes concerning the muḥkam and the mutashābih. The description of the Qur'an as having definite verses means that it is complete, its wording is most eloquent, and its meaning is most sound. No speech equals it in these two qualities. Its description as mutashābih is in His words ﴿a Book whose parts resemble one another﴾ (al-Zumar 39:23), meaning that some of it resembles others in kind and in confirmation. Here, however, mutashābih is that which admits of several meanings, and the mind is unable to distinguish between them, as in ﴿Indeed, the cows have become confused to us﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:70), and ﴿they were given it in resemblance﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:25), meaning: of differing tastes but similar appearance. From this comes the phrase "the two matters became confused" (ishtabaha al-amrān), when they are not distinguished from each other. Those who perform tricks are called "the people of confusions" (ashab al-shubah).

You may say: a word that is coined for a meaning that does not admit of anything other than it is a text (naṣṣ). Or it admits of two possibilities, one of which is preponderant over the other; then in relation to the preponderant it is apparent (ẓāhir), and in relation to the less preponderant it is interpreted (mu'awwal). Or it admits of possibilities without preponderance; then it is shared (mushtarak) in relation to both, and ambiguous (mujmal) in relation to each one of them. The common element between the text and the apparent is the muḥkam, and the common element between the ambiguous and the interpreted is the mutashābih, because lack of understanding occurs in both categories.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah, al-Rabi', and al-Dahhak said: The muḥkam is the abrogating (nāsikh), and the mutashābih is the abrogated (mansūkh). Mujahid and Ikrimah said: The muḥkam is that which Allah has made clear as lawful and unlawful, so its meanings are not confused. The mutashābih is that whose meanings are confused. Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, and al-Shafi'i said: The muḥkam is that which admits of only one aspect, and the mutashābih is that which admits of several aspects of interpretation. Ibn Zayd said: The muḥkam is that whose wording is not repeated, and the mutashābih is that whose wording is repeated. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Ibn Dhi'ab, and what is implied by the statement of al-Sha'bi, al-Thawri and others said: The muḥkam is that whose interpretation the scholars understand, and the mutashābih is that which Allah has kept knowledge of to Himself, such as the establishment of the Hour, the rising of the sun from its west, and the coming of Jesus.

Abu 'Uthman said: The muḥkam is al-Fatihah. Muhammad ibn al-Fadl said: It is Surat al-Ikhlas, since it contains only tawhid. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: The muḥkamat are those that have no alteration (taṣrīf) and no distortion (taḥrīf). Muqatil said: The muḥkamat are five hundred verses, because they expand their meanings, so they were the mother of branches, from which analogies were made and from which others were generated, like a mother from which offspring come. For this reason He called them "the Mother of the Book." The mutashābih are the stories and the parables.

Yahya ibn Ya'mur said: The muḥkam are the obligatory duties (farā'id), and the promise and the threat (al-wa'd wa al-wa'īd). The mutashābih are the stories and the parables. It has been said: the muḥkam is that which stands by itself and does not need inference, and the mutashābih is that whose meanings of rulings are not understood by reason, such as the numbers of the prayers, and the specification of fasting to the month of Ramadan rather than Sha'ban. It has been said: the muḥkam is the stories that are established in one wording, and the mutashābih is that whose wording varies, such as His words ﴿then suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:20), ﴿then suddenly it was a manifest serpent﴾ (al-A'raf 7:107), ﴿We said: "Load (it)"﴾ (Hud 11:40), and ﴿"Embark"﴾ (al-Mu'minun 23:27).

Abu Fakhitah said: The muḥkamat are the openings of the surahs, from which the surahs are derived, like (Alif Lam Mim) and (Alif Lam Mim Ra'). It has been said: the mutashābih are the openings of the surahs, the reverse of the first. It has been said: the muḥkamat are those in Surat al-An'am up to the end of the three verses, and the mutashābihat are (Alif Lam Mim) and (Alif Lam Mim Ra'), and what was confusing to the Jews of these and similar letters, when they heard (Alif Lam Mim) and said: by the abjad reckoning this is seventy-one, so it is the end of the term of this community. Then when they heard (Alif Lam Ra') and others, they were confused. Or it is what was confusing to the Christians from His words ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:171). It has been said: the mutashābihāt are what there is no way to know, such as the description of the face, the two hands, the hand, and the istiwa' (settling/establishment). It has been said: the muḥkam is what Allah commanded in every Book He sent down, such as His words ﴿Say: "Come, I will recite..."﴾ (al-An'am 6:151) and the verses following, and ﴿Your Lord has decreed...﴾ (al-Isra' 17:23) and the verses following. Everything other than the muḥkam is mutashābih. (p-382)

Most jurists said: The muḥkamat are those made definite by clarity, so when the listener hears them, he does not need to interpret them, because they are apparent and clear. The mutashābihat are what differ from that. Ibn Abi Najih said: The muḥkam is that which contains the lawful and the unlawful. Ibn Khuwayz Mindad said: The mutashābih is that which has several aspects and about which scholars differ, like the two verses concerning the pregnant woman whose husband has died. 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas say she observes the longer of the two terms; 'Umar, Zayd, and Ibn Mas'ud say it is the delivery of the child. Their disagreement concerns abrogation. Likewise there is disagreement concerning bequest to an heir, whether it has been abrogated or not. Likewise, the apparent conflict of two verses, as to which of them is to be given precedence when abrogation is not known, such as ﴿and lawful to you is what lies beyond that﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:24), which implies the combining of relatives by ownership of the right hand, and ﴿and that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:23), which prohibits that. Does the second prohibit this?

The meaning of "the Mother of the Book" (umm al-kitāb) is the majority of the Book, since the muḥkam among the verses of Allah is abundant and has been detailed. Yahya ibn Ya'mur said: This is like how Mecca is called "the Mother of the Cities" (umm al-qurā), Marw is called "the Mother of Khurasan," and the head is called "the Mother of the Head" (umm al-ra's) for the gathering place of the faculties, since it is the most vital place.

Ibn Zayd said: "jimā' al-Kitāb" (the main body of the Book). He did not say "ummahāt" (mothers, plural), because he treated the muhkamāt as one thing and the totality of the mutashābihāt as another, and one of them is the "umm" (origin) of the other. A parallel is ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50], where He did not say "two."

It is possible that (hunna) means each one of them, like ﴿flog them eighty lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 4], meaning each one of them. It has been said that it is also possible that the singular was used in place of the plural, as in ﴿and over their hearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7].

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Umm al-Kitāb" means the origin (asl) of the Book, to which the mutashābihāt are referred back and by which they are interpreted. Examples: ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ [al-An'am: 103], ﴿looking at their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 23], ﴿He does not command indecency﴾ [al-A'raf: 28], ﴿We commanded its affluent ones﴾ [al-Isra': 16]. End of quotation.

This is according to his Mu'tazili doctrine that Allah is not seen: he made the muhkam "No vision perceives Him," and the mutashābih "looking at their Lord." Ahl al-Sunnah reverse this, or distinguish between perception (idrak) and seeing (ru'yah). Among the muhkam is mentioned ﴿Your Lord was not forgetful﴾ [Maryam: 64] and ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52]; and among its mutashābih is ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67]. The apparent meaning of forgetting (nisyan) is the opposite of knowledge, and its less preponderant meaning is abandonment (tark).

The adherents of the schools differ regarding the muhkam and the mutashābih: whatever agrees with their school is muhkam for them, and whatever contradicts it is mutashābih. So ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [al-Kahf: 29] is muhkam according to the Mu'tazilah, and ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ [al-Insan: 30] is mutashābih; others are the reverse.

Turning a word from its preponderant meaning to its less preponderant meaning requires a separate (munfasil) proof. If the proof is verbal (lafzi), it is not complete except when a conflict occurs, and there is no preference in turning to one over the reverse. There is also no certainty in a verbal proof, whether it is a text (nass) or apparent (zahir), because it depends on speculative (zanni) matters, and that is not permissible in fundamental matters (al-masa'il al-usuliyyah). Therefore, moving to the less preponderant meaning does not occur through a decisive rational indication. When it is known that a word is diverted from its apparent meaning, there is no need to specify the intended meaning, because that would be preferring one metaphor (majaz) over another metaphor, and one interpretation (ta'wil) over another.

Among the heretics (mulahidah) is one who attacked the Qur'an for containing the mutashābih and said: They claim that the obligations of creation are tied to this Qur'an until the Day of Resurrection, yet we see every owner of a doctrine holding to it according to his doctrine. The determinist (Jabri) holds to verses of compulsion: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings﴾ [al-An'am: 25] and ﴿and in their ears deafness﴾ [al-An'am: 25]. The Qadari says: this is the doctrine of the disbelievers, mentioned in a context of blaming them, in His saying ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are in coverings from that to which you invite us, and in our ears is deafness"﴾ [Fussilat: 5], and in another place ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are uncircumcised"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 88].

Those who affirm the vision (of Allah) hold to His saying ﴿looking at their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 23], and the others hold to His saying ﴿No vision perceives Him﴾ [al-An'am: 103]. Those who affirm a direction (jihah) hold to His saying ﴿they fear their Lord above them﴾ [al-Nahl: 50] and His saying ﴿the Most Merciful, established above the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], and the others hold to His saying ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. So how is it fitting that the muhkam should be referred back to the less preponderant, in this manner? Thus ends the words of Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, and some of it has been summarized.

The scholars have mentioned benefits in the coming of the mutashābih, and the best of them is what al-Zamakhshari mentioned. He said: If you say, "Why was not the whole Qur'an muhkam?" I say: If all of it were muhkam, people would cling to it because of the ease of its meaning, and they would turn away from what requires investigation, reflection, and inquiry through reasoning and argument. Had they done so, they would have abandoned the path by which the knowledge of Allah and His Oneness is reached only through it. Also, there is the trial and distinguishing in the mutashābih between one who is steadfast upon the truth and one who wavers regarding it. And there is the benefit of the scholars competing and exerting their minds in extracting its meanings and referring them back to the muhkam, which contains great benefits, abundant sciences, and attaining high ranks with Allah. Moreover, the believer, who holds that there is no contradiction or discrepancy in the speech of Allah, when he sees in it what conflicts in its apparent sense, is concerned to seek what reconciles it and makes it run on one course. So he reflects and reviews his own understanding and that of others, and Allah grants him success, and the agreement of the mutashābih with the muhkam becomes clear to him. He then increases in tranquility toward his belief and in strength in mastering it. Thus ends the words of al-Zamakhshari, and it is a composition of what people have said about the benefit of the coming of the mutashābih in the Qur'an.

When He, exalted, mentioned at the beginning of the surah ﴿Allah, there is no god but Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting. He has sent down upon you the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 2], He mentioned here the manner of the Book, and used the relative pronoun (alladhi), since its relative clause refers back to the previous revelation (tanzil) and to something known in it. His saying ﴿He it is who has sent down upon you the Book; in it are verses that are muhkam...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7] to its end is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning that He left it in these two aspects, muhkam and mutashābih. The word (ayat) is in the nominative, functioning as the subject of the prepositional phrase (min-hu), since it has been relied upon; it is also permissible for it to be nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), and the sentence is then circumstantial. It is also possible that the sentence is a new independent sentence. The description of the verses as muhkam is true in that each verse is muhkam. As for His saying ﴿and others are mutashabihat﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7], ukhar is an adjective of a deleted noun, ayat. The description by similarity (tashabuh) is not valid for the singular of ukhar: if you said wa-ukhra mutashabihah, it would not be valid except in the sense that some of it resembles other parts of it. The intended meaning here is not this sense, because the resemblance intended here occurs only between two or more things. So this description is valid with the plural, since each of its units resembles the rest, though this does not apply to a single unit. It is like ﴿two men who fight﴾ [al-Qasas: 15], though one does not say rajul yaqtatil ("a man who fights"). The discussion of ukhar has already been covered in His saying ﴿then a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], so there is no need to repeat it here.

Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned that al-Mahdawi confused the matter of ukhar and spoiled the words of Sibawayh, so he paused at that part of al-Mahdawi's speech.

﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]: they are the Christians of Najran, because they confronted the Qur'an regarding the matter of Jesus, as said by al-Rabi'. Or they are the Jews, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi, because they asked that this verse of the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) be retained. Deviation (zaygh) here is their obstinacy.

Al-Tabari said: This is the most likely, and he mentioned the dialogue of Huyayy ibn Akhtab and his companions with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during the period of his mission, and their extracting the calculation of the time from the openings of the surahs, and their moving from one number to another, until they said: "It has confused us; we do not know whether to take the many or the few? And we do not believe in this." So Allah, exalted, sent down ﴿He it is who has sent down upon you the Book﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7], the verse.

Ibn Mas'ud and a group of the Companions, Mujahid, Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, and others interpreted deviation as the inclination away from guidance.

Qatadah said: They are those who deny the resurrection, for it says at its end ﴿and none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7], and that is nothing but the Day of Resurrection, for He concealed it from all creation. Qatadah also said: They are the Harurites (al-Haruriyyah), who are the Kharijites (al-Khawarij), and whoever interprets a verse not in its proper place. He also said: If the Harurites are not the Sabā'iyyah Kharijites, then I do not know who they are. Ibn Jurayj said: They are the hypocrites. It has been said: They are all the innovators (al-mubtadi'ah).

The apparent wording is general regarding those who deviate from the truth. Every group among those mentioned has deviated from the truth, so the wording includes them, even if it was revealed concerning a specific cause, because the lesson is in the generality of the wording.

﴿so they follow that of it which is mutashabih﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]. Al-Qurtubi said: Those who follow the mutashābih are either seekers of doubt, contradiction, and repetition; or seekers of the apparent meanings of the mutashābih, such as the anthropomorphists (al-mujassimah), who affirmed that He is a body and a form, with a face, an eye, a hand, a side, a leg, and a finger; or seekers of presenting an interpretation and clarification through direct observation. For example, a man asked Ibn 'Abbas about things that seemed to conflict in the Qur'an, such as ﴿and they will not ask one another﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 101], ﴿and they approached one another, questioning﴾ [al-Saffat: 27], ﴿and they will not conceal from Allah any statement﴾ [al-Nisa': 42], and ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23], and the like. Ibn 'Abbas answered him with what removed the contradiction from him. Or they are those who follow it and ask about it with a question meant to trap, as happened with Usaybigh and 'Umar, when 'Umar struck his head until blood ran down over his face. Thus ends his words, summarized.

﴿seeking discord and seeking its interpretation﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]: He gave two causes for their following the mutashābih. The first is seeking discord (al-fitnah). Al-Suddi, Rabi', Muqatil, and Ibn Qutaybah said: it is disbelief (kufr). Mujahid said: doubts and confusion (al-shubuhat wa-al-labs). Al-Zajjaj said: corrupting relations among people (ifsad dhat al-bayn). It was said: the doubts with which they argued against the delegation of Najran.

The second cause is seeking the interpretation (ta'wil). Ibn 'Abbas said: they sought knowledge of the duration of the Prophet's (ﷺ) mission. It was said: ta'wil means tafsir (explanation), as in ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not have patience﴾ [al-Kahf: 78]. Ibn 'Abbas also said: they sought the outcome of the affair of the believers, the final destiny of their Book, religion, and law, and the awaited end. Al-Zajjaj said: they sought the interpretation of their resurrection and revival. So Allah, exalted, informed that the interpretation of that and its time is ﴿the Day they see what they were promised﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35], namely the resurrection and the punishment; ﴿those who had forgotten it will say﴾ [al-A'raf: 53], meaning those who had neglected it; ﴿the messengers of our Lord had certainly come﴾ [al-A'raf: 53], meaning: we have now seen the interpretation of what the messengers had told us. Al-Suddi said: they wanted to know the outcomes of the Qur'an, which is its interpretation, namely when some of it would be abrogated (yunsakh, naskh). It was said: seeking its ta'wil is seeking the reality of its true nature and the depth of its meanings.

Al-Razi said words summarized as follows: the meaning of ta'wil here is that for which there is no evidence in the Book, such as "When is the Hour?" and the measures of reward and punishment for each responsible person.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿Those in whose hearts is deviation﴾ are the people of innovations (ahl al-bida'), so they follow the mutashābih, clinging to the mutashābih which admits what the innovator inclines to, that which does not match the muhkam, and admits what matches it from the saying of the people of truth. "Seeking discord" means seeking to tempt people away from their religion and mislead them, and "seeking its interpretation" means seeking to interpret it in the manner they desire. Thus ends his words, and it is a good statement.

(p. 383)

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 7:**

﴿No one knows its interpretation (ta'wil) except Allah, and those firmly grounded in knowledge say, "We believe in it."﴾ The sentence is complete at His words, "except Allah." Its meaning is that Allah alone has exclusive knowledge of the interpretation of the ambiguous verses (mutashabih). This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy, Ibn Abbas, Aisha, al-Hasan, Urwa, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Abu Nahik al-Asadi, Malik ibn Anas, al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Jubba'i, al-Akhfash, and Abu Ubayd. It is the view preferred by al-Khattabi and Fakhr al-Din al-Razi.

His words "and those firmly grounded" (al-rasikhun) would then be the subject (mubtada'), and "they say" (yaqulun) its predicate (khabar). It has also been said that "those firmly grounded" is joined to "Allah" (in the sense): "and those firmly grounded know its interpretation," and "they say" is a circumstantial clause (hal) describing them, meaning "saying." This view is also reported from Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, and most of the theologians (mutakallimun). The first view is preferred for the following reasons:

First, when the indicative evidence points to a meaning other than the apparent one, it is known that the intended meaning is one of the figurative senses (majaz). Preferring one figurative sense over another can only be done through verbal evidences, and these are speculative (zanni), and speculation is not sufficient for matters that are definitive (qat'i).

Second, what precedes the verse indicates a condemnation of those who seek the ambiguous verses. Had it been permissible, they would not have been condemned for seeking to know the time of the Hour. Restricting some of the ambiguous verses to a specific meaning is an abandonment of the apparent sense, which is not permissible.

Third, Allah praised those firmly grounded in knowledge by saying that they said, "We believe in it." Had they known the interpretation of the ambiguous verses in detail, there would be no praise in their believing in it, for whoever knows something in detail must believe in it. Rather, those firmly grounded know by rational proof that the intended meaning is other than the apparent one, and they leave the determination of the intended meaning to Allah's knowledge. They are certain that it is the truth, and the lack of determination did not lead them to abandon belief.

Fourth, if "those firmly grounded" were joined to "Allah," then "they say" would have to be the predicate of an implied subject, with the estimate "these people" or "they," which entails an implied pronoun, or it would be a circumstantial clause. The antecedent would be "Allah and those firmly grounded," so it would be a circumstantial clause for those firmly grounded alone, and this involves abandoning the apparent sense.

Fifth, His words "Each is from our Lord" (kullun min 'indi rabbina) imply a benefit, namely that they believed in what they knew in detail and in what they did not know. Had they known every detail, this benefit would be lost.

It was also reported from Ibn Abbas that the interpretation of the Qur'an is of four types:

An interpretation that no one can be ignorant of.

An interpretation that the Arabs know through their own language.

An interpretation that the scholars know.

An interpretation that none knows except Allah, the Exalted.

Malik was asked about the verse of establishment (istiwa'), and he said: "Establishment is known, the modality (kayfiyya) is unknown, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation." This concludes what was used to favor the first view. There is room for scrutiny in this. This view is supported by the recitation of Ubayy and Ibn Abbas, as transmitted by Tawus from him: "None knows its interpretation except Allah, and those firmly grounded in knowledge say, 'We believe in it.'" It is also supported by the recitation of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud): "Seeking its interpretation. Indeed its interpretation is only with Allah, and those firmly grounded in knowledge say..." Ibn Furak preferred the second view and elaborated on it at length.

In the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Ibn Abbas, "O Allah, give him understanding of the religion and teach him the interpretation," there is something that clarifies this, i.e., teach him the meanings of Your Book. When a difficulty occurred in the Book of Allah, Umar would summon Ibn Abbas and say to him, "Deep diver!" He would also gather the sons of the Emigrants and the Helpers and order them to reflect on the meanings of the Book.

Ibn Atiyya said: "If you reflect, you will see how close disagreement is to agreement. The Book is composed of the clear (muhkam) and the ambiguous (mutashabih). The clear is what is evident to anyone who understands the speech of the Arabs without reflection or confusion, and it is equally clear to the firmly grounded and to others. The ambiguous is what none knows except Allah, such as the matter of the Spirit, the time-limits of the unseen events reported as to occur, and other things. Among it is also what can be understood in several linguistic ways, so it is interpreted in the way that is correct, such as His words about Jesus, 'and a spirit from Him' (An-Nisa 4:171), and so on. No one is called firmly grounded except one who knows much of this type according to what has been decreed for him. Whoever knows only the clear is not firmly grounded."

So His words, "except Allah," necessarily imply by the plain intellect that He knows it in full, both of its two kinds. The firmly grounded know the second kind. The statement is sound according to the eloquence of the Arabs. They included the firmly grounded in the knowledge of interpretation by coordination (ʿatf), as when you say: "No one supported me except so-and-so and so-and-so," where one of them supported you by fighting alongside you and the other helped you with words only.

If we take "and those firmly grounded" as a separate subject, cut off from what precedes it, then calling them "firmly grounded" implies that they know more than the clear, which everyone who understands the speech of the Arabs knows equally. In what would their firmness consist if they know only what everyone knows? Is not firmness only the knowledge of the variations of speech, the sources of rulings, and the places of admonitions?

The grammatical analysis (i'rab) of "al-rasikhin" (the firmly grounded, in the accusative/genitive form) allows both views, and for this reason Ibn Abbas held both. As for one who interprets the ambiguous as only what Allah has exclusively known, his interpretation is not correct, because it restricts some of the ambiguous. This concludes the passage, which has been somewhat abridged. It also includes his preference that the phrase is joined to "Allah," and this is what al-Zamakhshari preferred. He said: "None can discern its true interpretation, which must be taken as its meaning, except Allah and His servants who are firmly grounded in knowledge, that is, those who are established in it, have settled in it, and have grasped it with a decisive molar." "They say" is a resumptive sentence clarifying the state of the firmly grounded, meaning: "These scholars of the interpretation say, 'We believe in it,'" that is, in the ambiguous. This concludes his words.

Two possibilities have emerged in the grammatical analysis of "and those firmly grounded":

The first: it is joined to His words "Allah," and then the grammatical analysis of "they say" has two possibilities. One is that it is the predicate of an elided subject. The second is that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause describing the firmly grounded, as when you say, "No one stood except Zayd and Hind laughing."

The second grammatical possibility for "and those firmly grounded" is that it is a subject (mubtada'), and "they say" must be its predicate, forming a coordination of sentences.

It has been said that "those firmly grounded in knowledge" (An-Nisa 4:162) refers to the believers among the People of the Book, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions, as evidenced by "but those firmly grounded in knowledge among them" (An-Nisa 4:162), meaning those firmly grounded in the knowledge of the Torah. This view is far-fetched. Firmness in knowledge has been explained by things that the language does not indicate. Rather, these are qualities that arise from firmness in knowledge, such as the saying of Nafi': "The firmly grounded is the one who is humble before Allah," and the saying of Malik: "The firmly grounded in knowledge is the one who acts on what he knows and follows it."

**"Each is from our Lord"** (kullun min 'indi rabbina) is part of what is said. The object of "they say" is His words: "We believe in it; each is from our Lord." Each clause is treated as though it were independently spoken, and for this reason they were not joined by a conjunction. Alternatively, the two are treated as merged in speech in the way of a single sentence, as in the verse of the poet:

*"How are you this morning, how are you this evening, from what plants love in the heart of the noble one."*

It is as if he said: "This speech is of what plants love." The pronoun in "bihi" (in it) may refer to the ambiguous, which is the apparent reading, and it may refer to the Book. The tanwin in "kullun" (each) is a substitute for the omitted element, so it may refer to the Book, meaning "all of it is from our Lord." It may also be estimated as: "Each of the clear and the ambiguous is from Allah." If it is from Allah, there is no contradiction and no discrepancy, and this is a truth that must be believed. He attributed the origin ("from") to "our Lord" rather than to any other of His names, because the word "Lord" (rabb) implies a consideration of the welfare of His servants. Had there been no benefit in the ambiguous, Allah would not have sent it down, and He would have made His whole Book clear.

**"But none will be mindful except people of understanding"** (Al 'Imran 3:7): that is, none is admonished by the revelation of the clear and the ambiguous except the people of intellect, since they are the ones who perceive the realities of things and place speech in its proper positions. He thereby indicated that what is ambiguous in the Qur'an requires reflection through the intellect, which was made the means of distinguishing the obligatory, the permissible, and the impossible. One must not stop at the apparent meaning of the wording; rather, thought must be exercised in this so that nothing unfitting is attributed to the Creator, the Exalted, nor to the rulings He has legislated anything that is impossible in reason. Ibn Atiyya said: "That is, whoever says this, believes in it, stops where it stops, and leaves off following the ambiguous, is none but a person of intellect." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is praise for the firmly grounded for applying the mind and for good reflection."

**"Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us"** (Al 'Imran 3:8). It may be that this is part of what is said, meaning: "They say, 'Our Lord...'" As they saw people divided into those who deviate and those who are mindful and believing, they called upon Allah, the Exalted, using the word "Lord," not to let their hearts deviate after their guidance, lest they join those in whose hearts is deviation. It may also be that the Exalted taught them this supplication, the estimate being: "Say, 'Our Lord...'"

The meaning of "deviation" (izagha) here is misguidance. Attributing this to Him, the Exalted, is a refutation of the Mu'tazila in their claim that Allah does not misguide, for if deviation were not from the Exalted, it would not be permissible to supplicate Him for the removal of what is not permissible for Him to do.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Do not burden us with a heavy worship by which our hearts would deviate." This view contains a safeguard against Allah creating deviation and misguidance in the heart of any of the servants. Ibn Kaysan said: "They asked not to deviate, lest Allah cause their hearts to deviate, as in His words, 'So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate' (As-Saff 61:5). That is: make us firm upon Your guidance, and let us not deviate, so that we would deserve that You cause our hearts to deviate." This is a Mu'tazilite inclination, as al-Jubba'i said: "He does not withhold from them the favors by which the heart continues in the attribute of faith. When He withheld the favors from them because of their deserving that, it was permissible to say that He caused them to deviate, and this is indicated by 'when they deviated.'" Al-Jubba'i also said: "Do not cause us to deviate from Your Garden and Your reward." Abu Muslim said: "Guard us from Satan and from the evil of our souls, so that we do not deviate." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Do not test us with trials in which our hearts deviate, or do not withhold Your kindnesses from us after You have been kind to us." This concludes his words.

This is a theological question: Does God create evil just as He creates good, or does He not create evil? The first is the view of the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna), and the second is the view of the Mu'tazila, and each interprets according to his own school.

Al-Siddiq, Abu Qa'ila and al-Jarrah read (لا تَزُغْ قُلُوبُنا) with a fatha on the tā' and a damma on the bā', [i.e., lā tazugh qulūbunā]. Some read (لا يَزُغْ) with a fatha on the yā', and a raf' on the bā' of (قُلُوبُنا), making it from zāgha and attributing it to the hearts. Its apparent meaning is a prohibition addressed to the hearts against swerving, but it is actually of the type of: "lā arayannaka hāhunā" (I shall not see you here), and the poet's line:

"Lā a'rifanna rabrabān ḥuwwaran madāmi'uh"
(I shall not recognize a gazelle with wide-set eyes whose tears...)

That is: "Do not make us swerve, so that our hearts swerve after You have guided us." Its apparent meaning is guidance, which is the opposite of misguidance. It has also been said: "after You have guided us" means guidance to knowledge of the clear (muḥkam) verses and submission to the ambiguous (mutashābih) verses of Your Book.

(إذْ) is originally a adverb of time, and here (بَعْدَ) has been prefixed to it, so it became a noun that is not a time adverb. Before it leaves the adverbial sense, it is followed by a clause, and its state of being prefixed to a clause is retained; the prefixing to it does not remove it from this ruling. Do you not see the Almighty's saying: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 119]? And ﴿a day when no soul shall control﴾ [al-Infitar: 19], according to the reading of the one who raised (يَوْمُ). And the poet's line:

"'Alā ḥīna 'ātabtu al-mashība 'alā al-ṣibā
'Alā ḥīna man tuktabu 'alayhi dhunūbuhu 'alā ḥīna al-kirāmi qalīl
Alā layta ayyāma al-ṣafā'i jadīd"

How did the adverb here leave its usual function, being used as a predicate, as a prepositional phrase, as the subject of "layta," and yet be prefixed to a clause?

﴿And grant us from Yourself mercy﴾: they asked using the word "grant" (hibah), which implies favour and kindness toward them without cause, deed or exchange, since a gift is of this kind. They specified that it is from Him. If mercy is one of the attributes of the Essence, then gift is not possible in it; rather the meaning would be: bounty, or reward issuing from mercy. Since what was asked for issues from mercy, it is valid to ask for mercy, treating the cause as if it were the effect. It has also been said: the meaning of "mercy" is success, rectitude and steadfastness in what we are upon of faith and guidance.

﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾: this is like the reason for their saying "grant." Like your saying: "Solve this difficult problem, for you are the knower of difficulties." He used the intensive form on the pattern fa'āl, though they had said "hawūb" for the sake of matching the verse-endings. In "anta" it is permissible to treat it as an emphatic pronoun, as a separator, or as a mubtada'.

﴿Our Lord, You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾: Since they asked Him, Exalted, not to make their hearts swerve after guidance, and the fruit of the absence of swerving and of guidance only appears on the Day of Resurrection, they informed that they are certain of the Day of Resurrection and of the raising therein for recompense, and that belief in the truth of the promise concerning it is what guided them to ask that He not make their hearts swerve. The meaning of "for a Day about which there is no doubt" is: for the recompense of a day. "There is no doubt in it" means there is no doubt about its existence, because of the truthfulness of the One who informed of it; and although doubt may befall one who denies it, he is in a state in which he should not have doubt.

It has also been said: the lām is in the sense of fī (in), i.e., "in a Day," and the object of gathering is not mentioned. The apparent meaning of this gathering is the resurrection from the graves for recompense; so it is an active participle with future meaning. What indicates that it refers to the future is the reading of Abu Hatim, "jāmi'un al-nāsa" with tanwīn and naṣb on "al-nās."

It has also been said: the meaning of gathering here is that He gathers them in the graves, and the lām seems to mean ilā (until), indicating the endpoint: He gathers them in the graves until the Day of Resurrection. The active participle here does not take account of time, since among mankind some have died and some have not, so the gathering is attributed to God without consideration of time. The pronoun in "fīhi" refers to the Day, since the clause is a qualifier of it. Whoever returns it to the gathering understood from "jāmi'" or to the recompense indicated by the meaning has gone too far.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾: the apparent shift from the second-person address to the third-person name indicates resumption, and that it is part of Allah's speech, not the speech of the firmly grounded who are supplicating. Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is that divinity is incompatible with breaking a promise, like your saying: "Indeed the generous does not disappoint the one who asks him." (al-mī'ād) means the appointed time. End of his words. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazili doctrine in his phrase "divinity is incompatible with breaking a promise." Al-Jubba'i cited this verse as proof for the certainty of threatening the sinners absolutely, whereas for us it is conditional upon the absence of pardon, as we and he agreed that it is conditional upon the absence of repentance; and both conditions are established by a separate proof. Even if we grant what they say, we do not grant that threat falls under promise.

Al-Wahidi said: it is permissible to take it as referring to the promise of the friends (of God) and not the threat against enemies, because breaking a threat is considered generosity among the Arabs, and for this reason they praise it. The poet said:

"Idhā wa'ada al-sarrā' anjaza wa'dahu
Wa in wa'ada al-darrā' fal-'afwu māni'uh"

It is also possible that this sentence is from the speech of the supplicants, and this would be a case of iltifat (shift of address), since it is a move from address to the third person, because mentioning Him by His greatest name carries majesty, grandeur and awe. And as if, when they continued the supplication with "Our Lord," they informed about God, Exalted, that He is faithful to His promise; and this statement includes belief in the resurrection, recompense, and fulfilment of what God, Exalted, has promised.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against Allah﴾: It has been said: the intended are the delegation of Najran, for it is narrated that Abu Harithah ibn 'Alqama said to his brother: "I know that he is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but if I declare that, the kings of Rome will take back from me what they gave me of wealth." It has also been said: the reference is to the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Ibn 'Abbas said: Qurayza and al-Nadir, who used to boast of their wealth and children. And the statement is general, encompassing every disbeliever.

The meaning of (min Allāh) is: from His punishment, both worldly and otherworldly. The meaning of aghnā 'anhu is: to repel and prevent it from him. Since wealth is more effective in the domain of defence, seeking nearness, and temptation than children, it is mentioned first in this verse, and in His saying: ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children will bring you near to Us in position﴾ [Saba': 37], and in His saying: ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ [al-Taghabun: 15], and in His saying: ﴿and competition in wealth and children﴾ [al-Hadid: 20], and in His saying: ﴿neither wealth nor sons will benefit﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 88]. This is unlike His saying: ﴿Adorned for mankind is love of desires: of women and sons, and heaped-up piles of gold and silver...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14], to the end, for there He mentioned the love of desires and placed women and sons before the mention of wealth. The discussion of that will come, God willing.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read (لَنْ يُغْنِيَ) with yā' in accordance with the masculine marking of the verb; 'Ali read (لَنْ يُغْنِي) with a sukūn on the yā'; al-Hasan read (لَنْ يُغْنِي) with yā' at the beginning and a sukūn yā' at the end, this being because of the difficulty of a vowel on a soft letter, and treating the accusative like the nominative. Some grammarians restrict this to poetic necessity, but it should not be restricted to it, since it is frequent in their speech.

(Min) is for the beginning of the endpoint according to al-Mubarrad, and in the sense of 'inda (with) according to Abu 'Ubayda, who likened it to His saying: ﴿He fed them against hunger and secured them against fear﴾ [Quraysh: 4]; he said: its meaning is "at hunger and at fear." That (min) means 'inda is very weak.

Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying "from Allah" is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, conjecture avails not against the truth at all﴾ [Yunus: 36]. The meaning: they will not avail them against God's mercy or obedience to God anything, i.e., in place of His mercy and His obedience, and in place of the truth. From this is: "and the wealth of the wealthy will not benefit him against You"; that is, his fortune and share of this world will not benefit him in that, i.e., in place of your obedience and worship and what is with You. In the same sense is His saying: ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children bring you near to Us in position﴾ [Saba': 37]. End of his words.

As for establishing that (min) means substitution, there is disagreement; our companions deny it, while others affirm it, and claim that it comes in the sense of substitution, citing His saying: ﴿Are you pleased with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ [al-Tawba: 38]; ﴿We would have made from you angels﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 60], i.e., in place of the Hereafter and in place of you. The poet said:

"Akhadhū al-makhāḍa min al-faṣīli ghulubbatan
Ẓulman wa yuktabu lil-amīri afīlā"

i.e., in place of the young camel. And "shay'an" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, as you say: "I struck a kind of striking." It is also possible that it is in the accusative as a direct object, since the sense of "lan tughnī" is "will not repel or prevent," so on this view "min" may be in the position of a circumstantial phrase relating to "shay'an," since if it had come after it, it would be in the position of a qualifier; when it precedes, it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial. In that case "min" is partitive.

So four views are summarized regarding (min): the beginning of the endpoint, which is the view of al-Mubarrad and al-Kalbi; its being in the sense of 'inda (with), which is the view of Abu 'Ubayda; substitution, which is the view of al-Zamakhshari; and partitiveness, which is what we have established.

﴿And they are the fuel of the Fire﴾: Since He mentioned earlier that the great number of their wealth and the support of their children will not avail those who disbelieved, He informed of their destination, and that the ultimate end of whoever disbelieves and denies the signs of Allah is the Fire. This sentence may be grammatically conjoined to the predicate of "inna," or it may be an independent sentence conjoined to the first sentence. He indicated (with ulā'ika) their remoteness, and used the word "hum," which implies exclusivity, and made them the very fuel itself, for emphasis on the burning, as if the Fire had nothing to kindle it but them. The discussion of "fuel" has already occurred in His saying: ﴿whose fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Baqara: 24].

Al-Hasan, Mujahid and others read (وُقُودُ) with a damma on the wāw, which is the verbal noun of: "the fire blazed, blazes, a blazing" (waqadat al-nār taqidu wuqūdan); and it may be according to an ellipsis: "the people of the fuel of the Fire," or "the wood of fuel," or he made them the fuel itself for emphasis, as you say: "Zayd is satisfaction."

It has also been said for the verbal noun: "wuqūd," with a fatha on the wāw, which is one of the verbal nouns that came on the pattern fa'ūl with fatha on the wāw, and this has been mentioned. "Hum" may be a mubtada', and it may be a separator (fasl).

﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾: Since He mentioned that whoever disbelieves and denies Allah ends up in the Fire, and his wealth and child will not avail him, He mentioned that the situation of these people in their denial of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the consequence of punishment for their disbelief is like the situation of the disbelieving nations who preceded them: they were seized for their sins and punished for them. He pointed to the people of Pharaoh because the discourse was with the Children of Israel, who knew what befell them when they denied Moses: their drowning, their eventual ending in the Fire, and the Children of Israel's victory over them and their inheritance of their dominion. In all this there is good news for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and for those who believe in him: that the disbelievers' end in this world is annihilation, and in the Hereafter the Fire, as happened to the people of Pharaoh, who were destroyed in this world and went on to the Fire.

They differed about the grammatical analysis of (كَدَأْبِ). It has been said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, so it is in the position of nominative; the estimate being: "their custom is like the custom of..." and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya began with this. It has been said: it is in the position of the accusative by (wuqūd), i.e., the Fire is kindled by them just as it is kindled by the people of Pharaoh, as you say: "Indeed you wrong people like the custom of your father," meaning "like the wrong of your father," as al-Zamakhshari said.

It has been said: it is by a verb estimated from the word "wuqūd," and the comparison is in the burning itself, as Ibn 'Atiyya said. It has been said: it is from its meaning, i.e., they were punished with a punishment like the custom of the people of Pharaoh, and the phrase "fuel of the Fire" indicates this.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 8–11 (part 2 of 3):

It has been said that it is governed by ﴿لَنْ تُغْنِيَ﴾ (*lan tughniya*, "will not avail"), meaning: "their wealth and children will not avail them against Allah, just as they did not avail those before them." This was said by al-Zamakhshari, but it is weak, because it separates the governing element (*'amil*) from the governed element (*ma'mul*) by the sentence ﴿وَأُولَئِكَ هُمْ وَقُودُ النَّارِ﴾ ("and those are the fuel of the Fire"). This is so under either of the two assessments we have made, namely whether it is coordinated with the predicate of *inna* (indeed), or with the sentence emphasized by *inna*. If you assess it as a parenthetical clause (*i'tirahiyya*), which is far-fetched, then what al-Zamakhshari said is permissible.

It has also been said that it is governed by a verb in the accusative that is implied by the meaning of ﴿لَنْ تُغْنِيَ﴾, meaning: their benefit from wealth and children was entirely nullified, as was the custom of the people of Pharaoh.

It has been said that it is an adjective (*na't*) of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), whose assessment is: *kufran* (disbelief) *ka-da'bi* (like the custom of). Its governing element is ﴿كَفَرُوا﴾ (*kafaru*, "they disbelieved"). This was said by al-Farra', and it is an error, because if it were governed by the relative clause (*sila*), it would be part of the relative clause, and it is not permissible for the relative pronoun to be given a predicate before it has completed its relative clause and its complements; here it has already been given a predicate, so it cannot be governed by what is within the relative clause.

It has also been said that it is governed by a verb omitted that is indicated by ﴿كَفَرُوا﴾, the assessment being: they disbelieved with a disbelief like the custom of the people of Pharaoh.

It has been said that the governing element of the *kaf* (like) is ﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ ("they denied Our signs"). On this view, the pronoun in *kadhdhabu* refers to the disbelievers of Makkah and others among the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: they denied with a denial like the custom of the people of Pharaoh.

It has been said that it is connected to the statement ﴿فَأَخَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾ ("so Allah seized them for their sins"), meaning: He seized them with a seizing like that with which He seized the people of Pharaoh. This is weak, because what follows the coordinating *fa'* (then) does not govern what precedes it. Some of our companions reported from the Kufans that they permitted: "Zaydan qumtu fa-darabtu" (Zayd, I stood up and then struck him), and according to this, this view is permissible. These are ten opinions about the governing element of the *kaf*.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: *al-da'b* (custom), with the hamza either vowelled with a sukun or with a fatha, is the verbal noun of *da'aba yad'abu*, when one persists in doing something and continues to exert effort at it; and *da'b* is also said of habit. Abu Hatim said: I heard Ya'qub mention *ka-da'bi* with a fatha on the hamza, and he said to me, while I was a little boy: "On what basis is it permissible?" I said to him: "I think it is from *da'iba yad'abu da'ban*." He accepted this from me and marvelled at the soundness of my assessment despite my youth, but I do not know whether it is said or not. Al-Nahhas said: *da'iba* is never said; rather it is said *da'aba yad'abu du'ubun*, as the grammarians have transmitted, including al-Farra', who related it in the book *al-Masadir* (The Verbal Nouns).

*Al ' Fir'awn* (the people of Pharaoh) means his partisans and followers.

﴿وَالَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ ("and those before them") refers to the disbelievers of earlier nations, such as the people of Nuh, the people of Hud, the people of Shu'ayb, and others. The pronoun on this view refers back to the people of Pharaoh. It is also possible that the pronoun refers back to ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ ("those who disbelieved"), who are the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The position of ﴿وَالَّذِينَ﴾ is genitive, coordinated with ﴿آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾.

﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ ("they denied Our signs"): this sentence is an explanation of *al-da'b* (custom), as if it was said: "What did they do, and what was done to them?" So it was said: "They denied Our signs." It is therefore as if it were the answer to an implied question. They also permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: denying. They also permitted that the speech is complete at ﴿كَدَأْبِ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ ("like the custom of the people of Pharaoh"), and then a new beginning is made: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ كَذَّبُوا﴾, so that ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*) and ﴿كَذَّبُوا﴾ is its predicate. In the phrase ﴿بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ there is an *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person), since before it there is ﴿مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ (from Allah), which is a third-person reference, and so it moves from it to the first person.

The signs (*ayat*) may be the recited ones in the books of Allah, and it may also be that they are the indications that point to the oneness of Allah and the truthfulness of His prophets.

﴿فَأَخَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾: it shifts from the first person to the third person. The meaning of seizing for a sin is punishment for it, and the *ba'* in *bi-dhunubihim* indicates cause.

﴿وَاللَّهُ شَدِيدُ الْعِقَابِ﴾ ("and Allah is severe in punishment"): the explanation of this has already been given before, and it contains an indication of the might of Allah against whoever disbelieves in His signs and denies them. It has been said: these verses contain, among the varieties of eloquence (*fasaha*), the beauty of ambiguity (*husn al-ibham*), which is found in what they begin with, in order to alert the mind to consider what follows in the speech.

The metaphorical use of comparison (*majaz al-tashbih*) occurs in several places, among them ﴿نَزَّلَ عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ ("He sent down to you the Book with truth"). The literal meaning of *nuzul* (descent) is the casting of a body from a height to a lower place. The Qur'an is established in the Preserved Tablet, and when it is established in the heart, it takes the place of a body cast from a height to a lower place, so it is likened to that, and the word *inzal* (sending down) is applied to it. And in His saying ﴿لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ﴾ ("confirming what was before it"), the Qur'an confirms what preceded it of the books; it is likened to a person who has in front of him something that he receives little by little. And in His saying ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ التَّوْرَاةَ وَالإِنْجِيلَ مِنْ قَبْلُ هُدًى لِلنَّاسِ وَأَنْزَلَ الْفُرْقَانَ﴾ ("and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel before, as guidance for mankind, and He sent down the Criterion"), He placed the verbal noun in the position of the active participle, so He made the Torah like a man who conceals from you a matter, that is, he hides it, because of the obscure meanings in it. The Gospel is likened, because of its breadth of encouragement and warning, its admonitions and humility, to the wide-eyed gazelle (*al-'ayn al-najla'*). He made it guidance because of the direction it gives, like the road that guides you to the place you seek. He likened the Criterion (*al-Furqan*) to a body that separates two bodies. And in His saying ﴿عَذَابٌ شَدِيدٌ﴾ ("a severe punishment"), He likened what the soul experiences of the constriction and pain of punishment to a person who is bound and confined. And in His saying ﴿يُصَوِّرُكُمْ﴾ ("He shapes you"), He likened His command, or the connection of His will to existence, to the highest degree of perfection and craftsmanship, to a craftsman who represents something: he joins one body to another and forms a figure from them. And in His saying ﴿مِنْهُ آيَاتٌ مُحْكَمَاتٌ﴾ ("in it are firm verses"), He made what is clear of the meanings of His Book, and whose traces of wisdom are apparent, firm (*muhkam*). He likened the firm verses, because of the fundamental meanings in them from which many branches derive, to the mother to which the offspring of her descendants return and which they resort to. And He likened what its meanings are obscure of, because of the variety of its aspects, such as the disjointed letters (*al-fawatih*), and words that carry many meanings, and the verses that indicate the matter of the return and the reckoning, to the ambiguous and confusing thing whose matter is so obscure that the intellect is baffled in describing it. And in His saying ﴿فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ زَيْغٌ﴾ ("in their hearts is deviation"), He likened the heart that inclines away from the right course to a thing that has strayed from its place. And in His saying ﴿وَهَبْ لَنَا مِنْ لَدُنْكَ رَحْمَةً﴾ ("grant us mercy from Yourself"), He likened the intelligible notion of mercy as a desire for good to the perceptible things of bodies, the gift and the thing given in a gift. And in His saying ﴿وَقُودُ النَّارِ﴾ ("the fuel of the Fire"), He likened them to firewood, which is of no use except as fuel. And the Exalted said: ﴿إِنَّكُمْ وَمَا تَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ حَصَبُ جَهَنَّمَ﴾ ("Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell," Q. 21:98), and *al-hasab* is firewood in the language of Abyssinia. And in His saying ﴿فَأَخَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾, He likened the encompassing of His punishment upon them to the one seized by the hand, which is disposed of by the judgment of the will to seize.

It has been said: all of these are metaphors (*isti'arat*), and there is no simile in them except ﴿كَدَأْبِ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾, since in it the particle of comparison is explicitly mentioned.

Particularization (*al-ikhtisas*) occurs in several places, among them in His saying ﴿نَزَّلَ عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ﴾ up to ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ الْفُرْقَانَ﴾, according to the one who interprets the Criterion as the Psalms (*Zabur*). He particularized the four and excluded the rest of what was sent down, because the people of books at that time were the believers, the Jews, and the Christians. And in His saying ﴿لَا يَخْفَى عَلَيْهِ شَيْءٌ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِي السَّمَاءِ﴾ ("nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Him"), He specified them because they are the largest of His created things that are apparent to us, because they are the abodes of rational beings, and because from them come most of the benefits particular to His servants. And in His saying ﴿وَالرَّاسِخُونَ﴾ ("and those firm in knowledge"), He singled them out by the particular quality of firmness in knowledge. And in His saying ﴿أُولُو الْأَلْبَابِ﴾ ("people of understanding"), because the rational have the particular quality of discernment, reflection, and consideration. And in His saying ﴿لَا تُزِغْ قُلُوبَنَا﴾ ("do not let our hearts deviate"), He specified the hearts, because the soundness and corruption of the body depend on them, which is not so for the rest of the organs, and because they are the place of faith and, according to those who hold this view, the place of the intellect. And in His saying ﴿إِنَّكَ جَامِعُ النَّاسِ لِيَوْمٍ﴾ ("You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day"), He is the gatherer of them in this world upon the surface of the earth alive and in its belly dead; but on that Day is the greatest gathering, which is the Resurrection, and it occurs only on that Day, and there is no gatherer except Him, exalted is He. And in His saying ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَنْ تُغْنِيَ عَنْهُمْ أَمْوَالُهُمْ وَلَا أَوْلَادُهُمْ﴾ ("indeed those who disbelieved, their wealth and their children will not avail them"), He specified the disbelievers, because the wealth of the believers, which they spend in the ways of righteousness, will avail them, for they will reap its fruit in the Hereafter; and their children will benefit them in the Hereafter: they will give them drink, they will be a shield for them from the Fire, they will intercede for them if they die young, and they will benefit them by righteous supplication when they are grown. All of this has been reported in a sound hadith.

And in His saying ﴿كَدَأْبِ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ ("like the custom of the people of Pharaoh"), He singled them out for mention and put them first, because they were the most tyrannical of the nations and the most obstinate toward their prophets, so they were the most severely punished.

Omission (*al-hadhf*) occurs in several places: in His saying ﴿لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ﴾ ("confirming what was before it"), meaning: of the books. And ﴿أَنْزَلَ التَّوْرَاةَ وَالإِنْجِيلَ﴾ ("He sent down the Torah and the Gospel"), meaning: and He sent down the Psalms (*Zabur*) and the Gospel, because the two descents were at different times (the omitted element is *al-Zabur*). ﴿هُدًى لِلنَّاسِ﴾ ("guidance for mankind"), meaning: those whom He willed to guide. ﴿عَذَابٌ شَدِيدٌ﴾ ("a severe punishment"), meaning: on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿ذُو انْتِقَامٍ﴾ ("Lord of retribution"), meaning: against whomever He wills to punish. ﴿فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِي السَّمَاءِ﴾, meaning: nor in anything other than these two. (*Al-'Aziz*), meaning: in His dominion. (*Al-Hakim*), meaning: in His making. (*Wa-ukhar*), meaning: and other verses. ﴿زَيْغٌ﴾ ("deviation"), meaning: from the truth. ﴿ابْتِغَاءَ الْفِتْنَةِ﴾ ("seeking discord"), meaning: for you. ﴿وَابْتِغَاءَ تَأْوِيلِهِ﴾ ("and seeking its interpretation"), meaning: according to other than the intended meaning of it. ﴿وَمَا يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَهُ﴾ ("and none knows its interpretation"), meaning: according to the true sought reality. (*Rabbana*), meaning: O our Lord. ﴿رَبَّنَا لَا تُزِغْ قُلُوبَنَا﴾ ("our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate"), meaning: from the truth. ﴿بَعْدَ إِذْ هَدَيْتَنَا﴾ ("after You have guided us"), meaning: to it. ﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ ("they denied Our signs"), meaning: those sent down upon the messengers, or those set up as proofs of the oneness (of Allah). ﴿بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾ ("for their sins"), meaning: those past.

Repetition (*al-takrar*): ﴿نَزَّلَ عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ﴾, ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ التَّوْرَاةَ﴾, ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ الْفُرْقَانَ﴾. It is repeated because of the difference in the sending down, its manner, and its time. With the signs of Allah, and Allah repeated His name, exalted is He, for magnification, because in mentioning the explicit noun there is a magnification that is not in the pronoun.

﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ﴾ ("there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting") (Q. 3:2); ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ الْعَزِيزُ﴾ ("there is no god but He, the Mighty") (Q. 3:6). He repeated the sentence to draw attention to the firm establishment of this in souls, and as a refutation of whoever claims that there is with Him another god. (*Ibtigha' ta'wilihi*) and ﴿وَمَا يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَهُ﴾ ("and none knows its interpretation") (Q. 3:7) are repeated because of the difference between the two interpretations, or for the magnification of the matter of interpretation.

﴿رَبَّنَا لَا تُزِغْ﴾ and ﴿رَبَّنَا إِنَّكَ﴾ ("our Lord, do not let... our Lord, indeed You"): He repeated the supplication, to alert to its constancy and to warn against neglecting it, because of what it contains of the manifestation of need.

Anteriority and posteriority (*al-taqdim wa-al-ta'khir*) occur in the mention of the sending down of the books: the report about it does not come in the order of time, for the Torah came first, then the Psalms, then the Gospel, then the Qur'an. The Qur'an was placed first because of its nobility, the greatness of its reward, its abrogation of what preceded it (*naskh*), its permanence, and the continuance of its ruling until the end of time. He placed the Torah second because of the many rulings in it, the narratives, and the hidden deductions.

Al-Mufaddal narrated that the Torah, when it was sent down, was seventy *wasq* (loads), then He made the Gospel a third, because it is a book containing admonitions and wisdom beyond counting, then He followed it with the Psalms, because it contains admonitions and wisdom that did not reach the level of the Gospel. This is if we say that the Criterion (*al-Furqan*) is the Psalms.

In His saying ﴿فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِي السَّمَاءِ﴾ ("on earth or in heaven"), He placed the earth before the heaven, even though the heaven is greater in worlds, greater in bodies, greater in signs and proofs, and more abundant in virtues because of the purity of its inhabitants, in contrast to the inhabitants of the earth. This was done in order to inform them of His awareness of the secrets of their affairs, and He gave importance to placing their location first, so that they might restrain themselves from their ugly deeds, because when it is made clear that Allah is not hidden from anything of their affair, they will feel shame before Him.

The shift (*al-iltifat*) in ﴿رَبَّنَا إِنَّكَ جَامِعُ﴾ ("our Lord, indeed You are the gatherer") is followed by ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ ("indeed Allah").
