And in His saying ﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ ("they denied Our signs") it is followed by ﴿وَاللَّهُ شَدِيدُ الْعِقَابِ﴾ ("and Allah is severe in punishment").

The emphasis (al-ta'kid): in ﴿And those — they are the fuel of the Fire﴾ he emphasized with the word "they" (hum), and he emphasized with his saying ﴿He is the One who forms you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 6] his saying ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 6]; and he emphasized with his saying ﴿He is the One who has sent down upon you the Book﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 7] his saying ﴿He has sent down upon you the Book﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 3].

The extension (al-tawassu'): by placing the verbal noun (masdar) in the position of the active participle (ism al-fa'il) in his saying "guidance" (huda) and "the Criterion" (al-furqan), meaning "guiding" (hadiyan) and "the one who distinguishes" (al-fariq). And by placing the particle in the position of the adverb of place (al-zarf) in his saying "from Allah" (min Allah), meaning "with Allah" ('inda Allah), according to the view of those who interpreted "min" as meaning "'inda" (with). And the paronomasia of different roots (al-tajnis al-mughayir) in his saying "grant" (wahab) and "the Bestower" (al-Wahhab).

This is a theological question: Does God create evil just as He creates good, or does He not create evil? The first is the view of the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna), and the second is the view of the Mu'tazila, and each interprets according to his own school.

Al-Siddiq, Abu Qa'ila and al-Jarrah read (لا تَزُغْ قُلُوبُنا) with a fatha on the tā' and a damma on the bā', [i.e., lā tazugh qulūbunā]. Some read (لا يَزُغْ) with a fatha on the yā', and a raf' on the bā' of (قُلُوبُنا), making it from zāgha and attributing it to the hearts. Its apparent meaning is a prohibition addressed to the hearts against swerving, but it is actually of the type of: "lā arayannaka hāhunā" (I shall not see you here), and the poet's line:

"Lā a'rifanna rabrabān ḥuwwaran madāmi'uh"
(I shall not recognize a gazelle with wide-set eyes whose tears...)

That is: "Do not make us swerve, so that our hearts swerve after You have guided us." Its apparent meaning is guidance, which is the opposite of misguidance. It has also been said: "after You have guided us" means guidance to knowledge of the clear (muḥkam) verses and submission to the ambiguous (mutashābih) verses of Your Book.

(إذْ) is originally a adverb of time, and here (بَعْدَ) has been prefixed to it, so it became a noun that is not a time adverb. Before it leaves the adverbial sense, it is followed by a clause, and its state of being prefixed to a clause is retained; the prefixing to it does not remove it from this ruling. Do you not see the Almighty's saying: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 119]? And ﴿a day when no soul shall control﴾ [al-Infitar: 19], according to the reading of the one who raised (يَوْمُ). And the poet's line:

"'Alā ḥīna 'ātabtu al-mashība 'alā al-ṣibā
'Alā ḥīna man tuktabu 'alayhi dhunūbuhu 'alā ḥīna al-kirāmi qalīl
Alā layta ayyāma al-ṣafā'i jadīd"

How did the adverb here leave its usual function, being used as a predicate, as a prepositional phrase, as the subject of "layta," and yet be prefixed to a clause?

﴿And grant us from Yourself mercy﴾: they asked using the word "grant" (hibah), which implies favour and kindness toward them without cause, deed or exchange, since a gift is of this kind. They specified that it is from Him. If mercy is one of the attributes of the Essence, then gift is not possible in it; rather the meaning would be: bounty, or reward issuing from mercy. Since what was asked for issues from mercy, it is valid to ask for mercy, treating the cause as if it were the effect. It has also been said: the meaning of "mercy" is success, rectitude and steadfastness in what we are upon of faith and guidance.

﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾: this is like the reason for their saying "grant." Like your saying: "Solve this difficult problem, for you are the knower of difficulties." He used the intensive form on the pattern fa'āl, though they had said "hawūb" for the sake of matching the verse-endings. In "anta" it is permissible to treat it as an emphatic pronoun, as a separator, or as a mubtada'.

﴿Our Lord, You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾: Since they asked Him, Exalted, not to make their hearts swerve after guidance, and the fruit of the absence of swerving and of guidance only appears on the Day of Resurrection, they informed that they are certain of the Day of Resurrection and of the raising therein for recompense, and that belief in the truth of the promise concerning it is what guided them to ask that He not make their hearts swerve. The meaning of "for a Day about which there is no doubt" is: for the recompense of a day. "There is no doubt in it" means there is no doubt about its existence, because of the truthfulness of the One who informed of it; and although doubt may befall one who denies it, he is in a state in which he should not have doubt.

It has also been said: the lām is in the sense of fī (in), i.e., "in a Day," and the object of gathering is not mentioned. The apparent meaning of this gathering is the resurrection from the graves for recompense; so it is an active participle with future meaning. What indicates that it refers to the future is the reading of Abu Hatim, "jāmi'un al-nāsa" with tanwīn and naṣb on "al-nās."

It has also been said: the meaning of gathering here is that He gathers them in the graves, and the lām seems to mean ilā (until), indicating the endpoint: He gathers them in the graves until the Day of Resurrection. The active participle here does not take account of time, since among mankind some have died and some have not, so the gathering is attributed to God without consideration of time. The pronoun in "fīhi" refers to the Day, since the clause is a qualifier of it. Whoever returns it to the gathering understood from "jāmi'" or to the recompense indicated by the meaning has gone too far.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾: the apparent shift from the second-person address to the third-person name indicates resumption, and that it is part of Allah's speech, not the speech of the firmly grounded who are supplicating. Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is that divinity is incompatible with breaking a promise, like your saying: "Indeed the generous does not disappoint the one who asks him." (al-mī'ād) means the appointed time. End of his words. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazili doctrine in his phrase "divinity is incompatible with breaking a promise." Al-Jubba'i cited this verse as proof for the certainty of threatening the sinners absolutely, whereas for us it is conditional upon the absence of pardon, as we and he agreed that it is conditional upon the absence of repentance; and both conditions are established by a separate proof. Even if we grant what they say, we do not grant that threat falls under promise.

Al-Wahidi said: it is permissible to take it as referring to the promise of the friends (of God) and not the threat against enemies, because breaking a threat is considered generosity among the Arabs, and for this reason they praise it. The poet said:

"Idhā wa'ada al-sarrā' anjaza wa'dahu
Wa in wa'ada al-darrā' fal-'afwu māni'uh"

It is also possible that this sentence is from the speech of the supplicants, and this would be a case of iltifat (shift of address), since it is a move from address to the third person, because mentioning Him by His greatest name carries majesty, grandeur and awe. And as if, when they continued the supplication with "Our Lord," they informed about God, Exalted, that He is faithful to His promise; and this statement includes belief in the resurrection, recompense, and fulfilment of what God, Exalted, has promised.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against Allah﴾: It has been said: the intended are the delegation of Najran, for it is narrated that Abu Harithah ibn 'Alqama said to his brother: "I know that he is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but if I declare that, the kings of Rome will take back from me what they gave me of wealth." It has also been said: the reference is to the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Ibn 'Abbas said: Qurayza and al-Nadir, who used to boast of their wealth and children. And the statement is general, encompassing every disbeliever.

The meaning of (min Allāh) is: from His punishment, both worldly and otherworldly. The meaning of aghnā 'anhu is: to repel and prevent it from him. Since wealth is more effective in the domain of defence, seeking nearness, and temptation than children, it is mentioned first in this verse, and in His saying: ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children will bring you near to Us in position﴾ [Saba': 37], and in His saying: ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ [al-Taghabun: 15], and in His saying: ﴿and competition in wealth and children﴾ [al-Hadid: 20], and in His saying: ﴿neither wealth nor sons will benefit﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 88]. This is unlike His saying: ﴿Adorned for mankind is love of desires: of women and sons, and heaped-up piles of gold and silver...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14], to the end, for there He mentioned the love of desires and placed women and sons before the mention of wealth. The discussion of that will come, God willing.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read (لَنْ يُغْنِيَ) with yā' in accordance with the masculine marking of the verb; 'Ali read (لَنْ يُغْنِي) with a sukūn on the yā'; al-Hasan read (لَنْ يُغْنِي) with yā' at the beginning and a sukūn yā' at the end, this being because of the difficulty of a vowel on a soft letter, and treating the accusative like the nominative. Some grammarians restrict this to poetic necessity, but it should not be restricted to it, since it is frequent in their speech.

(Min) is for the beginning of the endpoint according to al-Mubarrad, and in the sense of 'inda (with) according to Abu 'Ubayda, who likened it to His saying: ﴿He fed them against hunger and secured them against fear﴾ [Quraysh: 4]; he said: its meaning is "at hunger and at fear." That (min) means 'inda is very weak.

Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying "from Allah" is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, conjecture avails not against the truth at all﴾ [Yunus: 36]. The meaning: they will not avail them against God's mercy or obedience to God anything, i.e., in place of His mercy and His obedience, and in place of the truth. From this is: "and the wealth of the wealthy will not benefit him against You"; that is, his fortune and share of this world will not benefit him in that, i.e., in place of your obedience and worship and what is with You. In the same sense is His saying: ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children bring you near to Us in position﴾ [Saba': 37]. End of his words.

As for establishing that (min) means substitution, there is disagreement; our companions deny it, while others affirm it, and claim that it comes in the sense of substitution, citing His saying: ﴿Are you pleased with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ [al-Tawba: 38]; ﴿We would have made from you angels﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 60], i.e., in place of the Hereafter and in place of you. The poet said:

"Akhadhū al-makhāḍa min al-faṣīli ghulubbatan
Ẓulman wa yuktabu lil-amīri afīlā"

i.e., in place of the young camel. And "shay'an" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, as you say: "I struck a kind of striking." It is also possible that it is in the accusative as a direct object, since the sense of "lan tughnī" is "will not repel or prevent," so on this view "min" may be in the position of a circumstantial phrase relating to "shay'an," since if it had come after it, it would be in the position of a qualifier; when it precedes, it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial. In that case "min" is partitive.

So four views are summarized regarding (min): the beginning of the endpoint, which is the view of al-Mubarrad and al-Kalbi; its being in the sense of 'inda (with), which is the view of Abu 'Ubayda; substitution, which is the view of al-Zamakhshari; and partitiveness, which is what we have established.

﴿And they are the fuel of the Fire﴾: Since He mentioned earlier that the great number of their wealth and the support of their children will not avail those who disbelieved, He informed of their destination, and that the ultimate end of whoever disbelieves and denies the signs of Allah is the Fire. This sentence may be grammatically conjoined to the predicate of "inna," or it may be an independent sentence conjoined to the first sentence. He indicated (with ulā'ika) their remoteness, and used the word "hum," which implies exclusivity, and made them the very fuel itself, for emphasis on the burning, as if the Fire had nothing to kindle it but them. The discussion of "fuel" has already occurred in His saying: ﴿whose fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Baqara: 24].

Al-Hasan, Mujahid and others read (وُقُودُ) with a damma on the wāw, which is the verbal noun of: "the fire blazed, blazes, a blazing" (waqadat al-nār taqidu wuqūdan); and it may be according to an ellipsis: "the people of the fuel of the Fire," or "the wood of fuel," or he made them the fuel itself for emphasis, as you say: "Zayd is satisfaction."

It has also been said for the verbal noun: "wuqūd," with a fatha on the wāw, which is one of the verbal nouns that came on the pattern fa'ūl with fatha on the wāw, and this has been mentioned. "Hum" may be a mubtada', and it may be a separator (fasl).

﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾: Since He mentioned that whoever disbelieves and denies Allah ends up in the Fire, and his wealth and child will not avail him, He mentioned that the situation of these people in their denial of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the consequence of punishment for their disbelief is like the situation of the disbelieving nations who preceded them: they were seized for their sins and punished for them. He pointed to the people of Pharaoh because the discourse was with the Children of Israel, who knew what befell them when they denied Moses: their drowning, their eventual ending in the Fire, and the Children of Israel's victory over them and their inheritance of their dominion. In all this there is good news for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and for those who believe in him: that the disbelievers' end in this world is annihilation, and in the Hereafter the Fire, as happened to the people of Pharaoh, who were destroyed in this world and went on to the Fire.

They differed about the grammatical analysis of (كَدَأْبِ). It has been said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, so it is in the position of nominative; the estimate being: "their custom is like the custom of..." and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya began with this. It has been said: it is in the position of the accusative by (wuqūd), i.e., the Fire is kindled by them just as it is kindled by the people of Pharaoh, as you say: "Indeed you wrong people like the custom of your father," meaning "like the wrong of your father," as al-Zamakhshari said.

It has been said: it is by a verb estimated from the word "wuqūd," and the comparison is in the burning itself, as Ibn 'Atiyya said. It has been said: it is from its meaning, i.e., they were punished with a punishment like the custom of the people of Pharaoh, and the phrase "fuel of the Fire" indicates this.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 8–11 (part 2 of 3):

It has been said that it is governed by ﴿لَنْ تُغْنِيَ﴾ (*lan tughniya*, "will not avail"), meaning: "their wealth and children will not avail them against Allah, just as they did not avail those before them." This was said by al-Zamakhshari, but it is weak, because it separates the governing element (*'amil*) from the governed element (*ma'mul*) by the sentence ﴿وَأُولَئِكَ هُمْ وَقُودُ النَّارِ﴾ ("and those are the fuel of the Fire"). This is so under either of the two assessments we have made, namely whether it is coordinated with the predicate of *inna* (indeed), or with the sentence emphasized by *inna*. If you assess it as a parenthetical clause (*i'tirahiyya*), which is far-fetched, then what al-Zamakhshari said is permissible.

It has also been said that it is governed by a verb in the accusative that is implied by the meaning of ﴿لَنْ تُغْنِيَ﴾, meaning: their benefit from wealth and children was entirely nullified, as was the custom of the people of Pharaoh.

It has been said that it is an adjective (*na't*) of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), whose assessment is: *kufran* (disbelief) *ka-da'bi* (like the custom of). Its governing element is ﴿كَفَرُوا﴾ (*kafaru*, "they disbelieved"). This was said by al-Farra', and it is an error, because if it were governed by the relative clause (*sila*), it would be part of the relative clause, and it is not permissible for the relative pronoun to be given a predicate before it has completed its relative clause and its complements; here it has already been given a predicate, so it cannot be governed by what is within the relative clause.

It has also been said that it is governed by a verb omitted that is indicated by ﴿كَفَرُوا﴾, the assessment being: they disbelieved with a disbelief like the custom of the people of Pharaoh.

It has been said that the governing element of the *kaf* (like) is ﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ ("they denied Our signs"). On this view, the pronoun in *kadhdhabu* refers to the disbelievers of Makkah and others among the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: they denied with a denial like the custom of the people of Pharaoh.

It has been said that it is connected to the statement ﴿فَأَخَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾ ("so Allah seized them for their sins"), meaning: He seized them with a seizing like that with which He seized the people of Pharaoh. This is weak, because what follows the coordinating *fa'* (then) does not govern what precedes it. Some of our companions reported from the Kufans that they permitted: "Zaydan qumtu fa-darabtu" (Zayd, I stood up and then struck him), and according to this, this view is permissible. These are ten opinions about the governing element of the *kaf*.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: *al-da'b* (custom), with the hamza either vowelled with a sukun or with a fatha, is the verbal noun of *da'aba yad'abu*, when one persists in doing something and continues to exert effort at it; and *da'b* is also said of habit. Abu Hatim said: I heard Ya'qub mention *ka-da'bi* with a fatha on the hamza, and he said to me, while I was a little boy: "On what basis is it permissible?" I said to him: "I think it is from *da'iba yad'abu da'ban*." He accepted this from me and marvelled at the soundness of my assessment despite my youth, but I do not know whether it is said or not. Al-Nahhas said: *da'iba* is never said; rather it is said *da'aba yad'abu du'ubun*, as the grammarians have transmitted, including al-Farra', who related it in the book *al-Masadir* (The Verbal Nouns).

*Al ' Fir'awn* (the people of Pharaoh) means his partisans and followers.

﴿وَالَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ ("and those before them") refers to the disbelievers of earlier nations, such as the people of Nuh, the people of Hud, the people of Shu'ayb, and others. The pronoun on this view refers back to the people of Pharaoh. It is also possible that the pronoun refers back to ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ ("those who disbelieved"), who are the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The position of ﴿وَالَّذِينَ﴾ is genitive, coordinated with ﴿آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾.

﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ ("they denied Our signs"): this sentence is an explanation of *al-da'b* (custom), as if it was said: "What did they do, and what was done to them?" So it was said: "They denied Our signs." It is therefore as if it were the answer to an implied question. They also permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: denying. They also permitted that the speech is complete at ﴿كَدَأْبِ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ ("like the custom of the people of Pharaoh"), and then a new beginning is made: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ كَذَّبُوا﴾, so that ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*) and ﴿كَذَّبُوا﴾ is its predicate. In the phrase ﴿بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ there is an *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person), since before it there is ﴿مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ (from Allah), which is a third-person reference, and so it moves from it to the first person.

The signs (*ayat*) may be the recited ones in the books of Allah, and it may also be that they are the indications that point to the oneness of Allah and the truthfulness of His prophets.

﴿فَأَخَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾: it shifts from the first person to the third person. The meaning of seizing for a sin is punishment for it, and the *ba'* in *bi-dhunubihim* indicates cause.

﴿وَاللَّهُ شَدِيدُ الْعِقَابِ﴾ ("and Allah is severe in punishment"): the explanation of this has already been given before, and it contains an indication of the might of Allah against whoever disbelieves in His signs and denies them. It has been said: these verses contain, among the varieties of eloquence (*fasaha*), the beauty of ambiguity (*husn al-ibham*), which is found in what they begin with, in order to alert the mind to consider what follows in the speech.

The metaphorical use of comparison (*majaz al-tashbih*) occurs in several places, among them ﴿نَزَّلَ عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ ("He sent down to you the Book with truth"). The literal meaning of *nuzul* (descent) is the casting of a body from a height to a lower place. The Qur'an is established in the Preserved Tablet, and when it is established in the heart, it takes the place of a body cast from a height to a lower place, so it is likened to that, and the word *inzal* (sending down) is applied to it. And in His saying ﴿لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ﴾ ("confirming what was before it"), the Qur'an confirms what preceded it of the books; it is likened to a person who has in front of him something that he receives little by little. And in His saying ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ التَّوْرَاةَ وَالإِنْجِيلَ مِنْ قَبْلُ هُدًى لِلنَّاسِ وَأَنْزَلَ الْفُرْقَانَ﴾ ("and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel before, as guidance for mankind, and He sent down the Criterion"), He placed the verbal noun in the position of the active participle, so He made the Torah like a man who conceals from you a matter, that is, he hides it, because of the obscure meanings in it. The Gospel is likened, because of its breadth of encouragement and warning, its admonitions and humility, to the wide-eyed gazelle (*al-'ayn al-najla'*). He made it guidance because of the direction it gives, like the road that guides you to the place you seek. He likened the Criterion (*al-Furqan*) to a body that separates two bodies. And in His saying ﴿عَذَابٌ شَدِيدٌ﴾ ("a severe punishment"), He likened what the soul experiences of the constriction and pain of punishment to a person who is bound and confined. And in His saying ﴿يُصَوِّرُكُمْ﴾ ("He shapes you"), He likened His command, or the connection of His will to existence, to the highest degree of perfection and craftsmanship, to a craftsman who represents something: he joins one body to another and forms a figure from them. And in His saying ﴿مِنْهُ آيَاتٌ مُحْكَمَاتٌ﴾ ("in it are firm verses"), He made what is clear of the meanings of His Book, and whose traces of wisdom are apparent, firm (*muhkam*). He likened the firm verses, because of the fundamental meanings in them from which many branches derive, to the mother to which the offspring of her descendants return and which they resort to. And He likened what its meanings are obscure of, because of the variety of its aspects, such as the disjointed letters (*al-fawatih*), and words that carry many meanings, and the verses that indicate the matter of the return and the reckoning, to the ambiguous and confusing thing whose matter is so obscure that the intellect is baffled in describing it. And in His saying ﴿فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ زَيْغٌ﴾ ("in their hearts is deviation"), He likened the heart that inclines away from the right course to a thing that has strayed from its place. And in His saying ﴿وَهَبْ لَنَا مِنْ لَدُنْكَ رَحْمَةً﴾ ("grant us mercy from Yourself"), He likened the intelligible notion of mercy as a desire for good to the perceptible things of bodies, the gift and the thing given in a gift. And in His saying ﴿وَقُودُ النَّارِ﴾ ("the fuel of the Fire"), He likened them to firewood, which is of no use except as fuel. And the Exalted said: ﴿إِنَّكُمْ وَمَا تَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ حَصَبُ جَهَنَّمَ﴾ ("Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell," Q. 21:98), and *al-hasab* is firewood in the language of Abyssinia. And in His saying ﴿فَأَخَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾, He likened the encompassing of His punishment upon them to the one seized by the hand, which is disposed of by the judgment of the will to seize.

It has been said: all of these are metaphors (*isti'arat*), and there is no simile in them except ﴿كَدَأْبِ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾, since in it the particle of comparison is explicitly mentioned.

Particularization (*al-ikhtisas*) occurs in several places, among them in His saying ﴿نَزَّلَ عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ﴾ up to ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ الْفُرْقَانَ﴾, according to the one who interprets the Criterion as the Psalms (*Zabur*). He particularized the four and excluded the rest of what was sent down, because the people of books at that time were the believers, the Jews, and the Christians. And in His saying ﴿لَا يَخْفَى عَلَيْهِ شَيْءٌ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِي السَّمَاءِ﴾ ("nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Him"), He specified them because they are the largest of His created things that are apparent to us, because they are the abodes of rational beings, and because from them come most of the benefits particular to His servants. And in His saying ﴿وَالرَّاسِخُونَ﴾ ("and those firm in knowledge"), He singled them out by the particular quality of firmness in knowledge. And in His saying ﴿أُولُو الْأَلْبَابِ﴾ ("people of understanding"), because the rational have the particular quality of discernment, reflection, and consideration. And in His saying ﴿لَا تُزِغْ قُلُوبَنَا﴾ ("do not let our hearts deviate"), He specified the hearts, because the soundness and corruption of the body depend on them, which is not so for the rest of the organs, and because they are the place of faith and, according to those who hold this view, the place of the intellect. And in His saying ﴿إِنَّكَ جَامِعُ النَّاسِ لِيَوْمٍ﴾ ("You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day"), He is the gatherer of them in this world upon the surface of the earth alive and in its belly dead; but on that Day is the greatest gathering, which is the Resurrection, and it occurs only on that Day, and there is no gatherer except Him, exalted is He. And in His saying ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَنْ تُغْنِيَ عَنْهُمْ أَمْوَالُهُمْ وَلَا أَوْلَادُهُمْ﴾ ("indeed those who disbelieved, their wealth and their children will not avail them"), He specified the disbelievers, because the wealth of the believers, which they spend in the ways of righteousness, will avail them, for they will reap its fruit in the Hereafter; and their children will benefit them in the Hereafter: they will give them drink, they will be a shield for them from the Fire, they will intercede for them if they die young, and they will benefit them by righteous supplication when they are grown. All of this has been reported in a sound hadith.

And in His saying ﴿كَدَأْبِ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ ("like the custom of the people of Pharaoh"), He singled them out for mention and put them first, because they were the most tyrannical of the nations and the most obstinate toward their prophets, so they were the most severely punished.

Omission (*al-hadhf*) occurs in several places: in His saying ﴿لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ﴾ ("confirming what was before it"), meaning: of the books. And ﴿أَنْزَلَ التَّوْرَاةَ وَالإِنْجِيلَ﴾ ("He sent down the Torah and the Gospel"), meaning: and He sent down the Psalms (*Zabur*) and the Gospel, because the two descents were at different times (the omitted element is *al-Zabur*). ﴿هُدًى لِلنَّاسِ﴾ ("guidance for mankind"), meaning: those whom He willed to guide. ﴿عَذَابٌ شَدِيدٌ﴾ ("a severe punishment"), meaning: on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿ذُو انْتِقَامٍ﴾ ("Lord of retribution"), meaning: against whomever He wills to punish. ﴿فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِي السَّمَاءِ﴾, meaning: nor in anything other than these two. (*Al-'Aziz*), meaning: in His dominion. (*Al-Hakim*), meaning: in His making. (*Wa-ukhar*), meaning: and other verses. ﴿زَيْغٌ﴾ ("deviation"), meaning: from the truth. ﴿ابْتِغَاءَ الْفِتْنَةِ﴾ ("seeking discord"), meaning: for you. ﴿وَابْتِغَاءَ تَأْوِيلِهِ﴾ ("and seeking its interpretation"), meaning: according to other than the intended meaning of it. ﴿وَمَا يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَهُ﴾ ("and none knows its interpretation"), meaning: according to the true sought reality. (*Rabbana*), meaning: O our Lord. ﴿رَبَّنَا لَا تُزِغْ قُلُوبَنَا﴾ ("our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate"), meaning: from the truth. ﴿بَعْدَ إِذْ هَدَيْتَنَا﴾ ("after You have guided us"), meaning: to it. ﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ ("they denied Our signs"), meaning: those sent down upon the messengers, or those set up as proofs of the oneness (of Allah). ﴿بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾ ("for their sins"), meaning: those past.

Repetition (*al-takrar*): ﴿نَزَّلَ عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ﴾, ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ التَّوْرَاةَ﴾, ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ الْفُرْقَانَ﴾. It is repeated because of the difference in the sending down, its manner, and its time. With the signs of Allah, and Allah repeated His name, exalted is He, for magnification, because in mentioning the explicit noun there is a magnification that is not in the pronoun.

﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ﴾ ("there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting") (Q. 3:2); ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ الْعَزِيزُ﴾ ("there is no god but He, the Mighty") (Q. 3:6). He repeated the sentence to draw attention to the firm establishment of this in souls, and as a refutation of whoever claims that there is with Him another god. (*Ibtigha' ta'wilihi*) and ﴿وَمَا يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَهُ﴾ ("and none knows its interpretation") (Q. 3:7) are repeated because of the difference between the two interpretations, or for the magnification of the matter of interpretation.

﴿رَبَّنَا لَا تُزِغْ﴾ and ﴿رَبَّنَا إِنَّكَ﴾ ("our Lord, do not let... our Lord, indeed You"): He repeated the supplication, to alert to its constancy and to warn against neglecting it, because of what it contains of the manifestation of need.

Anteriority and posteriority (*al-taqdim wa-al-ta'khir*) occur in the mention of the sending down of the books: the report about it does not come in the order of time, for the Torah came first, then the Psalms, then the Gospel, then the Qur'an. The Qur'an was placed first because of its nobility, the greatness of its reward, its abrogation of what preceded it (*naskh*), its permanence, and the continuance of its ruling until the end of time. He placed the Torah second because of the many rulings in it, the narratives, and the hidden deductions.

Al-Mufaddal narrated that the Torah, when it was sent down, was seventy *wasq* (loads), then He made the Gospel a third, because it is a book containing admonitions and wisdom beyond counting, then He followed it with the Psalms, because it contains admonitions and wisdom that did not reach the level of the Gospel. This is if we say that the Criterion (*al-Furqan*) is the Psalms.

In His saying ﴿فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِي السَّمَاءِ﴾ ("on earth or in heaven"), He placed the earth before the heaven, even though the heaven is greater in worlds, greater in bodies, greater in signs and proofs, and more abundant in virtues because of the purity of its inhabitants, in contrast to the inhabitants of the earth. This was done in order to inform them of His awareness of the secrets of their affairs, and He gave importance to placing their location first, so that they might restrain themselves from their ugly deeds, because when it is made clear that Allah is not hidden from anything of their affair, they will feel shame before Him.

The shift (*al-iltifat*) in ﴿رَبَّنَا إِنَّكَ جَامِعُ﴾ ("our Lord, indeed You are the gatherer") is followed by ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ ("indeed Allah"). And in His saying ﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ ("they denied Our signs") it is followed by ﴿وَاللَّهُ شَدِيدُ الْعِقَابِ﴾ ("and Allah is severe in punishment").

The emphasis (al-ta'kid): in ﴿And those — they are the fuel of the Fire﴾ he emphasized with the word "they" (hum), and he emphasized with his saying ﴿He is the One who forms you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 6] his saying ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 6]; and he emphasized with his saying ﴿He is the One who has sent down upon you the Book﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 7] his saying ﴿He has sent down upon you the Book﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 3].

The extension (al-tawassu'): by placing the verbal noun (masdar) in the position of the active participle (ism al-fa'il) in his saying "guidance" (huda) and "the Criterion" (al-furqan), meaning "guiding" (hadiyan) and "the one who distinguishes" (al-fariq). And by placing the particle in the position of the adverb of place (al-zarf) in his saying "from Allah" (min Allah), meaning "with Allah" ('inda Allah), according to the view of those who interpreted "min" as meaning "'inda" (with). And the paronomasia of different roots (al-tajnis al-mughayir) in his saying "grant" (wahab) and "the Bestower" (al-Wahhab).

This is a theological question: Does God create evil just as He creates good, or does He not create evil? The first is the view of the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna), and the second is the view of the Mu'tazila, and each interprets according to his own school.

Al-Siddiq, Abu Qa'ila and al-Jarrah read (لا تَزُغْ قُلُوبُنا) with a fatha on the tā' and a damma on the bā', [i.e., lā tazugh qulūbunā]. Some read (لا يَزُغْ) with a fatha on the yā', and a raf' on the bā' of (قُلُوبُنا), making it from zāgha and attributing it to the hearts. Its apparent meaning is a prohibition addressed to the hearts against swerving, but it is actually of the type of: "lā arayannaka hāhunā" (I shall not see you here), and the poet's line:

"Lā a'rifanna rabrabān ḥuwwaran madāmi'uh"
(I shall not recognize a gazelle with wide-set eyes whose tears...)

That is: "Do not make us swerve, so that our hearts swerve after You have guided us." Its apparent meaning is guidance, which is the opposite of misguidance. It has also been said: "after You have guided us" means guidance to knowledge of the clear (muḥkam) verses and submission to the ambiguous (mutashābih) verses of Your Book.

(إذْ) is originally a adverb of time, and here (بَعْدَ) has been prefixed to it, so it became a noun that is not a time adverb. Before it leaves the adverbial sense, it is followed by a clause, and its state of being prefixed to a clause is retained; the prefixing to it does not remove it from this ruling. Do you not see the Almighty's saying: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 119]? And ﴿a day when no soul shall control﴾ [al-Infitar: 19], according to the reading of the one who raised (يَوْمُ). And the poet's line:

"'Alā ḥīna 'ātabtu al-mashība 'alā al-ṣibā
'Alā ḥīna man tuktabu 'alayhi dhunūbuhu 'alā ḥīna al-kirāmi qalīl
Alā layta ayyāma al-ṣafā'i jadīd"

How did the adverb here leave its usual function, being used as a predicate, as a prepositional phrase, as the subject of "layta," and yet be prefixed to a clause?

﴿And grant us from Yourself mercy﴾: they asked using the word "grant" (hibah), which implies favour and kindness toward them without cause, deed or exchange, since a gift is of this kind. They specified that it is from Him. If mercy is one of the attributes of the Essence, then gift is not possible in it; rather the meaning would be: bounty, or reward issuing from mercy. Since what was asked for issues from mercy, it is valid to ask for mercy, treating the cause as if it were the effect. It has also been said: the meaning of "mercy" is success, rectitude and steadfastness in what we are upon of faith and guidance.

﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾: this is like the reason for their saying "grant." Like your saying: "Solve this difficult problem, for you are the knower of difficulties." He used the intensive form on the pattern fa'āl, though they had said "hawūb" for the sake of matching the verse-endings. In "anta" it is permissible to treat it as an emphatic pronoun, as a separator, or as a mubtada'.

﴿Our Lord, You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾: Since they asked Him, Exalted, not to make their hearts swerve after guidance, and the fruit of the absence of swerving and of guidance only appears on the Day of Resurrection, they informed that they are certain of the Day of Resurrection and of the raising therein for recompense, and that belief in the truth of the promise concerning it is what guided them to ask that He not make their hearts swerve. The meaning of "for a Day about which there is no doubt" is: for the recompense of a day. "There is no doubt in it" means there is no doubt about its existence, because of the truthfulness of the One who informed of it; and although doubt may befall one who denies it, he is in a state in which he should not have doubt.

It has also been said: the lām is in the sense of fī (in), i.e., "in a Day," and the object of gathering is not mentioned. The apparent meaning of this gathering is the resurrection from the graves for recompense; so it is an active participle with future meaning. What indicates that it refers to the future is the reading of Abu Hatim, "jāmi'un al-nāsa" with tanwīn and naṣb on "al-nās."

It has also been said: the meaning of gathering here is that He gathers them in the graves, and the lām seems to mean ilā (until), indicating the endpoint: He gathers them in the graves until the Day of Resurrection. The active participle here does not take account of time, since among mankind some have died and some have not, so the gathering is attributed to God without consideration of time. The pronoun in "fīhi" refers to the Day, since the clause is a qualifier of it. Whoever returns it to the gathering understood from "jāmi'" or to the recompense indicated by the meaning has gone too far.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾: the apparent shift from the second-person address to the third-person name indicates resumption, and that it is part of Allah's speech, not the speech of the firmly grounded who are supplicating. Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is that divinity is incompatible with breaking a promise, like your saying: "Indeed the generous does not disappoint the one who asks him." (al-mī'ād) means the appointed time. End of his words. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazili doctrine in his phrase "divinity is incompatible with breaking a promise." Al-Jubba'i cited this verse as proof for the certainty of threatening the sinners absolutely, whereas for us it is conditional upon the absence of pardon, as we and he agreed that it is conditional upon the absence of repentance; and both conditions are established by a separate proof. Even if we grant what they say, we do not grant that threat falls under promise.

Al-Wahidi said: it is permissible to take it as referring to the promise of the friends (of God) and not the threat against enemies, because breaking a threat is considered generosity among the Arabs, and for this reason they praise it. The poet said:

"Idhā wa'ada al-sarrā' anjaza wa'dahu
Wa in wa'ada al-darrā' fal-'afwu māni'uh"

It is also possible that this sentence is from the speech of the supplicants, and this would be a case of iltifat (shift of address), since it is a move from address to the third person, because mentioning Him by His greatest name carries majesty, grandeur and awe. And as if, when they continued the supplication with "Our Lord," they informed about God, Exalted, that He is faithful to His promise; and this statement includes belief in the resurrection, recompense, and fulfilment of what God, Exalted, has promised.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against Allah﴾: It has been said: the intended are the delegation of Najran, for it is narrated that Abu Harithah ibn 'Alqama said to his brother: "I know that he is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but if I declare that, the kings of Rome will take back from me what they gave me of wealth." It has also been said: the reference is to the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Ibn 'Abbas said: Qurayza and al-Nadir, who used to boast of their wealth and children. And the statement is general, encompassing every disbeliever.

The meaning of (min Allāh) is: from His punishment, both worldly and otherworldly. The meaning of aghnā 'anhu is: to repel and prevent it from him. Since wealth is more effective in the domain of defence, seeking nearness, and temptation than children, it is mentioned first in this verse, and in His saying: ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children will bring you near to Us in position﴾ [Saba': 37], and in His saying: ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ [al-Taghabun: 15], and in His saying: ﴿and competition in wealth and children﴾ [al-Hadid: 20], and in His saying: ﴿neither wealth nor sons will benefit﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 88]. This is unlike His saying: ﴿Adorned for mankind is love of desires: of women and sons, and heaped-up piles of gold and silver...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14], to the end, for there He mentioned the love of desires and placed women and sons before the mention of wealth. The discussion of that will come, God willing.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read (لَنْ يُغْنِيَ) with yā' in accordance with the masculine marking of the verb; 'Ali read (لَنْ يُغْنِي) with a sukūn on the yā'; al-Hasan read (لَنْ يُغْنِي) with yā' at the beginning and a sukūn yā' at the end, this being because of the difficulty of a vowel on a soft letter, and treating the accusative like the nominative. Some grammarians restrict this to poetic necessity, but it should not be restricted to it, since it is frequent in their speech.

(Min) is for the beginning of the endpoint according to al-Mubarrad, and in the sense of 'inda (with) according to Abu 'Ubayda, who likened it to His saying: ﴿He fed them against hunger and secured them against fear﴾ [Quraysh: 4]; he said: its meaning is "at hunger and at fear." That (min) means 'inda is very weak.

Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying "from Allah" is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, conjecture avails not against the truth at all﴾ [Yunus: 36]. The meaning: they will not avail them against God's mercy or obedience to God anything, i.e., in place of His mercy and His obedience, and in place of the truth. From this is: "and the wealth of the wealthy will not benefit him against You"; that is, his fortune and share of this world will not benefit him in that, i.e., in place of your obedience and worship and what is with You. In the same sense is His saying: ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children bring you near to Us in position﴾ [Saba': 37]. End of his words.

As for establishing that (min) means substitution, there is disagreement; our companions deny it, while others affirm it, and claim that it comes in the sense of substitution, citing His saying: ﴿Are you pleased with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ [al-Tawba: 38]; ﴿We would have made from you angels﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 60], i.e., in place of the Hereafter and in place of you. The poet said:

"Akhadhū al-makhāḍa min al-faṣīli ghulubbatan
Ẓulman wa yuktabu lil-amīri afīlā"

i.e., in place of the young camel. And "shay'an" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, as you say: "I struck a kind of striking." It is also possible that it is in the accusative as a direct object, since the sense of "lan tughnī" is "will not repel or prevent," so on this view "min" may be in the position of a circumstantial phrase relating to "shay'an," since if it had come after it, it would be in the position of a qualifier; when it precedes, it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial. In that case "min" is partitive.

So four views are summarized regarding (min): the beginning of the endpoint, which is the view of al-Mubarrad and al-Kalbi; its being in the sense of 'inda (with), which is the view of Abu 'Ubayda; substitution, which is the view of al-Zamakhshari; and partitiveness, which is what we have established.

﴿And they are the fuel of the Fire﴾: Since He mentioned earlier that the great number of their wealth and the support of their children will not avail those who disbelieved, He informed of their destination, and that the ultimate end of whoever disbelieves and denies the signs of Allah is the Fire. This sentence may be grammatically conjoined to the predicate of "inna," or it may be an independent sentence conjoined to the first sentence. He indicated (with ulā'ika) their remoteness, and used the word "hum," which implies exclusivity, and made them the very fuel itself, for emphasis on the burning, as if the Fire had nothing to kindle it but them. The discussion of "fuel" has already occurred in His saying: ﴿whose fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Baqara: 24].

Al-Hasan, Mujahid and others read (وُقُودُ) with a damma on the wāw, which is the verbal noun of: "the fire blazed, blazes, a blazing" (waqadat al-nār taqidu wuqūdan); and it may be according to an ellipsis: "the people of the fuel of the Fire," or "the wood of fuel," or he made them the fuel itself for emphasis, as you say: "Zayd is satisfaction."

It has also been said for the verbal noun: "wuqūd," with a fatha on the wāw, which is one of the verbal nouns that came on the pattern fa'ūl with fatha on the wāw, and this has been mentioned. "Hum" may be a mubtada', and it may be a separator (fasl).

﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾: Since He mentioned that whoever disbelieves and denies Allah ends up in the Fire, and his wealth and child will not avail him, He mentioned that the situation of these people in their denial of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the consequence of punishment for their disbelief is like the situation of the disbelieving nations who preceded them: they were seized for their sins and punished for them. He pointed to the people of Pharaoh because the discourse was with the Children of Israel, who knew what befell them when they denied Moses: their drowning, their eventual ending in the Fire, and the Children of Israel's victory over them and their inheritance of their dominion. In all this there is good news for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and for those who believe in him: that the disbelievers' end in this world is annihilation, and in the Hereafter the Fire, as happened to the people of Pharaoh, who were destroyed in this world and went on to the Fire.

They differed about the grammatical analysis of (كَدَأْبِ). It has been said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, so it is in the position of nominative; the estimate being: "their custom is like the custom of..." and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya began with this. It has been said: it is in the position of the accusative by (wuqūd), i.e., the Fire is kindled by them just as it is kindled by the people of Pharaoh, as you say: "Indeed you wrong people like the custom of your father," meaning "like the wrong of your father," as al-Zamakhshari said.

It has been said: it is by a verb estimated from the word "wuqūd," and the comparison is in the burning itself, as Ibn 'Atiyya said. It has been said: it is from its meaning, i.e., they were punished with a punishment like the custom of the people of Pharaoh, and the phrase "fuel of the Fire" indicates this.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 8–11 (part 2 of 3):

It has been said that it is governed by ﴿لَنْ تُغْنِيَ﴾ (*lan tughniya*, "will not avail"), meaning: "their wealth and children will not avail them against Allah, just as they did not avail those before them." This was said by al-Zamakhshari, but it is weak, because it separates the governing element (*'amil*) from the governed element (*ma'mul*) by the sentence ﴿وَأُولَئِكَ هُمْ وَقُودُ النَّارِ﴾ ("and those are the fuel of the Fire"). This is so under either of the two assessments we have made, namely whether it is coordinated with the predicate of *inna* (indeed), or with the sentence emphasized by *inna*. If you assess it as a parenthetical clause (*i'tirahiyya*), which is far-fetched, then what al-Zamakhshari said is permissible.

It has also been said that it is governed by a verb in the accusative that is implied by the meaning of ﴿لَنْ تُغْنِيَ﴾, meaning: their benefit from wealth and children was entirely nullified, as was the custom of the people of Pharaoh.

It has been said that it is an adjective (*na't*) of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), whose assessment is: *kufran* (disbelief) *ka-da'bi* (like the custom of). Its governing element is ﴿كَفَرُوا﴾ (*kafaru*, "they disbelieved"). This was said by al-Farra', and it is an error, because if it were governed by the relative clause (*sila*), it would be part of the relative clause, and it is not permissible for the relative pronoun to be given a predicate before it has completed its relative clause and its complements; here it has already been given a predicate, so it cannot be governed by what is within the relative clause.

It has also been said that it is governed by a verb omitted that is indicated by ﴿كَفَرُوا﴾, the assessment being: they disbelieved with a disbelief like the custom of the people of Pharaoh.

It has been said that the governing element of the *kaf* (like) is ﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ ("they denied Our signs"). On this view, the pronoun in *kadhdhabu* refers to the disbelievers of Makkah and others among the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: they denied with a denial like the custom of the people of Pharaoh.

It has been said that it is connected to the statement ﴿فَأَخَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾ ("so Allah seized them for their sins"), meaning: He seized them with a seizing like that with which He seized the people of Pharaoh. This is weak, because what follows the coordinating *fa'* (then) does not govern what precedes it. Some of our companions reported from the Kufans that they permitted: "Zaydan qumtu fa-darabtu" (Zayd, I stood up and then struck him), and according to this, this view is permissible. These are ten opinions about the governing element of the *kaf*.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: *al-da'b* (custom), with the hamza either vowelled with a sukun or with a fatha, is the verbal noun of *da'aba yad'abu*, when one persists in doing something and continues to exert effort at it; and *da'b* is also said of habit. Abu Hatim said: I heard Ya'qub mention *ka-da'bi* with a fatha on the hamza, and he said to me, while I was a little boy: "On what basis is it permissible?" I said to him: "I think it is from *da'iba yad'abu da'ban*." He accepted this from me and marvelled at the soundness of my assessment despite my youth, but I do not know whether it is said or not. Al-Nahhas said: *da'iba* is never said; rather it is said *da'aba yad'abu du'ubun*, as the grammarians have transmitted, including al-Farra', who related it in the book *al-Masadir* (The Verbal Nouns).

*Al ' Fir'awn* (the people of Pharaoh) means his partisans and followers.

﴿وَالَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ ("and those before them") refers to the disbelievers of earlier nations, such as the people of Nuh, the people of Hud, the people of Shu'ayb, and others. The pronoun on this view refers back to the people of Pharaoh. It is also possible that the pronoun refers back to ﴿الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ ("those who disbelieved"), who are the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The position of ﴿وَالَّذِينَ﴾ is genitive, coordinated with ﴿آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾.

﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ ("they denied Our signs"): this sentence is an explanation of *al-da'b* (custom), as if it was said: "What did they do, and what was done to them?" So it was said: "They denied Our signs." It is therefore as if it were the answer to an implied question. They also permitted that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: denying. They also permitted that the speech is complete at ﴿كَدَأْبِ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ ("like the custom of the people of Pharaoh"), and then a new beginning is made: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِمْ كَذَّبُوا﴾, so that ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ is the subject (*mubtada'*) and ﴿كَذَّبُوا﴾ is its predicate. In the phrase ﴿بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ there is an *iltifat* (shift of grammatical person), since before it there is ﴿مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ (from Allah), which is a third-person reference, and so it moves from it to the first person.

The signs (*ayat*) may be the recited ones in the books of Allah, and it may also be that they are the indications that point to the oneness of Allah and the truthfulness of His prophets.

﴿فَأَخَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾: it shifts from the first person to the third person. The meaning of seizing for a sin is punishment for it, and the *ba'* in *bi-dhunubihim* indicates cause.

﴿وَاللَّهُ شَدِيدُ الْعِقَابِ﴾ ("and Allah is severe in punishment"): the explanation of this has already been given before, and it contains an indication of the might of Allah against whoever disbelieves in His signs and denies them. It has been said: these verses contain, among the varieties of eloquence (*fasaha*), the beauty of ambiguity (*husn al-ibham*), which is found in what they begin with, in order to alert the mind to consider what follows in the speech.

The metaphorical use of comparison (*majaz al-tashbih*) occurs in several places, among them ﴿نَزَّلَ عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ ("He sent down to you the Book with truth"). The literal meaning of *nuzul* (descent) is the casting of a body from a height to a lower place. The Qur'an is established in the Preserved Tablet, and when it is established in the heart, it takes the place of a body cast from a height to a lower place, so it is likened to that, and the word *inzal* (sending down) is applied to it. And in His saying ﴿لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ﴾ ("confirming what was before it"), the Qur'an confirms what preceded it of the books; it is likened to a person who has in front of him something that he receives little by little. And in His saying ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ التَّوْرَاةَ وَالإِنْجِيلَ مِنْ قَبْلُ هُدًى لِلنَّاسِ وَأَنْزَلَ الْفُرْقَانَ﴾ ("and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel before, as guidance for mankind, and He sent down the Criterion"), He placed the verbal noun in the position of the active participle, so He made the Torah like a man who conceals from you a matter, that is, he hides it, because of the obscure meanings in it. The Gospel is likened, because of its breadth of encouragement and warning, its admonitions and humility, to the wide-eyed gazelle (*al-'ayn al-najla'*). He made it guidance because of the direction it gives, like the road that guides you to the place you seek. He likened the Criterion (*al-Furqan*) to a body that separates two bodies. And in His saying ﴿عَذَابٌ شَدِيدٌ﴾ ("a severe punishment"), He likened what the soul experiences of the constriction and pain of punishment to a person who is bound and confined. And in His saying ﴿يُصَوِّرُكُمْ﴾ ("He shapes you"), He likened His command, or the connection of His will to existence, to the highest degree of perfection and craftsmanship, to a craftsman who represents something: he joins one body to another and forms a figure from them. And in His saying ﴿مِنْهُ آيَاتٌ مُحْكَمَاتٌ﴾ ("in it are firm verses"), He made what is clear of the meanings of His Book, and whose traces of wisdom are apparent, firm (*muhkam*). He likened the firm verses, because of the fundamental meanings in them from which many branches derive, to the mother to which the offspring of her descendants return and which they resort to. And He likened what its meanings are obscure of, because of the variety of its aspects, such as the disjointed letters (*al-fawatih*), and words that carry many meanings, and the verses that indicate the matter of the return and the reckoning, to the ambiguous and confusing thing whose matter is so obscure that the intellect is baffled in describing it. And in His saying ﴿فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ زَيْغٌ﴾ ("in their hearts is deviation"), He likened the heart that inclines away from the right course to a thing that has strayed from its place. And in His saying ﴿وَهَبْ لَنَا مِنْ لَدُنْكَ رَحْمَةً﴾ ("grant us mercy from Yourself"), He likened the intelligible notion of mercy as a desire for good to the perceptible things of bodies, the gift and the thing given in a gift. And in His saying ﴿وَقُودُ النَّارِ﴾ ("the fuel of the Fire"), He likened them to firewood, which is of no use except as fuel. And the Exalted said: ﴿إِنَّكُمْ وَمَا تَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ حَصَبُ جَهَنَّمَ﴾ ("Indeed you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell," Q. 21:98), and *al-hasab* is firewood in the language of Abyssinia. And in His saying ﴿فَأَخَذَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾, He likened the encompassing of His punishment upon them to the one seized by the hand, which is disposed of by the judgment of the will to seize.

It has been said: all of these are metaphors (*isti'arat*), and there is no simile in them except ﴿كَدَأْبِ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾, since in it the particle of comparison is explicitly mentioned.

Particularization (*al-ikhtisas*) occurs in several places, among them in His saying ﴿نَزَّلَ عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ﴾ up to ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ الْفُرْقَانَ﴾, according to the one who interprets the Criterion as the Psalms (*Zabur*). He particularized the four and excluded the rest of what was sent down, because the people of books at that time were the believers, the Jews, and the Christians. And in His saying ﴿لَا يَخْفَى عَلَيْهِ شَيْءٌ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِي السَّمَاءِ﴾ ("nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Him"), He specified them because they are the largest of His created things that are apparent to us, because they are the abodes of rational beings, and because from them come most of the benefits particular to His servants. And in His saying ﴿وَالرَّاسِخُونَ﴾ ("and those firm in knowledge"), He singled them out by the particular quality of firmness in knowledge. And in His saying ﴿أُولُو الْأَلْبَابِ﴾ ("people of understanding"), because the rational have the particular quality of discernment, reflection, and consideration. And in His saying ﴿لَا تُزِغْ قُلُوبَنَا﴾ ("do not let our hearts deviate"), He specified the hearts, because the soundness and corruption of the body depend on them, which is not so for the rest of the organs, and because they are the place of faith and, according to those who hold this view, the place of the intellect. And in His saying ﴿إِنَّكَ جَامِعُ النَّاسِ لِيَوْمٍ﴾ ("You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day"), He is the gatherer of them in this world upon the surface of the earth alive and in its belly dead; but on that Day is the greatest gathering, which is the Resurrection, and it occurs only on that Day, and there is no gatherer except Him, exalted is He. And in His saying ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لَنْ تُغْنِيَ عَنْهُمْ أَمْوَالُهُمْ وَلَا أَوْلَادُهُمْ﴾ ("indeed those who disbelieved, their wealth and their children will not avail them"), He specified the disbelievers, because the wealth of the believers, which they spend in the ways of righteousness, will avail them, for they will reap its fruit in the Hereafter; and their children will benefit them in the Hereafter: they will give them drink, they will be a shield for them from the Fire, they will intercede for them if they die young, and they will benefit them by righteous supplication when they are grown. All of this has been reported in a sound hadith.

And in His saying ﴿كَدَأْبِ آلِ فِرْعَوْنَ﴾ ("like the custom of the people of Pharaoh"), He singled them out for mention and put them first, because they were the most tyrannical of the nations and the most obstinate toward their prophets, so they were the most severely punished.

Omission (*al-hadhf*) occurs in several places: in His saying ﴿لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ﴾ ("confirming what was before it"), meaning: of the books. And ﴿أَنْزَلَ التَّوْرَاةَ وَالإِنْجِيلَ﴾ ("He sent down the Torah and the Gospel"), meaning: and He sent down the Psalms (*Zabur*) and the Gospel, because the two descents were at different times (the omitted element is *al-Zabur*). ﴿هُدًى لِلنَّاسِ﴾ ("guidance for mankind"), meaning: those whom He willed to guide. ﴿عَذَابٌ شَدِيدٌ﴾ ("a severe punishment"), meaning: on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿ذُو انْتِقَامٍ﴾ ("Lord of retribution"), meaning: against whomever He wills to punish. ﴿فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِي السَّمَاءِ﴾, meaning: nor in anything other than these two. (*Al-'Aziz*), meaning: in His dominion. (*Al-Hakim*), meaning: in His making. (*Wa-ukhar*), meaning: and other verses. ﴿زَيْغٌ﴾ ("deviation"), meaning: from the truth. ﴿ابْتِغَاءَ الْفِتْنَةِ﴾ ("seeking discord"), meaning: for you. ﴿وَابْتِغَاءَ تَأْوِيلِهِ﴾ ("and seeking its interpretation"), meaning: according to other than the intended meaning of it. ﴿وَمَا يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَهُ﴾ ("and none knows its interpretation"), meaning: according to the true sought reality. (*Rabbana*), meaning: O our Lord. ﴿رَبَّنَا لَا تُزِغْ قُلُوبَنَا﴾ ("our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate"), meaning: from the truth. ﴿بَعْدَ إِذْ هَدَيْتَنَا﴾ ("after You have guided us"), meaning: to it. ﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ ("they denied Our signs"), meaning: those sent down upon the messengers, or those set up as proofs of the oneness (of Allah). ﴿بِذُنُوبِهِمْ﴾ ("for their sins"), meaning: those past.

Repetition (*al-takrar*): ﴿نَزَّلَ عَلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ﴾, ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ التَّوْرَاةَ﴾, ﴿وَأَنْزَلَ الْفُرْقَانَ﴾. It is repeated because of the difference in the sending down, its manner, and its time. With the signs of Allah, and Allah repeated His name, exalted is He, for magnification, because in mentioning the explicit noun there is a magnification that is not in the pronoun.

﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ الْحَيُّ الْقَيُّومُ﴾ ("there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting") (Q. 3:2); ﴿لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا هُوَ الْعَزِيزُ﴾ ("there is no god but He, the Mighty") (Q. 3:6). He repeated the sentence to draw attention to the firm establishment of this in souls, and as a refutation of whoever claims that there is with Him another god. (*Ibtigha' ta'wilihi*) and ﴿وَمَا يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَهُ﴾ ("and none knows its interpretation") (Q. 3:7) are repeated because of the difference between the two interpretations, or for the magnification of the matter of interpretation.

﴿رَبَّنَا لَا تُزِغْ﴾ and ﴿رَبَّنَا إِنَّكَ﴾ ("our Lord, do not let... our Lord, indeed You"): He repeated the supplication, to alert to its constancy and to warn against neglecting it, because of what it contains of the manifestation of need.

Anteriority and posteriority (*al-taqdim wa-al-ta'khir*) occur in the mention of the sending down of the books: the report about it does not come in the order of time, for the Torah came first, then the Psalms, then the Gospel, then the Qur'an. The Qur'an was placed first because of its nobility, the greatness of its reward, its abrogation of what preceded it (*naskh*), its permanence, and the continuance of its ruling until the end of time. He placed the Torah second because of the many rulings in it, the narratives, and the hidden deductions.

Al-Mufaddal narrated that the Torah, when it was sent down, was seventy *wasq* (loads), then He made the Gospel a third, because it is a book containing admonitions and wisdom beyond counting, then He followed it with the Psalms, because it contains admonitions and wisdom that did not reach the level of the Gospel. This is if we say that the Criterion (*al-Furqan*) is the Psalms.

In His saying ﴿فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِي السَّمَاءِ﴾ ("on earth or in heaven"), He placed the earth before the heaven, even though the heaven is greater in worlds, greater in bodies, greater in signs and proofs, and more abundant in virtues because of the purity of its inhabitants, in contrast to the inhabitants of the earth. This was done in order to inform them of His awareness of the secrets of their affairs, and He gave importance to placing their location first, so that they might restrain themselves from their ugly deeds, because when it is made clear that Allah is not hidden from anything of their affair, they will feel shame before Him.

The shift (*al-iltifat*) in ﴿رَبَّنَا إِنَّكَ جَامِعُ﴾ ("our Lord, indeed You are the gatherer") is followed by ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ ("indeed Allah"). And in His saying ﴿كَذَّبُوا بِآيَاتِنَا﴾ ("they denied Our signs") it is followed by ﴿وَاللَّهُ شَدِيدُ الْعِقَابِ﴾ ("and Allah is severe in punishment").

The emphasis (al-ta'kid): in ﴿And those — they are the fuel of the Fire﴾ he emphasized with the word "they" (hum), and he emphasized with his saying ﴿He is the One who forms you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 6] his saying ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 6]; and he emphasized with his saying ﴿He is the One who has sent down upon you the Book﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 7] his saying ﴿He has sent down upon you the Book﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 3].

The extension (al-tawassu'): by placing the verbal noun (masdar) in the position of the active participle (ism al-fa'il) in his saying "guidance" (huda) and "the Criterion" (al-furqan), meaning "guiding" (hadiyan) and "the one who distinguishes" (al-fariq). And by placing the particle in the position of the adverb of place (al-zarf) in his saying "from Allah" (min Allah), meaning "with Allah" ('inda Allah), according to the view of those who interpreted "min" as meaning "'inda" (with). And the paronomasia of different roots (al-tajnis al-mughayir) in his saying "grant" (wahab) and "the Bestower" (al-Wahhab).

This is a theological question: Does God create evil just as He creates good, or does He not create evil? The first is the view of the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna), and the second is the view of the Mu'tazila, and each interprets according to his own school.

Al-Siddiq, Abu Qa'ila and al-Jarrah read (لا تَزُغْ قُلُوبُنا) with a fatha on the tā' and a damma on the bā', [i.e., lā tazugh qulūbunā]. Some read (لا يَزُغْ) with a fatha on the yā', and a raf' on the bā' of (قُلُوبُنا), making it from zāgha and attributing it to the hearts. Its apparent meaning is a prohibition addressed to the hearts against swerving, but it is actually of the type of: "lā arayannaka hāhunā" (I shall not see you here), and the poet's line:

"Lā a'rifanna rabrabān ḥuwwaran madāmi'uh"
(I shall not recognize a gazelle with wide-set eyes whose tears...)

That is: "Do not make us swerve, so that our hearts swerve after You have guided us." Its apparent meaning is guidance, which is the opposite of misguidance. It has also been said: "after You have guided us" means guidance to knowledge of the clear (muḥkam) verses and submission to the ambiguous (mutashābih) verses of Your Book.

(إذْ) is originally a adverb of time, and here (بَعْدَ) has been prefixed to it, so it became a noun that is not a time adverb. Before it leaves the adverbial sense, it is followed by a clause, and its state of being prefixed to a clause is retained; the prefixing to it does not remove it from this ruling. Do you not see the Almighty's saying: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will benefit﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 119]? And ﴿a day when no soul shall control﴾ [al-Infitar: 19], according to the reading of the one who raised (يَوْمُ). And the poet's line:

"'Alā ḥīna 'ātabtu al-mashība 'alā al-ṣibā
'Alā ḥīna man tuktabu 'alayhi dhunūbuhu 'alā ḥīna al-kirāmi qalīl
Alā layta ayyāma al-ṣafā'i jadīd"

How did the adverb here leave its usual function, being used as a predicate, as a prepositional phrase, as the subject of "layta," and yet be prefixed to a clause?

﴿And grant us from Yourself mercy﴾: they asked using the word "grant" (hibah), which implies favour and kindness toward them without cause, deed or exchange, since a gift is of this kind. They specified that it is from Him. If mercy is one of the attributes of the Essence, then gift is not possible in it; rather the meaning would be: bounty, or reward issuing from mercy. Since what was asked for issues from mercy, it is valid to ask for mercy, treating the cause as if it were the effect. It has also been said: the meaning of "mercy" is success, rectitude and steadfastness in what we are upon of faith and guidance.

﴿Indeed You are the Bestower﴾: this is like the reason for their saying "grant." Like your saying: "Solve this difficult problem, for you are the knower of difficulties." He used the intensive form on the pattern fa'āl, though they had said "hawūb" for the sake of matching the verse-endings. In "anta" it is permissible to treat it as an emphatic pronoun, as a separator, or as a mubtada'.

﴿Our Lord, You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾: Since they asked Him, Exalted, not to make their hearts swerve after guidance, and the fruit of the absence of swerving and of guidance only appears on the Day of Resurrection, they informed that they are certain of the Day of Resurrection and of the raising therein for recompense, and that belief in the truth of the promise concerning it is what guided them to ask that He not make their hearts swerve. The meaning of "for a Day about which there is no doubt" is: for the recompense of a day. "There is no doubt in it" means there is no doubt about its existence, because of the truthfulness of the One who informed of it; and although doubt may befall one who denies it, he is in a state in which he should not have doubt.

It has also been said: the lām is in the sense of fī (in), i.e., "in a Day," and the object of gathering is not mentioned. The apparent meaning of this gathering is the resurrection from the graves for recompense; so it is an active participle with future meaning. What indicates that it refers to the future is the reading of Abu Hatim, "jāmi'un al-nāsa" with tanwīn and naṣb on "al-nās."

It has also been said: the meaning of gathering here is that He gathers them in the graves, and the lām seems to mean ilā (until), indicating the endpoint: He gathers them in the graves until the Day of Resurrection. The active participle here does not take account of time, since among mankind some have died and some have not, so the gathering is attributed to God without consideration of time. The pronoun in "fīhi" refers to the Day, since the clause is a qualifier of it. Whoever returns it to the gathering understood from "jāmi'" or to the recompense indicated by the meaning has gone too far.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise﴾: the apparent shift from the second-person address to the third-person name indicates resumption, and that it is part of Allah's speech, not the speech of the firmly grounded who are supplicating. Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is that divinity is incompatible with breaking a promise, like your saying: "Indeed the generous does not disappoint the one who asks him." (al-mī'ād) means the appointed time. End of his words. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazili doctrine in his phrase "divinity is incompatible with breaking a promise." Al-Jubba'i cited this verse as proof for the certainty of threatening the sinners absolutely, whereas for us it is conditional upon the absence of pardon, as we and he agreed that it is conditional upon the absence of repentance; and both conditions are established by a separate proof. Even if we grant what they say, we do not grant that threat falls under promise.

Al-Wahidi said: it is permissible to take it as referring to the promise of the friends (of God) and not the threat against enemies, because breaking a threat is considered generosity among the Arabs, and for this reason they praise it. The poet said:

"Idhā wa'ada al-sarrā' anjaza wa'dahu
Wa in wa'ada al-darrā' fal-'afwu māni'uh"

It is also possible that this sentence is from the speech of the supplicants, and this would be a case of iltifat (shift of address), since it is a move from address to the third person, because mentioning Him by His greatest name carries majesty, grandeur and awe. And as if, when they continued the supplication with "Our Lord," they informed about God, Exalted, that He is faithful to His promise; and this statement includes belief in the resurrection, recompense, and fulfilment of what God, Exalted, has promised.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against Allah﴾: It has been said: the intended are the delegation of Najran, for it is narrated that Abu Harithah ibn 'Alqama said to his brother: "I know that he is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but if I declare that, the kings of Rome will take back from me what they gave me of wealth." It has also been said: the reference is to the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Ibn 'Abbas said: Qurayza and al-Nadir, who used to boast of their wealth and children. And the statement is general, encompassing every disbeliever.

The meaning of (min Allāh) is: from His punishment, both worldly and otherworldly. The meaning of aghnā 'anhu is: to repel and prevent it from him. Since wealth is more effective in the domain of defence, seeking nearness, and temptation than children, it is mentioned first in this verse, and in His saying: ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children will bring you near to Us in position﴾ [Saba': 37], and in His saying: ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ [al-Taghabun: 15], and in His saying: ﴿and competition in wealth and children﴾ [al-Hadid: 20], and in His saying: ﴿neither wealth nor sons will benefit﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 88]. This is unlike His saying: ﴿Adorned for mankind is love of desires: of women and sons, and heaped-up piles of gold and silver...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14], to the end, for there He mentioned the love of desires and placed women and sons before the mention of wealth. The discussion of that will come, God willing.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read (لَنْ يُغْنِيَ) with yā' in accordance with the masculine marking of the verb; 'Ali read (لَنْ يُغْنِي) with a sukūn on the yā'; al-Hasan read (لَنْ يُغْنِي) with yā' at the beginning and a sukūn yā' at the end, this being because of the difficulty of a vowel on a soft letter, and treating the accusative like the nominative. Some grammarians restrict this to poetic necessity, but it should not be restricted to it, since it is frequent in their speech.

(Min) is for the beginning of the endpoint according to al-Mubarrad, and in the sense of 'inda (with) according to Abu 'Ubayda, who likened it to His saying: ﴿He fed them against hunger and secured them against fear﴾ [Quraysh: 4]; he said: its meaning is "at hunger and at fear." That (min) means 'inda is very weak.

Al-Zamakhshari said: His saying "from Allah" is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, conjecture avails not against the truth at all﴾ [Yunus: 36]. The meaning: they will not avail them against God's mercy or obedience to God anything, i.e., in place of His mercy and His obedience, and in place of the truth. From this is: "and the wealth of the wealthy will not benefit him against You"; that is, his fortune and share of this world will not benefit him in that, i.e., in place of your obedience and worship and what is with You. In the same sense is His saying: ﴿Neither your wealth nor your children bring you near to Us in position﴾ [Saba': 37]. End of his words.

As for establishing that (min) means substitution, there is disagreement; our companions deny it, while others affirm it, and claim that it comes in the sense of substitution, citing His saying: ﴿Are you pleased with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ [al-Tawba: 38]; ﴿We would have made from you angels﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 60], i.e., in place of the Hereafter and in place of you. The poet said:

"Akhadhū al-makhāḍa min al-faṣīli ghulubbatan
Ẓulman wa yuktabu lil-amīri afīlā"

i.e., in place of the young camel. And "shay'an" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, as you say: "I struck a kind of striking." It is also possible that it is in the accusative as a direct object, since the sense of "lan tughnī" is "will not repel or prevent," so on this view "min" may be in the position of a circumstantial phrase relating to "shay'an," since if it had come after it, it would be in the position of a qualifier; when it precedes, it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial. In that case "min" is partitive.

So four views are summarized regarding (min): the beginning of the endpoint, which is the view of al-Mubarrad and al-Kalbi; its being in the sense of 'inda (with), which is the view of Abu 'Ubayda; substitution, which is the view of al-Zamakhshari; and partitiveness, which is what we have established.

﴿And they are the fuel of the Fire﴾: Since He mentioned earlier that the great number of their wealth and the support of their children will not avail those who disbelieved, He informed of their destination, and that the ultimate end of whoever disbelieves and denies the signs of Allah is the Fire. This sentence may be grammatically conjoined to the predicate of "inna," or it may be an independent sentence conjoined to the first sentence. He indicated (with ulā'ika) their remoteness, and used the word "hum," which implies exclusivity, and made them the very fuel itself, for emphasis on the burning, as if the Fire had nothing to kindle it but them. The discussion of "fuel" has already occurred in His saying: ﴿whose fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Baqara: 24].

Al-Hasan, Mujahid and others read (وُقُودُ) with a damma on the wāw, which is the verbal noun of: "the fire blazed, blazes, a blazing" (waqadat al-nār taqidu wuqūdan); and it may be according to an ellipsis: "the people of the fuel of the Fire," or "the wood of fuel," or he made them the fuel itself for emphasis, as you say: "Zayd is satisfaction."

It has also been said for the verbal noun: "wuqūd," with a fatha on the wāw, which is one of the verbal nouns that came on the pattern fa'ūl with fatha on the wāw, and this has been mentioned. "Hum" may be a mubtada', and it may be a separator (fasl).

﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾: Since He mentioned that whoever disbelieves and denies Allah ends up in the Fire, and his wealth and child will not avail him, He mentioned that the situation of these people in their denial of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the consequence of punishment for their disbelief is like the situation of the disbelieving nations who preceded them: they were seized for their sins and punished for them. He pointed to the people of Pharaoh because the discourse was with the Children of Israel, who knew what befell them when they denied Moses: their drowning, their eventual ending in the Fire, and the Children of Israel's victory over them and their inheritance of their dominion. In all this there is good news for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and for those who believe in him: that the disbelievers' end in this world is annihilation, and in the Hereafter the Fire, as happened to the people of Pharaoh, who were destroyed in this world and went on to the Fire.

They differed about the grammatical analysis of (كَدَأْبِ). It has been said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, so it is in the position of nominative; the estimate being: "their custom is like the custom of..." and al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya began with this.
