*Inna fī dhālika* ("Indeed in that"), that is, in the help. It was also said: in the seeing of the army as twice their number, *la-ʿibrah* ("is indeed a lesson"), that is, an admonition and a sign.

﴿for those endowed with insight﴾. If *ruʾya* is visual, the meaning is: for those who saw the two groups. If it is doxastic (belief), the meaning is: for those with sound minds that are capable of drawing lessons.

﴿Adorned for people is the love of desires, of women and children…﴾. The majority read *zuyyina* with passive voice, and the agent is omitted. It was said the agent is Allah, exalted is He. This was said by ʿUmar, because when this verse was revealed he said, "Now, O Lord, since You have adorned it!" Then the verse ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better?﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:15] was revealed. The meaning of adornment is His creating it and originating the natural disposition to incline towards it. This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them﴾ [al-Kahf 18:7]. So He adorned it for the sake of trial. This is supported by the reading *zayyana lil-nāsi ḥubba*, with active voice, whose subject is the pronoun referring to Allah in His saying ﴿And Allah strengthens﴾.

It was also said the one who adorns is Satan, which is the apparent view of al-Hasan. He said: "Who adorned it? No one is more critical of it than its Creator." Attributing the adornment to Allah is correct in terms of origination and preparing it for benefit, and attributing it to Satan is correct in terms of whispering and obtaining it by illegitimate means.

The verse alludes to the rebuke of the Jews and others among the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who were enthralled by this world. It attributes the verbal noun to its object, which is common in the Qur'an. It expresses the desired things by *shahawāt* ("desires") as an intensification, treating them as the very substances, and as an alert to their baseness, since desire is considered contemptible by intelligent people; its follower is blamed and is witnessed to be among the cattle. Enough to show its blame is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Fire is surrounded by desires, and Paradise is surrounded by hardships."

He first mentioned the desires in the plural, in a general way, then began to explain them one by one, to show that what is adorned is nothing but worldly desire and nothing else. In this there is a warning against it, a condemnation of its seeker, and of one who chooses it over what is with Allah. He began with the most important and then the next, starting with women, because they are the snares of Satan and are closest and most intermingled. "I have not left behind me a trial more harmful to men than women." And, "I have not seen among those deficient in intellect and religion anyone more capable of taking away the mind of a prudent man than you." It is said that in women there are two trials: severing kinship and gathering wealth from both lawful and unlawful means. In children there is one trial: gathering wealth. He mentioned children second because they are the fruits of women and offspring of them, and sisters to women in trials. "Children are a cause of miserliness and cowardice."

Poetry:
*Indeed our children among us
are our livers walking on the earth.*
*If the wind blows upon one of them,
my eye refuses to close in sleep.*

A man is captivated by his son and by his poetry. They were placed before wealth because a person's love for his child is greater than his love for his wealth. Wherever He mentioned bounty and favor, or aid and dominance, wealth was placed before children. The apparent meaning of *wal-banīn* ("and children") is males. It was said it includes females, and the masculine form predominated.

(p-397) **And heaped-up sums of gold and silver.** The qintar (a large unit of weight) is mentioned with the wealth because of the temptation in wealth, because most desires are fulfilled through it, and because a person risks dangers in acquiring it for his children.

Scholars have disagreed about the qintar: is it a specific quantity or not? It has been said to be one thousand and two hundred uqiyya (ounces). It has been said to be twelve thousand uqiyya. It has been said to be one thousand and two hundred dinars. All of these have been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ). The first was narrated by Ubayy and held by Mu'adh, Ibn Umar, Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, and al-Hasan in one narration. The second was narrated by Abu Hurayra and held by him. The third was narrated by al-Hasan, and al-'Awfi narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

It has been said: twelve thousand dirhams, or one thousand gold dinars. This is reported from Ibn Abbas, from al-Hasan, and from al-Dahhak. Ibn al-Musayyab said: eighty thousand. Mujahid, and one report from Ibn Umar, said: seventy thousand dinars. Al-Suddi said: eight thousand mithqals, which is one hundred ratls. Al-Kalbi said: one thousand mithqals of gold or silver. Qatada said: one hundred ratls of gold, or eighty thousand dirhams of silver. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrima said: one hundred thousand, one hundred mana, one hundred ratl, one hundred mithqal, or one hundred dirhams. Indeed, when Islam came, there were in Mecca a hundred men who had amassed qintars.

It has been said: forty uqiyya of gold or silver. Makki mentioned this, and Ibn Sida said it in al-Muhkam (The Firm/Precise). It has also been said: eight thousand mithqals, which is one hundred ratls.

Ibn Sida said in al-Muhkam: the qintar, in the language of the Berbers, is one thousand mithqals. Anas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), in explaining the verse ﴿and you had given one of them a qintar﴾ [al-Nisa': 20], that it was one thousand dinars. Al-Zajjaj related that it was said the qintar is a ratl of gold or silver. Ibn 'Atiyya said: I think this is a mistake, and the correct saying is one hundred ratls, so one hundred was dropped by the transmitter, end quote. Abu Hamza al-Thumali said: the qintar, in the language of Ifriqiya and al-Andalus, is eight thousand mithqals, and this was in the earlier time. As for now, with us it is one hundred ratls, and the ratl with us is sixteen uqiyya. Abu Basra and Abu 'Ubayda said: the filling of an ox's hide with gold. Ibn Sida said: it is likewise in Syriac. Ibn al-Kalbi said: it is likewise in the language of the Romans.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: the abundant wealth, some of it upon some. Ibn Kaysan said: the great wealth. Abu 'Ubayda said: the qintar, for the Arabs, is a weight without limit. Al-Hakam said: the qintar is whatever wealth lies between the sky and the earth. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the qintar is a standard by which something is weighed, just as the ratl is a standard.

It is said: when that weight reached a qintar, meaning it equals a qintar. The soundest of the sayings is the first. The qintar varies with variation of regions in the size of the uqiyya, end quote.

Al-Muqantara is a form of muf'alala or mufay'ala derived from qintar. Its meaning is "gathered together," as one says "the gathered thousands" and "the scattered purse." They derived from it a descriptive word for emphasis. It has been said: al-muqantara is "multiplied," said by Qatada and al-Tabari. It has been said: al-muqantara is nine qintars, since it is a plural of plural, said by al-Naqqash, but this is not correct. Ibn Kaysan said: al-muqantara is not less than nine. Al-Farra' said: it is not more than nine. All of this is arbitrary. Al-Suddi said: al-muqantara is what is minted into dinars or dirhams. Al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak said: it is what is piled up, one part over another. It has been said: it is what is stored and hoarded. Yaman said: it is what is buried and treasured. It has been said: it is what is present and ready, said by Ibn 'Atiyya. Marwan ibn al-Hakam said: wealth is only what the eye has seized.

﴿from gold and silver﴾: this clarifies the qintars, and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to them, meaning "consisting of gold and silver."

﴿and the branded horses﴾: that is, those grazing in the pastures. They "sawwama" means they pastured and took their fill of grazing, that is, their utmost effort, and they were not restricted to one state rather than another. So the verb has been made transitive by doubling (tadh'if), as it was made transitive by the hamza in their saying "asmatha-ha." This was said by Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza, Mujahid, and al-Rabi'. It was reported from Mujahid that they are the beautiful, well-proportioned ones. Al-Suddi said: they are the pleasing ones in appearance of beauty. Ikrima said: their sawm is beauty, and al-Nahhas preferred this, from their saying "rajul wasim" (a handsome man). This would not be possible due to the difference of the two roots, unless one claims metathesis (qalb). Abu 'Ubayda and al-Kisa'i said: those marked with markings.

It was reported from Ibn Abbas, and it is from the sawma, which is a mark. Abu Talib said:

"Trustworthy, loving to the servants, marked
With the seal of a pure Lord, for the seals."

Abu Zayd said: the origin of that is that one places upon it a tuft of wool or a sign that differs from the rest of its body, so that it may be distinguished from others in the pasture. Ibn Faris in al-Mujmal said: the musawwama is the one upon which its riders are sent. Ibn Zayd said: prepared for jihad. Ibn al-Mubarrad said: well known in the lands. Ibn Kaysan said: the piebald. It has been said: those with white markings from the forehead blaze and the leg whites. It has been said: they are the ones with long manes.

﴿and the cattle and the tilth﴾: it is possible that these are coordinated with what precedes, from "and the qintars" to the end, as an explanation coordinated with "the desires," meaning "and the love of qintars and so-and-so." It is also possible that it is coordinated with "of women," so that it falls within the desires. He did not pluralize "al-harth" (tilth) because it is originally a verbal noun. It has been said: it is meant in the sense of the object (maf'ul), and the discussion of it has already occurred under His saying ﴿and you do not water the tilth﴾ [al-Baqara: 71].

﴿That is the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾: He pointed with "dhalika," which is singular, to the previously mentioned things, which are many, because He meant "that mentioned," or "that previously mentioned." The meaning is belittling the matter of this world, and an indication of its passing and the passing of what is enjoyed in it. Abu 'Amr assimilated (idgham); in the great assimilation there is a thaʾ, and the harth in the dhal of dhalika. It was considered weak due to the soundness of the consonant before the thaʾ.

﴿And with Allah is the best return﴾: that is, the place of return. It is an indication of the bliss of the Hereafter, which does not perish or end.

Among the strange rulings deduced from this verse is that it indicates the obligation of zakat on grazing horses, because it is mentioned with what zakat or support (nafaqa) is obligatory upon. The women and the sons are included in support, and the rest are included in zakat. This was said by al-Maturidi.

They have mentioned in this verse types of eloquence and rhetoric: the general address, meaning the particular, in His saying ﴿to those who disbelieved﴾, according to the view of the majority of the commentators, that they are the Jews. This is a variation of address (talwin al-khitab), and the varied paronomasia (tajnis al-mughayir) in "you see them twice their number with the eye," and the caution (ihtiras) in "with the eye." They said: lest it be thought to be sight of the heart, so it is from the category of estimation and the prevalence of assumption. There is the ambiguity in "it was made attractive for people," and the identical paronomasia (tajnis al-mumathil) in "and the qintars of heaped-up," and the omission in various places, which is every place where one is compelled to correct the meaning by supposing an omitted element.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 12–14 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome and gathered into Hell, and wretched is the resting-place."﴾ ﴿There has already been a sign for you in the two hosts that met: one fighting in the way of Allah, and another disbelieving, whom they saw as twice their number with their own eyes. And Allah supports with His help whom He wills. Indeed in that is a lesson for those who have insight.﴾ ﴿Adorned for people is the love of desires: women, sons, heaped-up piles of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle, and tilled land. That is the enjoyment of the worldly life, but with Allah is the best return.﴾.

Al-'Ibrah (lesson, admonition): it means being warned by something. It is derived from the verb i'tabara, which means to infer one thing from another similar to it. Its root is from al-'ubur (crossing), which is passing from one thing to another. From this comes 'ibr al-nahr, meaning its bank, and al-mi'bar, meaning a boat. Also al-'ibarah, by which one conveys meanings to the addressee. 'Abartu al-ru'ya, in both its light and intensive forms, means: you conveyed what you knew of its interpretation to the dreamer or to another who is ignorant of it. I'tibar is a transition from the station of ignorance to the station of knowledge. From this comes al-'abrah, which is tears, because they pass over the eye.

Al-shahwah (desire): it is what the soul calls for. Its verb is ishtaha. It is pluralised with alif and ta' as shahawat. I found in Arab poetry its plural as shuhan, like nazwah and nuzan, and kawwah and kuwan, according to the view of those who claim that kuwan is the plural of kawwah with a fatha on the kaf. This, along with qaryah and qura, was mentioned by the grammarians among what came on the pattern fa'lah with a weak final radical and was pluralised as fu'al. I added shuhan myself. A woman from the Banu Nadr ibn Mu'awiyah said:

"Had it not been for desire, by Allah, I would have been worthy of leaving pleasures in every place."

Al-qintar (a large measure of wealth): it is fin'al, whose nun is additional, as Ibn Duraid said, so its pattern is fin'al from qatara yaqtur. It was also said that the nun is original, with the pattern fi'lal. There is a difference of opinion: does it refer to a specific number, or is it a measure that is not limited or confined? Those who say it is a specific number differ about that number, and this will come in the tafsir, Allah willing.

It is said from it: qannara li-rajul, when a man has qanatir or a qintar of wealth. Al-Zajjaj said: it is derived from qantartu al-shay', meaning I tied it and made it firm, and from this the bridge (qantarah) is named for its firmness. It was also said: qantartuh means I piled one thing upon another, and from this it is named qantarah. So the great wealth that is piled up, one part upon another, is likened to a bridge.

Al-dhahab (gold): it is well known, and it is feminine. Its plurals are dhihab and dhuhub. It was also said that al-dhahab is the plural of dhahabah.

Al-fiddah (silver): it is well known, and its plural is fidad. So al-dhahab is derived from al-dhahab (going away), and al-fiddah from infadda al-shay', meaning it scattered, and from this: fadadtu al-qawm, I dispersed the people.

Al-khayl (horses): it is a collective noun with no singular from its own form. Its singular is faras. It was also said its singular is khail, like rakib and rakb, as Abu 'Ubaydah said. It was named so for its strutting in its walk. It was also said its derivation is from al-takhayyul (imagining), because it is imagined in the form of something greater than itself. It was also said that ikhtiyal is derived from takhayyul.

Al-na'am (livestock): it is camels only. Al-Farra' said: it is masculine and is not feminised; they say "hadha na'amun warid." Al-Harawi said: al-na'am is masculine and feminine, and when pluralised it applies to camels, cows, and sheep. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-an'am are camels, cows, and sheep, its singular is na'am, and it is a collective noun with no singular from its own form. It was named so for the softness of its touch, which is its gentleness. From this come al-na'im (soft), al-na'amah (ostrich), and al-na'ami (the south wind), named so for the gentleness of its blowing.

Al-ma'ab (return): it is maf'al from aba ya'ub iyaban, meaning he returned. It can denote the verbal noun, the place, or the time.

﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome and gathered into Hell, and wretched is the resting-place."﴾ The occasion of its revelation: the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa' said after the battle of Badr: "The Quraysh were inexperienced; if you had fought us, you would have seen real men." It was also said: it was revealed concerning Quraysh two years before Badr, and Allah made that come true. It was also said: when He overcame Quraysh at Badr, the Jews said: "This is the awaited Prophet described in our book; his banner is never defeated." Then their devils said to them: "Do not hasten until we see his affair in another battle." When Uhud came, they all disbelieved and said: "He is not the victorious Prophet."

It was also said: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan and his people, who gathered against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ after Badr. Since Allah had earlier mentioned that those who disbelieve, their wealth and children will not avail them at all, and that they are fuel for the Fire, this true promise was fitting to be followed by this true promise, which is like an affirmation of what came before. So overcoming happens through their not benefiting from wealth and children, and their being gathered into Hell is the beginning of their becoming its fuel.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read yaghlibuna and yuhsharuna with the ya' (third person). The rest of the seven read with the ta' (second person, address), so the clause is then an object of "say." Whoever reads with ya' — the apparent referent of the pronoun is "those who disbelieve," and the clause is then not quoted by "qul" but by another statement. The implied sense is: "Say to them my word: they will be overcome," and my report that overcoming and defeat will befall them. As Allah said: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has passed will be forgiven for them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38]. With ta' He informs them of what He had informed them: that they will be overcome; with ya' He informs them with the very words by which He informed that they will be overcome. Some scholars, namely al-Farra', Ahmad ibn Yahya, and Ibn 'Atiyyah, permitted the possibility that in the reading with ta', the pronoun in "sa-yughlabuna" refers to Quraysh, meaning: say to the Jews, "Quraysh will be overcome." But this is far-fetched.

The apparent meaning is that "those who disbelieve" includes both groups, the polytheists and the Jews. Each was overcome by the sword, by the jizyah (poll tax), by humiliation, and by the manifestation of proofs and arguments. Its meaning includes the sense of endpoint (ila): Hell is the end of their gathering. Even further is the view of one who says that "ila" means "fi" (in), so the meaning would be: they will be gathered in Hell. "And wretched is the resting-place" may be part of what is said, or it may be a new statement from Him, as al-Raghib said. The thing that is the object of dispraise is omitted because what precedes it indicates it: the intended sense is "and wretched is the resting-place, Hell." It is often omitted when the meaning is understood. This is among what is cited in support of Sibawayh's school: that it is a subject (mubtada'), and the clause before it is in the position of the predicate. For if it were the predicate of an omitted subject, or a subject with an omitted predicate, it would necessarily follow that an entire clause is omitted without anything remaining to indicate it, which is not permissible, because omitting a single word is easier than omitting a whole clause. As for the one who makes "al-mihad" mean what they prepared for themselves, that is, "wretched is what they prepared for themselves," and the sense for him is "wretched is their deed that led them to Hell," this is far-fetched, and it is related from Mujahid.

﴿There has already been a sign for you in the two hosts that met.﴾ Al-Razi (in Ray al-Zam'an) said: the commentators agreed that it is the battle of Badr, and the address is to the believers, as Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan said. According to this, the meaning of the verse is to strengthen souls and encourage them, because when He commanded him to say to the disbelievers what he said, the hypocrites and some weak believers might find it hard to accept, just as one said on the day of the Trench: "Muhammad promises us the wealth of Kisra and Caesar, while we cannot even feel safe relieving ourselves." And as 'Adi ibn Hatim said when the Prophet ﷺ informed him of the security that would come, and he said to himself: "Where are the brigands of Tayy who set the lands ablaze?" — the hadith in full.

It was also said: the address is to the disbelievers, which is apparent, especially according to the reading of the one who reads sa-tughlabuna with ta'. This may be derived from the statement of Ibn 'Abbas. According to this, it is a warning to them and an announcement that Allah will support His religion, and He has shown you an example of this in what befell the polytheists of Quraysh of abandonment, killing, and capture.

It was also said: the address is to the Jews, as al-Farra', Ibn al-Anbari, and Ibn Jarir said. According to this, it is a warning to them, as if it was said: "Do not be deceived by your skill in war, the strength of your fortresses, or your alliance with the polytheists of Quraysh, for Allah will overcome you. You know what befell the people of Badr." The verb "kana" was not given a feminine ta' even though it is attached to a feminine noun, which is "ayah," because the feminine is metaphorical. Its beauty is increased by the separation (of the verb from its subject). If separation beautifies it with a real feminine, it is more so with a metaphorical feminine. From their speech: "The judge attended a woman and said:"

"A man whom one of you deceives, after me and after you, in this world, is indeed deceived."

It was also said: it was made masculine because the meaning of the verse is "bayan" (clarity). It is like the one who said:

"A tender, soft, delicate girl, like the shoot of the split willow" — he meant the branch (qadib).

In His words ﴿in two hosts﴾ there is an omitted element, its estimate being: "in the story of two hosts." The meaning of "met" (iltaqata) is for war and fighting.

﴿One fighting in the way of Allah, and another disbelieving﴾ That is: one believing host fighting in the way of Allah, and another host fighting in the way of Satan. He omitted from the first what He mentioned its counterpart in the second, and from the second what He mentioned its parallel in the first. So He mentioned in the first the necessary consequence of faith, which is fighting in the way of Allah. And He mentioned in the second the necessary consequence of fighting in the way of Satan, which is disbelief.

The majority read "fi'atun" in the nominative, as a cut-off (qat'), with the estimate "one of them (is fi'ah)." So "fi'atun" according to this is the predicate of an omitted subject, or the estimate is "from them," so it is the subject with an omitted predicate.

It was also said: the nominative is in apposition to the pronoun in "iltaqata."

Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, and Humayd read "fi'atin" in the genitive, as a detailed apposition, which is apposition of whole to whole, as the poet said:

"I was like one with two legs: one leg healthy, and the other leg which time struck so that it became paralysed."

Some read "kafiratun" in the nominative, and some read it in the genitive by coordination. According to this reading, the first "fi'ah" is a partial apposition (badal ba'd min kull), which requires an estimated pronoun, meaning "a host of them is fighting in the way of Allah." "Ukhra" is nominative in both possible cases of cut-off, either as a subject or as a predicate.

Ibn al-Sumayqi and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "fi'atan" in the accusative. They said: in praise. The complete statement of this view is that the first is accusative by praise and the second by dispraise, as if it was said: "I praise a host fighting in the way of Allah, and I dispraise another host that is disbelieving."

Al-Zamakhshari said: the accusative in "fi'atin" is by specification (ikhtisas), but this is not good, because the word in the accusative of specification cannot be indefinite or vague. He and others before him, such as al-Zajjaj, permitted that it be accusative as a state (hal) from the pronoun in "iltaqata," and that "fi'ah" is mentioned as a preparatory mention (tawti'ah).

The majority read "tuqatilu" with ta' in agreement with the feminine "fi'ah." Mujahid and Muqatil read "yuqatilu" with ya', in the masculine. They said: because the meaning of "fi'ah" is "a people," so it is returned to that meaning and follows its wording.

﴿They see them as twice their number with their own eyes.﴾ Nafi', Ya'qub, and Sahl read "taraunahum" with ta' (address). The rest of the seven read with ya' (third person). Ibn 'Abbas and Talhah read "turawnahum" with a damma on the ta' (address). Al-Sulami read with a damma on the ya' (third person). As for the one who reads with an open ta', it follows what precedes it of address. So the pronoun in "lakum" refers to the believers, and the pronoun of subject in "taraunahum" refers to the believers too. The object pronoun in "taraunahum," and the genitive pronoun in "mithlayhim," refer to the disbelievers. The estimate is: "You, O believers, see the disbelievers as twice your own number." This is more eloquent as a sign: that they saw the disbelievers at twice their number, and yet Allah gave them victory over them, and the Muslims inflicted upon them. This is the true meaning of support through victory, as in His words: ﴿How many a small host has overcome a large host by the permission of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249].

This meaning is considered unlikely, because they made this verse and the verse of al-Anfal one single story, and there is a text stating that He, exalted is He, made the polytheists appear few in the eyes of the believers. So this multiplication in this verse does not accord with that interpretation. It is possible, according to the one who reads with the *tāʾ* of address (*tarawnahum*), that the address is to the believers, that the object pronoun in *tarawnahum* refers to the disbelievers, and that the genitive pronoun refers to the believers. The implied meaning is: "You see, O believers, the disbelievers as twice the believers." This too is considered unlikely, since the construction would then require *tarawnahum mithlaykum* ("you see them as twice you").

It is answered that this is an *iltifāt* (a shift from second-person to third-person pronoun), like His saying: ﴿until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them with a good wind﴾ [Yunus 10:22]. It is also possible that the pronoun in *mithlayhim* refers to the fighting group in the way of Allah, meaning: "You see, O believers, the disbelieving group as twice the fighting group in the way of Allah, and they are themselves." The meaning is: "You see them as twice yourselves." This is an understatement if they were over a thousand while the Muslims were about a third of them. So Allah showed the Muslims the disbelievers as twice the Muslims, as established in His saying: ﴿if there are among you a hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal 8:66], so that you would be emboldened against them.

Then, if the pronoun in *lakum* refers to the disbelievers, and in *tarawnahum* the address is to them, with the object and genitive pronouns referring to the believers, the implied meaning is: "You, O disbelievers, see the believers as twice their own selves."

It is also possible that the genitive pronoun refers to the disbelieving group, meaning: "as twice the disbelieving group, and they are themselves." Then Allah, exalted is He, would have shown the polytheists the believers as many times the believers' own numbers, or as many times the disbelievers despite the believers' fewness, so that they would be awed by them and lose their nerve against them. That vision was a reinforcement (*madad*) from Allah to the believers, just as He reinforced them with the angels. If this and the verse of al-Anfal are about one single story, then combining this multiplication with that reduction is by consideration of two states: they were first made to appear few in the eyes of the disbelievers so that they would be emboldened to meet the believers, and then they were made to appear many at the moment of encounter until they prevailed and overcame. This is like His saying: ﴿stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ [al-Saffat 37:24], and ﴿no one will be asked about his sin, neither man nor jinn﴾ [al-Rahman 55:39].

As for the one who reads with the open *yāʾ*, the apparent sense is that the clause is a description of *wa-ukhrā kāfiratun* ("and another disbelieving group"). The raised pronoun refers back to it according to its meaning, since if it referred to the wording it would have been *tarāhum*. The object pronoun refers to *fiʾatun tuqātilu fī sabīl Allāh* ("a group fighting in the way of Allah"), and the genitive pronoun in *mithlayhim* also refers to a group, according to the meaning of "group." Otherwise, if it referred to the wording, the construction would be *tarāhā mithlayhā*, meaning: "the disbelieving group sees the believing group as twice the number of itself." That is: six hundred and some twenty, or twice the number of the disbelieving group itself, that is two thousand, or close to two thousand.

It is also possible that the subject pronoun refers to the believing group according to its meaning, and the object and genitive pronouns refer to the disbelieving group according to its meaning, meaning: "the believing group sees the disbelieving group as twice itself."

It is also possible that the genitive pronoun refers to the disbelieving group, meaning: "as twice the disbelieving group." In that case the clause is a description of *wa-ukhrā kāfiratun*. In the first reading the linking element is the *wāw*, and in this reading the linking element is the object pronoun.

If the pronoun in *lakum* refers to the Jews, then the verse is as Allah commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to say to them as an argument against them and as a confirmation of the image of the earlier promise that the disbelievers would be overcome. Whoever reads with the *tāʾ* means: "if you had been present," or "if you had indeed been present." This address is appropriate because the matter itself was clear and certain for every person of that era. Whoever reads with the *yāʾ*, the subject pronoun may refer to the believing group, or it may refer to the disbelieving group as explained above.

In these two readings the *ruʾya* (seeing) is visual (*baṣariyya*), transitive to one object, and *mithlayhim* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*). This was said by Abu ʿAli, Makki and Mahdawi. The apparent sense of His saying *raʾy al-ʿayn* ("the seeing of the eye") supports this, and its accusative here is the accusative of an emphatic verbal noun (*maṣdar*).

Al-Zamakhshari said: "A manifest, uncovered seeing, without ambiguity, a direct witnessing like other direct observations." It was also said: the seeing here is from the seeing of the heart (*ruʾyat al-qalb*), so it is transitive to two objects, and the second is *mithlayhim*. This was rejected on two grounds: first, His saying *raʾy al-ʿayn*; second, that the seeing of the heart is knowledge, and it is impossible for a thing to be known as two things.

The first ground is answered: its accusative is that of a comparative verbal noun, meaning "a seeing like the seeing of the eye," that is, it resembles the seeing of the eye without actually being it. The second is answered: the meaning of *ruʾya* here is belief (*iʿtiqād*), so this is not impossible. And since they applied the word "knowledge" (*ʿilm*) in the language to belief without certainty, it is even more appropriate that they apply *raʾy* to it. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿if you know them to be believers﴾ [al-Mumtahanah 60:10], meaning: "if you believe in their faith." This is indicated by the reading of those who read *tarawnahum* with a *ḍamma* on the *tāʾ* or on the *yāʾ*. They said: the meaning is that belief in the doubling of the number of the disbelievers or of the believers was an estimate and a guess, not a certainty.

For this reason the expression contains a kind of doubt. That is why *uriya* is read with a *ḍamm* on the *hamza*, meaning it is an opinion about which there is doubt. Since this is so, just as it is impossible to take *raʾy* here as knowledge, it is impossible to take it as seeing with the eye, because just as knowledge does not occur contrary to the known, visual seeing does not occur contrary to what is seen. The apparent sense is that this is by way of estimate and supposition, and because this was firmly established in their belief, it was likened to the seeing of the eye.

*Al-raʾy* is the verbal noun of *raʾā*. One says: *raʾā raʾyan*, *ruʾyatan*, and *ruʾyā*. *Ruʾyā* is predominantly used for a dream; *ruʾya* for visual seeing while awake; and *raʾy* for belief. One says: "This is the opinion of so-and-so." A poet said:

*The people saw, except for one who saw as he saw,*
*Kharijites, forsaking the paths of escape.*

The meaning of *mithlayhim* is: their measure twice over. Al-Farra' claimed that the meaning of *yarawnahum mithlayhim* is three times their number, like the speaker's saying: "I have a thousand, and I need twice that amount." Al-Zajjaj refuted him, saying: "The *mithl* of a thing is what is equal to it, and its *mithlān* are two equals." 

Ibn Kaysan said: Al-Farra' fell into this interpretation because the polytheists were three times the Muslims on the day of Badr, so he imagined that they could not have seen them except at their actual number. This is far-fetched, and it is not the meaning. The meaning is rather that Allah showed them a number other than their actual number for two reasons: first, He saw the benefit in that, since the hearts of the believers were strengthened by it; second, it was a sign of the Prophet (ﷺ). End of Ibn Kaysan's words.

Reports are consistent that the total number of disbelievers at Badr was about a thousand or nine hundred, and the believers were three hundred and fourteen. It was also said: three hundred and thirteen. But the Banu Zuhra returned with al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, and Talib ibn Abi Talib and his followers and many people returned, until there remained for the fighting only about two-thirds. So Allah mentioned the two-fold figure, since their situation was certain and no one disputed it. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that the polytheists in the fighting at Badr were six hundred and twenty-six. Al-Zajjaj and others held that they were about a thousand.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "On the day of Badr the people were a thousand." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "We looked at the polytheists and saw them increasing against us, then we looked at them again and did not see them exceed us by one man." In another report he said: "They were made to appear few in our eyes, so much so that I said to a man beside me, 'Do you see them as seventy?' He said, 'I see them as a hundred.' Then we took one of them prisoner and asked him, 'How many were you?' He said, 'A thousand.'" It is also reported that when the polytheists were taken prisoner, they said to the Muslims, "How many were you?" They said, "We were three hundred and thirteen." They said, "We did not see you except as doubling against us." The magnification of each group in the eyes of the other, and the diminishing of each relative to the other at two different times, is permissible, so there is no barrier to it.

*Wa-llāhu yuʾayyidu bi-naṣrihi man yashāʾ* ﴿And Allah strengthens with His help whom He wills﴾, that is, He strengthens him with His aid. It was also said: *naṣr* means proof. Attributing the strengthening to Him indicates that those strengthened are the believers. The object of *man yashāʾ* is omitted, meaning: whom He wills to help.

*Inna fī dhālika* ("Indeed in that"), that is, in the help. It was also said: in the seeing of the army as twice their number, *la-ʿibrah* ("is indeed a lesson"), that is, an admonition and a sign.

﴿for those endowed with insight﴾. If *ruʾya* is visual, the meaning is: for those who saw the two groups. If it is doxastic (belief), the meaning is: for those with sound minds that are capable of drawing lessons.

﴿Adorned for people is the love of desires, of women and children…﴾. The majority read *zuyyina* with passive voice, and the agent is omitted. It was said the agent is Allah, exalted is He. This was said by ʿUmar, because when this verse was revealed he said, "Now, O Lord, since You have adorned it!" Then the verse ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better?﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:15] was revealed. The meaning of adornment is His creating it and originating the natural disposition to incline towards it. This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it, that We may test them﴾ [al-Kahf 18:7]. So He adorned it for the sake of trial. This is supported by the reading *zayyana lil-nāsi ḥubba*, with active voice, whose subject is the pronoun referring to Allah in His saying ﴿And Allah strengthens﴾.

It was also said the one who adorns is Satan, which is the apparent view of al-Hasan. He said: "Who adorned it? No one is more critical of it than its Creator." Attributing the adornment to Allah is correct in terms of origination and preparing it for benefit, and attributing it to Satan is correct in terms of whispering and obtaining it by illegitimate means.

The verse alludes to the rebuke of the Jews and others among the contemporaries of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who were enthralled by this world. It attributes the verbal noun to its object, which is common in the Qur'an. It expresses the desired things by *shahawāt* ("desires") as an intensification, treating them as the very substances, and as an alert to their baseness, since desire is considered contemptible by intelligent people; its follower is blamed and is witnessed to be among the cattle. Enough to show its blame is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Fire is surrounded by desires, and Paradise is surrounded by hardships."

He first mentioned the desires in the plural, in a general way, then began to explain them one by one, to show that what is adorned is nothing but worldly desire and nothing else. In this there is a warning against it, a condemnation of its seeker, and of one who chooses it over what is with Allah. He began with the most important and then the next, starting with women, because they are the snares of Satan and are closest and most intermingled. "I have not left behind me a trial more harmful to men than women." And, "I have not seen among those deficient in intellect and religion anyone more capable of taking away the mind of a prudent man than you." It is said that in women there are two trials: severing kinship and gathering wealth from both lawful and unlawful means. In children there is one trial: gathering wealth. He mentioned children second because they are the fruits of women and offspring of them, and sisters to women in trials. "Children are a cause of miserliness and cowardice."

Poetry:
*Indeed our children among us
are our livers walking on the earth.*
*If the wind blows upon one of them,
my eye refuses to close in sleep.*

A man is captivated by his son and by his poetry. They were placed before wealth because a person's love for his child is greater than his love for his wealth. Wherever He mentioned bounty and favor, or aid and dominance, wealth was placed before children. The apparent meaning of *wal-banīn* ("and children") is males. It was said it includes females, and the masculine form predominated.

(p-397) **And heaped-up sums of gold and silver.** The qintar (a large unit of weight) is mentioned with the wealth because of the temptation in wealth, because most desires are fulfilled through it, and because a person risks dangers in acquiring it for his children.

Scholars have disagreed about the qintar: is it a specific quantity or not? It has been said to be one thousand and two hundred uqiyya (ounces). It has been said to be twelve thousand uqiyya. It has been said to be one thousand and two hundred dinars. All of these have been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ). The first was narrated by Ubayy and held by Mu'adh, Ibn Umar, Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, and al-Hasan in one narration. The second was narrated by Abu Hurayra and held by him. The third was narrated by al-Hasan, and al-'Awfi narrated it from Ibn Abbas.

It has been said: twelve thousand dirhams, or one thousand gold dinars. This is reported from Ibn Abbas, from al-Hasan, and from al-Dahhak. Ibn al-Musayyab said: eighty thousand. Mujahid, and one report from Ibn Umar, said: seventy thousand dinars. Al-Suddi said: eight thousand mithqals, which is one hundred ratls. Al-Kalbi said: one thousand mithqals of gold or silver. Qatada said: one hundred ratls of gold, or eighty thousand dirhams of silver. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrima said: one hundred thousand, one hundred mana, one hundred ratl, one hundred mithqal, or one hundred dirhams. Indeed, when Islam came, there were in Mecca a hundred men who had amassed qintars.

It has been said: forty uqiyya of gold or silver. Makki mentioned this, and Ibn Sida said it in al-Muhkam (The Firm/Precise). It has also been said: eight thousand mithqals, which is one hundred ratls.

Ibn Sida said in al-Muhkam: the qintar, in the language of the Berbers, is one thousand mithqals. Anas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), in explaining the verse ﴿and you had given one of them a qintar﴾ [al-Nisa': 20], that it was one thousand dinars. Al-Zajjaj related that it was said the qintar is a ratl of gold or silver. Ibn 'Atiyya said: I think this is a mistake, and the correct saying is one hundred ratls, so one hundred was dropped by the transmitter, end quote. Abu Hamza al-Thumali said: the qintar, in the language of Ifriqiya and al-Andalus, is eight thousand mithqals, and this was in the earlier time. As for now, with us it is one hundred ratls, and the ratl with us is sixteen uqiyya. Abu Basra and Abu 'Ubayda said: the filling of an ox's hide with gold. Ibn Sida said: it is likewise in Syriac. Ibn al-Kalbi said: it is likewise in the language of the Romans.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: the abundant wealth, some of it upon some. Ibn Kaysan said: the great wealth. Abu 'Ubayda said: the qintar, for the Arabs, is a weight without limit. Al-Hakam said: the qintar is whatever wealth lies between the sky and the earth. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the qintar is a standard by which something is weighed, just as the ratl is a standard.

It is said: when that weight reached a qintar, meaning it equals a qintar. The soundest of the sayings is the first. The qintar varies with variation of regions in the size of the uqiyya, end quote.

Al-Muqantara is a form of muf'alala or mufay'ala derived from qintar. Its meaning is "gathered together," as one says "the gathered thousands" and "the scattered purse." They derived from it a descriptive word for emphasis. It has been said: al-muqantara is "multiplied," said by Qatada and al-Tabari. It has been said: al-muqantara is nine qintars, since it is a plural of plural, said by al-Naqqash, but this is not correct. Ibn Kaysan said: al-muqantara is not less than nine. Al-Farra' said: it is not more than nine. All of this is arbitrary. Al-Suddi said: al-muqantara is what is minted into dinars or dirhams. Al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak said: it is what is piled up, one part over another. It has been said: it is what is stored and hoarded. Yaman said: it is what is buried and treasured. It has been said: it is what is present and ready, said by Ibn 'Atiyya. Marwan ibn al-Hakam said: wealth is only what the eye has seized.

﴿from gold and silver﴾: this clarifies the qintars, and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to them, meaning "consisting of gold and silver."

﴿and the branded horses﴾: that is, those grazing in the pastures. They "sawwama" means they pastured and took their fill of grazing, that is, their utmost effort, and they were not restricted to one state rather than another. So the verb has been made transitive by doubling (tadh'if), as it was made transitive by the hamza in their saying "asmatha-ha." This was said by Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza, Mujahid, and al-Rabi'. It was reported from Mujahid that they are the beautiful, well-proportioned ones. Al-Suddi said: they are the pleasing ones in appearance of beauty. Ikrima said: their sawm is beauty, and al-Nahhas preferred this, from their saying "rajul wasim" (a handsome man). This would not be possible due to the difference of the two roots, unless one claims metathesis (qalb). Abu 'Ubayda and al-Kisa'i said: those marked with markings.

It was reported from Ibn Abbas, and it is from the sawma, which is a mark. Abu Talib said:

"Trustworthy, loving to the servants, marked
With the seal of a pure Lord, for the seals."

Abu Zayd said: the origin of that is that one places upon it a tuft of wool or a sign that differs from the rest of its body, so that it may be distinguished from others in the pasture. Ibn Faris in al-Mujmal said: the musawwama is the one upon which its riders are sent. Ibn Zayd said: prepared for jihad. Ibn al-Mubarrad said: well known in the lands. Ibn Kaysan said: the piebald. It has been said: those with white markings from the forehead blaze and the leg whites. It has been said: they are the ones with long manes.

﴿and the cattle and the tilth﴾: it is possible that these are coordinated with what precedes, from "and the qintars" to the end, as an explanation coordinated with "the desires," meaning "and the love of qintars and so-and-so." It is also possible that it is coordinated with "of women," so that it falls within the desires. He did not pluralize "al-harth" (tilth) because it is originally a verbal noun. It has been said: it is meant in the sense of the object (maf'ul), and the discussion of it has already occurred under His saying ﴿and you do not water the tilth﴾ [al-Baqara: 71].

﴿That is the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾: He pointed with "dhalika," which is singular, to the previously mentioned things, which are many, because He meant "that mentioned," or "that previously mentioned." The meaning is belittling the matter of this world, and an indication of its passing and the passing of what is enjoyed in it. Abu 'Amr assimilated (idgham); in the great assimilation there is a thaʾ, and the harth in the dhal of dhalika. It was considered weak due to the soundness of the consonant before the thaʾ.

﴿And with Allah is the best return﴾: that is, the place of return. It is an indication of the bliss of the Hereafter, which does not perish or end.

Among the strange rulings deduced from this verse is that it indicates the obligation of zakat on grazing horses, because it is mentioned with what zakat or support (nafaqa) is obligatory upon. The women and the sons are included in support, and the rest are included in zakat. This was said by al-Maturidi.

They have mentioned in this verse types of eloquence and rhetoric: the general address, meaning the particular, in His saying ﴿to those who disbelieved﴾, according to the view of the majority of the commentators, that they are the Jews. This is a variation of address (talwin al-khitab), and the varied paronomasia (tajnis al-mughayir) in "you see them twice their number with the eye," and the caution (ihtiras) in "with the eye." They said: lest it be thought to be sight of the heart, so it is from the category of estimation and the prevalence of assumption. There is the ambiguity in "it was made attractive for people," and the identical paronomasia (tajnis al-mumathil) in "and the qintars of heaped-up," and the omission in various places, which is every place where one is compelled to correct the meaning by supposing an omitted element.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 15–17 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something better than that? For those who fear Allah, with their Lord are gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they will abide eternally, and purified spouses, and approval from Allah. And Allah is Seeing of [His] servants."﴾ ﴿Those who say, "Our Lord, indeed we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ ﴿[They are] the patient, the truthful, the devoutly obedient, the spenders, and those who seek forgiveness before dawn.﴾ ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no deity except Him, and [so do] the angels and those of knowledge, [maintaining] justice. There is no deity except Him, the Almighty, the Wise.﴾ [Al-'Imran: 18]. Al-Ridwan is a verbal noun from radiya (to be pleased). Its ra' may be vowelled with a kasra, which is the dialect of the Hijaz, or with a damma, which is the dialect of Tamim, Bakr, Qays and Ghaylan. It is said that the kasra is for the proper noun, as in Ridwan, the keeper of Paradise, while the damma is for the verbal noun.

Al-Sahar (the pre-dawn period) may be pronounced with a fatha or a sukun on the ha'. A group of scholars, including al-Zajjaj, said: it is the time before the break of dawn. From it comes the verb tasahhara, meaning he ate at that time, and istahara, meaning he travelled during it. He said:

*They set out early in the morning, and in the pre-dawn they travelled, so they are for the Wadi al-Rass like the hand to the mouth.*

Istahara al-tha'ir (the bird) also means it cried out and stirred within it. He said:

*Its cold teeth are cooled by it, when the stirring bird sings.*

Asḥara al-rajul and istahara also mean he entered the pre-dawn. He said:

*He travelled by night from Taybah in haste, and came to us when he had entered the pre-dawn.*

Some lexicographers said: al-sihr (the pre-dawn) is from the last third of the night until dawn. It is reported in some Arabic poetry that its ruling continues after dawn. It is also said that for the Arabs al-sahar is from the end of the night and continues until the morning light. The root meaning of sahar is concealment because of its subtlety, and from it come sihr and sahr (magic).

﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something better than that?"﴾ It was revealed when Umar said, when the verse "Adorned for people is the love of desires..." [Al-'Imran: 14] was revealed: "O Lord, now that You have adorned it..." Since the Exalted mentioned that "with Him is the best return" [Al-'Imran: 14], He mentioned the return and that it is better than the enjoyment of this world, because it is a good state free from the admixture of harms, and it is lasting and does not end. The hamza in "a'unabbi'ukum" — the first hamza is the interrogative hamza which entered upon the hamza of the present tense. In the seven canonical readings it is recited with both hamzas made clear without inserting an alif between them; with both made clear and an alif inserted between them; and with the second hamza eased without an alif between them. Warsh transferred the vowel to the lam and omitted the hamza. And [it is recited] with the second eased and an alif inserted between them. In this verse there is consolation regarding the adornments of this world, strengthening for the souls of those who abandon it, and honouring. The shift from the third person to the second person [occurs]. When He said "That is the enjoyment..." in the singular, He then said "something better than that," in the singular demonstrative, even though there was a referent previously mentioned, which is frequent. Here it refers to what was pointed to by "that." "Better" here is the comparative form, and it is not permissible that it means "a good thing among goods," with "than that" being a description of what would necessarily follow, namely that what they desired would be part of what they had renounced.

﴿For those who fear Allah, with their Lord are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ It is possible that "for those who fear Allah" is connected to "something better than that," and "gardens" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is gardens. Then "that" would be an explanation of what was left vague in "something better than that." This is supported by the reading of Ya'qub, "jannatin" in the genitive, in apposition to "bi-khayrin," as you say "marartu bi-rajulin Zaydin" with the nominative and the genitive. In Ya'qub's reading it is also permitted that "jannatun" is in the accusative by an implied "a'ni" (I mean), and in the accusative as an apposition to the position of "bi-khayrin," since it is in the accusative. It is also possible that "for those who fear Allah" is the predicate of "gardens," with "gardens" raised as the subject, and the sentence complete at "something better than that," and then it explains for whom that good is. In this case the governing element of "with their Lord" is the governing element of "for those who," and in the first view the governing element is "something better."

﴿Abiding therein, and purified spouses﴾ The explanation of this and what precedes it has already been given.

﴿And approval from Allah﴾ He first mentioned the abode, which is the gardens of which He said: "Therein is what the souls desire and the eyes delight in" [Az-Zukhruf: 71]. "Therein is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human being." Then He moved from mentioning them to mentioning what brings complete intimacy, namely the purified spouses. Then He moved from that to what is greater than all things, which is Allah's pleasure with them. Thus through the combination of all this there is physical pleasure and spiritual joy, since one knows that Allah is pleased with him. As in the hadith, that He, may He be exalted, "asks the people of Paradise: 'Are you pleased?' They say: 'What reason do we have not to be pleased, O Lord, when You have given us what You have not given anyone of Your creation?' He says: 'Shall I not give you something better than that?' They say: 'O Lord, and what is better than that?' He says: 'I shall make My approval descend upon you, and I shall never be angry with you again.'" So in this verse there is a movement from a high level to a higher level above it. For this reason, in Surat Bara'ah, after He mentioned the gardens and good dwellings, He said: "And approval from Allah is greater" [At-Tawbah: 72], meaning: greater than what was mentioned of the gardens and dwellings. Al-Maturidi said: the people of Paradise are purified, because defects in things are a sign of perishing, and they were created for permanence. He specified women with purity because of what they have in this world of excess blemishes and harm. Abu Bakr said: "wa-ridwanun" with a damma wherever it occurs, except in the second of the contracts (al-'Uqud), where there is a difference of opinion. The rest of the seven read it with a kasra, and we have mentioned that both are dialects.

* *

﴿And Allah is Seeing of [His] servants﴾ That is, He is seeing of their deeds, aware of them, and will recompense each according to his deed. Thus it includes both promise and warning. When He mentioned the God-fearing, He implied their opposites, and so He concluded the verse with this.

﴿Those who say, "Our Lord, indeed we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ When He mentioned that Paradise is for the God-fearing, He mentioned some of their attributes, beginning with faith, which is the head of piety. He mentioned their supplication to their Lord when reporting about themselves with faith, and emphasized the sentence with "indeed" for emphasis in the report. Then they asked for forgiveness and protection from punishment, arranging this upon bare faith, which shows that forgiveness is consequent upon faith, and that faith is not a term for all acts of obedience, as some hold, because whoever repents and obeys Allah will not be made to enter the Fire by His true promise. Then the request would be for Him not to do what is not fitting. A parallel is "Our Lord, indeed we have heard a caller..." [Al 'Imran: 193], and so the attributes that follow this are not conditions, but attributes that require the highest ranks.

Al-Maturidi said: He praised them by this statement, and in it there is self-purification through faith, while Allah forbade self-purification through acts of obedience, as He said: "So do not claim purity for yourselves" [An-Najm: 32]. If faith were a name for all acts of obedience, He would not have accepted from them self-purification by faith, just as He did not accept it by all other acts of obedience. So the verse is a proof for those who make acts of obedience part of faith, and in it there is evidence that inserting an exception ("if Allah wills") into faith is invalid, because He accepted it from them without exception. It was said: it indicates neither self-purification nor exception, because their saying "we have believed" is an acknowledgment of what they were commanded, so it is not self-purification on their part; and because the exception applies only to what a person dies upon, not to what he is characterized by; and no one holds that the faith by which a servant is characterized permits an exception, for that is rationally impossible.

It is parsed: "alladhina yaqulun" as a qualifier, as a substitute, and as a detached phrase, in the nominative or in the accusative. It would be among the followers of "alladhina ittaqaw" or among the followers of "al-'ibad." The first is more apparent.

﴿[They are] the patient, the truthful, the devoutly obedient, the spenders, and those who seek forgiveness before dawn﴾ When He mentioned faith by speech, He informed of the attribute indicating restraint of the soul upon what is burdensome for it of obligations: they were patient in performing obedience and in abstaining from what is forbidden. Then by the attribute indicating that belief in the heart corresponds to the tongue's utterance, they are truthful in what they report in their saying "Our Lord, indeed we have believed," and in everything they report.

It is also said: they are those whose intentions are true, and whose hearts and tongues are upright, in secret and in public. This goes back to the previous statement. Then by the attribute of devout obedience (qunut), whose explanation was given in His words "all are devoutly obedient to Him" [Al-Baqarah: 116], so there is no need to repeat it. Then by the attribute of spending, because what preceded are attributes whose benefit is confined to the one who possesses them and does not extend beyond him; so in this he brought an attribute that extends to others, which is spending. The objects of these attributes are omitted because they are known. The meaning is: patient in the obligations of their Lord, truthful in their statements, devoutly obedient to their Lord, spending their wealth in His obedience, and seeking forgiveness from Allah for their sins before dawn. When He mentioned that they arranged the request for forgiveness upon faith, which is the root of piety, He also informed that, when they are characterized by these noble attributes, they seek forgiveness before dawn. They do not see their being characterized by these noble attributes as something that removes the need to seek forgiveness. He singled out the pre-dawn for mention, though they seek forgiveness constantly, because it is a time of expected answer, as is established in the hadith: "He, exalted beyond the marks of createdness, descends when the last third of the night remains, and says: 'Who calls upon Me that I may respond to him? Who asks of Me that I may give him? Who seeks forgiveness from Me that I may forgive him?' He continues thus until dawn breaks." The Companions, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar and others, would seek out the pre-dawn hours to seek forgiveness in them. Seeking forgiveness at that time is recommended, because worship at that time is harder. Do you not see that they say that the dozing at dawn is among the sweetest sleep? And because at that time the soul is purer, the body less fatigued, and the mind more subtle and sharp, since the body is at rest from heavy physical and mental burdens, and the thought is left behind by immersion in the flow of sleep.

Al-Zamakhshari said: they used to perform the night prayer early, so it is good to ask for need at that time.

"To Him ascend the good word, and the righteous deed raises it" [Fatir: 10]. End. Its meaning, according to al-Hasan: these five attributes belong to one described person, namely the believers. They were joined with "wa" and were not left without conjunction, because each attribute is distinct from the other, as they do not have one meaning; so the difference and distinction of the attributes is treated as the difference of the essences, and thus they were conjoined. Al-Zamakhshari said: the "wa" placed between the attributes is to indicate their perfection in each of them. End. We do not know that conjunction with "wa" in an attribute indicates perfection.

The exegetes said regarding the patient: they were patient against sins. It is also said: they remained steadfast upon the first covenant. It is also said: they are those who fast. They said regarding the truthful: in statements. It is said: in speech, in action, and in intention. It is said: in secret and in public.

They said regarding the devoutly obedient: those who guard the unseen. Al-Zajjaj said: those who persist in worship. It is said: those who stand for the truth. It is said: those who supplicate and humble themselves. It is said: the humble. It is said: those who pray. They said regarding the spenders: those who bring out wealth in a lawful manner. It is said: in jihad. It is said: in all kinds of righteousness. Ibn Qutaybah said: in charities. They said regarding those who seek forgiveness: the askers, said by Ibn Abbas. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Umar, Anas and Qatadah said: those who ask for forgiveness at a time of leisure of mind and lightness of occupations. Qatadah also said: those who pray at the pre-dawn. Zayd ibn Aslam said: those who pray the dawn prayer in congregation. All of what they explained is closely related.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 15–17 (part 2 of 2):

﴿God bears witness that there is no god but Him, and so do the angels and those of knowledge, standing firm in justice.﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:18]. The occasion of its revelation: "Two rabbis (habr) from Syria came to Madina. One of them said to the other: 'How much this city resembles the city of the Prophet who will emerge at the end of time!' Then they recognised the Messenger of God (ﷺ) by his description and said: 'Are you Muhammad?' He said: 'Yes.' They said: 'Are you Ahmad?' He said: 'Yes.' They said: 'We will ask you about a testimony; if you inform us of it, we will believe.' He said: 'Ask me.' One of them said: 'Tell us about the greatest testimony in the Book of God.' So this verse was revealed, and they both embraced Islam."

Ibn Jubayr said: "Around the House (the Ka'ba) there were three hundred and sixty idols. When this verse was revealed, they fell down prostrate." It was also said: it was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran, when they disputed about the matter of 'Isa (Jesus). It was said: it concerns the Jews and Christians, when they abandoned the name of Islam and named themselves Judaism and Christianity. It was said: they said, "Our religion is better than your religion," and so it was revealed.

The root of shahida is "to be present" (ḥaḍara). Then the word was extended to the act of conveying what is firmly established in the mind, whatever the manner of that establishment, whether by presence or otherwise. It was said that the meaning of shahida here is "to make known" (a'lama). This was said by al-Mufaddal and others. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda said it means "to decree" (qaḍā). Mujahid said it means "to judge" (ḥakama). It was also said it means "to make clear" (bayyana). Ibn Kaysan said: shahida means by manifesting His handiwork.

The poet said:
"And in everything there is a sign that shows He is the One."

Al-Zamakhshari said: His indication of His oneness is likened to His particular acts which no other can perform, and to what He has revealed of His verses that declare His unity, such as the sura of Sincerity (al-Ikhlas), the Verse of the Throne (Ayat al-Kursi), and others, by the testimony of a witness in clarification and disclosure. Likewise is the affirmation of the angels and those of knowledge of this, and their argument for it. End of quotation. And it is good.

Al-Marwazi said: the mention of His testimony, glorified is He, is by way of honouring the testimony of those mentioned after Him, as in His saying: ﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: The spoils belong to God and the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal 8:1]. End of quotation.

*They set out early in the morning, and in the pre-dawn they travelled, so they are for the Wadi al-Rass like the hand to the mouth.*

Istahara al-tha'ir (the bird) also means it cried out and stirred within it. He said:

*Its cold teeth are cooled by it, when the stirring bird sings.*

Asḥara al-rajul and istahara also mean he entered the pre-dawn. He said:

[p. 403]

The sharing of the angels and the people of knowledge with God in testifying is by way of conjunction (ʿaṭf, coordination) with Him, because the attribution of making known is valid, or because the attribution of manifesting and clarifying is valid, even though the manner of manifesting and clarifying differs. God's manifesting is by creating the proofs, and the angels' manifesting is by confirming them to the Messengers, and the Messengers' to the people of knowledge. Al-Wahidi said: God's testimony is His clarifying and manifesting, and the witness (shāhid) is the knower who makes clear what he knows. God has made clear the indications of Oneness through everything He created. The testimony of the angels means affirmation (iqrār), as in His saying: ﴿They said, "We bear witness against ourselves"﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:130], that is, "We affirm." So He coordinated the angels' testimony with God's testimony, although they differ in meaning, because they are alike in wording, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, God and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 33:56], since from God it is mercy, and from the angels it is seeking forgiveness and supplication. The testimony of the people of knowledge may bear the meaning of affirmation and may bear the meaning of clarifying, because they affirmed and clarified. End of quotation.

Al-Muʾarrij said: "shahida Allāh" in the dialect of Qays ibn Ghaylān. As for ﴿ulū al-ʿilm﴾ (the people of knowledge), it was said: they are the Prophets. It was said: the scholars. It was said: the believers among the People of the Book. It was said: the Emigrants and the Helpers. It was said: the scholars among the believers. Al-Ḥasan said: the believers. What is meant by "the people of knowledge" is whoever among mankind has knowledge, because they are divided into knower and ignorant, unlike the angels, who are equal in knowledge.

﴿Annahu lā ilāha illā huwa﴾ is the object of "shahida" (object clause), and it was separated by it between the element coordinated upon and the coordinated element, to indicate attention to mentioning the object, and to indicate the difference in rank between the two conjoined elements, such that they are not coordinated while adjacent. He placed the angels before the people of knowledge from mankind, because they are the exalted assembly (al-malaʾ al-aʿlā), and all their knowledge is necessary (ḍarūrī, innate), unlike mankind, whose knowledge is both necessary and acquired (iktisābī).

Abū al-Shaʿthāʾ read "shuhida" with a damma on the shīn, in the passive voice, so "annahu" is in the position of a substitute (badal), meaning: it was witnessed that God is One and that He is the deity. In this reading, "al-malāʾikah" is in the nominative as the beginning (mubtadaʾ), and the predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "and the angels and the people of knowledge bear witness." The predicate was omitted because the meaning indicates it. It is also possible that it is the subject (fāʿil) with a verb omitted by implication, indicated by "shahida," because when the verb is made passive, before that it was active, and the estimate is: "And the angels and the people of knowledge bore witness to that."

Abū al-Muhallab, the paternal uncle of Muḥārib ibn Dithār, read: shuhadāʾa Allāh, on the pattern fuʿalāʾ, as a plural in the accusative. Ibn Jinnī said: it is in the accusative of circumstance (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "al-mustaghfirīn" (those who seek forgiveness). It was said: it is in the accusative of praise (madḥ), and it is the plural of shuhadāʾ, and the plural of shāhid like ẓurafāʾ and ʿulamāʾ. It is narrated from him and from Abū Nahīk: shuhadāʾu Allāh, with the nominative, meaning: they are the witnesses of God. In both readings, "shuhadāʾ" is in construct (muḍāf) with the name of God.

It is narrated from Abū al-Muhallab: shuhudun, with a damma on the shīn and the hāʾ, the plural of shahīd, like nadhīr and nudhur, and it is in the accusative of circumstance, and the name of God is in the accusative. Al-Naqqāsh mentioned that it was read likewise with a damma on the dāl, and with a fatḥa, in construct with the name of God in both readings. Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned that it was read: shuhadāʾu lillāh, with the hamza in the nominative and in the accusative, and with the lām of the genitive attached to the name of God. The accusative is the circumstance of those mentioned, and the nominative is by their being understood as an omitted subject. The nominative of "al-malāʾikah" in these two readings is by coordination upon the pronoun concealed in "shuhadāʾ," and that coordination was permitted because of the intervening separation between them. The nominative of "al-malāʾikah" was previously explained, either as subject or as beginning.

Abū ʿAmr, in one of the narrations from him, read with the assimilation (idghām) of the waw, and this is in the waw of "wa-al-malāʾikah." Ibn ʿAbbās read: (innahu lā ilāha illā huwa) with a kasra on the hamza in "innahu." This was explained on the basis that he treated "shahida" as "qāla" (said), because testimony has the meaning of speech, and therefore he made "inna" take the kasra. Or on the basis that the object of "shahida" is that the religion with God is Islam, and His saying: ﴿that there is no god but He﴾ is an interjected clause (jumlat iʿtirāḍ) between the element coordinated upon and the coordinated element, since in it is strengthening and reinforcement of the meaning of the speech. This is how they explained it. The pronoun in "annahu" may refer to "Allah," and it may be the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn). This is supported by the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: (shahida Allāhu anna lā ilāha illā huwa). In this reading it is necessarily the case that the omitted element, when you lighten it, is the pronoun of the matter, because when it is lightened it does not govern anything else except by necessity, and when it governs it, its omission is necessary.

They said: ﴿qāʾiman bi-al-qisṭ﴾ (standing in justice) is in the accusative as a circumstance from the name of God, or from "huwa," or from all of them, by consideration of each one individually, or as an accusative of praise, or it is an attribute of the negated element, as if it were said: "There is no god standing in justice except He." Or it is in the accusative as a detached (qaṭʿ) element, because its original form was "al-qāʾim." Likewise Ibn Masʿūd read it, so it is like His saying: ﴿and for Him is the religion, perpetual﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:52], that is, al-wāṣib. Abū Ḥanīfa read: qayyiman, and its accusative is on what has been mentioned.

Al-Sajāwandī mentioned that the reading of ʿAbd Allāh was qāʾimun (nominative). As for its accusative as a circumstance from the name of God, its governing element is "shahida," since it is what governs the circumstance, and in this aspect it is a necessary circumstance (ḥāl lāzima), because standing in justice is a fixed attribute of God, exalted is He. Al-Zamakhsharī said: its accusative is that it is a confirming circumstance (ḥāl muʾakkida) from Him, meaning from God, like His saying: ﴿and it is the truth, confirming﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:91]. End of quotation. But it is not of the confirming circumstance type, because it is not of the kind of: ﴿and the day he is raised alive﴾ [Maryam 19:15], nor of the kind of: "I am the servant of God, brave." So "qāʾiman bi-al-qisṭ" is not in the sense of "shahida," and it is not confirming the content of the preceding sentence, as in: "I am the servant of God, brave," and "He is Zayd, brave." But in this explanation there is awkwardness in the structure, since it becomes like your saying: "Zayd ate food, and ʿĀʾisha and Fāṭima, hungry." It then separates between the element coordinated upon and the coordinated element by the object, and between the circumstance and the one it describes by the object and the coordinated element, but with the proviso that all of them are governed by a single governor.

As for its accusative as a circumstance from the pronoun which is "huwa," al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya permitted it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you ask: "You have made it a circumstance from the subject of 'shahida'; can it be accusative as a circumstance from 'huwa' in ﴿there is no god but He﴾?" I say: Yes, because it is a confirming circumstance, and a confirming circumstance does not require that in the clause which it adds to the meaning there be a governor for it, as in His saying: "I am the servant of God, brave." End of quotation. He means that the confirming circumstance does not have as its governor, in its accusative, anything from the preceding sentence before it, but rather it is accusative by a hidden governor whose estimate is "aḥaqqu" (it is truly) or the like, hidden after the sentence. This is the opinion of the majority. The confirming circumstance of the content of the sentence is that which indicates a meaning necessarily attached to the predicated subject of the judgment, or resembling what is necessary. If the speaker of the sentence is informing about himself, the verb is estimated as "uḥaqqu," in the passive, like: "I am the servant of God, brave," that is, "I am truly brave." If he is informing about someone else, as in "He is Zayd, brave," its estimate is "uḥaqquhu, brave."

Al-Zajjāj held that the governor of this circumstance is the predicate, with what is implied of the meaning of naming (al-musammā). Ibn Kharūf held that it is the subject, with what is implied of the meaning of alerting (al-tanbīh). As for one who made it a circumstance from all of them, as has been mentioned, it was rejected on the ground that if that were permitted, it would be permitted to say: "The people came riding," meaning each one of them. And the Arabs do not say this.

As for its accusative as an accusative of praise, al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: Is it not the case that the accusative of praise must be definite, as in your saying: 'Praise be to God, the Praiseworthy,' and 'We, the company of the Prophets, do not leave inheritance' (hadith), and the verse: 'Indeed we, the sons of Nahshal, are not called after a father'?" I answer: It has come indefinite in the saying of the Hudhalī:

"And he resorts to women, bare of ornament, and disheveled, nursing like ghouls."

End of his question and answer. In this there is confusion, because he did not distinguish between the accusative of praise, or of blame, or of compassion, and the accusative of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), and he made their ruling one. He gave one example of the accusative of praise, which is: "Praise be to God, the Praiseworthy," and two examples of the accusative of specification, which are: "We, the company of the Prophets, do not leave inheritance," and "Indeed we, the sons of Nahshal, are not called after a father." What the grammarians mentioned is that the accusative of praise, blame, or compassion may be definite, and before it is a definite which may or may not serve as its qualifier, and it may be indefinite likewise, and it may be indefinite with a definite before it, so it cannot be an adjective of it, like the saying of al-Nābigha:

"I fight the clan of ʿAwf, and I seek no other than the faces of apes, whom you mock."

So "wujūha qurūd" is in the accusative of blame, and before it is a definite, which is his saying: "I fight the clan of ʿAwf." As for the accusative of specification, they explicitly stated that it is not indefinite nor ambiguous, and it is only definite by the article "al-" or by annexation, or by being a proper name, or by "ayyu," and it only comes after a first-person pronoun exclusive to the speaker or shared by him, and it sometimes comes after a second-person pronoun.

As for its accusative as an adjective of the negated element, al-Zamakhsharī said: "If you ask: Is it permissible that it be an adjective of the negated element, as if it were said: 'There is no god standing in justice except He'?" I answer: It is not far-fetched, for we have seen them being broad in separating between the adjective and the described. Then he said: And this is better than its being accusative from the subject of 'shahida,' and likewise its being accusative as an accusative of praise. End of quotation. He had given, in the separation between the adjective and the described, the example: "There is no man except ʿAbd Allāh, brave." He means that the accusative of "qāʾiman," as an adjective of "ilāha" or because it is in the accusative of praise, is better than its accusative as a circumstance from the subject of "shahida," which is God.

What he mentioned is not permissible, because he separated between the adjective and the described by a foreign element, namely the two coordinated items, which are "al-malāʾikah" and "ulū al-ʿilm," and they are not operands from the sentence "lā ilāha illā huwa" but rather they are operands of "shahida." This is like: "Zayd knew that Hind is going out, and ʿAmr and Jaʿfar, the Tamīmī woman." So he separates between Hind and "al-Tamīmiyya" by a foreign element that is not included in what governs them, and in their predicate, by a foreign element, which are ʿAmr and Jaʿfar, the two nominatives governed by "ʿarafa" (knew), coordinated upon Zayd. As for the example he gave, which is "There is no man except ʿAbd Allāh, brave," it is not an analogue of his explanation in the verse, because your saying "except ʿAbd Allāh" indicates the position of "lā rajul" (no man), so it is a follower in position, and so it is not foreign. Moreover, there is doubt about the permissibility of this construction, because it is a substitute (badal), and "shujāʿan" is a descriptive (waṣf), and the rule is that when the substitute and the descriptive are combined, the descriptive is placed before the substitute.
