The reason for that is that it is intended as a repetition of the governor according to the sound doctrine, so it becomes a separate sentence according to that doctrine.

As for its accusative as a detached element (qaṭʿ), it does not arise except according to the doctrine of the Kufans, and the Basrans have refuted it.

والأوْلى مِن هَذِهِ الأقْوالِ كُلِّها أنْ يَكُونَ مَنصُوبًا عَلى الحالِ (al-hal, the circumstantial accusative) مِنِ اسْمِ اللَّهِ، والعامِلُ فِيهِ: شَهِدَ، وهو قَوْلُ الجُمْهُورِ. وأمّا قِراءَةُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: القائِمُ بِالقِسْطِ، فَرَفْعُهُ عَلى أنَّهُ خَبَرُ مُبْتَدَأٍ مَحْذُوفٍ تَقْدِيرُهُ: هو القائِمُ بِالقِسْطِ. قالَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ وغَيْرُهُ: إنَّهُ بَدَلٌ (badal, substitute or apposition) مِن: هو، ولا يَجُوزُ ذَلِكَ، لِأنَّ فِيهِ فَصْلًا بَيْنَ البَدَلِ والمُبْدَلِ مِنهُ بِأجْنَبِيٍّ. وهو المَعْطُوفانِ، لِأنَّهُما مَعْمُولانِ لِغَيْرِ العامِلِ في المُبْدَلِ مِنهُ، ولَوْ كانَ العامِلُ في المَعْطُوفِ هو العامِلَ في المُبْدَلِ مِنهُ لَمْ يَجُزْ ذَلِكَ أيْضًا، لِأنَّهُ إذا (p-٤٠٦) اجْتَمَعَ العَطْفُ والبَدَلُ، قُدِّمَ البَدَلُ عَلى العَطْفِ، لَوْ قُلْتَ: جاءَ زَيْدٌ وعائِشَةُ أخُوكَ، لَمْ يَجُزْ. إنَّما الكَلامُ: جاءَ زَيْدٌ أخُوكَ وعائِشَةُ. وقالَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ: فَإنْ قُلْتَ: لِمَ جازَ إفْرادُهُ بِنَصْبِ الحالِ دُونَ المَعْطُوفَيْنِ عَلَيْهِ، ولَوْ قُلْتَ: جاءَنِي زَيْدٌ وعُمَرُ وراكِبًا لَمْ يَجُزْ؟ قُلْتُ: إنَّما جازَ هَذا لِعَدَمِ الإلْباسِ، كَما جازَ في قَوْلِهِ: ﴿ووَهَبْنا لَهُ إسْحاقَ ويَعْقُوبَ نافِلَةً﴾ [الأنبياء: ٧٢] إنِ انْتَصَبَ نافِلَةً حالًا، عَنْ يَعْقُوبَ، ولَوْ قُلْتَ: جاءَنِي زَيْدٌ وهِنْدٌ راكِبًا، جازَ لِتَمَيُّزِهِ بِالذُّكُورَةِ. انْتَهى كَلامُهُ.

وما ذَكَرَ مِن قَوْلِهِ في: جاءَنِي زَيْدٌ وعَمْرٌو راكِبًا، أنَّهُ لا يَجُوزُ، لَيْسَ كَما ذَكَرَ، بَلْ هَذا جائِزٌ، لِأنَّ الحالَ قُيِّدَ فِيمَن وقَعَ مِنهُ، أوْ بِهِ الفِعْلُ، أوْ ما أشْبَهَ ذَلِكَ، وإذا كانَ قَيْدًا فَإنَّهُ يُحْمَلُ عَلى أقْرَبِ مَذْكُورٍ، ويَكُونُ راكِبًا حالًا مِمّا يَلِيهِ، ولا فَرْقَ في ذَلِكَ بَيْنَ الحالِ والصِّفَةِ، لَوْ قُلْتَ: جاءَنِي زَيْدٌ وعَمْرٌو الطَّوِيلُ. لَكانَ: ”الطَّوِيلُ“ صِفَةً لِعَمْرٍو، ولا تَقُولُ: لا تَجُوزُ هَذِهِ المَسْألَةُ، لِأنَّهُ يَلْبَسُ، بَلْ لا لَبْسَ في هَذا، وهو جائِزٌ، فَكَذَلِكَ الحالُ.

وأمّا قَوْلُهُ في: نافِلَةً، إنَّهُ انْتَصَبَ حالًا عَنْ: يَعْقُوبَ، فَلا يَتَعَيَّنُ أنْ يَكُونَ حالًا عَنْ: يَعْقُوبَ، إذْ يُحْتَمَلُ أنْ يَكُونَ: نافِلَةً مَصْدَرًا كالعافِيَةِ والعاقِبَةِ. ومَعْناهُ: زِيادَةً، فَيَكُونُ ذَلِكَ شامِلًا لِإسْحاقَ ويَعْقُوبَ، لِأنَّهُما زِيدا لِإبْراهِيمَ بَعْدَ ابْنِهِ إسْماعِيلَ وغَيْرِهِ، إذْ كانَ إنَّما جاءَ لَهُ إسْحاقُ عَلى الكِبَرِ، وبَعْدَ أنْ عَجَزَتْ سارَّةُ وأيِسَتْ مِنَ الوِلادَةِ. وأوْلادُ إبْراهِيمَ غَيْرَ إسْماعِيلَ وإسْحاقَ: مَدْيانُ، ويُقالُ: مَدْيَنُ، ويُشْناقُ، وشُواحُ، وهو خاضِعُ، ورَمْرانُ، وهو مَحْدانُ، ومَدْنُ، ويَقْشانُ، وهو مُصْعَبُ، فَهَؤُلاءِ ولَدُ إبْراهِيمَ لِصُلْبِهِ. والعَقِبُ الباقِي مِنهم لِإسْماعِيلَ وإسْحاقَ لا غَيْرُ.

قالَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ: فَإنْ قُلْتَ: ما المُرادُ بِأُولِي العِلْمِ، الَّذِينَ عَظَّمَهم هَذا التَّعْظِيمَ، حَيْثُ جَمَعَهم مَعَهُ، ومَعَ المَلائِكَةِ في الشَّهادَةِ عَلى وحْدانِيَّتِهِ وعَدْلِهِ؟ قُلْتُ: هُمُ الَّذِينَ يُثْبِتُونَ وحْدانِيَّتَهُ وعَدْلَهُ بِالحُجَجِ القاطِعَةِ، والبَراهِينِ السّاطِعَةِ، وهم عُلَماءُ العَدْلِ والتَّوْحِيدِ. انْتَهى.

ويَعْنِي بِعُلَماءِ العَدْلِ والتَّوْحِيدِ المُعْتَزِلَةَ (al-Mu'tazila, the rationalist theological school)، وهم يُسَمُّونَ أنْفُسَهم بِهَذا الِاسْمِ، كَما أنْشَدَنا شَيْخُنا الإمامُ الحافِظُ أبُو مُحَمَّدٍ عَبْدُ المُؤْمِنِ بْنُ خَلَفٍ الدِّمْياطِيُّ، رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ، بِقِراءَتِي عَلَيْهِ. قالَ: أنْشَدَنا الصّاحِبُ أبُو حامِدٍ عَبْدُ الحُمَيْدِ بْنُ هِبَةَ بْنِ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ أبِي الحَدِيدِ المُعْتَزِلِيُّ بِبَغْدادَ لِنَفْسِهِ:

؎لَوْلا ثَلاثٌ لَمْ أُخْفِ صُرْعَتِي ∗∗∗ لَيْسَتْ كَما قالَ فَتى العَبْدِ
Had it not been for three things, I would not have hidden my downfall, which is not as the youth of al-Abd said.

؎أنْ أنْصُرَ التَّوْحِيدَ والعَدْلَ في ∗∗∗ كُلِّ مَقامٍ باذِلًا جُهْدِي
That I defend monotheism and justice in every situation, spending my utmost effort.

؎وأنْ أُناجِيَ اللَّهَ مُسْتَمْتِعًا ∗∗∗ بِخَلْوَةٍ أحْلى مِنَ الشَّهْدِ
And that I commune with God, enjoying a solitude sweeter than honey.

؎وإنَّ أتْيَهُ الدَّهْرَ كِبْرًا عَلى ∗∗∗ كُلِّ لَئِيمٍ أصْعَرِ الخَدِّ
And that I strut through time in pride over every base man with a averted cheek.

؎لِذاكَ أهْوى لا فَتاةَ ولا ∗∗∗ خَمْرَ ولا ذِي مَيْعَةٍ نَهْدِ
For this I long: neither a maiden, nor wine, nor one of youthful vigor and full breasts.

﴿لا إلَهَ إلّا هو العَزِيزُ الحَكِيمُ﴾ كُرِّرَ التَّهْلِيلُ تَوْكِيدًا. وقِيلَ: الأوَّلُ شَهادَةُ اللَّهِ، والثّانِي شَهادَةُ المَلائِكَةِ وأُولِي العِلْمِ. وهَذا بَعِيدٌ جِدًّا، لِأنَّهُ يُؤَدِّي إلى قَطْعِ المَلائِكَةِ عَنِ العَطْفِ عَلى اللَّهِ تَعالى، وعَلى إضْمارِ فِعْلٍ رافِعٍ، أوْ عَلى جَعْلِهِمْ مُبْتَدَأً، وعَلى الفَصْلِ بَيْنَ ما يَتَعَلَّقُ بِهِمْ وبَيْنَ التَّهْلِيلِ بِأجْنَبِيٍّ، وهو قَوْلُهُ: ﴿قائِمًا بِالقِسْطِ﴾. وقِيلَ: الأوَّلُ جارٍ مَجْرى الشَّهادَةِ، والثّانِي جارٍ مَجْرى الحُكْمِ. وقِيلَ: هَذا الكَلامُ يَنْطَوِي عَلى مُقَدِّمَتَيْنِ، وهَذا هو نَتِيجَتُهُما، فَكَأنَّهُ قالَ: شَهِدَ اللَّهُ والمَلائِكَةُ، وأُولُو العِلْمِ، وما شَهِدُوا بِهِ حَقٌّ، فَلا إلَهَ إلّا هو حَقٌّ، فَحَذَفَ إحْدى المُقَدِّمَتَيْنِ لِلدَّلالَةِ عَلَيْها. وهَذا التَّقْدِيرُ كُلُّهُ لا يُساعِدُ عَلَيْهِ اللَّفْظُ. وقالَ الرّاغِبُ: إنَّما كَرَّرَ ﴿لا إلَهَ إلّا هُوَ﴾، لِأنَّ صِفاتِ التَّنْزِيهِ أشْرَفُ مِن صِفاتِ التَّمْجِيدِ، لِأنَّ أكْثَرَها مُشارِكٌ في ألْفاظِها العَبِيدُ، فَيَصِحُّ وصْفُهم بِها، وكَذَلِكَ وردَتْ ألْفاظُ التَّنْزِيهِ في حَقِّهِ أكْثَرَ، وأبْلَغُ ما وُصِفَ بِهِ مِنَ التَّنْزِيهِ: لا إلَهَ إلّا اللَّهُ. فَتَكْرِيرُهُ هُنا لِأمْرَيْنِ: أحَدُهُما: لِكَوْنِ الثّانِي قَطْعًا لِلْحُكْمِ، كَقَوْلِكَ: (p-٤٠٧) أشْهَدُ أنَّ زَيْدًا خارِجٌ، وهو خارِجٌ. والثّانِي: لِئَلّا يَسْبِقَ بِذِكْرِ العَزِيزِ الحَكِيمِ إلى قَلْبِ السّامِعِ تَشْبِيهٌ، إذْ قَدْ يُوصَفُ بِهِما المَخْلُوقُ. انْتَهى. وقالَ الزَّمَخْشَرِيُّ: صِفَتانِ مُقَرِّرَتانِ لِما وصَفَ بِهِ ذاتَهُ مِنَ الوَحْدانِيَّةِ والعَدْلِ، يَعْنِي: أنَّهُ العَزِيزُ الَّذِي لا يُغالِبُهُ إلَهٌ آخَرُ، الحَكِيمُ الَّذِي لا يَعْدِلُ عَنِ العَدْلِ في أفْعالِهِ. انْتَهى.

وهُوَ تَحْوِيمٌ عَلى مَذْهَبِ المُعْتَزِلَةِ. وارْتَفَعَ: العَزِيزُ، عَلى أنَّهُ خَبَرُ مُبْتَدَأٍ مَحْذُوفٍ، أيْ: هو العَزِيزُ، عَلى الِاسْتِئْنافِ. قِيلَ: ولَيْسَ بِوَصْفٍ، لِأنَّ الضَّمِيرَ لا يُوصَفُ، ولَيْسَ هَذا بِالجَمْعِ عَلَيْهِ، بَلْ ذَهَبَ الكِسائِيُّ (al-Kisa'i) إلى أنَّ ضَمِيرَ الغائِبِ كَهَذا يُوصَفُ.

وجَوَّزُوا في إعْرابِ: العَزِيزُ، أنْ يَكُونَ بَدَلًا مِن: هو. ورُوِيَ في حَدِيثٍ عَنِ الأعْمَشِ (al-A'mash)، أنَّهُ قامَ يَتَهَجَّدُ، فَقَرَأ هَذِهِ الآيَةَ، ثُمَّ قالَ: وأنا أشْهَدُ بِما شَهِدَ اللَّهُ بِهِ، وأسْتَوْدِعُ اللَّهَ هَذِهِ الشَّهادَةَ، وهي لِي عِنْدَ اللَّهِ ودِيعَةٌ: إنَّ الدِّينَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ الإسْلامُ. قالَها مِرارًا، فَسُئِلَ، فَقالَ: حَدَّثَنِي أبُو وائِلٍ، عَنْ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ، قالَ: قالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ (ﷺ): «يُجاءُ بِصاحِبِها يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ، فَيَقُولُ اللَّهُ: عَبْدِي عَهِدَ إلَيَّ، وأنا أحَقُّ مَن وفى، أدْخِلُوا عَبْدِي الجَنَّةَ».

وقالَ أبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ عُمَرَ الرّازِيُّ: العَزِيزُ إشارَةٌ إلى كَمالِ القُدْرَةِ، والحَكِيمُ إشارَةٌ إلى كَمالِ العِلْمِ، وهُما الصِّفَتانِ اللَّتانِ يَمْتَنِعُ حُصُولُ الإلَهِيَّةِ إلّا مَعَهُما، لِأنَّ كَوْنَهُ ﴿قائِمًا بِالقِسْطِ﴾ لا يَتِمُّ إلّا إذا كانَ عالِمًا بِمَقادِيرِ الحاجاتِ، فَكانَ قادِرًا عَلى تَحْصِيلِ المُهِمّاتِ. وقُدِّمَ العَزِيزُ في الذِّكْرِ، لِأنَّ العِلْمَ بِكَوْنِهِ تَعالى قادِرًا مُتَقَدِّمٌ عَلى العِلْمِ بِكَوْنِهِ عالِمًا في طَرِيقِ المَعْرِفَةِ الِاسْتِدْلالِيَّةِ، وهَذا الخِطابُ مَعَ المُسْتَدِلِّ. انْتَهى كَلامُهُ.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 19:

﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam.﴾ That is: the creed and the law (al-milla wa'l-shar'). The meaning is: the religion that is accepted, or beneficial, or established. The majority (al-Jumhur) read *inna*, with a kasra on the hamza. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kisa'i, and Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-Asbahani read *anna*, with a fatha. The reading of Ibn 'Abbas, *shahida Allahu annahu* (Allah bears witness that He...), with a kasra on the hamza, has already been mentioned. As for the reading of the majority, it is an independent resumption (isti'naf, a new sentence), and it serves to emphasise the preceding sentence.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the benefit of this emphasis? I say: its benefit is that His saying *there is no god but Him* is a declaration of divine unity (tawhid), and His saying *standing in justice* is a declaration of justice (ta'dil). When it is followed by His saying *indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam*, it indicates that Islam is justice and monotheism, and that it is the religion with Allah, and that whatever is other than it is not, in His sight, any part of religion. And in it is (the implication) that whoever adheres to anthropomorphism (tashbih), or to what leads to it, such as permitting the vision of God (ijazat al-ru'ya), or adheres to determinism (al-jabr), which is pure injustice, is not upon the religion of Allah, which is Islam. This is clear and evident, as you see. End of his words.

This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah in denying the vision of God, and in their saying that the acts of the servant are created for him and not by Allah, the Exalted.

As for the reading of al-Kisa'i and those who agreed with him, with the *anna* in the accusative (*annahu* and *anna*), Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: If you wish, you may make it an apposition of a thing to a thing that is itself (badal al-shay' min al-shay' wa-huwa huwa), do you not see that the religion which is Islam includes monotheism and justice, and is identical with them in meaning? And if you wish, you may make it an apposition of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), because Islam comprises monotheism and justice.

He also said: And if you wish, you may make it an apposition of *al-qist* (justice), because the religion which is Islam is justice and equity, so it is likewise an apposition of a thing to a thing, and the two are of one referent. End of Abu 'Ali's explanations. He was a Mu'tazilite, and therefore his words include the terminology of the Mu'tazilah, such as monotheism and justice. He also made it an apposition to *annahu la ilaha illa huwa*. Others have also explained it this way, but it is not sound, because it leads to a remote construction, namely that something like it would come in Arabic speech, such as: *'arafa Zayd annahu la shuja'a illa huwa* (Zayd knew that there is no brave one except him), and: *Banu Tamim wa-Banu Darim mulaqiyan li'l-huruba la shuja'a illa huwa al-batalu al-muhami, inna al-khisla al-hamidah hiya al-basalah* (The Banu Tamim and the Banu Darim, encountering wars, there is no brave one but he, the champion who defends; indeed, the praiseworthy quality is valour).

The approximation of this example is: *daraba Zayd 'A'isha, wa'l-'Umaran hanaqa ukhtaka* (Zayd struck 'A'isha, and the two 'Umars choked your sister). So *hanaqa* is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to Zayd, and *ukhtaka* is an apposition (badal) to 'A'isha. Thus the apposition and the thing it substitutes are separated by a conjunction, which is not permitted; and it is separated by a circumstantial clause that does not belong to the thing substituted, which is also not permitted, because it is a separation by an alien element between the substituted noun and its apposition.

Al-Tabari explained it as the omission of the conjunctive particle, the implied sense being: *wa-anna al-din...* (and that the religion...). Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is weak, and he did not explain the reason for its weakness. The reason for its weakness is that the construction is discordant with the elision of the conjunctive particle, so that it separates the two coordinated nominatives (marfu'ayn) by an accusative object (maf'ul), and separates the two coordinated accusatives by a nominative that shares the agency of the agent (fa'iliyya), and by two parenthetical clauses (jumlatay al-i'tiraD). The construction then stands without observing the separation, like: *akala Zayd khubzan wa-'Amrun wa-samakan* (Zayd ate bread, and 'Amr and fish). The original construction is: *akala Zayd wa-'Amrun khubzan wa-samakan* (Zayd and 'Amr ate bread and fish). If we separate between your saying *wa-'Amrun* and your saying *wa-samakan*, a hideous construction results, and the elision of the conjunctive particle is not permitted according to the most correct view.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Both (*anna*) were read with a fatha, on the basis that the second is an apposition to the first, as if it were said: *shahida Allahu anna al-din 'inda Allahi al-Islam* (Allah bears witness that the religion with Allah is Islam). The apposition is, in meaning, the thing it substitutes, so it is a clear explanation, because the religion of Islam is monotheism and justice. End of his words.

This is a transmission of the words of Abu 'Ali without complete elaboration.

As for the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, it is explained as follows: *inna al-din 'inda Allahi al-Islam* is the object (ma'mul) of *shahida*, and there would be two parenthetical clauses in the speech: one between the coordinated element and the element it is coordinated with, namely *annahu la ilaha illa huwa* (that there is no god but He), and the second between the coordinated element and the circumstantial clause, and between the object of *shahida*, namely *la ilaha illa huwa al-'Aziz al-Hakim* (there is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise). And if we parse *al-'Aziz* as the predicate of an elided subject, then there are three parenthetical clauses. So consider these remote interpretations, which no one can match with a parallel from Arabic speech. This was imposed only by non-Arab (ajamiyya) origin, and by not thoroughly studying the constructions of Arabic speech and memorising its poetry.

As we indicated in the introduction of this book, grammar alone is not sufficient for knowing the eloquent speech of the Arabs; rather, one must be acquainted with Arabic speech, take on its natural disposition (tatabbu' bi-tibaiha), and increase one's exposure to it. The reading *anna al-din* with a fatha is explained by taking the sentence in the place of the object of *al-Hakim*, with the omission of the preposition, meaning *bi-anna* (that...), because *al-Hakim* is an intensive form (fa'il li'l-mubalaga) like *al-'Alim*, *al-Sami'*, and *al-Khabir*, as He said, the Exalted: ﴿from One Wise, All-Aware﴾ [Hud: 1], and He said: ﴿from One Wise, All-Knowing﴾ [al-Naml: 6]. The implied sense is: *la ilaha illa huwa al-'Aziz al-Hakimu anna al-din 'inda Allahi al-Islam* (there is no god but He, the Mighty, the one who judges that the religion with Allah is Islam).

When Allah, the Exalted, bore witness for Himself to His oneness, and the angels and those possessed of knowledge bore witness to it likewise, He decreed that the religion accepted with Allah is Islam, so no one should turn away from it. ﴿And whoever seeks a religion other than Islam, it will not be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85]. He turned from the form *al-Hakim* (judge) to *al-Hakim* (the Wise) for the sake of intensification and to match *al-'Aziz*. The meaning of intensification is the repetition of His judgment in regard to the laws: that the religion with Him is Islam, since He judged this in every law.

If you say: why did you take *al-Hakim* to be transferred from the active participle (fa'il) to the intensive form (fa'il for emphasis), and why not make it the form *fa'il* in the sense of *mufil* (causative), so that its meaning would be "the one who makes firm" (al-muhkim), as they said about *alim* (painful), that it means *mu'lim* (causing pain), and about *sami'* in the verse of the poet:

*Amin rayhanati al-da'i al-sami'*
*(Of the perfume of the caller who is the hearer?)*

That is, *al-musmi'* (the one who makes hear)?

The answer: We do not concede that *fa'il* comes in the sense of *mufil*. It may be interpreted that *alim* and *sami'* are not of the form *mufil*. Even if we concede that, it is among the rare, irregular and scarce usages that are not used as a general rule. As for *fa'il* transferred from *fa'il* for intensification, it is very common, beyond counting: like *'alim*, *sami'*, *qadir*, *khabir*, *hafiz*, in words that cannot be enumerated. Moreover, the pure Arab who retains his natural disposition did not understand from *hakim* except that it is transferred for intensification from *hakim* (judge). Do you not see that when he heard a reciter reciting: ﴿As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands as a recompense for what they earned, as an exemplary punishment from Allah﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 38], and *Allahu Ghafur Rahim* (Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful), he denied that the closing phrase of this preceding construction should be *wa-Allahu Ghafur Rahim*; then it was said to him by way of recitation: ﴿And Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 38]. He said: "Thus it should be: *'azza fa-hakama*" (He is mighty, so He judged). So he understood from *hakim* that it is transferred for intensification from *hakim* (judge). This Arab took this understanding as a decisive proof for what we have said. This explanation is easy and very acceptable, and it removes those artificialities and knotted constructions from which the Book of Allah should be cleared.

As for the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, we say likewise: we do not make *anna al-din* the object of *shahida*, as they understood; nor do we treat *annahu la ilaha illa huwa* as a parenthetical clause, with it lying between the coordinated element and the circumstantial clause, and between *anna al-din* another parenthetical clause, or two parenthetical clauses. Rather, we say: it is the object of *shahida*, and *innahu* with a kasra follows the line of one who explains that *shahida*, since it has the meaning of *qala* (to say), has what follows it kasra'd, treating it as a verb of saying. Or we say: it is its object, and it is suspended (mu'allaqa, i.e., the verb's effect is blocked): the lam was not admitted into the predicate because it is negated, unlike the case if it were affirmative, for you say: *shahidtu inna Zayda la-muntaliqun* (I bore witness that Zayd is indeed departing), where *inna* is suspended in the presence of the lam, because if there were no lam, *inna* would have been read with a fatha, and you would say: *shahidtu anna Zaydan muntaliqun*. So whoever reads *annahu* with a fatha did not intend suspension, and whoever reads with a kasra intended suspension. The lam was not admitted into the predicate because it is negated, as we have mentioned.

Islam here means faith (iman) and acts of obedience (ta'at). This was said by Abu al-'Aliyya, and it is the view of the majority of the theologians (mutakallimun). Qatada and Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr expressed it as faith (iman), and their meaning is that it is together with the deeds.

'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read: *inna al-din 'inda Allahi al-hanifiyya* (the religion with Allah is the hanifiyya, the pure monotheistic faith). Ibn al-Anbari said: It is not hidden from one who discerns that this is a statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) by way of explanation (tafsir), which some of those who transmit hadith have inserted into the readings. The discussion of Islam and faith has already preceded: are they one thing, or are they different? The distinction is clear in the hadith of Gabriel's question.

﴿And those who were given the Book did not differ﴾ That is: the Jews and the Christians, or they and the Magians. There are three views. According to the view that they are the Jews, which is the saying of al-Rabi' ibn Anas, it refers to those who differed concerning the Torah. He said: When death approached Musa (peace be upon him), he entrusted the Torah to seventy rabbis of the Children of Israel, giving each rabbi a portion, and he appointed Yusha' as successor. When three centuries had passed, division occurred among them. It is also said: it refers to those who differed concerning the prophethood of our Prophet (ﷺ): some of them said he was sent only to the Arabs, and some said he is not the prophet who was sent, because that was fulfilled among the Children of Isaac (Banu Ishaq). According to the view that they are the Christians, which is the saying of Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, what they differed about is: their religion, or the matter of 'Isa, or the religion of Islam. Three views.

Al-Zamakhshari said: They are the People of the Book from among the Jews and the Christians, and they differed, in that they abandoned Islam, which is monotheism and justice, after knowledge had come to them that it is the truth from which there is no turning away. So the Christians became trinitarian, ﴿and the Jews said: Ezra is the son of Allah﴾ [al-Tawba: 30], and they said: "We had more right that prophethood be among us than among the Quraysh, because they are unlettered, and we are People of the Book." This is an attribution of injustice to Allah, the Exalted. End of his words. Then he said: It is also said: their difference concerned the prophethood of Muhammad (peace be upon him), in that some believed in him and some disbelieved. It is also said: their difference concerned belief in the prophets, so some of them believed in Musa, and some believed in 'Isa. End of his words.

What appears is that the wording is general in ﴿those who were given the Book﴾, and that what they differed about is Islam, because He, the Exalted, established that the religion is Islam, then said: ﴿and those who were given the Book did not differ﴾, that is: concerning Islam, to the point that they turned away from it to other religions.

﴿except after knowledge had come to them﴾ which is the cause for following Islam, and for agreement upon believing in it and acting by it. But they were blind to the path of knowledge and its conduct, through the rebellion (baghy) that occurred among them, from envy and the monopolising of leadership, and each of them going off to a path that opposes Islam, until he became a leader to be followed in it. So they were among those who went astray with knowledge. Something similar to this has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿And none differed concerning it except those who were given it, after the clear proofs had come to them﴾ [al-Baqara: 213].

﴿out of rebellion among themselves﴾ As for the parsing of *baghyan*: after *illa* there came two things whose apparent status is that both are exceptions. The explanation of this has been given, so it suffices here without repetition.

﴿And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah, then indeed Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ This is general for every disbeliever in the signs of Allah, so it is not restricted to the disputing People of the Book, even though the conditional sentence came after mention of them. Here, *ayatihi* (His signs) is said to mean His proofs (hujaj). It is also said: the Torah and the Gospel and what is in them of the description of our Prophet (ﷺ). It is also said: the Qur'an. Al-Maturidi said: that is, from among the disputing parties. The explanation of *sari' al-hisab* (swift in reckoning) has already preceded, so it suffices without repetition. This sentence is the response to the conditional, and the returning pronoun to the conditional particle is elided, its implied sense being: *sari' al-hisab lahu* (swift in reckoning to him).

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 3, verse 20:

﴿If they argue with you, say: I have submitted my face to God.﴾ The pronoun in "they argue with you" (حاجُّوكَ, ḥājjūka) apparently refers to ﴿those who were given the Book﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 19]. Abu Muslim said it refers to all people, based on His saying after it: ﴿Say to those who were given the Book and to the unlettered [ummiyyīn]...﴾. It was also said that it refers to the Christians of Najran, who came to Medina to argue (li-l-muḥājjah). The apparent meaning of the argument (al-miḥājj) here is the religion of Islam, because it is the prior one. The answer to the conditional is: ﴿say: I have submitted my face to God﴾. The meaning is: I submitted, obeyed and humbled myself to God alone. He expressed the whole of the self by "the face," because the face is the most noble of the limbs, and when the face humbles itself, what is other than it is more humble.

Al-Marwazi, and al-Farrāʾ before him, said that the meaning of "I have submitted my face" is "my religion," because faith is to the deeds what the face is to the body, since it is the foundation.

Various statements were made in the tafsir: "I say to you," as Ibn Nuʿaym said: "You have agreed that he is right." ﴿He said: O my people, I am free of what you associate [with God]﴾ [al-Anʿām: 78]; ﴿I have turned my face toward Him who originated the heavens and the earth, as a ḥanīf, and I am not of those who associate partners [with God]﴾ [al-Anʿām: 79].

Al-Zamakhsharī said: "I have submitted my face," meaning: I have purified myself and my action for God alone. I did not make for Him a partner, by worshipping Him and calling upon another god along with Him. He means that my religion is monotheism (al-tawḥīd), which is the ancient religion whose soundness is established among you as it is established with me. I have not brought anything novel that you should dispute with me about it. Similar is ﴿Say: O People of the Book, come to a word...﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 64], and so it is a rebuttal of argument. End of his words.

In his tafsir, he applied "the face" to the self and the deed together, unless he intended an explanation of the meaning rather than an explanation of the word, in which case that is permissible for him.

Al-Rāzī said: There are two ways of understanding the manner in which this statement is delivered. The first: it is a turning away from argument, since He had already shown them the proof of its truth before the revelation of this verse, for this surah is Medinan, through the manifestation of miracles in the Qur'an and other than it. He had mentioned before this verse the proof in His saying ﴿the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 2], against the corruption of the Christians' view of the divinity of ʿĪsā; and in His saying ﴿He has sent down to you the Book﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 3], for the soundness of his prophethood. He mentioned the doubts of the people and answered them, and He mentioned other miracles, namely what they had witnessed on the day of Badr. He linked the affirmation of monotheism with His saying: ﴿God bears witness﴾. The second way: it is a manifestation of the proof, because they were affirming the Creator and His entitlement to worship. So it is as if He said: "I hold fast to this much on which there is agreement, and the disagreement lies beyond it, and the burden of proof is on the one who claims." Also, they used to revere Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, and that he was right, and he (the Prophet) was commanded to follow his creed; here he was commanded to say what he said, so this is by way of argument ad hominem, meaning: I hold to the path of one who is right in your view. Abu Muslim said this. Also, since it was previously stated that the religion is Islam, it was said to him: If they dispute with you, then say: the proof of it is that I have submitted my face to God. This is the complete fulfilment of the obligation of lordship and servanthood, so it is established that the perfect religion is Islam. Also, the verse is consistent with the saying of Ibrāhīm: ﴿Why do you worship what neither hears nor sees?﴾ [Maryam: 42], meaning worship is not permissible except for one who is beneficial and harmful and capable of all things, and ʿĪsā is not like that. Also, this is an allusion to the way of Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him: ﴿When his Lord said to him: Submit, he said: I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131]. This was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās. End of what has been summarised from al-Rāzī's words. The final parts of his words are not clearly within the intended meaning and implication of the verse.

The ya' in "wajhiya" (my face) is pronounced with a fatḥa here and in al-Anʿām by Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥafs; the rest read it with sukūn.

﴿And whoever follows me﴾. It was said: "man" (whoever) is in the nominative position; it was said: it is in the accusative position, as a maf'ūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment, "together with"); and it was said: it is in the genitive position, coordinated with the name of God. Its meaning: I have directed my intention in faith in Him and obedience to Him, and likewise for whoever follows me, by preserving it and by taking care to learn it and to keep it sound.

As for the nominative, it is coordinated with the subject in "I have submitted," as al-Zamakhsharī said, and he began with it, saying: it is good because of the separation (lil-fāṣil), meaning that it is coordinated with the attached pronoun, and according to the Basran grammarians coordination with an attached nominative pronoun is not permitted except in poetry. However, he separated between the pronoun and the coordinated noun, so it is acceptable. Ibn ʿAṭiyya also said this and began with it. It cannot be taken in its apparent sense, because if it is coordinated with the pronoun, as in: "I ate a loaf and Zayd," it would follow that they are partners in eating the loaf. Here that is not admissible, because the meaning is not that they and he, peace be upon him, submitted their faces to God; rather the meaning is that he, peace be upon him, submitted his face to God, and they submitted their faces to God. So what is strongest in the i'rāb (grammatical analysis) is that it is coordinated with a pronoun from which the object has been omitted, not a partner in the object of "I have submitted." The estimate: "and whoever follows me, [submits] his face." Or it is a subject whose predicate is omitted because the meaning indicates it, and "whoever follows me" is likewise: they submitted their faces to God, as you say: "Zayd fulfilled his vow and ʿAmr," meaning: and ʿAmr likewise, that is, fulfilled his vow.

Also, from the aspect that prevents the coordination of "wa-man" with the pronoun: if the statement is taken in its apparent sense without interpretation, it is impossible for "man" to be in the accusative as a maf'ūl maʿahu, because when you say: "I ate a loaf and ʿAmr," meaning "together with ʿAmr," that indicates he shares with you in eating the loaf. Al-Zamakhsharī permitted this possibility, but it is not permissible for the reasons we have mentioned in any case, because it is not possible to interpret it as the omission of the object together with the waw being the waw of accompaniment.

Abu ʿAmr and Nāfiʿ pronounced the ya' of "ittaba'anī" (follows me) in连 continuous speech, and the rest omitted it. Omitting it is better, because it accords with the orthography of the codex (muṣḥaf), and because it is the end of a verse (ra's āyah), like His saying ﴿akramani﴾ and ﴿ahānani﴾ [al-Fajr: 15–16], so it resembles the rhyming endings of poetry, as in the words of the poet:

"And will the wandering through lands prevent me from the fear of death, that it should come upon me?"

﴿And say to those who were given the Book﴾: they are the Jews and the Christians, by agreement. ﴿And the unlettered﴾: they are the polytheists of the Arabs, and everyone who has no book is included in that.

﴿Have you submitted?﴾ This is a question containing an implied command. Al-Zajjāj said it is a threat. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: this is better, because the meaning is: Have you submitted to Him or not? Al-Zamakhsharī said: meaning that there has come to you of clear proofs what necessitates submission and requires its occurrence without doubt; so have you submitted, or are you upon your disbelief? This is like your saying to someone to whom you have summarised a matter, leaving no path of explanation and clarification unfollowed: "Have you understood it, may you have no mother?" From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 91], after He mentioned the deterrents from wine and gambling. In this interrogation there is reproach, stubbornness, and a lack of fairness, because the fair person, when the proof becomes clear to him and his acceptance of the truth does not hesitate, and for the obstinate person after the proof becomes clear, there is something that places barriers between him and acceptance. Likewise, in "Have you understood it?" there is rebuke for dullness and sluggishness of mind, and in ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 91] there is rebuke for holding back from desisting and for intense eagerness to engage in what is forbidden. End of his words. It is good, and most of it is in the manner of rhetoric (khiṭābah).

﴿If they submit, then they are guided﴾: that is, if they enter Islam, then guidance has been attained for them. He expressed it with the past form accompanied by "qad," which indicates certainty, as an intensification in reporting the occurrence of guidance, and [a movement] from darkness to light. End.

﴿But if they turn away, then upon you is only the conveyance [of the message]﴾: that is, they cannot harm you by their turning away, and what is incumbent upon you is only to warn them by conveying to them the request that they submit and that they join in the worship of God alone. It was said: this is a verse of conciliation (āyat muwādaʿah) abrogated (mansūkhah) by the verse of the sword (āyat al-sayf), and it requires knowledge of the date of revelation. If you look at the occasion of revelation of these verses, which is the arrival of the delegation of Najran, then the meaning is: upon you is only the conveyance [of the message], by fighting or otherwise.

﴿And God is seeing of the servants﴾. In it there is a warning and a severe threat for whoever turns away from Islam, and a promise of good for whoever submits; its meaning is: God is aware of the conditions of His servants and will recompense them according to what His wisdom requires.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 21:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets﴾ etc.: It refers to the Jews and the Christians. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr and others. It describes those who turned away from Islam and disbelieved with three attributes. The first: their disbelief in the signs of Allah, even though they acknowledge the Creator. He made their disbelief in some of them like their disbelief in all of them. Or the "signs of Allah" is restricted to what understanding readily grasps from the Qur'an and the Messenger ﷺ. The second: their killing of the prophets. The manner of their killing has already been discussed in al-Baqarah, in His words ﴿and kill the prophets without right﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61]. The alif and lam in "al-nabiyyin" (the prophets) denote a known reference. The third: killing those who enjoin justice. These are three attributes, begun with the greatest and then the greatest, and with that which is the cause of the next. The first of them is disbelief in the signs of Allah, which is the strongest cause of indifference to the evil deeds that occur. The second of them: killing those who manifest the signs of Allah and argue by them.

The third: killing their followers from among those who enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil. This verse came as a threat to those who were in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, and for this reason the relative clause is in the future tense, and the fa' entered the predicate of "inna" because the relative pronoun was given the meaning of a conditional particle. Since they were following the practice of their forefathers in this, it was attributed to them. And because they intended to kill him ﷺ, the killing of his followers was attributed to them, so this was used for them figuratively, meaning: it is part of their character and their intention. It is possible that the fa' is superfluous according to the view of one who holds that, and that this sentence is a narration about the condition of their fathers and what they did in bygone times of these ugly attributes, and in that there is a debasement of whoever stands up in enmity to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, since they are following the way of their fathers. The meaning: Indeed your fathers, whose religion you hold fast to, were in the state you know of, characterized by these attributes, so it is proper for you to take a path other than theirs, for they were not upon the truth. He mentioned the ugliness of the attributes and the threat of punishment for them, which repels from them and urges adornment with their opposites: faith in the signs of Allah, and honouring His messengers and their followers.

Al-Hasan recited: "wa-yuqattiluna al-nabiyyin" with the shaddah, and the shaddah here is for intensification according to the context. Hamzah and a group outside the seven read: "wa-yuqatiluna" (the second). Al-A'mash read: "wa-qatalu alladhina", and likewise it is in the codex of Abdullah. Ubayy read: "yaqtuluna al-nabiyyina wa-alladhina ya'muruna". As for one who varies between the two verbs, its meaning is clear when he does not mention either of them by way of emphasis. As for one who omits, he suffices with mentioning one verb because they share in killing. As for one who repeats the verb, that is by way of conjoining sentences and presenting each sentence in the form of censure and reproach, because each sentence is independent in itself. Or, due to the difference in the rank of the punishment in relation to the one upon whom the act falls, the killing of the prophets is greater than the killing of those who enjoin good other than the prophets; so the killing was made, because of the difference in its rank, as if they were two different acts. It has been said: it is possible that one of the two killings is intended as the taking of life, and the other as humiliation and extinguishing of remembrance, so they would then be two different things. In this surah has come ﴿without right﴾ in indefinite form, and in al-Baqarah ﴿without the right﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61] in definite form, because the sentence here is presented in the manner of a conditional, which is general and not restricted, so it was fitting that the negated term be in indefinite form so that it is general. In al-Baqarah it came in the form of a report about known people, which is His words ﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without the right﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61], so it was fitting that it come in definite form, because the right by which the killing of souls was considered permissible among them was known, as in His words ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the soul is for the soul﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]. So the right here by which souls are killed is known and recognised, unlike what is in this surah. It has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah that His words ﴿without the right﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61] is a confirmatory circumstantial clause, since the killing of a prophet never occurs except without right, and we clarified that for you. So it suffices to not repeat and clarify it here. The meaning of "min al-nas" (from among the people): i.e., other than the prophets, since if He had said "those who enjoin justice," the prophets would have been included in that, because the wording applies to them. So "min al-nas" came with the meaning: other than the prophets. Al-Hasan said: the verse indicates that one who stands for enjoining good has a rank of greatness close to the rank of the prophets. And on the authority of his father, Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, which of the people will have the most severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection? He said: 'A man who killed a prophet, or a man who was ordered to enjoin good and forbid evil.'" Then he recited it. Then he said: "O Ubaydah, the Children of Israel killed forty-three prophets at the beginning of the day in one hour, and there arose one hundred and twelve men from the worshippers of the Children of Israel, and they commanded their killers with good and forbade them from evil, and they were all killed at the end of the day."

﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and it indicates that what is meant are his contemporaries, not their fathers, so the application of killing the prophets is figurative, since they did not kill prophets, but they approved of that and sought it. This sentence is the predicate of "inna," and the fa' entered because the relative pronoun includes the meaning of a conditional particle, as we have previously stated. This abrogating particle was not regarded, because it did not change the meaning of the inceptive, I mean "inna." Nevertheless, there is a difference of opinion on the matter: the correct view is the permissibility of the fa' entering the predicate of "inna" when its subject is given the meaning of a conditional particle, and the conditions for the permissibility of the fa' entering the predicate of the subject have already been mentioned, and those conditions apply here. Similar to this verse regarding the entry of the fa' are: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah, then die while they are disbelievers, Allah will not forgive them﴾ [Muhammad: 34]; ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," then remain steadfast, there will be no fear for them﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 13]; ﴿Indeed, those who persecute the believing men and believing women, then do not repent, for them is the punishment of Hell﴾ [al-Buruj: 10]. Whoever prevents that makes the fa' superfluous, and does not consider its superfluity analogical. It has been mentioned that "bushra" (good news) is the first report that is pleasing; when it is used with what is not pleasing, it is said that it is by way of mockery and derision, as in the saying:

"Their greeting among them is a painful blow."

That is: what takes the place of the pleasing report for them is the painful punishment. It has also been said that it is in the sense of the skin's being affected by that, so the condition of pleasure was not taken into account; rather, the sense of derivation was considered.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 22:**

﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter.﴾ The explanation of this sentence was given earlier, at His words ﴿And whoever of you turns back from his religion﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:217), so it is not repeated here. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-Sammal read *ḥabaṭat* with a fatḥah on the bāʾ (*ḥabaṭat*, not *ḥabiṭat*), and this is a dialectal variant (*lughah*).

﴿And they have no helpers.﴾ Using the plural here is better than the singular, for two reasons. First, it is the end of the verse (*ra's āyah*, the rhyme-ending of the verse). Second, it corresponds to the intercessors on the side of the believers, who are the angels, the prophets, and the righteous believers. That is, they have no one like these. The meaning is that with the negation of helpers, there is also the negation of the benefits and advantages that follow from help. If these benefits are negated from a group, then their negation from an individual is more fitting. And if a group cannot help, then it is even more certain that one individual cannot help. Since their disobedience was mentioned with three attributes, it was appropriate that their recompense be given in three parts, so that each attribute is matched with its counterpart. Since disbelief in the signs of Allah is greater, the announcing of a painful punishment is greater. The killing of the prophets is matched with the voiding of deeds in this world and the Hereafter. In this world, this is by killing, captivity, the seizure of property, and enslavement; in the Hereafter, it is by lasting punishment. The killing of those who command justice is matched with the negation of helpers for them when punishment descends upon them, just as those who commanded justice had no one to help them when the killing of the transgressors befell them. Likewise, the transgressors will have no helper when punishment descends upon them.

In His words ﴿Those (*ulā'ika*)﴾ there is an indication toward those who were previously described with those blameworthy attributes. They are referred to with *alladhīna* (the ones who), since this is more emphatic than referring to them with a verb. It also carries a kind of restriction (*inḥiṣār*). And making the verb a relative clause (*ṣilah*) indicates that it is known to the listener and familiar to him. So when you inform about a noun with a relative pronoun, the addressee understands that this known and familiar action belongs to the one referred to by the relative pronoun. This differs from informing with the verb itself, for you inform the addressee that the action of turning away is from the one about whom you are speaking, and that action is not known to him. If it is known to him, you make it the relative clause and inform about the noun with the relative pronoun.

It is said that these verses combine several kinds of eloquence (*faṣāḥah*) and rhetoric (*balāghah*). One is the fronting and postponing (*taqdīm wa ta'khīr*) in ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ (Āl ʿImrān 3:19). Ibn 'Abbas said the intended order is: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He﴾ and that the religion with Allah is Islam. For this reason, he read *innahu* with a kasrah (as a new sentence), and *anna al-dīn* with a fatḥah (as a clause governed by the witnessing).

The usage of the name of the cause for the effect (*iṭlāq ism al-sabab 'alā al-musabbab*) occurs in ﴿after knowledge had come to them﴾ (3:19). Here "knowledge" refers to the Torah and the Gospel, or to the Prophet (ﷺ), according to the disagreement that preceded.

The transfer of a verb to other than its doer (*isnād al-fi'l ilā ghayr fā'ilihi*) occurs in ﴿their deeds have become void﴾ and ﴿the companions of the Fire﴾.

The allusion (*īmā'*) in ﴿out of envy among themselves﴾ (3:19) indicates that the disbelief is widespread among them, and each group pulls at a part of it.

The use of the part for the whole (*ta'bīr bi-ba'ḍ 'an kull*) occurs in ﴿I have submitted my face﴾ (3:20).

The interrogative which is intended to affirm (*taqrīr*) or to rebuke and reproach (*tawbīkh wa taqrī'*) occurs in ﴿Have you submitted?﴾ (3:20).

The implied antithesis (*ṭibāq muqaddar*) occurs in ﴿If they submit, then they are guided; but if they turn away, then upon you is only the conveying﴾ (3:20). Its aspect is that submission means yielding to Islam and turning toward it, while turning away is the opposite of turning toward. The intended meaning is: "But if they turn away, then they have gone astray," and misguidance is the opposite of guidance.

The fine filler (*ḥashw ḥasan*) occurs in ﴿without right﴾ (3:21). No prophet was ever killed rightfully. This phrase was used only to emphasize the ugliness of killing the prophets and to magnify the matter in the heart of one who intends it.

The repetition in ﴿and kill those who﴾ (3:21) is for emphasis on the ugliness of that act.

The addition of the particle *fa-* in *fa-bashshirhum* ("so give them good tidings") is an announcement that the relative pronoun has been given the meaning of a conditional (*sharṭ*).

The omission (*ḥadhf*) in several places has been discussed in what preceded.

[p-415]

[p. 416]

**Gharra, yaghurru, ghurūran:** to deceive. *Al-ghirr* is the young (inexperienced) male, and *al-gharīrah* is the young female. They are so called because they are easily deceived through haste. *Al-ghirrah* derives from this: one says "he took him *ʿalā ghirrah*," meaning by surprise and deception. *Al-ghurrah* is whiteness on the face, and one says "a face that is *aghharr*," "a man who is *aghharr*," and "a woman who is *gharrāʾ*." The regular plural of these is *ghurr*. They also said that *ghurrān* is a plural, though it is not regular. The poet said:

*The garments of the Banū ʿAwf are pure and clean,*
*and their faces at gatherings are bright (ghurrān).*

**Naza`a, yanzaʿu:** to pull. *Tanāzaʿnā al-ḥadīth* means we pulled the conversation back and forth between us. From this comes *nizāʿ al-mayyit*, the death throes. *Nazaʿa ilā kadhā* means he inclined toward it and was drawn to it. Then the word is used figuratively for removal: one says "God *nazaʿa* evil from him," meaning He removed it.

**Walaja, yalij, wulūjan, walj, walajān (wa-wlijja):** to enter. *Walaja* has the forms *tawallaja* and *ittalaja*. The poet said:

*Indeed the rhymes (al-qawāfī) slip in as hidden passages (mawālij),*
*so narrow that the needle cannot pass through them.*

**Al-amad:** the limit or endpoint of a thing. Its plural is *āmād*.

**Allāhumma:** this is Allah, except that it is restricted to the vocative and is not used otherwise. According to the Basrans, the *mīm* attached to it is a substitute for the vocative particle, which is why it is not preceded by anything except in cases of poetic necessity. According to al-Farrāʾ, the *mīm* comes from the phrase *yā Allāh, umminnā bi-khayr* ("O Allah, grant us well"). The grammarians have rejected this accusative construction. The word became so frequently used that they dropped the *alif-lām* from it and said *lā humma*, meaning *allāhumma*. The poet al-Zājir said:

*O lā humma, I am ʿĀmir ibn Jahm,*
*who has entered the state of iḥrām for ḥajj in greasy garments.*

In some dialects its *mīm* is lightened, as in the verse:

*Like an oath from Abū Riyāḥ,*
*which the great ones (al-kubār) hear as "allāhum."*

**Al-ṣadr:** the chest, a known thing. Its plural is *ṣudūr*.

**"Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book" (Q 3:23).** Al-Suddī said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) invited the Jews to Islam. Al-Nuʿmān ibn Abī Awfā said to him: 'Come, let us bring our dispute before the rabbis.' He said: 'Rather, [bring it] to the Book of Allah.' He said: 'Rather, to the rabbis.'" So this was revealed. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) entered the houses of study (al-madāris) of the Jews and invited them to Allah. Nuʿaym ibn ʿAmr and al-Ḥārith ibn Zayd said: 'Upon what religion are you, O Muḥammad?' He said: 'Upon the religion of Ibrāhīm.' They said: 'Ibrāhīm was a Jew.' He said: 'Then come to the Torah.' They refused him," and so this was revealed. Al-Kalbī said: "A man among them committed adultery with a woman, and at that time stoning was not yet in our religion. So they referred the matter to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), seeking leniency for the two adulterers because of their nobility. He said: 'I only judge by your Book.' They denied stoning, so the Torah was brought. Their rabbi, Ibn Ṣūriyā, placed his hand over the verse of stoning. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām said: 'He has passed over it, O Messenger of Allah.' So he uncovered it, and they were stoned."

Al-Naqqāsh said: it was revealed concerning a group of Jews who denied his prophethood, and he said to them: "Come to the Torah, for in it is my description." Muqātil said: a group of Jews was invited to Islam, and they said: "We have more right to guidance than you, and Allah has sent no prophet except from the Children of Israel." He said: "Bring out the Torah, for it is written in it that I am a prophet." They refused, and so this was revealed. "Those who were given a portion of the Book" are the Jews, and "the Book" is the Torah.

Makkī and others said: it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ). It was also said that *min al-kitāb* is a genus referring to the revealed books. This was stated by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, and al-Zamakhsharī began with it. *Min* is partitive (tabʿīḍ). In His saying *naṣīban*, meaning a part, it implies only part of the Book, since they did not memorize it and did not know all of what is in it.

**"Who are invited to the Book of Allah" (Q 3:23).** The Book here is the Torah. Al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, and Ibn Jurayj said it is the Qur'an. *Yudʿawna* is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to *alladhīna*, and the governing verb is *tara*. The meaning is: "Do you not marvel at these people who are invited to the Book of Allah?" That is, in the state of being invited to the Book of Allah. **"That it may judge between them"**: that is, that the Book may judge. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Jaʿfar, and ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī read *liyuḥkama* in the passive voice. The matter judged concerning them is what was mentioned in the occasion of revelation.

**"Then a party of them turns away" (Q 3:23).** This is an expression of astonishment at their turning away after they have knowledge, since returning to the Book of Allah is obligatory. The turning away is attributed to "a party of them" and not to all of those addressed, because some of them accepted Islam and did not turn away, such as Ibn Salām and others.

**"While they are refusing" (Q 3:23).** This clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) that emphasizes, since turning away is refusal. Or it clarifies that the turning away is from the one who invites and the refusal is from what he invites to, so the object differs. Or it clarifies that the turning away is with the body and the refusal is with the heart. Or the turning away is from their scholars and the refusal is from their followers, as stated by Ibn al-Anbārī. Or it is a resumed sentence (jumlah mustaʾnafah) informing about them that they are a people for whom turning away from the truth and from its followers is a continuous habit and custom. In His saying *baynahum* ("between them") is evidence that the dispute was among them, not between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This contradicts what was mentioned in the occasions of revelation. If one of those occasions is authentic, the meaning is: "that He may judge between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." If none is authentic, it is understood as the disagreement occurring among those of their rabbis who accepted Islam and those who did not accept it. So they were invited to the Torah, about whose authenticity there is no disagreement among you, so that it might judge between the one who is right and the one who is wrong. Then whoever did not accept Islam turned away.

It was said: in this verse is evidence for the validity of the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because if they had not known what he claimed in their books concerning his description and the validity of his prophethood, they would not have turned away and hurried to oppose what is in their books, until they were exposed for the falsehood of his claim. In it is also evidence that whoever is called by his opponent to a just judgment must respond to him, because he has been called to the Book of Allah. This is supported by His saying: **"And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger that He may judge between them, behold, a party of them turns away"** (Q 24:48).

Al-Qurṭubī said: when someone is called to the Book of Allah and opposes it, it becomes obligatory to restrain him with discipline in proportion to the one who opposes and the one who is opposed. This ruling applies among us in al-Andalus and the lands of the Maghrib, but not in the Egyptian territories. Ibn Khuwayzimandād the Mālikī said: it is obligatory for one who is called to the court of judgment to respond, unless he knows that the judge is a sinner (fāsiq).

**"That is because they said: The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days" (Q 3:24).** The demonstrative *dhālika* refers to the turning away. That is: that turning away is caused by these false statements, by their making the punishment easy for themselves, and by their hope of leaving the Fire after a few days. Al-Zamakhsharī said: as the Jabriyyah and the Ḥashwiyyah hoped.

**"And their deception in their religion by what they used to fabricate" (Q 3:24).** That is, [their deception] by the claim that their forefathers, the prophets, would intercede for them. This is like how those (the Muʿtazilah?) were deceived by the intercession of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for their major sins. This is the end of his words. He is, as is his habit, persistent in reviling the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah), accusing them of anthropomorphism, and attacking them by any means he can.

The explanation of these numbered days has already been given in Sūrat al-Baqarah, so it is not necessary to repeat it here. However, there it came as *maʿdūdah*, and here as *maʿdūdāt*. Both are eloquent forms. You say "*jibāl shāmikhah*" and "*jibāl shāmikhāt*." You may treat the adjective of a broken plural of a masculine non-rational noun sometimes as an adjective for a feminine singular, and sometimes as an adjective for feminine plurals. Just as you say "*nisāʾ qāʾimāt*," so too you say "*jibāl rāsiyāt*," and this is a regular, consistent pattern.

**"And their deception in their religion by what they used to fabricate" (Q 3:24).** Mujāhid said: what they fabricated is their saying: "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days." Qatādah said: it is their saying: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved." It was also said: "No one will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian" (Q 2:111). It was also said: it is all of these sayings together.

*Dhālika* is in the nominative as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and *bi-annahum* is the predicate (khabar). The meaning is: that turning away and refusal belongs to them and is established by the cause of this saying, which is their claim that the Fire will touch them only for a few days, a small number that can be counted. It was also said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "their condition is that," that is, the turning away and refusal. This was stated by al-Zajjāj. According to this, *bi-annahum* is in the position of a ḥāl, meaning accompanied by this saying. The *mā* in *mā kānū* is either a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah) or a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah).

**"Then how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt" (Q 3:25).** This is an expression of wonder at their condition and an exaggeration of the greatness of their statement, since their hopes have diverged and the falsehood of their claim has become clear. They have come to a punishment for which they have no means of repelling it, as He, Exalted, said: **"Those are their wishful thinkings"** (Q 2:111). This expression is used to magnify the condition of a thing, as in: "How, then, when the angels take their souls?" The poet said:

*How then (for) a soul, whenever I said it had risen to recovery,*
*from a wound of Dahmāʾ its healing was broken.*

He also said:

*How then, when each one cannot pass beyond his appointed time,*
*and no man is delayed from what Allah has decreed?*

For **"fa-kayfa,"** it was said that it is in the accusative as a ḥāl, and the estimated meaning is: "How do they act?" Al-Ḥūfī estimated it as: "How will their condition be?" If he meant the complete (tāmmah) form of *kāna*, then it is in the accusative position as a ḥāl. If it is the incomplete (nāqiṣah) form, then it is in the accusative position as the predicate of *kāna*. The better view is that it is in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject, which the meaning indicates. The estimate is: "How is their condition?" The governing element for *idhā* is the verb that he estimated. The governing element for *kayfa*, when it is the predicate of the subject, if we say its accusative is the accusative of adverbs (ẓurūf), is the omitted subject we estimated, meaning: "How is their condition at that time?" If we say it is a noun other than an adverb, then the governing element for *idhā* is the omitted subject we estimated. This interrogative does not require an answer, and neither do most interrogatives in the Qur'an, because they belong to the realm of the observable (ʿālam al-shahādah). The interrogation of Allah, exalted is He, is a rebuke.

The *lām* in **"liyawmin"** is connected to *jamaʿnāhum*. The meaning is: "for the judgment of a day and its recompense," as in His saying: **"Indeed You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day"** (Q 3:9). Al-Naqqāsh said: "the Day" here means a time, and likewise **"numbered days"** and **"in two days"** (Q 2:203) and **"in four days"** (Q 41:10) are expressions for periods of time. Days and nights are only in this world according to us. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the correct view regarding the Day of Resurrection is that it is a day, because before it there is a night and in it there is a sun.

The meaning of **"about which there is no doubt"** is: in the reality of the matter, or according to the believer, or according to the one who informs about it, or at the time He gathers them in it. Or its meaning is "the matter," and there are five views.

**"And every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged" (Q 3:25).** The explanation of something like this has already been given in Sūrat al-Baqarah, at the end of the verses on usury.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 23–25 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Say: O Allah, Master of the kingdom﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. Al-Kalbi said: A rock appeared in the trench, and the Prophet (ﷺ) struck it, and a spark flashed, and he said "Allahu akbar." He did the same a second and a third time, and said: "With the first, the palaces of Persia were shown to me; with the second, the palaces of Rome; and with the third, the palaces of Yemen. Gabriel (peace be upon him) informed me that my community will prevail over all of them." The hypocrites mocked him, saying that he strikes with a pickaxe and digs the trench out of fear, and that he longs for the kingdom of Persia and Rome. Then this was revealed. Al-Sijawandi abridged it in this form, and it is a very lengthy occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul).

Ibn Abbas said: When Mecca was conquered, it weighed heavily on the polytheists, and they feared the conquest of the non-Arabs ('ajam). Abdullah ibn Ubayy said: "They are stronger and more powerful." Then this was revealed. Ibn Abbas and Anas said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) conquered Mecca, he promised his community the kingdom of Persia and Rome, and then this was revealed. It is also said: This reached the Jews, and they said: "Far-fetched, far-fetched!" Then this was revealed, and they were humiliated and sought a truce. Al-Hasan said: The Prophet (ﷺ) asked for the kingdom of Persia and Rome for his community, and this was revealed in the form of a prohibition. Something similar is narrated from Qatada, that this was mentioned to him. Abu Muslim al-Dimashqi said: The Jews said: "By Allah, we will not obey a man who has transferred prophethood from the Children of Israel to others." Then this was revealed. It is also said: It was revealed as a refutation of the Christians of Najran in their saying that 'Isa is Allah, though there is nothing in him of these attributes.

Here, the apparent meaning of "kingdom" (mulk) is authority and dominance, and the occasions of revelation accord with this interpretation. Mujahid said: "Kingdom" means prophethood, and this fits with Abu Muslim's account of the occasion of revelation. It is also said: it means wealth and slaves; and it is said: it means this world and the Hereafter.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Master of the servants and of what they possess." Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, "the possession of the genus of kingship," so that You dispose of it as owners dispose of what they own. Ibn Atiyya said the same. He spoke about the word "Allahumma" from the standpoint of grammar, and said: They agreed that its *h* is pronounced with a *damma* and its *m* is doubled and fatha-vowelled, and that it is a vocative (munada). The claim of consensus about doubling the *m* is not accurate, for al-Farra' transmitted that in some dialects its *m* is pronounced light (single). He said: Some have recited:

*Like the cry of Abu Riyah, which the great ones hear as "Allahumm."*

The one who refuted him said: Lightening the *m* is a gross error, especially according to al-Farra', because according to him it is the *m* of "ummana" (our mother), since the lightened form cannot allow that the *m* is a remnant of "ummana." He said: The correct narration is "*which the great ones hear as* lāhuhu" (his god). If this line is genuinely from the Arabs, there is another anomaly in it, in that it is used outside of the vocative. Do you not see that he made it the subject (fā'il) of the verb preceding it in this line? Abu Raja' al-Utaridi said: This letter *m* comprises seventy of His names. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: Whoever says "Allahumma" has called upon Allah with all of His names together. Al-Hasan said: "Allahumma" is the gathering-place of supplication.

The meaning of al-Nadr's statement is that "Allahumma" is "Allah," with an *m* added to it. It is thus the proper name that includes all the attributes of His essence, because when you say "Zayd has come," you have mentioned a specific name, which comprises all of his attributes that are in him: whether fair complexion, height, generosity, courage, or their opposites, and whatever is similar to that.

The accusative of "Master of the kingdom" is as a second vocative, meaning: "O Master of the kingdom." According to Sibawayh, "Allahumma" is not described by an adjective. Abu al-'Abbas and Abu Ishaq permitted it to be described by an adjective, so that it is an adjective of "Allahumm" according to them. This is a disputed issue discussed in the science of grammar (nahw).

﴿You give the kingdom to whom You will and You take the kingdom away from whom You will﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. The apparent meaning of "kingdom" is authority and dominance, just as the apparent meaning of the first "kingdom" is the same, so the first is general and these two are specific. The meaning is: You give some portion of the kingdom to whom You will, and You take some portion of the kingdom away from whom You will. Here "kingdom" has also been interpreted as prophethood, but this interpretation cannot apply to "You take away the kingdom," because Allah does not give prophethood to someone and then take it away from him, unless "take away" is used metaphorically in the sense of "withhold prophethood from whom You will," and then it is possible.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: It is dominion over the self and restraining it from following desire. It is also said: well-being; and it is said: contentment. It is said: dominance through religion and obedience. It is said: standing in prayer at night. Al-Shibli said: It is self-sufficiency through the Originator from the two worlds. Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya said: It is the subjugation of Iblis, just as he would flee from the shadow of Umar; and the opposite of this is one from whom Satan flows like blood. It is said: It is the kingdom of knowledge without a cause, as it came to the magicians of Pharaoh, and it was taken from Bal'am. Abu Uthman said: It is the granting of faith's success.

If we take it in its most apparent sense, which is sovereignty and dominance, and the one given it is the commanded and followed one, then the one to whom Allah gave the kingdom is Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, and those from whom it was taken are Persia and Rome. It is said: The one from whom it was taken is Abu Jahl and the chiefs of Quraysh. It is said: The Arabs and the caliphs of Islam and its kings are meant, and what was taken is Persia and Rome. Al-Suddi said: The prophets: the people were commanded to obey them; and what was taken from them are the tyrants, whom the people were commanded to oppose. It is said: Adam and his offspring, and what was taken from them is Iblis and his armies. It is said: David (peace be upon him), and what was taken from him was Talut. It is said: Sakhr, and what was taken from him was Sulayman during his trial. It is said: The meaning is that He gives the kingdom in Paradise to whom He wills, and takes away the kingdom from the kings of this world in the Hereafter from whom He wills. It is said: The kingdom is seclusion and withdrawal, and they named it "the unknown kingdom." These are confused opinions and particularizations for which nothing in the speech indicates; the better view is that it should be understood as an example and not as an exhaustive specification of what is meant.

﴿And You exalt whom You will and You abase whom You will﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. It is said: Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions, when they entered Mecca, twelve thousand strong, prevailing over it; and He humbled Abu Jahl and the chiefs of Quraysh, until their heads were cut off and they were thrown into the well. It is said: exaltation is by success and recognition, and abasement is by forsaking. Ata' said: exaltation is for the Muhajirun and the Ansar, and abasement is for Persia and Rome. It is said: exaltation is by obedience, and abasement is by disobedience. It is said: exaltation is by victory and spoils, and abasement is by killing and the poll-tax (jizya). It is said: exaltation is by sincerity, and abasement is by showing off. It is said: exaltation is by wealth, and abasement is by poverty. It is said: exaltation is by Paradise and the vision (of Allah), and abasement is by the veil and the Fire; this was said by al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl. It is said: exaltation is by subduing the self, and abasement is by following disgrace; this was said by al-Warraq. It is said: exaltation is by subduing Satan, and abasement is by Satan's subduing of him; this was said by al-Kattani. It is said: exaltation is by contentment and satisfaction, and abasement is by greed and covetousness.

These statements should be understood as examples, because there is no specifier in the verse. Rather, what exaltation and abasement are brought about by is left unstated. The Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazilites) have a discourse here that contradicts the discourse of the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna). Al-Ka'bi said: He gives the kingdom by way of entitlement to whoever establishes it, and He takes it away only from one who has committed wickedness (fisq). This is indicated by ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqara: 124], and ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you﴾ [al-Baqara: 247], where He made being chosen a cause of kingship. So it is not permissible that the kingship of wrongdoers is by Allah's giving it, though it may happen; and He has obligated them (p-٤٢٠) not to possess it. Thus it is established that the just kings are the ones specifically granted kingship by Allah, but the wrongdoers are not. As for taking away, it is the opposite: just as He takes it away from the just person for a reason, He may also take it away from the wrongdoer.

Qadi Abd al-Jabbar said: Exaltation attributed to Him, Exalted is He, occurs in religion through supporting with divine graces (alṭāf), praising them, and their dominance over enemies; and it occurs in the world through wealth and the granting of awe. The noblest kind of honor in religion is faith, and the most humiliating of things that cause humiliation is disbelief. So if the attainment of faith and disbelief came from the servant, then the servant's exalting himself by faith and his abasing himself by disbelief would be greater than Allah's exalting him and abasing him; and if that were so, his share of this attribute would be more complete than His share, glory be to Him, and that is absolutely false.

Al-Jubba'i said: He abases His enemies in this world and the Hereafter, and He does not abase His friends even if He makes them poor, sickens them, frightens them, or brings them to other needs, because that is for their honor in the Hereafter through reward or compensation. It is like bloodletting, which causes pain in the moment and yields benefit afterward. He said: The description of poverty as abasement is figurative, like His saying ﴿humble toward the believers﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 54]. And Allah's abasing of the falsifiers occurs in various ways: by blame and curse; by their being left without argument or support; by making them spoils for the people of His religion; and by their punishment in the Hereafter.

[p. 416]

**Gharra, yaghurru, ghurūran:** to deceive. *Al-ghirr* is the young (inexperienced) male, and *al-gharīrah* is the young female. They are so called because they are easily deceived through haste. *Al-ghirrah* derives from this: one says "he took him *ʿalā ghirrah*," meaning by surprise and deception. *Al-ghurrah* is whiteness on the face, and one says "a face that is *aghharr*," "a man who is *aghharr*," and "a woman who is *gharrāʾ*." The regular plural of these is *ghurr*. They also said that *ghurrān* is a plural, though it is not regular. The poet said:

*The garments of the Banū ʿAwf are pure and clean,*
*and their faces at gatherings are bright (ghurrān).*

**Naza`a, yanzaʿu:** to pull. *Tanāzaʿnā al-ḥadīth* means we pulled the conversation back and forth between us. From this comes *nizāʿ al-mayyit*, the death throes. *Nazaʿa ilā kadhā* means he inclined toward it and was drawn to it. Then the word is used figuratively for removal: one says "God *nazaʿa* evil from him," meaning He removed it.

**Walaja, yalij, wulūjan, walj, walajān (wa-wlijja):** to enter. *Walaja* has the forms *tawallaja* and *ittalaja*. The poet said:

*Indeed the rhymes (al-qawāfī) slip in as hidden passages (mawālij),*
*so narrow that the needle cannot pass through them.*

**Al-amad:** the limit or endpoint of a thing. Its plural is *āmād*.

**Allāhumma:** this is Allah, except that it is restricted to the vocative and is not used otherwise. According to the Basrans, the *mīm* attached to it is a substitute for the vocative particle, which is why it is not preceded by anything except in cases of poetic necessity. According to al-Farrāʾ, the *mīm* comes from the phrase *yā Allāh, umminnā bi-khayr* ("O Allah, grant us well"). The grammarians have rejected this accusative construction. The word became so frequently used that they dropped the *alif-lām* from it and said *lā humma*, meaning *allāhumma*. The poet al-Zājir said:

*O lā humma, I am ʿĀmir ibn Jahm,*
*who has entered the state of iḥrām for ḥajj in greasy garments.*

In some dialects its *mīm* is lightened, as in the verse:

*Like an oath from Abū Riyāḥ,*
*which the great ones (al-kubār) hear as "allāhum."*

**Al-ṣadr:** the chest, a known thing. Its plural is *ṣudūr*.

**"Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book" (Q 3:23).** Al-Suddī said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) invited the Jews to Islam. Al-Nuʿmān ibn Abī Awfā said to him: 'Come, let us bring our dispute before the rabbis.' He said: 'Rather, [bring it] to the Book of Allah.' He said: 'Rather, to the rabbis.'" So this was revealed. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) entered the houses of study (al-madāris) of the Jews and invited them to Allah. Nuʿaym ibn ʿAmr and al-Ḥārith ibn Zayd said: 'Upon what religion are you, O Muḥammad?' He said: 'Upon the religion of Ibrāhīm.' They said: 'Ibrāhīm was a Jew.' He said: 'Then come to the Torah.' They refused him," and so this was revealed. Al-Kalbī said: "A man among them committed adultery with a woman, and at that time stoning was not yet in our religion. So they referred the matter to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), seeking leniency for the two adulterers because of their nobility. He said: 'I only judge by your Book.' They denied stoning, so the Torah was brought. Their rabbi, Ibn Ṣūriyā, placed his hand over the verse of stoning. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām said: 'He has passed over it, O Messenger of Allah.' So he uncovered it, and they were stoned."

Al-Naqqāsh said: it was revealed concerning a group of Jews who denied his prophethood, and he said to them: "Come to the Torah, for in it is my description." Muqātil said: a group of Jews was invited to Islam, and they said: "We have more right to guidance than you, and Allah has sent no prophet except from the Children of Israel." He said: "Bring out the Torah, for it is written in it that I am a prophet." They refused, and so this was revealed. "Those who were given a portion of the Book" are the Jews, and "the Book" is the Torah.

Makkī and others said: it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ). It was also said that *min al-kitāb* is a genus referring to the revealed books. This was stated by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, and al-Zamakhsharī began with it. *Min* is partitive (tabʿīḍ). In His saying *naṣīban*, meaning a part, it implies only part of the Book, since they did not memorize it and did not know all of what is in it.

**"Who are invited to the Book of Allah" (Q 3:23).** The Book here is the Torah. Al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, and Ibn Jurayj said it is the Qur'an. *Yudʿawna* is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to *alladhīna*, and the governing verb is *tara*. The meaning is: "Do you not marvel at these people who are invited to the Book of Allah?" That is, in the state of being invited to the Book of Allah. **"That it may judge between them"**: that is, that the Book may judge. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Jaʿfar, and ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī read *liyuḥkama* in the passive voice. The matter judged concerning them is what was mentioned in the occasion of revelation.

**"Then a party of them turns away" (Q 3:23).** This is an expression of astonishment at their turning away after they have knowledge, since returning to the Book of Allah is obligatory. The turning away is attributed to "a party of them" and not to all of those addressed, because some of them accepted Islam and did not turn away, such as Ibn Salām and others.

**"While they are refusing" (Q 3:23).** This clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) that emphasizes, since turning away is refusal. Or it clarifies that the turning away is from the one who invites and the refusal is from what he invites to, so the object differs. Or it clarifies that the turning away is with the body and the refusal is with the heart. Or the turning away is from their scholars and the refusal is from their followers, as stated by Ibn al-Anbārī. Or it is a resumed sentence (jumlah mustaʾnafah) informing about them that they are a people for whom turning away from the truth and from its followers is a continuous habit and custom. In His saying *baynahum* ("between them") is evidence that the dispute was among them, not between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This contradicts what was mentioned in the occasions of revelation. If one of those occasions is authentic, the meaning is: "that He may judge between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." If none is authentic, it is understood as the disagreement occurring among those of their rabbis who accepted Islam and those who did not accept it. So they were invited to the Torah, about whose authenticity there is no disagreement among you, so that it might judge between the one who is right and the one who is wrong. Then whoever did not accept Islam turned away.

It was said: in this verse is evidence for the validity of the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because if they had not known what he claimed in their books concerning his description and the validity of his prophethood, they would not have turned away and hurried to oppose what is in their books, until they were exposed for the falsehood of his claim. In it is also evidence that whoever is called by his opponent to a just judgment must respond to him, because he has been called to the Book of Allah. This is supported by His saying: **"And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger that He may judge between them, behold, a party of them turns away"** (Q 24:48).

Al-Qurṭubī said: when someone is called to the Book of Allah and opposes it, it becomes obligatory to restrain him with discipline in proportion to the one who opposes and the one who is opposed.
