This ruling applies among us in al-Andalus and the lands of the Maghrib, but not in the Egyptian territories. Ibn Khuwayzimandād the Mālikī said: it is obligatory for one who is called to the court of judgment to respond, unless he knows that the judge is a sinner (fāsiq).

**"That is because they said: The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days" (Q 3:24).** The demonstrative *dhālika* refers to the turning away. That is: that turning away is caused by these false statements, by their making the punishment easy for themselves, and by their hope of leaving the Fire after a few days. Al-Zamakhsharī said: as the Jabriyyah and the Ḥashwiyyah hoped.

**"And their deception in their religion by what they used to fabricate" (Q 3:24).** That is, [their deception] by the claim that their forefathers, the prophets, would intercede for them. This is like how those (the Muʿtazilah?) were deceived by the intercession of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for their major sins. This is the end of his words. He is, as is his habit, persistent in reviling the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah), accusing them of anthropomorphism, and attacking them by any means he can.

The explanation of these numbered days has already been given in Sūrat al-Baqarah, so it is not necessary to repeat it here. However, there it came as *maʿdūdah*, and here as *maʿdūdāt*. Both are eloquent forms. You say "*jibāl shāmikhah*" and "*jibāl shāmikhāt*." You may treat the adjective of a broken plural of a masculine non-rational noun sometimes as an adjective for a feminine singular, and sometimes as an adjective for feminine plurals. Just as you say "*nisāʾ qāʾimāt*," so too you say "*jibāl rāsiyāt*," and this is a regular, consistent pattern.

**"And their deception in their religion by what they used to fabricate" (Q 3:24).** Mujāhid said: what they fabricated is their saying: "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days." Qatādah said: it is their saying: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved." It was also said: "No one will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian" (Q 2:111). It was also said: it is all of these sayings together.

*Dhālika* is in the nominative as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and *bi-annahum* is the predicate (khabar). The meaning is: that turning away and refusal belongs to them and is established by the cause of this saying, which is their claim that the Fire will touch them only for a few days, a small number that can be counted. It was also said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "their condition is that," that is, the turning away and refusal. This was stated by al-Zajjāj. According to this, *bi-annahum* is in the position of a ḥāl, meaning accompanied by this saying. The *mā* in *mā kānū* is either a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah) or a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah).

**"Then how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt" (Q 3:25).** This is an expression of wonder at their condition and an exaggeration of the greatness of their statement, since their hopes have diverged and the falsehood of their claim has become clear. They have come to a punishment for which they have no means of repelling it, as He, Exalted, said: **"Those are their wishful thinkings"** (Q 2:111). This expression is used to magnify the condition of a thing, as in: "How, then, when the angels take their souls?" The poet said:

*How then (for) a soul, whenever I said it had risen to recovery,*
*from a wound of Dahmāʾ its healing was broken.*

He also said:

*How then, when each one cannot pass beyond his appointed time,*
*and no man is delayed from what Allah has decreed?*

For **"fa-kayfa,"** it was said that it is in the accusative as a ḥāl, and the estimated meaning is: "How do they act?" Al-Ḥūfī estimated it as: "How will their condition be?" If he meant the complete (tāmmah) form of *kāna*, then it is in the accusative position as a ḥāl. If it is the incomplete (nāqiṣah) form, then it is in the accusative position as the predicate of *kāna*. The better view is that it is in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject, which the meaning indicates. The estimate is: "How is their condition?" The governing element for *idhā* is the verb that he estimated. The governing element for *kayfa*, when it is the predicate of the subject, if we say its accusative is the accusative of adverbs (ẓurūf), is the omitted subject we estimated, meaning: "How is their condition at that time?" If we say it is a noun other than an adverb, then the governing element for *idhā* is the omitted subject we estimated. This interrogative does not require an answer, and neither do most interrogatives in the Qur'an, because they belong to the realm of the observable (ʿālam al-shahādah). The interrogation of Allah, exalted is He, is a rebuke.

The *lām* in **"liyawmin"** is connected to *jamaʿnāhum*. The meaning is: "for the judgment of a day and its recompense," as in His saying: **"Indeed You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day"** (Q 3:9). Al-Naqqāsh said: "the Day" here means a time, and likewise **"numbered days"** and **"in two days"** (Q 2:203) and **"in four days"** (Q 41:10) are expressions for periods of time. Days and nights are only in this world according to us. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the correct view regarding the Day of Resurrection is that it is a day, because before it there is a night and in it there is a sun.

The meaning of **"about which there is no doubt"** is: in the reality of the matter, or according to the believer, or according to the one who informs about it, or at the time He gathers them in it. Or its meaning is "the matter," and there are five views.

**"And every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged" (Q 3:25).** The explanation of something like this has already been given in Sūrat al-Baqarah, at the end of the verses on usury.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 23–25 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Say: O Allah, Master of the kingdom﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. Al-Kalbi said: A rock appeared in the trench, and the Prophet (ﷺ) struck it, and a spark flashed, and he said "Allahu akbar." He did the same a second and a third time, and said: "With the first, the palaces of Persia were shown to me; with the second, the palaces of Rome; and with the third, the palaces of Yemen. Gabriel (peace be upon him) informed me that my community will prevail over all of them." The hypocrites mocked him, saying that he strikes with a pickaxe and digs the trench out of fear, and that he longs for the kingdom of Persia and Rome. Then this was revealed. Al-Sijawandi abridged it in this form, and it is a very lengthy occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul).

Ibn Abbas said: When Mecca was conquered, it weighed heavily on the polytheists, and they feared the conquest of the non-Arabs ('ajam). Abdullah ibn Ubayy said: "They are stronger and more powerful." Then this was revealed. Ibn Abbas and Anas said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) conquered Mecca, he promised his community the kingdom of Persia and Rome, and then this was revealed. It is also said: This reached the Jews, and they said: "Far-fetched, far-fetched!" Then this was revealed, and they were humiliated and sought a truce. Al-Hasan said: The Prophet (ﷺ) asked for the kingdom of Persia and Rome for his community, and this was revealed in the form of a prohibition. Something similar is narrated from Qatada, that this was mentioned to him. Abu Muslim al-Dimashqi said: The Jews said: "By Allah, we will not obey a man who has transferred prophethood from the Children of Israel to others." Then this was revealed. It is also said: It was revealed as a refutation of the Christians of Najran in their saying that 'Isa is Allah, though there is nothing in him of these attributes.

Here, the apparent meaning of "kingdom" (mulk) is authority and dominance, and the occasions of revelation accord with this interpretation. Mujahid said: "Kingdom" means prophethood, and this fits with Abu Muslim's account of the occasion of revelation. It is also said: it means wealth and slaves; and it is said: it means this world and the Hereafter.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Master of the servants and of what they possess." Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, "the possession of the genus of kingship," so that You dispose of it as owners dispose of what they own. Ibn Atiyya said the same. He spoke about the word "Allahumma" from the standpoint of grammar, and said: They agreed that its *h* is pronounced with a *damma* and its *m* is doubled and fatha-vowelled, and that it is a vocative (munada). The claim of consensus about doubling the *m* is not accurate, for al-Farra' transmitted that in some dialects its *m* is pronounced light (single). He said: Some have recited:

*Like the cry of Abu Riyah, which the great ones hear as "Allahumm."*

The one who refuted him said: Lightening the *m* is a gross error, especially according to al-Farra', because according to him it is the *m* of "ummana" (our mother), since the lightened form cannot allow that the *m* is a remnant of "ummana." He said: The correct narration is "*which the great ones hear as* lāhuhu" (his god). If this line is genuinely from the Arabs, there is another anomaly in it, in that it is used outside of the vocative. Do you not see that he made it the subject (fā'il) of the verb preceding it in this line? Abu Raja' al-Utaridi said: This letter *m* comprises seventy of His names. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: Whoever says "Allahumma" has called upon Allah with all of His names together. Al-Hasan said: "Allahumma" is the gathering-place of supplication.

The meaning of al-Nadr's statement is that "Allahumma" is "Allah," with an *m* added to it. It is thus the proper name that includes all the attributes of His essence, because when you say "Zayd has come," you have mentioned a specific name, which comprises all of his attributes that are in him: whether fair complexion, height, generosity, courage, or their opposites, and whatever is similar to that.

The accusative of "Master of the kingdom" is as a second vocative, meaning: "O Master of the kingdom." According to Sibawayh, "Allahumma" is not described by an adjective. Abu al-'Abbas and Abu Ishaq permitted it to be described by an adjective, so that it is an adjective of "Allahumm" according to them. This is a disputed issue discussed in the science of grammar (nahw).

﴿You give the kingdom to whom You will and You take the kingdom away from whom You will﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. The apparent meaning of "kingdom" is authority and dominance, just as the apparent meaning of the first "kingdom" is the same, so the first is general and these two are specific. The meaning is: You give some portion of the kingdom to whom You will, and You take some portion of the kingdom away from whom You will. Here "kingdom" has also been interpreted as prophethood, but this interpretation cannot apply to "You take away the kingdom," because Allah does not give prophethood to someone and then take it away from him, unless "take away" is used metaphorically in the sense of "withhold prophethood from whom You will," and then it is possible.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: It is dominion over the self and restraining it from following desire. It is also said: well-being; and it is said: contentment. It is said: dominance through religion and obedience. It is said: standing in prayer at night. Al-Shibli said: It is self-sufficiency through the Originator from the two worlds. Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya said: It is the subjugation of Iblis, just as he would flee from the shadow of Umar; and the opposite of this is one from whom Satan flows like blood. It is said: It is the kingdom of knowledge without a cause, as it came to the magicians of Pharaoh, and it was taken from Bal'am. Abu Uthman said: It is the granting of faith's success.

If we take it in its most apparent sense, which is sovereignty and dominance, and the one given it is the commanded and followed one, then the one to whom Allah gave the kingdom is Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, and those from whom it was taken are Persia and Rome. It is said: The one from whom it was taken is Abu Jahl and the chiefs of Quraysh. It is said: The Arabs and the caliphs of Islam and its kings are meant, and what was taken is Persia and Rome. Al-Suddi said: The prophets: the people were commanded to obey them; and what was taken from them are the tyrants, whom the people were commanded to oppose. It is said: Adam and his offspring, and what was taken from them is Iblis and his armies. It is said: David (peace be upon him), and what was taken from him was Talut. It is said: Sakhr, and what was taken from him was Sulayman during his trial. It is said: The meaning is that He gives the kingdom in Paradise to whom He wills, and takes away the kingdom from the kings of this world in the Hereafter from whom He wills. It is said: The kingdom is seclusion and withdrawal, and they named it "the unknown kingdom." These are confused opinions and particularizations for which nothing in the speech indicates; the better view is that it should be understood as an example and not as an exhaustive specification of what is meant.

﴿And You exalt whom You will and You abase whom You will﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. It is said: Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions, when they entered Mecca, twelve thousand strong, prevailing over it; and He humbled Abu Jahl and the chiefs of Quraysh, until their heads were cut off and they were thrown into the well. It is said: exaltation is by success and recognition, and abasement is by forsaking. Ata' said: exaltation is for the Muhajirun and the Ansar, and abasement is for Persia and Rome. It is said: exaltation is by obedience, and abasement is by disobedience. It is said: exaltation is by victory and spoils, and abasement is by killing and the poll-tax (jizya). It is said: exaltation is by sincerity, and abasement is by showing off. It is said: exaltation is by wealth, and abasement is by poverty. It is said: exaltation is by Paradise and the vision (of Allah), and abasement is by the veil and the Fire; this was said by al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl. It is said: exaltation is by subduing the self, and abasement is by following disgrace; this was said by al-Warraq. It is said: exaltation is by subduing Satan, and abasement is by Satan's subduing of him; this was said by al-Kattani. It is said: exaltation is by contentment and satisfaction, and abasement is by greed and covetousness.

These statements should be understood as examples, because there is no specifier in the verse. Rather, what exaltation and abasement are brought about by is left unstated. The Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazilites) have a discourse here that contradicts the discourse of the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna). Al-Ka'bi said: He gives the kingdom by way of entitlement to whoever establishes it, and He takes it away only from one who has committed wickedness (fisq). This is indicated by ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqara: 124], and ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you﴾ [al-Baqara: 247], where He made being chosen a cause of kingship. So it is not permissible that the kingship of wrongdoers is by Allah's giving it, though it may happen; and He has obligated them (p-٤٢٠) not to possess it. Thus it is established that the just kings are the ones specifically granted kingship by Allah, but the wrongdoers are not. As for taking away, it is the opposite: just as He takes it away from the just person for a reason, He may also take it away from the wrongdoer.

Qadi Abd al-Jabbar said: Exaltation attributed to Him, Exalted is He, occurs in religion through supporting with divine graces (alṭāf), praising them, and their dominance over enemies; and it occurs in the world through wealth and the granting of awe. The noblest kind of honor in religion is faith, and the most humiliating of things that cause humiliation is disbelief. So if the attainment of faith and disbelief came from the servant, then the servant's exalting himself by faith and his abasing himself by disbelief would be greater than Allah's exalting him and abasing him; and if that were so, his share of this attribute would be more complete than His share, glory be to Him, and that is absolutely false.

Al-Jubba'i said: He abases His enemies in this world and the Hereafter, and He does not abase His friends even if He makes them poor, sickens them, frightens them, or brings them to other needs, because that is for their honor in the Hereafter through reward or compensation. It is like bloodletting, which causes pain in the moment and yields benefit afterward. He said: The description of poverty as abasement is figurative, like His saying ﴿humble toward the believers﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 54]. And Allah's abasing of the falsifiers occurs in various ways: by blame and curse; by their being left without argument or support; by making them spoils for the people of His religion; and by their punishment in the Hereafter.

[p. 416]

**Gharra, yaghurru, ghurūran:** to deceive. *Al-ghirr* is the young (inexperienced) male, and *al-gharīrah* is the young female. They are so called because they are easily deceived through haste. *Al-ghirrah* derives from this: one says "he took him *ʿalā ghirrah*," meaning by surprise and deception. *Al-ghurrah* is whiteness on the face, and one says "a face that is *aghharr*," "a man who is *aghharr*," and "a woman who is *gharrāʾ*." The regular plural of these is *ghurr*. They also said that *ghurrān* is a plural, though it is not regular. The poet said:

*The garments of the Banū ʿAwf are pure and clean,*
*and their faces at gatherings are bright (ghurrān).*

**Naza`a, yanzaʿu:** to pull. *Tanāzaʿnā al-ḥadīth* means we pulled the conversation back and forth between us. From this comes *nizāʿ al-mayyit*, the death throes. *Nazaʿa ilā kadhā* means he inclined toward it and was drawn to it. Then the word is used figuratively for removal: one says "God *nazaʿa* evil from him," meaning He removed it.

**Walaja, yalij, wulūjan, walj, walajān (wa-wlijja):** to enter. *Walaja* has the forms *tawallaja* and *ittalaja*. The poet said:

*Indeed the rhymes (al-qawāfī) slip in as hidden passages (mawālij),*
*so narrow that the needle cannot pass through them.*

**Al-amad:** the limit or endpoint of a thing. Its plural is *āmād*.

**Allāhumma:** this is Allah, except that it is restricted to the vocative and is not used otherwise. According to the Basrans, the *mīm* attached to it is a substitute for the vocative particle, which is why it is not preceded by anything except in cases of poetic necessity. According to al-Farrāʾ, the *mīm* comes from the phrase *yā Allāh, umminnā bi-khayr* ("O Allah, grant us well"). The grammarians have rejected this accusative construction. The word became so frequently used that they dropped the *alif-lām* from it and said *lā humma*, meaning *allāhumma*. The poet al-Zājir said:

*O lā humma, I am ʿĀmir ibn Jahm,*
*who has entered the state of iḥrām for ḥajj in greasy garments.*

In some dialects its *mīm* is lightened, as in the verse:

*Like an oath from Abū Riyāḥ,*
*which the great ones (al-kubār) hear as "allāhum."*

**Al-ṣadr:** the chest, a known thing. Its plural is *ṣudūr*.

**"Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Book" (Q 3:23).** Al-Suddī said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) invited the Jews to Islam. Al-Nuʿmān ibn Abī Awfā said to him: 'Come, let us bring our dispute before the rabbis.' He said: 'Rather, [bring it] to the Book of Allah.' He said: 'Rather, to the rabbis.'" So this was revealed. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) entered the houses of study (al-madāris) of the Jews and invited them to Allah. Nuʿaym ibn ʿAmr and al-Ḥārith ibn Zayd said: 'Upon what religion are you, O Muḥammad?' He said: 'Upon the religion of Ibrāhīm.' They said: 'Ibrāhīm was a Jew.' He said: 'Then come to the Torah.' They refused him," and so this was revealed. Al-Kalbī said: "A man among them committed adultery with a woman, and at that time stoning was not yet in our religion. So they referred the matter to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), seeking leniency for the two adulterers because of their nobility. He said: 'I only judge by your Book.' They denied stoning, so the Torah was brought. Their rabbi, Ibn Ṣūriyā, placed his hand over the verse of stoning. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām said: 'He has passed over it, O Messenger of Allah.' So he uncovered it, and they were stoned."

Al-Naqqāsh said: it was revealed concerning a group of Jews who denied his prophethood, and he said to them: "Come to the Torah, for in it is my description." Muqātil said: a group of Jews was invited to Islam, and they said: "We have more right to guidance than you, and Allah has sent no prophet except from the Children of Israel." He said: "Bring out the Torah, for it is written in it that I am a prophet." They refused, and so this was revealed. "Those who were given a portion of the Book" are the Jews, and "the Book" is the Torah.

Makkī and others said: it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ). It was also said that *min al-kitāb* is a genus referring to the revealed books. This was stated by Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, and al-Zamakhsharī began with it. *Min* is partitive (tabʿīḍ). In His saying *naṣīban*, meaning a part, it implies only part of the Book, since they did not memorize it and did not know all of what is in it.

**"Who are invited to the Book of Allah" (Q 3:23).** The Book here is the Torah. Al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, and Ibn Jurayj said it is the Qur'an. *Yudʿawna* is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to *alladhīna*, and the governing verb is *tara*. The meaning is: "Do you not marvel at these people who are invited to the Book of Allah?" That is, in the state of being invited to the Book of Allah. **"That it may judge between them"**: that is, that the Book may judge. Al-Ḥasan, Abū Jaʿfar, and ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī read *liyuḥkama* in the passive voice. The matter judged concerning them is what was mentioned in the occasion of revelation.

**"Then a party of them turns away" (Q 3:23).** This is an expression of astonishment at their turning away after they have knowledge, since returning to the Book of Allah is obligatory. The turning away is attributed to "a party of them" and not to all of those addressed, because some of them accepted Islam and did not turn away, such as Ibn Salām and others.

**"While they are refusing" (Q 3:23).** This clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) that emphasizes, since turning away is refusal. Or it clarifies that the turning away is from the one who invites and the refusal is from what he invites to, so the object differs. Or it clarifies that the turning away is with the body and the refusal is with the heart. Or the turning away is from their scholars and the refusal is from their followers, as stated by Ibn al-Anbārī. Or it is a resumed sentence (jumlah mustaʾnafah) informing about them that they are a people for whom turning away from the truth and from its followers is a continuous habit and custom. In His saying *baynahum* ("between them") is evidence that the dispute was among them, not between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This contradicts what was mentioned in the occasions of revelation. If one of those occasions is authentic, the meaning is: "that He may judge between them and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." If none is authentic, it is understood as the disagreement occurring among those of their rabbis who accepted Islam and those who did not accept it. So they were invited to the Torah, about whose authenticity there is no disagreement among you, so that it might judge between the one who is right and the one who is wrong. Then whoever did not accept Islam turned away.

It was said: in this verse is evidence for the validity of the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because if they had not known what he claimed in their books concerning his description and the validity of his prophethood, they would not have turned away and hurried to oppose what is in their books, until they were exposed for the falsehood of his claim. In it is also evidence that whoever is called by his opponent to a just judgment must respond to him, because he has been called to the Book of Allah. This is supported by His saying: **"And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger that He may judge between them, behold, a party of them turns away"** (Q 24:48).

Al-Qurṭubī said: when someone is called to the Book of Allah and opposes it, it becomes obligatory to restrain him with discipline in proportion to the one who opposes and the one who is opposed. This ruling applies among us in al-Andalus and the lands of the Maghrib, but not in the Egyptian territories. Ibn Khuwayzimandād the Mālikī said: it is obligatory for one who is called to the court of judgment to respond, unless he knows that the judge is a sinner (fāsiq).

**"That is because they said: The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days" (Q 3:24).** The demonstrative *dhālika* refers to the turning away. That is: that turning away is caused by these false statements, by their making the punishment easy for themselves, and by their hope of leaving the Fire after a few days. Al-Zamakhsharī said: as the Jabriyyah and the Ḥashwiyyah hoped.

**"And their deception in their religion by what they used to fabricate" (Q 3:24).** That is, [their deception] by the claim that their forefathers, the prophets, would intercede for them. This is like how those (the Muʿtazilah?) were deceived by the intercession of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for their major sins. This is the end of his words. He is, as is his habit, persistent in reviling the People of the Sunnah and the Community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jamāʿah), accusing them of anthropomorphism, and attacking them by any means he can.

The explanation of these numbered days has already been given in Sūrat al-Baqarah, so it is not necessary to repeat it here. However, there it came as *maʿdūdah*, and here as *maʿdūdāt*. Both are eloquent forms. You say "*jibāl shāmikhah*" and "*jibāl shāmikhāt*." You may treat the adjective of a broken plural of a masculine non-rational noun sometimes as an adjective for a feminine singular, and sometimes as an adjective for feminine plurals. Just as you say "*nisāʾ qāʾimāt*," so too you say "*jibāl rāsiyāt*," and this is a regular, consistent pattern.

**"And their deception in their religion by what they used to fabricate" (Q 3:24).** Mujāhid said: what they fabricated is their saying: "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days." Qatādah said: it is their saying: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved." It was also said: "No one will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian" (Q 2:111). It was also said: it is all of these sayings together.

*Dhālika* is in the nominative as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and *bi-annahum* is the predicate (khabar). The meaning is: that turning away and refusal belongs to them and is established by the cause of this saying, which is their claim that the Fire will touch them only for a few days, a small number that can be counted. It was also said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "their condition is that," that is, the turning away and refusal. This was stated by al-Zajjāj. According to this, *bi-annahum* is in the position of a ḥāl, meaning accompanied by this saying. The *mā* in *mā kānū* is either a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah) or a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah).

**"Then how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt" (Q 3:25).** This is an expression of wonder at their condition and an exaggeration of the greatness of their statement, since their hopes have diverged and the falsehood of their claim has become clear. They have come to a punishment for which they have no means of repelling it, as He, Exalted, said: **"Those are their wishful thinkings"** (Q 2:111). This expression is used to magnify the condition of a thing, as in: "How, then, when the angels take their souls?" The poet said:

*How then (for) a soul, whenever I said it had risen to recovery,*
*from a wound of Dahmāʾ its healing was broken.*

He also said:

*How then, when each one cannot pass beyond his appointed time,*
*and no man is delayed from what Allah has decreed?*

For **"fa-kayfa,"** it was said that it is in the accusative as a ḥāl, and the estimated meaning is: "How do they act?" Al-Ḥūfī estimated it as: "How will their condition be?" If he meant the complete (tāmmah) form of *kāna*, then it is in the accusative position as a ḥāl. If it is the incomplete (nāqiṣah) form, then it is in the accusative position as the predicate of *kāna*. The better view is that it is in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject, which the meaning indicates. The estimate is: "How is their condition?" The governing element for *idhā* is the verb that he estimated. The governing element for *kayfa*, when it is the predicate of the subject, if we say its accusative is the accusative of adverbs (ẓurūf), is the omitted subject we estimated, meaning: "How is their condition at that time?" If we say it is a noun other than an adverb, then the governing element for *idhā* is the omitted subject we estimated. This interrogative does not require an answer, and neither do most interrogatives in the Qur'an, because they belong to the realm of the observable (ʿālam al-shahādah). The interrogation of Allah, exalted is He, is a rebuke.

The *lām* in **"liyawmin"** is connected to *jamaʿnāhum*. The meaning is: "for the judgment of a day and its recompense," as in His saying: **"Indeed You are the gatherer of mankind for a Day"** (Q 3:9). Al-Naqqāsh said: "the Day" here means a time, and likewise **"numbered days"** and **"in two days"** (Q 2:203) and **"in four days"** (Q 41:10) are expressions for periods of time. Days and nights are only in this world according to us. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the correct view regarding the Day of Resurrection is that it is a day, because before it there is a night and in it there is a sun.

The meaning of **"about which there is no doubt"** is: in the reality of the matter, or according to the believer, or according to the one who informs about it, or at the time He gathers them in it. Or its meaning is "the matter," and there are five views.

**"And every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged" (Q 3:25).** The explanation of something like this has already been given in Sūrat al-Baqarah, at the end of the verses on usury.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 23–25 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Say: O Allah, Master of the kingdom﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. Al-Kalbi said: A rock appeared in the trench, and the Prophet (ﷺ) struck it, and a spark flashed, and he said "Allahu akbar." He did the same a second and a third time, and said: "With the first, the palaces of Persia were shown to me; with the second, the palaces of Rome; and with the third, the palaces of Yemen. Gabriel (peace be upon him) informed me that my community will prevail over all of them." The hypocrites mocked him, saying that he strikes with a pickaxe and digs the trench out of fear, and that he longs for the kingdom of Persia and Rome. Then this was revealed. Al-Sijawandi abridged it in this form, and it is a very lengthy occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul).

Ibn Abbas said: When Mecca was conquered, it weighed heavily on the polytheists, and they feared the conquest of the non-Arabs ('ajam). Abdullah ibn Ubayy said: "They are stronger and more powerful." Then this was revealed. Ibn Abbas and Anas said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) conquered Mecca, he promised his community the kingdom of Persia and Rome, and then this was revealed. It is also said: This reached the Jews, and they said: "Far-fetched, far-fetched!" Then this was revealed, and they were humiliated and sought a truce. Al-Hasan said: The Prophet (ﷺ) asked for the kingdom of Persia and Rome for his community, and this was revealed in the form of a prohibition. Something similar is narrated from Qatada, that this was mentioned to him. Abu Muslim al-Dimashqi said: The Jews said: "By Allah, we will not obey a man who has transferred prophethood from the Children of Israel to others." Then this was revealed. It is also said: It was revealed as a refutation of the Christians of Najran in their saying that 'Isa is Allah, though there is nothing in him of these attributes.

Here, the apparent meaning of "kingdom" (mulk) is authority and dominance, and the occasions of revelation accord with this interpretation. Mujahid said: "Kingdom" means prophethood, and this fits with Abu Muslim's account of the occasion of revelation. It is also said: it means wealth and slaves; and it is said: it means this world and the Hereafter.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Master of the servants and of what they possess." Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, "the possession of the genus of kingship," so that You dispose of it as owners dispose of what they own. Ibn Atiyya said the same. He spoke about the word "Allahumma" from the standpoint of grammar, and said: They agreed that its *h* is pronounced with a *damma* and its *m* is doubled and fatha-vowelled, and that it is a vocative (munada). The claim of consensus about doubling the *m* is not accurate, for al-Farra' transmitted that in some dialects its *m* is pronounced light (single). He said: Some have recited:

*Like the cry of Abu Riyah, which the great ones hear as "Allahumm."*

The one who refuted him said: Lightening the *m* is a gross error, especially according to al-Farra', because according to him it is the *m* of "ummana" (our mother), since the lightened form cannot allow that the *m* is a remnant of "ummana." He said: The correct narration is "*which the great ones hear as* lāhuhu" (his god). If this line is genuinely from the Arabs, there is another anomaly in it, in that it is used outside of the vocative. Do you not see that he made it the subject (fā'il) of the verb preceding it in this line? Abu Raja' al-Utaridi said: This letter *m* comprises seventy of His names. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: Whoever says "Allahumma" has called upon Allah with all of His names together. Al-Hasan said: "Allahumma" is the gathering-place of supplication.

The meaning of al-Nadr's statement is that "Allahumma" is "Allah," with an *m* added to it. It is thus the proper name that includes all the attributes of His essence, because when you say "Zayd has come," you have mentioned a specific name, which comprises all of his attributes that are in him: whether fair complexion, height, generosity, courage, or their opposites, and whatever is similar to that.

The accusative of "Master of the kingdom" is as a second vocative, meaning: "O Master of the kingdom." According to Sibawayh, "Allahumma" is not described by an adjective. Abu al-'Abbas and Abu Ishaq permitted it to be described by an adjective, so that it is an adjective of "Allahumm" according to them. This is a disputed issue discussed in the science of grammar (nahw).

﴿You give the kingdom to whom You will and You take the kingdom away from whom You will﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. The apparent meaning of "kingdom" is authority and dominance, just as the apparent meaning of the first "kingdom" is the same, so the first is general and these two are specific. The meaning is: You give some portion of the kingdom to whom You will, and You take some portion of the kingdom away from whom You will. Here "kingdom" has also been interpreted as prophethood, but this interpretation cannot apply to "You take away the kingdom," because Allah does not give prophethood to someone and then take it away from him, unless "take away" is used metaphorically in the sense of "withhold prophethood from whom You will," and then it is possible.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: It is dominion over the self and restraining it from following desire. It is also said: well-being; and it is said: contentment. It is said: dominance through religion and obedience. It is said: standing in prayer at night. Al-Shibli said: It is self-sufficiency through the Originator from the two worlds. Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya said: It is the subjugation of Iblis, just as he would flee from the shadow of Umar; and the opposite of this is one from whom Satan flows like blood. It is said: It is the kingdom of knowledge without a cause, as it came to the magicians of Pharaoh, and it was taken from Bal'am. Abu Uthman said: It is the granting of faith's success.

If we take it in its most apparent sense, which is sovereignty and dominance, and the one given it is the commanded and followed one, then the one to whom Allah gave the kingdom is Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, and those from whom it was taken are Persia and Rome. It is said: The one from whom it was taken is Abu Jahl and the chiefs of Quraysh. It is said: The Arabs and the caliphs of Islam and its kings are meant, and what was taken is Persia and Rome. Al-Suddi said: The prophets: the people were commanded to obey them; and what was taken from them are the tyrants, whom the people were commanded to oppose. It is said: Adam and his offspring, and what was taken from them is Iblis and his armies. It is said: David (peace be upon him), and what was taken from him was Talut. It is said: Sakhr, and what was taken from him was Sulayman during his trial. It is said: The meaning is that He gives the kingdom in Paradise to whom He wills, and takes away the kingdom from the kings of this world in the Hereafter from whom He wills. It is said: The kingdom is seclusion and withdrawal, and they named it "the unknown kingdom." These are confused opinions and particularizations for which nothing in the speech indicates; the better view is that it should be understood as an example and not as an exhaustive specification of what is meant.

﴿And You exalt whom You will and You abase whom You will﴾ [Al 'Imran: 26]. It is said: Muhammad (ﷺ) and his companions, when they entered Mecca, twelve thousand strong, prevailing over it; and He humbled Abu Jahl and the chiefs of Quraysh, until their heads were cut off and they were thrown into the well. It is said: exaltation is by success and recognition, and abasement is by forsaking. Ata' said: exaltation is for the Muhajirun and the Ansar, and abasement is for Persia and Rome. It is said: exaltation is by obedience, and abasement is by disobedience. It is said: exaltation is by victory and spoils, and abasement is by killing and the poll-tax (jizya). It is said: exaltation is by sincerity, and abasement is by showing off. It is said: exaltation is by wealth, and abasement is by poverty. It is said: exaltation is by Paradise and the vision (of Allah), and abasement is by the veil and the Fire; this was said by al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl. It is said: exaltation is by subduing the self, and abasement is by following disgrace; this was said by al-Warraq. It is said: exaltation is by subduing Satan, and abasement is by Satan's subduing of him; this was said by al-Kattani. It is said: exaltation is by contentment and satisfaction, and abasement is by greed and covetousness.

These statements should be understood as examples, because there is no specifier in the verse. Rather, what exaltation and abasement are brought about by is left unstated. The Mu'tazila (the Mu'tazilites) have a discourse here that contradicts the discourse of the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna). Al-Ka'bi said: He gives the kingdom by way of entitlement to whoever establishes it, and He takes it away only from one who has committed wickedness (fisq). This is indicated by ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqara: 124], and ﴿Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you﴾ [al-Baqara: 247], where He made being chosen a cause of kingship. So it is not permissible that the kingship of wrongdoers is by Allah's giving it, though it may happen; and He has obligated them (p-٤٢٠) not to possess it. Thus it is established that the just kings are the ones specifically granted kingship by Allah, but the wrongdoers are not. As for taking away, it is the opposite: just as He takes it away from the just person for a reason, He may also take it away from the wrongdoer.

Qadi Abd al-Jabbar said: Exaltation attributed to Him, Exalted is He, occurs in religion through supporting with divine graces (alṭāf), praising them, and their dominance over enemies; and it occurs in the world through wealth and the granting of awe. The noblest kind of honor in religion is faith, and the most humiliating of things that cause humiliation is disbelief. So if the attainment of faith and disbelief came from the servant, then the servant's exalting himself by faith and his abasing himself by disbelief would be greater than Allah's exalting him and abasing him; and if that were so, his share of this attribute would be more complete than His share, glory be to Him, and that is absolutely false.

Al-Jubba'i said: He abases His enemies in this world and the Hereafter, and He does not abase His friends even if He makes them poor, sickens them, frightens them, or brings them to other needs, because that is for their honor in the Hereafter through reward or compensation. It is like bloodletting, which causes pain in the moment and yields benefit afterward. He said: The description of poverty as abasement is figurative, like His saying ﴿humble toward the believers﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 54]. And Allah's abasing of the falsifiers occurs in various ways: by blame and curse; by their being left without argument or support; by making them spoils for the people of His religion; and by their punishment in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 26–27 (part 1 of 2):

﴿In Your hand is the good.﴾ That is: by Your power and decree the good comes to be. The existence of a hand in the sense of a bodily limb is impossible for God, exalted is He. It has been said: the meaning is "and the evil," as in ﴿He protects you from the heat﴾, meaning "and the cold." Omitting the coordinated term is permissible when the meaning is understood, since one of two opposites implies the other. God has mentioned the giving of sovereignty and its removal, and the granting of honour and the bringing of humiliation, and that is good for some people and evil for others. Therefore the implied meaning is: "In Your hand is the good and the evil." Then He concluded with His saying ﴿Indeed You are over all things competent﴾, so this general statement, which includes the attributes mentioned earlier, came in, and it encompasses the goods and the evils. Mentioning only the good is a teaching for us on how to praise: by mentioning the best of qualities.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, how did He say ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾, mentioning the good without the evil? I answer: because the discourse was concerned with the good that He bestows upon the believers, and that is what the disbelievers denied. So He said ﴿In Your hand is the good﴾, You give it to Your allies in spite of Your enemies. And because all of God's acts, whether beneficial or harmful, proceed from wisdom and benefit, so all of it is good." End of his words. But his final statement contradicts his first, because in the question he asked why He mentioned only the good and not the evil.

He answered with the first answer, which indicates that the good and the evil are in His hand, and that the restriction to the good was because the discourse concerned what He bestows of good upon the believers, so restricting the mention to the good alone was appropriate. He answered with the second answer, which indicates that all of His acts are good, with nothing evil in them, and this answer contradicts the first.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He singled out the good for mention, though everything is in His hand, because the verse has the sense of supplication and desire. So the meaning is: "In Your hand is the good, so grant me abundantly of it."

Al-Raghib said: Since the context is praise and thanks, not judgment, He mentioned the good, since it is what is thanked for.

Al-Razi said: The word "the good" has the definite article ال, which indicates generality. The fronting of "in Your hand" indicates exclusivity, so it indicates that there is no good except by His hand. The best of goods is faith, so it must be by God's creation. Also, the agent of the most noble is most noble, and faith is most noble.

﴿You cause the night to enter into the day and You cause the day to enter into the night.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that what is lost from the day is added to the night, and what is lost from the night is added to the day, in continuous succession for each season of the year. It has been said: until the shorter reaches nine hours and the longer fifteen hours. One of our contemporaries mentioned: the people of astronomy agree that the increase of night and day, by each taking thirty degrees from the other, results in the increase of the night over the day reaching fourteen hours, and likewise the reverse. Al-Mawardi mentioned that the meaning of "entering" here is the covering of the night by the day when the day comes, and the covering of the day by the night when the night comes, so the becoming of each of them within the time of the other is like entering into it. Ibn ʿAtiyyah put forward this view as a possibility, saying: "The wording of the verse may include the alternation of night and day, and the departure of one is the entering of the other."

﴿You bring the living out of the dead and You bring the dead out of the living.﴾ The meaning of "bringing out" here is "creating." Literally, bringing out is removing a thing from a container. Ibn Masʿud, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibrahim, al-Suddi, Ismaʿil ibn Abi Khalid, and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: it means bringing an animal out of a drop of semen, which is dead when the drop separates from the animal, and bringing the drop, which is dead, out of a man who is alive. On this view, "death" is metaphorical, since the drop never had life before, and the meaning is: You bring the living out of what life does not inhabit, and You bring what life does not inhabit out of the living. "Bringing out" is an expression for a change of state.

ʿIkrimah and al-Kalbi said: that is, the chick out of the egg, and the egg out of the bird. Here too death is metaphorical and bringing out is literal. Abu Malik said: the palm tree out of the date-stone, the ear of grain out of the seed, the date-stone out of the palm tree, and the seed out of the ear of grain; and life and death in this are metaphorical. Al-Hasan said, and something similar is narrated from Salman al-Farisi: You bring the believer out of the disbeliever and the disbeliever out of the believer; these too are metaphorical. In a hadith: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Glory be to God, who brings the living out of the dead," and he saw a righteous woman whose father had died a disbeliever; she was Khalidah bint al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth.

Al-Zajjaj said: He brings out tender, fresh vegetation from the seed, and He brings the dry seed out of living vegetation. It has been said: the good out of the evil, and the evil out of the good. Al-Mawardi said: It is possible that it means: He brings the clever, intelligent person out of the dull, incapable one, and the reverse, because intelligence is the life of perception and dullness is its death. It has been said: He brings wisdom out of the heart of the wicked, because it does not settle in it, and a slip out of the tongue of the knowledgeable one. All these are distant metaphors.

The more evident meaning of His saying ﴿the living out of the dead﴾ is the imagining of two things. It has been said that by this He meant one thing in which the state changes, so that it is dead and then lives, and living and then dies, like your saying: "There came from so-and-so a lion." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The majority of scholars held that life and death here are both literal, with no metaphor in them, and then they differed about the example by which they explained it. He mentioned the statement of Ibn Masʿud and the statement of ʿIkrimah mentioned above, and that in those cases it is not possible to take it literally at all, and likewise with death.

Hafs, Nafiʿ, Hamzah and al-Kisaʾi read al-mayyit (with shaddah on the yaʾ) in this verse. In al-Anʿam, al-Aʿraf, Yunus, al-Rum and Fatir, Nafiʿ additionally read the shaddah on the yaʾ in ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life﴾ [al-Anʿam 6:122] in al-Anʿam, in ﴿a dead land﴾ [Yasin 36:33] in Yasin, and in ﴿the flesh of his dead brother﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:12] in al-Hujurat. The rest read these without the shaddah. There is no difference between the shaddah and its absence in usage, just as you say layyin and layn, and hayyin and hayn. Whoever claims that the unshaddah form is for what has died, and the shaddah form is for what has died and what has not yet died, needs proof.

﴿You provide for whom You will without account.﴾ Its like has been explained earlier in His saying ﴿God provides for whom He wills without account﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:37], and ﴿Mankind were one community﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:213], so repeating it here is unnecessary.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He mentioned His dazzling power. He mentioned the state of night and day in their alternation, and the state of the living and the dead in the bringing out of one from the other, and He conjoined with it His provision without account, as an indication that whoever is able to do those mighty acts, which bewilder minds, and then is able to provide without account for whomever He wills among His servants, is able to remove sovereignty from the non-Arabs and humble them, and to give it to the Arabs and honour them. End of his words. It is good.

It has been said: these verses contain kinds of eloquence, rhetoric and figurative embellishment. The interrogative whose meaning is wonder in ﴿Have you not seen those who﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:23]. The reference in ﴿a share of the Book﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:23]: the insertion of min (of) indicates that they had not comprehended the Torah in knowledge or in memorisation, and this is an indication of belittling them, diminishing their status and blaming them, since they claim that they are the good and they are the opposite of that. In His saying ﴿That is because they﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:24] there is an indication of their turning away and aversion, whose cause was their fabrication. In ﴿and every soul will be paid in full﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:25] there is an indication that the recompense for their deeds is not diminished in any way.

Repetition occurs in ﴿a share of the Book﴾ and ﴿they are called to the Book of God﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:23], either in both wording and meaning if the referent is one, or in wording only if the referent differs. Likewise in "turning away" and "aversion" if they have one meaning. In ﴿Owner of sovereignty﴾, ﴿You give sovereignty﴾, and ﴿You remove sovereignty﴾, the repetition in sentences serves to magnify and exalt, if the intended meaning is one; if it differs, it is repetition of wording only. There is also the repetition of ﴿whom You will﴾, in ﴿You cause to enter﴾, in ﴿You bring out﴾, and in their two objects.

There is the extension of using fi (in) to mean ʿala (upon), according to the view of one who claims this in His saying ﴿You cause the night to enter into the day﴾, meaning "upon the day," and ﴿You cause the day to enter into the night﴾, meaning "upon the night."

The term "entering" (al-iyla) is used as an expression for elevation and covering. The negation that implies a command in ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:25], according to al-Zajjaj's view, means: "Do not doubt in it." There is paronomasia (tajnis) of the similar kind in ﴿Owner of sovereignty﴾; antithesis (tibaq) in "You give" and "You remove," "You honour" and "You humble," in night and day, and in living and dead. There is the return of the final part to the beginning (radd al-ʿajz ʿala al-sadr) in "You cause to enter" and what follows it. There is ellipsis (hadhf), which in several places is such that understanding the discourse depends on supplying it, as in His saying ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾, meaning "to whom You will to give it." There is metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi) in ﴿that He may judge between them﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:23], where judgment is attributed to the Book, because it makes the rulings clear, so it is the cause of the judgment.

It is narrated in a hadith: "Whoever wants to pay off his debt should recite every day: ﴿Say: O God, Owner of sovereignty﴾ until ﴿without account,﴾ and say: 'O Merciful of this world and the next, and Compassionate to both, You give from both to whom You will: settle my debt for me.' Even if it were as much gold as fills the earth, God would pay it."

﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies, rather than the believers﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:28]. It has been said: it was revealed concerning ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit, who had allies among the Jews, and he wanted to gain support from them against the enemy. It has been said: it was concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, who used to befriend the Jews. It has been said: it was concerning a group of Jews, namely al-Hajjaj ibn ʿAmr, Kahmas ibn Abi al-Huqayq, and Qays ibn Yazid, who used to secretly associate with a group of the Ansar, tempting them away from their religion; a group of Muslims forbade them and said: "Avoid these Jews," but they refused, so it was revealed. These statements are reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. It has been said: it was concerning Hatib ibn Balta'ah and others who used to show affection toward the disbelievers of Quraysh, so it was revealed.

The meaning of taking them as allies is showing kindness to them in companionship, whether because of kinship or friendship before Islam, or because of a previous favour, or otherwise. This, as it appears, is what they were forbidden from. As for taking them into one's heart and intention, a believer does not do that. The ones addressed here were already established in faith, so the prohibition here means only the prohibition of showing kindness to them and inclining toward them. Kindness is general in all ages, and this has been repeated in the Qur'an.

What suffices in this regard is His exalted saying: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in God and the Last Day loving those who oppose God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadilah 58:22], and the love for God and hatred for God are a great foundation of the principles of the religion. The majority read ﴿Let not take﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:28] in the jussive as a prohibition. al-Daba'i read it with a damma on the dhal, as a negation whose meaning is a prohibition, and al-Kisa'i permitted the damma as in the reading of al-Daba'i.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it: when He mentioned what the believer must hold of exalting God and praising Him by the acts that are peculiar to Him, He mentioned what the believer must do in dealing with creation. The preceding verses concerned the disbelievers, so they were forbidden from allying with them, and were commanded to desire what is with Him and with His allies rather than His enemies, since He, exalted is He, is the Owner of sovereignty.

The apparent meaning of the verse requires the prohibition of allying with them, except what has been permitted to us of it: taking them as slaves, seeking help from them as the mighty seeks help from the lowly, the higher from the lower, and marrying among them. All of this is a kind of alliance (p. 423) that we have been permitted, and we are not prohibited from it. So the prohibition is not general.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 26–27 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Rather than the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28]. The explanation of "min dun" (from besides/apart from) has already been given in His saying, ﴿And call your witnesses, apart from Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], so there is no need to repeat it here.

"Yattakhidh" (take, adopt) here is transitive to two objects. "Min dun" is connected to the verb "la yattakhidh" (let not take). The "min" is for the starting point of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: That is, do not make the starting point of allegiance (wilayah) from a place other than the place of the believers.

On this view, "death" is metaphorical, since the drop never had life before, and the meaning is: You bring the living out of what life does not inhabit, and You bring what life does not inhabit out of the living. "Bringing out" is an expression for a change of state.

ʿIkrimah and al-Kalbi said: that is, the chick out of the egg, and the egg out of the bird. Here too death is metaphorical and bringing out is literal. Abu Malik said: the palm tree out of the date-stone, the ear of grain out of the seed, the date-stone out of the palm tree, and the seed out of the ear of grain; and life and death in this are metaphorical. Al-Hasan said, and something similar is narrated from Salman al-Farisi: You bring the believer out of the disbeliever and the disbeliever out of the believer; these too are metaphorical. In a hadith: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Glory be to God, who brings the living out of the dead," and he saw a righteous woman whose father had died a disbeliever; she was Khalidah bint al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth.

Al-Zajjaj said: He brings out tender, fresh vegetation from the seed, and He brings the dry seed out of living vegetation. It has been said: the good out of the evil, and the evil out of the good. Al-Mawardi said: It is possible that it means: He brings the clever, intelligent person out of the dull, incapable one, and the reverse, because intelligence is the life of perception and dullness is its death. It has been said: He brings wisdom out of the heart of the wicked, because it does not settle in it, and a slip out of the tongue of the knowledgeable one. All these are distant metaphors.

The more evident meaning of His saying ﴿the living out of the dead﴾ is the imagining of two things. It has been said that by this He meant one thing in which the state changes, so that it is dead and then lives, and living and then dies, like your saying: "There came from so-and-so a lion." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The majority of scholars held that life and death here are both literal, with no metaphor in them, and then they differed about the example by which they explained it. He mentioned the statement of Ibn Masʿud and the statement of ʿIkrimah mentioned above, and that in those cases it is not possible to take it literally at all, and likewise with death.

Hafs, Nafiʿ, Hamzah and al-Kisaʾi read al-mayyit (with shaddah on the yaʾ) in this verse. In al-Anʿam, al-Aʿraf, Yunus, al-Rum and Fatir, Nafiʿ additionally read the shaddah on the yaʾ in ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life﴾ [al-Anʿam 6:122] in al-Anʿam, in ﴿a dead land﴾ [Yasin 36:33] in Yasin, and in ﴿the flesh of his dead brother﴾ [al-Hujurat 49:12] in al-Hujurat. The rest read these without the shaddah. There is no difference between the shaddah and its absence in usage, just as you say layyin and layn, and hayyin and hayn. Whoever claims that the unshaddah form is for what has died, and the shaddah form is for what has died and what has not yet died, needs proof.

﴿You provide for whom You will without account.﴾ Its like has been explained earlier in His saying ﴿God provides for whom He wills without account﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:37], and ﴿Mankind were one community﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:213], so repeating it here is unnecessary.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He mentioned His dazzling power. He mentioned the state of night and day in their alternation, and the state of the living and the dead in the bringing out of one from the other, and He conjoined with it His provision without account, as an indication that whoever is able to do those mighty acts, which bewilder minds, and then is able to provide without account for whomever He wills among His servants, is able to remove sovereignty from the non-Arabs and humble them, and to give it to the Arabs and honour them. End of his words. It is good.

It has been said: these verses contain kinds of eloquence, rhetoric and figurative embellishment. The interrogative whose meaning is wonder in ﴿Have you not seen those who﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:23]. The reference in ﴿a share of the Book﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:23]: the insertion of min (of) indicates that they had not comprehended the Torah in knowledge or in memorisation, and this is an indication of belittling them, diminishing their status and blaming them, since they claim that they are the good and they are the opposite of that. In His saying ﴿That is because they﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:24] there is an indication of their turning away and aversion, whose cause was their fabrication. In ﴿and every soul will be paid in full﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:25] there is an indication that the recompense for their deeds is not diminished in any way.

Repetition occurs in ﴿a share of the Book﴾ and ﴿they are called to the Book of God﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:23], either in both wording and meaning if the referent is one, or in wording only if the referent differs. Likewise in "turning away" and "aversion" if they have one meaning. In ﴿Owner of sovereignty﴾, ﴿You give sovereignty﴾, and ﴿You remove sovereignty﴾, the repetition in sentences serves to magnify and exalt, if the intended meaning is one; if it differs, it is repetition of wording only. There is also the repetition of ﴿whom You will﴾, in ﴿You cause to enter﴾, in ﴿You bring out﴾, and in their two objects.

There is the extension of using fi (in) to mean ʿala (upon), according to the view of one who claims this in His saying ﴿You cause the night to enter into the day﴾, meaning "upon the day," and ﴿You cause the day to enter into the night﴾, meaning "upon the night."

The term "entering" (al-iyla) is used as an expression for elevation and covering. The negation that implies a command in ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:25], according to al-Zajjaj's view, means: "Do not doubt in it." There is paronomasia (tajnis) of the similar kind in ﴿Owner of sovereignty﴾; antithesis (tibaq) in "You give" and "You remove," "You honour" and "You humble," in night and day, and in living and dead. There is the return of the final part to the beginning (radd al-ʿajz ʿala al-sadr) in "You cause to enter" and what follows it. There is ellipsis (hadhf), which in several places is such that understanding the discourse depends on supplying it, as in His saying ﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will﴾, meaning "to whom You will to give it." There is metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi) in ﴿that He may judge between them﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:23], where judgment is attributed to the Book, because it makes the rulings clear, so it is the cause of the judgment.

It is narrated in a hadith: "Whoever wants to pay off his debt should recite every day: ﴿Say: O God, Owner of sovereignty﴾ until ﴿without account,﴾ and say: 'O Merciful of this world and the next, and Compassionate to both, You give from both to whom You will: settle my debt for me.' Even if it were as much gold as fills the earth, God would pay it."

﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies, rather than the believers﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:28]. It has been said: it was revealed concerning ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit, who had allies among the Jews, and he wanted to gain support from them against the enemy. It has been said: it was concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, who used to befriend the Jews. It has been said: it was concerning a group of Jews, namely al-Hajjaj ibn ʿAmr, Kahmas ibn Abi al-Huqayq, and Qays ibn Yazid, who used to secretly associate with a group of the Ansar, tempting them away from their religion; a group of Muslims forbade them and said: "Avoid these Jews," but they refused, so it was revealed. These statements are reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. It has been said: it was concerning Hatib ibn Balta'ah and others who used to show affection toward the disbelievers of Quraysh, so it was revealed.

The meaning of taking them as allies is showing kindness to them in companionship, whether because of kinship or friendship before Islam, or because of a previous favour, or otherwise. This, as it appears, is what they were forbidden from. As for taking them into one's heart and intention, a believer does not do that. The ones addressed here were already established in faith, so the prohibition here means only the prohibition of showing kindness to them and inclining toward them. Kindness is general in all ages, and this has been repeated in the Qur'an.

What suffices in this regard is His exalted saying: ﴿You will not find a people who believe in God and the Last Day loving those who oppose God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Mujadilah 58:22], and the love for God and hatred for God are a great foundation of the principles of the religion. The majority read ﴿Let not take﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:28] in the jussive as a prohibition. al-Daba'i read it with a damma on the dhal, as a negation whose meaning is a prohibition, and al-Kisa'i permitted the damma as in the reading of al-Daba'i.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it: when He mentioned what the believer must hold of exalting God and praising Him by the acts that are peculiar to Him, He mentioned what the believer must do in dealing with creation. The preceding verses concerned the disbelievers, so they were forbidden from allying with them, and were commanded to desire what is with Him and with His allies rather than His enemies, since He, exalted is He, is the Owner of sovereignty.

The apparent meaning of the verse requires the prohibition of allying with them, except what has been permitted to us of it: taking them as slaves, seeking help from them as the mighty seeks help from the lowly, the higher from the lower, and marrying among them. All of this is a kind of alliance (p. 423) that we have been permitted, and we are not prohibited from it. So the prohibition is not general.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 26–27 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Rather than the believers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 28]. The explanation of "min dun" (from besides/apart from) has already been given in His saying, ﴿And call your witnesses, apart from Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], so there is no need to repeat it here.

"Yattakhidh" (take, adopt) here is transitive to two objects. "Min dun" is connected to the verb "la yattakhidh" (let not take). The "min" is for the starting point of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: That is, do not make the starting point of allegiance (wilayah) from a place other than the place of the believers.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 28:

﴿Whoever does that has nothing to do with Allah at all.﴾ "That" refers to their taking them as allies (awliya'), and this indicates the extreme emphasis on abandoning loyalty (muwalah), since He negated from the one who takes them as allies that he has anything of Allah. In the sentence there is an elided modifier (mudaf mahdhuf), meaning: "then he has nothing of Allah's guardianship (wilayah)." It was also said: "of His religion." It was said: "of His worship." It was said: "of His party."

The predicate (khabar) of laysa is what the meaning is complete with, namely "fi shay'" (in anything). "Min Allah" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), because if it were postponed it would be an attribute of "shay'." The estimate is: "so he is not in anything of Allah's guardianship." The "min" is partitive (tab'idiyyah), negating Allah's guardianship from one who takes His enemy as an ally, because the two guardianships are mutually exclusive. He said:

*You wish my enemy, then you claim that I am your friend; the folly is not far from you.*

As for the one who likened the verse to the line of al-Nabigha:

*If you attempt against the lion some wickedness, then I am not of you and you are not of me.*

That is not good, because "minka" and "minni" are the predicate of laysa, and the meaning is complete with them. In the verse, the predicate is his saying "fi shay'," so the line is not like the verse. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "*So he has nothing of Allah*" means: "in anything pleasing to Him in perfection and correctness," and this is like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever cheats us is not of us." In the sentence there is an elided modifier, its estimate being: "so he has nothing of drawing near to Allah and seeking closeness." Similar to this is his saying "fi shay'," which is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in His saying "*so he has nothing of Allah*." End of his words. But this is a confused statement, because its estimate, "so he has nothing of drawing near to Allah," requires that "min Allah" not be the predicate of laysa, since it would not then be complete. And his saying "fi shay'" being in the accusative as a circumstantial clause requires that it not be the predicate, leaving "laysa" without a predicate according to his view, and that is not permissible. Comparing it to the saying of the Prophet (peace be upon him), "Whoever cheats us is not of us," is not good, for the difference between it and the verse has been explained in the line of al-Nabigha.

﴿Except when you fear a danger from them﴾ (illa an tattaqu minhum tuqatan). This is an exception derived from the object of purpose (maf'ul lahu); the meaning is: they should not take an unbeliever as an ally for any reason except for the sake of taqiyyah (precautionary dissimulation), so it is permissible to show loyalty by word and deed, without what the heart and inner self hold. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: "The taqiyyah referred to is outward courtesy (mudarah zahirah)." He also said: "It occurs when one is with the unbelievers or among them, so he guards himself with his tongue, while there is no affection for them in his heart." Qatadah said: "When the unbelievers are dominant, or the believers are among an unbelieving people who they fear, then they may make alliances with them and be courteous to them to avert harm, while their hearts remain at peace with faith." Ibn Mas'ud said: "Mix with people, keep company with them, and deal with them in what they desire, but do not damage your religion." Sa'sa'ah ibn Suhan said to Usamah ibn Zayd: "Be sincere to the believer and be courteous to the unbeliever, for the unbeliever is satisfied from you with good character." Al-Sadiq said: "Taqiyyah is obligatory. I hear a man in the mosque insulting me, so I hide from him behind the pillar, lest he see me." He also said: "Showing off before a believer is polytheism, and before a hypocrite it is worship."

Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Mujahid said: "Taqiyyah existed in the early days of Islam, before the religion was firmly established and the Muslims were strong. But today Allah has honored the Muslims so that they need not practice taqiyyah against them, by guarding themselves against their enemy." Al-Hasan said: "Taqiyyah is permissible until the Day of Resurrection, but there is no taqiyyah in killing." Mujahid said: "Except that you guard against severing the ties of kinship, so mix with them in worldly affairs."

In His saying "*except when you fear*" there is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person), for it moves from the third person to the second person. Had it come in the pattern of the first, it would have been: "except that they fear," with the letter ya' dotted from below. This kind of expression is at the height of eloquence, because when the believers were forbidden to do what is not permitted, that prohibition was expressed in the third person, so they were not confronted directly with the prohibition; and when leniency and permission were granted in part of that, they were addressed with it, as a notice of Allah's kindness toward them and an honoring by His address to them.

The majority read *tuqatan*, and its original form is *wuqyatan*; the waw was changed to ta', as they changed it in *tujahin* and *tukahin*, and the ya' became alif because it was vowelled and the letter before it was open. It is a verbal noun on the pattern *fi'lah*, like *tu'dah* and *tukhmah*; and a verbal noun on the pattern *fi'l* or *fi'lah* is rare. It came as a verbal noun not of the regular form, for if it had come on the regular pattern it would have been *ittiqa'* and its like, as in the Exalted saying: "*And devote yourself to Him with complete devotion*" (al-Muzzammil 8), and the poet's saying:

*And there appeared beside the two mountains from him a heap, digging up the earth with digging.*

The meaning is: "except that you fear them with fear." Al-Kisa'i inclined *tuqatan* and *haqqa tuqatihi*, and Hamzah agreed with him here; Warsh read between the two pronunciations, and the rest read with a fatha.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Except that you fear from their side a matter that must be guarded against." It was also read *taqiyyatan*. It was said that the one who guards himself is called *tuqat* and *taqiyyah*, like their saying: "the striking of the commander is for his struck one." End of his words. So he made *tuqatan* a verbal noun in the place of the passive participle, so its accusative is as an object, not as a verbal noun; for this reason he estimated it as "except that you fear a matter." Abu 'Ali said: "It is permissible that *tuqatan*, like *rumatan*, be a circumstantial clause from *tattaqu*, and it is the plural of *fa'il*, even though *fa'il* is not used from it; and it is permissible that it be the plural of *taqiyy*." End of his words.

The circumstantial clause is emphatic, because its meaning has already been understood from His saying "*except that you guard against them*." And allowing it to be a plural is very weak; if it were the plural of *taqiyy* it would be *atqiya'*, like *ghaniyy* and *aghniya'*; and their saying *kamiyy* and *kamah* is anomalous, so it is not to be derived from it. What confirms that it is a verbal noun is His saying: "*Fear Allah with the fear due to Him*" (Al 'Imran 102), meaning "with the fear of guarding." It is fitting that the verbal noun come in this triliteral form, since they have dropped *ittaqa*, so that it became *taqiya, yattaqi, taqi Allah*, and so it became as if it were a verbal noun of a triliteral verb.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Raja', Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Abu Haywah, Ya'qub, Sahl, Humayd ibn Qays, and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read *taqiyyatan*, on the pattern of *matiyyah* and *janiyyah*; it is a verbal noun on the pattern *fa'iliyyah*, which is rare, like *al-namimah*. For it to be from *if'ala* is very rare.

The apparent meaning of the verse permits showing loyalty to them when one fears them. The exegetes spoke here about taqiyyah, since it is connected to the verse. They said: As for loyalty of the heart, there is no disagreement among the Muslims about its prohibition; likewise loyalty by word and deed without taqiyyah. The texts of the Qur'an and the Sunnah indicate this. The consideration of taqiyyah concerns: from whom one guards oneself; what permits it; and with what kinds of words and deeds it may occur. As for from whom: every powerful dominant person who forces one through injustice, so this includes unbelievers, oppressive rulers, highwaymen, and the powerful people of the cities. Malik said: "A woman's husband may also be a source of compulsion." As for what permits it: killing, fear for the limbs, being struck with a whip, threat, and the enmity of oppressive people of influence. As for with what kinds of words: with unbelief or less than it, such as selling, gifting, and other things. As for deeds: every prohibited act.

Masruq said: "If one does not do it until he dies, he enters the Fire," but this is anomalous. A group of the people of knowledge said: taqiyyah occurs in words but not in deeds; this was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak. The companions of Abu Hanifah said: taqiyyah is a concession from Allah the Exalted, and abandoning it is more excellent; so if one is compelled to unbelief and does not do it until he is killed, he is more excellent than one who manifests it, and likewise every matter in which the honor of religion is involved: advancing toward it until one is killed is more excellent than taking the concession. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, when it was said to him, "If you are presented with the sword, will you answer?" said: "No." And he said: "If the scholar answers by taqiyyah, and the ignorant man remains ignorant, then when will the truth become clear?" What has reached us, generation after generation, is that the Companions and their Followers gave up their lives for the sake of Allah, and that they were not deterred in Allah's cause by the blame of any blamer, nor by the violence of an unjust tyrant. Al-Razi said: taqiyyah is permissible only in what concerns the manifestation of the truth and the religion; as for what necessarily harms others, such as killing, adultery, seizing property, false testimony, slandering chaste women, and revealing the weaknesses of the Muslims to the unbelievers, it is absolutely impermissible.

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that it applies with dominant unbelievers. However, the position of al-Shafi'i is that if the situation among Muslims resembles the situation among polytheists, taqiyyah is permitted to defend oneself, and it is permissible for the preservation of life and property. End of his words. It was said: the verse also indicates that an unbeliever has no guardianship over a Muslim in any matter; so if he has a young son who is a Muslim through his mother's Islam, he has no guardianship over him in disposing of his affairs, nor in marriage, nor otherwise. It was said: it also indicates that a dhimmi does not bear the blood-money (diyah) for a Muslim's crime, and likewise a Muslim does not bear the blood-money for his crime, because that belongs to loyalty, support and assistance.

﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "His seizure (batsh)." al-Zajjaj said: "Himself," that is, Him the Exalted Himself, as al-A'sha said:

*On a day more generous in gift from him, when the self of the miser has frowned at its request.*

He meant: when the miser frowned at his request. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is address according to what humans commonly understand, and "self" in such a case refers to the essence. In the sentence there is an elided modifier, because warning is only from punishment, chastisement and the like. So Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: "And Allah warns you of His punishment." End of his words. When the Exalted forbade them to take unbelievers as allies, He warned them against opposing Him by loyalty to His enemies. He said: ﴿And to Allah is the final return﴾, that is, your ultimate destination and your return; so He will requite you if you commit loyalty to them after the prohibition. In this there is a severe threat and warning.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 29–32 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Say: "Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it."﴾ The explanation of the like of this verse has already been given at the end of the verses of al-Baqarah. There the revealing (*al-ibda'*) was placed before the concealing (*al-ikhfa'*), while here the concealing has been placed before the revealing. Both have the location "what is in the breasts," and the answer of the condition is His saying: ﴿Allah knows it.﴾ This is from the variety (*al-tafannun*) in eloquence. What is understood is that the Creator, exalted is He, is aware of what is in the hearts; His knowledge of their hidden matters does not vary.
