Reason does not reach knowledge of Allah's rulings concerning acts of worship nor concerning anything else; rather His Messenger (ﷺ) is the one who clarifies that. So following him in what he brought is a safeguard for whoever wishes to act in obedience to Allah.

Al-Jumhūr (the majority) read *tuḥibbūna* and *yuḥbibkumu* from the form *aḥabba*. Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿUṭāridī read *taḥibbūna* and *yaḥbibkum* with a fatḥa on the *tāʾ* and the *yāʾ*, from *ḥabba*; both are dialects, and they were mentioned earlier. Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned that it was also read *yaḥubbukum* with a fatḥa on the *yāʾ* and assimilation (*idghām*).

Al-Zuhrī read *fa-ittabaʿūnnī* with a shadda on the *nūn*: he attached the emphatic *nūn* (*nūn al-tawkīd*) to the imperative verb and assimilated it into the *nūn* of protection (*nūn al-wiqāya*), and did not delete the *wāw*, by analogy with *atuḥājjūnnī* (Qurʾān 6:80). This is an irregular (shādhdh) reading. Al-Zamakhsharī said: he meant to give their claim a confirmation through action. Whoever claims to love Him and opposes the practice (*sunna*) of His Messenger is a liar, and the Book of Allah refutes him.

Then he mentioned those who speak of Allah's love while clapping their hands as they mention it, become ecstatic, sway, and clap; ugly is the one who does this, and rebuked is the doer of this, with what is found in His Book.

It is reported from Abū ʿAmr that he assimilated the *rāʾ* of *wa-yaghfir lakum* into the *lām* of *lakum*. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reported from al-Zajjāj that this is an error and a mistake on the part of whoever transmitted it from Abū ʿAmr. We have previously discussed this, and we noted that the leading figures of Kufa, namely Abū Jaʿfar al-Rawāsī, al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ, transmitted this from the Arabs, and two leading figures of Basra, namely Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb, read it and transmitted it. So no attention should be paid to whoever disagrees with that.

﴿قُلْ أطِيعُوا اللَّهَ والرَّسُولَ﴾ ("Say: Obey Allah and the Messenger"). This is an emphasis on His saying: "follow me." It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that when ﴿قُلْ إنْ كُنْتُمْ تُحِبُّونَ اللَّهَ فاتَّبِعُونِي يُحْبِبْكُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ was revealed, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy said to his companions: "Muḥammad makes his obedience like the obedience of Allah, and commands that we love him as the Christians loved ʿĪsā ibn Maryam." So it was revealed: ﴿قُلْ أطِيعُوا اللَّهَ﴾.

﴿فَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا فَإنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُحِبُّ الكافِرِينَ﴾ ("But if they turn away, then indeed Allah does not love the disbelievers"). It may be that *tawallaw* is a past tense verb. It may also be a present tense verb from which the *tāʾ* has been dropped, meaning *fa-in tatawallaw*. The meaning is: if they turn away from what they were commanded, namely following and obeying him, then Allah does not love those who are disbelievers. He treated one who does not follow him and does not obey him as a disbeliever. The restriction of the negation of Allah's love to this attribute, which is disbelief, indicates causation; so a believer who is disobedient is not included in that.

It is said: in these verses there are types of eloquence and branches of rhetoric. The general address whose cause is specific, in His saying ﴿لا يَتَّخِذِ المُؤْمِنُونَ الكافِرِينَ﴾ ("Let not the believers take the disbelievers," Qurʾān 3:28). The repetition, in His saying "the believers," instead of "the believers" (in a different form), and in His saying ﴿مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ ("from Allah," 3:28), ﴿ويُحَذِّرُكُمُ اللَّهُ نَفْسَهُ﴾, ﴿وإلى اللَّهِ﴾ ("and to Allah," 3:28); in ﴿يَعْلَمْهُ اللَّهُ﴾ ("Allah knows it"), (and "He knows"); and in His saying ﴿يَعْلَمْهُ اللَّهُ﴾, ﴿واللَّهُ عَلى﴾ ("and Allah is over"); and in His saying ﴿ما عَمِلَتْ﴾, ﴿وما عَمِلَتْ﴾ ("what it did"); and in His saying ﴿اللَّهُ نَفْسَهُ﴾ ("Allah, Himself"), (and "Allah"); and in His saying ﴿ويُحَذِّرُكُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ (3:28), ﴿واللَّهُ رَءُوفٌ﴾ ("And Allah is Kind"); and in His saying ﴿تُحِبُّونَ اللَّهَ﴾ ("you love Allah"), ﴿يُحْبِبْكُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ ("Allah will love you"), (and "Allah is Forgiving"), ﴿قُلْ أطِيعُوا اللَّهَ﴾ ("Say: obey Allah"), ﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ ("then indeed Allah").

Paronomasia (*tajnīs*) of the same root appears in *tuḥibbūna* and *yuḥbibkum*. Paronomasia of different roots appears in ﴿تَتَّقُوا مِنهم تُقاةً﴾ ("guard yourselves against them, a guarding," 3:28), and in *yaghfir lakum* and *Ghafūr*.

Antithesis (*ṭibāq*) appears in *tukhfū* and *tubdūhu* ("you conceal" and "you reveal"), and in *min khayrin* and *min sūʾin* ("good" and "evil"), and in *muḥḍaran* and *baʿīdan* ("present" and "far").

Figurative expression by place for the thing (*al-taʿbīr bil-maḥall*) appears in His saying *mā fī ṣudūrikum* ("what is in your breasts"), by which He expressed the hearts; He says: ﴿فَإنَّها لا تَعْمى الأبْصارُ﴾ ("for indeed it is not the eyes that go blind," Qurʾān 22:46), the verse.

Allusion (*ishāra*) appears in His saying ﴿ومَن يَفْعَلْ ذَلِكَ﴾ ("whoever does that," 3:28), the verse. He alluded to their having severed themselves from Allah's guardianship.

Restriction (*ikhtiṣāṣ*) appears in His saying ﴿ما في صُدُورِكُمْ﴾ ("what is in your breasts," 3:154), and in His saying ﴿ما في السَّماواتِ وما في الأرْضِ﴾ ("what is in the heavens and what is in the earth").

Reassurance after alarm (*al-ta'nīs baʿda al-īḥāsh*) appears in His saying: "And Allah is Most Kind to His servants." Omission (*al-ḥadhf*) appears in several places whose mention has preceded in the exegesis.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 29–32 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Say: "Whether you conceal what is in your breasts or reveal it, Allah knows it."﴾ The explanation of the like of this verse has already been given at the end of the verses of al-Baqarah. There the revealing (*al-ibda'*) was placed before the concealing (*al-ikhfa'*), while here the concealing has been placed before the revealing. Both have the location "what is in the breasts," and the answer of the condition is His saying: ﴿Allah knows it.﴾ This is from the variety (*al-tafannun*) in eloquence. What is understood is that the Creator, exalted is He, is aware of what is in the hearts; His knowledge of their hidden matters does not vary. On what is in them is based reward and punishment: if it is good, then good; and if it is evil, then evil. In this there is an emphasis on not taking allies (*al-muwalah*) and a warning against it.

﴿And He knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth.﴾ This is evidence of the breadth of His knowledge and of the mention of a generality after a specific. So His knowledge of what is in their breasts is mentioned twice, by way of emphasis: one time specifically, and the other time generally, since they are among those who are on the earth.

﴿And Allah is Able over all things.﴾ In this there is a warning of what follows from His knowledge, exalted is He, of their conditions, namely recompense for what their breasts harbor. Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is an explanation of His saying ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾, because His self (*nafsahu*), which is His essence distinguished from all other essences, is characterized by an essential knowledge that is not restricted to one known thing over another. Thus He is related to all the known things, and by an essential power that is not restricted to one thing able over another. Thus He is able over all the things that are able to be done. So it is right that He be feared and guarded against, so that no one dares to do an abomination or falls short of an obligation, for that is certainly known to Him, and punishment will inevitably overtake him." End of quote. This is a good statement, and in it is an explicit affirmation of the attributes of knowledge and power for Allah, exalted is He. This is contrary to what his teachers among the Mu'tazilah held, and it agrees with the People of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*) in affirming the attributes.

﴿On the Day every soul will find what it has done of good present, and what it has done of evil, it will wish that between itself and that were a long distance.﴾ [p. 426] There has been disagreement about the governing element (*al-'amil*) of "the Day" (*yawma*). Al-Zajjaj said: its governing element is "and warns you," and he preferred this. He also said: its governing element is "the destination" (*al-masir*). Makki ibn Abi Talib said: its governing element is "able" (*qadir*). He also said: there is a hidden verb in it whose estimate is "remember." Ibn Jarir said: its estimate is "fear" (*ittaqu*). Its being in the accusative is weak with His saying "and warns you," because of the long separation. This is from the standpoint of wording. As for the standpoint of meaning, the warning is present, while the Day is promised, so it is not correct for it to govern it. Its being in the accusative with "the destination" is weak, because of the separation between the verbal noun and its object. Its being in the accusative with "able" is weak, because His ability over all things is not restricted to one day over another; rather, He, exalted is He, is always characterized by ability. As for its being in the accusative by a hidden verb, the hiding is contrary to the original rule.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿On the Day every soul finds﴾ is in the accusative by 'it will wish' (*tawaddu*), and the pronoun in 'between it and that' refers to the Day of Resurrection, when every soul finds its good and its evil present, and it wishes that between itself and that Day, which is far from it, were a long distance." End of this explanation.

What is apparent at first glance is its goodness and its preference, since it appears that there is nothing in it of the weakening factors of the previous opinions. But regarding the permissibility of this issue and its like, there is a disagreement among the grammarians. It is this: when the subject is a pronoun referring back to something that is attached to the object of the verb, as in: *ghulama Hindin darabtu* ("the boy of Hind, I struck"), *thawba akhawayka yalbasani* ("the garments of your two brothers, they wear"), and *malu Zaydin ukhidha* ("the wealth of Zayd was taken"). Al-Kisa'i, Hisham, and the majority of the Basrans went to the permissibility of these cases. Among them is the verse according to al-Zamakhshari's explanation, because the subject of "it wishes" is a pronoun referring back to something attached to the object of "it wishes," which is "the Day," since "the Day" is an annexation to "every soul finds." The estimate is: "the Day of the finding of every soul what it has done of good present, and what it has done of evil, it wishes."

Al-Farra', Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash, and others from the Basrans went to the view that these cases and their like are not permissible, because this object is a superfluous element (*fadlah*), so it can be dispensed with, and returning the pronoun to what is attached to it in these cases takes it out of that status, because it requires mentioning the object so that the subject pronoun may return to what is attached to it. For this reason, "Zayd, he struck" and "Zayd, he thought standing" are prohibited. The correct view is the permissibility of that. A poet said:

*The term of a man is hastened, and he does not know, when he seeks the attainment of his hopes.*

That is: the man, at the time of his seeking the attainment of his hopes, is hastening his term while not perceiving it.

As for "you find" (*tajidu*): the apparent is that it is transitive to one object, which is "what they have done," so it means "portion" (*nasib*), and "present" (*muhdaran*) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. It was said: "you find" here means "you know," so it is transitive to two objects, and "present" is in the accusative as its second object. "What" in "what they have done" is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun in the relative clause is omitted. It is also permissible for it to be a verbal (*masdariyyah*) "what," meaning "their action," and by this is meant the object, that is, "what is acted upon," so His saying "what they have done" is by omitting an annexed word, meaning "the recompense of what they have done and its reward."

It was said: the meaning of "present," on this view, is "complete, not diminished." It was also said: "you see what they have done written in the records present to them," as good news for them, so that the reward comes after witnessing the deed. The majority read *muhdaran* with a fatha on the *dad*, as a passive participle. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read *muhdiran* with a kasra on the *dad*, meaning "bringing (it) present," that is, bringing Paradise present, or "bringing it quickly to Paradise," from their saying *ahdara al-faras*, when the horse ran and hastened.

"And what they have done of evil" may be in the accusative position, coordinated with "what they have done of good." Then the second object is, if "you find" is transitive to both, or it is a circumstantial state if it is transitive to one omitted object, meaning: "and what they have done of evil present." This is like: *zanantu Zaydan qa'iman wa 'Amran*, when you intend "and 'Amr standing." On this aspect, "it wishes" may be a new sentence. It may also be that "it wishes" is in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: "wishing, it distances what is between it and what it has done of evil." Then the pronoun in "between it" refers back to "what it has done of evil."

Al-Zamakhshari went too far in making it refer to the Day, because one of the two parts that were presented on that Day is the good that it did, and the distancing of the time of presenting the good is not sought except by a figurative usage, if it includes the presenting of the good and the evil. So "it wishes its distancing" means that it wishes to be safe from the evil, and let it be that good does not come to it.

The more preferable is that it refers back to "what it has done of evil," because it is the nearest thing mentioned, since the meaning is that evil wishes on that Day to be far from it. This is the preference for coordinating "what it has done of evil" with "what it has done of good," and al-Tabari went to the view that "it wishes" is in the position of a circumstantial state. It is also permissible that "what it has done of evil" be a relative clause in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence. "It wishes" is a sentence in the position of the predicate of *ma*, the estimate being: "and what it has done of evil, it wishes it were that between it and it there was a distance." By this aspect Al-Zamakhshari began, and Ibn 'Atiyyah followed him in it, and both agreed that "and what it has done of evil" cannot be a conditional clause. Al-Zamakhshari said: "because of the raising of 'it wishes.'" Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "because the verb is a nominative future that requires its jussive, unless some omitted element is estimated in the speech, meaning: 'so it wishes'; and in that there is weakness." End of his words.

It is apparent from their two statements that the conditional is prohibited because of the raising of "it wishes." This issue was asked of me by the Chief Judge Abu al-'Abbas Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn 'Abd al-Ghani al-Surujj al-Hanafi, may Allah have mercy on him, and he found al-Zamakhshari's statement problematic and said: "It should be permissible; at most this is like the saying of Zuhayr:

*And if a friend comes to him on a day of asking, he says: 'Neither is my wealth absent, nor am I forbidden.'*"

I wrote the answer to what he asked me in my large book called (*al-Tadhkirah*). Here we mention what is needed from that after we first present what should be presented in this issue. We say: when the verb of the condition is past, and what follows it is a present verb completing the conditional and its answer, the present verb may be jussive, and it may be nominative. An example of that: *in qama Zaydun yaqum 'Amrun* and *in qama Zaydun yaqumu 'Amrun*. As for the jussive, it is because it is the answer of the condition, and we know of no disagreement about the permissibility of that, and that it is eloquent, except what the author of the book (*al-I'rab*) mentioned from some grammarians, that it does not occur in eloquent speech, and that it occurs only with *kana*, due to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We will pay them their deeds in it﴾ [Hud: 15], because it is the origin of verbs, and it is not permissible with other than it. The apparent of Sibawayh's statement, and the explicit statement of the group, is that this is not restricted to *kana*; rather, all other verbs are like *kana* in that. Sibawayh recited to al-Farazdaq:

*She sent a messenger that the people, if they have power over you, will heal breasts with rage.*

And he also said:

*Come, if you covenant with me, do not betray me, we will be like those who accompany one another, O wolf.*

As for the nominative, it is heard abundantly from the tongue of the Arabs. One of our companions said: "It is better than the jussive, and from it is the verse of Zuhayr mentioned earlier, which is his saying also:

*And if the best of the group is drawn out in fear, he says openly: 'Woe to you, do not flee!'*"

Abu Sakhr said:

*Nor with the one who, if his beloved departs from him, says and hides patience: "Indeed I am distraught."*

Another said:

*And if they are far, they do not feel safe from its approach, the eagerness of the people of the absent one awaited.*

Another said:

*And if he is not pleased with you until you return me to my region, I do not think you are pleased.*

Another said:

*If they ask for good, they give it; and if they are informed in hardship, the good news is attained from them.*

So this nominative, as you see, is abundant, and the statements of the leading scholars are on its permissibility in speech, even if their interpretations differ, as we will mention. Our companion Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Rashid al-Maliqi, the author of (*Wasf al-Mabani*), may Allah have mercy on him, said: "I know of nothing of it that came in speech, and if it came, its analogy is the jussive, because it is the original governing of the present verb, whether the past precedes it or follows it." He interpreted this heard form as having the *fa'* omitted, and making it like the poet's saying:

*Indeed, if your brother is struck down, you will be struck down.*

according to the view of those who held the *fa'* there to be omitted.

As for the earlier scholars, they differed in the analysis of the nominative. Sibawayh went to the view that this is by way of fronting (*al-taqdim*). As for the answer of the condition, it is omitted in his view. The Kufans and Abu al-'Abbas went to the view that it is the answer, with the *fa'* omitted. Others went to the view that, since the effect of the conditional particle does not appear on the verb of the condition because it is past, it is too weak to govern the verb of the answer. It is, in their view, an answer that is neither by an omitted *fa'* nor by intention of fronting. This view and the one before it are both weak.

It is concluded from what we have said that the raising of the present verb does not prevent what precedes it from being a conditional. But "and what they have done" is prohibited from being a conditional for another reason, not because "it wishes" is raised. That is according to what we establish on Sibawayh's view, that the intention in the nominative is fronting, and then it would be evidence of the answer, not the answer itself. So we say: if "it wishes" is intended with fronting, that leads to the pronoun preceding its explicit referent, outside the exceptional cases recognized in Arabic grammar. Do you not see that the pronoun in His saying "between it and it" refers back to the conditional noun, which is *ma*? So the estimate becomes: "Every soul wishes, if between it and it there were a long distance, what it has done of evil?" This estimate requires the pronoun to precede its explicit referent, and that is not permissible.

If you ask: why would that not be permissible, given that the pronoun has been placed after the conditional noun? If its intention is anteriority, then the pronoun has returned to the apparent noun before it, as in the example *ḍaraba Zaydan ghulāmuhu* ("Zayd's servant struck him"). There the agent (*fā'il*, the doer of the action) should by rank come first, but it must be placed after the verb so that the pronoun can correctly refer back. The answer is that when the conditional noun's pronoun appears within the response clause, the pronoun must follow the conditional noun in order to refer back to it. This entails that the conditional clause requires the clause of the response (*dalīl*), whereas the conditional clause only requires the clause of the consequent (*jawāb*), not its own explanatory clause. Consider that it does not operate within the explanatory clause; rather, it operates only on the consequent clause, and the explanatory clause has no place in the grammatical structure. Since that is the case, the matter contradicts itself: as an explanatory clause, it is not required by the conditional verb, but insofar as the pronoun refers back to the conditional noun, it is required by it, so the two conflict. This is different from *ḍaraba Zaydan ghulāmuhu*, which is a single clause in which the verb governs both the agent and the object, and each of them requires the other. For this reason some grammarians permitted *ḍaraba ghulāmuhā Hindan* ("her servant struck Hind"), because the agent, which is joined to a pronoun, and the object to which the pronoun refers share the same governing verb. But *ḍaraba ghulāmuhā jāra Hindin* ("her servant struck the neighbour of Hind") is disallowed, because there is no shared governing verb. This is the difference between the two cases.

The construction *awaddu law annī ukrimuhu ayyā ḍarabat Hindun* ("I wish that I would honour him, whomever Hind struck") is not attested in the speech of the Arabs, because it would entail placing a pronoun before its explanatory noun in situations other than those the grammarians have mentioned. Therefore it is not permitted to postpone it.

ʿAbdullāh (Ibn Masʿūd) and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read: *min sūʾin waddat law anna* ("from evil that it wishes that..."). On this reading, *mā* may be a conditional particle in the accusative position, and so it governs. Or it may be in the nominative position, with the pronoun *hā'* of *ʿamilat* ("it did") understood, according to the view of al-Farrāʾ, who permits this with the conditional noun in eloquent speech. Then *waddat* is the response of the condition. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "But treating it as a subject and predicate (*mubtadaʾ* and *khabar*) is more apt in meaning, because it is a description of what exists on that day, and it is more firmly established as matching the reading of the common people (the majority)."

*Law* here is a particle for what would have happened on account of the occurrence of something else. Its response is omitted, and the object of *tawaddu* ("she wishes") is omitted. The implied sense is: she wishes the distance between them, that between it and her there were a long period, she would be glad of that. This parsing and estimation is the familiar one for *law*, with *anna* and what follows it in the position of a subject according to Sībawayh, and in the position of an agent according to Abū al-ʿAbbās (al-Mubarrad). As for the view of those who hold that *law* means *an* (that) and is a verbal-nominal particle, it is remote here, because *anna*, which is a verbal particle, follows it, and a verbal particle does not directly precede another verbal particle except rarely, as in the Qurʾānic verse ﴿مِثْلَ ما أنَّكم تَنْطِقُونَ﴾ ("like your speaking," Qurʾān 51:23). What the meaning requires is that *law anna* and what follows it is the object of *tawaddu*, in the position of the direct object. Al-Ḥasan said: "One of them would be glad never to meet his deed, that is its meaning." The meaning of *amadan baʿīdan* ("a far-off term") is an extended duration; it is said to be the measure of its appointed term, and it is said to be the distance between the east and the west.

﴿وَيُحَذِّرُكُمُ اللَّهُ نَفْسَهُ﴾ ("And Allah warns you of Himself"). He repeated the warning for emphasis and to incite fear of Allah, so that they would obey His command and prohibition.

﴿وَاللَّهُ رَءُوفٌ بِالعِبادِ﴾ ("And Allah is Most Kind to His servants"). When He mentioned the attribute of warning and repeated it, that was alarming to hearts and a reminder of the occurrence of what is feared, together with what is joined to it of His knowledge of the hidden depths of deeds and His presenting them on the Day of Reckoning. This is the attribute of knowledge and power, by which one must be warned. Then He mentioned the attribute of mercy, so that one would hope for His goodness and extend hope for His bounties. This is part of the principle that when a statement indicates severity, it is followed by a statement indicating the vastness of mercy, as in the verse ﴿إنَّ رَبَّكَ لَسَرِيعُ العِقابِ وإنَّهُ لَغَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful," Qurʾān 7:167). This clause is more eloquent as a description than the clause of warning, because the clause of warning came with a verb that implies an unrestricted sense and in which the name of Allah was not repeated, and the one warned was specifically the addressee alone. This clause came as a nominal sentence, so the name of Allah is repeated in it, since the adjective may take His pronoun. The predicate came in the pattern *faʿūl*, which implies intensity and multiplicity. It came with the most specific of the words for mercy, which is *raʾūf*. Its complement came general, to include the addressee and others, and with the word *ʿibād* ("servants"), to indicate complete goodness, because the owner is good to his servant and regards him with the best regard, since the servant is his possession.

They said: it is possible that it refers to the warning, meaning: His warning of Himself, and His making known to them the state of His knowledge and power, is from His great compassion for His servants, because when they know Him with true knowledge and beware, that calls them to seek His pleasure and avoid His wrath. From al-Ḥasan: "Among His compassion for them is that He warned them of Himself." Al-Ḥūfī said: "He made their warning of Him and their fear of His punishment a sign of compassion for them, and He did not leave them in blindness regarding their affairs." This same meaning is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās. The statement can bear this, but the more apparent is the first, namely that the beginning of His informing them of this attribute is by way of comfort and encouragement, so that He does not overdo the threat upon the heart of the believer.

﴿قُلْ إنْ كُنْتُمْ تُحِبُّونَ اللَّهَ فاتَّبِعُونِي يُحْبِبْكُمُ اللَّهُ ويَغْفِرْ لَكم ذُنُوبَكم واللَّهُ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ ("Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful"). It was revealed concerning the Jews, who said: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved" (Qurʾān 5:18). Or it was revealed concerning the words of the polytheists: "We only worship them so that they may bring us near to Allah in nearness" (Qurʾān 39:3). They said that, while Quraysh had set up their idols to prostrate to them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O assembly of Quraysh, you have certainly opposed the creed of your father Ibrāhīm (Abraham)." Both of these reports are from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Jurayj said: it was revealed concerning a people who said: "Indeed we love our Lord with a fierce love." Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr said: it was revealed concerning the delegation of Najrān, when they said: "Indeed we magnify the Messiah out of love for Allah."

The wording of the verse covers everyone who claims love for Allah. The servant's love for Allah is an expression of his heart's inclination toward what He has prescribed and commanded him, acting upon it, and devoting worship to Him alone. Allah's love for the servant has already been discussed earlier, and whether it is one of the essential attributes or one of the attributes of action, so there is no need to repeat it. Allah ordered, as a consequence of their love for Him, that His love for them be [conditioned on] following His Messenger. That is because the path leading to His pleasure is only learned from His Prophet, for he is the one who explains about Allah. Reason does not reach knowledge of Allah's rulings concerning acts of worship nor concerning anything else; rather His Messenger (ﷺ) is the one who clarifies that. So following him in what he brought is a safeguard for whoever wishes to act in obedience to Allah.

Al-Jumhūr (the majority) read *tuḥibbūna* and *yuḥbibkumu* from the form *aḥabba*. Abū Rajāʾ al-ʿUṭāridī read *taḥibbūna* and *yaḥbibkum* with a fatḥa on the *tāʾ* and the *yāʾ*, from *ḥabba*; both are dialects, and they were mentioned earlier. Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned that it was also read *yaḥubbukum* with a fatḥa on the *yāʾ* and assimilation (*idghām*).

Al-Zuhrī read *fa-ittabaʿūnnī* with a shadda on the *nūn*: he attached the emphatic *nūn* (*nūn al-tawkīd*) to the imperative verb and assimilated it into the *nūn* of protection (*nūn al-wiqāya*), and did not delete the *wāw*, by analogy with *atuḥājjūnnī* (Qurʾān 6:80). This is an irregular (shādhdh) reading. Al-Zamakhsharī said: he meant to give their claim a confirmation through action. Whoever claims to love Him and opposes the practice (*sunna*) of His Messenger is a liar, and the Book of Allah refutes him.

Then he mentioned those who speak of Allah's love while clapping their hands as they mention it, become ecstatic, sway, and clap; ugly is the one who does this, and rebuked is the doer of this, with what is found in His Book.

It is reported from Abū ʿAmr that he assimilated the *rāʾ* of *wa-yaghfir lakum* into the *lām* of *lakum*. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reported from al-Zajjāj that this is an error and a mistake on the part of whoever transmitted it from Abū ʿAmr. We have previously discussed this, and we noted that the leading figures of Kufa, namely Abū Jaʿfar al-Rawāsī, al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ, transmitted this from the Arabs, and two leading figures of Basra, namely Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb, read it and transmitted it. So no attention should be paid to whoever disagrees with that.

﴿قُلْ أطِيعُوا اللَّهَ والرَّسُولَ﴾ ("Say: Obey Allah and the Messenger"). This is an emphasis on His saying: "follow me." It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that when ﴿قُلْ إنْ كُنْتُمْ تُحِبُّونَ اللَّهَ فاتَّبِعُونِي يُحْبِبْكُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ was revealed, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy said to his companions: "Muḥammad makes his obedience like the obedience of Allah, and commands that we love him as the Christians loved ʿĪsā ibn Maryam." So it was revealed: ﴿قُلْ أطِيعُوا اللَّهَ﴾.

﴿فَإنْ تَوَلَّوْا فَإنَّ اللَّهَ لا يُحِبُّ الكافِرِينَ﴾ ("But if they turn away, then indeed Allah does not love the disbelievers"). It may be that *tawallaw* is a past tense verb. It may also be a present tense verb from which the *tāʾ* has been dropped, meaning *fa-in tatawallaw*. The meaning is: if they turn away from what they were commanded, namely following and obeying him, then Allah does not love those who are disbelievers. He treated one who does not follow him and does not obey him as a disbeliever. The restriction of the negation of Allah's love to this attribute, which is disbelief, indicates causation; so a believer who is disobedient is not included in that.

It is said: in these verses there are types of eloquence and branches of rhetoric. The general address whose cause is specific, in His saying ﴿لا يَتَّخِذِ المُؤْمِنُونَ الكافِرِينَ﴾ ("Let not the believers take the disbelievers," Qurʾān 3:28). The repetition, in His saying "the believers," instead of "the believers" (in a different form), and in His saying ﴿مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ ("from Allah," 3:28), ﴿ويُحَذِّرُكُمُ اللَّهُ نَفْسَهُ﴾, ﴿وإلى اللَّهِ﴾ ("and to Allah," 3:28); in ﴿يَعْلَمْهُ اللَّهُ﴾ ("Allah knows it"), (and "He knows"); and in His saying ﴿يَعْلَمْهُ اللَّهُ﴾, ﴿واللَّهُ عَلى﴾ ("and Allah is over"); and in His saying ﴿ما عَمِلَتْ﴾, ﴿وما عَمِلَتْ﴾ ("what it did"); and in His saying ﴿اللَّهُ نَفْسَهُ﴾ ("Allah, Himself"), (and "Allah"); and in His saying ﴿ويُحَذِّرُكُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ (3:28), ﴿واللَّهُ رَءُوفٌ﴾ ("And Allah is Kind"); and in His saying ﴿تُحِبُّونَ اللَّهَ﴾ ("you love Allah"), ﴿يُحْبِبْكُمُ اللَّهُ﴾ ("Allah will love you"), (and "Allah is Forgiving"), ﴿قُلْ أطِيعُوا اللَّهَ﴾ ("Say: obey Allah"), ﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ﴾ ("then indeed Allah").

Paronomasia (*tajnīs*) of the same root appears in *tuḥibbūna* and *yuḥbibkum*. Paronomasia of different roots appears in ﴿تَتَّقُوا مِنهم تُقاةً﴾ ("guard yourselves against them, a guarding," 3:28), and in *yaghfir lakum* and *Ghafūr*.

Antithesis (*ṭibāq*) appears in *tukhfū* and *tubdūhu* ("you conceal" and "you reveal"), and in *min khayrin* and *min sūʾin* ("good" and "evil"), and in *muḥḍaran* and *baʿīdan* ("present" and "far").

Figurative expression by place for the thing (*al-taʿbīr bil-maḥall*) appears in His saying *mā fī ṣudūrikum* ("what is in your breasts"), by which He expressed the hearts; He says: ﴿فَإنَّها لا تَعْمى الأبْصارُ﴾ ("for indeed it is not the eyes that go blind," Qurʾān 22:46), the verse.

Allusion (*ishāra*) appears in His saying ﴿ومَن يَفْعَلْ ذَلِكَ﴾ ("whoever does that," 3:28), the verse. He alluded to their having severed themselves from Allah's guardianship.

Restriction (*ikhtiṣāṣ*) appears in His saying ﴿ما في صُدُورِكُمْ﴾ ("what is in your breasts," 3:154), and in His saying ﴿ما في السَّماواتِ وما في الأرْضِ﴾ ("what is in the heavens and what is in the earth").

Reassurance after alarm (*al-ta'nīs baʿda al-īḥāsh*) appears in His saying: "And Allah is Most Kind to His servants." Omission (*al-ḥadhf*) appears in several places whose mention has preceded in the exegesis.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 33–34 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of ʿImran over the worlds.﴾ ﴿Descendants, one of another; and Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿When the wife of ʿImran said: "My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb as a dedicated one, so accept it from me. Indeed, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 35] ﴿So when she delivered her, she said: "My Lord, I have delivered her as a female" – and Allah knows best what she delivered – "and the male is not like the female. And I have named her Maryam, and I seek refuge for her in You and for her offspring from the accursed Satan."﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 36] ﴿So her Lord accepted her with a good acceptance and caused her to grow in a good growth, and Zakariyya took charge of her. Every time Zakariyya entered upon her in the sanctuary (mihrab), he found with her provision. He said: "O Maryam, from where is this for you?" She said: "It is from Allah. Indeed, Allah provides for whom He wills without account."﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 37] ﴿There Zakariyya prayed to his Lord. He said: "My Lord, grant me from Yourself good offspring. Indeed, You are the Hearer of supplication."﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 38] ﴿So the angels called him while he was standing in prayer in the sanctuary: "Indeed, Allah gives you good news of Yahya, confirming a word from Allah, and a master, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous."﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 39] ﴿He said: "My Lord, how can I have a boy when old age has overtaken me and my wife is barren?" He said: "Thus Allah does what He wills."﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 40] ﴿He said: "My Lord, make for me a sign." He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three days except by gestures. And remember your Lord much and glorify Him in the evening and the morning."﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 41]

Noah: a non-Arabic (aʿjamī) name, declined (maṣrūf) according to the majority, although it has what would require it to be non-declined, namely the status of a proper name (ʿalamiyya) and the personal non-Arabic character (ʿujma). The reason it is declined is the lightness of its form, being triliteral with a quiescent middle letter, to which no other cause is added. Whoever permitted both forms (declined and non-declined) did so by analogy with this, not by transmission (samāʿ). As for the one who held that it is derived from al-nawāḥ (wailing), his view is weak, because derivation from Arabic does not apply to non-Arabic words, unless he claims that it is among the words in which the Arabic and the non-Arabic languages coincide, and then that is possible. It is said that he is the second Adam, and his name was al-Sakan, as said by more than one scholar. He is the son of Malik ibn Mutawshalakh ibn Akhnukh ibn Sarid ibn Mahlabil ibn Qaynan ibn Anush ibn Shith ibn Adam.

ʿImran: a non-Arabic name, not declined because of its proper-name status and non-Arabic origin. Even if it were Arabic, it would still be non-declined because of its proper-name status and the addition of the alif and nun; its derivation from ʿumr (life) would then be clear.

Muharraran (dedicated): a passive participle from ḥarrara (to free). The disagreement of the exegetes regarding its meaning in the verse will come. Taḥrīr means manumission (ʿitq), which is making a slave free.

Waḍʿ (delivery): lowering and placing down. You say waḍaʿa yaḍaʿu waḍʿan waḍaʿatan, and from it comes mawḍiʿ (place).

Unthā (female) and dhakar (male) are both well-known. The alif of unthā is for feminine marking. It is pluralized as ināth, like ruba and rabāb. The analogical plural is unāthā, like ḥublā and ḥubālā. The plural of dhakar is dhukūr and dhukrān.

Maryam: a Hebrew name. It is also said to be Arabic, having come irregularly, like Madyan. Its analogical form would be marām, like manāl. Its meaning in Arabic is the one who flirts with young men. The rajiz (poet) said:

"I said to Zayd: Maryamuhu did not reach him"

ʿādha bi-kadhā: he sought refuge in it, taking shelter (ʿawdan, ʿiyādhan, or muʿādhan, or muʿādhatan). Its meaning is he sought refuge and took protection. It is also said that its derivation is from al-ʿawdh, which is a tuft to which grass takes refuge in the direction of the wind.

Rajama: he threw and hurled. From it is ﴿a guess at the unseen﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], meaning throwing without certainty. A "mirjam" saying is one that is conjectured, meaning a thing that is only supposed and has no certainty.

Al-Rajīm may be an intensive form of the agent (fāʿil), meaning that it throws and hurls evil and disobedience into the heart of the son of Adam. It may also mean "stoned" (marjūm), that is, it is pelted with meteors or is driven away and expelled.

Al-Kafāla: guarantee (ḍamān). One says kafala yakfulu, so he is kāfil and kafīl. This is its origin, and then it is borrowed for nurturing and taking charge of a thing.

Zakariyya: a non-Arabic name, assimilated to the forms that have an extended alif and a shortened alif, so it is both extended and shortened. For this reason its indefinite form is not declined. These two forms in it are according to the people of the Ḥijāz. Had its non-declension been due to proper-name status and non-Arabic origin, it would be declined when indefinite. Abu Ḥatim went to this view, and it is a mistake on his part. It is also said Dhikrā, with the alif deleted, and at its end a yā like the yā of Bukhtī, indefinite, so it is declined. This is the dialect of Najd. Its basis, according to Abu ʿAli, is that he deleted the two yās of the extended and shortened forms and attached the two yās of the nisba (relative adjective). This is shown by its being declined. Had the two yās been those that were in Zakariyya, it would have been necessary for it not to be declined due to non-Arabic origin and definiteness. End of his words.

It is also reported: Dhukar on the pattern of ʿUmar, and al-Akhfash related it. Miḥrāb: Abu ʿUbayda said it is the master of gatherings, its most noble and foremost place, and likewise it is of the mosque. Al-Aṣmaʿī said it is the upper room (ghurfa). He said:

"And what is upon him if I am reminded or forgotten, like gazelles of sand in the sanctuaries of Aqyal?"

The commentators explained it as "upper rooms of Aqyal." Al-Zajjaj said it is the high, noble place. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ said it is the palace, because of its nobility and height. It is said it is the mosque. It is said its known miḥrāb was so named because people compete for it and vie over it, and it is the place of the imam in the mosque.

Hunā (there): a demonstrative noun for a near place. It is obligatorily used as a locative adverb, but it can be governed by a preposition. If you attach the kāf of address to it, it indicates a distant place. The tribe of Banū Tamīm says hunāka. The particle of alerting (ḥarf al-tanbīh) may be prefixed to it when the lām is not present in it, and it may be intended for temporal adverbs.

Al-Nidāʾ: raising the voice. Fulān is andā ṣawtan, that is, higher-voiced. Dār al-Nadwa (the Council House) is named so because their voices were raised in it. Al-Muntadā and al-Nādī are the gathering place of the people. One says nādā munādāh, nidāʾ, and nudāʾ, with a kasra or ḍamma on the nūn. It is said: with the kasra it is the verbal noun (maṣdar), and with the ḍamma it is a noun. Most vocal sounds come with a ḍamma, like the call (duʿāʾ), the bleating (rughāʾ), and the crying (ṣurākh). Yaʿqūb said: it is extended with a kasra on the nūn, and shortened with a ḍamma. Al-Nadā means rain, from which one says nadā yandā nadan.

Yaḥyā: a non-Arabic name, not declined due to non-Arabic origin and proper-name status. It is also said that it is Arabic, and it is an imperfect verb from ḥayiya. It was named with it, so it is not declined due to proper-name status and the pattern of the verb. According to both views, its plural is yaḥyawna, with the alif deleted and the letter before it given a fatḥa, according to the view of al-Khalīl and Sībawayh. It is transmitted from the Kufans: if it is Arabic, the yā is given a fatḥa; if it is non-Arabic, the yā is given a ḍamma.

Sayyid (master): on the pattern fayʿil from sāda, meaning he surpassed in nobility. The discussion of its counterpart has preceded. Its plural on the pattern faʿla is sādah, which is irregular. Al-Rāghib said: he is the one who manages the common people, that is, most of them, and for this reason one says "the master of the slave" but not "the master of the garment." End of his words.

Al-Ḥaṣūr: on the pattern faʿūl from al-ḥaṣr (restraint), and it is for intensity from ḥāṣara. It is also said it is faʿūl in the sense of mafʿūl, that is, maḥṣūr (restrained). In the verse it means the one who does not approach women.

Al-Ghulām: a young man among people, the one whose moustache has grown. It is applied to a child by way of optimism, and to an elderly man. From it is the saying of Layla al-Akhyaliyya:

"He is healed from the stubborn illness that is in her by a youth who, when he shakes the spear, gives her drink."

It is a naming by what he was before old age. It comes from al-ghulma and al-ightilām, which is the intensity of the desire for marriage. One says ightalama al-faḥl: the stallion became excited from the intensity of the desire for mating. And ightalama al-baḥr: the sea became agitated and its waves surged. Its plural ghulma is irregular. Its analogical plural for the few is aghlima. For the many it is pluralized as ghilmān, and this is its analogy.

Al-Kibar: the verbal noun of kabura yakburu in age. He said:

"Two small ones grazing the bahm (thistles): O that we had not grown up, nor had the thistles grown up!"

Al-ʿĀqir (barren): the one who has no offspring from a man or a woman. Its verb is intransitive. Al-ʿāqir is the active participle from ʿaqara, meaning he killed, which is transitive.

Al-Ramz: a gesture with the hand, the head, or other things. Its origin is movement. One says irtamaza: he moved. From it the sea is called al-rāmūz.

Al-ʿAshiyy: the singular of ʿashiyya, like rakiyy and rakiyya. Al-ʿashiyya is the end of the day, and its lām is a wāw, so it is like maṭiyy.

Al-Ibkār: the verbal noun of abkara. One says abkara: he went out early in the morning.

﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of ʿImran over the worlds.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: the Jews said, "We are the sons of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and we are upon their religion," so this was revealed. It is also said: it concerns the Christians of Najran when they exaggerated regarding ʿIsa, made him the son of Allah, the Exalted, and took him as a god. It was revealed as a refutation of them and an announcement that ʿIsa is from the descendants of mankind, who moved through the stages that are impossible for God. It digressed from this to the birth of his mother, then to his own birth. This is the connection of these verses to what precedes them. Also, since it was previously said: ﴿Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 31], and it followed with ﴿Say: Obey Allah and the Messenger﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 32], and concluded with ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 32], He mentioned the chosen ones whose following He loves. He began first with the first of them in existence and origin, and then followed with Noah (peace be upon him), since he is the younger Adam; there is no one on the face of the earth except from his offspring. Then He came third with the family of Abraham, within which is included the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who is commanded to be followed and obeyed, and Moses (peace be upon him). Then He came fourth with the family of ʿImran, within which are included Maryam and ʿIsa (peace be upon them both). He specified the family of Abraham because of the particularity of the Jews with them, and the family of ʿImran because of the particularity of the Christians with them. Thus Allah mentioned the making of these a chosen elite, that is, selected, pure. The meaning is that He purified them from turbidity, and this is an example of the known explained through the perceptible.

The choosing of Adam is by several aspects. Among them: his creation as the first of this noble species, his being made a khalīfa (successor) on earth, the angels' prostration to him, his dwelling in His garden, and other things by which He honored him. The choosing of Noah (peace be upon him) is by several things. Among them: that he was the first messenger sent to the people of the earth with the prohibition of daughters, sisters, paternal and maternal aunts, and the rest of the forbidden relatives, and that he is the father of mankind after Adam, and other things. The choosing of the family of Abraham (peace be upon him) is by His placing prophethood and the Book among them. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Ḥasan said: the family of Abraham are those who were upon his religion. Muqatil said: his family are Ismaʿil, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes. It is also said: what is meant by the family of Abraham is Abraham himself. Some of the discussion on this has preceded us in His words: ﴿And a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind﴾ [al-Baqara: 248].

Ali Imran (the person to whom "Aal" is attributed): it is said he is Imran ibn Matan, a descendant of Sulayman ibn Dawud (Solomon, son of David), and he is the father of Maryam the virgin, mother of 'Isa (peace be upon him). This was said by al-Hasan and Wahb. It is also said he is Imran, father of Musa and Harun, namely Imran ibn Nusayr, as said by Muqatil. According to the first view, the "family" (Aal) is 'Isa, as said by al-Hasan; according to the second, the family is Musa and Harun, as said by Muqatil. It is also said that by "the family of Imran" is meant Imran himself. The apparent reading of "Imran" is that he is the father of Maryam, because of His words after this, ﴿When the wife of Imran said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35], and then He mentions the story of Maryam and her son 'Isa, and states explicitly that Allah chose her with His words ﴿The angels said: O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 42]. So His words ﴿When the wife of Imran said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35] are like an explanation of the manner of the choosing, corresponding to His words "and the family of Imran", and it becomes like the repetition of a name in two clauses, so the mind jumps to the idea that the second is the first, as in: "Zayd was honoured by a righteous man." If the intended second is other than the first, this would cause confusion for the listener. The other view has been preferred on the grounds that Musa is frequently mentioned together with Ibrahim, and there is no way for the understanding to reach that the second Imran is the father of Musa and Harun, even though he had a daughter called Maryam who was older than Musa and Harun, because of the explicit statement that Maryam daughter of Imran ibn Matan bore 'Isa, and that Zakariyya was the guardian of Maryam, mother of 'Isa. Zakariyya had married the sister of Maryam, Ishaa daughter of Imran ibn (p-435) Matan, so Yahya and 'Isa were cousins through their mothers, and between the two Imrans and the two Maryams there are many generations. It is said that between the two Imrans there are a thousand years and eight hundred years.

The apparent meaning: "Aal" refers to those who return to the person by kinship or by creed. The apparent meaning is that He explicitly named these here in the choosing, for the excellences which Allah placed in them. The chief judge in al-Andalus, Abu al-Hakam Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballluti, may Allah have mercy on him and be pleased with him, held that the mention of Adam and Nuh included an indication to the believers between them, and that "the family" means the followers. So the meaning is that Allah chose the believers over the disbelievers, and these were singled out for mention to honour them, and because the discourse concerns the story of some of them. End of his summarised words. His statement is similar in meaning to that of one who interpreted His words "Adam" and what follows as having an omitted genitive construction, meaning: Allah chose the religion of Adam. This meaning was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the intended meaning is that He chose their religion over the other religions, and al-Farra' preferred it. Al-Tibrizi said: this is weak, because if there were an omitted genitive, it would be "and Nuh" in the genitive case, since the position of Adam is genitive by annexation. What al-Tibrizi said is nothing, and had it not been written down in books I would not have mentioned it. For it is not necessary that the annexed noun be put in the genitive when the annexing noun is omitted, so that what is conjoined to it must be genitive; rather the annexed noun takes the i'rab of the omitted annexing noun. Do you not see His words ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]? As for keeping it in the genitive, it is not permissible except under a condition mentioned in the science of grammar.

﴿عَلى العالَمِينَ﴾ ("over the worlds") is connected to "isṭafā" (chose), which has been made to include the meaning of "faḍḍala" (favoured), so it takes "ʿalā". Had it not been given the meaning of "faḍḍala", it would have taken "min". It is said: the meaning is "over the worlds of their time", and the wording is general while the intended meaning is particular, as Jarir said:
"And the worlds will come to him as dependants"
And al-Hutay'a said:
"May Allah relieve the worlds of you"
And as you interpret His words ﴿and that I favoured you over the worlds﴾ [al-Baqara: 47]. Al-Qatibi said: every age has its world, and it is possible that it is restricted to those other than these, and that Muhammad is included in His words "and the family of Ibrahim," so the meaning is that these were favoured over those other than them among the worlds. Their sharing in the common measure of preference does not indicate equality in the degrees of preference, just as you say: Zayd, Umar and Khalid are wealthy; their sharing in the common measure of wealth does not indicate equality in the degrees of wealth. When we take "the worlds" to mean those other than these, this indicates the preference of humans over angels, since they are among those other than these chosen ones, and the verse has been used as evidence for that. It is not possible to take "the worlds" in its generality, because of contradiction: if a large group is described such that each one of them is better than all the worlds, it would follow that each one of them is better than the other, which is impossible. ʿAbd Allah read: "and the family of Muhammad over the worlds."

﴿ذُرِّيَّةً بَعْضُها مِن بَعْضٍ﴾ ("offspring, some of them from others"): they permitted two possibilities for the accusative of "dhurriyyatan". The first: that it is a substitute (badal). Al-Zamakhshari said: from "the family of Ibrahim and the family of Imran", meaning that the two families are one offspring. Others said it is a substitute for Nuh and those conjoined to him among the names. Abu al-Baqa' said: it cannot be a substitute for Adam, because he is not an offspring. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is not proper to say of a parent of this one that he is an offspring of his child. Al-Raghib said: "dhurriyya" is said of the one, the plural, the origin and the progeny, as in His words ﴿We carried their offspring﴾ [Ya Sin: 41], meaning their forefathers, and it is said of women: "dharari". The author of al-Nazm said: the verse requires that fathers be offspring of sons and sons be offspring of fathers, and this is permissible because it derives from "dhara'a Allahu al-khalq" (Allah created creation): the father is one from whom the child was created, and the child was created from the father. Al-Naqqash said the same. According to the view of al-Raghib and the author of al-Nazm, it is permissible for "dhurriyyatan" to be a substitute for Adam and those conjoined to him. They also permitted the accusative of "dhurriyyatan" as a state (hal), which is the second of the two possibilities; al-Zamakhshari did not mention it, but Ibn 'Atiyya did, and said it is more apparent than the substitute. The discussion of "dhurriyya" in terms of meaning, derivation and form has already preceded, so it is sufficient and there is no need to repeat it.

End of his words.

It is also reported: Dhukar on the pattern of ʿUmar, and al-Akhfash related it. Miḥrāb: Abu ʿUbayda said it is the master of gatherings, its most noble and foremost place, and likewise it is of the mosque. Al-Aṣmaʿī said it is the upper room (ghurfa). He said:

"And what is upon him if I am reminded or forgotten, like gazelles of sand in the sanctuaries of Aqyal?"

The commentators explained it as "upper rooms of Aqyal." Al-Zajjaj said it is the high, noble place. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ said it is the palace, because of its nobility and height. It is said it is the mosque. It is said its known miḥrāb was so named because people compete for it and vie over it, and it is the place of the imam in the mosque.

Hunā (there): a demonstrative noun for a near place. It is obligatorily used as a locative adverb, but it can be governed by a preposition. If you attach the kāf of address to it, it indicates a distant place. The tribe of Banū Tamīm says hunāka. The particle of alerting (ḥarf al-tanbīh) may be prefixed to it when the lām is not present in it, and it may be intended for temporal adverbs.

Al-Nidāʾ: raising the voice. Fulān is andā ṣawtan, that is, higher-voiced. Dār al-Nadwa (the Council House) is named so because their voices were raised in it. Al-Muntadā and al-Nādī are the gathering place of the people. One says nādā munādāh, nidāʾ, and nudāʾ, with a kasra or ḍamma on the nūn. It is said: with the kasra it is the verbal noun (maṣdar), and with the ḍamma it is a noun. Most vocal sounds come with a ḍamma, like the call (duʿāʾ), the bleating (rughāʾ), and the crying (ṣurākh). Yaʿqūb said: it is extended with a kasra on the nūn, and shortened with a ḍamma. Al-Nadā means rain, from which one says nadā yandā nadan.

Yaḥyā: a non-Arabic name, not declined due to non-Arabic origin and proper-name status. It is also said that it is Arabic, and it is an imperfect verb from ḥayiya. It was named with it, so it is not declined due to proper-name status and the pattern of the verb. According to both views, its plural is yaḥyawna, with the alif deleted and the letter before it given a fatḥa, according to the view of al-Khalīl and Sībawayh. It is transmitted from the Kufans: if it is Arabic, the yā is given a fatḥa; if it is non-Arabic, the yā is given a ḍamma.

Sayyid (master): on the pattern fayʿil from sāda, meaning he surpassed in nobility. The discussion of its counterpart has preceded. Its plural on the pattern faʿla is sādah, which is irregular. Al-Rāghib said: he is the one who manages the common people, that is, most of them, and for this reason one says "the master of the slave" but not "the master of the garment." End of his words.

Al-Ḥaṣūr: on the pattern faʿūl from al-ḥaṣr (restraint), and it is for intensity from ḥāṣara. It is also said it is faʿūl in the sense of mafʿūl, that is, maḥṣūr (restrained). In the verse it means the one who does not approach women.

Al-Ghulām: a young man among people, the one whose moustache has grown. It is applied to a child by way of optimism, and to an elderly man. From it is the saying of Layla al-Akhyaliyya:

"He is healed from the stubborn illness that is in her by a youth who, when he shakes the spear, gives her drink."

It is a naming by what he was before old age. It comes from al-ghulma and al-ightilām, which is the intensity of the desire for marriage. One says ightalama al-faḥl: the stallion became excited from the intensity of the desire for mating. And ightalama al-baḥr: the sea became agitated and its waves surged. Its plural ghulma is irregular. Its analogical plural for the few is aghlima. For the many it is pluralized as ghilmān, and this is its analogy.

Al-Kibar: the verbal noun of kabura yakburu in age. He said:

"Two small ones grazing the bahm (thistles): O that we had not grown up, nor had the thistles grown up!"

Al-ʿĀqir (barren): the one who has no offspring from a man or a woman. Its verb is intransitive. Al-ʿāqir is the active participle from ʿaqara, meaning he killed, which is transitive.

Al-Ramz: a gesture with the hand, the head, or other things. Its origin is movement. One says irtamaza: he moved. From it the sea is called al-rāmūz.

Al-ʿAshiyy: the singular of ʿashiyya, like rakiyy and rakiyya. Al-ʿashiyya is the end of the day, and its lām is a wāw, so it is like maṭiyy.

Al-Ibkār: the verbal noun of abkara. One says abkara: he went out early in the morning.

﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of ʿImran over the worlds.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: the Jews said, "We are the sons of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and we are upon their religion," so this was revealed. It is also said: it concerns the Christians of Najran when they exaggerated regarding ʿIsa, made him the son of Allah, the Exalted, and took him as a god. It was revealed as a refutation of them and an announcement that ʿIsa is from the descendants of mankind, who moved through the stages that are impossible for God. It digressed from this to the birth of his mother, then to his own birth. This is the connection of these verses to what precedes them. Also, since it was previously said: ﴿Say: If you love Allah, then follow me; Allah will love you﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 31], and it followed with ﴿Say: Obey Allah and the Messenger﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 32], and concluded with ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 32], He mentioned the chosen ones whose following He loves. He began first with the first of them in existence and origin, and then followed with Noah (peace be upon him), since he is the younger Adam; there is no one on the face of the earth except from his offspring. Then He came third with the family of Abraham, within which is included the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who is commanded to be followed and obeyed, and Moses (peace be upon him). Then He came fourth with the family of ʿImran, within which are included Maryam and ʿIsa (peace be upon them both). He specified the family of Abraham because of the particularity of the Jews with them, and the family of ʿImran because of the particularity of the Christians with them. Thus Allah mentioned the making of these a chosen elite, that is, selected, pure. The meaning is that He purified them from turbidity, and this is an example of the known explained through the perceptible.

The choosing of Adam is by several aspects. Among them: his creation as the first of this noble species, his being made a khalīfa (successor) on earth, the angels' prostration to him, his dwelling in His garden, and other things by which He honored him. The choosing of Noah (peace be upon him) is by several things. Among them: that he was the first messenger sent to the people of the earth with the prohibition of daughters, sisters, paternal and maternal aunts, and the rest of the forbidden relatives, and that he is the father of mankind after Adam, and other things. The choosing of the family of Abraham (peace be upon him) is by His placing prophethood and the Book among them. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Ḥasan said: the family of Abraham are those who were upon his religion. Muqatil said: his family are Ismaʿil, Isaac, Jacob, and the Tribes. It is also said: what is meant by the family of Abraham is Abraham himself. Some of the discussion on this has preceded us in His words: ﴿And a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind﴾ [al-Baqara: 248].

Ali Imran (the person to whom "Aal" is attributed): it is said he is Imran ibn Matan, a descendant of Sulayman ibn Dawud (Solomon, son of David), and he is the father of Maryam the virgin, mother of 'Isa (peace be upon him). This was said by al-Hasan and Wahb. It is also said he is Imran, father of Musa and Harun, namely Imran ibn Nusayr, as said by Muqatil. According to the first view, the "family" (Aal) is 'Isa, as said by al-Hasan; according to the second, the family is Musa and Harun, as said by Muqatil. It is also said that by "the family of Imran" is meant Imran himself. The apparent reading of "Imran" is that he is the father of Maryam, because of His words after this, ﴿When the wife of Imran said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35], and then He mentions the story of Maryam and her son 'Isa, and states explicitly that Allah chose her with His words ﴿The angels said: O Maryam, indeed Allah has chosen you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 42]. So His words ﴿When the wife of Imran said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 35] are like an explanation of the manner of the choosing, corresponding to His words "and the family of Imran", and it becomes like the repetition of a name in two clauses, so the mind jumps to the idea that the second is the first, as in: "Zayd was honoured by a righteous man." If the intended second is other than the first, this would cause confusion for the listener. The other view has been preferred on the grounds that Musa is frequently mentioned together with Ibrahim, and there is no way for the understanding to reach that the second Imran is the father of Musa and Harun, even though he had a daughter called Maryam who was older than Musa and Harun, because of the explicit statement that Maryam daughter of Imran ibn Matan bore 'Isa, and that Zakariyya was the guardian of Maryam, mother of 'Isa. Zakariyya had married the sister of Maryam, Ishaa daughter of Imran ibn (p-435) Matan, so Yahya and 'Isa were cousins through their mothers, and between the two Imrans and the two Maryams there are many generations. It is said that between the two Imrans there are a thousand years and eight hundred years.

The apparent meaning: "Aal" refers to those who return to the person by kinship or by creed. The apparent meaning is that He explicitly named these here in the choosing, for the excellences which Allah placed in them. The chief judge in al-Andalus, Abu al-Hakam Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballluti, may Allah have mercy on him and be pleased with him, held that the mention of Adam and Nuh included an indication to the believers between them, and that "the family" means the followers. So the meaning is that Allah chose the believers over the disbelievers, and these were singled out for mention to honour them, and because the discourse concerns the story of some of them. End of his summarised words. His statement is similar in meaning to that of one who interpreted His words "Adam" and what follows as having an omitted genitive construction, meaning: Allah chose the religion of Adam. This meaning was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the intended meaning is that He chose their religion over the other religions, and al-Farra' preferred it. Al-Tibrizi said: this is weak, because if there were an omitted genitive, it would be "and Nuh" in the genitive case, since the position of Adam is genitive by annexation. What al-Tibrizi said is nothing, and had it not been written down in books I would not have mentioned it. For it is not necessary that the annexed noun be put in the genitive when the annexing noun is omitted, so that what is conjoined to it must be genitive; rather the annexed noun takes the i'rab of the omitted annexing noun. Do you not see His words ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]? As for keeping it in the genitive, it is not permissible except under a condition mentioned in the science of grammar.

﴿عَلى العالَمِينَ﴾ ("over the worlds") is connected to "isṭafā" (chose), which has been made to include the meaning of "faḍḍala" (favoured), so it takes "ʿalā". Had it not been given the meaning of "faḍḍala", it would have taken "min". It is said: the meaning is "over the worlds of their time", and the wording is general while the intended meaning is particular, as Jarir said:
"And the worlds will come to him as dependants"
And al-Hutay'a said:
"May Allah relieve the worlds of you"
And as you interpret His words ﴿and that I favoured you over the worlds﴾ [al-Baqara: 47]. Al-Qatibi said: every age has its world, and it is possible that it is restricted to those other than these, and that Muhammad is included in His words "and the family of Ibrahim," so the meaning is that these were favoured over those other than them among the worlds. Their sharing in the common measure of preference does not indicate equality in the degrees of preference, just as you say: Zayd, Umar and Khalid are wealthy; their sharing in the common measure of wealth does not indicate equality in the degrees of wealth. When we take "the worlds" to mean those other than these, this indicates the preference of humans over angels, since they are among those other than these chosen ones, and the verse has been used as evidence for that. It is not possible to take "the worlds" in its generality, because of contradiction: if a large group is described such that each one of them is better than all the worlds, it would follow that each one of them is better than the other, which is impossible. ʿAbd Allah read: "and the family of Muhammad over the worlds."

﴿ذُرِّيَّةً بَعْضُها مِن بَعْضٍ﴾ ("offspring, some of them from others"): they permitted two possibilities for the accusative of "dhurriyyatan". The first: that it is a substitute (badal). Al-Zamakhshari said: from "the family of Ibrahim and the family of Imran", meaning that the two families are one offspring. Others said it is a substitute for Nuh and those conjoined to him among the names. Abu al-Baqa' said: it cannot be a substitute for Adam, because he is not an offspring. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is not proper to say of a parent of this one that he is an offspring of his child. Al-Raghib said: "dhurriyya" is said of the one, the plural, the origin and the progeny, as in His words ﴿We carried their offspring﴾ [Ya Sin: 41], meaning their forefathers, and it is said of women: "dharari". The author of al-Nazm said: the verse requires that fathers be offspring of sons and sons be offspring of fathers, and this is permissible because it derives from "dhara'a Allahu al-khalq" (Allah created creation): the father is one from whom the child was created, and the child was created from the father. Al-Naqqash said the same. According to the view of al-Raghib and the author of al-Nazm, it is permissible for "dhurriyyatan" to be a substitute for Adam and those conjoined to him. They also permitted the accusative of "dhurriyyatan" as a state (hal), which is the second of the two possibilities; al-Zamakhshari did not mention it, but Ibn 'Atiyya did, and said it is more apparent than the substitute. The discussion of "dhurriyya" in terms of meaning, derivation and form has already preceded, so it is sufficient and there is no need to repeat it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 35 (part 1 of 2):

Zayd ibn Thabit and al-Dahhak read *dhurriyyatan* with a kasra on the dhal, while the majority read it with a damma.

﴿some of them are from others﴾ is a clause in the position of a qualifier (ṣifa) for *dhurriyyatan*. *Min* here is partitive in its literal sense, meaning that they are branching out, some from others, through descent. If *Imran* is interpreted as the father of Musa and Harun, then they are from him. He is from Yaṣhar, Yaṣhar is from Qahith, Qahith is from Lawi, Lawi is from Ya'qub, Ya'qub is from Ishaq, and Ishaq is from Ibrahim, peace be upon them. If *Imran* is interpreted as the father of Maryam, mother of Isa, then Isa is from Maryam, and Maryam is from Imran ibn Mathan. He is from the descendants of Sulayman ibn Dawud, and Sulayman is from the descendants of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered the family of Ibrahim (ﷺ). It was also said that *min* is partitive in a metaphorical sense, meaning: some from others in faith, obedience, and the favour of prophethood bestowed upon them. Al-Hasan went in a similar direction and said: some from others in supporting the religion. Abu Rawq said: some of them are upon the religion of others. Qatada said: in intention, action, sincerity, and monotheism.

﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ means: He hears what creatures say and knows what they conceal. Or: He hears what the wife of Imran says and knows what she intends. Or: He hears what the offspring say and knows what they conceal. These are three opinions. Al-Zamakhshari said: He knows who is fit for being chosen, or He knows that some of them are from others in religion, end of quote.

What appears to be the case is that ending this verse with ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ is appropriate to His saying ﴿and the family of Ibrahim and the family of Imran﴾, because Ibrahim, peace be upon him, supplicated to his Lord in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in an uncultivated valley﴾, and in His saying: ﴿So make hearts among the people incline toward them and provide for them from the fruits﴾. He praised his Lord, the Exalted, and said: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has granted me in old age Ismail and Ishaq﴾, and he said, informing about his Lord: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Hearer of supplication﴾. Then he supplicated his Lord to make him and his offspring establishers of prayer. When he and Ismail were building the Kaaba, he said: ﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾, and went on through the rest of what he supplicated for, up to His saying: ﴿And send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses﴾. For this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I am the answer to the prayer of Ibrahim." Since there came from Ibrahim supplications and invocations to his Lord, the Exalted, concerning his family and offspring, it was appropriate to end with His saying: ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾. Likewise the family of Imran: the wife of Imran supplicated for the acceptance of what she had vowed to Allah, the Exalted, so it was also appropriate to mention the two attributes. For this reason, when she mentioned the vow and supplicated for its acceptance, she informed about her Lord that He is ﴿the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, that is: the All-Hearing of her supplication, the All-Knowing of the sincerity of her intention in vowing what is in her womb to Allah, the Exalted.

﴿When the wife of Imran said: My Lord, indeed I have vowed to You﴾, up to the verse. When He mentioned that He, the Exalted, had chosen the family of Imran, and since the greater part of the opening of this surah concerns the Christians of the delegation of Najran, He mentioned at the outset the condition of the family of Imran. The name of the wife of Imran was Hannah, with a ḥa' (unpointed), a nun with shadda, both vowelled with a fatḥa, and ending with a *tā' marbūṭa* (feminine ending). It is a Hebrew name. She was Hannah daughter of Faqud. The monastery of Hannah in Syria is well known, and there is another monastery known as the Monastery of Hannah. Abu Nawas mentioned the Monastery of Hannah in his poetry, saying:

O Monastery of Hannah, from the side of al-Akayrah, whoever is sober about you, for I am not sober.

The tomb of Hannah, grandmother of Isa, is on the outskirts of Damascus. Al-Qurtubi said: The name Hannah is not known in Arabic as a woman's name. Abd al-Ghani ibn Sa'id, the ḥāfiẓ, mentioned: Hannah, mother of Umar, and Ibn Juraij narrates her hadith. Hannah is also found alongside Habbah, with an unpointed ḥa' and a single dot below the bā', and Ḥayyah, with an unpointed ḥa' and two dots below the yā'. Both are names of people. Alongside Khabbah, with a dotted khā' and a single dot below the bā', is Khabbah daughter of Yahya ibn Akthum the judge, mother of Muhammad ibn Nasr. Alongside Jannah, with a jīm and a nun, is Abu Jannah, maternal uncle of Dhu al-Rummah the poet; we know of no one else by this name. Hannah did not suffice with the intention of the vow until she made it manifest by utterance, and she addressed it to Allah, the Exalted, and before pronouncing that, she preceded it with her call to Him, the Exalted, using the word *Rabb*, which is the Owner of her and the Owner of everything. The meaning of *nadhr* has already been mentioned: it is seeking to avert what is feared by means of an act of righteousness that a person binds upon himself. It was also said: it is what a person makes obligatory upon himself, either conditionally or unconditionally. The poet said:

So would that men who vowed my blood concerning you, O Buthayn, and intended to kill me, would meet me!

(p-437) The *lām* in *laka* is the lām of cause, and it is with an omitted estimate: for the service of Your House, or to be detained in obedience to You.

﴿what is in my womb﴾: she was certain of the vow on the assumption that it would be a male, or hoping that it would be a male.

(*Muharraran*) its meaning is freed from every occupation of worldly affairs, so it is derived from the word *hurriyyah* (freedom). Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: or a servant of the church. This was said by Mujahid. Or: devoted to worship, said by al-Sha'bi. Khusayf narrated it from Ikrima and Mujahid. She used the word *ma* rather than *man*, because the fetus at that time was not characterized by reason, or because *ma* is indefinite, applying to everything, so it may stand in the place of *man*. This was attributed to Sibawayh.

﴿So accept from me﴾: she supplicated Allah, the Exalted, to accept from her what she had vowed to Him. *Taqabbul* is taking a thing with approval of it, and its root is reciprocating with reward. *Tqabbal* here has the meaning of *qabila* (accepted), so it is one of those forms of *tafa''ala* used with the meaning of the bare verb, like their saying: *ta'addā al-shay'* and *'addāhu* (he passed over the thing and made it pass). This is one of the meanings for which *tafa''ala* has come.

﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾: it was concluded with these two attributes because she had resolved the vow, bound it by her intention, uttered it, and supplicated for its acceptance, so mentioning these two attributes was appropriate. The governing element in *idh* is an implied verb whose estimate is: *udhkur* (remember), as said by al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad. Or the meaning of *al-istifa'* (choosing), the estimate being: and He chose the family of Imran. This was said by al-Zajjaj. On this view, *wa-āla 'Imrān* is treated as coordination of clauses, not of single words. This is because if it were treated as coordination of single words, the governing element for it would have to be *iṣṭafā Ādam* (He chose Adam), and this is not permissible, since the time of this choosing differs from the time of the statement of the wife of Imran, so its governing does not hold for it. Al-Tabari said something to the effect that the governing element for it is *samī'*, which is the apparent view of al-Zamakhshari; or *samī' 'alīm*, because of the statement and intention of the wife of Imran, and *idh* is in the accusative by it, end of quote. This is not correct, because His saying *'alīm* is either a predicate after a predicate, or a qualifier of *samī'*. If it is a predicate, then it is not permissible to separate the governing element from the governed by it, since it is foreign to both of them. If it is a qualifier, then *samī'* cannot govern the adverbial phrase, since it has already been qualified. The active participle and what is like it, when it has been qualified before taking its object, does not permit governing in that case, in contrast to some of the Kufans on this matter. Also, His being described as All-Hearing, All-Knowing is not restricted to that time.

Abu Ubayda held that *idh* is superfluous, the meaning being: the wife of Imran said. A parallel to this view had preceded him in several places, and Abu Ubayda used to be weak in grammar.

*Muharraran* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). It was said: it is from *mā*, so the governing element is *nadhartu* (I vowed). It was also said: from the pronoun in *istaqarra*, and the governing element for the prepositional phrase is *istaqarra*. Makki said: whoever puts it in the accusative as an adjective (na't) of an implied object, estimating it as: a boy freed (ghulāman muḥarraran). Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: In this there is a consideration, meaning that *nadhara* has already taken its object, which is *mā fī baṭnī* (what is in my womb), so it does not transitively extend to a further object. *Muharraran* may be in the accusative as a verbal noun in the sense of *taḥrīran* (liberating), since a verbal noun may be of the form of the passive participle from any verb of more than three radicals, as the poet said:

Do you not know that my verses are sent forth, so there is no difficulty in them nor any effort in bringing them?

The estimate is: *tasrīḥī al-qawāfī* (my sending forth of the verses). In that case it is by omitting a noun in the genitive construction, meaning: she vowed liberation (*nadhara taḥrīran*). Or it is a verbal noun from the meaning of *nadhartu*, since the meaning of "I vowed to You what is in my womb" is: I liberated for You, by the vow, what is in my womb. The apparent view is the first opinion, which is that it is a circumstantial state of *mā*. In that case it is a future circumstantial state if the intended meaning of *muharraran* is a servant of the church, and a simultaneous circumstantial state if the intended meaning is freed, since freeing what is in the womb is permissible.
