They wrote *imra'at 'Imrān* with a *tā'* and not a *hā'*, and likewise *imra'at al-'Azīz* in two places, *imra'at Nūḥ*, *imra'at Lūṭ*, and *imra'at Fir'awn*. That makes seven places. The people of Madina stop with a *tā'*, following the orthography of the Mushaf, although it is a dialect of some Arabs who stop on *Ṭalḥah* as *Ṭalḥat* with a *tā'*. Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i stopped with a *hā'* and did not follow the orthography of the Mushaf in that, and this is the dialect of most Arabs.

The exegetes mentioned the reason for this pregnancy that befell the wife of Imran. It was narrated that she was barren, and they were a household that had a station with Allah. One day she was in the shade of a tree, and she saw a bird feeding its chick, so her soul was stirred toward having a child, and she called upon Allah, the Exalted, to grant her a child. Then she conceived. Imran, her husband, died while she was pregnant, so she considered the pregnancy to be a child, and she vowed it to Allah as one dedicated to serving the church or Bayt al-Maqdis. It was among their customs to draw near to Allah by dedicating their children to their houses of worship. The sons of Mathan were the chiefs, kings, and rabbis of the Children of Israel, and not one of them was without a descendant who was freed for Bayt al-Maqdis among the boys, while a girl was not suited for this. It was permissible in their law, and their children were obligated to obey them. When a servant of the church was freed, he would serve by sweeping and lighting the lamps until he reached maturity, and then he was given the choice: if he wished to remain in the church, he remained there, and he had no right to leave after that; and if he wished to go, he went wherever he wished. Not one of the prophets or scholars was without a descendant who was freed for Bayt al-Maqdis.

﴿So when she delivered her, she said: My Lord, indeed I have delivered her as a female﴾ [Aal Imran: 36]. The pronoun in *waḍa'at-hā* was made feminine in agreement with the meaning of *mā*, because what was in her womb was a female in the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: in agreement with the one who was born (*al-mawjidah*), and to raise the wording of *mā* in her saying *mā fī baṭnī* (what is in my womb). Al-Zamakhshari said: or in accordance with the interpretation of the nature (*al-jiblla*), or the soul (*al-nafs*), or the living being (*al-nasamah*). The answer to *lammā* is: she said, and she addressed her Lord out of a sense of regret over what had escaped her of her hope, and contrary to what she had estimated, because she had hoped to bear a male suitable for service, and for this reason she had vowed him as freed. In His saying *innī waḍa'tu-hā* (I have delivered her), the pronoun came feminine. If it is in accordance with the meaning of the living being or the soul, then it is clear, since the circumstantial state in her saying *unthā* (female) is then specifying, for the living being and the soul apply to both male and female. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, how is it permissible for *unthā* to be in the accusative as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in *waḍa'tu-hā*, when it is like your saying: "She delivered the female, a female"?

Ibn Abi Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) said: I say: The original is "wada'athu unthā" (she gave birth to it, a female), and the feminine was used because of the feminine gender of the circumstance (al-hal), since the circumstance and the one in that circumstance are one thing. This is like the noun being made feminine in "man kanat ummuka?" (who was your mother?) because of the feminine gender of the predicate (al-khabar). A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they were two (females)﴾ [an-Nisa': 176]. End of quote.

Its outcome is that "unthā" (female) becomes an emphatic circumstance (hal mu'akkida), and its being feminine because of the feminine gender of the circumstance does not prevent the circumstance from being emphatic.

As for his comparison of that with His saying "man kanat ummuka", where the pronoun returns to the meaning of "man", this is not a parallel to "wada'tuha unthā", because that is agreement with the meaning of "man", since the meaning is: "whatever woman was your mother", i.e., she was which woman your mother was. So the feminine is not because of the feminine gender of the predicate, but is from the category of agreement with the meaning of "man". Even if we supposed that the feminine is for the noun because of the feminine gender of the predicate, it would not be a parallel to "wada'tuhā unthā", because the predicate is specified by its being in construct with the pronoun, so something is gained from the predicate that is not gained from the noun. Unlike "unthā", which is merely for emphasis.

As for his using as a parallel His saying "fa-in kanatāithnatayn" [an-Nisa': 176], he means that he made the noun dual to match the dual of the predicate. The discussion of it will come in its place, for it is one of the difficult matters. So the best option is to make the pronoun in "wada'tuhā unthā" refer to the soul (nasama) or the self (nafs), so that the circumstance is descriptive (mabniyya) and not emphatic.

It has also been said: she addressed God, exalted is He, with this, as an apology and a disclaimer from having vowed what is not suitable for serving the sanctuary, since a female was not suitable for that in their law. It has also been said: Maryam was the most beautiful and most perfect of the women of her time.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 36–38 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And God knows best what she gave birth to.﴾ Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Bakr and Yaʿqub read waḍaʿat with a ḍamma on the tāʾ (waḍaʿtu), and in that case this and what follows is part of the speech of Umm Maryam, as though she were addressing herself by saying "God knows best." She did not use the form "my Lord" (rabbi), for had she done so she would have said, "And You know best what I gave birth to." Rather, she addressed herself by way of consolation for the male child (al-dhakar) she had hoped for, and the knowledge of God, His foreordained power and His wisdom, would lead her to not grieve or fret over what had escaped her of the purpose, since His will must be the will that is to be done. The male she had sought and hoped for is not like the female whom He knew, willed and decreed. Perhaps this female will be better than a male, since God willed her, and so she consoled herself with this.

The alif and lam in "al-dhakar" may be for specificity (ʿahd), in which case her intent is to prefer this female, who is a gift from God, over what she had hoped, that it would be a male. It may also be understood that her intent was that the male is not like the female in excellence, rank and virtue, because the male is fit for dedication and for continuing in service at the place of worship, and because he is stronger for service, and no defect or suspicion attaches to him in service or in mixing with people. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "like the female in the impermissibility of vowing her, since the female menstruates and is not fit for companionship with the monks," as stated by Qatadah, al-Rabiʿ, al-Suddi, ʿIkrimah and others. She began with the matter most important to her, and otherwise the natural sequence of speech would be, "the female is not like the male," placing the negating particle with the thing she possesses and negating from it the attributes of perfection for the intended purpose, end of quote. On this understanding the alif and lam in "al-dhakar" are for the genus.

The rest of the seven readers read bimā waḍaʿat, with the feminine tāʾ sukūn, as a statement from God that He is most knowing of what she gave birth to, that is, of its condition and what this female's affair will become. Her saying "I gave birth to her as a female" shows that she knew of her only this much: that this offspring had come as a female unfit for dedication. So God informed that He knows best about this one who was born, using the comparative form, which implies knowledge of the details of the conditions, and this is for the sake of magnifying this one who was born and informing of the great matters attached to her and her son, since He made her and her son a sign for the worlds. Her mother was ignorant of this and knew nothing of it. Ibn ʿAbbas read bimā waḍaʿti, with a kasra on the tāʾ of address, meaning God addressed her thus: "You do not know the worth of this gifted one, nor what God knows of her great station and her exalted rank." Mā is a relative pronoun meaning "that which" or "she who," and it is stated with the word mā, as in His words, ﴿I vowed to You what is in my womb﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 35]. The returning pronoun is omitted in every reading.

﴿And I have named her Maryam﴾. Maryam, in their language, means "the worshipper." By this naming she sought an omen of good for her and drew near to God, Exalted is He, and humbled herself before Him, that her conduct would correspond to her name and that her hope for her would be fulfilled. Do you not see her seeking refuge in God for her and for her offspring from Satan? She addressed God with these words because the seeking of refuge follows from them. Her sole right to the naming indicates that her father ʿImran had died, as it is reported that he died while she was pregnant. Yet it is possible, since she was a female, that the mother alone named her, out of the dislike of men for daughters. The verse includes naming the child near the time of birth. In a hadith: "A child was born to me last night, and I named him after my father Ibrahim." And in a hadith it is said that a sacrifice is made for a newborn on the seventh day and he is named.

This sentence is joined to what came before it in her speech, and all of it falls under "she said" on the reading of those who read waḍaʿtu with a ḍamma on the tāʾ. As for those who read waḍaʿat with a sukūn on the tāʾ or with a kasra, al-Zamakhshari said: it is joined to "I have given birth to her as a female," and what lies between them is two parenthetical clauses, like His words, ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 76], end of his words. It is not necessarily the case that these are two parenthetical clauses, since it is possible that ﴿and the male is not like the female﴾ in this reading is part of her speech, and the parenthetical would be a single clause, as it was part of her speech in the reading of those who read waḍaʿtu with a ḍamma. Rather, this should be the definite view, because the parenthesis of two clauses is disputed according to the view of Abu ʿAli, who held that two clauses do not intervene; and we have already discussed this. Furthermore, his comparison of these two clauses with which he claims a parenthesis is made between the conjunct and the conjoined, with his words ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 76], is not an exact parallel to the verse, because two clauses did not intervene between a seeker and a sought. Rather, a single clause, His words ﴿if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 76], intervened between the oath, which is ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 75], and its answer, which is ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 77]. But it came within the parenthetical clause, between some of its parts and others, a parenthesis by a clause, namely His words ﴿if you only knew﴾, which intervened between the modified, "a mighty oath," and its modifier, "mighty." This is a parenthesis within a parenthesis, so it is not a separation by two parenthetical clauses in His words, "God knows best what she gave birth to, and the male is not like the female."

He named (sammā) among the verbs that take one object directly and another through a preposition, which may be dropped, though keeping it is the original form: one says "I named my son Zayd" and "I named him Zayd." The poet said:

"I named Kaʿb 'Bishr al-ʿIẓam,' and your father used to be named al-Jaʿl."

That is: "I was named Kaʿb," and "he is named al-Jaʿl." This is a restricted usage that depends on transmission, and there is a difference of opinion about it from al-Akhfash al-Saghir; the detailed discussion belongs to the science of grammar.

﴿And I seek refuge for her with You, and for her offspring, from the accursed Satan.﴾ The predicate of inna is in the present tense, "u'īdhuhā," because her intent is the continuity of seeking refuge and its recurrence, unlike "I gave birth to her" and "I named her," which are past acts that have ended. She placed the object of seeking refuge before the conjoined noun following the pronoun for the sake of emphasis. Then she went on to mention her offspring, and her addressing God with the earlier direct speech was only a means to this seeking of refuge, just as a person puts before his purpose something that draws down the goodness of the one he is addressing, and then after that mentions the purpose itself. It is related in a hadith, from Abu Hurayrah: "Every child of the sons of Adam is touched by Satan at birth, and with that touch the child cries out, except Maryam the daughter of ʿImran and her son. For her mother said when she gave birth to her: ﴿And I seek refuge for her with You, and for her offspring, from the accursed Satan﴾. So a veil was set between them, and Satan struck the veil."

The wordings of this hadith have varied across several chains, while the meaning is one. The judge ʿAbd al-Jabbar criticized this hadith, saying: it is a solitary report (khabar wahid) contrary to the evidence, and so it must be rejected. It is contrary to the evidence because Satan only calls to evil those who know good and evil, and the infant is not such; and because if he could reach this touch he would do more than that, such as destroying the righteous and other things, since it specified Maryam and her son ʿIsa over the rest of the prophets; and because if he touched them, its trace would be visible, and if it were visible the screaming and weeping would continue, but since this is not so, we know the falsity of this hadith. Al-Zamakhshari said: as for what is narrated in the hadith: "No child is born except that Satan touches him at his birth, and he cries out from the touch of Satan, except Maryam and her son," God knows best its soundness. If it is sound, its meaning is that every child is one whom Satan hopes to mislead, except Maryam and her son, for they were protected. Likewise everyone who shares their attributes, according to His words: ﴿And I will surely mislead them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 39], ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [al-Hijr: 40]. The crying out from his touch is imaginative and figurative, owing to Satan's hope for him, as though he touches him and strikes his hand on him, saying, "This is one of those I will mislead." Of the same figurative kind is the saying of Ibn al-Rumi:

"For what the world announces of its calamities, the crying of the infant at the hour of his birth is what it means."

As for the literal reality of touch and pricking, as the ignorant of the literalist school imagine, no: even if Iblis were empowered over people to prick them, the world would be filled with shrieking and wailing from what he would test us with by his pricking, end of his words. This proceeds along the path of the Mu'tazilites, and we have already passed some discussion of this in His words: ﴿like one whom Satan has confused by touch﴾ [al-Baqara: 275].

﴿So her Lord accepted her with a goodly acceptance.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: the original is "fa-tqabbalahā bi-tqabbulin ḥasanin," but qabūlin is taken as qabilahā qabūlan, one says qabila al-shay' qabūlan when he is pleased with it, and the measure for it is the ḍamma, like duḫūl and khurūj, but it came with a fatḥa. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj permitted a ḍamma on the qāf, and Ibn al-Aʿrabi transmitted it, saying: qabiltuhu qabūlan and qubūlan. Ibn ʿAbbas said: its meaning is that He took her on the path of the blessed. Others said: He undertook her upbringing and attending to her affairs. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is that He did not punish her for a single hour of night or day. On these views, "tqabbala" is in the sense of "istaqbala," so that "tafaʿʿala" is in the sense of "istafʿala," meaning: her Lord received her, like "ta'ajjaltu al-shay' fa-isti'jaltuhu" and "taqassaytu al-shay' wa-istaqsaytuhu," from their saying istaqbala al-amr, that is, he took it at its beginning. The poet said:

"The best of affairs is what you receive from its outset, and not what you pursue after it has passed."

That is: He took her at the beginning of her affair, the moment she was born. It is also said: the meaning is "fa-qabilahā," that is, He was pleased with her in the vow in place of the male, as her mother had vowed, and He accepted her supplication in her words: ﴿So accept from me, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, and no female was accepted before Maryam in this way. In this case "tafaʿʿala" is in the sense of the bare verb, as in taʿajjaba and ʿajiba, and tabarraʾa and bari'a. The bāʾ in "bi-qabūlin" is said by some to be extra, and then it is in the accusative as an infinitive not of its own verb; others say it is not extra.

Qabūl is the name of what by which something is accepted, like suʿūṭ and ludūd, for what is put into the nose and what is poured into the mouth. It refers to her being singled out by His making her stand in place of the male in the vow. Or it is a verbal noun with an omitted modifier, meaning "with one who has goodly acceptance," that is, "with a matter of goodly acceptance," which is the singling out.

﴿And He caused her to grow in a goodly growth.﴾ This is an expression for goodness of upbringing and excellence in form and character, so He raised her in obedience and worship. Ibn ʿAbbas said: when she reached nine years of age she fasted by day and stood in prayer by night until she surpassed the rabbis. It is said: no sin ever befell her. Qatadah said: we have been told that she never committed sins as the sons of Adam do. It is also said the meaning of "wa-anbatahā nabātan ḥasanan" is that He made her fruit like ʿIsa. "Nabātan" is in the accusative either as an infinitive not of its own verb, or as an infinitive for an omitted verb, meaning "so she grew a goodly growth." It is also said: the acceptance is her being raised upon the attribute of purity, until she said: ﴿I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing﴾ [Maryam: 18]. The goodly growth is steadfastness in obedience and preferring God's pleasure at all times.

﴿And Zakariyya took charge of her.﴾ Qatadah said: he took her to himself. Abu ʿUbayda said: he undertook (ḍamina) the care of her, and among the goodly acceptance and the goodly growth is that God made her guardian, the one in charge of her affairs and her protection, a prophet. God revealed to Dawud, peace be upon him: "When you see one seeking Me, be a servant to him."

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 3, verses 36–38 (part 2 of 3):

The Kufans read "wa-kaffalahā" (﴿وكَفَّلَها﴾) with a doubled fa' (tashdid), and the rest of the seven readers read it with a single fa' (takhfif). Ubayy read "wa-akfalahā" (﴿وأكْفَلَها﴾), and Mujahid read "fa-taqabbal-hā" (﴿فَتَقَبَّلْها﴾) with a sukun on the lam. "Rabbahā" was read with a fatha, as a vocative (ʿalā al-nidāʾ). "Wa-anbitha-hā" was read with a kasra on the ba' and a sukun on the ta'. "Wa-kaffil-hā" was read with a kasra on the fa' with tashdid and a sukun on the lam, as a supplication from Umm Maryam, addressed to Maryam. ʿAbd Allah al-Muzani read "wa-kafila-hā" with a kasra on the fa', which is a dialect form: it is said kafila yakfalu and kafala yakfulu, like ʿalima yaʿlamu. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read "Zakariyyā" with a short vowel (maqsur), while the rest of the seven read it as a long form (mamdud). The dialectal forms of this word have been mentioned before.

It is related that when Hannah gave birth to Maryam, she wrapped her in a piece of cloth and took her to the mosque, and placed her with the rabbis, the sons of Harun, who in Bayt al-Maqdis were like the custodians (al-hajabah) of the Ka'bah. She said to them: "Take this offering (al-nadhirah), and compete for her," because she was the daughter of their imam and the one who offered their sacrifices. The Banu Mathan were the leaders of the Children of Israel, their rabbis and their kings. Zakariyya said to them: "I have the greatest right to her; her aunt is with me." They said: "No, until we draw lots over her." So they went off, and they were twenty-seven, to a river. It is said it was the river Jordan, and this is the view of the majority. It is also said it was a spring of water there. They cast their pens into it, and the pen of Zakariyya rose up while their pens sank, and so he took charge of her. It is said that he also arranged a wet-nurse for her. Al-Hasan said: she never took a breast at all. ʿIkrimah said: they cast their pens, and the pen of Zakariyya moved against the current of the water, while their pens went along with the current. It is also said that they floated along with the water, lying flat, and Zakariyya's pen remained standing, as if it had been fixed in mud. Ibn Ishaq said: Zakariyya had married her aunt, for he and ʿImran were brothers-in-law through two sisters. The wife of Zakariyya bore Yahya, and the wife of ʿImran bore Maryam. al-Suddi and others said: Zakariyya had married another daughter of ʿImran. This view is supported by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ about Yahya and ʿIsa: "The sons of the maternal aunt." It is also said that he took charge of her only because her mother had died, and her father had died while she was still in her mother's womb. It is also said that Zakariyya was her paternal cousin, and her sister was his wife. Ibn Ishaq said: she grew up, and the Children of Israel suffered a famine. Zakariyya said to them: "I have become unable to provide for Maryam." So they cast lots over who would take charge of her, and they did so. A man called Jurayj came out to them, and he began to provide for her. This "istihām" (drawing of lots) is different from the first one: the purpose of this one was to hand her over for the provision of her maintenance, while the purpose of the first was to take her into his care. According to this view, Zakariyya had taken charge of her from childhood without a lottery. But what the people hold to is that Zakariyya took charge of her by lot, and the Qur'an does not indicate that anyone other than Zakariyya took charge of her. Zakariyya was the more deserving of her guardianship, because he was among her relatives on her father's side, and because her aunt or her sister was his wife (depending on the two views), and because he was a prophet, so he was the most deserving of her for his infallibility (ʿiṣmah). Zakariyya is the son of Adhn ibn Muslim, of the descendants of Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them. But the genealogist Abu al-Barakat al-Jawwani, the naqib, mentioned that Yahya ibn Zakariyya, al-Yasaʿ, Ilyas and al-ʿUzayr were of the descendants of Harun, the brother of Musa. On this view, Zakariyya would not be of the descendants of Sulayman, and would not be the cousin of Maryam, because Maryam is of the descendants of Sulayman, peace be upon him, and Sulayman was of Yahudha ibn Yaʿqub, while Musa and Harun were the sons of Lawi ibn Yaʿqub.

Ibn Ishaq said: he placed her with her aunt, the mother of Yahya, until she grew up and reached the age of women. He built a niche (mihrab) for her in the mosque, and placed its door in its middle, so that it could not be reached except by a ladder, like the door of the Ka'bah, and no one but him could climb up to her. It is also said that when he went out he would lock seven doors on her. Muqatil said: he would lock the door on her with the key in his hand, and would not entrust it to anyone. When she menstruated he would take her out to his house, to be with her aunt the mother of Yahya or her sister; when she became clean he would return her to Bayt al-Maqdis. It is also said that she was purified from menstruation.

﴿Every time Zakariyya entered upon her in the mihrab, he found provision with her﴾. Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: he found with her winter fruit in summer, and summer fruit in winter. al-Hasan said: she spoke in the cradle, and never took a breast at all, and her provision used to come to her from Paradise. What is related in the Sahih is that the ones who spoke in the cradle were three: ʿIsa, the companion of Jurayj, and the son of the woman, and a unique (shadhdh) narration mentions the companion of the trench (al-Ukhdud). The most surprising thing is that Maryam is among them. It is said that Jurayj was a carpenter, whose name was Yusuf ibn Yaʿqub, and he was a cousin of Maryam when he took charge of her by lottery. Zakariyya had become too weak to carry out this task, so Jurayj would bring her something light from his earnings, according to his capacity, and it would increase and multiply. Then Zakariyya would enter upon her and realise that it was beyond Jurayj's means, and would ask her. This indicates that this happened after she had grown up, and this is the closer view to the truth. It is also said that she was provided with food from outside the provision of their land: Ibn ʿAbbas said it was grapes in a basket, though no grapes grew in that land; this was also said by Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. It is also said that some of the righteous used to bring her provision.

What the apparent meaning of the verse indicates is that the one who took charge of her by upbringing was Zakariyya and no one else, for Allah the Exalted sufficed him, when he took charge of her, the burden of her provision, and by his good guardianship removed from him the hardship of effort. "Kullama" (every time) requires repetition, and so it indicates the abundance of his care and attentiveness to her circumstances. The verse indicates that the provision was present with her at every time he entered upon her. The meaning is that it was nourishment eaten by her which he had not known to be with her, and which he had not himself brought. Far removed is the one who explained "rizq" here as an overflow that came to her from Allah of knowledge and wisdom without human teaching, and so called it "rizq." al-Raghib said: the word admits this, end of quote. This resembles the interpretation of the Batiniyyah.

﴿He said: O Maryam, from where is this for you? She said: it is from Allah﴾. Zakariyya was surprised at the presence of the provision with her, when he had not brought it, and since it repeatedly appeared with her every time he entered upon her, he asked, in the manner of one wondering, about the arrival of this provision to her, and how it had come. "Anna" is a question about the manner, about the place, and about the time, and the most apparent is that it is a question about the direction, as though he said: from what direction has this provision come to you? For this reason Abu ʿUbaydah said: its meaning is "from where?" It is not far-fetched that it is a question about the manner, that is: how did the arrival of this provision to you come about? al-Kumayt said:

"From where, and from what direction has joy come to you, from a place with neither youthful folly nor joy?"

Her reply to his question, that it is "from Allah," apparently means that no human being brought it at all; rather it is provision which Allah the Exalted takes charge of for me. Its apparent meaning is that he used to ask every time he found provision with her, because it is permissible in the act that this second instance comes from a direction other than the one that came before. So she answers him that it is from Allah, and refers him to the Causer of causes and the Bringer of things from pure non-existence into pure existence. At this, the heart of Zakariyya was at rest, because no one had preceded him in caring for Maryam, and because he was witnessing a noble station and a subtle care for the one whom Allah the Exalted had chosen by placing her in his guardianship. It is said that this great marvel came about through Zakariyya's supplication for her for provision, and so it would be one of the special qualities of Zakariyya. It is also said that it was a foundation for the prophethood of her son ʿIsa. These two views resemble the views of the Mu'tazilah, in that they deny the existence of a marvel at the hand of someone other than a prophet, unless it occurs in the time of a prophet, in which case it is a miracle for that prophet. The apparent view is that it was a karamah (noble gift) which Allah singled out for Maryam. Had it been a marvel on account of Zakariyya, Zakariyya would not have asked about it. As for it being on account of the prophethood of ʿIsa, he had not yet been created.

al-Zajjaj said: this marvel is one of the signs of which Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91]. al-Jubbai said: it is possible that it was one of the miracles of Zakariyya, who prayed for her in general terms that her provision be delivered to her, and perhaps he was unaware of the details of that; then, when he saw a specific thing at a specific time, he asked about it, and so knew that it was a miracle, and he prayed for it, or asked about it out of fear that the one who brought it might be a human being; so she informed him that it was ﴿from Allah﴾. It may also be that it came through the hands of the believers, and he asked lest it should be in a way that is not fitting.

﴿Indeed Allah provides for whomever He wills without reckoning﴾. The explanation of this sentence has been given before. The apparent view is that it is part of Maryam's speech. al-Tabari said: it is not part of Maryam's speech, but a statement from Allah the Exalted to Muhammad ﷺ. Jabir related a lengthy hadith in which bread and meat were multiplied in a manner that breaks the usual course, for Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He asked her: "From where is this for you?" She said: "It is from Allah." So he praised Allah and said: "All praise is to Allah who made you resemble the mistress of the women of the Children of Israel."

It is said: in these verses there are types of eloquence. The generality that is intended to be particular, in His saying "over the worlds"; and the specification in His saying "Adam, Nuh, the family of Ibrahim, and the family of ʿImran." The use of the name of the branch for the root, and of the effect for the cause, in the word "dhurriyyah," according to the one who said the meaning is the fathers. The ambiguity in His saying "what is in my womb": when it was impossible for her to know what was in her womb, she used the word "ma," which applies to both male and female. The emphasis in His saying "Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing." The report intended as an excuse in her saying: "I have given birth to a female," and the parenthetical insertion in His saying "and Allah knows best what she has given birth to," in the reading of the one who vocalised the ta' with a sukun or a kasra. The shifting of address and what is derived from it in His saying "and Allah knows best what you have given birth to," in the reading of the one who read the ta' with a kasra: it moved from the third person of "fa-lamma waḍaʿat-hā" to the second person of direct address in "bi-mā waḍaʿt." The repetition in "wa-anna," and in "Zakariyya, Zakariyya," and in "from the presence of Allah," "inna Allah." The paronomasia (tajnis) of differing kinds in "fa-taqabbalahā rabbuhā bi-qabūl, wa-anbatahā nabātan," and in "rizqan" and "yarzuqu." The allusion, which is to express a hidden meaning by an apparent expression, in His saying "it is from Allah," meaning it is a provision which no one can bring at that time except Allah. In His saying "rizqan," he used it indefinitely, indicating that it is not of one kind, but of many kinds, because an indefinite noun implies multiplicity and abundance. And there is ellipsis in several places, where the meaning would not be correct without taking it into account.

﴿There Zakariya called upon his Lord﴾. The origin of *hunalika* is that it indicates a place, though it may also be used for a time. Some have said both are meant in this verse: that is, in that place Zakariya called upon Him, or at that time, when he saw this great miraculous sign regarding Maryam, and that she was among those whom Allah had chosen. He was moved to ask for a child, and he needed one because of his advanced age, and so that he might inherit from him and from the family of Ya'qub, as Allah related in Surah Maryam. The fact that his wife was barren did not prevent him from making this request, since he had seen in Maryam's condition something outside the ordinary. So it is not far-fetched that Allah would grant him a child even though his wife was barren, for Hannah had been granted Maryam after she had despaired of having children. The word *hunalika* is governed by the verb *da'a* (called). It occurs in al-Sajawandi's commentary that *hunaka* is for place and *hunalika* for time, but this is a mistake. Rather, the principle is that it is used for place, whether it is joined with the *lam* and the *kaf*, with the *kaf* alone, or with neither. It may be used figuratively for place to mean time, just as the basic meaning of *'inda* (at, with) is place, and then it is used figuratively for time, as when you say: "I will come to you at (*'inda*) sunrise." It has been said that the *lam* in *hunalika* indicates the great distance between the supplication and the answer, for the commentators have reported that there were forty years between his supplication and its answer. It has also been said that the *lam* was added to indicate that this matter is far from ordinary reach, because it breaks the normal course of things, just as the *lam* was added in His words: ﴿That is the Book﴾ (2:2), to indicate its remoteness of reach and its great elevation and nobility. Al-Maturidi said: His soul was speaking to him that Allah might grant him a child through whom the remembrance would endure until the Day of Resurrection, but he did not call upon Him out of regard for good manners, since good manners require that one not ask for a desire except for what is normally possible. Although Allah is capable of all things, when he saw there something that breaks the normal course, this led him to supplicate for a child that is not customary. End of quote.

As for his saying that his soul was speaking to him about this, it needs a transmission. In His words ﴿There called he﴾ there is an indication that the servant should seek out blessed places and honored times for his supplication.

﴿He said: My Lord, grant me from Yourself offspring that is good﴾. This sentence is an explanation and elaboration of the supplication. He addressed Him with the title "My Lord," since He is the One who nurtures him and sets his affairs right. The request came with the word *hab* (grant), because a gift is pure bounty, having no return that would serve as compensation for the giver. Since this was almost by way of no cause at all, neither from the father because of his old age, nor from the mother because she was barren and could not bear children, his existence was like existence without any cause. So it came as a pure gift attributed to Allah the Exalted by His words "from Yourself," meaning from the very source of Your power without any intermediary cause. It has been mentioned that *ladun* is used for what is near, while *'inda* is used for both what is near and what is far, and *ladun* is less vague than *'inda*. Do you not see that *'inda* can be an answer to "where" (*ayna*), while *ladun* cannot be an answer to it? "From Yourself" (*min ladunka*) is connected to *hab*. It has been said that it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) for *dhurriyyatan* (offspring), because if it had been placed after it, it would have been an attribute. On this view it is connected to an omitted element. *Dhurriyyah* is a collective noun that applies to one or more. Al-Tabari said: By *dhurriyyah* here he meant one person, as evidence for which is that he asked for one heir, and did not ask for heirs. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: There is an objection to what al-Tabari said, for *dhurriyyah* and *waliyy* (heir, protector) are collective nouns that apply to one and to more, and this is how Zakariya's request was. End of quote.

He interpreted *tayyibah* (good) as meaning sound in character and in religion, pious. Al-Raghib said: righteous. The use of *al-salih* for *al-tayyib* is like the use of *al-khabith* for its opposite, though *al-tayyib* carries an additional meaning beyond *al-salih*. It has been said that he meant: with a good one, that she would reach in religion the rank of prophethood. If he meant by *dhurriyyah* its meaning as a collective noun, not restricted to unity, then describing it as *tayyibah* is clear. If he meant one male, then he used the feminine because of the feminine form of the word, as the poet said:

*Your father is a caliph, whom another (woman) bore,*
*Silent when he bites, not toothless.*

And as another said:

*Your father is a caliph, whom another (woman) bore,*
*And you are a caliph, that is perfection.*

In His words ﴿grant me﴾ there is an indication of seeking a righteous child and supplicating for its coming into being, and this is the practice of the messengers, the truthful ones, and the righteous.

﴿Indeed You are Hearer of supplication﴾. When he asked his Lord that He grant him a righteous child, he informed Him that He is the Answerer of supplication. The meaning is not hearing in the usual sense, but like His saying: "Allah hears whoever praises Him." He expressed by hearing the answering of the purpose, and in this he followed his great forefather Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me in old age Isma'il and Ishaq; indeed my Lord is Hearer of supplication﴾ (14:39). So Allah answered his supplication and provided him in old age, just as He provided Ibrahim in old age, and he had become accustomed to Allah's answering his supplications. Do you not see His words: ﴿And I have never been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord﴾ (19:4)?

It has been said: He mentioned in the manner of his supplication three formulations. The first is this one. The second is: ﴿Indeed my bones have weakened within me﴾ (19:4) to the end of the verse. The third is: ﴿My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors﴾ (21:89). This indicates that the supplication was repeated from him three times, with these three formulations, and it indicates that there was an interval of time between the supplication and the answer. End of quote. But the repetition of the supplication does not indicate this, as it has been said, because in the narration of the situation this may have been related in the manner of brevity in His words ﴿My Lord, do not leave me alone﴾ (21:89), and in Surah Maryam in the manner of elaboration, and in this surah in the manner of moderation. This narration of these formulations is only in meaning, since their language was not Arabic. What indicates that it was a single supplication followed by the good tidings is the conjunction with *fa* (then) in His words: ﴿So the angels called him﴾ (3:39), and in His words: ﴿So We answered him and granted him Yahya﴾ (21:90). The apparent meaning of His words in Maryam: ﴿O Zakariya, We give you good tidings﴾ (19:7) is that the good tidings came immediately after the supplication, not that they were delayed after it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 36–38 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And God knows best what she gave birth to.﴾ Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Bakr and Yaʿqub read waḍaʿat with a ḍamma on the tāʾ (waḍaʿtu), and in that case this and what follows is part of the speech of Umm Maryam, as though she were addressing herself by saying "God knows best." She did not use the form "my Lord" (rabbi), for had she done so she would have said, "And You know best what I gave birth to." Rather, she addressed herself by way of consolation for the male child (al-dhakar) she had hoped for, and the knowledge of God, His foreordained power and His wisdom, would lead her to not grieve or fret over what had escaped her of the purpose, since His will must be the will that is to be done. The male she had sought and hoped for is not like the female whom He knew, willed and decreed. Perhaps this female will be better than a male, since God willed her, and so she consoled herself with this.

The alif and lam in "al-dhakar" may be for specificity (ʿahd), in which case her intent is to prefer this female, who is a gift from God, over what she had hoped, that it would be a male. It may also be understood that her intent was that the male is not like the female in excellence, rank and virtue, because the male is fit for dedication and for continuing in service at the place of worship, and because he is stronger for service, and no defect or suspicion attaches to him in service or in mixing with people. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "like the female in the impermissibility of vowing her, since the female menstruates and is not fit for companionship with the monks," as stated by Qatadah, al-Rabiʿ, al-Suddi, ʿIkrimah and others. She began with the matter most important to her, and otherwise the natural sequence of speech would be, "the female is not like the male," placing the negating particle with the thing she possesses and negating from it the attributes of perfection for the intended purpose, end of quote. On this understanding the alif and lam in "al-dhakar" are for the genus.

The rest of the seven readers read bimā waḍaʿat, with the feminine tāʾ sukūn, as a statement from God that He is most knowing of what she gave birth to, that is, of its condition and what this female's affair will become. Her saying "I gave birth to her as a female" shows that she knew of her only this much: that this offspring had come as a female unfit for dedication. So God informed that He knows best about this one who was born, using the comparative form, which implies knowledge of the details of the conditions, and this is for the sake of magnifying this one who was born and informing of the great matters attached to her and her son, since He made her and her son a sign for the worlds. Her mother was ignorant of this and knew nothing of it. Ibn ʿAbbas read bimā waḍaʿti, with a kasra on the tāʾ of address, meaning God addressed her thus: "You do not know the worth of this gifted one, nor what God knows of her great station and her exalted rank." Mā is a relative pronoun meaning "that which" or "she who," and it is stated with the word mā, as in His words, ﴿I vowed to You what is in my womb﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 35]. The returning pronoun is omitted in every reading.

﴿And I have named her Maryam﴾. Maryam, in their language, means "the worshipper." By this naming she sought an omen of good for her and drew near to God, Exalted is He, and humbled herself before Him, that her conduct would correspond to her name and that her hope for her would be fulfilled. Do you not see her seeking refuge in God for her and for her offspring from Satan? She addressed God with these words because the seeking of refuge follows from them. Her sole right to the naming indicates that her father ʿImran had died, as it is reported that he died while she was pregnant. Yet it is possible, since she was a female, that the mother alone named her, out of the dislike of men for daughters. The verse includes naming the child near the time of birth. In a hadith: "A child was born to me last night, and I named him after my father Ibrahim." And in a hadith it is said that a sacrifice is made for a newborn on the seventh day and he is named.

This sentence is joined to what came before it in her speech, and all of it falls under "she said" on the reading of those who read waḍaʿtu with a ḍamma on the tāʾ. As for those who read waḍaʿat with a sukūn on the tāʾ or with a kasra, al-Zamakhshari said: it is joined to "I have given birth to her as a female," and what lies between them is two parenthetical clauses, like His words, ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 76], end of his words. It is not necessarily the case that these are two parenthetical clauses, since it is possible that ﴿and the male is not like the female﴾ in this reading is part of her speech, and the parenthetical would be a single clause, as it was part of her speech in the reading of those who read waḍaʿtu with a ḍamma. Rather, this should be the definite view, because the parenthesis of two clauses is disputed according to the view of Abu ʿAli, who held that two clauses do not intervene; and we have already discussed this. Furthermore, his comparison of these two clauses with which he claims a parenthesis is made between the conjunct and the conjoined, with his words ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 76], is not an exact parallel to the verse, because two clauses did not intervene between a seeker and a sought. Rather, a single clause, His words ﴿if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 76], intervened between the oath, which is ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 75], and its answer, which is ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 77]. But it came within the parenthetical clause, between some of its parts and others, a parenthesis by a clause, namely His words ﴿if you only knew﴾, which intervened between the modified, "a mighty oath," and its modifier, "mighty." This is a parenthesis within a parenthesis, so it is not a separation by two parenthetical clauses in His words, "God knows best what she gave birth to, and the male is not like the female."

He named (sammā) among the verbs that take one object directly and another through a preposition, which may be dropped, though keeping it is the original form: one says "I named my son Zayd" and "I named him Zayd." The poet said:

"I named Kaʿb 'Bishr al-ʿIẓam,' and your father used to be named al-Jaʿl."

That is: "I was named Kaʿb," and "he is named al-Jaʿl." This is a restricted usage that depends on transmission, and there is a difference of opinion about it from al-Akhfash al-Saghir; the detailed discussion belongs to the science of grammar.

﴿And I seek refuge for her with You, and for her offspring, from the accursed Satan.﴾ The predicate of inna is in the present tense, "u'īdhuhā," because her intent is the continuity of seeking refuge and its recurrence, unlike "I gave birth to her" and "I named her," which are past acts that have ended. She placed the object of seeking refuge before the conjoined noun following the pronoun for the sake of emphasis. Then she went on to mention her offspring, and her addressing God with the earlier direct speech was only a means to this seeking of refuge, just as a person puts before his purpose something that draws down the goodness of the one he is addressing, and then after that mentions the purpose itself. It is related in a hadith, from Abu Hurayrah: "Every child of the sons of Adam is touched by Satan at birth, and with that touch the child cries out, except Maryam the daughter of ʿImran and her son. For her mother said when she gave birth to her: ﴿And I seek refuge for her with You, and for her offspring, from the accursed Satan﴾. So a veil was set between them, and Satan struck the veil."

The wordings of this hadith have varied across several chains, while the meaning is one. The judge ʿAbd al-Jabbar criticized this hadith, saying: it is a solitary report (khabar wahid) contrary to the evidence, and so it must be rejected. It is contrary to the evidence because Satan only calls to evil those who know good and evil, and the infant is not such; and because if he could reach this touch he would do more than that, such as destroying the righteous and other things, since it specified Maryam and her son ʿIsa over the rest of the prophets; and because if he touched them, its trace would be visible, and if it were visible the screaming and weeping would continue, but since this is not so, we know the falsity of this hadith. Al-Zamakhshari said: as for what is narrated in the hadith: "No child is born except that Satan touches him at his birth, and he cries out from the touch of Satan, except Maryam and her son," God knows best its soundness. If it is sound, its meaning is that every child is one whom Satan hopes to mislead, except Maryam and her son, for they were protected. Likewise everyone who shares their attributes, according to His words: ﴿And I will surely mislead them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 39], ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [al-Hijr: 40]. The crying out from his touch is imaginative and figurative, owing to Satan's hope for him, as though he touches him and strikes his hand on him, saying, "This is one of those I will mislead." Of the same figurative kind is the saying of Ibn al-Rumi:

"For what the world announces of its calamities, the crying of the infant at the hour of his birth is what it means."

As for the literal reality of touch and pricking, as the ignorant of the literalist school imagine, no: even if Iblis were empowered over people to prick them, the world would be filled with shrieking and wailing from what he would test us with by his pricking, end of his words. This proceeds along the path of the Mu'tazilites, and we have already passed some discussion of this in His words: ﴿like one whom Satan has confused by touch﴾ [al-Baqara: 275].

﴿So her Lord accepted her with a goodly acceptance.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: the original is "fa-tqabbalahā bi-tqabbulin ḥasanin," but qabūlin is taken as qabilahā qabūlan, one says qabila al-shay' qabūlan when he is pleased with it, and the measure for it is the ḍamma, like duḫūl and khurūj, but it came with a fatḥa. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj permitted a ḍamma on the qāf, and Ibn al-Aʿrabi transmitted it, saying: qabiltuhu qabūlan and qubūlan. Ibn ʿAbbas said: its meaning is that He took her on the path of the blessed. Others said: He undertook her upbringing and attending to her affairs. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is that He did not punish her for a single hour of night or day. On these views, "tqabbala" is in the sense of "istaqbala," so that "tafaʿʿala" is in the sense of "istafʿala," meaning: her Lord received her, like "ta'ajjaltu al-shay' fa-isti'jaltuhu" and "taqassaytu al-shay' wa-istaqsaytuhu," from their saying istaqbala al-amr, that is, he took it at its beginning. The poet said:

"The best of affairs is what you receive from its outset, and not what you pursue after it has passed."

That is: He took her at the beginning of her affair, the moment she was born. It is also said: the meaning is "fa-qabilahā," that is, He was pleased with her in the vow in place of the male, as her mother had vowed, and He accepted her supplication in her words: ﴿So accept from me, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, and no female was accepted before Maryam in this way. In this case "tafaʿʿala" is in the sense of the bare verb, as in taʿajjaba and ʿajiba, and tabarraʾa and bari'a. The bāʾ in "bi-qabūlin" is said by some to be extra, and then it is in the accusative as an infinitive not of its own verb; others say it is not extra.

Qabūl is the name of what by which something is accepted, like suʿūṭ and ludūd, for what is put into the nose and what is poured into the mouth. It refers to her being singled out by His making her stand in place of the male in the vow. Or it is a verbal noun with an omitted modifier, meaning "with one who has goodly acceptance," that is, "with a matter of goodly acceptance," which is the singling out.

﴿And He caused her to grow in a goodly growth.﴾ This is an expression for goodness of upbringing and excellence in form and character, so He raised her in obedience and worship. Ibn ʿAbbas said: when she reached nine years of age she fasted by day and stood in prayer by night until she surpassed the rabbis. It is said: no sin ever befell her. Qatadah said: we have been told that she never committed sins as the sons of Adam do. It is also said the meaning of "wa-anbatahā nabātan ḥasanan" is that He made her fruit like ʿIsa. "Nabātan" is in the accusative either as an infinitive not of its own verb, or as an infinitive for an omitted verb, meaning "so she grew a goodly growth." It is also said: the acceptance is her being raised upon the attribute of purity, until she said: ﴿I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing﴾ [Maryam: 18]. The goodly growth is steadfastness in obedience and preferring God's pleasure at all times.

﴿And Zakariyya took charge of her.﴾ Qatadah said: he took her to himself. Abu ʿUbayda said: he undertook (ḍamina) the care of her, and among the goodly acceptance and the goodly growth is that God made her guardian, the one in charge of her affairs and her protection, a prophet. God revealed to Dawud, peace be upon him: "When you see one seeking Me, be a servant to him."

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 3, verses 36–38 (part 2 of 3):

The Kufans read "wa-kaffalahā" (﴿وكَفَّلَها﴾) with a doubled fa' (tashdid), and the rest of the seven readers read it with a single fa' (takhfif). Ubayy read "wa-akfalahā" (﴿وأكْفَلَها﴾), and Mujahid read "fa-taqabbal-hā" (﴿فَتَقَبَّلْها﴾) with a sukun on the lam. "Rabbahā" was read with a fatha, as a vocative (ʿalā al-nidāʾ). "Wa-anbitha-hā" was read with a kasra on the ba' and a sukun on the ta'. "Wa-kaffil-hā" was read with a kasra on the fa' with tashdid and a sukun on the lam, as a supplication from Umm Maryam, addressed to Maryam. ʿAbd Allah al-Muzani read "wa-kafila-hā" with a kasra on the fa', which is a dialect form: it is said kafila yakfalu and kafala yakfulu, like ʿalima yaʿlamu. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read "Zakariyyā" with a short vowel (maqsur), while the rest of the seven read it as a long form (mamdud). The dialectal forms of this word have been mentioned before.

It is related that when Hannah gave birth to Maryam, she wrapped her in a piece of cloth and took her to the mosque, and placed her with the rabbis, the sons of Harun, who in Bayt al-Maqdis were like the custodians (al-hajabah) of the Ka'bah. She said to them: "Take this offering (al-nadhirah), and compete for her," because she was the daughter of their imam and the one who offered their sacrifices. The Banu Mathan were the leaders of the Children of Israel, their rabbis and their kings. Zakariyya said to them: "I have the greatest right to her; her aunt is with me." They said: "No, until we draw lots over her." So they went off, and they were twenty-seven, to a river. It is said it was the river Jordan, and this is the view of the majority. It is also said it was a spring of water there. They cast their pens into it, and the pen of Zakariyya rose up while their pens sank, and so he took charge of her. It is said that he also arranged a wet-nurse for her. Al-Hasan said: she never took a breast at all. ʿIkrimah said: they cast their pens, and the pen of Zakariyya moved against the current of the water, while their pens went along with the current. It is also said that they floated along with the water, lying flat, and Zakariyya's pen remained standing, as if it had been fixed in mud. Ibn Ishaq said: Zakariyya had married her aunt, for he and ʿImran were brothers-in-law through two sisters. The wife of Zakariyya bore Yahya, and the wife of ʿImran bore Maryam. al-Suddi and others said: Zakariyya had married another daughter of ʿImran. This view is supported by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ about Yahya and ʿIsa: "The sons of the maternal aunt." It is also said that he took charge of her only because her mother had died, and her father had died while she was still in her mother's womb. It is also said that Zakariyya was her paternal cousin, and her sister was his wife. Ibn Ishaq said: she grew up, and the Children of Israel suffered a famine. Zakariyya said to them: "I have become unable to provide for Maryam." So they cast lots over who would take charge of her, and they did so. A man called Jurayj came out to them, and he began to provide for her. This "istihām" (drawing of lots) is different from the first one: the purpose of this one was to hand her over for the provision of her maintenance, while the purpose of the first was to take her into his care. According to this view, Zakariyya had taken charge of her from childhood without a lottery. But what the people hold to is that Zakariyya took charge of her by lot, and the Qur'an does not indicate that anyone other than Zakariyya took charge of her. Zakariyya was the more deserving of her guardianship, because he was among her relatives on her father's side, and because her aunt or her sister was his wife (depending on the two views), and because he was a prophet, so he was the most deserving of her for his infallibility (ʿiṣmah). Zakariyya is the son of Adhn ibn Muslim, of the descendants of Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them. But the genealogist Abu al-Barakat al-Jawwani, the naqib, mentioned that Yahya ibn Zakariyya, al-Yasaʿ, Ilyas and al-ʿUzayr were of the descendants of Harun, the brother of Musa. On this view, Zakariyya would not be of the descendants of Sulayman, and would not be the cousin of Maryam, because Maryam is of the descendants of Sulayman, peace be upon him, and Sulayman was of Yahudha ibn Yaʿqub, while Musa and Harun were the sons of Lawi ibn Yaʿqub.

Ibn Ishaq said: he placed her with her aunt, the mother of Yahya, until she grew up and reached the age of women. He built a niche (mihrab) for her in the mosque, and placed its door in its middle, so that it could not be reached except by a ladder, like the door of the Ka'bah, and no one but him could climb up to her. It is also said that when he went out he would lock seven doors on her. Muqatil said: he would lock the door on her with the key in his hand, and would not entrust it to anyone. When she menstruated he would take her out to his house, to be with her aunt the mother of Yahya or her sister; when she became clean he would return her to Bayt al-Maqdis. It is also said that she was purified from menstruation.

﴿Every time Zakariyya entered upon her in the mihrab, he found provision with her﴾. Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: he found with her winter fruit in summer, and summer fruit in winter. al-Hasan said: she spoke in the cradle, and never took a breast at all, and her provision used to come to her from Paradise. What is related in the Sahih is that the ones who spoke in the cradle were three: ʿIsa, the companion of Jurayj, and the son of the woman, and a unique (shadhdh) narration mentions the companion of the trench (al-Ukhdud). The most surprising thing is that Maryam is among them. It is said that Jurayj was a carpenter, whose name was Yusuf ibn Yaʿqub, and he was a cousin of Maryam when he took charge of her by lottery. Zakariyya had become too weak to carry out this task, so Jurayj would bring her something light from his earnings, according to his capacity, and it would increase and multiply. Then Zakariyya would enter upon her and realise that it was beyond Jurayj's means, and would ask her. This indicates that this happened after she had grown up, and this is the closer view to the truth. It is also said that she was provided with food from outside the provision of their land: Ibn ʿAbbas said it was grapes in a basket, though no grapes grew in that land; this was also said by Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. It is also said that some of the righteous used to bring her provision.

What the apparent meaning of the verse indicates is that the one who took charge of her by upbringing was Zakariyya and no one else, for Allah the Exalted sufficed him, when he took charge of her, the burden of her provision, and by his good guardianship removed from him the hardship of effort. "Kullama" (every time) requires repetition, and so it indicates the abundance of his care and attentiveness to her circumstances. The verse indicates that the provision was present with her at every time he entered upon her. The meaning is that it was nourishment eaten by her which he had not known to be with her, and which he had not himself brought. Far removed is the one who explained "rizq" here as an overflow that came to her from Allah of knowledge and wisdom without human teaching, and so called it "rizq." al-Raghib said: the word admits this, end of quote. This resembles the interpretation of the Batiniyyah.

﴿He said: O Maryam, from where is this for you? She said: it is from Allah﴾. Zakariyya was surprised at the presence of the provision with her, when he had not brought it, and since it repeatedly appeared with her every time he entered upon her, he asked, in the manner of one wondering, about the arrival of this provision to her, and how it had come. "Anna" is a question about the manner, about the place, and about the time, and the most apparent is that it is a question about the direction, as though he said: from what direction has this provision come to you? For this reason Abu ʿUbaydah said: its meaning is "from where?" It is not far-fetched that it is a question about the manner, that is: how did the arrival of this provision to you come about? al-Kumayt said:

"From where, and from what direction has joy come to you, from a place with neither youthful folly nor joy?"

Her reply to his question, that it is "from Allah," apparently means that no human being brought it at all; rather it is provision which Allah the Exalted takes charge of for me. Its apparent meaning is that he used to ask every time he found provision with her, because it is permissible in the act that this second instance comes from a direction other than the one that came before. So she answers him that it is from Allah, and refers him to the Causer of causes and the Bringer of things from pure non-existence into pure existence. At this, the heart of Zakariyya was at rest, because no one had preceded him in caring for Maryam, and because he was witnessing a noble station and a subtle care for the one whom Allah the Exalted had chosen by placing her in his guardianship. It is said that this great marvel came about through Zakariyya's supplication for her for provision, and so it would be one of the special qualities of Zakariyya. It is also said that it was a foundation for the prophethood of her son ʿIsa. These two views resemble the views of the Mu'tazilah, in that they deny the existence of a marvel at the hand of someone other than a prophet, unless it occurs in the time of a prophet, in which case it is a miracle for that prophet. The apparent view is that it was a karamah (noble gift) which Allah singled out for Maryam. Had it been a marvel on account of Zakariyya, Zakariyya would not have asked about it. As for it being on account of the prophethood of ʿIsa, he had not yet been created.

al-Zajjaj said: this marvel is one of the signs of which Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91]. al-Jubbai said: it is possible that it was one of the miracles of Zakariyya, who prayed for her in general terms that her provision be delivered to her, and perhaps he was unaware of the details of that; then, when he saw a specific thing at a specific time, he asked about it, and so knew that it was a miracle, and he prayed for it, or asked about it out of fear that the one who brought it might be a human being; so she informed him that it was ﴿from Allah﴾. It may also be that it came through the hands of the believers, and he asked lest it should be in a way that is not fitting.

﴿Indeed Allah provides for whomever He wills without reckoning﴾. The explanation of this sentence has been given before. The apparent view is that it is part of Maryam's speech. al-Tabari said: it is not part of Maryam's speech, but a statement from Allah the Exalted to Muhammad ﷺ. Jabir related a lengthy hadith in which bread and meat were multiplied in a manner that breaks the usual course, for Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He asked her: "From where is this for you?" She said: "It is from Allah." So he praised Allah and said: "All praise is to Allah who made you resemble the mistress of the women of the Children of Israel."

It is said: in these verses there are types of eloquence. The generality that is intended to be particular, in His saying "over the worlds"; and the specification in His saying "Adam, Nuh, the family of Ibrahim, and the family of ʿImran." The use of the name of the branch for the root, and of the effect for the cause, in the word "dhurriyyah," according to the one who said the meaning is the fathers. The ambiguity in His saying "what is in my womb": when it was impossible for her to know what was in her womb, she used the word "ma," which applies to both male and female. The emphasis in His saying "Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing." The report intended as an excuse in her saying: "I have given birth to a female," and the parenthetical insertion in His saying "and Allah knows best what she has given birth to," in the reading of the one who vocalised the ta' with a sukun or a kasra. The shifting of address and what is derived from it in His saying "and Allah knows best what you have given birth to," in the reading of the one who read the ta' with a kasra: it moved from the third person of "fa-lamma waḍaʿat-hā" to the second person of direct address in "bi-mā waḍaʿt." The repetition in "wa-anna," and in "Zakariyya, Zakariyya," and in "from the presence of Allah," "inna Allah." The paronomasia (tajnis) of differing kinds in "fa-taqabbalahā rabbuhā bi-qabūl, wa-anbatahā nabātan," and in "rizqan" and "yarzuqu." The allusion, which is to express a hidden meaning by an apparent expression, in His saying "it is from Allah," meaning it is a provision which no one can bring at that time except Allah. In His saying "rizqan," he used it indefinitely, indicating that it is not of one kind, but of many kinds, because an indefinite noun implies multiplicity and abundance. And there is ellipsis in several places, where the meaning would not be correct without taking it into account.

﴿There Zakariya called upon his Lord﴾. The origin of *hunalika* is that it indicates a place, though it may also be used for a time. Some have said both are meant in this verse: that is, in that place Zakariya called upon Him, or at that time, when he saw this great miraculous sign regarding Maryam, and that she was among those whom Allah had chosen. He was moved to ask for a child, and he needed one because of his advanced age, and so that he might inherit from him and from the family of Ya'qub, as Allah related in Surah Maryam. The fact that his wife was barren did not prevent him from making this request, since he had seen in Maryam's condition something outside the ordinary. So it is not far-fetched that Allah would grant him a child even though his wife was barren, for Hannah had been granted Maryam after she had despaired of having children. The word *hunalika* is governed by the verb *da'a* (called). It occurs in al-Sajawandi's commentary that *hunaka* is for place and *hunalika* for time, but this is a mistake. Rather, the principle is that it is used for place, whether it is joined with the *lam* and the *kaf*, with the *kaf* alone, or with neither. It may be used figuratively for place to mean time, just as the basic meaning of *'inda* (at, with) is place, and then it is used figuratively for time, as when you say: "I will come to you at (*'inda*) sunrise." It has been said that the *lam* in *hunalika* indicates the great distance between the supplication and the answer, for the commentators have reported that there were forty years between his supplication and its answer. It has also been said that the *lam* was added to indicate that this matter is far from ordinary reach, because it breaks the normal course of things, just as the *lam* was added in His words: ﴿That is the Book﴾ (2:2), to indicate its remoteness of reach and its great elevation and nobility. Al-Maturidi said: His soul was speaking to him that Allah might grant him a child through whom the remembrance would endure until the Day of Resurrection, but he did not call upon Him out of regard for good manners, since good manners require that one not ask for a desire except for what is normally possible. Although Allah is capable of all things, when he saw there something that breaks the normal course, this led him to supplicate for a child that is not customary. End of quote.

As for his saying that his soul was speaking to him about this, it needs a transmission. In His words ﴿There called he﴾ there is an indication that the servant should seek out blessed places and honored times for his supplication.

﴿He said: My Lord, grant me from Yourself offspring that is good﴾. This sentence is an explanation and elaboration of the supplication. He addressed Him with the title "My Lord," since He is the One who nurtures him and sets his affairs right. The request came with the word *hab* (grant), because a gift is pure bounty, having no return that would serve as compensation for the giver. Since this was almost by way of no cause at all, neither from the father because of his old age, nor from the mother because she was barren and could not bear children, his existence was like existence without any cause. So it came as a pure gift attributed to Allah the Exalted by His words "from Yourself," meaning from the very source of Your power without any intermediary cause. It has been mentioned that *ladun* is used for what is near, while *'inda* is used for both what is near and what is far, and *ladun* is less vague than *'inda*. Do you not see that *'inda* can be an answer to "where" (*ayna*), while *ladun* cannot be an answer to it? "From Yourself" (*min ladunka*) is connected to *hab*. It has been said that it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) for *dhurriyyatan* (offspring), because if it had been placed after it, it would have been an attribute. On this view it is connected to an omitted element. *Dhurriyyah* is a collective noun that applies to one or more. Al-Tabari said: By *dhurriyyah* here he meant one person, as evidence for which is that he asked for one heir, and did not ask for heirs. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: There is an objection to what al-Tabari said, for *dhurriyyah* and *waliyy* (heir, protector) are collective nouns that apply to one and to more, and this is how Zakariya's request was. End of quote.

He interpreted *tayyibah* (good) as meaning sound in character and in religion, pious. Al-Raghib said: righteous. The use of *al-salih* for *al-tayyib* is like the use of *al-khabith* for its opposite, though *al-tayyib* carries an additional meaning beyond *al-salih*. It has been said that he meant: with a good one, that she would reach in religion the rank of prophethood. If he meant by *dhurriyyah* its meaning as a collective noun, not restricted to unity, then describing it as *tayyibah* is clear. If he meant one male, then he used the feminine because of the feminine form of the word, as the poet said:

*Your father is a caliph, whom another (woman) bore,*
*Silent when he bites, not toothless.*

And as another said:

*Your father is a caliph, whom another (woman) bore,*
*And you are a caliph, that is perfection.*

In His words ﴿grant me﴾ there is an indication of seeking a righteous child and supplicating for its coming into being, and this is the practice of the messengers, the truthful ones, and the righteous.

﴿Indeed You are Hearer of supplication﴾. When he asked his Lord that He grant him a righteous child, he informed Him that He is the Answerer of supplication. The meaning is not hearing in the usual sense, but like His saying: "Allah hears whoever praises Him." He expressed by hearing the answering of the purpose, and in this he followed his great forefather Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me in old age Isma'il and Ishaq; indeed my Lord is Hearer of supplication﴾ (14:39). So Allah answered his supplication and provided him in old age, just as He provided Ibrahim in old age, and he had become accustomed to Allah's answering his supplications. Do you not see His words: ﴿And I have never been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord﴾ (19:4)?

It has been said: He mentioned in the manner of his supplication three formulations. The first is this one. The second is: ﴿Indeed my bones have weakened within me﴾ (19:4) to the end of the verse. The third is: ﴿My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors﴾ (21:89). This indicates that the supplication was repeated from him three times, with these three formulations, and it indicates that there was an interval of time between the supplication and the answer. End of quote. But the repetition of the supplication does not indicate this, as it has been said, because in the narration of the situation this may have been related in the manner of brevity in His words ﴿My Lord, do not leave me alone﴾ (21:89), and in Surah Maryam in the manner of elaboration, and in this surah in the manner of moderation. This narration of these formulations is only in meaning, since their language was not Arabic. What indicates that it was a single supplication followed by the good tidings is the conjunction with *fa* (then) in His words: ﴿So the angels called him﴾ (3:39), and in His words: ﴿So We answered him and granted him Yahya﴾ (21:90). The apparent meaning of His words in Maryam: ﴿O Zakariya, We give you good tidings﴾ (19:7) is that the good tidings came immediately after the supplication, not that they were delayed after it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 36–38 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And God knows best what she gave birth to.﴾ Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Bakr and Yaʿqub read waḍaʿat with a ḍamma on the tāʾ (waḍaʿtu), and in that case this and what follows is part of the speech of Umm Maryam, as though she were addressing herself by saying "God knows best." She did not use the form "my Lord" (rabbi), for had she done so she would have said, "And You know best what I gave birth to." Rather, she addressed herself by way of consolation for the male child (al-dhakar) she had hoped for, and the knowledge of God, His foreordained power and His wisdom, would lead her to not grieve or fret over what had escaped her of the purpose, since His will must be the will that is to be done. The male she had sought and hoped for is not like the female whom He knew, willed and decreed. Perhaps this female will be better than a male, since God willed her, and so she consoled herself with this.

The alif and lam in "al-dhakar" may be for specificity (ʿahd), in which case her intent is to prefer this female, who is a gift from God, over what she had hoped, that it would be a male. It may also be understood that her intent was that the male is not like the female in excellence, rank and virtue, because the male is fit for dedication and for continuing in service at the place of worship, and because he is stronger for service, and no defect or suspicion attaches to him in service or in mixing with people. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "like the female in the impermissibility of vowing her, since the female menstruates and is not fit for companionship with the monks," as stated by Qatadah, al-Rabiʿ, al-Suddi, ʿIkrimah and others. She began with the matter most important to her, and otherwise the natural sequence of speech would be, "the female is not like the male," placing the negating particle with the thing she possesses and negating from it the attributes of perfection for the intended purpose, end of quote. On this understanding the alif and lam in "al-dhakar" are for the genus.

The rest of the seven readers read bimā waḍaʿat, with the feminine tāʾ sukūn, as a statement from God that He is most knowing of what she gave birth to, that is, of its condition and what this female's affair will become. Her saying "I gave birth to her as a female" shows that she knew of her only this much: that this offspring had come as a female unfit for dedication. So God informed that He knows best about this one who was born, using the comparative form, which implies knowledge of the details of the conditions, and this is for the sake of magnifying this one who was born and informing of the great matters attached to her and her son, since He made her and her son a sign for the worlds. Her mother was ignorant of this and knew nothing of it. Ibn ʿAbbas read bimā waḍaʿti, with a kasra on the tāʾ of address, meaning God addressed her thus: "You do not know the worth of this gifted one, nor what God knows of her great station and her exalted rank." Mā is a relative pronoun meaning "that which" or "she who," and it is stated with the word mā, as in His words, ﴿I vowed to You what is in my womb﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 35]. The returning pronoun is omitted in every reading.

﴿And I have named her Maryam﴾. Maryam, in their language, means "the worshipper." By this naming she sought an omen of good for her and drew near to God, Exalted is He, and humbled herself before Him, that her conduct would correspond to her name and that her hope for her would be fulfilled. Do you not see her seeking refuge in God for her and for her offspring from Satan? She addressed God with these words because the seeking of refuge follows from them. Her sole right to the naming indicates that her father ʿImran had died, as it is reported that he died while she was pregnant. Yet it is possible, since she was a female, that the mother alone named her, out of the dislike of men for daughters. The verse includes naming the child near the time of birth. In a hadith: "A child was born to me last night, and I named him after my father Ibrahim." And in a hadith it is said that a sacrifice is made for a newborn on the seventh day and he is named.

This sentence is joined to what came before it in her speech, and all of it falls under "she said" on the reading of those who read waḍaʿtu with a ḍamma on the tāʾ. As for those who read waḍaʿat with a sukūn on the tāʾ or with a kasra, al-Zamakhshari said: it is joined to "I have given birth to her as a female," and what lies between them is two parenthetical clauses, like His words, ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 76], end of his words. It is not necessarily the case that these are two parenthetical clauses, since it is possible that ﴿and the male is not like the female﴾ in this reading is part of her speech, and the parenthetical would be a single clause, as it was part of her speech in the reading of those who read waḍaʿtu with a ḍamma. Rather, this should be the definite view, because the parenthesis of two clauses is disputed according to the view of Abu ʿAli, who held that two clauses do not intervene; and we have already discussed this. Furthermore, his comparison of these two clauses with which he claims a parenthesis is made between the conjunct and the conjoined, with his words ﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 76], is not an exact parallel to the verse, because two clauses did not intervene between a seeker and a sought. Rather, a single clause, His words ﴿if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 76], intervened between the oath, which is ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 75], and its answer, which is ﴿Indeed it is a noble Qur'an﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 77].
