But it came within the parenthetical clause, between some of its parts and others, a parenthesis by a clause, namely His words ﴿if you only knew﴾, which intervened between the modified, "a mighty oath," and its modifier, "mighty." This is a parenthesis within a parenthesis, so it is not a separation by two parenthetical clauses in His words, "God knows best what she gave birth to, and the male is not like the female."

He named (sammā) among the verbs that take one object directly and another through a preposition, which may be dropped, though keeping it is the original form: one says "I named my son Zayd" and "I named him Zayd." The poet said:

"I named Kaʿb 'Bishr al-ʿIẓam,' and your father used to be named al-Jaʿl."

That is: "I was named Kaʿb," and "he is named al-Jaʿl." This is a restricted usage that depends on transmission, and there is a difference of opinion about it from al-Akhfash al-Saghir; the detailed discussion belongs to the science of grammar.

﴿And I seek refuge for her with You, and for her offspring, from the accursed Satan.﴾ The predicate of inna is in the present tense, "u'īdhuhā," because her intent is the continuity of seeking refuge and its recurrence, unlike "I gave birth to her" and "I named her," which are past acts that have ended. She placed the object of seeking refuge before the conjoined noun following the pronoun for the sake of emphasis. Then she went on to mention her offspring, and her addressing God with the earlier direct speech was only a means to this seeking of refuge, just as a person puts before his purpose something that draws down the goodness of the one he is addressing, and then after that mentions the purpose itself. It is related in a hadith, from Abu Hurayrah: "Every child of the sons of Adam is touched by Satan at birth, and with that touch the child cries out, except Maryam the daughter of ʿImran and her son. For her mother said when she gave birth to her: ﴿And I seek refuge for her with You, and for her offspring, from the accursed Satan﴾. So a veil was set between them, and Satan struck the veil."

The wordings of this hadith have varied across several chains, while the meaning is one. The judge ʿAbd al-Jabbar criticized this hadith, saying: it is a solitary report (khabar wahid) contrary to the evidence, and so it must be rejected. It is contrary to the evidence because Satan only calls to evil those who know good and evil, and the infant is not such; and because if he could reach this touch he would do more than that, such as destroying the righteous and other things, since it specified Maryam and her son ʿIsa over the rest of the prophets; and because if he touched them, its trace would be visible, and if it were visible the screaming and weeping would continue, but since this is not so, we know the falsity of this hadith. Al-Zamakhshari said: as for what is narrated in the hadith: "No child is born except that Satan touches him at his birth, and he cries out from the touch of Satan, except Maryam and her son," God knows best its soundness. If it is sound, its meaning is that every child is one whom Satan hopes to mislead, except Maryam and her son, for they were protected. Likewise everyone who shares their attributes, according to His words: ﴿And I will surely mislead them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 39], ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ [al-Hijr: 40]. The crying out from his touch is imaginative and figurative, owing to Satan's hope for him, as though he touches him and strikes his hand on him, saying, "This is one of those I will mislead." Of the same figurative kind is the saying of Ibn al-Rumi:

"For what the world announces of its calamities, the crying of the infant at the hour of his birth is what it means."

As for the literal reality of touch and pricking, as the ignorant of the literalist school imagine, no: even if Iblis were empowered over people to prick them, the world would be filled with shrieking and wailing from what he would test us with by his pricking, end of his words. This proceeds along the path of the Mu'tazilites, and we have already passed some discussion of this in His words: ﴿like one whom Satan has confused by touch﴾ [al-Baqara: 275].

﴿So her Lord accepted her with a goodly acceptance.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: the original is "fa-tqabbalahā bi-tqabbulin ḥasanin," but qabūlin is taken as qabilahā qabūlan, one says qabila al-shay' qabūlan when he is pleased with it, and the measure for it is the ḍamma, like duḫūl and khurūj, but it came with a fatḥa. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj permitted a ḍamma on the qāf, and Ibn al-Aʿrabi transmitted it, saying: qabiltuhu qabūlan and qubūlan. Ibn ʿAbbas said: its meaning is that He took her on the path of the blessed. Others said: He undertook her upbringing and attending to her affairs. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is that He did not punish her for a single hour of night or day. On these views, "tqabbala" is in the sense of "istaqbala," so that "tafaʿʿala" is in the sense of "istafʿala," meaning: her Lord received her, like "ta'ajjaltu al-shay' fa-isti'jaltuhu" and "taqassaytu al-shay' wa-istaqsaytuhu," from their saying istaqbala al-amr, that is, he took it at its beginning. The poet said:

"The best of affairs is what you receive from its outset, and not what you pursue after it has passed."

That is: He took her at the beginning of her affair, the moment she was born. It is also said: the meaning is "fa-qabilahā," that is, He was pleased with her in the vow in place of the male, as her mother had vowed, and He accepted her supplication in her words: ﴿So accept from me, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾, and no female was accepted before Maryam in this way. In this case "tafaʿʿala" is in the sense of the bare verb, as in taʿajjaba and ʿajiba, and tabarraʾa and bari'a. The bāʾ in "bi-qabūlin" is said by some to be extra, and then it is in the accusative as an infinitive not of its own verb; others say it is not extra.

Qabūl is the name of what by which something is accepted, like suʿūṭ and ludūd, for what is put into the nose and what is poured into the mouth. It refers to her being singled out by His making her stand in place of the male in the vow. Or it is a verbal noun with an omitted modifier, meaning "with one who has goodly acceptance," that is, "with a matter of goodly acceptance," which is the singling out.

﴿And He caused her to grow in a goodly growth.﴾ This is an expression for goodness of upbringing and excellence in form and character, so He raised her in obedience and worship. Ibn ʿAbbas said: when she reached nine years of age she fasted by day and stood in prayer by night until she surpassed the rabbis. It is said: no sin ever befell her. Qatadah said: we have been told that she never committed sins as the sons of Adam do. It is also said the meaning of "wa-anbatahā nabātan ḥasanan" is that He made her fruit like ʿIsa. "Nabātan" is in the accusative either as an infinitive not of its own verb, or as an infinitive for an omitted verb, meaning "so she grew a goodly growth." It is also said: the acceptance is her being raised upon the attribute of purity, until she said: ﴿I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing﴾ [Maryam: 18]. The goodly growth is steadfastness in obedience and preferring God's pleasure at all times.

﴿And Zakariyya took charge of her.﴾ Qatadah said: he took her to himself. Abu ʿUbayda said: he undertook (ḍamina) the care of her, and among the goodly acceptance and the goodly growth is that God made her guardian, the one in charge of her affairs and her protection, a prophet. God revealed to Dawud, peace be upon him: "When you see one seeking Me, be a servant to him."

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 3, verses 36–38 (part 2 of 3):

The Kufans read "wa-kaffalahā" (﴿وكَفَّلَها﴾) with a doubled fa' (tashdid), and the rest of the seven readers read it with a single fa' (takhfif). Ubayy read "wa-akfalahā" (﴿وأكْفَلَها﴾), and Mujahid read "fa-taqabbal-hā" (﴿فَتَقَبَّلْها﴾) with a sukun on the lam. "Rabbahā" was read with a fatha, as a vocative (ʿalā al-nidāʾ). "Wa-anbitha-hā" was read with a kasra on the ba' and a sukun on the ta'. "Wa-kaffil-hā" was read with a kasra on the fa' with tashdid and a sukun on the lam, as a supplication from Umm Maryam, addressed to Maryam. ʿAbd Allah al-Muzani read "wa-kafila-hā" with a kasra on the fa', which is a dialect form: it is said kafila yakfalu and kafala yakfulu, like ʿalima yaʿlamu. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read "Zakariyyā" with a short vowel (maqsur), while the rest of the seven read it as a long form (mamdud). The dialectal forms of this word have been mentioned before.

It is related that when Hannah gave birth to Maryam, she wrapped her in a piece of cloth and took her to the mosque, and placed her with the rabbis, the sons of Harun, who in Bayt al-Maqdis were like the custodians (al-hajabah) of the Ka'bah. She said to them: "Take this offering (al-nadhirah), and compete for her," because she was the daughter of their imam and the one who offered their sacrifices. The Banu Mathan were the leaders of the Children of Israel, their rabbis and their kings. Zakariyya said to them: "I have the greatest right to her; her aunt is with me." They said: "No, until we draw lots over her." So they went off, and they were twenty-seven, to a river. It is said it was the river Jordan, and this is the view of the majority. It is also said it was a spring of water there. They cast their pens into it, and the pen of Zakariyya rose up while their pens sank, and so he took charge of her. It is said that he also arranged a wet-nurse for her. Al-Hasan said: she never took a breast at all. ʿIkrimah said: they cast their pens, and the pen of Zakariyya moved against the current of the water, while their pens went along with the current. It is also said that they floated along with the water, lying flat, and Zakariyya's pen remained standing, as if it had been fixed in mud. Ibn Ishaq said: Zakariyya had married her aunt, for he and ʿImran were brothers-in-law through two sisters. The wife of Zakariyya bore Yahya, and the wife of ʿImran bore Maryam. al-Suddi and others said: Zakariyya had married another daughter of ʿImran. This view is supported by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ about Yahya and ʿIsa: "The sons of the maternal aunt." It is also said that he took charge of her only because her mother had died, and her father had died while she was still in her mother's womb. It is also said that Zakariyya was her paternal cousin, and her sister was his wife. Ibn Ishaq said: she grew up, and the Children of Israel suffered a famine. Zakariyya said to them: "I have become unable to provide for Maryam." So they cast lots over who would take charge of her, and they did so. A man called Jurayj came out to them, and he began to provide for her. This "istihām" (drawing of lots) is different from the first one: the purpose of this one was to hand her over for the provision of her maintenance, while the purpose of the first was to take her into his care. According to this view, Zakariyya had taken charge of her from childhood without a lottery. But what the people hold to is that Zakariyya took charge of her by lot, and the Qur'an does not indicate that anyone other than Zakariyya took charge of her. Zakariyya was the more deserving of her guardianship, because he was among her relatives on her father's side, and because her aunt or her sister was his wife (depending on the two views), and because he was a prophet, so he was the most deserving of her for his infallibility (ʿiṣmah). Zakariyya is the son of Adhn ibn Muslim, of the descendants of Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them. But the genealogist Abu al-Barakat al-Jawwani, the naqib, mentioned that Yahya ibn Zakariyya, al-Yasaʿ, Ilyas and al-ʿUzayr were of the descendants of Harun, the brother of Musa. On this view, Zakariyya would not be of the descendants of Sulayman, and would not be the cousin of Maryam, because Maryam is of the descendants of Sulayman, peace be upon him, and Sulayman was of Yahudha ibn Yaʿqub, while Musa and Harun were the sons of Lawi ibn Yaʿqub.

Ibn Ishaq said: he placed her with her aunt, the mother of Yahya, until she grew up and reached the age of women. He built a niche (mihrab) for her in the mosque, and placed its door in its middle, so that it could not be reached except by a ladder, like the door of the Ka'bah, and no one but him could climb up to her. It is also said that when he went out he would lock seven doors on her. Muqatil said: he would lock the door on her with the key in his hand, and would not entrust it to anyone. When she menstruated he would take her out to his house, to be with her aunt the mother of Yahya or her sister; when she became clean he would return her to Bayt al-Maqdis. It is also said that she was purified from menstruation.

﴿Every time Zakariyya entered upon her in the mihrab, he found provision with her﴾. Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: he found with her winter fruit in summer, and summer fruit in winter. al-Hasan said: she spoke in the cradle, and never took a breast at all, and her provision used to come to her from Paradise. What is related in the Sahih is that the ones who spoke in the cradle were three: ʿIsa, the companion of Jurayj, and the son of the woman, and a unique (shadhdh) narration mentions the companion of the trench (al-Ukhdud). The most surprising thing is that Maryam is among them. It is said that Jurayj was a carpenter, whose name was Yusuf ibn Yaʿqub, and he was a cousin of Maryam when he took charge of her by lottery. Zakariyya had become too weak to carry out this task, so Jurayj would bring her something light from his earnings, according to his capacity, and it would increase and multiply. Then Zakariyya would enter upon her and realise that it was beyond Jurayj's means, and would ask her. This indicates that this happened after she had grown up, and this is the closer view to the truth. It is also said that she was provided with food from outside the provision of their land: Ibn ʿAbbas said it was grapes in a basket, though no grapes grew in that land; this was also said by Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid. It is also said that some of the righteous used to bring her provision.

What the apparent meaning of the verse indicates is that the one who took charge of her by upbringing was Zakariyya and no one else, for Allah the Exalted sufficed him, when he took charge of her, the burden of her provision, and by his good guardianship removed from him the hardship of effort. "Kullama" (every time) requires repetition, and so it indicates the abundance of his care and attentiveness to her circumstances. The verse indicates that the provision was present with her at every time he entered upon her. The meaning is that it was nourishment eaten by her which he had not known to be with her, and which he had not himself brought. Far removed is the one who explained "rizq" here as an overflow that came to her from Allah of knowledge and wisdom without human teaching, and so called it "rizq." al-Raghib said: the word admits this, end of quote. This resembles the interpretation of the Batiniyyah.

﴿He said: O Maryam, from where is this for you? She said: it is from Allah﴾. Zakariyya was surprised at the presence of the provision with her, when he had not brought it, and since it repeatedly appeared with her every time he entered upon her, he asked, in the manner of one wondering, about the arrival of this provision to her, and how it had come. "Anna" is a question about the manner, about the place, and about the time, and the most apparent is that it is a question about the direction, as though he said: from what direction has this provision come to you? For this reason Abu ʿUbaydah said: its meaning is "from where?" It is not far-fetched that it is a question about the manner, that is: how did the arrival of this provision to you come about? al-Kumayt said:

"From where, and from what direction has joy come to you, from a place with neither youthful folly nor joy?"

Her reply to his question, that it is "from Allah," apparently means that no human being brought it at all; rather it is provision which Allah the Exalted takes charge of for me. Its apparent meaning is that he used to ask every time he found provision with her, because it is permissible in the act that this second instance comes from a direction other than the one that came before. So she answers him that it is from Allah, and refers him to the Causer of causes and the Bringer of things from pure non-existence into pure existence. At this, the heart of Zakariyya was at rest, because no one had preceded him in caring for Maryam, and because he was witnessing a noble station and a subtle care for the one whom Allah the Exalted had chosen by placing her in his guardianship. It is said that this great marvel came about through Zakariyya's supplication for her for provision, and so it would be one of the special qualities of Zakariyya. It is also said that it was a foundation for the prophethood of her son ʿIsa. These two views resemble the views of the Mu'tazilah, in that they deny the existence of a marvel at the hand of someone other than a prophet, unless it occurs in the time of a prophet, in which case it is a miracle for that prophet. The apparent view is that it was a karamah (noble gift) which Allah singled out for Maryam. Had it been a marvel on account of Zakariyya, Zakariyya would not have asked about it. As for it being on account of the prophethood of ʿIsa, he had not yet been created.

al-Zajjaj said: this marvel is one of the signs of which Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91]. al-Jubbai said: it is possible that it was one of the miracles of Zakariyya, who prayed for her in general terms that her provision be delivered to her, and perhaps he was unaware of the details of that; then, when he saw a specific thing at a specific time, he asked about it, and so knew that it was a miracle, and he prayed for it, or asked about it out of fear that the one who brought it might be a human being; so she informed him that it was ﴿from Allah﴾. It may also be that it came through the hands of the believers, and he asked lest it should be in a way that is not fitting.

﴿Indeed Allah provides for whomever He wills without reckoning﴾. The explanation of this sentence has been given before. The apparent view is that it is part of Maryam's speech. al-Tabari said: it is not part of Maryam's speech, but a statement from Allah the Exalted to Muhammad ﷺ. Jabir related a lengthy hadith in which bread and meat were multiplied in a manner that breaks the usual course, for Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He asked her: "From where is this for you?" She said: "It is from Allah." So he praised Allah and said: "All praise is to Allah who made you resemble the mistress of the women of the Children of Israel."

It is said: in these verses there are types of eloquence. The generality that is intended to be particular, in His saying "over the worlds"; and the specification in His saying "Adam, Nuh, the family of Ibrahim, and the family of ʿImran." The use of the name of the branch for the root, and of the effect for the cause, in the word "dhurriyyah," according to the one who said the meaning is the fathers. The ambiguity in His saying "what is in my womb": when it was impossible for her to know what was in her womb, she used the word "ma," which applies to both male and female. The emphasis in His saying "Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing." The report intended as an excuse in her saying: "I have given birth to a female," and the parenthetical insertion in His saying "and Allah knows best what she has given birth to," in the reading of the one who vocalised the ta' with a sukun or a kasra. The shifting of address and what is derived from it in His saying "and Allah knows best what you have given birth to," in the reading of the one who read the ta' with a kasra: it moved from the third person of "fa-lamma waḍaʿat-hā" to the second person of direct address in "bi-mā waḍaʿt." The repetition in "wa-anna," and in "Zakariyya, Zakariyya," and in "from the presence of Allah," "inna Allah." The paronomasia (tajnis) of differing kinds in "fa-taqabbalahā rabbuhā bi-qabūl, wa-anbatahā nabātan," and in "rizqan" and "yarzuqu." The allusion, which is to express a hidden meaning by an apparent expression, in His saying "it is from Allah," meaning it is a provision which no one can bring at that time except Allah. In His saying "rizqan," he used it indefinitely, indicating that it is not of one kind, but of many kinds, because an indefinite noun implies multiplicity and abundance. And there is ellipsis in several places, where the meaning would not be correct without taking it into account.

﴿There Zakariya called upon his Lord﴾. The origin of *hunalika* is that it indicates a place, though it may also be used for a time. Some have said both are meant in this verse: that is, in that place Zakariya called upon Him, or at that time, when he saw this great miraculous sign regarding Maryam, and that she was among those whom Allah had chosen. He was moved to ask for a child, and he needed one because of his advanced age, and so that he might inherit from him and from the family of Ya'qub, as Allah related in Surah Maryam. The fact that his wife was barren did not prevent him from making this request, since he had seen in Maryam's condition something outside the ordinary. So it is not far-fetched that Allah would grant him a child even though his wife was barren, for Hannah had been granted Maryam after she had despaired of having children. The word *hunalika* is governed by the verb *da'a* (called). It occurs in al-Sajawandi's commentary that *hunaka* is for place and *hunalika* for time, but this is a mistake. Rather, the principle is that it is used for place, whether it is joined with the *lam* and the *kaf*, with the *kaf* alone, or with neither. It may be used figuratively for place to mean time, just as the basic meaning of *'inda* (at, with) is place, and then it is used figuratively for time, as when you say: "I will come to you at (*'inda*) sunrise." It has been said that the *lam* in *hunalika* indicates the great distance between the supplication and the answer, for the commentators have reported that there were forty years between his supplication and its answer. It has also been said that the *lam* was added to indicate that this matter is far from ordinary reach, because it breaks the normal course of things, just as the *lam* was added in His words: ﴿That is the Book﴾ (2:2), to indicate its remoteness of reach and its great elevation and nobility. Al-Maturidi said: His soul was speaking to him that Allah might grant him a child through whom the remembrance would endure until the Day of Resurrection, but he did not call upon Him out of regard for good manners, since good manners require that one not ask for a desire except for what is normally possible. Although Allah is capable of all things, when he saw there something that breaks the normal course, this led him to supplicate for a child that is not customary. End of quote.

As for his saying that his soul was speaking to him about this, it needs a transmission. In His words ﴿There called he﴾ there is an indication that the servant should seek out blessed places and honored times for his supplication.

﴿He said: My Lord, grant me from Yourself offspring that is good﴾. This sentence is an explanation and elaboration of the supplication. He addressed Him with the title "My Lord," since He is the One who nurtures him and sets his affairs right. The request came with the word *hab* (grant), because a gift is pure bounty, having no return that would serve as compensation for the giver. Since this was almost by way of no cause at all, neither from the father because of his old age, nor from the mother because she was barren and could not bear children, his existence was like existence without any cause. So it came as a pure gift attributed to Allah the Exalted by His words "from Yourself," meaning from the very source of Your power without any intermediary cause. It has been mentioned that *ladun* is used for what is near, while *'inda* is used for both what is near and what is far, and *ladun* is less vague than *'inda*. Do you not see that *'inda* can be an answer to "where" (*ayna*), while *ladun* cannot be an answer to it? "From Yourself" (*min ladunka*) is connected to *hab*. It has been said that it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) for *dhurriyyatan* (offspring), because if it had been placed after it, it would have been an attribute. On this view it is connected to an omitted element. *Dhurriyyah* is a collective noun that applies to one or more. Al-Tabari said: By *dhurriyyah* here he meant one person, as evidence for which is that he asked for one heir, and did not ask for heirs. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: There is an objection to what al-Tabari said, for *dhurriyyah* and *waliyy* (heir, protector) are collective nouns that apply to one and to more, and this is how Zakariya's request was. End of quote.

He interpreted *tayyibah* (good) as meaning sound in character and in religion, pious. Al-Raghib said: righteous. The use of *al-salih* for *al-tayyib* is like the use of *al-khabith* for its opposite, though *al-tayyib* carries an additional meaning beyond *al-salih*. It has been said that he meant: with a good one, that she would reach in religion the rank of prophethood. If he meant by *dhurriyyah* its meaning as a collective noun, not restricted to unity, then describing it as *tayyibah* is clear. If he meant one male, then he used the feminine because of the feminine form of the word, as the poet said:

*Your father is a caliph, whom another (woman) bore,*
*Silent when he bites, not toothless.*

And as another said:

*Your father is a caliph, whom another (woman) bore,*
*And you are a caliph, that is perfection.*

In His words ﴿grant me﴾ there is an indication of seeking a righteous child and supplicating for its coming into being, and this is the practice of the messengers, the truthful ones, and the righteous.

﴿Indeed You are Hearer of supplication﴾. When he asked his Lord that He grant him a righteous child, he informed Him that He is the Answerer of supplication. The meaning is not hearing in the usual sense, but like His saying: "Allah hears whoever praises Him." He expressed by hearing the answering of the purpose, and in this he followed his great forefather Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has granted me in old age Isma'il and Ishaq; indeed my Lord is Hearer of supplication﴾ (14:39). So Allah answered his supplication and provided him in old age, just as He provided Ibrahim in old age, and he had become accustomed to Allah's answering his supplications. Do you not see His words: ﴿And I have never been unblessed in my supplication to You, my Lord﴾ (19:4)?

It has been said: He mentioned in the manner of his supplication three formulations. The first is this one. The second is: ﴿Indeed my bones have weakened within me﴾ (19:4) to the end of the verse. The third is: ﴿My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors﴾ (21:89). This indicates that the supplication was repeated from him three times, with these three formulations, and it indicates that there was an interval of time between the supplication and the answer. End of quote. But the repetition of the supplication does not indicate this, as it has been said, because in the narration of the situation this may have been related in the manner of brevity in His words ﴿My Lord, do not leave me alone﴾ (21:89), and in Surah Maryam in the manner of elaboration, and in this surah in the manner of moderation. This narration of these formulations is only in meaning, since their language was not Arabic. What indicates that it was a single supplication followed by the good tidings is the conjunction with *fa* (then) in His words: ﴿So the angels called him﴾ (3:39), and in His words: ﴿So We answered him and granted him Yahya﴾ (21:90). The apparent meaning of His words in Maryam: ﴿O Zakariya, We give you good tidings﴾ (19:7) is that the good tidings came immediately after the supplication, not that they were delayed after it.

﴿Then the angels called to him﴾. It has been said that the word *nida'* (calling out) is used for good news, and for something that should be hastened and conveyed to the hearer so that he is gladdened by it. So this was not an announcement from the angels in the manner of revelation, but a calling out, like the Ansari man who called out to Ka'b ibn Malik from the top of a mountain. This was said by Ibn 'Atiyya and others. But this does not appear correct. Rather, calling out (*munada*) is used for good news and for distress, and for other purposes, as has come: "O people of the Fire, there is eternal abiding without death." And it has come: ﴿O Haman, build me a tower﴾ [Ghafir: 36]. The sense of good news in the verse is understood only from their words ﴿Indeed, Allah gives you good news﴾ [Al 'Imran: 45], not because the wording *nadat-hu* (they called to him) indicates it, neither by its lexical form nor by its usage. It is also possible that their calling to him was by way of revelation, meaning: it was revealed to them that they should call to him. Or they called to him on their own initiative, as one would say to you: "Inform Zayd of such-and-such," and you say to him: "O Zayd, such-and-such has happened." These are two opinions among the exegetes. In the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: Allah accepted his supplication, granted him Yahya, and sent the angels to him with this news, and so they called to him.

It is mentioned that there was a period of forty years between his supplication and the response to it, but the apparent sense is contrary to that. The apparent sense is that his caller was a group of angels, by the form of the wording. Indeed, Allah the Exalted sent angels to the people of Lut, and to Ibrahim, and in other places than those He related. Most scholars mention that the caller was Jibril alone, and this is supported by the reading of 'Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) and his codex: "Then Jibril called to him while he was standing." Al-Zamakhshari said: The word "angels" was used only in the manner of their saying: "So-and-so rides horses," meaning that the one who called to him was of the kind of the angels, not that he intends the plurality specifically, just as their saying "So-and-so rides horses" does not intend the plurality specifically, but intends that his mount is of this kind. This is how the reference of those whom "the people" said to (in the verse about Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud) is explained. Al-Fadl said: The leader is spoken of with plural expressions, because his companions are with him, or because of the gathering of beautiful qualities in him which are scattered in others. So it was expressed with plurality for this reason. It has been said: Jibril is the chief of the angels.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *fa-nada-hu* with *imala* (inclination of the vowel). The rest of the seven read *fa-nadat-hu* with the feminine *ta'*, and *al-malaikah* (the angels) is a broken plural, so it is permissible that the feminine marker be attached and permissible that it not be attached. One says: *qama al-rijal* (the men stood) and *qamat al-rijal*. Attaching the marker has been said to be better; do you not see: *idh qalat al-malaikah* (when the angels said), and *lamma ja'at rusuluna* (when Our messengers came)? What makes the omission good here is the separation by the object.

﴿While he was standing, praying in the *mihrab*﴾. Al-Baghawi mentions that Zakariyya was the great rabbi who would offer the sacrifice and open the door of the altar, so they would not enter until he gave permission. So while he was standing praying in the *mihrab*, meaning the place of worship beside the altar, while the people were waiting for permission to enter, behold, a man in white garments appeared to him, and he was frightened by him. Then he called to him, and he was Jibril: "O Zakariyya, indeed Allah gives you good news." It has been said: the *mihrab* is the place of the imam's standing in the mosque, and this is the saying of the majority of exegetes. It has also been said: it is the *qiblah*. The apparent sense is that this *mihrab* is the same *mihrab* mentioned before it in the statement: ﴿Whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the *mihrab*﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37]. So in the place where he saw the breaking of custom, there he supplicated, and there the good news came to him. This indicates the legitimacy of prayer in their law. It has also been said: "prayer" here means supplication. And in the verse is evidence for the permissibility of calling to and addressing one who is engaged in prayer, even if that distracts him from his prayer.

This clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun of the object, or from the angels. As for *yusalli* (praying): it is possible that it is a qualifier of *qa'im* (standing). It is possible that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun concealed in *qa'im*, or from the pronoun of the object, according to the view of one who permits two circumstantial clauses from one qualified thing. It is possible that it is a second predicate of *huwa* (he), according to the view of one who permits multiple predicates for a single subject, even if they are not in the meaning of a single predicate. The phrase *fi al-mihrab* (in the *mihrab*) is connected to *yusalli*, and it is not permissible that it be connected to *qa'im* in any of the possibilities of the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of *yusalli* except in one: that *yusalli* be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun concealed in *qa'im*, in which case it is permissible. Because then the governing element of both is the same, namely *qa'im*, since the governing element of the circumstantial clause is *qa'im*, being the governor of the qualified thing, and by it the prepositional phrase is connected.

From His saying ﴿standing, praying in the *mihrab*﴾, they said: it is evidence for the permissibility of the imam standing in his *mihrab*. Abu Hanifa disliked this, and said: that was a law for those before us. Warsh pronounced the *ra'* of *al-mihrab* with thinness, and Ibn Dhakwan inclined the *ra'* when *al-mihrab* is in the genitive case. Abu 'Ali attributed this to Ibn 'Amir, and he did not restrict it to the genitive.

﴿Indeed Allah gives you good news of Yahya﴾. Ibn 'Amir and Hamza read *inna Allah* with a kasra on the hamza. According to the Basrans, the kasra is by implying a verb of saying, meaning: "and she said." According to the Kufans, there is no implied verb, because other than saying, things of the same meaning, such as calling and supplicating, take the place of saying in reporting speech. So *nadat-hu* was given kasra, because its meaning is "she said to him." The rest read with a fatha on the hamza, and it is governed by an elided *ba'* (with) originally, meaning "with good news." When it was elided, the position is accusative by the verb, or genitive by the elided *ba'*. These are two opinions that have already been stated in more than one place in this book.

'Abdullah read: "O Zakariyya, indeed Allah..." So his saying *ya Zakariyya* is the object of the calling. It is therefore in the accusative position, and it is not permissible to read *inna* with a fatha in this reading, because the verb has already taken its two objects, which are the pronoun and the vocative. The conveying of good news through the messenger to the one to whom he is sent is not good news from the messenger, but from the sender. Do you not see the attribution of this to Him in His saying: "He gives you good news"? And He said in Surat Maryam: ﴿O Zakariyya, indeed We give you good news﴾ [Maryam: 7], attributing it to Him, the Exalted. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *yubashshiruka* in both places in the story of Zakariyya and the story of Maryam, and in al-Isra', al-Kahf, and al-Shura, from *bashara*, unstressed. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr agreed with them, and in al-Shura Hamza added in al-Hijr: ﴿Then for what do you give me good news?﴾ and in Maryam. The rest read *yubashshiru*, from *bashshara* with the doubled middle radical. 'Abdullah read *yubshiru* throughout the Qur'an, from *absharа*. These are three dialects, mentioned by more than one lexicographer. A poet said:

*I gave good news to my dependants when I saw a letter that came to you from al-Hajjaj, whose contents are read.*

Another said:

*O Bishr, your face has the right to be glad-tidings; would that you were angry for us while you are a commander!*

*Bi-Yahya* (of Yahya) is connected to *nubashshiruka* (We give you good news), and the meaning is: of the birth of Yahya from you and from your wife. If it is non-Arabic, its prohibition from declension is due to being a proper name and being foreign. If it is Arabic, it is due to being a proper name and the weight of the verb, like *ya'mur*. We have already mentioned this. This which many exegetes have adopted takes into account the sense of derivation from *hayah* (life). Qatada said: Allah named him Yahya because He gave him life through faith. Al-Hasan ibn al-Mufaddal said: he lived through preservation from sin and obedience. Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib said: he was named Yahya because he was martyred, and martyrs are living. It has been related in a hadith: "Among the lowliness of this world before Allah is that Yahya ibn Zakariyya was killed by a woman." Muqatil said: he was named Yahya because He gave him life between an old man and an old woman. Al-Zajjaj said: he lived by the knowledge and wisdom which he was given. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah gave life through him to the womb of his mother. It has also been said: the meaning is that he will die, so he was named Yahya optimistically, like *al-mafazah* and *al-salim* (names given by hope). It has also been said: because Allah gave life through him to people by guidance.

﴿Confirming a word from Allah﴾. The majority hold that the "word" is 'Isa, and the reason he is called a word will come later. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi, and others. Al-Rabi' and others said: Yahya was the first to believe in 'Isa and to testify that he was a word from Allah. Yahya was older than 'Isa by six months, as the majority say. It is said: by three years. He was killed before 'Isa was raised. The mother of Yahya used to say to Maryam: "Indeed I find that which is in my belly moves," and in another report: "prostrates," and in another report: "bows his head to what is in your belly." That is his confirmation, and it is the first confirmation. Abu 'Ubaydah and others said: ﴿a word from Allah﴾ means a book from Allah: the Torah, the Gospel, and others. The singular was used in the place of the plural, so *al-kalimah* is a generic noun. The Arabs called a poem a *kalimah*. It is related that al-Huwaydirah was mentioned to Hassan, and he said: "May Allah curse his *kalimah*," meaning his poem. In a hadith: "The truest word a poet has spoken is the word of Labid: 'Surely everything except Allah is vain, and every bliss will certainly vanish.'" It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿a word from Allah﴾ here is a promise from Allah. Abu al-Sammal al-'Adawi read *bi-kilmah* with a kasra on the kaf and sukun on the lam throughout the Qur'an. This is an eloquent dialect like *katf* and *kitf* (shoulder). Its basis is that he made the first letter of the word follow its middle letter, so that two kasras rarely come together, and so he made the middle letter sukun. Some of them make it sukun with a fatha on the first letter, finding the kasra on the middle letter burdensome.

*Musaddiqan* (confirming) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is an emphatic circumstantial clause, according to the condition of these prophets, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them.

﴿And a master﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-sayyid* (master) is the noble. Qatada said: the forbearing, and from it is the saying of the poet:

*A master whose bounty is not forfeited, the sudden outbursts of the ignorant even when they act ignorantly.*

'Ikrimah said: one whom anger does not overcome. al-Dahhak said: one of good character. Salim said: the pious. Ibn Zayd said: the noble. Ibn al-Musayyab said: the jurist, the learned. Ahmad ibn 'Asim said: the one content with Allah's decree. al-Khalil said: the one obeyed, surpassing his peers. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: the one who relies upon Allah. al-Tirmidhi said: the one of great aspiration. al-Thawri said: the master is one who does not envy, from their saying: "The envious does not become a master." Abu Ishaq said: the master is one who surpasses his people in goodness.

Some lexicographers said: *al-sayyid* is the owner whose obedience is obligatory. For this reason the husband is called *sayyid*, and it is said: "the master of the boy." Salamah related from al-Farra': *al-sayyid* is the owner, the chief, the wise, and the generous.

A hadith has come: "The master is one who is given wealth and granted generosity, so he brings the poor near, and his complaints among people are few." And in its meaning: one who gives his kindness and restrains his harm. In a hadith he (ﷺ) said to Banu Salamah, when he asked them: "Who is your master?" They said: "al-Jadd ibn Qays, despite his stinginess." He (ﷺ) said: "And what disease is more harmful than stinginess? Your master is 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh." It is also said that Sa'd ibn Mu'adh was called "master" in his saying (ﷺ): "Stand up for your master." That is: your chief, the one obeyed among you. Al-Hasan ibn 'Ali was called "master" in his saying (ﷺ): "Indeed this son of mine is a master, and perhaps Allah will reconcile through him between two great groups of the Muslims." Al-Zamakhshari said: the master is one who leads his people, that is, surpasses them in nobility. Yahya was standing for his people, standing for all people in that he never committed a sin at all. And what a mastery is this! So ends his words.

Ibn 'Atiyya said, in summary: Allah singled him out by mention of leadership (*su'dud*), which is striving for the pleasure of people in the noblest manner, without falling into falsehood. Its detail is: giving generously, which is generosity; restraining harm, which is chastity in the private parts, hand, and tongue; and bearing great burdens, and here it is forbearance in bearing debts, mending the broken, and rescuing from ruin. There may be found among the trustworthy scholars one who does not excel in these qualities, and there may be found one who excels in them, and he is called a master, even if he falls short in a recommended matter, and is contentious in a right, and little concerned with blame. Ibn 'Umar said: "I have not seen anyone blacker than Mu'awiya." It was said to him: "And Abu Bakr and 'Umar?" He said: "They are better than him, and Mu'awiya is blacker than both of them." So ends his words.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 39–40 (part 2 of 3):

All these opinions that were mentioned in the tafsir of al-Sayyid can serve as an explanation of the description of Yahya (peace be upon him), and the people most deserving of the attributes of perfection are the prophets. In His saying "and sayyid (a chief/master)," there is an indication that this name is applied to one who possesses leadership (siyadah), and it is among the descriptions of praise. It is not said of an oppressor, a hypocrite, or a disbeliever.

It has been reported that there is a prohibition: "Do not call the hypocrite a sayyid (chief)." As for His saying ﴿We obeyed our chiefs (sadatana)﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67], it refers to what they believed and claimed. It has been said: As for what came in the hadith of the delegation of Bani Amir, when they said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "You are our sayyid, and the one of favour over us," and he said: "The sayyid is Allah; speak with your speech," it is to be understood as meaning that he saw them being artificial in that, or that this was before he came to know that he was the sayyid of mankind. He (ﷺ) also named al-Hasan ibn Ali a sayyid, and likewise Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Amr ibn al-Jamuh.

﴿Hasuran﴾ is the one who does not approach women although he has the ability to do so; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Ata', Abu al-Sha'tha', al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd. The poet said:
"And a hasur who does not desire marriage, nor seeks the bright-faced women."

It has been narrated that he nevertheless married, so that he would be more restrained in his gaze. It was also said: the hasir is one who restrains himself from desires; it was said: from the disobedience of Allah; and it was said: the hasur is the timid (hayub). Ibn Mas'ud also said, as did Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, and al-Musayyib: he is the impotent one who has no male organ by which marriage can be consummated, and who does not ejaculate. The mention of hasur as a description in the context of praise is generally only for an acquired act rather than an innate disposition, and what the station of Yahya (peace be upon him) requires is that he restrained himself from the desires of this world, including women and others; perhaps his abandoning women was an asceticism regarding them, and that was their law at that time.

Mujahid said: The food of Yahya was herbs, and he would weep out of fear of Allah, so much that if there were pitch over his eyes he would have pierced it, and tears had made a channel in his face. It has been said: whoever is in this state is occupied away from women and other worldly desires. It was also said: the hasur is the one who does not enter with the people into gambling (maysir). The poet al-Akhtal said:
"And a drinker who delights me with the cup, not one who is hasur, nor one who leaves its remnants."

So it is borrowed for one who does not take part in play and amusement. It has been narrated that he passed, while still a child, by some boys who invited him to play, and he said: "For play was I not created." And hasur and hasir mean one who keeps a secret; Jarir said:
"Indeed the slanderers have brought me down, and they found in you, O Umayyim, one who is hasir (secretive) with your secret, and stingy."

It has come in a hadith from Ibn al-As, with the meaning: that Yahya did not have what men have except like this twig, pointing to a small stick. And in the narration of Abu Hurayrah: his male organ was like this speck, pointing to a speck of dirt he took from the ground. And whoever holds that devotion to voluntary acts of worship is better than occupation with marriage, which is the view of the majority, has taken evidence from His saying ﴿hasuran﴾, unlike the view of Abu Hanifah, for he holds the opposite.

﴿And a prophet (nabiyyan)﴾: this is the most noble description and the highest of the descriptions. He first mentioned the description upon which the following descriptions are built, which is affirmation (tasdiq), which is faith (iman); then he mentioned sayyidship (siyadah), which is the quality by which he surpasses his people; then he mentioned asceticism, especially regarding that from which one hardly abstains, which is women; then he mentioned the highest rank, which is the rank of prophethood. In these descriptions there is a resemblance to the descriptions of Maryam (peace be upon her), for when Zakariyya saw what Maryam possessed of beautiful qualities and what Allah had specially granted her of extraordinary things beyond custom, he prayed to his Lord to grant him good offspring, and He answered him and gave him Yahya according to what he asked. So affirmation is shared between Maryam and Yahya; Maryam was the sayyida (mistress) of the Children of Israel by the explicit text of the Messenger in the hadith about Fatimah, and Yahya was a sayyid, so they shared in this description. Maryam was a virgin, chaste, whom no human had touched, and Yahya did not approach women. Maryam had the angel come to her as a messenger from Allah, and they conversed about Allah in many discourses, to the extent that some claimed she was a prophetess; and Yahya was a prophet, and the reality of prophethood is that Allah reveals to him, so they shared in this description.

﴿Among the righteous (al-salihin)﴾: this may have two meanings. One: that it means from the loins of the prophets, as He said: ﴿offspring, one from another﴾ [Al Imran: 34]. The other possibility is that it means: and righteous, one of the company of the righteous, as Allah the Exalted said in describing Ibrahim: ﴿and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130]. Ibn al-Anbari said: its meaning is among those righteous in state with Allah. al-Kirmani said: the prophets were singled out for mention of righteousness because no opposite of that intrudes upon their righteousness. al-Zajjaj said: the righteous is one who performs what is obligatory upon him and the rights of people towards them, end quote.

Sulayman said, after prophethood had been granted to him: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾ [al-Naml: 19]. It has been said: the realization of this is that the prophets have a measure of righteousness, which if diminished, prophethood would be negated; then after they share in that measure, their ranks vary in the increase above that measure, so whoever has the greater share of righteousness has the higher rank. al-Maturidi said: righteousness is realized in every prophet in all respects, while in others it is realized only in some of them; and although the name applies to all, the reason for the name being deserved by the prophets is the realization of righteousness in all respects, while in others it is in some of them. So He specified it by mention, so that the possibility of prophethood being permissible in general believers is cut off; thus restricting it by the name of righteousness was beneficial. It has also been said: among the righteous in this world and the Hereafter, so it is an indication of persistence in faith and security from fear of the bad end.

﴿He said: My Lord, how can I have a son when old age has overtaken me and my wife is barren?﴾ His previous request to his Lord had preceded: ﴿My Lord, grant me from Yourself good offspring﴾ [Al Imran: 38]. There is no doubt about the possibility and permissibility of that; and if it was possible, and the angels gave him good news of it, what is the purpose of this question?

It has been answered in several ways. One: that it is a question about the manner, and the meaning is: will a child be born to me at the age of old age and with my wife being barren? That is, she has reached the age of one who does not bear children; he had reached ninety-nine years, and his wife had reached ninety-eight years. Ibn Abbas said: he was one hundred and twenty when he was given the good news; al-Kalbi said: he was ninety-two years old.

Or: shall I and my wife be restored to the age of youth and the state of one who has children? It was answered: he will be given a child in this state. This meaning was said by al-Hasan and al-Asamm. The second: that when he was given the good news of a child, he sought to know: would that child be from his own loins or from his sons?

The third: that he had forgotten the question, and between the question and the announcement there were forty years; and it is narrated from Sufyan that between them there were sixty years. The fourth: that this inquiry was by way of magnifying the power of Allah the Exalted; it occurs upon witnessing the signs, and its meaning comes back to what some said: that it was from intense joy, for he was like one astonished when what he was accustomed to considering impossible came to pass. The fifth: he only asked because he was incapable of intercourse due to his old age, so he asked his Lord: will He strengthen him for intercourse, and will his wife accept it in her state of old age? The sixth: he asked whether the child would be granted from his barren wife, or from another.

The seventh: that when he was given the good news of a child, Satan came to him to cloud the blessing of his Lord for him, and said to him: Do you know who called you? He said: The angels of my Lord. He said: No, it was that Satan; and if this were from your Lord, He would have concealed it from you as you concealed your call. So a whisper mixed with his heart, and he said: ﴿How can I have a son?﴾ so that Allah would make clear to him that it was from revelation. This was said by Ikrimah and al-Suddi. The judge said: if the speech of the angel were confused for the speech of Satan to the messengers, the trust in all the laws would not remain.

It is answered: what he said does not follow, because it is possible that a miracle establishes the revelation regarding matters of religion, while matters pertaining to the worldly interests may not be confirmed by a miracle, so the possibility remains, and he seeks its removal. al-Zamakhshari said: it is a remote inference from the standpoint of custom, just as Maryam said. End quote. But according to what he said: if it were a remote inference, he would not have asked it by saying: ﴿grant me from Yourself good offspring﴾ [Al Imran: 38], for one does not ask except for what is possible, especially prophets, since breaking custom for them occurs frequently.

And: "yakun" may be a complete verb with "ghulam" as its subject, meaning: how will a boy come to be born to me? It may also be a defective (incomplete) verb, and in that case the predicate does not necessarily have to precede the subject, because it has been said: the entry of kana makes valid the beginning with an indefinite noun, since the preceding of the interrogative particle justifies beginning with an indefinite noun. The two clauses after each of them are circumstantial (hal), and the governing element in both is "yakun" if it is complete, or the governing element in "li" if it is defective.

It has been said: "wa-imra'ati 'aqir" is a circumstantial clause of the object in "balaghani," and the governing element is "balaghani." The first clause was verbal because old age renews itself little by little, so it was not an inherent description; and the second was nominal with the predicate "'aqir," because her being barren is a necessary matter for her and not an accidental attribute, so it was fitting that the first be a verbal clause and that the second be a nominal clause. The meaning of "balaghani al-kibar" is: it affected me. The real meaning of reaching is in physical bodies, namely that the one who reaches moves to the place reached.

He attributed the reaching to old age as a broadening of speech, as though old age were seeking him, since events befall a person, so they are as though seeking him, and he is the one sought. It has been said: it is of the inverted kind, as came: ﴿and I have indeed reached from old age a withering﴾ [Maryam: 8], and as the poet said:
"Like the hedgehogs, scuttling, they have reached Najran, or their private parts have reached Hajar."

al-Raghib said: when you reach old age, old age has reached you, end quote. Here he put his own condition first and delayed his wife's condition, whereas in Maryam he reversed this. al-Maturidi said: the wording is not observed in narration; rather the meanings contained in the wording are observed. Others said: the opening of the verses in Maryam conforms to this order here, for there he mentioned that the bone had weakened in him, ﴿and the head glistened with grey hair﴾ [Maryam: 4]. And he said: ﴿and indeed I feared my successors after me, and my wife has been barren﴾ [Maryam: 5]; so when he repeated her mention in the inquiry, he delayed the mention of old age so that "itiyya" would match the rhyme endings, and this is a principle sought in eloquence, preferred when it does not impair the meaning. The conjunction here is "wa," so the placing first and last does not indicate a precedence in time; rather this is from the category of placing first what fits better in the eloquence of speech.

﴿He said: Thus Allah does what He wills.﴾ The kaf is for comparison, and "dhalika" refers to the act, that is: like that act, which is the formation of a child between one who has aged and a barren woman. Allah does what He wills of strange acts; so this is a report from Allah that He does the things to which His will relates as an act like that act; nothing can frustrate Him, and the cause of its existence is the attachment of His will, whether it be among the acts that follow custom or among those that do not follow custom.

(p-451) Since Allah (exalted is He) brings things into existence from pure non-existence, without material or cause, how much more so for things that have a material and a cause, even if that is contrary to the custom? In this case, the kaf (ka, "like") occupies a position of accusative (naṣb) as an attribute (ṣifah) of a deleted verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: an act like that act; or it occupies the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the deleted maṣdar in "yafʿalu" (he does). This is according to the view of Sibawayh, and a similar matter has already been mentioned by us. It is also possible that "kadhalika Allah" is a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar), with a deleted modifier (muḍāf) in between, meaning: the wondrous handiwork of Allah is like that handiwork. In this case, "yafʿalu ma yashā'" is an explanation (sharḥ) of the ambiguity (ibhām) in the demonstrative (ism al-ishārah). Al-Zamakhshari estimated it, in a similar manner to this attribute, as: Allah. He said: "(yafʿalu ma yashā')" is an elucidation (bayān) of it, i.e., He does what He wills of the acts that break customary norms, end quote.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: That is, like this wondrous power, the power of Allah is [the same]. End quote. According to this possibility, the kaf is in the position of nominative (rafʿ), because the prepositional phrase and its object are in the position of the predicate of the subject, and the statement consists of two clauses. According to the first interpretation, the statement is one single clause.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah and others said, and the wording is Ibn ʿAtiyyah's: It is possible that the demonstrative "bi-dhalika" refers to the condition of Zakariyya and the condition of his wife, as if he said: "My Lord, in what manner will we have a boy, while we are in such a state?" So He said to him: "Just as you are, a boy will be born to you." The statement is complete according to this interpretation at His saying "kadhalika," and His saying "Allah does what He wills" is a clause that explains and firmly establishes in the soul the occurrence of this wondrous matter, end quote of his words. Thus "kadhalika" is related to a deleted element. Al-Raghib explained the meaning, saying: He grants you a son while you are in your state.

The apparent view among these three opinions is the first.

﴿Then the angels called to him﴾. It has been said that the word *nida'* (calling out) is used for good news, and for something that should be hastened and conveyed to the hearer so that he is gladdened by it. So this was not an announcement from the angels in the manner of revelation, but a calling out, like the Ansari man who called out to Ka'b ibn Malik from the top of a mountain. This was said by Ibn 'Atiyya and others. But this does not appear correct. Rather, calling out (*munada*) is used for good news and for distress, and for other purposes, as has come: "O people of the Fire, there is eternal abiding without death." And it has come: ﴿O Haman, build me a tower﴾ [Ghafir: 36]. The sense of good news in the verse is understood only from their words ﴿Indeed, Allah gives you good news﴾ [Al 'Imran: 45], not because the wording *nadat-hu* (they called to him) indicates it, neither by its lexical form nor by its usage. It is also possible that their calling to him was by way of revelation, meaning: it was revealed to them that they should call to him. Or they called to him on their own initiative, as one would say to you: "Inform Zayd of such-and-such," and you say to him: "O Zayd, such-and-such has happened." These are two opinions among the exegetes. In the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: Allah accepted his supplication, granted him Yahya, and sent the angels to him with this news, and so they called to him.

It is mentioned that there was a period of forty years between his supplication and the response to it, but the apparent sense is contrary to that. The apparent sense is that his caller was a group of angels, by the form of the wording. Indeed, Allah the Exalted sent angels to the people of Lut, and to Ibrahim, and in other places than those He related. Most scholars mention that the caller was Jibril alone, and this is supported by the reading of 'Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) and his codex: "Then Jibril called to him while he was standing." Al-Zamakhshari said: The word "angels" was used only in the manner of their saying: "So-and-so rides horses," meaning that the one who called to him was of the kind of the angels, not that he intends the plurality specifically, just as their saying "So-and-so rides horses" does not intend the plurality specifically, but intends that his mount is of this kind. This is how the reference of those whom "the people" said to (in the verse about Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud) is explained. Al-Fadl said: The leader is spoken of with plural expressions, because his companions are with him, or because of the gathering of beautiful qualities in him which are scattered in others. So it was expressed with plurality for this reason. It has been said: Jibril is the chief of the angels.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *fa-nada-hu* with *imala* (inclination of the vowel). The rest of the seven read *fa-nadat-hu* with the feminine *ta'*, and *al-malaikah* (the angels) is a broken plural, so it is permissible that the feminine marker be attached and permissible that it not be attached. One says: *qama al-rijal* (the men stood) and *qamat al-rijal*. Attaching the marker has been said to be better; do you not see: *idh qalat al-malaikah* (when the angels said), and *lamma ja'at rusuluna* (when Our messengers came)? What makes the omission good here is the separation by the object.

﴿While he was standing, praying in the *mihrab*﴾. Al-Baghawi mentions that Zakariyya was the great rabbi who would offer the sacrifice and open the door of the altar, so they would not enter until he gave permission. So while he was standing praying in the *mihrab*, meaning the place of worship beside the altar, while the people were waiting for permission to enter, behold, a man in white garments appeared to him, and he was frightened by him. Then he called to him, and he was Jibril: "O Zakariyya, indeed Allah gives you good news." It has been said: the *mihrab* is the place of the imam's standing in the mosque, and this is the saying of the majority of exegetes. It has also been said: it is the *qiblah*. The apparent sense is that this *mihrab* is the same *mihrab* mentioned before it in the statement: ﴿Whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the *mihrab*﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37]. So in the place where he saw the breaking of custom, there he supplicated, and there the good news came to him. This indicates the legitimacy of prayer in their law. It has also been said: "prayer" here means supplication. And in the verse is evidence for the permissibility of calling to and addressing one who is engaged in prayer, even if that distracts him from his prayer.

This clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun of the object, or from the angels. As for *yusalli* (praying): it is possible that it is a qualifier of *qa'im* (standing). It is possible that it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun concealed in *qa'im*, or from the pronoun of the object, according to the view of one who permits two circumstantial clauses from one qualified thing. It is possible that it is a second predicate of *huwa* (he), according to the view of one who permits multiple predicates for a single subject, even if they are not in the meaning of a single predicate. The phrase *fi al-mihrab* (in the *mihrab*) is connected to *yusalli*, and it is not permissible that it be connected to *qa'im* in any of the possibilities of the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of *yusalli* except in one: that *yusalli* be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun concealed in *qa'im*, in which case it is permissible. Because then the governing element of both is the same, namely *qa'im*, since the governing element of the circumstantial clause is *qa'im*, being the governor of the qualified thing, and by it the prepositional phrase is connected.

From His saying ﴿standing, praying in the *mihrab*﴾, they said: it is evidence for the permissibility of the imam standing in his *mihrab*. Abu Hanifa disliked this, and said: that was a law for those before us. Warsh pronounced the *ra'* of *al-mihrab* with thinness, and Ibn Dhakwan inclined the *ra'* when *al-mihrab* is in the genitive case. Abu 'Ali attributed this to Ibn 'Amir, and he did not restrict it to the genitive.

﴿Indeed Allah gives you good news of Yahya﴾. Ibn 'Amir and Hamza read *inna Allah* with a kasra on the hamza. According to the Basrans, the kasra is by implying a verb of saying, meaning: "and she said." According to the Kufans, there is no implied verb, because other than saying, things of the same meaning, such as calling and supplicating, take the place of saying in reporting speech. So *nadat-hu* was given kasra, because its meaning is "she said to him." The rest read with a fatha on the hamza, and it is governed by an elided *ba'* (with) originally, meaning "with good news." When it was elided, the position is accusative by the verb, or genitive by the elided *ba'*. These are two opinions that have already been stated in more than one place in this book.

'Abdullah read: "O Zakariyya, indeed Allah..." So his saying *ya Zakariyya* is the object of the calling. It is therefore in the accusative position, and it is not permissible to read *inna* with a fatha in this reading, because the verb has already taken its two objects, which are the pronoun and the vocative. The conveying of good news through the messenger to the one to whom he is sent is not good news from the messenger, but from the sender. Do you not see the attribution of this to Him in His saying: "He gives you good news"? And He said in Surat Maryam: ﴿O Zakariyya, indeed We give you good news﴾ [Maryam: 7], attributing it to Him, the Exalted. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *yubashshiruka* in both places in the story of Zakariyya and the story of Maryam, and in al-Isra', al-Kahf, and al-Shura, from *bashara*, unstressed. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr agreed with them, and in al-Shura Hamza added in al-Hijr: ﴿Then for what do you give me good news?﴾ and in Maryam. The rest read *yubashshiru*, from *bashshara* with the doubled middle radical. 'Abdullah read *yubshiru* throughout the Qur'an, from *absharа*. These are three dialects, mentioned by more than one lexicographer. A poet said:

*I gave good news to my dependants when I saw a letter that came to you from al-Hajjaj, whose contents are read.*

Another said:

*O Bishr, your face has the right to be glad-tidings; would that you were angry for us while you are a commander!*

*Bi-Yahya* (of Yahya) is connected to *nubashshiruka* (We give you good news), and the meaning is: of the birth of Yahya from you and from your wife. If it is non-Arabic, its prohibition from declension is due to being a proper name and being foreign. If it is Arabic, it is due to being a proper name and the weight of the verb, like *ya'mur*. We have already mentioned this. This which many exegetes have adopted takes into account the sense of derivation from *hayah* (life). Qatada said: Allah named him Yahya because He gave him life through faith. Al-Hasan ibn al-Mufaddal said: he lived through preservation from sin and obedience. Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib said: he was named Yahya because he was martyred, and martyrs are living. It has been related in a hadith: "Among the lowliness of this world before Allah is that Yahya ibn Zakariyya was killed by a woman." Muqatil said: he was named Yahya because He gave him life between an old man and an old woman. Al-Zajjaj said: he lived by the knowledge and wisdom which he was given. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah gave life through him to the womb of his mother. It has also been said: the meaning is that he will die, so he was named Yahya optimistically, like *al-mafazah* and *al-salim* (names given by hope). It has also been said: because Allah gave life through him to people by guidance.

﴿Confirming a word from Allah﴾. The majority hold that the "word" is 'Isa, and the reason he is called a word will come later. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi, and others. Al-Rabi' and others said: Yahya was the first to believe in 'Isa and to testify that he was a word from Allah. Yahya was older than 'Isa by six months, as the majority say. It is said: by three years. He was killed before 'Isa was raised. The mother of Yahya used to say to Maryam: "Indeed I find that which is in my belly moves," and in another report: "prostrates," and in another report: "bows his head to what is in your belly." That is his confirmation, and it is the first confirmation. Abu 'Ubaydah and others said: ﴿a word from Allah﴾ means a book from Allah: the Torah, the Gospel, and others. The singular was used in the place of the plural, so *al-kalimah* is a generic noun. The Arabs called a poem a *kalimah*. It is related that al-Huwaydirah was mentioned to Hassan, and he said: "May Allah curse his *kalimah*," meaning his poem. In a hadith: "The truest word a poet has spoken is the word of Labid: 'Surely everything except Allah is vain, and every bliss will certainly vanish.'" It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿a word from Allah﴾ here is a promise from Allah. Abu al-Sammal al-'Adawi read *bi-kilmah* with a kasra on the kaf and sukun on the lam throughout the Qur'an. This is an eloquent dialect like *katf* and *kitf* (shoulder). Its basis is that he made the first letter of the word follow its middle letter, so that two kasras rarely come together, and so he made the middle letter sukun. Some of them make it sukun with a fatha on the first letter, finding the kasra on the middle letter burdensome.

*Musaddiqan* (confirming) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is an emphatic circumstantial clause, according to the condition of these prophets, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them.

﴿And a master﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: *al-sayyid* (master) is the noble. Qatada said: the forbearing, and from it is the saying of the poet:

*A master whose bounty is not forfeited, the sudden outbursts of the ignorant even when they act ignorantly.*

'Ikrimah said: one whom anger does not overcome. al-Dahhak said: one of good character. Salim said: the pious. Ibn Zayd said: the noble. Ibn al-Musayyab said: the jurist, the learned. Ahmad ibn 'Asim said: the one content with Allah's decree. al-Khalil said: the one obeyed, surpassing his peers. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: the one who relies upon Allah. al-Tirmidhi said: the one of great aspiration. al-Thawri said: the master is one who does not envy, from their saying: "The envious does not become a master." Abu Ishaq said: the master is one who surpasses his people in goodness.

Some lexicographers said: *al-sayyid* is the owner whose obedience is obligatory. For this reason the husband is called *sayyid*, and it is said: "the master of the boy." Salamah related from al-Farra': *al-sayyid* is the owner, the chief, the wise, and the generous.

A hadith has come: "The master is one who is given wealth and granted generosity, so he brings the poor near, and his complaints among people are few." And in its meaning: one who gives his kindness and restrains his harm. In a hadith he (ﷺ) said to Banu Salamah, when he asked them: "Who is your master?" They said: "al-Jadd ibn Qays, despite his stinginess." He (ﷺ) said: "And what disease is more harmful than stinginess? Your master is 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh." It is also said that Sa'd ibn Mu'adh was called "master" in his saying (ﷺ): "Stand up for your master." That is: your chief, the one obeyed among you. Al-Hasan ibn 'Ali was called "master" in his saying (ﷺ): "Indeed this son of mine is a master, and perhaps Allah will reconcile through him between two great groups of the Muslims." Al-Zamakhshari said: the master is one who leads his people, that is, surpasses them in nobility. Yahya was standing for his people, standing for all people in that he never committed a sin at all. And what a mastery is this! So ends his words.

Ibn 'Atiyya said, in summary: Allah singled him out by mention of leadership (*su'dud*), which is striving for the pleasure of people in the noblest manner, without falling into falsehood. Its detail is: giving generously, which is generosity; restraining harm, which is chastity in the private parts, hand, and tongue; and bearing great burdens, and here it is forbearance in bearing debts, mending the broken, and rescuing from ruin. There may be found among the trustworthy scholars one who does not excel in these qualities, and there may be found one who excels in them, and he is called a master, even if he falls short in a recommended matter, and is contentious in a right, and little concerned with blame. Ibn 'Umar said: "I have not seen anyone blacker than Mu'awiya." It was said to him: "And Abu Bakr and 'Umar?" He said: "They are better than him, and Mu'awiya is blacker than both of them." So ends his words.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 39–40 (part 2 of 3):

All these opinions that were mentioned in the tafsir of al-Sayyid can serve as an explanation of the description of Yahya (peace be upon him), and the people most deserving of the attributes of perfection are the prophets. In His saying "and sayyid (a chief/master)," there is an indication that this name is applied to one who possesses leadership (siyadah), and it is among the descriptions of praise. It is not said of an oppressor, a hypocrite, or a disbeliever.

It has been reported that there is a prohibition: "Do not call the hypocrite a sayyid (chief)." As for His saying ﴿We obeyed our chiefs (sadatana)﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67], it refers to what they believed and claimed. It has been said: As for what came in the hadith of the delegation of Bani Amir, when they said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "You are our sayyid, and the one of favour over us," and he said: "The sayyid is Allah; speak with your speech," it is to be understood as meaning that he saw them being artificial in that, or that this was before he came to know that he was the sayyid of mankind. He (ﷺ) also named al-Hasan ibn Ali a sayyid, and likewise Sa'd ibn Mu'adh and Amr ibn al-Jamuh.

﴿Hasuran﴾ is the one who does not approach women although he has the ability to do so; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, Ata', Abu al-Sha'tha', al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd. The poet said:
"And a hasur who does not desire marriage, nor seeks the bright-faced women."

It has been narrated that he nevertheless married, so that he would be more restrained in his gaze. It was also said: the hasir is one who restrains himself from desires; it was said: from the disobedience of Allah; and it was said: the hasur is the timid (hayub). Ibn Mas'ud also said, as did Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, and al-Musayyib: he is the impotent one who has no male organ by which marriage can be consummated, and who does not ejaculate. The mention of hasur as a description in the context of praise is generally only for an acquired act rather than an innate disposition, and what the station of Yahya (peace be upon him) requires is that he restrained himself from the desires of this world, including women and others; perhaps his abandoning women was an asceticism regarding them, and that was their law at that time.

Mujahid said: The food of Yahya was herbs, and he would weep out of fear of Allah, so much that if there were pitch over his eyes he would have pierced it, and tears had made a channel in his face. It has been said: whoever is in this state is occupied away from women and other worldly desires. It was also said: the hasur is the one who does not enter with the people into gambling (maysir). The poet al-Akhtal said:
"And a drinker who delights me with the cup, not one who is hasur, nor one who leaves its remnants."

So it is borrowed for one who does not take part in play and amusement. It has been narrated that he passed, while still a child, by some boys who invited him to play, and he said: "For play was I not created." And hasur and hasir mean one who keeps a secret; Jarir said:
"Indeed the slanderers have brought me down, and they found in you, O Umayyim, one who is hasir (secretive) with your secret, and stingy."

It has come in a hadith from Ibn al-As, with the meaning: that Yahya did not have what men have except like this twig, pointing to a small stick. And in the narration of Abu Hurayrah: his male organ was like this speck, pointing to a speck of dirt he took from the ground. And whoever holds that devotion to voluntary acts of worship is better than occupation with marriage, which is the view of the majority, has taken evidence from His saying ﴿hasuran﴾, unlike the view of Abu Hanifah, for he holds the opposite.

﴿And a prophet (nabiyyan)﴾: this is the most noble description and the highest of the descriptions. He first mentioned the description upon which the following descriptions are built, which is affirmation (tasdiq), which is faith (iman); then he mentioned sayyidship (siyadah), which is the quality by which he surpasses his people; then he mentioned asceticism, especially regarding that from which one hardly abstains, which is women; then he mentioned the highest rank, which is the rank of prophethood. In these descriptions there is a resemblance to the descriptions of Maryam (peace be upon her), for when Zakariyya saw what Maryam possessed of beautiful qualities and what Allah had specially granted her of extraordinary things beyond custom, he prayed to his Lord to grant him good offspring, and He answered him and gave him Yahya according to what he asked. So affirmation is shared between Maryam and Yahya; Maryam was the sayyida (mistress) of the Children of Israel by the explicit text of the Messenger in the hadith about Fatimah, and Yahya was a sayyid, so they shared in this description. Maryam was a virgin, chaste, whom no human had touched, and Yahya did not approach women. Maryam had the angel come to her as a messenger from Allah, and they conversed about Allah in many discourses, to the extent that some claimed she was a prophetess; and Yahya was a prophet, and the reality of prophethood is that Allah reveals to him, so they shared in this description.

﴿Among the righteous (al-salihin)﴾: this may have two meanings. One: that it means from the loins of the prophets, as He said: ﴿offspring, one from another﴾ [Al Imran: 34]. The other possibility is that it means: and righteous, one of the company of the righteous, as Allah the Exalted said in describing Ibrahim: ﴿and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130].
