Or: because of the camels wiping him, meaning their passing over him, as the poet said:

*"On the face of Mayy is a trace of beauty."*

Or: because of a wiping away of the filth that afflicts newborns, for his mother did not menstruate and was not defiled by postpartum blood. These are seven opinions. ﴿فَعِيل﴾ (fa'il, a pattern) here has the meaning of the passive participle (maf'ul), and the ﴿الألِفُ واللّامُ﴾ (al-alif wa al-lam, the definite article) in ﴿المَسِيحِ﴾ is for dominance (al-ghalaba), like it is in al-Dabaran and al-'Ayyuq (names of stars). Ibn 'Abbas said: he was named so because he would not wipe with his hand anyone afflicted with a defect except that he was healed. Based on this, ﴿فَعِيل﴾ is a form for intensification (mubalagha), like ﴿عَلِيم﴾ (ʿalīm, "all-knowing"), and it is among the patterns that were changed from the active participle (fa'il) to fa'il for intensification. It was said: it comes from measuring (al-misaha), and he used to travel through the land, so it is as if he were measuring it. It was said: it is a form of ﴿مُفْعِل﴾ (muf'il) from sāḥa yasīḥu, meaning travel (al-siyaha). Mujahid and al-Nakha'i said: al-Masih means the truthful one (al-siddiq). Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: al-Masih means the king, named so because he possessed the reviving of the dead and other signs. Abu 'Ubayd said: its origin in Hebrew is mashiah, which was altered. Based on this, it is a name coined (murtajal), and is not derived from wiping nor from travel.

﴿'Isa son of Maryam﴾: Sons are attributed to fathers, and he was attributed to her. Although the address was to her, this informs that he would be born without a father, so he is not attributed except to her.

The apparent meaning is that his name is al-Masih, so ﴿اسْمُهُ المَسِيحُ﴾ is a subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar). As for ﴿عِيسى﴾ ('Isa), they permitted that it be a predicate after a predicate, a substitute (badal), or an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan). Some grammarians prohibited it from being a predicate after a predicate, and said: it would have required that he say "his names" in terms of meaning, or "her names" according to the wording of "the word." It is permissible that ﴿عِيسى﴾ be a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: he is 'Isa son of Maryam. Ibn 'Atiyya said: what calls to this is that ﴿ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ (ibn Maryam, "son of Maryam") is an attribute (sifa) of ﴿عِيسى﴾, since people have agreed to write it without the alif. As for it being a substitute or explanatory apposition, then ﴿ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ cannot be an attribute of ﴿عِيسى﴾, because the name here is not intended to refer to the person. This is the view of Abu 'Ali, and there is an issue in the beginning of his speech. End of his words. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, why was it said ﴿اسْمُهُ المَسِيحُ عِيسى بْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾, when these are three things, the name among them is 'Isa, while al-Masih and "son" are a title (laqab) and an attribute (sifa)? I say: the name is a sign for the named by which it is known and distinguished from others; it is as if it were said: that by which he is known and distinguished from others is the combination of these three. End of his words. It appears from his words that his name is the combination of these three, so the three are predicates of the statement "his name," and it is of the type: "this is sweet-sour," and "this is: difficult-easy." Thus none of them on this basis is independently a predicate. A parallel to this in the case of two things, or things, being in the ruling of one thing is the saying of the poet:

*"How did you rise? How did you spend the evening? Of what plants the affection in the heart of the generous one?"*

That is: the combination of this is what plants affection. Since it is permissible for the subject to be multiple without a conjunction when the meaning is on the combination, likewise it is permissible for the predicate. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: he is the son of Maryam; and it is not permissible that it be a substitute for what precedes it, nor an attribute, because ﴿ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ is not a name. Do you not see that you do not say: "the name of this man is son of 'Amr," unless it is a proper name for him? End of his words.

Some said: whoever says that al-Masih is an attribute of 'Isa, then there is in the speech an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), its estimate being: "his name is 'Isa al-Masih," because the attribute follows what it describes. End of his words. It is not correct that al-Masih in this construction be an attribute, because what is predicated by this wording and al-Masih is an attribute of the referent (al-madlul), not an attribute of the signifier (al-dal), since the word 'Isa is not al-Masih. Whoever says: they are two names, al-Masih came before 'Isa because of its fame. Ibn al-Anbari said: He began with his title because al-Masih is more famous than 'Isa, since it rarely applies to a namesake who might be confused with him, whereas 'Isa may apply to a large number of people, so he put it first because of its fame. Do you not see that the titles of the caliphs are more famous than their names? This indicates that according to Ibn al-Anbari al-Masih is a title, not a name. Al-Zajjaj said: 'Isa is an arabized form of Ayshu', and if you make it Arabic it would not take nunation in definite or indefinite form, because it has the feminine alif; and it would be derived from 'asa ya'usu, meaning to govern and to stand over. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is derived from al-'Is, like a drawing in water.

﴿Honored in this world and the Hereafter﴾: Ibn Qutayba said: the wajih is one who has rank (dhu al-jah); it is said: the man was made honored (wujiha al-rajul yujahu wijaha). Ibn Duraid said: the wajih is the beloved and accepted. Al-Akhfash said: the noble one of high rank and standing. It was said: the one who is esteemed by whoever asks him, because he does not refuse him, out of the nobility of his face. Its meaning regarding 'Isa is that his honor in this world is by his prophethood, and in the Hereafter by the loftiness of his rank. It was said: in this world by obedience, and in the Hereafter by intercession. It was said: in this world by bringing the dead to life and healing the blind and the leper, and in the Hereafter by intercession. It was said: in this world he is noble, whose face is not refused, and in the Hereafter he is among the elite of the messengers. Al-Zamakhshari said: honor in this world is prophethood and precedence over people, and in the Hereafter it is intercession and high rank in Paradise. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the honor of 'Isa in this world is his prophethood, his mention, and his elevation, and in the Hereafter his station, his favor, and his intercession.

﴿And of those brought near﴾: Its meaning is: from Allah, Exalted is He. Al-Zamakhshari said: his being among those brought near is that He raised him to the heaven and the angels accompanied him. Qatada said: and among those brought near to Allah on the Day of Resurrection. It was said: among the people by acceptance and response; this was said by al-Mawardi. It was said: its meaning is: one who is greatly brought near, because ﴿فَعُلَ﴾ (fa'ula) is a form of intensification, so one says: he brought him near (qarraba), meaning he greatly brought him near. End of his words. ﴿فَعُلَ﴾ is not here a form of intensification, because the doubling here is for transitivity; it occurs for intensification only in examples like: I wounded Zayd (jarraḥtu Zaydan), and he killed the people (mawwata al-nas). End of quote.

﴿And of those brought near﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿وجِيهًا﴾ (wajihan), and its estimate is: "and brought near, from among those brought near." He informed that there are those brought near, and that 'Isa is among them. A parallel to this conjunction is His saying: ﴿وإنَّكم لَتَمُرُّونَ عَلَيْهِمْ مُصْبِحِينَ وبِاللَّيْلِ﴾ [al-Saffat 37:137–138] ("You pass by them in the morning, and by night"). Here ﴿وبِاللَّيْلِ﴾ (wa bil-layl, "and by night") is a prepositional phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is conjoined to ﴿مُصْبِحِينَ﴾ (musbiḥin, "in the morning"). This circumstantial clause came in this form because it is a closing word (fasila, the rhyme ending of a verse), so if it had come as ﴿ومُقَرَّبًا﴾ (wa muqarraban), it would not have been a closing word. Also, He informed that 'Isa is brought near from among those brought near, and nearness is a sublime, great attribute. Do you not see His saying: ﴿ولا المَلائِكَةُ المُقَرَّبُونَ﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:172] ("nor the angels who are brought near")? And His saying: ﴿فَأمّا إنْ كانَ مِنَ المُقَرَّبِينَ فَرَوْحٌ﴾ [al-Waqi'a 56:88] ("But if he is of those brought near, then there is rest and provision")? It is a nearness from Allah, Exalted is He, in standing, nobility, and elevation of rank.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on Surah Al 'Imran 3:44–46 (part 2 of 2)

﴿And he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity.﴾ He conjoined "and he will speak" (wa-yukallimu), which is also a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a state or condition of the subject) like "distinguished" (wajīhan). Its parallel is ﴿at the birds above them, spreading and folding [their wings]﴾ [al-Mulk: 19], meaning "spreading and folding." Likewise, "and he will speak" means "and speaking." The first state is expressed by a noun, because the noun signifies permanence. The second state is a prepositional phrase with its object, because it is restricted by a noun. The third state is a clause, because it comes in the third rank. Do you not see that the circumstantial state is, in meaning, a description? Just as the best and most common usage in the Arabic language is that when several different descriptions are combined, one begins with the noun, then the prepositional phrase, then the clause, as in His saying: ﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said﴾ [Ghafir: 28], the same applies to the circumstantial states: one begins with the noun, then the prepositional phrase, then the clause. This clause is verbal, because the verb indicates renewal, just as the noun indicates permanence. "In the cradle" is linked to an implied element, since it is in the position of a circumstantial state. The estimate is: "existing in the cradle and in maturity," coordinated with this state, as if it were said: "as a child and as a mature man." So the explicit circumstantial state is coordinated with the prepositional phrase that occupies the position of a state. Its reverse parallel is ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning and at night﴾ [al-Saffat: 137]. Whoever claims that "and in maturity" is coordinated with "distinguished" has gone far astray.

Al-mahd (the cradle) is the place where the infant rests while nursing. Its origin is a verbal noun that became a name. It is said: "I prepared (mahhadtu) for myself," with the letter ha' lightened or doubled, meaning "I made ready." It is also said: "amhada al-shay'," meaning "it rose." The linguistic explanation of al-kahl (maturity) has already been given. Mujahid said: al-kahl is "the forbearing one." This is generally an explanation by a necessary concomitant, because the mature man's reason, understanding and experience become strong, so he is not like the youth. The Arabs take pride in maturity. One poet said:

"Nor does it harm one whose remnants are like us:
youth that aspired to lofty heights, and maturity."

For this reason this age was singled out in the verse rather than the rest of life, because it is the middle stage in the firmness of reason and soundness of judgment. In His saying "and in maturity" there is good news that he will live until the age of maturity, as al-Rabi' said. It is said that Maryam bore him after eight months, and whoever is born at that time does not live, so this was a glad tiding to her that he would live to this age. It was also said that the custom was that whoever spoke in the cradle would die. In His saying ﴿in the cradle and in maturity﴾ there is an indication of the changing of conditions upon him and a refutation of the Christians' claim of his divinity. Ibn Kaysan said: He mentioned this before He created him, informing that he would reach maturity. When Maryam was informed of it, it was known that it was from the knowledge of the unseen.

It is disputed concerning his speech in the cradle: was it for a single moment, after which he did not speak until he reached the stage of speech? Or did he speak continually in the cradle until he reached the time of speech? There are two opinions. The first is from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Tha'alibi reported several things he said to his mother while he was still nursing. The apparent meaning is that when he spoke to the people in the cradle, he was a prophet, because of His saying ﴿Indeed I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 30], and because this miracle appeared from him with a challenge therein. It was also said that he was not a prophet at that time, and that the speech was a foundation for his prophethood. Then His saying ﴿and made me a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 30] is an announcement of what would become of him, based on His saying ﴿and He has enjoined upon me prayer and zakat﴾ [Maryam: 31]. It does not address the time of his speech when he was mature. It was said that his speech before being raised to the heaven was addressing them with revelation and messengership.

It was also said: he will descend from the heaven as a mature man of thirty-three years, and will say to them: "Indeed I am the servant of Allah," as he said in the cradle. This is the benefit of His saying "and in maturity": it informs that he will descend when he kills the Dajjal (the Antichrist), as Ibn Zayd said.

Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is: "and he will speak to the people in these two conditions with the speech of the prophets, without any difference between the state of childhood and the state of maturity, in which reason is firm and in which prophets are commissioned."

It is said: seven spoke in the cradle: 'Isa, Yahya, the witness of Yusuf, the companion of Jurayj, the child of the hairdresser of Pharaoh's wife, the companion of the tyrant, and the companion of the trench (al-Ukhdud). The stories of these are transmitted. What has come limiting those who spoke as infants to three does not contradict this, because that was a report made before the others were made known, so it reported according to what was first made known to it, and then the others were made known.

﴿And of the righteous﴾, i.e., "and righteous, among the company of the righteous." The meaning of the righteousness with which the prophets are described has already been explained. The accusative of "distinguished" and what is coordinated with it is a circumstantial state of "a word from Him." This is permissible even though it is indefinite, because it is described by His saying "from Him," and by His saying "from Him," and by His saying "whose name is the Messiah."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 44–46 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And you were not with them when they disputed﴾: That is, concerning Maryam. It is possible that this dispute was the casting of lots, and that it was another dispute after it. The intent is the intensity of their desire to take charge of her affairs. The governing element of ﴿إذْ﴾ (idh, "when") is the element governing ﴿لَدَيْهِمْ﴾ (ladayhim, "with them"), or ﴿كُنْتَ﴾ (kunta, "you were"), according to the view of Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) regarding ﴿إذْ يُلْقُونَ﴾ (idh yulqun, "when they cast"). This verse contains, among the kinds of eloquence, repetition in ﴿اصْطَفاكِ﴾ (isṭafāki, "has chosen you"), in ﴿يا مَرْيَمُ﴾ (Yā Maryam, "O Maryam"), and in ﴿ما كُنْتَ لَدَيْهِمْ﴾ (mā kunta ladayhim, "you were not with them"). It was said that there is also inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir, the placing of a word earlier or later than its expected order) in ﴿واسْجُدِي وارْكَعِي﴾ (wasjudī warka'ī, "prostrate and bow"), according to some opinions. There is also metaphor (isti'ara), according to those who held that ﴿القُنُوتَ والسُّجُودَ والرُّكُوعَ﴾ (al-qunut, al-sujud, al-ruku', "devotion, prostration, and bowing") are not a metonymy (kinaya) for the postures of prayer. The allusion to that is among the reports of the unseen. There is generality intended as specificity in ﴿نِساءِ العالَمِينَ﴾ (nisa' al-'alamin, "the women of the worlds"), according to one of the two interpretations. There is simile in ﴿أقْلامِهِمْ﴾ (aqlamahum, "their pens"), if we say he meant the arrows (al-qidah). There is ellipsis in several places.

﴿When the angels said: O Maryam, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him﴾: The governing element of ﴿إذا﴾ (idh) is ﴿اذْكُرْ﴾ (udhkur, "remember"), or ﴿يَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾ (yakhtasimun, "they dispute"), or ﴿إذْ﴾ (idh) is a substitute (badal) for ﴿إذْ﴾ in His saying ﴿إذْ يَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾, or for ﴿وإذْ قالَتِ المَلائِكَةُ﴾. These are opinions. The two middle opinions require that the time of the dispute and the time of the angels' speech be the same, and this is far-fetched; it is the opinion of al-Zajjaj. The fourth is distant because of the long separation between the substitute and what it substitutes. The fourth is the choice of al-Zamakhshari, and with it he began. The disagreement concerning ﴿المَلائِكَةُ﴾ (al-malā'ika, "the angels") is whether they are a group of angels, or Jibril alone, as was previously mentioned in their address to Zakariyya and to Maryam. The speech of the angels was mentioned before this good tidings, with mention of her selection, her purification by Allah, and the assurance of worship of Him, as a means of gentleness and kindness, so that this would be a preface to this good tidings of this wondrous, extraordinary matter that had not happened to any woman before her, and will not happen to any woman after her: that she would conceive without a male touching her. The occurrence of that extraordinary matter was also, as a provision from Allah for her, a means of comforting her regarding this extraordinary matter.

Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Umar recited: ﴿وإذْ قالَ المَلائِكَةُ﴾ (wa idh qāla al-malā'ika). The ﴿الكَلِمَةُ﴾ (al-kalima, "the word") from Allah is 'Isa, peace be upon him. He was called a word because of his coming into being through the word "Be" (kun), without a father. This was said by Qatada. It was also said: because he was named al-Masih, and he is a word from Allah, that is, from the speech of Allah. It was also said: because of Allah's promise concerning him in His book, the Torah and the previous scriptures. In the Torah: "Allah came from Sinai, and shone forth from Sa'ir, and appeared from the mountains of Paran." Sa'ir is the place from which the Messiah was sent. It was also said: because Allah guides by His word. It was also said: because it came in accordance with the word of Jibril, which is: ﴿إنَّما أنا رَسُولُ رَبِّكِ لِأهَبَ لَكِ غُلامًا زَكِيًّا﴾ [Maryam 19:19] ("I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy"), so it came in the attribute that was described. It was also said: Allah named him by this, just as He names whomever He wills among the rest of His creation with whatever names He wills. Based on this, it is a proper noun set for him, in which no suitable aspect is considered. It was also said: the word here does not mean 'Isa; rather the "word" is the angels' good tidings to Maryam about 'Isa. It was also said: it is the good tidings of the Prophet to her.

﴿Whose name is al-Masih, 'Isa son of Maryam﴾: The pronoun in ﴿اسْمُهُ﴾ (ismuhu, "his name") refers to ﴿الكَلِمَةُ﴾ (the word), in the sense: We give you good tidings of one brought into being from Him, or of one existing from Allah. He was named al-Masih (the Messiah) because he was anointed with blessing; this was said by al-Hasan, Sa'id, and Shamir. Or: because of the oil with which the prophets are anointed; he came out of his mother's womb anointed with it, and it is a fragrant oil, such that when a person is anointed with it, it is known that he is a prophet. Or: because of purification from sins. Or: because Jibril wiped him with his wing. Or: because he wiped his feet, for there was no hollow in them, and the hollow (al-akhmas) is that part of the sole of the foot that does not touch the ground. 'Isa had a flat foot with no hollow. The poet said:

*"He spent the night struggling with her, a boy like an arrow-shaft, with firm, thick shins, and a flat foot."*

Or: because of the camels wiping him, meaning their passing over him, as the poet said:

*"On the face of Mayy is a trace of beauty."*

Or: because of a wiping away of the filth that afflicts newborns, for his mother did not menstruate and was not defiled by postpartum blood. Based on this, ﴿فَعِيل﴾ is a form for intensification (mubalagha), like ﴿عَلِيم﴾ (ʿalīm, "all-knowing"), and it is among the patterns that were changed from the active participle (fa'il) to fa'il for intensification. It was said: it comes from measuring (al-misaha), and he used to travel through the land, so it is as if he were measuring it. It was said: it is a form of ﴿مُفْعِل﴾ (muf'il) from sāḥa yasīḥu, meaning travel (al-siyaha). Mujahid and al-Nakha'i said: al-Masih means the truthful one (al-siddiq). Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: al-Masih means the king, named so because he possessed the reviving of the dead and other signs. Abu 'Ubayd said: its origin in Hebrew is mashiah, which was altered. Based on this, it is a name coined (murtajal), and is not derived from wiping nor from travel.

﴿'Isa son of Maryam﴾: Sons are attributed to fathers, and he was attributed to her. Although the address was to her, this informs that he would be born without a father, so he is not attributed except to her.

The apparent meaning is that his name is al-Masih, so ﴿اسْمُهُ المَسِيحُ﴾ is a subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar). As for ﴿عِيسى﴾ ('Isa), they permitted that it be a predicate after a predicate, a substitute (badal), or an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan). Some grammarians prohibited it from being a predicate after a predicate, and said: it would have required that he say "his names" in terms of meaning, or "her names" according to the wording of "the word." It is permissible that ﴿عِيسى﴾ be a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: he is 'Isa son of Maryam. Ibn 'Atiyya said: what calls to this is that ﴿ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ (ibn Maryam, "son of Maryam") is an attribute (sifa) of ﴿عِيسى﴾, since people have agreed to write it without the alif. As for it being a substitute or explanatory apposition, then ﴿ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ cannot be an attribute of ﴿عِيسى﴾, because the name here is not intended to refer to the person. This is the view of Abu 'Ali, and there is an issue in the beginning of his speech. End of his words. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, why was it said ﴿اسْمُهُ المَسِيحُ عِيسى بْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾, when these are three things, the name among them is 'Isa, while al-Masih and "son" are a title (laqab) and an attribute (sifa)? I say: the name is a sign for the named by which it is known and distinguished from others; it is as if it were said: that by which he is known and distinguished from others is the combination of these three. End of his words. It appears from his words that his name is the combination of these three, so the three are predicates of the statement "his name," and it is of the type: "this is sweet-sour," and "this is: difficult-easy." Thus none of them on this basis is independently a predicate. A parallel to this in the case of two things, or things, being in the ruling of one thing is the saying of the poet:

*"How did you rise? How did you spend the evening? Of what plants the affection in the heart of the generous one?"*

That is: the combination of this is what plants affection. Since it is permissible for the subject to be multiple without a conjunction when the meaning is on the combination, likewise it is permissible for the predicate. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: he is the son of Maryam; and it is not permissible that it be a substitute for what precedes it, nor an attribute, because ﴿ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ is not a name. Do you not see that you do not say: "the name of this man is son of 'Amr," unless it is a proper name for him? End of his words.

Some said: whoever says that al-Masih is an attribute of 'Isa, then there is in the speech an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), its estimate being: "his name is 'Isa al-Masih," because the attribute follows what it describes. End of his words. It is not correct that al-Masih in this construction be an attribute, because what is predicated by this wording and al-Masih is an attribute of the referent (al-madlul), not an attribute of the signifier (al-dal), since the word 'Isa is not al-Masih. Whoever says: they are two names, al-Masih came before 'Isa because of its fame. Ibn al-Anbari said: He began with his title because al-Masih is more famous than 'Isa, since it rarely applies to a namesake who might be confused with him, whereas 'Isa may apply to a large number of people, so he put it first because of its fame. Do you not see that the titles of the caliphs are more famous than their names? This indicates that according to Ibn al-Anbari al-Masih is a title, not a name. Al-Zajjaj said: 'Isa is an arabized form of Ayshu', and if you make it Arabic it would not take nunation in definite or indefinite form, because it has the feminine alif; and it would be derived from 'asa ya'usu, meaning to govern and to stand over. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is derived from al-'Is, like a drawing in water.

﴿Honored in this world and the Hereafter﴾: Ibn Qutayba said: the wajih is one who has rank (dhu al-jah); it is said: the man was made honored (wujiha al-rajul yujahu wijaha). Ibn Duraid said: the wajih is the beloved and accepted. Al-Akhfash said: the noble one of high rank and standing. It was said: the one who is esteemed by whoever asks him, because he does not refuse him, out of the nobility of his face. Its meaning regarding 'Isa is that his honor in this world is by his prophethood, and in the Hereafter by the loftiness of his rank. It was said: in this world by obedience, and in the Hereafter by intercession. It was said: in this world by bringing the dead to life and healing the blind and the leper, and in the Hereafter by intercession. It was said: in this world he is noble, whose face is not refused, and in the Hereafter he is among the elite of the messengers. Al-Zamakhshari said: honor in this world is prophethood and precedence over people, and in the Hereafter it is intercession and high rank in Paradise. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the honor of 'Isa in this world is his prophethood, his mention, and his elevation, and in the Hereafter his station, his favor, and his intercession.

﴿And of those brought near﴾: Its meaning is: from Allah, Exalted is He. Al-Zamakhshari said: his being among those brought near is that He raised him to the heaven and the angels accompanied him. Qatada said: and among those brought near to Allah on the Day of Resurrection. It was said: among the people by acceptance and response; this was said by al-Mawardi. It was said: its meaning is: one who is greatly brought near, because ﴿فَعُلَ﴾ (fa'ula) is a form of intensification, so one says: he brought him near (qarraba), meaning he greatly brought him near. End of his words. ﴿فَعُلَ﴾ is not here a form of intensification, because the doubling here is for transitivity; it occurs for intensification only in examples like: I wounded Zayd (jarraḥtu Zaydan), and he killed the people (mawwata al-nas). End of quote.

﴿And of those brought near﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿وجِيهًا﴾ (wajihan), and its estimate is: "and brought near, from among those brought near." He informed that there are those brought near, and that 'Isa is among them. A parallel to this conjunction is His saying: ﴿وإنَّكم لَتَمُرُّونَ عَلَيْهِمْ مُصْبِحِينَ وبِاللَّيْلِ﴾ [al-Saffat 37:137–138] ("You pass by them in the morning, and by night"). Here ﴿وبِاللَّيْلِ﴾ (wa bil-layl, "and by night") is a prepositional phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is conjoined to ﴿مُصْبِحِينَ﴾ (musbiḥin, "in the morning"). This circumstantial clause came in this form because it is a closing word (fasila, the rhyme ending of a verse), so if it had come as ﴿ومُقَرَّبًا﴾ (wa muqarraban), it would not have been a closing word. Also, He informed that 'Isa is brought near from among those brought near, and nearness is a sublime, great attribute. Do you not see His saying: ﴿ولا المَلائِكَةُ المُقَرَّبُونَ﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:172] ("nor the angels who are brought near")? And His saying: ﴿فَأمّا إنْ كانَ مِنَ المُقَرَّبِينَ فَرَوْحٌ﴾ [al-Waqi'a 56:88] ("But if he is of those brought near, then there is rest and provision")? It is a nearness from Allah, Exalted is He, in standing, nobility, and elevation of rank.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on Surah Al 'Imran 3:44–46 (part 2 of 2)

﴿And he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity.﴾ He conjoined "and he will speak" (wa-yukallimu), which is also a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a state or condition of the subject) like "distinguished" (wajīhan). Its parallel is ﴿at the birds above them, spreading and folding [their wings]﴾ [al-Mulk: 19], meaning "spreading and folding." Likewise, "and he will speak" means "and speaking." The first state is expressed by a noun, because the noun signifies permanence. The second state is a prepositional phrase with its object, because it is restricted by a noun. The third state is a clause, because it comes in the third rank. Do you not see that the circumstantial state is, in meaning, a description? Just as the best and most common usage in the Arabic language is that when several different descriptions are combined, one begins with the noun, then the prepositional phrase, then the clause, as in His saying: ﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said﴾ [Ghafir: 28], the same applies to the circumstantial states: one begins with the noun, then the prepositional phrase, then the clause. This clause is verbal, because the verb indicates renewal, just as the noun indicates permanence. "In the cradle" is linked to an implied element, since it is in the position of a circumstantial state. The estimate is: "existing in the cradle and in maturity," coordinated with this state, as if it were said: "as a child and as a mature man." So the explicit circumstantial state is coordinated with the prepositional phrase that occupies the position of a state. Its reverse parallel is ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning and at night﴾ [al-Saffat: 137]. Whoever claims that "and in maturity" is coordinated with "distinguished" has gone far astray.

Al-mahd (the cradle) is the place where the infant rests while nursing. Its origin is a verbal noun that became a name. It is said: "I prepared (mahhadtu) for myself," with the letter ha' lightened or doubled, meaning "I made ready." It is also said: "amhada al-shay'," meaning "it rose." The linguistic explanation of al-kahl (maturity) has already been given. Mujahid said: al-kahl is "the forbearing one." This is generally an explanation by a necessary concomitant, because the mature man's reason, understanding and experience become strong, so he is not like the youth. The Arabs take pride in maturity. One poet said:

"Nor does it harm one whose remnants are like us:
youth that aspired to lofty heights, and maturity."

For this reason this age was singled out in the verse rather than the rest of life, because it is the middle stage in the firmness of reason and soundness of judgment. In His saying "and in maturity" there is good news that he will live until the age of maturity, as al-Rabi' said. It is said that Maryam bore him after eight months, and whoever is born at that time does not live, so this was a glad tiding to her that he would live to this age. It was also said that the custom was that whoever spoke in the cradle would die. In His saying ﴿in the cradle and in maturity﴾ there is an indication of the changing of conditions upon him and a refutation of the Christians' claim of his divinity. Ibn Kaysan said: He mentioned this before He created him, informing that he would reach maturity. When Maryam was informed of it, it was known that it was from the knowledge of the unseen.

It is disputed concerning his speech in the cradle: was it for a single moment, after which he did not speak until he reached the stage of speech? Or did he speak continually in the cradle until he reached the time of speech? There are two opinions. The first is from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Tha'alibi reported several things he said to his mother while he was still nursing. The apparent meaning is that when he spoke to the people in the cradle, he was a prophet, because of His saying ﴿Indeed I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 30], and because this miracle appeared from him with a challenge therein. It was also said that he was not a prophet at that time, and that the speech was a foundation for his prophethood. Then His saying ﴿and made me a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 30] is an announcement of what would become of him, based on His saying ﴿and He has enjoined upon me prayer and zakat﴾ [Maryam: 31]. It does not address the time of his speech when he was mature. It was said that his speech before being raised to the heaven was addressing them with revelation and messengership.

It was also said: he will descend from the heaven as a mature man of thirty-three years, and will say to them: "Indeed I am the servant of Allah," as he said in the cradle. This is the benefit of His saying "and in maturity": it informs that he will descend when he kills the Dajjal (the Antichrist), as Ibn Zayd said.

Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is: "and he will speak to the people in these two conditions with the speech of the prophets, without any difference between the state of childhood and the state of maturity, in which reason is firm and in which prophets are commissioned."

It is said: seven spoke in the cradle: 'Isa, Yahya, the witness of Yusuf, the companion of Jurayj, the child of the hairdresser of Pharaoh's wife, the companion of the tyrant, and the companion of the trench (al-Ukhdud). The stories of these are transmitted. What has come limiting those who spoke as infants to three does not contradict this, because that was a report made before the others were made known, so it reported according to what was first made known to it, and then the others were made known.

﴿And of the righteous﴾, i.e., "and righteous, among the company of the righteous." The meaning of the righteousness with which the prophets are described has already been explained. The accusative of "distinguished" and what is coordinated with it is a circumstantial state of "a word from Him." This is permissible even though it is indefinite, because it is described by His saying "from Him," and by His saying "from Him," and by His saying "whose name is the Messiah."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 44–46 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And you were not with them when they disputed﴾: That is, concerning Maryam. It is possible that this dispute was the casting of lots, and that it was another dispute after it. The intent is the intensity of their desire to take charge of her affairs. The governing element of ﴿إذْ﴾ (idh, "when") is the element governing ﴿لَدَيْهِمْ﴾ (ladayhim, "with them"), or ﴿كُنْتَ﴾ (kunta, "you were"), according to the view of Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) regarding ﴿إذْ يُلْقُونَ﴾ (idh yulqun, "when they cast"). This verse contains, among the kinds of eloquence, repetition in ﴿اصْطَفاكِ﴾ (isṭafāki, "has chosen you"), in ﴿يا مَرْيَمُ﴾ (Yā Maryam, "O Maryam"), and in ﴿ما كُنْتَ لَدَيْهِمْ﴾ (mā kunta ladayhim, "you were not with them"). It was said that there is also inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir, the placing of a word earlier or later than its expected order) in ﴿واسْجُدِي وارْكَعِي﴾ (wasjudī warka'ī, "prostrate and bow"), according to some opinions. There is also metaphor (isti'ara), according to those who held that ﴿القُنُوتَ والسُّجُودَ والرُّكُوعَ﴾ (al-qunut, al-sujud, al-ruku', "devotion, prostration, and bowing") are not a metonymy (kinaya) for the postures of prayer. The allusion to that is among the reports of the unseen. There is generality intended as specificity in ﴿نِساءِ العالَمِينَ﴾ (nisa' al-'alamin, "the women of the worlds"), according to one of the two interpretations. There is simile in ﴿أقْلامِهِمْ﴾ (aqlamahum, "their pens"), if we say he meant the arrows (al-qidah). There is ellipsis in several places.

﴿When the angels said: O Maryam, indeed Allah gives you good tidings of a word from Him﴾: The governing element of ﴿إذا﴾ (idh) is ﴿اذْكُرْ﴾ (udhkur, "remember"), or ﴿يَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾ (yakhtasimun, "they dispute"), or ﴿إذْ﴾ (idh) is a substitute (badal) for ﴿إذْ﴾ in His saying ﴿إذْ يَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾, or for ﴿وإذْ قالَتِ المَلائِكَةُ﴾. These are opinions. The two middle opinions require that the time of the dispute and the time of the angels' speech be the same, and this is far-fetched; it is the opinion of al-Zajjaj. The fourth is distant because of the long separation between the substitute and what it substitutes. The fourth is the choice of al-Zamakhshari, and with it he began. The disagreement concerning ﴿المَلائِكَةُ﴾ (al-malā'ika, "the angels") is whether they are a group of angels, or Jibril alone, as was previously mentioned in their address to Zakariyya and to Maryam. The speech of the angels was mentioned before this good tidings, with mention of her selection, her purification by Allah, and the assurance of worship of Him, as a means of gentleness and kindness, so that this would be a preface to this good tidings of this wondrous, extraordinary matter that had not happened to any woman before her, and will not happen to any woman after her: that she would conceive without a male touching her. The occurrence of that extraordinary matter was also, as a provision from Allah for her, a means of comforting her regarding this extraordinary matter.

Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Umar recited: ﴿وإذْ قالَ المَلائِكَةُ﴾ (wa idh qāla al-malā'ika). The ﴿الكَلِمَةُ﴾ (al-kalima, "the word") from Allah is 'Isa, peace be upon him. He was called a word because of his coming into being through the word "Be" (kun), without a father. This was said by Qatada. It was also said: because he was named al-Masih, and he is a word from Allah, that is, from the speech of Allah. It was also said: because of Allah's promise concerning him in His book, the Torah and the previous scriptures. In the Torah: "Allah came from Sinai, and shone forth from Sa'ir, and appeared from the mountains of Paran." Sa'ir is the place from which the Messiah was sent. It was also said: because Allah guides by His word. It was also said: because it came in accordance with the word of Jibril, which is: ﴿إنَّما أنا رَسُولُ رَبِّكِ لِأهَبَ لَكِ غُلامًا زَكِيًّا﴾ [Maryam 19:19] ("I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy"), so it came in the attribute that was described. It was also said: Allah named him by this, just as He names whomever He wills among the rest of His creation with whatever names He wills. Based on this, it is a proper noun set for him, in which no suitable aspect is considered. It was also said: the word here does not mean 'Isa; rather the "word" is the angels' good tidings to Maryam about 'Isa. It was also said: it is the good tidings of the Prophet to her.

﴿Whose name is al-Masih, 'Isa son of Maryam﴾: The pronoun in ﴿اسْمُهُ﴾ (ismuhu, "his name") refers to ﴿الكَلِمَةُ﴾ (the word), in the sense: We give you good tidings of one brought into being from Him, or of one existing from Allah. He was named al-Masih (the Messiah) because he was anointed with blessing; this was said by al-Hasan, Sa'id, and Shamir. Or: because of the oil with which the prophets are anointed; he came out of his mother's womb anointed with it, and it is a fragrant oil, such that when a person is anointed with it, it is known that he is a prophet. Or: because of purification from sins. Or: because Jibril wiped him with his wing. Or: because he wiped his feet, for there was no hollow in them, and the hollow (al-akhmas) is that part of the sole of the foot that does not touch the ground. 'Isa had a flat foot with no hollow. The poet said:

*"He spent the night struggling with her, a boy like an arrow-shaft, with firm, thick shins, and a flat foot."*

Or: because of the camels wiping him, meaning their passing over him, as the poet said:

*"On the face of Mayy is a trace of beauty."*

Or: because of a wiping away of the filth that afflicts newborns, for his mother did not menstruate and was not defiled by postpartum blood. These are seven opinions. ﴿فَعِيل﴾ (fa'il, a pattern) here has the meaning of the passive participle (maf'ul), and the ﴿الألِفُ واللّامُ﴾ (al-alif wa al-lam, the definite article) in ﴿المَسِيحِ﴾ is for dominance (al-ghalaba), like it is in al-Dabaran and al-'Ayyuq (names of stars). Ibn 'Abbas said: he was named so because he would not wipe with his hand anyone afflicted with a defect except that he was healed. Based on this, ﴿فَعِيل﴾ is a form for intensification (mubalagha), like ﴿عَلِيم﴾ (ʿalīm, "all-knowing"), and it is among the patterns that were changed from the active participle (fa'il) to fa'il for intensification. It was said: it comes from measuring (al-misaha), and he used to travel through the land, so it is as if he were measuring it. It was said: it is a form of ﴿مُفْعِل﴾ (muf'il) from sāḥa yasīḥu, meaning travel (al-siyaha). Mujahid and al-Nakha'i said: al-Masih means the truthful one (al-siddiq). Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: al-Masih means the king, named so because he possessed the reviving of the dead and other signs. Abu 'Ubayd said: its origin in Hebrew is mashiah, which was altered. Based on this, it is a name coined (murtajal), and is not derived from wiping nor from travel.

﴿'Isa son of Maryam﴾: Sons are attributed to fathers, and he was attributed to her. Although the address was to her, this informs that he would be born without a father, so he is not attributed except to her.

The apparent meaning is that his name is al-Masih, so ﴿اسْمُهُ المَسِيحُ﴾ is a subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar). As for ﴿عِيسى﴾ ('Isa), they permitted that it be a predicate after a predicate, a substitute (badal), or an explanatory apposition ('atf bayan). Some grammarians prohibited it from being a predicate after a predicate, and said: it would have required that he say "his names" in terms of meaning, or "her names" according to the wording of "the word." It is permissible that ﴿عِيسى﴾ be a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: he is 'Isa son of Maryam. Ibn 'Atiyya said: what calls to this is that ﴿ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ (ibn Maryam, "son of Maryam") is an attribute (sifa) of ﴿عِيسى﴾, since people have agreed to write it without the alif. As for it being a substitute or explanatory apposition, then ﴿ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ cannot be an attribute of ﴿عِيسى﴾, because the name here is not intended to refer to the person. This is the view of Abu 'Ali, and there is an issue in the beginning of his speech. End of his words. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, why was it said ﴿اسْمُهُ المَسِيحُ عِيسى بْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾, when these are three things, the name among them is 'Isa, while al-Masih and "son" are a title (laqab) and an attribute (sifa)? I say: the name is a sign for the named by which it is known and distinguished from others; it is as if it were said: that by which he is known and distinguished from others is the combination of these three. End of his words. It appears from his words that his name is the combination of these three, so the three are predicates of the statement "his name," and it is of the type: "this is sweet-sour," and "this is: difficult-easy." Thus none of them on this basis is independently a predicate. A parallel to this in the case of two things, or things, being in the ruling of one thing is the saying of the poet:

*"How did you rise? How did you spend the evening? Of what plants the affection in the heart of the generous one?"*

That is: the combination of this is what plants affection. Since it is permissible for the subject to be multiple without a conjunction when the meaning is on the combination, likewise it is permissible for the predicate. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: he is the son of Maryam; and it is not permissible that it be a substitute for what precedes it, nor an attribute, because ﴿ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ is not a name. Do you not see that you do not say: "the name of this man is son of 'Amr," unless it is a proper name for him? End of his words.

Some said: whoever says that al-Masih is an attribute of 'Isa, then there is in the speech an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), its estimate being: "his name is 'Isa al-Masih," because the attribute follows what it describes. End of his words. It is not correct that al-Masih in this construction be an attribute, because what is predicated by this wording and al-Masih is an attribute of the referent (al-madlul), not an attribute of the signifier (al-dal), since the word 'Isa is not al-Masih. Whoever says: they are two names, al-Masih came before 'Isa because of its fame. Ibn al-Anbari said: He began with his title because al-Masih is more famous than 'Isa, since it rarely applies to a namesake who might be confused with him, whereas 'Isa may apply to a large number of people, so he put it first because of its fame. Do you not see that the titles of the caliphs are more famous than their names? This indicates that according to Ibn al-Anbari al-Masih is a title, not a name. Al-Zajjaj said: 'Isa is an arabized form of Ayshu', and if you make it Arabic it would not take nunation in definite or indefinite form, because it has the feminine alif; and it would be derived from 'asa ya'usu, meaning to govern and to stand over. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is derived from al-'Is, like a drawing in water.

﴿Honored in this world and the Hereafter﴾: Ibn Qutayba said: the wajih is one who has rank (dhu al-jah); it is said: the man was made honored (wujiha al-rajul yujahu wijaha). Ibn Duraid said: the wajih is the beloved and accepted. Al-Akhfash said: the noble one of high rank and standing. It was said: the one who is esteemed by whoever asks him, because he does not refuse him, out of the nobility of his face. Its meaning regarding 'Isa is that his honor in this world is by his prophethood, and in the Hereafter by the loftiness of his rank. It was said: in this world by obedience, and in the Hereafter by intercession. It was said: in this world by bringing the dead to life and healing the blind and the leper, and in the Hereafter by intercession. It was said: in this world he is noble, whose face is not refused, and in the Hereafter he is among the elite of the messengers. Al-Zamakhshari said: honor in this world is prophethood and precedence over people, and in the Hereafter it is intercession and high rank in Paradise. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the honor of 'Isa in this world is his prophethood, his mention, and his elevation, and in the Hereafter his station, his favor, and his intercession.

﴿And of those brought near﴾: Its meaning is: from Allah, Exalted is He. Al-Zamakhshari said: his being among those brought near is that He raised him to the heaven and the angels accompanied him. Qatada said: and among those brought near to Allah on the Day of Resurrection. It was said: among the people by acceptance and response; this was said by al-Mawardi. It was said: its meaning is: one who is greatly brought near, because ﴿فَعُلَ﴾ (fa'ula) is a form of intensification, so one says: he brought him near (qarraba), meaning he greatly brought him near. End of his words. ﴿فَعُلَ﴾ is not here a form of intensification, because the doubling here is for transitivity; it occurs for intensification only in examples like: I wounded Zayd (jarraḥtu Zaydan), and he killed the people (mawwata al-nas). End of quote.

﴿And of those brought near﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿وجِيهًا﴾ (wajihan), and its estimate is: "and brought near, from among those brought near." He informed that there are those brought near, and that 'Isa is among them. A parallel to this conjunction is His saying: ﴿وإنَّكم لَتَمُرُّونَ عَلَيْهِمْ مُصْبِحِينَ وبِاللَّيْلِ﴾ [al-Saffat 37:137–138] ("You pass by them in the morning, and by night"). Here ﴿وبِاللَّيْلِ﴾ (wa bil-layl, "and by night") is a prepositional phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is conjoined to ﴿مُصْبِحِينَ﴾ (musbiḥin, "in the morning"). This circumstantial clause came in this form because it is a closing word (fasila, the rhyme ending of a verse), so if it had come as ﴿ومُقَرَّبًا﴾ (wa muqarraban), it would not have been a closing word. Also, He informed that 'Isa is brought near from among those brought near, and nearness is a sublime, great attribute. Do you not see His saying: ﴿ولا المَلائِكَةُ المُقَرَّبُونَ﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:172] ("nor the angels who are brought near")? And His saying: ﴿فَأمّا إنْ كانَ مِنَ المُقَرَّبِينَ فَرَوْحٌ﴾ [al-Waqi'a 56:88] ("But if he is of those brought near, then there is rest and provision")? It is a nearness from Allah, Exalted is He, in standing, nobility, and elevation of rank.

Abu Hayyan's commentary on Surah Al 'Imran 3:44–46 (part 2 of 2)

﴿And he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity.﴾ He conjoined "and he will speak" (wa-yukallimu), which is also a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a state or condition of the subject) like "distinguished" (wajīhan). Its parallel is ﴿at the birds above them, spreading and folding [their wings]﴾ [al-Mulk: 19], meaning "spreading and folding." Likewise, "and he will speak" means "and speaking." The first state is expressed by a noun, because the noun signifies permanence. The second state is a prepositional phrase with its object, because it is restricted by a noun. The third state is a clause, because it comes in the third rank. Do you not see that the circumstantial state is, in meaning, a description? Just as the best and most common usage in the Arabic language is that when several different descriptions are combined, one begins with the noun, then the prepositional phrase, then the clause, as in His saying: ﴿And a believing man from the family of Pharaoh, who concealed his faith, said﴾ [Ghafir: 28], the same applies to the circumstantial states: one begins with the noun, then the prepositional phrase, then the clause. This clause is verbal, because the verb indicates renewal, just as the noun indicates permanence. "In the cradle" is linked to an implied element, since it is in the position of a circumstantial state. The estimate is: "existing in the cradle and in maturity," coordinated with this state, as if it were said: "as a child and as a mature man." So the explicit circumstantial state is coordinated with the prepositional phrase that occupies the position of a state. Its reverse parallel is ﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning and at night﴾ [al-Saffat: 137]. Whoever claims that "and in maturity" is coordinated with "distinguished" has gone far astray.

Al-mahd (the cradle) is the place where the infant rests while nursing. Its origin is a verbal noun that became a name. It is said: "I prepared (mahhadtu) for myself," with the letter ha' lightened or doubled, meaning "I made ready." It is also said: "amhada al-shay'," meaning "it rose." The linguistic explanation of al-kahl (maturity) has already been given. Mujahid said: al-kahl is "the forbearing one." This is generally an explanation by a necessary concomitant, because the mature man's reason, understanding and experience become strong, so he is not like the youth. The Arabs take pride in maturity. One poet said:

"Nor does it harm one whose remnants are like us:
youth that aspired to lofty heights, and maturity."

For this reason this age was singled out in the verse rather than the rest of life, because it is the middle stage in the firmness of reason and soundness of judgment. In His saying "and in maturity" there is good news that he will live until the age of maturity, as al-Rabi' said. It is said that Maryam bore him after eight months, and whoever is born at that time does not live, so this was a glad tiding to her that he would live to this age. It was also said that the custom was that whoever spoke in the cradle would die. In His saying ﴿in the cradle and in maturity﴾ there is an indication of the changing of conditions upon him and a refutation of the Christians' claim of his divinity. Ibn Kaysan said: He mentioned this before He created him, informing that he would reach maturity. When Maryam was informed of it, it was known that it was from the knowledge of the unseen.

It is disputed concerning his speech in the cradle: was it for a single moment, after which he did not speak until he reached the stage of speech? Or did he speak continually in the cradle until he reached the time of speech? There are two opinions. The first is from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Tha'alibi reported several things he said to his mother while he was still nursing. The apparent meaning is that when he spoke to the people in the cradle, he was a prophet, because of His saying ﴿Indeed I am the servant of Allah. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 30], and because this miracle appeared from him with a challenge therein. It was also said that he was not a prophet at that time, and that the speech was a foundation for his prophethood. Then His saying ﴿and made me a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 30] is an announcement of what would become of him, based on His saying ﴿and He has enjoined upon me prayer and zakat﴾ [Maryam: 31]. It does not address the time of his speech when he was mature. It was said that his speech before being raised to the heaven was addressing them with revelation and messengership.

It was also said: he will descend from the heaven as a mature man of thirty-three years, and will say to them: "Indeed I am the servant of Allah," as he said in the cradle. This is the benefit of His saying "and in maturity": it informs that he will descend when he kills the Dajjal (the Antichrist), as Ibn Zayd said.

Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is: "and he will speak to the people in these two conditions with the speech of the prophets, without any difference between the state of childhood and the state of maturity, in which reason is firm and in which prophets are commissioned."

It is said: seven spoke in the cradle: 'Isa, Yahya, the witness of Yusuf, the companion of Jurayj, the child of the hairdresser of Pharaoh's wife, the companion of the tyrant, and the companion of the trench (al-Ukhdud). The stories of these are transmitted. What has come limiting those who spoke as infants to three does not contradict this, because that was a report made before the others were made known, so it reported according to what was first made known to it, and then the others were made known.

﴿And of the righteous﴾, i.e., "and righteous, among the company of the righteous." The meaning of the righteousness with which the prophets are described has already been explained. The accusative of "distinguished" and what is coordinated with it is a circumstantial state of "a word from Him." This is permissible even though it is indefinite, because it is described by His saying "from Him," and by His saying "from Him," and by His saying "whose name is the Messiah."

﴿She said, "My Lord, how can I have a son when no man has touched me?"﴾ When the angels informed her that God had given her good news of al-Masih, she called out to her Lord, who is God, asking in wonder at the birth of a child without a father. This is one of the things that call for wonder. This case is more remarkable than the case of Zakariyya, because in Zakariyya's case the child came from a man and a woman, whereas here it came from a woman without any human intermediary. For this reason she said, ﴿and no man has touched me﴾.

It has also been said that she was asking about the manner (kayfiyya) of the birth, just as Zakariyya asked about the manner. The sense would be: "Will this happen according to the customary course of intercourse first, or by a command of God's power?" Al-Anbari said: When Jibril addressed her, she thought him to be a human being who intended harm to her, and for this reason she said, ﴿I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing﴾ [Maryam: 18]. When he gave her the good news, she did not become certain of the truth of his words, because she did not know that he was an angel, so she said, ﴿My Lord, how can I have a son?﴾

As for those who hold that her saying "My Lord" and Zakariyya's saying "My Lord" were only an address to Jibril when he gave them good news, its meaning being "O my master," this view is far-fetched. Al-Zamakhshari said: This is one of the strange (bida') interpretations. The word Rabb may be taken as the incomplete (nāqisa) or the complete (tamma) form, as was mentioned earlier in the story of Zakariyya.

﴿And no man has touched me﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumla ḥāliyya). Here al-masis is a metaphor (kināya) for intercourse. This is a general negation, that no one has touched her in any way, whether by marriage or otherwise. The word bashar (human being) is applied to the singular and the plural, and here the intended sense is the general negation. It is called bashar because of the visibility of its bashra, which is its skin. One says: bashartu al-adim, meaning I peeled the surface of the hide. Absharat al-ard means the earth brought forth its plants. Tabashir al-subh are the first appearances of its light.

﴿He said, "Thus God creates what He wills"﴾. The discussion of its like has preceded in the story of Zakariyya, except that in that story the words are ﴿He does what He wills﴾ [Al 'Imran: 40]. The reason is that Zakariyya's case falls within the ordinary possibility that is commonly known, even if rare, whereas in the story of Maryam the word is "creates," because the like of this is not commonly known, namely the existence of a child without a parent. This is origination and invention without an ordinary cause, and for this reason the word "creates," which indicates this meaning, is used.

Some Arabs whose speech is cited as evidence composed a riddle, saying:

Is there not many a child with no father, and one who has a child whom no two parents bore?

He means 'Isa and Adam.

﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾. The discussion of this sentence has been given in al-Baqara, in respect of lexicography, interpretation, recitation, and grammatical analysis (i'rab), so that suffices and need not be repeated.

﴿And He will teach him the Book and the Wisdom, and the Torah and the Gospel﴾. Here al-Kitab is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning that He will teach him writing with the hand. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jurayj, and a group. It has also been said that al-Kitab is a certain unknown book which God taught 'Isa along with the Torah and the Gospel. It has also been said that it means the revealed books of God. The alif and lam here are for the genus. It has further been said that it means the Torah and the Gospel. They said: the waw in "and the Torah" is superfluous (muqhama), and al-Kitab is an expression for the written. His teaching it to him is said to be by inspiration (ilham), or by revelation (wahy), or by granting success and guidance to learning. Al-Hikma (wisdom) has been explained earlier, and here it has been explained as the practices (sunan) of the prophets, as what He legislated of religion, as prophethood, as correctness in speech and action, as reason, as kinds of knowledge. Together with what has preceded, these make seven sayings.

It is related that 'Isa used to recite the Torah by heart. It is said that no one memorized it by heart except Musa, Yusha', 'Uzayr, and 'Isa. The Gospel was mentioned to Maryam though it had not yet been revealed, and it was not yet a book mentioned among the prophets and scholars, and it was to be revealed later.

Nafi', 'Asim, Ya'qub, and Sahl read ﴿wa-yu'allimuhu﴾ with the ya' (third person). The rest read it with the nun (first person plural). In both readings it is coordinated with the statement that was spoken, because His saying "thus He said" has the pronoun in "He said" referring to the Lord, and the sentence after it is the statement that was spoken. Whether the word Allah is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate precedes it, which requires the subject and predicate to be "He creates" in accordance with the i'rab mentioned in ﴿Thus God does what He wills﴾ [Al 'Imran: 40], so that this is part of what was said to Maryam, or whether it is in the manner of rejoicing and giving good news of this child whom God brings into existence from her, it may also be coordinated with "He creates," whether it is a report from God or an explanation of what precedes it, if you parse the word "Allah" as the subject and what precedes it as the predicate. All of this is clear in the reading with the ya'.

As for the reading with the nun, it is an instance of iltifat (shift of pronoun), moving from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun for the sake of the majesty this carries. Abu 'Ali said: al-Zamakhshari and others permitted that "wa-yu'allimuhu" is coordinated with "yubashshiruki" (He gives you good news). This is very far-fetched because of the long separation between the coordinated and that which it is coordinated with. Ibn 'Atiyya and others permitted that it is coordinated with "wa-yukallimu" (and he speaks). Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it is coordinated with "wajihan" (honored), so on these two views it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (hal). On what Abu 'Ali and al-Zamakhshari permitted, it is in the nominative position, because it is coordinated with the predicate of inna (indeed). These two views too are far-fetched, because of the long separation between the coordinated and that which it is coordinated with, and such a thing does not occur in the speech of the Arabs.

Some said: "wa-nu'allimuhu" with the nun is governed by His saying ﴿We reveal it to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 44]. If by governing they mean coordination, nothing is further from this construction. If by governing they mean that it is an instance of iltifat, that is correct. Al-Zamakhshari said: Or it is an independent sentence (kalam mubtada'), meaning His saying "wa-nu'allimuhu." He permitted it to be coordinated with "yubashshiruki," and with "wajihan," and with "yakhluqu," then he said "or it is an independent sentence," meaning that it is not coordinated with any of those mentioned. If by this he means that it is a resumptive report about God, or from God according to the difference of the two readings, then because of the presence of the waw it must be coordinated with something before it, so it cannot be an independent beginning of speech unless one claims that the waw in "wa-yu'allimuhu" is superfluous, in which case it could be an independent beginning. If he means that it is not coordinated with what was mentioned, then he should have explained what it is coordinated with, and that which it is coordinated with should be an independent beginning of speech, so that the coordinated is likewise.

Al-Tabari said: The reading with the ya' is coordinated with His saying ﴿He creates what He wills﴾, and the reading with the nun is coordinated with His saying ﴿We reveal it to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 44]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This statement, which he made regarding both readings, corrupts the meaning. Ibn 'Atiyya did not explain the manner in which it corrupts the meaning. As for the reading with the nun, the corruption of its coordination with "nuhiihi" is evident both in terms of wording and in terms of meaning. In terms of wording, such a construction does not occur in the speech of the Arabs, because of the extreme length of separation, the complication of the structure, and the discordance of the speech. In terms of meaning, the item coordinated with the waw is a partner of that which it is coordinated with, so the meaning of His saying "that" would be: the reports of the unseen, namely your report, O Muhammad, of the story of the wife of 'Imran, her giving birth to Maryam, the guardianship of Zakariyya, his story concerning the birth of Yahya to him, and the angels' good news to Maryam of her being chosen and purified. All of this is among the reports of the unseen. "We teach him," that is, We teach 'Isa the Book. This statement's meaning does not fit with the meaning of what precedes it. As for the reading with the ya', and the coordination of "wa-yu'allimuhu" with "yakhluqu," it does not corrupt the meaning. Rather it is preferable, and the most appropriate way to understand "wa-yu'allimuhu" as coordinated is because of the closeness of its wording and the soundness of its meaning. We have already mentioned its permissibility earlier. God has informed Maryam that He, may He be exalted, creates strange things in which no custom has been established, like what He created for you, a child without a father. He, may He be exalted, also teaches this child whom He creates for you what He had not taught before, of the Book, the Wisdom, the Torah and the Gospel. In this report there is therefore the greatest good news for her concerning this child and the manifestation of his blessing, and that he does not resemble the children of people among the Children of Israel, but differs from them in the very origin of his creation and in the knowledge God teaches him. This appears to me to be the best way to understand the coordination of "wa-yu'allimuhu."
