Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 49 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And a messenger to the Children of Israel, [saying], "Indeed, I have come to you with a sign from your Lord"﴾ Scholars differed regarding: rasulan (a messenger) here. It was said: it is an attributive noun with the meaning of "one who is sent" according to its apparent understanding. It was also said: it is a verbal noun (masdar) meaning "risalah" (mission), since it is established that rasul can mean risalah. Among those who permitted this here were al-Hufi and Abu al-Baqa', and they said: it is conjoined to al-kitab, meaning: "and He will teach him the risalah to the Children of Israel," so risalah will be included among what Allah teaches Jesus. Abu al-Baqa' also permitted, in this case, that it be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal). As for the first view, they stated several possibilities for its i'rab (grammatical analysis).

The first: that it is in the accusative by an implied verb, its estimated form being: "and He will make him a messenger to the Children of Israel." They said: this is like his saying:
"Would that your husband had become one girded with a sword and a spear"
meaning: "and armed with a spear." Since it was not possible to make it coordinated with the accusatives before it in terms of the governing verb, which is "yu'allimuhu" (He will teach him), a governing verb was implied for it by which the meaning is correct. This was said by Ibn 'Atiyyah and others. The second: that it is conjoined to "yu'allimuhu" (He will teach him), so that it becomes a circumstantial qualifier, the estimate being: "and teaching the Book," so all of this is a coordination in meaning with his saying "wajihan" (distinguished). This was said by al-Zamakhshari, and Ibn 'Atiyyah followed him and began with it, and it is based on the i'rab of "wa-yu'allimuhu." We have already shown the weakness of the i'rab of those who say that "wa-yu'allimuhu" is conjoined to "wajihan," because of the excessive separation between the two conjoined elements. The third: that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun concealed in "wa-yukallimu" (and he will speak), so it is conjoined to his saying "wa-kahlan" (and in maturity), meaning: "and he will speak to people in infancy and in maturity, and as a messenger to the Children of Israel." This was said by Ibn 'Atiyyah, and it is very far-fetched because of the long separation between the two conjoined elements. The fourth: that the waw is superfluous, and it is a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in "wa-yu'allimuhu," said by al-Akhfash, and it is weak because of the addition of the waw, which does not occur in their speech: "came Zayd and laughing," meaning: "laughing." The fifth: that it is in the accusative by an implied verb derived from the word "rasulan," and that verb is governed by a saying from Jesus. The estimate is: "and you say: I have been sent as a messenger to the Children of Israel." He needed all this estimation because of his saying: ﴿that I have indeed come to you﴾ and his saying: ﴿confirming what is before me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 50], since it is not valid, on the apparent reading, to take it as governed by what precedes it of accusatives, due to the difference of pronouns: what precedes it is a third-person pronoun, while these are a first-person pronoun, so this implication was necessary to make the meaning sound. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, who said: it is one of the "difficult passages," meaning one of the places in which there is a problem. This view is weak, for it involves implying the saying and its governed element, which is "ursiltu" (I have been sent), and dispensing with both by a noun in the accusative as an emphatic circumstantial qualifier, since "ursiltu" implies that he is a messenger, so on this estimate it is an emphatic circumstantial qualifier. These are five possibilities for the i'rab of "wa-rasulan," the first of which is the best, since it involves only the implication of a verb indicated by the meaning, namely "wa-yaj'aluhu rasulan" (and He will make him a messenger), and "anni qad ji'tukum" (that I have indeed come to you) being governed by "rasulan," meaning: speaking that I have indeed come to you, according to the reading of the majority, and governed by an implied saying according to the reading of those who read the hamza with kasra, which is an anomalous reading, meaning: saying that I have indeed come to you. It may also be that it is reported by the verb "rasulan," because it carries the sense of saying, and this is according to the school of the Kufans. Al-Yazidi read "wa-rasulin" with a genitive, and al-Zamakhshari explained it as conjoined to "bi-kalimatin minhu" (with a word from Him), and it is an anomalous reading in terms of analogy, because of the long distance between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined.

Jesus was sent to the Children of Israel confirming the ruling of the Torah, calling them to act upon it, and making lawful some things that had been forbidden in it, such as fat (al-thurub), the flesh of camels, and some things of fish and birds. Jesus's mother had fled with him from her people to Egypt when they isolated their children, forbade them from associating with him, and confined them in a house. Jesus came seeking them, and they said: "They are not here." He said: "What is in this house?" They said: "Swine." He said: "Thus they shall be." They opened it for him and they were swine. This spread among the Children of Israel, and they intended to harm him, so his mother fled with him to the land of Egypt. When he reached twelve years of age, Allah revealed to her: "Set out for al-Sham (Syria)," and she did so. When he reached thirty years of age, revelation came to him at the age of thirty, so his prophethood lasted three years, and then Allah raised him to Himself. The first of the prophets of the Children of Israel was Yusuf (Joseph), and it was said: Musa (Moses), and the last of them was Jesus.

The apparent view is that his saying: ﴿that I have indeed come to you with a sign﴾ up to his saying "straight" (mustaqim) is connected to his saying ﴿and a messenger to the Children of Israel﴾ and governed by it, so that it falls under the preceding saying. The address to Mary is in his saying: "Thus said Allah," so Mary will have been given good news of things Allah will do for her son Jesus, from teaching him what has been mentioned, and from making him a messenger speaking of what will come from him when he is sent, from his coming with signs and the manifestation of extraordinary events at his hands, and other things mentioned up to his saying "straight." And it will be after his saying "straight." It was said that his saying "fa-lamma ahassa" (then when he perceived) is an implied element indicated by it, and the meaning requires its estimate: "So Jesus came to the Children of Israel, and as a messenger, and he said to them what has been mentioned before, and brought the extraordinary things he had spoken of, but they disbelieved in him and conspired to kill him and harm him," ﴿then when Jesus perceived disbelief from them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52].

It was also said: it is possible that the speech was complete at his saying ﴿and a messenger to the Children of Israel﴾, and that ﴿that I have indeed come to you﴾ is not connected to what precedes it, nor included under the saying, and the address to Mary is not in it. The implied element here would be not after his saying "straight," and the estimate would be: "So Jesus came, as Allah had given good news, a messenger to the Children of Israel, that I have indeed come to you with a sign from your Lord."

The majority read "bi-annahu" in the singular, and likewise in ﴿and I have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran: 50]. In the codex of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), it is "bi-ayatin" in the plural in both places. It is permissible that "min rabbikum" (from your Lord) be in the position of a qualifier, because it is connected to an implied element, and it is permissible that it be connected to "wa-ji'tukum" (and I have come to you), meaning: I have come to you from your Lord with a sign.

﴿That I create for you from clay the form of a bird, then I breathe into it and it becomes a bird by Allah's permission﴾ The majority read "annI akhluqu" with a fatha on the hamza, so that it is a substitute for "ayah" (sign), in which case it is in the genitive position; or a substitute for his saying "annI qad ji'tukum," in which case it is in the accusative or genitive position according to the disagreement; or as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning: "it is," i.e., the sign is "that I create," in which case it is in the nominative position. Nafi' read it with a kasra, as a resumption, or by implying a saying, or as an explanation of the sign, just as he explained the likeness in his saying: ﴿the likeness of Adam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59] by his saying: ﴿He created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. The meaning of "akhluqu" is: I estimate and prepare. Creation (khalq) may mean bringing a thing into existence and making it appear from pure non-existence into existence; this is only for Allah the Exalted. It may also mean estimating and shaping, and for this reason they call the maker of leather and the like "khaliq," because he estimates, and its origin is in physical bodies, and they have transferred it to meanings. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿and you fabricate a lie﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 17]. Among what has the word khuluq in the sense of estimating is His saying: ﴿So blessed be Allah, the best of creators﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 14], meaning: the best of those who estimate. The poet said:
"Indeed you alter what you create, and some people create but do not alter."

The "lam" in "lakum" (for you) signifies causation. "From clay" is a restriction indicating that it is not produced from pure non-existence, but rather mentions the material from which he forms an image. The majority read "ka-hay'at" on the pattern of "jay'at." Al-Zuhri read "ka-hiyyat" with a kasra on the ha' and a doubled, fatha-vowelled ya', followed by the feminine ta'. The kaf in "ka-hay'at" is a noun according to the view of Abu al-Hasan, and so it is the object of "akhluqu." On the view of the majority, it is an attribute of an implied object, its estimate being: "a form like the form," and "hay'at" is a verbal noun in the sense of the object, meaning: a prepared model like. The majority read "al-tayr" (the bird); Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "ka-hay'ati al-ta'ir," and the intended meaning is the genus. "Fa-anfukhu fihi" (then I breathe into it): the pronoun in "fihi" refers to the kaf, or to its described noun, according to the two views mentioned. Some readers read "fa-anfukhuha," referring the pronoun to the implied form, since the estimate is: "a form like the form of a bird," or to the kaf according to its meaning, since it is in the sense of "similar to the form of a bird," so the feminine here is as it is in al-Ma'idah in his saying: ﴿then you breathe into it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110], and in this reading the preposition has been dropped, as in the poet's words:
"No pocket was torn for you, nor did a mourning woman lament you, nor did steeds weep for you at the spoils of war."
He means: "nor stood over you." This is an anomalous reading transmitted by al-Farra'. The poet al-Nabighah said:
"Like the Hibraqi who withdrew, blowing upon the coals"
"Like the Barqi who withdrew, blowing upon the coals."
So "nafakha" transitively governs an accusative object, and it may be that the preposition is dropped, or that it is by transference, meaning: he kindles the coal by blowing, so here it is a defective verb (naqisah) in its own category, or in the sense of "becomes."

Nafi' and Ya'qub read "ta'iran" here and in al-Ma'idah, while the rest read "tayran." Its accusative is as the predicate of "yakunu" (becomes). Whoever makes "yakunu" a complete verb here, with "ta'iran" as a circumstantial qualifier, has gone too far. "By Allah's permission": it was said that it is connected to "yakunu," and it was said to "ta'iran." The meaning of "by Allah's permission" is by His enabling and His knowledge that I do this. Jesus's undertaking the shaping with his hand, and the breathing into that form, is a clarification of his being endowed with the miracle, and an explanation that it comes from him. As for the creation of life in that clay form, it is from Allah alone. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that his creating this was not at their suggestion; rather these extraordinary acts came as an explanation of his saying: ﴿that I have indeed come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾. It was also said that it was at their suggestion: they asked him to create for them a bat as a way of obstinacy, in keeping with their customs with their prophets. They singled out the bat because it is wondrous in creation, and it is the most complete of birds in its make-up: it has teats, teeth, ears, and an udder from which milk flows; it cannot see in the light of day nor in the darkness of night; it sees only in two hours: an hour after sunset and an hour after the break of dawn, before it becomes very bright; it laughs as humans laugh; it flies without feathers; and its female menstruates and gives birth.

It is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that he said to them: "What do you want?" They said: "The bat." They asked him for the strangest of birds in creation, for it flies without feathers. It is said: "He made nothing but the bat," and it is said: "He did this first while he was with his teacher in the Book." The transmission from the exegetes is consistent that the bird Jesus created would fly as long as people were watching it, and when it disappeared from their eyes it would fall dead, so that the act of the created would be distinguished from the act of the Creator. The Children of Israel, despite witnessing that bird fly, would say of Jesus: "This is a sorcerer."

﴿And I heal the blind and the leper﴾ Their explanations were mentioned earlier in the Mufradat. Mujahid said: the akmah (born blind) is the one with cataracts (al-a'sha). 'Ikrimah said: he is the one with weak eyes (al-a'mash). Al-Zamakhshari said: he is the one born blind. It was said: he is the one whose eye is smoothed over. No one in this community was akmah except Qatadah ibn Di'amah al-Sadusi, the author of the tafsir. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi said: he is the blind man in the absolute sense. Al-Naqqash related that the akmah is the mute who neither understands nor is understood, the dead-hearted. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Qatadah: he is the one born blind with his eyes closed.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 49 (part 2 of 2):

It is said: Isa used to cure every illness by his supplication and by passing his hand over the afflicted. But the proof (hujjah) against the Children of Israel regarding the meaning of prophethood would only be established by curing the diseases that physicians are unable to cure, so that his doing of that would be a breach of customary norms (kharq lil-'adat). Curing blear-eyedness (al-'asha) and weak-sightedness (al-'amash) is not a breach of norms. As for blindness ('ama), the most eloquent (al-abligh) example is curing the blindness of one whose eye was wiped. It is narrated that there would gather around him perhaps fifty thousand of the sick; whoever was able came to him, and whoever was not able, Isa came to him. His healing was by supplication alone. He specifically mentioned the blind from birth (al-kamah) and the leper (al-baras), because these are two stubborn afflictions from which none can heal except Allah the Exalted. In the time of Isa, medicine was dominant, so Allah showed them the miracle within the kind of their knowledge, just as He showed the people of Musa, when magic was dominant among them, the miracle of the staff and the white hand; and just as He showed the Arabs, when eloquence was dominant among them, the miracle of the Qur'an. It is narrated that Galen (Jalinus) was in the time of Isa, and that he travelled to him from Rome to Syria to meet him, but died on the way.

﴿And I heal the blind and the leper, and I bring the dead to life, by the permission of Allah﴾. The leading scholars of tafsir related that he brought four to life: 'Azar, who had been his friend, three days after he died; he rose from his grave dripping its fat (wadak), and lived until he had a child. The son of the widow, who was on his bier; he descended from the shoulders of the men, carried his bier, and lived until he had a child. The daughter of the tenth man: she enjoyed her child after she had been brought back to life. And they asked him to bring Sam ibn Nuh back to life, so that he might inform them about the state of the Ark. He came out of his grave and said: "Has the Hour already come?" Half of his head had turned grey, though he had been a youth of five hundred years. He said: "The terror of the Day of Resurrection has greyed me." It is also narrated that in bringing the dead to life he would strike the dead person, or the grave, or the skull, with his staff, and the person would rise, speak to him, and live. It is said that they would die quickly again.

It is narrated from al-Zuhri that he said: "It has reached me that Isa went out, he and those of his disciples (hawariyyun) who were with him, until they reached al-Andalus," and he mentioned a lengthy story whose content is that he brought a dead man to life by it, and when they asked him, he was from the people of 'Ad. Many accounts have come concerning the bringing to life of a great multitude at the hands of Isa, and they mentioned things he used to supplicate with when he brought someone to life; Allah knows best their authenticity.

﴿And I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses﴾. Al-Suddi, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ata', and Ibn Ishaq said: From his earliest childhood, when he was in the kuttab (Qur'anic school), Isa would inform the boys of what their fathers were doing, and of what food was eaten and what was stored, until he was made a prophet; and he would say to whoever asked him: "You ate such-and-such yesterday, and you stored such-and-such." It is also said that this was after prophethood, when he brought the dead to life for them, and they asked him for another sign, saying: "Inform us of what we eat and what we store for tomorrow," and he informed them. Qatadah said: This was at the revelation of the Table (al-ma'idah); he charged them to eat from it and not to hide or store anything, but they disobeyed, so Isa would inform them of what they had eaten and what they had stored in their houses, and they were punished for that. He brought these four breaches of norms preceded by the present tense (al-mudari'), which indicates renewal and a continuing state, and he began with creation, since it is greatest in miraculous power; then he followed with curing the blind and the leper; third he mentioned bringing the dead to life, which is a breach of norms in which others shared with him by the permission of Allah the Exalted; and he repeated "by the permission of Allah" to repel anyone who might imagine divinity in him. In the phrase "by the permission of Allah" it came directly after his words "that I create", and he joined to it "and I heal the blind and the leper" without mentioning "by the permission of Allah", being satisfied with it in the greatest breach of norms. He followed his words "and I bring the dead to life" with "by the permission of Allah", and joined to it "and I inform you", without mentioning it there, because bringing the dead to life is greater than informing of unseen matters, so he was satisfied with it in the greatest breach of norms as well. Thus each of the two greatest breaches was qualified by "by the permission of Allah", and there was no need for that in what was joined to them, being satisfied with the first, since all these breaches occur only by the permission of Allah.

And: "ma" in "ma ta'kulun wa ma tadda'irun" is a relative noun (mawsulah ismiyyah), which is the apparent reading. It is also said to be a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyyah).

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "taddakhirun" with a shaddah on the dal, and its origin is "idhtakhara", from al-dhukhr (storing). The ta' was changed to dal, so it became "idhdakhara"; then the dhal was assimilated into the dal, and it became "iddakhara", as it is said "iddakarahu". Mujahid, al-Zuhri, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, and Abu al-Sammal read "tadhkhirun", with an unvowelled dhal and an open kha'. Abu Shu'ayb al-Susi, in a transmission from him, read "wa ma tadhdakhirun", with an unvowelled dhal and an open dal, without assimilation, and this unassimilated form is permissible. The majority's reading with assimilation is better. It is also permissible to make the dal a dhal and assimilate, so one says "idhdakhara" with a marked dhal and shaddah.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers﴾. The apparent meaning of this sentence is that it is from the speech of Isa, since it is enclosed by his speech before and after it, relayed by Allah about him. It is also said that it is from the speech of Allah the Exalted, a resumptive statement (isti'naf) whose form is that of a report but whose meaning is rebuke and reproach, and by "that" is indicated what preceded: the making of clay into a bird, and the curing, the bringing to life, and the informing. It has been mentioned that in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads "la-ayat" in the plural. Whoever uses the singular intends the genus, which is suitable for few and many, and the context, verbal, semantic, and circumstantial, determines the intended meaning. Whoever uses the plural follows the original form, since they are "ayat", and each one is in itself a sign, whether they believed or disbelieved. It is possible that there is an omitted qualifier, so that the conditional linkage with this condition makes sense, meaning: "a beneficial, guiding sign for you, if you believe"; and it would be an address to those who have not yet believed. If it is an address to those who have believed, it is by way of reinforcement, steadying the soul and stirring it. Just as you say to your son: "Obey me if you are my son," while it is known he is your son, but you want to stir him by mentioning what is certain. He mentioned what was made conditional on what precedes it, in the manner that it might come about.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on surah 3, verses 50–51:

﴿And confirming what is before me of the Torah﴾. "Wa-musaddiqan" is coordinated with his words "bi-ayatin" (with a sign), since the *ba'* there is for circumstance (*al-hal*, the circumstantial clause), and it cannot be for transitivity (*al-ta'diyah*), because that would corrupt the meaning. So the meaning is: "I have come to you accompanied by a sign from your Lord, and confirming what is before me." They rejected that "wa-musaddiqan" is coordinated with "rasulan ila Bani Isra'il" (a messenger to the Children of Israel), or with "wajihan" (honoured), because it would require the pronoun in "lima bayna yadayya" (what is before me) to be third person, so it would have to say "lima bayna yadayhi." We have already mentioned that "rasulan" may be in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "and I have been sent as a messenger." On this reading, "wa-musaddiqan" is coordinated with "wa-rasulan." The meaning of his confirming the Torah is believing in it, even though his law differs from it in some matters. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "He used to observe the Sabbath, and he faced Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) in prayer."

﴿And to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾. Ibn Jurayj said: "He made lawful for them the flesh of camels and the fats." Al-Rabi' said: "And some kinds of fish, and birds that have no crop (*dah'dah*), and that was forbidden in the Torah." Some exegetes said: "'Hurrima 'alaykum' (what was forbidden to you) refers to what the rabbis (*al-ahbar*) forbade after Musa and then legislated, so 'Isa returned the rulings of the Torah to their true realities, which had come down from Allah." End of his words. They differed about his making the Sabbath lawful for them. 'Ikrimah read "ma harrama 'alaykum" in the active voice, with the subject being a pronoun referring to "ma" in "lima bayna yadayya," or referring to Allah, the sender of the Torah, or to Musa, the bearer of the Torah. The first is more apparent, because it has been mentioned. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read "harama" on the pattern of "karuma." The intended meaning of "ba'd" (some) is its common signification. Abu 'Ubaydah claimed that "ba'd" here means "every error," because it would follow that He would make lawful for them killing, adultery and theft, since these are forbidden to them. His evidence that *ba'd* can mean *kull* (all) is the verse of Labid:

*Tarrak amkinatin idha lam arduha, aw tartabit ba'd al-nufus hamamuha*
"I abandon places when I do not like them, or when death binds some souls."

This is not correct, because *ba'd* keeps its meaning here, since he means *nafsahu* (himself), so it is a valid partitive. The same applies to the argument of one who cited the verse:

*Inna al-umura idha al-ahdathu dabbaraha, dunna al-shuyukhi tara fi ba'diha khalalan*
"Indeed, when the young men manage affairs without the elders, you see a flaw in some of them."

This is for the validity of the partitive, since not everything managed by the young contains a flaw. Some said: *ba'd* does not stand in place of *kull* unless a clear indication (*qarinah*) shows it, such as his saying:

*Aba Mundhirin afnayta fa-istabqi ba'dana, hananayka ba'd al-sharri ahwan min ba'd*
"O Abu Mundhir, you have destroyed, so spare some of us. Mercy upon you! Some evil is easier than some other evil."

He means: "Some evil is easier than all of it." End of his words. There is an objection to this.

The *lam* in "wa-li-uhilla lakum" is the *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*), and there is no preceding element that permits coordinating it with what came before in terms of wording. So it was said that it is coordinated with the meaning: the meaning of "musaddiqan" is "li-usaddiqa ma bayna yadayya min al-Tawrah, wa-li-uhilla lakum" (so that I confirm what is before me of the Torah, and so that I make lawful for you). This is coordination by assumption (*al-'atf 'ala al-tawahhum*), and this is not that, because the intelligibility of the circumstantial clause differs from the intelligibility of the causal clause, and coordination by assumption must have a single meaning shared by the coordinated and the element coordinated with.

Do you not see his words: "fa-asaddaqa wa-akun" (so that I may give charity and be among the righteous), how the meaning was unified in respect of being suitable as an answer to the exhortation (*tahdid*)? Likewise his words:

*Taqiyyun naqiyyun lam yukthir ghanimatan, bi-nakhati dhi qurba wa-la bi-khafladi*
"Pious and pure, he did not accumulate spoils, by the reproach of a relative nor by a stingy one."

How is the meaning of negation unified in "lam yukthir" and in "wa-la bi-khafladi"? That is, he is neither accumulating nor stingy. Likewise is whatever comes of this type. It was said: the *lam* is attached to an implied verb after the *waw*, which the meaning clarifies: that is, "and I came to you in order to make lawful for you." It was said: the *lam* is attached to his words "wa-ati'un" (and obey me), and the meaning is: "follow me in order to make lawful for you." This is very far-fetched. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is coordinated with an omitted element whose estimate is "li-ukhaffifa 'ankum" (in order to lighten for you), or something similar. Al-Zamakhshari said: "wa-li-uhilla" is a return to his words "bi-ayatin min rabbikum" (with a sign from your Lord), meaning: "I came to you with a sign from your Lord," because "bi-ayatin" is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and "wa-li-uhilla" is a causal clause. The coordination of a causal clause upon a circumstantial clause is not valid, because coordination with a particle that shares the ruling requires sharing the genus of the coordinated element. So if you coordinate upon a verbal noun, or a direct object, or an adverb of place or time, or a circumstantial clause, or a causal clause, or anything else, it shares that with the element coordinated.

﴿And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, so fear Allah and obey me. Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him﴾. The apparent meaning of the wording is that his words "wa-ji'tukum bi-ayatin min rabbikum" are for establishing (*al-ta'sis*), not for emphasis (*al-tawkid*), in view of his words "qad ji'tukum bi-ayatin min rabbikum" (I have indeed come to you with a sign from your Lord). This verse is his words "Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him," because this statement is evidence of the validity of his mission, since all the messengers were upon it and did not differ concerning it. This statement was made a sign and proof, because he is a messenger like the other messengers, in that He guided him to reflect upon the proofs of reason and to reason. The kasra of "inna" on this reading is because a statement before it is omitted, and that statement is an apposition to the sign, so it is governed by the apposition. Whoever reads "anna" with a fatha, it is in apposition to "ayah," and the sentence beginning with "inna" with a kasra cannot be taken as a new sentence on this estimate with an implied "qala" (he said), and his words "fa-ittaqu Allah wa-ati'un" (so fear Allah and obey me) are a parenthetical clause (*jumla i'tiradiyya*) between the apposition and the thing apposed.

It was said: the first sign in his words "qad ji'tukum bi-ayatin" (I have come to you with a sign) [Ali Imran: 49] is a miracle (*mu'jizah*). In his words "wa-ji'tukum bi-ayatin," it is the sign from the Gospel. So the object of the coming differs. It is permissible that "wa-ji'tukum bi-ayatin min rabbikum" is repeated for emphasis, meaning: "I have come to you with one sign after another of what I have mentioned to you: the creation of the bird, the healing, the raising of the dead, the telling of hidden things, and other things, including my birth without a father, my speaking in the cradle, and the rest of the signs." On this reading, whoever reads "inna" with a kasra does so as a new sentence, and whoever reads it with a fatha, it is said the estimate is "li-anna Allah rabbi wa-rabbukum fa-u'budhu" (because Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him), so it is connected to his words "fa-u'budhu," like His words "li-ilaf Quraysh" (for the familiarity of Quraysh) [Quraysh: 1], then He said "fa-l-ya'budu" (so let them worship). So he put "anna" before its governing element. As for whoever permitted that "anna" be placed before, with the governing element after it, as in "hadha ghayru musib" (this is not correct), it is not permitted to say "anna Zaydan munṭaliqun 'arftu" (that Zayd is departing, I knew). Sibawayh and others stated this explicitly. It is permissible that the meaning be: "I have come to you with a sign, on the basis that Allah is my Lord and your Lord," and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the estimate is "ati'uni" (obey me), because Allah is my Lord and your Lord. End of his words. His statement is not apparent.

The command to piety and obedience is a warning and a supplication. The meaning is that he displayed proofs and extraordinary signs confirming his truthfulness, so fear Allah in opposing me, and obey me in my command and my prohibition. It was also said: fear Allah in what He commanded you and forbade you in His Book which He sent down to Musa, and obey me in what I call you to, namely confirming me in what He sent me with to you. The repetition of "Rabbi wa-rabbukum" (my Lord and your Lord) is more emphatic in committing to servitude than saying "Rabbuna" (our Lord), and it is more indicative of disavowing lordship.

﴿This is a straight path﴾. That is: a clear road for whoever walks it, with no crookedness in it. The reference of "hadha" (this) is to his words "Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him," meaning: singling out Allah alone for worship is the straight path. The word "ibadah" (worship) includes faith and acts of obedience.

In these verses there are kinds of eloquence and rhetorical embellishment (*al-badi'*): the attribution of the verb to the one who commands it rather than to its doer, in his words "Inna Allaha yubashshiruka" (Allah gives you good news), since they are the ones addressed with the good news, and Allah is the one who commands it. Similar to this: "The sultan proclaimed in the land such-and-such," and the application of the name of the cause to the effect in his words "bi-kalimatin minhu" (with a word from Him), according to the disagreement over the interpretation of "kalimah."

The precaution (*al-ihtiras*) is in his words "wa-kahlan" (and in maturity): what is customary, that one who speaks in childhood does not live.

The metonymy (*al-kinayah*) is in his words "wa-lam yamsasni basharun" (no human has touched me) [Ali Imran: 47], where "al-mass" (touching) is a metonymy for sexual intercourse, as it is also expressed by "al-harth" (tilling), "al-libas" (clothing) and "al-mubashara" (intimate contact).

The question and answer are in "qalat al-malaikah" (the angels said) and in "anna yakunu" (how will there be). The repetition is in "ji'tukum bi-ayatin" and in "anni akhluqu lakum" (that I create for you) [Ali Imran: 49], and in "al-tayr" (the birds), and in "bi-idhni Allah" (by the permission of Allah), and in "rabbi wa-rabbukum," and in "ma" in his words "bima ta'kulun wa-ma" (what you eat and what you store).

The expression of a plural by a singular occurs in the verse, and in "al-akmah wa-al-abrasa" (the blind and the leper), and in "idha qada amran" (when He decrees a matter).

Antithesis (*al-tibaq*) occurs in "wa-uhyi al-mawta" (and I give life to the dead), and in "li-uhilla" (to make lawful) and "hurrima" (was forbidden). Turning (*al-iltifat*) occurs in "wa-nu'allimuhu" (and We teach him), according to whoever reads it with the *nun*. Explanation after ambiguity occurs in the statement of whoever said: "The Book is ambiguous and not specified, and the Torah and the Gospel are its explanation." Ellipsis (*al-hadhf*) occurs in a number of places.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on surah 3, verses 50–51:

﴿And confirming what is before me of the Torah﴾. "Wa-musaddiqan" is coordinated with his words "bi-ayatin" (with a sign), since the *ba'* there is for circumstance (*al-hal*, the circumstantial clause), and it cannot be for transitivity (*al-ta'diyah*), because that would corrupt the meaning. So the meaning is: "I have come to you accompanied by a sign from your Lord, and confirming what is before me." They rejected that "wa-musaddiqan" is coordinated with "rasulan ila Bani Isra'il" (a messenger to the Children of Israel), or with "wajihan" (honoured), because it would require the pronoun in "lima bayna yadayya" (what is before me) to be third person, so it would have to say "lima bayna yadayhi." We have already mentioned that "rasulan" may be in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning "and I have been sent as a messenger." On this reading, "wa-musaddiqan" is coordinated with "wa-rasulan." The meaning of his confirming the Torah is believing in it, even though his law differs from it in some matters. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "He used to observe the Sabbath, and he faced Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) in prayer."

﴿And to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you﴾. Ibn Jurayj said: "He made lawful for them the flesh of camels and the fats." Al-Rabi' said: "And some kinds of fish, and birds that have no crop (*dah'dah*), and that was forbidden in the Torah." Some exegetes said: "'Hurrima 'alaykum' (what was forbidden to you) refers to what the rabbis (*al-ahbar*) forbade after Musa and then legislated, so 'Isa returned the rulings of the Torah to their true realities, which had come down from Allah." End of his words. They differed about his making the Sabbath lawful for them. 'Ikrimah read "ma harrama 'alaykum" in the active voice, with the subject being a pronoun referring to "ma" in "lima bayna yadayya," or referring to Allah, the sender of the Torah, or to Musa, the bearer of the Torah. The first is more apparent, because it has been mentioned. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i read "harama" on the pattern of "karuma." The intended meaning of "ba'd" (some) is its common signification. Abu 'Ubaydah claimed that "ba'd" here means "every error," because it would follow that He would make lawful for them killing, adultery and theft, since these are forbidden to them. His evidence that *ba'd* can mean *kull* (all) is the verse of Labid:

*Tarrak amkinatin idha lam arduha, aw tartabit ba'd al-nufus hamamuha*
"I abandon places when I do not like them, or when death binds some souls."

This is not correct, because *ba'd* keeps its meaning here, since he means *nafsahu* (himself), so it is a valid partitive. The same applies to the argument of one who cited the verse:

*Inna al-umura idha al-ahdathu dabbaraha, dunna al-shuyukhi tara fi ba'diha khalalan*
"Indeed, when the young men manage affairs without the elders, you see a flaw in some of them."

This is for the validity of the partitive, since not everything managed by the young contains a flaw. Some said: *ba'd* does not stand in place of *kull* unless a clear indication (*qarinah*) shows it, such as his saying:

*Aba Mundhirin afnayta fa-istabqi ba'dana, hananayka ba'd al-sharri ahwan min ba'd*
"O Abu Mundhir, you have destroyed, so spare some of us. Mercy upon you! Some evil is easier than some other evil."

He means: "Some evil is easier than all of it." End of his words. There is an objection to this.

The *lam* in "wa-li-uhilla lakum" is the *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*), and there is no preceding element that permits coordinating it with what came before in terms of wording. So it was said that it is coordinated with the meaning: the meaning of "musaddiqan" is "li-usaddiqa ma bayna yadayya min al-Tawrah, wa-li-uhilla lakum" (so that I confirm what is before me of the Torah, and so that I make lawful for you). This is coordination by assumption (*al-'atf 'ala al-tawahhum*), and this is not that, because the intelligibility of the circumstantial clause differs from the intelligibility of the causal clause, and coordination by assumption must have a single meaning shared by the coordinated and the element coordinated with.

Do you not see his words: "fa-asaddaqa wa-akun" (so that I may give charity and be among the righteous), how the meaning was unified in respect of being suitable as an answer to the exhortation (*tahdid*)? Likewise his words:

*Taqiyyun naqiyyun lam yukthir ghanimatan, bi-nakhati dhi qurba wa-la bi-khafladi*
"Pious and pure, he did not accumulate spoils, by the reproach of a relative nor by a stingy one."

How is the meaning of negation unified in "lam yukthir" and in "wa-la bi-khafladi"? That is, he is neither accumulating nor stingy. Likewise is whatever comes of this type. It was said: the *lam* is attached to an implied verb after the *waw*, which the meaning clarifies: that is, "and I came to you in order to make lawful for you." It was said: the *lam* is attached to his words "wa-ati'un" (and obey me), and the meaning is: "follow me in order to make lawful for you." This is very far-fetched. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is coordinated with an omitted element whose estimate is "li-ukhaffifa 'ankum" (in order to lighten for you), or something similar. Al-Zamakhshari said: "wa-li-uhilla" is a return to his words "bi-ayatin min rabbikum" (with a sign from your Lord), meaning: "I came to you with a sign from your Lord," because "bi-ayatin" is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and "wa-li-uhilla" is a causal clause. The coordination of a causal clause upon a circumstantial clause is not valid, because coordination with a particle that shares the ruling requires sharing the genus of the coordinated element. So if you coordinate upon a verbal noun, or a direct object, or an adverb of place or time, or a circumstantial clause, or a causal clause, or anything else, it shares that with the element coordinated.

﴿And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, so fear Allah and obey me. Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him﴾. The apparent meaning of the wording is that his words "wa-ji'tukum bi-ayatin min rabbikum" are for establishing (*al-ta'sis*), not for emphasis (*al-tawkid*), in view of his words "qad ji'tukum bi-ayatin min rabbikum" (I have indeed come to you with a sign from your Lord). This verse is his words "Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him," because this statement is evidence of the validity of his mission, since all the messengers were upon it and did not differ concerning it. This statement was made a sign and proof, because he is a messenger like the other messengers, in that He guided him to reflect upon the proofs of reason and to reason. The kasra of "inna" on this reading is because a statement before it is omitted, and that statement is an apposition to the sign, so it is governed by the apposition. Whoever reads "anna" with a fatha, it is in apposition to "ayah," and the sentence beginning with "inna" with a kasra cannot be taken as a new sentence on this estimate with an implied "qala" (he said), and his words "fa-ittaqu Allah wa-ati'un" (so fear Allah and obey me) are a parenthetical clause (*jumla i'tiradiyya*) between the apposition and the thing apposed.

It was said: the first sign in his words "qad ji'tukum bi-ayatin" (I have come to you with a sign) [Ali Imran: 49] is a miracle (*mu'jizah*). In his words "wa-ji'tukum bi-ayatin," it is the sign from the Gospel. So the object of the coming differs. It is permissible that "wa-ji'tukum bi-ayatin min rabbikum" is repeated for emphasis, meaning: "I have come to you with one sign after another of what I have mentioned to you: the creation of the bird, the healing, the raising of the dead, the telling of hidden things, and other things, including my birth without a father, my speaking in the cradle, and the rest of the signs." On this reading, whoever reads "inna" with a kasra does so as a new sentence, and whoever reads it with a fatha, it is said the estimate is "li-anna Allah rabbi wa-rabbukum fa-u'budhu" (because Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him), so it is connected to his words "fa-u'budhu," like His words "li-ilaf Quraysh" (for the familiarity of Quraysh) [Quraysh: 1], then He said "fa-l-ya'budu" (so let them worship). So he put "anna" before its governing element. As for whoever permitted that "anna" be placed before, with the governing element after it, as in "hadha ghayru musib" (this is not correct), it is not permitted to say "anna Zaydan munṭaliqun 'arftu" (that Zayd is departing, I knew). Sibawayh and others stated this explicitly. It is permissible that the meaning be: "I have come to you with a sign, on the basis that Allah is my Lord and your Lord," and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the estimate is "ati'uni" (obey me), because Allah is my Lord and your Lord. End of his words. His statement is not apparent.

The command to piety and obedience is a warning and a supplication. The meaning is that he displayed proofs and extraordinary signs confirming his truthfulness, so fear Allah in opposing me, and obey me in my command and my prohibition. It was also said: fear Allah in what He commanded you and forbade you in His Book which He sent down to Musa, and obey me in what I call you to, namely confirming me in what He sent me with to you. The repetition of "Rabbi wa-rabbukum" (my Lord and your Lord) is more emphatic in committing to servitude than saying "Rabbuna" (our Lord), and it is more indicative of disavowing lordship.

﴿This is a straight path﴾. That is: a clear road for whoever walks it, with no crookedness in it. The reference of "hadha" (this) is to his words "Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him," meaning: singling out Allah alone for worship is the straight path. The word "ibadah" (worship) includes faith and acts of obedience.

In these verses there are kinds of eloquence and rhetorical embellishment (*al-badi'*): the attribution of the verb to the one who commands it rather than to its doer, in his words "Inna Allaha yubashshiruka" (Allah gives you good news), since they are the ones addressed with the good news, and Allah is the one who commands it. Similar to this: "The sultan proclaimed in the land such-and-such," and the application of the name of the cause to the effect in his words "bi-kalimatin minhu" (with a word from Him), according to the disagreement over the interpretation of "kalimah."

The precaution (*al-ihtiras*) is in his words "wa-kahlan" (and in maturity): what is customary, that one who speaks in childhood does not live.

The metonymy (*al-kinayah*) is in his words "wa-lam yamsasni basharun" (no human has touched me) [Ali Imran: 47], where "al-mass" (touching) is a metonymy for sexual intercourse, as it is also expressed by "al-harth" (tilling), "al-libas" (clothing) and "al-mubashara" (intimate contact).

The question and answer are in "qalat al-malaikah" (the angels said) and in "anna yakunu" (how will there be). The repetition is in "ji'tukum bi-ayatin" and in "anni akhluqu lakum" (that I create for you) [Ali Imran: 49], and in "al-tayr" (the birds), and in "bi-idhni Allah" (by the permission of Allah), and in "rabbi wa-rabbukum," and in "ma" in his words "bima ta'kulun wa-ma" (what you eat and what you store).

The expression of a plural by a singular occurs in the verse, and in "al-akmah wa-al-abrasa" (the blind and the leper), and in "idha qada amran" (when He decrees a matter).

Antithesis (*al-tibaq*) occurs in "wa-uhyi al-mawta" (and I give life to the dead), and in "li-uhilla" (to make lawful) and "hurrima" (was forbidden). Turning (*al-iltifat*) occurs in "wa-nu'allimuhu" (and We teach him), according to whoever reads it with the *nun*. Explanation after ambiguity occurs in the statement of whoever said: "The Book is ambiguous and not specified, and the Torah and the Gospel are its explanation." Ellipsis (*al-hadhf*) occurs in a number of places.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 52:**

﴿Then when Jesus sensed disbelief from them, he said, "Who are my helpers in the cause of God?" The disciples (al-Hawariyyun) said, "We are the helpers of God. We believe in God, and bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, we believe in what You have sent down and have followed the Messenger, so write us down among the witnesses."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 53] ﴿And they schemed, and God schemed, and God is the best of schemers.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54] ﴿When God said, "O Jesus, I will take you and raise you to Me, and purify you from those who disbelieve, and I will make those who follow you superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection. Then to Me will be your return, and I will judge between you concerning that over which you used to differ."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55] ﴿As for those who disbelieved, I will punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 56] ﴿And as for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will give them their rewards in full. And God does not love the wrongdoers.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 57] ﴿That which We recite to you is of the signs and the wise Reminder.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 58] ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with God is like the likeness of Adam. He created him from dust, then said to him, "Be," and he was.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59] ﴿The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 60] ﴿Whoever argues with you about it after knowledge has come to you, say, "Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, and ourselves and yourselves, then let us invoke earnestly and place the curse of God upon the liars."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 61].

**Al-ihsas (الإحساس):** perception through one of the five senses, which are hearing, sight, smell, taste and touch. It is said: *ahsastu al-shay'* and *hassastu bihi*. Its first *sin* may be changed to a *ya'*, so one says *hasaytu bihi*, or the first of its two *sin*s may be dropped from *ahsastu*, so one says *ahsatu*. The poet said:

*Except that the noble mounts among the riding beasts sensed it, and so they are alert toward it.*

Sibawayh said: What is anomalous among the doubled verbs, meaning in the dropping, resembles the pattern of *aqamtu*. This is their saying *ahsatu* and *ahsatna*, meaning *ahsastu* and *ahsastna*. The same is done with every form in which the final radical of the verb is vowelled with sukun and the movement does not reach it. When you say *lam uhissa*, nothing is dropped.

**Al-hawari (الحواري):** the choice and inner circle of a man. From this comes the saying: "the urban women are *hawariyyat*," because of the purity of their complexions and their cleanliness. Abu Jaladhah al-Yashkuri said:

*So say to the hawariyyat: "You weep for others, and only the barking dogs weep for us."*

Similar in form is *al-hawali*, for the one who is very resourceful. The *ya'* in both is not the *ya'* of relation. It is derived from *al-hawar*, which is whiteness. *Hawwartu al-thawb* means I whitened the garment.

**Al-makr (المكر):** deceit and malice. Its origin is concealment. It is said: *makara al-layl* when the night grew dark. Its derivation is from *al-makr*, which is a densely intertwined tree, so the one deceived is enveloped by the deceit and encompassed by it. It is said: *imra'ah mamkurah* for a woman whose build is compact. *Al-makr* is also a kind of plant.

**Ta'ala (تعالى):** a form of *tafā'ala* from *al-'uluww* (height). It is a verb, because of the attachment of the raised pronouns to it. Its meaning is summoning the one called from his place to the place of the caller. It is a word originally intended to beautify manners with the one addressed. Then its use became common, so that a person says it to his enemy, to his beast, and the like.

**Al-ibtihal (الابتهال):** his saying *bahlat Allah 'ala al-kadhib* means the curse of God upon the liar. *Al-bahlah*, with a *fatha* or a *damma*, means a curse. It is said *bahalahu Allah*, meaning He cursed him and removed him far away, from your saying *abhalahu* when he left him neglected. A she-camel that is *bahilah* is one that is not harmed. The origin of *al-ibtihal* is this. Then it was used for every supplication made with effort, even if it was not a mutual curse. Labid said:

*From the chieftains of noble lords among their people, whom time looked upon and then made earnest supplication.*

(p. 471) **"Then when Jesus sensed disbelief from them" (فلما أحس عيسى منهم الكفر):** The arrangement of this sentence after what precedes it has been mentioned. Is the omission after His saying "a straight path" (Al 'Imran: 51) or after His saying "and a messenger to the Children of Israel" (Al 'Imran: 49)? That is at the explanation of "and a messenger to the Children of Israel" (Al 'Imran: 49).

Muqatil said: *ahassa* here means he saw, either by sight or by the heart. Al-Farra' said: *ahassa* means he found. Abu 'Ubaydah said: he knew. It has been said: he knew. It has been said: he feared. *Al-kufr* here means denying his prophethood and rejecting his miracles. *Minhum* is connected to *ahassa*. It has been said that it may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from *al-kufr*.

**"He said, 'Who are my helpers in the cause of God?'" (قال من أنصاري إلى الله):** When they intended to kill him, he sought help against them. Mujahid said, and others said: he sought help when they disbelieved in him and drove him out of their town. It has been said: he sought their help to establish the truth.

Al-Maghribi said: Jesus only said "Who are my helpers in the cause of God?" after his being raised to heaven and his return to earth, and after he had gathered the twelve disciples and dispersed them across the horizons calling to the truth. What was said, that this statement came after what was mentioned, is very distant and no one else mentioned it, rather what is transmitted is otherwise. The apparent meaning is that he said this before his being raised to heaven. As-Suddi said: Who are my helpers alongside God? Al-Hasan said: Who are my helpers on the path to God? Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said that the meaning of *ila Allah* is *li-Allah*, like His saying "guides to the truth" (Yunus: 35), meaning "guides to the truth." It has been said: who will help me toward the victory of God? It has been said: who will be cut off with me for God? This was said by Ibn Bahr. It has been said: who will help me until I make the command of God clear? Abu 'Ubaydah said: who are my helpers in God's essence? Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Who are my helpers toward God?" is an expression of Jesus's state in seeking someone who would stand up for the religion, believe in the law and protect it, just as Muhammad (ﷺ) would present himself to the tribes and approach the clans in the seasons. End of quotation. Al-Zamakhshari said: *ila Allah* is connected to *ansari*, implying the meaning of attribution, as if it were said: who are those who attribute themselves to God and help me as God helps me? Or it is connected to an omitted word as a circumstantial clause from the *ya'*, meaning: who are my helpers going toward God, seeking refuge in Him? End of quotation.

**"The disciples said" (قال الحواريون):** that is, the chosen ones of Jesus. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Or: his intimates, said by al-Farra'. Or the white-garmented ones, narrated by Ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. Or the launderers, named so because they whiten garments, that is, they make them white. This was said by al-Dahhak and Muqatil. Or: the fighters. Or: the fishermen. Jesus, peace be upon our Prophet and upon him, said to them: "Will you not walk with me to catch people for God?" So they answered. Mus'ab said: they were twelve men who traveled with him, and what they needed came out of the earth for them. They said: who is better than us? We eat from wherever we wish. Jesus said: who works with his hand and eats from his earnings? So they became launderers. Ibn al-Anbari related: *al-hawariyyun* means kings. Al-Dahhak and Abu Artah said: the washers. Ibn al-Mubarak said: *al-hawar* is light, and they were attributed to it because of the mark of worship and its light in their faces. Taj al-Qurra' said: *al-hawari* is the truthful one.

It has been said: when He showed them the signs, He set before them various colours from one grain, and they believed in it and followed him.

The majority read *al-hawariyyun* with a shadda on the *ya'*. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Abu Bakr al-Thaqafi read it with the *ya'* unshaddah throughout the Qur'an. The Arabs find the *damma* on a *ya'* preceded by a kasra, as in *al-qadiyyun*, heavy, so they move the *damma* onto the preceding letter and drop the *ya'* because it meets a following sakin. Based on this, the analogical form would be *al-hawarun*. But the *damma* was kept, and this does not indicate that the shadda is intended, since the shadda may carry a *damma*, as al-Akhfash held in *yastahziun*, where he changed the hamza into a *ya'*, and the *damma* carried the memory of the state of the hamza that was intended in it.

**"We are the helpers of God" (نحن أنصار الله):** that is, the helpers of His religion, His law, and the one who calls to it.

**"We believe in God, and bear witness that we are Muslims" (آمنا بالله واشهد بأنا مسلمون):** When they mentioned that they are the helpers of God, they mentioned the basis of this attribution, which is belief in God. They asked Jesus to bear witness to their submission, in order to confirm their faith, because the submission of the limbs follows the submission of the heart and its affirmation. The messengers bear witness on the Day of Resurrection for their peoples and against them. This indicates that Jesus, peace be upon him, was upon the religion of Islam, and God cleared him of all other religions, just as He cleared Abraham, by His saying: "Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian" (Al 'Imran: 67), (p. 472) and so on. It is possible that *wash-had* is an address to God, Most High, meaning: "and bear witness, O our Lord." In this there is a rebuke to the Christians of Najran, since God related the statement of their forebears who believed in Jesus. So their saying about him and their claim of his divinity is not like what they said about him.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 53–55 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down﴾, that is: of the signs that indicate the truthfulness of Your prophets. Or: what You sent down of Your speech to the messengers, or the Gospel.

﴿and we have followed the Messenger﴾ is Jesus, according to the majority opinion.

﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾. They are Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, because they bear witness for the messengers that they conveyed the message, and Muhammad (ﷺ) bears witness for them as to their truthfulness. This was related by Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas. Or: those who believed before them, related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. Or: the prophets, because every prophet is a witness over his nation. Or: the truthful, said by Muqatil. Or: those who bear witness to the prophets by confirming them, said by al-Zajjaj. Or: those who witness to the support of Your messengers, or those who bear witness to the truth before You. They desired to be in His reckoning among those who bear witness to the truth from the believers of the nations. They expressed God's act of this with them by the wording "so write us," since writing (kitaba) restricts and secures what needs to be verified and known at a later state.

﴿And they schemed, and God schemed﴾. The pronoun in "they schemed" refers back to those to whom the pronoun in "When Jesus sensed disbelief from them" [Al-Imran: 52] refers, namely the Children of Israel. Their scheming was their plotting to kill Jesus, by appointing someone to kill him secretly. The account of how they besieged him and his companions in one place, their intention to kill him, the casting of his likeness upon another man, and the killing and crucifixion of that man in his place, will come later, God willing.

﴿And God schemed﴾: His requiting them for their scheming, which He named "scheming" because the requital for them arose from scheming, as in His saying: ﴿The recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], and His saying ﴿Whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in like manner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194]. Often punishment is named by the name of the sin, even if it is not of the same meaning. It has been said: God's scheming against them is His turning them back from what they wanted, by raising Jesus to heaven and casting his likeness upon the one who intended to assassinate him, until he was killed. Al-Asamm said: God's scheming against them is that He empowered over them the people of Persia, who killed them and took their offspring captive. Ibn Ishaq mentioned that the Jews raided the disciples after the raising of Jesus, seized them and tortured them. The king of the Romans heard of this, and the king of the Jews was among his subjects, so he rescued them. He then raided the Children of Israel, and became a Christian, but did not make this public. Then another king ruled after him and raided Bayt al-Maqdis about forty years after the raising of Jesus, leaving not a stone upon another in it. At that time Qurayza and al-Nadir went out to the Hijaz.

Al-Mufaddal said: "They plotted (dabbaru), and God plotted (dabbara)." Scheming (al-makr) is subtle arrangement. Ibn Isa said: scheming is ugly, and it was only permitted to be attributed to God's attributes on account of the pairing of speech. It has been said: God's scheming against them is the exaltation of His religion and their subjugation through humiliation, and their scheming is their insistence on nullifying His religion. Scheming is an expression for the contriving of bringing harm in secret, and this is not impossible (for God). It has been said: scheming is seizing someone who deserves it while he is heedless. A man asked al-Junayd: "How did God, glorified be He, consent to scheming for Himself, when He has disparaged it in others?" He said: "I do not know what you are saying, but a certain al-Zahrani recited to me:

*"Whoever else does the deed, I find it ugly; yet you do it, and it becomes beautiful from you."*

Then he said: "I have answered you, if you understand."

﴿And God is the best of schemers﴾: its meaning is that He is the best of those who requite. He requites the people of good with grace, and the people of injustice with justice, because He is the doer of truth in this, whereas the schemer among humans is generally a doer of falsehood. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God is stronger in might and stronger in punishment﴾ [al-Nisa: 84]. It has been said: "best" (khayr) here is not comparative, but is like its use in His saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day are better in resting place﴾ [al-Furqan: 24], and Hassan said:

*"So your evil is for the sake of your good: the ransom."*

In this verse there are figures of eloquence: the metaphor in "sensed" (ahassa), since one senses only what is embodied, and disbelief is not perceptible; it is known and understood through insight, and is not apprehended by the senses, unless "sensed" means "saw," or means "heard from them the word of disbelief," in which case "sensed" is not a metaphor, since he perceived it from them by the faculty of sight or the faculty of hearing. Also there is the naming of a thing by the name of its fruit. The majority said: he sensed from them killing, and killing a prophet is among the greatest fruits of disbelief.

The question and answer in: ﴿He said: "Who are my helpers toward God?" The disciples said﴾ [Al-Imran: 52]; and the repetition in: "Who are my helpers toward God?" and "the helpers of God," and "we have believed in God," and "we have believed in what You have sent down," and "they schemed" and "God schemed," and "the schemers." In this is the paronomasia (tajnis), both the identical and the contrasting, and ellipsis in several places.

﴿When God said: "O Jesus, I will take you back"﴾. The governing element of "when" (idh) is "God schemed," said al-Tabari; or "remember," said some grammarians; or "the best of schemers," said al-Zamakhshari. This statement was through an angel, because Jesus was not speaking, said Ibn Atiyya. It has been said: forty years. End of quotation.

It has been said: to a place in which no one holds judgement in reality, nor apparently except Me, unlike the earth, where created beings may exercise judgements apparently. It has been said: to the place of your reward. Al-Raghib said: "taking you back" is taking you away from your desires, and "raising you to Me" is raising you away from your desires; it was not a physical raising, but an elevation of rank, even though he was raised to heaven. Abu Muslim said: rescue and purification are one, except that the word "purification" (tahhir) contains an elevation for the one addressed, just as witnessing and presence are one, but witnessing contains elevation. ﴿And We shall make those who follow you﴾. The "you" (ka) is a pronoun for Jesus, like the preceding "you." It has been said: it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab). The statement ends. This view is not apparent. The meaning of "followed you" (ittaba'uka): in religion and law, and they are the Muslims, because they follow him in the basics of Islam, even if the laws differ.

﴿above those who disbelieved﴾: they will dominate them with proof, and in most circumstances with proof and with the sword. "Those who disbelieved" are those who denied him and lied about him among the Jews and Christians, said al-Zamakhshari, with an inversion of order in his speech.

Thus they are above the Jews, so there will be no kingdom for them as there is for the Christians. The verse, according to this view, is informing of the humiliation and punishment of the Jews, that the Christians are above them in all regions of the earth until the Day of Resurrection. The statement of Ibn Jurayj appears to indicate that his followers are those in the time of his help, namely the disciples. God made them above the disbelievers because He honoured them and preserved for them a good remembrance among the righteous. (p-475) ﴿To the Day of Resurrection﴾. The apparent view is that "ila" (to) is connected to an omitted element, which is the governing element of "fawq" (above), and it is the second object of "jā'il" (one who makes), since the meaning of "jā'il" here is "muṣayyir" (one who makes [them] become). So the meaning is: "being above them until the Day of Resurrection." This is based on the figurative (majāz) sense of "fawqiyyah" (superiority/above). But if "fawqiyyah" is taken literally, meaning being above them in Paradise, then "ila" is not connected to that omitted element, but rather to what preceded it: "mutawaffika" (causing you to die), or "rāfi'uka" (raising you), or "muṭahhiruka" (purifying you), since it can be connected to each one of them. As for "rāfi'uka" or "muṭahhiruka," it is clear. As for "mutawaffika," it is so according to some opinions. These four statements are in the utmost eloquence in their arrangement. He began first by informing Jesus that God would cause him to die, so those who plot against him have no power over him and no way to reach him. Then He gave him a second glad tidings of raising him to His heaven, dwelling with His angels there, and worshipping there, and the length of his life in worship of his Lord. Then third, by raising him to His heaven by purifying him from the disbelievers, thereby encompassing all of his time when He raised him and when He will send him down at the end of the world. So it is a great glad tidings for him that he is purified from the disbelievers, both first and last. Since "tawaffi" and "raf'" are each specific to a time, they were mentioned first. Since "tathhīr" is general, encompassing all times, it was mentioned after them. When He gave him these three glad tidings, which are attributes of himself, He gave him the glad tidings of the elevation of his followers above every disbeliever, so that his eye would be comforted and his heart gladdened.

Since this attribute of the superiority of his followers over the disbelievers is one of the attributes of his followers, it was placed after the three attributes that pertain to himself, for beginning with the attributes pertaining to the self is more important. Then this fourth attribute was followed up as a glad tiding about the state of his followers in this world, in order to complete his joy in what he was given and what his followers were given of good.

﴿Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that over which you used to differ﴾. This is an information about the gathering and resurrection, and the meaning is: then to My judgment. In my view this is an instance of iltifat (shift of address); because the mention of his deniers, namely the Jews, and the mention of those who believed in him, namely the disciples (al-Hawariyyun), had preceded. Following that was His saying: ﴿And We will make those who followed you superior to those who disbelieved﴾, so He mentioned his followers and the disbelievers. Had it come in the pattern of this preceding statement, the construction would have been: "Then to Me is their return," but instead He shifted to address all of them, so that the information would be more forceful in warning and more stringent in restraining those who are restrained. Then He mentioned the expression "ilayya" (to Me) and the expression "fa-ahkum" (so I will judge) with the first-person pronoun, so that it would be known that the judge there is one from whom nothing is hidden; and He mentioned that He will judge concerning what they differed about regarding the matter of the prophets and following their laws, and He brought the judgment in general terms, then detailed the judged among them into believer and disbeliever, and mentioned the recompense of each one of them.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Your return" — the address is to Jesus, and what is intended is the information about the Resurrection and gathering; therefore the wording came general in terms of the matter itself, which does not concern Jesus alone, so He addressed him as one addresses a group, since he is one of them, and since they are intended in meaning. End of his words. But in my view the better position is that it is part of iltifat, as I have mentioned.

It has been said: "above those who disbelieved" on the Day of Resurrection, in the Garden, as they are in the high chambers, while those who disbelieved are in the lowest depths of the Fire.
