As for superiority: it is either literal, and that is by the Garden and the Fire; or figurative, meaning by proof and evidence, in which case it is religious; or by might and victory, in which case it is worldly; or by both.

(p-475) ﴿To the Day of Resurrection﴾. The apparent view is that "ila" (to) is connected to an omitted element, which is the governing element of "fawq" (above), and it is the second object of "jā'il" (one who makes), since the meaning of "jā'il" here is "muṣayyir" (one who makes [them] become). So the meaning is: "being above them until the Day of Resurrection." This is based on the figurative (majāz) sense of "fawqiyyah" (superiority/above). But if "fawqiyyah" is taken literally, meaning being above them in Paradise, then "ila" is not connected to that omitted element, but rather to what preceded it: "mutawaffika" (causing you to die), or "rāfi'uka" (raising you), or "muṭahhiruka" (purifying you), since it can be connected to each one of them. As for "rāfi'uka" or "muṭahhiruka," it is clear. As for "mutawaffika," it is so according to some opinions. These four statements are in the utmost eloquence in their arrangement. He began first by informing Jesus that God would cause him to die, so those who plot against him have no power over him and no way to reach him. Then He gave him a second glad tidings of raising him to His heaven, dwelling with His angels there, and worshipping there, and the length of his life in worship of his Lord. Then third, by raising him to His heaven by purifying him from the disbelievers, thereby encompassing all of his time when He raised him and when He will send him down at the end of the world. So it is a great glad tidings for him that he is purified from the disbelievers, both first and last. Since "tawaffi" and "raf'" are each specific to a time, they were mentioned first. Since "tathhīr" is general, encompassing all times, it was mentioned after them. When He gave him these three glad tidings, which are attributes of himself, He gave him the glad tidings of the elevation of his followers above every disbeliever, so that his eye would be comforted and his heart gladdened.

Since this attribute of the superiority of his followers over the disbelievers is one of the attributes of his followers, it was placed after the three attributes that pertain to himself, for beginning with the attributes pertaining to the self is more important. Then this fourth attribute was followed up as a glad tiding about the state of his followers in this world, in order to complete his joy in what he was given and what his followers were given of good.

﴿Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that over which you used to differ﴾. This is an information about the gathering and resurrection, and the meaning is: then to My judgment. In my view this is an instance of iltifat (shift of address); because the mention of his deniers, namely the Jews, and the mention of those who believed in him, namely the disciples (al-Hawariyyun), had preceded. Following that was His saying: ﴿And We will make those who followed you superior to those who disbelieved﴾, so He mentioned his followers and the disbelievers. Had it come in the pattern of this preceding statement, the construction would have been: "Then to Me is their return," but instead He shifted to address all of them, so that the information would be more forceful in warning and more stringent in restraining those who are restrained. Then He mentioned the expression "ilayya" (to Me) and the expression "fa-ahkum" (so I will judge) with the first-person pronoun, so that it would be known that the judge there is one from whom nothing is hidden; and He mentioned that He will judge concerning what they differed about regarding the matter of the prophets and following their laws, and He brought the judgment in general terms, then detailed the judged among them into believer and disbeliever, and mentioned the recompense of each one of them.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Your return" — the address is to Jesus, and what is intended is the information about the Resurrection and gathering; therefore the wording came general in terms of the matter itself, which does not concern Jesus alone, so He addressed him as one addresses a group, since he is one of them, and since they are intended in meaning. End of his words. But in my view the better position is that it is part of iltifat, as I have mentioned.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 53–55 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Our Lord, we have believed in what You have sent down﴾, that is: of the signs that indicate the truthfulness of Your prophets. Or: what You sent down of Your speech to the messengers, or the Gospel.

﴿and we have followed the Messenger﴾ is Jesus, according to the majority opinion.

﴿so write us among the witnesses﴾. They are Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, because they bear witness for the messengers that they conveyed the message, and Muhammad (ﷺ) bears witness for them as to their truthfulness. This was related by Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas. Or: those who believed before them, related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. Or: the prophets, because every prophet is a witness over his nation. Or: the truthful, said by Muqatil. Or: those who bear witness to the prophets by confirming them, said by al-Zajjaj. Or: those who witness to the support of Your messengers, or those who bear witness to the truth before You. They desired to be in His reckoning among those who bear witness to the truth from the believers of the nations. They expressed God's act of this with them by the wording "so write us," since writing (kitaba) restricts and secures what needs to be verified and known at a later state.

﴿And they schemed, and God schemed﴾. The pronoun in "they schemed" refers back to those to whom the pronoun in "When Jesus sensed disbelief from them" [Al-Imran: 52] refers, namely the Children of Israel. Their scheming was their plotting to kill Jesus, by appointing someone to kill him secretly. The account of how they besieged him and his companions in one place, their intention to kill him, the casting of his likeness upon another man, and the killing and crucifixion of that man in his place, will come later, God willing.

﴿And God schemed﴾: His requiting them for their scheming, which He named "scheming" because the requital for them arose from scheming, as in His saying: ﴿The recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], and His saying ﴿Whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in like manner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194]. Often punishment is named by the name of the sin, even if it is not of the same meaning. It has been said: God's scheming against them is His turning them back from what they wanted, by raising Jesus to heaven and casting his likeness upon the one who intended to assassinate him, until he was killed. Al-Asamm said: God's scheming against them is that He empowered over them the people of Persia, who killed them and took their offspring captive. Ibn Ishaq mentioned that the Jews raided the disciples after the raising of Jesus, seized them and tortured them. The king of the Romans heard of this, and the king of the Jews was among his subjects, so he rescued them. He then raided the Children of Israel, and became a Christian, but did not make this public. Then another king ruled after him and raided Bayt al-Maqdis about forty years after the raising of Jesus, leaving not a stone upon another in it. At that time Qurayza and al-Nadir went out to the Hijaz.

Al-Mufaddal said: "They plotted (dabbaru), and God plotted (dabbara)." Scheming (al-makr) is subtle arrangement. Ibn Isa said: scheming is ugly, and it was only permitted to be attributed to God's attributes on account of the pairing of speech. It has been said: God's scheming against them is the exaltation of His religion and their subjugation through humiliation, and their scheming is their insistence on nullifying His religion. Scheming is an expression for the contriving of bringing harm in secret, and this is not impossible (for God). It has been said: scheming is seizing someone who deserves it while he is heedless. A man asked al-Junayd: "How did God, glorified be He, consent to scheming for Himself, when He has disparaged it in others?" He said: "I do not know what you are saying, but a certain al-Zahrani recited to me:

*"Whoever else does the deed, I find it ugly; yet you do it, and it becomes beautiful from you."*

Then he said: "I have answered you, if you understand."

﴿And God is the best of schemers﴾: its meaning is that He is the best of those who requite. He requites the people of good with grace, and the people of injustice with justice, because He is the doer of truth in this, whereas the schemer among humans is generally a doer of falsehood. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God is stronger in might and stronger in punishment﴾ [al-Nisa: 84]. It has been said: "best" (khayr) here is not comparative, but is like its use in His saying: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that Day are better in resting place﴾ [al-Furqan: 24], and Hassan said:

*"So your evil is for the sake of your good: the ransom."*

In this verse there are figures of eloquence: the metaphor in "sensed" (ahassa), since one senses only what is embodied, and disbelief is not perceptible; it is known and understood through insight, and is not apprehended by the senses, unless "sensed" means "saw," or means "heard from them the word of disbelief," in which case "sensed" is not a metaphor, since he perceived it from them by the faculty of sight or the faculty of hearing. Also there is the naming of a thing by the name of its fruit. The majority said: he sensed from them killing, and killing a prophet is among the greatest fruits of disbelief.

The question and answer in: ﴿He said: "Who are my helpers toward God?" The disciples said﴾ [Al-Imran: 52]; and the repetition in: "Who are my helpers toward God?" and "the helpers of God," and "we have believed in God," and "we have believed in what You have sent down," and "they schemed" and "God schemed," and "the schemers." In this is the paronomasia (tajnis), both the identical and the contrasting, and ellipsis in several places.

﴿When God said: "O Jesus, I will take you back"﴾. The governing element of "when" (idh) is "God schemed," said al-Tabari; or "remember," said some grammarians; or "the best of schemers," said al-Zamakhshari. This statement was through an angel, because Jesus was not speaking, said Ibn Atiyya. "I will take you back" (mutawaffika): it is a taking back (wafa) on the day God raised him in his sleep, said al-Rabi', from His saying: ﴿It is He who takes you back at night﴾ [al-An'am: 60], meaning: "I will raise you while you sleep, so that no fear reaches you, and you awaken while you are in heaven, secure and brought near." Or: it is a taking back of death, said Ibn Abbas. Wahb said: he died for three hours, during which He raised him, then God revived him after that in heaven; and in some books it is said: seven hours. Al-Farra said: it is a taking back of death, but the meaning is: "I will take you back at the end of your term, at your descent and your killing of the Antichrist (al-Dajjal)," and there is an inversion of order in the speech. Al-Zamakhshari said: "one who completes your term," meaning: "one who protects you from the disbelievers killing you, and who delays you until a term that I have decreed for you, and who causes you to die a natural death (hatf anfika), not killed by their hands." It has been said: "I will take you back" means: "one who takes you from the earth without death," said al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Jurayj, Mattar al-Warraq, and Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, from "I took back (tawaffaytu) my due from so-and-so" when you receive it in full.

It has been said: "I will make you like one who is taken back," because by raising he resembles him. It has been said: "I will take you in full with your spirit and your body." It has been said: "I will take you back" means: "one who accepts your deed." This is weak on linguistic grounds. Abu Bakr al-Wasiti said: "I will take you back from your desires." Ibn Atiyya said: the community has agreed on what is contained in the widely transmitted hadith (mutawatir, a report transmitted by so many narrators that its falsehood is inconceivable): "That Jesus is alive in heaven, and that he will descend at the end of time, and will kill the pig, break the cross, kill the Antichrist, justice will spread, and the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) will prevail through him, and he will perform the Hajj and the 'umrah, and will remain on earth for twenty-four years." It has been said: forty years. End of quotation.

﴿And I will raise you to Me﴾. Raising (al-raf') is a transfer from a low place to a high one. "To Me" is an idiom of honour. The meaning: to My heaven and the abode of My angels. It is known that the Exalted Creator is not confined to a direction, but the anthropomorphists (al-Mushabbiha, those who liken God to creation) have clung to this in asserting that God has a place. It has been said: to a place in which no one holds judgement in reality, nor apparently except Me, unlike the earth, where created beings may exercise judgements apparently. It has been said: to the place of your reward. Ibn Abbas said: His raising to heaven, the lowest heaven, where He swims with the angels; then God will send him down at the appearance of the Antichrist to the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis. It has been said: Jesus was on Mount Sinai, and a wind blew, so Jesus hastened, and God raised him in his haste, while he was wearing a woollen garment. Al-Zajjaj said: Jesus was in a house that had a window, and a man entered to kill him, so Jesus was raised from the house, and the man went out in Jesus' likeness, informing them that Jesus was not in the house, so they killed him. Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba related from Ibn Abbas that he said: God raised Jesus from a window that was in the house.

﴿And purify you from those who disbelieved﴾. He made those who disbelieved filthy and unclean, and purified him from them, because the company of the wicked and the mixing with the sinful are like filth on a garment. The meaning: He, exalted is He, rescues him from them, so He expressed his removal from them and his rescue by "purifying." He used the apparent noun "those who disbelieved" rather than a pronoun, indicating the cause of the filth and uncleanness, which is disbelief, as He said: ﴿The polytheists are only unclean﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28], and as came in the hadith: "The believer does not become unclean," so He made the cause of his purification faith.

It has been said: "purifying you from the harm of the disbelievers." It has been said: "from disbelief and immoralities." It has been said: "from what they said about you and your mother." It has been said: "and purifier of you," i.e., one who purifies through you the face of the people from the filth of disbelief and disobedience. Al-Raghib said: "taking you back" is taking you away from your desires, and "raising you to Me" is raising you away from your desires; it was not a physical raising, but an elevation of rank, even though he was raised to heaven. His purification from the disbelievers is his removal from among them. It has been said: rescuing him from their killing, because that is uncleanness from which God purified him. Abu Muslim said: rescue and purification are one, except that the word "purification" (tahhir) contains an elevation for the one addressed, just as witnessing and presence are one, but witnessing contains elevation. That is why God mentioned it regarding the believers, and mentioned presence and bringing forth regarding the disbelievers. (p-473)(p-474)

﴿And We shall make those who follow you﴾. The "you" (ka) is a pronoun for Jesus, like the preceding "you." It has been said: it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab). The statement ends. This view is not apparent. The meaning of "followed you" (ittaba'uka): in religion and law, and they are the Muslims, because they follow him in the basics of Islam, even if the laws differ.

﴿above those who disbelieved﴾: they will dominate them with proof, and in most circumstances with proof and with the sword. "Those who disbelieved" are those who denied him and lied about him among the Jews and Christians, said al-Zamakhshari, with an inversion of order in his speech.

So superiority here is by proof and evidence, said al-Hasan; or by might and protection, said Ibn Zayd. Thus they are above the Jews, so there will be no kingdom for them as there is for the Christians. The verse, according to this view, is informing of the humiliation and punishment of the Jews, that the Christians are above them in all regions of the earth until the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Zayd specified "the followers" and "the disbelievers," and made it a worldly ruling with no merit in it for the followers who are disbelievers; rather their being above the Jews is a punishment for the Jews. The majority said: "the followers" is general, so the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) enters into this, as Qatadah stated explicitly, and "the disbelievers" is general.

The verse implies informing Jesus that those who believe in him, as he loves, are above those who disbelieved, by proof, evidence, might, protection and victory. The statement of Ibn Jurayj appears to indicate that his followers are those in the time of his help, namely the disciples. God made them above the disbelievers because He honoured them and preserved for them a good remembrance among the righteous. So they are above them by proof and evidence, and by the good pleasure of God that appeared upon them.

It has been said: "above those who disbelieved" on the Day of Resurrection, in the Garden, as they are in the high chambers, while those who disbelieved are in the lowest depths of the Fire. It is summarized from the sayings of these exegetes that his followers are those who follow him in the basics of Islam, so this is general for Muslims and general for disbelievers; or his followers are those who claim adherence to his law even if they do not truly follow it, and the disbelievers are specifically the Jews; or his followers are the disciples, and the disbelievers are whoever disbelieved in him. As for superiority: it is either literal, and that is by the Garden and the Fire; or figurative, meaning by proof and evidence, in which case it is religious; or by might and victory, in which case it is worldly; or by both.

(p-475) ﴿To the Day of Resurrection﴾. The apparent view is that "ila" (to) is connected to an omitted element, which is the governing element of "fawq" (above), and it is the second object of "jā'il" (one who makes), since the meaning of "jā'il" here is "muṣayyir" (one who makes [them] become). So the meaning is: "being above them until the Day of Resurrection." This is based on the figurative (majāz) sense of "fawqiyyah" (superiority/above). But if "fawqiyyah" is taken literally, meaning being above them in Paradise, then "ila" is not connected to that omitted element, but rather to what preceded it: "mutawaffika" (causing you to die), or "rāfi'uka" (raising you), or "muṭahhiruka" (purifying you), since it can be connected to each one of them. As for "rāfi'uka" or "muṭahhiruka," it is clear. As for "mutawaffika," it is so according to some opinions. These four statements are in the utmost eloquence in their arrangement. He began first by informing Jesus that God would cause him to die, so those who plot against him have no power over him and no way to reach him. Then He gave him a second glad tidings of raising him to His heaven, dwelling with His angels there, and worshipping there, and the length of his life in worship of his Lord. Then third, by raising him to His heaven by purifying him from the disbelievers, thereby encompassing all of his time when He raised him and when He will send him down at the end of the world. So it is a great glad tidings for him that he is purified from the disbelievers, both first and last. Since "tawaffi" and "raf'" are each specific to a time, they were mentioned first. Since "tathhīr" is general, encompassing all times, it was mentioned after them. When He gave him these three glad tidings, which are attributes of himself, He gave him the glad tidings of the elevation of his followers above every disbeliever, so that his eye would be comforted and his heart gladdened.

Since this attribute of the superiority of his followers over the disbelievers is one of the attributes of his followers, it was placed after the three attributes that pertain to himself, for beginning with the attributes pertaining to the self is more important. Then this fourth attribute was followed up as a glad tiding about the state of his followers in this world, in order to complete his joy in what he was given and what his followers were given of good.

﴿Then to Me is your return, and I will judge between you concerning that over which you used to differ﴾. This is an information about the gathering and resurrection, and the meaning is: then to My judgment. In my view this is an instance of iltifat (shift of address); because the mention of his deniers, namely the Jews, and the mention of those who believed in him, namely the disciples (al-Hawariyyun), had preceded. Following that was His saying: ﴿And We will make those who followed you superior to those who disbelieved﴾, so He mentioned his followers and the disbelievers. Had it come in the pattern of this preceding statement, the construction would have been: "Then to Me is their return," but instead He shifted to address all of them, so that the information would be more forceful in warning and more stringent in restraining those who are restrained. Then He mentioned the expression "ilayya" (to Me) and the expression "fa-ahkum" (so I will judge) with the first-person pronoun, so that it would be known that the judge there is one from whom nothing is hidden; and He mentioned that He will judge concerning what they differed about regarding the matter of the prophets and following their laws, and He brought the judgment in general terms, then detailed the judged among them into believer and disbeliever, and mentioned the recompense of each one of them.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Your return" — the address is to Jesus, and what is intended is the information about the Resurrection and gathering; therefore the wording came general in terms of the matter itself, which does not concern Jesus alone, so He addressed him as one addresses a group, since he is one of them, and since they are intended in meaning. End of his words. But in my view the better position is that it is part of iltifat, as I have mentioned.

(p-٤٧٦)

﴿As for those who disbelieve﴾. It has been said: it is possible that this is specific, meaning those who disbelieved in you and denied your prophethood. The apparent meaning is generality. It is permissible for *alladhina* (the ones who) to be the subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical topic), and it is permissible for it to be in the accusative, governed by a verb that is omitted and explained by what follows it, in which case it falls under the construction called *al-ishtighal* (the grammatical construction in which a noun is preceded by a verb that is omitted and whose object-pronoun is attached to the noun, so that the noun is governed by the omitted verb).

﴿Then I will punish them with a severe punishment﴾. The punishment is described as severe because it is multiplied and increases. It has also been said: because its kinds differ.

﴿In this world﴾: by captivity, killing, the poll-tax (*jizya*), and humiliation. Whoever is not struck by any of these is in a state of apprehension, since he knows that Islam seeks him out.

(And the Hereafter): by the punishment of the Fire. This is a report from Him, exalted is He, about what He does to the disbeliever from the beginning of his affair in his worldly life to the end of his affair in his final abode.

﴿And they will have no helpers﴾. The explanation of this clause has already been given in this surah, so repeating it here is unnecessary.

﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will pay them their rewards in full﴾. He began first with the category of the disbelievers, because what precedes it, the mention of His judgment among them, is in the manner of threat and warning to the disbelievers and a report of their recompense, so it was appropriate to begin with them. Also, they are closer in mention, by His saying ﴿above those who disbelieved﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55], and because the discourse was with the Jews who disbelieved in Jesus and sought to kill him. Then He came second with the mention of the believers, and there He tied the punishment to mere disbelief, while here He tied the full payment of reward to belief and doing righteous deeds, as an alert to the degree of perfection in faith and an invitation to it. *Al-tawfiya* (full payment) is giving a thing in full without deficiency, and *al-ujur* (the rewards) are the recompense of deeds; He likened it to the worker whose wage is paid in full upon completion of his work. The full payment of rewards is the apportioning of ranks in Paradise according to deeds, as He, exalted is He, has arranged them. In the verse before it He said (﴿fa-U'adhdhibuhum﴾, "then I will punish them"), attributing the verb to the first-person singular speaker alone, in order to match His saying ﴿fa-ahkumu baynakum﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55], "then I will judge between you." In this verse He said *fa-yuwaffihim* with the *ya'* (third person), according to the reading of Hafs and Ruways; this is by way of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person), moving from the first-person speaker to the third-person absent, for variety in eloquence. The majority read *fa-nuwaffihim* with the *nun* indicating the speaker of exalted status, and did not use the *hamza* as in that verse, in order to differ in the report regarding the attribution of what He does to the disbeliever and to the believer, just as it differed in the verb. Also, because the believer who does righteous deeds is great before God, so the report about the one being recompensed was suited to the *nun* of greatness. It is also permissible for *alladhina amanu* (those who believed) to be the subject, and it is permissible for it to be in the accusative, governed by an omitted verb explained by what follows it, and that would fall under *al-ishtighal*, like His saying ﴿and as for Thamud, We guided them﴾ [Fussilat: 17], according to the one who put the *dal* in the accusative.

﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾. The explanation of something similar to this has already been given, namely His saying ﴿and if they turn away, then indeed Allah does not love the disbelievers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 32]. The Mu'tazila used this as evidence that He, exalted is He, does not will disbelief and sins, because whoever wills a thing loves it when that thing is among the acts; love and will differ only when they are connected to persons, so one says "I love Zayd" but one does not say "I will him"; but as for acts, they are one in them. So His saying "does not love" means "does not will the wrongdoing of the wrongdoers." This is how 'Abd al-Jabbar established it. But according to our companions (the Ash'arite scholars), love is an expression for willing to bestow good upon someone; so He, exalted is He, even if He wills the disbelief of the disbeliever, does not will to bestow reward upon him.

(p-٤٧٦) ﴿That is what We recite to you of the signs and the wise Reminder﴾. *Dhalika* (that) refers to what preceded of the report about Jesus, Zechariah, and others. *Natluhu* (We recite it) means: We relate it and mention it one thing after another. He attributed the recitation to Himself, even though the angel is the one who recites, as an honoring of him; He made the recitation of the one commanded the recitation of the One who commands. In *natluhu* there is an *iltifat* (shift of person), because before it there was a third-person pronoun in His saying "does not love." *Natluhu* means "We recited it," like His saying ﴿and they followed what the devils recited﴾ [Al-Baqara: 102]. It is also permissible for it to be understood in its apparent sense of the present, because the story of Jesus had not yet been concluded, and that would have the same meaning as this.

*Al-ayat* (the signs) here: the apparent meaning is that the verses of the Qur'an are meant by them. It is possible that the miracles and wondrous matters are meant, that is: We bring them these unseen matters from Our side and through Our recitation, while you are unlettered, who does not read and does not associate with the People of the Book, so they are signs of your prophethood. Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said: *al-dhikr* (the Reminder) is the Qur'an, and *al-hakim* (the wise) means the judge (*hakim*, one who judges); it came in the form of intensive emphasis, and it was described with the attribute of One who is the cause of it, which is Allah, exalted is He; or: it is as though it speaks with wisdom because of the abundance of its judgments. Al-Zajjaj said: because it is full of wisdom in its composition and arrangement. It is also permissible for it to mean *al-muhkam* (the perfected, firmly structured), as the majority said: it is made firm against the paths of flaw. From this is His saying ﴿whose verses have been perfected﴾ [Hud: 1]. In this case *fa'il* (*hakim*) would have the meaning of *maf'al* (*muhkam*), which is rare; from it come "I thickened the honey, so it is *mu'qad* and *'aqid*," and "I dedicated a horse to the way of Allah, so it is *muhbas* and *habis*."

It has also been said that *al-dhikr* here means the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*), from which all the books of Allah revealed to the prophets were copied. He reported that He sent down these narratives from what was written there.

*Dhalika* is the subject (*mubtada'*), and *natluhu* is the predicate (*khabar*). *Min al-ayat* is related to an omitted element, because it is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), that is: being among the signs. The *min* here is for partitive meaning (*tab'id*), because this recited matter is part of the signs and the Reminder. (p-٤٧٦)

﴿Then I will punish them with a severe punishment﴾. The punishment is described as severe because it is multiplied and increases. It has also been said: because its kinds differ.

﴿In this world﴾: by captivity, killing, the poll-tax (*jizya*), and humiliation. Whoever is not struck by any of these is in a state of apprehension, since he knows that Islam seeks him out.

(And the Hereafter): by the punishment of the Fire. This is a report from Him, exalted is He, about what He does to the disbeliever from the beginning of his affair in his worldly life to the end of his affair in his final abode.

﴿And they will have no helpers﴾. The explanation of this clause has already been given in this surah, so repeating it here is unnecessary.

﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, He will pay them their rewards in full﴾. He began first with the category of the disbelievers, because what precedes it, the mention of His judgment among them, is in the manner of threat and warning to the disbelievers and a report of their recompense, so it was appropriate to begin with them. Also, they are closer in mention, by His saying ﴿above those who disbelieved﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55], and because the discourse was with the Jews who disbelieved in Jesus and sought to kill him. Also, because the believer who does righteous deeds is great before God, so the report about the one being recompensed was suited to the *nun* of greatness. ﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾. So His saying "does not love" means "does not will the wrongdoing of the wrongdoers." This is how 'Abd al-Jabbar established it. But according to our companions (the Ash'arite scholars), love is an expression for willing to bestow good upon someone; so He, exalted is He, even if He wills the disbelief of the disbeliever, does not will to bestow reward upon him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 59–60 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus before God is like the likeness of Adam﴾. Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Suddi and others said: "The delegation of Najran (Wafd Najran) argued with the Prophet ﷺ about the matter of Jesus. They said: 'We have heard that you revile our companion and say that he is a servant.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'What harm does that do to Jesus? Yes, he is the servant of Allah, and His word which He cast to Mary, and a spirit from Him.' They said: 'Have you ever seen a human being come into existence without a father, or have you heard of such?' Then they left, and the verse was revealed. In some reports they said: 'If you are truthful, then show us the like of him,' and the verse was revealed."

Waki' narrated from Mubarak, from al-Hasan, who said: "The two monks of Najran came to him and he invited them to Islam. One of them said: 'We had already submitted before you.' He said: 'You are lying. Three things prevent you from Islam: your worship of the cross, your eating of pork, and your saying that Allah has a son.' They said: 'Who is the father of Jesus?' He did not hasten, until his Lord commanded him. Then He revealed: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus﴾."

The discussion of a structure similar to this one has already been given in the explanation of His words: ﴿Their likeness is like the likeness of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17].

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The matter and the strange condition of Jesus is like the matter of Adam, so 'mathal' is used with the meaning of 'matter' and 'condition'." This returns to the view of those who said that "mathal" here means "attribute," as in His words: ﴿the likeness of Paradise﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35]. In this view, the kaf in His words ﴿like the likeness of Adam﴾ retains its meaning of comparison.

Ibn Atiyyah said, regarding the view of those who said that "mathal" here means "attribute": "This, in my view, is an error and a weakness in understanding the speech. The meaning is that the likeness that souls and minds conceive of regarding Jesus is like what is conceived of regarding Adam, since all people agree that God Most High created him from earth without a male." Likewise, ﴿the likeness of Paradise﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35] is an expression for what is conceived of it. In this verse there is the validity of analogy (qiyas), i.e., when the matter of Adam is conceived, the permissibility of the matter of Jesus is analogically drawn from it. The kaf in ﴿like the likeness of Adam﴾ is a noun, according to what we have mentioned of the meaning. End of his words.

It does not appear to me that there is any difference between his statement and the statement of those who made "mathal" mean "matter and condition," or "attribute." In Ray al-Zam'an (it is said): "Mathal" means "attribute," and your saying "the attribute of Jesus is like the attribute of Adam" is a consistent statement. Most of the linguists and exegetes hold this view. Abu Ali al-Farisi opposed all of them and said: "'Mathal' in the sense of 'attribute' cannot be validated in the language; rather, 'mathal' means resemblance (shabah)." On this the derivations of the word revolve, and there is no meaning of descriptiveness in resemblance. A "mathal" is a saying which its speaker utters for a wise purpose, by which he likens matters and compares conditions. End of his words.

As for the one who made "mathal" here synonymous with "mithl" (likeness), like "shabah" and "shibh," he said: "It combined two particles of comparison as a way of emphasizing the resemblance, and as an alert to the greatness of its significance and rank." Some of these said: "The kaf is superfluous." Some said: "'Mathal' is superfluous." Some of them made "mithl" here of the kind of "daraba al-amthal" (coining parables). He said: "The Arabs coin parables to clarify what is hidden in meaning and subtle in explanation. When the secret of Jesus's birth without a father was hidden, because it contradicted what is known, God coined the parable with Adam, who is established in minds, and it is known that he was brought into existence without a father or a mother. Likewise the creation of Jesus without a father. There must be a meaningful sharing between the one by whom the parable is coined and the one for whom the parable is coined, in one respect or in several respects; it is not required that they share all attributes. The meaning in which Adam and Jesus share is that each of them was created without a father." Some scholars of knowledge said: "The sharing between Adam and Jesus is in fifteen attributes: in the act of bringing into being (takwin); in creation from the elements from which God composed the world; in servitude; in prophethood; in trial, Jesus with the Jews and Adam with Iblis; in their eating of food and drink; in need of God; in form; in being raised to heaven and sent down from it to earth; in inspiration: Adam sneezed and was inspired, so he said 'Praise be to Allah,' and Jesus was inspired when he was brought out of his mother's womb and said: ﴿Indeed, I am the servant of Allah﴾ [Maryam: 30]; in knowledge: He said: ﴿And He taught Adam the names﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31], and He said: ﴿and He will teach him the Book and wisdom﴾ [Al 'Imran: 48]; in the breathing of the spirit into both of them (﴿So I breathed into him of My spirit﴾), and ﴿So We breathed into her of Our spirit﴾ [al-Tahrim: 12]; in death; and in the loss of a father."

The meaning of ﴿عِنْدَ اللَّهِ﴾ ("before God") is: in the sight of the One who knows the reality of the matter and how it is; that is, the matter is thus regarding what is hidden from you, and you have not comprehended its essence. The element governing "ʿinda" is the element governing the kaf of comparison. This comparison is from one of the two sides, as has preceded, and it is existence without a father. The two are alike in that each of them was brought into being by God outside what is established and continuous in custom regarding the creation of a human being born of a male and a female, as He Most High said: ﴿O mankind, indeed We created you from male and female﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]. Existence without father or mother is stranger in custom than existence without a father. ﴿Then let us lay the curse of Allah upon the liars﴾. That is, each of us says: "May Allah curse the liar among us concerning the matter of Jesus." This indicates the permissibility of cursing whoever persists in his disbelief, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did curse the Jews. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: "The verse is evidence that al-Hasan and al-Husayn were the sons of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Abu Ahmad ibn 'Aylan said: "They were then of age (mukallaf), because mubahala (mutual imprecation) is not valid according to him except from one who is of age." [p. 480] The exegetes have lengthened their accounts with what they narrated about the story of the mubahala. Its substance is that he invited them to the mubahala, and he went out with al-Hasan, al-Husayn, Fatima and 'Ali to the appointed place. They refrained from it and agreed to remain upon their religion and to pay the jizya (poll tax). Their rabbis told them that if they engaged in mubahala they would be punished, and he (ﷺ) informed them that if they engaged in it they would be punished. The Christians' abstention from the mutual curse, given their knowledge of his prophethood, is a great witness to the truth of his prophethood.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: his invitation to the mubahala was only to distinguish the liar from himself and his opponent, and that is a matter specific to him and to the one who lies against him, so what is the meaning of including the sons and the women?"

I say: That is more emphatic in showing his confidence in his own state and his certainty of his truthfulness, since he ventured to expose himself to it, and his confidence in the lie of his opponent, to the point that he would destroy his opponent along with his beloved ones and his dear ones, with a total destruction if the mubahala were completed. He singled out the sons and the women because they are the dearest of the family and the closest to the hearts. A man may often ransom them with his own self and fight in their defense until he is killed. For this reason they used to drive their camel-litters (zaʿa'in) with themselves in wars, so that they would prevent them from fleeing, and they called those who defend them with their lives "the protectors of the realities" (hummat al-haqa'iq). He mentioned them before the selves (anfus) in the text to draw attention to the nobility of their position and the nearness of their rank, and to indicate that they are preferred over the selves, to be ransomed by them. In this there is evidence, with nothing stronger than it, of the excellence of the People of the Cloak, upon them be peace. And in it is a clear proof of the truth of the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), because no one, whether from among the agreeing or the opposing, saw that they responded to that. End of his words.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "What the narrators related, that they abandoned the mutual curse out of knowledge of his prophethood, is a stronger argument for us against all the disbelievers, and more fitting to the state of Muhammad (ﷺ). The invocation of the women and the sons for the mutual curse is more moving to the souls and more likely to call upon Allah's mercy, or His wrath upon the falsifiers. The apparent meaning of the command is that the Prophet (ﷺ) brought them what is specific to him. Had they resolved, he would have summoned the believers with their sons and their women. It is possible that he would have been content with himself and his close family alone." End.

In the verse there is evidence of the use of a miracle-challenge (muzaharah bi-tariq al-i'jaz) against one who claims falsehood after the proof has become clear, by way of analogy. Among the most strange of the arguments is what Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Himsi used as evidence from the verse, and he was a theologian according to the path of the Twelver Shi'a (al-Ithna 'Ashariyya). [He argued] that 'Ali is more excellent than all the prophets except Muhammad (ﷺ). He said: "That is because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and our selves and your selves﴾ does not mean the self of Muhammad (ﷺ), since a person does not invite his own self; rather the intended one is other than him. They agreed that the one who is other than him is 'Ali. The verse therefore indicates that his self is the self of the Messenger, and it is not possible that it be his very self, so what is meant is its likeness. That requires generality, except that the excellence of prophethood was excluded in respect of the right of prophethood because of the existence of evidence. Consensus indicates that he (ﷺ) was more excellent than all other prophets, so it follows that 'Ali is likewise."

He said: "What confirms this is the hadith transmitted from him, reported by both those who agree and those who disagree: 'Whoever wishes to see Adam in his knowledge, Noah in his obedience, Abraham in his forbearance, Moses in his people, and Jesus in his purity, let him look at 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.' This indicates that there was gathered in him what was dispersed among them."

He said: "That indicates that he is more excellent than all the prophets and the Companions."

Al-Razi replied: "The consensus is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) is more excellent than one who is not a prophet, and 'Ali was not a prophet, so it is necessary to affirm with certainty that he is excluded in respect of all the prophets."

Al-Razi also said: "The argument of al-Himsi is corrupt in several respects. Among them is his saying that a person does not invite his own self. Rather, it is permissible for a person to invite his own self; the Arabs say, 'I invited myself to such-and-such, but it did not answer me.' This is what Abu 'Ali calls tajrid (abstraction, i.e., speaking of oneself as if another).

"Among them is his saying: 'They agreed that the one who is other than him is 'Ali.' This is not correct, by the evidence of the sayings that were brought in the meaning of His words ﴿and our selves﴾.

"Among them is his saying: 'So his self is like his self.' Likeness does not require that it be in all things; it suffices that there be likeness in some respect. This is what the people of the language (ahl al-lugha) hold, not what the theologians (mutakallimun) say, that likeness must be in all the attributes of the self. That is a technical convention of theirs, not a linguistic usage. On this basis, likeness in one single attribute suffices, which is that he is from the Banu Hashim. The Arabs say, 'This is from ourselves,' meaning from our tribe.

"As for the hadith he used as evidence, it is fabricated (mawdu') with no basis. This whim (nazghah) to which this al-Himsi went, that 'Ali is more excellent than the prophets, peace be upon them, other than Muhammad (ﷺ), was seized upon by some who affiliate with the discourse of the Sufis, and they widened the scope of it. They claimed that the saint (wali) is more excellent than the prophet, and they did not restrict that to one saint, as al-Himsi restricted it, but claimed that the rank of sainthood which has no prophethood with it is more excellent than the rank of prophethood. He said: 'Because the saint takes from Allah without an intermediary, while the prophet takes from Allah through an intermediary, and whoever takes without an intermediary is more excellent than whoever takes through one.' This doctrine opposes the doctrines of the People of Islam. We seek refuge in Allah from that. No one is more lying than one who claims that the saint takes from Allah without an intermediary. The believer shudders at hearing this slander. One whom I do not accuse related to me, concerning one of those who claim affiliation to the righteous, that a book was seen in his hand which he was reading, and he was asked about it. He said: 'In it is what I took from the Messenger of Allah, and in it is what I took from Allah orally, or He spoke to me with it'—the doubt is from the listener. Look at the audacity of this liar against Allah, in that he claimed the station of one whom Allah spoke to, like Moses and Muhammad, upon them both be prayer and peace, and upon all the prophets."

It has been said: In this verse there are kinds of eloquence (balagha). Among them is the attribution of the verb to other than its doer, namely ﴿when Allah said: O Jesus﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55], whereas Allah did not speak to him directly with that, but through the reporting of Jibril or another of the angels. There is metaphor (isti'ara) in ﴿taking you in full﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55] and in ﴿above those who disbelieved﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55]. There is detailing of what was stated in summary in ﴿to Me is your return, and I will judge﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55] by His saying: "As for ... and as for ...". There is the addition for the increase of meaning in ﴿from helpers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 56], or the "likeness" in His saying ﴿the likeness of Jesus﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. There is figurative usage (tajawwuz) by placing the present for the past in His saying ﴿We recite it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 58] and in ﴿then he is﴾, and by joining two particles of comparison according to one opinion in ﴿like the likeness of Adam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. There is figurative usage by naming a thing with the name of its origin in ﴿created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. There is address to a specific person while the intended meaning is another, in ﴿so do not be among the doubters﴾ [Al 'Imran: 60]. The general is intended in the sense of the particular in ﴿we will call our sons﴾ and the verse, and there is figurative usage by placing the cousin in the position of the self according to the most well-known opinions, and omission in many places.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 62:

﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative.﴾ This is a report from Allah, a firm and emphatic affirmation, by which a separation is made between the disputants. The reference (ishara) is to the Qur'an according to the view of the majority (al-jumhur). The apparent meaning, however, is that it refers to what preceded of the reports about ʿIsa (Jesus), and his being created without a father. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd, and others. That is: this is the truth, not what the Christians claim about him, that he is God or the Son of God, nor what the Jews claim about him. (p-482) It has also been said that this refers to what follows it, namely His words ﴿There is no god except Allah﴾. This view is weak, because this sentence is not a narrative (qasas), and because of the presence of the conjunction particle in His words "wa ma" (and no). Some have said: unless by "qasas" one means "khabar" (report), in which case it is valid, and the sense would be: "Indeed the true report is that there is no god except Allah." End of quote. But what prevents this interpretation is the presence of the conjunctive waw and the lam in "lahuwa," which entered upon the separator (fasl). "Al-qasas" is the predicate of "inna," "al-haqq" is its adjective, and "al-qasas" is a verbal noun (masdar), or a verb in the sense of a passive participle, meaning "al-maqsus" (the narrated), like "al-qabd" in the sense of "al-maqbud." It is also permissible that "huwa" be the subject (mubtada') and "al-qasas" its predicate, with the whole clause in the position of the predicate of "inna." The description of the narrative as "true" is a reference to the false narrative brought by the Christians of Najran and others concerning the matter of ʿIsa and his divinity.

﴿There is no god except Allah﴾. That is: the one exclusively deserving divinity is Allah alone. In this is a refutation of the Dualists (al-thanawiyya), the Christians, and everyone who claims a god other than Allah.

"Min" is additional (za'ida), for the generalization of the genus (li-istighraq al-jins). "Ilah" is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, and "Allah" is a substitute (badal) for it according to its position (ʿala al-mawdi'), and substitution according to its wording (ʿala al-lafz) is not permissible, because it would necessitate the addition of "min" in an obligatory position. In Arabic, in this type of construction, it is permissible to put in the accusative what follows "illa," as in "ma min shuja'in illa Zaydan" (there is no brave man except Zayd). The accusative was not read in this verse, although the accusative as an exception (istithna') is permissible in Arabic.

﴿And indeed Allah is the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾. This is a reference to the two attributes of divinity: power, arising from dominance, so nothing can resist Him, and knowledge, expressed by wisdom in what He made, and perfection in what He originated, so nothing is hidden from Him. These two attributes are denied of ʿIsa. "Lahuwa" may be parsed in the same ways as "lahuwa al-qasas," and the purpose of the separator (fasl) has been mentioned previously.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 63:

﴿Then if they turn away, indeed Allah is All-Knowing of the corrupters.﴾ Muqatil said: "Then if they turn away" means: turn away from the mula'anah (the mutual imprecation). Al-Zajjaj said: from the clarification (bayan) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made clear. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: from acknowledging the Oneness (wahdaniyyah) and from declaring Allah free of having a consort or offspring. Al-Mursi said: from this reminder (dhikr). And it was said: from faith (iman).

As for "tawallaw" (they turn away): it is either a past or a present verb whose initial ta' has been elided (the original form being "tatawallaw"). The apparent response of the conditional clause is the sentence ﴿indeed Allah is All-Knowing of the corruptors﴾. The meaning is: what follows from His knowledge of the corruptors, namely His punishment of them. He expressed the punishment by the knowledge from which their punishment arises, and He drew attention to the cause that necessitates punishment, which is corruption (ifsad). For this reason He used the apparent noun rather than a pronoun, and He used it in the plural, to indicate a general scope that includes those who turned away and others besides them, and because it is the end of a verse. It also indicates that their turning away is corruption of the utmost kind.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 64:

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you."﴾ It was revealed concerning the delegation of Najran; this is what al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said. Ibn Zayd said: When the people of Najran refused what they were invited to of mubahala (mutual imprecation), they were invited to something easier than that, which is "the equitable word." Ibn 'Abbas said: It was revealed concerning the priests and monks. The Prophet ﷺ sent it to Ja'far and his companions in Abyssinia, and Ja'far recited it while the Negus was sitting with the nobles of Abyssinia. Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Ibn Jurayj said: It concerns the Jews of Madinah, who are the ones who disputed about Abraham. It has also been said: It was revealed concerning the Jews and the Christians, who said: "O Muhammad, you want nothing from us except that we say about you what the Jews said about 'Uzayr?"

The expression "O People of the Scripture" encompasses everyone who was given a Scripture, and for this reason the Messenger of Allah ﷺ invited the Jews with this verse. The closer view, however, is to restrict it to the Christians, because the proof was directed at them and the mutual imprecation was with them. He addressed them as "O People of the Scripture" to stir them to listen to what is conveyed to them, and to alert them that whoever is a people of Scripture from Allah ought to follow the Book of Allah. When he had silenced them with clear proofs and they did not submit, and he invited them to mubahala and they refused, he turned to a kind of gentleness, which is inviting them to a word in which there is fairness between them. Abu al-Sammal read "kalmatin" like "darbatin," and "kilmatin" like "sidratin." This was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿confirming a word﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39]. The "kalimah" is what is explained by what follows. Abu al-'Aliyah said: "(There is no god but Allah)," and this is an explanation of the meaning. He expressed "kalimah" as "kalimat" (words) because the Arabs may use "kalimah" for speech, and al-Zajjaj went to this view, either by placing the singular in the position of the plural, as the poet said:

*Therein are the carcasses of the exhausted; as for their bones, they are white, and as for their skins, they are hard.*

Or because the words are linked to one another, so they are in the status of a single word: if one part of it is defective, the word is defective, since the word of tawhid, "There is no god but Allah," consists of words in which the intended attribution, restricting divinity to Allah, is not complete except by their totality.

Al-Jumhur read "sawa'in" in the genitive, as an adjective. Al-Hasan read "sawa'an" in the accusative, and al-Hufi and al-Zamakhshari construed it as a verbal noun. Al-Zamakhshari said: With the meaning "they became equal in equality," so "sawa'in" means "istiwa'" (equality). It may also be in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier of "kalimah," even though it is indefinite, and Sibawayh permitted this and analogized it. The circumstantial and the attributive meet in meaning, whereas the verbal noun requires a supplied verb, and an interpretation of "sawa'" as "istiwa'." The more common usage is "sawa'" in the sense of the active participle, i.e., "mustawin" (equal). The discussion of "sawa'" was already given at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah. Qatadah, al-Rabi' and al-Zajjaj said: Here "sawa'" means justice, and it is from "istawa al-shay'" (the thing became even). Zuhayr said:

*Show me a plan in which there is no injustice, in which equity makes us even.*

The meaning is: to a word that is just between us and you. Abu 'Ubaydah said: The Arabs say: "So-and-so has invited you to sawa', so accept from him." In the Codex of 'Abdullah: "to a word of justice between us and you." Ibn 'Abbas said: That is, a straight word, i.e., an upright one. It has also been said: to a word of purpose. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: What I say about the word "sawa'" is that it should be explained by a particular explanation specific to this place, namely that He invited them to meanings in which all people are equal, young and old, and the practice of those invited was that some of them took others as lords, so they were not in a state of equality. So He invited them with this verse to what souls are familiar with as a right in which people do not differ, so "sawa'" according to this interpretation is like your saying to another: "This is my partner in property, equal between me and him." The difference between this explanation and the explanation of the word as justice is that if you invited a captive of yours to embrace Islam or have his neck struck, you would have invited him to the "sawa'" which is justice. On this measure the word "sawa'" came in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then throw back to them on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal: 58], according to some interpretations. And if you invited your captive to believe so that he would become free, sharing your living with you, you would have invited him to the "sawa'" which is equality of condition as I have explained. The word in every interpretation carries the meaning of justice, but I have not seen any of the predecessors who held that the word includes the meaning of intending equality of condition, though it is good in my view, because souls are familiar with it, and Allah is the granter of success to what is right. End of his words; it is an excess with no real benefit beneath it. The apparent view is that the adverbial phrase is accusative governed by "sawa'."

"That we not worship except Allah": the position of "an" is genitive as an apposition to "kalimah," an appositive of one thing to another. It may also be in the nominative position as the predicate of a deleted subject, i.e., "it is that we not worship except Allah." They also permitted that the sentence is complete at His saying "sawa'," and that "an la na'bud" is nominative by being the subject, with the predicate being "bayننا wa bayنكم" (between us and you). They said: The clause is an attribute of "kalimah." This is an error, since the clause lacks a connecting pronoun linking it to the modified noun. They also permitted that "an la na'bud" be nominative by the adverbial phrase, and this is valid only according to the view of al-Akhfash and the Kufans, who permitted the adverb to operate without a preceding head, whereas the Basrans prohibit this. 'Ali ibn 'Isa permitted that the estimation be: "to a word, equal between us and you, in which is the refraining from worshipping other than Allah." According to this, "an la na'bud" is in the nominative position as the agent of "sawa'," except that this involves omitting the connecting pronoun, namely "fiha" (in it), and this is weak.

The meaning is: that we single out Allah alone for worship, and do not associate anything with Him, i.e., do not make for Him a partner. "Shay'an" may be a direct object, or it may be a verbal noun, i.e., "something of associating." The verb is in the context of negation, so it generalizes its complements: object, verbal noun, time, place, and manner.

(p-484) ﴿And that some of us do not take others as lords besides Allah﴾, i.e., we do not take them as lords, so that we believe in their divinity and worship them on that basis, like 'Uzayr and 'Isa. This was said by Muqatil, al-Zajjaj and 'Ikrimah.

It has been said concerning it: it is that some of them prostrate to others; or that we do not obey the bishops and leaders in what they command of disbelief and sins, and make their obedience a law. This was said by Ibn Jurayj, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and also the Messiah son of Mary﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31]. And from 'Adi ibn Hatim: "We did not worship them, O Messenger of Allah. He said: 'Did they not make lawful for you and make unlawful, and you followed their word?' He said: Yes. He said: 'That is it.'" In His saying "some of us to some" there is a subtle indication, namely that being a partner in humanity contradicts divinity, since it is like it in humanity, and what is like you cannot be a god. If they regarded following one who shares their humanity as improbable, for the sake of exclusivity in prophethood, in their saying: ﴿You are only human like us﴾ [Ibrahim: 10], ﴿We are only human like you﴾ [Ibrahim: 11], ﴿Shall we believe two humans like us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 47], then ascribing divinity to them should be even more improbable for them. These verbs governed by the negative particle are close in meaning, each reinforcing the other, since the exclusivity of worship to Allah entails the negation of association and the negation of taking lords besides Allah. But the position calls for emphasis, elaboration and extension of speech, because they were excessive in holding fast to worship other than Allah, so the emphasis in negating that was fitting. The Christians combined all three acts: they worshipped 'Isa, associated partners with Him by saying "third of three," and took their rabbis as lords in obedience to them in permitting and forbidding, and in prostrating to them.

Al-Tabari said: In His saying ﴿lords besides Allah﴾, they placed them in the station of their Lord in accepting prohibition and permission for what Allah had neither forbidden nor permitted. This indicates the falsity of the view of mere istihsan (juristic preference) that is not based on a legal proof, such as estimations without basis, and the view that the followers must accept the word of the Imam without a legal basis being shown, as the Rafidah held. End of his words. There is some abridgment in it.

﴿Then if they turn away, say: "Bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ That is: if they turn away from the equitable word, then call them to witness that you are submitting to it. This is an emphasis in disavowing them, i.e., if you turn away from this word, then we are accepting it and obeying. He expressed knowledge by testimony as an emphasis, since that moves it from the realm of the intelligible to the realm of the observed, which is what is present to the senses. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is a command to inform them of your opposition and to confront them with it, and to call them to witness it, in the sense of rebuke and threat, i.e., you will see, O turners-away, what the outcome of your turning away will be. End of his words.

Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, the proof has become binding upon you, so you must acknowledge and concede that we are Muslims in preference to you, as the victor says to the vanquished in a debate or a contest or other, "Acknowledge that I am the victor, and concede victory to me." It may also be from the mode of allusion, and its meaning: "Bear witness and acknowledge that you are disbelievers, since you have turned away from the truth after its manifestation." End of his words. This verse is in the letter that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent with Dihyah to the great one of Busra, who passed it to Heraclius.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 65:

﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him? Will you not then use your reason?﴾ It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and others that the Jews said, "Abraham was a Jew," and the Christians said, "He was a Christian." So God revealed it, rebuking them. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan said: Abraham had asked God to grant him a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations, and God answered his supplication, so that every sect claimed him.

And: "mā" in His saying "li-mā" is an interrogative particle whose alif was dropped together with the preposition, and there is a grammatical reason for this that is mentioned in the grammar books. The "lām" is connected to "tuḥājjūna" (you argue). The meaning of this interrogation is denial. The meaning of "in Abraham" is: in his law (sharīʿa) and his religion, and what he was upon. The meaning of "muḥājjah" (argumentation) is that each of the two groups claims that he belongs to them, and they dispute about that. God refuted this claim by pointing out that the law of the Jews and the Christians is later than Abraham, while he came before both of them, and it is impossible to attribute the earlier to the later. Because the corruption of this claim is evident, He said: ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ That is, this is the speech of one who does not reason, since reason prevents such a thing.

It is also not fitting that he should be in agreement with them, neither in beliefs nor in rulings. As for beliefs, they worship ʿĪsā and claim that he is God, or the son of God, or the third of three. And the Jews claim that ʿUzayr is the son of God, though neither of these two existed in the time of Abraham.

As for rulings, the Torah and the Gospel contain rulings that contradict the rulings upon which the law of Abraham was based. Among that is His saying: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who judaized, We forbade them good things which had been made lawful for them﴾ [al-Nisāʾ: 160], and His saying: ﴿The Sabbath was only enjoined upon those who differed concerning it﴾ [al-Naḥl: 124], and other such things. So it is impossible that Abraham was upon a religion that came into being long after him, after lengthy periods of time. The historians mention that between Abraham and Moses there were a thousand years, and between him and Jesus two thousand. Abu Salih related from Ibn ʿAbbas that between Abraham and Moses there were five hundred and seventy-five years, and between Moses and Jesus there were one thousand six hundred and thirty-two years.

Ibn Ishaq said: Between Abraham and Moses there were five hundred and sixty-five years, and between Moses and Jesus there were one thousand nine hundred and twenty-five years. The "wāw" in ﴿and the Torah was not revealed﴾ is for conjoining one sentence to another, so they mentioned. What appears to be the case is that it is for the state (ḥāl), as it is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why do you disbelieve in the signs of God while you witness [them]?﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 70], and His saying ﴿Why do you mix truth with falsehood?﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 71], then He said ﴿while you know﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 71], and His saying: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ [al-Baqara: 28]. He denounced their claim that Abraham was upon the law of the Jews or the Christians, while the state is that their two laws are later than him in existence, so how could he be upon them while he preceded them?

As for ḥanīfiyya (uprightness) and Islam, they are among the attributes that belong to every adherent of a true religion. For this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the religion with God is Islam﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 19], since the ḥanīf is the one who inclines toward the truth, and the Muslim is the one who submits to the truth. The Qur'an has informed us that Abraham was a ḥanīf and a Muslim. In His saying: ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ there is a rebuke for the impossibility of their statement, and an alert to what reveals their error and their obstinacy.

**The people who have knowledge about it** refers to their religion, which they found in their books and whose authenticity was established for them. **That about which they have no knowledge** refers to the matter and religion of Abraham, which is not present in their books, and which their prophets did not bring to them, nor did they witness it so as to know it. This is the view of Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Rabi', and others. It is also the apparent meaning, given the narratives about Abraham that surround it before and after. Ibn 'Atiyya attributed this view to al-Tabari and said: "He overlooked that where this is the case, there is no need to argue with them about it, because they would find it with Muhammad ﷺ as it was there, in its true form."

It was also said: **That about which they have knowledge** refers to the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, because they found his description in their books, but they argued with falsehood. **That about which they have no knowledge** refers to the matter of Abraham. The apparent meaning of ﴿about which you have knowledge﴾ is the affirmation of knowledge for them. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "About which you have knowledge, according to your claim." The meaning is: about what resembles your claim, and the rational proof would refute you. Qatada also said: "You argued about what you witnessed and saw, so why do you argue about what you have not witnessed and do not know?" Al-Razi said: ﴿Here you are, these are the ones...﴾ (the verse), meaning: you claimed that the law of the Torah and the Gospel contradicts the law of the Qur'an, so how can you argue about what you have no knowledge of? This is their claim that the law of Abraham contradicts the law of Muhammad ﷺ. It is possible that His saying ﴿about which you have knowledge﴾ means: you claim knowledge of it, not that He actually described them as having knowledge. So how can they argue about what they have absolutely no knowledge of?

The Kufans, Ibn 'Amir, and al-Bazzi read ﴿ha antum﴾ with an alif after the hā' and the hamzah after it fully articulated (*antum*, with a clear hamzah). Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ya'qub read it with a hā' followed by an alif and then a hamzah that is softened to a state between hamzah and alif (*bayn bayn*). Some transmitted the hamzah as a pure alif for Warsh. *Ha* is used for alerting the listener (*tanbih*), since it frequently occurs with the nominative pronouns when they are separated from the demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*), where there is no question. Its original position is to come directly before the demonstrative, but the alerting particle was given importance and placed first. An example is the Arabs' saying: *ha ana dha qa'iman* ("here I am standing"), *ha anta dha taṣnau kadha* ("here you are, doing such and such"), and *ha huwa dha qa'iman* ("here he is standing"). Here the address does not alert the one addressed to the existence of his essence, but rather alerts him to a state he has neglected because of his preoccupation with what he has become involved in. That state is that they argued about what they do not know, and the Torah and the Gospel did not mention it. So it is as if you were saying to them: "Suppose you argue about what you claim was mentioned in the earlier books of God; why do you argue about what is not so?" The sentence is then declarative (*khabariyya*), which is the original form, since argument did indeed proceed from them about what they knew. For this reason He denounced them after their argument about what they had no knowledge of. On this view, *ha* has been repeated with the demonstrative for emphasis. In Qunbul's reading, he dropped the alif of *ha*, just as someone who pauses on *ayyuhā al-thaqalān* ("O you two burdens") says *ayyuh* with a sukun. Dropping it is not analogically strong.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash said: the original form of *ha antum* is *a-antum* (an interrogative). The first hamzah, which is the interrogative particle, was replaced with a *hā'*, because it is its sibling. Al-Nahhas found this preferable. Replacing hamzah with hā' is attested in certain words but is not analogically productive. It is not heard in the interrogative hamzah; nothing is preserved from their speech like *hatadribu zaydan* ("are you hitting Zayd?") except in a rare line of verse in which *ha* replaces the interrogative hamzah, namely:

*"Her companions came and said: 'This is the one who gave love to others besides us and deprived us.'"*

Then separating the hā' substituted for the interrogative hamzah from the hamzah of *antum* does not fit, because separation is only done to avoid the heaviness of two hamzahs together. Here the heaviness has already been removed by replacing the first with a hā'. Do you not see that they dropped the hamzah in such words as *uriquhu* ("I pour it out"), whose original form is *a-uriquhu?* When they replaced it with hā', they did not drop it; rather they said *ahriquhu*. They have explained Qunbul's reading as the hā' being a substitute for the interrogative hamzah because it is a hā' with no alif after it. On this view, whoever maintains the alif takes it that there is a separation between the hā' substituted for the interrogative hamzah and the hamzah of *antum*, treating the substitute in the separation as if it were the thing substituted for. The interrogative on this view means astonishment at their foolishness. As for the one who softens the hamzah, it is because it is a hamzah after an alif, following their manner of softening it in *hayya'ahu* ("he prepared it"). Its full articulation is the original form. Its replacement with an alif has already been discussed in the explanation of His words ﴿Whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:6].

*Antum* is the subject (*mubtada'*), and *ha'ula'* is the predicate (*khabar*). *Hajajtum* is a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*), like the saying *ha anta dha qa'iman*. It is among the states that cannot be dispensed with, like His saying ﴿Then you are these, killing one another﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:85], according to the best analysis of its grammatical structure. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Antum* is the subject, *ha'ula'* is its predicate, and *hajajtum* is a new sentence explaining the first sentence. That is: you are these foolish individuals. The explanation of your foolishness and the weakness of your minds is that you argued about what you have knowledge of from what the Torah and the Gospel recite, so why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of and no mention of in your two books, namely the religion of Abraham?" End of quote.

They permitted *ha'ula'* to be a substitute (*badal*) or an explicative apposition (*'atf bayan*), with *hajajtum* as the predicate. They also permitted *ha'ula'* to be a relative pronoun meaning *alladhi* ("the one who"), which is the predicate of the subject, or *hajajtum* as its relative clause (*sila*). This is the view of the Kufans. They also permitted it to be a vocative, meaning *ya ha'ula'* ("O these"), with the vocative particle omitted. Omitting the vocative particle before a demonstrative is not permitted according to the Basrans, but is permitted according to the Kufans. Its omission occurs in poetry, though rarely, like the saying of a man of Tayy:

*"Indeed, those who described my people to them... so they are: 'Hold fast to this, and you will find the one who opposes you humiliated.'"*

And another said:

*"Let not these people deceive you with an inclination toward peace; it is a deception."*

He meant: "O this man, hold fast," and "O these people."

﴿And God knows, while you do not know﴾, meaning: God knows the religion of Abraham about which you argued, and how the laws stand in agreement and disagreement, while you do not know that. This is an emphasis of what came before, namely the denial of their knowledge concerning Abraham's matter. In His saying ﴿And God knows﴾ there is a call to them to listen, just as you say to someone you are informing about something he does not know: "Listen, for I know what you do not know."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 67:

﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a hanif, a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists.﴾ God, exalted is He, informed of Abraham's freedom from these religions, and began with the negation of Judaism because the law of the Jews is older than the law of the Christians. He repeated *lā* (neither/nor) not for emphasis of the negation regarding each of the two religions. Then He corrected [the negation] with a statement of what Abraham was upon, in His words ﴿but he was a hanif, a Muslim﴾. The particle *lākin* (but) is used here in its best position, since it falls between two opposites with respect to the belief in truth and falsehood. Because the discourse was with the Jews and the Christians, the correction came after the mention of the negation regarding their laws. Then He negated, by way of completion, to disassociate him from all other religions, that he was among the *mushrikūn* (polytheists), namely the worshippers of idols, such as the Arabs who used to claim that they were upon the religion of Abraham, and such as the Magians (*majūs*), the worshippers of fire, and the Sabians (*ṣābiʾa*), the worshippers of the stars. He did not specify their details, because *shirk* (associationism) encompasses them.

It has been said: by the *mushrikūn* He meant the Jews and the Christians, because they associated with Him ʿUzayr and the Messiah. In that case this clause is an emphasis of what came before it, His words ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾. And the phrase *min al-mushrikīn* (of the polytheists) came, rather than *wa-mā kāna mushrikan* (and he was not a polytheist), so that it would correspond to the negation before it, because it is the *raʾs āya* (the end of the verse, i.e., the final word of the verse that forms its rhyme).

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: He negated from him Judaism, Christianity, and *shirk*, which is the worship of idols. And included in that is the *shirk* that Judaism and Christianity contain. The arrangement of the negation came in the utmost eloquence: He negated the very communities (*milal*), then affirmed the good condition, then negated with a negation through which He made clear that those communities contain this corruption, which is *shirk*. This is like your saying: "I did not take any wealth for you, rather I guarded it, and I was not a thief," so you have negated the worst of what could be in the taking. The end of his words.

Summarizing what has preceded: regarding His words ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾, there are three opinions. The first: the polytheists are the worshippers of idols, fire, and stars. The second: they are the Jews and the Christians. The third: they are the worshippers of idols, together with the Jews and the Christians.

ʿAbd al-Jabbar said: the meaning of ﴿he was not a Jew nor a Christian﴾ is that he was not upon the religion that these disputants adhere to, but he was upon the way of the religion that the Muslims adhere to. The intent is not that the laws of Moses and Jesus were not sound. ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā said: Abraham should not be described as a Jew or a Christian, because these are terms of blame, since they are specific to two misguided sects, and they are two paths distorted from the religion of Moses and Jesus. His being a Muslim does not necessitate that he was upon the law of Muhammad (ﷺ), but rather he was upon the way of Islam.

The *ḥanīf* is a name for one who faces the Kaaba in his prayer, makes the pilgrimage to it, sacrifices, and circumcises. Then whoever was upon the religion of Abraham was called a *ḥanīf*. The end.

In the hadith of Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl: he set out to Syria seeking the religion, and he met a scholar of the Jews, then a scholar of the Christians.
