The Jewish one said to him: "You will not be upon our religion until you take your share of the wrath of God." The Christian said to him: "You will not be upon our religion until you take your share of the curse of God." Zayd said: "I only flee from the wrath of God and from His curse. So will you two direct me to a religion in which there is none of this?" They said: "We do not know of one except that you be a *ḥanīf*." He said: "And what is the *ḥanīf*?" They said: "The religion of Abraham. He was neither a Jew nor a Christian, and he did not worship anyone but God alone." So Zayd kept raising his hands to the sky and said: "O God, I call You to witness that I am upon the religion of Abraham."

Al-Razi said, in summary: if the negation concerns the fundamentals (*uṣūl*), then it is in agreement with the Jews and Christians of the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), because they had changed, and said: "The Messiah is the son of God," and "ʿUzayr is the son of God." It is not regarding the fundamentals upon which the Jews and Christians were, who were upon what Moses and Jesus brought, and all the prophets agree in the fundamentals. If the negation concerns the subsidiary matters (*furūʿ*), then it is because God abrogated the law of Abraham by the law of Moses and Jesus. As for his agreement with the law of Muhammad (ﷺ), if it is in the fundamentals then it is evident, and if it is in the subsidiary matters then the agreement is in the majority, and if he differed in the minority, that does not detract from the agreement.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 68:**

﴿Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him, and this Prophet and those who believe. And Allah is the Ally of the believers.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbās said: The leaders of the Jews said, "By Allah, O Muhammad, you know that we are more entitled than you and others to the religion of Abraham, and that he was a Jew. What prevents you is only envy." So this was revealed. A lengthy report is also narrated about the gathering of Jaʿfar and his companions, and ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and his companions, before the Najāshī (the Negus). In it, the Najāshī said, "There is no *dahwara* (harm or ruin) today upon the party of Abraham," meaning: no fear and no consequence. ʿAmr said, "Who is the party of Abraham?" The Najāshī said, "These men and their leader," meaning Jaʿfar and his companions. And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every prophet has allies among the prophets, and my ally among them is my father and the friend of my Lord, Abraham." Then he recited this verse.

The meaning of *awlā al-nās* ("the most entitled of people") is: those most specially associated with him and closest to him, from *al-walī*, which is closeness. *Alladhīna ittabaʿūhu* ("those who followed him") includes everyone who followed him in his own time and beyond it, so it includes his followers in the periods of interval (*fatarāt*). By "followers" is meant those who followed his law (*sharīʿa*).

ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā said: "most worthy of his support," that is, with aid and with proof. Whoever followed him in his time supported him with aid against those who opposed him. Muhammad and the believers supported him with proof, by showing that he was truthful and free from defamations. *Wa-hādhā al-nabiyy* ("and this Prophet") refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), and he was singled out from among all who followed him for his distinction and excellence, as in His words: ﴿Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqara: 98] (i.e., whoever is an enemy to Gabriel and Michael, Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers).

*Wa-alladhīna āmanū* ("and those who believe"): it is said they are the believers of the community of Muhammad, and they were also singled out for mention to honor them, since they are the best of the followers of the messengers, just as their Messenger is the best of the messengers. It is also said that they are the believers in every age. *Wa-hādhā al-nabiyy* is coordinated (*ʿuṭifa*) with the predicate of *inna*. As for one who parsed it as (*wa-hādhā al-nabiyy wa-alladhīna āmanū maʿahu*) as a subject (*mubtadaʾ*), with the predicate being "they are the ones who follow him," then he has burdened the sentence with an implied element (*iḍmār*) for which there is no necessity.

It was also read *wa-hādhā al-nabiyya* with a *naṣb* (accusative), coordinated with the *hāʾ* in *ittabaʿūhu*, so that it is "followed" (*mutabaʿan*) and not "following" (*mutabiʿan*). The meaning is: the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him and Muhammad, may Allah bless both of them and grant them peace. Then *wa-alladhīna āmanū* is coordinated with the predicate of *inna*, so it is in the nominative position.

It was also read *wa-hādhā al-nabiyyi* with a *jarr* (genitive). It was explained that it is coordinated with *Ibrāhīm*, so the meaning is: indeed the people most worthy of Abraham and of this Prophet are those who followed Abraham. As for *al-nabiyy*, they said it is a substitute (*badal*) for *hādhā*, or a qualifier (*naʿt*), or an explanatory appositive (*ʿaṭf bayān*).

He drew attention to the attribute by which Allah is an ally to His servants, which is faith. So He said *walī al-mu'minīn* ("Ally of the believers") and did not say *waliyyuhum*. This is a promise to them of victory in this world and success in the Hereafter. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah is the Ally of those who believe﴾ [al-Baqara: 257].

It is said that these verses combine rhetorical features: alerting (*tanbīh*), pointing (*ishāra*), and joining the two emphasis particles; and with separation (*faṣl*) in His words ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 62], and in ﴿And indeed Allah is the Mighty﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 62]; and specification (*ikhtiṣāṣ*) in ﴿Knowing of the corrupters﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 63] and in ﴿Ally of the believers﴾; and metonymy by using the name of the singular for the plural in ﴿to a word that is equitable﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 64]; and by using the name of a genus for its species in ﴿O People of the Scripture﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 70], if it is interpreted as referring to the Jews; and repetition in *illā Allāh* ("except Allah") and *inna Allāh* ("indeed Allah"), and in *yā ahla al-kitāb taʿālaw* ("O People of the Scripture, come"), *yā ahla al-kitāb lima* ("O People of the Scripture, why"), and in *Ibrāhīm*, *mā kāna Ibrāhīm* ("Abraham was not"), and *inna awlā al-nās bi-Ibrāhīm* ("indeed the people most worthy of Abraham"). And there is simile (*tashbīh*) in *arbāban* ("lords"): when they obeyed them in permitting and forbidding, and submitted to them, He applied to them the term *arbāban*, likening them to the Lord who deserves worship and lordship. And there is generality in the address in *yā ahla al-kitāb taʿālaw* and *yā ahla al-kitāb lima tuḥājjūna* ("O People of the Scripture, why do you argue"), like the saying of Abraham: ﴿O my father, O my father﴾ [Maryam: 44]. And like the saying of the poet:

*Patience, cousins of ours, patience, our allies; do not dig up between us what was buried.*

And like the saying of another:

*Cousins of ours, do not stir up evil between us, for how many an ember has become a flame from it.*

And there is paronomasia (*tajnīs*) of similar form (*al-mumāthil*) in *awlā* and *walī*.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 69:

﴿A party of the People of the Book wish that they could lead you astray﴾ The exegetes unanimously agree that it was revealed concerning Mu'adh, Hudhayfah and Ammar, when the Jews of the Banu al-Nadir, Qurayzah and Qaynuqa' invited them to their religion. It was also said: a group of the people of Najran and of the Jews invited them. Ibn Abbas said: they were the Jews, who said to Mu'adh and Ammar, "You have abandoned your religion and followed the religion of Muhammad," and so it was revealed. It was also said: the Jews reproached them over the battle of Uhud.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: "wadda" means "tamanna" (to wish), so it is used with "law" (if only) and "an" (that), and sometimes the two are combined, so one says: "wadadtu an law fa'ala" (I wished that if he had done). Its verbal noun is al-widadah, and its noun form is wudd, and the two may overlap in the verbal noun and the noun. Al-Raghib said: when wadda means "ahabba" (to love), it is never permissible to insert "law" into it. Ali ibn Isa said: when wadda means "tamanna" (to wish), it is suitable for the past, present and future; when it means love and desire, it is not suitable for the past, because desire is like requesting an action. When it refers to the present and future, both "an" and "law" are permissible; when it refers to the past, "an" is not permissible, because "an" is for the future. What he said is open to question. Do you not see that "an" is connected to a past verb, as in: "sarrani an qumta" (it pleased me that you stood)?

(p-489) ﴿from among the People of the Book﴾ is in the position of a qualifier for "a party," and "al-ta'ifah" refers to their leaders and rabbis. Ibn Atiyyah said: it is possible that "min" is explanatory of the genus, and that "al-ta'ifah" is all the People of the Book. What he said is remote from the indication of the wording. Here "law" is said to mean "an," so that it is verbal (masdariyyah), but the majority of the Basran grammarians do not hold this view, and the better course is to keep it in its original usage. The object of "wadda" is omitted, and the answer to "law" is omitted; from each of the two clauses what the meaning points to has been omitted. The sense is: they wish for your misguidance; if they could mislead you, they would rejoice at it. We have already discussed a similar case at length in His words: ﴿Each of them would love to be given a life of a thousand years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 96], so refer to it there. The meaning of "yudillunakum" is "yaruddunakum ila kufrikum" (they will return you to your disbelief), as said by Ibn Abbas. It was also said: "yuhlikunakum" (they will destroy you), as said by Ibn Jarir and al-Dimashqi. Ibn Atiyyah said: Ibn Jarir al-Tabari relied on the verse of Jarir:

*You were a speck of dust in a green, foaming wave, which the flood cast about, and so it went astray in utter error.*

And on the words of al-Nabigha:

*So its misleaders returned with clear eyes, and wisdom and bounty were left behind at al-Jawlan.*

He said: this is not a conclusive interpretation, nor is it specific to the word; it is only consistent for him because this "dalal" (going astray) in the verse, in the two lines, is associated with destruction. As for interpreting the word "dalal" as "halak" (destruction), it is not sound. End of quote.

Someone other than Ibn Atiyyah said: the root meaning of "adall al-dalal" in the language is destruction, from their saying: "dalla al-laban fi al-ma'" (the milk was lost in the water) when it becomes dissolved in it. It was also said: its meaning is that they cause you to fall into error, and they cast at you what makes you doubt your religion, as said by Abu Ali.

﴿And they mislead none but themselves﴾ If its meaning is destruction, then the meaning is that they destroy themselves and their followers, since by their preference for destroying the believers they deserve the wrath and anger of God. If the meaning is removal from the religion, then that is realized for them by denying the prophethood of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and altering his description; by this they became disbelievers and departed from the creed of Moses and Jesus. If the meaning is causing one to fall into error, then that is realized for them even though they are able to follow guidance through the clarification of proofs, the sending down of books, and the sending of messengers. Ibn Atiyyah said: it is an announcement that the evil of their deed returns upon them, and that it keeps them far from Islam. Al-Zamakhshari said: the harm of misguidance returns only upon them, because the punishment is doubled for them on account of their going astray and their leading others astray; or: they have no power to mislead the Muslims, and they only mislead their like among their followers. End of quote.

﴿And they do not perceive﴾ That this misguidance is peculiar to them, i.e. they do not notice it, because its matter is subtle and hidden from them, due to the hardness that has overtaken their hearts; so they do not know that they are misleading themselves. This indicates that whoever errs from the truth out of ignorance is astray. Or: ﴿and they do not perceive﴾ that they will not reach the misguidance of you; or: they do not notice the soundness of Islam, and it is obligatory upon them to know it, due to the manifestness of the proofs and evidences; this was mentioned by al-Qurtubi. Or: they do not perceive that God guides the Muslims to their state and informs them of their scheming and their error; this was mentioned by Ibn al-Jawzi. And in His words "they do not perceive" there is an intensification of their blame, in that they have lost the benefit of their senses.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 70:

﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: They are the Torah and the Gospel, concerning the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) and belief in him, as is made clear in His words: ﴿They find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 157]. This was said by Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Rabiʿ and Ibn Jurayj. Or it is the Qur'an, in view of their saying: ﴿It is only a human who teaches him﴾ [al-Nahl: 103], ﴿This is nothing but a falsehood﴾ [al-Furqan: 4], ﴿tales of the ancients﴾ [al-Anʿam: 25]; and the signs that he manifested at their hands, such as the splitting of the moon, the moaning of the trunk, the glorification of the pebbles, and other things. Or it is Muhammad and Islam, as Qatadah said. Or it is what he recited of the secrets of their books and the strange reports about them, as Ibn Bahr said. Or it is the Books of Allah. Or it is the signs in which He makes clear to them the truthfulness of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the soundness of his prophethood, and in which they were commanded to follow him, as Abu ʿAli said.

﴿while you bear witness﴾ is a circumstantial clause, by which He rebukes them for their disbelief in the signs of Allah while they themselves bear witness that they are the signs of Allah. The object of the witnessing is omitted and is to be supplied according to the interpretation of "the signs"; so it is supplied with what suits the explanation given. Therefore Qatadah, al-Suddi and al-Rabiʿ said: "while you bear witness, by what indicates their soundness, from your Book, in which there is good news."

It was also said: you bear witness to something like them from the signs of the prophets which you acknowledge. It was said: by the proof that is against you in it. It was said: your books are true, yet you do not follow what was sent down in them. It was said: by their soundness when you are alone. In that case, "you bear witness" means "you acknowledge and confess." Al-Raghib said: Or He means what will be of their testimony on the Day when their tongues, hands and feet bear witness against them.

It was also said: "you disbelieve in the signs of Allah" means: you deny that the Qur'an is inimitable; then "you bear witness" with your hearts and minds that it is inimitable.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 71:

﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you mix up the truth with falsehood and conceal the truth while you know?﴾ The interpretation of the like of this has already passed in His words: ﴿And do not mix up the truth with falsehood﴾ [al-Baqarah: 42], and mixing up (al-labs) was explained as blending and covering. The exegetes spoke here and interpreted the truth as what they find in their books concerning the description of the Messenger, and the falsehood as what they write with their own hands and alter. This is the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. It was also said: it is the showing of Islam and the nullification of Judaism and Christianity; this is the view of Qatadah, Ibn Jarir and al-Tha'labi. It was said: it is belief in Musa and Isa while disbelieving in the Messenger. Abu 'Ali said: they distort the verses that indicate the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ away from their proper interpretation, so that what appears to the common people is the opposite of what they actually are, while you know the falsehood of what you say. It was said: it refers to what He mentioned after that, His words: ﴿Believe in what has been revealed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 72]. It was said: it is their acknowledgment of some of the matter of the Prophet ﷺ, and the falsehood is their concealment of some of his matter; these two views are from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: it is their acknowledgment of his prophethood and messengership, and the falsehood is the saying of their rabbis: "He is not a messenger to us; rather our law is perpetual." 

Yahya ibn Wathhab recited: ﴿talbisūna﴾ with a fatha on the ba', the present tense of labisa, treating the truth as if it were a garment they put on; the ba' in ﴿bil-bāṭil﴾ is for accompaniment, meaning accompanied by falsehood.

Abu Mijlaz recited: ﴿tulabbisūna﴾ with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the doubled ba', and the doubling here is for intensification, like their saying jarraḥtu and qattaltu. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj permitted the accusative for ﴿wa-yaktumūna﴾, so that the nun is dropped according to the Arabic usage in your saying: "Why do you gather this and that?" It would then be in the subjunctive by conversion (al-sarf) according to the Kufans, and by the implied "an" according to the Basrans. Abu 'Ali denied this and said: the interrogative fell only on the mixing up. As for ﴿wa-yaktumūna﴾, it is a definite statement that permits only the nominative, in the sense that it is not coordinated with ﴿talbisūna﴾ but is a resumptive statement telling about them that they conceal the truth while knowing that it is the truth. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Abu 'Ali said: conversion is ugly here, and likewise the implied "an", because ﴿yaktumūna﴾ is coordinated with an affirmed affirmative clause, not with something asked about; the question concerned only the cause of the mixing up, and the mixing up is an affirmed fact. So the verse is not like the saying: "Do not eat fish and drink milk," nor like your saying: "Will you stand so that I may stand?" Coordination with an affirmed, established affirmative is ugly when put in the subjunctive, except in poetic necessity, as is reported:

*And I join with the Hijaz so that I may rest.*

Sibawayh has said: in your saying, "You travelled until you enter it," only the subjunctive is permitted in "tadkhula," because the travel is questioned about and is not affirmed. But if we say, "Which of them travelled until he enters it?", it is put in the nominative, because the travel is affirmed and the interrogation falls on something other than it. End of what Ibn 'Atiyyah transmitted from Abu 'Ali. The apparent meaning conflicts with what preceded it, because what preceded it says that the interrogation fell only on the mixing up, while as for ﴿yaktumūna﴾ it is a definite statement permitting only the nominative; whereas in what Ibn 'Atiyyah transmitted, ﴿yaktumūna﴾ is coordinated with an affirmed affirmative clause and is not asked about, so the coordination indicates their sharing in the question about the cause of the two affirmed matters, the mixing up and the concealing. He distinguished between this meaning and the case where ﴿wa-yaktumūna﴾ is a purely informative statement that does not share with the mixing up in asking about the cause. Ibn Malik followed Abu 'Ali in the view that when the interrogative implies the occurrence of the verb, the verb is not put in the subjunctive by an implied "an" in its answer. In al-Tashil, when enumerating what requires an implied "an" necessarily in the answer, he said: "or for an interrogative that does not imply the occurrence of the verb; if it implies the occurrence of the verb, the subjunctive is not permitted according to him," such as: "Why did you strike Zayd, so that he will requite you?" because the striking has occurred. None of our companions known to me has stipulated this condition which Abu 'Ali mentioned, and Ibn Malik followed him in it regarding the interrogative. Rather, when it is impossible to form a verbal noun from what precedes, either because there is no verb nor anything with its meaning from which one can be formed, or because forming a verbal noun referring to the future is impossible due to the past tense of the verb, then the verbal noun of its future reference is estimated from what the meaning indicates. So when one says, "Why did you strike Zayd, so that I may strike you?", the meaning is: let there be from you an informing about the striking of Zayd, so that there is a striking from us. What Abu 'Ali responded with against Abu Ishaq is not convincing, because His words ﴿Why do you mix up﴾ are not explicit that the present tense is meant as the past in actual fact, since the future may be denied for the certainty of its occurrence, especially with a person from whom the like has already occurred. Even if we assume it is actually past, there is no refutation of Abu Ishaq in it, because, as we established earlier, when it is not possible to form a future verbal noun from the sentence, we form it from the sentence's necessary consequence.

Abu al-Hasan ibn Kaysan reported the accusative of a verb asked about whose occurrence is certain, as in: "Where did Zayd go, so that we may follow him?" and likewise in "What is your wealth, so that we may know it?" and "Who is your father, so that we may honor him?" However, it is explained by what was mentioned earlier: the estimate is "let there be from you an informing about Zayd's going, so that there is following from us"; "let there be from you an informing about the amount of your wealth, so that there is knowing from us"; "let there be from you an informing about your father, so that there is honoring from us to him."

Ubayd ibn 'Umayr recited: ﴿limā talbisū﴾ and ﴿wa-taktumū﴾ without the nun in both, and they said that this is jazm (apocopation). They said: there is no basis for it except the view held by an anomalous group of grammarians that "lima" is assimilated to "lam" in governing the jussive. al-Sajawandi said: there is no basis for it except that "lima" apocopates the verb according to some people. The established usage of the Arabic language is that "lima" does not apocopate what follows it, and I have not seen any of the grammarians mention that "lima" operates like "lam" in jazm except what the exegetes mentioned here. In my view, this is rather a case of dropping the nun in the nominative, which has occurred in prose very rarely, namely in the reading of Abu 'Amr, and in some of his transmissions: "sahiranī tazzāharān," with the doubling of the zay, meaning "you two are sorcerers who support each other," so that the ta' is assimilated into the zay and the nun is dropped. As for verse, it is like the words of the rajaz poet:

*I spend the night humming while you spend the night rubbing me.*

He means: "wa-tabītīna tudallikīna." And he said:

*If a people are pleased by what you have done, they will milk them, a pregnant she-camel not barren.*

The apparent meaning is that He rebuked them for mixing up the truth with falsehood and for concealing the truth, as though the truth were divided into two parts: a part in which they mixed falsehood so that it cannot be distinguished, and a part which they concealed entirely so that it does not appear.

﴿And you know﴾ is a circumstantial clause, reproaching them for what they were engaged in of mixing up the truth with falsehood and concealing it; that is, it is not fitting for one who knows the truth to conceal it or to mix it with falsehood. The question about the cause is a question about the effect, so when the cause is denied, the effect is denied all the more. The previous verse ended with His words ﴿while you witness﴾ [Al 'Imran: 70], and this one with His words ﴿while you know﴾, because the thing condemned in that one is disbelief in the signs of God, which is more specific than the truth, since the signs of God are a part of the truth, and witnessing is more specific than knowing; so the more specific matched the more specific. Here, the truth is more general than the signs and other things, and knowledge is more general than witnessing; so the more general matched the more general. They said concerning His words ﴿while you know﴾: that is, that he is a true prophet and that what he brought is from God. It was said: He said ﴿while you know﴾ so that the matter by which the obligation is valid and the proof is established against them becomes clear to them. It was said: ﴿while you know﴾ the truth by what you have recognized from your books and what you have heard from the tongues of your prophets.

In these verses there are kinds of rhetorical ornamentation: the antithesis in His words "the truth with falsehood"; the semantic antithesis in His words "why do you disbelieve while you witness," since witnessing is affirmation and manifestation, and disbelief is concealment. The paronomasia of likeness in "yudilluunakum" and "ma yudilluna." The repetition in "People of the Scripture." And ellipsis in several places that have been explained.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 3, verse 72:

﴿And a faction of the People of the Book said: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, so that perhaps they will turn back."﴾ Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: Twelve rabbis (ḥibr, plural aḥbār, learned Jewish scholars) of the Jews of Khaybar and the villages of ʿUrayna conspired together, and some of them said to others: "Enter the religion of Muhammad at the beginning of the day with your tongues only, without belief in your hearts, and disbelieve in him at the end of the day. Say: 'We examined our books and consulted our scholars, and we found that Muhammad is not as he claims, and his falsehood and the invalidity of his religion have become clear to us.' When you do this, his companions will doubt their religion and say: 'They are the People of the Book, so they know better than us,' and they will turn back from their religion to your religion." So this verse was revealed.

Mujahid, Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: This concerns the qibla. When the direction of prayer was changed to the Kaʿba, this was difficult for the Jews, so Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and his companions said: "Pray towards it at the beginning of the day, and return to your Kaʿba, the Rock, at its end." So this verse was revealed.

Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid said: They prayed with the Prophet ﷺ the dawn prayer, then they returned at the end of the day and prayed their prayer (their own way), so that people would see that misguidance had appeared in them from him after they had followed him. So this verse was revealed.

Al-Suddi said: The Jews said to their lowly ones: "Believe in Muhammad at the beginning of the day, and when evening comes, say: 'Our scholars have informed us that you are not upon anything,'" so this verse was revealed. Ibn ʿAtiyya related from al-Hasan that the Jews of Khaybar said this to the Jews of Medina, end quote. The Jews made this occasion a means of deceiving the Muslims.

The one addressed (al-maqūl lahum) is omitted. It is possible that some of this faction said it to others, and it is possible that those addressed were not from this faction. What is meant by "Believe" (āminū) is: show belief (aẓhirū al-īmān), and it is not possible that it means affirmation of truth (taṣdīq). In the words ﴿in what has been revealed to those who believe﴾ there is an omission, meaning: "according to their claim," for otherwise they are liars and do not believe that God revealed anything to the believers.

The phrase "wajh al-nahār" (the face of the day) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf, adverbial accusative), and its meaning is "the beginning of the day." It is likened to the face of a person, since it is the first part of him that one faces. Al-Rabiʿ ibn Ziyad al-Absi said, concerning Malik ibn Zuhayr ibn Khuzayma al-Absi:

"Whoever was glad at the killing of Malik, let him come to our women at the face of the day."

The pronoun in "ākhirahu" refers to "al-nahār," meaning: the end of the day. The governing verb for the first adverb is "āminū," and for the last is "ukfurū." It has been said that the governing verb for "wajh al-nahār" is "unzila," meaning: "in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day," and the pronoun in "ākhirahu" refers to "alladhī unzila," meaning: "disbelieve at the end of what was revealed." This view is remote and contrary to the occasions of revelation (asbāb al-nuzūl). The object of "yarjiʿūn" (they return) is omitted, meaning: they turn back from their religion.

The apparent meaning of the verse supports this view. As for the carrying out of the command by those to whom it was addressed, the verse is silent about whether it occurred, while the occasions of revelation indicate that it did occur. In this statement they hoped that the Arabs would be deceived by it, or that one of them would say: "These are People of the Book of old, with excellent judgment and knowledge; they entered into this matter and then turned back from it." It also serves to strengthen their weak ones in their religion. (p-494)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 73 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And do not believe except in one who follows your religion.﴾ The lam in *liman* (for one who): it was said that it is superfluous (*za'idah*, grammatically extra) for emphasis, as in His words ﴿It may be that some of what you seek to hasten has drawn close behind you﴾ [an-Naml: 72], meaning *radifakum* (has drawn close to you). The poet says:

*"I was never deceived by a friend through his friendship, until a friend became deceitful to me."*

He meant: "I was never deceiving the friend." However, the better view is that the lam is not superfluous. Rather, *amana* (to believe) is taken to include the meaning of *aqarra* (to acknowledge) and *i'tarafa* (to confess), so it is transitive with the lam. Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: "*Amana* has also been used with the lam in His words ﴿But none believed in Musa except some of his people﴾ [Yunus: 83] (and *amantum lahu*, you believed in him), and in ﴿He believes in Allah and believes for the believers﴾ [at-Tawbah: 61]." End of quote. The better view is what we have mentioned: it is taken to include the meaning of acknowledgment, and the object of belief is omitted.

The apparent sense of His words ﴿And do not believe except in one who follows your religion﴾ is that it is part of the speech of a group of the Jews, since it is joined to their statement. For this reason Ibn Atiyya said: "There is no disagreement among the people of interpretation that this statement is part of the speech of the group." This is not so. Rather, among the exegetes are those who held that this is the speech of Allah, by which He strengthens the hearts of the believers so that they do not doubt when the Jews deceive and falsify. But if it is part of the speech of the group of Jews, then the apparent sense is that their speech ends there, since there is no disagreement and no doubt that His words ﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah﴾ are the speech of Allah addressing His Prophet ﷺ, and what follows it clearly appears to be the speech of Allah, and part of what He said to His Prophet.

*An yu'ta* (that one be given) is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*, an object indicating the reason for the action). The sense of the sentence is: "Say, O Muhammad, to those Jews who said: 'Indeed guidance is the guidance of Allah,' not what you intended of deception by that statement and that action, out of fear ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given, or that they dispute with you before your Lord﴾. You said that statement and plotted that scheme, i.e., you did so out of envy and fear that your leadership would go away, and that someone would share with you in what you were given of the excellence of knowledge, or that they would dispute with you before your Lord, i.e., they would establish the proof against you before Allah, since your Book is full of the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and obligates you to believe in him and follow him." This meaning is supported by His words ﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills﴾ to the end of the verse. This meaning is also supported by the reading of Ibn Kathir: *an yu'ta* with an interrogative form that carries the sense of rebuke against them, reproach and censure. The interrogative that carries the sense of denial is affirmative in meaning. That is: "Out of fear that anyone be given the like of what you were given? Or that they dispute with you before your Lord? You said that and did it?" Then *aw yuhajjukum* (or that they dispute with you) is coordinated with *yu'ta*, and *aw* is for classification (*lil-tanwi'*, indicating distinct categories).

They also allowed that *huda Allah* (the guidance of Allah) be in apposition (*badal*) to *al-huda* (the guidance), not the predicate of *inna*. The predicate would be His words ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given﴾, meaning: indeed, the guidance of Allah is that anyone be given the like of what you were given of knowledge. Then *aw yuhajjukum* would be in the subjunctive by an implied *an*, after *aw* in the sense of *hatta* (until), meaning: until they dispute with you before your Lord and overcome you and refute your argument before Allah, because you know the truth of the religion of Islam and that following this Prophet is obligatory for you. *Aw yuhajjukum* cannot be coordinated with *yu'ta* and included in the predicate of *inna*. As for *ahad* (anyone) in these two views, it is not the one that comes in generalization (*'umum*), because the condition for that is that it be in a negation or in the predicate of a negation. Rather, *ahad* here means *wahid* (one), and it is singular, since by it is meant the Messenger ﷺ. The pronoun in *yuhajjukum* is plural only because it refers to the Messenger and his followers, since the message implies following.

Some grammarians said: *inna* here is for negation in the sense of *la* (no). The sense is: "No one is given the like of what you were given." This is also reported from al-Farra'. Then *aw* means *illa* (except), and the meaning then is: "No one is given the like of what you were given except that they dispute with you, for his being given what you were given is linked to contending with you and disputing with you before your Lord, because whoever Allah gives revelation must dispute with them before their Lord about their not following him. So *aw yuhajjukum* is a necessary circumstantial clause in meaning, since Allah does not reveal to a Messenger except that he disputes with those who oppose him." In this view, *ahad* is the one that is general, because the negation precedes it. The pronoun in *yuhajjukum* is plural, taking *ahad* in its sense, as in His words ﴿Then not one of you could withhold him from it﴾ [al-Haqqah: 47], where *hajizin* is plural, taking *ahad* in its sense and not its wording; if it had been taken by its wording it would have been singular. But in this view there is the claim that *an* with a fatha is used for negation in the sense of *la*, and no evidence for this has been established from Arabic speech. The address in *ututum* and in *yuhajjukum*, in these three views, is to the group previously mentioned, who said ﴿Believe in what has been sent down to those who believed at the beginning of the day﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 72].

Some grammarians allowed that the meaning be: *an la yu'ta ahad* (that no one be given), with *la* deleted, because the sentence contains evidence of the deletion. He said, as in His words ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [an-Nisa': 176], meaning: *an la tadillu* (that you not go astray). Abu al-Abbas (al-Mubarrad) rejected this and said: "*La* is not deleted. The meaning is: out of dislike that you go astray." Likewise here: out of dislike that anyone be given the like of what you were given, i.e., from among those who opposed the religion of Islam, because Allah does not guide one who is a liar and a disbeliever. So the guidance of Allah is far from non-believers.

The address in *ututum* and *yuhajjukum* is to the community of Muhammad ﷺ. In this case, *an yu'ta* is an object of purpose with *karahata* (out of dislike) omitted, and it requires an implied governing verb, which is difficult to supply, since before it is a clause in which the attribution does not show the reason as dislike of the giving mentioned.

Ibn Atiyya said: "It is possible that His words *an yu'ta* are a substitute (*badal*) for His words *huda Allah*, and the meaning would be: 'Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah,' and it is that anyone be given like what came to us. And His words *aw yuhajjukum* would mean: *aw falyuhajjukum* (or let them dispute with you), for indeed they will overcome you." End of quote. In this statement there is jussive mood through the imperative lam, which is omitted, and this is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans except in poetic necessity.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is permissible that *an yu'ta* be in the accusative by a hidden verb indicated by His words ﴿And do not believe except in one who follows your religion﴾, as if it were said: ﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah﴾, so do not deny that anyone be given the like of what they were given." End of his words. This is far-fetched, because it involves deleting the particle of prohibition and its object, and this is not known from their speech.

They also allowed that His words ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given, or that they dispute with you before your Lord﴾ are not included under His words "Say," but are part of the speech of the group, connected to His words ﴿And do not believe except in one who follows your religion﴾, and that His words ﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah﴾ be a parenthetical clause (*jumlah i'tiradiyyah*, an interjected sentence) between what precedes it and what follows it.

This statement admits several aspects:

First: the meaning is: "Do not believe with true belief and do not have faith except in one who came with the like of your religion, out of fear that anyone be given the prophethood and honor like what you were given, and out of fear that they dispute with you by your believing in them before your Lord if they do not persist in it." This statement, in this meaning, is the fruit of envy and disbelief along with knowledge of the truth of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ.

Second: the intended meaning is: *an la yu'ta* (that no one be given), so *la* is deleted due to what the sentence indicates, and this is negated and included within the scope of *illa* (except), not presumed to enter before it. The meaning: "Do not believe in anyone regarding anything except one who follows your religion, given that no one is given the like of what you were given, and that they will not dispute with you before your Lord," i.e., except with the negation of such and such.

Third: the intended meaning is: *bi-an yu'ta* (by the giving that someone is given), and it is connected to *tu'minu* (believe), and it is not included within the scope of *illa*. The meaning: "Do not believe, by the giving that anyone is given the like of what you were given, except in one who follows your religion, came with its like, and supports it, for that is not given to anyone but you." The meaning of *aw yuhajjukum 'inda rabbikum* (or they dispute with you before your Lord) is in the sense of *illa an yuhajjukum* (except that they dispute with you), as you say: "I will not leave you unless you pay me my right." This statement, in this meaning, is the fruit of denial of Muhammad ﷺ, based on their belief that prophethood exists only among the Children of Israel.

Fourth: the meaning is: "Do not believe in Muhammad and acknowledge his prophethood, though you know its truth, except to the Jews who are of you," (p-496) and *an yu'ta ahad mithla ma utitum* (that anyone be given the like of what you were given) is a description of the state of Muhammad ﷺ. So the meaning is: "Conceal your acknowledgment that someone has been given the like of what you were given," or, "they mean the Arabs, who will dispute with you by acknowledgment before your Lord."

Al-Zamakhshari said regarding this aspect, beginning with it, the following text: "*Wa la tu'minu* is connected to His words *an yu'ta ahad*, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause, meaning: 'Do not display your belief that anyone is given the like of what you were given, except to the people of your religion alone, not to others. They intended: conceal your belief that the Muslims have been given the like of what you were given, and do not spread it except to your partisans alone, not to the Muslims, lest it increase them in steadfastness, and not to the polytheists, lest it call them to Islam.' *Aw yuhajjukum 'inda rabbikum* is coordinated with *an yu'ta*, and the pronoun in *yuhajjukum* refers to *ahad*, since it has the sense of the plural, meaning: 'Do not believe except to others who follow you, that the Muslims will dispute with you on the Day of Resurrection with the truth, and overcome you before Allah with the proof.'" End of his words.

As for *ahad* in these views: if it is the one that is general, and what precedes it is presumed to be negated, as in the statement of some of them that the meaning is "no one is given," or "the meaning is: that no one be given," then it follows the familiar usage of the Arabic language, that it comes only in negation or what resembles negation, such as prohibition. If the verb is affirmative, it can enter here, because the negation came at the beginning of the sentence, just as *min* entered in His words ﴿that any good be sent down to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105] because of the negation before it in His words ﴿Those who disbelieve do not wish﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105].

The meaning of the parenthetical objection in these aspects is that He, exalted is He, informs that what they aimed for of plotting and deception by their saying ﴿Believe in what has been sent down to those who believed at the beginning of the day﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 72], and so on, will not avail anything, and does not turn away from faith the one whom Allah wills to have faith, because the guidance is the guidance of Allah. So it is not for anyone to bring it to someone, nor to deny it of anyone.

Ibn Kathir recited *an yu'ta ahadun* with a long alif (*al-madd*) as a question (*al-istifham*). Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) explained it as part of the speech of the group (*qawl al-ta'ifa*). It cannot be linked to the verb before it, because the interrogative particle cuts off the connection. It is therefore in the nominative position as a subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is omitted. The implied sense is: "Do you believe in it," or "Do you acknowledge it," or "Do you mention it to others," or something similar that the context indicates. *Yuhajjukum* is coordinated with *an yu'ta*. Abu 'Ali said: The position of *an* could also be accusative, so the meaning would be: "Do you spread the word," or "Do you mention that anyone has been given the like of what you have been given?" This would mean: "Do you tell them about what Allah has opened to you?" On both readings, the meaning of the verse is a rebuke from the rabbis to the followers for their belief that Muhammad is a prophet sent by God. *Aw yuhajjukum* would then be in the sense of the particle *an* being implied, meaning: "Or do you want them to argue with you?" Abu 'Ali also said: *Ahad* (anyone), according to Ibn Kathir's reading, is the word that does not indicate plurality. The interrogative cut-off prevents it from being used in negation, because it cannot enter into the negation at the beginning of the sentence. Therefore only *ahad* remains, as in your saying *ahad wa-'ishrun* (twenty-one), and it occurs in affirmative statements because it means "one." Its pronoun in *aw yuhajjukum* is made plural by taking account of the meaning, since the intended sense of "the like of prophethood" refers to followers, so the meaning is plural. Abu 'Ali said: This is a place where the reading of other than Ibn Kathir should be preferred over Ibn Kathir's reading, because singular nouns do not necessarily indicate plurality. This concludes Abu 'Ali's explanation of Ibn Kathir's reading. The explanation of his reading was previously given, where *an yu'ta* is an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*), on the basis that it falls under the speech of the group. This is more apparent than taking it as the speech of the group.

The early scholars (*al-salaf*) differed concerning this verse. Al-Suddi and others held that the whole statement, from His words ﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah﴾ to the end of the verse, is what Allah commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to say to his community.

Qatada and al-Rabi' held that all of this is the speech of Allah, Who commanded him to say it to the group that said ﴿And do not believe except for those who follow your religion﴾. Mujahid and others held that His words ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given, or that they argue with you before your Lord﴾ are entirely the speech of the group to their followers, and His words ﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah﴾ are a parenthetical insertion between what comes before and what comes after, which is the speech of the group to their followers. Ibn Juraij held that His words ﴿that anyone be given the like of what you were given﴾ fall under the command "Say," which the Messenger says to the Jews, and his speech ends at His words "you were given." As for His words ﴿or that they argue with you before your Lord﴾, it is connected to the speech of the group, ﴿And do not believe except for those who follow your religion﴾. The previous interpretations are arranged according to these approaches.

(p. 497) Al-A'mash and Shu'ayb ibn Ubayy read *in yu'ta* with a kasra on the hamza, meaning: "No one has been given the like of the honour you have been given." This reading may be understood as speech from the group that said it, so that their words "or that they argue with you" mean "or let them argue with you." This is in the sense of insisting that no one will be given the like of what was given to you, or it may mean "unless they argue with you," which allows that anyone may be given that if the proof is established for him. This is Ibn 'Atiyya's explanation of this reading, and it is based on the assumption that it is the speech of the group.

Ibn 'Atiyya also said in explaining it: It is as though he (ﷺ) is informing his community that Allah does not give anyone, nor has He given anyone in the past, the like of what He gave to the community of Muhammad, namely that it is a middle community (*wasatan*). This explanation holds that it is the speech of Muhammad (ﷺ) to his community, and falls under "Say." According to the first explanation, al-Zamakhshari interpreted it. He said: It is also read as *an yu'ta ahadun* with *an* as a negative particle (*an al-nafiya*), and it is connected to the speech of the People of the Book, meaning: "And do not believe except for those who follow your religion," and "Say to them: No one is given the like of what you were given, until they argue with you before your Lord," that is, they do not give the like of it, so they do not argue with you.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: al-Hasan read *an yu'tiya ahadun*, with a kasra on the ta' and the verb ascribed to *ahadun*, and the meaning is that Allah's bounty is not like the bounty of any of His creatures. The clearest reading of this form is that it is an address from Muhammad (ﷺ) to his community, and the object is omitted; its implied form is: *an yu'tiya ahadun ahadan* ("that anyone give anyone"). Ibn 'Atiyya did not address whether the *an* in this reading is with a kasra or a fatha.

Al-Sajawandi said: al-A'mash read *an yu'tiya*, and al-Hasan read *an yu'tiya ahadan*, making *an* a negative particle, even though it does not come after *illa* (except), as in His words ﴿in that which We have established you in﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 26]. *Aw* here means *illa an* (unless). This may be the speech of Allah, but with an objection: "Say" is the speech of the Jews.

There are two views on the meaning of *al-huda* (guidance) here. The first: what believers are given of faith in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The second: success (*tawfiq*) and guidance toward good until one becomes Muslim or remains steadfast in Islam.

*'Inda rabbikum* ("before your Lord") may have two meanings. The first: that this takes place in the Hereafter. The second: before the books of your Lord that testify against you and for you. He ascribed this to "the Lord" as an honour, and the meaning would be: "or they argue with you before the Truth." The interpretations of the verse revolve around these two meanings, and each is taken according to what suits these two meanings.

* *

﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills﴾. This is an emphasis on the meaning of ﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of Allah﴾. In it is a refutation of the Jews, who said that the law of Moses is eternal and that Allah would never give anyone the like of what the Children of Israel were given of prophethood. "Bounty is in the hand of Allah" means that He disposes of it, as a thing is in the hand, and this is a figurative expression (*kinaya*) for the power to dispose of something and to have authority over it. The Creator, exalted is He, is free from having a bodily limb (*jariha*). Then He informed that He gives it to whomever He wills, so His singling out of someone with bounty is caused solely by His will. Here "bounty" is interpreted as prophethood, though it is more general, and prophethood is the most noble of its kinds.

﴿And Allah is All-Embracing, All-Knowing﴾. Its explanation has already been given.

﴿He singles out for His mercy whomever He wills.﴾ Al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Rabi' said: He singles out for His prophethood whomever He wills. Ibn Juraij said: by Islam and the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: Islam. It was also said: by frequent remembrance of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾ The explanation of this, and of what precedes it, has already been given at the end of the verse: ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Scripture do not wish that any good be sent down to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105]. These verses contain, from the rhetorical embellishments (al-badi', the science of rhetorical ornamentation), identical paronomasia (al-tajnis al-mumathil) and repetition in: آمنوا (āmanū, "they believed") and آمِنوا (āminū, "believe!"), and in al-huda (guidance) and huda Allah (the guidance of Allah), and in: يُؤتى (yu'tā, "is given") and أوتيتم (ūtītum, "you were given"), and in: inna al-fadl (indeed the bounty) and dhu al-fadl (the possessor of bounty). There is also repetition of the name of Allah in four places. Antithesis (al-tibaq) appears in: āminū and ukfurū (ākfurū, "disbelieve"), and in: wajh al-nahar (the face of the day) and in: ākhirahu (its end). The specification (al-ikhtisas) appears in: wajh al-nahar, because it is the time they gather with the believers, pretending to them; and in: ākhirahu, because it is the time of their seclusion with their like among the disbelievers. And there is ellipsis (al-hadhf) in several places.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 75 (part 1 of 2):

(p-498) ﴿Among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you; and among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you unless you keep standing over him. That is because they say, "There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered (ummiyyin)." And they speak falsely against Allah while they know.﴾ ﴿Yes! Whoever fulfils his covenant and fears Allah – indeed Allah loves those who fear Him.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 76] ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price – those will have no share in the Hereafter, and Allah will not speak to them, nor look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify them, and they will have a painful punishment.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 77] ﴿And indeed among them is a group who distort their tongues with the Book so that you may think it is from the Book, but it is not from the Book. And they say, "It is from Allah," but it is not from Allah. And they speak falsely against Allah while they know.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 78] ﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Book, the judgment and the prophethood, and then he should say to the people, "Be servants of me rather than of Allah." Rather, [he would say], "Be masters devoted (rabbaniyyin) to the Lord, by what you have taught of the Book and by what you have studied."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 79].

Al-dinar (dinar): a known coin. It is twenty-four qirat, and the qirat is three grains from the middle of a barley grain; so its total is seventy-two grains, and this is agreed upon. Its fa' (ف) is a substitution for a nun (ن), indicated by the plural of it: they say dananir (دنانير). Its original form is dinnar (دِنّار), and the first of the two identical letters was replaced, just as they replaced a nun in the third of the repeated forms with a ya' in: tazannaytu (تَظَنَّيْتُ). Its original form is tazannantu (تَظَنَّنْتُ), because it is from al-zann (الظَّنّ), and this is a transmitted (samu') substitution. And al-dinar is a non-Arabic word (a'jami) which the Arabs inflected and assimilated into the vocabulary of their speech.

Dama (دام): it remained (thabata). Its present tense is yadumu (يَدُومُ), so its pattern is fa'ala (فَعَلَ), like qala (قالَ) – yaqulu (يَقُولُ). Al-Farra' said: this is the dialect of the Hijaz and Tamim; they say dimta (دِمْتَ), with a kasra on the dal. He said: and they agree on the present tense: they say yadumu. Abu Ishaq said: "yaqulu" – "dumta tadamu," like "nimta tanamu," and this is a dialect. So according to this, the pattern of "dama" is fa'ila (فَعِلَ) with a kasra on the 'ayn, like khafa (خافَ) – yakhafu (يَخافُ). Al-tadwim (التَّدْوِيم) is revolving around something. From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"And the sun is bewildered, in the air is its tadwim."

And 'Alqama said describing wine:

"It cures the headache, and its pourer does not harm you, and there is no tadwim in the head from mixing with it."

Al-dawwam (الدَّوام) is dizziness (al-dawwar), which seizes a person's head so that he sees things revolving around him. And the tadwim of a bird in the sky is its remaining still when it spreads its wings and circles. From it: standing water (al-ma' al-da'im), as if it turns around its centre. Lawa al-habl and iltawa: he twisted the rope; then it was used for wriggling away in arguments and disputes. From it: liyan al-gharim (لِيانُ الغَرِيمِ), which is pushing him off and delaying him. From it: khasm alwa (خَصْمٌ ألْوى), a very fierce adversary; meanings were likened to physical bodies.

Al-lisan (اللِّسان): the well-known organ. Abu 'Amr said: al-lisan is masculine and feminine; whoever makes it masculine plurals it as alsina (ألْسِنَةً), and whoever makes it feminine plurals it as alsun (ألْسُنًا). Al-Farra' said: "al-lisan" itself, we have not heard it from the Arabs except as masculine. End. It is used figuratively for speech, and it too is masculine and feminine when that is what is meant.

Al-rabbani (الرَّبّانِيُّ): a relative adjective to al-Rabb, and the alif and nun were added for emphasis (mubalagha), as they said: lihyani (لَحْيانِيٌّ), sha'rani (شَعْرانِيٌّ), and raqbani (رَقْبانِيٌّ). They do not isolate this addition from the ya' of relation. Some said: it is a relative adjective to Rabban, who is the teacher and governor of the people, and the alif and nun in it are like those in ghadban and 'atshan; then a relative was made from it, and they said rabbani; according to this it is a relative in the adjective, as they said: ahmari (أحْمَرِيٌّ) from ahmar, and dawwari (دَوّارِيٌّ) from dawwar; and both opinions are anomalous and not to be analogised upon. Darasa al-kitab yadrusuhu (دَرَسَ الكِتابَ يَدْرُسُهُ): he persisted in reading and repeating it. Darasa al-manzil (دَرَسَ المَنزِلُ): it faded away; and talal darisun (طَلَلٌ دارِسٌ): a faded trace.

﴿Among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you; and among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you unless you keep standing over him.﴾ The majority hold that the People of the Book are the Jews and the Christians; Allah informs about the blaming of the treacherous among them. Its apparent meaning is that among the Jews and Christians there is one who is entrusted and is faithful, and one who is entrusted and betrays. It was said: "the People of the Book" is meant to refer to the People of the Qur'an, related by Ibn Jurayj. This is very weak, because of what follows it of their saying: ﴿That is because they say, "There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered."﴾ It was also said: the intended People of the Book are the Jews, because this statement, "There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered," was not said nor believed except by the Jews.

It was said: ﴿one who, if you entrust him with a qintar﴾ refers to the Christians, due to the predominance of trustworthiness among them; and ﴿one who, if you entrust him with a dinar﴾ refers to the Jews, due to the predominance of betrayal among them. Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions were specified from among them. It was also said: ﴿one who, if you entrust him with a qintar﴾ are those among the People of the Book who embraced Islam, and ﴿one who, if you entrust him with a dinar﴾ are those among them who did not embrace Islam.

It is narrated that some Arabs traded with some Jews, and they deposited with them; the Jews betrayed those who had embraced Islam and said: "You have left your religion upon which we contracted with you, and in our Book there is no sanctity for your property." So Allah refuted them. It was said: this is the occasion of revelation of this verse. From Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it﴾ is 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, a man of Quraysh deposited with him a thousand and two hundred uqiyya of gold, and he returned it to him. And ﴿one who, if you entrust him with a dinar﴾ is Finhas ibn 'Azura, a man of Quraysh deposited with him a dinar, and he denied it and betrayed him. End. The condition is not restricted to those two specified individuals; rather each of them is an instance of those included under "man" (مَن). Do you not see how it was made plural in His saying: ﴿That is because they say, "There is no blame upon us"﴾ – "they say"? And the addressee in His saying "you entrust him" is the Prophet ﷺ without dispute, and it is possible that the listener is from among the Muslims; and their saying ﴿There is no blame upon us regarding the unlettered﴾ clarifies this, so it gathers "the unlettered," who are the followers of the unlettered Prophet.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: tid'manhu (تِئْمَنهُ) in both places, and tid'manna (تِئْمَنّا) in Yusuf. Ibn Mas'ud, al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, and Ibn Wathhab read: timanhu (تِيمَنهُ), with a kasra on the ta' and a sakin ya' after it; al-Dani said: this is the dialect of Tamim. As for the replacement of the hamza with ya' in tid'manhu (تِئْمَنهُ), it is due to the kasra before it, as they replaced it in bi'r (بِئْرٍ).

We have already discussed the letters of the present tense of a verb, and those beginning with a hamzat al-wasl, when discussing His saying ﴿nasta'in (نَسْتَعِينُ)﴾ [al-Fatiha: 5], so there is no need to repeat it. Ibn 'Atiyya, when mentioning Ubayy's reading, said: "I do not think it is anything but a Qurashi dialect, which is the kasra of the plural nun, as in nasta'inu, and the alif of the speaker, as in the saying of Ibn 'Umar: 'la ikhalahu,' and the ta' of the addressee, as in this verse; and they do not kasra the ya' of the third person, and Ubayy read tid'manhu with it." End. He did not clarify by a general rule what vowels of the present-tense prefixes are kasra'd, and his assumption that it is a Qurashi dialect is not as he thought. We have clarified this at ﴿nasta'in﴾ [al-Fatiha: 5]. The explanation of al-qintar was already given in His saying: ﴿and the heaped-up piles of gold and silver﴾ [Al 'Imran: 14].

The majority read: yu'addihi (يُؤَدِّهِ) with a kasra on the ha' and connecting it with a ya'. Qalun read with ikhtilas (reduced vowel). Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr, Hamza, and al-A'mash read with sukun. Abu Ishaq said: this sukun narrated from these is a manifest error, because the ha' should not be jazm'd, and if it is not jazm'd, it is not permissible for it to be sakin in connected speech. As for Abu 'Amr, I think he used to reduce the kasra, so it was wrongly attributed to him, as he was wrongly attributed in bari'kum (بارِئِكم); Sibawayh narrated from him, and he is a reliable source for such matters, that he used to give a light kasra. End of Ibn Ishaq's words. What Abu Ishaq held, that sukun is an error, is nothing, since it is a reading among the seven, and it is mutawatir; and it suffices that it is transmitted from the imam of the Basrans, Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', for he is a pure Arab, a hearer of the language, and an imam in grammar, and it would not have escaped him that such a thing is permissible.

Al-Farra' permitted this, and he is an imam in grammar and language, and he related it as a dialect of some Arabs who apply jazm in connection and in pause. Al-Kisa'i related that the dialect of 'Uqayl and Kilab is that they reduce the vowel in this ha' when it follows a moving letter, and that they also make it sakin. Al-Kisa'i said: I heard the Bedouins of 'Uqayl and Kilab say: ﴿li-rabbihi la-kanud﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 6] with jazm, and "li-rabbihi la-kanud" without completion; and "lahu mal." Other than 'Uqayl and Kilab, there is no reduction or sukun in "lahu" and its like in their speech, except in poetic necessity, such as the saying:

"lahu zajal ka'anahu sawtun hadd"

And he said:

"illa li-anna 'uyunahu sayl wadiha"

Some of our companions stated that the vowel of this ha', after a verb from which a letter has been dropped for pause or jazm, may be lengthened (ishba'), may be reduced (ikhtilas), and may be sakin. As for Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj, it is said of him that he was not an imam in language, and for this reason he objected to Tha'lab in his book al-Fasih regarding places he claimed the Arabs do not say; people refuted Abu Ishaq in his objection and transmitted them from the language of the Arabs. Among those who refuted him was Abu Mansur al-Jawaliqi; Tha'lab was an imam in language and an imam in grammar according to the Kufan school. They also transmitted two readings: one with a damma on the ha' and connecting it with a waw, which is the reading of al-Zuhri, and the other with a damma without connection, and Salam read with it.

The ba' in bi-qintar and in bi-dinar: it was said it is for ilsaq (attachment). It was said it means 'ala (على), since the basic construction is to transitive with 'ala, as Malik said: ﴿Do we not trust you with Yusuf?﴾ [Yusuf: 11] and he said: ﴿Shall I trust you with him except as I trusted you with his brother?﴾ [Yusuf: 64]. It was said it means fi (في), i.e., in the safekeeping of a qintar, and in the safekeeping of a dinar. What appears is that the qintar and the dinar are two examples of the great and the small, so more than a qintar and less are included, and in the dinar there is less than it.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: it may be intended that its tibq (equivalent) is meant, i.e., regarding the dinar, it is not permissible except for a dinar or more; and he did not mention the treacherous ones in "less," since they are rabble and dregs. End.

* *

As for the meaning of ﴿unless you keep standing over him﴾: Qatada, Mujahid, al-Zajjaj, al-Farra', and Ibn Qutayba said: persistently demanding with all kinds of demand, through urging, and litigation before the judges. So the intention is not the posture of standing; rather it is from a person's standing over his affairs, i.e., his striving in them.

Al-Suddi and others said: standing over his head, which is the well-known posture, and that is the extreme of urging, because the meaning of that is that he is busy with another matter and wants to attend to him. A group of jurists adopted this interpretation and derived from the verse the permissibility of imprisonment, because the one who stands over his debtor prevents him from his dealings except through judgment, and there is no difference between preventing dealings and imprisonment. It was said: standing over him with your face toward him, and he is shy of you. It was said: the meaning of "you kept standing over him" is "upon him," i.e., dominating; so if your side softens, he will not return your trust.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan, Talha, and others read: dimta (دِمْتَ) with a kasra on the dal, and it was mentioned earlier that this is the dialect of Tamim, and the disagreement regarding its present tense was mentioned earlier. The "ma" in "ma dumta" is a verbal-temporal (masdariyya zarfiyya) particle. "Dumta" is a defective verb (naqisa), so its predicate is "qa'iman." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "ma" be only verbal (masdariyya) and not temporal, so it is construed with a verbal noun, and that verbal noun is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal); so that is an exception from circumstances, not from times. He said: the meaning is "except in the state of your constant attendance upon him." According to this, "qa'iman" is accusative as a circumstantial state, not as the predicate of "dama," because the condition for "dama" being defective is that it be a relative clause (silla) to a temporal verbal "ma."

That is because they said, "There is no blame on us regarding the *ummiyyin*." It is narrated that the Children of Israel used to hold it lawful to seize the wealth of the Arabs, because they were people of idols. When Islam came and some of the Arabs embraced it, the Jews remained upon that belief, so this verse was revealed to forbid it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Everything from the affairs of the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam) is under my feet, except trustworthiness, for it is to be returned to the righteous and the wicked." The reference of "that" is to the non-fulfilment of the trust, which the phrase "he will not return it" indicates. That is, their not returning the trust was due to their saying.

As for the pronoun in *bi-annahum*, it is said to refer to the Jews, and it is said to refer to the whole mass of the Children of Israel. The more apparent view is that it refers to *man* in His words, "Among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you." It is put in the plural by taking the sense into account: that is, he abandoned returning a dinar or less, and what is more than that is due to the statement of the one who withholds the return and betrays, "There is no blame on us regarding the *ummiyyin*." The *ummiyyin* are those who are not of the People of the Book, namely the Arabs. Their being called *ummiyyin* has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

As for *al-sabil* (the way, or blame), it is said to mean reproach and blame. It is also said to mean argument or proof, as in the verse of Humayd ibn Thawr:

"And am I, if I console myself with a shade-tree of the acacias, one for whom the way is closed?"

His words, "Against such there is no way (*sabil*)," are of this meaning, and this usage is frequent in the Qur'an and in the speech of the Arabs. It is also said that *al-sabil* here means the act that leads to sin. The meaning is: there is no way (of blame) upon them concerning what they make lawful of the wealth of the believing *ummiyyin*. He said: The reason for their permitting themselves the wealth of the *ummiyyin* is that they regarded them as polytheists, and after their conversion they remained upon what they had been upon. This is due to the Jews' denial of the Qur'an and of the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also said: this is because the covenant that existed between them was broken by their conversion, so they became like combatants, and thus they made their wealth lawful. It is also said: this is because in their scripture it is permitted to take the property of whoever opposes them.

Al-Kalbi said: The Jews said, "All the wealth was ours, so whatever is in the hands of the Arabs of it is ours, and they wronged us and usurped it, so there is no way (of blame) upon us in taking our wealth from them." Abd al-Razzaq narrated, from Ma'mar, from Abu Ishaq al-Hamdani, from Sa'sa'ah, that a man said to Ibn Abbas, "We take, in raiding, sheep and chickens from the wealth of the *ahl al-dhimmah* (protected non-Muslim subjects), and they say, 'There is no harm on us in that.'" He said to him: "This is like what the People of the Book said: 'There is no way (of blame) upon us regarding the *ummiyyin*.' When they pay the *jizyah* (the poll tax levied on protected non-Muslims), their wealth is not lawful to you except with their willing consent." Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyyah also mentioned this report, and in it, after mention of the sheep or the chicken, he said: "They say, 'What did he say?' He says: 'There is no harm on us in that.'"

* *

"And they speak falsehood against God." That is, they utter a false statement which they fabricate against God, by their claim that this is in their scripture. Al-Suddi, Ibn Jurayj and others said: a group among the People of the Book claimed that the Torah contains a permission for them to take the wealth of the *ummiyyin*, a lie that they fabricated, while knowing it was false. Thus the falsehood spoken here is this specific lie in this passage. The apparent meaning, however, is more general than this, and this is included within it: they lie against God in many matters, while being aware of the place of truth.

It has been permitted that *'alayna* be the predicate of *laysa*, and that the predicate be *fi al-ummiyyin*. Some people held that *laysa* operates on the prepositional phrase, so on this view it may be connected to it.

It is said: it is also permissible that *sabil* be raised by *'alayna*, with a pronoun of the matter in *laysa*, and that *'ala Allah* be connected to *yaqulun* in the sense of *yaftaruna* (they fabricate). It is said: it is also permissible that it be a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from *al-kadhib* placed before it, and not connected to *al-kadhib*. It is said: because the relative clause (*silah*) does not precede the relative pronoun.

"And they know." This is a circumstantial clause that censures the ugliness of the lying they commit. That is, knowledge of a thing makes it remote and ugly to lie about it; so their lying is not from heedlessness or ignorance, but from knowledge.

(Bala) is an answer to their statement: ﴿There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered (ummiyyin) [Qur'an 3:75]﴾, and this contradicts their claim. The meaning is: Yes, there is blame upon them concerning the unlettered. The discussion of "bala" has already been given in His words ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed [Qur'an 2:81]﴾, so there is no need to repeat it here.

﴿Whoever fulfils his covenant and fears God, then indeed God loves those who are God-fearing﴾. God, exalted is He, informs that whoever fulfils the covenant and fears God in breaking it, then he is beloved to God. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Taqwa (God-consciousness) here means avoiding shirk (associating partners with God)." This sentence confirms the omitted sentence after "bala". As for "man" (whoever), it may be a relative pronoun, but the more apparent reading is that it is conditional. "Awfa" is the dialect of the Hijaz, "wafa" (light form) is the dialect of Najd, and "waffa" (intensive form) is also a dialect. These dialects have already been mentioned. The apparent reading of "bi-'ahdihi" is that the pronoun refers back to "man". It has also been said that it refers back to God, exalted is He. Included in fulfilling the covenant is the greatest covenant taken from them in their scripture, namely belief in the Messenger of God (ﷺ), whether the covenant is attributed to "man" or to God. The conditions apply to the declarative or the conditional sentence, with "man" being general in meaning, as is the case with "al-muttaqin", or what precedes it, being an instance of its instances. It is also possible that the predicate is omitted, its meaning being indicated, the estimated sense being: "God loves him." Then He said, ﴿indeed God loves those who are God-fearing﴾, using the general term "al-muttaqin" to honour God-consciousness and to encourage it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 77:

﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price﴾ It was revealed concerning the rabbis of the Jews: Abu Rafi', Kinana ibn Abi al-Huqayq, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and Huyayy ibn Akhtab. This was said by Ikrimah. Or: it refers to those among the Jews who distorted his description (ﷺ), said by al-Hasan. Or: it was revealed concerning the dispute of al-Ash'ath ibn Qays with a Jew, or with some of his relatives. Or: it was revealed concerning a man who swore over a commodity in the evening that he would give such-and-such for it at the start of the day, a false oath. This was said by Mujahid and al-Sha'bi.

The genitive construction in ﴿covenant of Allah﴾ may be either the subjective or the objective genitive, meaning: the covenant of Allah with them concerning belief in the Messenger who was sent confirming what is with them, and their oaths which they swore that "we will certainly believe in him and certainly support him," or "the covenant of Allah." The word "purchasing" (al-ishtira') here is metaphorical, and the "small price" is the enjoyment of this worldly life, such as bribes, flattery, and the like. The apparent meaning is that it refers to the People of the Book, because of what surrounds it of the verses before it and the verses after it.

﴿Those will have no share in the Hereafter﴾ That is: they have no portion in the Hereafter. They have exchanged the transient little for the lasting bliss. We mean: they have no portion of good, denying them any share of good.

﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾ al-Tabari said: that is, with what would please them. Others said: He will not speak to them at all; rather, the angels will call them to account. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Some people said: it is an expression for anger, that is, He does not regard them and is not pleased with them, and this was said by Ibn Bahr. The explanation of ﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾ was already mentioned in al-Baqarah [2:174].

﴿And will not look at them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ al-Zamakhshari said: "And will not look at them" is a metaphor for contempt toward them and wrath against them. You say: "So-and-so does not look at so-and-so," meaning the denial of his regard for him and his kindness toward him. If you ask: what is the difference between using it for one to whom looking is applicable and one to whom it is not applicable? I say: its original usage for one to whom looking is applicable is a kinaya (metonymy), because whoever regards a person turns toward him and lends him the look of his eyes; then it became common until it became an expression for regard and kindness even where there is no looking. Then it came to be used for one to whom looking is not applicable, purely to mean kindness, as a metaphor for what had occurred as a kinaya for one to whom looking is applicable. End of his words. Others said: "and will not look" means: will not show mercy. He said:

"So I said: 'Look, O most beautiful of all people, at one with a burning thirst, whom longing has wasted.'"

﴿And will not purify them﴾ And will not praise them, or will not increase their deeds (so that it is growth for them), or will not cleanse them of sins. These are three opinions, and their explanation was previously given in al-Baqarah.

﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ Its explanation was also previously given.

﴿Wa-inna minhum lafariqan﴾: that is, of the Jews. This is the view of al-Hasan. Or: of the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas: they are the Jews who came to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. They altered the Torah and wrote a book in which they changed the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then Quraydhah took what they had written and mixed it with the Book that was in their possession.

﴿Yalwuna alsinatahum bil-kitabi li-tahsabuhu mina al-kitab﴾: that is, they twist their tongues with its recitation, away from the correct reading toward the altered one. This is the view of al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: they distort (p-503) and devise tricks to change the meanings, by means of the similarity and shared usage of words and the diversity of interpretations they admit. An example of this is their saying "ra'ina" and "isma' ghayra musma'" and similar expressions. This is not pure substitution (al-tabdil al-mahd). End of quotation.

What appears to be the case is that the twisting (al-layy) occurred in the Book, that is, in its words and not in its meanings alone, as some people claim. Rather, the distortion and substitution occurred in the words, and the meanings follow the words. Whoever studies the Torah knows with certainty that the substitution occurred in both words and meanings, because it contains things that a rational person is certain are not from Allah. It is also not plausible that such things would occur in a divine Book, given the great number of contradictions in its reports and numbers, its attribution to Allah, exalted is He, of things such as eating and wrestling and the like, and its attribution to the prophets of lying, drunkenness from wine, committing adultery with their daughters, and other vile acts from which a rational person would keep himself free, let alone one who holds the station of prophethood.

Shaykh 'Ala' al-Din 'Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Khattab al-Baji, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, wrote a book titled "Questions on the Words and Meanings of the Torah" (al-Su'alat 'ala alfaz al-Tawrah wa ma'anihi). Whoever studies that book sees in it wonders and oddities, and it affirms the substitution of the words and meanings of the Torah. This is despite the fact that it is empty of mention of the Last Day, resurrection, gathering, spreading forth (of deeds), and the punishment and bliss of the Hereafter, and of the good news of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). How far is this from the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who enjoins on them what is right and forbids them what is wrong, makes lawful for them the good things and makes unlawful for them the evil things, and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:157), and His saying, and He mentioned His Messenger and his companions.
