﴿Dhalika mathaluhum fi al-Tawrah﴾ (Al-Fath 48:29).

The Exalted has stated in the Qur'an what necessitates their concealment of much of the Torah. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: Who revealed the Book that Moses brought, a light and guidance for mankind, which you make into scattered pages, showing some and concealing much?﴾ (Al-An'am 6:91). And He, the Exalted, said: ﴿O People of the Book, there has come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Book﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:15). These two verses indicate that what they concealed of the Book is much, and by the implication of the qualifier, what they disclosed of the Book is little.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿yalwuna﴾, the present tense of lawa. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa', Shaybah ibn Nassah, and Abu Hatim, from Nafi', read ﴿yulawwuna﴾ with shaddah, the present tense of lawwa, intensified. Al-Zamakhshari attributed this reading to the people of Madinah. The doubling (al-tadh'if) is for intensity and frequency of the action, not for transitivity. Humayd read ﴿yulunu﴾ with a dammah on the lam, and al-Zamakhshari attributed it to a narration from Mujahid and Ibn Kathir. It is explained on the basis that the original form was ﴿yalwuna﴾, then the waw was changed to a hamzah, then its vowel was transferred to the preceding unvowelled consonant and the hamzah itself was dropped. Here "al-kitab" means the Torah. The addressee in ﴿li-tahsabuhu﴾ is the Muslims. It is also read ﴿li-yahsabuhu﴾ with a ya', and the subject then refers to those who twist their tongues, meaning that the Muslims would suppose it. The pronoun object in ﴿li-yahsabuhu﴾ refers to what is indicated by what precedes it, namely the altered text, meaning "so that they would suppose the altered text to be from the Book."

It is possible that His saying ﴿bil-kitab﴾ involves an omitted noun, meaning "they twist their tongues with something resembling the Book." The pronoun then refers to that omitted noun, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or like darkness in a deep sea, covered by a wave﴾ (Al-Nur 24:40), meaning "or like those in darkness," so the object pronoun in ﴿yaghshahu﴾ refers back to the omitted ﴿dhi﴾.

﴿Wa ma huwa mina al-kitab﴾: that is, what they twisted with their tongues, the altered and substituted text, is not from the Torah. So do not suppose that it is from the Torah.

﴿Wa yaquluna huwa min 'indi Allah﴾: this emphasizes what they intended, namely that the Muslims would suppose it to be from the Book. It is also a great slander against Allah, since they did not suffice with this vile act of substitution and alteration but reinforced it with speech, so that the act would match the statement. This indicates that they do not hesitate about this and do not feel shame, but openly declare that it is thus in the Torah and that Allah revealed it to Moses in this form. This is due to their extreme audacity toward Allah and their despair of the Hereafter.

﴿Wa ma huwa min 'indi Allah﴾: this is a rebuttal of them in their report of falsehood. It emphasizes His saying ﴿wa ma huwa mina al-kitab﴾, the first negation, which is more specific, since the reasoning given there was specific. The negation here is more general, because their claim was more general. For its being from Allah (p-504) is more general than its being in the Torah or in something else.

Abu Bakr al-Razi said: this verse indicates that sins are not from Allah and not of His doing, for if they were of His doing they would be from Him, and Allah has generally negated that sins are from Him. End of quotation. This is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), and al-Razi inclined toward their doctrine.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: ﴿Wa ma huwa min 'indi Allah﴾ negates that it was revealed, as they claimed, though it is from Allah by creation, origination, and bringing into existence, and from them by acquisition (al-taksub). The verse means only the sense of revelation, so the attachment of the Qadariyyah (those who affirm human power over acts) to the apparent wording of His saying ﴿wa ma huwa min 'indi Allah﴾ is refuted.

﴿Wa yaquluna 'ala Allahi al-kadhiba wa hum ya'lamun﴾: the explanation of the like of this has preceded a short while ago.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 79:

﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Scripture and the wisdom and prophethood, and then he should say to the people, "Be servants of mine rather than of Allah."﴾ It is narrated that Abu Rafi' al-Qurazi said to the Prophet ﷺ, when the rabbis of the Jews and the delegation of the Christians of Najran had gathered: "O Muhammad, you only want us to worship you and take you as a god, just as the Christians worshipped 'Isa." The leader of the Christians of Najran said: "Is that what you want, O Muhammad, and is that what you call us to?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "God forbid! That is not what I was commanded, nor to it did I call," and so it was revealed. It was also said: a man said, "O Messenger of Allah, shall we greet you as some of us greet others, and shall we not prostrate to you?" He said: "It is not fitting that anyone be prostrated to besides Allah, but honor your Prophet and recognize the right of those who deserve it."

The exegetes differed as to whom the reference in His words ﴿It is not for a human being﴾ points. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Rabi' and Ibn Jurayj, and a group, said: it refers to Muhammad ﷺ, and they mentioned the occasion of revelation mentioned above.

Al-Naqqash and others said: it refers to 'Isa, and the verse is a refutation of the Christians who said that 'Isa is a god, and claimed that his worship is a law based on his commands. The meaning of ﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him﴾ and what is similar to it is that it negates the occurrence (al-kawn) of the matter, and the intended meaning is negation of the report, and this is of two kinds.

The first: that the negation is from the standpoint of reason, and it is expressed as the complete negation (al-nafy al-tamm). Its example is His saying: ﴿It was not for you to cause its trees to grow﴾ [al-Naml: 60] and ﴿It is not for any soul to die except by the permission of Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 145].

The second: that the negation is by way of probability (al-intifa' 'ala sabil al-intifa'), and it is expressed as the non-complete negation (al-nafy ghayr al-tamm). Its example is the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "It is not for the son of Abu Quhafa to advance and lead the prayer in front of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ."

The apprehension of both kinds is known only through the context of the speech in which the negation occurs, and this verse is of the first kind, because we know that Allah does not give [the Scripture, wisdom and prophethood] to liars and to those who claim prophethood. In this verse there is also an indication of the infallibility ('ismah) of the prophets, peace be upon them.

Here "al-Kitab" is a generic noun (ism jins). As for "al-hukm," it is said to mean "wisdom (al-hikmah)," as in the saying "Indeed, among poetry there is wisdom (hukman)." It is also said that "al-hukm" here means the Sunnah, meaning in contrast to the Book. The apparent meaning, however, is that "al-hukm" here means judgment and the deciding of disputes among people. This is of the manner of ascent (min bab al-taraqqi): He begins with the Book, which is knowledge, then ascends to authority (al-tamkin), which is the deciding among people, then ascends to the highest rank, which is prophethood, the gathering place of all good. Then "thumma yaqula li-n-nas" (then he should say to the people).

He used the particle "thumma" (then), which indicates a lapse of time, to magnify this saying. If this saying is negated after a lapse of time, its negation without that interval is more fitting and more certain; that is, this great bestowal does not combine with this saying, even if it comes after an interval following this great favor.

﴿Be servants of mine rather than of Allah.﴾ "'Ibadan" is the plural of "'abd." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: among its plurals are "'abid" and "'ibaddi." Some philologists said: all these plurals have the same meaning. Others said: "'ibad" is for Allah, and "'abid" is for human beings. Others said: "'ibaddi" is used only for "'abid" in the sense of "slaves of slaves," as if it is an intensification implying total submission in servitude.

What has been established from the usage of the word "'ibad" is that it is the plural of "'abd" whenever the word is used in a context of elevation and indication of obedience, without any connotation of belittlement or diminishing of status. Consider His saying, exalted is He: "Allah is Kind to His servants" (ra'uf bi-l-'ibad), "and honored servants" (wa-'ibad mukramun), and ﴿O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], and the words of 'Isa in the sense of intercession and allusion: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 118]. As for "'abid," it is used for belittlement, and from it is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"Say to Dudan, slaves of the staff, what deceived you about the brave lion?"

And from it is the saying of Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib: "Are you anything but slaves of my father?" And from it is ﴿and your Lord is not unjust to the servants (lil-'abid)﴾ [Fussilat: 46], because it is a place of dividing and informing of their scant victory and capability, and that He, exalted is He, is not unjust to them despite that. And since the word "'ibad" entails obedience, it does not occur here; and for this reason it is familiar in His saying: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves﴾ [al-Zumar: 53]. This kind of reflection leads you along the path of wonders within the domain of the eloquence of the Glorious Qur'an according to the sound Arabic manner. The meaning of His saying ﴿Be servants of mine rather than of Allah﴾ is: worship me and make me a god. End of the words of Ibn 'Atiyyah. In it there is some disputation.

As for his saying, "and from its plurals: 'abid, and 'ibaddi": as for "'abid," the more correct view is that it is a plural. It is also said it is a collective noun (ism jam'). As for "'ibaddi," it is a collective noun, and its alif is for feminine marking. As for what he inferred from induction, that "'ibad" is used in the context of elevation and indication of obedience without any connotation of belittlement or diminution, and his bringing words in the Qur'an with the form "'ibad," and his saying, "As for 'abid, it is used for belittlement," and his citing the verse of Imru' al-Qays, the saying of Hamzah, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿unjust to the servants (lil-'abid)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 182], this is not a sound induction. The use of "'ibad" became more common than "'abid" only because the pattern fi'al is the regular (muttarid) plural pattern of fa'l with a non-ya'i middle radical, whereas the plural of fa'l on fa'il does not follow a regular pattern.

Sibawayh said: it sometimes comes as fa'il, but this is rare, like "al-kulayb" and "al-'abid." End of the words. Since fi'al is the regular plural pattern of "'abd," "'ibad" came frequently. As for ﴿and your Lord is not unjust to the servants (lil-'abid)﴾ [Fussilat: 46], its occurrence here is fitting, even though it is not the regular form, because it came to match the rhyme (tawakhi al-fawasil). Do you not see that before it is ﴿They are called from a far place﴾ [Fussilat: 44], and after it ﴿They will say: We have informed You that none of us is a witness﴾ [Fussilat: 47]? So its occurrence with the word "'abid" fits the matching of these two verse-endings. A parallel to this is His saying in Surat Qaf: ﴿And I am not unjust to the servants (lil-'abid)﴾ [Qaf: 29], because before it (He said: ﴿They will say: We have informed You that none of us is a witness﴾ [Fussilat: 47]) and after it ﴿On the Day We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ [Qaf: 30]. As for its meaning, the meaning of "'abid" and "'ibad" is the same.

As for the verse of Imru' al-Qays, the meaning of belittlement is not understood from the word "'abid" itself; it is understood from their being attributed to the staff, and from the whole verse. Likewise the saying of Hamzah: the meaning of belittlement is understood from it only through the situational context in which it was said, and it came in the verse, and in the saying of Hamzah, according to one of the two permissible readings.

The majority read ﴿thumma yaqula﴾ in the accusative (naṣb), as a conjunction with "an yu'tiyahu." Shibl, from Ibn Kathir, and Mahbub, from Abu 'Amr, read it in the nominative (raf') as a new clause (al-qat'), meaning: "then he himself says." The majority read "'ibadan li," with the ya' of possession (ya' al-idafah) sukun. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read it with fath.

﴿But rather, be rabbaniyyin﴾: this is by implying a verb of saying, its estimated form being: "but rather he says: be rabbaniyyin." The rabbani is the wise, knowledgeable one; this was said by Qatadah and Abu Razin. Or the jurist (faqih), said by 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid. Or the knowledgeable and forbearing one, said by Qatadah and others. Or the wise jurist, said by Ibn 'Abbas. Or the knowledgeable jurist, said by al-Hasan and al-Dahhak. Or the ruler of the affair who trains them and sets them right, said by Ibn Zayd. Or the wise and pious one, said by Ibn Jubayr. Or the teacher, said by al-Zajjaj. Or the scholar, said by al-Mubarrad. Or one who turns repentant to his Lord, said by al-Mu'arrij. Or one who holds most firmly to the religion of Allah and His obedience, said by al-Zamakhshari. Or the wise scholar who sincerely advises Allah concerning His creation, said by 'Ata'. Or the scholar who acts upon his knowledge, said by Ibn Jubayr. Or the scholar who teaches, said by some. These sayings are close to one another.

The Sufis have many other interpretations besides these. Mujahid said: the rabbani is above the habr, since the habr is the scholar, whereas the rabbani is one who, in addition to knowledge and jurisprudence, looks into governance and management, and undertakes the affairs of the subjects and what sets them right in their religion and their worldly life. In al-Bukhari: the rabbani is one who trains people with the minor points of knowledge before its major points. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the sum of what is said about the rabbani is that he is the scholar who is correct in judging, among the sayings and deeds, what he attempts among the people. When Ibn 'Abbas died, Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: Today the rabbani of this Ummah has died.

﴿Because you used to teach the Scripture and because you used to study﴾: the "ba'" is causal (li-l-sabab). As for "ma," the apparent view is that it is a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyyah). "Tu'allimun" is transitive to one object according to the reading of the two Harams and Abu 'Amr, since they read the imperfect of 'alima (lightened). As for the reading of the rest of the Seven, with a dammah on the ta', fath on the 'ayn, and shaddah on the kasra lam, it is transitive to two objects, since it is transferred by doubling from what is transitive to one; the first object is omitted, its estimated form being: "you teach people the Scripture." They spoke at length about preferring one of the two readings over the other, and I have previously stated that I see none of these preferences, since all of them are transmitted by mutawatir chains as Qur'an, so there is no preference of one reading over the other.

Mujahid and al-Hasan read "ta'allamun," with fath on the ta', 'ayn, and the shaddah lam; it is an imperfect from which the ta' has been omitted, the estimated form being "tata'allamun," and the disagreement about what is omitted from either has already been mentioned.

Abu Haywa read "tadrusun" with kasra on the ra'. It is narrated from him: "tudarrisun," with dammah on the ta', fath on the dal, and shaddah kasra on the ra', meaning "you teach others the knowledge"; it is possible that the doubling is for intensity, not for transitivity. It was also read "tadrusun," from "adrasa," in the sense of "darrasa," like "akrama" and "karrama," and "anzala" and "nazzala." Al-Zamakhshari said: it necessitates that leadership, which is the strength of holding to obedience to Allah, be a consequence of knowledge and study, and that is sufficient evidence of the failure of the effort of one who exerts himself and wearies his soul in gathering knowledge but does not make it a means to action; he is like one who plants a beautiful tree which delights him with its appearance but does not benefit him with its fruit. He then said, a few lines later: In it is that whoever knows and studies knowledge but does not act upon it has nothing of Allah in him, and that the connection between him and his Lord is cut, since attribution to Him is established only for those who hold to His obedience. End of his words. In it there is the subtle trace of Mu'tazilism, namely that one is not a believing scholar except through action, and that action is a condition for the soundness of faith.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 80:

﴿Nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords.﴾ The two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr), the two grammarians (al-Kisa'i and Hamza? no) — 

Let me give the translation precisely as follows.

﴿Nor would He command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords.﴾ The two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), the two grammarians (Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i), al-A'sha and al-Barjami read it with a raised ra' (yamurukum, with damma), as a new sentence (qat'). Abu 'Amr elides the vowel (yakhtalisu) according to his usual practice, and the subject is a concealed pronoun in "yaʾmuru" referring to Allah, as said by Sibawayh and al-Zajjaj. Ibn Jurayj said it refers to "basharin" (a human being), described with what preceded it, namely Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning according to this reading is that it is not possible for a human being described with what he was described with to make himself a lord to be worshipped, nor does he command the taking of others, angels and prophets, as lords; thus it is negated that he would call people to himself or to others. If the pronoun refers to Allah, it is then a report from Allah that He did not command this, so the command of Allah and the command of His prophets to this are both negated.

Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamza read "wa la yamurakum" with a fatha on the ra', and Abu 'Ali and others explained it as meaning: "nor is it for him to command you," so that an implied "an" (that) is assumed after la, and la is emphasizing the preceding negation, as you say: "There was no coming from Zayd, nor standing," meaning that neither of them was from Zayd; so la is for emphasis of the preceding negation, and the meaning becomes: "There was from Zayd neither coming nor from him standing."

Al-Tabari said: His saying "wa la yamurakum" with the accusative is coordinated with His saying "thumma yaqula" (then he would say). Ibn 'Atiyya said: "This is an error that does not fit the meaning," end of his words. He did not explain the nature of the error, nor the lack of fit of the meaning with it. The nature of the error is that if it is coordinated with "thumma yaqula," and la is for establishing the negation (ta'sis al-nafy), then it is not possible except that the governing element is assumed before la, which is "an," so that from "an" and the negated verb there results a negated verbal noun, and the meaning becomes: "It is not for a human being described with what he was described with that there be a negation of his command to take the angels and prophets as lords." And if there is no negation for him, there is affirmation for him, so he becomes one who commands taking them as lords, which is an error. But if you make la for emphasizing the preceding negation, the negation extends over the two assumed verbal nouns, so His saying "Be servants to Me" (Aal 'Imran 79) and His command to take the angels and prophets as lords are both negated. This meaning is clarified by the placement of ghayr in place of la: when you say, "Zayd has no jurisprudence nor grammar," la is for emphasizing the negation and both attributes are denied of him; but if you made la for establishing the negation, it would mean ghayr, so the meaning becomes the negation of jurisprudence from him and the affirmation of grammar for him, since if you said, "Zayd has no jurisprudence, and other than grammar," that would affirm grammar for him, as if you said, "He has nothing but grammar." Do you not see that when you say "I came without provision," the meaning is "I came without provision," but when you say "I did not come without provision," its meaning is that you came with provision? Because la here is for establishing the negation. And it is possible that the one who coordinates the negated item with la to the affirmed item to which negation applies is like: "I do not want you to be ignorant, nor that you not learn," meaning: "I do not want you not to learn."

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that la be for establishing the negation. He first mentioned that it is superfluous for emphasizing the meaning of negation, then said: "The second is that he makes la not superfluous, and the meaning is: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to forbid the Quraysh from worshipping the angels, and the Jews and Christians from worshipping 'Uzayr and the Messiah. When they said to him, 'Shall we take you as a lord?', it was said to them: 'It is not for a human being that Allah should give him prophethood, then he would command people to worship him, and forbid you from worshipping the angels and prophets.'"

He said: "The reading with the raised ra' as the beginning of a sentence is more evident, and the reading of 'Abd Allah supports it: 'wa lan yamurakum'," end of al-Zamakhshari's words.

﴿Would he command you to disbelief after you have become Muslims?﴾ This is a rhetorical question of denunciation, and its being after they have become Muslims is more vile and more ugly, since commanding disbelief is in every state reprehensible. Its meaning is that he does not command disbelief, neither after Islam nor before it, whether the commander is Allah or the one Allah has made a prophet.

In this verse there is an indication that those addressed were Muslims, and an indication that disbelief is one religion (millah wahidah), since those who took the angels as lords, then the Sabians and idol worshippers, and those who took the prophets as lords, namely the Jews, Christians and Magians, despite this difference, Allah named all of them disbelief. "Ba'da" (after) is governed by "al-kufr" (disbelief), or by "yamurakum," and "idh" (when) is attached to the nominal clause, as in His saying: ﴿And remember when you were few﴾ (al-Anfal 26), and "ba'da" is attached to it, and only a time-noun is attached to it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 81 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when God took the covenant of the Prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, and then there comes to you a Messenger confirming what is with you, you shall believe in him and you shall surely help him."﴾ The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when God negated from the People of the Book their evil sayings and deeds, and among what He had mentioned last was their trading the signs of God for a small price and what their affair would come to in the Hereafter, and that among them were those who altered and changed in His Book, He described the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and declared His Messenger free from being commanded to worship him or anyone else, rather God alone is singled out for worship. Then He began to establish the proof against the People of the Book and others who denied his prophethood and religion. So He mentioned the taking of the covenant from their prophets to believe in the Messenger of God (ﷺ), to confirm him, and to stand by his support, and their acknowledgment of that, their testimony against themselves, and God's testimony against them concerning that. This covenant is mentioned in their books, and their prophets bear witness to it.

Ubayy and Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited: "the covenant of those who were given the Book" instead of "the Prophets," and it is so in their two mushafs (copies of the Qur'an). It is narrated from Mujahid that he said: "This is how the Qur'an is, and the mention of 'the Prophets' is an error by the scribe." This does not hold from him, because the trustworthy narrators related from him that he recited "the Prophets" like Abd Allah ibn Kathir and others. And even if it is established from someone else, it is an error that is rejected by the ijma' (scholarly consensus) of the Companions upon the mushaf of Uthman.

The address in His words "And when He took" may be directed to the Prophet (ﷺ), commanding him to remind the People of the Book of what is in their books concerning the taking of the covenant from the Prophets. It may also be directed to the People of the Book, who were commanded to recall that. On both of these assessments the governing element is "remember" (udhkur) or "remember" (udhkuru, plural). It is also possible that the governing element of "idh" is "qal" (said) in His words: ﴿He said: "Do you acknowledge and accept my covenant?"﴾ and this is good, since there is no strain in it.

It has been said: it is also possible that it is coordinated with the earlier "idh," whose governing element is "istafa" (chose), but this is very far-fetched. The apparent sense of the speech indicates that God is the One who takes the covenant of the Prophets. It is narrated from Ali, Ibn Abbas, Tawus, al-Hasan and al-Suddi that those whose covenant was taken were the Prophets themselves, not their nations. He took from them that some of them should confirm others and that some should support others. The support of each Prophet for those after him is a charge to whoever believed in him that he should support him if he reaches his time. What goes against this meaning is the phrase: ﴿Then there comes to you a Messenger﴾ to the end of the statement. Ibn Abbas also said, in what is narrated from him: (p-509) He took the covenant of the Prophets and their nations to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) and support him, and he sufficed with mentioning the Prophets rather than mentioning their nations, because the nations are followers of the Prophets. This is supported by the saying of Ali, may God ennoble his face: "God did not send a Prophet except that He took from him the covenant concerning Muhammad (ﷺ), and commanded him to take the covenant from his people concerning him, that they should believe in him and support him if they reach his time." It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas: that when God brought forth the offspring of Adam from his loins, He took the covenant from all the messengers that they should acknowledge Muhammad (ﷺ). On these two views, His words "Then there comes to you a Messenger" refer to one individual, namely Muhammad (ﷺ), and not to a category. The statement of Ibn Abbas that the covenant was taken when He brought them out from Adam's back like tiny particles is far-fetched.

Hamza recited: "lamma ataynakum" (with "atayna" for "ataytu"), because the apparent meaning is that this happened after the giving of the Book and wisdom. The word "covenant" is in construct with "the Prophets," so it is possible that the Prophets are the ones who bind their nations to the covenant, and it is possible that they are the ones bound by it. What indicates this is what precedes the verse, namely His words: ﴿It is not for a human that God should give him the Scripture﴾ [Al 'Imran: 79], to the end of the verse, and what follows it, namely His words: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85]. The meaning of His words "Then there comes to you a Messenger" is Muhammad (ﷺ), and for this reason he came confirming what is with you. Our Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) is very often described with this attribute in the Qur'an. Do you not see His words: ﴿And when there came to them a Messenger from God confirming what was with them, a group among those who were given the Book threw away the Book of God behind their backs﴾ [al-Baqara: 101]? Likewise the description of His Book as confirming what is in their books. Given this, the figurative sense is in the beginning of the verse, so it is by omitting a noun: that is, "And when God took the covenant of the followers of the Prophets from among the People of the Book," or "the covenant of the sons of the Prophets." This accords the beginning of the verse with what follows it. And it has been made a covenant for the Prophets as a way of magnifying this covenant. Alternatively, the one upon whom the covenant is taken is understood to be after "the Prophets," the meaning being: "And when God took the covenant of the Prophets upon their nations." The reading of Ubayy and Abd Allah, "the covenant of those who were given the Book," clarifies this interpretation. It also clarifies that the covenant was upon the nations, by His words: ﴿Then whoever turns away after that, those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 82]. This supposition is impossible with respect to the Prophets; it applies only to the followers.

The majority of the Seven Readers recited "lamma" with a fatha on the lam and a light mim. Hamza recited "lima" with a kasra on the lam. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan recited "lamma" with a shadda on the mim. As for the justification of the majority's reading, there are four opinions.

The first: that "ma" is a conditional particle, in the accusative as the object of the verb after it, and the lam before it is a preparatory lam (muwatta'a) that prepares for "ma" to come after it as the answer of an oath, and that is "akhadha Allahu mithaqa" (God took the covenant of). "Min" in His words "min kitab" (of Scripture) is like it is in His words: ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate﴾ [al-Baqara: 106]. The verb after "ma," being past in form, has a future meaning because the conditional "ma" precedes it. His words "thumma ja'akum" (then there comes to you) are coordinated with the verb after "ma," so it falls within the scope of the condition, and there must be in His words "thumma ja'akum" a pronoun linking it to what it is coordinated with, because "ja'akum" is coordinated with the verb after "ma." His words "la-tu'minunna bihi" (you shall surely believe in him) are the answer to His words: "God took the covenant of the Prophets." A parallel example of this construction is: "I swear by whomever I accompanied, then a Tamimi man did him good, I shall surely do good to him," meaning: "I shall surely do good to the Tamimi man." So "la-uhsinanna" is the answer of the oath, and the answer of the condition is omitted, because the answer of the oath indicates it. Likewise in the verse the answer of the condition is omitted, because the answer of the oath indicates it. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "rasul" (messenger). This view, that "ma" is conditional, is the view of al-Kisa'i.

Sibawayh asked al-Khalil about this verse, and he said, and this is his wording: "Ma here is in the position of alladhi (who), and the lam entered it as it entered 'in' (if), when you say: 'By God, if you do it, I will surely do it.' So the lam in 'ma' is like this lam which is in 'in,' and the lam which is in the verb is like this lam which is in the verb here." End of quote. Then Sibawayh said: "Like this is: ﴿Whoever of them follows you, I will surely fill Hell﴾ [al-A'raf: 18]; the lam entered on the intention of an oath." End of quote.

Abu Ali said: al-Khalil did not mean by his words "in the position of alladhi" that it is a relative pronoun, but that it is a noun, just as alladhi is a noun. He acknowledged that it could be a particle, as it came as a particle in: ﴿Surely each of them, your Lord will certainly repay them in full﴾ [Hud: 111], and in His words: ﴿And surely all that is but the enjoyment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 35]. End of quote.

What emerges from the words of al-Khalil and Sibawayh is that "ma" in "lama atayna-kum" is conditional. Others than these also construed it as conditional: such as al-Mazini, al-Zajjaj, Abu Ali, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya. There is a very subtle objection to this: when it is conditional, the answer is omitted because the answer of the oath indicates it. And when this is so, the omitted element is of the same type as the stated element, and its complements are its complements. So when you say, "By God, whoever comes to me, I will surely honor him," the answer of "man" is omitted, the meaning being: "whoever comes to me, I will honor him." In the verse, the conditional noun is "ma," and its answer is omitted and must be of the same type as the answer of the oath, which is the verb sworn to, and the complement of the verb is the pronoun of the Messenger by means of the preposition, not the pronoun of the supposed "ma." So if the supposed answer of "ma" is of the same type as the answer of the oath, that is not permissible, because it is an overreach. And the answer clause then would be of a pronoun returning to the conditional noun. And if it is not of the same type as the answer of the oath, how does the answer of the oath indicate it, when it is not of its type? And it may not be omitted except when it is of the same type as the answer of the oath. Do you not see that if you said, "By God, if Zayd strikes me, I will surely strike him"? How would you construe it: "If Zayd strikes me, I will strike him"? And it is not permissible that the construction be: "By God, if Zayd strikes me, I will complain to him, I will surely strike him," because "la-adribannahu" does not indicate "ashkuhu" (I will complain to him). So this is the objection to the view of those who construe "ma" as conditional.

As for al-Zamakhshari's statement: "la-tu'minunna" serves in place of the answer of both the oath and the condition together, this is a statement whose apparent sense contradicts the view of those who made "ma" conditional, because they stated explicitly that the answer of the condition is omitted, indicated by the answer of the oath. Unless he meant that from the standpoint of interpreting the meaning, not interpreting the grammar, it serves in place of both, and that could be said. But from the standpoint of grammatical analysis (i'rab), it is not correct, because each of the two, that is the condition and the oath, requires an answer of its own, and it is not possible for this to be governed by both, because the condition requires it in the manner of governing it, so it would be in the position of jazm (jussive mood), while the oath requires it through a semantic connection with it without governing it, so it has no grammatical position. And it is impossible for one thing to have a grammatical position and to have no grammatical position.

The second view, stated by Abu Ali al-Farisi and others: that "ma" is a relative pronoun, a subject (mubtada'), and its relative clause is "atayna-kum," with the returning pronoun omitted, the meaning being "atayna-kumuhu" (We gave you it). "Thumma ja'akum" is coordinated with the relative clause, and the pronoun returning from it to the relative pronoun is omitted, the meaning being "thumma ja'akum rasulun bihi" (then there came to you a messenger with it), so it is omitted because the meaning indicates it. This is how they construed it, and they claimed this is according to the school of Sibawayh. They construed it according to the school of al-Akhfash: the linking of this clause that lacks a pronoun is achieved by His words "limā ma'akum" (confirming what is with you), because that is the relative clause, so it is as if it were said: "then there came to you a messenger confirming it." The linking in a relative clause without a pronoun has occurred, but it is rare. Abu Sa'id, whom I narrated from al-Khudri, related from their speech, meaning: "I narrated from him," and he said:

"O Lord of Layla, You are in every place,
and You are the One in the mercy of God I hope."

He means: "in His mercy I hope." The predicate of the subject which is "ma" is the clause consisting of the omitted oath and its answer, which is "la-tu'minunna bihi." The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the relative pronoun which is the subject, and does not refer to "rasul," lest the clause that serves as the predicate be left without a linking element connecting it to the subject. The initial clause "lama atayna-kum" to the end is the clause that receives what is treated as the oath, which is His words: "And when God took the covenant of the Prophets."

The third view: stated by some scholars, that "ma" is a relative pronoun, the object of the verb which is the answer of the oath, the meaning being: "la-tablughunna ma atayna-kum min kitab wa hikmah" (you will surely convey what We have given you of Scripture and wisdom). He said: but he omitted "la-tablughunna" because of the indication of it, since the lam of the oath falls only on the verb. When this lam indicated this verb, it was omitted. Then He said, exalted is He: "Then there came to you a messenger confirming what is with you," which is Muhammad (ﷺ), "you shall surely believe in him and surely help him." On this supposition the composition is sound. End of quote. What he means is that "la-tu'minunna bihi" is the answer of an omitted oath. This is very far-fetched and is not known from their speech. "By God, Zayd, you desire," is a parallel: the meaning is "la-yadribanna Zaydan" (he will surely strike Zayd).

The fourth opinion was stated by Ibn Abi Ishaq: that *lamā* is a lightened form of *lammā*, with the meaning "when [I gave you]." The explanation of the heavy-stressed reading will follow. As for the explanation of Hamzah's reading, the *lām* is for causation (*lām al-ta'līl*), *mā* is a relative pronoun linked to *ātaynākum*, and the returning pronoun is omitted. *Thumma jā'akum* is coordinated with the relative clause (*ṣilah*), and the link between the clause and the relative pronoun is either a suppressed pronoun, as is attributed to Sibawayh, or this apparent noun *limā ma'akum*, since in meaning it is the relative pronoun according to the view of Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash).

Al-Zamakhshari's statement is that the answer to "He took the covenant of the prophets" is *latu'minunna bihi* ("you shall surely believe in him"), with the pronoun in *bihi* returning to *rasūl*. It is permissible to separate the oath from the thing sworn by a prepositional phrase like this one. If you say, "I swear by the report that reached me about 'Umar, and I will surely be kind to him," it is permissible. Al-Zamakhshari also permitted, in the reading of Hamzah, that *mā* be a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyyah*), and he began with this in explaining the reading. He said: its meaning is "for the sake of My giving you some of the Book and wisdom, and then for the coming of a messenger confirming what is with you, you shall surely believe in him," with *mā* being a verbal-noun particle, and the two verbs with it, namely *ātaynākum* and *jā'akum*, having the sense of two verbal nouns. The *lām* is for causation, in the sense that He took their covenant "so that they would surely believe in the Messenger and surely support him, because I gave you wisdom, and the Messenger whom I commanded you to believe in and support agrees with you and does not oppose you." That is the end of his words.

However, the apparent meaning of this causation that he mentioned, and this estimate he made, is that it is a causation for the sworn action. If this apparent meaning is intended, it contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse, because the apparent meaning of the verse requires that it be a causation for the taking of the covenant, not for its object, which is belief. The *lām* then relates to *akhadha* ("took"). But on the apparent reading of al-Zamakhshari's estimate, it would relate to his words *latu'minunna bihi*, and this is impossible, because the *lām* that introduces the oath does not govern what comes after it on what precedes it. You say, "By God, I will surely strike Zayd," so it is not permissible to say, "By God, Zayd I will surely strike." Accordingly, the *lām* in *lamā* cannot relate to *latu'minunna bihi*. Some grammarians have permitted, for the object of the answer when it is an adverbial or a prepositional phrase, that it precede it, and from this they counted the words of "lā nataffaraq" ("we will not separate") and the Exalted saying: ﴿'ammā qalīlin layuṣbiḥunna nādimīn﴾ ("After a little while they will surely become regretful") [al-Mu'minun: 40]. On this view it is permissible for the *lām* to relate to his words *latu'minunna bihi*. The details of this question are mentioned in the science of grammar.

Al-Sajawandi reported, from the author of *al-Nazm*, that this *lām* in the reading of Hamzah has the meaning of *ba'da* ("after"), like the words of al-Nabigha:

*"I imagined signs in them, so I recognized them, after six years, and this year is the seventh."*

On this view the *lām* in *limā* is not for causation. As for the explanation of the reading of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan, *lammā*, Abu Ishaq said: that is, "When He gave you the Book and wisdom, He took the covenant," and *lammā* here comes to function as a conditional (*jazā'*), as you say, "When you came to me, I honored you." That is the end of his words.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it appears that this *lammā* is the temporal one, meaning: "When you were in this state, the leaders and nobles of the people, He took the covenant from you, since the covenant is taken from leaders." Thus it comes, on this meaning, like the meaning in the reading of Hamzah.

Al-Zamakhshari said: *lammā*, with the doubling, means "when I gave you some of the Book and wisdom, and then a messenger confirming came to you, it became obligatory upon you to believe in him and support him." That is the end of his words. Ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Zamakhshari agreed that *lammā* is temporal, but they differed on the estimate of the answer governing *lammā*, according to their own claims. Ibn 'Atiyyah estimated it from the oath, and al-Zamakhshari estimated it from the answer of the oath. Both of their opinions contradict the school of Sibawayh regarding *lammā*, which requires an answer, for according to Sibawayh it is a particle of necessity for necessity, not temporal in the sense of *ḥīn* ("when") or any other meaning. Only Abu 'Ali al-Farisi went to its temporal character.

We have discussed this at length in the book *al-Takmil li-Sharh al-Tashil*, and we showed that the correct view is the school of Sibawayh.

Ibn Jinni, in explaining this reading, went to the view that its original form was *lamin mā*, with *min* added in the affirmative according to the school of al-Akhfash, and then it was assimilated as is required in such cases, so it became *lammā*. Three *mīms* together were heavy, so the first *mīm* was deleted, leaving *lammā*.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the explanation of this reading, according to this supplementary explanation, is the explanation of *lamā* with a light *mīm*, and this has already been mentioned. The apparent sense of his words is that *min* in his saying *lamin mā* is an additional affirmative particle according to the view of al-Akhfash. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned this estimate in explaining the reading of *lammā* with the doubling, but did not attribute it to anyone. He said: "It was said its original form is *lamin mā*, so they found the combination of three *mīms* heavy, namely the two *mīms* and the *nūn* changed into a *mīm* by its assimilation into the *mīm*, so they deleted one of them, and it became *lammā*. Its meaning is: *lamin ajli mā ātaynākum latu'minunna bihi*, and this is similar in meaning to the reading of Hamzah." That is the end of his words.

This contradicts the words of Ibn Jinni regarding *min*, estimated to enter upon *mā*, for the apparent sense of Ibn Jinni's words is that it is additional, while the apparent sense of al-Zamakhshari's words is that it is not additional, since he made it for causation.

In al-Zamakhshari's statement "they deleted one of them," there is vagueness about what was deleted, and Ibn Jinni specified it: the deleted one is the first. This explanation for the reading with the doubling is extremely far-fetched, and the speech of the Arabs should be held above such a thing coming in it, so how about the speech of God the Exalted? Ibn Jinni was very tolerant in accepting things from the speech of the Arabs.

According to what al-Zamakhshari established, it would follow that in this *lammā* the *lām* in *lamin mā ātaynākum* is additional, and it is not the *lām* of the anticipatory oath (*al-lām al-muwaṭṭi'ah*), because the anticipatory *lām* enters upon conditional particles, not upon a preposition. If you say, "I swear by God, *lamin ajlika la-adribanna 'Amran*," it is not permissible. It is called "anticipatory" because it prepares what is suitable to be the answer of a condition for the oath, so the answer of the condition in that case becomes deleted, because the answer of the oath indicates it.

Nafi' read *ātaynākum* in the plural of majesty, treating the single one as if it were a plural. The majority read *ātaytukum* in the singular, and this is the one consistent with what comes before and after it, since before it is ﴿wa-idh akhadha Allāh﴾ ("and when God took"), and after it comes ﴿iṣrī﴾ ("My covenant").

'Abdullah read *rasūlun muṣaddiqan* with the accusative as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*), and this is permissible from an indefinite noun even if the indefinite noun precedes it. We have mentioned that Sibawayh analogized it. What makes this reading good is that it is indefinite in wording but definite in meaning, since what is meant is Muhammad ﷺ according to the view of the majority. As for his words "*limā ātaytukum*," if all the prophets are intended, which is the apparent wording, then if giving means sending down, not all of them had a book sent down to them, so this is an address to all by the address to its noblest type, and the generalization regarding the prophets is then metaphorical. If by giving is meant being guided by it and calling to act upon it, this is valid for all the prophets, and the generalization is literal. Likewise, if the prophets are taken metaphorically to mean their communities, their being given the Book is God's making it a guidance and call for them.

* *

﴿Thumma jā'akum rasūlun muṣaddiqun limā ma'akum﴾ ("Then there came to you a messenger confirming what is with you"): that is, then he came in your time. The meaning of confirmation is his agreeing in monotheism, prophethood, and the fundamentals of the laws. All of them agree that the truth in the time of each prophet is his law. In the words "a messenger" there is an indication that the covenant taken is what has been established in the intellects by the proofs that necessitate submission to God's command. In His saying "confirming what is with you" there is an indication that the covenant is His describing the attributes of the Messenger in the books of the prophets. These two aspects are both possible. He made belief obligatory first and support second, and this is a clear ordering.

﴿Qāla a-aqrartum wa-akhadtum 'alā dhālikum iṣrī﴾ ("He said: Do you acknowledge and accept My covenant on that condition?"): its apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *qāla* returns to God the Exalted, and in *a-aqrartum* the address is to the prophets from whom the covenant was taken, according to the disagreement: is it on its apparent sense, or is there an omitted genitive, or is it something omitted after "the prophets," the estimate being "the covenant of the prophets with their communities"? He did not suffice with taking the covenant until He made it speak by acknowledging belief in Him and support for Him.

It was said: it is possible that the pronoun in *qāla* refers to each single prophet individually, meaning: each prophet said to his community, "Do you acknowledge?" The meaning of this statement on this possibility is affirmation and emphasis. They did not limit themselves to taking the covenant from the communities, but demanded of them acknowledgment of acceptance.

*Iṣrī* ("My covenant") on the apparent reading is attached to God the Exalted, and on this second statement it is attached to the prophet. *Al-iṣr* means the pact, because it is something that is bound (*yu'ṣaru*), that is, tied and knotted. It was read with a *ḍamma* on the *hamzah*, and this is narrated from Abu Bakr from 'Asim, so it is possible that this is a dialectal form of *aṣarra*, just as they said *nāqatun asfārun 'ubrun* and *'ubru asfārin*, meaning the one prepared for journeys. It is possible that it is a plural of *āṣār*, like *izār* and *uzur*. The meaning of "taking" here is acceptance.

﴿Qālū aqrarnā﴾ ("They said: We acknowledge"): its meaning is that we acknowledge belief in Him and support for Him, and we accept that and bind ourselves to it. There is an omitted clause there, that is: "We acknowledge and have accepted that covenant," and it was omitted because what precedes it indicates it.

﴿Qāla fa-shhadū﴾ ("He said: Then bear witness"): the apparent meaning is that the Exalted said to the prophets from whom the covenant was taken, "Then bear witness," and its meaning from testimony is: let some of you bear witness against others to the acknowledgment and the acceptance of the covenant. This was said by Muqatil. It was said: *fa-shhadū* is an address to the angels, said by Ibn al-Musayyab. It was said: the meaning of *fa-shhadū* is "make this covenant clear to the elite and the common, so that no one has an excuse in ignorance of it." The root of this is that the witness is the one who makes clear the truth of the claim, said by al-Zajjaj, and *ishhadū* here means "perform" (*addū*), not "undertake" (*taḥammalū*). It was said: its meaning is "be certain of what I have established upon you of this covenant, and be in it as one who sees a thing and witnesses it directly," said by Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: *fa-shhadū* is an address to the prophets, if we say that the taking of the covenant was upon their followers; they were commanded to be witnesses over their communities. This was narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.

On the view that the meaning of *qāla a-aqrartum* is "each prophet said," the meaning is: to each prophet for his community, then *fa-shhadū* means "let some of you bear witness against others." The phrase *fa-shhadū* is coordinated with an omitted element, the estimate being: "He said: 'Did you acknowledge? Then bear witness.'" So the *fā'* entered for coordination. A parallel to this is the saying: "Did you meet Zayd?" He said: "I met him." He said: "Then be good to him." The estimate: "You met Zayd, so be good to him." So what contains the *fā'* is part of the speech, and it is not permissible that it be all of the speech because of the *fā'*. Do you not see that "He said: did you acknowledge?" and "They said: we acknowledge?" — when it was all of the speech the *fā'* did not enter.

﴿Wa-anā ma'akum mina al-shāhidīn﴾ ("And I am with you among the witnesses"): it may be a resumed sentence for emphasis, and it may be a circumstantial clause (*jumlah ḥāliyyah*).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 82:

﴿Then whoever turns away after that, those are the defiant transgressors (al-fasiqun).﴾ That is: whoever turns away from faith in this Messenger, and from supporting him, after the covenant was taken, after the acknowledgment and the binding of the pledge. This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib and others. Ibn Atiyya said: It is possible that it means after the testimony of the nations to this covenant, on the basis that His saying, ﴿so bear witness﴾, is a command to fulfil it. Clearly, the conditional particle (sharta, the conditional) is the subject of the verse, and the clause beginning with ﴿those are﴾ and what follows it is the response (jaza'). It is also possible that the particle is a relative pronoun (mawsula). He repeated the pronoun in "turns away" in the singular, following the wording of "whoever" (man), and he used the plural in "those are", following the meaning. This clause indicates that those from whom the covenant was taken are the followers of the Prophets, because He, exalted is He, ruled that defiance applies to whoever turns away after that. This ruling only befits the nations of the Prophets. Also, the Prophets, peace be upon them, had died by the time of his mission (ba'th), which informs us that those upon whom the covenant was taken are their nations.

They mentioned in this verse several kinds of eloquence (fasaha). Among them:

- Antithesis (tibaq) in ﴿a great amount of wealth (qintar)﴾ and ﴿a dinar﴾, since by them both is meant the little and the much. Also in ﴿يُؤَدِّهِ﴾ (yu'addihi, "he returns it") and ﴿لا يُؤَدِّهِ﴾ (la yu'addihi, "he does not return it"), because the meaning of return (ada') is giving, and its absence means withholding, and these two are opposites.
- Paronomasia (tajnis) of the differing kind in ﴿بِالكُفْرِ﴾ (bil-kufr, "with disbelief") and ﴿مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ (muslimun, "submitting"). Also in ﴿اتَّقى﴾ (ittaqa, "feared/guarded against") and ﴿المُتَّقِينَ﴾ (al-muttaqin, "the righteous"), and in ﴿فاشْهَدُوا﴾ (fashhadu, "so bear witness") and ﴿الشّاهِدِينَ﴾ (ash-shahidin, "the witnesses").
- Paronomasia of the similar kind (tajnis al-mumathil) in ﴿ولا يَأْمُرَكم﴾ (wa la ya'murakum, "and he does not command you") and ﴿أيَأْمُرُكم﴾ (a-ya'murukum, "does he command you?"), and in ﴿أأقْرَرْتُمْ﴾ (a-aqrartum, "did you acknowledge?") and ﴿وأقْرَرْنا﴾ (wa-aqrarna, "we acknowledge").
- Demonstration (ishara) in His saying ﴿that﴾ (dhalika) in ﴿بِأنَّهم﴾ (bi-annahum, "because they"), and in ﴿أُولَئِكَ لا خَلاقَ لَهم﴾ (ulaika la khalaqa lahum, "those have no share"), where ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ is the demonstrative.
- Question and answer (su'al wa jawab), which occurs in ﴿قالَ أأقْرَرْتُمْ؟﴾ (qala a-aqrartum?, "He said: Did you acknowledge?"), then ﴿قالُوا أقْرَرْنا﴾ (qalu aqrarna, "They said: We acknowledge").
- Specification (ikhtisas) in ﴿يُحِبُّ المُتَّقِينَ﴾ (yuhibbu al-muttaqin, "Allah loves the righteous"), and in ﴿يَوْمِ القِيامَةِ﴾ (yawm al-qiyama, "the Day of Resurrection"). He specified it by mention, because it is the day on which the requital for deeds becomes manifest.
- Repetition (takrar) in ﴿يُؤَدِّهِ﴾ and ﴿لا يُؤَدِّهِ﴾, in the divine name (Allah) in several places, and in ﴿مِنَ الكِتابِ﴾ (min al-kitab, "from the Book") and ﴿وما هو مِنَ الكِتابِ﴾ (wa ma huwa min al-kitab, "and it is not from the Book").
- Metaphor (isti'ara) in ﴿يَشْتَرُونَ بِعَهْدِ اللَّهِ﴾ (yashtaruna bi-ahdi Allah, "they sell the covenant of Allah").
- Iltifat (shift in grammatical person) in ﴿لَما آتَيْتُكم﴾ (lama ataytukum, "what I have given you"). It is an address (khitab) after His saying ﴿the Prophets﴾ (al-nabiyyin), which is in the third person (ghaib).
- Ellipsis (hadhf) in several places that were mentioned earlier.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 83–86 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah, while to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and to Him they will be returned?﴾ ﴿Say: "We believe in Allah, and in what was sent down to us, and what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and what was given to Moses and Jesus and the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting."﴾ ﴿Whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him, and in the Hereafter he will be among the losers.﴾ ﴿How could Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief, and had testified that the Messenger is true, and clear proofs had come to them? Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ ﴿Their recompense is that upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together.﴾ [Al-Imran: 87] ﴿Abiding therein; their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be reprieved.﴾ [Al-Imran: 88] ﴿Except those who repent after that and make amends, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [Al-Imran: 89] ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief, their repentance will never be accepted, and those are the astray.﴾ [Al-Imran: 90] ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, from any one of them will not be accepted the earth filled with gold even if he offered it as ransom. For them is a painful punishment, and they will have no helpers.﴾ [Al-Imran: 91]

Al-mil' (الملء): the quantity that fills something. It is a noun that has a dual and a plural. One says: milu' al-qadah (مِلْءَ القَدَحِ) and milo'hu (مِلْأهُ), and thalathata amlā'ihi (ثَلاثَةَ أمْلائِهِ). With a fatha on the mim (بِفَتْحِ المِيمِ), it is the verbal noun (المَصْدَرُ): one says malaʼtu al-shay' amla'uhu mal'an. Al-mulā'ah (المُلاءَةُ), which is worn, is the mulḥafah (المُلْحَفَةُ), with a damma on the mim and a hamza. This root was discussed previously in the explanation of al-mala' (المَلَأِ).

﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?﴾ It was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas: "The People of the Book disputed, and each sect claimed that it had the better right to the religion of Abraham. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Both groups are free from the religion of Abraham.' They became angry and said: 'By Allah, we are not content with your judgment, nor will we take up your religion.' So this verse was revealed." The connection of this verse with what precedes it is quite clear. (p. 515)

The hamza in "afa-ghayra" (أفَغَيْرَ) is for denunciation and for drawing attention to the error of turning away and withdrawing. The religion is attributed to Allah because He is the One who legislated it and imposed worship of it upon creation. The meaning of "tabghūna" (تَبْغُونَ) is "you seek," and here it means "you adhere to a religion," because they are clothed in a religion other than the religion of Allah, not seeking it. The verb of seeking is used to indicate that they are at all times searching for it, extracting it and seeking it out. Al-Maturidi said: "If it is said: every intelligent person seeks the religion of Allah and claims that what he follows is the religion of Allah. The answer is in two respects. First: since he fell short in the seeking, he is treated, in meaning, as one who seeks other than the religion of Allah, for if he were truly seeking he would have strived hard in seeking it by the way that leads to it. So he is not, in meaning, seeking, though he is in outward appearance. Second: it has become clear to some in their seeking what the truth is, owing to the manifest proofs and signs, yet they refused except obstinacy, so he is one who seeks other than the religion of Allah, and the verse is about the obstinate." End of his words.

Abu ʿAmr, Hafs, ʿAyyash, Yaʿqub and Sahl read "yabghūna" (يَبْغُونَ) with the ya' (third person, the absent form). Ibn ʿAtiyyah attributes this to Abu ʿAmr and to ʿAsim in full. The rest read it with the ta' (second person, addressing). The ya' is in sequence with "hum al-fasiqun" (هُمُ الفاسِقُونَ), and the ta' is an iltifat (a shift) from the absent to the addressed form. The fa' is for coordinating this sentence with what came before it, and the hamza is placed first out of concern for the interrogation. The implied sense is: "fa-ghayra" (فَأغَيْرَ)? Al-Zamakhshari permitted this view, and it is the view of all grammarians before him. He said: "It is also permissible that it be coordinated with an omitted element whose assumed sense is: 'Do they turn away, so they seek other than the religion of Allah?'" End of his words. This has already been mentioned, and the discussion of his position on it, we have thoroughly examined in our book "al-Takmil" (التَّكْمِيلِ).

"Ghayra" (غَيْرَ) is in the accusative as the object of "yabghūna," and it was placed before its verb because it is more important, in that the denunciation which is the meaning of the hamza is directed at the falsely worshipped deity. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. There is no precision in this, because the denunciation which is the meaning of the hamza is not directed at essences; it is directed at actions that relate to essences. What is denounced is the seeking whose object is other than the religion of Allah. The fronting of the object here is only a matter of latitude (al-ittisaʿ), and "yabghūna" is likened to the rhyme-final position at the end of the verb.

﴿And to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly.﴾ According to the majority, "aslama" (أسْلَمَ) means: to surrender and submit. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "He submitted willingly through his speaking state when the covenant was taken from him, and unwillingly when the prophets called them to Islam." Mujahid said: "The prostration of the shadow of the believer is willing, and the prostration of the shadow of the disbeliever is unwilling," as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shadows at the mornings and evenings.﴾ [Al-Raʿd: 15]. Mujahid also said, as did Abu al-ʿAliyah and al-Shaʿbi, something close to this meaning: "Aslama" means he acknowledged the Creatorship and the servitude; even if among them there were those who associated others in worship, the one who associated submitted unwillingly, while the one who was sincere submitted willingly. Al-Hasan said: "Some people submitted willingly, and some people out of fear of the sword." Matar al-Warraq said: "Whoever is in the heavens submitted willingly, and likewise the Ansar, the Banu Sulaym and ʿAbd al-Qays, and the rest of the people submitted unwillingly, fearing battle and the sword." According to this view, faith is included within submission. Qatadah said: "Submission unwillingly is the submission of the disbeliever at the time of death and the witnessing of it, when it no longer benefits him." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "It follows from this that every disbeliever does so, and this is not found except in individual cases." ʿIkrimah said: "Willingly, through the compulsion of the proof." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Willingly, through reflecting on the evidences and being fair to oneself; and unwillingly, by the sword, or by witnessing what compels one to Islam, such as the lifting of the mountain over the Children of Israel, and the drowning overtaking Pharaoh, and being on the verge of death ﴿so when they saw Our might, they said: We believe in Allah alone﴾ [Ghafir: 84]." End of his words. Al-Zamakhshari thus combined the explanation of "willingly" from the saying of ʿIkrimah, and the explanation of his words "and unwillingly" from the saying of Matar al-Warraq and the saying of Qatadah. Al-Kalbi said: "Willingly, by being born upon Islam; and unwillingly, by the sword."

Ibn Kaysan said: "The meaning is: to Him submits whoever is in the heavens and the earth, in what He has fashioned them in and arranged them upon, and in what He brings about among them; they do not resist Him. Whether they dislike it or love it, whether they are pleased by it or resent it. This is the meaning of the saying of al-Zajjaj: Islam here is the submission to the executing of His command in their natural constitution; no one is able to resist what he has been created upon, nor to change it." What appears is the generality of those in the heavens, and the particularity of those on the earth. "Taw" (الطَّوْعُ) is that in which there is no compulsion, and "karh" (الكَرْهُ) is that which involves hardship. So the submission of those in the heavens is pure willingness, since they are free of the desires that call to opposition. As for the submission of those on the earth: whoever among them is protected (maʿṣūm) it is willing, and whoever is not protected, it is unwilling, in the sense that he is in hardship, because the obligations came in opposition to the psychic desires. Had a messenger from Allah not come, bringing good tidings of reward and warning of punishment, a person would not have bound himself to any of the obligations.

These statements do not remove "aslama" from being understood as surrender, as belief, as verbal affirmation, and as commitment to the rulings. All of this has been said.

The sentence "wa-lahu aslama" (وَلَهُ أسْلَمَ) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyyah). "Ṭawʿan wa-karhan" (طَوْعًا وكَرْهًا) are two verbal nouns in the position of a circumstantial qualifier, meaning: willingly and unwillingly. It is said that they are two verbal nouns used contrary to the usual form. Al-Aʿmash read "kurhan" (كُرْهًا) with a damma on the kaf, while the majority read it with a fatha.

﴿And to Him they will be returned.﴾ This is a great threat to whoever follows and seeks other than the religion of Allah. The meaning of returning to Him has already been discussed. It is possible that it is coordinated with His saying "wa-lahu aslama," so that it shares the circumstantial status with it, and it is as though He reproached them for seeking other than the religion of the One to whom all the obligated submit and to whom their return is, so He will recompense them for their deeds. The meaning: whoever has these two attributes does not seek a religion other than His. It is also possible that it is a new sentence (istiʾnaf) and information that their destination and final return is to Him, so He will recompense them for their deeds.

Hafs, ʿAbbas, Yaʿqub and Sahl read "yarjiʿūna" (يَرْجِعُونَ) with the ya' (absent form). It is possible that it refers back to whoever submitted, and it is possible that it refers to a pronoun other than that of "yabghūna." In that case it would be an iltifat according to the reading of the one who read "tabghūna" with the ta', since it would have shifted from address to absence. The rest read it with the ta'. If the pronoun refers to "man" (whoever), it is an iltifat; if it refers to the pronoun of "tabghūna," it is an iltifat according to the reading of the one who read "yabghūna" with the ya'; or it is a shift from absence to address.

﴿Say: "We believe in Allah, and in what was sent down to us, and what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and what was given to Moses and Jesus and the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting."﴾ This verse agrees with what is in al-Baqarah except in: "Say" (قُلْ), in: "sent down to us" (عَلَيْنا), and in: "Jesus and the prophets" (عِيسى والنَّبِيُّونَ). The explanation of what is in al-Baqarah has already been given, so it is not necessary to repeat it here, except regarding what has been disputed. We say: the apparent meaning of "Say" is that it is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, commanded to inform about himself and about his community with the saying: "We believe in Him." What strengthens that it is information about him and his community is His saying at the end: "and to Him we are submitting." He addressed him in the singular with "Say" because his mention preceded in the taking of the covenant in the saying: ﴿Then there came to you a messenger﴾ [Al-Imran: 81], so He specified him in this obligation to make manifest that he confirms what is with the prophets whose covenant was taken from them. He said "We believe," to indicate that this obligation is not peculiar to him, but is binding on all believers. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Each believed in Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285], after His saying: ﴿The Messenger believes in what was sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285].

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that he be commanded to speak about himself, as kings speak, out of honor from Allah for the rank of His Prophet." Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "The meaning: 'Say, O Muhammad: you and your community believe in Allah.'" Thus it appears from the words of Ibn ʿAtiyyah that there is an omitted coordinated element, and that the command is directed to the Prophet ﷺ and his community.

As for the transitive use of "unzila" (أُنْزِلَ) here with "ʿalā" (عَلى), and in al-Baqarah with "ilā" (إلى), Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "The sending down upon the Prophet of a community is a sending down upon that community."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: why was 'unzila' in this verse transitive by the preposition of elevation, while in what preceded of its like it was by the preposition of terminus?" I say: for the existence of both meanings together, since revelation descends from above and ends at the messengers. So it came sometimes with one of the two meanings and at other times with the other. Al-Raghib said: "He only said here 'ʿalā' because that was a direct address to the Prophet ﷺ, and it reached him from the Highest Assembly without human intermediary, so the word 'ʿalā,' which is specific to height, is more appropriate to it. And there, since it was an address to the community, and it reached them through the Prophet ﷺ, the word 'ilā,' which is specific to conveyance, is more appropriate. It is also permissible to say: 'unzila ʿalayhi' (it was sent down upon him) in regard to what he was commanded to convey to others, and 'unzila ilayhi' (it was sent down to him) in regard to what he was specially given in himself. The terminus of sending down is to Him, and on this basis He said: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down upon you the Book being recited to them?﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 51]. And He said: ﴿And We sent down to you the Reminder, that you may make clear to the people what was sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl: 44]. Here it was specified with 'ilā' because it was specified with the mention, which is the explanation of what was sent down." End of his words, and this is a statement about what is preferable, not about what is obligatory.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that whoever said this distinction has strained the meaning, and he said: "Do you not see His saying: ﴿with what was sent down to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 4], ﴿And We sent down to you the Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48], and His saying: ﴿Believe in what was sent down to those who believed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 72]?" End of quotation. As for the repetition of the phrase "and what was given" (wa-ma ughiya), it is because the wording of the address is general, and among the wisdoms of addressing a general category is elaboration rather than brevity; but since the address here is specific, brevity suffices.

﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾. Regarding "Islam" here, it has been said that it means submission to God and entrusting oneself to Him, which is required in every era, place and law; for this reason al-Zamakhshari explained it as monotheism and the submission of the face to God. It has also been said that what is meant by Islam is the law of Muhammad (ﷺ): God made clear that whoever, after his mission, seeks a law other than his law, that is not accepted from him, and this is the religion which agrees in its beliefs with the religion of the prophets mentioned.

It is said that Ibn 'Abbas said: when the verse ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews and the Christians﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62] was revealed, God then sent down after it: ﴿And whoever seeks﴾ (the verse). This is an indication of the abrogation of ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾. And from 'Ikrimah: when it was revealed, they said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We submitted before you and we are the Muslims." God said to him: "Argue with them, O Muhammad," and He sent down ﴿And due to God from the people is the pilgrimage to the House﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97], so the Muslims performed the pilgrimage and the disbelievers sat back.

It is said that it was revealed concerning al-Harith ibn Suwayd, whose story will come after this. Acceptance of the deed is His being pleased with it and rewarding its doer for it. "Dinan" (religion) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) for "ghayr" (other than), because "ghayr" is vague, so it is specified by "dinan," just as "mithlan" is vague and is likewise specified. This is like their saying: "We have other than it, camels and sheep." The object of "yabtaghi" is "ghayr"; it has also been said that "dinan" is the object and "ghayr" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), because if it came after it would be an adjective. It has also been said that "dinan" is a substitute (badal) for "ghayr." The majority pronounce the two ghayns distinctly, and it is transmitted from Abu 'Amr that he assimilated them (idgham).

﴿And he, in the Hereafter, is among the losers﴾. Loss in the Hereafter is the deprivation of reward and the incurring of punishment. It is likened, in the wasting of his time in this world by following other than Islam, to one who has lost his merchandise. It is possible that this sentence is conjoined to the answer of the condition, so that refusal of acceptance and loss are consequences of seeking other than Islam as a religion. It is also possible that it is not conjoined to it, but is rather a resumed statement about his state in the Hereafter.

"Fi al-akhirah" (in the Hereafter) is related to an omitted element indicated by what follows it, i.e., "and he is a loser in the Hereafter"; or by the supposition of "a'ni" (I mean); or to "al-khasirin" (the losers), on the basis that the alif and lam are not relative but definite, as in "al-rajul" (the man); or to it on the basis that they are relative, and leniency is allowed with the adverbial phrase and the prepositional phrase, because more latitude is permitted with them than with other things. Each is transmitted, and a parallel to it has been mentioned before for us.

﴿How will God guide a people who disbelieved after their belief and had testified that the Messenger is true and clear proofs had come to them? And God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾. It was revealed concerning the People of the Book, who believed in the Torah and the Gospel, and in them is mention of Muhammad (ﷺ), but they altered it and disbelieved after their belief in his prophethood. This was said by al-Hasan, and 'Atiyyah narrated something close to it from Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil said: concerning ten men who apostatized, among them al-Harith ibn Suwayd al-Ansari; he regretted and returned. Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid and al-Suddi mentioned that al-Harith used to show Islam; when the day of Uhud came, he killed al-Mujaddar ibn Ziyad for a blood debt he had against him, and killed Zayd ibn Qays, and apostatized and joined the polytheists. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered 'Umar to kill him if he got hold of him, but he escaped. Then he sent to his brother in Makkah seeking repentance, and the verses were revealed up to His saying: ﴿except those who repent﴾ [Al 'Imran: 89]. His people wrote them to him, and he returned repentant.

'Ikrimah narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, without naming him, and mentioned only that he was a man of the Ansar who apostatized, joined the polytheists; al-Nasa'i recorded it from Ibn 'Abbas at length. It has been said that he joined the Romans. It has been said that al-Harith apostatized with eleven men; al-Zamakhshari named among them Ta'mah ibn Ubayriq, al-Harith ibn Suwayd ibn al-Samit, and Wahwah ibn al-Aslat. 'Ikrimah mentioned that they were twelve, and named among them Abu 'Amir the monk, al-Harith, and some notables. Al-Naqqash said: it was revealed concerning Ta'mah ibn Ubayriq. The wording of the verse includes all who were mentioned and others. It has been said that it is about the polytheists in general. Mujahid said: a man from his people carried the verses to al-Harith and recited them to him; al-Harith said to him: "By God, as far as I know, you are truthful, and the Messenger of God is more truthful than you, and God, Exalted is He, is the most truthful of the three." He said: al-Harith returned, embraced Islam, and his Islam was good.

"Kayfa" (how): a question about states; here it is for wonder and magnification, because of their disbelief after belief; that is, how does one deserve guidance who has done what contradicts it after being entangled with it and after its clarity to him? So its attainment for them is deemed unlikely given the severity of their crimes, as the poet said: "How will a nation prosper that has bloodied the face of its prophet?"

Al-Zamakhshari said: How would He show them kindness, when they are not of the people of kindness, given what God knows of their determination in their disbelief? End of quotation. This is a Mu'tazili tendency, for the meaning in his view is not that God creates guidance in them, just as He does not create misguidance in them, but rather both are created for the servant.

It has been said: the interrogative here is meant as denial, and the meaning is: "it is not guidance." Its parallel is the saying of the poet:
"These are swords, O Sadiyy ibn Malik, many; but where is the striker with the sword?"
And the saying of another:
"How can I sleep on the bed, when a fierce raid overwhelms Syria?"

Guidance here is toward faith and the following of truth. He who claimed that the meaning is: He does not guide them to Paradise, except by figurative usage, calling the cause by the name of its effect, is far off, because entry into Paradise is caused by faith; so it returns to the first saying. "And they testified" (wa-shahidu): its apparent sense is that it is conjoined to their saying "disbelieved" (kafaru); this was said by al-Hufi and Ibn 'Atiyyah, and Makki rejected it, saying: it is not permissible to conjoin "they testified" to "they disbelieved," because the meaning is corrupt; he did not explain from what angle the meaning is corrupt, and it seems he presumed sequence, so the meaning became corrupt in his view. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the meaning understood is that the testimony was before the disbelief, and the conjunction particle (waw) does not indicate sequence. A group, including Makki and al-Zamakhshari, permitted that it be conjoined to the verbal sense in "their belief," since the meaning is: after they believed and testified. Al-Zamakhshari and others permitted that the waw be circumstantial rather than conjunctive; the sense: they disbelieved after their belief, while they had testified, and the governing element of it is "disbelieved." "The Messenger" here is Muhammad (ﷺ), as the majority said; it was permitted that "the Messenger" here means the message, but this is remote.

"Al-bayyinat" (the clear proofs): they are the evidences of the Qur'an and the miracles which prophets bring the like of.

﴿And God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾: that is, He does not create guidance in their hearts. "Al-zalimin" (the wrongdoers) is general in wording but specific in meaning; that is, He does not guide those whom He has decreed will die in disbelief. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is possible that it intends to inform that the wrongdoer, in his wrongdoing, is not upon guidance from God, so the verse comes general in its full generality. End of quotation. This meaning he mentioned is not supported by the wording of the verse. Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-zalimin" means the obstinate ones whom God knows kindness will not benefit, end of quotation; and he interpreted it according to his Mu'tazili method.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 83–86 (part 1 of 2):
