"Al-dallun" means: those who have erred from the path of truth and salvation in the Hereafter, or: those who perish; from "dalla al-laban fi al-ma'" when it becomes perished. The waw in "wa-ulaika" is for coordination, either upon the predicate of inna, so the clause is in a place of raf', or upon the clause consisting of inna and its two objects, in which case it has no place in the i'rab.

Al-Raghib mentioned a saying: that the waw in "wa-ulaika" is the waw of the state (waw al-hal), and the meaning: "their repentance from sins will never be accepted while they are astray," so repentance and error are mutually contradictory and do not come together. End of this saying. This meaning is refuted by this construction, for if this meaning were intended, the demonstrative would not have been used; and the hum may be a separator (fasl), an inchoative (ibtida'), or a substitute (badal).

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers—never will there be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth with gold﴾. Ikrimah read: "fa-lan naqbala" with the nun and "mil'a" with the accusative. It was also read: "fa-lan yaqbala" with the ya', in the active voice, i.e., "then Allah will never accept," and "mil'a" in the accusative. Abu Ja'far and Abu al-Sammal read: "milla al-ardi," without hamza. It was transmitted from Nafi' as well, and its explanation: he transferred the vowel of the hamza to the preceding unvowelled letter, which is the lam, and the hamza was deleted; this is a regular analogy in every case like this. And He used the wording "ahadihim" and did not use the wording "minhum," because that is more emphatic and more explicit in the intended meaning, since "minhum" could be understood as with the condition of the whole group. The accusative of "dhahaban" is by way of tamyiz; there is a disagreement about the governing word of the tamyiz. Al-Farra' called it an explanation (tafsir), because the quantity is known while the thing by which it is measured is general. Al-Kisa'i said: it is accusative by the implied "min" (of), i.e., "min dhahabin," like His saying: ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95], i.e., "min siyam" (of fasting). Al-A'mash read: "dhahabun" in the nominative. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a reference back to "mil'a," as one says: "I have twenty persons, men," End of his words. By "reference back" he means apposition, and it would be an apposition of an indefinite from a definite, since "mil'a al-ardi" is definite; for this reason the expert grammarians pointed the saying "Laka al-hamdu mil'u al-samawati wa-l-ardi" with the nominative as an attribute of "al-hamd," and they avoided its accusative as a circumstantial (hal) because it is definite.

﴿Even if he offers it as ransom﴾. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "law iftada bihi" without the waw, and "law" here has the meaning of the conditional "in" and not of "law" which indicates what would have occurred because of the occurrence of something else; because "law" here is connected to the future, namely "fa-lan yuqbila," while that other is connected to the past. As for the reading of Ibn Abi 'Ablah, he made the ransoming a condition for non-acceptance, so the negation of the existence of acceptance is not generalized. As for the reading of the majority with the waw, it was said: the waw is superfluous, and this is weak, and the meaning in that case would be the meaning of Ibn Abi 'Ablah's reading. It was also said: it is not superfluous.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: what is the position of His saying ﴿even if he offers it as ransom﴾? I say: it is a statement understood by meaning, as if it were said: 'then there will never be accepted from any of them a ransom, even if he ransoms himself with the filling of (p-521) the earth in gold.'" End of his words. This meaning is refuted by this construction and it does not bear it; what this construction requires, and what it should be understood as, is that Allah the Exalted informed that whoever dies in disbelief, there will not be accepted from him what fills the earth of gold, in any state he intends, even in the state of ransoming himself from the punishment with it; because the state of ransoming is a state in which the ransomer is not favored over the one ransomed from him, since it is a state of compulsion from the one ransomed from upon the ransomer. We have already established in similar constructions that "law" comes to alert that what precedes it came by way of exhaustive enumeration, and what follows it came as an explicit mention of the state which is supposed not to be included in what precedes it, as in his saying: "Give to the beggar even if he comes on a horse, and turn away the beggar even with a burnt hoof." As if these things were ones that should not be given; for the beggar being on a horse shows his wealth, so it is not appropriate that a filling of the earth of gold be accepted from him, but it is not accepted. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿and you will not be a believer to us even if we were truthful﴾ [Yusuf: 17], because they negated that he would believe them in every state, even in the state of their truthfulness, which is the state in which they should be believed. So the word "law" here is for generalizing the negation and for emphasizing it; and we have mentioned the benefit of its coming. Al-Zajjaj went to the view that the meaning is: there will never be accepted from any one of them his expenditure and his acts of nearness in this world, even if he spent the filling of the earth in gold, and even if he ransomed himself with it in the Hereafter, it would not be accepted from him. He said: So Allah informed that He does not reward them for their good deeds, nor does He accept from them ransom from the punishment. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a good saying. End of his words.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that it be intended: "there will never be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth in gold, even if he had given it in charity; and even if he ransomed himself with it, it would not be accepted from him either." End of his words. This is the meaning of al-Zajjaj's saying, except that he did not restrict the ransoming to the Hereafter. Ṣāḥib Rayy al-Ẓam'ān and others reported from al-Zajjaj that he said: the meaning of the verse: even if he ransoms himself with it in this world while persisting in disbelief, it will not be accepted from him. What appears is that the non-acceptance even by way of ransom occurs only in the Hereafter. What clarifies this is what is established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from the hadith of Anas: that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The disbeliever will be called to account on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said to him: 'Tell me, if you had the filling of the earth in gold, would you ransom yourself with it?' He will say: 'Yes.' It will be said to him: 'You were asked for something easier than that.'" This hadith shows that His saying ﴿so there will never be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth in gold, and even if he ransoms himself with it﴾ (p-522) is by way of supposition and hypothesis, i.e., if the disbeliever were to possess the most precious things, and then were to be able to give it, he would be unable to use that as a means to deliver himself from the punishment of Allah. The meaning is that they are despairing of delivering themselves from the punishment. It is thus like His saying: ﴿And if those who wronged had all that is on the earth entirely﴾ [al-Zumar: 47], and like His saying: ﴿The criminal would wish to ransom himself﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 11], the two verses. And on this basis, what al-Zajjaj said is far-fetched, namely that the meaning is: that if they spent the filling of the earth in gold in this world, that would not be accepted; because obedience alongside disbelief is not accepted.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 87–91 (part 2 of 2):

"Wa-ftada" (وافْتَدى): it is of the form "ifta'ala" from "al-fidyah" (ransom). It has been said that it has the same meaning as "fa'ala", like "shawa" and "ishtawa" (both meaning to roast), and its object is omitted. Making "iftada" transitive requires a hearing from the Arabs. The pronoun in "bihi" (بِهِ) refers to "mil' al-ard" (filling of the earth), which is the quantity that would fill it. It is found in some tafsirs that it refers to "al-mil'" (the filling), or to "al-dhahab" (the gold). It has been said that the reference to "al-dhahab" is an error.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that what is meant is: 'Even if he ransomed himself with its like,' because of His saying: ﴿Even if those who did wrong had whatever is on the earth entirely and the like of it with it﴾ [al-Zumar: 47]. The word "mithl" (like) is often omitted in their speech, as when you say: 'I struck the strike of Zayd,' meaning: 'the like of his strike,' and 'Abu Yusuf is Abu Hanifa,' meaning: 'his like.'"

[Poetry]
"Nor does Haytham tonight [mourn] for the riding beasts"
And the case of "wa-la Aba Hasanin lahā" [nor Abu Hasan has her], you mean: "nor [the like of] Haytham, nor the like of Abu Hasan," just as it is intended in phrases such as their saying: "Mithlaka la yaf'alu kadha" [one like you does not do such a thing], you mean: "you yourself and that [is not so]." This is because two like things, one of them stands in place of the other, so they are in the ruling of one thing. End of his words.

There is no need to assume "mithl" in His saying ﴿even if he ransomed himself with it﴾. Al-Zamakhshari imagined that what is denied acceptance cannot be ransomed with, so he needed to supply "mithl" in order to distinguish between what is denied acceptance and what is used as ransom. This is not so, because that, as we have mentioned, is by way of supposition, and the meaning is: it is customarily impossible that anyone possesses the filling of the earth with gold such that, if he were to spend it in any way whatsoever, it would not be accepted from him. Rather, even if that were possible, there would be no need to assume "mithl," because He denied its acceptance even in the state of ransoming. What is supplied in the verse is not like the example he gave, because this supposition is not needed, has no meaning, and neither in the wording nor in the meaning is there anything indicating it, so it is not supplied. As for the examples he gave, "I struck the strike of Zayd" and "Abu Yusuf is Abu Hanifa," by the necessity of reason we know that "mithl" must be supplied, since your striking cannot be the striking of Zayd, and the person of Abu Yusuf cannot be the person of Abu Hanifa. As for:

[Poetry]
"Nor does Haytham tonight [mourn] for the riding beasts"

it indicates an omission, as is established in the Arabic language, that "la" which denotes the negation of the genus does not enter upon proper nouns and affect them, so one needs to supply "mithl" in order to keep it within what is established for it, since it is established that it governs only the genus, because definiteness as a proper name contradicts the generality of the genus. As for his words: "just as it may be added in: 'Mithlaka la yaf'alu kadha,' meaning 'anta' (you)," this is a view that has been stated, but the preferred view among the skilled grammarians is that nouns are not added (as extra words), and for establishing that "one like you does not do such a thing," "mithl" is not there as an extra word in place of anything other than this.

﴿Those, for them is a painful punishment﴾. This is a second report about the one who died while a disbeliever. When Almighty God explained in the first report that nothing is accepted from him until he ransoms his soul with it, He explained in this report what punishment he has, described with intensity in pain for him, since ransoming and spending wealth only happens in response to the pains that will befall the one who ransoms, so that he will spend the most precious things to be freed from that. As He said: ﴿The criminal would wish to ransom himself from the punishment of that Day with his children﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 11], and so on. The raising of "adhab" (punishment) is as the subject of the preceding prepositional phrase, since it relies on "ula'ika" (those), it being its predicate. It is also permissible for it to be raised as the subject of an inceptive (mubtada').

﴿And for them there are no helpers﴾. The construction of this phrase has been explained before. This is a third report. When He explained that there is no escape for him from the punishment by spending wealth, He also explained that there is no escape for him from it by means of help, and included in this is help by force and help by intercession.

This verse contains kinds of rhetorical ornamentation (badi'): antithesis (tibaq) in His saying "tau'an wa-karhan" (willingly or unwillingly), and in "kafaru ba'da imanihim" in two places; repetition (takrar) in "yahdi" and "la yahdi," and in "kafaru ba'da imanihim"; and paronomasia of the different kind (tajnis mughayir) in "kafaru" and "kafaru." Emphasis by the pronoun "hum" appears in His saying: "wa-ula'ika humu al-dallun" (those are the astray), it is said. Also the simile in "thumma izdadu kufran," where He likened their persistence in disbelief and their crimes to offenses that are added one upon another, and this is comparing the intelligible to the perceptible. Also the change from "mif'al" to "fa'il" in "adhabun alim," because of the intensity found in "fa'il." And omission in several places.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 87–91 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those—their recompense is that upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein; the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.﴾ The tafsir of the like of this sentence has already passed. As for the reading of al-Hasan, "wa-l-nasu ajma'una" (the nominative form), its explanation was given in Surat al-Baqarah, so it suffices from repeating it. However, here it is ﴿Those—their recompense﴾, i.e., the recompense of their disbelief, whereas there it is ﴿Those—upon them is the curse of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 161]; because there the statement concerns those who died in disbelief, so the curse was made certain upon them, whereas here it is not so. Do you not consider the occasion of revelation? And that most of the sayings are that it was revealed concerning a people who apostatized and then returned to Islam? Therefore the exception came, which is His saying: ﴿except those who repent after that﴾, and it is an exception of the connected kind (istithna' muttasil), and therefore He said ﴿after that﴾, (p-519) i.e., after that great disbelief.

(Wa-aslahu) means: they amended what they had corrupted, or: they entered into righteousness, as you say "Amsa Zayd," i.e., he entered the evening. It was also said: the meaning of aslahu is: they made clear that they had been in error. The explanation of this word has already passed in al-Baqarah in His saying ﴿except those who repent and amend and make clear﴾ [al-Baqarah: 160].

﴿Then indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ "Forgiving" means for their disbelief; "Merciful" means for accepting their repentance; and these are two intensive forms indicating the vastness of His mercy.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief, then increase in disbelief—their repentance will never be accepted, and those are the astray.﴾ It was revealed concerning the Jews, who disbelieved in Jesus and the Gospel after their belief in their prophets, then increased in disbelief by their disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ after their belief in his description; this was said by Qatadah and al-Hasan. It was also said: concerning the Jews who disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ after their belief in his attributes and their acknowledgment that they were in the Torah; then they increased in disbelief through the sins they committed in opposing the Prophet ﷺ, such as slander, calumny, and striving against Islam; this was said by Abu al-'Aliyah. Or the meaning is: then they increased in disbelief, they persisted in their disbelief and reached death in it; this includes the Jews and the apostates; this was said by Mujahid, and al-Suddi said something similar. It was also said: it was revealed concerning those among the companions of al-Harith ibn Suwayd who died in disbelief, for they said: "We will remain in Mecca and await for Muhammad ﷺ the vicissitudes of fate (rayb al-manun)"; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The meaning of the increase in disbelief is explained by these sayings, and it is according to its objects, since belief and disbelief, in reality, do not increase or decrease; rather, the increase and decrease occur in their objects, and so that is attributed to them by way of metaphor. "Izdadu" is of the form "iftaʿalu" from increase, and "kufran" is in the accusative as a tamyiz transferred from the agent; the meaning: "then the disbelief of them increased," and the first dal is a substitute for the ta' of the iftiʿal.

The saying ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾ may admit two aspects. One: that there is a repentance from them, but it is not accepted—although it is known that the repentance of every disbeliever is accepted, whether he disbelieved after belief and increased in disbelief, or was a disbeliever from the first time. Thus, in this there is need for a specification. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid, and al-Suddi said: the denial of their repentance is specific to the death-rattle, the gurgling, and the moment of seeing (the angels). Al-Nahhas said: this is a good saying, like His saying: ﴿and repentance is not for those who do evil deeds﴾ [al-Nisa': 18], etc. Abu al-'Aliyah said: "their repentance will never be accepted" refers to the sins they committed together with their persistence in disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾, because it is a repentance that is not sincere, since they are apostates and resolved to display repentance to conceal their states, while disbelief is in their inner selves. Mujahid said: their repentance will never be accepted after death if they die in disbelief. It was also said: their repentance will never be accepted which they repented before they disbelieved, because disbelief has nullified it. It was also said: their repentance will never be accepted if they repent from one disbelief to another disbelief; it is accepted only if they repent to Islam. The distinguishing principle of this specification is that it is a specification by time, or it is described in the repentance.

The second aspect: that the meaning be: there is no repentance for them so that it might be accepted; so the acceptance is negated, while the intended meaning is the negation of repentance itself, and thus it is of the type of the saying:

"On a road whose landmarks are not guided by"

i.e., there is no landmark for it by which one is guided; and this would be concerning a specific people whom Allah has decreed to disbelief, i.e., they have no repentance, so they will inevitably die in disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah have indicated this meaning. The particle fa' did not enter upon "lan tuqbila" here, but it entered upon "fa-lan tuqbila" (in 91), because the fa' indicates entitlement by the preceding attribute; and there he said: "and they died while they were disbelievers," whereas here he did not state this condition explicitly.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: since the meaning of ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾ is in the sense of dying in disbelief, why was not dying in disbelief made the consequence of their apostasy and their increase in disbelief, because of what that involves of hardness of hearts, the mounting of rust, and its leading to dying in disbelief?" I say: because how many an apostate who increased in disbelief returns to Islam and does not die in disbelief? If you say: then what is the benefit of this kinaya (metaphor), I mean if he alludes to dying in disbelief by the impossibility of accepting repentance? I say: the benefit in it is great: it is the intensification concerning that group of disbelievers, and the portrayal of their state (p-520) in the form of the state of those who despair of mercy, which is the most severe and intense of states. Do you not see that dying in disbelief is feared only because of despair of mercy? End of his words.

Ikrimah read: "lan naqbala tawbatahum" with the nun and the accusative tawbatahum. "Al-dallun" means: those who have erred from the path of truth and salvation in the Hereafter, or: those who perish; from "dalla al-laban fi al-ma'" when it becomes perished. The waw in "wa-ulaika" is for coordination, either upon the predicate of inna, so the clause is in a place of raf', or upon the clause consisting of inna and its two objects, in which case it has no place in the i'rab.

Al-Raghib mentioned a saying: that the waw in "wa-ulaika" is the waw of the state (waw al-hal), and the meaning: "their repentance from sins will never be accepted while they are astray," so repentance and error are mutually contradictory and do not come together. End of this saying. This meaning is refuted by this construction, for if this meaning were intended, the demonstrative would not have been used; and the hum may be a separator (fasl), an inchoative (ibtida'), or a substitute (badal).

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers—never will there be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth with gold﴾. Ikrimah read: "fa-lan naqbala" with the nun and "mil'a" with the accusative. It was also read: "fa-lan yaqbala" with the ya', in the active voice, i.e., "then Allah will never accept," and "mil'a" in the accusative. Abu Ja'far and Abu al-Sammal read: "milla al-ardi," without hamza. It was transmitted from Nafi' as well, and its explanation: he transferred the vowel of the hamza to the preceding unvowelled letter, which is the lam, and the hamza was deleted; this is a regular analogy in every case like this. And He used the wording "ahadihim" and did not use the wording "minhum," because that is more emphatic and more explicit in the intended meaning, since "minhum" could be understood as with the condition of the whole group. The accusative of "dhahaban" is by way of tamyiz; there is a disagreement about the governing word of the tamyiz. Al-Farra' called it an explanation (tafsir), because the quantity is known while the thing by which it is measured is general. Al-Kisa'i said: it is accusative by the implied "min" (of), i.e., "min dhahabin," like His saying: ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95], i.e., "min siyam" (of fasting). Al-A'mash read: "dhahabun" in the nominative. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a reference back to "mil'a," as one says: "I have twenty persons, men," End of his words. By "reference back" he means apposition, and it would be an apposition of an indefinite from a definite, since "mil'a al-ardi" is definite; for this reason the expert grammarians pointed the saying "Laka al-hamdu mil'u al-samawati wa-l-ardi" with the nominative as an attribute of "al-hamd," and they avoided its accusative as a circumstantial (hal) because it is definite.

﴿Even if he offers it as ransom﴾. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "law iftada bihi" without the waw, and "law" here has the meaning of the conditional "in" and not of "law" which indicates what would have occurred because of the occurrence of something else; because "law" here is connected to the future, namely "fa-lan yuqbila," while that other is connected to the past. As for the reading of Ibn Abi 'Ablah, he made the ransoming a condition for non-acceptance, so the negation of the existence of acceptance is not generalized. As for the reading of the majority with the waw, it was said: the waw is superfluous, and this is weak, and the meaning in that case would be the meaning of Ibn Abi 'Ablah's reading. It was also said: it is not superfluous.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: what is the position of His saying ﴿even if he offers it as ransom﴾? I say: it is a statement understood by meaning, as if it were said: 'then there will never be accepted from any of them a ransom, even if he ransoms himself with the filling of (p-521) the earth in gold.'" End of his words. This meaning is refuted by this construction and it does not bear it; what this construction requires, and what it should be understood as, is that Allah the Exalted informed that whoever dies in disbelief, there will not be accepted from him what fills the earth of gold, in any state he intends, even in the state of ransoming himself from the punishment with it; because the state of ransoming is a state in which the ransomer is not favored over the one ransomed from him, since it is a state of compulsion from the one ransomed from upon the ransomer. We have already established in similar constructions that "law" comes to alert that what precedes it came by way of exhaustive enumeration, and what follows it came as an explicit mention of the state which is supposed not to be included in what precedes it, as in his saying: "Give to the beggar even if he comes on a horse, and turn away the beggar even with a burnt hoof." As if these things were ones that should not be given; for the beggar being on a horse shows his wealth, so it is not appropriate that a filling of the earth of gold be accepted from him, but it is not accepted. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿and you will not be a believer to us even if we were truthful﴾ [Yusuf: 17], because they negated that he would believe them in every state, even in the state of their truthfulness, which is the state in which they should be believed. So the word "law" here is for generalizing the negation and for emphasizing it; and we have mentioned the benefit of its coming. Al-Zajjaj went to the view that the meaning is: there will never be accepted from any one of them his expenditure and his acts of nearness in this world, even if he spent the filling of the earth in gold, and even if he ransomed himself with it in the Hereafter, it would not be accepted from him. He said: So Allah informed that He does not reward them for their good deeds, nor does He accept from them ransom from the punishment. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a good saying. End of his words.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that it be intended: "there will never be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth in gold, even if he had given it in charity; and even if he ransomed himself with it, it would not be accepted from him either." End of his words. This is the meaning of al-Zajjaj's saying, except that he did not restrict the ransoming to the Hereafter. Ṣāḥib Rayy al-Ẓam'ān and others reported from al-Zajjaj that he said: the meaning of the verse: even if he ransoms himself with it in this world while persisting in disbelief, it will not be accepted from him. What appears is that the non-acceptance even by way of ransom occurs only in the Hereafter. What clarifies this is what is established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from the hadith of Anas: that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The disbeliever will be called to account on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said to him: 'Tell me, if you had the filling of the earth in gold, would you ransom yourself with it?' He will say: 'Yes.' It will be said to him: 'You were asked for something easier than that.'" This hadith shows that His saying ﴿so there will never be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth in gold, and even if he ransoms himself with it﴾ (p-522) is by way of supposition and hypothesis, i.e., if the disbeliever were to possess the most precious things, and then were to be able to give it, he would be unable to use that as a means to deliver himself from the punishment of Allah. The meaning is that they are despairing of delivering themselves from the punishment. It is thus like His saying: ﴿And if those who wronged had all that is on the earth entirely﴾ [al-Zumar: 47], and like His saying: ﴿The criminal would wish to ransom himself﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 11], the two verses. And on this basis, what al-Zajjaj said is far-fetched, namely that the meaning is: that if they spent the filling of the earth in gold in this world, that would not be accepted; because obedience alongside disbelief is not accepted.

The saying ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾ may admit two aspects. One: that there is a repentance from them, but it is not accepted—although it is known that the repentance of every disbeliever is accepted, whether he disbelieved after belief and increased in disbelief, or was a disbeliever from the first time. Thus, in this there is need for a specification. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid, and al-Suddi said: the denial of their repentance is specific to the death-rattle, the gurgling, and the moment of seeing (the angels). Al-Nahhas said: this is a good saying, like His saying: ﴿and repentance is not for those who do evil deeds﴾ [al-Nisa': 18], etc. Abu al-'Aliyah said: "their repentance will never be accepted" refers to the sins they committed together with their persistence in disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾, because it is a repentance that is not sincere, since they are apostates and resolved to display repentance to conceal their states, while disbelief is in their inner selves. Mujahid said: their repentance will never be accepted after death if they die in disbelief. It was also said: their repentance will never be accepted which they repented before they disbelieved, because disbelief has nullified it. It was also said: their repentance will never be accepted if they repent from one disbelief to another disbelief; it is accepted only if they repent to Islam. The distinguishing principle of this specification is that it is a specification by time, or it is described in the repentance.

The second aspect: that the meaning be: there is no repentance for them so that it might be accepted; so the acceptance is negated, while the intended meaning is the negation of repentance itself, and thus it is of the type of the saying:

"On a road whose landmarks are not guided by"

i.e., there is no landmark for it by which one is guided; and this would be concerning a specific people whom Allah has decreed to disbelief, i.e., they have no repentance, so they will inevitably die in disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah have indicated this meaning. The particle fa' did not enter upon "lan tuqbila" here, but it entered upon "fa-lan tuqbila" (in 91), because the fa' indicates entitlement by the preceding attribute; and there he said: "and they died while they were disbelievers," whereas here he did not state this condition explicitly.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: since the meaning of ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾ is in the sense of dying in disbelief, why was not dying in disbelief made the consequence of their apostasy and their increase in disbelief, because of what that involves of hardness of hearts, the mounting of rust, and its leading to dying in disbelief?" I say: because how many an apostate who increased in disbelief returns to Islam and does not die in disbelief? If you say: then what is the benefit of this kinaya (metaphor), I mean if he alludes to dying in disbelief by the impossibility of accepting repentance? I say: the benefit in it is great: it is the intensification concerning that group of disbelievers, and the portrayal of their state (p-520) in the form of the state of those who despair of mercy, which is the most severe and intense of states. Do you not see that dying in disbelief is feared only because of despair of mercy? End of his words.

Ikrimah read: "lan naqbala tawbatahum" with the nun and the accusative tawbatahum. "Al-dallun" means: those who have erred from the path of truth and salvation in the Hereafter, or: those who perish; from "dalla al-laban fi al-ma'" when it becomes perished. The waw in "wa-ulaika" is for coordination, either upon the predicate of inna, so the clause is in a place of raf', or upon the clause consisting of inna and its two objects, in which case it has no place in the i'rab.

Al-Raghib mentioned a saying: that the waw in "wa-ulaika" is the waw of the state (waw al-hal), and the meaning: "their repentance from sins will never be accepted while they are astray," so repentance and error are mutually contradictory and do not come together. End of this saying. This meaning is refuted by this construction, for if this meaning were intended, the demonstrative would not have been used; and the hum may be a separator (fasl), an inchoative (ibtida'), or a substitute (badal).

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers—never will there be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth with gold﴾. Ikrimah read: "fa-lan naqbala" with the nun and "mil'a" with the accusative. It was also read: "fa-lan yaqbala" with the ya', in the active voice, i.e., "then Allah will never accept," and "mil'a" in the accusative. Abu Ja'far and Abu al-Sammal read: "milla al-ardi," without hamza. It was transmitted from Nafi' as well, and its explanation: he transferred the vowel of the hamza to the preceding unvowelled letter, which is the lam, and the hamza was deleted; this is a regular analogy in every case like this. And He used the wording "ahadihim" and did not use the wording "minhum," because that is more emphatic and more explicit in the intended meaning, since "minhum" could be understood as with the condition of the whole group. The accusative of "dhahaban" is by way of tamyiz; there is a disagreement about the governing word of the tamyiz. Al-Farra' called it an explanation (tafsir), because the quantity is known while the thing by which it is measured is general. Al-Kisa'i said: it is accusative by the implied "min" (of), i.e., "min dhahabin," like His saying: ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95], i.e., "min siyam" (of fasting). Al-A'mash read: "dhahabun" in the nominative. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a reference back to "mil'a," as one says: "I have twenty persons, men," End of his words. By "reference back" he means apposition, and it would be an apposition of an indefinite from a definite, since "mil'a al-ardi" is definite; for this reason the expert grammarians pointed the saying "Laka al-hamdu mil'u al-samawati wa-l-ardi" with the nominative as an attribute of "al-hamd," and they avoided its accusative as a circumstantial (hal) because it is definite.

﴿Even if he offers it as ransom﴾. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "law iftada bihi" without the waw, and "law" here has the meaning of the conditional "in" and not of "law" which indicates what would have occurred because of the occurrence of something else; because "law" here is connected to the future, namely "fa-lan yuqbila," while that other is connected to the past. As for the reading of Ibn Abi 'Ablah, he made the ransoming a condition for non-acceptance, so the negation of the existence of acceptance is not generalized. As for the reading of the majority with the waw, it was said: the waw is superfluous, and this is weak, and the meaning in that case would be the meaning of Ibn Abi 'Ablah's reading. It was also said: it is not superfluous.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: what is the position of His saying ﴿even if he offers it as ransom﴾? I say: it is a statement understood by meaning, as if it were said: 'then there will never be accepted from any of them a ransom, even if he ransoms himself with the filling of (p-521) the earth in gold.'" End of his words. This meaning is refuted by this construction and it does not bear it; what this construction requires, and what it should be understood as, is that Allah the Exalted informed that whoever dies in disbelief, there will not be accepted from him what fills the earth of gold, in any state he intends, even in the state of ransoming himself from the punishment with it; because the state of ransoming is a state in which the ransomer is not favored over the one ransomed from him, since it is a state of compulsion from the one ransomed from upon the ransomer. We have already established in similar constructions that "law" comes to alert that what precedes it came by way of exhaustive enumeration, and what follows it came as an explicit mention of the state which is supposed not to be included in what precedes it, as in his saying: "Give to the beggar even if he comes on a horse, and turn away the beggar even with a burnt hoof." As if these things were ones that should not be given; for the beggar being on a horse shows his wealth, so it is not appropriate that a filling of the earth of gold be accepted from him, but it is not accepted. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿and you will not be a believer to us even if we were truthful﴾ [Yusuf: 17], because they negated that he would believe them in every state, even in the state of their truthfulness, which is the state in which they should be believed. So the word "law" here is for generalizing the negation and for emphasizing it; and we have mentioned the benefit of its coming. Al-Zajjaj went to the view that the meaning is: there will never be accepted from any one of them his expenditure and his acts of nearness in this world, even if he spent the filling of the earth in gold, and even if he ransomed himself with it in the Hereafter, it would not be accepted from him. He said: So Allah informed that He does not reward them for their good deeds, nor does He accept from them ransom from the punishment. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a good saying. End of his words.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that it be intended: "there will never be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth in gold, even if he had given it in charity; and even if he ransomed himself with it, it would not be accepted from him either." End of his words. This is the meaning of al-Zajjaj's saying, except that he did not restrict the ransoming to the Hereafter. Ṣāḥib Rayy al-Ẓam'ān and others reported from al-Zajjaj that he said: the meaning of the verse: even if he ransoms himself with it in this world while persisting in disbelief, it will not be accepted from him. What appears is that the non-acceptance even by way of ransom occurs only in the Hereafter. What clarifies this is what is established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from the hadith of Anas: that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The disbeliever will be called to account on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said to him: 'Tell me, if you had the filling of the earth in gold, would you ransom yourself with it?' He will say: 'Yes.' It will be said to him: 'You were asked for something easier than that.'" This hadith shows that His saying ﴿so there will never be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth in gold, and even if he ransoms himself with it﴾ (p-522) is by way of supposition and hypothesis, i.e., if the disbeliever were to possess the most precious things, and then were to be able to give it, he would be unable to use that as a means to deliver himself from the punishment of Allah. The meaning is that they are despairing of delivering themselves from the punishment. It is thus like His saying: ﴿And if those who wronged had all that is on the earth entirely﴾ [al-Zumar: 47], and like His saying: ﴿The criminal would wish to ransom himself﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 11], the two verses. And on this basis, what al-Zajjaj said is far-fetched, namely that the meaning is: that if they spent the filling of the earth in gold in this world, that would not be accepted; because obedience alongside disbelief is not accepted.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 87–91 (part 2 of 2):

"Wa-ftada" (وافْتَدى): it is of the form "ifta'ala" from "al-fidyah" (ransom). It has been said that it has the same meaning as "fa'ala", like "shawa" and "ishtawa" (both meaning to roast), and its object is omitted. Making "iftada" transitive requires a hearing from the Arabs. The pronoun in "bihi" (بِهِ) refers to "mil' al-ard" (filling of the earth), which is the quantity that would fill it. It is found in some tafsirs that it refers to "al-mil'" (the filling), or to "al-dhahab" (the gold). It has been said that the reference to "al-dhahab" is an error.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that what is meant is: 'Even if he ransomed himself with its like,' because of His saying: ﴿Even if those who did wrong had whatever is on the earth entirely and the like of it with it﴾ [al-Zumar: 47]. The word "mithl" (like) is often omitted in their speech, as when you say: 'I struck the strike of Zayd,' meaning: 'the like of his strike,' and 'Abu Yusuf is Abu Hanifa,' meaning: 'his like.'"

[Poetry]
"Nor does Haytham tonight [mourn] for the riding beasts"
And the case of "wa-la Aba Hasanin lahā" [nor Abu Hasan has her], you mean: "nor [the like of] Haytham, nor the like of Abu Hasan," just as it is intended in phrases such as their saying: "Mithlaka la yaf'alu kadha" [one like you does not do such a thing], you mean: "you yourself and that [is not so]." This is because two like things, one of them stands in place of the other, so they are in the ruling of one thing. End of his words.

There is no need to assume "mithl" in His saying ﴿even if he ransomed himself with it﴾. Al-Zamakhshari imagined that what is denied acceptance cannot be ransomed with, so he needed to supply "mithl" in order to distinguish between what is denied acceptance and what is used as ransom. This is not so, because that, as we have mentioned, is by way of supposition, and the meaning is: it is customarily impossible that anyone possesses the filling of the earth with gold such that, if he were to spend it in any way whatsoever, it would not be accepted from him. Rather, even if that were possible, there would be no need to assume "mithl," because He denied its acceptance even in the state of ransoming. What is supplied in the verse is not like the example he gave, because this supposition is not needed, has no meaning, and neither in the wording nor in the meaning is there anything indicating it, so it is not supplied. As for the examples he gave, "I struck the strike of Zayd" and "Abu Yusuf is Abu Hanifa," by the necessity of reason we know that "mithl" must be supplied, since your striking cannot be the striking of Zayd, and the person of Abu Yusuf cannot be the person of Abu Hanifa. As for:

[Poetry]
"Nor does Haytham tonight [mourn] for the riding beasts"

it indicates an omission, as is established in the Arabic language, that "la" which denotes the negation of the genus does not enter upon proper nouns and affect them, so one needs to supply "mithl" in order to keep it within what is established for it, since it is established that it governs only the genus, because definiteness as a proper name contradicts the generality of the genus. As for his words: "just as it may be added in: 'Mithlaka la yaf'alu kadha,' meaning 'anta' (you)," this is a view that has been stated, but the preferred view among the skilled grammarians is that nouns are not added (as extra words), and for establishing that "one like you does not do such a thing," "mithl" is not there as an extra word in place of anything other than this.

﴿Those, for them is a painful punishment﴾. This is a second report about the one who died while a disbeliever. When Almighty God explained in the first report that nothing is accepted from him until he ransoms his soul with it, He explained in this report what punishment he has, described with intensity in pain for him, since ransoming and spending wealth only happens in response to the pains that will befall the one who ransoms, so that he will spend the most precious things to be freed from that. As He said: ﴿The criminal would wish to ransom himself from the punishment of that Day with his children﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 11], and so on. The raising of "adhab" (punishment) is as the subject of the preceding prepositional phrase, since it relies on "ula'ika" (those), it being its predicate. It is also permissible for it to be raised as the subject of an inceptive (mubtada').

﴿And for them there are no helpers﴾. The construction of this phrase has been explained before. This is a third report. When He explained that there is no escape for him from the punishment by spending wealth, He also explained that there is no escape for him from it by means of help, and included in this is help by force and help by intercession.

This verse contains kinds of rhetorical ornamentation (badi'): antithesis (tibaq) in His saying "tau'an wa-karhan" (willingly or unwillingly), and in "kafaru ba'da imanihim" in two places; repetition (takrar) in "yahdi" and "la yahdi," and in "kafaru ba'da imanihim"; and paronomasia of the different kind (tajnis mughayir) in "kafaru" and "kafaru." Emphasis by the pronoun "hum" appears in His saying: "wa-ula'ika humu al-dallun" (those are the astray), it is said. Also the simile in "thumma izdadu kufran," where He likened their persistence in disbelief and their crimes to offenses that are added one upon another, and this is comparing the intelligible to the perceptible. Also the change from "mif'al" to "fa'il" in "adhabun alim," because of the intensity found in "fa'il." And omission in several places.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 87–91 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those—their recompense is that upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein; the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.﴾ The tafsir of the like of this sentence has already passed. As for the reading of al-Hasan, "wa-l-nasu ajma'una" (the nominative form), its explanation was given in Surat al-Baqarah, so it suffices from repeating it. However, here it is ﴿Those—their recompense﴾, i.e., the recompense of their disbelief, whereas there it is ﴿Those—upon them is the curse of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 161]; because there the statement concerns those who died in disbelief, so the curse was made certain upon them, whereas here it is not so. Do you not consider the occasion of revelation? And that most of the sayings are that it was revealed concerning a people who apostatized and then returned to Islam? Therefore the exception came, which is His saying: ﴿except those who repent after that﴾, and it is an exception of the connected kind (istithna' muttasil), and therefore He said ﴿after that﴾, (p-519) i.e., after that great disbelief.

(Wa-aslahu) means: they amended what they had corrupted, or: they entered into righteousness, as you say "Amsa Zayd," i.e., he entered the evening. It was also said: the meaning of aslahu is: they made clear that they had been in error. The explanation of this word has already passed in al-Baqarah in His saying ﴿except those who repent and amend and make clear﴾ [al-Baqarah: 160].

﴿Then indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ "Forgiving" means for their disbelief; "Merciful" means for accepting their repentance; and these are two intensive forms indicating the vastness of His mercy.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief, then increase in disbelief—their repentance will never be accepted, and those are the astray.﴾ It was revealed concerning the Jews, who disbelieved in Jesus and the Gospel after their belief in their prophets, then increased in disbelief by their disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ after their belief in his description; this was said by Qatadah and al-Hasan. It was also said: concerning the Jews who disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ after their belief in his attributes and their acknowledgment that they were in the Torah; then they increased in disbelief through the sins they committed in opposing the Prophet ﷺ, such as slander, calumny, and striving against Islam; this was said by Abu al-'Aliyah. Or the meaning is: then they increased in disbelief, they persisted in their disbelief and reached death in it; this includes the Jews and the apostates; this was said by Mujahid, and al-Suddi said something similar. It was also said: it was revealed concerning those among the companions of al-Harith ibn Suwayd who died in disbelief, for they said: "We will remain in Mecca and await for Muhammad ﷺ the vicissitudes of fate (rayb al-manun)"; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The meaning of the increase in disbelief is explained by these sayings, and it is according to its objects, since belief and disbelief, in reality, do not increase or decrease; rather, the increase and decrease occur in their objects, and so that is attributed to them by way of metaphor. "Izdadu" is of the form "iftaʿalu" from increase, and "kufran" is in the accusative as a tamyiz transferred from the agent; the meaning: "then the disbelief of them increased," and the first dal is a substitute for the ta' of the iftiʿal.

The second aspect: that the meaning be: there is no repentance for them so that it might be accepted; so the acceptance is negated, while the intended meaning is the negation of repentance itself, and thus it is of the type of the saying:

"On a road whose landmarks are not guided by"

i.e., there is no landmark for it by which one is guided; and this would be concerning a specific people whom Allah has decreed to disbelief, i.e., they have no repentance, so they will inevitably die in disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that it be intended: "there will never be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth in gold, even if he had given it in charity; and even if he ransomed himself with it, it would not be accepted from him either." End of his words. This is the meaning of al-Zajjaj's saying, except that he did not restrict the ransoming to the Hereafter. Ṣāḥib Rayy al-Ẓam'ān and others reported from al-Zajjaj that he said: the meaning of the verse: even if he ransoms himself with it in this world while persisting in disbelief, it will not be accepted from him. What appears is that the non-acceptance even by way of ransom occurs only in the Hereafter. What clarifies this is what is established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from the hadith of Anas: that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The disbeliever will be called to account on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said to him: 'Tell me, if you had the filling of the earth in gold, would you ransom yourself with it?' He will say: 'Yes.' It will be said to him: 'You were asked for something easier than that.'" This hadith shows that His saying ﴿so there will never be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth in gold, and even if he ransoms himself with it﴾ (p-522) is by way of supposition and hypothesis, i.e., if the disbeliever were to possess the most precious things, and then were to be able to give it, he would be unable to use that as a means to deliver himself from the punishment of Allah. The meaning is that they are despairing of delivering themselves from the punishment. It is thus like His saying: ﴿And if those who wronged had all that is on the earth entirely﴾ [al-Zumar: 47], and like His saying: ﴿The criminal would wish to ransom himself﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 11], the two verses. And on this basis, what al-Zajjaj said is far-fetched, namely that the meaning is: that if they spent the filling of the earth in gold in this world, that would not be accepted; because obedience alongside disbelief is not accepted.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 87–91 (part 2 of 2):

"Wa-ftada" (وافْتَدى): it is of the form "ifta'ala" from "al-fidyah" (ransom). It has been said that it has the same meaning as "fa'ala", like "shawa" and "ishtawa" (both meaning to roast), and its object is omitted. Making "iftada" transitive requires a hearing from the Arabs. The pronoun in "bihi" (بِهِ) refers to "mil' al-ard" (filling of the earth), which is the quantity that would fill it. It is found in some tafsirs that it refers to "al-mil'" (the filling), or to "al-dhahab" (the gold). It has been said that the reference to "al-dhahab" is an error.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that what is meant is: 'Even if he ransomed himself with its like,' because of His saying: ﴿Even if those who did wrong had whatever is on the earth entirely and the like of it with it﴾ [al-Zumar: 47]. The word "mithl" (like) is often omitted in their speech, as when you say: 'I struck the strike of Zayd,' meaning: 'the like of his strike,' and 'Abu Yusuf is Abu Hanifa,' meaning: 'his like.'"

[Poetry]
"Nor does Haytham tonight [mourn] for the riding beasts"
And the case of "wa-la Aba Hasanin lahā" [nor Abu Hasan has her], you mean: "nor [the like of] Haytham, nor the like of Abu Hasan," just as it is intended in phrases such as their saying: "Mithlaka la yaf'alu kadha" [one like you does not do such a thing], you mean: "you yourself and that [is not so]." This is because two like things, one of them stands in place of the other, so they are in the ruling of one thing. End of his words.

There is no need to assume "mithl" in His saying ﴿even if he ransomed himself with it﴾. Al-Zamakhshari imagined that what is denied acceptance cannot be ransomed with, so he needed to supply "mithl" in order to distinguish between what is denied acceptance and what is used as ransom. This is not so, because that, as we have mentioned, is by way of supposition, and the meaning is: it is customarily impossible that anyone possesses the filling of the earth with gold such that, if he were to spend it in any way whatsoever, it would not be accepted from him. Rather, even if that were possible, there would be no need to assume "mithl," because He denied its acceptance even in the state of ransoming. What is supplied in the verse is not like the example he gave, because this supposition is not needed, has no meaning, and neither in the wording nor in the meaning is there anything indicating it, so it is not supplied. As for the examples he gave, "I struck the strike of Zayd" and "Abu Yusuf is Abu Hanifa," by the necessity of reason we know that "mithl" must be supplied, since your striking cannot be the striking of Zayd, and the person of Abu Yusuf cannot be the person of Abu Hanifa. As for:

[Poetry]
"Nor does Haytham tonight [mourn] for the riding beasts"

it indicates an omission, as is established in the Arabic language, that "la" which denotes the negation of the genus does not enter upon proper nouns and affect them, so one needs to supply "mithl" in order to keep it within what is established for it, since it is established that it governs only the genus, because definiteness as a proper name contradicts the generality of the genus. As for his words: "just as it may be added in: 'Mithlaka la yaf'alu kadha,' meaning 'anta' (you)," this is a view that has been stated, but the preferred view among the skilled grammarians is that nouns are not added (as extra words), and for establishing that "one like you does not do such a thing," "mithl" is not there as an extra word in place of anything other than this.

﴿Those, for them is a painful punishment﴾. This is a second report about the one who died while a disbeliever. When Almighty God explained in the first report that nothing is accepted from him until he ransoms his soul with it, He explained in this report what punishment he has, described with intensity in pain for him, since ransoming and spending wealth only happens in response to the pains that will befall the one who ransoms, so that he will spend the most precious things to be freed from that. As He said: ﴿The criminal would wish to ransom himself from the punishment of that Day with his children﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 11], and so on. The raising of "adhab" (punishment) is as the subject of the preceding prepositional phrase, since it relies on "ula'ika" (those), it being its predicate. It is also permissible for it to be raised as the subject of an inceptive (mubtada').

﴿And for them there are no helpers﴾. The construction of this phrase has been explained before. This is a third report. When He explained that there is no escape for him from the punishment by spending wealth, He also explained that there is no escape for him from it by means of help, and included in this is help by force and help by intercession.

This verse contains kinds of rhetorical ornamentation (badi'): antithesis (tibaq) in His saying "tau'an wa-karhan" (willingly or unwillingly), and in "kafaru ba'da imanihim" in two places; repetition (takrar) in "yahdi" and "la yahdi," and in "kafaru ba'da imanihim"; and paronomasia of the different kind (tajnis mughayir) in "kafaru" and "kafaru." Emphasis by the pronoun "hum" appears in His saying: "wa-ula'ika humu al-dallun" (those are the astray), it is said. Also the simile in "thumma izdadu kufran," where He likened their persistence in disbelief and their crimes to offenses that are added one upon another, and this is comparing the intelligible to the perceptible. Also the change from "mif'al" to "fa'il" in "adhabun alim," because of the intensity found in "fa'il." And omission in several places.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 87–91 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those—their recompense is that upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein; the punishment will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved.﴾ The tafsir of the like of this sentence has already passed. As for the reading of al-Hasan, "wa-l-nasu ajma'una" (the nominative form), its explanation was given in Surat al-Baqarah, so it suffices from repeating it. However, here it is ﴿Those—their recompense﴾, i.e., the recompense of their disbelief, whereas there it is ﴿Those—upon them is the curse of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 161]; because there the statement concerns those who died in disbelief, so the curse was made certain upon them, whereas here it is not so. Do you not consider the occasion of revelation? And that most of the sayings are that it was revealed concerning a people who apostatized and then returned to Islam? Therefore the exception came, which is His saying: ﴿except those who repent after that﴾, and it is an exception of the connected kind (istithna' muttasil), and therefore He said ﴿after that﴾, (p-519) i.e., after that great disbelief.

(Wa-aslahu) means: they amended what they had corrupted, or: they entered into righteousness, as you say "Amsa Zayd," i.e., he entered the evening. It was also said: the meaning of aslahu is: they made clear that they had been in error. The explanation of this word has already passed in al-Baqarah in His saying ﴿except those who repent and amend and make clear﴾ [al-Baqarah: 160].

﴿Then indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ "Forgiving" means for their disbelief; "Merciful" means for accepting their repentance; and these are two intensive forms indicating the vastness of His mercy.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief, then increase in disbelief—their repentance will never be accepted, and those are the astray.﴾ It was revealed concerning the Jews, who disbelieved in Jesus and the Gospel after their belief in their prophets, then increased in disbelief by their disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ after their belief in his description; this was said by Qatadah and al-Hasan. It was also said: concerning the Jews who disbelieved in Muhammad ﷺ after their belief in his attributes and their acknowledgment that they were in the Torah; then they increased in disbelief through the sins they committed in opposing the Prophet ﷺ, such as slander, calumny, and striving against Islam; this was said by Abu al-'Aliyah. Or the meaning is: then they increased in disbelief, they persisted in their disbelief and reached death in it; this includes the Jews and the apostates; this was said by Mujahid, and al-Suddi said something similar. It was also said: it was revealed concerning those among the companions of al-Harith ibn Suwayd who died in disbelief, for they said: "We will remain in Mecca and await for Muhammad ﷺ the vicissitudes of fate (rayb al-manun)"; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The meaning of the increase in disbelief is explained by these sayings, and it is according to its objects, since belief and disbelief, in reality, do not increase or decrease; rather, the increase and decrease occur in their objects, and so that is attributed to them by way of metaphor. "Izdadu" is of the form "iftaʿalu" from increase, and "kufran" is in the accusative as a tamyiz transferred from the agent; the meaning: "then the disbelief of them increased," and the first dal is a substitute for the ta' of the iftiʿal.

The saying ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾ may admit two aspects. One: that there is a repentance from them, but it is not accepted—although it is known that the repentance of every disbeliever is accepted, whether he disbelieved after belief and increased in disbelief, or was a disbeliever from the first time. Thus, in this there is need for a specification. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid, and al-Suddi said: the denial of their repentance is specific to the death-rattle, the gurgling, and the moment of seeing (the angels). Al-Nahhas said: this is a good saying, like His saying: ﴿and repentance is not for those who do evil deeds﴾ [al-Nisa': 18], etc. Abu al-'Aliyah said: "their repentance will never be accepted" refers to the sins they committed together with their persistence in disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾, because it is a repentance that is not sincere, since they are apostates and resolved to display repentance to conceal their states, while disbelief is in their inner selves. Mujahid said: their repentance will never be accepted after death if they die in disbelief. It was also said: their repentance will never be accepted which they repented before they disbelieved, because disbelief has nullified it. It was also said: their repentance will never be accepted if they repent from one disbelief to another disbelief; it is accepted only if they repent to Islam. The distinguishing principle of this specification is that it is a specification by time, or it is described in the repentance.

The second aspect: that the meaning be: there is no repentance for them so that it might be accepted; so the acceptance is negated, while the intended meaning is the negation of repentance itself, and thus it is of the type of the saying:

"On a road whose landmarks are not guided by"

i.e., there is no landmark for it by which one is guided; and this would be concerning a specific people whom Allah has decreed to disbelief, i.e., they have no repentance, so they will inevitably die in disbelief. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah have indicated this meaning. The particle fa' did not enter upon "lan tuqbila" here, but it entered upon "fa-lan tuqbila" (in 91), because the fa' indicates entitlement by the preceding attribute; and there he said: "and they died while they were disbelievers," whereas here he did not state this condition explicitly.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: since the meaning of ﴿their repentance will never be accepted﴾ is in the sense of dying in disbelief, why was not dying in disbelief made the consequence of their apostasy and their increase in disbelief, because of what that involves of hardness of hearts, the mounting of rust, and its leading to dying in disbelief?" I say: because how many an apostate who increased in disbelief returns to Islam and does not die in disbelief? If you say: then what is the benefit of this kinaya (metaphor), I mean if he alludes to dying in disbelief by the impossibility of accepting repentance? I say: the benefit in it is great: it is the intensification concerning that group of disbelievers, and the portrayal of their state (p-520) in the form of the state of those who despair of mercy, which is the most severe and intense of states. Do you not see that dying in disbelief is feared only because of despair of mercy? End of his words.

Ikrimah read: "lan naqbala tawbatahum" with the nun and the accusative tawbatahum. "Al-dallun" means: those who have erred from the path of truth and salvation in the Hereafter, or: those who perish; from "dalla al-laban fi al-ma'" when it becomes perished. The waw in "wa-ulaika" is for coordination, either upon the predicate of inna, so the clause is in a place of raf', or upon the clause consisting of inna and its two objects, in which case it has no place in the i'rab.

Al-Raghib mentioned a saying: that the waw in "wa-ulaika" is the waw of the state (waw al-hal), and the meaning: "their repentance from sins will never be accepted while they are astray," so repentance and error are mutually contradictory and do not come together. End of this saying. This meaning is refuted by this construction, for if this meaning were intended, the demonstrative would not have been used; and the hum may be a separator (fasl), an inchoative (ibtida'), or a substitute (badal).

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers—never will there be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth with gold﴾. Ikrimah read: "fa-lan naqbala" with the nun and "mil'a" with the accusative. It was also read: "fa-lan yaqbala" with the ya', in the active voice, i.e., "then Allah will never accept," and "mil'a" in the accusative. Abu Ja'far and Abu al-Sammal read: "milla al-ardi," without hamza. It was transmitted from Nafi' as well, and its explanation: he transferred the vowel of the hamza to the preceding unvowelled letter, which is the lam, and the hamza was deleted; this is a regular analogy in every case like this. And He used the wording "ahadihim" and did not use the wording "minhum," because that is more emphatic and more explicit in the intended meaning, since "minhum" could be understood as with the condition of the whole group. The accusative of "dhahaban" is by way of tamyiz; there is a disagreement about the governing word of the tamyiz. Al-Farra' called it an explanation (tafsir), because the quantity is known while the thing by which it is measured is general. Al-Kisa'i said: it is accusative by the implied "min" (of), i.e., "min dhahabin," like His saying: ﴿or its equivalent in fasting﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 95], i.e., "min siyam" (of fasting). Al-A'mash read: "dhahabun" in the nominative. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a reference back to "mil'a," as one says: "I have twenty persons, men," End of his words. By "reference back" he means apposition, and it would be an apposition of an indefinite from a definite, since "mil'a al-ardi" is definite; for this reason the expert grammarians pointed the saying "Laka al-hamdu mil'u al-samawati wa-l-ardi" with the nominative as an attribute of "al-hamd," and they avoided its accusative as a circumstantial (hal) because it is definite.

﴿Even if he offers it as ransom﴾. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "law iftada bihi" without the waw, and "law" here has the meaning of the conditional "in" and not of "law" which indicates what would have occurred because of the occurrence of something else; because "law" here is connected to the future, namely "fa-lan yuqbila," while that other is connected to the past. As for the reading of Ibn Abi 'Ablah, he made the ransoming a condition for non-acceptance, so the negation of the existence of acceptance is not generalized. As for the reading of the majority with the waw, it was said: the waw is superfluous, and this is weak, and the meaning in that case would be the meaning of Ibn Abi 'Ablah's reading. It was also said: it is not superfluous.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: what is the position of His saying ﴿even if he offers it as ransom﴾? I say: it is a statement understood by meaning, as if it were said: 'then there will never be accepted from any of them a ransom, even if he ransoms himself with the filling of (p-521) the earth in gold.'" End of his words. This meaning is refuted by this construction and it does not bear it; what this construction requires, and what it should be understood as, is that Allah the Exalted informed that whoever dies in disbelief, there will not be accepted from him what fills the earth of gold, in any state he intends, even in the state of ransoming himself from the punishment with it; because the state of ransoming is a state in which the ransomer is not favored over the one ransomed from him, since it is a state of compulsion from the one ransomed from upon the ransomer. We have already established in similar constructions that "law" comes to alert that what precedes it came by way of exhaustive enumeration, and what follows it came as an explicit mention of the state which is supposed not to be included in what precedes it, as in his saying: "Give to the beggar even if he comes on a horse, and turn away the beggar even with a burnt hoof." As if these things were ones that should not be given; for the beggar being on a horse shows his wealth, so it is not appropriate that a filling of the earth of gold be accepted from him, but it is not accepted. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿and you will not be a believer to us even if we were truthful﴾ [Yusuf: 17], because they negated that he would believe them in every state, even in the state of their truthfulness, which is the state in which they should be believed. So the word "law" here is for generalizing the negation and for emphasizing it; and we have mentioned the benefit of its coming. Al-Zajjaj went to the view that the meaning is: there will never be accepted from any one of them his expenditure and his acts of nearness in this world, even if he spent the filling of the earth in gold, and even if he ransomed himself with it in the Hereafter, it would not be accepted from him. He said: So Allah informed that He does not reward them for their good deeds, nor does He accept from them ransom from the punishment. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this is a good saying. End of his words.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is possible that it be intended: "there will never be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth in gold, even if he had given it in charity; and even if he ransomed himself with it, it would not be accepted from him either." End of his words. This is the meaning of al-Zajjaj's saying, except that he did not restrict the ransoming to the Hereafter. Ṣāḥib Rayy al-Ẓam'ān and others reported from al-Zajjaj that he said: the meaning of the verse: even if he ransoms himself with it in this world while persisting in disbelief, it will not be accepted from him. What appears is that the non-acceptance even by way of ransom occurs only in the Hereafter. What clarifies this is what is established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from the hadith of Anas: that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The disbeliever will be called to account on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said to him: 'Tell me, if you had the filling of the earth in gold, would you ransom yourself with it?' He will say: 'Yes.' It will be said to him: 'You were asked for something easier than that.'" This hadith shows that His saying ﴿so there will never be accepted from any one of them the filling of the earth in gold, and even if he ransoms himself with it﴾ (p-522) is by way of supposition and hypothesis, i.e., if the disbeliever were to possess the most precious things, and then were to be able to give it, he would be unable to use that as a means to deliver himself from the punishment of Allah. The meaning is that they are despairing of delivering themselves from the punishment. It is thus like His saying: ﴿And if those who wronged had all that is on the earth entirely﴾ [al-Zumar: 47], and like His saying: ﴿The criminal would wish to ransom himself﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 11], the two verses. And on this basis, what al-Zajjaj said is far-fetched, namely that the meaning is: that if they spent the filling of the earth in gold in this world, that would not be accepted; because obedience alongside disbelief is not accepted.
