**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 92:**

﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love. And whatever you spend, indeed Allah knows it.﴾ ﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel (Ya'qub) had made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed. Say: "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 93] ﴿So whoever fabricates a lie against Allah after this, those are the wrongdoers.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 94] ﴿Say: "Allah has spoken the truth. So follow the religion of Ibrahim, a upright monotheist, and he was not among the polytheists."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 95] ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is the one at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 96] ﴿In it are clear signs: the Station of Ibrahim. Whoever enters it is safe. And pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to Allah by the people who are able to make their way to it. And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need from the worlds.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97] ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah, while Allah is Witness over what you do?"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 98] ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you bar from the way of Allah those who believe, seeking to make it crooked, while you are witnesses? And Allah is not unaware of what you do."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 99] ﴿O you who believe, if you obey a group of those who were given the Scripture, they will return you, after your belief, to disbelief.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 100] ﴿And how can you disbelieve while the verses of Allah are recited to you and His Messenger is among you? And whoever holds fast to Allah has been guided to a straight path.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 101]

**al-Nayl (نَيْل)** (attaining): reaching a thing and encountering it. Its verb is nala yanalu. It has been said that al-nayl also means a gift.

**al-Wad' (وَضْع)** (placing, establishing): casting something down. One says wada'a al-shay' (he put the thing down), i.e., alqāhu (he threw it down). Wadat ma fi batniha means she gave birth to what was in her womb. The verb is wada'a yada'u wad'an wadi'atan. Al-mawdi' is the place where something is put. Fulan yada' al-hadith means he fabricates speech on his own authority without transmission, inventing it.

**Bakkah (بَكَّة):** a synonym for Makkah, as said by Mujahid and al-Zajjaj. The Arabs interchange the letters ba' and mim, and they say lazim and razim, and al-numayt, and in these words [they use] the ba'. It has been said that it is the name of the interior (batn) of Makkah, as said by Abu 'Ubayda. It has been said that it is the name of the place of the House (the Ka'bah), as said by al-Nakha'i. It has been said that it is the name of the Mosque specifically, as said by Ibn Shihab. It has been said: what indicates this is that al-bakk is the pushing of people against one another and their crowding, and this occurs in the Mosque during circumambulation, not in other places. The discussion of the word Makkah will come, God willing.

**al-Barakah (بَرَكَة)** (blessing): increase. Its verb is baraka, which is transitive. From it: ﴿that blessed is whoever is in the Fire﴾ [al-Naml: 8]. It is construed with the meaning of what is transitive with "ʿalā," due to his saying: "and bless upon Muhammad." Tabāraka is intransitive.

**al-'Iwaj (عِوَج)** (crookedness): inclination. Abu 'Ubayda said: in religion, speech, and action. With a fatha on the ʿayn (ʿaja) it is used for a wall and a trunk. Al-Zajjaj said the same in meaning, adding: for what we do not see as a figure (shakhs), and with fatha for what has a figure. Ibn Faris said: with fatha for everything upright like a wall. Al-ʿiwaj is what is in a carpet, or in religion, or in land, or in livelihood.

**al-'Asm (عَصْم)** (protection): prevention. I'tasama and istaʿsama mean to refrain. I'tasamtu fulānan means I prepared for him what he could hold on to for protection. Everyone who holds fast to something is muʿtasim, and everything that prevents something is ʿasim. To this meaning belong al-aʿsam, al-miʿsam, and al-ʿiṣām. Bread is called ʿāṣim because it prevents hunger.

﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾: the connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He informed about the one who died as a disbeliever, that what he spent in this world, or what he brought forward to free himself in the Hereafter, would not be accepted, according to the disagreement that preceded, He urged the believer to give charity, and clarified that he will never reach righteousness (al-birr) until he spends from what he loves. Al-birr here, said Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and 'Amr ibn Maymun, is Paradise. Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said it is the obligatory charity. Abu Rawq said it is all good. It has been said it is truthfulness. It has been said it is the noblest of religion, said by 'Ata'. Ibn 'Atiyyah said it is obedience. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said it is piety. Al-Zajjaj said it is every good deed by which one draws near to Allah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said the same in meaning. Abu Muslim said: it has several usages, so it is said: al-sidq is al-birr, and from it: "You spoke truly and you were righteous (bararta)," and "noble (kiram) righteous ones (barara)." It also means kindness, and from it: "I was dutiful (barartu) to my parents." It also means gentleness and attentiveness, and from it: "He is good (yabirru) to his companions when he visits and attends to them." It also means gift and charity: "He gave him (barrahu) such-and-such when he gave it to him as a gift."

He said: It is possible that "You will never attain the righteousness of Allah toward you" means His mercy and kindness, end of quote. This is the view of Abu Bakr al-Warraq, who said: the meaning of the verse is "You will never attain My righteousness toward you except by your righteousness toward your brothers, and spending upon them from your wealth and your standing." 'Ali ibn Jarir narrated something similar. It is possible that it means: you will never attain the degree of perfection in performing righteousness until you are righteous, except by spending in addition to your other deeds, as said by Ibn 'Atiyyah. The explanation of al-birr was already given in His saying: ﴿Do you order people to righteousness?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 44], but we have done what people said regarding the specificity of this passage.

The "min" in "mimma tuhibbun" is partitive (lil-tab'īḍ). This is indicated by the reading of ʿAbd Allah: "until you spend some of what you love." The "mā" is relative (mawṣūlah), and the returning pronoun is omitted. The apparent meaning is that love here is the inclination of the soul and its complete attachment to the one who spends, so giving it away is harder and more difficult than giving away what the soul is not so attached to. For this reason al-Hasan and al-Dahhak explained it as beloved wealth, like His saying: ﴿and they give food, despite their love for it﴾ [al-Insan: 8]. For this reason, it is narrated from a group that, on account of this verse, they gave in charity the thing most beloved to them. Abu Talhah gave away Bayraha'; Zayd ibn Haritha gave away a horse of his that he loved; Ibn 'Umar gave away sugar and almonds because he loved them; Abu Dharr gave away the stallion of his best camels and a burnus to one who was cold, and recited the verse; al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham gave away sugar because of his love for it; 'Umar freed a slave-girl who pleased him; and his son 'Abd Allah freed a slave-girl who was the most pleasing thing to him.

It has been said: the meaning of "what you love" is the choicest and best of wealth, not its inferior and bad part. It has been said: what is needed by him. It has been said: everything that the Muslim spends from his wealth, seeking thereby the face of Allah.

The word "tuhibbun" (you love) does not fit these sayings, and what appears is that spending here is recommended (nadb), because the one who pays zakat is not obligated to give out his most excellent wealth or the most beloved to him. Those who went far afield claimed that this verse is abrogated (naskh), because encouragement toward what is recommended for the sake of Allah does not contradict zakat. Some of them said: this verse indicates that speech becomes poetry by several things, among them: the speaker's intention to make it poetry, because this verse is on the meter of the bayt al-ramal, called al-mujazz and al-musabba', which is:

*O my two companions, halt and ask about the abode of the worn-out dwelling, of a tribe that is lawful...*

*a trace at 'Usfan.*

It is not permissible to say that there is poetry in the Qur'an.

﴿And whatever you spend of anything, indeed Allah knows it﴾: the explanation of the like of this has already preceded.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

*"All food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed."* (Al 'Imran 3:93)

Abu Rawq and Ibn al-Sa'ib said: It was revealed when the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I am upon the religion (millah) of Abraham." The Jews said: "How (can you be)? You eat the flesh of camels and drink their milk." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "That is lawful for the father of Abraham, and we make it lawful." The Jews said: "Everything we forbid today was forbidden to Noah and Abraham until it reached us." So God revealed this as a refutation of them.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it, and what unites them, is that He, exalted is He, informed that a person does not attain righteousness (al-birr) except by spending from what he loves. The Prophet of God, Israel, is reported in a hadith that he fell into a severe illness, and his sickness lingered, so he made a vow (nadhr) to God that if God healed him from his sickness, he would forbid, or he would certainly forbid, the food and drink he loved most. The food he loved most was camel meat, and the drink he loved most was its milk, so he did that seeking nearness to God. Thus this verse and what precedes it share the point that each of them concerns leaving what a person loves and prefers, in the way of drawing near to God, exalted is He. Both are forms of general expression (sigha al-'umum).

*Al-ta'am* (food): its origin is a verbal noun (masdar) used in place of the passive participle, and it is a term for everything that is eaten and consumed. Some followers of Abu Hanifa claimed that it refers specifically to wheat. Al-Razi said: The verse refutes this, because it makes an exception from it of what Israel forbade for himself. They agreed that it is something other than wheat and other than what is made from it. What confirms this is His saying regarding water: "and whoever does not taste it" (al-Baqarah 2:249). And He said: "The food of those who were given the Book is lawful for you" (al-Ma'idah: 5), meaning the slaughtered animals. End of his words.

It is answered regarding the exception that it is disjunctive (munqati'), so it does not fall under "food." Al-Qaffal said: It has not reached us that carrion and swine were permitted to them, even though they are food. So it is possible that this refers to the foods which the Jews, at the time of the Messenger (ﷺ), claimed had been forbidden to Abraham. Thus the problem disappears, meaning the problem of generality.

*Al-hill* (lawful): it is the same as *al-halal*, and it is a verbal noun of *halla*, like *'azza 'izzan*. From it is His saying: "and you are lawful (hill) in this city" (al-Balad: 2), meaning lawful in it. In a hadith from 'Aishah: "I used to perfume the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for his lawful state (lihillihi) and his sacred state (lihurmihi)." For this reason it is used uniformly for the singular and plural, the masculine and feminine. He said: "They are not lawful for them (la hunna hillun lahum)" (al-Mumtahanah: 10), and it is like *hurum*, meaning *haram* (forbidden). *Al-libs* means the clothing (al-libas).

Israel is Jacob, and his discussion has already been mentioned. It has already been mentioned that what Israel forbade was the flesh of camels and their milk. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is the opinion of al-Hasan, 'Ata', Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, and 'Abdullah ibn Kathir among others. It was also said: the veins (al-'uruq). This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas. It is also the opinion of Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and Abu Mijlaz among others.

Ibn 'Abbas said: A sciatic ailment (al-anasa') afflicted him, and it weakened him, so he vowed to God that if He cured him of that, he would not eat a vein. He said: For this reason the Jews remove the veins from the meat. There is no nearness to God in forbidding the veins, as far as is apparent. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he forbade the veins and the flesh of camels. It was also said: the fat around the liver, the two kidneys, and the fat except what is on the back. This was said by Ikrimah. The reason for its prohibition, by what he prohibited, has already been mentioned.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: There is no disagreement, as far as I know, that the cause of the prohibition was an illness that afflicted him, so he made the forbidding of that a thanksgiving to God, exalted is He, if he was healed. It was also said: it was the pain of sciatica (irq al-nasa). This exception may be either connected (muttasil) or disconnected (munqati'). If it is connected, the meaning is: "except what Israel forbade for himself," and so it was forbidden to them in the Torah. Thus the additions which they invented and claimed were forbidden are not in it. If it is disconnected, the meaning is: "but Israel forbade that for himself alone, and God did not forbid it for the Children of Israel." The connected reading is more apparent. The apparent meaning of His saying "for himself" (ʿala nafsihi) is that it was by his own ijtihad (independent reasoning), not by a prohibition from God, exalted is He. It has been cited as evidence that prophets may forbid by ijtihad. It was also said: his prohibition was by the permission of God, exalted is He. It was also said: it is possible that the prohibition in his law was like the nadhr (vow) in our law. Al-Asamm said: Perhaps his soul inclined toward those kinds, so he refrained from eating them, subduing the soul and seeking the pleasure of God, as many ascetics do, so he expressed that refraining as prohibition.

They differed regarding the cause of the prohibition of the food which Israel forbade for his sons and those after them among the Jews, and this applies if we say the exception is connected. As for if it is disconnected, then it was not forbidden to them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He forbade them by Israel's prohibition, and it was not forbidden in the Torah. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that Jacob said: "If God cures me, my son shall never eat it." Al-Dahhak said: They agreed with their father in its prohibition, not that it was forbidden to them by the shari'ah (sacred law). Then they attributed its prohibition to the shari'ah, so God, exalted is He, refuted them. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: God forbade it to them after the Torah, not in it. Whenever they committed a great sin, a good food was made forbidden to them because of it, or a punishment was poured upon them. This is confirmed by the verse "for the wrongdoing of those who judaized, We forbade them good things" (al-Nisa' 4:160).

It was also said: it was not forbidden to them before the revelation of the Torah nor after it, nor by Israel's prohibition for them, nor by their agreeing with him. Rather, they said that merely by conjecture and fabrication. Al-Suddi said: When God revealed the Torah, He forbade them what they used to forbid themselves before its revelation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is that all foods had remained lawful to the Children of Israel from before the revelation of the Torah, and the prohibition of what was forbidden to them from among them came because of their wrongdoing and transgression. Before that, nothing was forbidden from among them except the one food which their father Israel forbade for himself, and they followed him in forbidding it. This is a rejection of the Jews and a denial of them, since they wanted to clear themselves of what was reproached against them in His saying: "for the wrongdoing of those who judaized, We forbade them good things" (al-Nisa' 4:160), and the verse. They denied what angered them, repelled them, and disgusted them, in what the Qur'an stated about the prohibition of good things upon them because of their transgression and wrongdoing. So they said: "We are not the first to whom it was forbidden. This is only an ancient prohibition. It was forbidden to Noah, Abraham, those after him among the Children of Israel, and so on, until the prohibition reached us, so it became forbidden to us just as it was forbidden to those before us." Their aim was to deny God's testimony against them of transgression, wrongdoing, hindering from the way of God, consuming usury, and taking people's wealth falsely, and what was enumerated of their evil deeds, for every great sin they committed, a kind of good things was forbidden to them as punishment. End of his words.

"*min qabli an tunazzala al-Tawrah*" (from before the Torah was revealed). Abu al-Baqa' said: "min" is connected to "harrama" (forbade), meaning in His saying "except what Israel forbade for himself." This is far-fetched, since it is informing of the obvious, because it is known that what Israel forbade for himself was before the revelation of the Torah, necessarily, given the great distance between the existence of Israel and the revelation of the Torah. It appears that it is connected to His saying "was lawful to the Children of Israel," meaning: "from before the Torah was revealed," and it was separated by the exception, since that separation is permissible. This is according to the view of al-Kisa'i and Abu al-Hasan regarding the permissibility of the element before "illa" (except) governing what comes after it when it is an adverbial phrase, a prepositional phrase, or a circumstantial clause, such as: "He was not detained except Zayd with you," "Amr did not take refuge except to you," and "Zayd did not come except laughing." Al-Kisa'i permitted this in an accusative object generally, such as: "Zayd did not strike except 'Amr." He and Ibn al-Anbari permitted this in a nominative subject, such as: "'Amr did not strike except Zayd." As for its derivation according to the view other than al-Kisa'i and Abu al-Hasan, a governing element of the same kind as what precedes it is supposed for it, and its estimate here is: "lawful from before the Torah was revealed."

*"Qul fa'tu bi'l-Tawrati fa'tluhaa in kuntum sadiqin"* (Say: "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful") (Al 'Imran 3:93). "*Qul*" (say): an address to the Prophet (ﷺ). It was also said: "*fa'tu*" (bring) has an omitted element whose estimate is: "This is the truth, not your claim, O assembly of Jews." "*Fa'tu*" is the greatest argument: that they be commanded to bring their book in which their law is, for there is nothing in it of what they claimed. Rather, it confirms what he (ﷺ) informed, that those foods were lawful for them from long ago, and that the prohibition was a later innovation. It was narrated that they did not dare to bring the Torah, because the disgrace of bringing it was evident to them. Rather, they were confounded, and that was their habit in many of their conditions. In demanding the Torah from them and reciting it lies the clear proof of the truthfulness of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), since he, peace be upon him, was the unlettered Prophet who had not read the books nor known the reports of the earlier nations. Then he began to argue with them and call upon what is in their books as evidence against them, and they could find no escape from his denial.

In the verse there is evidence for the permissibility of *naskh* (abrogation) in the shari'ahs, while they deny that. His saying "*in kuntum sadiqin*" (if you are truthful) came in the form of a supposition, though their falsehood was known. This is by way of mocking them, like your saying: "If you are brave, then strike me," while it is known to you that he is not brave, but you mocked him, since you made this attribute something that could be ascribed to him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 94:

﴿Whoever fabricates a lie against Allah after that, those are the wrongdoers.﴾ It is possible that this falls under the preceding statement, and it is possible that it is the beginning of a fresh report from Allah about that. His fabrication of a lie is his claim that that (food) had been forbidden to the Children of Israel before the Torah was revealed. As for the reference of "that" (dhalika), it has been said that it may have three aspects. The first: that it refers to the recitation (tilawah), since its content is the clarification of their position and the establishment of the decisive, conclusive proof; and the fabrication of a lie would then be attributing to the books of Allah what is not in them. The second: that it refers to the establishment of the prohibition in the Torah, since the meaning is: "except what Israel forbade for himself," and then the Torah forbade it to them as a punishment for them. The fabrication of a lie would then be adding to the prohibited things what is not among them. The third: that it refers to the situation after Israel forbade it upon himself and before the revelation of the Torah, from the practice of Ya'qub, and that this was legislated without permission from Allah. This possibility is supported by His saying: ﴿Because of the wrongdoing of those who became Jews﴾ [al-Nisa': 160], the verse, where He stated explicitly that they had a wrongdoing in the sense of permitting and forbidding, and they used to be strict, so Allah made it strict upon them, as they did in the matter of the cow. Our Shari'ah came contrary to this: "The religion of Allah is ease; be easy and do not make things difficult, and I have been sent with the tolerant, upright monotheism."

﴿And He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship﴾ [al-Hajj: 78]. The more apparent reading of "min" (in "min") is that it is conditional (shartiyyah), though it may also be relative (mawsulah). The plural is used in "fa-ulaika" in consideration of the meaning. As for "hum": it may be a separator (fasl), a subject (mubtada'), or an appositive (badal). Al-zulm (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place. It has been said that here it means disbelief (kufr).

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 95–96:**

﴿Say: "God has spoken the truth."﴾ God commanded His Prophet to declare their falsehood openly. That is, the true matter is what God has reported, not the lies they fabricated. By this He indicated that what He reported, including His saying ﴿All food﴾ [Al 'Imran: 93] and everything mentioned before it, is true, and that it is the creed (millah) of Abraham. The better view is that His saying "﴿Say: God has spoken the truth﴾" means: in all that He reported in His revealed books. It was also said that it refers to the claim that Muhammad (ﷺ) follows the creed of Abraham, and that Abraham was a Muslim. It was said regarding His saying "﴿All food﴾" [Al 'Imran: 93] and the verse, related by Ibn al-Sa'ib. It was also said that it refers to the claim that Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian. This was said by Muqatil and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Then He commanded them to follow the creed of Abraham, saying:

﴿Follow the creed of Abraham, a man of pure faith, and he was not of the polytheists.﴾ This is the creed of Islam, upon which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers with him stood, so that they would be freed from the creed of Judaism. By His saying "and he was not of the polytheists," He hinted that they are polytheists in taking some of them as lords besides God. The discussion of the parallel of this clause in Surat al-Baqarah has already been covered, both in exegesis (tafsir) and in grammatical analysis (i'rab), so there is no need to repeat it.

Aban ibn Tha'lab read ﴿qad sadaqa﴾ (Say: "sadaqa") with the assimilation (idgham, the merging of one letter into the next) of the lam into the sad, and ﴿qul siru﴾ [al-An'am: 11] with the assimilation of the lam into the sin. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hisham assimilated the lam in ﴿bal sawwalat﴾ [Yusuf: 18]. Ibn Jinni said: the reason for this is that these two letters are spread widely in the mouth and the sound produced by them extends, so they come close to the place of articulation of the lam, and so it is permissible to assimilate the lam into them, end of his words. This returns to the sense of Sibawayh's statement. Sibawayh said: "Assimilation, meaning the assimilation of the lam with the ta', the sad and their sisters, is permissible, but it is not as frequent as with the ra', because these letters are farther from it, and they are from the front teeth (thana). And the permissibility of assimilation is because the last point of articulation of the lam is close to their point of articulation." End of his words.

﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah﴾. It was narrated from Mujahid that the Muslims and the Jews boasted, and the Jews said: "The House of the Holy Sanctuary (Bayt al-Maqdis) is more excellent and greater than the Ka'bah, because it is the place of migration of the prophets and it is in the holy land." The Muslims said: "Rather, the Ka'bah is more excellent," and so this verse was revealed. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is clear: when God commanded following the creed of Abraham, and the pilgrimage (hajj) to the House was among the greatest rites of Abraham's creed and among the particular features of his religion, He began to mention the House and its virtues, in order to build upon that the mention of the pilgrimage and its obligation. Also, when the qiblah was changed to the Ka'bah, the Jews criticized the prophethood of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "The House of the Holy Sanctuary is more excellent and more worthy of facing, because it was established before the Ka'bah, and it is the land of the gathering (al-mahshar), and the qiblah of all the prophets." So God refuted them in that claim by His saying: "﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah﴾," just as He refuted their earlier claim that the forbidding of certain things to them was only what had been forbidden to Jacob before the Torah was revealed. Also, every sect of the Jews and Christians claimed to be upon the creed of Abraham, and among the rites of his creed is the pilgrimage to the Ka'bah, yet they do not make pilgrimage to it. So God refuted them in that claim. "The first" (awwal) is the single one that precedes others. The discussion of the word "awwal" has already been given in His saying: "﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾" [al-Baqarah: 41], and the clause was placed in the position of a qualifier (sifah).

The scholars differed about the meaning of its being "the first House established for mankind." It was said: it is the first house that appeared upon the surface of the water when the heavens and the earth were created; it was created two thousand years before the earth, and it was a white foam upon the water, and the earth was spread out beneath it. It was said: it is the first house built by Adam on the earth. It was said: when Adam was sent down, the angels said to him: "Circumambulate this House, for we circumambulated it before you by two thousand years." At its location, before Adam, there was a house called al-Durah, which was lifted up to the fourth heaven during the Flood, where the angels of the heavens circumambulate it. The noble Abu al-Barakat As'ad ibn 'Ali ibn Abi al-Ghana'im al-Husayni al-Juwani, the genealogist (nassabah), mentioned that Shith ibn Adam is the one who built the Ka'bah from clay and stones, upon the location of the tent which God had placed for Adam from Paradise. According to these sayings, "the first House established for mankind" is to be understood literally. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the first house to be pilgrimaged to after the Flood, so the priority here is with respect to this attribute of pilgrimage, since there were houses before it. It was narrated from 'Ali that a man asked him: "Is it the first house?" 'Ali said: "No, there were houses before it, but it is the first house established for mankind as blessed, containing guidance, mercy and blessing." So he took the priority with the restriction of this condition. It was said: the first who built it was Abraham, then a people of the Arabs from Jurhum, then it was demolished and the Amalekites built it, then it was demolished and the Quraysh built it. Abu Dharr said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, which mosque was established first?' He said: 'The Sacred Mosque.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'The Farthest Mosque.' I said: 'How long was between them?' He said: 'Forty years.'" The apparent meaning of this hadith is that it was established by Abraham, and it contradicts what was mentioned in the previous sayings, unless "establishment" is taken to mean renewal (tajdid), in which case the two can be reconciled. The apparent meaning of Abu Dharr's hadith weakens the view of al-Zajjaj that the House of the Holy Sanctuary was built by Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them both. Rather, it appears from it that it was established by Abraham, so just as he established the Ka'bah, he established the House of the Holy Sanctuary. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained that between the two establishments there were forty years. "And where is the time of Abraham from the time of Sulayman!"

The meaning of "established for mankind" is: a place of worship (muta'abbad) in which people share in worship, since the other houses are specific to their owners, whereas the place shared by people is the site of their obedience, worship and qiblah. Most readers read ﴿wudi'a﴾ in the passive voice. 'Ikrimah and Ibn al-Sumayqa' read ﴿wada'a﴾ in the active voice, which may refer back to God, or may refer back to Abraham. The latter is closer in mention, more fitting, and more in agreement with the hadith of Abu Dharr. "For mankind" (lil-nas) is connected to "established" (wada'a), and the lam in it indicates purpose. "For the one at Bakkah" is the predicate of "inna." The meaning: "for the House which is at Bakkah." The predication is emphasized by two emphasizers: inna and the lam. Here the predicate is about an indefinite noun, "﴿first House﴾," because it is specified by the genitive construction and by the qualifier which is "established" (wad'), either for it or for what it is attached to, since specifying it makes it definite. And the predicate "for the one at Bakkah" specifies it, because the intention is to inform about the first house established for mankind. The presence of "inna" makes it acceptable to predicate about an indefinite noun by a definite one. Among Sibawayh's examples: "Inna qariban minka Zayd" (Indeed, one near you is Zayd). Here "qarib" (near) is specified by the phrase "minka" (from you), so the predication about it is acceptable. It has also come without specification, and this is permissible by choice (fi al-ikhtiyar). He said:

*"And indeed it is forbidden for me to revile Mujashi' with my noble, lofty, generous fathers."*

The "ba'" in "bi-Bakkah" is adverbial of place, like your saying: "Zayd is in Basra." It is weak to say that Bakkah is the Mosque itself, because this would require that a thing be a container for itself, which is not valid.

﴿Blessed and a guidance for the worlds﴾. As for its blessing, it is due to the reward that is obtained in it and the expiation of sins for whoever makes pilgrimage to it, performs 'umrah, circumambulates it, and remains in devotion near it. Al-Qaffal said: its blessing may be what was mentioned in His saying: "﴿To which are brought the fruits of every thing﴾" [al-Qasas: 57]. It was said: its blessing is the continuance of worship in it and the constancy of it, because blessing (barakah) has two meanings: one is growth, the other is stability; from it comes "barakah" for the stability of water in it. "Al-barak" is the chest, due to the stability of memory in it; "al-baraka'" is steadfastness in fighting; and "tabaraka Allah" means God endured and never ceased. It was said: its blessing is the multiplication of reward in it. Ibn 'Umar narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever circumambulates the House, does not raise one foot nor put down the other except that God writes for him a good deed by it and raises him a degree by it." Al-Farra' said: it was called "blessed" because it is forgiveness of sins. Ibn Jarir said: its blessing is its purification from sins. It was said: its blessing is that whoever enters it is safe, even the wild animals, so that the gazelle and the dog gather in it. As for its being a guidance: since it is an establishing and reforming (muqawwiman musliḥan), there is guidance in it. The predicate "guidance" is used in an exaggerated way, or it is by omission of an attribute, meaning: "and it is one of guidance." It was said: the meaning of "guidance" is qiblah. It was said: mercy. It was said: righteousness. It was said: a clarification and an indication toward God through the signs in it, which none other than God, the Exalted, is able to produce. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "guidance" here may be understood in the sense of supplication (du'a'), meaning: from where the worlds call to it. The accusative "blessed" is a circumstantial (hal). They permitted that it be a circumstantial from the pronoun concealed in "wudi'a," with the verb "wudi'a" governing it, meaning: "Indeed the first House, blessed, in this state, is the one at Bakkah." This construction is not permissible, because you have separated the governing element of the circumstantial from the circumstantial by a foreign element, namely the predicate, since it is a complement of "inna," a predicate for it. If you supply "wudi'a" after the predicate, it becomes possible for it to govern the circumstantial, and its construction would be: "The one at Bakkah was established blessed." On this construction, the interpretation of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib mentioned above should be understood, when he noticed in this House that it was established first with the condition of this state.

(p-7) They also permitted that the governing element of the circumstantial be the governing element of "bi-Bakkah," meaning: "he settled at Bakkah in the state of its blessing." This is a plainly permissible view, and al-Zamakhshari mentioned no other. As for "guidance," its apparent meaning is that it is conjoined to "blessed," and what is conjoined to a circumstantial is also circumstantial. Some permitted that it be nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "and it is a guidance." There is no need to strain with this omission.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 95–96:**

﴿Say: "God has spoken the truth."﴾ God commanded His Prophet to declare their falsehood openly. That is, the true matter is what God has reported, not the lies they fabricated. By this He indicated that what He reported, including His saying ﴿All food﴾ [Al 'Imran: 93] and everything mentioned before it, is true, and that it is the creed (millah) of Abraham. The better view is that His saying "﴿Say: God has spoken the truth﴾" means: in all that He reported in His revealed books. It was also said that it refers to the claim that Muhammad (ﷺ) follows the creed of Abraham, and that Abraham was a Muslim. It was said regarding His saying "﴿All food﴾" [Al 'Imran: 93] and the verse, related by Ibn al-Sa'ib. It was also said that it refers to the claim that Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian. This was said by Muqatil and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Then He commanded them to follow the creed of Abraham, saying:

﴿Follow the creed of Abraham, a man of pure faith, and he was not of the polytheists.﴾ This is the creed of Islam, upon which the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers with him stood, so that they would be freed from the creed of Judaism. By His saying "and he was not of the polytheists," He hinted that they are polytheists in taking some of them as lords besides God. The discussion of the parallel of this clause in Surat al-Baqarah has already been covered, both in exegesis (tafsir) and in grammatical analysis (i'rab), so there is no need to repeat it.

Aban ibn Tha'lab read ﴿qad sadaqa﴾ (Say: "sadaqa") with the assimilation (idgham, the merging of one letter into the next) of the lam into the sad, and ﴿qul siru﴾ [al-An'am: 11] with the assimilation of the lam into the sin. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hisham assimilated the lam in ﴿bal sawwalat﴾ [Yusuf: 18]. Ibn Jinni said: the reason for this is that these two letters are spread widely in the mouth and the sound produced by them extends, so they come close to the place of articulation of the lam, and so it is permissible to assimilate the lam into them, end of his words. This returns to the sense of Sibawayh's statement. Sibawayh said: "Assimilation, meaning the assimilation of the lam with the ta', the sad and their sisters, is permissible, but it is not as frequent as with the ra', because these letters are farther from it, and they are from the front teeth (thana). And the permissibility of assimilation is because the last point of articulation of the lam is close to their point of articulation." End of his words.

﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah﴾. It was narrated from Mujahid that the Muslims and the Jews boasted, and the Jews said: "The House of the Holy Sanctuary (Bayt al-Maqdis) is more excellent and greater than the Ka'bah, because it is the place of migration of the prophets and it is in the holy land." The Muslims said: "Rather, the Ka'bah is more excellent," and so this verse was revealed. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is clear: when God commanded following the creed of Abraham, and the pilgrimage (hajj) to the House was among the greatest rites of Abraham's creed and among the particular features of his religion, He began to mention the House and its virtues, in order to build upon that the mention of the pilgrimage and its obligation. Also, when the qiblah was changed to the Ka'bah, the Jews criticized the prophethood of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "The House of the Holy Sanctuary is more excellent and more worthy of facing, because it was established before the Ka'bah, and it is the land of the gathering (al-mahshar), and the qiblah of all the prophets." Also, every sect of the Jews and Christians claimed to be upon the creed of Abraham, and among the rites of his creed is the pilgrimage to the Ka'bah, yet they do not make pilgrimage to it. So God refuted them in that claim. "The first" (awwal) is the single one that precedes others. It was said: it is the first house that appeared upon the surface of the water when the heavens and the earth were created; it was created two thousand years before the earth, and it was a white foam upon the water, and the earth was spread out beneath it. It was said: it is the first house built by Adam on the earth. It was said: when Adam was sent down, the angels said to him: "Circumambulate this House, for we circumambulated it before you by two thousand years." At its location, before Adam, there was a house called al-Durah, which was lifted up to the fourth heaven during the Flood, where the angels of the heavens circumambulate it. The noble Abu al-Barakat As'ad ibn 'Ali ibn Abi al-Ghana'im al-Husayni al-Juwani, the genealogist (nassabah), mentioned that Shith ibn Adam is the one who built the Ka'bah from clay and stones, upon the location of the tent which God had placed for Adam from Paradise. According to these sayings, "the first House established for mankind" is to be understood literally. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the first house to be pilgrimaged to after the Flood, so the priority here is with respect to this attribute of pilgrimage, since there were houses before it. It was narrated from 'Ali that a man asked him: "Is it the first house?" 'Ali said: "No, there were houses before it, but it is the first house established for mankind as blessed, containing guidance, mercy and blessing." So he took the priority with the restriction of this condition. It was said: the first who built it was Abraham, then a people of the Arabs from Jurhum, then it was demolished and the Amalekites built it, then it was demolished and the Quraysh built it. Abu Dharr said: "I said: 'O Messenger of God, which mosque was established first?' He said: 'The Sacred Mosque.' I said: 'Then which?' He said: 'The Farthest Mosque.' I said: 'How long was between them?' He said: 'Forty years.'" The apparent meaning of this hadith is that it was established by Abraham, and it contradicts what was mentioned in the previous sayings, unless "establishment" is taken to mean renewal (tajdid), in which case the two can be reconciled. The apparent meaning of Abu Dharr's hadith weakens the view of al-Zajjaj that the House of the Holy Sanctuary was built by Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them both. Rather, it appears from it that it was established by Abraham, so just as he established the Ka'bah, he established the House of the Holy Sanctuary. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained that between the two establishments there were forty years. "And where is the time of Abraham from the time of Sulayman!"

The meaning of "established for mankind" is: a place of worship (muta'abbad) in which people share in worship, since the other houses are specific to their owners, whereas the place shared by people is the site of their obedience, worship and qiblah. Most readers read ﴿wudi'a﴾ in the passive voice. 'Ikrimah and Ibn al-Sumayqa' read ﴿wada'a﴾ in the active voice, which may refer back to God, or may refer back to Abraham.
