Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 97 (part 1 of 3):

﴿In it are clear signs﴾, that is, manifest indications, among them: the Station of Ibrahim (Maqam Ibrahim), the stone on which he stood, the Black Stone, which is one of the stones of the Ka'bah and is the Right Hand of Allah on earth, testifying for whoever touches it; al-Hatim; Zamzam; the security of the one who fears, and its awe and magnification in the hearts of people; the affair of the Elephant; the casting down upon it of the birds of Allah with stones of sijjil; the restraint of tyrants from it throughout the ages; the submission of the souls of the Arabs to venerating this place without anyone forbidding or restraining them; the gathering of provisions to it, although it is in a valley without crops; and its protection from torrents. Also, the fact that rain comes to it from all its sides indicates the fertility of the horizons of the earth, for if the rain came from one side, the horizon adjacent to it would be made fertile. Makki and others mentioned that among its signs is that birds do not fly over it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is weak, for birds are observed flying high, and the eagle has flown over it, having seized the snake that was overlooking its wall, and that was among its signs." End of quote. And whoever ascends over it is freed (from slavery). Hastening punishment upon whoever transgresses within it, answering the supplication of one who prays beneath the spout (al-Mizab), the multiplication of the reward of the one who prays, and other signs.

As for His saying, "in it are clear signs": the pronoun in "fihi" refers to the House, so it would seem that among the signs only those that are in the House should be mentioned. However, they have extended the use of the adverbial sense (zarfiyyah), since it is not possible to take it literally, for that would require the signs to be inside the walls. The basis of the extension is that the House was established together with its sanctuary (haram) and all its virtues, so they are "in it" in a metaphorical manner. Therefore the commentators counted signs in the sanctuary and matters that were made obligatory in our Shari'ah, such as the prohibition of cutting its trees and the prohibition of hunting within it. What the verse specifically addresses is the Station of Ibrahim, because it is a sign that remains throughout the ages. That is because when Ibrahim stood upon the stone of the Station at the time of raising the foundations of the House, the building grew tall for him; whenever the wall rose, the stone rose with him into the air. He continued building while standing upon it, and Isma'il handed him the stones and the clay until the wall was completed. Then Allah willed to preserve that as a sign for the worlds: He softened the stone so that the feet of Ibrahim sank into it as if into clay, and that (p-٨) trace remains to this day. All the Arabs transmitted this in the Jahiliyyah across the ages. Abu Talib said concerning it:

"And the treading place of Ibrahim upon the rock, soft, with his two feet, barefoot, not sandaled."

No one is known to have disputed this statement. It was also said: the cause of the trace of his two feet in this stone was that he came to Makkah as a visitor from Syria, and Isma'il's wife said to him: "Descend until I wash your head." He refused to descend, so she brought this stone from the side of its right part, and he placed his foot upon it until she washed one side of his head; then she turned it to its left side until she washed the other side, and the trace of his two feet remained in it.

The "ayat" is in the nominative as the subject of the preposition-phrase preceding it, so the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the governing element is omitted; that omitted element is in reality the circumstance. Attributing the circumstantial character to the adverb and the prepositional phrase is metaphorical, like attributing the predicate to them when you say: "Zayd is in the house" or "with you." Therefore some of our companions said: what is attributed to the adverb of predication and of governing, the more correct view is that it belongs to its governing element, and that "fihi" is in the position of a presumed circumstance, whether the governing element in it is the governing element in "bi-Bakkata" (Qur'an 3:96), or whether the governing element in it is "wudi'a" (was placed), as they parsed it, or as we parsed it. It is also permissible that it is an independent sentence, in which Allah the Exalted informs that in it are clear signs.

"Maqam Ibrahim": maqam is a noun of place from qiyam (standing). The majority read "ayat bayyinat" in the plural. Ubayy, 'Amr ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Abu Ja'far in the transmission of Qutaybah read "ayah bayyinah" in the singular. According to the reading of the majority, they parsed "Maqam Ibrahim" as an apposition (badal), a badal of the whole from the whole, from the phrase "ayat"; and they parsed it as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are the Station of Ibrahim. But according to what they parsed, how can a singular be substituted for a plural, or be predicated of a plural? It was answered in two ways: The first: that it is taken alone as equivalent to many signs, because of the prominence of its matter and the strength of its indication of the power of Allah and the prophethood of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, from the effect of his foot in solid rock, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "Indeed Ibrahim was a nation, devoutly obedient" (Qur'an 16:120). The second: that it includes several signs, for the trace of the foot in the hard rock is a sign, his sinking into it up to the ankles is a sign, the softening of part of the rock and not another part is a sign, its preservation apart from the rest of the signs of the prophets is a sign specific to Ibrahim, and its preservation despite the great number of his enemies among the polytheists, the People of the Book and the heretics for thousands of years is a sign. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also permissible that what is meant by 'in it are clear signs' is the Station of Ibrahim and the security of whoever enters it, because the two signs are a type of plurality, like three and four." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "What is preferred in my view is that the Station and the security of the one who enters were made examples of the signs in the sanctuary of Allah, and were singled out for mention because of their greatness, and because proof is established against the disbelievers by them, since they perceive these two signs with their senses." The apparent meaning of his words and of al-Zamakhshari's words before him is that the Station of Ibrahim and the security of the one who enters are an explanation of the signs, which are plural; but the security of the one who enters is not mentioned in the verse as a grammatical explanation. Rather, "whoever enters it is secure" comes as a clause of condition and consequence, or as a subject and predicate, not in the manner of being a singular noun coordinated with his saying "Maqam Ibrahim," so that it would be a grammatical explanation. Rather, after His saying "clear signs," nothing came except a singular, which is "Maqam Ibrahim," so he said: If you say: how did you permit that "Maqam Ibrahim" and the security be an apposition, and his saying "whoever enters it is secure" be an independent sentence, either initial or conditional? I say: I permitted that from the standpoint of meaning, because his saying "whoever enters it is secure" indicates the security of the one who enters, so it is as if it were said: in it are clear signs: the Station of Ibrahim and the security of its entrant. Do you not see that if you said: "In it is a clear sign: whoever enters it is secure," it would be correct, because it means: in it is a clear sign, the security of whoever enters it. End of his question and answer. It is not clear, because his assumption "and the security of the entrant" is in the nominative, coordinated with "Maqam Ibrahim," and they explained the signs by the two. The clause "whoever enters it is secure" has no place in grammatical analysis, so the two contradict each other, unless one believes that this is a coordinated, omitted element indicated by what follows, in which case the interpretation is possible. So "whoever enters it is secure" is not taken to mean "and the security of its entrant" except in terms of explaining the meaning, not the grammatical analysis. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that these two signs be mentioned and mention of others be omitted, as an indication of the multiplicity of signs, as if it were said: in it are clear signs: the Station of Ibrahim, and the security of whoever enters it, and many others besides them. Similar to this in omitted mention is the verse of Jarir:

"Hanifah was in thirds, a third of them from the slaves, and a third from its clients."

And from it is his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "Three things have been made beloved to me of your world: perfume, women, and the coolness of my eyes is in prayer." End of his words. In this there is the omission of two coordinated elements. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention in parsing "Maqam Ibrahim" anything except that it is an apposition to "ayat bayyinat." This was rejected against him, because "ayat" is indefinite and "Maqam Ibrahim" is definite, and it is not permissible for an apposition to differ in this way. His statement contradicts the consensus of the Kufans and the Basrans, so it is not to be heeded. The rule of apposition according to the Kufans is the rule of the attribute, so the indefinite follows the indefinite and the definite follows the definite; and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi followed them in this. But according to the Basrans, it is not permissible unless both are definite, and it is not permissible for both to be indefinite. What the Kufans and those who agree with them parsed as an apposition, an indefinite following an indefinite before it, the Basrans parsed as a badal; and there is no proof for specifying that apposition applies to an indefinite, so it should not be permissible. The more appropriate and correct parsing of "Maqam Ibrahim" is that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is: one of them, that is, one of those clear signs is the Station of Ibrahim; or an omitted-predicate subject whose estimate is: of them, that is, of the clear signs is the Station of Ibrahim. The mention of the Station is due to its greatness, its fame among them, its being visible to them without change, and its reminding them of the religion of their father Ibrahim. As for the reading of the one who read "ayah bayyinah" in the singular, its parsing is a badal, a badal of a definite from an indefinite qualified noun, like His saying, Exalted is He: "And indeed you guide to a straight path, the path of Allah" (Qur'an 42:52). Allah the Exalted has informed concerning this one great sign alone, which is the Station of Ibrahim, for the reason we have mentioned, even though there are many signs in the House.

They differed in the interpretation of "Maqam Ibrahim." The majority said: it is the well-known stone. Others said: the whole House is the Station of Ibrahim, because he built it and stood in all its regions. Others said: all of Makkah is the Station of Ibrahim. Others said: the whole sanctuary. The sanctuary, on the side adjacent to Madinah, extends about four miles to the end of al-Tan'im; on the side adjacent to Iraq, about eight miles, called al-Maqta'; and on the side adjacent to 'Arafah, nine miles to the end of al-Hudaybiyyah.

The pronoun in "wa-man dakhalahu" ("and whoever enters it") refers to the House, since it is the subject being described, and it is the one qualified by those attributes of blessing, guidance, and the clear signs, including the Station of Ibrahim and others. It cannot refer to the Station of Ibrahim if we interpret that as the stone. The apparent meaning of the verse and the context of the discourse indicate that this sentence explains some of the signs of the House and reminds the Arabs of what they used to do in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period) regarding the reverence of this House and the safety of whoever entered it, even those guilty of crimes. The Arabs would raid one another, and people were snatched away through killing, the seizure of property, and various kinds of injustice, except within the sanctuary (haram), as in His saying: ﴿Have they not seen that We made a secure sanctuary, while people are being snatched away all around them?﴾ [al-Ankabut: 67]. This was by the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure city﴾ [al-Baqarah: 126]. As for in Islam, whoever commits a prescribed offence (hadd), the sanctuary does not protect him. This view was held by ʿAta', Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and others. So whoever commits adultery, theft, or murder has the prescribed punishment carried out against him. Many who held this view considered it good that whoever is liable to execution should leave for the area outside the sanctuary (al-hill) and be executed there.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: whoever commits an offence and seeks refuge in the House is safe. The matter in Islam is as it was in the Jahiliyyah: no one may confront the killer of his guardian (wali). However, it is obligatory upon the Muslims not to sell to him, not to speak with him, and not to shelter him, until he becomes wearied, leaves the sanctuary, and the prescribed punishment is carried out upon him. ʿAta' also held this view, as did al-Shaʿbi, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, al-Suddi, Ibn Jubayr, and others. However, most of them said: this applies to one who is killed outside the sanctuary and then takes refuge in the sanctuary; but whoever is killed within it, the prescribed punishment is carried out against him within it.

The jurists of the major cities (fuqahaʾ al-amsar) differed: if someone commits a crime outside the sanctuary and then takes refuge in it, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, Muhammad, Zufar, al-Hasan ibn Ziyad, and Ahmad in a narration transmitted by Hanbal from him said: if the offence was against a person (life), retaliation (qisas) is not carried out against him, and he is not to be mixed with; if it was for something less than a life, retaliation is carried out against him within the sanctuary. Malik, in one narration, said: retaliation is not carried out against him there, neither by killing nor for anything less than a life, and he is not to be mixed with.

They said: consensus (ijmaʿ) has been established that whoever commits an offence within it is not granted safety, because he has violated the sanctity of the sanctuary and rejected its security. Thus the ruling of the verse remains for one who committed an offence outside it and then took refuge in it. They also said: this is a report whose meaning is a command, i.e. "and whoever enters it, grant him safety." It is general regarding one who committed an offence within it or elsewhere and then entered it, but the consensus has prevented acting upon it for one who committed an offence within it, and the ruling of the verse remains specific to one who committed an offence outside it and then entered it.

Yahya ibn Jaʿdah and others said: "safe" means safe from the Fire. And there must be a restriction in "﴿And whoever enters it shall be safe﴾": i.e. whoever enters it as a pilgrim, or whoever enters it sincerely in his entering. It was also said that the meaning is: whoever entered it in the year of the ʿUmrat al-Qadaʾ with the Prophet ﷺ, based on His saying: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if God wills, in security﴾ [al-Fath: 27]. Jaʿfar al-Sadiq said: whoever enters it and ascends al-Safa is safe with the safety of the prophets.

The apparent meaning of the verse is what we began with first, and all these other statements are far-fetched (mutakallafat); the wording rejects them, and some of them contradict the apparent meanings of the verses and the principles of the Sharia.

﴿And for God, upon the people, is the pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find a way to it.﴾ ʿIkrimah narrated: "When the verse was revealed: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion﴾ [Al ʿImran: 85], the Jews said: we are upon Islam. So the verse was revealed: ﴿And for God, upon the people, is the pilgrimage to the House﴾ ..." up to the end of the verse. It was said to them: perform the pilgrimage, O Muhammad, if they are upon the creed of Ibrahim, which is Islam; let them perform the pilgrimage if they are Muslims. The Jews said: we will never perform it.

This verse emphasises the obligation of the pilgrimage (hajj), since it came with His saying "for God" (li-llah), which indicates that it belongs to Him, and it came with "upon" (ʿala), which denotes obligation, and it came attached to "the people" in general terms, though the intended meaning is specific, so that whoever is obligated to it is mentioned twice. Al-Zamakhshari said: in this statement there are several kinds of emphasis and stress. Among them is His saying ﴿And for God, upon the people, is the pilgrimage to the House﴾, meaning that it is a binding right of God upon the necks of people, from which they cannot be released except by fulfilling it and discharging their duty. Among them is that He mentioned "the people" and then substituted for it ﴿whoever is able to find a way to it﴾; in this there are two forms of emphasis. One is that the substitution serves as an alert to the intended meaning and a repetition of it. The second is that clarification after ambiguity and detail after generality is presenting it in two different forms. End of his words, and they are good.

Hamzah, al-Kisaʾi, and Hafs read "ḥijj" with a kasra on the ḥa', and the rest read it with a fatḥa. Both are dialects: the kasra is the dialect of Najd, and the fatḥa is the dialect of the people of al-ʿAliyah. Sibawayh made ḥijj with the kasra a verbal noun (maṣdar), like "dhakara dhikran". Al-Zajjaj made it a noun of action (ism al-ʿamal). They did not disagree that with the fatḥa it is a verbal noun. "Ḥajj" is the subject (mubtadaʾ), and its predicate is in the prepositional phrase "li-llah"; "ʿala al-nas" is related to the element that governs the prepositional phrase which is the predicate. It is permitted that "ʿala al-nas" be a circumstantial clause (ḥal), and that it be the predicate of "ḥajj". "Li-llah" cannot be a circumstantial clause, because that would entail its preceding the implicit governing element. "Ḥajj" is a verbal noun, annexed to the object which is "al-bayt", and the definite article in it is for previous reference, since ﴿Indeed, the first house established for people is that at Bakkah﴾ [Al ʿImran: 96] has already been mentioned. This is the original usage, and then it became a proper name by dominance. Whenever "the House" is mentioned, nothing comes to the mind except that it is the Kaʿbah, and it has become like the Pleiades (al-Thurayya) for the star. The poet said:

*By my life, you are indeed the House; I honour its people,*
*and I sit among its precincts in the evenings.*

In this verse, the only condition for its obligation is ability (istitaʿah). They mentioned that its conditions are: sanity, puberty, freedom, Islam, and ability. The apparent meaning of His saying "﴿for God, upon the people﴾" is that it is obligatory upon the slave, and he is addressed by it; this is the view of Dawud. The majority said: he is not addressed by it, because he is not able, since his master prevents him from this worship for the sake of his rights. They said: likewise the child. So if a slave performs the pilgrimage while in bondage, or a child before reaching puberty, and then the slave is freed and the child reaches puberty, then the obligatory pilgrimage of Islam (ḥajjat al-Islam) is incumbent upon both of them. The apparent meaning is sufficiency with one pilgrimage, and consensus of the majority is established on this, unlike some of the Zahiris who said it is obligatory every five years; the sound hadith refutes him.

The apparent meaning is that its condition is the capacity to reach it by any means one is able to, whether walking, begging, riding a ship, or hiring oneself out for service. Men and women are equal in this, and the stipulation is unrestricted ability. The verse contains no ambiguous terms (mujmalat) requiring explanation. The verse does not address whether the pilgrimage is obligatory immediately (ʿalal-fawr) or may be delayed (ʿalal-tarakhi), but the apparent meaning is that it is obligatory at the time ability is attained. There are two opinions on this from the Hanafis and the Malikis. Abu ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: what indicates delay is the consensus of the scholars on not declaring a person who is able to perform the pilgrimage a sinner (fasiq) if he postpones it from the year in which it became obligatory for him, unlike someone who missed a prayer until its time expired and then made it up. They also agreed that it is not said to someone who performed the pilgrimage years after his ability: "you are a debtor (qadin)." Everyone who holds the view of delay finds no limit for it except what was narrated from Sahnun, that if someone exceeds sixty years while able and has neglected it, he is a sinner. A similar report was transmitted from Ibn al-Qasim.

Regarding the grammatical analysis (iʿrab) of "man" there is disagreement. Most scholars held that it is a partitive substitute (badal baʿḍ min kull), so "man" is a relative pronoun in a genitive position, and a partitive substitute necessarily requires a pronoun, which here is elided, its estimated form being: "whoever among them is able to find a way to it." Al-Kisaʾi and others said: "man" is conditional, so it is in the nominative position as the subject. This requires the elision of the connecting pronoun linking this clause to what precedes it, and the elision of the response (jawab) of the conditional, since the estimate would be: "whoever among them is able to find a way to it, then the pilgrimage is incumbent upon him, or then that is incumbent upon him." The first view is preferable, because the elision in it is less, and its elision is more frequent in the latter. The conditional is suited by the conditional coming after it in His saying ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾. It was also said: "man" is a relative pronoun in the nominative position as the predicate of an elided subject, its estimate being: "they are whoever is able to find a way to it." Some Basrans said: "man" is a relative pronoun in the nominative position as the agent of the verbal noun "ḥajj", so that the verbal noun is annexed to its object and its agent is raised by it, like: "I was amazed at the drinking of honey by Zayd." This view is weak in terms of both wording and meaning. As for wording, the annexation of a verbal noun to its object while raising the agent by it is rare in the language and is hardly found in the speech of the Arabs except in poetry; some even claimed it is not permitted except in poetry. As for meaning, it is not valid, because the meaning would be: God obligated the people, both its able and its unable, to perform the pilgrimage to the House, the able among them. But the element upon which obligation falls is only the able person, not people in general. The pronoun in "ilayhi" refers to the House; it was also said it refers to the pilgrimage. "Ilayhi" is related to "istaṭāʿa", and "sabīlan" is the object of "istaṭāʿa", since it is a transitive verb. He said: ﴿They are not able to help you﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 197]. And everything that leads to something is a way (sabīl) to it.

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates the obligation of Hajj upon those who are able to find a way to the House, and capacity (istita'ah) is not among the ambiguous terms (mujmalat) as we have previously mentioned. 

ʿUmar, his son, Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿAṭā', and Ibn Jubayr said: it is the condition of the one who finds provision and a mount (rahilah). This is the view of most scholars. Ibn al-Zubayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: if one is able without hardship upon himself, it is obligatory upon him. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: if he is able to hire himself out, then he is capable. It was said to him regarding this, "If some people had an inheritance in Mecca, would he leave it? Rather, he would set out to it even crawling on his hands and knees. Likewise, Hajj is obligatory upon him." (p-12) Al-Ḥasan said: whoever finds something that will convey him, it has become obligatory upon him. ʿIkrimah said: the capacity for the way is health. The position of Mālik is that if a man trusts in his strength, it is binding upon him, and it is also reported from him that it is according to the measure of one's ability. Someone may find provision and a mount yet be unable to travel, and someone may be able to travel without a mount or provision. Ibn ʿAbbas said: whoever possesses three hundred dirhams, that is the way to it. Al-Shāfiʿī said: capacity is of two kinds. First, by oneself: whoever is prevented by illness or a valid excuse, while possessing wealth, must appoint someone to perform Hajj on his behalf, and he is considered capable for that purpose.

The opinion of Mālik differed regarding one who begs while going and returning, from one whose custom is not that during his residence. Ibn Wahb reported from him: there is no harm in that. Ibn al-Qāsim reported from him: I do not regard that, and one should not set out for Hajj or military campaign as a beggar. Mālik disliked that women perform Hajj by sea. It was differed upon from him regarding women performing Hajj on foot when they are able to do so. There is no Hajj obligation upon a woman unless she has with her a mahram (a close male relative who is forbidden to her in marriage). It was differed upon if she lacks one. Al-Ḥasan, al-Nakhaʿī, Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions, Aḥmad, and Isḥāq said: the mahram is part of the way, and there is no Hajj obligation upon her except with a mahram. Abū Ḥanīfa said: this applies when the distance between her and Mecca is a three-day journey or more. And if she finds a mahram, is it permissible for her husband to prevent her from performing the obligatory Hajj? Al-Shāfiʿī said: he may prevent her. Regarding Mālik there are two reports: prevention and non-prevention. A mahram is one whom it is never permissible for her to marry permanently, by kinship, by fosterage, or by affinity. Free and slave, Muslim and dhimmī (non-Muslim protected subject) are equal in this, except that if he is a Magian who believes it lawful to marry her, or a Muslim who is not trustworthy, then she may not go out nor travel with him. Mālik said: she goes out with a group of women. Al-Shāfiʿī said: with a trustworthy, Muslim free woman. Ibn Sīrīn said: with a trustworthy man from among the Muslims. Al-Awzāʿī said: with a group of upright people, and she should take a ladder to climb up and down on, and no man should approach her.

They differed regarding the obligation of Hajj in the presence of unlawful tolls (mukus) and levies (gharamah). Sufyān al-Thawrī said: if the toll is even a single dirham, the obligation of Hajj falls from the people. ʿAbd al-Wahhāb said: if the levy is large and ruinous, the obligation falls. The apparent meaning of his statement is that if it is large but not ruinous to him, given the abundance of his wealth, then it does not fall. This is the view of a group of the people of knowledge, and the ages have proceeded upon it. They agreed that the sick and the incapacitated (maʿdūb) are not obligated to journey to Hajj. Mālik said: the obligation of Hajj falls from the incapacitated, and no one performs Hajj on his behalf during his lifetime. If he bequeaths that Hajj be performed on his behalf after his death, it is performed from one-third of his estate, and it is considered voluntary. Al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfa and his companions, Ibn al-Mubārak, Aḥmad, and Isḥāq said: if he is able to pay money with which to hire someone, it is binding upon him to do so. If someone offers him his personal service and proxy (niyābah), it is binding upon him by the offer of service according to al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, and Isḥāq. Abū Ḥanīfa said: Hajj is not obligatory upon him by an offer of service, and even if someone offers him money, the sound position is that he is not obligated to accept it. The subsidiary issues of istiṭāʿah are many and are mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (fiqh).

* *

﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is Free of need from the worlds﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: [this refers to] the obligation of Hajj; whoever claims it is not obligatory upon him has disbelieved. The same was said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAṭā', al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, and ʿImrān al-Qaṭṭān. Ibn ʿUmar and others said: "And whoever disbelieves in Allah and the Last Day." Ibn Zayd said: "And whoever disbelieves in these signs that are in the House." Al-Suddī and a group said: "And whoever disbelieves" by failing to perform Hajj when he finds the means to do so; this is disbelief of disobedience (kufr maʿṣiyah), unlike the first view, which is disbelief of denial (kufr juḥūd). According to al-Suddī's view it follows, based on his saying: "Whoever abandons the prayer has disbelieved," and "Do not revert after me to disbelief, striking one another's necks," according to one of the two interpretations. Al-Zamakhsharī said: among the forms of emphasis and intensification is His saying "and whoever disbelieves," in place of "and whoever does not perform Hajj," as a severe warning to the one who abandons Hajj. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever dies without having performed Hajj, let him die, if he wishes, as a Jew or a Christian." And similar to this severity is: whoever abandons the prayer deliberately has disbelieved. The end of his words. This is in the sense of al-Suddī's statement. Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab said: "And whoever disbelieves" regarding the House being the direction of truth. According to this, it refers to the Jews who said when the qiblah was changed: ﴿What has turned them away from their qiblah which they had been upon?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142], and they disbelieved in it and said: "We will never perform Hajj toward it."

"Whoever" (man) is a conditional particle, and the answer to the condition is the clause introduced by the fāʾ (the particle of consequence). The link connecting it to the conditional clause is the generality in His saying "the worlds," since whoever disbelieves is included under this generality. In this expression there is a severe warning for whoever disbelieves. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: the intended meaning of the speech is "indeed Allah is free of need of them," but the expression was generalized so that the meaning would be comprehensive, and the mind would be alerted to the power and sovereignty of Allah and His independence from all aspects, such that there is no need in Him for anything, there being no lord besides Him. The end of his words. Al-Zamakhsharī said: among the forms of emphasis is the mention of His independence from it [i.e., from Hajj], which indicates abhorrence, wrath, and abandonment. Among them is His saying "from the worlds" rather than "from it," and what it contains of indication of independence from it, by proof: since if He is independent of the worlds, independence from it is necessarily included, and because it indicates complete independence, it is more indicative of the magnitude of the wrath which is expressed by it. It was said: there is an elided element in the speech, its estimate being: "indeed Allah is free of need of the Hajj of the worlds."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 98:

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of Allah while Allah is witness over what you do?"﴾ Al-Tabari said: The occasion of its revelation, and the revelation of what follows it up to His saying, ﴿And for them is a great punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 105], is that a man from the Jews tried to incite discord between the Aws and the Khazraj. His name was Shas ibn Qays, and he was a blind man, intensely full of rancor and envy toward the Muslims. He saw the unity of the Aws and the Khazraj, and said: "We will have no place of settlement in this land while the assembly of the Banu Qaylah is gathered." So he ordered a young Jew to remind them of the Day of Bu'ath and what took place in it of war, and of what they had said in poetry about it. He did so, and they spoke until they rose up to arms at al-Harrah. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Is it the calls of the Jahiliyyah while I am among you?" And he admonished them, and they returned, and some of them embraced one another. This is its summary, and they related it at length. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Suddi said: It was revealed concerning the rabbis of the Jews who used to turn the Muslims away from Islam by telling them: "Muhammad is not the one described in our Book." The apparent meaning is that the address is to the People of the Scripture in general and to the common people, even if they did not know; the proof stands against them just as it stands against the elite. It is as though, by abandoning reasoning and turning to blind imitation, they are in the position of one who knows and then denies. It was also said: The intended ones are the scholars of the People of the Scripture who knew the truth of his prophethood, and this was deduced from His saying: ﴿while you are witnesses﴾ [Al 'Imran: 99]. End of this view. He singled out the People of the Scripture for mention, apart from the rest of the disbelievers, because they are the ones addressed at the beginning of this verse, for whom the proofs from the Torah and the Gospel on the truth of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) are presented, and whose doubts on this matter are answered. Also, their knowledge of the signs of Allah is stronger, due to their prior acknowledgment of monotheism and the basis of prophethood, and due to their knowledge of what is in their books of testimony to the Messenger and good tidings of him. When the Exalted mentioned that in the House there are clear signs and made its pilgrimage obligatory, then said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is free of need from the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran: 97], it was fitting to rebuke the disbelievers for their disbelief in the signs of Allah. So He addressed them as ﴿O People of the Scripture﴾, to alert them that they are the People of the Scripture, so it is not fitting for one who ascribes himself to the Book of Allah to disbelieve in its signs; rather, obedience to it and belief in it should be befitting, since he has a source of knowledge to which he returns when a doubt afflicts him.

And "the signs" (al-ayat) are the indications which Allah has set up as evidence of the truth. It was also said: The signs of Allah are verses from the Torah in which the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) is found. The Qur'an and the miracle of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) are also possible.

﴿And Allah is witness over what you do﴾ is a circumstantial clause containing a threat and a warning. That is: whoever is such that Allah is aware of his deeds and observes him in all his states, it is not fitting for him to disbelieve in His signs. Thus the knowledge that Allah is aware of all the deeds of disbelief in the signs of Allah does not combine with it; for whoever is certain that Allah will requite him rarely commits disbelief, which is the greatest of the major sins. The form "shahid" (witness) comes to indicate intensification with respect to its object, because witnessing is meant in relation to Allah as knowledge, and His attributes, in themselves, do not admit of increase or decrease. So when an attribute of His comes in the intensive form, it is according to its objects. The discussion of "li-ma" (why) and the deletion of the alif from "ma" (what) when the preposition precedes it has already been treated. His saying "﴿over what you do﴾" is connected to "shahid," and "ma" is a relative pronoun. They also permitted that it be a verbal noun (masdariyyah), meaning "over your deed."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 99:

﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, why do you bar from the way of Allah those who have believed, seeking to make it crooked, while you are witnesses? And Allah is not unaware of what you do."﴾

When He denounced their disbelief and misguidance within themselves, and they were not content with that but strove to lead astray those who had believed, He denounced this as well from Him, Exalted is He. Thus they combined misguidance with leading others into misguidance. [This is in line with the hadith]: "Whoever establishes an evil practice, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it."

"Ṣadda" is both intransitive and transitive. It is said: ṣadda ʿan kadhā (he turned away from such-and-such), and ṣadda ghayrahu ʿan kadhā (he turned another away from such-and-such). The reading of the majority is yaṣuddūna, in the triliteral form, which is transitive, and its object is "man āmana" (those who believed). Al-Ḥasan read taṣuddūna from aṣadda, which makes the intransitive ṣadda transitive by means of the hamza; both are two dialects.

Dhu al-Rummah said:

*"People who turned the people away from them by the sword"*

The meaning of ṣadda here is "turned away" (ṣarafa). "The way of Allah" is the religion of Allah and the path of His law, and it has previously been mentioned that it may be masculine or feminine. As an example of the feminine usage, he said:

*"So do not be distant, for every youth of the people / will soon be walking that path."*

Al-Raghib said: The phrase "O People of the Scripture" [Āl ʿImrān: 98] came without "Qul," whereas here "Qul" is present. Without "Qul," it is an invitation from Him, Exalted is He, to them toward the truth; so making His address to them a gentle appeal to the people makes them more inclined to submit. When He intended to belittle them, He mentioned "Qul" as an alert that they are not worthy that He address them Himself, though both addresses reached them through the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ). The phrase "People of the Scripture" is used in praise at times and in blame at others. "People of the Qur'an and the Sunnah" is used only in praise, because "the Book" may refer to what they fabricated rather than what Allah revealed, as in: "They write the Book with their own hands" [al-Baqarah: 79], and it may also refer to what Allah revealed. Furthermore, it may be said in a tone of blame and mockery, as if one said "O People of the Scripture" to someone who does not act upon its requirements. End of the summarized portion of his words.

The pronoun in "yabghūnahā" refers to "the way." Al-Zajjaj and al-Ṭabarī said: they seek for it crookedness. The Arabs say: ibghinī kadhā (with a joined alif), meaning "seek it for me"; and abghinī (with a cut alif), meaning "help me in seeking it."

Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say) how can they seek it crooked, when that is impossible? (I say) it has two meanings. The first: you confuse people until you make them imagine that it has crookedness, by your saying that the law of Moses is not abrogated, and by altering the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from its true form, and similar things. The second: you exhaust yourselves in concealing the truth and seeking crookedness in what is more upright than every straight thing, which is not possible for you to achieve. End of his words. It was also said: "yabghūna" here is from baghy, meaning transgression, that is, they transgress against it or within it; and "ʿiwajan" in this interpretation is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in "tabghūn," meaning crooked from you and without uprightness. End of his words. According to the first interpretation, "ʿiwajan" is the direct object, and the clause "tabghūnahā ʿiwajan" may be taken as a new sentence, or as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "taṣuddūn" or from "sabīl Allāh," since it contains two pronouns referring to them.

"And you are witnesses," meaning: by reason, as in "Or he gives ear while he is a witness" [Qāf: 37], meaning one who knows by his intellect; sometimes by action, as in "He said: Bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses" [Āl ʿImrān: 81]; and sometimes by establishing that, meaning you bore witness to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) before his mission, according to the description and truthfulness of him found in the Torah. Al-Zamakhshari said: "And you are witnesses" that it is the way of Allah, which none turns away from except one who is astray and misleads. Or: "And you are witnesses" among the people of your religion, upright, whom they trust in your words, and whom they call upon as witnesses in their great matters, and they are the rabbis. End of his words. It was said: In His words "and you are witnesses" there is an indication that the testimony of some of them against others is permissible, since He called them "witnesses," and this designation applies only to one who has testimony. Their testimony against Muslims is not permissible by consensus, so it is determined that they are described as those whose testimony against one another is permissible; this is the view of Abu Hanifa and a group. Most scholars hold that their testimony is never accepted in any case, and that they are not among the people of testimony.

﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ This is a severe warning to them. The explanation of this sentence has already been given earlier, so it is sufficient and need not be repeated.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 100:

﴿O you who have believed, if you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture, they will return you, after your belief, to disbelief.﴾ When Allah, exalted is He, denied them (the People of the Book) the ability to turn the believers away from Islam, He warned the believers against the seduction and misguidance of the disbelievers, and He addressed them by the description of faith, to draw attention to the difference between them and the disbelievers. He did not use the word "Say" (qul), so that this would be direct address from Him, exalted is He, to them, and a reassurance to them. He expressed His prohibition against agreeing with them and obeying them in the form of a conditional sentence, because their obedience to them had not actually occurred. The address "O you who have believed" refers to the Aws and the Khazraj, because of the uproar caused by Shas ibn Qays. He left the obedience unrestricted in order to indicate the generality of the case, that is, that any obedience at all may come from you in anything at all of what they attempt of your misguidance. He did not restrict the obedience to the story of the Aws and the Khazraj, as mentioned in the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul, the specific event that prompted the verse). "Return" (radd) here means "make," that is, they will make you. The disbelief referred to here is not disbelief in its true sense, because the occasion of revelation concerns the sowing of enmity between the Aws and the Khazraj. Had that happened, it would have been disobedience, not disbelief, unless they did it considering it lawful. It may be that this occurs through the People of the Book beautifying things for them, one prohibited matter after another, and luring them little by little until they leave Islam and become disbelievers in the true sense. The accusative of "disbelievers" (kafirin) is as a second object (maf'ul thani, the second object of a verb) of "yaruddu," because here it carries the meaning of "make," as in the saying of the poet:

"He made their black hair white, and made their white faces black."

It has been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal, a word describing the condition of the subject at the time of the action), but the first view is more evident.

﴿And how can you disbelieve while the verses of Allah are being recited to you and among you is His Messenger?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 101] This is a question expressing astonishment at the occurrence of disbelief from them in these two circumstances: the recitation of the Book of Allah to them, which is the Qur'an, manifest in its inimitability, and the presence of the Messenger among them, through whose hands the extraordinary signs became manifest. The existence of these two circumstances contradicts disbelief and does not coexist with it, so no disbelief can reach them while these two conditions remain. The meaning is not that disbelief had actually occurred from them so that they were rebuked for its occurrence, because they are believers; for this reason they were addressed with His saying: "O you who have believed." So this is not like His saying: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah while you were dead?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. The Messenger here is Muhammad (ﷺ), without any disagreement. The address, according to al-Zajjaj, is specifically to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), because the Prophet (ﷺ) was among them and they were witnessing him. It has been said that it is addressed to the whole nation, because his traces and his sunnah are among them, even though they did not witness him. Qatada said: In this verse there are two clear signs: the Book of Allah and the Prophet of Allah. As for the Prophet of Allah, he has passed away; as for the Book of Allah, Allah has preserved it among them out of mercy from Him and as a blessing upon them, its lawful and its unlawful, its obedience and its disobedience. It has been said that the address is to the Aws and the Khazraj, whose case is the occasion of the revelation of this verse concerning what passed between them, as mentioned by the majority of scholars. The majority read "tutla" with a "ta" (feminine). Al-Hasan and al-A'mash read "yutla" with a "ya," on account of the separation, and because the feminine marking is not real, and because the verses are the Qur'an. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "And among you is His Messenger" is a locative expression of presence and witnessing of his person (ﷺ), and he is among his nation until the Day of Resurrection through his sayings and his traces. Al-Zamakhshari said: "And how can you disbelieve" has in it the meaning of interrogation, carrying denial and wonder, and the meaning is: from where could disbelief reach you, when the signs of Allah, which are the inimitable Qur'an, are being recited to you upon the tongue of the Messenger, fresh and new, and among you is the Messenger of Allah, who admonishes you, advises you, and removes your doubts?

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 101:

﴿Whoever holds fast to Allah, has indeed been guided to a straight path.﴾ Ibn Jurayj said: "Whoever believes in Allah." This statement is consistent with His saying: ﴿And how can you disbelieve?﴾ It was also said: "He clings to the Qur'an." And it was said: "He takes refuge in it (Allah)," so according to this view, it is a matter of seeking refuge in Allah to repel the evils of the disbelievers. The answer to "man" (the conditional particle) is "faqad hudiya" ("has indeed been guided"), which is past in wording but future in meaning. "Qad" (indeed) is used here to express expectation (tawaqqu', anticipation), because the one who holds fast to Allah is expecting guidance.

They mentioned, in these verses, some of the aspects of eloquence and rhetorical excellence (funun al-balaghah wa al-fasahah): the interrogative (istifham) used to express denunciation (inkar) in ﴿Why do you disbelieve?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 98], ﴿Why do you bar?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 99], and ﴿And how can you disbelieve?﴾; the repetition (takrar) in "﴿O People of the Scripture﴾" [Al 'Imran: 98], and in the name of Allah in several places, and in "what they do"; the antithesis (tibaq) in "faith and disbelief," in "disbelief, since it is misguidance," and "guidance," and in "crookedness" and "uprightness"; and the figurative usage (tajawwuz) through the use of a collective noun (ism al-jam') in ﴿a group from those who were given the Scripture﴾ [Al 'Imran: 100]. It was said: he is an unspecified Jew. It was also said: he is Shas ibn Qays, the Jew. The use of a general term while meaning a specific one (itlaq al-'umum wa al-murad al-khusus) is in "O you who have believed," according to the majority of scholars, that it is addressed to the Aws and the Khazraj. And there is ellipsis (hadhf) in several places.

(p-١٦)

﴿O you who believe, fear God as He should be feared, and do not die except as Muslims﴾ ﴿And hold fast together to the rope of God, all of you, and do not divide. Remember God's blessing upon you: when you were enemies, He joined your hearts, so by His blessing you became brothers; and you were on the brink of a pit of Fire, and He rescued you from it. Thus God makes clear His signs to you, that you may be guided﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 103] ﴿Let there be among you a community that invites to good, enjoins what is right, and forbids what is wrong. Those are the successful﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 104] ﴿And do not be like those who divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them. For them is a great punishment﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 105] ﴿On the Day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black. As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 106] ﴿As for those whose faces turn white, they will be in God's mercy, therein they will abide forever﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 107] ﴿These are the signs of God, which We recite to you in truth. God does not intend any injustice to the worlds﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 108] ﴿To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to God all matters are returned﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 109] ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind: you enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in God. Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them; among them are believers, but most of them are defiant transgressors﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 110] ﴿They will not harm you except with some annoyance. If they fight you, they will turn their backs to you, then they will not be helped﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 111] ﴿Humiliation is decreed upon them wherever they are found, except with a rope from God and a rope from men. They have earned anger from God, and poverty is decreed upon them. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God and kill the prophets without right. That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 112].

Aṣbaḥa (أصبح): one of the "incomplete" (nāqiṣa) verbs, indicating that the subject is characterized by the attribute at morning time. It may also mean ṣāra (to become), which is likewise incomplete, and it may also be used intransitively (lāzima), as in: aṣbaḥtu, meaning "I entered the morning." One says: aṣbaḥa Zayd, meaning "Zayd stayed in the morning." From this is the saying: "When you hear the night-journey of the smith, know that he is staying up in the morning," i.e., remaining in the morning.

Shafā (شفا) al-shay': its edge and its brink. It is from the weak-radical (dhawāt al-wāw) class, its dual is shafawān, and it is the edge of every precipice that has a drop, such as a pit, a well, a cliff, a roof, or a wall. In usage it is attached to the upper part, as in shafā jurufin (the brink of a precipice), and to the lower part, as in shafā ḥufratin (the brink of a pit). One says: ashfā 'alā kadhā, meaning "he came close to it." From this: ashfā al-marīḍu 'alā al-mawt, "the sick person came close to death." Ya'qūb said: One says of a man at his death, of the moon at its waning, and of the sun at its setting: "Nothing remained of him or of it except shafā," meaning little.

Al-ḥufra: known, and it is the singular of ḥufar; it is a form fi'la in the sense of maf'ūla, like ghurfa (a handful) of water. Anqadha: rescued.

Ibyiḍāḍ (white) and isweddād (black) are well known; one says: bayyaḍa, so he is abyaḍ (white), and sawwada, so he is aswad (black). It is said that they are the origins of colors. Dhāqa al-shay': he tasted it; its original sense is with the mouth, then it was borrowed for everything that is sensed and perceived, by way of comparison with what is known through taste. The Arabs say: "I have tasted the honor of so-and-so, which makes me desire to visit him." They also say: "Taste the difference and know what he has." Tamīm ibn Muqbil said:

"Or like the swaying of a Rudaynī spear, which the hands of merchants have tested, so they increased its shaft in softness."

Another said:

"Indeed God tested the wisdom of Qays *** then when He saw its lightness, He rejected it."

By "taste" they mean knowledge, whether through the senses or otherwise. Thaqiftu al-rajul: I overcame the man and prevailed over him.

﴿O you who believe, fear God as He should be feared﴾. When He warned them against the misguidance of those who wish to mislead them, He commanded them with the comprehensive forms of obedience. He first instilled awe in them by saying "fear God" (ittaqū Allāh), since taqwā (God-consciousness) indicates fear of God's punishment. Then He made it the cause for the command to hold fast to God's religion. Then He followed the awe with hope, which is His saying: ﴿And remember God's blessing upon you﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 103]. He followed the command to fear God and the command to hold fast with another prohibition, which is part of holding fast.

Ibn Mas'ūd, al-Rabī', Qatāda and al-Ḥasan said: "as He should be feared" means that He is obeyed and not disobeyed, remembered and not forgotten, thanked and not denied. This was also narrated as a marfū' report (traced to the Prophet ﷺ). It was said: "as He should be feared" means fearing all of His disobediences.

Qatāda, al-Suddī, Ibn Zayd and al-Rabī' said: this verse is abrogated (mansūkha, naskh) by His saying: ﴿So fear God as much as you are able﴾ [Surah al-Taghābun: 16]. They were first commanded with the utmost degree of taqwā, so that no shortfall would occur in anything, and then it was abrogated. Ibn 'Abbās and Ṭāwūs said: it is definitive (muḥkama, not abrogated).

﴿So fear God as much as you are able﴾ [Surah al-Taghābun: 16] is an explanation of His saying: "Fear God as He should be feared." It was also said: it means that one does not let the blame of the blamer deter him regarding God, and that he upholds justice even against himself, his son, or his father. It was said: a servant does not fear God as He should be feared until he guards his tongue. Ibn 'Abbās said: the meaning is "strive for God as He should be striven for." Al-Mātrīdī said: in the reading of Ḥafṣa (her codex): "Worship God as He should be worshipped."

Tuqāt (تُقاة) here is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and the discussion of it has already preceded in ﴿except that you fear them with some caution﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 28].

Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: It is possible that tuqāt in this verse is the plural of fā'il, although the verb is not conjugated from it, so it would be like rummāt (plural of rāmin, archers) and rāmin (archer); or it is the plural of taqiyy, since fa'īl and fā'il are equivalent. The meaning according to this is: "Fear God as it is fitting that His God-fearing people, those specific to Him, should fear Him; and for this reason they are attributed to God's pronoun." End of his words. This meaning is refuted by this wording, since the apparent sense is that His saying "as He should be feared" (ḥaqqa tuqātihi) is of the type of attributive construction (idāfat al-ṣifa ila mawṣūfihā), as when you say: "I struck Zayd, very severely," meaning "a severe striking." Likewise here: "Fear God with true fear," meaning the fear that is right, that is, obligatory and firm. But if tuqāt is made a plural, the construction becomes like: "Strike Zayd as his strikings are due," and this construction does not indicate the meaning: "Strike Zayd as it is fitting that his striking should be." Rather, even if this construction were stated explicitly, understanding its meaning would require supplying matters by which the meaning becomes sound, and the supplied sense would be: "Strike Zayd a true striking, as it is fitting that the striking of his striking should be." There is no need to burden the expression with what is not its apparent meaning, or to strain toward supposed implications that the apparent wording does not indicate.

﴿And do not die except as Muslims﴾. Its apparent meaning is a prohibition against dying except while clothed in Islam. The meaning is: persist in Islam until death comes to you while you are upon it. A parallel to this is what Sībawayh reported of their saying: "I will not see you here," when what is meant is: "Do not be here, so that I see you." This meaning has already been discussed thoroughly in Surat al-Baqara, in His saying: ﴿Indeed God has chosen for you this religion﴾ [Surah al-Baqara: 132], and so on. The clause "while you are Muslims" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyya), and the exception is a sub-branch of the circumstances. The meaning: "Do not die in any state except the state of Islam." Its coming as a nominal sentence is more emphatic because of the repetition of the pronoun, and for the directness of address within it. Some claimed that the more apparent reading of the sentence is that the state is already present beforehand and continuing. But if it had been said "Muslims" (muslimīn), it would indicate concurrence with death only, neither preceding nor following it.

[p-18] ﴿Hold fast, all of you, to the rope of Allah﴾. That is, cling to it and seek its protection. The "rope of Allah" (ḥabl Allāh) has been interpreted as the covenant, or the Qur'an, or the religion, or obedience, or sincere repentance, or the community (al-jamā'ah), or sincere monotheism (ikhlāṣ al-tawḥīd), or Islam. These are sayings of the early generations (al-salaf), and some of them are close to one another. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Book of Allah is the rope of Allah, stretched from the heaven to the earth." It is also reported from him that he said: "The Qur'an is the firm rope of Allah. Its wonders never cease, and it does not wear out through much repetition. Whoever speaks by it speaks truly, whoever acts by it is guided aright, and whoever holds fast to it is guided to the straight path." The saying "I held fast to the rope of so-and-so" may be figurative (tamthīl), like one who relies on a strong rope held by one who hangs from a high place, trusting that the rope will not break. It may also be a metaphor (isti'ārah), in which the rope is used for the covenant and holding fast is used for trust in the covenant. The word "jamī'an" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in "wa'taṣimū."

﴿And do not be divided﴾. They were forbidden from dividing and differing in the religion, as the Jews and Christians differed. It was also said: they were forbidden from the enmity and hostility they had in the time of ignorance (jāhiliyyah). It was further said: they were forbidden from introducing what necessitates division and that removes unity. This verse has been used by two groups: those who reject analogical reasoning (qiyās) and independent legal reasoning (ijtihād), such as al-Naẓẓām and others of the Shi'ah, and those who affirm qiyās and ijtihād. The first group said: it is not permissible for division and difference to be a religion of Allah, the Exalted, when Allah has forbidden it. The others said: the division that is forbidden is in the fundamentals of the religion and of Islam.

﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you, when you were enemies and He joined your hearts, so that by His favour you became brothers; and you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He saved you from it﴾. The address is to the polytheist Arabs. This was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatādah, meaning those among them who believed, since the strong would prey upon the weak. It was also said that the address is to the Aws and the Khazraj. This is preferred because, at the time this verse was revealed, the Arabs were not united upon Islam nor bound in their hearts by it, whereas the Aws and the Khazraj had come together upon Islam and had been brought together by it after their excessive enmity and the wars that had been between them. Moreover, since He had earlier commanded them to hold fast to the rope of Allah, which is the religion, and forbade them from division, which is a command and a prohibition aimed at the continuance of what they were upon (since they were holding fast and united), He reminded them that what they were upon, of holding fast to the religion of Islam and the joining of hearts, was caused by Allah's bestowing this upon them. For Allah the Exalted created that motivation in their hearts, which necessarily results in the act. Thus He reminded them of the worldly and the otherworldly favour. As for the worldly favour, it is the joining of their hearts and their becoming brothers in Allah, showing mercy to one another, after they had lived in war and fighting for about one hundred and twenty years, until Allah joined them together through Islam. Their two grandfathers, I mean of the Aws and the Khazraj, were full brothers, of the same father and mother. As for the otherworldly favour, it is their rescue from the Fire after they had been on the brink of entering it. He began with mention of the worldly favour first, because it precedes in action and because of its connection with His saying: "and do not be divided." This is similar to: ﴿On the Day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black; as for those whose faces turn black﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 106]. The meaning of "fa-aṣbaḥtum" is "you became." "Aṣbaḥa," as we mentioned in al-Mufradāt (the book on Qur'anic vocabulary), is used to mean that the subject is characterized by its attribute at the time of morning, and it is also used in the sense of "ṣāra" (became), in which case the time of morning is not intended, but only the general transition and becoming from one state to another. On this usage is his saying:

"I have become one who no longer carries a weapon, nor owns the bridle of a camel if it bolts."

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "fa-aṣbaḥtum" is an expression for continuity, even though the word is specific to a certain time. This word was specifically used in this meaning because the morning is the beginning of the day, and in it begins the day's activities. So the state a person considers himself to be in at the start of the day is generally the state in which his day continues. On this is the saying of al-Rabīʿ ibn Ḍabʿ:

"I have become one who no longer carries a weapon, nor owns the bridle of a camel if it bolts."

[p-19] What he mentioned, that "aṣbaḥa" is for continuity, and the reason he gave for it, I do not know of any of the grammarians who held this. They only mentioned that it is used in the two senses I have mentioned. Al-Ḥawfī permitted "idh" to be governed by "udhkurū" (remember). Others permitted it to be governed by "niʿmah" (favour), meaning the bestowal of Allah, and by the element governing "ʿalaykum." They permitted "ʿalaykum" to be a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of "niʿmah," and they also permitted "ʿalaykum" to be connected to "niʿmah." They permitted "aṣbaḥtum" to be a defective verb (nāqiṣah) with the predicate being "bi-niʿmatihi," with the "bāʾ" being adverbial of time, and "ikhwānan" being a circumstantial state governed by "aṣbaḥa" or by what the prepositional phrase depends upon. They also permitted "ikhwānan" to be the predicate of "aṣbaḥa," with the prepositional phrase being a circumstantial state governed by "aṣbaḥa," or a circumstantial state of "ikhwānan," since it is a qualifier of it that preceded it, or the governing element being what is in it of the meaning of "taʾākhaytum bi-niʿmatihi" (you became brothers through His favour). They also permitted "aṣbaḥtum" to be a complete verb (tāmmah), with "bi-niʿmatihi" connected to it, or in the position of a circumstantial state of the subject of "aṣbaḥtum" or of "ikhwānan," with "ikhwānan" as a circumstantial state. What appears correct is that "aṣbaḥa" is defective, "ikhwānan" is the predicate, "bi-niʿmatihi" is connected to "aṣbaḥtum," and the "bāʾ" is causal, not adverbial of time.

Some people said: the brother in religion is pluralized as "ikhwān," and the brother by lineage as "ikhwah." This is how their usage became common. In the Book of Allah the Exalted: ﴿The believers are only brothers﴾ [al-Ḥujurāt: 10]. The correct view is that both terms are used for lineage and for religion. Sibawayh did not accept that the plural of "akh" is "ikhwah," rather for him "ikhwah" is a collective noun (ism jamʿ), because the pattern "fiʿālan" is pluralized as "fiʿlah." Ibn al-Sarrāj held that "fiʿlah," when it conveys plurality, is a collective noun, because "fiʿlah" is not regularly used as a plural of anything.

The pronoun in "minhā" refers to the Fire, which is the nearest antecedent, or it refers to the pit. Al-Ṭabarī related that some people said it refers to the brink (shafā), and the feminine "min" is used because the brink is attached to a feminine noun, as Jarīr said:

"I see that the passing years have taken from me as the waning has taken from the crescent."

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: The matter is not as they mentioned, because there is no need in the verse for this grammatical treatment, unless there were no antecedent for the pronoun except the brink. Here we have a feminine noun with which the pronoun agrees, and the meaning under discussion supports it, so there is no need for that grammatical explanation. End of quotation. I say: it is not good for the pronoun to refer to anything but the brink, because their standing on the brink is one of the two parts of the predication (isnād), so the pronoun can only refer to it. As for the mention of the pit, it came only as an annexation to it. Do you not see that if you say: "Zayd was the servant of Jaʿfar," Jaʿfar is not the one spoken about, and is not one of the two parts of the predication? Likewise, if you say: "Zayd struck the servant of Hind," you have not said anything about Hind, but you have mentioned Hind only to specify the one spoken about. As for the mention of the Fire, it was brought only to specify the pit, and it is not one of the two parts of the predication, nor is it the one spoken about. Furthermore, rescue from the brink is more eloquent than rescue from the pit and from the Fire, because rescue from the brink necessarily entails rescue from the pit and from the Fire, while rescue from those two does not necessarily entail rescue from the brink. Therefore, referring the pronoun to the brink is the apparent meaning both in wording and in sense. Their life, after which falling into the Fire is expected, was depicted as sitting on the edge of its precipice, being about to fall into it. It was also said: Allah, the Exalted, likened their disbelief, in which they were, and their war against Medina, to the brink of death, because they were constantly falling into Hell, and Allah rescued them through Islam. al-Suddī said: "through Muḥammad (ﷺ)." A Bedouin said to Ibn ʿAbbās while he was explaining this verse: "By Allah, He did not rescue them from it, but He wants to throw them into it!" Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Take it from one who is not a jurist." The commentators also mentioned here the story of the beginning of the Anṣār's Islam, and what had been between them after Islam, and the removal of that by the blessings of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿Thus Allah makes His signs clear to you, that you may be guided﴾. The discussion of a similar sentence has already preceded, except that the end of this one is concluded with guidance, in keeping with what came before it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "﴿that you may be guided﴾" means the intention that you may increase in guidance. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: His saying "that you may be guided" concerns humankind, that is, whoever among you reflects upon the situation hoping to be guided. So al-Zamakhsharī made the expression of hope a metaphor for Allah's will to increase guidance, while Ibn ʿAṭiyyah kept the expression of hope on its literal meaning, but he made it with reference to humans, not to Allah the Exalted, since hope is impossible for Allah the Exalted. In both views there is metaphor. In al-Zamakhsharī's view it is because he made the expression of hope mean Allah's will, and in Ibn ʿAṭiyyah's view it is because he attributed to humans what apparently is attributed to Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 104–105:

﴿Let there be among you a community who call to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. It is they who are the successful.﴾ The command is directed at those to whom the address is addressed. It has been said: they are the Aws and the Khazraj, as the majority (al-Jumhur) has reported. His command to them to do this is a command to all the believers and to those who follow them until the Day of Resurrection. It is therefore a specific address that is intended in a general sense. It is also possible that the address is general, so that the Aws and the Khazraj are included within it. The apparent meaning of His words "from among you" (minkum) indicates partiality (al-tab'id), as said by al-Dahhak and al-Tabari, because calling to good, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong are only suitable for one who knows what is right and what is wrong. How could he arrange the command in its establishment, and how could he carry it out? For the ignorant person may enjoin what is wrong and forbid what is right, and perhaps he knows a ruling in his own school of law that contradicts the school of another, so he forbids what is not wrong and enjoins what is not right, and he may be harsh in places where gentleness is required, and vice versa. Accordingly, "min" is partitive, and the command applies to a part of the community, namely those who are fit for it. Al-Zajjaj held that "min" is for explaining the genus (li-bayan al-jins), and he brought, according to his claim, parallels from the Qur'an and the speech of the Arabs. In that case the command applies to the whole community, who would call the entire world to good: the disbelievers to Islam and the disobedient to obedience. The apparent sense of this command is obligation (al-far'iyya), and the majority hold that it is a communal obligation (fard kifaya), so that when some of them perform it, it is dropped from the rest. A group of scholars held that it is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn), so that it becomes incumbent upon every Muslim to enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong whenever he is able and has the capacity for it. They differed concerning what removes the obligation. Some people said: fear for one's own soul; anything other than that does not remove it. Others said: if beating, imprisonment, or humiliation is certain, the obligation falls from him and he moves to the recommended (al-nadb) level, and the commanding and forbidding become optional. Although these two (enjoining and forbidding) are stated in absolute terms in the Qur'an, they have been restricted by the Sunnah through his saying (ﷺ): "Whoever among you sees a wrong, let him change it with his hand; if he cannot, then with his tongue; if he cannot, then with his heart, and that is the weakest of faith." No scholar of this community, neither among its predecessors nor its successors, has denied the obligation of this, except the most stupid of the Hashawiyya and the ignorant of the people of hadith. For they denied the action of the rebellious faction, and the enjoining of what is right and the forbidding of what is wrong by the sword, despite what they heard of His words, exalted is He: ﴿So fight the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of Allah﴾ [49:9]. They claimed that the ruler may not be censured for injustice, oppression, and killing a soul that Allah has forbidden; rather, censure is only directed at others than the ruler, by speech or by hand without weapons. Abu Bakr al-Razi, in his Ahkam, mentioned an extensive section on enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, in which he stated that the blood of the owners of taxes and tolls (al-darā'ib wa al-mukus) is permitted, that it is obligatory for the Muslims to kill them, and that each one of the people may kill whoever of them he is able to, without giving him warning or prior notice in words.

"Calling to good" (yad'una ila al-khayr): it is Islam. This was said by Muqatil; or it is acting in obedience to Allah, said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi; or it is jihad and Islam. The majority read "wal-takun" with a sunna-vowel on the lam (sukun). Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and Abu Haywa read it with a kasra, and the reason for its being built on the kasra is mentioned in grammar (al-nahw). They permitted, for "wal-takun", that it be a complete verb (tamma), in which case "minkum" is related to it, or to an omitted word on the basis that it is a circumstantial phrase (hal), since if it were postponed it would be an attribute of "ummah". And that it be a incomplete verb (naqisa), with "yad'una" as its predicate, and "min" is related on the two previously mentioned aspects. They also permitted that "minkum" be the predicate and "yad'una" be an attribute. The locus of the benefit (mahat al-fa'ida) is only in "yad'una", for it is the predicate.

Some of them interpreted "what is right" as monotheism (tawhid) and "what is wrong" as disbelief (kufr). There is no doubt that monotheism is the head of what is right, and disbelief is the head of what is wrong. However, the apparent sense is generality, covering every right that is commanded in the Shari'a and every wrong that is forbidden in the Shari'a. The exegetes mentioned hadiths related about the virtue of one who enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong, and about the sin of one who abandons that, and reports from the Companions and others concerning that. And (they discussed) the path to the obligation: is hearing alone sufficient, as Abu Hashim held, or hearing and reason, as his father Abu 'Ali held? This is according to the opinions of the Mu'tazila. As for the conditions of forbidding and obligation, who carries it out, the manner of carrying it out, and whether one forbids what he himself commits, the verse does not address any of that, and the subject of all of this is the science of jurisprudence (fiqh).

In it there is an allusion to the harm that afflicts the one who enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and be patient over what afflicts you﴾ [31:17].

﴿And it is they who are the successful﴾ [2:5]. The discussion of this sentence has preceded at the beginning of al-Baqara. It is a great glad tiding and a generous promise to those who possess the qualities mentioned before this sentence.

This and the verse before it are like an explanation of His words: ﴿And hold fast together to the rope of Allah, all of you, and do not separate﴾ [3:103]. So He explained holding fast to the rope of Allah by His words: ﴿Let there be among you a community﴾, especially according to the view of al-Zajjaj. And He explained ﴿and do not separate﴾ [3:103] by His words: ﴿And do not be like those who separated﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the earlier nations who split in religion. al-Hasan said: they are the Jews and the Christians, who differed and became sects. Qatada said: they are the people of innovations (ahl al-bid'a) from this community. al-Zamakhshari added: and they are the anthropomorphists (al-mushabbiha), the determinists (al-mujabbira), the Hashawiyya, and their likes. Abu Umama said: they are the Harurites (al-Haruriyya), and a hadith has been related concerning that. One of our contemporaries said: there is something to consider in the words of Qatada and Abu Umama, for the innovators of this community and the Harurites did not exist until a time after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ). How would Allah forbid the believers to be like a people whose division and innovations did not appear until after the cessation of revelation and the death of the Prophet (ﷺ)? For you do not forbid Zayd from being like 'Amr except after a prior disliked act has taken place from 'Amr, and there is no meaning for their two statements except that "they separated and differed" is in the past tense meaning the future, so the meaning would be: "And do not be like those who separate and differ." Then this would be among the miracles of the Qur'an, and its informing of what had not yet happened and then happened. End of his speech.

The "clear proofs" (al-bayyinat), according to the words of Ibn 'Abbas, are the signs of Allah that were sent down to the people of every religion. According to al-Hasan, it is the Torah. According to Qatada and Abu Umama, it is the Qur'an.

﴿On a day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black﴾ [3:106]. The majority hold that the whitening and blackening of the faces are according to the literal colour. White is from light, and black from darkness. al-Zamakhshari said: whoever is among the people of the light of religion is marked by whiteness of colour, its brightness and radiance, and his record turns white and radiant, and the light runs before him and on his right. "For the miser, over his wealth, are excuses: blue-eyed, and upon them are faces black."

"And a white one, the clouds are sought through his face."

Imru' al-Qays said:

"And their faces, at the assemblies, are bright."

Zuhayr said:

"And a white, bountiful one, whose hands are a cloud."

It was also said: the faces of the People of the Sunna and the faces of the People of Innovation. 'Ata' said: the faces of the sincere and the faces of the hypocrites. It was said: the faces of the believers and the faces of the People of the Book and the hypocrites. It was said: the faces of the fighters in jihad and the faces of those who fled from the battle line. His command to them to do this is a command to all the believers and to those who follow them until the Day of Resurrection. It is therefore a specific address that is intended in a general sense. It is also possible that the address is general, so that the Aws and the Khazraj are included within it. The apparent meaning of His words "from among you" (minkum) indicates partiality (al-tab'id), as said by al-Dahhak and al-Tabari, because calling to good, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong are only suitable for one who knows what is right and what is wrong. How could he arrange the command in its establishment, and how could he carry it out? For the ignorant person may enjoin what is wrong and forbid what is right, and perhaps he knows a ruling in his own school of law that contradicts the school of another, so he forbids what is not wrong and enjoins what is not right, and he may be harsh in places where gentleness is required, and vice versa. Accordingly, "min" is partitive, and the command applies to a part of the community, namely those who are fit for it. Al-Zajjaj held that "min" is for explaining the genus (li-bayan al-jins), and he brought, according to his claim, parallels from the Qur'an and the speech of the Arabs.
