﴿فَأمّا الَّذِينَ اسْوَدَّتْ وُجُوهُهم أكَفَرْتُمْ بَعْدَ إيمانِكم فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾ ﴿As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your faith? Then taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve."﴾ This is a detailed division of the rulings concerning those whose faces become white and those whose faces become black. The description of those whose faces turned black is given first, for the sake of emphasis on warning against their condition, and because of its proximity to His saying: ﴿وتَسْوَدُّ وُجُوهٌ﴾ (and faces will turn black). It also begins with the believers and ends with their ruling, so the opening and closing of the speech are both something that gladdens the soul and expands the breast. The discussion of ﴿أمّا﴾ (amma, a conditional particle) has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqarah, and that it is a conditional particle which requires a response. For this reason the fa' (فاء) entered the predicate after the subject (mubtada', the subject of a nominal sentence), and the predicate here is omitted because it is known. The estimate is: "Then it will be said to them: 'Did you disbelieve?'" just as the saying (qawl) is omitted in many places, such as His saying: ﴿والمَلائِكَةُ يَدْخُلُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ مِن كُلِّ بابٍ﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 23] ﴿سَلامٌ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 24], meaning: they say, "Peace be upon you." When the predicate is omitted, the fa' is omitted too, although its omission outside this context occurs only in poetry, such as the saying:

؎As for fighting, there is no fighting among you, but rather a march through the broad ranks of the processions.

He means: "then there is no fighting." The Shaykh Kamal al-Din Abd al-Wahid ibn Abd Allah ibn Khalaf al-Ansari said in his book titled "Nihayat al-Ta'mil fi Asrar al-Tanzil" (The End of Interpretation in the Secrets of the Revelation): "An objection has been raised against the grammarians in their saying, regarding what has been omitted, 'It is said,' that the fa' has been omitted, by His saying: ﴿وأمّا الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا أفَلَمْ تَكُنْ آياتِي تُتْلى عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 31] (And as for those who disbelieved: 'Were not My verses recited to you?'). Its estimate is: 'Then it will be said to them: Were not My verses recited to you?' So 'then it will be said' has been omitted, but the fa' was not omitted. When this has been refuted, it is necessarily the case that the response is: ﴿فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾ (then taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve), and so this falls as a response to it, and to His saying: 'Did you disbelieve?'. It is part of the Arabic style that when they mention a particle which requires a response, they dispense with its response until they mention another particle which requires a response, and then they make one response for both, as in His saying: ﴿فَإمّا يَأْتِيَنَّكم مِنِّي هُدًى فَمَن تَبِعَ هُدايَ فَلا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ ولا هم يَحْزَنُونَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38] (If guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance, no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve). So His saying: ﴿فَلا خَوْفَ عَلَيْهِمْ ولا هم يَحْزَنُونَ﴾ (no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve) is the response to both conditions. And ﴿أفَلَمْ﴾ (Then did not...) is not the response to ﴿أمّا﴾; rather the fa' is conjunctive upon an estimated element, and the estimate is: (p-24) 'Did I neglect you, so that I did not recite My verses to you?'" End of what was quoted from this man, and it is the words of a man of letters, not of a grammarian. ؎People die, or their youth grows old, and the young one grows up.

He means: "and the young one grows up." And the saying of another:

؎When he sought with a great hand, its wrong was done, so I left its upper skin swinging.

He means: "I left." And Zuhayr said:

When He mentioned the punishment, He gave its cause as their deed, but here He did not specify the cause of their being in mercy. Abu al-Jawza' and Ibn Ya'mur read: "فَأمّا الَّذِينَ اسْوادَّتْ" and "وأمّا الَّذِينَ ابْياضَّتْ" with an alif. The origin of "if'alla" is "if'alala," which is shown by "uswaddat" and "ihmarrat." It occurs for a color or a sensory defect, like "aswad" (black), "a'waj" (crooked), and "a'waz" (in need). It does not occur from a geminate root, like "ahamm," nor from a defective final-radical root, like "alma," nor for the reflexive (mutawa'ah). The response to "أمّا" is "fa-fi al-jannah" (then in Paradise), and the prepositional phrase is the predicate of the subject, meaning: then they are settled in Paradise. ؎As for fighting, there is no fighting among you, but rather a march through the broad ranks of the processions.

He means: "then there is no fighting." I say: it is in the position of a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), as if it was said: "How will they be therein?" So it was said: "They abide therein forever, they will not depart from it nor die." End. And it is good. It was also said: the response to "أمّا" is "fa-fi al-jannah," and "هم فِيها خالِدُونَ" (they abide therein forever) is a subject and predicate. And "khalidun" is the governing element for both adverbial phrases, and it was repeated for emphasis, because of what it indicates of the call and the arousing of desire toward the enduring bliss.

﴿فَأمّا الَّذِينَ اسْوَدَّتْ وُجُوهُهم أكَفَرْتُمْ بَعْدَ إيمانِكم فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾ ﴿As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your faith? Then taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve."﴾ This is a detailed division of the rulings concerning those whose faces become white and those whose faces become black. The description of those whose faces turned black is given first, for the sake of emphasis on warning against their condition, and because of its proximity to His saying: ﴿وتَسْوَدُّ وُجُوهٌ﴾ (and faces will turn black). It also begins with the believers and ends with their ruling, so the opening and closing of the speech are both something that gladdens the soul and expands the breast. The discussion of ﴿أمّا﴾ (amma, a conditional particle) has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqarah, and that it is a conditional particle which requires a response. For this reason the fa' (فاء) entered the predicate after the subject (mubtada', the subject of a nominal sentence), and the predicate here is omitted because it is known. The estimate is: "Then it will be said to them: 'Did you disbelieve?'" just as the saying (qawl) is omitted in many places, such as His saying: ﴿والمَلائِكَةُ يَدْخُلُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ مِن كُلِّ بابٍ﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 23] ﴿سَلامٌ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 24], meaning: they say, "Peace be upon you." When the predicate is omitted, the fa' is omitted too, although its omission outside this context occurs only in poetry, such as the saying:

؎As for fighting, there is no fighting among you, but rather a march through the broad ranks of the processions.

He means: "then there is no fighting." The Shaykh Kamal al-Din Abd al-Wahid ibn Abd Allah ibn Khalaf al-Ansari said in his book titled "Nihayat al-Ta'mil fi Asrar al-Tanzil" (The End of Interpretation in the Secrets of the Revelation): "An objection has been raised against the grammarians in their saying, regarding what has been omitted, 'It is said,' that the fa' has been omitted, by His saying: ﴿وأمّا الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا أفَلَمْ تَكُنْ آياتِي تُتْلى عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 31] (And as for those who disbelieved: 'Were not My verses recited to you?'). Its estimate is: 'Then it will be said to them: Were not My verses recited to you?' So 'then it will be said' has been omitted, but the fa' was not omitted. When this has been refuted, it is necessarily the case that the response is: ﴿فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ بِما كُنْتُمْ تَكْفُرُونَ﴾ (then taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve), and so this falls as a response to it, and to His saying: 'Did you disbelieve?'. It is part of the Arabic style that when they mention a particle which requires a response, they dispense with its response until they mention another particle which requires a response, and then they make one response for both, as in His saying: ﴿فَإمّا يَأْتِيَنَّكم مِنِّي هُدًى فَمَن تَبِعَ هُدايَ فَلا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ ولا هم يَحْزَنُونَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38] (If guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance, no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve). So His saying: ﴿فَلا خَوْفَ عَلَيْهِمْ ولا هم يَحْزَنُونَ﴾ (no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve) is the response to both conditions. And ﴿أفَلَمْ﴾ (Then did not...) is not the response to ﴿أمّا﴾; rather the fa' is conjunctive upon an estimated element, and the estimate is: (p-24) 'Did I neglect you, so that I did not recite My verses to you?'" End of what was quoted from this man, and it is the words of a man of letters, not of a grammarian. As for his saying, "An objection has been raised against the grammarians," it suffices to refute this objection that it is an objection against all grammarians, for there is no grammarian who did not interpret the verse as having an omitted element, so that it is said to them: "Did you disbelieve?" They said: this is the very meaning of the discourse (fahwa al-khitab), which is that there is something estimated in the speech without which the meaning is not complete. Therefore, holding otherwise contradicts the consensus (ijma', the agreement of scholars), so there is no regard for it. As for what he raised as an objection, from His saying: ﴿وأمّا الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا أفَلَمْ تَكُنْ آياتِي﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 31] and that they estimated it as "Then it will be said to them: Were not My verses...", so "then it will be said" was omitted but the fa' was not omitted, which shows the invalidity of this estimate, this is not correct. Rather, this fa' that comes after the interrogative hamza in "أفَلَمْ" is not the fa' of "then it will be said," which is the response to ﴿أمّا﴾, such that one could say: "'then it will be said' was omitted and the fa' remained." Rather, the fa' which is the response to ﴿أمّا﴾ is the one, and "it will be said" after it is omitted. The fa' of "أفَلَمْ" may have two possible readings. One of them is that it is superfluous (za'idah). The grammarians have cited, as evidence for the superfluity of the fa', the saying of the poet:

؎People die, or their youth grows old, and the young one grows up.

He means: "and the young one grows up." And the saying of another:

؎When he sought with a great hand, its wrong was done, so I left its upper skin swinging.

He means: "I left." And Zuhayr said:

؎I see myself, when I spend the night, spending it in desire, then when I rise in the morning, I rise departing.

He means: "then when." And the saying of al-Akhfash: "They claim that they say 'akhuka fa-wujida' (your brother, so he was found)," meaning "akhuka wujida" (your brother was found). The second reading, or the mistaken one: its deliberate form. "With the mistakes, an arrow strikes true" is said of one who makes many errors but sometimes hits the mark. And "khata'at al-qidr bi-zabadiha" (the pot erred with its foam) is like something omitted being construed as a circumstantial state (hal), since if it were postponed it would be an attribute of "ummah" (a community). And it may be that the fa' is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), and the discourse has already mentioned what distresses them: "Then did not My verses...", and then attention was given to the interrogative hamza, so it preceded the explanatory fa', just as it precedes the fa' which indicates sequence, as in His saying: ﴿أفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا في الأرْضِ﴾ [Yusuf: 109] (Have they not traveled in the land?). This is according to the view of those who affirm that the fa' may be explanatory, as in: "Zayd performed ablution, so he washed his face and his hands..." up to the end of the acts of ablution. So the fa' here is not sequential, but explanatory of the ablution. Likewise in ﴿أفَلَمْ تَكُنْ آياتِي تُتْلى عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 31] it explains the saying that distresses them. As for this man's saying, "When this has been refuted," meaning: that the response is "taste" (fa-dhuqu), i.e., the invalidity of omitting what the grammarians estimated, "Then it will be said to them," is established because of the presence of this fa' in "Did not...", and we have already made clear that this estimate has not been refuted, and that it is equal in both verses. Since that is so, the response to ﴿أمّا﴾ is "then it will be said" in both places, and the meaning of the speech is upon it. As for his estimate: "Did I neglect you, so My verses were not...", this is a Zamakhsharian tendency, because al-Zamakhshari estimates between the interrogative hamza and the fa' a verb to which what follows can be conjoined, and it is not believed that the fa', the waw, and thumma, when the hamza enters upon them, originally precede the hamza; rather, attention is given to the interrogative, so it precedes the conjunctive particles, as Sibawayh and others among the grammarians hold. Al-Zamakhshari eventually returned to the view of the majority on this matter, and the invalidity of his first statement is mentioned in grammar. And his view on this has been mentioned earlier in this book. According to this man's estimate, "Did I neglect you?", it is necessary to posit an implied saying and estimate it, so that it is said: "Did I neglect you?", because this estimated element is the predicate of the subject, and the fa' is the response of ﴿أمّا﴾. This is what the speech indicates and what it necessarily requires. As for this man's saying: "So that became a response to it and to His saying: 'Did you disbelieve?'", meaning that "﴿فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ﴾ (taste the punishment)" is a response to ﴿أمّا﴾ and to "Did you disbelieve?", the interrogative here has no response; it is only an interrogative in the manner of rebuke and contempt toward them. As for this man's saying: "And from the arrangement of the Arabs..." to the end, the speech of the Arabs is not as he claims. Rather (p-25) for every response a response is made, and if it is not apparent it is estimated, and they do not make one response for two. As for his claim about His saying: ﴿فَإمّا يَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38] and the verse, and his assertion that His saying ﴿فَلا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38] is a response to both conditions, this is a view transmitted from al-Kisa'i. Some people have held that the response to the first condition is omitted, its estimate being: "then follow it." The correct view is that the second condition and its response are the response to the first condition. These three views were mentioned earlier at the discussion of His saying: ﴿فَإمّا يَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38] and the verse. The hamza in (أكَفَرْتُمْ) (Did you disbelieve?) is for affirmation (taqrir), rebuke, and expressing wonder at their condition. The address in "Did you disbelieve?" and what follows branches off from the disagreement concerning those whose faces turned black. If they are the disbelievers, the estimate is: "after you believed, when the covenant was taken from you while you were in the loins of Adam like atoms," and if they are the people of innovation (ahl al-bida'), then the innovation is that which removes one from faith. If they are the Qurayzah and al-Nadir, then their faith in him was before his mission and their disbelief in him after it, or their faith in the Torah and what came in it about his prophethood, his description, and the command to follow him. If they are the hypocrites, then the intended disbelief is the disbelief of their hearts, and the intended faith is faith of the tongue. If they are the Harurites or the apostates, then faith had truly occurred from them (p-26). In His saying "(Did you disbelieve?)" they said: this is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab), which is one of the types of iltifat (shift in grammatical person), because His saying "As for those whose faces turned black" is third-person absence, and "Did you disbelieve?" is second-person direct address. "بِما كُنْتُمْ" — the ba' is causal (sababiyyah) and ma is verbal-noun (masdariyyah).

﴿وأمّا الَّذِينَ ابْيَضَّتْ وُجُوهُهم فَفي رَحْمَةِ اللَّهِ هم فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ﴿And as for those whose faces turn white, they are in the mercy of Allah; therein they will abide forever.﴾ Note the difference between the two divisions. There, those whose faces turned black were combined between reproach by speech and punishment, while here He made them settled in mercy, so mercy is a receptacle for them and it encompasses them. When He informed that they are settled in the mercy of Allah, He made clear that this settlement is by way of eternity, without cessation or removal, and by the word "mercy" He pointed to His prior care for them, and that the servant, however much his obedience increases, does not enter Paradise except by the mercy of Allah the Exalted. Ibn Abbas said: what is meant by "mercy" here is Paradise. He mentioned eternity for the believer and did not mention it for the disbeliever, to indicate that the aspect of mercy is predominant. He attributed "mercy" here to Himself, and did not attribute the punishment to Himself; rather He said: ﴿فَذُوقُوا العَذابَ﴾ (taste the punishment). When He mentioned the punishment, He gave its cause as their deed, but here He did not specify the cause of their being in mercy. Abu al-Jawza' and Ibn Ya'mur read: "فَأمّا الَّذِينَ اسْوادَّتْ" and "وأمّا الَّذِينَ ابْياضَّتْ" with an alif. The origin of "if'alla" is "if'alala," which is shown by "uswaddat" and "ihmarrat." It occurs for a color or a sensory defect, like "aswad" (black), "a'waj" (crooked), and "a'waz" (in need). It does not occur from a geminate root, like "ahamm," nor from a defective final-radical root, like "alma," nor for the reflexive (mutawa'ah). Exceptions occur, such as "inqadda al-ha'it" (the wall collapsed), "ibharra al-layl" (the night became dark), "ish'arra al-rajul" (the man's hair parted), and the anomalous "irʿawa," since it is defective in its final radical, without color or defect, reflexive to "ra'awtuhu" in the sense of "kaffatuhu" (I restrained him). As for the insertion of the alif: most often it is intended to indicate that the meaning is incidental when it is brought in, and that it is permanent when it is not. The reverse may also occur. From the intention of permanence with the alif's presence is His saying: ﴿مُدْهامَّتانِ﴾ [al-Rahman: 64] (dark green). From the intention of incidental meaning without the alif is His saying: "tazawwara 'an kahfihim" (turning away from their cave), "wa-hmarra khajalan" (he reddened with shame). The response to "أمّا" is "fa-fi al-jannah" (then in Paradise), and the prepositional phrase is the predicate of the subject, meaning: then they are settled in Paradise. "وهم فِيها خالِدُونَ" (And they therein abide forever) is an independent nominal sentence, of a subject and predicate, which has not entered the scope of ﴿أمّا﴾, nor into the grammatical analysis of what follows it. It indicates that this settlement is by way of eternity. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say, what is the position of His saying: '﴿هم فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 39]' after His saying: 'fa-fi rahmat Allah'?" I say: it is in the position of a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), as if it was said: "How will they be therein?" So it was said: "They abide therein forever, they will not depart from it nor die." End. And it is good. It was also said: the response to "أمّا" is "fa-fi al-jannah," and "هم فِيها خالِدُونَ" (they abide therein forever) is a subject and predicate. And "khalidun" is the governing element for both adverbial phrases, and it was repeated for emphasis, because of what it indicates of the call and the arousing of desire toward the enduring bliss.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 109:

﴿Those are the verses of God, which We recite to you in truth; and God does not desire injustice toward the worlds.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 108] The demonstrative "those" (tilka) is said to refer to the entire Qur'an. It is also said to refer to the verses revealed about the Aws and the Khazraj and the Jews who plotted against them, and to the admonition to avoid division. God revealed to the believers the state of those people and the state of their enemies through His words: ﴿On the day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 106]. It is also said that "those" means "these," and that once the events had passed they seemed distant. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Those are the verses of God that came concerning promise and threat," and Ibn 'Atiyya said the same. He said: "The demonstrative 'those' refers to these preceding verses, which include the punishment of the disbelievers and the blessing of the believers."

The majority of readers recited "natluwuha" (We recite it) with the nun, as a shift (iltifat, a sudden change of grammatical person) because attributing the recitation to the Majestic Himself carries grandeur and honour. Abu Nahik recited it with the ya' (yatluwuha, He recites it). The better view is that in this reading the implied subject of "yatluwuha" refers to God, so that the pronoun is unified, and there is no iltifat in it, because it is a third-person pronoun referring back to a third-person noun. The meaning of recitation (tilawa) is reading one thing after another. Attributing it to God is a metaphor, since the actual reciter is Gabriel, and when He commanded him to recite, it was as though He Himself were the reciter. It is also said that "yatluwuha" may mean "He sends it down successively, one thing after another." For Abu Nahik's reading, they allowed the subject pronoun to refer to Gabriel, even though he has not been mentioned, since he is known.

"Bi-l-haqq" means "with true reports." It is also said the meaning is: containing deeds which are themselves true, such as the honouring of one people and the punishment of (p-27) others. "Tilka" is the subject and "ayatu Allah" its predicate, and "natluwuha" is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya). They said the governing element in it is the demonstrative. They also allowed that "ayatu Allah" could be an apposition, with "natluwuha" as the predicate. Al-Zajjaj said: "There is an omission in the sentence; its estimated form is: 'Those are the verses of the Qur'an mentioned, the proofs and evidences of God.'" End of quotation. According to this estimate, the predicate of the subject is omitted, because by this estimate the meaning of the verse is complete. There is no need to posit this omitted element, since the sentence is self-sufficient and complete in itself. The "ba'" in "bi-l-haqq" is the ba' of accompaniment, so it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the object, meaning: "accompanied by truth." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Accompanied by truth and justice, in the recompense of the good-doer and the wrongdoer according to what each deserves." End of quotation. In his words "according to what each deserves" he inserted a Mu'tazili insinuation (a rationalist Mu'tazili doctrine). Then God informed that He does not desire injustice, and if He does not desire it, it does not come from Him to anyone. Therefore what came from Him of blessing one people and punishing two others is not of the category of injustice, and injustice is placing a thing in other than its proper place. Abu Dharr narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said, relating from his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, that He said: "O My servants, I have forbidden injustice to Myself and made it forbidden among you, so do not wrong one another." It is also in the sound hadith that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God does not wrong a believer. A good deed is given to him in this world and rewarded for it in the Hereafter. As for the disbeliever, he is fed with his good deeds in this world for what he did for God; when he reaches the Hereafter, he has no good deed for which he is rewarded." It is also said the meaning is: He does not increase the evil-doer's evil nor reduce the good-doer's good, and in this is an indication that blackening faces is justice. End of quotation.

"Lil-'alamin" occupies the position of the object of the verbal noun "zulm" (injustice), and the subject is omitted together with the verbal noun. The estimate is: "its injustice," and the returning pronoun is the pronoun of God, Exalted. That is: God does not desire to wrong any of the worlds. He made "zulman" indefinite because it is in a negative context, so it is general. It is also said the meaning is that God does not desire that the worlds wrong one another. The wording rejects this meaning, since if this meaning were intended, "min" (from) would have been more appropriate for it, and the construction would have been: "wa-ma Allahu yuridu zulman min al-'alamin" (God does not desire injustice from the worlds). Al-Zamakhshari said: "And God does not desire injustice, so that He would seize anyone without guilt, or increase the punishment of a sinner, or diminish the reward of a good-doer." Then he said: "Glory be to Him who forbears toward one who describes Him as desiring abominations and being content with them." End of his words, following his Mu'tazili doctrine. We say to him: "Glory be to Him who forbears toward one who describes Him as having in His dominion what He does not desire, and that the will of the servant overcomes the will of the Lord. Exalted is God above that."

﴿To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to God all matters are returned﴾. When He mentioned the states of the disbelievers and the believers, and that He specially favours the deeds of one who believes, so He shows mercy to them by it, and specially punishes the deeds of one who disbelieves, so He punishes them, He drew attention to the fact that this disposition is in what He owns, so there is no objection to Him, Exalted. The verse indicates the vastness of His dominion, and that the return of all matters is to Him. So He is free from injustice, because injustice occurs only in what is specific to the unjust person in contrast to Him. The explanation of these two sentences has already preceded, so repeating it is unnecessary.

They said: These verses include antithesis (tibaq) in: "(tabyaddu) (and tasawwadd)," in "iswaddat" and "ibyadda," in "akafartum ba'da iymanikum" (did you disbelieve after your belief), and in "bi-l-haqq" and "zulman." They include detailed explanation (tafsil) in "fa-amma" and "amma." They include paronomasia of the perfect kind (tajnis tamthil) in "akafartum" and "takfurun." They include emphasis of the explicit noun by the pronoun in "fa-fi rahmati Allahi hum fiha khalidun" (so in God's mercy they abide therein forever). They include repetition in the word "Allah," and its embellishment is that it occurs in sentences of differing meanings. It is known in the language of the Arabs that when sentences differ, they repeat the explicit noun, not the pronoun, because mentioning it indicates the magnification and exaltation of the matter. This is not like the verse:

*I do not see death overtaking death by anything*

since that is a single sentence. Yet the explicit noun may sometimes be used in a single sentence deliberately for magnification. They also include the demonstrative in His words "tilka," the shift of address (talwin al-khitab) in: ﴿As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 106], the simile and the figurative image in: ﴿tabyaddu﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 106] ﴿wa-tasawwaddu﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 106], when that is an expression of radiance and gloom. And they include omission (hadhf) in several places.

(p-28) **"You are the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, and believing in God."** Ikrimah and Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfah, and Mu'adh ibn Jabal. Some of the Jews had said to them: "Our religion is better than what you call us to, and we are better and more excellent." It was also said: it was revealed concerning the Muhajirun (the Emigrants).

What appears to be the case is that it is part of the completion of the first address, in His words: ﴿O you who believe, fear God﴾ (3:102). After this, the addresses to the believers continued with commands and prohibitions. He had digressed from that to mention those whose faces turn white and those whose faces turn black, and some of their conditions in the Hereafter, then returned to the first address. So He said, Exalted is He: ﴿You are the best nation﴾, urging by this information toward submission and obedience.

Apparently the address is directed to those to whom it was first addressed, namely the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Thus the word "nation" (ummah) refers to a specific nation, namely the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the Companions are its best.

Al-Hasan, Mujahid and a group said: the address is to the entire Ummah, that they are the best of nations. This interpretation is supported by their being ﴿witnesses over mankind﴾ (2:143), and by the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "We are the last and the foremost," the hadith. And by his saying (ﷺ): "We will complete seventy nations on the Day of Resurrection; we are the last of them and the best of them."

The apparent function of kana here is that of the incomplete (naqisah) copular verb ("was"), and ﴿the best nation﴾ is its predicate (khabar). It is not intended here to indicate the passing of time and the cessation of the attribution, as in your saying: "Zayd was standing." Rather, the intent is the continuance of the attribution, as in His words: ﴿God is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾ (4:96), and ﴿Do not approach fornication; indeed it is an abomination and an evil way﴾ (17:32).

That kana indicates continuance and that its synonym lam yazal ("has not ceased") is a weak opinion. Rather, the more correct view is that it, like the other verbs, indicates cessation, though it is sometimes used where cessation is not intended.

It was said that kana here means sara ("became"), i.e., "you became the best nation." It was said that kana here is a complete verb (tammah), and "the best nation" is a circumstantial state (hal). He who held that it is superfluous (za'idah) was far off the mark, because the superfluous kana cannot be the first word of a speech and has no governing effect.

Al-Zamakhshari said: kana is an expression for the existence of a thing at a past time in an indefinite manner, and there is no indication in it of a prior non-existence nor of a sudden cessation. From it is His saying: ﴿God is ever Forgiving﴾ (4:96). And from it is His saying: ﴿You were the best nation﴾, as if it were said: "You were found to be the best nation." End of his words.

His saying that it does not indicate a prior non-existence applies when it is not in the sense of sara. When it is in the sense of sara, it does indicate a prior non-existence. So when you say "Zayd was knowledgeable" in the sense of sara, it indicates that he moved from the state of ignorance to the state of knowledge.

As for his saying "nor a sudden cessation": we have mentioned before that the correct view is that it is like the other verbs, and its past form indicates cessation, though it is sometimes used where there is no cessation. There is a difference between indication (dalalah) and usage (isti'mal). Do you not see that you say, "This word indicates generality," and then it is used where generality is not intended, rather the particular is meant?

His saying "as if it were said: you were found to be the best nation" contradicts his claim that it is like His saying ﴿God was ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾ (4:96), because his estimate "you were found" indicates that it is a complete verb and that "the best nation" is a circumstantial state. As for His saying ﴿God was ever Forgiving﴾ (4:96), there is no doubt that kana there is the incomplete one, so the two conflict.

It was said: the meaning is "you were in God's knowledge." It was said: "in the Preserved Tablet." It was said: "in what the earlier nations were informed about you." It was said: it is in the mode of narration (hikayah), and it is connected to His saying: ﴿As for those whose faces are white, they will be in God's mercy, therein they abide forever﴾ (3:107), meaning: it will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection, "You were in the world the best nation." This is a far-fetched opinion given the context of the speech.

Khayr (best) is annexed to an indefinite noun (ummah), and it is an elative (af'al al-tafdil). Therefore it must be singular and masculine, even if the noun it qualifies is plural. The meaning is that when nations are ranked one by one, this nation is the best of them. It was judged that they are the best nation, but the wording did not specify the aspect of their excellence, which is their precedence in belief in the Messenger of God (ﷺ), their hastening to support him, their transmission from him of the knowledge of the Shari'ah, and their conquest of lands. These are virtues specific to them, in addition to the other virtues they possess.

Whoever acts well after them has a like reward, because they are the cause of its existence, since they are the ones who established it and made its path clear. "Whoever establishes a good practice (sunnah hasanah), he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection, without that diminishing their reward in anything."

The meaning of ukhrijat ("brought forth") is "made manifest and displayed." The one who brought it forth is God, Exalted is He, and the agent is omitted because it is known. Ibn Abbas said: it was brought forth from Mecca to Medina.

It is a clause in the place of an attribute (sifah) of "nation," meaning "the best nation brought forth." It is also permissible that it be in the place of an attribute of "best nation," in which case it occupies the accusative position, meaning "brought forth." On this latter view, the form of the third person (ghaybah) is observed here, and the form of address is not observed.

These are two methods of the Arabs. When a present pronoun of a speaker or addressee precedes, then its predicate comes as a noun, and after that comes what may serve as a description, sometimes the state of that pronoun is observed, so the suitable description follows the pronoun. You say: "I am a man who enjoins right," and "You are a man who enjoins right." From it: ﴿Nay, you are a people being tested﴾ (27:47), and the hadith: "Indeed you are a man in whom is jahiliyyah (the spirit of pre-Islamic ignorance)." And the poem:

"You are a man whose beard has grown thick for you, as if you were sitting in a sack of it."

And sometimes the state of that noun is observed, so the suitable description follows its third-person form. You say: "I am a man who enjoins right," and "You are a man who enjoins right" (with the third person). From it: ﴿You were the best nation brought forth﴾.

Had it come as ﴿you were brought forth﴾ (second person), observing the pronoun of address in kuntum ("you were"), it would have been correct and eloquent Arabic. The better view is to make ﴿brought forth for mankind﴾ an attribute of "nation," not of "best," so as to harmonize the address in "you were the best nation" with the address in "you enjoin" and what follows.

The apparent meaning of His saying "for mankind" (li-l-nas) is that it is connected to "brought forth." It was said that it is connected to "best." On this interpretation, it does not necessarily follow that they are the best of nations from this wording itself, but from another place. It was said that it is connected to "enjoin" (ta'murun), and the estimate is "you enjoin people to what is right." When the object was fronted, it was governed by the preposition lam (to), as in His words: ﴿If you are interpreters of dreams﴾ (12:43), meaning "you interpret dreams." This view is far-fetched.

"You enjoin what is right" is a statement that came in the mode of praise from God, said by al-Rabi'. Or it came in the mode of a condition regarding the superiority in goodness. This meaning was reported from Amr, Mujahid, and al-Zajjaj. It was said that it is a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf), by which He explains that they are the best nation, as you say: "Zayd is generous: he feeds people, clothes them, and attends to their affairs."

Ibn Atiyyah said: "you enjoin" and what follows are circumstantial clauses in the accusative position. End. Al-Raghib said the same. But the resumptive sentence is more apt and more laudatory. Al-Hawfi permitted that "you enjoin" be a predicate following another predicate, or that it be an attribute of "best nation."

It was said: He placed enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong before belief, because belief is shared among all nations, so it is not the factor that produces this added excellence. Rather, the producing factor is that they are stronger in state regarding commanding and forbidding. Belief is a condition for that effect, since as long as it is not present, no act of obedience would make a difference to the attribute of excellence. And the agent is closer to the effect than the condition of the effect is. He sufficed with mentioning belief in God rather than belief in prophethood, because it entails it. End. This is from the words of Muhammad ibn Umar al-Razi.

Al-Zamakhshari said: belief in everything that must be believed in is considered belief in God, because whoever believes in only some of what must be believed in, whether a messenger, a book, resurrection, reckoning, punishment, reward, or other things, his belief is not counted, so he is as if he does not believe in God. And they say: "We believe in part of the verse." End.

It was said: it is by the elision of a noun, meaning "and you believe in the Messenger of God."

The apparent meaning of al-ma'ruf (what is right) and al-munkar (what is wrong) is generality. Ibn Abbas said: al-ma'ruf is the Messenger, and al-munkar is the worship of idols. Abu al-Aliyah said: al-ma'ruf is monotheism, and al-munkar is polytheism.

﴿Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them﴾, meaning: had all of them, their common people and the rest of them, believed. It refers to complete and beneficial belief. The subject of kana is a pronoun returning to the verbal noun (masdar) understood from "believed," as one says: "Whoever believes, it is better for him," meaning "it would be [belief] that is better for him." He made belief's being better for them conditional upon its occurrence, as a reproach combined with His counsel to them, that if they believed they would save themselves from God's punishment.

Khayr here is the elative, and the meaning is: "it would be better for them than what they are upon." For they either preferred their own religion over the religion of Islam out of love for leadership and for having followers among the common people; so for them in this there is a worldly portion. Their belief would bring them a worldly portion, by making them leaders in Islam, and a great otherworldly portion through what they were promised for believing: that God would give them their reward twice.

Ibn Atiyyah said: the word khayr is an elative form, and there is no sharing between their disbelief and their belief in goodness; this is permissible because of the commonness of the word khayr and the branching of its meanings. Likewise with afdal ("more excellent") and ahabb ("more beloved") and what runs in that manner. End of his words. It is preferable to keep the word on its original meaning when that is possible, and it is possible here, since the goodness is unrestricted, so it is obtained with the least degree of sharing.

﴿Among them are believers, and most of them are deviators﴾. The apparent meaning of the active participle (ism al-fa'il) is being characterized by the act. So He informed that among the People of the Book are those characterized by belief, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his brother, Tha'labah ibn Sa'id, and whoever of the Jews embraced Islam; and like al-Najashi, Bahirah, and whoever of the Christians embraced Islam, since they affirmed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) before he was sent and after. This indicates that the intent of ﴿If the People of the Book had believed﴾ is particular, namely the rest of the People of the Book, since a group of them had already attained belief.

It was said that the intent of the active participle here is the future: among them are those who will believe. Then the intent of "the People of the Book" is general, and His saying ﴿Among them are believers﴾ is information about the unseen, that belief will occur among some of them, and they will not all remain in disbelief.

He informed that most of them are deviators, which indicates that the believers among them are few. The definite article (al) in "the believers" (al-mu'minun) and "the deviators" (al-fasiqun) indicates exaggeration and completeness in the two attributes. This is evident, since whoever believed in his book and in the Qur'an is complete in his belief; and whoever denied his book, not following what it contains of belief in the Messenger of God, and denied the Qur'an, is also complete in his deviance, obstinate in his disbelief.

These two clauses convey two future-tense predictions. The first is that their harm to you will be nothing but a small injury (*adha*), meaning something that causes you discomfort, not harm that brings them victory and total destruction. Accordingly, if they fight you, they will be abandoned and you will be given victory. Both of these things happened to the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). None of the People of the Book harmed them in a way that mattered, and whenever they targeted an unbeliever, they were granted victory over him and dominance.

Apparently, the phrase *illa adha* ("except harm") is a connected exception (*istithna' muttasil*, an exception that belongs to the same category as what precedes it), specifically an exception from a deleted verbal noun (*masdar*). The implied meaning is: "They will not harm you with any harm, except a slight harm that does not inflict damage or cause serious loss." Al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, al-Tabari and others said it is a disjunct exception (*istithna' munqati'*, an exception that does not belong to the same category as what precedes it), and the meaning is: "They will not harm you, but there will be only harm through the tongue." Some said this refers to hearing words of disbelief. Others said it refers to their slander and distortion of the text. Others said it refers to threats and defamation. And others said it refers to lies they fabricate against God. This was stated by al-Hasan and Qatada.

This sentence indicates encouragement for the believers to remain firm in their religion and steadfast in it, and it demeans the status of the unbelievers, since they have no harm to inflict on the Muslims beyond what reaches them through speaking an evil word.

﴿وإنْ يُقاتِلُوكم يُوَلُّوكُمُ الأدْبارَ﴾ This is an intensification of the point that the unbelievers do not stand up to the believers when they want to fight them. Rather, as soon as the confrontation takes place, they turn their backs. They are not among those who are overcome and killed while facing their opponent, not turning away from him. This clause comes as an emphatic confirmation of the clause before it, since it conveys that they will not have victory, domination, or authority over the believers. That is because achieving such things comes either from sincere fighting and steadfastness in it, or from the victory that is sought from God, and neither of these is available to them.

The word *al-adbar* ("backs") is used instead of *al-zuhur* ("backs" in a different sense, in the sense of the back as a whole), because mentioning the backs carries more humiliation than the other term, and because this is more emphatic about defeat and flight. For this reason it occurs in the Qur'an in this form rather than with the word *al-zuhur*, as in His saying: ﴿سَيُهْزَمُ الجَمْعُ ويُوَلُّونَ الدُّبُرَ﴾ [al-Qamar: 45], and ﴿ومَن يُوَلِّهِمْ يَوْمَئِذٍ دُبُرَهُ﴾ [al-Anfal: 16].

﴿ثُمَّ لا يُنْصَرُونَ﴾ This is a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*, a new clause that begins a fresh statement) informing that they will never be helped. It is not joined to the conditional clause in the jussive form, because it is not dependent on the condition. Rather, turning their backs is dependent on the fighting. The negation of their being helped applies to them forever, whether they fight or do not fight, since the cause of being denied help is disbelief. Thus this is a clause coordinated with the conditional clause and its response, just as the conditional clause and its response are coordinated with ﴿لَنْ يَضُرُّوكم إلّا أذًى﴾.

The reason the jussive form is not used for them is not, as some claimed, that the response of the condition occurs immediately after the conditioned act. That person claimed that *thumma* (then) indicates delay, and therefore it is not suitable in the response of the condition, and what is coordinated with the response is like the response. What that person claimed is an error, because what he said is impermissible has come in the most eloquent speech. God the Exalted said: ﴿وإنْ تَتَوَلَّوْا يَسْتَبْدِلْ قَوْمًا غَيْرَكم ثُمَّ لا يَكُونُوا أمْثالَكُمْ﴾ [Muhammad: 38], where the jussive form is used for what is coordinated with *thumma* after the response of the condition. Here *thumma* does not indicate a delay in time. Rather, it indicates a delay in the statement. Informing them of their turning their backs in battle, their humiliation, and their being overcome is more delightful and more pleasing to the soul. Then He informed after that that they would be absolutely denied help.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "The delay is in rank, because the information about God imposing humiliation upon them is greater than the information about their turning their backs." (If you ask) what is the position of the two clauses, I mean "they will turn their backs" and "they will not harm you," in relation to what comes before about the believers? (I answer) they are two statements that come by way of digression when the mention of the People of the Book is brought up, as a speaker says: "And regarding so-and-so, his situation is such-and-such." For this reason, it came without a conjunction.

﴿ضُرِبَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الذِّلَّةُ﴾ The explanation of this clause has already been given. It describes a state that was established upon the Jews in the regions of the earth before the coming of Islam. Al-Hasan said: "When Islam came, the Magians were collecting the poll tax (*jizya*) from the Jews, and they had no zeal or protection except in Yathrib, Khaybar, and that land. Islam removed them, and no banner of theirs remained on earth."

﴿أيْنَ ما ثُقِفُوا﴾ This is general regarding places. It is a conditional particle, *ma* is an extra particle after it, and *thuqifu* is in a jussive position. The response of the condition is deleted, indicated by what precedes it. According to the one who permits placing the response of the condition before it, he said that *duribat* ("was imposed") is the response, and it follows from this that the imposing of humiliation is future. According to the first view, it is a past form that indicates the future, meaning: "Humiliation was imposed upon them," and wherever they are found and encountered, it will be imposed upon them. The mention of the past indicates the future, as it does in the verse of the poet:

Many a drinking companion increases the cup's pleasure—I have given him to drink when the stars have set.

The meaning is: "I have given him to drink and will give him to drink when the stars set."

﴿إلّا بِحَبْلٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ وحَبْلٍ مِنَ النّاسِ﴾ This is an exception whose apparent character is disjunction, and this is the view of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, and Ibn 'Atiyya preferred it, because humiliation does not leave them. Al-Farra' estimated it as: "Unless they hold fast to a rope from God," so he omitted what the prepositional phrase depends on, as Humayd ibn Nur al-Hilali said:

She saw me with her two ropes and turned away out of fear...

Ibn 'Atiyya compared it to His saying: ﴿وما كانَ لِمُؤْمِنٍ أنْ يَقْتُلَ مُؤْمِنًا إلّا خَطَأً﴾ [al-Nisa': 92]. He said: "Because at first glance it suggests that he may kill by mistake, and that the rope from God and from people removes the imposition of humiliation, and the matter is not like that. Rather, the statement contains an implied element that the listener and the one who looks into the matter will understand, and its estimate is: 'In our community, there is no escape from death except by a rope.'" End of his statement. According to what he estimated, it is not a disjunct exception, because it is an exception from an implied sentence, which is his saying: "There is no escape from death," and it is connected according to this estimate, so it is not a disjunct exception from the first, since a single exception cannot be both connected and disjunct. A disjunct exception, as established in the science of grammar (*'ilm al-nahw*), is of two kinds: one kind that the governing element can apply to, and another kind to which that does not apply. This verse, on the assumption of disjunction, is of the second kind, since the estimate is: "But their holding fast to a rope from God and a rope from people will save them from being killed, captured, having their children taken captive, and having their wealth destroyed." And it is indicated that the report is disjunct by His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿وضُرِبَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الذِّلَّةُ والمَسْكَنَةُ وباءُوا بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61], where there is no exception there.

Al-Zamakhshari and others held that it is a connected exception. He said: "It is an exception from the most general of general states, and the meaning is: humiliation was imposed upon them in all general conditions, except in the condition of holding fast to a rope from God and a rope from people, meaning the protection of God and the protection of the Muslims. That is, they have no honor at all except this one, which is their seeking refuge in protection in return for what they accepted of the poll tax." End of his statement. This is a sound view. He likened the covenant to a rope, because it connects one people with another, just as a rope does with physical objects. Regarding the repetition of "rope," the apparent meaning is that two ropes are intended. The rope of God is interpreted as Islam, and the rope of people as covenant and protection. It was also said: the rope of God is what God specified regarding the collection of the poll tax, and the second is what is left to the judgment of the ruler, who may increase or decrease it according to his reasoning. It was also said: what is meant is one rope, since the rope of the believers is the rope of God, and it is the covenant.

﴿وباءُوا بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ وضُرِبَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ المَسْكَنَةُ ذَلِكَ بِأنَّهم كانُوا يَكْفُرُونَ بِآياتِ اللَّهِ ويَقْتُلُونَ الأنْبِياءَ بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ ذَلِكَ بِما عَصَوْا وكانُوا يَعْتَدُونَ﴾ The explanation of similar sentences has already been given, so there is no need to repeat it here.

It was also said: what is meant is one rope, since the rope of the believers is the rope of God, and it is the covenant.

﴿وباءُوا بِغَضَبٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ وضُرِبَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ المَسْكَنَةُ ذَلِكَ بِأنَّهم كانُوا يَكْفُرُونَ بِآياتِ اللَّهِ ويَقْتُلُونَ الأنْبِياءَ بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ ذَلِكَ بِما عَصَوْا وكانُوا يَعْتَدُونَ﴾ The explanation of similar sentences has already been given, so there is no need to repeat it here.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 3, verses 113–118 (part 1 of 4):**

﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is a upright community who recite the signs of God in the night hours, and they prostrate.﴾ ﴿They believe in God and the Last Day, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds. These are among the righteous.﴾ ﴿Whatever good they do, they will not be denied its reward. God is Knowing of the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿Indeed, as for those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against God. They are the companions of the Fire, and they will abide in it forever.﴾ ﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life is like a wind containing bitter cold that strikes the tilth of a people who wronged themselves, and destroys it. God did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, do not take intimate companions from outside your own ranks. They will not fail to corrupt you; they wish you to suffer. Hatred has already shown from their mouths, and what their chests conceal is greater. We have already made the signs clear to you, if you understand.﴾ ﴿Here you are, loving them, though they do not love you, and you believe in the whole Scripture. When they meet you they say, "We believe," but when they are alone they bite their fingertips at you in rage. Say, "Die in your rage. Indeed God knows what is in the breasts."﴾ [Al-Imran: 119] ﴿If good touches you, it grieves them; if an evil befalls you, they rejoice at it. But if you are patient and God-fearing, their scheming will not harm you at all. Indeed God encompasses what they do.﴾ [Al-Imran: 120].

**Lexical notes:**

*Al-ānā'* (الآناء): the hours. The singular has several forms: *anyun* (أنْيٌ) like *ma'yun*, *anan* (أنى) like *fata*, *ann* (أنّى) like *nahhā*, *anyun* (أنْيٌ) like *zaby*, and *anwun* (أنْوٌ) like *jarw*.

*Al-ṣarr* (الصَّرُّ): intense, burning cold. It is also said that it means cold in the sense of *al-ṣarṣar* (the violent wind), as the poet said:
*"Do not wrong the Atawiyyin by striking them with a violent wind against the people of the encampments."*
Layla al-Akhyaliyya said:
*"He did not overcome the fierce adversary, nor fill the bowls with fat meat on a day of a violent, roaring wind."*
Ibn Kaysan said it is the sound of the flame of fire, which is the view preferred by al-Zajjaj, from *al-ṣarīr* (creaking). This is the sound in the saying *ṣarra al-shay'* (the thing creaked), and from it comes *al-rīḥ al-ṣarṣar* (the violent wind). Al-Zajjaj said: *al-ṣarr* is the sound of the fire that is in the wind.

*Al-biṭāna* (البِطانَة): the lining of a garment, opposite to the outer layer. It is used metaphorically for the one whom a person chooses for close intimacy, like the undergarment and the covering. One says *baṭana fulān min fulān buṭūnan wa biṭāna* when he is particularly close to him and involved in his affairs. The poet said:
*"Those are my close friends, indeed my inner circle, and they are my trusted confidants above all relatives."*

*Alawtu fī al-amr* (ألوْتُ في الأمْرِ): I fell short in the matter. Zuhayr said:
*"After them came a people seeking to overtake them, but they did not do it, and they did not fall short."*
That is, they did not fail to act.

*Al-khabāl* and *al-khabal* (الخَبالُ والخَبَلُ): corruption affecting an animal. One says there is *khabal* in the legs of a horse, meaning a defect from unsteadiness, impairment, or madness. One says *khabalahu al-ḥubb*, meaning love corrupted him.

*Al-baghḍā'* (البَغْضاءُ): a verbal noun like *al-sarrā'* and *al-ba'sā'*. One says *bughida al-rajul* (the man was hated), so he is *baghīḍ*, and *abghaḍtuhu* (I hated him), meaning my dislike for him became intense.

*Al-afwāh* (الأفْواهُ): the mouths. Its singular in origin is *fūh*, but the Arabs did not use it; they said *fam*. There are nine dialect forms of *fam* mentioned in some grammar books.

*Al-‘aḍḍ* (العَضُّ): placing the teeth on something with force. The verb of this form is *ʿaḍḍa* with a kasra on the ʿayn, and it is with the *ḍād*. As for *ʿaẓẓ al-zamān* and *ʿaẓẓ al-ḥarb*, these are with the *ẓā'*, the sister of the *ṭā'*. The poet said:
*"And the biting of time, O son of Marwan, has left no wealth except what is stripped or shaven."*
*Al-ʿuḍḍ* (with a ḍamma on the ʿayn) is the fodder of city dwellers, like the dried produce and crushed date pits. One says *aʿaḍḍa al-qawm* when their camels eat *al-ʿaḍḍ*. A camel described as *ʿuḍāḍī* is fat, as if it were ascribed to that. *Al-ʿiḍḍ* (with a kasra) means a cunning man.

*Al-anāmil* (الأنامِلُ): plural of *unmula*, also pronounced with a fatha or ḍamma on the mīm. It means the fingertips. Ibn ʿĪsā said its origin is the known ant (*al-naml*), and it is compared to it in fineness and in quick movement. From it comes *rajul namil*, meaning a tale-bearer.

*Al-ghayḍ* (الغَيْضُ): verbal noun of *ghāḍa*. *Ghayḍ* is also a proper name.

*Al-faraḥ* (الفَرَحُ): joy, known. One says *fariḥa* with a kasra on the ʿayn.

*Al-kayd* (الكَيْدُ): cunning. *Kādahu yakīduhu* means he schemed against him, that is, deceived him by falsehood. Ibn Qutayba said its origin is hardship, from the saying *fulān yakīdu bi-nafsihi*, meaning he struggles with the pains of the death agony and the throes of death.

**Commentary on the verses:**

﴿They are not all alike, among the People of the Book, a upright community.﴾

*The occasion of revelation*: the conversion of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and others of the Jews, and the statement of the disbelievers among their rabbis: "None believed in Muhammad except our worst people; if they were the best, they would not have abandoned the religion of their fathers." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and Ibn Jurayj.

The *wāw* in *"they are not"* (لَيْسُوا) refers to the People of the Book mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿If the People of the Book had believed, it would have been better for them. Some of them are believers, but most of them are defiant transgressors.﴾ [Al-Imran: 110]. The more correct view is that the *wāw* is a pronoun referring to the People of the Book, and *sawā'an* (سَواءً) is the predicate of *laysa*. The meaning: the People of the Book are not equal; among them are those who believed in their Scripture and in the Qur'an, from those who reached the law of Islam, or who were upright and died before they reached it.

﴿Among the People of the Book, a upright community﴾ is a subject and predicate. Al-Farrāʾ said: *ummatun* (أُمَّةٌ) is raised by *sawāʾ*, meaning the People of the Book are not equal. Among the People of the Book is a community described by what was mentioned, and a disbelieving community. This second clause, which balances the first, was omitted, and the first part indicates it, as in his saying:
*"I disobeyed the heart concerning her, though I listen to its command; I do not know whether its pursuit is right guidance."*
The estimated words are: *am ghayy* (or is it error), and it was omitted because *arushd* (is it right guidance) indicates it. He also said:
*"I see you; I do not know whether it is a worry I hold, while the one with worry has long been humbled and subdued."*
The estimate is: *am ghayruhu* (or is it something else). Al-Farrāʾ said: equality requires two things, as in ﴿equal for those who dwell there and the visitor﴾ [Al-Hajj: 25] and ﴿equal their living and their dying﴾ [Al-Jathiya: 21].

The view of al-Farrāʾ is weak in terms of the omission, and in terms of placing an apparent noun in place of a pronoun, since the estimate would be: "They are not equal; among them is a community that is upright, and a disbelieving community."

Abu ʿUbayda held that the *wāw* in *"laysū"* is a plural marker, not a pronoun, like its use in the poet's words:
*"They blame me for buying camels, my people, and all of them are most blameworthy."*
The subject of *laysa* is *ummatun qā'ima* (an upright community), meaning: it is not equal; among the People of the Book is an upright community described by what was mentioned, and a disbelieving community.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: what Abu ʿUbayda said is an error, rejected. End. He did not clarify the nature of the error, and it seems he thought the subject of *laysa* is only *ummatun qā'ima*, with nothing omitted. Then, since the purpose is not the difference among the upright community that follows, if an omitted element is estimated there, Abu ʿUbayda's view is not an error to be rejected. It was said: what Abu ʿUbayda said follows the dialect of *"akalūnī al-barāghīth"* (the fleas ate me), which is a poor dialect, and the Arabs are against it, so it should not be applied to it, along with its contradiction of the apparent meaning. End. Al-Suhaylī disputed the grammarians' statement that it is a weak dialect, noting that it appears often in the Hadith. The first parsing is the apparent one, namely that *"among the People of the Book is an upright community"* is a resumptive clause explaining the negation of equality, as in ﴿They enjoin what is right﴾ [Al-Tawba: 71] explaining His saying ﴿You are the best community﴾ [Al-Imran: 110]. The People of the Book here means the Jews and the Christians.

*Ummatun qā'ima* (an upright community), that is, one that is upright, from *aqamtu al-ʿūd fa-qāma* (I set the stick straight and it stood), meaning it became straight. Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and Ibn Jurayj said: just. Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda and al-Rabīʿ said: upright in the Book of God and its limits, guided. Al-Suddī said: obedient and devoted. All of these go back to the first view.

Ibn Masʿūd and al-Suddī said: the pronoun in *"laysū"* refers to the Jews and the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), since the mention of the Jews and of this community preceded in His saying: ﴿You are the best community﴾ [Al-Imran: 110]. On this view, "the Book" means the category of God's books, not only the known Torah and Gospel. The phrase *"among the People of the Book is an upright community"* means the people of the Qur'an. The apparent reading is that the pronoun refers to the People of the Book mentioned in His saying ﴿If the People of the Book had believed﴾ [Al-Imran: 110], because the pronouns referring to them follow one another, so the pronoun in *laysū* is likewise.

ʿAṭāʾ said: *"among the People of the Book is an upright community"* and the verse in full, meaning forty men from the people of Najran from the Arabs, thirty-two from the Abyssinians, and eight from the Romans, who were upon the religion of ʿĪsā and believed in Muhammad (ﷺ). Some of the Ansar were monotheists who performed ritual bathing from impurity, and they practised what they knew of the laws of the *ḥanīfiyya* (the pure monotheism) before the coming of the Prophet (ﷺ), until As'ad ibn Zurāra, al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr, Muḥammad ibn Maslama, and Qays ibn Ṣirma ibn Anas came to them from him.

﴿They recite the signs of God in the night hours, and they prostrate.﴾

He described the upright community as reciting the signs of God, and He expressed the recitation during the hours of the night as the *tahajjud* (night prayer) with the Qur'an. His saying *"and they prostrate"* is also a clause in the position of a description, conjoined to *"recite"*. He described them by reciting the Qur'an and by prostrating. The recitation of the Qur'an is done while standing, while in prostration recitation is not prescribed. The second description came as a nominal sentence to indicate emphasis through the repetition of the pronoun *"hum"*, and the *wāw* in *"yasjudūn"*, since a servant is nearest to his Lord when he is prostrating. He reported about the subject with the present tense. The first description also came in the present tense to indicate renewal. The second was joined to the first by *wāw* to show that that recitation was in prayer, so the recitation was not alone, nor was the prostration alone.

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿in the watches of the night﴾ is that it refers to all the hours of the night. Thus it is unlikely that this (I mean the recitation and the prostration) would come from every single person, and it would only come from a group. Some people stand in prayer at the beginning of the night, some at its end, and some after a sleep, then return to their sleep. So from all of them, in the cities and communities, the hours of the night are covered by standing in prayer, reciting the Qur'an, and prostrating. This was the practice of the early part of this community. People knew of standing in prayer during the first third of the last part of the night, or slightly before it, and few stood the whole night. Among the righteous there were those who made it a constant practice, and God mentioned moderation in this at the beginning of Surat al-Muzzammil. The "watches of the night" (āna' al-layl) means its hours. This was said by al-Rabi' and Qatada and others. Al-Suddi said it means its middle portion, which is the use of the whole for a part, since the middle is one member of the plural. It is reported from Mansur that it was revealed concerning those who prayed between the two evening prayers, which contradicts the apparent meaning of His words ﴿they recite the verses of God in the watches of the night﴾. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that it refers to the prayer of 'atama (the night prayer). He mentioned that the cause of its revelation was that the Prophet (ﷺ) was delayed in the 'atama prayer and was at the house of one of his wives. He did not come until the night had passed. When he came, some of us were praying and some were lying down, and he said: "Rejoice, for none of the People of the Book pray this prayer." For this reason Ibn Mas'ud mentioned that His words ﴿they are not all alike﴾ refer to the Jews and this community, which contradicts the apparent meaning. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿while they prostrate﴾ is that it refers to prostration in the prayer. It was said that prostration is used to express prayer, naming the whole by a noble part of it, just as prayer is expressed by bowing (ruku'). This was said by Muqatil, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, because recitation is not done in bowing or in prostration. According to this, the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), meaning they recite the verses of God while engaged in prayer. It was also said that it refers to the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa). It was said that prostration means humility and submission. Al-Tabari and others held that it is a conjoined clause from the first statement, informing that they are also people of prostration. What makes this good is that the recitation was outside of prayer. According to this interpretation, outside of prayer, it is also a descriptive qualifier enumerated with the conjunction "wa", as you say: "Zayd the generous and the intelligent came to me." Some permitted, regarding His words ﴿and they prostrate﴾, that it be a circumstantial phrase both from the pronoun in (qā'ima) and from (umma), since it has been described as (qā'ima). So two views are established regarding this clause. One is that it has no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) and is a new independent sentence. The other view is that it has a place in the i'rab, either in the nominative, being in the position of a qualifier, or in the accusative, being in the position of a circumstantial phrase, either from the pronoun in (yatlūna), or from the pronoun in (qā'ima), or from (umma). This verse indicates encouragement to stand in prayer at night. There has come in the Book of God: ﴿And from the night, pray with it as a supererogatory act for you﴾ [al-Isra' 79], ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing﴾ [al-Zumar 9], ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ [al-Muzzammil 1], ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil 2]. And in the hadith: "O servant of God, do not be like so-and-so; he used to stand in prayer at night, then he abandoned it." And in it: "What a fine man is the servant of God, except that he does not stand in prayer at night." And much else. It is reported from a man of the Banu Shayba who used to study the scriptures: "We find a statement from the words of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic: Does the shepherd of camels and sheep think, when the night covers him, that he lies down [to sleep] like one who stands and prostrates in the night?"

(They believe in God and the Last Day, and enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.) The explanation of such phrases has already been given.

﴿And they hasten to good deeds.﴾ Hastening to good arises from an intense desire for it, because whoever desires a matter rushes to it and to doing it, and prefers promptness over delay. There has come in a hadith: "Seize five before five: your youth before your old age, your health before your sickness, your leisure before your preoccupation, your life before your death, and your wealth before your poverty."

He, the Exalted, described them as those who, when called to something good, such as supporting the oppressed, relieving the distressed, or worshipping God, hasten to do it. The apparent sense of "they believe" is that it is a qualifying description, meaning reciting and believing. They allowed that the clause be a new independent sentence, or in the position of a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun in "they prostrate", or that it be an apposition to the prostration. It was said: because prostration here means faith. Al-Zamakhshari said: He described them with characteristics that were not found among the Jews, namely reciting the verses of God at night while prostrating, and believing in God, because their belief in Him was no belief at all, since they associated 'Uzayr with Him and disbelieved in some of the books and messengers but not others; and belief in the Last Day, because they described it contrary to its reality; and enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, because they were compromisers; and hastening to good deeds, because they were slow to them and not eager for them. End of his words, and it is good.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned this community, He described it with six attributes. The first: that they are steadfast (qā'ima), meaning upright on the straight path. Since steadfastness is a fixed attribute that does not change, it came in the form of the active participle. The second: the prayer at night, expressed by recitation and prostration, which is the worship by which one shows devotion to communing with God at night. The third: belief in God and the Last Day, which is what drives worship of God. He mentioned the Last Day because in it appear the effects of worshipping God through the great reward. Belief in the Last Day includes belief in the prophets, since they are the ones who informed about the existence and occurrence of this, which is possible in reason, so belief in it became obligatory. The fourth: enjoining what is right. The fifth: forbidding what is wrong. When they perfected themselves, they strove to perfect others through these two attributes. The sixth: hastening to good deeds, an attribute that includes their own particular deeds and the deeds that extend from them to others. These three attributes also arise from belief. Observe the excellent arrangement of these attributes: belief is placed in the middle, the attribute specific to the person in himself, namely prayer at night, is placed before it, and the two transitive attributes and the shared attribute come after it, all of them being results of belief.

﴿And those are among the righteous.﴾ This refers to those who combined these six attributes, meaning those described by these qualities who are among those whose conditions are good in the sight of God. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that by "the righteous" he means the Muslims. End of his words. His statement resembles the statement of Ibn 'Abbas from among the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). In what al-Zamakhshari said afterward: Rather, the apparent meaning is that describing someone as righteous carries an added value beyond describing him as a Muslim; that is why some prophets asked for this rank. God, the Exalted, said, relating about Solomon, upon our prophet and upon him be the best of prayers and the most complete peace: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾ [al-Naml 19]. And God, the Exalted, said concerning Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And We had chosen him in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾ [al-Baqara 130]. And God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift, and We made each of them righteous﴾ [al-Anbiya' 72]. And God, the Exalted, said after mentioning Ishmael: ﴿And Idris and Dhu al-Kifl, all of them were of the patient﴾ [al-Anbiya' 85]. ﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy; indeed they were among the righteous﴾ [al-Anbiya' 86]. And He said: ﴿And the martyrs and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisa' 69].

The "min" (in "from the righteous") is partitive. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is also good for it to be for explaining the kind. End. Nothing had preceded it containing ambiguity that would make its kind clear.

﴿And whatever good they do, they will not be denied its reward.﴾ Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr read both verbs with the letter "ta'" (you), as address. They differed about who is addressed. Abu Hatim said: It refers back to His words ﴿you are the best nation﴾ [Al 'Imran 110], so it is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab) and its deviation. Makki said: The "ta'" in them is general, covering the whole community. What appears to be the case is that it is a turn (iltifat) to His words "a steadfast community". When He described them with noble attributes, He turned to them to reassure them and to win their affection, addressing them that whatever good you do, you will not be deprived of its reward. For this reason He limited it to "good" and did not mention evil, because this is a place of kindness toward them and compassion, while it is known that everything done, good or evil, has its promised consequence. This turn is supported, and that it refers back to ﴿a steadfast community﴾, by the reading with "ya'" (they), which is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, and 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr, and the choice of Abu 'Ubayd; the rest of Abu 'Amr's transmitters allowed a choice between "ta'" and "ya'". It is known in this reading that the pronoun refers to ﴿a steadfast community﴾, just as it refers in His words "they recite" and what follows. Kafara (to deny/reject) is transitive to one object, as in "kafara al-ni'ma" (he denied the favor). Here it has been used with the meaning of "hurma" (to be deprived), meaning you will not be deprived of its reward. And since His description as "Shakur" (Most Appreciative) has come in the sense of fully paying the reward, He negated of Himself the opposite of appreciation, which is denying the reward, meaning depriving of it.

﴿And God is Knowing of the righteous.﴾ Since the verse was about those described with beautiful attributes, and He informed that He rewards the doing of good, it was fitting to end the verse by mentioning His knowledge of the righteous, although He knows both the righteous and their opposites. The meaning of "Knowing of them" is that He will recompense them for their piety. In this there is a promise to the righteous and a warning to the negligent.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will never avail them against God at all.﴾ [Al 'Imran 10] The explanation of this sentence has already been given at the beginning of this surah.

﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ The explanation of a parallel to this sentence has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqara. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is clear: when He mentioned some of the conditions of the believers, He mentioned some of the conditions of the disbelievers, so that the difference between the two groups would become clear.

﴿The example of what they spend in this worldly life is like the example of a wind containing frost which strikes the crops of a people who have wronged themselves and destroys them.﴾ When He, the Exalted, mentioned that what the believers do of good is not denied its reward, but they will reap in the Hereafter the fruit of what they planted in this world, He began to explain the spending of the disbelievers, and gave for it a parable which required its nullification and its going to waste without return. Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning the expenditures and charities of the disbelievers. Muqatil said: concerning the spending of the lowly Jews on their scholars. It was said: concerning the spending of the polytheists on the day of Badr. It was said: concerning the spending of the hypocrites when they went out with the Muslims to fight the polytheists. Al-Zamakhshari said: He likened what they used to spend of their wealth in pursuit of nobility, glory, gaining praise, and good repute among people, not seeking thereby the face of God, to a crop that the cold has struck so that it became debris. It was said: it is what they draw near to God by, along with their disbelief. It was said: what they spent in hostility to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), because they did not achieve by spending it what they spent it for. End of his words.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is the image that forms in the mind of their spending, which they regard as an act of nearness to God, a seeking of reward, and a means of obtaining merit. Their spending will be nullified on the Day of Resurrection and become "scattered dust." Its disappearance is like the image that forms in the mind of a people's crop that has grown green and flourished, so that their hope in it was strengthened, and then a biting, scorching wind struck it and destroyed it. End of quotation. The apparent reading is that what is in His words, ﴿the likeness of what they spend﴾, is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and its returning pronoun (a'id) is omitted, meaning "what they spend" (yunfiquna-hu). The apparent reading is that what they spend is likened to the wind, and the meaning is that its likeness is to the tilth (harth). It was said that this is a compound simile (tashbih murakkab), in which the singular is not matched with the singular. A parallel to this has already passed in His words, ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:17]. For this reason Tha'lab said: he began with the wind, while the meaning is referred to the tilth. This is the preference of al-Zamakhshari. It was also said: the comparison occurs between two things and two things. He mentioned one of the two compared items and left out the other. Then he mentioned one of the two things used for comparison, but not the one that corresponds to the first mentioned item, and left out the other. The two mentioned items point to the two omitted ones. This is the preference of Ibn 'Atiyya, who said: this is the utmost of eloquence and inimitability. Similar to this is His words, ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:171]. End of quotation. It is also permissible that there is an omitted modifying noun (mudaf) in the first part, its estimate being: "the likeness of the destruction of what they spend," or in the second part, its estimate being: "like the likeness of the destruction of a wind." It was said: it is permissible for "mā" to be verbal-noun (maṣdariyya), meaning "the likeness of their spending," so the intelligible is compared to the sensible, since the spending is compared to the wind. The apparent sense of His words "they spend" is that it refers to spending wealth. As-Suddi said: its meaning is that they spend from their words, which they conceal the opposite of. This is weakened by the fact that this verse concerns the disbelievers who openly declare, not the hypocrites who conceal.
