When He, the Exalted, mentioned this community, He described it with six attributes. The first: that they are steadfast (qā'ima), meaning upright on the straight path. Since steadfastness is a fixed attribute that does not change, it came in the form of the active participle. The second: the prayer at night, expressed by recitation and prostration, which is the worship by which one shows devotion to communing with God at night. The third: belief in God and the Last Day, which is what drives worship of God. He mentioned the Last Day because in it appear the effects of worshipping God through the great reward. Belief in the Last Day includes belief in the prophets, since they are the ones who informed about the existence and occurrence of this, which is possible in reason, so belief in it became obligatory. The fourth: enjoining what is right. The fifth: forbidding what is wrong. When they perfected themselves, they strove to perfect others through these two attributes. The sixth: hastening to good deeds, an attribute that includes their own particular deeds and the deeds that extend from them to others. These three attributes also arise from belief. Observe the excellent arrangement of these attributes: belief is placed in the middle, the attribute specific to the person in himself, namely prayer at night, is placed before it, and the two transitive attributes and the shared attribute come after it, all of them being results of belief.

﴿And those are among the righteous.﴾ This refers to those who combined these six attributes, meaning those described by these qualities who are among those whose conditions are good in the sight of God. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that by "the righteous" he means the Muslims. End of his words. His statement resembles the statement of Ibn 'Abbas from among the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). In what al-Zamakhshari said afterward: Rather, the apparent meaning is that describing someone as righteous carries an added value beyond describing him as a Muslim; that is why some prophets asked for this rank. God, the Exalted, said, relating about Solomon, upon our prophet and upon him be the best of prayers and the most complete peace: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾ [al-Naml 19]. And God, the Exalted, said concerning Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And We had chosen him in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾ [al-Baqara 130]. And God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift, and We made each of them righteous﴾ [al-Anbiya' 72]. And God, the Exalted, said after mentioning Ishmael: ﴿And Idris and Dhu al-Kifl, all of them were of the patient﴾ [al-Anbiya' 85]. ﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy; indeed they were among the righteous﴾ [al-Anbiya' 86]. And He said: ﴿And the martyrs and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisa' 69].

The "min" (in "from the righteous") is partitive. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is also good for it to be for explaining the kind. End. Nothing had preceded it containing ambiguity that would make its kind clear.

﴿And whatever good they do, they will not be denied its reward.﴾ Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr read both verbs with the letter "ta'" (you), as address. They differed about who is addressed. Abu Hatim said: It refers back to His words ﴿you are the best nation﴾ [Al 'Imran 110], so it is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab) and its deviation. Makki said: The "ta'" in them is general, covering the whole community. What appears to be the case is that it is a turn (iltifat) to His words "a steadfast community". When He described them with noble attributes, He turned to them to reassure them and to win their affection, addressing them that whatever good you do, you will not be deprived of its reward. For this reason He limited it to "good" and did not mention evil, because this is a place of kindness toward them and compassion, while it is known that everything done, good or evil, has its promised consequence. This turn is supported, and that it refers back to ﴿a steadfast community﴾, by the reading with "ya'" (they), which is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, and 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr, and the choice of Abu 'Ubayd; the rest of Abu 'Amr's transmitters allowed a choice between "ta'" and "ya'". It is known in this reading that the pronoun refers to ﴿a steadfast community﴾, just as it refers in His words "they recite" and what follows. Kafara (to deny/reject) is transitive to one object, as in "kafara al-ni'ma" (he denied the favor). Here it has been used with the meaning of "hurma" (to be deprived), meaning you will not be deprived of its reward. And since His description as "Shakur" (Most Appreciative) has come in the sense of fully paying the reward, He negated of Himself the opposite of appreciation, which is denying the reward, meaning depriving of it.

﴿And God is Knowing of the righteous.﴾ Since the verse was about those described with beautiful attributes, and He informed that He rewards the doing of good, it was fitting to end the verse by mentioning His knowledge of the righteous, although He knows both the righteous and their opposites. The meaning of "Knowing of them" is that He will recompense them for their piety. In this there is a promise to the righteous and a warning to the negligent.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will never avail them against God at all.﴾ [Al 'Imran 10] The explanation of this sentence has already been given at the beginning of this surah.

﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ The explanation of a parallel to this sentence has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqara. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is clear: when He mentioned some of the conditions of the believers, He mentioned some of the conditions of the disbelievers, so that the difference between the two groups would become clear.

﴿The example of what they spend in this worldly life is like the example of a wind containing frost which strikes the crops of a people who have wronged themselves and destroys them.﴾ When He, the Exalted, mentioned that what the believers do of good is not denied its reward, but they will reap in the Hereafter the fruit of what they planted in this world, He began to explain the spending of the disbelievers, and gave for it a parable which required its nullification and its going to waste without return. Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning the expenditures and charities of the disbelievers. Muqatil said: concerning the spending of the lowly Jews on their scholars. It was said: concerning the spending of the polytheists on the day of Badr. It was said: concerning the spending of the hypocrites when they went out with the Muslims to fight the polytheists. Al-Zamakhshari said: He likened what they used to spend of their wealth in pursuit of nobility, glory, gaining praise, and good repute among people, not seeking thereby the face of God, to a crop that the cold has struck so that it became debris. It was said: it is what they draw near to God by, along with their disbelief. It was said: what they spent in hostility to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), because they did not achieve by spending it what they spent it for. End of his words.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is the image that forms in the mind of their spending, which they regard as an act of nearness to God, a seeking of reward, and a means of obtaining merit. Their spending will be nullified on the Day of Resurrection and become "scattered dust." Its disappearance is like the image that forms in the mind of a people's crop that has grown green and flourished, so that their hope in it was strengthened, and then a biting, scorching wind struck it and destroyed it. End of quotation. The apparent reading is that what is in His words, ﴿the likeness of what they spend﴾, is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and its returning pronoun (a'id) is omitted, meaning "what they spend" (yunfiquna-hu). The apparent reading is that what they spend is likened to the wind, and the meaning is that its likeness is to the tilth (harth). It was said that this is a compound simile (tashbih murakkab), in which the singular is not matched with the singular. A parallel to this has already passed in His words, ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:17]. For this reason Tha'lab said: he began with the wind, while the meaning is referred to the tilth. This is the preference of al-Zamakhshari. It was also said: the comparison occurs between two things and two things. He mentioned one of the two compared items and left out the other. Then he mentioned one of the two things used for comparison, but not the one that corresponds to the first mentioned item, and left out the other. The two mentioned items point to the two omitted ones. This is the preference of Ibn 'Atiyya, who said: this is the utmost of eloquence and inimitability. Similar to this is His words, ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:171]. End of quotation. It is also permissible that there is an omitted modifying noun (mudaf) in the first part, its estimate being: "the likeness of the destruction of what they spend," or in the second part, its estimate being: "like the likeness of the destruction of a wind." It was said: it is permissible for "mā" to be verbal-noun (maṣdariyya), meaning "the likeness of their spending," so the intelligible is compared to the sensible, since the spending is compared to the wind. The apparent sense of His words "they spend" is that it refers to spending wealth. As-Suddi said: its meaning is that they spend from their words, which they conceal the opposite of. This is weakened by the fact that this verse concerns the disbelievers who openly declare, not the hypocrites who conceal. It was said: the object of the spending is their deeds, including disbelief and the like. These are like the wind in which is a biting cold, which nullified their deeds, every kinship they had and their acts of devotion through freeing slaves, just as the wind destroys the crop. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is a good view, were it not for the remoteness of the metaphor (isti'ara) in the word "spending." End of quotation. Al-Raghib said: some have said that "what they spend" is an expression for all their deeds, but he singled out spending because it is more apparent and more common. End of quotation.

Ibn Hurmuz and al-A'raj read tunfiquna with a "ta" (second-person address), on the sense of "say to them," and they used the singular for "wind" because it is specific to punishment, just as it is used singularly in His words, ﴿Rather, it is what you were hasting for: a wind﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:24], ﴿And if We sent a wind﴾ [al-Rum 30:51], ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind﴾ [al-Qamar 54:19], and ﴿the barren wind﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:41]. Likewise, the plural is specific to mercy: ﴿that He sends the winds as bringers of good tidings﴾ [al-Rum 30:46], ﴿And We sent the fertilizing winds﴾ [al-Hijr 15:22], ﴿He sends the winds as good news﴾ [al-A'raf 7:57]. For this reason it has been related: "O God, make them winds, and do not make them a wind." The word ṣirr is nominative as the subject of the preposition-phrase before it, since it is dependent on being an attribute (ṣifa) of the wind. If ṣirr means cold, which is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and as-Suddi, or the sound of the flame of fire, or the sound of a violent wind, then it is apparent that it is in the wind. If ṣirr is an attribute of the wind like ṣarṣar, then the meaning is that in it is a coldness, ṣirr, as you say "cold, cold" (bard bārid). The qualified noun is omitted and the attribute takes its place. Or the adverbial sense is a metaphor, in which the qualified noun is made a container for the attribute, as in the line: "And in the Most Merciful is sufficiency for the weak." And the saying of people: "If so-and-so wrongs me, then in God is sufficiency." The meaning is: "the Most Merciful is sufficient, and God is sufficient." This is remote.

His words ﴿that struck the tilth of a people﴾ are in the position of an attribute of the wind. He began first with the attribute by the preposition-phrase, then with the attribute by a clause. His words ﴿who wronged themselves﴾ are a clause in the position of an attribute of "a people." Its apparent meaning is that they wronged themselves through their sins, so the destruction was more severe, since it was a punishment for them.

A group of the people of knowledge have held that the calamities of this world are only due to the servant's sins. This is inferred from more than one verse of the Qur'an, so it follows from this that every tilth that the wind destroys belongs to one who has wronged himself. It was said: "they wronged themselves" means they sowed outside the season of sowing, that is, they placed the actions of cultivation outside their proper place, either in time or in the manner of work. These were singled out for mention because the tilth in such a case is more complete and more firmly established. Al-Mahdawi inclined to this view.

﴿And God did not wrong them﴾: al-Zamakhshari and others permitted that the pronoun returns to the spenders, meaning He did not wrong them by not accepting their expenditures, and that it returns to the owners of the tilth, meaning He did not wrong them by destroying their tilth, but they wronged themselves by committing sins. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the pronoun in "wronged them" refers to the disbelievers whose pronoun was mentioned in "they spend," and it does not refer to the people who own the tilth, because they were not mentioned so that it would return to them, nor to clarify their wrongdoing. Also His words, ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:57], indicate the present-tense action of those present. End of quotation. This is a good preference. It is read irregularly as wa-lākinna (with shadda), with its noun being "themselves," and the predicate "they wrong." The meaning is: they wrong themselves. The omission of this pronoun, though its omission in such a construction is rare, is made good by its being the end-rhyme (fāṣila) of a verse, for if it were stated explicitly this meaning would disappear. It is not permissible to think that the noun of lākinna is a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n) that was omitted, with "themselves" being an object of "they wrong," because the omission of this pronoun is specific to poetry.

﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimates (biṭāna) those outside your own who will not spare you corruption﴾. It was revealed concerning men from among the believers who associated with men of the Jews because of neighborliness, alliance, and foster-suckling. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said. He also said, with Qatada, as-Suddi and ar-Rabi': it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. God forbade the believers from them. He likened the close friend (ṣiddīq) of intimate sincerity to the garment that touches the inside of a person's body. It is called biṭāna (inner garment) and walīja (intimate). His words ﴿from outside your own﴾ are in the position of an attribute of biṭāna. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "from outside the sons of your kind," and they are the Muslims. It was said: "from" is connected to His words "do not take." It was also said: "from" is extra (zā'ida), meaning "intimates outside you." The meaning is that they were forbidden to take as confidants (aṣfiyā') non-believers. This prohibition indicates the prohibition of employing protected non-Muslims (ahl al-dhimma) as secretaries, and of entrusting them with buying and selling, or appointing them as deputies. Umar reproached Abu Musa for employing a dhimmi as a scribe, and recited this verse to him. It was also said to Umar about a skilled scribe from the Christians of al-Hira: "Will he not write for you?" He said: "Then I would be taking an intimate."

The clause ﴿who will not spare you corruption﴾ has no place in grammatical analysis, since it came as an explanation of the state of the disbelieving intimate, together with the clauses that follow it, to repel the believers from taking them as intimates. Whoever holds that it is an attribute of "intimates" or a state (ḥāl) of what "from" is connected to is far from the understanding of eloquent speech, because they were forbidden from taking disbelieving intimates, and then He drew attention to things they were doing: seeking to cause harm to the believers, wishing them hardship, and the manifestation of their hatred. The restriction by an attribute or by a state indicates the permissibility of taking them when those are absent. "Ala" is transitive to one object by means of a preposition: one says "I did not fall short in the matter" (mā alawtu fī al-amr), meaning I did not fall short in it. It was said: "khabālan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz) transferred from the object, like His words, ﴿And We caused the earth to gush forth springs﴾ [al-Qamar 54:12]. The estimate is: "they will not spare you corruption," meaning "in your corruption." So the original form of this object was the preposition. It was said: its accusative is by dropping a preposition, the estimate being: "they will not spare you in causing you confusion." It was said: its accusative is as a verbal noun in the position of a state. Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is that they do not fall short for you in what would be corruption for you. On this view, the verb has taken the pronoun directly by dropping the preposition "li," and "khabāl" by dropping "fī." Al-Zamakhshari said: one says "alā fī al-amr yaṣlū" when one falls short in it, then it was used with two objects in their saying "lā ālūka nuṣḥan" and "lā ālūka juhdan," by way of tadmīn (implicit meaning). The meaning is: I do not withhold from you sincere advice, and I do not diminish it for you. End of quotation.

﴿They wish for you what distresses you﴾. Ibn Jarir said: they wish your misguidance. Al-Zajjaj said: your hardship. Al-Raghib said: al-mu'ānada and al-mu'ānata are close in meaning, but mu'ānada is resistance, while mu'ānata is seeking hardship along with resistance. End of quotation. It is said "'anita" with the kasra on the "n," and its original sense is the re-breaking of a bone after it has been set. The "mā" in His words "mā 'anittum" is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyya), and this clause is a resumptive sentence (mustaʾnafa), as we have said of the one before it. They permitted that it be an attribute of "intimates," and a state of the pronoun in "they will not spare you," with "qad" implied along with it.

﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾. Abdullah read "qad badā" (with a masculine verb), because the subject is feminine in a metaphorical sense, or because it refers to the meaning of hatred (al-bughḍ). That is, they are not content with hating you in their hearts, until they declare it with their mouths. He mentioned "mouths" and not "tongues" to indicate that what they uttered fills their mouths, as one says "a word that fills the mouth" when one speaks boastfully with it. It was said: the meaning is that they cannot contain themselves, despite their restraint of themselves and their effort against it, so that what makes their hatred of the Muslims known does not escape their tongues. End of quotation.

When He mentioned what they hid of their love for the hardship of the believers, which is a report about an inner act, He mentioned what that inner act produced of a bodily act, namely the manifestation of hatred toward the believers in their speech. Thus they combined the hatred of the hearts with the spitefulness of the tongues. Then He mentioned that what they concealed of evil, harm to the believers, and hatred of them is greater than what appeared of them, so He said:

﴿What their breasts conceal is greater﴾, meaning more than what has appeared from them. The apparent meaning is that the manifestation of hatred from them is directed at the believers, meaning they showed hatred toward the believers. Qatada said: "hatred has already appeared" to their allies from among the hypocrites and disbelievers, because some of them became aware of it in others. It was said: it appeared by their acknowledgment after denial, and this is the description of one who openly declares. He attributed the concealment to the breasts figuratively, since they are the places of the hearts, which are what is concealed, as He said: ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded, but it is hearts within breasts that are blinded﴾ [al-Hajj 22:46].

﴿We have already made the signs clear to you﴾, meaning those that indicate the obligation of sincerity in religion, loyalty to the believers, and enmity toward the disbelievers.

﴿If you should use reason﴾, meaning: act upon what has been made clear to you. Or: if you are people of reason. God already knows that they are people of reason, but He attached it to this condition as a way of stirring the souls, like your saying "If you are a man, then do such-and-such." Ibn Jarir said: its meaning is: if you understand from God His command and His prohibition. It was said: if you understand, then do not befriend them, but treat them as enemies. It was said: the meaning of "in" (in) is the meaning of "idh" (since), meaning: since you are people of reason.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 113–118 (part 4 of 4):

﴿Here you are, you love them, yet they do not love you, while you believe in the whole Book.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 119] The discussion of its parallel, "Antum ula'i" (أنتم أولاء) in His saying: ﴿Here you are, you are the ones who argued﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 66], has already preceded, in terms of recitation (qira'a) and grammatical analysis (i'rab). Its summary here is that "ula'i" (أولاء) is a predicate (khabar) of "antum" (أنتم), and "tuhibbunahum" (تحبونهم) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), or a circumstantial clause (hal), or a relative clause (sila), provided that "ula'i" is a relative pronoun (mawsul) or a predicate of "antum", with "ula'i" being a vocative (munada); or "ula'i" is a second subject (mubtada' thani), with "tuhibbunahum" as its predicate, and the whole clause is a predicate of the first subject; or "ula'i" is in the accusative position, as in the example: "Ana Zaydan darabtuhu" (I, Zayd, I struck him), in which case it is an instance of "ishtighal" (the construction in which a verb is occupied with a pronoun referring back to the noun before it). In these two constructions, the demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah) refers to something other than what "antum" refers to, because "antum" addresses the believers, while "ula'i" points to the disbelievers. In the preceding possibilities, its referent and the referent of "antum" are one and the same, namely the believers.

On the reading of "tuhibbunahum" as a resumptive clause, nothing forms a subject and predicate with what precedes it except by supposing an implied descriptive phrase, whose estimate is: "You are those who err in befriending non-believers, since you love them while they do not love you." This is an explanation of their error in their allegiance, in that they give love to those who hate them. The pronoun of the object in "tuhibbunahum" was said by some to refer to the hypocrites among the Jews, and in al-Zamakhshari, to the hypocrites among the People of the Book. What appears to be the case is that it refers to a close circle (bitana) from among those other than the believers, so it is every hypocrite, including the hypocrites among the polytheists.

The love (mahabba) here is the natural inclination (al-mayl bil-tab') toward kinship, fosterage and alliance; this was said by Ibn Abbas. Or it is for the sake of displaying faith and doing good to the believers; this was said by Abu al-Aliya. Or it is mercy toward them because of the sins that they commit; this was said by Qatada. Or it is the desire for their Islam; this was said by al-Mufaddal and al-Zajjaj. This last view is not good, because a rebuke does not occur on the basis of desiring the Islam of a disbeliever, or of friendship (al-musafat), since these are fruits of love.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 3, verses 113–118 (part 1 of 4):**

﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is a upright community who recite the signs of God in the night hours, and they prostrate.﴾ ﴿They believe in God and the Last Day, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds. These are among the righteous.﴾ ﴿Whatever good they do, they will not be denied its reward. God is Knowing of the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿Indeed, as for those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against God. They are the companions of the Fire, and they will abide in it forever.﴾ ﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life is like a wind containing bitter cold that strikes the tilth of a people who wronged themselves, and destroys it. God did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, do not take intimate companions from outside your own ranks. They will not fail to corrupt you; they wish you to suffer. Hatred has already shown from their mouths, and what their chests conceal is greater. We have already made the signs clear to you, if you understand.﴾ ﴿Here you are, loving them, though they do not love you, and you believe in the whole Scripture. When they meet you they say, "We believe," but when they are alone they bite their fingertips at you in rage. Say, "Die in your rage. Indeed God knows what is in the breasts."﴾ [Al-Imran: 119] ﴿If good touches you, it grieves them; if an evil befalls you, they rejoice at it. But if you are patient and God-fearing, their scheming will not harm you at all. Indeed God encompasses what they do.﴾ [Al-Imran: 120].

**Lexical notes:**

*Al-ānā'* (الآناء): the hours. The singular has several forms: *anyun* (أنْيٌ) like *ma'yun*, *anan* (أنى) like *fata*, *ann* (أنّى) like *nahhā*, *anyun* (أنْيٌ) like *zaby*, and *anwun* (أنْوٌ) like *jarw*.

*Al-ṣarr* (الصَّرُّ): intense, burning cold. It is also said that it means cold in the sense of *al-ṣarṣar* (the violent wind), as the poet said:
*"Do not wrong the Atawiyyin by striking them with a violent wind against the people of the encampments."*
Layla al-Akhyaliyya said:
*"He did not overcome the fierce adversary, nor fill the bowls with fat meat on a day of a violent, roaring wind."*
Ibn Kaysan said it is the sound of the flame of fire, which is the view preferred by al-Zajjaj, from *al-ṣarīr* (creaking). This is the sound in the saying *ṣarra al-shay'* (the thing creaked), and from it comes *al-rīḥ al-ṣarṣar* (the violent wind). Al-Zajjaj said: *al-ṣarr* is the sound of the fire that is in the wind.

*Al-biṭāna* (البِطانَة): the lining of a garment, opposite to the outer layer. It is used metaphorically for the one whom a person chooses for close intimacy, like the undergarment and the covering. One says *baṭana fulān min fulān buṭūnan wa biṭāna* when he is particularly close to him and involved in his affairs. The poet said:
*"Those are my close friends, indeed my inner circle, and they are my trusted confidants above all relatives."*

*Alawtu fī al-amr* (ألوْتُ في الأمْرِ): I fell short in the matter. Zuhayr said:
*"After them came a people seeking to overtake them, but they did not do it, and they did not fall short."*
That is, they did not fail to act.

*Al-khabāl* and *al-khabal* (الخَبالُ والخَبَلُ): corruption affecting an animal. One says there is *khabal* in the legs of a horse, meaning a defect from unsteadiness, impairment, or madness. One says *khabalahu al-ḥubb*, meaning love corrupted him.

*Al-baghḍā'* (البَغْضاءُ): a verbal noun like *al-sarrā'* and *al-ba'sā'*. One says *bughida al-rajul* (the man was hated), so he is *baghīḍ*, and *abghaḍtuhu* (I hated him), meaning my dislike for him became intense.

*Al-afwāh* (الأفْواهُ): the mouths. Its singular in origin is *fūh*, but the Arabs did not use it; they said *fam*. There are nine dialect forms of *fam* mentioned in some grammar books.

*Al-‘aḍḍ* (العَضُّ): placing the teeth on something with force. The verb of this form is *ʿaḍḍa* with a kasra on the ʿayn, and it is with the *ḍād*. As for *ʿaẓẓ al-zamān* and *ʿaẓẓ al-ḥarb*, these are with the *ẓā'*, the sister of the *ṭā'*. The poet said:
*"And the biting of time, O son of Marwan, has left no wealth except what is stripped or shaven."*
*Al-ʿuḍḍ* (with a ḍamma on the ʿayn) is the fodder of city dwellers, like the dried produce and crushed date pits. One says *aʿaḍḍa al-qawm* when their camels eat *al-ʿaḍḍ*. A camel described as *ʿuḍāḍī* is fat, as if it were ascribed to that. *Al-ʿiḍḍ* (with a kasra) means a cunning man.

*Al-anāmil* (الأنامِلُ): plural of *unmula*, also pronounced with a fatha or ḍamma on the mīm. It means the fingertips. Ibn ʿĪsā said its origin is the known ant (*al-naml*), and it is compared to it in fineness and in quick movement. From it comes *rajul namil*, meaning a tale-bearer.

*Al-ghayḍ* (الغَيْضُ): verbal noun of *ghāḍa*. *Ghayḍ* is also a proper name.

*Al-faraḥ* (الفَرَحُ): joy, known. One says *fariḥa* with a kasra on the ʿayn.

*Al-kayd* (الكَيْدُ): cunning. *Kādahu yakīduhu* means he schemed against him, that is, deceived him by falsehood. Ibn Qutayba said its origin is hardship, from the saying *fulān yakīdu bi-nafsihi*, meaning he struggles with the pains of the death agony and the throes of death.

**Commentary on the verses:**

﴿They are not all alike, among the People of the Book, a upright community.﴾

*The occasion of revelation*: the conversion of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām and others of the Jews, and the statement of the disbelievers among their rabbis: "None believed in Muhammad except our worst people; if they were the best, they would not have abandoned the religion of their fathers." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and Ibn Jurayj.

The *wāw* in *"they are not"* (لَيْسُوا) refers to the People of the Book mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿If the People of the Book had believed, it would have been better for them. Some of them are believers, but most of them are defiant transgressors.﴾ [Al-Imran: 110]. The more correct view is that the *wāw* is a pronoun referring to the People of the Book, and *sawā'an* (سَواءً) is the predicate of *laysa*. The meaning: the People of the Book are not equal; among them are those who believed in their Scripture and in the Qur'an, from those who reached the law of Islam, or who were upright and died before they reached it.

﴿Among the People of the Book, a upright community﴾ is a subject and predicate. Al-Farrāʾ said: *ummatun* (أُمَّةٌ) is raised by *sawāʾ*, meaning the People of the Book are not equal. Among the People of the Book is a community described by what was mentioned, and a disbelieving community. This second clause, which balances the first, was omitted, and the first part indicates it, as in his saying:
*"I disobeyed the heart concerning her, though I listen to its command; I do not know whether its pursuit is right guidance."*
The estimated words are: *am ghayy* (or is it error), and it was omitted because *arushd* (is it right guidance) indicates it. He also said:
*"I see you; I do not know whether it is a worry I hold, while the one with worry has long been humbled and subdued."*
The estimate is: *am ghayruhu* (or is it something else). Al-Farrāʾ said: equality requires two things, as in ﴿equal for those who dwell there and the visitor﴾ [Al-Hajj: 25] and ﴿equal their living and their dying﴾ [Al-Jathiya: 21].

The view of al-Farrāʾ is weak in terms of the omission, and in terms of placing an apparent noun in place of a pronoun, since the estimate would be: "They are not equal; among them is a community that is upright, and a disbelieving community."

Abu ʿUbayda held that the *wāw* in *"laysū"* is a plural marker, not a pronoun, like its use in the poet's words:
*"They blame me for buying camels, my people, and all of them are most blameworthy."*
The subject of *laysa* is *ummatun qā'ima* (an upright community), meaning: it is not equal; among the People of the Book is an upright community described by what was mentioned, and a disbelieving community.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: what Abu ʿUbayda said is an error, rejected. End. He did not clarify the nature of the error, and it seems he thought the subject of *laysa* is only *ummatun qā'ima*, with nothing omitted. Then, since the purpose is not the difference among the upright community that follows, if an omitted element is estimated there, Abu ʿUbayda's view is not an error to be rejected. It was said: what Abu ʿUbayda said follows the dialect of *"akalūnī al-barāghīth"* (the fleas ate me), which is a poor dialect, and the Arabs are against it, so it should not be applied to it, along with its contradiction of the apparent meaning. End. Al-Suhaylī disputed the grammarians' statement that it is a weak dialect, noting that it appears often in the Hadith. The first parsing is the apparent one, namely that *"among the People of the Book is an upright community"* is a resumptive clause explaining the negation of equality, as in ﴿They enjoin what is right﴾ [Al-Tawba: 71] explaining His saying ﴿You are the best community﴾ [Al-Imran: 110]. The People of the Book here means the Jews and the Christians.

*Ummatun qā'ima* (an upright community), that is, one that is upright, from *aqamtu al-ʿūd fa-qāma* (I set the stick straight and it stood), meaning it became straight. Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and Ibn Jurayj said: just. Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda and al-Rabīʿ said: upright in the Book of God and its limits, guided. Al-Suddī said: obedient and devoted. All of these go back to the first view.

Ibn Masʿūd and al-Suddī said: the pronoun in *"laysū"* refers to the Jews and the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), since the mention of the Jews and of this community preceded in His saying: ﴿You are the best community﴾ [Al-Imran: 110]. On this view, "the Book" means the category of God's books, not only the known Torah and Gospel. The phrase *"among the People of the Book is an upright community"* means the people of the Qur'an. The apparent reading is that the pronoun refers to the People of the Book mentioned in His saying ﴿If the People of the Book had believed﴾ [Al-Imran: 110], because the pronouns referring to them follow one another, so the pronoun in *laysū* is likewise.

ʿAṭāʾ said: *"among the People of the Book is an upright community"* and the verse in full, meaning forty men from the people of Najran from the Arabs, thirty-two from the Abyssinians, and eight from the Romans, who were upon the religion of ʿĪsā and believed in Muhammad (ﷺ). Some of the Ansar were monotheists who performed ritual bathing from impurity, and they practised what they knew of the laws of the *ḥanīfiyya* (the pure monotheism) before the coming of the Prophet (ﷺ), until As'ad ibn Zurāra, al-Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr, Muḥammad ibn Maslama, and Qays ibn Ṣirma ibn Anas came to them from him.

﴿They recite the signs of God in the night hours, and they prostrate.﴾

He described the upright community as reciting the signs of God, and He expressed the recitation during the hours of the night as the *tahajjud* (night prayer) with the Qur'an. His saying *"and they prostrate"* is also a clause in the position of a description, conjoined to *"recite"*. He described them by reciting the Qur'an and by prostrating. The recitation of the Qur'an is done while standing, while in prostration recitation is not prescribed. The second description came as a nominal sentence to indicate emphasis through the repetition of the pronoun *"hum"*, and the *wāw* in *"yasjudūn"*, since a servant is nearest to his Lord when he is prostrating. He reported about the subject with the present tense. The first description also came in the present tense to indicate renewal. The second was joined to the first by *wāw* to show that that recitation was in prayer, so the recitation was not alone, nor was the prostration alone.

The apparent meaning of His words ﴿in the watches of the night﴾ is that it refers to all the hours of the night. Thus it is unlikely that this (I mean the recitation and the prostration) would come from every single person, and it would only come from a group. Some people stand in prayer at the beginning of the night, some at its end, and some after a sleep, then return to their sleep. So from all of them, in the cities and communities, the hours of the night are covered by standing in prayer, reciting the Qur'an, and prostrating. This was the practice of the early part of this community. People knew of standing in prayer during the first third of the last part of the night, or slightly before it, and few stood the whole night. Among the righteous there were those who made it a constant practice, and God mentioned moderation in this at the beginning of Surat al-Muzzammil. The "watches of the night" (āna' al-layl) means its hours. This was said by al-Rabi' and Qatada and others. Al-Suddi said it means its middle portion, which is the use of the whole for a part, since the middle is one member of the plural. It is reported from Mansur that it was revealed concerning those who prayed between the two evening prayers, which contradicts the apparent meaning of His words ﴿they recite the verses of God in the watches of the night﴾. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that it refers to the prayer of 'atama (the night prayer). He mentioned that the cause of its revelation was that the Prophet (ﷺ) was delayed in the 'atama prayer and was at the house of one of his wives. He did not come until the night had passed. When he came, some of us were praying and some were lying down, and he said: "Rejoice, for none of the People of the Book pray this prayer." For this reason Ibn Mas'ud mentioned that His words ﴿they are not all alike﴾ refer to the Jews and this community, which contradicts the apparent meaning. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿while they prostrate﴾ is that it refers to prostration in the prayer. It was said that prostration is used to express prayer, naming the whole by a noble part of it, just as prayer is expressed by bowing (ruku'). This was said by Muqatil, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, because recitation is not done in bowing or in prostration. According to this, the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), meaning they recite the verses of God while engaged in prayer. It was also said that it refers to the prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa). It was said that prostration means humility and submission. Al-Tabari and others held that it is a conjoined clause from the first statement, informing that they are also people of prostration. What makes this good is that the recitation was outside of prayer. According to this interpretation, outside of prayer, it is also a descriptive qualifier enumerated with the conjunction "wa", as you say: "Zayd the generous and the intelligent came to me." Some permitted, regarding His words ﴿and they prostrate﴾, that it be a circumstantial phrase both from the pronoun in (qā'ima) and from (umma), since it has been described as (qā'ima). So two views are established regarding this clause. One is that it has no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) and is a new independent sentence. The other view is that it has a place in the i'rab, either in the nominative, being in the position of a qualifier, or in the accusative, being in the position of a circumstantial phrase, either from the pronoun in (yatlūna), or from the pronoun in (qā'ima), or from (umma). This verse indicates encouragement to stand in prayer at night. There has come in the Book of God: ﴿And from the night, pray with it as a supererogatory act for you﴾ [al-Isra' 79], ﴿Is one who is devoutly obedient during the hours of the night, prostrating and standing﴾ [al-Zumar 9], ﴿O you who are wrapped up﴾ [al-Muzzammil 1], ﴿Stand [in prayer] through the night﴾ [al-Muzzammil 2]. And in the hadith: "O servant of God, do not be like so-and-so; he used to stand in prayer at night, then he abandoned it." And in it: "What a fine man is the servant of God, except that he does not stand in prayer at night." And much else. It is reported from a man of the Banu Shayba who used to study the scriptures: "We find a statement from the words of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic: Does the shepherd of camels and sheep think, when the night covers him, that he lies down [to sleep] like one who stands and prostrates in the night?"

(They believe in God and the Last Day, and enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong.) The explanation of such phrases has already been given.

﴿And they hasten to good deeds.﴾ Hastening to good arises from an intense desire for it, because whoever desires a matter rushes to it and to doing it, and prefers promptness over delay. There has come in a hadith: "Seize five before five: your youth before your old age, your health before your sickness, your leisure before your preoccupation, your life before your death, and your wealth before your poverty."

He, the Exalted, described them as those who, when called to something good, such as supporting the oppressed, relieving the distressed, or worshipping God, hasten to do it. The apparent sense of "they believe" is that it is a qualifying description, meaning reciting and believing. They allowed that the clause be a new independent sentence, or in the position of a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun in "they prostrate", or that it be an apposition to the prostration. It was said: because prostration here means faith. Al-Zamakhshari said: He described them with characteristics that were not found among the Jews, namely reciting the verses of God at night while prostrating, and believing in God, because their belief in Him was no belief at all, since they associated 'Uzayr with Him and disbelieved in some of the books and messengers but not others; and belief in the Last Day, because they described it contrary to its reality; and enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, because they were compromisers; and hastening to good deeds, because they were slow to them and not eager for them. End of his words, and it is good.

When He, the Exalted, mentioned this community, He described it with six attributes. The first: that they are steadfast (qā'ima), meaning upright on the straight path. Since steadfastness is a fixed attribute that does not change, it came in the form of the active participle. The second: the prayer at night, expressed by recitation and prostration, which is the worship by which one shows devotion to communing with God at night. The third: belief in God and the Last Day, which is what drives worship of God. He mentioned the Last Day because in it appear the effects of worshipping God through the great reward. Belief in the Last Day includes belief in the prophets, since they are the ones who informed about the existence and occurrence of this, which is possible in reason, so belief in it became obligatory. The fourth: enjoining what is right. The fifth: forbidding what is wrong. When they perfected themselves, they strove to perfect others through these two attributes. The sixth: hastening to good deeds, an attribute that includes their own particular deeds and the deeds that extend from them to others. These three attributes also arise from belief. Observe the excellent arrangement of these attributes: belief is placed in the middle, the attribute specific to the person in himself, namely prayer at night, is placed before it, and the two transitive attributes and the shared attribute come after it, all of them being results of belief.

﴿And those are among the righteous.﴾ This refers to those who combined these six attributes, meaning those described by these qualities who are among those whose conditions are good in the sight of God. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that by "the righteous" he means the Muslims. End of his words. His statement resembles the statement of Ibn 'Abbas from among the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). In what al-Zamakhshari said afterward: Rather, the apparent meaning is that describing someone as righteous carries an added value beyond describing him as a Muslim; that is why some prophets asked for this rank. God, the Exalted, said, relating about Solomon, upon our prophet and upon him be the best of prayers and the most complete peace: ﴿And admit me by Your mercy among Your righteous servants﴾ [al-Naml 19]. And God, the Exalted, said concerning Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And We had chosen him in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾ [al-Baqara 130]. And God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift, and We made each of them righteous﴾ [al-Anbiya' 72]. And God, the Exalted, said after mentioning Ishmael: ﴿And Idris and Dhu al-Kifl, all of them were of the patient﴾ [al-Anbiya' 85]. ﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy; indeed they were among the righteous﴾ [al-Anbiya' 86]. And He said: ﴿And the martyrs and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisa' 69].

The "min" (in "from the righteous") is partitive. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is also good for it to be for explaining the kind. End. Nothing had preceded it containing ambiguity that would make its kind clear.

﴿And whatever good they do, they will not be denied its reward.﴾ Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr read both verbs with the letter "ta'" (you), as address. They differed about who is addressed. Abu Hatim said: It refers back to His words ﴿you are the best nation﴾ [Al 'Imran 110], so it is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab) and its deviation. Makki said: The "ta'" in them is general, covering the whole community. What appears to be the case is that it is a turn (iltifat) to His words "a steadfast community". When He described them with noble attributes, He turned to them to reassure them and to win their affection, addressing them that whatever good you do, you will not be deprived of its reward. For this reason He limited it to "good" and did not mention evil, because this is a place of kindness toward them and compassion, while it is known that everything done, good or evil, has its promised consequence. This turn is supported, and that it refers back to ﴿a steadfast community﴾, by the reading with "ya'" (they), which is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, and 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr, and the choice of Abu 'Ubayd; the rest of Abu 'Amr's transmitters allowed a choice between "ta'" and "ya'". It is known in this reading that the pronoun refers to ﴿a steadfast community﴾, just as it refers in His words "they recite" and what follows. Kafara (to deny/reject) is transitive to one object, as in "kafara al-ni'ma" (he denied the favor). Here it has been used with the meaning of "hurma" (to be deprived), meaning you will not be deprived of its reward. And since His description as "Shakur" (Most Appreciative) has come in the sense of fully paying the reward, He negated of Himself the opposite of appreciation, which is denying the reward, meaning depriving of it.

﴿And God is Knowing of the righteous.﴾ Since the verse was about those described with beautiful attributes, and He informed that He rewards the doing of good, it was fitting to end the verse by mentioning His knowledge of the righteous, although He knows both the righteous and their opposites. The meaning of "Knowing of them" is that He will recompense them for their piety. In this there is a promise to the righteous and a warning to the negligent.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, their wealth and their children will never avail them against God at all.﴾ [Al 'Imran 10] The explanation of this sentence has already been given at the beginning of this surah.

﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ The explanation of a parallel to this sentence has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqara. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is clear: when He mentioned some of the conditions of the believers, He mentioned some of the conditions of the disbelievers, so that the difference between the two groups would become clear.

﴿The example of what they spend in this worldly life is like the example of a wind containing frost which strikes the crops of a people who have wronged themselves and destroys them.﴾ When He, the Exalted, mentioned that what the believers do of good is not denied its reward, but they will reap in the Hereafter the fruit of what they planted in this world, He began to explain the spending of the disbelievers, and gave for it a parable which required its nullification and its going to waste without return. Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning the expenditures and charities of the disbelievers. Muqatil said: concerning the spending of the lowly Jews on their scholars. It was said: concerning the spending of the polytheists on the day of Badr. It was said: concerning the spending of the hypocrites when they went out with the Muslims to fight the polytheists. Al-Zamakhshari said: He likened what they used to spend of their wealth in pursuit of nobility, glory, gaining praise, and good repute among people, not seeking thereby the face of God, to a crop that the cold has struck so that it became debris. It was said: it is what they draw near to God by, along with their disbelief. It was said: what they spent in hostility to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), because they did not achieve by spending it what they spent it for. End of his words.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is the image that forms in the mind of their spending, which they regard as an act of nearness to God, a seeking of reward, and a means of obtaining merit. Their spending will be nullified on the Day of Resurrection and become "scattered dust." Its disappearance is like the image that forms in the mind of a people's crop that has grown green and flourished, so that their hope in it was strengthened, and then a biting, scorching wind struck it and destroyed it. End of quotation. The apparent reading is that what is in His words, ﴿the likeness of what they spend﴾, is a relative pronoun (mawsula), and its returning pronoun (a'id) is omitted, meaning "what they spend" (yunfiquna-hu). The apparent reading is that what they spend is likened to the wind, and the meaning is that its likeness is to the tilth (harth). It was said that this is a compound simile (tashbih murakkab), in which the singular is not matched with the singular. A parallel to this has already passed in His words, ﴿Their likeness is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:17]. For this reason Tha'lab said: he began with the wind, while the meaning is referred to the tilth. This is the preference of al-Zamakhshari. It was also said: the comparison occurs between two things and two things. He mentioned one of the two compared items and left out the other. Then he mentioned one of the two things used for comparison, but not the one that corresponds to the first mentioned item, and left out the other. The two mentioned items point to the two omitted ones. This is the preference of Ibn 'Atiyya, who said: this is the utmost of eloquence and inimitability. Similar to this is His words, ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:171]. End of quotation. It is also permissible that there is an omitted modifying noun (mudaf) in the first part, its estimate being: "the likeness of the destruction of what they spend," or in the second part, its estimate being: "like the likeness of the destruction of a wind." It was said: it is permissible for "mā" to be verbal-noun (maṣdariyya), meaning "the likeness of their spending," so the intelligible is compared to the sensible, since the spending is compared to the wind. The apparent sense of His words "they spend" is that it refers to spending wealth. As-Suddi said: its meaning is that they spend from their words, which they conceal the opposite of. This is weakened by the fact that this verse concerns the disbelievers who openly declare, not the hypocrites who conceal. It was said: the object of the spending is their deeds, including disbelief and the like. These are like the wind in which is a biting cold, which nullified their deeds, every kinship they had and their acts of devotion through freeing slaves, just as the wind destroys the crop. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is a good view, were it not for the remoteness of the metaphor (isti'ara) in the word "spending." End of quotation. Al-Raghib said: some have said that "what they spend" is an expression for all their deeds, but he singled out spending because it is more apparent and more common. End of quotation.

Ibn Hurmuz and al-A'raj read tunfiquna with a "ta" (second-person address), on the sense of "say to them," and they used the singular for "wind" because it is specific to punishment, just as it is used singularly in His words, ﴿Rather, it is what you were hasting for: a wind﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:24], ﴿And if We sent a wind﴾ [al-Rum 30:51], ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a violent wind﴾ [al-Qamar 54:19], and ﴿the barren wind﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:41]. Likewise, the plural is specific to mercy: ﴿that He sends the winds as bringers of good tidings﴾ [al-Rum 30:46], ﴿And We sent the fertilizing winds﴾ [al-Hijr 15:22], ﴿He sends the winds as good news﴾ [al-A'raf 7:57]. For this reason it has been related: "O God, make them winds, and do not make them a wind." The word ṣirr is nominative as the subject of the preposition-phrase before it, since it is dependent on being an attribute (ṣifa) of the wind. If ṣirr means cold, which is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and as-Suddi, or the sound of the flame of fire, or the sound of a violent wind, then it is apparent that it is in the wind. If ṣirr is an attribute of the wind like ṣarṣar, then the meaning is that in it is a coldness, ṣirr, as you say "cold, cold" (bard bārid). The qualified noun is omitted and the attribute takes its place. Or the adverbial sense is a metaphor, in which the qualified noun is made a container for the attribute, as in the line: "And in the Most Merciful is sufficiency for the weak." And the saying of people: "If so-and-so wrongs me, then in God is sufficiency." The meaning is: "the Most Merciful is sufficient, and God is sufficient." This is remote.

His words ﴿that struck the tilth of a people﴾ are in the position of an attribute of the wind. He began first with the attribute by the preposition-phrase, then with the attribute by a clause. His words ﴿who wronged themselves﴾ are a clause in the position of an attribute of "a people." Its apparent meaning is that they wronged themselves through their sins, so the destruction was more severe, since it was a punishment for them.

A group of the people of knowledge have held that the calamities of this world are only due to the servant's sins. This is inferred from more than one verse of the Qur'an, so it follows from this that every tilth that the wind destroys belongs to one who has wronged himself. It was said: "they wronged themselves" means they sowed outside the season of sowing, that is, they placed the actions of cultivation outside their proper place, either in time or in the manner of work. These were singled out for mention because the tilth in such a case is more complete and more firmly established. Al-Mahdawi inclined to this view.

﴿And God did not wrong them﴾: al-Zamakhshari and others permitted that the pronoun returns to the spenders, meaning He did not wrong them by not accepting their expenditures, and that it returns to the owners of the tilth, meaning He did not wrong them by destroying their tilth, but they wronged themselves by committing sins. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the pronoun in "wronged them" refers to the disbelievers whose pronoun was mentioned in "they spend," and it does not refer to the people who own the tilth, because they were not mentioned so that it would return to them, nor to clarify their wrongdoing. Also His words, ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:57], indicate the present-tense action of those present. End of quotation. This is a good preference. It is read irregularly as wa-lākinna (with shadda), with its noun being "themselves," and the predicate "they wrong." The meaning is: they wrong themselves. The omission of this pronoun, though its omission in such a construction is rare, is made good by its being the end-rhyme (fāṣila) of a verse, for if it were stated explicitly this meaning would disappear. It is not permissible to think that the noun of lākinna is a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n) that was omitted, with "themselves" being an object of "they wrong," because the omission of this pronoun is specific to poetry.

﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimates (biṭāna) those outside your own who will not spare you corruption﴾. It was revealed concerning men from among the believers who associated with men of the Jews because of neighborliness, alliance, and foster-suckling. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said. He also said, with Qatada, as-Suddi and ar-Rabi': it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. God forbade the believers from them. He likened the close friend (ṣiddīq) of intimate sincerity to the garment that touches the inside of a person's body. It is called biṭāna (inner garment) and walīja (intimate). His words ﴿from outside your own﴾ are in the position of an attribute of biṭāna. Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "from outside the sons of your kind," and they are the Muslims. It was said: "from" is connected to His words "do not take." It was also said: "from" is extra (zā'ida), meaning "intimates outside you." The meaning is that they were forbidden to take as confidants (aṣfiyā') non-believers. This prohibition indicates the prohibition of employing protected non-Muslims (ahl al-dhimma) as secretaries, and of entrusting them with buying and selling, or appointing them as deputies. Umar reproached Abu Musa for employing a dhimmi as a scribe, and recited this verse to him. It was also said to Umar about a skilled scribe from the Christians of al-Hira: "Will he not write for you?" He said: "Then I would be taking an intimate."

The clause ﴿who will not spare you corruption﴾ has no place in grammatical analysis, since it came as an explanation of the state of the disbelieving intimate, together with the clauses that follow it, to repel the believers from taking them as intimates. Whoever holds that it is an attribute of "intimates" or a state (ḥāl) of what "from" is connected to is far from the understanding of eloquent speech, because they were forbidden from taking disbelieving intimates, and then He drew attention to things they were doing: seeking to cause harm to the believers, wishing them hardship, and the manifestation of their hatred. The restriction by an attribute or by a state indicates the permissibility of taking them when those are absent. "Ala" is transitive to one object by means of a preposition: one says "I did not fall short in the matter" (mā alawtu fī al-amr), meaning I did not fall short in it. It was said: "khabālan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz) transferred from the object, like His words, ﴿And We caused the earth to gush forth springs﴾ [al-Qamar 54:12]. The estimate is: "they will not spare you corruption," meaning "in your corruption." So the original form of this object was the preposition. It was said: its accusative is by dropping a preposition, the estimate being: "they will not spare you in causing you confusion." It was said: its accusative is as a verbal noun in the position of a state. Ibn 'Atiyya said: its meaning is that they do not fall short for you in what would be corruption for you. On this view, the verb has taken the pronoun directly by dropping the preposition "li," and "khabāl" by dropping "fī." Al-Zamakhshari said: one says "alā fī al-amr yaṣlū" when one falls short in it, then it was used with two objects in their saying "lā ālūka nuṣḥan" and "lā ālūka juhdan," by way of tadmīn (implicit meaning). The meaning is: I do not withhold from you sincere advice, and I do not diminish it for you. End of quotation.

﴿They wish for you what distresses you﴾. Ibn Jarir said: they wish your misguidance. Al-Zajjaj said: your hardship. Al-Raghib said: al-mu'ānada and al-mu'ānata are close in meaning, but mu'ānada is resistance, while mu'ānata is seeking hardship along with resistance. End of quotation. It is said "'anita" with the kasra on the "n," and its original sense is the re-breaking of a bone after it has been set. The "mā" in His words "mā 'anittum" is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyya), and this clause is a resumptive sentence (mustaʾnafa), as we have said of the one before it. They permitted that it be an attribute of "intimates," and a state of the pronoun in "they will not spare you," with "qad" implied along with it.

﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾. Abdullah read "qad badā" (with a masculine verb), because the subject is feminine in a metaphorical sense, or because it refers to the meaning of hatred (al-bughḍ). That is, they are not content with hating you in their hearts, until they declare it with their mouths. He mentioned "mouths" and not "tongues" to indicate that what they uttered fills their mouths, as one says "a word that fills the mouth" when one speaks boastfully with it. It was said: the meaning is that they cannot contain themselves, despite their restraint of themselves and their effort against it, so that what makes their hatred of the Muslims known does not escape their tongues. End of quotation.

When He mentioned what they hid of their love for the hardship of the believers, which is a report about an inner act, He mentioned what that inner act produced of a bodily act, namely the manifestation of hatred toward the believers in their speech. Thus they combined the hatred of the hearts with the spitefulness of the tongues. Then He mentioned that what they concealed of evil, harm to the believers, and hatred of them is greater than what appeared of them, so He said:

﴿What their breasts conceal is greater﴾, meaning more than what has appeared from them. The apparent meaning is that the manifestation of hatred from them is directed at the believers, meaning they showed hatred toward the believers. Qatada said: "hatred has already appeared" to their allies from among the hypocrites and disbelievers, because some of them became aware of it in others. It was said: it appeared by their acknowledgment after denial, and this is the description of one who openly declares. He attributed the concealment to the breasts figuratively, since they are the places of the hearts, which are what is concealed, as He said: ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded, but it is hearts within breasts that are blinded﴾ [al-Hajj 22:46].

﴿We have already made the signs clear to you﴾, meaning those that indicate the obligation of sincerity in religion, loyalty to the believers, and enmity toward the disbelievers.

﴿If you should use reason﴾, meaning: act upon what has been made clear to you. Or: if you are people of reason. God already knows that they are people of reason, but He attached it to this condition as a way of stirring the souls, like your saying "If you are a man, then do such-and-such." Ibn Jarir said: its meaning is: if you understand from God His command and His prohibition. It was said: if you understand, then do not befriend them, but treat them as enemies. It was said: the meaning of "in" (in) is the meaning of "idh" (since), meaning: since you are people of reason.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 113–118 (part 4 of 4):

﴿Here you are, you love them, yet they do not love you, while you believe in the whole Book.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 119] The discussion of its parallel, "Antum ula'i" (أنتم أولاء) in His saying: ﴿Here you are, you are the ones who argued﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 66], has already preceded, in terms of recitation (qira'a) and grammatical analysis (i'rab). Its summary here is that "ula'i" (أولاء) is a predicate (khabar) of "antum" (أنتم), and "tuhibbunahum" (تحبونهم) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), or a circumstantial clause (hal), or a relative clause (sila), provided that "ula'i" is a relative pronoun (mawsul) or a predicate of "antum", with "ula'i" being a vocative (munada); or "ula'i" is a second subject (mubtada' thani), with "tuhibbunahum" as its predicate, and the whole clause is a predicate of the first subject; or "ula'i" is in the accusative position, as in the example: "Ana Zaydan darabtuhu" (I, Zayd, I struck him), in which case it is an instance of "ishtighal" (the construction in which a verb is occupied with a pronoun referring back to the noun before it). In these two constructions, the demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah) refers to something other than what "antum" refers to, because "antum" addresses the believers, while "ula'i" points to the disbelievers. In the preceding possibilities, its referent and the referent of "antum" are one and the same, namely the believers.

On the reading of "tuhibbunahum" as a resumptive clause, nothing forms a subject and predicate with what precedes it except by supposing an implied descriptive phrase, whose estimate is: "You are those who err in befriending non-believers, since you love them while they do not love you." This is an explanation of their error in their allegiance, in that they give love to those who hate them. The pronoun of the object in "tuhibbunahum" was said by some to refer to the hypocrites among the Jews, and in al-Zamakhshari, to the hypocrites among the People of the Book. What appears to be the case is that it refers to a close circle (bitana) from among those other than the believers, so it is every hypocrite, including the hypocrites among the polytheists.

The love (mahabba) here is the natural inclination (al-mayl bil-tab') toward kinship, fosterage and alliance; this was said by Ibn Abbas. Or it is for the sake of displaying faith and doing good to the believers; this was said by Abu al-Aliya. Or it is mercy toward them because of the sins that they commit; this was said by Qatada. Or it is the desire for their Islam; this was said by al-Mufaddal and al-Zajjaj. This last view is not good, because a rebuke does not occur on the basis of desiring the Islam of a disbeliever, or of friendship (al-musafat), since these are fruits of love.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 119:

﴿And you believe in the Book, all of it﴾. Al-Kitab (the Book) is a generic noun, meaning the revealed books; this is what Ibn 'Abbas said. Whether it refers to the Torah and the Gospel, or to the Torah alone, there are three opinions. There is also an omitted clause, whose estimated sense is: "and you do not believe in it, all of it; rather, they say: we believe in part and disbelieve in part." What indicates this is the affirmation of the counterpart in "you love them, but they do not love you." The waw in "wa-tu'minuna" is for conjunction with "tuhibbunahum," so it has whatever i'rab (grammatical analysis) belongs to it. Al-Zamakhshari said: the waw in "wa-tu'minuna" is for the state (hal), and its position as an accusative is from "la yuhibbunakum," meaning: they do not love you, while the state is that you believe in their Book, all of it, and yet they hate you. So why do you love them when they do not believe in any part of your Book? In this there is severe rebuke, that they are firmer in their falsehood than you are in your truth, and the like. [Quran 4:104]: ﴿Indeed they feel pain as you feel pain, and you hope from Allah for what they do not hope.﴾ End of his words. And it is good. However, it contains grammatical craft that weakens it: he made the waw in "wa-tu'minuna" a waw of the state, and that it is in the accusative from (p-41) "la yuhibbunakum." A affirmative present-tense verb, when it occurs as a state, does not take the waw of the state. You say: "Zayd came laughing (jaa'a Zaydun yadhhaku)," and it is not permitted to say "wa-yadhhaku." As for their saying "qumtu wa-asukku 'aynahu (I stood up while I was striking his eye)," it is in the extreme of rarity. It has been interpreted as an omitted subject, meaning: "I stood up while I was striking his eye," so the clause becomes a nominal clause. This interpretation may apply here too, meaning: "they do not love you while you believe in the Book, all of it," but the preferable reading is what we mentioned, that it is for conjunction. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "wa-tu'minuna bil-kitabi kullihi" requires that the verse concerns the hypocrites among the Jews, not the hypocrites of the Arabs. This is objected to: the hypocrites of the Jews are not known to have professed belief outwardly in an absolute way while disbelieving inwardly, as the hypocrites of the Arabs did, except what is reported about the matter of Zayd ibn al-Sayf al-Qaynuqa'i. So nothing remains except that their saying "amanna" means "we affirm that he is a prophet sent to you." That is: "remain upon your religion, and we are your allies and brothers, and we conceal toward you nothing but affection." For this reason some believers would take them as intimate companions (bitana). This is a position that is known to have been held by many Jews. What indicates this interpretation is that the counterpart to their saying "amanna" is biting the fingertips out of rage, and there is nothing in it that requires apostasy, as in His saying: ﴿And when they meet with those who believe, they say: we believe; but when they are alone with their devils, they say: indeed we are with you﴾ [2:14]; rather, it indicates hatred and lack of affection. Abu al-Jawza, when he recited this verse, would say: "They are the Ibadiyya." This attribute may continue to apply to people of innovation until the Day of Resurrection. End of his words.

What he mentioned, that it is not known of the Jewish hypocrites that they professed belief outwardly in an absolute way while disbelieving inwardly, except what is reported about Zayd's matter, is open to question, for it has been reported that a group of them relied upon this; al-Bayhaqi and others mentioned it. Even if this were reported only of Zayd al-Qaynuqa'i, there would still be blame on them for it, since it was found in their kind. The Arabs often praise or blame a whole tribe for the act of one of its members. Confirming that this came from the Jews is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And a group of the People of the Book said: believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end﴾ [3:72].

﴿And when they meet you, they say: we believe﴾. This statement follows from their dispute over the Torah, their concealment, and their wickedness, since they did not mention the object of belief, but they give the believers the impression by this wording that they are believers.

﴿And when they are alone﴾: that is, some of them are alone with others and withdraw without you. The meaning: their gatherings are empty of you, so the being alone is attributed to them by way of metaphor (majaz).

﴿They bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾. Its apparent meaning is that this act occurs, and that biting of the fingertips does happen from them because of intense rage while unable to carry out what they wish. From this is the saying of Abu Talib:

"They have made peace with a people against us, stingy ones who bite behind us with their thumbs."

Another said:

"When they see me, may Allah prolong their rage, they bite from anger the tips of the thumbs."

Another said:

"Qays witnessed, yet their help was not for Qutayba except biting it with the thumbs."

Al-Harith ibn Zalim al-Murri said:

"And there came to us low, base, humbled peoples who bite from rage the heads of the thumbs."

The enraged and the regretful are described by biting the fingertips, the fingers, and the thumbs. This biting is with the teeth, and it is a bodily posture that follows the state of an angry soul, just as striking one hand upon the other follows the state of a soul distressed over something about to escape, and as the grinding of the teeth is a posture that follows the state of a regretful soul, and beyond that, such as counting pebbles or drawing lines on the ground for one who is grieved, and the like. It is possible that there is no actual biting of fingertips, and that it is a figurative expression (majaz al-tamthil), by which is expressed intense rage and grief over what escapes them of harming you. By this verse Allah draws attention that whoever has these attributes, namely hatred of the believers, disbelief in the Qur'an, and show-off by displaying what his inner self does not hold, is worthy of not being taken as a friend.

﴿Say: die in your rage﴾. Its apparent meaning is that he was commanded to say this to them. It is an imperative form, and its meaning is supplication: Allah permitted His Prophet to invoke against them when he despaired of their faith. This is the view of al-Tabari. Many exegetes said: he may supplicate against them directly. It was also said: he and his community were commanded to confront them with this. On this view the meaning of supplication disappears and the meaning of reproach remains, as Ibn 'Atiyya said. It was also said: its form is an imperative, but its meaning is a statement, and the "bi" (with) is for the state, meaning: you will die while your rage is with you, and this is by way of censure for the evil they have done. Al-Zamakhshari said: he invoked against them that their rage increase until they perish by it. What is meant by the increase of rage is what angers them of the strength of Islam and the honor of its people, and what they have of humiliation, disgrace and ruin in that. End of his words.

What he explained is not the apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿Say: die in your rage﴾; and what al-Zamakhshari said resembles the saying: "die of your disease," meaning: may Allah keep your disease until you die of it. But in al-Zamakhshari's wording there is an addition of the increase of rage, which the wording of the Qur'an does not indicate. Some of our shaykhs said: this is not a definite command, because if it were a command they would have died at once, as it came: ﴿Then Allah said to them: die﴾ [2:243]. Nor is it a supplication, because if he had been commanded to supplicate they would all have died in this state, for his supplication is not rejected; yet many of them believed after this verse. Nor is it a statement, because if it were a statement of an event with a ruling it would inform of it, meaning that no one had believed after it; rather it is a command whose meaning is reproach and rebuke, like His saying: ﴿Do what you will﴾ [41:40], and "If you feel no shame, then do what you like." It was said: it may also be that there is no saying at all, but that it is a command to good spirits, strong hope, and rejoicing in the promise of Allah that they will perish of rage at the strengthening of Islam and their humiliation by it, as if it were said: speak to yourself with this.

﴿Indeed Allah is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾. It was said: it may be part of what is said, and the meaning: inform them of what they conceal of biting their fingertips out of rage when they are alone, and say to them: indeed Allah knows what is more hidden than what you conceal among yourselves, namely the secrets within the breasts, so do not think that any of your secrets is hidden from Him. It may also be that it is not included in the saying, and its meaning: say that to them, and do not marvel at my informing you of what they conceal, for I know what is more hidden than that, namely the secrets of their breasts, which they have not shown by their tongues. The first is the apparent one, and it is given as a threat addressed to them.

The word dhat is a homonym (mushtarak), and its meaning here is that it is the feminine of "dhu" in the sense of "possessor." So its original form here is: "Knowing of the hidden things that possess the breasts," then the modified noun was omitted and the attribute came to stand in its place. The meaning of "companion of the breasts" is that it clings to them and never separates from them, as you say: "So-and-so is the companion of so-and-so," and from this: "the companions of Paradise, the companions of the Fire." They differed over stopping on "dhat." Al-Akhfash, al-Farra' and Ibn Kaysan said: with a taa (ت), out of regard for the orthography of the Mushaf. Al-Kisa'i and al-Jirmi said: with a haa (ه), because it is the taa of feminine marking.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 3, verse 120:**

﴿If good befalls you, it distresses them; and if evil befalls you, they rejoice at it.﴾ *Al-hasanah* (the good) here means whatever pleases, such as ease, abundance, victory, spoils of war, and similar benefits. *Al-sayyi'ah* (the evil) is the opposite of that. By this, God, exalted is He, explained the extent of their enmity: they are distressed by whatever good reaches the believers, and they rejoice at whatever hardship befalls them. Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-mass* (touching) is used metaphorically for the meaning of *al-isabah* (reaching), so the meaning is one. Do you not see His saying: ﴿If good reaches you, it distresses them; and if a calamity reaches you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 50], and ﴿Whatever good reaches you is from God, and whatever evil reaches you is from yourself﴾ [al-Nisa': 79], and ﴿When evil touches him, he is distressed; and when good touches him, he withholds﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 20]? Ibn 'Atiyyah said: God mentioned *al-mass* with the good so as to show that even the slightest touch of good causes distress to the souls of these haters. Then He balanced this with the word *al-isabah* for the evil, which is an expression for taking hold (*al-tamakkun*), because a thing that reaches another thing has power over it or is in it. This eloquent form indicates the intensity of enmity, for it is a rancour that does not depart even when hardships descend; rather, they rejoice at the descent of hardships upon the believers. End of his words.

The indefinite noun here, in the context of a conditional, is general in the sense of distributive generality (*'umum al-badal*). It was not made definite, to convey the vagueness of a specific reference and to convey all-inclusive generality. He set *al-hasanah* against *al-sayyi'ah*, and *al-masa'ah* (distress) against *al-farah* (rejoicing), which is a striking antithesis.

Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Ibn Juraij said: the good is your victory over the enemy, spoils taken from them, the successive entry of people into your religion, and the prosperity of your livelihood. The evil is the failure of a detachment from you, or an enemy's striking at some of you, or discord among you. Al-Hasan said: the good is harmony and unity of word, and the evil is the enemy's striking and disunity of word. Ibn Qutaybah said: *al-hasanah* is blessing, and *al-sayyi'ah* is calamity. These statements are by way of example, not by way of specification.

﴿But if you are patient and mindful of God, their scheming will not harm you at all.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: if you are patient under their harm and mindful of God, and do not despair, and do not weary of their harm, even when it is repeated. Muqatil said: if you are patient in obeying God's command and mindful of their secret dealings (*mubatanatahum*). Ibn 'Abbas also said: if you are patient in faith and mindful of polytheism. It was also said: if you are patient in obedience and mindful of sins. And it was said: if you are patient in fighting them.
