What appears to be the case is that the object of the patience and the object of the mindfulness are not mentioned here. Patience is restraining the self upon what is disliked, and mindfulness is taking a protection against the punishment of God. So it is fitting that the omitted object be estimated to be of the same kind as what is indicated by the word *al-sabr* (patience) and the word *al-taqwa* (mindfulness). In this there is good news for the believers, strengthening of their souls, and guidance toward seeking help against the enemy's scheming through patience and mindfulness.

The majority read ﴿tamsaskum﴾ with a *ta'* (feminine). Al-Sulami read it with a *ya'* dotted from below, because the feminine gender of *hasanah* is metaphorical. The two Harami imams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), Abu 'Amr, and Hamza in one transmission read ﴿la yadurrukum﴾ from *dara yadiru* (to harm). It is also said *dara yadooru*, and both have the meaning of *darra* (to harm). The Kufans and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿la yadurrukum﴾ with a *damma* on the *dad* and a shadda on the *ra'*, from *darra yadurru*. It has been disputed whether the vowel on the *ra'* is a grammatical inflection (*i'rab*, the marking of case) indicating that the verb is indicative (marfu'), or a vowel of harmonisation (*harakat ittiba'*) with the *damma* of the *dad*, in which case the verb is jussive (majzum), like your saying *madda* (?). This was attributed to Sibawayh, and the inflection then came out as an anticipation (*al-taqdim*), with the estimate: ﴿it will not harm you that you be patient﴾; and this view was attributed to Sibawayh. It also came out on the basis that *la* means *laysa* (is not), with the *fa'* (then) omitted, and the estimate: ﴿so it does not harm you﴾; this was said by al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i. 'Asim, as transmitted by Abu Zayd from al-Mufaddal from him, read with a *damma* on the *dad* and a *fatha* on the shadda'd *ra'*. This is better than the reading with a *damma* on the *ra'*, like *lam yarudda Zayd* (Zayd did not return), and the *fatha* is the more common and widely used. Al-Dahhak read with a *damma* on the *dad* and a *kasra* on the shadda'd *ra'*, on the basis of the meeting of two consonants (*iltiqa' al-sakinayn*). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: as for the *kasra*, I do not know it as a reading; al-Zajjaj's expression on this is figurative, for it appears from the course of his speech that it is a reading. End of his words. It is indeed a reading, as we mentioned from al-Dahhak. Ubayy read ﴿la yadrurkum﴾ without assimilation (*fakk al-idgham*), and this is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and according to it in the verse is ﴿tamsaskum﴾. The dialect of the rest of the Arabs is assimilation in all of this.

﴿Indeed God is encompassing of what they do.﴾ Whoever reads with the *ya'* (*ya'maluna*, "they do") it is a warning, and the meaning is: His requital encompasses them. He expressed by *al-ihatah* (encompassing) complete awareness, power and dominion. Whoever reads with the *ta'* (*ta'maluna*, "you do") — and this is al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan — then it is by *al-iltifat* (the shift of address) to the disbelievers, or by an implied "say to them, O Muhammad", or on the basis that it is an address to the believers that includes a threat against them for taking a *bitanah* (inner circle of confidants) from among the disbelievers.

They said: these verses include various types of eloquence and fluency. Among them: the joining and separation (*al-wasl wa al-qat'*) in ﴿They are not all alike: of the People of the Book is a upright community﴾ [Al 'Imran: 113]. The repetition in ﴿They are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Al 'Imran: 116]. The turning away from the active participle to another form in *yatluna* (they recite) and what follows it, and in *yazlimun* (they wrong). The sufficiency of mentioning part of a thing instead of the whole when there is an indication of the rest in ﴿They believe in God and the Last Day﴾ [Al 'Imran: 114]. The antithesis (*al-muqabalah*) in *ta'murun* (you enjoin) and *tunhawna* (you are forbidden), and in *al-ma'ruf* (the right) and *al-munkar* (the wrong). It may be a moral antithesis (*tibaq ma'nawi*), and in *hasanah* and *sayyi'ah*, and in *tasu'hum* (it distresses them) and *yafrahu* (they rejoice). The specification in ﴿Knower of what is in the breasts﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119]. The simile in ﴿the likeness of what they spend﴾ [Al 'Imran: 117], and in *bitanah* [Al 'Imran: 118], and in ﴿they bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119] according to one of the two interpretations, and in ﴿if good touches you﴾ and ﴿if evil reaches you﴾. Their occurrence was likened to touching and reaching, and this is from the type of likening the intelligible to the perceptible; and the correct view is that this is a metaphor. In *muhit* (encompassing), the power over things and the knowledge of them was likened to a thing surrounding another thing from all its sides, and this is from (p-44) the likening of the intelligible to the perceptible. The paronomasia of identical roots (*al-tajnis al-mumathil*) in ﴿zalamahum﴾ and ﴿yazlimun﴾, and in ﴿you love them and they do not love you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119], in *tu'minun* (you believe) and *amanna* (we believed), and in ﴿out of rage﴾ and ﴿in your rage﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119]. The *iltifat* (shift of address): in ﴿whatever good you do, it will not be denied you﴾ according to the reading of him who reads with the *ta'*, and in ﴿what you do is encompassing﴾ [Hud: 92] according to one of the two aspects. The naming of a thing by the name of its place in ﴿out of their mouths﴾ [Al 'Imran: 118], where he expressed by it the tongues, because they are the place of them. And ellipsis in several places.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 121:

﴿And when you set out in the morning from your family to station the believers at their positions for the battle, and Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿When two groups among you were about to lose heart, though Allah was their ally; and in Allah let the believers put their trust.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 122] ﴿Allah had already given you victory at Badr, when you were weak. So be mindful of Allah, that you may give thanks.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 123] ﴿When you said to the believers, "Will it not suffice you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 124] ﴿Yes! If you are patient and mindful, and they come at you suddenly, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels, marked out.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 125] ﴿Allah did not make this except as good news for you, and so that your hearts might be at rest; and victory comes only from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 126] ﴿That He might cut off a part of those who disbelieved, or subdue them, so that they turn back frustrated.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 127].

Ghada al-rajulu (غَدا الرَّجُلُ): he went out in the early morning (ghudwa). Al-ghudu (الغُدُوُّ) occurs at the beginning of the day. Regarding the use of ghada in the sense of "became" (ṣāra), there is a difference of opinion as to whether it is then a defective (nāqiṣ) verb.

Al-hamm (الهَمُّ): what falls short of resolve; its verb is hamma yahummu. The Arabs say hamamtu and hamtu, dropping one of the two doubled letters, just as they say amasttu, zaltu and ahastu for massastu, zalaltu and ahsastu. The first thing that passes through the heart is called khāṭir (passing thought). If it recurs, it becomes ḥadīth al-nafs (inner speech). If its doing becomes preponderant, it becomes hamm (intention). If it grows strong and intense, it becomes ʿazm (resolve). When resolve grows strong and intense, the act or the utterance takes place.

Al-fashal (الفَشَلُ): in the body, it is exhaustion (iʿyāʾ); in war, cowardice and feebleness; in judgement, incapacity and corruption. Its verb is fashila, with the shīn vowelled with kasra.

Al-tawakkul (التَّوَكُّلُ): a form of tafaʿʿul from wakkala amrahu ilā fulān, when he entrusted his affair to him. Ibn Faris said: it is the display of incapacity and reliance on another; one says, "Fulān is wakala tukala," meaning he is helpless in all his affairs and depends on another. It has also been said that it derives from wikāla, which is the entrusting of an affair to another out of confidence in his good management.

Badr (بَدْرٌ) in the verse: a proper name for the place between Makkah and Madinah. It was so named for its clearness (ṣafāʾ), or because the full moon (al-badr) was seen there for its clearness, or for its roundness (istidāra). It is said that it was named after its owner, Badr ibn Kaladah. It is said, rather, [after] Badr ibn Bajil ibn al-Nadr ibn Kinanah. It is said it is a well belonging to Ghifar. It is said it is the name of the valley of al-Ṣafrāʾ. It is said it is the name of a village between Madinah and al-Jār.

Al-fawr (الفَوْرُ): haste and hurry. One says, "Do this at once (ʿalā al-fawr)." Its origin is from fārat al-qidr, when the cooking pot boils intensely and what is in it hastens to come out; and it is said, "fāra ghaḍabuhu," when his anger surges and moves. One says, "He went out at once (min fawrihi)," meaning immediately, without delay. Al-fawr was used metaphorically for speed, and then that state was named by it, the state in which there is no doubt and no turning aside to anything by its doer.

Al-khamsah (الخَمْسَةُ): a known rank of number, and from it the derived form fāʿala is formed; one says, "I made the four into five (khammastu al-arbaʿata)," meaning I made them into a group of five.

Al-ṭarf (الطَّرْفُ): the last edge of a thing; then it is used for a piece of a thing, even if it is not a final edge. Al-kabt (الكَبْتُ): defeat. It has been said: felling on the face or onto the two hands. Al-Naqqash and others said: the tāʾ (in yakbitahum) is a substitute for a dāl; its origin is kabbadahu, meaning he did an act that harmed his liver (kabid). Al-khaybah (الخَيْبَةُ): the failure to attain what is sought.

﴿And when you set out in the morning from your family to station the believers at their positions for the battle﴾. Al-Miswar ibn Makhramah said: I said to ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, "O uncle, tell me about your story on the day of Uhud." He said: "Recite the hundred and twentieth [verse] of Al 'Imran, and you will find: ﴿And when you set out in the morning from your family﴾ up to ﴿Then He sent down upon you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 154]."

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He forbade them from taking intimate companions from among the disbelievers, and promised them that if they were patient and mindful, their plot would not harm them, He reminded them of a situation in which some of them complied and followed some of the hypocrites. This was what happened on the day of Uhud, when ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul withdrew from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and about three hundred men from the hypocrites followed him in withdrawing, along with others from the believers. The majority hold that this occurred in the battle of Uhud, and in it all these verses were revealed; this is the view of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, al-Zuhri, al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq. Al-Hasan said: this going out was in the battle of the Confederates (al-Aḥzab). This is the view of (p-45) Mujahid and Muqatil, and it is weak, because on the day of the Confederates the believers were victorious, and nothing of what is mentioned in these verses occurred in it; rather, the two accounts are different. Al-Hasan also said: this going out was on the day of Badr. The exegetes mentioned the story of the battle of Uhud, and it is fully recorded in the books of biography (al-siyar); we will mention from it only what is related to the wording of the verse, to some extent, when explaining it. The apparent meaning of His words, "﴿And when you set out﴾", is his going out in the morning from among his family. It has been explained as his going out from the chamber of ʿAʾishah on Friday in the morning, when he consulted the people. Some advised remaining and not going out to fight, and that if the polytheists came they would fight them in Madinah, and this was his own opinion; and some advised going out, a group of the righteous believers who had missed the battle of Badr. According to this view, the stationing of the believers at their positions for the battle means dividing the sides of Madinah among the tribes of the Ansar. It has also been said: his going out was his rising on Friday after the prayer, and his stationing them at the time of the presence of battle; he called it "going out" because he had resolved upon it in the morning. It has been said: his going out was on Saturday for the battle. Since that night did not coincide with the going out, it is as if he was with his family. The governing element of "idh" (when) is "udhkur" (remember). It has been said: it is coordinated with His words, ﴿There has been a sign for you in the two hosts that met﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 13], meaning "and a sign, when you set out." This is extremely remote, and were it not recorded in the books I would not have mentioned it. Likewise is the view of one who makes "min" mean "maʿa" (with), meaning "and when you set out with your family." These are interpretations which he proposes and transmits by way of conjecture, by one who has no insight into the language of the Arabs.

The meaning of tubawwi' (تُبَوِّئُ) is "you lodge," from al-mabaʾah, which is the place of return. From it is His words, ﴿We will surely lodge them in the Garden in lofty chambers﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 58], and "let him take his seat in the Fire" (fal-yatabawwa' maqʿadahu min al-nār). The poet said:

How many a righteous companion of mine I lodged with my own hands in the grave (laḥd).

And al-Aʿsha said:

And the Merciful did not lodge your house in a dwelling / to the east of the heights of al-Ṣafa and al-Muḥarram.

Maqāʿid (مَقاعِدُ) is the plural of maqʿad, which there means the place of sitting. The meaning is: positions and stations. Al-maqʿad and al-maqām have been used in the sense of place, as in: ﴿in a seat of truth﴾ [al-Qamar: 55] and ﴿before you rise from your place﴾ [al-Naml: 39].

Al-Zamakhshari said: qaʿada and qāma have been extended until they are treated as ṣāra (to become). End of quotation. As for treating qaʿada as ṣāra, our companions (the grammarians) said: it occurs only in one word, which is anomalous and does not extend; it is in their saying, "He sharpened his blade until it became (qaʿadat) like a spear," meaning it became. The Zamakhshari's interpretation of His words, ﴿so that you sit reproached﴾ [al-Isra': 29], as meaning "so that you become," has been criticised, because that does not apply generally according to the grammarians. In Abu ʿUmar al-Zahid's al-Yawaqit, Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: al-qaʿd means becoming, and the Arabs say, "Fulan sat as a commander after he had been commanded," meaning he became. As for treating qāma as ṣāra, I know of no one who counted it among the sisters of kāna, nor who mentioned that it comes in the sense of ṣāra, nor who mentioned a predicate for it except Abu ʿAbd Allah ibn Hisham al-Hadrawi, who said, regarding the verse of the poet:

Upon what he has risen, a base man reviles me.

that it is one of the verbs of approximation. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the word al-quʿūd is more indicative of permanence, especially since the archers were only seated, and likewise the rows of the Muslims were at first; while the duellers and the vanguard were moving about. He used the plural maqāʿid because He designated for them positions in which they would stand, such as the right wing, the left wing, the centre, and the advance guard, and He made clear for each group their place where they would stand.

He (ﷺ) went out after the Friday prayer, and at dawn on Saturday, on the fifteenth of Shawwal, he was at the glen (al-shiʿb). He walked on foot and began arranging his companions for battle as if he were straightening arrows with an arrow-shaft. If he saw a man protruding, he said, "Step back." His descent was at the lower part of the valley, and he placed his back and his army toward Uhud, and he appointed ʿAbd Allah ibn Jubayr over the archers, and said to them, "Shoot arrows at them to repel them from us; let them not come at us from behind."

﴿Tubawwi'﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the addressee. It has been said: it is a presumed circumstance (ḥāl muqaddarah), meaning you went out intending the lodging, because the time of the going out was not the time of the lodging. Al-Jumhur read tubawwi' from bawwa'a. ʿAbd Allah read tubwi' from abwa'a; the majority treat it as transitive by doubling, while ʿAbd Allah treats it as transitive by the hamzah. Yahya ibn Wathhab read tabwā, on the pattern of taḥyā, making it transitive by the hamzah, and he eased the lām of the verb by changing the hamzah into a yā', like yuqri for yuqri'. ʿAbd Allah read "lil-mu'minin" with the genitive particle lām, in the sense of "you arrange and prepare." It appears that the original is that it is transitive to one object by itself and to the other by the lām, since its triliteral form is not transitive by itself but only by a preposition.

Al-Ashhab read "maqāʿida al-qitāl" with an annexation (iḍāfah), and the accusative of "maqāʿid" is that it is the second object of "tubawwi'". Whoever reads "lil-mu'minin" makes it the first object of "tubawwi'", transitivised by the lām, as in His words, ﴿And when We lodged Ibrahim at the site of the House﴾ [al-Hajj: 26]. It has been said: the lām in "li-Ibrahim" is superfluous, and the lām in "lil-qitāl" is the lām of cause, governed by "tubawwi'". It has been said: it is in the position of a qualifier of "maqāʿid". In the verse there is evidence that the leaders (al-a'immah) are those who take charge of the armies and select places for them for war, and that the soldiers must obey them. This was said by al-Maturidi, and it is apparent.

﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾: that is, All-Hearing of your words, All-Knowing of your intentions. These two attributes came here because at the beginning of this battle there was consultation and response with differing opinions, and an inner state of disturbed intentions, as His account of the story of the battle of Uhud contains.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 122:

﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart﴾. The two parties (al-ta'ifatan) were Banu Salamah of the Khazraj and Banu Harithah of the Aws, and they are the two wings (al-junahan). This was said by Ibn Abbas, Jabir, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Rabi' and al-Suddi, and it is the view of the majority of the exegetes (jumhur al-mufassirin). It was also said that the two parties were from the Ansar and the Muhajirun.

It is narrated that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out with a thousand men, and it was said nine hundred and fifty, while the polytheists numbered three thousand, and he had promised them victory if they remained steadfast." Then 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy withdrew with a third of the people. The cause of his withdrawal was that he had advised the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to remain in Medina when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) consulted him, and he had not consulted him before that. So he advised him to stay in Medina, but he did not do so and went out. 'Abdullah became angry and said: "He obeyed them and disobeyed me." He said: "O people, why should we kill ourselves and our children?" 'Amr ibn Hazm al-Ansari followed them, and in another narration it was Abu Jabir al-Salami, and said: "I implore you by Allah regarding your Prophet and yourselves." 'Abdullah said: "If we knew there would be fighting, we would have followed you." The coward then intended to follow 'Abdullah, but Allah protected them, and they went on with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Ibn Abbas said: "They had concealed that they would turn back, so Allah resolved for them upon right guidance, and they remained steadfast." This intention was not something for which they are held accountable, since it was not a firm resolve; it was merely an inclination without determination.

There is no doubt that the soul, when it meets wars and one who grapples with them, is afflicted with some weakness in facing them, and then its companion prepares it for fighting, so it stands firm and settles. Do you not see the words of the poet:

"My saying, whenever I am stirred and it stirs, is: 'Stay where you are, you will be praised or you will rest.'"

Idh hammat is a substitution (badal) for "idh ghadawta" (when you went out in the morning). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or the meaning of 'Sami' alim' [al-Baqarah: 224] operated in it." End of quote. This is not precisely stated, because an operator cannot be composed of two descriptions; its precise formulation would be: "or the meaning of sami' or 'alim operated in it," and the matter would then fall under the category of tanazu' (competition between governors). He also permitted that it be governed by "tubawwi'" [Al 'Imran: 121] and by "ghadawta" [Al 'Imran: 121]. Hamma is transitive with the preposition ba', so the estimate is: "bi-an tafshalа," and the meaning is: "that you would lose heart in fighting." How excellent is the poet's saying in urging fighting and forbidding cowardice:

"Fight the people with deception, and let not cowardice take you away from fighting them.
The people are like you: they have hair on the head that does not spread out when they are slain."

The seven readers assimilated the ta' of the feminine marker into the ta' (ṭāʾ) [of tafshalā]. There is a difference reported from Qalun, which we mentioned in our work "'Iqd al-La'ali fi al-Qira'at al-Sab' al-'Awali" (p. 47), which is our composition. The apparent meaning is that this intention occurred at the time the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) placed the fighters in their positions for battle, and the withdrawal of 'Abdullah with those who withdrew. It was also said: when they urged him to go out and opposed 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy.

In His saying "two parties" (ta'ifatan) there is a subtle allusion to concealment (kinayah) regarding the one from whom what is unbecoming proceeds, and to veiling him; for He did not specify the two parties themselves, nor did He name the tribes from which the intention came, out of veiling over them.

﴿And Allah is their guardian﴾. The meaning of guardianship (wilayah) here is support and victory, so they should not lose heart. It was also said: He made them among His allies who persevere in obedience to Him. In al-Bukhari, from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah al-Ansari, who said: "It was regarding us that this was revealed: ﴿When two parties among you were about to lose heart, and Allah is their guardian﴾." He said: "We are the two parties, Banu Harithah and Banu Salamah. And we would not wish that it had not been revealed, because of the saying of Allah: ﴿And Allah is their guardian.﴾" Jabir said this out of extreme joy at the honour they had gained through Allah's praise and His sending down of a verse in their regard clearly affirming the validity of this guardianship, and that this intention, which was pardoned because it was not a firm resolve, was the cause of its revelation. 'Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) read: "wallahu waliyyuhum" (with the pronoun in the plural), referring the pronoun to the meaning rather than the wording of the dual, as in His saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9] and ﴿These two are two adversaries who dispute﴾ [al-Hajj: 19]. This sentence has no place in i'rab; rather it came as a resumed statement (mustanafah) in praise of Allah for these two parties.

﴿And upon Allah let the believers rely﴾. When He, exalted is He, mentioned what the two parties had intended of loss of heart, and informed that He is their guardian, and whoever Allah is his guardian should not entrust his affair except to Him, He commanded them to rely upon Him. He placed the prepositional phrase first to give attention to the one upon whom reliance is placed, or for exclusivity according to the view of those who hold that. He drew attention to the attribute that necessitates this, which is faith, because whoever believes in Allah is most fitting that his reliance be upon none but Him; for this reason He said: ﴿And upon Allah rely, if you are believers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 23]. He stated it generally so that the two concerned parties and others would be included in this command, and that its object is whoever has faith. In this command there is an encouragement to envy (taghbit) for what the two parties did in following the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and marching with him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 123–124:

﴿And God had already given you victory at Badr, when you were weak.﴾ When He had commanded them to rely upon Him (tawakkul), He reminded them of what necessitates reliance upon Him, namely what He facilitated and made easy for them of conquest and victory on the day of Badr, when they were in a state of paucity and weakness, since that victory was the fruit of reliance upon Him and trust in Him. As for the victory referred to at Badr, there are several opinions: that it was by means of the angels, or by casting terror (ru'b), or by the handful of pebbles which the Messenger of God ﷺ threw, or by the will of God, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And victory is only from God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 126].

The clause "and you were weak" (wa-antum adhillah) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object in "nasarakum" (He gave you victory). The meaning is: "and you were weak in the eyes of others, while they were mighty in their own estimation, and in comparison to their enemy and all the disbelievers in the regions of the earth they were, in the view of the one who reflects, defeated." The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "O God, if this band perishes, You will not be worshipped."

Al-adhillah is the plural of dhalil. The plural of abundance is dhillan, so it came in the form of the plural of paucity to indicate that they were few in number. The weakness that appeared to others was what they had of frailty, scarcity of weapons, wealth and mounts. They set out on water-camels, several men taking turns on a single camel, and they had no more horses than a single horse, while their enemy had a hundred horses. The number of Muslims was three hundred and thirteen men: seventy-seven of the Emigrants (Muhajirun), whose standard-bearer was 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and two hundred and thirty-six of the Helpers (Ansar), whose standard-bearer was Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah. It is also said: three hundred and sixteen men. It is said: three hundred and fourteen men. And in one report: three hundred and some ten men. Their enemy, in a state of abundance, numbered about a thousand fighters.

How excellent is the saying of the poet:

Someone said: "What has befallen the family of 'Adiyy, that they have perished while few of them remain and they are obscure?"

They reproach us that our number is small, so I said to her: "Indeed, the noble are few."

And what harms us that we are few, while our neighbor is mighty, and the neighbor of the many is humbled?

The victory at Badr is the well-known one in which the chieftains of Quraysh were killed, and Islam was founded upon the day of Badr. It was on Friday, the seventeenth of Ramadan, in the eighteenth month after the Hijra.

﴿So fear God, that you may be grateful.﴾ He commanded taqwa in an unrestricted manner. It is also said: [it refers] to steadfastness alongside the Messenger of God ﷺ, and His hoping for gratitude, either for the previous favour of victory at Badr, or for a favour hoped to occur. It is as if it were said: "Perhaps He will bestow upon you another favour, and you will be grateful for it." He placed gratitude in the place of favour, because it is its cause.

﴿When you said to the believers: "Is it not sufficient for you that your Lord should reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?" Yes…﴾ The apparent connection of this verse with what precedes it, and that it belongs to the account of Badr, is the view of the majority; thus "idh" (when) is governed by "nasarakum" (He gave you victory). It is also said: this is part of the account of Uhud, so the saying "And God had already given you victory at Badr" is parenthetical between the two statements, because of the exhortation in it to reliance and steadfastness for battle. The argument of this view is that at Badr the reinforcement by angels was one thousand, whereas here it is three thousand and five thousand. The disbelievers at Badr were a thousand, and the Muslims were a third of that; so the number of disbelievers was three thousand, and they were promised three thousand angels. He also said: "and they will come upon you immediately," i.e., the reinforcement. On the day of Badr the Muslims went out against them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: how is it valid for Him to say this to them on the day of Uhud, when angels did not descend in it?" I say: He said it to them together with the condition of patience and taqwa upon them. They did not persevere against the spoils and did not fear God, since they opposed the command of the Messenger of God ﷺ; therefore the angels did not descend. Had they remained steadfast in what was stipulated upon them, they would have descended. He advanced the promise of the descent of the angels only so that their hearts might be strengthened, they might resolve upon steadfastness, and they might trust in God's victory." End of his words.

As for his saying "the angels did not descend in it," this is not agreed upon; rather Mujahid said: the angels were present in it but did not fight, so according to Mujahid's view the question falls away. As for his saying "He said it to them together with the condition of patience and taqwa upon them, and they did not persevere against the spoils, nor did they fear God…" to the end, the reinforcement of five thousand is what was conditioned upon patience and taqwa. As for the first reinforcement, which was three thousand, it was not conditioned; and it does not follow from the non-descent of five thousand, due to the failure of its condition, that three thousand, or any part of them, would not descend. It has been answered regarding the non-descent of three thousand that it was a promise from the Messenger of God ﷺ to the believers whom he placed in positions for battle and commanded to remain still and steadfast in them; thus this promise was conditioned upon steadfastness in those positions. When they neglected the condition, the conditioned thing did not occur. End. There is no concealing the weakness of this answer. Al-Dahhak said: this promise and saying were addressed to the believers on the day of Uhud; the people fled and turned back, so God did not guide them, and they were only reinforced on the day of Badr with one thousand angels. Ibn Zayd said: they did not persevere. 'Ikrimah said: they did not persevere and did not fear God on the day of Uhud, so they were not reinforced; and had they been reinforced, they would not have been defeated. The promise of reinforcement was on the day of Badr, and it is preferred that He said this on the day of Badr: the apparent continuity of the discourse supports this; and because scarcity of numbers and equipment was on the day of Badr, so they were more in need of strengthening their hearts with the promise; and because the promise of three thousand was unconditioned, so its fulfilment was necessary. And it occurred on the day of Badr. As for the combining of one thousand and three thousand, that was unconditioned, so its fulfilment was necessary; and what occurred on the day of Badr was that they were first reinforced with one thousand, then two thousand more were added to them, making three thousand. Or they were first reinforced with one thousand, then news reached them of the reinforcement of the polytheists with a large number, so He promised five thousand in accordance with the reinforcement of the disbelievers. But the disbelievers were not reinforced, so He dispensed with reinforcing the Muslims.

The apparent reading of these numbers is that the lesser is included in the greater: they were promised one thousand, then two thousand was added to it, then two thousand more, making five. Whoever adds the lesser to the greater and places this in the account of Uhud, they would have been promised eight thousand; or in the account of Badr, they would have been promised nine thousand. The noble verse does not address the descent of the angels nor their fighting the polytheists and killing them; rather that is a matter left unstated in the verse. The reports have converged and mutually supported the view that the angels were present at Badr and fought. Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned this from a group of the Companions in what can be consulted in his book. Since the verse does not address it, we have not burdened our book by transmitting it. Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned that al-Sha'bi said: the believers were not reinforced with angels on the day of Badr; the angels used to attend the battles of the Prophet ﷺ as reinforcements afterwards, and they attend the battles of the Muslims until the Day of Resurrection. He said: the people disagreed with al-Sha'bi in this statement. Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Razi mentioned the following text: "The exegetes and biographers agreed that God sent down the angels on the day of Badr, and that they fought the disbelievers." Then he said: As for Abu Bakr al-Asamm, he denied this most strongly, and reports of his arguments were mentioned; then he said: all these doubts befit one who denies the Qur'an and prophethood, because the Qur'an and the Sunnah speak clearly of this, meaning the sending down of the angels. Then he said: they differed regarding the support of the angels. It was said: by fighting. It was said: by strengthening the souls of the believers and casting terror into the hearts of the disbelievers. The apparent meaning of reinforcement is that they join the army in fighting, and that their mere presence would suffice. End of his words.

The interrogative particle entered upon the negative particle as a form of rebuke, because the sufficiency of this number of angels is denied. The negative particle "lan" was used, which is more emphatic in future negation than "la," indicating that they, because of their scarcity, weakness, the multitude of their enemy and his might, were as those who had despaired of victory.

"Bala" (Yes): an affirmation of what follows "lan," meaning: "Yes, the reinforcement with them suffices for you," so it affirmed sufficiency. In the codex of Ubayy: "Alā yakfiyakum." End. Most of this is from al-Zamakhshari's words.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Alan yakfiyakum" is an affirmation of their belief in the sufficiency of this number of angels; and since the matter was clear in itself, that the angels are sufficient, the speaker hastened to an answer so as to build what he would continue to say upon it, so he said: "Bala," which is the answer of those who affirm. This is fitting in clear matters from which there is no escape in answering, and similar to it is His saying: ﴿Say: What thing is greatest in testimony? Say: God﴾ [al-An'am: 19]. End. Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi said: "Alan yakfiyakum" is the answer of the Companions when they said: "Why did you not inform us of the fighting so that we might prepare?" The Prophet ﷺ said to them: "Alan yakfiyakum." Ibn 'Isa said: sufficiency is the measure that fills the need, and reinforcement is giving a thing time after time. End.

al-Hasan recited: "bi-thalathah alfin" (with three thousand), pausing on the ha', and likewise "bi-khamsati alfin." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the basis of this reading is weak, because the mudaf and the mudaf ilayhi require connection, as they are like a single word, and the second is the completion of the first; the ha' is merely a sign of pause, so a pause applied in a place that is meant for connection. But similar things have come from the Arabs in various places. Among them is what al-Farra' related: they say "akaltu lahman shatan" (I ate meat of a sheep), meaning "lahma shatin," so they prolonged the fatha until an alif arose from it, just as they say in pause "qala" (he said) meaning "qala," and they prolonged the fatha in rhymes and the like at places of rhyme and deliberation. Among such in poetry is the saying of the poet:

Yanba'u min dhifra ghadubin jasratan / zayyanatin mithla al-'atiqi al-mukram

He means "yanba'a," so he prolonged. And from it is the saying of another:

Aqulu idh kharrat 'ala al-kalkali / ya naqata ma julti min majali

He means "al-kalkala," so he prolonged. And from it is the saying of another:

Fa-anta min al-ghawa'ili hina turma / wa-min dhamma al-rijala bi-muntazah

He means "bi-muntazih." Abu al-Fath said: since this prolonging is permissible between the parts of a single word, prolonging and deliberation between the mudaf and the mudaf ilayhi is permissible, since they are in reality two. End of his words. This is an excess of illustration and comparison with what is not appropriate; what is appropriate for the justification of this irregular reading is that it is from applying the rules of pause to continuity: he changed it into a ha' in continuity, just as they changed it into a ha' in pause, and it is found in their speech to apply the rules of continuity to pause and the rules of pause to continuity. As for his saying "but such things have come from the Arabs in various places," all that was mentioned belongs to the category of prolonging the vowel (ishba' al-harakah). Prolonging the vowel is not like changing the taa' into a ha' in continuity; rather it is analogous to their saying "thalathah arba'ah," where the taa' is changed into a ha', then the vowel of the hamza of "arba'ah" is transferred to it and the hamza is dropped, thereby applying the rules of pause to continuity in the change. Because of continuity the transfer occurred, for this transfer would not occur except in continuity.

It was read irregularly "bi-thalathah alfin" with a kasra on the taa' in continuity, applying the rules of pause. They differed regarding this quiescent taa': is it a substitute for the ha' with which one pauses, or is it the taa' of feminine gender itself, which is pronounced with taa' when pausing as it is? It is a dialect.

al-Jumhur read "munzalin" with light pronunciation, in the passive voice, and Ibn 'Amir with doubling, also in the passive voice; the hamza and the doubling are for transitivity, so both are the same. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "munazzilin" with doubling of the zay and a kasra, in the active voice. Some readers read it with a light zay and a kasra, also in the active voice, and the meaning is: they send down victory.

Then he said: they differed regarding the support of the angels. It was said: by fighting. It was said: by strengthening the souls of the believers and casting terror into the hearts of the disbelievers. The apparent meaning of reinforcement is that they join the army in fighting, and that their mere presence would suffice. End of his words.

The interrogative particle entered upon the negative particle as a form of rebuke, because the sufficiency of this number of angels is denied. The negative particle "lan" was used, which is more emphatic in future negation than "la," indicating that they, because of their scarcity, weakness, the multitude of their enemy and his might, were as those who had despaired of victory.

"Bala" (Yes): an affirmation of what follows "lan," meaning: "Yes, the reinforcement with them suffices for you," so it affirmed sufficiency. In the codex of Ubayy: "Alā yakfiyakum." End. Most of this is from al-Zamakhshari's words.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Alan yakfiyakum" is an affirmation of their belief in the sufficiency of this number of angels; and since the matter was clear in itself, that the angels are sufficient, the speaker hastened to an answer so as to build what he would continue to say upon it, so he said: "Bala," which is the answer of those who affirm. This is fitting in clear matters from which there is no escape in answering, and similar to it is His saying: ﴿Say: What thing is greatest in testimony? Say: God﴾ [al-An'am: 19]. End. Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi said: "Alan yakfiyakum" is the answer of the Companions when they said: "Why did you not inform us of the fighting so that we might prepare?" The Prophet ﷺ said to them: "Alan yakfiyakum." Ibn 'Isa said: sufficiency is the measure that fills the need, and reinforcement is giving a thing time after time. End.

al-Hasan recited: "bi-thalathah alfin" (with three thousand), pausing on the ha', and likewise "bi-khamsati alfin." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the basis of this reading is weak, because the mudaf and the mudaf ilayhi require connection, as they are like a single word, and the second is the completion of the first; the ha' is merely a sign of pause, so a pause applied in a place that is meant for connection. But similar things have come from the Arabs in various places. Among them is what al-Farra' related: they say "akaltu lahman shatan" (I ate meat of a sheep), meaning "lahma shatin," so they prolonged the fatha until an alif arose from it, just as they say in pause "qala" (he said) meaning "qala," and they prolonged the fatha in rhymes and the like at places of rhyme and deliberation. Among such in poetry is the saying of the poet:

Yanba'u min dhifra ghadubin jasratan / zayyanatin mithla al-'atiqi al-mukram

He means "yanba'a," so he prolonged. And from it is the saying of another:

Aqulu idh kharrat 'ala al-kalkali / ya naqata ma julti min majali

He means "al-kalkala," so he prolonged. And from it is the saying of another:

Fa-anta min al-ghawa'ili hina turma / wa-min dhamma al-rijala bi-muntazah

He means "bi-muntazih." Abu al-Fath said: since this prolonging is permissible between the parts of a single word, prolonging and deliberation between the mudaf and the mudaf ilayhi is permissible, since they are in reality two. End of his words. This is an excess of illustration and comparison with what is not appropriate; what is appropriate for the justification of this irregular reading is that it is from applying the rules of pause to continuity: he changed it into a ha' in continuity, just as they changed it into a ha' in pause, and it is found in their speech to apply the rules of continuity to pause and the rules of pause to continuity. As for his saying "but such things have come from the Arabs in various places," all that was mentioned belongs to the category of prolonging the vowel (ishba' al-harakah). Prolonging the vowel is not like changing the taa' into a ha' in continuity; rather it is analogous to their saying "thalathah arba'ah," where the taa' is changed into a ha', then the vowel of the hamza of "arba'ah" is transferred to it and the hamza is dropped, thereby applying the rules of pause to continuity in the change. Because of continuity the transfer occurred, for this transfer would not occur except in continuity.

It was read irregularly "bi-thalathah alfin" with a kasra on the taa' in continuity, applying the rules of pause. They differed regarding this quiescent taa': is it a substitute for the ha' with which one pauses, or is it the taa' of feminine gender itself, which is pronounced with taa' when pausing as it is? It is a dialect.

al-Jumhur read "munzalin" with light pronunciation, in the passive voice, and Ibn 'Amir with doubling, also in the passive voice; the hamza and the doubling are for transitivity, so both are the same. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "munazzilin" with doubling of the zay and a kasra, in the active voice. Some readers read it with a light zay and a kasra, also in the active voice, and the meaning is: they send down victory.

ﷻ﴿Yes, if you are steadfast and god-fearing, and they come upon you suddenly this very moment, your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels, marked out.﴾ 

He, exalted is He, made the aid He gives the believers, with more than the previous number, conditional upon the combination of steadfastness and God-consciousness, and upon their coming at once in that same instant with the number [mentioned], and He tied it to the presence of these [conditions], such that the descent of the angels does not lag behind their being adorned with the three attributes. The meaning of "min fawrihim" ("at once", "suddenly") is: "from their journey" (min safarihim); this is what Ibn 'Abbas said. Or: "from their face" (min wajhihim); this is what al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi said. It was said: this is the dialect of Hudhayl, Qays, Ghaylan and Kinanah. Or: "from their anger" (min ghadabihim); this is what Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak and Abu Salih, the mawla of Umm Hani', said. Or its meaning is: "in this their rising" (fi nahdatihim hadhihi); this is what Ibn 'Atiyyah said. Or the meaning is: "from this very hour of theirs" (min sa'atihim hadhihi); this is what al-Zamakhshari said.

The word al-fawr (immediacy) indicates swiftness and haste; one says: "Do this immediately (ala al-fawr), not at leisure (ala al-tarakhi)." From it comes the immediacy (al-fawr) in the Hajj and in ablution (wudu'). In attributing the reinforcement to the word "your Lord" (rabbukum) rather than any other of Allah's names there is an indication of goodly regard for them and gentleness toward them.

The two Companions (Abu 'Amr? no—Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah? the reciters Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah) and the two brothers, namely al-Kisa'i... 

Note: The recitation list here is given as in the text: the two Companions and the two brothers read "musawwimin" with a fatha on the waw, while Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and 'Asim read it with a kasra on it. It was said: it is from al-sawm, which is the mark placed on a sheep or other animal, a colour made to differ from its own colour so that it may be recognised. It was also said: it is from al-sawm, which is leaving the beast to graze. According to the first, it was narrated that the angels wore white turbans, except Jibril, who wore a yellow turban like al-Zubayr. This was said by Ibn Ishaq and al-Zajjaj. It was said: [they wore] yellow turbans like al-Zubayr; this was said by 'Urwah and 'Abd Allah, the two sons of al-Zubayr, 'Abbad ibn Hamzah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, and al-Kalbi, who added: hanging down upon their shoulders. It was said: they were on piebald horses, and their mark was [as] Mujahid said: their horses' forelocks and tails were shorn, marked with wool and dyed fleece. Qatadah and al-Rabi' said their mark was [their horses]. With fatha on the waw: "mu'allamin" (marked), and with kasra: "mu'allimin" (marking themselves or their horses). Al-Tabari preferred the reading with kasra, on the ground that he (peace be upon him) said on the day of Badr: "Mark yourselves, for the angels have marked themselves." On the second view, which is al-sawm, the meaning of "musawwimin" with a kasra on the waw is: they let their horses graze, i.e. gave them freedom of movement and running for battle, and from it comes "sa'imat al-mashiyah" (grazing livestock). As for the fatha on the waw, this meaning is also valid for it, as said by al-Mahdawi and Ibn Furak; i.e., Allah made them roam and run for battle. Abu Zayd said: "sawwama al-rajul khaylahu" means he sent his horses out on a raid. Some Basran scholars related: "sawwama al-rajul ghulamahu" means he sent his slave off and let him go his way; for this reason al-Akhfash said: the meaning of "musawwimin" is "sent forth." The verse contains evidence for the permissibility of adopting a distinguishing mark for tribes and battalions, so that each tribe and battalion may be distinguished in war.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 126:

﴿And Allah did not make it except as good tidings for you, and so that your hearts might be reassured thereby.﴾ The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿jaʿalahu﴾ refers to the verbal noun understood from "﴿yumdidkum﴾ [Aal ʿImran: 125]", which is al-imdad (the provision of aid). It has also been permitted that it refers to the taswim (marking of the horses), or to the victory (al-nasr), or to the sending down (al-tanzil), or to the number (al-ʿadad), or to the promise (al-waʿd).

﴿Illa bushra﴾ is an exception from the object of purpose (al-maf'ul lahu), meaning: Allah did not make it for any thing except as good tidings for you. This is an exceptive construction (istithna' farigh) in which the governing verb is left without its object, and bushra is a maf'ul min ajlihi (object of purpose), and the conditions for its accusative case are present, namely that it is a verbal noun (masdar) and that the agent and the time are unified. ﴿Wa-li-tatma'inna﴾ is conjoined to the position (mahall) of bushra, since its original form is li-bushra. Because the agent differed in ﴿wa-li-tatma'inna﴾, the lam was brought, as the condition of unity of agent was lost; for the agent of bushra is Allah, while the agent of ﴿tatma'innu﴾ is ﴿qulubukum﴾ (your hearts). ﴿Tatma'innu﴾ is in the subjunctive by the hidden ʾan after the lam of kay (lam al-ta'lil, the lam of purpose), so it is conjunction of a noun upon an assumed position of another noun (ʿatf al-ism ʿala tawahhum mawdiʿ ismin akhar), and ﴿jaʿala﴾ on this estimation is transitive to one object.

Al-Hawfi said: ﴿Illa bushra﴾ is in the accusative position as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun, and it refers to the promise of reinforcement. It has been said: bushra is the second object of ﴿jaʿalahu﴾ (Allah made it). On these two opinions, the lam in ﴿li-tatma'inna﴾ is linked to a deleted element, since there is no conjunction preceding it to be conjoined to. They said: its estimate is "wa-li-tatma'inna qulubukum bihi bashsharakum" (and so that your hearts might be reassured thereby; He gave you good tidings). Bushra is a ﴿fuʿla﴾ form verbal noun like ﴿rujʿa﴾, and it is a masdar of the triliteral bare verb bashara, and the pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ refers to what it referred to in ﴿jaʿlahu﴾, according to the preceding disagreement. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: the lam in ﴿wa-li-tatma'inna﴾ is connected to a hidden verb indicated by ﴿jaʿalahu﴾. The meaning of the verse: "This aid was not except so that you would rejoice thereby and your hearts would be reassured thereby." End of quotation. It seems that he saw that it was not possible in his view to conjoin ﴿wa-li-tatma'inna﴾ upon bushra according to the position, because one of the conditions of conjoining upon the position, according to our companions, is that there be a marker of the position (muhriz lil-mawdiʿ), and there is no marker here, since the governing element of the genitive is absent. Whoever does not stipulate the marker, that is permitted according to his school; otherwise it falls under conjunction upon assumption (ʿatf ʿala al-tawahhum), as we mentioned at the beginning.

Abu ʿAbd Allah Muhammad ibn ʿUmar al-Razi said: Some of them said: the waw in ﴿wa-li-tatma'inna﴾ is superfluous (za'ida). He also said: in the mention of the aid there are two aims. One of them: bringing joy into their hearts, which is what is meant by His saying: ﴿illa bushra﴾. The second: the attainment of tranquility through victory, so that they do not lose courage; and this is the principal aim. So he distinguished between these two expressions, as an alert to the occurrence of difference between the two matters, and so he conjoined the verb upon the noun. And since attaining tranquility was the stronger, he introduced the particle of causation. End of quotation. In it there is some disorder and a dispute regarding his statement "so he conjoined the verb upon the noun," since it is not conjoining a verb upon a noun; and regarding his statement "he introduced the particle of causation," since that is not for the reason he mentioned.

﴿And victory is not except from the presence of Allah, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ He restricted the existence of victory to His direction, not that it comes from increasing the fighters in number, nor from the reinforcement of the angels. He mentioned the reinforcement by the angels to strengthen the hope of victory for them and to firm up their hearts. He mentioned the attribute of ʿIzza (might), which is the attribute indicating dominance, and the attribute of Hikma (wisdom), which is the attribute indicating placing things in their proper places, such as victory and abandonment and other than that.

The commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 3, verse 127:

﴿That He might cut off a part of those who disbelieved, or subdue them so that they turn back defeated﴾. Al-ṭaraf (the part, the portion): those who were killed at Badr, who were seventy of the leaders of Quraysh, or those who were killed at Uhud, who were twenty-two men according to the sound opinion. Al-Suddi said eighteen. Or it refers to the total of those killed in the two battles. These are three opinions. He referred to the group by the word ṭaraf because those whom the Muslims killed in a battle are a part of the disbelievers, since they are the ones nearest to the slayers, so they are an edge (ḥāshiya) of them. All the disbelievers were a company (rufqa), and these slain were a portion of it. It was said: it is possible that by His words ṭaraf is meant dābir, that is, the last, which returns to the meaning of ṭaraf, because the last of a thing is a part of it. (Or subdue them) means to humiliate them and enrage them, so that they return without gaining anything of what they had hoped for. Whenever victory falls upon the disbelievers, it is either by killing, or by disappointment, or by both. It is like His words: ﴿And Allah repelled those who disbelieved in their rage; they gained no good﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 25]. 

The majority recited ”أوْ تَكْبِتَهم“ with a tā' (تَكْبِتَهم). Lāḥiq ibn Ḥumayd recited ”أوْ يَكْبِدَهم“ with a dāl in place of the tā', and the meaning is: grief reaches their liver (kabid). Among the exegetes there are opinions regarding ﴿yakbitahum﴾: it means He defeats them, said by Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Zajjāj; or He humiliates them, said by Qatāda and Muqātil; or He throws them down, said by Abū ʿUbayda and al-Yazīdī; or He destroys them, said by Abū ʿUbayda; or He curses them, said by al-Suddi; or He grants them victory over them, said by al-Mubarrad; or He enrages them, said by al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl and preferred by Ibn Qutayba. As for the recitation of Lāḥiq, it is from the substitution of the dāl for the tā', as they said: hawata al-thawb wa-harada-hu (he tore the garment), meaning if he burned it; and sabata raʾsahu wa-sabada-hu, meaning if he shaved it. Likewise, kabata al-ʿaduww wa-kabada-hu means he struck his liver.

The lām in ”لِيَقْطَعَ“ (li-yaqṭaʿa): it is said that it is connected to an omitted element whose estimate is: He aided you or He gave you victory. Al-Ḥawfī said: it is connected to His words ﴿And Allah had already given you victory﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 123], meaning He gave you victory so that He might cut off. He said: it is also permissible that it be connected to His words ﴿And victory is only from Allah﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 126]. It is also permissible that it be connected to yumdidkum (will reinforce you). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is possible that the lām is connected to ”جَعَلَهُ“ (jaʿalahu, He made it). It was also said that it is conjoined to His words ”ولِتَطْمَئِنَّ“ (wa-li-taṭmaʾinna, and so that they might be reassured), and the conjunction particle was omitted from it; the estimate is: and so that your hearts might be reassured by it, and so that He might cut off. In that case the sentence ﴿And victory is only from Allah﴾ would be a parenthetical sentence between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. What appears to be correct is that it is connected to the nearest preceding mention, which is the element governing ﴿from the presence of Allah﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 126], which is the predicate of the subject. As if the estimate is: and victory is only existing from the presence of Allah, not from the presence of anyone else, for one of two matters: either cutting off a part of the disbelievers by killing and capture, or by humiliation and returning in disappointment. The alif and lām in ”النَّصْرُ“ (al-naṣr, victory) are not for the specific known (ʿahd) of a particular victory, but for generality, meaning: there is no victory, any victory from Allah for the Muslims over the disbelievers, except for one of two matters.

[p-53]

ﷻ﴿Not for you is any part of the affair﴾. There is disagreement about the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), and its summary is as follows: that he (ﷺ) cursed some people, or a specific person whom he named as ʿUtbah ibn Abi Waqqas; or specific persons against whom he invoked curses and who were named: Abu Sufyan, al-Harith ibn Hisham, and Safwan ibn Umayya; or tribes, of which he named: Liḥyan, Ri'l, Dhakwan, and ʿAṣiyya. Or they were (revealed) because of those who fled on the day of Uhud. Or he sought permission from his Lord to invoke (curses). He invoked (curses) on the day of Uhud when his face was wounded, his lower front tooth (rubāʿiyya) was broken, and he was struck with stones, until he fell on his side; then some of their men (fullāḥ) pursued him, and he inclined toward wishing that Allah would uproot them and relieve him of them, and then (this verse) was revealed. Based on these occasions, the meaning of the verse is: a reminder that all matters belong only to Allah, and this includes the guidance of these people or their remaining in their state. In his address there is evidence that an order issued from him, or an intention toward one, or a request for permission to supplicate, as has been mentioned, and that the outcomes of matters are in the hand of Allah. The Kufans said: this verse abrogated (nasakhat) the qunūt (supplication in prayer) against Ri'l, Dhakwan, ʿAṣiyya, and others of the polytheists. Al-Sakhawi said: this is not a condition of the abrogating text (al-nāsikh), because it did not abrogate a Qur'an.

﴿or He will turn to them in forgiveness or punish them, for indeed they are wrongdoers﴾. It was said: this is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon what precedes it of the verbs in the accusative (manṣūba). And His saying "Not for you is any part of the affair" would be a parenthetical clause (jumla iʿtiraḍiyya), and the meaning is that Allah is the owner of their affair; so either He destroys them, or defeats them, or turns to them in forgiveness if they embrace Islam, or punishes them if they persist in disbelief. It was also said: "an" (that) is implied after "aw" (or), with the meaning "illā an" (except that), which is the one in their saying: "la-ulzimannaka aw taqḍīnī ḥaqqī" (I will certainly hold you to it, or you will settle my right), and the meaning is that he has no part of their affair except that Allah turns to them in forgiveness through Islam, so he is gladdened by their guidance, or that He punishes them with killing and capture in this world, or with fire in the Hereafter, so he is healed by that and finds relief. On this interpretation, the negated sentence is for establishing (ta'sīs) a new meaning, not for emphasis (ta'kīd). It was also said: "aw yatūba" is conjoined to "al-amr" (the affair). And it was said: conjoined to "shay'" (thing). That is: not for you is any part of the affair, or of their repentance, or of their punishment, any part. Or: not for you is any part of the affair or their punishment. The most apparent of these four analyses is the first. He who went to the view that "﴿not for you is any part of the affair﴾" means the affair of the two groups who had intended to lose heart is far off the mark.

Ibn Bahr said: "min al-amr" means "from this victory," and it is only from Allah, as He said: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾ [al-Anfal: 17]. It was also said: the intended "affair" is the affair of fighting. The apparent reading is to take it in its general sense, and all affairs belong to Allah the Exalted.

Ubayy recited: "aw yatūbu ʿalayhim aw yuʿadhdhibuhum" with both verbs in the nominative (marfūʿ), meaning: "or He turns to them in forgiveness, or He punishes them," then he drew attention to the cause that calls for the punishment in His saying: ﴿for indeed they are wrongdoers﴾, and used "inna," which indicates emphasis, in attributing wrongdoing to them.

﴿To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ When He had said, "﴿You have no say in the matter﴾" (Q 3:128), He made clear that affairs belong only to the One who has dominion, and dominion belongs to Him. He brought this sentence to confirm the preceding one. The explanation of this sentence has already been given. *Ma* (whatever) refers to the totality of the world and its make-up, which is why *ma* is appropriate here.

﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.﴾ When He had mentioned, "﴿or He will turn to them in mercy or punish them﴾," He followed with this sentence to clarify that His actions follow His will. Beginning with forgiveness and then following with punishment suits what came earlier: "﴿or He will turn to them in mercy or punish them﴾" (Q 3:128). Here He did not make repentance a condition for forgiveness, since God forgives whom He wills, whether he repents or not, except for shirk, which He excluded. Al-Zamakhshari said, quoting al-Hasan, may God have mercy on him, the following: "He forgives whom He wills through repentance, and He wills to forgive only the penitent. He punishes whom He wills, and He wills to punish only those who deserve punishment." And from Ata': "He forgives those who turn to Him, and punishes those who meet Him as wrongdoers." His following words, "﴿for they are wrongdoers﴾" (Q 3:128), are a clear explanation of "whom He wills," since they are either those for whom He turns in mercy or those who are wrongdoers. But the people of desires and innovations (*ahl al-ahwa' wa'l-bida'*) feign deafness and blindness to the signs of God, so they stumble about blindly, and they console themselves with what they invent. From Ibn Abbas, from their saying: "He grants the great sin to whom He wills, and punishes whom He wills for the small sin." End of his words. This is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school), because whoever dies persisting in a major sin, God does not forgive him. What he attributed to al-Hasan is not authentic at all. The doctrine of the People of the Sunna (Sunni orthodoxy) is that God forgives whom He wills, even if he dies persisting in a major sin without repenting of it.

﴿And God is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ In this sentence is an emphasis on the aspect of kindness and bounty.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 130:

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume usury, doubled and multiplied﴾ Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: This prohibition on consuming usury (ribā) came in the midst of the story of Uhud, and I do not know of anything transmitted on this matter. End of quote.

The connection of this verse to what precedes it, and its coming in the midst of the narrative, is as follows: when He forbade the believers from taking intimate companions (biṭānah) from outside their own community, and digressed to mention the story of Uhud, and since the disbelievers conducted most of their dealings through usury both with their own kind and with the believers, and this dealing leads to mixing with the disbelievers, they were forbidden from this dealing, which is usury, decisively, because of mixing with the disbelievers, their affection, and taking them as close friends. This is especially so since the believers, at the beginning of Islam, were in a state of hardship, while the disbelievers, from among the Jews and others, were in a state of ease. Also, consuming what is unlawful has a great effect on the non-acceptance of good deeds and supplications, as came in the hadith: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, does not respond to one whose food is unlawful and whose drink is unlawful when he supplicates, and indeed the one who consumes the unlawful, when he performs Hajj, says: 'Labbayka wa saʿdayka' (Here I am at Your service and happiness). Then Allah says to him: 'No labbayka and no saʿdayka; your Hajj is rejected upon you.'" So the mention of this verse here is appropriate.

It was also said: the interjection of this sentence here is appropriate because He, exalted is He, promised the believers victory and reinforcement coupled with patience and piety, so He began with the most important of these, which is what they were engaged in of consuming wealth falsely, and commanded piety, then obedience. It was also said: when Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 129], and clarified that whatever is in them of existing things is His possession, and it is not permissible to dispose of any of them except with His permission in the manner He prescribed, and the one who consumes usury disposes of his wealth in other than the manner He commanded, He drew attention to this and forbade what they were persisting in during Islam of the judgment of the Jahiliyyah. Usury has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The word ﴿ʾaḍʿāfan﴾ (multiplied) is in the accusative. They were forbidden from the abominable condition in which they imposed usury: the creditor would say, "Will you pay or will you increase (the debt)?" Often a small amount would consume the debtor's property, since if he could not repay, he would increase the debt and increase the principal. By His saying ﴿mudāʿafah﴾ (doubled) He indicated that they would repeat the doubling year after year. Usury is prohibited in all its forms, so this condition has no implied restriction (mafhūm) and is not a qualifying condition on the prohibition, since what does not occur as "multiplied manifold" is equal in prohibition to what occurs as "multiplied manifold." The discussion regarding the attribution of consuming to usury has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah.

It was also said: "mudāʿafah" refers to wealth. If the usury concerned animals of age, they would raise a bint makhāḍ to a bint labūn, then a ḥiqqah, then a jadhʿah, then a rubāʿ, and so on upward. If it concerned money, a hundred would become two hundred the following year, and if he did not pay both, then four hundred. "Al-ʾaḍʿāf" is the plural of "ḍiʿf" (double), and it is one of the plurals of paucity (jumūʿ al-qillah); therefore He followed it with "mudāʿafah."

﴿And fear Allah that you may be successful﴾ When He forbade them from a matter that was difficult for them to give up, namely usury, He commanded the fear of Allah, since it is what drives one to oppose what a person has become accustomed to of what the Law has forbidden. Then He mentioned that piety is a cause for hoping for success (falāḥ), which is attainment of victory, and He commanded it absolutely, not restricted to the act of usury; because when He forbade usury, the believers were the swiftest of all to obey Allah, exalted is He. So He did not say "fear Allah regarding consuming usury," but rather they were commanded with piety in general, not in relation to a specific thing they had been prevented from by the Law.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 131–132:

﴿وَاتَّقُوا النَّارَ الَّتِي أُعِدَّتْ لِلْكَافِرِينَ﴾ (And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers). Its preceding context is "وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ" (And fear Allah). Since essences (al-dhawat) are not feared, what is feared (al-muttaqa) is omitted, and this verse makes it clear when it says: "وَاتَّقُوا النَّارَ" (and fear the Fire). The alif and lam in "النَّارِ" (the Fire) denote the genus (lil-jins). Therefore, the fire promised to the consumer of riba (usury) may be lighter than the fire of the disbeliever, meaning that its genus has been prepared for the disbelievers. It may also be for a specific reference (lil-'ahd), so that the consumer of riba has been threatened with the particular Fire by which the disbeliever is punished. It has been said that the consumers of riba are threatened with the fire of the disbelievers, since the Fire has seven levels (tabaqat): the highest of them is Jahannam for the disobedient, the five for the disbelievers, and the lowest level (al-darak al-asfal) for the hypocrites. Thus the consumers of riba are punished with the fire of the disbelievers, not with the fire of the disobedient. Ibn 'Abbas said: this is a warning to the believers, lest they consider riba lawful.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "fear lest you make lawful what Allah has forbidden, and thus disbelieve." It has also been said: "fear the deed that strips you of faith and makes you deserving of the Fire." Abu Hanifa used to say: this is the most frightening verse in the Qur'an, since Allah threatens the believers with the Fire prepared for the disbelievers if they do not guard themselves against Him by avoiding His prohibitions. Al-Zamakhshari said: He has reinforced that with what follows it, namely the linking of the believer's hope for His mercy to his devotion to His obedience and the obedience of His Messenger. Whoever reflects on these verses and their like will not entertain empty hopes or wishful thinking about Allah, the Exalted. In His mention of "لَعَلَّ" (perhaps) and "عَسَى" (it may be) in such contexts, and despite what people have said, there is much that is not hidden from the discerning knower: the subtlety of the path of taqwa (God-consciousness), the difficulty of attaining the pleasure of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the rarity of reaching His mercy and reward. End of his words. This is in line with his doctrine of despairing the disobedient non-penitent of the mercy of his Lord, and his zeal for his doctrine leads him to impose on the words of the Qur'an what they do not bear, or what is far from them. The explanation of "أُعِدَّتْ لِلْكَافِرِينَ" has already been given at the beginning of al-Baqara.

﴿وَأَطِيعُوا اللَّهَ وَالرَّسُولَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُرْحَمُونَ﴾ (And obey Allah and the Messenger, that you may receive mercy). It has been said: obey Allah in the obligatory duties (fara'id), and the Messenger in the sunan (the recommended practices of the Prophet). It has been said: [obey Allah and the Messenger] regarding the prohibition of riba, and the Messenger regarding what he conveyed to you of the prohibition. It has also been said: "And obey Allah and the Messenger in what they command you and forbid you." For obedience to the Messenger is obedience to Allah, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [al-Nisa': 80]. Al-Mahdawi said: the mention of the Messenger is an addition for clarification, emphasis, and to make known that his obedience is the obedience of Allah. Ibn Ishaq said: this verse is the beginning of the reproach concerning the affair of Uhud, the defeat of those who fled, and the departure of the archers from their position. It has been said: its form is an imperative, but its meaning is a reproach upon the believers for what occurred among them of consuming riba and of opposition on the day of Uhud. Mercy from Allah is His desire for good for His servants, or His reward for their deeds.

These verses also contain various kinds of eloquence and rhetorical embellishment (badi'). Among them is the general term intended as a specific one (al-'amm al-murad bihi al-khass) in "﴿مِن أَهْلِكَ﴾" (from your family) [Al 'Imran: 121]. The majority said that it refers to the house of 'A'isha. The specificity appears in: "﴿وَاللَّهُ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾" (And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing) [Al 'Imran: 121]; in "﴿فَلْيَتَوَكَّلِ الْمُؤْمِنُونَ﴾" (so let the believers rely upon Allah) [Al 'Imran: 122]; in "﴿مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾" (whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth) [Al 'Imran: 129]; and in "﴿يَغْفِرُ لِمَن يَشَاءُ وَيُعَذِّبُ مَن يَشَاءُ﴾" (He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills) [Al 'Imran: 129], where He singles out Himself with this, like His saying: "﴿وَمَن يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ﴾" (And who forgives sins except Allah) [Al 'Imran: 135], and "﴿نَبِّئْ عِبَادِي أَنِّي أَنَا الْغَفُورُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾" (Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful) [al-Hijr: 49], and in "﴿الْعَزِيزِ الْحَكِيمِ﴾" (the Mighty, the Wise) [Al 'Imran: 126], because might is among the fruits of victory, and good planning is among the fruits of wisdom.

As for simile (tashbih): in "﴿لِيَقْطَعَ طَرَفًا﴾" (that He might cut off a part) [Al 'Imran: 127], He likened those among them who were killed and scattered to a severed piece whose parts have been separated and whose order has been broken. In "﴿وَلِتَطْمَئِنَّ قُلُوبُكُمْ﴾" (and that your hearts may be reassured) [Al 'Imran: 126], He likened the departure of fear from the heart and its settling from its agitation to the calm of a man who is still in motion. In "﴿فَيَنْقَلِبُوا خَائِبِينَ﴾" (so that they might return disappointed) [Al 'Imran: 127], He likened their return without victory or spoils to a man who hoped for good from a person, went to him, and whose hope and aim were frustrated. Antithesis (tibaq) appears in "نَصَرَكُمْ" (He helped you) and "أَنتُمْ أَذِلَّةٌ" (while you were humble): victory is honor, which is the opposite of humiliation. And in "يَغْفِرُ" (forgives) and "يُعَذِّبُ" (punishes): forgiveness is leaving off taking to account, and punishment is taking to account for the sin. There is a figurative usage (tajawwuz) in the use of the dual for the plural in "أَن يَفْشَلَا" (that the two of them would lose heart). And there is the placing of the lam in place of "إلى" (to) in "﴿لَيْسَ لَكَ﴾" (It is not for you) [Al 'Imran: 128], meaning "إِلَيْكَ" (to you), or in place of "عَلى" (upon), meaning "لَيْسَ عَلَيْكَ" (not upon you). There is ellipsis (hadhf) and parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh) in places where the context required them. There is the matching paronomasia (tajnis al-mumathil) in "﴿أَضْعَافًا مُضَاعَفَةً﴾" (multiplied manifold) [Al 'Imran: 130]. And there is naming a thing by what it will become, in "لَا تَأْكُلُوا" (do not consume): the taking [of riba] was called eating, because it leads to it.

﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Paradise whose breadth is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the God-conscious,﴾ ﴿who spend in ease and in hardship, who restrain their anger and pardon people. And these days We alternate among people, that God may know those who believe and take martyrs from among you — and God does not love the wrongdoers.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140] ﴿And that God may purify those who believe and destroy the disbelievers.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 141]

(p-56) Al-kazm (restraint, the act of holding back) is holding oneself in check over anger or grief. Al-kazim is one who is filled with grief, and it is the same as al-makzum. Abdul-Muttalib said:

"So I roused my people and sought reward in fighting them, while the people were restrained (kuzzam) from fear of death."

The restraint of anger is returning it into the inner self when it would otherwise come out because of its intensity; so controlling it and preventing it is kazm (restraint) for it. It is said: kazama the waterskin when he tied it while it was full. Al-kizam is the strap tied over its mouth. Kazama the camel its cud: he returned it into its belly, or held it back before sending it up to its mouth. It is said: the camel and the she-camel kazama when they do not chew the cud, and from this is the saying of al-Ra'i:

"Then, after their restraint, they poured forth a cud from the valleys of Dhu al-Abatih when they grazed Haqil."

Haqil is a place, and haqil is also a plant. It is said: camels do not withhold their cud except at times of hardship and fear, so they do not chew. From this is the saying of A'sha Bahila describing the slaughterer of camels:

"He restrains the young camel when he sees it, until its chewing is cut off in its bellies."

Al-israr (persistence) is firm resolve to continue upon a matter, and not giving up on it; from sarra al-dananir (he tied the dinars), meaning he tied them up. Abu al-Sammal said:

"God knows that it is from me a bond (sirran)."

That is: a resolve. Al-Hutay'a, describing horses, said:

"Frowning, with the disheveled brave ones, when they seek their hooves with the racing ones, they persisted (asarrat)."

That is, they remained steadfast in their running. Another said:

"He persists by night while his tracks are concealed; woe to every heart that persists, a deceiver."

Al-sunnah is the way. Al-Mufaddal said: it is the community (ummah), and he recited:

"No people have seen such excellence as your excellence, nor have they seen its like in the past sunan."

The sunnah of a person is what he does and persists in, like the saying of Khalid al-Hudhali to Abu Dhu'ayb:

"So do not grieve over a sunnah you have traveled upon; the first to be content with a sunnah is the one who travels it."

Sulayman ibn Qutayba said:

"Indeed those of the most gentle of the family of Hashim who followed the example (ta'assaw), so they established for the noble the example (ta'assi)."

Labid said:

"From a community whose fathers established for them, and for every people there is a sunnah and its imam."

Al-Khalil said: sanna the thing means he shaped it; al-masnun is the shaped. Sanna upon them evil means he poured it; he poured water and the coat of mail. The derivation of sunnah may be from one of these two meanings, or from sanna the spear and the blade: he sharpened them on the whetstone, or from sanna the camels: when he grazed them well. Al-sayr fi al-ardh is going.

Wahana al-shay' means it became weak, and wahanahu al-shay' means it weakened him; it is both transitive and intransitive. In a hadith: "The fever of Yathrib weakened them." Al-wahn is weakness. Zuhayr said:

"So the rope became frayed and worn."

Al-qarh and al-qurh are two dialects, like al-du'f and al-du'f, and al-kurh and al-kurh. The fatha form is the Hijazi dialect and means a wound. Hunduj said:

"And I was given a bleeding wound after health, perhaps our deaths have turned into miseries."

Al-Akhfash said: both are verbal nouns. Whoever says al-qarh with fatha is a wound and with damma is pus must provide authentic transmission from the Arabs. The root meaning of the word is purity, and from it: clear water (ma' qira') with no turbidity, clear land (ard qira') pure in its clay, and the nature (qarihat) of a man is the purity of his disposition.

Al-mudawalah is repetition, which is passing around (al-mu'ahadah) time after time. It is said: dawalt bayna-hum al-shay' fa-tadawaluhu, I passed the thing among them and they passed it around. He said:

"He comes to the waters and does not stop being passed around among people, between recitation and hearing."

And adaltuhu: I made for him a turn and alternation. Al-dawlah with damma is the verbal noun, and with fatha is a single occurrence; therefore one says "in the dawlah of so-and-so," because it is once in time. Al-dawr and al-dawl are close in meaning, but al-dawr is more general, for al-dawlah is only said of worldly fortune.

Al-mahs is like al-fahs, but al-fahs is said of bringing out a thing from among separate things, while al-mahs is bringing it out from things attached to it. Al-Khalil said: al-tamhis is purification from defects. It is said: mahhasa al-habl (he purified the rope) when it became free of its fiber from much passing over the hand, and became smooth. Thus al-Zajjaj narrated the expression "al-habl". Al-Naqqash narrated it as: mahhasa al-jamal when it became free of its hair and smooth. Hanif al-Hanatim said: "He came to a water named Tuwayla'; you are indeed a smooth rope, far from the watering place, overlooking the enemies."
