The meaning: because of its distance, its rope becomes smooth from the passing of hands.

* *

﴿And hasten to forgiveness from your Lord and a Paradise whose breadth is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the God-conscious﴾: Ibn 'Amir and Nafi' read "sari'u" (hasten) without a waw, as a new sentence; the rest read it with the waw, as a conjunction. When they were commanded to be wary of the Fire, they were commanded to hasten to the causes of forgiveness and Paradise. Al-Duri, in the reading of al-Kisa'i, inclined "wa-sari'u" because of the kasra on the ra'. Ubayy and Abdullah read "wa-sabiqu" (and race). Al-musara'ah (hastening) is a form of mufa'alah (reciprocal action), since each of the people reaches [the goal] before others, so there is a mutual contest among them in that. Do you not see His saying: ﴿So race to good deeds﴾ [al-Baqarah: 148]. The hastening to the cause of forgiveness is sincerity, said by Uthman; or performing the obligatory duties, said by Ali; or Islam, said by Ibn 'Abbas; or the first takbir of the prayer with the imam, said by Anas and Makhul; or obedience, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr; or repentance, said by Ikrimah; or emigration, said by Abu al-'Aliyah; or jihad, said by al-Dahhak; or the five daily prayers, said by Yaman; or righteous deeds, said by Muqatil. These sayings should be taken as examples, not as specification or restriction.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of hastening to forgiveness and Paradise is turning toward what deserves them both. End. In the mention of deserving there is a hidden trace of Mu'tazilite doctrine. The mention of forgiveness precedes Paradise because it is the cause that leads to Paradise. The modifier is omitted from "al-samawat", meaning "the breadth of the heavens", after the omission of the particle of comparison, meaning "like the breadth". After this supposition they differed: is it a real comparison, or is it taken to mean great vastness? Since Paradise is at the utmost extent of expansiveness, as the heavens and the earth are the widest and most extensive of the created things known to people, and breadth was specified because it is usually less than length for emphasis, then according to this no literal breadth or length is meant, as said by al-Zajjaj. The Arabs say: "bilad 'ariydah", meaning wide lands. A poet said:

"As if the lands of God, though wide, upon the fearful one who is pursued were the palm of a fowler."

The first saying is from Ibn 'Abbas and others. Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and the majority said: the heavens and the earth are joined one to another as cloths are spread out; that is the breadth of Paradise, and none knows its length but God. End. This is not denied, for what has come in the hadith describing Paradise and its vastness supports this. Ibn 'Atiyya cited many such things in his book. According to this saying, Paradise is greater than the heavens, and it extends in length wherever God wills. Breadth was specified for mention because it indicates length, and length when mentioned does not indicate the vastness of breadth, since breadth may be small like the breadth of a thread.

Some people said: its meaning is like the breadth of the heavens and the earth laid in layers, not joined like the spreading of cloths. So Paradise is in the heaven and its breadth is like its breadth, and the breadth of what corresponds to it of the earths up to the seventh. This indicates greatness, and mention of breadth sufficed without mention of length. Ibn Furak said: Paradise is in the heaven, and it will be increased on the Day of Resurrection. The discussion has preceded concerning Paradise: was it created? That is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the explicit sound prophetic reports; or has it not yet been created (p-58)? That is the saying of the Mu'tazila, and our scholars from our land agreed with them, Qadi Mundhir ibn Sa'id. As for Ibn Furak's saying that it will be increased, it requires authentic transmission from the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Kalbi said: Gardens are four: the Garden of Eden, the Garden of Refuge, the Garden of Firdaws, and the Garden of Bliss. Each garden among them is like the breadth of the heavens and the earth; if some were joined to others, none would know their length except God. Ibn Bahr said: it is from the "'ard" of goods for sale, not the breadth opposite to length. That is: if they were offered for exchange, the share of each one of you would equal it. Its preparation is for the God-conscious, and they were singled out for mention as an honor for them and to inform that they are the foundation of this, while others follow them in its preparation. If by the God-conscious is meant those who are conscious of shirk, it becomes general to every Muslim, obedient or disobedient.

**Those who spend in ease and in hardship:** Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Kalbī and Muqātil said: *al-sarrāʾ* is ease, and *al-ḍarrāʾ* is hardship. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: prosperity and adversity. It was also said: in life and after death, by making a bequest. It was said: in joy and in sorrow. It was said: in what gladdens, such as spending on children and relatives, and in what harms, such as spending on enemies. It was said: in hosting the wealthy and giving gifts to them, and in what one spends on the needy and gives in charity to them. It was said: in times of eagerness and in times of reluctance. It is possible to restrict it to these two states, and it is possible that it means all circumstances, since the one who spends is never free of one of these two states. The meaning is: neither a state of joy nor a state of trial prevents them from giving in kindness. It is narrated from ʿĀʾishah that she gave away a single grape, and from one of the *salaf* (the early pious predecessors) that he gave away an onion. The verse begins with the attribute of *taqwā* (God-consciousness), which encompasses all noble qualities, and then follows it with the attribute of giving, since it is harder on the soul and more indicative of sincerity, and it is among the greatest of deeds, because of the need for it in jihad and in aiding the poor. In "الَّذِينَ" both *al-itbāʿ* (agreeing with the preceding word as an adjective) and *al-qaṭʿ* (breaking off into a separate clause) are permissible, for the nominative (*rafʿ*) and the accusative (*naṣb*).

**And those who restrain anger:** that is, those who hold back within themselves the anger they feel, through patience, so that no trace of it appears. *Al-ghayẓ* is the root of anger (*al-ghaḍab*), and the two often accompany each other; for this reason some commentators here explained it as anger.

*Al-ghayẓ* is an inner state that does not show on the limbs, whereas *al-ghaḍab* is a state in which the limbs show visible signs and some action necessarily follows. For this reason it is attributed to Allah, the Exalted, since it is an expression of His actions toward those who have earned His wrath (*al-maghḍūb ʿalayhim*), whereas *al-ghayẓ* is not attributed to Him. Many hadiths have been transmitted about restraining anger, and it is among the greatest acts of worship. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever restrains anger while able to act upon it, Allah will fill his heart with security and faith." And from him (peace be upon him): "No sip that a servant swallows is better for him or greater in reward than a sip of anger swallowed for the sake of Allah." And from ʿĀʾishah: a servant of hers angered her, and she said: "By Allah, how wonderful is *taqwā*! It leaves no cure for the one who is angry." Muqātil said: "We have been informed that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said about this verse: 'Those who do this in my nation are few, though they were more numerous among the earlier nations.'" Abū al-Qāsim ibn Ḥabīb recited:

Whenever you are angered, be dignified and restrain your anger; you will see clearly what you say, and you will hear.

So it is honour enough, a moment of patience, through which the God is pleased with you and repels harm.

**And those who pardon people:** that is, the wrongdoers and the offenders. Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū al-ʿĀliyah and al-Rabīʿ said: the slaves. This is an example, since slaves commit many wrongs due to their ignorance and constant closeness, and it is easy to inflict punishment upon them because one has power over them. Al-Ḥasan said: "those who restrain anger" toward slaves, and "those who pardon people" when they act ignorantly toward them. Prophetic reports about pardon have been transmitted, among them: "On the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: 'Where are those whose reward is upon Allah? Let them enter Paradise.' It will be asked: 'Who has a reward upon Allah?' None will stand except those who pardoned." Abū Sufyān narrated this to al-Rashīd when he was angry with a man, and so al-Rashīd let him go. In "الكاظِمِينَ والعافِينَ" the accusative (*naṣb*) and the agreeing form (*itbāʿ*) are permissible, on the condition that it agrees with "الَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ".

**And Allah loves the good-doers:** The *alif* and *lām* here are for the category (*li-l-jins*), so it includes every good-doer. Or they are for a known reference (*li-l-ʿahd*), in which case it refers to those already mentioned who possess these qualities. The first is more apparent, so it includes these and others. This verse concerns what is recommended (*al-mandūb ilayhi*). Do you not see the hadith of Jibrīl (peace be upon him): "What is faith?" And he (ﷺ) explained to him the creedal articles (*ʿaqāʾid*). "What is Islam?" And he explained to him the obligatory duties (*farāʾiḍ*). "What is *iḥsān*?" He said: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him." The meaning is that Allah loves the good-doers, those who perform righteous deeds while being mindful of Allah as though they are witnessing Him. Al-Ḥasan said: *iḥsān* is that you extend benefit generally and do not restrict it, like the wind, the rain, the sun and the moon. Al-Thawrī said: *iḥsān* is that you show kindness to the one who wrongs you, for kindness toward him is a settlement, like the exchange in the market: take from me and give to me.

(p-59)

﴿Those who, when they commit an indecency or wrong themselves, remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins﴾ was revealed, according to the majority view, concerning Manhal al-Tammar, who was known by the kunya Abu Muqbil. A woman came to him to buy dates, and he embraced her and kissed her, then regretted it. It was also said that he struck her buttocks.

The conjunction with "and" (al-'atf bi'l-waw) indicates difference. When He mentioned the highest category, those who are God-conscious (al-muttaqun), described with those beautiful attributes, He mentioned those below them who committed sins, then repented and gave them up. This is not a case of conjoining attributes of a single described subject. It was also said that it is a conjunction of attributes, and that it is a description of the God-conscious; this was narrated from al-Hasan.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "The indecency (al-fahisha) is adultery, and wronging oneself is what falls short of it, such as looking and touching." Muqatil said: "The indecency is adultery, and wronging oneself is all other sins." Al-Nakha'i said: "The indecency is the vile deeds, and wronging oneself is part of the indecency; it is for the sake of additional clarification." It was said: "It is all sins, and wronging oneself is acting without knowledge or proof." al-Baqir said: "The indecency is looking at actions, and wronging oneself is seeing salvation as coming through deeds." It was said: "The indecency is the major sin, and wronging oneself is the minor sin." It was said: "The indecency is the sin that is openly displayed, and it was said: it is what is hidden." Muqatil and al-Kalbi said: "The indecency is what falls short of adultery, such as a kiss, a touch, or a look at what is not lawful, and wronging oneself is disobedience." It was also said: "The indecency is the sin which involves a consequence for created beings, and wronging oneself is what lies between the servant and his Lord." These are specifications that require evidence. The word "indecency" is most commonly used for adultery; for this reason Jabir, when he heard the verse, said: "They committed adultery, by the Lord of the Ka'ba!"

The meaning of "remember Allah" is: they remembered His threat (wa'idahu). This was said by Ibn Jarir and others. It was also said: it means being presented before Allah, as said by al-Dahhak; or being questioned about Him on the Day of Resurrection, as said by al-Kalbi, Muqatil and al-Waqidi. It was said: it means His prohibition. It was said: His forgiveness. It was said: they brought His remembrance to their hearts so that it would move them to repentance. It was said: His great pardon, so they hoped for His forgiveness. It was said: His kindness, so they felt shame before Him for their wrongdoing. All of these views hold that the remembrance is of the heart. It was also said that it is by the tongue, and that is seeking forgiveness. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra, 'Ata' and others said: they remembered Allah in their hearts, saying: "O Allah, forgive us our sins." It was narrated from Abu Hurayra: "I have not seen anyone who sought forgiveness more than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Along with the remembrance of the tongue, there must be agreement of the heart; otherwise, this seeking of forgiveness has no weight. Whoever seeks forgiveness while persisting in sin, his seeking forgiveness itself requires seeking forgiveness. Seeking forgiveness (al-istighfar) is asking Allah for forgiveness after repentance.

It was said: they regretted, even if they did not ask. The apparent meaning is the first. The object of "they sought forgiveness from Allah" is omitted because the meaning is understood; that is, "they sought forgiveness from Him for their sins." This verb and its transitivity have already been discussed.

* *

﴿And who forgives sins but Allah?﴾ This is a parenthetical clause (jumla i'tiradiyya) placed between the conjoined elements, or between the circumstantial element and the circumstance (dhu'l-hal wa'l-hal). The grammatical analysis (i'rab) of a parallel of this clause has already been discussed in His words: ﴿And who turns away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself?﴾ [al-Baqara: 130]. This parenthetical clause contains a softening of the soul, an incitement to hope in Allah and in the vastness of His pardon, and the singling out of Him for forgiving sins. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It describes His essence with vast mercy and the nearness of forgiveness, that the one who repents from sin is with Him as one who has no sin, that there is no refuge for sinners except His grace and generosity, and that His justice requires forgiveness for the repentant, because when the servant comes in apology and self-exoneration with the utmost of what he can, pardon and overlooking become obligatory." In this there is consolation for the souls of the servants, encouragement to repentance and urging towards it, and deterrence from despair and hopelessness; and that sins, however great, His pardon is greater, and His generosity is more immense. The meaning is that He alone possesses the conditions that make forgiveness valid." End of quote. This is a fine statement, except that it does not depart from the expressions of the Mu'tazila in his words "His justice requires forgiveness for the repentant," and in his words "pardon and overlooking become obligatory." Had we not known that his school is Mu'tazilism, we would have interpreted his words to mean that this obligation is through the true promise, so it is from the perspective of revelation (al-sam') and not from the perspective of reason alone. (p-60)

﴿And they did not persist in what they had done while they knew﴾ That is, they did not continue in their vile deed. This clause is conjoined to "they sought forgiveness," so it is part of the consequent (jaza') that follows the condition (shart). It is also permissible for the "waw" to be the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and for it to be a circumstance of the subject in "they sought forgiveness," so it would be part of the consequent: "they sought forgiveness for their sins, not persisting." The "ma" may be a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) or a verbal-masdar (masdariyya).

Qatada said: "Persistence (al-israr) is continuing in sin, going on with it." al-Hasan said: "It is committing the sin again and again until one repents." Mujahid said: "They did not persist: they did not continue." al-Suddi said: "It is abandoning seeking forgiveness and remaining silent about it while in sin." The clause "while they knew" — al-Zamakhshari said: it is a circumstance of the act of persistence, and the negation particle applies to both together. The meaning is: "They are not among those who persist in sins while knowing their ugliness, and the prohibition against them, and the threat for them; for one who does not know the ugliness of the ugly may be excused."

In these verses there is a decisive explanation that those who believe are in three categories: the God-conscious, the repentant, and the persistent. Paradise is for the God-conscious and the repentant among them, not for the persistent. Whoever disagrees on this has opposed his own reason and defied his Lord. End of his words, and its ending follows his Mu'tazilite method, that whoever dies persisting enters the Fire and never leaves it forever. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "﴿while they knew﴾ [al-Baqara: 75]" could be a circumstance of the pronoun in "they sought forgiveness." If we parse "they did not persist" as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "they sought forgiveness," then "while they knew" may also be a circumstance of it. If "they did not persist" is conjoined to "they sought forgiveness," then what Abu al-Baqa' said is far-fetched, because of the separation between the circumstantial element and the circumstance by the clause. As for the object of knowledge, it has been mentioned in al-Zamakhshari's words.

Abu al-Baqa' said: "They know the consequence of it, or Allah's pardon for it." Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: "They know that leaving it is better than persisting in it." Mujahid and Abu 'Umara said: "They know that Allah accepts the repentance of whoever repents." al-Suddi and Muqatil said: "They know that they have sinned." It was said: "They remember their sins and repent of them," the name of knowledge being applied to remembrance because it is one of its fruits. Ibn Ishaq said: "They know what I have forbidden to them." al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: "They know that they have a Lord who forgives sins." Ibn Bahr said: "They know through the sin." It was said: "They know the pardon for sins, however many they are."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 136:

﴿Those—their reward is forgiveness from their Lord and gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever.﴾ "Ulā'ika" (those) is a demonstrative referring to the two categories (al-ṣinfayn). It is also permissible that it refers specifically to the second category, with ﴿those who, when they commit an indecency﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 135] being the subject (mubtada'), "Ulā'ika" and what follows it being its predicate (khabar), and ﴿their reward is forgiveness﴾ being a subject and predicate in the place of the predicate of "Ulā'ika." There is an omitted element, i.e., "the reward of their deeds is forgiveness from their Lord for their sins."

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: By this truthful report He has obligated Himself to accept the repentance of the penitent. Nothing is obligatory upon Him, exalted is He, by way of reason; rather, He acts by the authority of sovereignty, and none can challenge His command. Al-Zamakhsharī said: He said "ajr al-ʿāmilīn" (the reward of the workers) after His saying "jazā'uhum" (their reward), because the two have one meaning; He varied between the two expressions only to add emphasis to the point that this is a reward that is due for a deed, and a wage that is deserved for it, not as the falsifiers (al-mubṭilūn) say. It is reported that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed to Moses, peace be upon him: "How little shame has one who hopes for My Paradise without works! How shall I be generous with My mercy to one who is miserly with My obedience?" And from Shahr ibn Ḥawshab: Seeking Paradise without works is a sin among sins, awaiting intercession without cause is a kind of delusion, and hoping for mercy from one who is not obeyed is foolishness and ignorance. And from al-Ḥasan: Allah says on the Day of Resurrection: "Cross the Ṣirāt by My pardon, enter Paradise by My mercy, and divide it by your deeds." And from Rābiʿa al-Baṣriyya that she used to recite:

Hoping for salvation without treading its paths,
Indeed the ship does not run on dry land.

End of what he mentioned. The verse that Rābiʿa used to recite belongs to ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak. Al-Zamakhsharī's statement follows his Muʿtazilī doctrine that faith without deeds does not benefit in the Hereafter. (p-61)

﴿And excellent is the reward of the workers﴾: the object of praise (al-makhṣūṣ bi-l-madḥ) is omitted; its estimated form is: "And excellent is the reward of the workers—that, i.e., the forgiveness and the Paradise."

The address is to the believers. The meaning is that if the unbelievers prevailed over you at Uhud, the good end belongs to the God-fearing, and if the unbelievers were overcome, the end belongs to the believers. "And likewise, these unbelievers of yours, their end is destruction." Al-Naqqash said: the address is to the unbelievers, because of His saying afterward "(and do not weaken)." When God, exalted is He, mentioned the intervening clauses in the story of Uhud, He returned to its completion, addressing them that if the unbelievers' overcoming occurred, the end belongs to the believers. The meaning: "They have passed and gone."

Al-Zajjaj said: *ahl sunan*, that is, "ways" (*taraʾiq*) or "nations" (*umam*), according to the explanation of al-Mufaddal that *al-sunnah* means the nation. Al-Hasan said: *sunnah* means the decrees concerning the destruction of the earlier nations, such as ʿAd, Thamud and others. Ibn Zayd said: *amthal* (examples). Ibn ʿAbbas said: events, and the request to travel in the earth, although the circumstances of those who came before are known through reports rather than travel, because reports come only from one who traveled and witnessed, and are transmitted from him. So He asked them for the more complete way, since direct observation has a stronger effect than hearing. It was said: the travel here is a metaphor (*majaz*) for reflection, and this is from likening the intelligible to the sensible (*tashbih al-maʿqul bi-l-mahsus*). The majority said: the looking here is looking with the eye. Some people said: it is with thought.

The interrogative clause is in the position of the object of "look" (*unẓurū*), because it is suspended (*muʿallaqah*), and "how" (*kayfa*) is in the position of the accusative as the predicate of *kāna*. The meaning: what is God's way (*sunnat Allah*) among the unbelieving nations, in terms of its events, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So We seized each one for his sin﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 40] and ﴿and they were killed with a killing, the way of God concerning those who passed away before﴾ [al-Ahzab: 61].

In this verse is evidence of the permissibility of travel across the wide paths of the earth for the purpose of taking lessons (*iʿtibar*), observing what it contains of the wonders of God's creation, visiting the righteous, and visiting honored places, as the travelers of this community do. Also permitted is looking into the books of historians, because they are a way to knowing the histories of the world and what befell its peoples of calamities.

This is an explanation for mankind and a guidance and admonition for the God-fearing. Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ibn Juraij and al-Rabi' said: the reference is to the Qur'an. It was also said: the reference is to His words, ﴿Certainly, ways (sunan) have passed before you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 137]. This was said by Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari, and a group of others. That is: this is an explanation for mankind, if they accept it. Al-Sha'bi said: this is a clarification for mankind from blindness. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a clarification for mankind, an elucidation of the evil end of what they are upon of denial. He means: it urges them to reflect on the evil consequences for those who denied before them, and to take warning from what they witness of the traces of their destruction. ﴿And a guidance and an admonition for the God-fearing﴾. He means: although it is a clarification and a warning to the deniers, it is also an increase, a confirmation and an admonition for those among the believers who fear God. It is permissible that the phrase ﴿Certainly, ways have passed﴾ is a parenthetical clause urging towards faith and towards what deserves the reward mentioned for those who act. And his saying ﴿This is a clarification﴾ would be a reference to what he summarized and made clear regarding the state of the God-fearing, the repentant and the persistent. End of his words. And it is good. Since it was evident and clear, he said: a clarification for mankind. And since guidance and admonition are only for those who fear God, he specified the God-fearing with them, because whoever's understanding is blind and whose heart is hard does not find guidance nor take admonition, so it is not fitting for guidance and admonition to be attributed to him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 139:

﴿Do not be weak, nor grieve, for you will be the superior ones if you are believers.﴾ When those among the believers who fled had fled, Khalid [ibn al-Walid] came, intending to climb the mountain. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Let him not rise above us. O Allah, we have no strength except through You." Then this verse was revealed. This was related by Ibn Abbas. Al-Waqidi added that the archers of the Muslims climbed the mountain and shot at the horses of the polytheists until they routed them, and that this is the meaning of His words: "and you will be the superior ones." Al-Qurtubi said: "and you will be the victorious after Uhud. They did not set out after that except that they were victorious in every army that existed in his time (peace be upon him) and in every army that existed after him, even if there was only one of the Companions among them." Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed after Uhud, when they were commanded to pursue the enemy despite the wounds that had afflicted them, and he (the Prophet) said: "None shall set out except those who were with us yesterday." This was hard on the Muslims, so this verse was revealed. It forbade them from becoming weak in striving against their enemies and from grieving over those among their brothers who had been martyred, for they had gone to the honour of Allah. This was related by Ibn Abbas. Or it refers to their defeat and the killing of them on the day of Uhud; this was said by Muqatil. Or it refers to what befell the Prophet (ﷺ) of wounds to his head and the breaking of his front tooth; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Or it refers to what escaped them of the spoils; this was mentioned by Ahmad al-Naysaburi. Or it refers to all of that together. He consoled them with His words: "﴿and you will be the superior ones﴾", meaning the victorious and those who have the final outcome. It is a report of the elevation of the word of Islam. This was said by the majority, and it is the apparent meaning.

It was also said: "﴿and you will be the superior ones﴾" means that you had inflicted on them at Badr double what they had inflicted on you at Uhud, in captives and in killing. In this case "﴿and you will be the superior ones﴾" is in the accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial clause, "state" of the subject), meaning: do not grieve while you are superior, i.e., victorious over your enemy. End of quote. As for it being from their ascent of the mountain, as was indicated in the occasion of revelation, this was related from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Jubayr. Ibn Atiyya said: "It is from nobility of character that a person should not be weak in his war and his disputes, nor yield when he is in the right, and that he should exhaust all his capability, and not humble himself even if he dies. Gentleness is only fitting in peace and contentment. From this is his (peace be upon him) saying: 'The believer is gentle and easy-going, and the believers are gentle and easy-going.'" Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: "By this verse it is obligatory that one not make a truce with the enemy as long as the Muslims have strength and might. If they are in some region in other than this condition, then the Imam (ruler) considers what is most beneficial for them." End of quote.

In His words "﴿and you will be the superior ones﴾" there is an indication of the excellence of this Ummah, since He addressed them with the same as He addressed Moses, His interlocutor (Kalim), upon our Prophet and him (peace be upon them), when He said to him: "﴿Do not fear; indeed, you are the superior one﴾ [Ta-Ha: 68]." His words "﴿if you are believers﴾" are connected to the prohibition, so that this becomes a stirring of souls which necessitates strength of heart, trust in the handiwork of Allah, and little concern for the enemies. Or it is connected to the declarative sentence, meaning: if you affirm what He promised you and gave you good news of, namely victory. The conditional here remains on its original footing, and through it there is a rebuke of those whose hypocrisy became evident on that day, meaning: victory and superiority belong only to the believers, so hold fast to faith.

This is a translation request for a classical tafsir passage, so I'll render it into English following your formatting rules.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 140:**

﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has already touched the people﴾. The meaning: if they inflicted a wound on you on the Day of Uhud, then you inflicted one on them on the Day of Badr, and they did not weaken when they fought you after that, so do not you weaken. Or: a similar wound touched the people during the battle of Uhud, before the disobedience of the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the like, so they feel pain as you feel pain, but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope for. This is consolation from Him, may He be exalted, to the believers, and taking the example of others is the greatest consolation. Al-Khansa said:

"Were it not for the abundance of those weeping around me over their brothers, I would have killed myself.
And they do not weep like my brother, but I console myself for him by taking the example of others."

Likeness (al-mithliyyah) is true with even the slightest resemblance. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: what befell the believers on the Day of Uhud was like what befell the polytheists on the Day of Badr; seventy of the believers were martyred on the Day of Uhud. Al-Zamakhshari said: on that day, that is the Day of Uhud, a number of the disbelievers were killed. Do you not see His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿when you were killing them by His permission﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152]? According to his view, "a similar wound touched the people" refers to the Day of Badr. He who held that "the people" here refers to the earlier nations that had passed away is far off the mark, meaning that their believers suffered harm from their disbelievers similar to what you suffered from your enemies. Then the final outcome was for the believers, so you have in them an example. Your taking them as an example is something that lightens your pain and makes your feet firm at the encounter.

The two brothers (al-Akhawan), Abu Bakr and al-A'mash through his transmission, read "qurh" with a damma on the qaf in both places, and the rest of the seven read it with a fatha. The seven read the ra' with sukun. Abu 'Ali said: the fatha is preferred. End of quote. There is no preference, since both are mutawatir. Abu al-Sammal and Ibn al-Sumaiqa read "qarh" with fatha on the qaf and ra', which is a dialect, like al-tard and al-tarad, and al-shall and al-shalal. Al-A'mash read: "in yamsaskum" with the ta' from above, "qurooh" in the plural, and the answer of the conditional is omitted, its estimate being: then be consoled, for a wound has touched the people; because the past tense in meaning cannot be the answer of the condition. Whoever claims that the answer of the condition is "faqad massa" is confused.

﴿And these days We alternate among the people﴾. He, may He be exalted, informed by way of consolation that the days, since ancient times, do not remain for people in one state. By "the days" are meant the times of dominance and victory, which Allah turns as He wills, sometimes for these and sometimes for those, as war is a series of alternating turns. He said:

"One day is against us and one day is for us,
and one day we are distressed and one day we are delighted."

Some of the pure Arabs heard a reciter recite this verse and said: it is only "nudawiluha bayna al-'Arab" (among the Arabs). It was said to him: it is only "bayna al-nas" (among the people). He said: Surely we belong to Allah; the kingdom of the Arabs has gone, by the Lord of the Ka'bah. It was read irregularly as "yudawiluha" with the ya'. It accords with the third person before and after it. The reading with the nun in it is an iltifat (shift of person) and a report with the royal "we" suitable to the alternation of the days. "Al-ayyam" is an attribute of "tilka," or a substitute, or an explicative apposition. The predicate is "nudawiluha," or the predicate of "tilka," and "nudawiluha" is a circumstantial clause.

﴿And that Allah may know those who believed﴾. This is the lam of purpose (lam kay), preceded by the conjunction, so it is connected to an omitted later element, meaning: We did that, namely the alternation, or the disbelievers' inflicting harm on you. Or it is connected to an omitted cause and its governing element, meaning: We did that so that it would be such-and-such and so that Allah would know. Al-Zamakhshari and others estimated it this way, but did not specify the agent of the omitted cause; he referred to it only with "such-and-such," and one does not refer to a thing by a pronoun until it is known. So in this view there is omission of the cause, omission of its governing element, and vagueness about its agent. The first view is more apparent, since it involves only omission of the governing element. "Yalam" here apparently takes one object, so it is like "'arafa" (to know). It was said: it takes two objects, the second being omitted, its estimate being: distinguished by faith from others. That is, the wisdom in this alternation is that those who believed become distinguished from those who claim faith, through their patience and steadfastness in Islam.

The knowledge of Allah, may He be exalted, does not renew; rather He has always known things before they exist. This is by way of figurative speech, meaning: We did that as one who wishes to know, among you, those who are steadfast in faith from those who are not. It was said: its meaning is that the faith of those whom He knew from eternity would believe may become manifest in existence, and that His knowledge accords with their faith and existence; otherwise their knowledge would be lost in eternity, since His knowledge is not subject to change. Similar to this is a ruler who strikes a man and then explains the reason for the striking and says: I did this explanation so that I might strike him deservedly. Its meaning: so that it might be manifest that my act accorded with his deserving. It was said: its meaning is "and that He might know them with a knowledge on which reward depends," which is that He knows them as existing, with steadfastness present in them. It was said: the knowledge remains on its signified meaning, and it is by omitting a modifier, the estimate being: and that He might know the friends of Allah, but He attributed that to Himself in exaltation.

﴿And that He may take martyrs from among you﴾: that is, by being killed in His cause, so He honors them with martyrdom. This refers to the Day of Uhud. Many verses and hadiths have been transmitted about the virtue of the martyr. Or it means witnesses over the people on the Day of Resurrection, that is, that He may take from among you those who are fit to bear witness over the nations on the Day of Resurrection, by what He tests your patience through in hardships, from His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. The first view is more apparent and more fitting to the story of Uhud.

﴿And Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 57]: that is, He does not love one who is not steadfast in faith and patient in jihad. In this is an indication that whoever deserted on the Day of Uhud, like 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his followers among the hypocrites, by their desertion their faith was not made clear, rather their hypocrisy appeared, and they were not fit to be taken as martyrs by being killed in the cause of Allah. This is also an indication that what was done in terms of the disbelievers' alternation over the believers was not caused by His love, rather by the benefits mentioned, namely the manifestation and steadfastness of the believer's faith, and His choosing whom He wills among the believers for martyrdom. This sentence is placed as a parenthetical insertion between some causes and others, because of the emphasis and reinforcement it carries. The basis of the absence of love is wrongdoing, and this indicates its vileness and ugliness above all other evil attributes.

*Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 141:*

﴿And that Allah may purify those who believe﴾, i.e., cleanse them from sins, free them from defects, and purify them. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Suddi, Muqatil, Ibn Qutayba and others said: *al-tamhis* (purification through testing) means trial and examination. The poet said:

*"I saw Fudayl as something wrapped up, until testing (al-tamhis) uncovered him and he appeared clear to me."*

Al-Zajjaj said: it means cleansing and purging. He reported this from al-Mubarrad and al-Khalil. It was also said: it means purification. Al-Farra' said: it is by ellipsis of a noun (*hadhf mudaf*), meaning: "And that Allah may purify the sins of those who believe."

﴿And destroy the disbelievers﴾, i.e., destroy them little by little. The meaning is: if victory belongs to the disbelievers over the believers, it becomes a cause for distinguishing the believer from others, a cause for the martyrdom of those among them who are killed, and a cause for purifying the believer from sin. It thus combines many benefits for the believers. If, however, victory belongs to the believers over the disbelievers, it becomes a cause for their complete annihilation and uprooting. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn 'Abbas also said: it means diminishing and reducing them; al-Farra' said the same. Muqatil said: it means removing their call (their da'wa). It was also said: it means nullifying their deeds; al-Zajjaj mentioned this, and it is then by ellipsis of a noun.

The apparent meaning is that by "the disbelievers" here is meant a specific group, namely those who fought the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because He, exalted is He, did not destroy every disbeliever; many of them remained upon their disbelief. Thus the word "the disbelievers" is general, but what is intended is the specific (*al-'amm yurad bihi al-khass*, a general term used to mean a specific). It was said: He contrasted the purification of the believer with the destruction of the disbeliever, because purification (*al-tamhis*) is the destruction of sins, and destruction (*al-mahq*) is the destruction of souls; this is a subtle contrast in meaning. End. Mentioning what befalls the believer when the disbelievers gain the upper hand is a consolation for them and good news of these great benefits, and that this turn of fortune was not out of contempt for them, nor does it lower their status, but rather for what Allah, exalted is He, has mentioned.

These verses contain various kinds of eloquence, rhetoric and figurative expression. Among them is the *i'tiraḍ* (parenthetical insertion) in "﴿And Allah loves the good-doers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134]", in "﴿And who forgives sins except Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 135]", and in "﴿Allah does not love the wrongdoers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 57]". There is also naming a thing by the name of its cause (*tasmiyat al-shay' bi-ism sababihi*) in "﴿forgiveness from your Lord﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]", and the simile in "﴿whose breadth is the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]". It was said: this is a metaphor (*isti'ara*), and the attribution of the ruling to the majority in "﴿prepared for the God-conscious﴾" is a case where it is prepared for them and for others among the disobedient. There is antithesis (*tibaq*) in "the times of adversity and prosperity (al-sarra' wa-l-darra')", and in "﴿do not weaken﴾" and "﴿you will be the superior ones (al-a'lawn)﴾", because weakness and superiority are opposites. And in "﴿believed﴾" and "﴿the wrongdoers﴾", because here the wrongdoers are the disbelievers; and in "﴿believed﴾" and "﴿destroy the disbelievers﴾". The general term used to mean the specific occurs in "﴿and those who pardon people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134]", meaning those who wronged them or the slaves. Repetition occurs in "﴿and fear Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 200]", "﴿and fear the Fire﴾ [Al 'Imran: 131]", in the word of majesty (*lafz al-jalala*, the name Allah), in "﴿Allah loves﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134]", "﴿remembered Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 135]", in "﴿that Allah may know﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140]", "﴿Allah does not love﴾ [Al 'Imran: 57]", "﴿and that Allah may purify﴾", and in "those who spend" and "those who, when they do". Restriction (*al-ikhtisas*) occurs in "﴿loves the good-doers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134]", in "﴿while they know﴾ [Al 'Imran: 75]", in "﴿the end of the deniers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 137]", in "an admonition for the God-conscious", in "﴿if you are believers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 175]", in "﴿does not love the wrongdoers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140]", in "﴿and that Allah may purify those who believe﴾", and in "﴿and destroy the disbelievers﴾". Metaphor occurs in "so travel (fa-sirū)", taken as the travel of thought rather than of the feet; in "﴿and you will be the superior ones﴾ [Al 'Imran: 139]", if it is not about height of place; in "those days We alternate them", and in "that Allah may purify" and "﴿and destroy﴾", and the indication in this is clarification. And in "﴿those days﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140]". The insertion of the conditional particle with a matter that is certain, as in "﴿if you are believers﴾ [Al Baqara: 91]", when the prohibition and the omission are attached to it, occurs in a number of places.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 142:**

﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and known the steadfast?﴾ ﴿Indeed, you used to wish for death before you met it. Now you have seen it, while you were looking on.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 143] ﴿Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers have passed away before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels? Whoever turns back on his heels will not harm Allah at all, and Allah will reward the grateful.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 144] ﴿No soul may die except by Allah's permission, at an appointed term. Whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him of it, and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him of it, and We will reward the grateful.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 145] ﴿How many a prophet has fought, and with him many devoted followers (ribbiyyun). They did not falter for what befell them in the way of Allah, nor did they weaken or submit. Allah loves the steadfast.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 146] ﴿Their only words were: "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excesses in our affair, make our feet firm, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 147] ﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter. Allah loves the doers of good.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 148] ﴿O you who have believed, if you obey those who disbelieve, they will turn you back on your heels, and you will become losers.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 149] ﴿Rather, Allah is your Protector, and He is the best of helpers.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 150] ﴿We will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved, because they associated with Allah that for which He had sent down no authority. Their refuge is the Fire, and wretched is the abode of the wrongdoers.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 151] ﴿And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission, until when you lost courage, disputed about the matter, and disobeyed after He had shown you what you love. Among you were those who desired this world, and among you were those who desired the Hereafter. Then He turned you away from them to test you. He has certainly pardoned you, and Allah is full of bounty toward the believers.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152]

(p-65) "Ka'ayyin" (how many) is a word used for multiplication, meaning "kam" (how many) in an informative sense, and it is rarely used in a interrogative sense. The "ka" is for comparison (tashbih); it entered upon "ayy," and the meaning of comparison disappeared. This is the position of Sibawayh and al-Khalil, and according to their view it is pausing without tanwin. Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) claimed that the pattern (wazn) of "ayy" is "fi'l," being the verbal noun of "awa, ya'wi," meaning to gather and come together; its origin is "awa," and it underwent what happened to the verbal noun "tayy" of "tawa." All of this is a claim for which no proof stands. What appears to be correct is that it is a simple, indeclinable noun with no composition in it, used for multiplication like "kam." It has several dialectal forms: the first is the one mentioned above; "ka'in" (kā'in) and the claim that this is the active participle of "kana" is far-fetched; "ka'a'an" on the pattern of "ka'an," "ka'ayyin," and "kayayyin." It is pausing on it with a nun. Its specification (tamyiz) most often comes accompanied by "min" (of). Ibn 'Usfur erred in his statement that it necessarily requires "min," and that when it is omitted the specification is in the accusative whether or not it immediately follows it, as in the words of the poet:

"I drive away despair with hope, for how many a pain has overtaken one whose ease came after hardship."

And the words of another:

"How many a favor and blessing we have had over you of old, and you do not know of any benefactor."

Al-Ru'b: fear. One says "ra'abtuhu," and he is "marub" (terrified). Its origin is from filling. One says: "a flood (sayl ra'ib) fills the valley," and "ra'abtu al-hawd" means "I filled the basin."

Al-Sultan: proof and evidence; from it the ruler is called "sultan." It has been said that the derivation of "sultan" is from "salit," which is what the lamp is lit with from sesame oil. It has been said: "salit" is iron, and "salata" is sharpness, and "salata" is from "taslit" which is domination, and "sultan" derives from that, so the nun is augmentative. "Salita" is a loud-voiced woman, and "salit" is an eloquent man.

Al-Mathwa: a noun of place from "thawa, yathwi," meaning to dwell. It can be a verbal noun, a noun of time, and a noun of place. "Al-thawa'" is residing in a place.

Al-Hass: a devastating killing. One says: "hassahu, yahussuhu." The poet said:

"We struck them with the sword in a striking, and their remnant became scattered and dispersed."

A locust that is "mahsus" is one killed by cold, and a year that is "hasus" is one that destroyed everything.

Al-Tanazu': disagreement; it is from "naz'," which is pulling. "Naza'a, yanza'u" means to pull, and it is transitive to one object. "Nazi'a" is transitive to two objects, and "tanazi'a" is transitive to one object. He said:

"When we contended over the talk and it turned sweet, I bent down a branch with clusters, swaying."

﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while Allah has not yet known those of you who strove and known the steadfast?﴾ This verse and what follows is severe reproach toward those who committed lapses on the Day of Uhud. The interrogation is in the manner of denunciation: that anyone should suppose he could enter Paradise while he neglects what has been made obligatory upon him of jihad and steadfastness in it. The intended meaning of the negation of knowledge is the negation of its object, because it is negated by the negation of that, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾ [al-Anfal: 23]. The meaning is: there was no good in them, because what Allah the Exalted's knowledge does not attach to does not exist, and what does not exist will never exist.

"Am" here is disconnected (munqati'ah) according to the majority, being estimated as "bal" (rather), and the hamza is as established in grammar. It has been said: it has the meaning of the hamza. It has been said: "am" is connected (muttasilah). Ibn Bahr said: it is the equivalent of a hamza that is estimated from the meaning of what precedes it, because His saying: ﴿If a wound touches you, a similar wound has touched the people﴾ [Al 'Imran: 140] through the end of the story requires that what follows be: "Do you know that obligation requires this, or do you suppose that you would enter Paradise without testing and enduring hardship, and that you would strive so that Allah would know it from you as actual?" End of his words. What we have already mentioned refutes this kind of view. This interrogation whose meaning includes denial, and the turning away (idrab) which it also includes, is leaving what precedes without nullifying it and moving on to what follows.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: "﴿Or did you think﴾" is a prohibition expressed in the form of an interrogation that is used for rebuke. Its summary: "Do not suppose that you would enter Paradise while jihad has not occurred from you." When He said: ﴿Do not weaken and do not grieve﴾ [Al 'Imran: 139], it was in the sense of: "Do you know that this is as you are commanded, or do you suppose that you would enter Paradise without striving and steadfastness?" This is considered far-fetched because Allah the Exalted made jihad obligatory before this event, and made steadfastness obligatory in bearing its hardships, and clarified the aspects of its benefits in religion and worldly life. Given this, it is far-fetched that a person should attain happiness and Paradise while neglecting this principle. End of his words. Its apparent sense is that "am" is connected, and "hasibtum" here means "zanantum" (you supposed) in the sense of preponderance, and "an" and what follows fill the place of its two objects according to the school of Sibawayh, and fill the place of one object with the second omitted according to the school of Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash).

﴿while Allah has not yet known﴾ is a circumstantial clause (jumlah hāliyyah), and it is a emphatic negation in contrast to the affirmative emphasized with "qad." When you say: "qad qama Zayd" (Zayd has indeed stood), there is in it affirmation and emphasis that is not in your saying "qama Zayd" (Zayd stood). When you negate it you say: "lamma yaqum Zayd." And when you say "qama Zayd," its negation is "lam yaqum Zayd," as Sibawayh and others said. al-Zamakhshari said: "lamma" has the meaning of "lam," except that in it there is a kind of expectation (tawaqquʿ), so it indicates the negation of jihad regarding the past, and the expectation of it regarding the future. You say: "He promised me to do such-and-such, lamma yurid (he has not yet wished), and he did not do it, and I am expecting his doing it." End of his words. What he said about "lamma," that it indicates the expectation of the verb negated by it in the future, I know of no grammarian who mentioned it. Rather, they mentioned that when you say "lamma yakhruj Zayd," it indicates the negation of going out in the past, its negation continuing up to the time of speaking. As for its indicating expectation of it in the future, no. However, I found in the words of al-Farra' something close to what al-Zamakhshari said. He said: "lamma" is for presenting the existence, unlike "lam."

The majority read with a kasra on the mim, because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. Ibn Wathhab and al-Nakha'i read it with a fatha, and it has been interpreted as assimilation (ittiba') to the fatha of the lam, and as intending the light nun and deleting it, as the poet said:

"Do not humiliate the poor man, lest you one day bow down while Time has raised him."

The majority read "wa-ya'lama" with a damma on the mim. It has been said: it is jussed (majzum), and the mim was made to follow the lam in fatha, like the reading of one who read "﴿wa-lamma ya'lama﴾" with a fatha on the mim, according to one of the two interpretations. It has been said: it is in the accusative (mansub). According to the school of the Basrans, it is by hidden "an" after waw together with the like of: "do not eat the fish and drink the milk." According to the school of the Kufans, it is by the waw of "sarf" (the waw meaning "with," in the sense of the waw that turns the sense away), and the presentation of the two schools is in the science of grammar. al-Hasan, Ibn Ya'mur, Abu Hayawah, and Amr ibn 'Ubayd read it with a kasra on the mim, conjoining it to "﴿wa-lamma ya'lam﴾." Abd al-Warith on the authority of Abu Amr read "wa-ya'lamu" with a damma on the mim. al-Zamakhshari said: on the basis that the waw is for the circumstantial (hal), as if it were said: "and while you are not striving and you are steadfast." End of his words. What he said is not sound, because the waw of circumstance does not enter upon the present tense. One may say: "Zayd came and laughs," meaning "Zayd came laughing," because the present tense stands in the position of the active participle. Just as "Zayd came and laughing" is not permitted, so "Zayd came and laughs" is not permitted. If it is interpreted as the present tense being the predicate of a omitted subject, it is possible, the estimate being: "and He knows the steadfast," as they interpreted His saying: "I was saved and I pledge to them Malik," meaning "and I pledge to them." Other than al-Zamakhshari interpreted the reading with a damma as the resumption of information, meaning: "and He knows the steadfast."

In Allah's denunciation of those who supposed that entering Paradise occurs with the absence of jihad and steadfastness at the encounter with the enemy, there is evidence of the obligation of jihad at that time and of steadfastness against the enemy. It has been mentioned in a hadith: "Turning away at the time of the advancing army is among the seven destructive sins."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 143:

﴿And you had certainly wished for death before you met it; so you have now seen it while you were looking on.﴾ The address is to the believers. Its apparent meaning is generality, but the intended meaning is particularity. That is because a group of the believers did not attend the Battle of Badr, since the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had set out only hastily, intending a caravan of Quraysh, so they did not expect a battle. The people of Badr won what they won of honour in this world and the Hereafter, so they wished to meet the enemy so that they too might have a day like the Day of Badr. They were the ones who urged going out to Uhud. When on the Day of Uhud there occurred what occurred, namely the killing by Abdullah ibn Qami'ah of Mus'ab ibn Umayr, who was defending the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), supposing him to be the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "I have killed Muhammad," and a crier cried out with that, and it spread among the people, they turned back fleeing. The Messenger (ﷺ) called out to them: "To me, servants of Allah!" until a group rallied to him, and they made excuses for their retreat, saying: "The news of your killing reached us, so our hearts were terrified, and we turned back in flight." Then this verse was revealed, rebuking them for what proceeded from them, along with what they had resolved upon themselves of wishing for death. He expressed meeting men and fighting them with iron by death, since that is a state which in most cases includes death, so none wishes for it except one whose soul is content with death. One who wishes for death in jihad is not wishing for the victory of the disbelievers over the Muslims; that comes only incidentally and is not intended. Rather his aim is to attain the rank of martyrdom, because of the honour it has with Allah. Abdullah ibn Rawahah recited, when he had risen toward his death, and he said to them: "May Allah return you," then he said:

Yet I ask the Merciful for forgiveness
and a striking blow with a gushing wound that scatters foam,
So that when they pass by my grave they say:
"May Allah guide him, a warrior who has been rightly guided."

﴿Before you met it⦆ i.e., before you witnessed its hardships and its straits. The pronoun of the object in "talqawhu" refers to death, and it was said to refer to the enemy, and it is left implicit because the context indicates it. The first is more apparent, since it refers to something already mentioned. An-Nakha'i and az-Zuhri read "tulaqunahu," and its meaning and the meaning of "talqawhu" are the same, in that the meaning of "laqiya" includes that it is between two parties, even if it is not on the pattern of "faa'ala." Mujahid read "min qablu" with a damma on the lam, cut off from the annexation, so the position of "an talqawhu" is in the accusative as a substitute of inclusion for "al-mawt." ﴿So you have now seen it⦆ i.e., you have witnessed its causes, which is the blazing war, as he said:

Indeed I have seen death before tasting it

And he said:

I found the scent of death from their direction
in a narrow strait while the horses had not scattered

It was said: the meaning of seeing here is knowing, and it requires the omission of the second object, i.e., "you have known death to be present," and it was omitted because the meaning indicates it. The omission of one of the two objects of "zanna" and its sisters is very rare; therefore the grammarians disagreed about it. Talhah ibn Musarrif read "falaqad ra'aytumuhu" with a lam. ﴿While you were looking on⦆ is a circumstantial clause for emphasis, and it removed what "ra'aytumuhu" may bear of metaphor, or of the shared sense between seeing with the heart and seeing with the eye, i.e., you were witnessing and observing it when those among your brethren and relatives who were killed were killed before your eyes, and you were close to being killed yourselves. On this view the object of the looking is the object of the seeing, and this is the view of al-Akhfash, and it is the apparent one. It was said: "while you were discerning," i.e., there was no defect in your eyes. Its meaning returns to the first view, and az-Zajjaj and al-Akhfash also said it. It was said: "you are looking at Muhammad (ﷺ) and what was done to him." It was said: "you are looking with the look of contemplation after seeing." It was said: "you are looking into the means of salvation and flight, and into the matter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whether he was killed or not." It was said: "you are looking at what you wished for," and it returns to death. (p-68) It was said: "you are looking at your deeds now after the end of the war, whether you have fulfilled or opposed." On this meaning the clause is not circumstantial, but a resumed informative clause, brought by way of reproach. As if it were said: "and you are reckoners of your own selves, so consider the ugliness of your deed." Although this verse's form is that of a report, its meaning is reproach and denunciation of those who fled on the Day of Uhud. In it there is an ellipsis at the end after His saying "so you have now seen it while you were looking on," i.e., their dispersal after seeing its causes and the unveiling of the unseen, that the object of your wish is what you turned away from. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is said that the meaning of "ra'aytumuhu" is "you faced it while you were looking with your eyes," and for this reason looking is mentioned after seeing when their meanings differ, because the first means confronting and facing, and the second means seeing with the eye. End. In that case "while you were looking" would be a clause in the position of a descriptive circumstance, not an emphatic one; except that the well-known usage in the language is that seeing is perceiving by sight, not confronting and facing.

This is a continuation of their reproach, another point: Muhammad is a messenger like those who passed before him from among the messengers, who conveyed from God as they conveyed. The continued existence of the messengers is not a condition for the continued existence of their laws (shara'i'), rather they die, and their laws remain, which their followers adhere to. Just as the messengers passed away and departed, so too their ruling in this matter is one.

The majority of readers recited "al-Rusul" (the messengers) with the definite article, for the purpose of glorifying the messengers and highlighting them according to their status with God. In the Mushaf (codex) of Abd Allah, it is "Rusul" (messengers) in the indefinite form, and Ibn Abbas and Qahtan ibn Abd Allah recited it this way. Its rationale is that it is a place of giving good news regarding the Prophet's matter concerning the meaning of life, and a place of equalizing him with mankind in that. Thus, it connects in places requiring this with the thing and from it: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ (34:13), ﴿And none believed with him except a few﴾ (11:40), and so on. Abu al-Fath mentioned this distinction between the definite and the indefinite in this kind of context, but the definite reading is more preferable, since it indicates that everyone is equal in creation and death, so this messenger is like them in that.

﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ When it was shouted that Muhammad had been killed, the feet of the believers trembled, their hearts were terrified, and they went to great lengths in fleeing. They were in three groups. One group said: "What use is life after the Messenger of God (ﷺ)? Fight for what he fought for," so they fought until they were killed, among them Anas ibn al-Nadr. Another group said: "We will lay down our arms before them, for they are our people and our paternal cousins." And another group displayed hypocrisy and said: "Return to your original religion; if Muhammad were a prophet, he would not have been killed."

The apparent meaning of "turning back on the heels" is apostasy (irtidad). It was also said that it means fleeing, not apostasy. This expression has come in the sense of apostasy and disbelief in His saying: "﴿That We may know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾" (2:143). This alif is the hamzat al-istifham (interrogative hamza), whose meaning is denial. The fa' is for conjunction (al-'atf), and its original position is at the front, since the estimated form is: "fa-'a-in mata." But they give importance to the interrogative and place it before the conjunctive particle, and we have previously mentioned something similar to this and al-Zamakhshari's disagreement about it. Al-Khatib Kamal al-Din al-Zamalkani said: "The more likely is that something omitted is estimated after the hamza, and it was said that it is the fa', which is conjunctive to it. If it were stated explicitly, it would be said: 'Do you believe in him during his lifetime, then if he dies, you will apostatize, thereby opposing the customs of following the prophets before you in their steadfastness upon the creeds of their prophets after their death.'" End of quote. This is a Zamakhshari tendency, and the discussion with him regarding such matters has already been covered. The fa' here only conjoins the interrogative clause to the declarative clause before it, and the interrogative hamza enters upon the conditional clause and its apodosis. Its apodosis is "turned back" (inqalabtum), so the interrogative hamza changes nothing of the rules of the conditional and its apodosis. If both are in the present tense, both are jussive, like: "A-in ta'tini ata'ika" (Will you come to me, I will come to you?). Yunus held that the second verb is built upon the interrogative particle, so the fronting is intended with it necessarily; in that case the first verb must be in the past tense, because the answer to the condition is omitted, and the answer is not omitted except when the conditional verb shows no effect of the conditional particle. Thus, according to him, one must say: "A-in akramtani ukrimka" (Did you honor me? I will honor you). The estimate here is: "Ukrimka in akramtani" (I will honor you if you honor me), and according to him it is not permissible to say "in tukrimni ukrimka" with both jussive at all, nor "in tukrimni ukrimuka" with the first jussive and the second marfu', except in poetic necessity. The discussion of this issue is complete in the science of grammar (nahw).

According to Yunus's view, the interrogative hamza entered in estimation upon "inqalabtum," which is in the past tense but its meaning is the future, since it is restricted by death or killing. The answer to the condition according to Yunus is omitted. Many exegetes said regarding the verse: the alif of interrogation entered in a place other than its proper place, since the purpose is: "Will you turn back on your heels if Muhammad dies?" And "in" (if) here entered upon the certain, and this is not its proper place, because it was presented in the position of the doubtful, due to the uncertainty between death and killing, and the possibility of his being killed according to most of the addressees. Do you not see that when they heard that he had been killed, they were agitated and fled, and divided into three groups, and whoever remained steadfast among them fought until he was killed? Some of them said: "O people, if Muhammad has been killed, the Lord of Muhammad has not been killed; die upon what he died upon." And some of them said: "If Muhammad has been killed, he has indeed conveyed the message, so fight for your religion." This shows the possibility, according to most of the addressees, that he could be killed. As for the knowledge that he will not be killed, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾ (5:67), this is specific to the scholars among the believers and those among them with insight, and to whoever heard this verse and knew the occasion of its revelation.

﴿And whoever turns back on his heels, he will not harm God at all﴾, meaning: whoever returns to disbelief or apostatizes, fleeing from the fighting and from what the Messenger (ﷺ) was upon regarding the matter of jihad, according to the two previous interpretations. This conditional sentence is general in that everyone who turns back on his heels harms only himself, and nothing of that reaches God, exalted is He, because harm from the servant cannot reach Him. No apostasy occurred from anyone among the Muslims on that day except what was said by the hypocrites.

The majority recited "﴿'alá 'aqibayhi﴾" (on his two heels) in the dual. Ibn Abi Ishaq recited "'alá 'aqibihi" in the singular. The accusative of "shay'an" is as a masdar (verbal noun), meaning: any harm at all, neither little nor much. "Turning back on the heels," whether on "al-a'qab," "al-'aqibayn," or "al-'aqib," is a figurative expression, like one who returns to his original religion described as one who turns back on his heels. This sentence contains a severe threat.

﴿And God will reward the grateful﴾, a great promise of reward. It is introduced with "sa-" (surely), which some say is an indicator of the future tense in interpretation, meaning: God's reward to them will not be delayed from them. The grateful are those who endured in His religion, were truthful to God in what they promised Him, and remained firm, thanking God's favor upon them with Islam and not denying it, like Anas ibn al-Nadr, Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', the Ansari man who was writhing in his blood, and others who remained firm that day.

"The grateful" is a general term encompassing every grateful person by deed and word. Discussion of gratitude has already been covered. The apparent meaning of this reward is in the Hereafter. It was also said: in this world, through provision and establishment on the earth. They interpreted "the grateful" here as those who remained steadfast upon their religion, as stated by Ali. He and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "Abu Bakr is the leader of the grateful," alluding to his steadfastness on the day the Messenger of God (ﷺ) died, the agitation of the people at that time, his steadfastness in the matter of apostasy, and what he undertook of the burdens of Islam. It was also interpreted as "the obedient."

(p-70) Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 145:

﴿It is not for any soul to die except by God's permission﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning is that the death of souls is impossible to occur except by God's will. He expressed it in the form of an act that no one should undertake unless God permits him to do so, as a figure of speech (tamthil). Also, the Angel of Death is the one entrusted with this, so he may not seize a soul except with permission from God. This has two meanings. The first: urging them to jihad and encouraging them to meet the enemy, by informing them that caution does not benefit, and that no one dies before reaching his appointed term, even if he plunges into destruction and storms the battles. The second: mentioning what God Most High did for His Messenger when the enemy prevailed and gathered around him, and when his people abandoned him, which was a prize for those who would snatch away from the protection and safeguarding and the postponement of the term. End of al-Zamakhshari's words. It is good, and it expands on what others among the exegetes (mufassirun) said: that no soul dies except at a decreed term. Cowardice does not add to life, and bravery does not subtract from it. In this sentence there is strengthening of souls (p-70) for jihad, and in it there is consolation for the death of the Prophet ﷺ.

The Arabs' saying "ma kana li-Zaydin an yaf'ala" (it was not for Zayd to do such-and-such) means the negation of the act from Zayd and his being prevented from it. Sometimes the prohibition in this construction is because it is impossible rationally, as in God's words: ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35], and His words: ﴿It was not for you to grow its trees﴾ [al-Naml: 60]. Sometimes it is because it is customarily impossible, as in: "It was not for Zayd to fly." Sometimes it is because it is prohibited by the Law (shar'), as in God's words: ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer﴾ [al-Nisa': 92]. Sometimes it is because it is improper (adab), as in the saying of Abu Bakr: "It was not for the son of Abu Quhafa to lead the prayer in front of the Messenger of God ﷺ." This is understood from the context of speech. This formula does not contain a prohibition, as some have said.

His words "li-nafsin" (for a soul) mean the genus, not one particular soul. "Illa bi-idhni Allah" (except by God's permission) means by His enabling and allowing that. The explanation of permission (idhn) has already been given, and the best view concerning it is that it is an enabling of a thing together with knowledge of it; if a statement is added to that, it becomes a command. The meaning is: except by God's permission to the angel entrusted with the seizing. The phrase "an tamuta" (that it die) is in the position of the subject of kana, and "li-nafsin" is in the position of the predicate, so it is connected to an omitted element. Some considered "kana" to be superfluous (za'ida), so that "an tamuta" is in the position of a subject and "li-nafsin" in the position of its predicate. Al-Zajjaj estimated it according to the meaning, saying: "And a soul was not such that it would die," so he made "ma kana" a predicate and what was the predicate a subject; he did not mean this as grammatical analysis (i'rab), but explained it from the standpoint of meaning. Abu al-Baqa' said: the lam in "li-nafsin" is for specification (tabyin), connected to kana. End of his words. This works only if kana is complete (tamma), and the view of one who said it is connected to an omitted element, its estimate being: "And death was not for a soul," with "an tamuta" as an explanation of the omitted element, is rejected, because the subject of kana, if it is incomplete, or the agent if it is complete, may not be omitted; and because of what would follow from omitting it, namely omitting the verbal noun (masdar) and leaving its complement, which is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans.

﴿A decreed term﴾ (kitaban mu'ajjalan): i.e., it has a term that does not advance or delay. In this there is a refutation of the Mu'tazila in their saying that there are two terms. The "writing" here is an expression for decree (qada'), and it was said: written in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), clarified therein. This statement may be an answer to their saying: ﴿If they had been with us they would not have died or been killed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156]. The accusative of "kitaban" is that it is a verbal noun emphasizing the content of the preceding sentence, and the estimate is: "God wrote a decreed writing." Similar to it: ﴿The Book of God upon you﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], ﴿The handiwork of God﴾ [al-Naml: 88], and ﴿God's promise﴾ [al-Nisa': 95]. It was said that it is in the accusative by incitement (ighra'), i.e., "Hold fast to and believe in the decree," but this is far-fetched. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "kitaban" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz), but this is not clear, for the specification, as the grammarians divided it, is of two kinds, transferred and non-transferred, and its types are limited in both kinds, and this is not one of them.

﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him from it; and whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him from it﴾: This is an allusion to those who desired the spoils on the day of Uhud and busied themselves with them, and to those who stood firm in fighting on that day and were not diverted by anything from supporting the religion. This reward, God's giving to whoever desires the reward of this world, is conditioned on God Most High's will, as in the other verse: ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We desire﴾ [al-Isra': 18].

His words "nu'tihi" (We will give him) with the nun in both places, and in "﴿We will reward﴾" [al-An'am: 157], is the reading of the majority, and it is a shift (iltifat), since it is a move from the third person absence to first person plural of majesty. Al-A'mash read "yu'tihi" with the ya' in both places and in "sayajzi," and this follows the preceding absence. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is by omitting the agent, due to what the speech indicates. End of his words. This is an error; the correct view is that the agent is implied, and the pronoun refers to God. The apparent division requires that each category be specific to what was desired, because whoever's intention is restricted to seeking his worldly life has no share in the Hereafter, but whoever's intention is restricted to seeking the Hereafter may be given a share of this world.

The exegetes have several views on it: "We will give him a share of the spoils for his fighting the unbelievers," or "We will not deprive him of what We have apportioned for him," since whoever seeks this world by an act of the Hereafter, We will give him from it, and he has no share in the Hereafter. Or it is specific to the people of Uhud. Or whoever desires the reward of this world by engaging in it through supererogatory acts together with committing grave sins, will be recompensed for them in this world and the Hereafter.

﴿And We will reward the grateful﴾: a promise to those who give thanks for God's blessings, whose concern and intention are restricted to seeking the reward of the Hereafter. Ibn Furak said: In this (p-71) there is an indication that God will bless them with the blessings of this world, and not restrict them to the blessings of the Hereafter. Al-Haramayn, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir in some transmissions of the narration of Hisham and Ibn Dhakwan made the dal of "yurid" clear before "thawab," and assimilated it in connected speech. Qalun and al-Halwani from Hisham through one route read with ikhtilas (reduction of the vowel), and the rest read with ishba' (full vowel). In pause, all read with sukun. The rationale for sukun is that the ha' occupied the position of an omitted element which, had it not been a letter of weakness (glide), would have been quiescent, so the ha' was given what it deserves of quiescence. The rationale for ikhtilas is that it retained what the ha' had before the ya' was deleted, because before deletion its original form was "yu'tihi," and the deletion is incidental, so it is not counted. The rationale for ishba' is that it is permissible considering the wording, even though the ha' is attached to a vowel. The preferable course is to leave these explanations aside, for the reduction of the damma and kasra after a moving letter is a dialect recorded by al-Kisa'i from the tribes of Banu 'Uqayl and Banu Kilab. Al-Kisa'i said: I heard the Bedouins of Kilab and 'Uqayl say: ﴿Indeed, man is ungrateful to his Lord﴾ [al-'Adiyat: 6] as "li-rabbihi lakanud" without full vowel, and "lahu mal" and "lahu mal." Other than the Banu Kilab and Banu 'Uqayl, reduction is not found in their speech, nor is sukun in "lahu" and its like except in poetic necessity, such as the saying of the poet:

"For him is a roar as if it were the voice of a driver when he seeks the herd, or the sound of a flute."

And the saying of another:

"And I drink the water, though I have no thirst for it, except because its springs are the flood of its valley."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 146 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And how many a prophet fought, and with him many devoted servants (ribbiyyun). They did not falter for what befell them in the way of Allah, nor did they weaken, nor did they submit.﴾: (p-72) When what occurred among the believers occurred on the Day of Uhud, and Allah reproached them for what He had warned them about in the verses that preceded, He informed them that many of the earlier nations had killed their prophets, or that many devoted servants (ribbiyyun) had been killed alongside them. Thus they did not suffer the weakness and feebleness that befell you, and the grief over the killing of their prophets, or the killing of their devoted servants, did not turn them away from fighting. Rather, they pressed forward in support of their religion, patient over what had befallen them. The killing of a prophet or of his followers is among the greatest of calamities, so it was fitting for you to take as an example those righteous ones of the earlier nations who passed on. Moreover, you are the best of nations and your Prophet is the best of prophets. In this sentence there is also a rebuke to those who fled from the Prophet (ﷺ).

The majority read "wa-ka'ayyin" (وكَأيِّنْ).
