They said: this is the original form of the word, since it is "ayy" (أيٌّ) to which the particle of comparison "ka" (كاف التشبيه, the particle of comparison) was attached, and it is written with a nun in the Mushaf. Abu 'Amr pronounced it with a pause on it. Suwra ibn al-Mubarak reported from al-Kisa'i a reading with a ya' without a nun, and the majority paused on the nun, following the orthography. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi gave a justification for this with what is pronounced as a pause in speech, as is the custom of those who give reasons. Among what came in this dialect is the verse of the poet:

Wa-ka'ayyin fi al-ma'asiri min unasin akhuhum fawqahum wa-hum kiramun
(And how many among people in hardships, whose brother is above them, and they are noble.)

Ibn Kathir read "wa-ka'in" (وكائِنْ), which is more common in the language of the Arabs and their poetry. He said:

Wa-ka'in radadna 'ankum min mudajjajin
(And how many an armored warrior did we turn back from you.)

Ibn Muhaysin and al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read "wa-ka'ayyin" on the pattern of "ka'ayyin." Some of the non-canonical readers read "kay'in," which is the inverse of Ibn Muhaysin's reading. Ibn Muhaysin also read, as transmitted by al-Dani, "kan" on the pattern of "ka'," and the poet said:

Kana sadiqun khiltuhu sadiqa al-akha abana ikhtibari annahu li mudahinu
(A friend I thought to be a true brother; my testing revealed that he is a flatterer toward me.)

Al-Hasan read "kayyin" with a kaf followed by a kasra-ya' with tanwin. The exegetes, Ibn 'Atiyya and others, went at length in explaining these variations in "ka'ayyin" and what has operated upon it; therefore we have turned away from mentioning it briefly.

The two Harams and Abu 'Amr read "qutTila" (قُتِّلَ) in the passive voice, and Qatada likewise, except that he doubled the ta'. The rest of the seven read "qatala" (قاتَلَ) with an alif, as a past active verb. In each of these readings it is possible for the verb to be attributed to the pronoun, so that the subject of the pronoun is the one who was killed or was made to be killed, in the sense of multiplicity relative to the multitude of persons, not relative to each individual, since killing does not multiply in each individual. Or it is "qatala" (fought), and his saying "ma'ahu ribbiyyun" (with him were devoted servants) may be a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), so that "ribbiyyun" is the subject of the nominal sentence and the adverbial phrase before it is its predicate; it did not need a waw because of the pronoun in "ma'ahu" referring back to the one in the circumstance. It is also possible that "ribbiyyun" is the agent of the adverbial phrase, and the adverbial phrase itself is the circumstance, with the estimate: "being with him were devoted servants." This is the better view, since a circumstance that is a single word is better than one that is a clause. The adverbial phrase has been relied upon because it occurs as a circumstance and so governs, and it is a narrated circumstance; therefore "ribbiyyun" is raised by the adverbial phrase, even though the governing element is past, because it narrates the circumstance, as in His saying: ﴿and their dog stretching out his forelegs﴾ [al-Kahf: 18]. This is according to the school of the Basrans. As for al-Kisa'i and Hisham, they permit, according to them, the active participle in the past tense not defined with al-alif wa-al-lam to govern without interpretation, by making it a narration of a circumstance, and it is possible that the verb is attributed to "ribbiyyun," so there is no pronoun in it, and the ribbiyyun are those who were killed, or were made to be killed, or fought. The position of "ka'ayyin" is nominative, as the subject of a nominal sentence. The apparent view is that its predicate is the clause from His saying "qutila," "qutTila," or "qatala," whether the verb takes the pronoun or the ribbiyyun as its subject. They permitted that "qutila," when the pronoun is the subject, is in the position of a qualifier for "nabiyyin" and "ma'ahu ribbiyyun" is in the position of the predicate, as you say: "How many a righteous man with him is wealth." Or it is in the position of a qualifier, so that it is described as being killed, or made to be killed, or fighting, and as having with him many devoted servants. Then the predicate of "ka'ayyin" would be omitted, its estimate being: "in the world," or "has passed." This is weak, since the sentence is self-contained and does not need the burden of an implied element. As for when the apparent noun is the subject, they permitted that the verbal clause of "qutila" and its complements is in the position of a qualifier for "nabiyyin," with the predicate omitted. This, as we have said, is weak.

When they mentioned that the origin of "ka'ayyin" is "ayyin," to which the particle of comparison entered, governing it in the genitive, so that it governs it, just as it entered upon "dha" in their saying: "Lahu 'indi kadha" (he has with me such-and-such), and as it entered upon "anna" in their saying "ka'anna," most of them claimed that in "ka'anna" the kaf remained with the meaning of comparison, while in "kadha" and "ka'anna" the meaning of comparison has departed from them. Based on this, the kaf is attached to nothing, and the meaning of "ka'ayyin" becomes the meaning of "kam" (how many), so it indicates no comparison whatsoever. Al-Hawfi said: As for the governing element of the kaf, if we take it according to the rule of the original, then it is carried on the meaning, and the meaning is: your affliction is like the affliction of those prophets and their companions who preceded. And if we take the rule to be the transfer to the meaning of "kam," then the governing element is by estimate the inchoative, and it is in the position of nominative, and "qutila" is the predicate. "Min" is attached to the sense of settledness, and the first estimate is clearer, because it carries the sentence on the wording rather than the meaning, with the required genitive of "ayyin." And when "ayyin" is on its own track of treating the wording, then "min" is attached to what the kaf was attached to in the meaning that is indicated. End of his words, and they are words with strangeness in them. What led them into confusion over this word is their claim that it is compounded of the particle of comparison, and that its origin is "ayy," so it was put in the genitive by the particle of comparison; this is a claim for which no proof stands in its favor. We have mentioned our opinion on it: that it is simple, built on quiescence, and the nun is part of the root of the word and not tanwin, and it was treated in its building as analogous to its counterpart "kam," and that the verb is attributed to the pronoun.

Al-Tabari and a group went to this view and preferred it, reasoning that the story is the cause of the expedition of Uhud and the desertion of the believers when Muhammad (ﷺ) was killed, so the example was struck with a prophet who was killed. This preference is supported by His saying: ﴿Then if he dies or is killed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 144]. Ibn 'Abbas said, regarding His saying: ﴿It is not for a prophet to defraud﴾ [Al 'Imran: 161]: The prophet is killed, so how could he not be betrayed? If it is attributed to other than the prophet, the meaning is only the strengthening of the believers for the loss of those among them who were lost. To the view that the verb is attributed to the ribbiyyun went al-Hasan and a group. He and Ibn Jubayr said: No prophet was ever killed in battle. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The reading of one who reads "qatala" is more general in praise, since it includes those who were killed and those who remained. In my view, on this reading it is good to attribute the verb to the ribbiyyun, and on the reading "qutila" to attribute it to "nabiyyin." End of his words. We say: "qutila" appears to be praise, and it is more eloquent in the intended purpose of the address, since it is explicit in the occurrence of killing and it entails fighting. "Qatala" does not indicate killing, since fighting does not necessarily entail the occurrence of killing; there may be fighting without any killing. As for what he mentioned, that it is good in his view, its goodness does not appear clearly; rather, both readings admit both aspects. Abu al-Fath ibn Jinni said: In the reading of Qatada, it is not good for the verb to be attributed to the ribbiyyun, because of the meaning of multiplicity it carries, which cannot be used of the killing of a single person. If it is said: it is attributed to "nabiyyin" in observance of the meaning of "ka'ayyin," the answer is: the wording has proceeded in the singular form in His saying "min nabiyyin," and the singular pronoun in "ma'ahu" indicates that the intention is only the illustration with one individual after another, so the speech came out in the meaning of "ka'ayyin." Abu al-Fath said: This reading strengthens the view of one who said, regarding those who were killed and those who fought: it is only attributed to the ribbiyyun. End of his words, and it is not apparent; for "ka'ayyin" is like "kam," and you know that when you say "kam min 'anin fakakatuhu" (how many a captive I freed), you use the singular, observing the wording of "kam," while its meaning is plural. When you say "kam min 'anin fakakatuhum" (how many a captive I freed), you observe the meaning of "kam," not its wording. The observance of the wording is nothing other than that you use the singular pronoun while meaning the plural, so there is no difference in meaning between "fakakatuhu" and "fakakatuhum," and similarly there is no difference between "qutilu ma'ahum ribbiyyun" and "qutila ma'ahu ribbiyyun." Observing the wording at one time and observing the meaning at another is permissible because the referent of "kam" and "ka'ayyin" is many, and the meaning is a great multitude. When you report about a great multitude, sometimes you use the singular in observance of the wording, and sometimes you use the plural in observance of the meaning, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿Or do they say: We are a united host, victorious?﴾ [al-Qamar: 44] ﴿The host will be routed and they will turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45]. He said "munTasir" (victorious) in the singular, and said "yuwallun" (they will turn) in the plural, so He used the singular for "munTasir" and the plural for "yuwallun." As for Abu al-Fath's answer to the objection he posed, namely that the wording proceeded in the singular in "min nabiyyin," meaning the wording of "ka'ayyin" was observed because its specification came in the singular, so when it was specified by a singular it was fitting that its wording be observed, while the meaning is plural; and his saying that the singular pronoun in "ma'ahu" indicates that the intention is only the illustration with one individual after another, this intention is shared between using the singular pronoun or the plural, because the singular pronoun here does not mean singling out its referent; rather there is no difference between it as singular and as plural in meaning. Since there is no difference, its signification is general, namely its signification of every single individual. As for his saying "the speech came out of the meaning of ka'ayyin," the speech did not come out of the meaning of ka'ayyin; it came out only of the plurality of the pronoun in accordance with the meaning of ka'ayyin and not its wording, for when it is used singular in wording its referent is not singular, but rather plural, as they say: "He is the best of the youths and their most beautiful," meaning: "and their most beautiful." As for the one who attributes "qutila" or "qutTila" to ribbiyyun, the meaning according to him is: some of them were killed, as you say: "The sons of so-and-so were killed in such-and-such a battle," meaning a group of them.

The rabbiyyun (the followers of a rabbi, or the worshippers of the Lord). The vowel of the rā' was changed in the relative form (taghyīr al-nisab, the alteration of the relative/nisba form), as they said amsiyy in the relative form of ams (yesterday). This is the view of al-Akhfash. Or it means "the group," as Abu 'Ubayda said. Or it is a relative noun derived from al-rabbah, which means "the group," and then it was made plural with the wāw and nūn, as al-Zajjaj said. Or it means "the large group," as Yunus ibn Habib said. Rabbiyyūn is the plural relative form derived from it. Qutrub said: "The scholars agree with Yunus' view." As for the exegetes, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas said: "They are thousands." Al-Farra' and others preferred this view. Some exegetes counted them and said: "They are ten thousand." Ibn 'Abbas, in one narration, and Mujahid, 'Ikrima, al-Dahhak, Qatada, al-Suddi and al-Rabi' said: "They are the large groups," and Ibn Qutayba preferred this. Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of al-Hasan, said: "They are the pious scholars who are patient over what befalls them," and al-Yazidi and al-Zajjaj preferred this. Ibn Zayd said: "They are the followers, and the rabbaniyyun are the rulers." Ibn Faris said: "They are the righteous who know God." It was also said: "They are the ministers of the prophets." Al-Dahhak said: "One rabbiyyah is a thousand, and rabbiyyun is its plural." Al-Kalbi said: "One rabbiyyah is ten thousand." Al-Naqqash said: "They are those who have abundant knowledge," from their saying: rabā al-shay'u yarbū, meaning "the thing increased." But this is not sound, because the two roots differ: the root of rabā is rā', bā' and wāw, while the root of this word is rā', bā' and bā'.

The majority of readers read it with a kasra on the rā'. 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib read it with a ḍamma on the rā', and this is from the alteration of the relative form, as they said duhriyy with a ḍamma on the dāl, meaning "relating to the long age," derived from al-dahr al-ṭawīl. Ibn 'Abbas, as Qatada narrated from him, read it with a fatḥa on the rā'. Ibn Jinni said: "It is the dialect of Tamim, and all of these are dialects." The pronoun in "wahanū" refers to the rabbiyyūn, if the pronoun in "qutila" refers to the Prophet ﷺ. If rabbiyyūn is the subject of the verb, and the verb is in the active voice (mabnī lil-fā'il, built for the doer), then it is the same. If it is in the passive voice (mabnī lil-maf'ūl, built for the object), then the pronoun refers to those among them who remained, since the meaning indicates this, because it is not sound for it to refer to rabbiyyūn because of the conjunction with fa' (then), "for what befell them in the way of God, by the killing of their prophets or their rabbiyyūn."

The majority read: "﴿wahanū﴾" with a fatḥa on the hā'. Al-A'mash, al-Hasan and Abu al-Sammal read it with a kasra on it. Both are dialects: wahana yahinu like wa'ada ya'idu, and wahana yawhanu like wajila yawjalu. 'Ikrima and Abu al-Sammal also read: "wahnū" with the hā' sukūn (unvocalized), as they said ni'm for na'am and shahd for shahida. Tamim pronounce the 'ayn of fa'ala with sukūn.

"﴿Wa-mā ḍa'ufū﴾" means they did not become weak in jihad after what befell them. It was also said: their certainty did not weaken, and their resolve did not dissolve. The root meaning of al-ḍa'f is loss of strength, and then it is used for opinion and intellect. It was also read "ḍa'afū" with a fatḥa on the 'ayn, and al-Kisa'i transmitted it as a dialect.

"﴿Wa-mā istakānū﴾": Ibn Ishaq said: they did not sit back from jihad in their religion. Al-Suddi said: they were not humiliated. 'Ata' said: they did not humble themselves. Muqatil said: they did not surrender. Abu al-'Aliya said: they were not cowardly. Al-Mufaddal said: they were not humble. Qatada and al-Rabi' said: they did not abandon their support for their religion, but they fought for what their prophet fought for until they joined their Lord. All these sayings are close in meaning. This is an allusion to what befell them on the day of Uhud of weakness and breaking, when the rumor of the killing of the Messenger of God ﷺ spread, and to their weakness at that time in striving against the polytheists and their submission to them, when some of them wanted to seek the support of the hypocrite 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy in seeking security from Abu Sufyan.

The apparent form of istakāna is that it is istaf'ala (the form X verb) from al-kawn (existence), so the original of its alif is wāw. Or it derives from the Arabs' saying: "Fulan died in a bad kīna," meaning in a bad state. And "kānahu yakīnuhu" means when he subjugated him. Al-Azhari and Abu 'Ali said this. According to their view, the original of the alif is yā'. Al-Farra' and a group of grammarians said: it is ifta'ala (another verb form) from al-sukūn (stillness), and the fatḥa was lengthened, so an alif was produced from it, as the poet said: "I seek refuge in God from al-'aqrāb," meaning from al-'aqrab (the scorpion). This lengthening occurs only in poetry. This word in all its inflections is built on this letter, you say: istakāna yastakīnu, so he is mustakīn and mustakānun lahu. The lengthening does not occur in this manner.

"﴿Wa-llāhu yuḥibbu al-ṣābirīn﴾": meaning, patient in fighting their enemy. This is what the majority said. Or patient in their religion and in fighting the disbelievers. The apparent meaning is general, for every patient person over what befalls him of killing in the way of God, or wounding, or trial, or harm that reaches him by word or deed, or a calamity in his self, his family, or his property, or what runs in the same course as that. The Arabs often praised themselves for patience and were eager for it, as Tarafa ibn al-'Abd said:

"And the soul complains of what has befallen it, so be patient, for you are of a people who are patient."

"If you meet a sarsar (a dangerous place), we shall reach its joy and good, and you will not stumble in harm."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 147:

﴿And their saying was only that they said, "Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excess in our affair, and make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾ When He mentioned what they had of steadfastness, patience, not weakening, and not submitting to the enemy, all of which are inward acts whose effect appears upon the limbs, He mentioned what they had of turning back (to Allah), seeking forgiveness, and taking refuge in Allah the Exalted through supplication. He restricted their saying to that statement, so they had no refuge and no recourse except Allah the Exalted, and no speech except this speech. (This is) unlike what you were doing on the Day of Uhud of agitation and disagreement in statements: some said, "Let us take safe-conduct from Abu Sufyan," some said, "Let us return to our religion," and some said what he said when he fled. These people had been stricken by the death of their Prophet or of their rabbis (ribbiyyun), yet they did not weaken; rather they were patient and said this statement, and they were rabbis (ribbiyyun, scholars). (They did this) out of humbling themselves, and to indicate that the afflictions of this world come only because of sins committed by humans, as was the case in the story of Uhud, through the disobedience of those who disobeyed.

Al-Jumhur read "qawlahum" with the accusative (naṣb), as the predicate (khabar) of kāna, and "an qālū" is in the position of the subject (ism). They made what kāna is more definite as the subject, because "inna" and its complement function as a pronoun. And "qawlahum" is attached to a pronoun, which functions as a proper noun (ʿilm). A group among them, Hammad ibn Salama on the authority of Ibn Kathir, and Abu Bakr on the authority of ʿAsim, as mentioned by al-Mahdawi, read "qawluhum" with the nominative (raf'), making it the subject of kāna and "an qālū" the predicate. Both constructions are eloquent, though the first is more common. It has also been recited, "﴿thumma lam takun fitnatuhum﴾ [al-An'am: 23]," in both ways among the seven (readings). He placed the request for forgiveness before the request for making firm the feet and for victory, so that their request to Allah would proceed from purity and cleanliness, and thus their request for firmness, by placing the seeking of forgiveness first, would be worthy of being answered. "Dhunubana" and "israfana" are close in meaning, so this came by way of emphasis.

It was said: the dhunub are what falls short of the major sins, and the israf are the major sins. Abu ʿUbayda said: the dhunub are the sins (khataya), and "israfana" means our neglect (tafrit). Al-Dahhak said: "dhunub" is general, while "israf fi'l-amr" refers specifically to the major sins.

Here, "al-aqdam" (the feet) was said to be literal: they supplicated for the firmness of the feet in the places of battle and in meeting the enemy, so that they would not slip. It was said that the meaning is: encourage our hearts to meet the enemy. It was said: make firm our hearts upon Your religion. The better view is to take it literally, because it is its proper context. The firmness of the foot in war is only from the firmness of its owner in the religion. This expression frequently occurs in the context of war and together with victory, as in His saying: "﴿Pour upon us patience and make firm our feet and help us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 250]," and "﴿If you help Allah, He will help you and make firm your feet﴾ [Muhammad: 7]." It was also said: "Forgive us our sins" refers to disobedience, "our excess in our affair" to defeat, "make firm our feet" through steadfastness, and "help us against the disbelieving people" through striving.

Ibn Fawrak said: in this supplication there is a refutation of the Qadariyya, because of their saying that Allah does not create the actions of the servant; if that were so, it would not be proper to ask (Allah) for what He did not do. In this there is evidence for the legitimacy of supplication at the meeting of the enemy, and that one may supplicate with this specific supplication. Indeed, the Qur'an contains supplications (p-76) whose answer Allah has followed up with acceptance.

﴿So Allah gave them the reward of this world and the excellent reward of the Hereafter﴾: al-Jahdari recited ﴿fa-athabahum﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 85], from al-ithaba (bestowing a reward). Since their supplication had already included what would be answered with both rewards, namely their saying ﴿Forgive us our sins and our excesses﴾, which encompasses the reward of the Hereafter, and ﴿Make our feet firm and help us against the disbelieving people﴾, which encompasses the reward of this world, Allah informed them that He had granted them both rewards. There, they began their request with what was most important to them, which is what results in the reward of the Hereafter. Here, He informed them of what He had given them, mentioning it first. He mentioned the reward of this world so that it would be a sign to them that their supplication had been accepted and their request granted; and because that reward comes earlier in time than the reward of the Hereafter. Qatadah, Ibn Ishaq and others said: the reward of this world is victory over their enemy. Ibn Juraij said: it is triumph and booty. Al-Zamakhshari said: the reward of this world consists of support, booty, honor and a good reputation. Al-Naqqash said: it is nothing but triumph and victory, because booty was not made lawful except for this community. This is correct, as established in the authentic hadith: "Booty has been made lawful for me, and it was not made lawful for anyone before me," and it is one of the five things with which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was favored and which no one before him was given. The excellent reward of the Hereafter is Paradise, without any disagreement. This was stated by Ibn Atiyyah. It was also said: it is the wage and forgiveness. He specified the reward of the Hereafter with the adjective "excellent" to indicate its virtue and precedence, and that it is the one that truly counts in His sight ﴿You desire the goods of this world, while Allah desires the Hereafter﴾ [al-Anfal: 67], and to encourage seeking what it is obtained through righteous deeds, and as an appropriate conclusion to the verse. Ali said: whoever works for his worldly life harms his Hereafter, and whoever works for his Hereafter harms his worldly life, though Allah may combine both for some people.

﴿And Allah loves the doers of good﴾: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained ihsan (excellence in faith and conduct) when he was asked about its reality, in the hadith of Jibril's question: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him." The exegetes explained it here in one of two ways: that it refers to one who does best in what lies between him and his Lord by adhering to His obedience, or one who stands firm in fighting alongside his Prophet until he is killed or achieves victory.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 149:

﴿O you who have believed, if you obey those who disbelieve, they will turn you back on your heels, and you will become losers﴾: The address is general, encompassing the people of Uhud and others. The disbelievers have never ceased to persist in trying to turn the believers back from their religion: ﴿They wish that you would disbelieve as they disbelieved, and that you would be equal﴾ [al-Nisa: 89]. ﴿And they wish that you would disbelieve﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 2], ﴿Your relatives will not benefit you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 3], ﴿Many of the People of the Scripture wish they could return you to disbelief after your belief﴾ [al-Baqarah: 109].

﴿A group of the People of the Scripture wish they could mislead you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 69]. It has also been said: the address is specific to those among the believers who were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the day of Uhud. According to the first view, He attached turning back on one's heels and turning over into loss to the mere obedience to them, and this is an utmost degree of caution regarding them and of keeping away from them, so they are not to be obeyed in anything nor consulted, because that would draw one toward agreeing with them. Here ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ is general. According to the second view, ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ is specific. ʿAli and Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are the hypocrites, who said to the believers when they returned from Uhud: "If he were a prophet, what befell him would not have befallen him; so return to your brothers." Ibn Jurayj said: they are the Jews and Christians, and al-Hasan said the same, and he also reported: "If you seek the counsel of the Jews and Christians and accept from them," because they used to seduce them, cast doubts upon them, and say: "If you had a true prophet, he would not have been defeated, and what befell him and his companions would not have befallen them. He is only a man whose condition is like the condition of other people: a day for him and a day against him."

al-Suddi said: they are Abu Sufyan and his companions from the idol-worshippers. al-Hasan also said: it is Kaʿb and his companions. Abu Bakr al-Razi said: in it is an indication of the prohibition of obeying the disbelievers absolutely, but the Muslims have agreed that it does not include those whose counsel we trust from among them, such as the spy, the guide (al-khirrit) who shows the way, the person of sound opinion with apparent benefit, and a wife who advises what is right. The "turning back on the heels" here is a metaphor (kinaya) for returning to disbelief. And "losers" means: defrauded, by your exchanging the Hereafter.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 150:

﴿Nay, Allah is your Protector (mawlakum)﴾ "Bal" (بَلْ): used to leave the previous statement without cancelling it and to move on to a different statement. The meaning is: the disbelievers are not allies (awliya') who are to be obeyed in anything; rather, Allah is your Protector (mawlakum). Al-Hasan read the word Allah in the accusative (بِنَصْبِ الجَلالَةِ), with the meaning: "Nay, obey Allah," because the preceding conditional clause implies the sense of a prohibition, i.e., "Do not obey the disbelievers so that you become disbelievers; rather, obey Allah, your Protector."

﴿And He is the best of helpers (khayr al-nasirin)﴾: When He mentioned that He is their Protector (mawlahum), i.e., their Helper (nasirihim), He mentioned that He is the best of helpers, with whom there is no need for the help or the guardianship of anyone else. In this is an indication that whoever fights to support the religion of Allah will not be forsaken or defeated, because Allah is his Protector. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If you help Allah, He will help you﴾ [Muhammad: 7] ﴿If Allah helps you, none can overcome you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 160].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 151:

﴿We shall cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieved﴾: that is, these disbelievers, even though they prevailed over you on the Day of Uhud, We shall humiliate them by casting terror into their hearts. He used the sin (sawf) of near future, and so it happened. Allah cast terror into their hearts on the Day of Uhud, and they fled to Makkah without any cause from the Muslims, although at that time they had strength and dominance. It is said: they went toward Makkah, and when they were part of the way they said, "We have achieved nothing. We killed some of them and then left them while we were the conquerors. Return and uproot them completely." When they resolved upon that, Allah cast terror into their hearts, and they held back. The verb "to cast" (al-ilqa') is literally applied to physical bodies, and here it is used metaphorically for "placing." A parallel to this is ﴿And those who accuse chaste women﴾ [An-Nur: 4], and similar to it is the saying of the poet:

*They two blew into my mouth from their two mouths*
*upon the barking, howling one, a most forceful throwing.*

The majority of readers recited "sanulqi" with the nun, which indicates the greatness of what is cast, since it is attributed to the speaker by the nun of majesty (nun al-'azamah, the first-person plural "we" used to express grandeur). Ayyub al-Sikhtiyani recited "sayulqi" with the ya', following the preceding third-person pronoun in His saying ﴿And He is the best of helpers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 150]. He placed "in their hearts" first, though it is in the genitive case functioning as the object, to give importance to the place where it is cast before mentioning what is cast. Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read "al-ru'ub" with a damma on the 'ayn, while the rest read it with a sukun. It is said: both are dialectal variants. It is said: the original is with sukun, and the damma was applied for ease (ittiba'), like "al-subh" and "al-subuh." It is said: the original is with damma, and it was made sukun for lightness, like "al-rusl" and "al-rusul."

They mentioned, regarding the casting of terror into the hearts of the disbelievers on the Day of Uhud, a long story, which we wished not to leave out of the book entirely, so we summarize from it that 'Ali informed the Messenger that Abu Sufyan and his companions, when they departed, rode the camels and led the horses by the reins, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was pleased by that. Then the Messenger returned to Madinah, prepared himself, and pursued the polytheists as far as Hamra' al-Asad. And that Ma'bad al-Khuza'i came to the Messenger (ﷺ) while he was still a disbeliever, distressed by what had befallen the Muslims, and the Khuza'ah tended toward the Messenger (ﷺ). And the polytheists had resolved to return to fighting, but Safwan ibn Umayyah and Ma'bad discouraged them. Ma'bad said: "They went out burning with rage against you, in a host the like of which I have never seen. I saw nothing but the foreheads of their horses coming toward you." And what I saw moved me to compose a poem about that, and he recited:

*My mount almost broke from the sounds*
*when the earth flowed with the swarming, scattered flocks.*

*Riding with noble lions, not weak-bodied,*
*nor lean and deficient at the time of meeting.*

*So I kept running, thinking the earth was tilting*
*when they set out with a leader who is not forsaken.*

Until the end of the poem, and so terror fell into the hearts of the disbelievers. His saying "We shall cast" is a promise to the believers of victory after Uhud and of triumph. He (ﷺ) also said: "I have been made victorious through terror over a distance of a month's march." In this is evidence for the truthfulness of the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since he reported from Allah that He would cast terror into their hearts, and it happened as he had reported.

﴿Because they associated with Allah that for which He had sent down no authority﴾: The particle "bi" indicates cause, and "ma" is a verbal-masdar particle: that is, because of their associating with Allah gods for whose association He had sent down no proof or evidence. The negation is applied to the sending down (al-inzal), while the intended meaning is the negation of authority, that is: gods for whose association there is no authority. This is like the saying:

*on a clear path whose landmarks cannot guide one*

that is, there is no landmark for it by which one could be guided. And like the saying:

*and you do not see the lizard entering its burrow therein*

that is, the lizard does not enter its burrow so that it could be seen there. The intended meaning is the negation of both authority and sending down together. Association with Allah was a cause for the casting of terror, because they hated death and preferred the life of this world, since their hopes were not attached to the Hereafter, nor to reward or punishment therein. So their belief in this became an influence on their desire for the life of this world, as they said: ﴿There is none but our life of this world; we die and we live, and we will not be resurrected﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 37]. In His saying "﴿for which He had sent down no authority﴾" there is evidence for the invalidity of taqlid (blind imitation), since there is no proof with one who merely imitates.

﴿And their refuge is the Fire﴾: He, exalted is He, informed that their final destination and return is to the Fire. So they are terrified in this world and punished in the Hereafter, because of their associating partners with Allah. Thus it brings them evil in this world and the Hereafter.

﴿And wretched is the abode of the wrongdoers﴾: He exaggerated in censuring their abode, and the one to whom the censure is directed is omitted, that is: "and wretched is the abode of the wrongdoers, the Fire." He made the Fire their refuge (ma'wa) and their abode (mathwa). He began with "refuge," which is the place to which a person retreats, and it does not necessarily entail lasting residence, because "thawa'" (abiding) indicates settlement. So He made it both refuge and abode, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿And the Fire is an abode for them﴾ [Muhammad: 12]. He drew attention to the attribute by which they deserved the Fire, which is wrongdoing and transgressing the limit, since they associated others with Allah, as He said: ﴿Indeed, associating partners with Allah is a great wrongdoing﴾ [Luqman: 13].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 152:

﴿And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission, until when you lost courage and disputed about the matter and disobeyed after He had shown you that which you love.﴾ This is an answer to those of the believers who returned to Madinah. They said: "Allah promised us victory and reinforcement with the angels, so from what direction have we been struck?" So this was revealed to inform them that He, the Exalted, had fulfilled His promise to them and granted them victory over their enemies at first, and that the reinforcement was conditional upon patience and piety. Some of them committed the act of disobedience that Allah stated in His Book, and the address came in the plural pronoun referring to the believers in these verses, although not everyone among them committed what deserves reproach. This follows the manner of the Arabs in attributing what occurs from some of them to all of them by way of figurative speech. In this there is also a concealment of the one who did it, since he was not specified, and a deterrent for the one who did not do it, so that he would not do it.

The fulfilment of the promise: it was that they defeated the polytheists at first. Ali ibn Abi Talib, Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, al-Zubayr, Abu Dujana and Asim ibn Abi al-Aflah had great trial on that day, and it is mentioned in the biographies (al-siyar). The polytheists numbered three thousand, and with them were two hundred horses, while the Muslims numbered seven hundred men. The verb "sadaqa" (to fulfil/be true to) here takes two objects, and it may take the second with a prepositional particle; you say: "sadaqtu Zaydan al-hadith" (I told Zayd the truth of the speech) and "sadaqtu Zaydan fi al-hadith." Some grammarians mentioned this in the chapter of verbs that take two objects. It may also take the second with the particle of genitive, in which case it is of the category of "istaghfara" (to seek forgiveness) and "ikhtara" (to choose). The governing element of "idh" (when) is "sadaqakum" (He fulfilled to you).

The meaning of "tahussunahum" is: you kill them. They had killed twenty-two men of the polytheists. Ubayd ibn Umayr read "tuhussunahum" as a quadriliteral from "ihsas" (sensation), meaning you deprive them of their sense by killing. Wishing for killing at the time of failure (fashal) is: cowardice and weakness.

Tanazu' (dispute) is: pulling against one another regarding the matter. This dispute issued from the archers. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had stationed the archers at the mouth of the valley and said: "Hold your positions, and if you see us defeating them, we will not cease to be victorious as long as you remain in your positions." He promised them victory if they adhered to his command. When the polytheists were routed, some of the archers said: "They have been defeated, so what is our position here? The spoils, the spoils! Join the Muslims." Others said: "Rather we shall remain in our position as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us." It was said: the dispute is what issued from the Muslims of disagreement when it was shouted that Muhammad had been killed.

Disobedience (i'syan) is: the departure of those archers who left their place seeking plunder and spoils. Khalid, when he saw the scarcity of the archers, shouted to his cavalry and charged against those who remained of the archers, killing them, and charged against the army of the Muslims, so the polytheists turned back, and seventy men of the Muslims were struck on that day.

"Min ba'di ma arakum ma tuhibbun" (after He had shown you that which you love): this is the victory and triumph of the believers. Al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam said: "I saw myself looking at the servants of Hind and her companions, lifting their garments and fleeing, with nothing held back from taking them, great or small; when the archers inclined toward the army seeking plunder and left our backs exposed to the cavalry, we were attacked from our rear, a crier cried out: 'Verily Muhammad has been killed!' and we turned back and the enemy turned back upon us."

Regarding "idha" in His saying "idha fashiltum": it was said that it means "idh" (when). "Hatta" is a preposition, and there is no answer for it at that point; it is connected to "tahussunahum," meaning: you were killing them up to this time. It was also said: "hatta" is a particle of beginning that has entered upon a conditional sentence, as it enters upon nominal sentences. The answer is stated explicitly, which is His saying "wa tanazi'tum" (and you disputed), with the extra "wa"; this was said by al-Farra' and others, and "thumma sarafakum" (then He turned you away) with the extra "thumma." These two opinions and the two before them are weak. The correct view is that the answer is omitted, as the meaning indicates it. Ibn Atiyyah estimated it as: "you were defeated"; al-Zamakhshari: "He withheld His victory from you"; and others: "you were tested." The estimates are close in meaning. Omitting the answer of a conditional when the meaning is understood is permissible, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth or a ladder into the sky to bring them a sign...﴾ [al-An'am: 35], its estimate being: "then do it." It appears that the omitted answer is other than what they estimated, namely: "you divided into two groups," and what follows indicates it, and it is similar to: ﴿Then when He delivered them to the land, among them is one who is moderate﴾ [Luqman: 32], the estimate being: "they divided into two groups: among them is one who is moderate." It is not said: how can it be said "they divided" regarding those who failed, disputed and disobeyed? Because these actions did not issue from all of them, but from some of them, as we mentioned at the beginning of the discussion of this verse.

Abu Bakr al-Razi said: this verse indicates the prior promise of Allah, the Exalted, to the believers of victory over their enemy as long as they did not disobey by their dispute and their failure. It occurred as He had informed: they defeated them and killed. This indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the Prophet, because the reporting of the unseen is among the specific attributes of lordship and the qualities of divinity, which no one comprehends except one whom Allah has informed of it, and its knowledge does not reach us except through the tongue of a messenger who reports it from Allah, the Exalted.

﴿Among you are those who desire the world, and among you are those who desire the Hereafter.﴾ Ibn Abbas and the majority of the exegetes said: "the world" means the spoils. Ibn Mas'ud said: "We did not perceive that any of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) desired the world until the day of Uhud." Those who desired the Hereafter were those who remained firm in their station with their commander Abdullah ibn Jubayr, in a band of fewer than ten, all of whom were killed. The archers were fifty, of whom more than forty departed for the plunder and disobeyed the command. Among those who desired the Hereafter were those who remained steady after the Muslims were thrown into confusion, and fought until they were killed, such as Anas ibn al-Nadr and others, who did not waver in their fighting or in their religion. These two sentences are a parenthetical insertion between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined.

* *

﴿Then He turned you away from them﴾: that is, He made you turn away. (*li-yabtaliyakum*): that is, that He might test your patience under calamities and your steadfastness in faith at that time. It was said: "He turned you away from them," meaning the defeat did not continue upon you so that they would annihilate you. It was said: the meaning is that He did not impose upon you the pursuit of them immediately after their withdrawal. The Mu'tazila interpreted it to mean: "then you turned away from them," so its attribution to Allah, the Exalted, is by His bringing terror into the hearts of the disbelievers as a trial for the believers. It was said: the meaning of *li-yabtaliyakum* is that He might send upon you that calamity of killing and purification (*tamhis*).

﴿And certainly He pardoned you﴾: it was said: "from the punishment for your fleeing," and He did not take you to account for it. It was said: "by repelling the enemy from you." It was said: "by not commanding you to return to fighting them immediately." It was said: "by not uprooting you after the disobedience and opposition." So the meaning of "'afa 'ankum" (He pardoned you) is: "He spared you."

Al-Hasan said: "Among them a group was killed, seventy; the uncle of the Prophet (ﷺ) was killed, his face was split, and his front tooth was broken. The pardon was only that these did not uproot them in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They were in the path of Allah, enraged for the sake of Allah, fighting the enemies of Allah. They were forbidden from a thing and they neglected it. By Allah, they were not left until they were afflicted with this affliction. O wickedness of the wicked! Today he makes lawful every great sin, mounts every calamity, drags his garments over it, and claims there is no harm upon him; so he will soon know." End of al-Hasan's speech. The apparent meaning is that the pardon is only regarding the sin, that is, He did not take them to account for the disobedience. This is indicated by the context of His saying "and you disobeyed." The meaning: the sin deserved more than what befell you, so He pardoned you; thus it is an announcement of pardon for what the sin deserved of punishment. Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Ishaq and a group said this. With this, there is also a warning.

﴿And Allah is Bountiful to the believers﴾: that is, in their circumstances, or by the pardon.

These verses contain various kinds of rhetorical embellishment (al-bayan wa al-badi'). Among them: the interrogative whose meaning is denial in "am hasibtum" (did you think...). Paronomasia of identical form in "inqalabtum" and "man yanqalib," and in "thawab al-dunya" and "husn thawab." Paronomasia of differing form in the saying "illa an qalu." The naming of a thing by the name of its cause in "tamannawna al-mawt" (you wished for death), meaning jihad in the path of Allah; and in His saying "wa thabbit aqdamana," for those who interpreted it as the hearts, because firmness of feet results from firmness of hearts. The turn of address (iltifat) in "wa sanajzi al-shakirin." Repetition in "wa lamma ya'lam" and "ya'lam," due to the difference in the object, or to alert to the excellence of the patient. In "afa-in mata aw qutila," because the custom regarding death differs from the custom regarding killing, while the meaning is: the separation of the soul from the body, which is one. "Man" in "wa man yurid thawab" in both sentences; and in "dhunubana wa israfana" in the saying of one who equated them; and in "thawab" and "husn al-thawab." In the word "al-Jalala" (the Majesty, Allah). In "minkum man yurid," both sentences. The division in "wa man yurid" [Al 'Imran: 145] and in "minkum man yurid." The restriction (ikhtisas) in "al-shakirin," "al-sabirin," and "al-mu'minin." Antithesis (tibaq) in "in tuti'u alladhina kafaru" [Al 'Imran: 149]. Simile (tashbih) in "yaruddukum 'ala a'qabikum," in which the turning back from the religion is likened to one who retreats backward, and the one whose deeds are nullified by disbelief is likened to the losing merchant whose profit and capital are lost, and to one who returns by one road and goes in another; and in His saying "sanalqa." It was said: all of this is metaphor (isti'ara). Omission (hadhf) in a number of places.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 153 (part 1 of 2):

﴿When you were climbing away and not turning back for anyone, while the Messenger was calling you from behind you. So He repaid you with grief upon grief, so that you would not grieve over what had escaped you nor over what had befallen you. And Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾ ﴿Then after the grief He sent down security upon you, a drowsiness that overcame a group of you, while another group was concerned only for themselves. They thought about Allah other than the truth, the thinking of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance). They said, "Do we have any say in the matter?" Say: "Indeed the matter belongs entirely to Allah." They conceal within themselves what they do not reveal to you. They say, "If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here." Say: "Even if you had been in your houses, those destined for killing would have gone out to their places of death, so that Allah might test what is in your breasts and purify what is in your hearts. And Allah knows what is in the breasts."﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 154] ﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met, only Satan caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned. And Allah has already pardoned them. Indeed Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 155] ﴿O you who have believed, do not be like those who disbelieved and said of their brothers when they travelled in the land or went out to fight, "If they had remained with us they would not have died or been killed," so that Allah may make that a regret in their hearts. Allah gives life and causes death, and Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 156] ﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah or die, forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they accumulate.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 157] ﴿And if you die or are killed, indeed to Allah you will be gathered.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 158] ﴿It is by a mercy from Allah that you were gentle with them. Had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you. So pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter. And when you have decided, rely upon Allah. Indeed Allah loves those who rely upon Him.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 159] ﴿If Allah helps you, none can overcome you. And if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him? And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 160] ﴿It is not for a Prophet to misappropriate. And whoever misappropriates will bring what he misappropriated on the Day of Resurrection. Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 161] ﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah like one who incurs wrath from Allah, whose refuge is Hell? And wretched is the destination.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 162] ﴿They are of varying ranks with Allah, and Allah is Seeing of what they do.﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 163]

(p-81) al-is'ad (the setting out, the departure) means the beginning of a journey and the place of departure. As for al-su'ud (ascent), it is the verbal noun of sa'ida, meaning he climbed up from a low place to a high place; this is the view of al-Farra', Abu Hatim and al-Zajjaj. Al-Qutabi said: aş'ada means he went far away in departing, so it is like going far away, as in the sense of rising high. He said:

"Ala ayyuha-l-sa'ili 'ayna şa'idta fa-inna laha fi ardi Yathriba mau'idan
(Oh you who ask where you went up, indeed for her there is an appointment in the land of Yathrib.)

Abu 'Ubayda recited:

Qad kunta tubkini 'ala-l-is'adi *** fa-l-yawma sarahtu wa şaha al-hadi
(You used to make me weep over the departure, but today I have set off and the driver has cried out.)

Al-Mufaddal said: sa'ida, a'sada and sa'ada have one meaning. Al-sa'id is the surface of the earth. Sa'ada is one of the names of the earth. And a'sada means he entered into the sa'id.

Fat al-shay'(the thing escaped) means its attainment was beyond reach. It is transitive, and its verbal noun is fawt, which is the standard pattern for a transitive verb.

Al-nu'as is light sleep. It is said: na'isa yan'as nu'asan, fa-huwa na'is, and one does not say na'san. Al-Farra' said: I have heard it, but I do not favour it.

Al-madja' is the place on which one reclines for sleep, and from it comes Allah's words: ﴿and forsake them in the beds﴾ [al-Nisa': 34]. Al-madaji' also means al-masari', which are places of killing, named so after the fallen person lying down (yad'ja'ah) there.

Al-ghazw is intent, and likewise al-maghza. Then it was applied to a specific intent, which is attacking the enemy. You say: ghaza bani fulan, meaning he struck them with killing, plunder and whatever resembles that. Ghuzzan is the plural of ghazin, like 'afin and 'afa. They also said ghuzza', with a long vowel. Both are not regular. The plural of the active participle of a defective final-radical verb was treated as if it were sound, like rukka' and suwwam. The regular form would be fu'ala, like qadin and qudat. It is said: aghzat al-naqatu, meaning her conception was difficult; and atanun mughziyatun, meaning a she-ass whose delivery was delayed and then gave birth.

It is said: li'a al-shay' yalin, so it is layyin. The verbal noun is layn and layan with a fatha on the lam. Its original sense is in physical bodies, namely their smoothness and the absence of roughness, and it is perceived only by touch. Then they extended it and transferred it to meanings.

Al-fazaza is harshness in dealing with people, in speech and in action. A poet said about his daughter:

Akhsha fazaza 'ammin aw jafa'a akhin *** wa kuntu akhsha 'alayha min adha al-kalimi
(I fear the harshness of a paternal cousin, or the coldness of a brother, and I used to fear for her from the harm of words.)

Al-ghilazh originally refers to bodies, namely the abundance of their parts. Then it is used for little reaction, little compassion and little mercy, as he said:

Yabki 'alayna wa la nabki 'ala ahadin *** lanahnu aghlazu akbadan mina al-ibili
(He weeps for us, and we do not weep for anyone; indeed we are harder of livers than camels.)

Al-infid'ad is dispersal. Fadadtu al-shay' means I broke it, and it is the separation of its parts.

Al-khadhl and al-khidhlan mean abandonment in a place where one who is abandoned needs the one who leaves. Its origin is from khadhl al-zabyi (the gazelle's fawn being left behind). For this reason it is said of her, khadhil, when her mother has left her. This is on the pattern of attribution, meaning one who has khadhl, because the one left behind is the khadhil, in the sense of makhdhul (forsaken). It is also said khadhila. The poet said:

Bi-jidi mughzilatin adma'a khadhilatin *** mina al-zaba tura'i shadinan kharaqa
(With the neck of a slender, brown-skinned, forsaken [female gazelle] from among the gazelles, watching over a young gazelle that is sprightly.)

It is also said of her khadhul, on the pattern of fa'ul, in the sense of maf'ul. He said:

Khadhulun tura'i rabraban bi-khamilatin *** tanawalu atrafa al-barid wa tartadi
(A forsaken [female] watching over a wild cow in a thicket, reaching for the ends of the mail and wrapping herself.)

Al-ghulul is taking property from the spoils secretly. Its verb is ghalla yaghullu, with a damma on the ghayn. Al-ghill is resentment, and its verb is ghalla yaghillu, with a kasra on the ghayn. Abu 'Ali said: The Arabs say aghalla al-rajulu ighlalan, meaning he betrayed the trust. Al-Namir said:

Jaza Allahu 'anni jamrata bna nawfalin *** jaza'a mughillin bi-l-amanati kadhibi
(May Allah repay on my behalf Jamrah ibn Nawfal the recompense of a betrayer of trust who lies.)

Some grammarians said: al-ghulul is derived from al-ghalal, which is the water flowing at the roots of trees and the spirit. It is also said of ghulul: aghalla ighlalan, and aghalla al-harizu, meaning he stole some meat along with the skin. It is also said: aghallahu, meaning he found him to be a betrayer, as when you say abkhaltuhu, you found him stingy.

Al-sukhţ is the verbal noun of sakhita, and it follows the regular pattern. It is also said: al-sukhţ with a damma on the sin and a sukun on the kha'. It is said: mata fulanun fi sukhtati al-maliki, meaning in the king's displeasure. Al-sukhţ is extreme dislike, and its opposite is approval (al-rida).

﴿When you were climbing away and not turning back for anyone, while the Messenger was calling you from behind you﴾: these sentences contain severe reproach and strong reproof. This is a reminder of the flight of those who fled and went to extremes in running away, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was calling them back. Because of the intensity of their flight and their preoccupation with themselves, while they were seeking their own salvation, they did not heed the Messenger's call. This is among the greatest reproaches, since they fled while the Messenger of Allah was calling them back.

(p-82) The majority read tus'idun, the present tense of as'ada, and the hamza in as'ada indicates entering. That is, you entered the sa'id, meaning you went into it, just as you say: asbaha Zayd, meaning he entered the morning. So the meaning is: when you were going into the land. This is clarified by the reading of Ubayy: "When you were climbing into the valley." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Yazidi read tus'idun from sa'ida fi al-jabal, when one climbs up a mountain. Abu Hayra read tasa''adun from tasa''ada fi al-sullam, climbing the ladder, whose original form is tatasa''adun, and one of the two taus was dropped, according to the disagreement on that point: is it the taw of the present tense, or the taw of tafa''ala? The combination of these is that first they went up into the valley when the enemy's attack overwhelmed them, and then they climbed the mountain. Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir in the narration of Shibl read yas'idun, with the ya', shifting from address to the third person absent. The operator of idh is: udhkur (remember) understood, or 'asaytum (you disobeyed), or tana'atum (you disputed), or fashiltum (you lost heart), or 'afa 'ankum (He pardoned you), or liyabtaliyakum (in order to test you), or sarafakum (He turned you away). The last two are from al-Zamakhshari, and the rest are from Ibn 'Atiyya. All of these before it are distant because of the long separation. The first is good, because what comes before idh are independent sentences that are fine to stop at, so they have no grammatical connection to what follows. They are connected to it only because the whole context is one story. Its connection to sarafakum is good in meaning, and its connection to 'afa 'ankum is good in closeness.

The meaning of ﴿and not turning back for anyone﴾ is: you did not return to anyone because of the intensity of the flight. Law bi-kadha means he went off with it, and law 'alayhi means he turned back upon it and inclined to it. This is more emphatic than the line of verse:

Akhu al-jahdi la yalwi 'ala man ta'adhdhara
(The one who is in extreme hardship does not turn back for anyone who has become incapable.)

Because in the verse it is a general negation, while in this line it is a specific negation, namely "for one who has become incapable." Durayd ibn al-Simma said:

Wa hal yaruddu al-munhazima shay'un
(And does anything turn back the one who has fled in defeat?)

It was read as talu'una with the waw changed to a hamza, because of the dislike of two consecutive waws. The analogy for this damma-vowelled waw is that it should not be changed into a hamza, because the damma on it is incidental. Whenever a waw that is not initial takes a damma, it is not permissible to change it into a hamza except under two conditions: first, that the damma is required; second, that it cannot be lightened by making it sukun. An example is fawuwj and fawul and ghawur. In these cases fa'uwj, qa'ul and gha'ur are permissible with a hamza. An example of the damma being incidental is: hadha dulukun. An example of the damma being lightened by sukun is: hadha sur and nur, plural of suwar and nuwar. You say in both: sur and nur. One of our companions pointed out another condition that is indispensable: that it is not assimilated into a following letter, as in ta'uudhu, so taqu'udhu with the damma-vowelled waw changed to hamza is not permissible. Some grammarians added another condition: that the waw is not an added letter, as in al-tarahwuk. This condition is not agreed upon.

Al-Hasan read talunna, and they explained it on the basis of the reading of the one who changed the damma-vowelled waw into a hamza, then moved its vowel to the lam and dropped the hamza. Ibn 'Atiyya said: One of the two sukun waws was dropped. He had said about this reading: it is a composite reading based on the reading of one who made the damma-vowelled waw a hamza, then the vowel of the hamza was moved to the lam. End of quote. This is a strange statement. This man imagined that the vowel had been moved to the lam, so two sukun waws came together: one of them the waw that is the root letter of the word, and the other the waw of the pronoun, so one of the two waws was dropped because they were both sukun. This is the view of one who did not study grammar deeply, because if it is composed on the dialect of one who made the waw a hamza, and then moved its vowel to the lam, then the hamza in that case is dropped, and two sukun waws do not meet. Had he said: the damma was made heavy on the waw, because the damma is as if it were a waw, so it is as if three waws had been gathered, and the damma is then moved to the lam; thus two sukun letters meet, and the first of them is dropped, and had he not left the phrase "one of the two waws" unspecified, that would have made sense in explaining this anomalous reading. But to base it on the dialect of one who made the hamza, by his assumption, is not conceivable.

It is possible that it is the present tense of waliya, and it is transitive with 'ala, on the basis of implying the meaning of turning back. That is: you do not turn back to anyone. Al-A'mash and Abu Bakr in a narration from 'Asim read tulwuna, from alwa, which is a dialect of lawa. The apparent meaning of his words "for anyone" is generality.

It is said: the intended one is the Prophet (ﷺ), and he expressed it as "anyone" to honour him and to protect his name from being mentioned when they went away from him. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi.

Humayd ibn Qays read "upon Uhud" with a damma on the hamza and the ha', and this is the mountain. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the well-known reading is stronger, because the Prophet (ﷺ) was not on the mountain except after the people had fled from him, and this state of their climbing was while he was calling them. End of quote. Others said: the address in it is to those who went far in flight and did not climb the mountain, over those who climbed. It is possible that by his words "and not turning back for Uhud" he meant those who were on the mountain of Uhud, namely the Prophet (ﷺ) and those with him who had climbed. And talwuna is from the twisting of the neck, because whoever turns to something twists his neck, or the reins of his mount.

The alif and lam in al-Rasul are for a known referent. The call of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is reported: he used to say, "Come to me, servants of Allah," while the people were fleeing from him. It is also reported: "O servants of Allah, return!" This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. In another narration: "Return to me, for I am the Messenger of Allah; whoever attacks for him, Paradise (is his)." This is the view of al-Suddi and al-Rabi'. Al-Qurtubi said: His calling was a change of the wrong, and it is impossible that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would see the wrong, which is the rout, and then not forbid it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 153 (part 2 of 2):

The meaning of "in your rear" (fi ukhrakum) is: in your rearguard and your other, later body, which is the one at the back. It is said: "I came at the end of the people and their rear (akhrahum)," just as you say "at their front (awwalihim) and their first (ula)," with the interpretation of their vanguard and their first body. In His saying "in your rear" there is a great indication of the courage of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), for standing at the heels of the brave when they are fleeing, and remaining firm in that position, belongs only to the valiant heroes. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was the bravest of people. Salamah said: "When the fighting grew fierce, we would take shelter behind the Messenger of God (ﷺ)."

﴿So He rewarded you with grief upon grief﴾: the agent of "rewarded you" (athabakum) is God, exalted is He. Al-Farra' said: "The word ithabah (reward) here means ghalabah (overpowering)." End of quote. The grief was called a "reward" in the sense that it stood in this calamity in the place of the reward that would have been obtained had they not fled. It is like His saying:
"A greeting among them is a painful blow,"
and His saying:
"I fear that Ziyad's gift may be black shackles or dark-skinned, dragged chains,"
he made the fetters and whips a gift, and "muhadrajah" means "mudahrajah" (rolled). The "ba'" in "with grief" (bighammin) may be either for accompaniment or for causation. If it is for accompaniment, which some of them expressed by the meaning "with" (ma'a), the meaning is: grief accompanied by grief. Then the two griefs belong to them. The first is what befell them of defeat and killing; the second is Khalid's approach upon them with the cavalry of the polytheists. This is related from Ibn Abbas and Muqatil. It was said: the first grief was caused by their first flight, and the second was caused by their fleeing when they heard that Muhammad had been killed. This is related from Mujahid. It was said: the first is what they lost of the spoils and what afflicted them of wounds and killing; the second is when they heard that the Prophet (ﷺ) had been killed. This is related from Qatadah and al-Rabi'. It was said that the reverse of this order is the case, and Ibn Atiyyah attributed it to Qatadah and Mujahid. It was said: the first is what they lost of spoils and victory; the second is Abu Sufyan's approach upon them, mentioned by al-Tha'labi. It was said: the first is their killing, their wounds, and everything that occurred in that narrow place; the second is Abu Sufyan's approach upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and those with him, related by al-Suddi, Mujahid also, and others. Al-Zamakhshari expressed this meaning, namely the accumulation of the two griefs upon them, by saying: "grief after grief," and "grief connected to grief," from the distress caused by what was spread about the killing of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the wounding, the killing, the victory of the polytheists, the loss of the spoils, and the victory. End of his words. His saying "grief after grief" is an explanation of the meaning, not a grammatical explanation, because the "ba'" does not carry the meaning of "after"; although some of them went to that, and therefore some of them said that the meaning is "grief upon grief," so it should be taken as an explanation of the meaning, though some of them went to that as well. If the "ba'" is for causation, which some of them expressed as meaning "in return for," then the first grief belongs to the Companions. As for the second, al-Hasan and others said its referent is the polytheists on the day of Badr. The meaning is: He rewarded you with grief in return for the grief that was inflicted upon the disbelievers at your hands on the day of Badr. Ibn Atiyyah said: the "ba'" on this view is the "ba'" of equivalence, as Abu Sufyan said on the day of Badr: "War is a matter of turns." Some people, including al-Zajjaj, and al-Zamakhshari following him, said: its referent is the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the meaning is: He recompensed you with grief because of the grief you caused the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and all the believers through your cowardice, your disputing, and your disobedience. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also possible that the pronoun in "so He rewarded you" refers to the Messenger, meaning He consoled you in grief, and just as what befell him of the breaking of his incisor and the wound to his head and other things grieved him, what befell you grieved him, so He rewarded you for what he had grieved over on your account, because of a grief you caused him, and he did not turn against you for your disobedience and your opposition, but he did this only to console you and relieve you, so that you would not grieve over what you had lost of God's help, nor over what had befallen you of the enemy's victory. End of his words. This is contrary to the apparent meaning, because the subject of the preceding verbs is God, exalted is He, as in His saying: ﴿And God had certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152], and His saying: ﴿Then He turned you away from them to test you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152], ﴿And God certainly pardoned you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152]. So His saying "so He rewarded you" is attributed to God, exalted is He. The mention of the Messenger came only in a circumstantial clause, which censured them for their flight while those who were guided through him were calling them. So it was not intended to be spoken of as the main subject; the clause in which it is mentioned is in the place of a single word, since it is a circumstantial clause. Al-Zamakhshari said: "so He rewarded you" is coordinated with "He turned you away." End of his words. This is far-fetched, because of the long separation between the two coordinated items. What appears is that it is coordinated with "﴿you were going up and not turning back﴾," because it is a present verb in the sense of the past, since "idh" (when) turns the present into the past, as it is an adverb of what has passed. The meaning is: when you went up and did not turn back on anyone, so He rewarded you.

﴿So that you would not grieve over what escaped you, nor over what befell you﴾: the "lam" is the "lam" of purpose (kay), and it is connected to His saying "so He rewarded you." It was said: "la" is extra, because it does not follow from being grieved that grief is absent. The meaning is: on the basis that He grieved them so that He might make them grieve, as a punishment for them for their failure to comply with them. This was said by Abu al-Baqa' and others. It is like His saying: ﴿So that the People of the Book may not know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29], since its estimated meaning is: so that the People of the Book may know. He made them know this as a rebuke to them and a deterrent against returning to the like. Most scholars hold that "la" retains its meaning of negation. They differ about the reasoning for the reward being the absence of grief over what has been mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿So that you would not grieve﴾" means: so that you would become accustomed to swallowing griefs and be trained to endure hardships, so that you would not grieve afterward over a lost benefit, nor over a harm that struck you. End of his words. Thus he made the reason, in reality, a positive one, namely training in swallowing griefs and habituation to enduring hardships, and he made the absence of grief follow from that, and he made the time of the grief a future time not connected to the story of Uhud, but so that grief would be absent from you after this story. Ibn Atiyyah said: the meaning is: so that you would know that what befell you was only because of your own offense, for you harmed yourselves. The habit of humankind is that the one who commits a wrong endures punishment, and most of the distress and grief of the one punished arises only when he thinks himself innocent. End of his words. This is an interpretation contrary to that of al-Zamakhshari.

Among the exegetes is one who held that His saying "so that you would not grieve" is connected to His saying: ﴿And God certainly pardoned you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152], and God informed them of this as a consolation for their calamity and a compensation for them for the grief that had befallen them, because His pardon removes every grief. But there is distance in this because of the long separation, and because its apparent connection is with what is adjacent to it, which is "so He rewarded you."

Ibn Abbas said: what escaped them was the spoils, and what befell them was the failure and the defeat. Among what this verse may bear is that when He mentioned their going up and fleeing eagerly in flight, while the Messenger (ﷺ) was calling them to return from fleeing and to withdraw to his group, the eagerness to flee became a cause for griefs to be linked to them, and their preoccupation with themselves in seeking to be saved from death. So that, that is, their preoccupation with themselves and the griefs that were linked to them from the direction of fear of being killed, became a cause for the absence of grief over what had escaped them of the spoils and what had befallen their brothers of wounds and killing. As if it were said: they came into a state of being so occupied and concerned with the salvation of themselves that no grief over any lost thing, nor any affliction, however great, came to their minds. Thus He preoccupied them with themselves so that grief would be absent from them.

﴿And God is Aware of what you do﴾: this sentence implies a threat. He specified "doing" here, although He, exalted is He, is Aware of all states, including actions, words, and intentions, to draw attention to their deeds: turning their backs and their extreme haste in flight. These are deeds whose consequences and punishment are to be feared.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 154 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Then He sent down upon you, after distress, security in the form of drowsiness﴾: al-amanah (security) means al-amn (security), as said by Ibn Qutaybah and others. Others made a distinction, saying: al-amanah occurs while the causes of fear still remain, whereas al-amn occurs when those causes have been removed. Al-Jumhur (the majority) read amanatan with a fatha on the mim, on the basis that it means al-amn, or that it is the plural of amin, like barr and baraha, and its i'rab (grammatical analysis) will come. al-Nakha'i and Ibn Muhaysin read "amnatan" with a sukun on the mim, meaning al-amn. The meaning of the verse is God's favour upon them in granting them security after fear and distress, such that they came to sleep in security, for one who is in intense fear and distress can hardly sleep. The exegetes related what the Companions reported about the overpowering sleep that overcame them, such as Abu Talhah, al-Zubayr, and Ibn Mas'ud. They differed about the time at which the drowsiness overcame them.

Al-Jumhur said: it was when Abu Sufyan departed from the battlefield. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Ali, who was among those who had withdrawn to him: "Go and look at the people. If they have led their horses away, they are heading for Makkah; and if they are still upon their horses, they are returning to Madinah. So fear God and be patient," and prepare them for fighting. Ali went, then returned and reported that they had led their horses away and sat upon their baggage, hastening. So the believers who affirmed the Messenger of God (ﷺ) became secure, and God, may He be exalted, cast drowsiness upon them. But the hypocrites, in whose hearts is a disease, remained and did not believe; rather, they thought that Abu Sufyan was heading for Madinah, so no sleep fell upon any of them, and their concern was only for their worldly affairs. It is established in al-Bukhari from the hadith of Abu Talhah, who said: "Drowsiness overtook us while we were in our ranks on the day of Uhud, and it kept falling from my hand, and I would pick it up, and it would fall and I would pick it up again." In another route: "I raised my head and I saw no one of the people except that he was swaying beneath his shield." This indicates that drowsiness overtook them while they were in their ranks. The context of the verse and the first hadith indicate otherwise. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿So He rewarded you with grief upon grief﴾ [Al 'Imran: 153]. The grief came after they had been broken and scattered from their ranks, and the polytheists had departed from them. The reconciliation of these two views is that the ranks of which Abu Talhah spoke were on the mountain after the defeat; Abu Sufyan looked down upon them from above with a great number of horses, and those of the Companions who had withdrawn to the mountain pelted them with stones, and Umar was there and remained until they brought them down. They remained in their ranks until news came to them from Quraysh that they had resolved to return to Makkah, and then God sent down drowsiness upon them in that place, so they became secure, while the hypocrites did not become secure.

The subject of "anzala" (sent down) is a pronoun referring to God, the Exalted, and it is coordinated with "fa-athabakum." "Alaykum" (upon you) indicates the enveloping, dominating and overpowering character of the drowsiness, and attributing the sending down is metaphorical, since its literal sense applies to physical bodies. They parsed "amanatan" as a direct object of anzala, and nu'asan as a substitute (badal) from it, a badal al-ishtimal (substitution by inclusion), because each of the two may conceive of including the other, or one may conceive of the agent including both, according to the disagreement on this matter. Or it is an explicative apposition ('atf bayan), but this is not permissible according to the view of the Basran majority, since a condition of explicative apposition for them is that it be among the definites. Or it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), which is weak, because of the failure of one of the conditions, namely the unity of the agent, for the agent of sending down is God, the Exalted, while the agent of drowsiness is the one who sends it down upon them; and this condition is according to the school of the majority of grammarians. It has been said: nu'asan is the object of anzala, and amanatan is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from it, because originally it was an indefinite qualifier which was placed before its noun and so became accusative as a circumstantial. The estimate is: nu'asan dha amanatin (drowsiness possessing security), because drowsiness is not security. Or it is a circumstantial from the genitive pronoun, with the estimate: dhawi amanatin (possessors of security). Or it is the plural of amin, meaning aminin (secure ones). Or it is an object of purpose, meaning li-amanatin (for security), as said by al-Zamakhshari, and this is weak for the same reason by which we showed the weakness of the view that parsed nu'asan as an object of purpose.

﴿It overcomes a group among you﴾: they are the believers. This indicates that His saying "then He sent down upon you" is general with a specific intent, for in reality He sent it down only upon those who had believed.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "taghsha" with a ta', taking it according to the wording of amanatan. So they said: and the clause is in the position of a qualifier. This is not clear, because the grammarians have stated that the qualifier precedes the substitute and the explicative apposition when they are combined. So whoever parsed nu'asan as a substitute or explicative apposition does not complete this, since it contradicts this rule; and whoever parsed it as an object of purpose also has in it the separation between the qualifier and the qualified by this superfluous element. There is a question about the permissibility of this, together with what we have pointed out regarding the failure of the condition, namely the unity of the agent. If you make "taghsha" a resumed clause, as if it were an answer to one who asks: what is the ruling on this security? Then He, the Exalted, informs: it overcomes a group among you, that is permissible. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the verb is ascribed to the pronoun of the substituted noun. End.

When he parsed nu'asan as a substitute from amanatan, the analogy would have been to speak about the substitute and not about the substituted noun, yet here he spoke about the substituted noun. When you say: inna Hindan husnuha fatinun (indeed Hind, her beauty is captivating), the predicate concerns her beauty; this is the well-known usage of the Arabs. Some of our companions permitted predicating about the substituted noun, as Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted in the verse, and they cited as evidence the verse:

Indeed the swords, their morning and their evening, have left Hawazin like the horn of the hornless one.

And the verse of another:

And as if he had on his back a white mark, as if his two eyebrows were marked with blackness.
