He said: "taraka" (has left), and did not say "taraka" in dual; and "mu'ayyan" (marked), and did not say "mu'ayyanan" (two marked). So he returned the pronoun to the substituted noun, which is "al-suyuf" (the swords). The pronoun in "ka-annahu" and "lam" did not return to the substitute, which is "ghuduwwuha wa rawahuha" and "hajibayhi." "Ma" is superfluous between the substituted noun and the substitute. There is no proof in what they cited, since it is possible that the accusative of "ghuduwwuha wa rawahiha" is as an adverbial of time and not as a substitute, and it is possible that "mu'ayyan" is a predicate about "hajibayhi," because it is permissible to predicate about two things that cannot be separated from one another, such as the hands, the feet, the eyes, and the eyebrows, predicating about one as in what he said:

For whom is a slippery path, on which the two eyes flow with tears.

And he said:

And as if in the two eyes is a grain of clove, or an ear of grain, with which they were kohled and so they flowed.

He said: "tanhallu" (flows), and "kuhilat bihi" (were kohled with it), and did not say "tanhallani" or "kuhhilata bihi." This is like what they permitted, that one of these two be predicated of as if it were the dual, as he said:

When my two eyes recall the time that passed, in the desert of Falj, they both shed tears.

He said: "zallatan" (they both remained), and did not say "zallat takif" (one remained shedding).

Those remaining read "yaghsha" with the ya', taking it according to the wording of nu'asan.

* *

﴿And a group, their own selves had caused them concern, thinking about God other than the truth, the thought of the Jahiliyyah. They say: "Is there anything for us in the matter?" Say: "Indeed the matter, all of it, belongs to God."﴾ Makki said: The exegetes agreed that this group were the hypocrites, and they said: drowsiness overtook the people of faith and sincerity, so it was a cause of their security and steadfastness, and it left the people of hypocrisy and doubt bare, so it was a cause of their panic and their exposure in their ranks. End.

It is said: "ahammani al-shay'" means the thing was of my concern and aim, i.e., something I cared about or intended. "Ahammani al-amr" means the matter made me anxious and brought me into worry, that is, grief. On this basis the exegetes differed about "qad ahammathum anfusuhum." Qatadah, al-Rabi' and Ibn Ishaq and most of them said: it means grief, and the meaning is that their sick selves and evil thoughts brought them the fear of death; this is the meaning of al-Zamakhshari's statement, or: their own selves and what befell them had cast them into griefs and sorrows, so they were in lamentation. Some exegetes said: it is from "hamma bi al-shay'," meaning he intended to do it. The meaning is: their own selves made them intend to abandon the faith and to renounce religion. This view is held by those who said: Muhammad has been killed, so let us return to our former religion, and similar sayings. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding His words "qad ahammathum anfusuhum": they were concerned only with the concern of their own selves, not the concern of religion, nor the concern of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the Muslims. End. So it would be from their saying: "ahammani al-shay'," meaning it was of my concern and will. The meaning is: the concern of their own deliverance alone occupied them, that is, their concern and will was only the deliverance of their selves, and they thought without truth that Islam is not true, and that the affair of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would go away and vanish.

The meaning of "thann al-jahiliyyah" according to the majority is: the ancient period of ignorance before Islam, as He said: ﴿the zealotry of the jahiliyyah﴾ [al-Fath: 26], ﴿and do not display yourselves in the display of the jahiliyyah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33], and as you say: "poetry of the jahiliyyah." Ibn 'Abbas said: I heard my father in the jahiliyyah say: "Give us a cup full to the brim." Some exegetes said: the meaning is the thought of the ignorant faction, the reference being to Abu Sufyan and those with him, and Qatadah and al-Tabari inclined to this view. Muqatil said: they thought that his affair was falling apart. al-Zajjaj said: indeed his period has ended. al-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas: they thought that Muhammad (ﷺ) had been killed. It has been said: the thought of the jahiliyyah is the nullification of prophethoods and laws. It has been said: their despair of God's help and their doubt about His earlier promise of victory. It has been said: they thought that the truth is what the unbelievers held, and therefore they were victorious. It has been said: they denied predestination. Al-Zamakhshari said: "thann al-jahiliyyah" is like your saying: "Hatim of generosity" and "a man of truthfulness," meaning the thought specific to the jahili creed. It is permissible that what is meant is the thought of the people of jahiliyyah, that is, none would think such a thought except the idolaters who are ignorant of God. End.

The apparent meaning of His saying "Is there anything for us in the matter?" is interrogation. It has been said: they asked the Messenger (ﷺ): is there for us, the company of Muslims, any share of victory and dominance over the enemy? They were answered with His saying: "Say: indeed the matter, all of it, belongs to God," that is, victory and dominance. ﴿God has decreed: "Surely I shall prevail, I and My messengers"﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 21]; ﴿and indeed Our host, they are the victorious﴾ [al-Saffat: 173]. It has been said: the meaning is that victory is not ours, but belongs to the polytheists. Qatadah and Ibn Juraij said: it was said to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul: the Banu al-Khazraj have been killed. He said: "Is there anything for us in the matter?" meaning that the opinion was not ours, and if there had been any of it for us, our opinion would have been heeded and we would not have gone out, and none of us would have been killed. This from them is a statement with two terms. Al-Mahdawi and Ibn Fawrak mentioned that the meaning is: we are not upon the truth in following Muhammad. This interpretation is weakened by the reply to them with His saying "Say," so understand that their speech was in fact an expression of the bad opinion about going out, and that had he not gone out, none would have been killed.

According to this meaning and what precedes it from the view of Qatadah and Ibn Juraij, the interrogation has the sense of negation. Since emphasis was added in their speech by the insertion of "min" in "min shay'," the reply came emphasized with "inna," and the emphasis of generality was intensified by His saying "kulluhu li-llah," so the answer was more eloquent.

The address in "Say" is directed to the Messenger without dispute. What appears is that it is an interrogation remaining on its literal sense, because they were answered with His saying: "Say: indeed the matter, all of it, belongs to God." Had its meaning been negation, they would not have been answered thus, since one who denies that anything of the matter belongs to him is not answered in this way, unless one estimates together with the negative clause an affirmative clause concerning others, so the meaning would be: nothing of the matter is ours, but it belongs to others, such as those who compelled us to go out and forced us to it; so this answer may be a reply to this estimated clause. This answering clause is a parenthesis between the clauses through which God informed about them.

The waw in His saying ﴿وطائِفَةٌ﴾ (wa-ṭā'ifatun) is the waw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl). ﴿وطائِفَةٌ﴾ is a mubtada' (the subject of a nominal sentence), and the clause connected to it is its khabar (predicate). The beginning of a sentence with an indefinite noun (nakira) is permitted here, because there are two justifications (musawwighān) for it. The first is the waw of circumstance, which some scholars have listed among the justifications, though most of our companions (aṣḥābunā) did not mention it. A poet said:

*We travelled while a star had shone, but when your face appeared, its light hid every dawn-bright star.*

The second justification is that the context is one of differentiation (tafṣīl). The meaning is: He covers a group of you, and a group had not slept. This is like the poet's words:

*When she wept from behind her, she turned toward him with one side, and the other side, in our view, was not turned.*

Putting ﴿طائِفَةً﴾ in the accusative (naṣb) on this reading, with the construction being one of ishtighāl (where a verb is occupied with a pronoun referring back to the noun, so the noun is governed by a verb supplied by implication), is permissible in terms of i'rāb (grammatical inflection). It is also permissible for ﴿قَدْ أهَمَّتْهُمْ﴾ (qad ahammathum) to be in the position of a descriptive clause (ṣifa), with ﴿يَظُنُّونَ﴾ (yaẓunnūna) as the predicate. It is permissible for the predicate to be omitted, with both clauses being descriptive, the sense being: "and among you is a group." It is also permissible for ﴿يَظُنُّونَ﴾ to be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿أهَمَّتْهم﴾. The accusative of ﴿غَيْرَ الحَقِّ﴾ (ghayra al-ḥaqq) is explained as follows. Abu al-Baqa' said that it is the first object of ﴿تَظُنُّونَ﴾, meaning "a matter other than the truth," and "bi-Allāh" is the second. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "ghayra al-ḥaqq" has the force of a verbal noun (maṣdar), and its meaning is: "they think about God the thought of the Jāhiliyya (the age of ignorance)." "Ghayra al-ḥaqq" is an emphatic (ta'kīd) for ﴿يَظُنُّونَ﴾, like your saying, "this statement is not what you say," and "this statement is not your statement." End of his words. On this view, ﴿يَظُنُّونَ﴾ is not stated with two objects, and the bāʼ is locative (ẓarfiyya), as when you say, "I thought about Zayd (ẓanantu bi-Zaydin)." When that is so, ẓanantu does not take two objects, and the meaning is: "I put Zayd in place of my thought." The grammarians have explicitly stated this. On this is the poet's line:

*So I said to them: "Think of two thousand armoured men, their chieftains in the woven mail."*

That is, "Set in place of your thought two thousand armoured men." The accusative of ﴿ظَنَّ﴾ (ẓanna) is as a verbal noun of comparison (maṣdar tashbīhī), meaning: "a thought like the thought of the Jāhiliyya." ﴿يَقُولُونَ﴾ (yaqūlūna) may be a descriptive clause, or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿يَظُنُّونَ﴾, or a second predicate after a predicate, according to the view of those who permit enumerating predicates, in a case where they have not agreed on the permissibility of enumerating them. ﴿مِن شَيْءٍ﴾ (min shay') is in the position of a subject (mubtada'), since ﴿مِن﴾ is extra (zā'ida), and its predicate is in ﴿لَنا﴾ (lanā). ﴿مِنَ الأمْرِ﴾ (min al-amr) is in the position of a circumstantial clause, because if it were placed after "shay'," it would be a qualifier (na't) for it, and it would be governed by something omitted. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿مِنَ الأمْرِ﴾ be the predicate, with ﴿لَنا﴾ as an explanation (tabyīn), and the benefit completed by it, as in His saying: ﴿ولَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ كُفُوًا أحَدٌ﴾ [al-Ikhlāṣ: 4]. This is not permissible, because what comes as an explanation has an operative element that is supposed, and its supposed form is: "I mean, to us," which is another clause, so that the subject and predicate remain a clause that does not stand on its own for the benefit, and that is not permissible. As for his citing His saying ﴿ولَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ كُفُوًا أحَدٌ﴾, the two are not the same, because ﴿لَهُ﴾ is a complement of ﴿كُفُوًا﴾, and it is not an explanation, so its operative element would be supposed, and the meaning is: "No one was a match for Him," that is, equal to Him. So it is like "he was not one striking for ʿAmr (lam yakun lahu ḍāriban li-ʿamr)," where "li-ʿamr" is not an explanation, but a complement of ḍārib (striking). Abu 'Amr read ﴿كُلُّهُ﴾ (kulluhu) with a nominative, as a subject. It is also permissible for it to be parsed as an emphatic (tawkīd) for the matter, on the position (maḥall) of the noun, according to the view of those who permit that, namely al-Jarmī, al-Zajjāj, and al-Farrā'. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "People have preferred the reading of the majority (al-jumhūr), because the emphatic is more fitting with the word 'kull'." End of his words. There is no preference here, since each of the two readings is mutawātir (transmitted by a multiple chain, certain), and beginning with "kull" is common in the speech of the Arabs.

(p-89)

* *

﴿يُخْفُونَ في أنْفُسِهِمْ ما لا يُبْدُونَ لَكَ﴾: It was said: the meaning is that they conceal themselves behind these statements, which are not pure disbelief but ignorance. It may be that this is a report of what they conceal of disbelief, which they cannot manifest beyond these slips. It was also said: what they concealed was their saying: "If we had been in our houses, we would not have been killed here." It was also said: it is regret at their presence with the Muslims at Uhud.

﴿يَقُولُونَ لَوْ كانَ لَنا مِنَ الأمْرِ شَيْءٌ ما قُتِلْنا هاهُنا﴾ Al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwām said, in what al-Ṭabarī transmitted from him: "By God, it is as if I hear the saying of Muʿattib ibn Qushayr, brother of the Banū ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf, while sleep was covering me. I heard it only like a dream, when he said: 'If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here.'" This Muʿattib was present at Badr, as Ibn Isḥāq and others mentioned, and he was suspected of hypocrisy (nifāq). The meaning is: "Our nobles and our best were not killed." This is the use of the name of the whole for a part, by way of metaphor (majāz).

His saying ﴿يَقُولُونَ﴾ may be what they concealed, so it is an explanation after the vagueness of ﴿ما لا يُبْدُونَ لَكَ﴾. Its meaning is: "They say within themselves, or some of them say to others."

His saying ﴿مِنَ الأمْرِ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 128]: "al-amr" is explained here by what was explained in the saying of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl: "Do we have any say in the matter?" It was said: the meaning is: "If the matter were as Muḥammad said, that the whole matter belongs to God and to His friends, and that they are the victorious, we would never have been defeated, and none of the Muslims who were killed in this battle would have been killed." It was also said: "al-amr" means opinion and planning. It was also said: it means the religion of Muḥammad, that is, "we are not upon the truth in following it."

The answer (jawāb) to "law" (if) is the negated clause with mā. When you negate with mā, the eloquent usage is not to put the lām (of emphasis) before it.

It was said: there is confusion in the story of Uhud. At its beginning, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ubayy and those with him from the hypocrites turned back and did not witness Uhud. On this view, they said this in Medina, and none of them or their companions was killed in Medina; rather they were killed at Uhud. So how does His saying "here" (hāhunā) come? And the report of al-Zubayr hearing Muʿattib saying that is evidence that Muʿattib was present at Uhud! If the report of al-Zubayr is sound, then some of the hypocrites separated from ʿAbd Allāh and were present at Uhud, so His saying "here" is apt. If it is not sound, then His saying "here" is directed to the fact that it is a pointing to Uhud, the pointing of one near and present, because Uhud is near Medina.

﴿قُلْ لَوْ كُنْتُمْ في بُيُوتِكم لَبَرَزَ الَّذِينَ كُتِبَ عَلَيْهِمُ القَتْلُ إلى مَضاجِعِهِمْ﴾ This type is called, among the scholars of rhetoric (ʿulamāʾ al-bayān), "theoretical argumentation" (al-iḥtijāj al-naẓarī), which is that the speaker mentions a meaning and argues for it with kinds of rational proof, such as: ﴿لَوْ كانَ فِيهِما آلِهَةٌ إلّا اللَّهُ لَفَسَدَتا﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 22]; ﴿قُلْ يُحْيِيها الَّذِي أنْشَأها أوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ﴾ [Yāsīn: 79]; ﴿أوَلَيْسَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ السَّماواتِ والأرْضَ بِقادِرٍ﴾ [Yāsīn: 81]. Some call it the dialectical method (al-madhhab al-kalāmī). From it is the poet's saying:

*The decree has run with what is in it; so if you are blamed, there is no blame for what was written with the pen.*

"Kataba" here means: decreed (faraḍa), or determined and made certain (qaḍā wa-ḥatama), or inscribed on the tablet (khaṭṭa fī al-lawḥ), or that the angel wrote it for them while they were still embryos (ajinna). These are the views. The meaning of the verse: if you had stayed behind in the houses, those whose killing was made certain would have gone out to the place of their fall and been killed there. This is a refutation of Muʿattib's saying, and evidence that each person has one term (ajal) which he does not exceed. If it is said: that is the term that was preceded in eternity, and otherwise he would die at that term, and there is no difference between his death and his soul's departure by killing, or by any causes of illness, or if it came upon him without illness: it is one term for each person, even if the causes multiply. Al-Zamakhsharī spoke here with long-winded phrases, as is his habit. He said: "If you had been in your houses," meaning: whoever God knew would be killed and fall in these places of fall, and He wrote that in the Preserved Tablet, there would have been no alternative to its existence. So if you had sat in your houses, there would have come forth from among you those whom God knew would be killed to their "maḍāji'" (lying places), which are their places of fall, so that what He knew would happen would happen. The meaning: God wrote on the tablet the killing of those of the believers who are killed, and wrote along with that that they are the victorious, because He knew that the outcome in victory is theirs, and that the religion of Islam will prevail over all religion. They are only struck at certain times, for purification (tamḥīṣ) for them, and to encourage them to martyrdom, and their eagerness for martyrdom is among what urges them to jihad, so victory is achieved. End of his words. This is a kind of oratory, and the meaning of the verse is very clear and does not (p-90) need this lengthy elaboration.

The majority read ﴿لَبَرَزَ﴾ as a triliteral active verb (thulāthī mabnī li-l-fāʿil), meaning: they would have come out into the open (al-barāz) from the earth. Abū Ḥaywa read ﴿لَبُرِّزَ﴾ as passive with a doubled rāʾ, making the verb transitive through doubling. The majority read ﴿كُتِبَ﴾ as passive, with ﴿القَتْلُ﴾ in the nominative. It is also read ﴿كَتَبَ﴾ as active, with ﴿القَتْلُ﴾ in the accusative. Al-Ḥasan and al-Zuhrī read ﴿القِتالُ﴾ (al-qitāl) in the nominative. This reading may imply independence from the hypocrites, meaning: even if you had stayed behind, the obedient believers upon whom fighting was obligated would have come out willingly to the places of their martyrdom, and He would have done without you.

﴿ولِيَبْتَلِيَ اللَّهُ ما في صُدُورِكم ولِيُمَحِّصَ ما في قُلُوبِكُمْ﴾ The meanings of testing (ibtilāʾ) and purging (tamḥīṣ) have already been mentioned. It was said: the meaning is that God made fighting obligatory upon you and did not give you victory on the day of Uhud, in order to test your patience, and to purge from you your misdeeds if you repented and were sincere. It was also said: so that He may deal with you as one who is tested. It was said: so that there may occur among you the witnessing of His knowledge unseen, as in His saying: ﴿فَيَنْظُرَ كَيْفَ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 129]. It was said: it has an elided modifier (muḍāf maḥdhūf), meaning: "and that the friends of God may test what is in your breasts," and He attributed it to Himself to magnify its importance. The waw is said to be extra (zāʾida). It was said: it is for coordination (ʿaṭf) upon an elided cause, meaning: "so that God may decree His command, and that He may test." Ibn Baḥr said: it is coordinated upon ﴿لِيَبْتَلِيَكُمْ﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 152]; when the speech was lengthy, He repeated it and then coordinated upon it with "li-yumaḥḥiṣa." It was said: the lām is attached to a later verb, the supposed meaning being: "and that He may test and purge, the doing of these events that occurred." The object of the testing is what the breasts contain, which is the hearts, as He said: ﴿ولَكِنْ تَعْمى القُلُوبُ الَّتِي في الصُّدُورِ﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 46]. The object of purging, which is clarifying and purifying, is what the hearts contain of intentions and beliefs.

﴿واللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِذاتِ الصُّدُورِ﴾: The explanation of this kind of clause has already been given. It comes after His saying "and that He may purge what is in your hearts," with the meaning that He knows what the breasts contain and what they conceal of beliefs, so He purges from them what He wishes to purge.

﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met, Satan only caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned.﴾ ʿUmar delivered a Friday sermon and recited Surat Al ʿImran, and it pleased him to recite it when he preached. When he reached this verse, he said: "On the day of Uhud we were defeated. I fled until I climbed the mountain. I saw myself scrambling like a mountain goat, while the people were saying, 'Muhammad has been killed.' I said, 'I will not find anyone saying, "Muhammad has been killed" except that I will kill him.' Then we gathered on the mountain, and this whole verse was revealed." ʿIkrimah said: "It was revealed concerning those among the believers who fled in great flight, among them Rafiʿ ibn al-Muʿallā, Abu Hudhayfah ibn ʿUtbah, and another man."

*Alladhina tawallaw* (those who turned away): this refers to everyone who turned their backs to the polytheists on the day of Uhud. This is the view of ʿUmar, Qatadah and al-Rabiʿ. Or it refers to everyone who was near Medina at the time of the defeat, the view of al-Suddi. Or it refers to specific men, the view of Ibn Ishaq. Among them were ʿUtbah ibn ʿUthman al-Zuraqi, his brother Saʿd, and others. They reached al-Jalʿab, a mountain on the outskirts of Medina near al-Aʿwas, and stayed there three days. Then they returned to the Messenger of God ﷺ, who said to them: "You have gone a wide way in it." On that day, only thirteen men remained with the Messenger of God ﷺ: Abu Bakr, ʿAli, Talhah, Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, and the rest of them were from the Ansar, among them Abu Talhah. The apparent sense of *tawallaw* indicates the general act of turning away on the day of the encounter, whether one fled to Medina or climbed the mountain.

*Al-jamʿ* (the two hosts) is an *ism al-jamʿ* (collective noun). The grammarians stated that a collective noun is not made dual, but here it is used with the intended meaning of the group-sense of the collective noun, indeed of some specifics of it, that is, the group of believers and the group of polytheists, and therefore its dual form is valid. A parallel to this is the poet's words:

*Each of the two companions of every saddle, even if they grasp the spear, their two tribes are brothers.*

Here he made *qawm* (people) dual, because he intended the sense of tribe.

*Istazalla* here is form X (*istafʿala*) meaning seeking, i.e., he sought from them the slip and invited them to it, because that is what his whispering and intimidation require. This is what they said. However, seeking a thing and inviting it does not necessarily mean it occurred. The better view is that *istafʿala* here has the meaning of *afʿala* (form IV), so the meaning is: "Satan caused them to slip," which indicates that the slip occurred. Then *istazalla* and *azalla* have one meaning, like *istabāna* and *abāna*, and *istaballa* and *aballa*, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Then Satan caused them both to slip from it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36] according to one of its interpretations. Satan's causing them to slip was prior to the time of turning away, meaning that they had obeyed Satan and committed sins before, which prevented them from victory, so they fled. It was also said: the slip is their turning away on that day. That is, "Satan only caused them to slip into turning away because of some sins that had previously been recorded against them, since sin leads to sin, and this is similar to *bi-mā ʿaṣaw* (because of what they disobeyed)." In these two views, *some of what they earned* is their abandonment of the position where the Messenger of God ﷺ had commanded them to remain steadfast, which led them to defeat. But this does not appear to be correct, because the archers who abandoned the position were fewer than forty, so it would be a case of referring to the whole by a part. Al-Mahdawi said: "*Some of what they earned*" is their love of booty and their greed for life. Al-Zajjaj and others held that the meaning is that Satan reminded them of previous sins, so they disliked dying before repenting of them and giving them up, so they delayed jihad until they could set their affairs right and fight in a state pleasing to God. This view does not appear to be correct either, because they were able to repent before the fighting and during the fighting, and "the one who repents of a sin is like one who has no sin." The apparent meaning of *tawallī* is turning away in retreat and fleeing from the battle, so it does not include those who climbed the mountain, because they were withdrawing toward a position in which the Messenger of God ﷺ and those who remained with him had gathered. The apparent sense of this turning away is that it was an act of disobedience, as indicated by the mention of Satan causing them to slip and God's pardon of them. As for those who hold that this turning away was not disobedience, because they intended to seek refuge in Medina and to cut off the enemy's hope of them when they heard that Muhammad had been killed, or because they did not hear the Prophet's ﷺ call, "Come to me, servants of God!" due to the terror they were in, or because they were seven hundred while the enemy was three thousand, and in such a case fleeing is permissible, or because they thought the Messenger had not withdrawn to the mountain and that he was making Medina his back, then this view contradicts the apparent sense, and these circumstances are such that fleeing is permissible in them. But God, exalted is He, mentioned Satan causing them to slip and His pardon of them, and that would not apply to what is permissible to do. The phrase *bi-baʿḍi mā kasabū* (because of some of what they earned) came, and not *bi-mā kasabū* (because of what they earned), because He, exalted is He, pardons much, as He said, exalted is He: ﴿and He pardons much﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 15]. So the slipping was caused by some sins that He did not pardon, and these were made the cause of the slipping. Had they been pardoned, they would not have been the cause of the slipping.

﴿And God has certainly pardoned them.﴾ The majority hold that the meaning of pardon here is the removal of consequences in this world and the Hereafter. ʿUthman interpreted it in this way in a discussion between him and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf. ʿAbd al-Rahman said to him: "You had turned away with those who turned away on the day of the gathering," meaning the day of Uhud. ʿUthman said to him: "God said: '﴿And God has certainly pardoned them﴾,' so I was among those whom God pardoned." Likewise Ibn ʿUmar, with the Iraqi man, when he adjured him by the sanctity of this House: "Do you know that ʿUthman fled on the day of Uhud?" He replied that he testifies that God had pardoned him.

Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning of "God pardoned them" is that He did not punish them. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: fleeing from the battle line is one of the major sins by consensus, as far as I know, and the Messenger of God ﷺ counted it among the destructive sins, along with associating partners with God, killing a soul, and others. End of quotation. Since the view of al-Zamakhshari is that pardon and forgiveness of a sin occur only for one who repents, and that if a sin is not repented of, pardon does not accompany it, he slipped his view into this sentence and said: "And God has certainly pardoned them because of their repentance and their apology." End of quotation.

﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾ That is, He is Forgiver of sins and Forbearing, who does not hasten punishment. This sentence came as a justification for His, exalted is He, pardon of those who turned away on the day of Uhud, because God, exalted is He, has vast forgiveness and vast forbearance.

[p. 92] When the statement of the hypocrites was mentioned, "If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here," and God reported about them that they "said to their brethren, while they stayed behind, 'Had they obeyed us, they would not have been killed'" [Al 'Imran: 168], and this was a false statement and a corrupt belief, God forbade the believers from being like them in this corrupt statement and evil belief. This is the belief that whoever travels for trade or the like and dies, or fights and is killed, would have lived and not died at that time if he had stayed in his house, the time at which he exposed himself to travel or to fighting. This is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah in affirming the "two terms" (al-ajalayn, the two lifespans, one of the predetermined term and one of the term of the cause). As for the unbelievers who said this, it was said: it refers to all of them, meaning that this belief was held by all of them; this was said by Ibn Ishaq and others. Or it refers to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions, from whom this statement was heard; this was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi and others. Or it refers to him, Mu'attib, Jadd ibn Qays and their companions.

The lam in "li-ikhwanihim" is the lam of causation (lam al-sabab), meaning "on account of their brethren," and it is not the lam of reporting (lam al-tabligh), as in "I said to you." The brotherhood here is brotherhood of lineage, since the dead at Uhud were from the Ansar, most of them from the Khazraj, and only four, or it is said five, of the Muhajirun were killed. The speakers would then be hypocrites of the Ansar, gathered by a near or distant father. Or it is brotherhood of creed and affection, as in His saying: "and by His favour you became brothers" [Al 'Imran: 103], and as the poet said:

"We pardoned the Banu Dhuhl, and we said, 'The people are brothers.'"

Striking in the land means going far away in it and departing for a person's need. al-Suddi said: striking here means travel for trade. Ibn Ishaq said: travel in acts of obedience.

"Idha" is a temporal adverb referring to the future, and "qalu" is in the past tense, so it cannot govern it. Some therefore stripped it of the sense of the future and made it refer to unspecified time, meaning "when," so that "qalu" governs it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "idha" has entered, and it is a particle of the future, because "alladhina" is a term of ambiguity that includes those who spoke in the past and those who speak in the future, and because this event can be imagined in future time. al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, how is 'idha darabu fi al-ard' said together with 'qalu'?" I answer: it is the narration of a past situation, like your saying, "When you strike in the land." End of his words. It is possible to keep "idha" in its established sense of the future, with the governing element being a omitted future-referring noun phrase, and there must be an omitted noun governing it; at most we estimate it as a future noun, so that it governs the future temporal adverb. But the pronoun in His saying "law kanu" then refers to "ikhwanihim" verbally and to others in meaning, like His saying: "Nor is any man given a long life, nor is any of his life shortened" [Fatir: 11], and the Arab saying, "I have a dirham and its half," and the poet's saying:

"She said, 'Would that this dove were for us, to our dove, and its half is lost.'"

The meaning: of another man who was given a long life, and half of another dirham, and half of another dove. The pronoun returned to dirham and dove verbally, not in meaning. Likewise the pronoun in "law kanu" refers to "ikhwanihim" verbally. The meaning: "had our other brethren been..." The meaning of the verse then is: they said, out of fear for the destruction of their brethren, when they struck in the land or were raiding: "Had our other brethren, those whose death and killing came before, been with us, meaning residing and not travelling, they would not have died or been killed." This statement would be a discouragement to their remaining brethren from striking in the land and from raiding, and a suggestion to them that they would suffer what their other brethren suffered, whose death and killing came from striking in the land and raiding. In that case the governing element of "idha" is "halak" (destruction), a verbal noun that is resolved into "an" plus the present tense, meaning: lest their remaining brethren be destroyed when they strike in the land or go raiding. This is more eloquent in meaning, since they presented the living with residence, so that they would not suffer what befell those who died or were killed. They said: it is also possible that "waqalu" means "wa-yaqulun" (and they say), and it governs "idha," and it is possible that "idha" means "idh" (when), so that "waqalu" remains in the past. In that case there is an omission in the sentence, estimated as: "When they struck in the land and died, or were raiding and were killed." I know no one more ignorant than he who claims that were it not for striking in the land and raiding and abandoning sitting in the homeland, the traveller and the warrior would not have died. How far is the intellect of these people from the intellect of Abu Dhu'ayb, in his pre-Islamic ignorance, when he says:

"They say to me, 'Had he been in the sand, Nushayba would not have died, and al-Turraq's report lies.'"

"And had I entrusted him to the sun, the causes of death would have climbed up to him, its eye and its messenger."

Al-Razi said: He mentioned raiding after striking, because some raiding is not striking, since striking means going far away, while holy struggle may be at a short distance; therefore he singled out raiding from striking. End of his words. He means that between them there is a general and specific relation, so they are distinct, and it is correct to single it out, since it is not included under the other in any respect. It was also said: raiding is not understood from striking, and it was mentioned first because of its frequency, as God said: "And others strike in the land seeking of God's bounty, and others fight in God's way" [al-Muzzammil: 20].

Al-Jumhur read "ghuzza" with a doubled zay. al-Hasan and al-Zuhri read it with a single zay. This is explained as the omission of one of the two doubled letters for lightness, or as the omission of the ta' marbuta, and the meaning is "ghuzat" (raiders). One who explained it as the omission of the ta' said it is Ibn 'Atiyyah, who said: this omission is frequent in their speech, and from it is the poet's saying, praising al-Kisa'i:

"Blame refused the character of al-Kisa'i, and glory inclined to him, the character of the fathers of the precedents."

He means "al-ubuwwa," the plural of "ab" (father), just as "al-umumah" is the plural of "amm" (paternal uncle), and "al-bunuwwa" is the plural of "ibn" (son). They also said "ibn" and "bunuw." End of his words. His saying "this omission is frequent in their speech" is not as he mentioned. Rather, there is nothing like "rami" and "rama," nor "hami" and "hama," meaning "ruma" and "huma." If he meant that omitting the ta' is frequent in their speech in general, then the claim is only that the omission occurs in its verbal form, and we do not say that omitting it, meaning the ta', is frequent in their speech, because that would suggest that the plural pattern was built upon it and then frequently dropped, which is not so. Rather the plural came in the pattern "fu'ul," like "amm" and "umum," and "fahl" and "fuhul," and then the ta' was added to emphasize the sense of plurality. So we do not say of "umum" that the ta' was frequently dropped from it, because the plural was not built upon it. This differs from "qudat" and "rumat," where the plural was built upon it. The grammarians were compelled to include it in what should not include it, saying that it is for the emphasis of plurality, because they saw a superfluous element with no meaning and said that it came for the sense of emphasis, like superfluous elements whose meaning is understood only as emphasis. As for the verse, the grammarians say that it is among the irregular plurals that were not altered, so it is said "aba," as they said "asa" for "asa" (staff). It is in their view a plural on the pattern "fu'ul," and its origin is not "ubuwa." "Ibn" is not pluralized as "bunuwwa," for these are two verbal nouns. The clause of "law" and its answer is the object of the verb of saying, so it is in the accusative position as an object. It came in the order that follows "idha," placing the negation of death before the negation of killing, just as it placed striking before raiding. The pronoun in "law kanu" refers to the dead of Uhud; this was said by the majority. Or it refers to the expedition whose members were killed at Bi'r Ma'unah; this was said by Bakr ibn Sahl al-Dimyati. Al-Jumhur read "wa-ma qutilu" with a light ta'. al-Hasan read it with a doubled ta', for multiplicity in places, not in relation to a single place, since multiplicity cannot be meant in a single place.

"Li-yaj'ala Allahu dhalika hasratan fi qulubihim" (That God may make that a grief in their hearts). They differed about this lam. It was said: it is the lam of purpose (lam kay). It was said: it is the lam of result (lam al-sayrurah). If it is the lam of purpose, then to what does it attach? And to what does "dhalika" refer? Some held that it attaches to an omitted element indicated by the meaning and context of the speech. The estimate: "God caused that," meaning the saying and the belief, to be in their hearts, so that He might make it a grief upon them. The omitted element is needed because the lam cannot attach as the lam of purpose; one would say: they did not say that statement so that God would make that a grief in their hearts, so this cannot be a motive for their saying; they only said it to discourage the believers from holy struggle. Nor can it attach to the prohibition, "do not be like those who disbelieved," because God making that a grief in their hearts is not a cause for God's prohibition of the believers from resembling the unbelievers.

al-Zamakhshari said: He also raised an objection to what "li-yaja'a" attaches to, saying: "Or 'la yakunu' means: do not be like them in uttering that saying and believing in it, so that God may make it a grief in their hearts specifically, and may guard your hearts from it." End of his words. This is the words of a shaykh with no verification, because making the grief a cause of the prohibition is not so, as we said. It is rather a cause for the obtaining of obedience to the prohibition, which is the absence of resemblance. The obtaining of that absence and difference in what they say and believe results in what enrages and distresses them, since you did not agree with them in what they said and believed. So do not strike in the land and do not raid. Al-Zamakhshari was confused between seeking the absence of resemblance as a cause of the absence itself, and understanding this is obscure and subtle. Ibn 'Isa and others said: the lam is attached to "kawn" (being), meaning: "Do not be like these, so that God may make that a grief in their hearts and not in yours." End of his words. From this al-Zamakhshari took his words. But Ibn 'Isa specified what the lam attaches to, and al-Zamakhshari did not. We have already shown the corruption of this view.

If it is the lam of result and consequence, then it attaches to "qalu," and the meaning is: they did not say it in order to make a grief, but they said that for a reason, and so its outcome came to be grief and regret. They compared it to His saying: "Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he might become for them an enemy and a sorrow" [al-Qasas: 8], though they did not pick him up for that, but his affair ended in that. Most of our companions do not affirm this meaning for the lam, I mean that the lam signifies result and outcome, and they attribute this view to al-Akhfash. As for "bi-dhalika" (with that), al-Zajjaj said: it refers to the supposition, namely that if they supposed that had they not attended they would not have been killed, their grief over those among them who were killed would be greater. al-Zamakhshari said, in substance, that it refers to the uttering and believing of the saying. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "bi-dhalika" refers to this belief they hold, that God made it a grief, since one who is certain that every death and killing is by a predetermined term finds the coolness of despair and submission to God in his heart, while one who believes that his close one would not have died had he stayed at home grieves and laments. End of his words. These statements agree on what "that" refers to. It was also said: "that" refers to God's prohibition against being like the unbelievers in this belief, because when they see that God has marked them with a belief and commanded the opposite of their beliefs, that would be a grief in their hearts. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: In my view it is also possible that the reference is to the prohibition and the cessation together, so consider it. End of his words.

These are all sayings that contradict the apparent meaning. What the apparent meaning of the verse requires is that the reference is to the verbal noun (maṣdar) understood from "qālū" (they said), and that the lam is of result (lam al-ṣayrūrah), so the meaning is: they uttered this statement intending to discourage (tathbīṭ) from jihad and to be distant in the land (al-ibʿād fī al-arḍ), whether they believed its truth or did not believe it, since many of the disbelievers say that there is one fixed term (ajal) [for all]. So this intention failed, and God made that saying a regret (ḥasrah) in their hearts, meaning a grief over what had escaped them, since they did not attain their aim of discouraging [the believers] from jihad. The apparent sense of "making" the regret and its occurrence is that it happens in this world, namely the grief that befalls them over what they missed of attaining their aim. It has been said: the making takes place on the Day of Resurrection, due to the disgrace and remorse they are in, and due to what the Muslims enjoy of bliss and honour. The making is attributed to God because He is the one who places grief and regret in their hearts as a punishment for them for this corrupt saying.

﴿Wa-llāhu yuḥyī wa-yumītu﴾ [And God gives life and causes death]: a refutation of them in that corrupt statement. Rather, that is by His decisive decree, and the command is in His hand: He may give life to the traveler and the warrior, and cause death to the one who stays home and the one who sits. Khālid ibn al-Walīd said at his death: "There is not a hand's breadth on me without a blow or a thrust in it, and here I am dying as a camel dies. So may the eyes of cowards never sleep." It has also been said: this clause is connected to His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who disbelieved and said﴾, meaning: do not say the like of their saying, for God is the Giver of life; whoever He decrees life for will not be killed in jihad, and the Causer of death; whoever He decrees death for will not remain even if he does not fight. This was said by al-Rāzī, who also said: the purpose of it is to nullify their doubt, meaning there is no effect of anything else on life and death, because His decree does not change. This does not necessarily apply to actions, because He may do what He wills. End of quote. This distinction between death and life and the rest of actions was refuted, because the rest of actions are likewise settled, like death and life: whatever is decreed to occur of them must occur, and whatever is not decreed is impossible to occur, so there is then no distinction.

﴿Wa-llāhu bimā taʿmalūna baṣīr﴾ [And God is Seeing of what you do]: al-Rāghib said: He attached this to sight (baṣar) and not to hearing (samʿ), even though what proceeded from them was a heard statement and not a seen act, because that statement from the disbeliever was intended toward an action they were attempting, so He singled out sight for it, like your saying to one who says something while intending an act he is trying to accomplish: "I see what you are doing." Ibn Kathīr and the two brothers (al-Akhawān) read "bimā yaʿmalūna" with the yāʾ, in the third person (al-ghaybah), and it is a threat to the hypocrites. The rest read it with the tāʾ, addressing the believers, as in His saying: "do not be," so it is an emphasis of the prohibition, a threat to whoever opposes it, and a promise to whoever complies.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 157–158:

﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah or you die, surely forgiveness from Allah and mercy are better than what they amass.﴾ Before this, the disbelievers' claim was refuted, that whoever dies or is killed while travelling or on a military expedition would not have died or been killed had he stayed at home. He forbade the believers from saying the like of this statement, because it is a cause of holding back from the expedition. In this sentence, he informed them that if what they fear of being killed in the way of Allah or dying therein comes to pass, then what they obtain of the forgiveness of Allah and His mercy because of that is better than what they amass of the fleeting goods and benefits of this world, had they not perished by killing or death. He emphasised this with an oath, because the lam in "la-in" (la-'in, the lam of oath preceding the conditional) is the lam that prepares for the oath, and the answer of the oath is "lamaghfiratun" (surely forgiveness). It came indefinite (nakirah) to indicate that the least part of forgiveness and mercy is better than the world, and that it is sufficient for the believer's success. Beginning with it was permitted (jawaza al-ibtida' bihi) because it is qualified by his saying "min Allah" (from Allah), and it is coordinated with an indefinite noun (nakirah) after it, and what justifies beginning with indefinites (musawwigh al-ibtida' bi-ha) is that it is coordinated with something that itself justifies beginning. Or [it is justified by] its being implicitly qualified, since the estimate is: "and mercy from Him." There is another omitted qualifier which must be assumed, and its estimate is: "and mercy for you." "Khayr" (better) here is on its original basis as a superlative (af'al tafdil), as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "better than the earth filled with red gold." The nominative case of "khayr" is because it is the predicate of "lamaghfiratun."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The verse may admit that his saying "lamaghfiratun" refers to being killed or dying in the way of Allah, so He named that forgiveness and mercy, since both are joined to it. The estimate for this would be: "forgiveness and mercy." "Maghfiratun" is nominative as the predicate of an assumed inchoative. And his saying "khayr" is a qualifier, not the predicate of an inchoative. End of his words. This is contrary to the apparent meaning. The answer of the conditional, which is "in qutiltum" (if you are killed), is omitted, because the answer of the oath indicates it. As for al-Zamakhshari's saying: "it took the place of the answer of the conditional" — if he means that it is omitted because it is indicated by it, then it is correct; and if he means that it needs no estimate, then it is not correct. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that forgiveness and mercy are made for whoever is granted one of these two: being killed in the way of Allah, or dying therein.

Al-Razi said: "lamaghfiratun min Allah" refers to his worship out of fear of His punishment, and "rahmatun" refers to his worship seeking His reward. End of his words. It is not the apparent meaning. He put killing first here because it is the beginning of information, so he put first the more noble and more important in obtaining forgiveness and mercy, since being killed in the way of Allah is greater in reward than dying in His way.

Al-Raghib said: These two verses contain a binding argument which operates in the manner of two conditional syllogisms that require eagerness for being killed in the way of Allah. Its representation: "If you are killed in the way of Allah or you die, forgiveness and mercy are obtained for you, and they are better than what you amass. Therefore, death and killing in the way of Allah are better than what you amass. And if you die or are killed, the gathering (to Allah) is certainly obtained by you. And if death and killing are unavoidable, and so is the gathering, then the result is that the killing and death which entail forgiveness and mercy are better than the killing and death which do not entail them." End of his words.

The readers Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far (al-Ibnan wa al-Abawan) read "mutum" with a damma on the mim throughout the Qur'an, and Hafs in these two places: "aw mutum" and "wa-la'in mutum." The rest read it with a kasra. The damma is more analogical and more well-known. The kasra is commonly used, and it is anomalous in analogy; al-Mazini made it from fa'ala yaf'alu, like duma tadumu and fadhdhalta tufadhdhilu, and likewise Abu 'Ali, so both judged it anomalous. Others have transmitted two dialects for it: the first is fa'ala yaf'ulu, so one says "mata yamutu"; the second is fa'ala yaf'alu, like "mata yamatu," whose origin is "mawata," so according to this it is not anomalous, since it is like "khafa yakhafu," whose origin is "mawata yamutu." So whoever reads with the kasra does so according to this dialect, and there is no anomaly in it. It is the dialect of the Hijaz, who say "mutum" from "mata yamatu," as the poet said:

"Live, and do not be wary that you will die"

And the lower Mudar say "mutum" with a damma on the mim from "mata yamutu"; the Kufans transmitted this.

The majority read "tajma'un" with the ta' in accordance with the address in His saying "wa-la'in qutiltum." Some people, among them Hafs from 'Asim, read it with the ya', meaning: what the disbelieving hypocrites and others amass.

﴿And if you die or are killed, surely to Allah you will be gathered.﴾ This is a general address to the believer and the disbeliever. In it He informed that the return of all is to Him, so He recompenses each for his deed, so said some of them. It seems that when he saw that death and killing were stated without being restricted by mention of the way of Allah, as they were restricted in the verse, he understood that this is general. The apparent meaning is that it is an address to the believers, like the preceding address; for this reason al-Zamakhshari estimated it: "surely to the Merciful, the Wide in Mercy, the Giver of Death, the Mighty in Reward you will be gathered." He said: The occurrence of the name of Allah in this position, with its being placed first and the lam entering on the particle connected to it, both are equal, and it is not obscure. End of his words. By this he points to his doctrine that placing first indicates restriction, so the meaning for him is: "then to Allah alone, not other than Him, you will be gathered." It does not, according to us, indicate this by its linguistic form; rather, placing first indicates attention to a thing and concern with mentioning it, as Sibawayh said. What adds beauty here is that the postponement of the verb here is a closing rhyme (fasila), so if the prepositional phrase were postponed this purpose would be lost. The verse includes belittling the matter of this world and eagerness for martyrdom, and that the destiny of the whole world is to Allah; so meeting Allah while in martyrdom is more excellent for a person, so that he secures its reward and finds it at the time of gathering. He placed death first before killing here, because it is a verse of admonition regarding the Hereafter and the gathering, and of renunciation of this world and its life, and death in it is absolute, not restricted by anything. So either the address is specific to those previously addressed, or it is general and those people are included in it; so it was placed first because of its generality, and also because death is more prevalent among people than killing. So these are three positions. "Ma matu wa-ma qutilu" (Aal 'Imran 3:156), where he placed death before killing for the sake of its fit with what precedes it, his saying "idha darabu fi al-ardi aw kanu ghuzzan" (Aal 'Imran 3:156). Killing was placed before death afterwards, because it is a place of exhortation to jihad, so he placed first the more important and more noble. He placed death first here because it is more prevalent, and the verb that is the answer of the omitted oath was not emphasised, because it is separated between the lam to which the oath is attached and it by the prepositional phrase. Had it been postponed it would have been "la-tuhsharunna ilayhi," like His saying "liyaqulunna ma yahbisuhu." Whether the separation is by a complement of the verb, as here, or by "sawfa," like His saying "fa-lasawfa ta'lamun" (al-Shu'ara' 26:49), or by "qad," as the poet's saying:

"You have lied, indeed I hunt over a man's wife, and I forbid my wife that the idle one should be with her"

Abu 'Ali said: The original is the entry of the nun, to distinguish between the lam of oath and the lam of inchoative; and the lam of inchoative does not enter on complements, so by the entry of the lam of oath on a complement the separation occurred, so the nun was not needed. And by its entry on "sawfa" the distinction occurred, so the nun was not needed; because the lam of inchoative does not enter on the verb except when it is present, but when it is future it does not.

He forbade the believers from saying the like of this statement, because it is a cause of holding back from the expedition. In this sentence, he informed them that if what they fear of being killed in the way of Allah or dying therein comes to pass, then what they obtain of the forgiveness of Allah and His mercy because of that is better than what they amass of the fleeting goods and benefits of this world, had they not perished by killing or death. He emphasised this with an oath, because the lam in "la-in" (la-'in, the lam of oath preceding the conditional) is the lam that prepares for the oath, and the answer of the oath is "lamaghfiratun" (surely forgiveness). It came indefinite (nakirah) to indicate that the least part of forgiveness and mercy is better than the world, and that it is sufficient for the believer's success. Beginning with it was permitted (jawaza al-ibtida' bihi) because it is qualified by his saying "min Allah" (from Allah), and it is coordinated with an indefinite noun (nakirah) after it, and what justifies beginning with indefinites (musawwigh al-ibtida' bi-ha) is that it is coordinated with something that itself justifies beginning. Or [it is justified by] its being implicitly qualified, since the estimate is: "and mercy from Him." There is another omitted qualifier which must be assumed, and its estimate is: "and mercy for you." "Khayr" (better) here is on its original basis as a superlative (af'al tafdil), as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "better than the earth filled with red gold." The nominative case of "khayr" is because it is the predicate of "lamaghfiratun."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 159:

﴿So by a mercy from Allah you were gentle with them﴾. The object of the mercy (muta'allaq al-rahmah) is "the believers." The meaning is: "So by a mercy from Allah upon them, you were gentle with them," so that the mercy is one by which He bestowed favour upon them. That is, your character became gentle and your side was lowered towards them after they had opposed your command and disobeyed you in this recitation, and that was by the mercy of Allah towards them. It was also said: the object of the mercy is the one addressed, i.e., by Allah's mercy towards you He made you gentle of side and easy of disposition, so you showed them mercy and were gentle with them, and did not take them to account for disobedience, fleeing, and leaving you alone to face the enemies; and this would be a favour upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It is also possible that the object of the mercy is the Prophet ﷺ, in that He made him upon a great character, and sent him to perfect the noble qualities of character, and [made him gentle] towards the believers by making him gentle towards them.

The "ma" here is a superfluous particle for emphasis (za'idah li-l-ta'kid), and its insertion between the preposition ba' and 'an, min and the kaf, and between its genitives, is a known feature of the language, established in the science of Arabic grammar. Some people held that it is an indefinite complete noun (nakirah tammah), and "rahmah" is a substitute (badal) from it, as if it were said: "by something left vague, then substituted for clarification, [namely] 'mercy'." It seems that the one who says this flees from the description of it as superfluous. It was also said: "ma" here is interrogative (istifhamiyyah). Al-Razi said: The scholars who verify matters said: the entry of a word of no defined function (muhmal al-wad') into the speech of the Most Wise of the Wise is not permissible. Here it is permissible for "ma" to be an interrogative of wonder (istifham li-l-ta'ajjub), its estimate being: "By what kind of mercy from Allah you were gentle with them," because their offence was great, (p-98) then he did not at all show any harshness in speech or roughness in words; they knew that this could not come about except by a Lordly support before that. End of his words. What the scholars who verify matters said is correct, but the superfluity of "ma" for emphasis is not denied in its places by anyone who has the least connection with Arabic, let alone one who undertakes the exegesis of the speech of Allah, and what is in this place is not something anyone would imagine to be without function, so there is no need to interpret it as an interrogative of wonder. Moreover, its estimate "by what kind of mercy" is evidence that he made "ma" an annexing noun (mudafah) to "rahmah," and what he went to is an error in two respects: First, the interrogative "ma" is not annexed, nor are interrogative nouns other than "ayy" annexed, without dispute, and "kam" according to the view of Abu Ishaq. Second, if it is not correct as an annexation, then its i'rab is as a substitute, and if it is a substitute for an interrogative noun, then the interrogative hamzah must be repeated in the substitute. This man attended to the meaning and did not heed what is established in the science of grammar regarding the rulings of words; and what would have spared him this confusion, this climbing to what he does not do well, and this leaping upon it, is al-Zajjaj's statement about this "ma": that it is a connecting particle (silah) containing the meaning of emphasis, by the consensus of the grammarians.

﴿And had you been harsh, hard-hearted, they would have dispersed from around you﴾: Allah the Exalted explained that the fruit of gentleness is love and gathering around him. Its opposite, from coarseness and roughness, leads to dispersal. The meaning: had I rebuked them in person for what proceeded from them of opposition and fleeing, they would have scattered from around you out of awe and shame of you, and that would have been a cause for the dispersal of the word of Islam and the weakening of its foundation, and an encouragement to the enemy; so gentleness and kindness are what did not lead to neglecting any right of the rights of Allah the Exalted. Allah the Exalted said concerning the disbelievers: ﴿And be harsh upon them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73], and in describing him in the revealed books that he is not coarse nor harsh, nor loud in the markets. The two descriptions were said to have one meaning, so they were combined for emphasis. It was also said: fazz (fazzah) is coarseness in speech and deed. Hardness of heart (ghilazh al-qalb) is an expression for his being created solid, not softening and not being affected, and from hardness arises coarseness; what is apparent to the senses is mentioned before what is hidden, and it is known only by the manifestation of its effect.

﴿So pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the matter﴾: Allah the Exalted commanded him to pardon them, in what was specifically his own right against them, and to seek forgiveness for them in what is specifically the right of Allah the Exalted, and to consult them. In this there are benefits: consoling their hearts; elevating their rank by his sincere heart towards them, since he qualified them for consultation and made them the elite after what proceeded from them; legislating consultation for those after him; seeking support in their opinion in matters on which no revelation has descended, for they may have in worldly affairs what benefits him; testing their minds so that he places them in their proper stations; and their striving in what contains the way of righteousness. It follows the methods and customs of the Arabs in consulting in affairs, and when he did not consult anyone of them, something would arise in his soul; for this reason it weighed heavily upon ʿAli and the People of the House that he had been unilateral regarding consultation in the caliphate of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with them all. As to what he was commanded to consult them about: it was said: in matters of war and worldly affairs. It was also said: in religion and worldly affairs where no text has come; for this reason he consulted about the captives of Badr.

The apparent sense of these commands implies that he was commanded to do these things, and they do not indicate a chronological sequence. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: he was commanded with eloquent gradation (tadrij baligh): he was commanded to pardon them in what concerns him (p-99), so when they reached this rank, he was commanded to seek forgiveness for what concerns Allah; when they reached this rank, they became fit for consultation in affairs. End of his words. There is some abridgement in it, and this gradation does not appear from the wording, but this is the wisdom of placing these commands in this order relative to one another. He first commanded pardon for them, since his pardon of them removes his right and is evidence of his contentment with them and his not holding them to account. When his right fell away through his pardon, he asked Allah's forgiveness for them, so that his forgiveness and Allah's forgiveness of them would be complete, and they would obtain his contentment and the contentment of Allah the Exalted. When the obligations were removed from them on both sides, he consulted them, as a declaration that they are worthy of sincere love and advising friendship, since a person does not consult anyone except one whom he believes to have affection, intellect and experience. The apparent meaning of his saying "so pardon them" is a command to him to pardon. It was said: its meaning is "ask me to pardon them so that I may pardon them," and the one pardoned and the one asked to seek forgiveness on their behalf are the ones concerned. It was said: [the offence was] their fleeing on the day of Uhud, their not answering him, and the archers leaving their positions. It was said: what they showed of their slips and what their tongues uttered of the lapses they did not hold as belief, such as their calling out from behind the chambers. And the saying of some of them: "Ibn 'ammatik" (the son of your paternal aunt), and his pulling of his cloak until it affected his neck, and other things that happened from them by way of slip. Among the strange reports and sayings, and the weak ones from which the Qur'an is to be exonerated, is the saying of some: that His saying, the Exalted, "﴿and consult them in the matter﴾" is inverted (maqlub), and the meaning is: "and let them consult you in the matter." The exegetes mentioned here a number of what has come concerning consultation from verses, hadiths and reports. Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned: consultation is among the foundations of the Shari'ah and firm rulings, and whoever does not consult the people of knowledge and religion, his removal is obligatory; this is something on which there is no disagreement. The one consulted in religion must be a scholar of religion, and this is rarely found except in a sound-minded person. Al-Hasan said: the religion of a man is not complete if his intellect is not complete; and in worldly matters, a sound-minded, experienced man is suitable for the one who seeks counsel. End of Ibn 'Atiyyah's words, and there is some abridgement in it. The reading of the majority: "﴿in the matter﴾ [Al 'Imran: 152]," and it is not general, since one does not consult in what is lawful and unlawful. "Al-amr" is a noun of genus which applies to the whole and to a part. Ibn 'Abbas read: "in some of the matter."

﴿So when you have resolved, then put your trust in Allah﴾: that is, when you have fixed your heart upon a matter after consultation, then make your reliance in it upon Allah the Exalted, for He is the one who knows what is most right for you and most rightly guided for your affair, which he who advised you does not know. In this verse is evidence for consultation, the testing and refining of opinion, and reflection upon it, and that this is required by the Shari'ah, unlike what some of the Arabs did of abandoning consultation and acting unilaterally on their opinion without thought for the outcome, as one said:

Whenever he resolves, he casts his resolve before his eyes and turns aside from remembering the consequences,

And he does not consult anyone about his opinion but himself, and is not pleased except with a companion who is the sword's edge.

The majority read "ʿazamta" in the second person, as the preceding. ʿIkrimah, Jabir ibn Zayd, Abu Nahik and Jaʿfar al-Sadiq read "ʿazamtu" with a damma on the ta', as a pronoun for Allah the Exalted, and the meaning is: "when I have resolved for you upon something," i.e., I guided you to it and made you aim at it; and His saying "upon Allah" is an instance of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), since if it had followed the pattern of the damma on the ta', it would have been "then rely upon Me." A parallel for attributing resolve to Allah by way of metaphor is Umm Salamah's saying: "then Allah resolved."

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who rely upon Him﴾: this urges reliance upon Allah, since He informed that He loves whoever relies upon Him, and a person strives in what brings him the love of Allah the Exalted.

These verses contain varieties of rhetoric (bayan) and figures of speech (badi'), and of ambiguity (ibham) in: "﴿and do not turn aside for anyone﴾ [Al 'Imran: 153]." Whoever said it refers to the Messenger left it vague out of reverence for his rank, and because stating it explicitly would diminish his standing. Paronomasia of identical type (tajnis mumathil) in: "﴿grief upon grief﴾ [Al 'Imran: 153]," "﴿then He sent down upon you after the grief﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]." Antithesis (tibaq) in: "yukhfuna" and "yubdun," and in: "fatakum" and "asabakum." Paronomasia of different type (tajnis mughayir) in: "tazunnun" and "zanna," and in: "fatawakkal" and "al-mutawakkilin." Some mentioned that in "fazzan" and "infaddu," but it is not of this kind, since the two roots differ. Explanation after ambiguity in: "what they do not show" — "they say." Discursive argument (ihtijaj nazari) in: "﴿If you had been in your houses﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]," and interpolation (i'tiraD) in: "﴿Say: indeed the affair is entirely Allah's﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]." Restriction (ikhtisas) in: "﴿with what is in the breasts﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]," and in: "﴿Allah is Seer of what you do﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156]," and in: "﴿Allah loves those who rely upon Him﴾." Allusion (ishara) in His saying: "﴿so that Allah may make that a regret﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156]." Metaphor (isti'arah) in: "﴿when they travel in the land﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156]," and in: "lintа" (you were gentle), and in: "﴿harsh of heart﴾." Repetition (takrir) in: "﴿whether they died or were killed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156]," and what follows them, and in: "upon Allah, indeed Allah." Insertion of a letter for emphasis in: "﴿So by what mercy﴾." Shift (iltifat) and omission (hadhf) in a number of places.

(p-101)

﴿If Allah helps you, none can overcome you; and if He forsakes you, who is there that can help you after Him?﴾ This is an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), since it moves from the third person (absence) to direct address. When He had commanded the Prophet to consult them and to put his trust in Him, He made clear that whatever victory or defeat occurs is subject to what He wills. Whenever Allah grants you victory, no one can overcome you. Whenever He forsakes you, there is no helper for you in whatever victory you achieved or whatever defeat befell you, as on the days of Badr and Uhud, because that is by His will. This is a consolation for them over the flight that had befallen them. Then He commanded them to rely upon Him, and attached the command to the believers, thereby pointing out the attribute that fits with reliance, which is faith (iman), because the believer affirms that Allah is the Doer who chooses, and that victory and defeat are in His hand. He also associated them with their Prophet in the requirement of reliance, which means attributing affairs to Allah Most High and entrusting them to Him.

Reliance upon Allah is one of the obligations of faith, but it is accompanied by exerting oneself in obedience, by utmost resolve and striving to the limit, and by taking the means of protection. Casting oneself down and neglecting what must be observed is not reliance. Rather, it is as he said: "Tie it down and rely upon Allah." A parallel to this verse is: ﴿Whatever mercy Allah opens to people, none can withhold it; and whatever He withholds, none can release after Him﴾ [Fatir: 2]. The pronoun in "min ba'dihi" ("after Him") refers to Allah Most High. It may be taken as an elided construction, meaning "after His forsaking," that is, after the one who is helped is forsaken. Or there may be no need to posit this elision, and the meaning would be: if you go beyond Him to another while He has forsaken you, then who is there whom you can turn to so that he helps you? It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the verbal noun implied by "﴿and if He forsakes you﴾", meaning "after the forsaking."

The answer to "﴿If Allah helps you﴾" came as a clear general negation, while the answer to "﴿and if He forsakes you﴾" contains a negation in the form of a question. This is a variation of speech for eloquence and for gentleness toward the believers, so that it is not stated plainly to them that they have no helper. Rather, this was presented in the form of a question, which asks about the helper, though the meaning is the negation of any helper. However, a distinction is maintained between the explicit and the implicit, so the believers were not placed in the same position as the disbelievers, concerning whom it was stated explicitly that they have no helper, as in His saying: ﴿We destroyed them, and they had no helper﴾ [Muhammad: 13].

The apparent sense of nasr (help) is support in meeting the enemy, aid in confronting him, and gaining control over him. Most exegetes took nasr to mean a decisive proof and ultimate outcome in the Hereafter. They said the meaning is: if you obtain help, do not regard the worldly accidents that occur in some circumstances as defeat; and if He forsakes you in that, do not regard the worldly subjugation that befalls you as help. Thus victory and defeat are judged by their final outcome. In His saying "﴿If Allah helps you﴾" there is an indication of encouragement to obey Allah, because He had earlier shown that whoever fears Allah, He helps him.

Al-Zamakhshari said, concerning His saying "and upon Allah": "So that the believers may single out their Lord for reliance and for entrusting their affairs to Him, He taught them that there is no helper besides Him; and because your faith requires this and demands it." The end of his statement. He derived the exclusivity from the fronting of the prepositional phrase, following his method that fronting the object implies restriction and exclusivity.

The majority read ﴿yakhdhulukum﴾ from khadhala. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read ﴿yakhdhulukum﴾ from akhdhala in the quadriliteral form, in which the hamza indicates making, i.e., "yaj'aluku" (He makes you).

﴿It is not for a Prophet to commit ghulul (embezzlement of spoils)﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah, and Ibn Jubayr said: a red woolen cloak was lost from the spoils on the day of Badr. Some of those with the Prophet ﷺ said: "Perhaps the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took it." So this verse was revealed. The one who said that was a believer who did not think it was a sin. It was also said that he was a hypocrite. It is narrated that the missing item was a sword. Al-Naqqash said: on the day of Uhud the archers said: "The spoils, the spoils, O people! We fear that the Prophet ﷺ will say: whoever takes something, it is his." When they mentioned this, he said: "Did you fear that we would embezzle?" So this verse was revealed. A similar report is narrated from al-Kalbi and Muqatil. Others have said other things. Among these, Ibn Ishaq said: it was revealed only to inform that the Prophet ﷺ did not conceal anything of what he was commanded to convey.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that it contains a ruling about the spoils in jihad, and embezzlement is among the sins for which the Fire is threatened, as occurred in the story of Mid'am. So He warned them against it. The discussion of the meaning of "﴿It is not for Zayd to do﴾" has already passed earlier.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, and ʿAsim read ﴿an yaghulla﴾ from ghalla, in the active voice. The meaning is that such a thing is not possible for him, because ghulul is an act of disobedience, and the Prophet ﷺ is protected from sins, so it is not possible for him to fall into any of them. This negation is an indication that one should not imagine such a thing concerning him, nor attribute any of it to him.

Ibn Masʿud and the rest of the seven read ﴿an yughalla﴾ with a dammah on the yaʾ and a fathah on the ghayn, in the passive voice. The majority said it is from ghalla, and the meaning is that no one has the right to betray him concerning the spoils. So it is a prohibition to people against embezzlement of the spoils. The Prophet ﷺ was singled out for mention, although it is forbidden for others as well, because disobedience in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ is more heinous, owing to the obligation to honor and revere him, just as disobedience in a sacred place or on a glorified day is more heinous. It was also said that it is from aghalla (in the quadriliteral form), and the meaning is that he is found to be a ghall (embezzler), as one says: "ahmada al-rajul" meaning he was found to be praiseworthy. ﴿And whoever embezzles will come on the Day of Resurrection with what he embezzled﴾. The apparent meaning of this is that he will come with the very thing he embezzled. This is reported in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim. In the hadith, he mentioned embezzlement and magnified it and magnified its matter, then said: "Let me not find any of you coming on the Day of Resurrection with a camel on his neck, which has a bellow, and he says: 'O Messenger of Allah, help me!' Similarly, in the hadith of Ibn al-Lutbiyyah: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, no one takes anything from it except that he will carry it on his neck on the Day of Resurrection: if it is a camel with a bellow, or a cow with a lowing, or a sheep that bleats." It is also narrated from him: "or a horse that neighs." Al-Kalbi said: that thing which he embezzled will be displayed to him in the Fire, and then it will be said to him: "Come down and take it." He will come down and carry it on his back, and when he reaches his watchtower, he will fall into the Fire, and then he will be ordered to come down to it and bring it out. This is done to him repeatedly. It was also said: he will come bearing the sin of what he embezzled. It was also said: it will be taken from his good deeds in exchange for what he embezzled. Many hadiths have been transmitted concerning the magnification of embezzlement and the threat against it.

﴿Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged﴾. This sentence is conjoined to the conditional sentence. Having mentioned the matter of embezzlement and what befalls its perpetrator on the Day of Resurrection, He mentions that this recompense is not specific to the one who embezzles; rather, every soul is paid in full the recompense of what it earned without injustice. The explanation of this sentence has already passed, so there is no need to repeat it here.
