Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 162–163:

﴿Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah like one who incurs wrath from Allah, whose refuge is Hell? And wretched is the destination.﴾ This interrogative (istifham) means negation. That is: one who follows the pleasure of Allah, complying with His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, is not like one who disobeys Him and so incurs His wrath. This is a striking metaphor (istiʿara badiʿiyya). He made what Allah legislated like the guide that one who is guided follows, and He made the disobedient like a person who was commanded to follow something, turned away from following it, and returned accompanied by what contradicts following. In terms of meaning, the verse contains an ellipsis (hadhf), and the implied sense is: Is one who follows what leads to Allah's pleasure with him, and so returns with His pleasure, like one who does not follow that and so returns with His wrath? Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and the majority said: Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah by not misappropriating (lam yaghull) like one who incurs wrath from Allah by misappropriating (hina ghall)? Al-Zajjaj said: Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah by following the Messenger on the day of Uhud like one who incurs wrath from Allah by staying behind, and they were a group of the hypocrites? Al-Zajjaj also said: The pleasure of Allah is jihad, and the wrath is fleeing. It was also said: The pleasure of Allah is obedience to Him, and His wrath is His punishment. It was also said: His wrath is His disobedience; this was said by Ibn Ishaq. What al-Zamakhshari claims, namely assuming a conjunction (maʿtuf) between the interrogative hamza and the conjunction particle in a construction like this, is difficult, and his supposition is excessively contrived. The opinion of the majority then prevails, that the fa' (fa, "then") originally belongs before the hamza, but the hamza was placed first because interrogation has precedence at the beginning of speech. The readers' differences regarding "riḍwān" were discussed at the beginning of this surah, and the apparent reading is that this is a new sentence (istiʾnaf).

﴿And his refuge is Hell﴾: He informed that whoever incurs wrath from Allah, his place to which he returns is Hell. This implies that its counterpart, namely one who follows the pleasure of Allah, has the Garden as his refuge. It is possible that the phrase is in the relative clause (silla) of "man", so He connected it with His saying "bāʾa" (incurred). With this clause the meaning is: like one who incurs the wrath of Allah and ends up in the Fire. "And wretched is the destination": that is, Hell.

﴿They are of degrees﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan said: For each there are degrees, of the Garden and of the Fire. Abu ʿUbayda said, as in His saying: they are categories (tabaqat). Mujahid and Qatadah said: That is, they possess degrees, since some believers are superior to others. It was also said: It refers to the one who misappropriates and the one who abstains from misappropriation, and the daraja (degree) is rank. Al-Razi said: Its implied sense is: For them are degrees. Some of the authors, responding to him, said: Al-Razi followed most of the exegetes in this, through his ignorance and their ignorance of the Arabic language, because the omission of the preposition lam (the lam of genitive/dative) here has no justification, since the lam of jarr is only omitted in cases of necessity (ḍarura) or because of frequent usage, and this is not one of those cases. Moreover, the meaning without omitting it is good and very sound, because when He said: Is one who follows the pleasure of Allah like one who incurs the wrath of Allah, and it is as if he were awaiting an answer, He was told in reply: No, they are not equal; rather, they are of degrees (ʿinda Allah) according to their deeds. This is a correct meaning that does not need the assumption of an omitted lam, even if that were permissible, and how could it be, since it is not permissible. The author's words end here. The explanation of Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan bears the meaning that: For each there are degrees of the Garden and the Fire, according to an interpretation of the meaning rather than an interpretation of the grammatical (iʿrabi) wording. From their statement "they are degrees," the apparent sense is that the pronoun refers to all of them, so they vary in reward and punishment, and variation in punishment has come just as variation in reward has. The meaning of "ʿinda Allah" according to this view is: in the judgment of Allah. It was also said: The pronoun refers to the people of the pleasure of Allah, so "ʿinda Allah" in that case means honour and status, not place. Like His saying: ﴿in the presence of a Sovereign, All-Powerful﴾ [al-Qamar: 55]. In that case the degrees are specific to the Garden, and this is the meaning of the view of Ibn Jubayr, Abu Salih and Muqatil, and the apparent sense of what Mujahid and al-Suddi said. The degrees are stations, some higher than others, either in distance or in honour. al-Jumhur read "darajat" (in the plural), which agrees with the word "hum." al-Nakhaʿi read "darajatan" in the singular.

﴿And Allah is All-Seeing of what they do﴾: That is, He knows their deeds and their degrees, so He will recompense them according to them. These verses contain antithesis (ṭibāq) in: ﴿He helps you or forsakes you﴾, and in "riḍwān Allah" and "bi-sakhaṭ" (with wrath). Repetition (takrār) in: "yanṣurukum" and "yanṣurukum", and in the divine name (al-jalala) in several places. Paronomasia (tajnis mumāthil, a perfect pun) in: "yaghull" and "mā ghall". The interrogation whose meaning is in: "Is one who follows" and the verse. Restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ) in: "let the believers put their trust," and in: "It is not for a Prophet," and in: "of what they do." The deeds were singled out over speech, because deeds are the main thing upon which recompense is based. Ellipsis (ḥadhf) occurs in several places.

**(p-103)** The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when Allah, the Exalted, mentioned the two groups, the group of good pleasure and the group of wrath, and that they are "degrees with Allah" in general terms without detail, He then explained their conditions in detail, beginning with the believers. He mentioned the favour He bestowed upon them by sending them a Messenger, reciting to them the signs of Allah, showing them the way of guidance, purifying them from the defilements of polytheism, and rescuing them from the depths of error after they had been in it. He also consoled them for what befell them at the Battle of Uhud of defeat, killing and wounding, in return for what He had granted them at the Battle of Badr of victory and spoils. Then He detailed the condition of the hypocrites, who are the people of wrath, in what Allah, the Exalted, explicitly stated.

The meaning of "manna" (*manna*) is to bestow favour and grace. He singled out the believers because they are the ones who benefit from his being sent, though its apparent scope is general. On this reading, "from themselves" (*min anfusihim*) means from among their own community, as He said: ﴿Certainly there has come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128]. The meaning is: of the same kind as the children of Adam. The favour lies in the fact that he is familiar to them, being of mankind, so that they feel at ease with him and receive from him more easily, and the natural estrangement and aversion that exists between two different kinds is removed, and they know the capacities of their own kind. When the miracle appears, they realise that it is not within the capacities of the children of Adam, so they know that it is from Allah, and that becomes a summons to respond. Had the Messenger been of a different kind, it could have been imagined that that miracle was in his nature. Al-Maturidi (al-Maturidi, a theologian and exegete) pointed out this reason.

It has been said that the intended meaning of "the believers" is the Arabs, because there is no tribe of the Arabs except that he has kinship with them through his mothers, except the Banu Taghlib, because of their Christianity. This was said by al-Naqqash, so his being sent among them became an honour for them over all the other nations.

The meaning of "from themselves" would then be: that is, of their own kind, Arab like them. It has also been said: from the descendants of Ishmael, just as they are his descendants. Ibn Abbas and Qatada said: He said "from themselves" because he was well known in lineage among them, well known for trustworthiness and truthfulness. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: so that teaching from him would be easy for them, due to the agreement of language. Al-Mawardi said: because their honour is completed by the emergence of a prophet from among them. End of quotation.

The favour upon them through his being from themselves is that the tongue is one, so it is easy for them to take what must be taken from him. They were also aware of his circumstances in truthfulness and trustworthiness, and that was closer to their believing him and trusting in him. It was read irregularly (*shadhdh*, a reading not accepted as Qur'anic): ﴿li-min manna Allahu ʿala al-mu'minin﴾ **(p-104)** with *min* as a preposition governing *manna*, in place of "qad manna". Al-Zamakhshari said: In this there are two possibilities: that it means "for [the one] whom Allah bestowed favour upon the believers from him or his sending among them," the object being omitted because the indication is clear; or that *idh* ("when") is in the position of a nominative, like *idha* in your saying: "The emir is at his most eloquent when he is standing," meaning: "for whom Allah bestowed favour upon the believers at the time of sending him." End of quotation.

As for the first possibility, it is permissible, and the subject has been omitted together with *min* in several places, among them: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him﴾ [al-Nisa': 159]; ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164]; ﴿And among us are some who are otherwise﴾ [al-Jinn: 11], according to one view. As for the second possibility, it is corrupt, because he made *idh* a subject-initial, and the Arabs never used it in this way at all. It is only a time-adverb, or it is followed by a noun of time, and it can be an object of "udhkur" (remember), according to one view. As for its being used as a subject, that is not established in the language of the Arabs; there is nothing in their speech like: "idh qama Zayd tawil" ("when Zayd stood tall") and you, meaning "at the time of Zayd's standing tall." Abu Ali al-Farisi said: *idh* and *idha* do not occur in the speech of the Arabs except as adverbs of time, and they are not used as a subject or object, nor as subject-initials. End of his words. As for his saying "in the position of a nominative, like *idha*", this comparison is corrupt, because the thing compared is nominative by being a subject-initial, whereas the thing compared to it is not a subject-initial; it is rather an adverb in the position of the predicate according to the view of those who hold that. In reality it is not in a nominative position, but in an accusative position governed by a deleted verb, and that governing element is itself nominative. So when the grammarians say "this adverb which occurs as a predicate is in a nominative position," they mean that since it has taken the place of the nominative, it has come to occupy its position, though in reality it is in an accusative position as we have mentioned. As for his saying "the emir is at his most eloquent when he is standing," this is utterly corrupt, because this adverb, according to the view of the one who makes it stand in the position of the predicate of the subject-initial which is "at his most eloquent," does not allow it to be pronounced; it is merely a presumed matter. The proponents of this view, who hold that "at his most eloquent" is a subject-initial, stated that this state took the place of the predicate, and that it is one of the things where the predicate must be deleted because this state takes its place. There are four views on the explanation of this predicate, mentioned in the detailed works of grammar.

The majority read "min anfusihim" with a *damma* on the *fa'*, the plural of *nafs* ("self"). Fatima, ʿAisha, al-Dahhak and Abu al-Jawza read "min anfasihim" with a *fatha* on the *fa'*, from *nafasa* ("preciousness") and "a precious thing." It was related from Anas that he heard it so from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). "ʿAli narrated from him, peace be upon him: 'I am from the most precious of you in lineage, in nobility and in marriage alliance, and there is no illegitimate union in my forefathers from Adam until the day I was born; all of them are lawful marriages, and praise be to Allah.'"

It has been said: the meaning is "from the most noble of them," because ʿAdnan is the summit of the descendants of Ishmael, Mudar is the summit of Nizar ibn Ma'add ibn ʿAdnan, Khindif is the summit of Mudar, Mudrika is the summit of Khindif, Quraysh is the summit of Mudrika, and the summit of Quraysh is Muhammad (ﷺ). In what Abu Talib spoke at the marriage of Khadija, may Allah be pleased with her, when the Banu Hashim and the chiefs of Mudar were present with him: "Praise be to Allah who made us of the offspring of Abraham, the seed of Ishmael, the origin of Ma'add, and the stock of Mudar, and made us the guardians of His House and the keepers of His sanctuary, and gave us a House to be visited and a secure sanctuary, and made us the rulers over the people. Then, this nephew of mine, Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allah, is one with whom no young man of Quraysh can be weighed without his outweighing him; and by Allah, after this he will have a great news and a lofty standing." Ibn Abbas said: Allah did not create a soul more honoured by Allah than Muhammad, His Messenger (ﷺ), and He did not swear by the life of anyone other than him, saying: ﴿By your life﴾ [al-Hijr: 72].

﴿He recites to them His signs and purifies them and teaches them the Book and the wisdom﴾: The explanation of these clauses has already preceded.

﴿And indeed they were before in clear error﴾: that is, before his sending. **(p-105)** That is, clear bewilderment, and He guided them through him. Here *in* (*inna*) is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and the discussion of it and of the *lam* in His saying: ﴿And indeed it was a great [matter]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], and the disagreement on that, has already preceded, so it suffices from repeating it here. Al-Zamakhshari said: *in* is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and the *lam* is the distinguishing particle between it and the negative *in*, and the implied sense is: and indeed the matter and the report was that they were before in manifest error. End of quotation. Makki said: He mentioned that *in* before it is negative, and the *lam* has the sense of *illa* ("except"), that is: and they were not before except in manifest error. He said: This is the view of the Kufans. As for Sibawayh, he said: *in* is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and its subject is a pronoun, and the implied sense in his view is: and indeed they were before in manifest error. From al-Zamakhshari's words it becomes clear that when it was lightened, its subject, which is the pronoun of the matter and the report, was deleted, and from Makki's words that when it was lightened its subject, which is a pronoun referring back to the believers, was deleted; and we do not know either of these two views as having been held grammatically. What is established for us in the books of grammar and from the teachers is that if you say: "inna Zaydan qa'im" and then lighten it, the view of the Basrans regarding it at that time has two possibilities: one of them is the permissibility of its governing, and its state while lightened is like its state when heavy, except that it does not govern a pronoun. The Kufans prohibited this, and they are refuted by the established evidence from the language of the Arabs. The second possibility, which is the more prevalent among them, is that it be disregarded and not govern, neither an explicit noun nor a pronoun, neither pronounced nor presumed at all. If a nominal sentence follows it, it takes the nominative by the subject-initial and the predicate, and the *lam* must be attached to the second of its two propositions if it is not negated, and to the first of them if it is postponed. So we say: "in Zayd la-qa'im" ("indeed Zayd is standing"), and its meaning is the meaning of "inna Zaydan qa'im." If a verbal sentence follows it, then according to the Basrans it must be one of the initiating verbs of the subject-initial. If the verb comes from other than these, it is anomalous and is not analogised upon according to the majority of them. The clause "and they were" is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), and the apparent view is that its governing element is "wa-yu'allimuhum" ("and teaches them"), so it is a circumstantial state of the object.

[Quran 3:165] "Why is it that when a calamity struck you, though you had inflicted twice as much (on them), you said, 'How is this?'"

The hamza (ألف الاستفهام / *hamzat al-istifham*, the interrogative particle) here carries the meaning of disapproval.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: The alif of interrogation (*alif al-taqrir*, the alif of affirmation or confrontation) has entered upon it, to mean that the believers are being held to account for this statement in this situation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Lammā*" is governed by "*qultum*" (you said), and "*aṣābatkum*" (it struck you) is in a genitive position as the object of "*lammā*," whose implied sense is: "Did you say (it) when it struck you?" And "*anná hādhā*" is in the accusative, because it is the thing said (*maqūl*). The hamza is for affirmation and rebuke.

(If you ask): On what does the conjunction *wāw* in this clause depend? (I say): It depends on what preceded, from the story of Uhud, in His words: ﴿And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 152]. It is also permissible that it be conjoined to an omitted element, so that it is as if He said: "Did you do such-and-such, and then say such-and-such at that time?" End of quote.

As for the conjunction upon what preceded from the story of Uhud, in His words, "﴿And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 152]," this is far-fetched, and it is unlikely that the like of it occurs in the Qur'an. As for the conjunction upon an omitted element, it follows what has been established in more than one place in his school of thought, and we have refuted it. As for the position of the majority—Sibawayh and others—they said: the original arrangement is that it is placed first, and the interrogative clause is conjoined to what precedes it. As for his statement, "*Lammā* is governed..." to the end, and its implied sense, "And you said at that time such-and-such," he made *lammā* mean *ḥīna* (when), and this is not the view of Sibawayh; it is only the view of Abu ʿAli al-Farisi. He claimed that *lammā* is a temporal adverb meaning *ḥīna*, and the clause after it is in a genitive position with it, so he counted it among the adverbs which must be followed by clauses, and he made it governed by the verb that occurs as its response, as in: "*Lammā jāʾa Zaydun jāʾa ʿAmrun*" (When Zayd came, ʿAmr came), so that *lammā* is in the accusative position governed by "*jāʾa*" from your saying "*jāʾa ʿAmrun*." As for the view of Sibawayh, *lammā* is a particle, not an adverb, and it is a particle of necessity for necessity, and the view of Sibawayh is the correct one. We have made clear the corruption of Abu ʿAli's view in several respects in our book called *al-Takmīl*.

The "calamity" (*muṣība*) is what befell the believers on the day of Uhud: the slaying of seventy of them and their being turned back from steadfastness in fighting. The attribution of "striking" (*iṣāba*) to the calamity is a metaphor (*majāz*), like the attribution of "wanting" (*irāda*) to a wall. As for the two equal (*mithlān*) amounts which they had inflicted, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatada, al-Rabīʿ, and a group said: it is their slaying of seventy on the day of Badr and their capture of seventy. So the equivalence occurs in the number of men struck. Al-Zajjaj said: their slaying of seventy on the day of Badr, and their slaying of twenty-two on the day of Uhud—so it is slaying for slaying. The captives have no place in the verse, because they were ransomed, so there is no equivalence between their condition and the slaying of seventy of the believers. It was also said: the equivalence is in the defeat. The believers defeated the unbelievers on the day of Badr, and they (the unbelievers) defeated them at first on the day of Uhud, and the polytheists defeated them at the end of the day of Uhud.

The summary of this: Is the equivalence in the striking the slaying and capture, or the slaying only, or the defeat? Three opinions. The most evident is the first, because His words, "*qad aṣabtum mithlayhā*" (though you had inflicted twice as much), are in the manner of a favour from Him, may He be exalted, upon the believers, by granting them victory over the unbelievers, and a consolation for them over what had struck them. So this is most eloquent as consolation, and alerting them to the fact that they slew seventy of the enemy and captured seventy is more eloquent in terms of favour and consolation, and more apt to make them remember the blessings of Allah upon them in the past, and to forget what befell them on the day of Uhud.

"*Anná hādhā*" (How is this?): it is a sentence of subject and predicate, and it is in an accusative position as the object of His words "*qultum*" (you said). They said this as an expression of wonder and disapproval at what struck them. The meaning: How has this struck us when we are fighting the enemies of Allah, and we were promised victory and the reinforcement of the angels? So they asked, in wonder, about that. "*Anná*" here is a question about the state (*ḥāl*), and it is not appropriate here to mean "where" or "when," because the question did not concern place or time here; rather the question concerned the condition which brought about that for them, and they asked about it in wonder. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Anná hādhā*" means "From where is this?" like His saying "*Anná laka hādhā*" (From where is this for you?), in view of His words "from your own selves" and His words "from Allah." End of his statement. An adverb which occurs as a predicate of a subject may not be taken as governed by a preposition other than "*fī*" (in). As for taking "*min*" (from) as governing it, that is not permissible, because it is in the accusative only through the omission of "*fī*." Likewise, when the adverb is implicit, the verb reaches it through the intermediary of "*fī*," unless the verb is given wider scope so that it is put in the accusative in the manner of a direct object. So al-Zamakhshari's estimate, "*Anná hādhā*: from where is this," is an unacceptable estimate. His reasoning for this estimate, through his words "from your own selves" and "from Allah," is a holding to the correspondence of the answer to the question in wording, and a neglect of this rule which we have mentioned. As for what we have established, the answer came in observance of the meaning, not in matching the answer to the question in wording. It is established in the science of Arabic that the answer comes according to the question, matching it in wording, while the meaning is what is observed, not the wording. The question with "*anná*" is a question about specifying the manner in which this matter came about, and the answer in His words "from your own selves" includes specifying the manner, because by specifying the cause the manner is specified in terms of meaning. If it were said in wonder and disapproval, "How is it that Zayd the righteous does not perform the pilgrimage?", the answer would be given: "Because he is not able," and thereby the answer is obtained and the meaning is complete that he does not perform the pilgrimage, being unable to do so.

﴿Say: It is from your own selves﴾. The pronoun in "*huwa*" (it) refers to the calamity in meaning, not in wording. The interpretation of the calamity has already been given in the explanation of the equivalent of the two amounts: Is it the slaying which corresponds to the slaying and capture, or which corresponds to the slaying alone, or the defeat which corresponds to the two defeats? The meaning: the cause of this calamity came from your own selves. It was said: it is the ransom which they preferred over slaying on the day of Badr without the permission of Allah, the Exalted. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, ʿAlī, and al-Ḥasan said this. ʿAlī narrated concerning that: "When the defeat of the polytheists on the day of Badr was over, Jibril came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'O Muhammad, Allah has disliked what your people did in taking the ransom of the captives, and He has commanded you to offer them a choice between two matters: that they bring forward the captives so their necks are struck, or that they take the ransom on condition that a number of your companions equal to these captives be slain.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then called the people and mentioned that to them. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, our clans and brothers—we take their ransom so that we may strengthen ourselves with it against the fighting of our enemy, and from us a number of martyrs will be made equal to them; so there is nothing in that which we dislike.' So seventy men of them were slain on the day of Uhud." The majority said: it is the opposition to the Messenger in opinion, when he saw that he should remain in Medina and leave the unbelievers to the worst of gatherings; but they opposed him and went out, until the story took its course. A group, including Ibn ʿAbbas and Muqatil, said: it is the disobedience of the archers and their causing the defeat of the believers. Al-Zamakhshari summarized these three opinions in the finest summary, saying: The meaning is that you were the cause of what struck you, by your choosing to go out of Medina, or by your leaving the centre (*markaz*) unguarded. And from ʿAlī: by your taking the ransom from the captives of Badr before permission had been given to you. End of quote. Allah, the Exalted, did not specify what the cause was, out of gentleness toward the believers in His address to them. The apparent meaning of His words "*anná hādhā*" is that it is a question from the believers, in the manner of wonder.

Al-Razi mentioned that when Allah related the hypocrites' attack on the Messenger, in that they attributed to him embezzlement and betrayal, He related from them another doubt in this verse, which is their saying: "If he were a messenger from Allah, his army would not have been defeated on the day of Uhud," and this is what is meant by their saying: "*Anná hādhā*." So He answered it with His words: "Say: it is from your own selves," meaning: this defeat only occurred through the ill-omen of your disobedience. End of his statement. This indicates that His words "*anná hādhā*" are the words of the hypocrites. Al-Maturidi also said: it is the words of the hypocrites. The apparent meaning, as we have said, is that it is the words of the believers, and they are the ones addressed by His words "*Why is it that when a calamity struck you*," because the hypocrites had not been struck by a calamity, since they had turned back with ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and had not attended the fighting—unless "*aṣābatkum muṣība*" (a calamity struck you) is taken as a figurative expression meaning that it struck your relatives and brothers, and this is possible but far-fetched.

﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent﴾: that is, Able to grant victory and to withhold it, and able to let a calamity strike you at one time and to let it strike them at another. By this He alerts that what befell them was due to a weakness in their religion, not to a deficiency in the power of Allah, because the One who is competent over all things is competent to repel them in every condition.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 166–167 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Whatever befell you on the day the two hosts met, it was by the permission of God.﴾ It is the day of Uhud. "The two hosts" are the host of the Prophet ﷺ and the disbelievers of Quraysh, and the address is to the believers. "Ma" (whatever) is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) serving as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the phrase "fa-bi-idhni Allah" (then by the permission of God). This is according to an elided construction (idmar), meaning: "then it is by the permission of God."

As for the entry of the "fa" (then) here, al-Hawfi said: "*lamma* (when) in the sentence carries the sense of a conditional (shart), because it demands a verb." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The *fa* entered as a linking particle that firms up the meaning, because of the indefiniteness in *ma*, so the sentence resembled a conditional, and this is as Sibawayh said: 'The one who stood up, then for him are two dirhams.' It is good for the *fa* to enter when standing up is the cause of the giving." That is the end of his words. And this is better than the words of al-Hawfi, because al-Hawfi claimed that the sentence carries the sense of a conditional, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya said: "the sentence resembled a conditional."

The entry of the *fa* according to what the majority have said and established is problematic here. They established that in permitting the entry of the *fa* on the predicate of a relative pronoun, the relative clause (sila) must be self-contained. Thus they do not permit: "The one who stood up yesterday, then for him is a dirham," because this *fa* entered the predicate of the relative pronoun only because of its resemblance to the conditional. Just as the verb of the conditional (fi'l al-shart) cannot be past in meaning, so too the relative clause.

Yet "that which befell them on the day the two hosts met" is truly past, so it is a report about something past in meaning. Given what they established, the entry of the *fa* here is problematic. What we hold is that it is permissible for the *fa* to enter the predicate when the relative clause is past in meaning, due to the occurrence of this verse, and due to God's saying: ﴿And what God gave back from them to His Messenger, you did not press forward against it with horse or camel﴾ [al-Hashr: 6]. It is well known that this is past in meaning, certainly occurring as relative clause and predicate. This is understood as: "and what is clearly shown to be its striking you." Just as they interpreted: ﴿if his shirt is torn﴾ [Yusuf: 26], meaning: if it is shown that his shirt is torn. Once this is established, the following should be understood in the same way: God's saying ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ [al-Nisa': 79], and ﴿Whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 30]. For the apparent sense of all of these is a report about past matters, and the meaning becomes "according to what is future-clarified."

The "permission" (idhn) here has been explained as "knowledge," and it was expressed by it because knowledge is one of its requirements. This is said by al-Zajjaj. Or it is explained as God's enabling and leaving the two hosts to face each other; this is said by al-Qaffal. Or as "in sight and hearing," or as "by His decree and destiny." al-Zamakhshari said: "So it occurs by the permission of God; He borrowed 'permission' for the disbelievers' being left free, and that He did not prevent them from them, in order to test them, because the one who permits leaves the one permitted free to pursue his desire." That is the end of his words. In this there is a hidden trace of Mu'tazilism, because the killing of believers by disbelievers is ugly according to him, so there is no permission in it.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is good for the *fa* to enter when there is a cause of giving, and likewise is the arrangement of this verse. The meaning is: it is only that whatever God permitted is what struck, but He put first what was more important in their souls and closer to their perception. The *idhn* (permission) is enabling someone to do something together with knowledge of it." That is the end of his words. Since in meaning the striking is consequent upon God's enabling, from this he took the verse to mean that, and claimed inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir). But the verse does not need that, because it is not a conditional and consequent that would require such a thing. Rather, this is of the type of reporting something past, and the report is correct. God informed that what struck them on the day of Uhud was, without doubt, by the permission of God. This is a correct report and a correct meaning, so we do not strain toward inversion, and we make it of the type of conditional and consequent.

* *

﴿And that He might know the believers﴾ and ﴿that He might know those who were hypocrites﴾: this is with an elided genitive (hadhf mudaf), meaning: "and that He might know the faith of the believers, and know the hypocrisy of those who were hypocrites." Or the meaning is: "and that He might distinguish the actual persons of the believers from the actual persons of the hypocrites." It has been said: "so that knowledge, with the existence of the believers and the hypocrites, would be coextensive with the knowledge that has never ceased and will never cease." It has also been said: "that He might make manifest the faith of these and the hypocrisy of those." The interpretation of a similar expression has already been given in His saying: ﴿that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. They said: the verse is connected to an omitted element, meaning: "and for such-and-such reason He did that." What appears is that it is conjoined to His saying "by the permission of God," conjoining cause to cause. There is no difference between *ba'* (by) and *lam* (that/for), so it is connected to what *ba'* was connected to from His saying: "it is in existence." Those who were hypocrites here are Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions.

﴿And it was said to them: Come, fight in the way of God, or repel﴾: the speaker was the Messenger of God ﷺ. It has also been said: Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn Haram al-Ansari, the father of Jabir ibn Abdullah. When Abdullah ibn Ubayy withdrew with about three hundred men, Abdullah [ibn 'Amr] followed them and said to them: "Fear God, and do not abandon your Prophet, and fight in the way of God, or repel," and similar words. Abdullah ibn Ubayy said: "I do not think there will be fighting; if we knew there would be fighting, we would be with you." When Abdullah [ibn 'Amr] despaired of them, he said: "Go, enemies of God, God will suffice without you," and he went on until he was martyred. al-Suddi, Ibn Juraij, Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and al-Farra' said: its meaning is: "increase the number, and even if you do not fight, you repel the people by multiplying." Abu 'Awn al-Ansari said its meaning is: "stand guard (ribat)," and this is close to the first, because the one who stands guard on the frontiers repels the enemy, for were it not for him, the enemy would attack them. Anas said: "I saw Abdullah ibn Umm Maktum on the day of al-Qadisiyya, wearing armor whose edges trailed, and in his hand a black banner. It was said to him: 'Has not God made your excuse?' He said: 'Yes, but I increase the Muslims by myself.'" It has also been said: fighting is with the souls, and repelling is with the wealth. It has also been said: the meaning is "or repel out of zeal," because when He first called them to fight in the way of God, He found their resolve loosened from that, since they had no motive for it, due to their hypocrisy; so He sought from them that they repel from the sacred enclosure, and He alerted them to what one fights for: either to exalt the religion, or to protect what must be defended. Do you not see the saying of Qazman: "By God, I fought only for the honor of my people"; and the saying of the Ansari when he saw Quraysh grazing the crops of his spear: "Do you graze the crops of Banu Qaylah while they have not yet been struck?" Even though He ordered that no one should fight until He commanded him.

The "aw" (or) is in its proper sense, meaning one of two things. It has also been said: it may be in the sense of the "wa" (and), so that He demanded of them two things: fighting in the way of God, and repelling from the sanctuary, family, and wealth. For the disbelievers of Quraysh do not distinguish between believer and hypocrite in killing, captivity, and plunder. The apparent sense is that His saying "and it was said to them" is a resumed statement. He divided the matter upon them, between fighting for the Hereafter or repelling for their own selves, families, and wealth. God related what indicates their hypocrisy in this question and answer. It is possible that His saying "and it was said to them" is conjoined to "were hypocrites," so that it would be part of the relative clause.

﴿They said: If we knew there would be fighting, we would certainly follow you﴾: the reason why no *fa* was used is that this is an answer to a question that their summons to fighting called for, as if it were said: "What did they say?" and it was answered: "They said: if we knew..." When it is in the sense of the conditional *in* (if), it makes the present tense refer to the future. The import of this answer is that they made following conditional upon the supposition of the existence of knowledge of fighting, and their knowledge of fighting is nonexistent, so following is nonexistent. Their report that knowledge of fighting was absent from them is either by way of obstinacy and lying, since it is known that when two armies emerge and meet, one of them intending the other from a far distance, with a great number and equipment, and the other army came out to them from their own town to meet them before they reached their town, trusting in God's victory and fighting in the way of God, even if they were fewer than those, there would inevitably arise fighting between them. So they denied knowledge of this outright, because of their hypocrisy, deceit, and joy at gaining control over the believers. It was not so; it was rather casting themselves into destruction, since they had no power to resist the disbelievers' war because of their numbers and the believers' fewness. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 166–167 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Whatever befell you on the day the two hosts met, it was by the permission of God.﴾ It is the day of Uhud. "The two hosts" are the host of the Prophet ﷺ and the disbelievers of Quraysh, and the address is to the believers. "Ma" (whatever) is a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) serving as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is the phrase "fa-bi-idhni Allah" (then by the permission of God). This is according to an elided construction (idmar), meaning: "then it is by the permission of God."

As for the entry of the "fa" (then) here, al-Hawfi said: "*lamma* (when) in the sentence carries the sense of a conditional (shart), because it demands a verb." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The *fa* entered as a linking particle that firms up the meaning, because of the indefiniteness in *ma*, so the sentence resembled a conditional, and this is as Sibawayh said: 'The one who stood up, then for him are two dirhams.' It is good for the *fa* to enter when standing up is the cause of the giving." That is the end of his words. And this is better than the words of al-Hawfi, because al-Hawfi claimed that the sentence carries the sense of a conditional, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya said: "the sentence resembled a conditional."

The entry of the *fa* according to what the majority have said and established is problematic here. They established that in permitting the entry of the *fa* on the predicate of a relative pronoun, the relative clause (sila) must be self-contained. Thus they do not permit: "The one who stood up yesterday, then for him is a dirham," because this *fa* entered the predicate of the relative pronoun only because of its resemblance to the conditional. Just as the verb of the conditional (fi'l al-shart) cannot be past in meaning, so too the relative clause.

Yet "that which befell them on the day the two hosts met" is truly past, so it is a report about something past in meaning. Given what they established, the entry of the *fa* here is problematic. What we hold is that it is permissible for the *fa* to enter the predicate when the relative clause is past in meaning, due to the occurrence of this verse, and due to God's saying: ﴿And what God gave back from them to His Messenger, you did not press forward against it with horse or camel﴾ [al-Hashr: 6]. It is well known that this is past in meaning, certainly occurring as relative clause and predicate. This is understood as: "and what is clearly shown to be its striking you." Just as they interpreted: ﴿if his shirt is torn﴾ [Yusuf: 26], meaning: if it is shown that his shirt is torn. Once this is established, the following should be understood in the same way: God's saying ﴿Whatever good befalls you is from God, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself﴾ [al-Nisa': 79], and ﴿Whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 30]. For the apparent sense of all of these is a report about past matters, and the meaning becomes "according to what is future-clarified."

The "permission" (idhn) here has been explained as "knowledge," and it was expressed by it because knowledge is one of its requirements. This is said by al-Zajjaj. Or it is explained as God's enabling and leaving the two hosts to face each other; this is said by al-Qaffal. Or as "in sight and hearing," or as "by His decree and destiny." al-Zamakhshari said: "So it occurs by the permission of God; He borrowed 'permission' for the disbelievers' being left free, and that He did not prevent them from them, in order to test them, because the one who permits leaves the one permitted free to pursue his desire." That is the end of his words. In this there is a hidden trace of Mu'tazilism, because the killing of believers by disbelievers is ugly according to him, so there is no permission in it.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is good for the *fa* to enter when there is a cause of giving, and likewise is the arrangement of this verse. The meaning is: it is only that whatever God permitted is what struck, but He put first what was more important in their souls and closer to their perception. The *idhn* (permission) is enabling someone to do something together with knowledge of it." That is the end of his words. Since in meaning the striking is consequent upon God's enabling, from this he took the verse to mean that, and claimed inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir). But the verse does not need that, because it is not a conditional and consequent that would require such a thing. Rather, this is of the type of reporting something past, and the report is correct. God informed that what struck them on the day of Uhud was, without doubt, by the permission of God. This is a correct report and a correct meaning, so we do not strain toward inversion, and we make it of the type of conditional and consequent.

* *

﴿And that He might know the believers﴾ and ﴿that He might know those who were hypocrites﴾: this is with an elided genitive (hadhf mudaf), meaning: "and that He might know the faith of the believers, and know the hypocrisy of those who were hypocrites." It has been said: "so that knowledge, with the existence of the believers and the hypocrites, would be coextensive with the knowledge that has never ceased and will never cease." Those who were hypocrites here are Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions.
