**Those who said to their brothers while they sat [at home], "If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed."** This verse is similar to His saying: "﴿And they said to their brothers when they traveled in the land...﴾ [Al ʿImran: 156]" and the rest of it. The word "brothers" (al-ikhwan) is explained here as it was explained there. The lam of the preposition (lam al-jarr, the particle "li") can carry the same possibilities it carried there. Scholars also permitted several analyses (i'rab, grammatical parsing) of the word "those who" (alladhina):
- In the nominative, as an adjective (naʿt) for "those who were hypocrites."
- In the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject.
- In the nominative, as an apposition (badal) of the waw in "they conceal."
- In the accusative, as a verb of dispraise, meaning "I dispraise those who..."
- In the genitive, as an apposition of the pronoun in "in their mouths" or "in their hearts."

The clause "and they sat" (wa qaʿadu) is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "while they had sat." The use of a past-tense verb as a circumstantial clause in this construction, accompanied by *qad*, or by the waw, or by both, or without them, is established in the Arabic language through transmitted usage (al-sama', attested usage). The object of "obeyed" (ta'a) is abstaining from going out. "Sitting" here is as they themselves sat. This statement from them is a claim covering both possibilities: that is, "If they had agreed with us in staying behind and sitting, they would not have been killed, just as we were not killed." Al-Hasan read *qutilu* with the doubled letter (tashdid), i.e., *quttilu*.

**Say: "Then avert death from yourselves, if you are truthful."** God refuted them in their claim. It is as if it were said: killing is a form of death. If you have a way to repel it from yourselves through a deliberate action, then repel death from yourselves; and if you do not, that shows that you are liars in your claim. "Repelling" (al-darʾ) means pushing away, and its root was mentioned in His saying "﴿and you disputed about it﴾" (fa-idaraʾtum fīha). Daghfal al-Nassabah (the genealogist) said:

*The repelling of the flood met one who pushed it back,*
*and the burden neither knows it nor lifts it.*

The meaning is: if you are truthful in your claim that cunning and caution save from death, then strive yourselves to repel it. But you will not find a way to that, and indeed some of the causes of death must reach you. Suppose that, by your assumption, you repelled this particular cause by sitting at home; then repel all the other causes of death. This is absolutely impossible for you.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: they were truthful in that they repelled killing from themselves by sitting, so what is the meaning of His saying 'if you are truthful'?" I answer: its meaning is that deliverance from killing may have as its cause sitting out of fighting, or it may have another cause, since the causes of deliverance are many. A man's fighting may be his deliverance, and had he not fought, he would have been killed. So how do you know that the cause of your deliverance is sitting, and that you are truthful in your fighting, and that you do not deny that the cause could be something else?

Another interpretation: "if you are truthful in your saying, 'If they had obeyed us and sat, they would not have been killed'," meaning: if they had obeyed you and sat, they would have been killed sitting, just as they were killed fighting. His saying "then avert death from yourselves" is mockery of them, meaning: if you are men who repel the causes of death, then repel all its causes so that you do not die. End of his words. It is good, despite its length.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 169:

﴿And do not think that those who were killed in the way of Allah are dead; rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for.﴾ (p-112) It was said: they are the slain of Uhud. It was also said: they are the martyrs of Bi'r Ma'una. And it was said: they are the martyrs of Badr. The cause of this (revelation) is said to be either the words of one who was martyred, having entered Paradise and eaten of its fruits, who said: "Whoever conveys from us to our brothers that we are in Paradise, being provided for, do not shun jihad." Then Allah said: "I will convey it on your behalf," and so this was revealed. Or (it was) the words of one who had not been martyred, among the relatives of the martyrs: "When a blessing befalls them, we are in blessing and joy, while our fathers, our sons and our brothers are in graves," and so this was revealed.

The majority read "wa la tahsabanna" with a ta' (tā'), meaning: "and do not think, O hearer." Al-Zamakhshari said: the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone. Hamid ibn Qays and Hisham, with a variant from him, read it with a ya' (yā'), meaning: "and let him not think," that is, a single thinker. Ibn 'Atiyya said: I consider this reading to be with a damma on the ya', so the meaning is: "and let people not be thought (to be dead)." End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible that "alladhina qutilu" be the subject, and the implied sense is: "and let those who were killed not think them dead," meaning: let not those who killed themselves think them dead. (If you say:) how is the omission of the first object permitted? (I say:) it is originally a subject, so it was omitted just as the subject is omitted in His words "ahya'un" (alive). The meaning is: they are alive, by the indication of the speech upon it. End of his words. What he held, that the implied sense is "wa la tahsabannahumu alladhina qutilu amwatan," is not permissible, because it involves placing a pronoun before its explanatory noun, which is restricted to places that do not extend: the chapter of rubba without dispute, as in: rubbahu rajulan akramtuhu; and the chapter of ni'ma and bi'sa, as in: ni'ma rajulan Zayd, according to the school of the Basrans; and the chapter of tanazu', according to the school of Sibawayh, as in: darabani wa darabtu al-zaydayn; and the pronoun of the matter and affair, which is called the unknown (majhul) according to the Kufans, as in: huwa Zayd munțaliq; and the chapter of substitution, with disagreement among the Basrans on it, as in: marartu bihi Zayd. Some of our companions added that the explicit explanatory noun be a predicate of the pronoun, and from it is taken His words, exalted is He: ﴿wa qalu in hiya illa hayatuna al-dunya﴾ [al-An'am: 29], its implied sense for him being: "What is life but our worldly life." What al-Zamakhshari estimated is not one of these mentioned places. As for his question and its answer, it may be consistent with the opinion of the majority that it is permissible to omit one of the two objects of zanna and its sisters by way of abbreviation; omission by abbreviation is for understanding the meaning, but according to them it is very rare. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: its omission is very rare, just as omitting the predicate of kana is so, though the aspects of ugliness differ. End of the words of Abu 'Ali. Ustadh Abu Ishaq Ibrahim ibn Malkun al-Hadrami al-Ishbili went to prohibit that by way of abbreviation, and the argument for it and against it is mentioned in the science of grammar. What is in this position, prohibited according to some and rare in its omission according to the majority, should not be attributed to the speech of Allah, exalted is He. So the interpretation of one who took the subject as a hidden pronoun explained by the meaning, that is: "let him not think" (huwa), that is, let no one think, or a thinker of any kind. The two readings agree that the subject is a pronoun, though they differ in address and third person.

The discussion of the meaning of the death and life of the martyrs (p-113) has already been covered in His words: ﴿wa la taqulu liman yuqtalu fi sabil Allah amwat bal ahya'﴾ [al-Baqarah: 154], so that suffices here without repeating it. Al-Hasan and Ibn 'Amir read "quttilu" with the doubled letter. It is narrated from 'Asim: "qatalu." The majority read "qutilu" lightened. The majority read "bal ahya'un" with the raf' (damma), as the predicate of an omitted subject whose estimate is: "bal hum ahya'un." Ibn Abi 'Abla read "ahya'an" with the nasb (fatha). Al-Zamakhshari said: according to the meaning: "bal uhsibhum ahya'an" (rather, consider them alive). End of quote. Al-Zajjaj followed him in implying this verb. Al-Zajjaj said: the nasb is also permissible according to the meaning: "bal uhsibhum ahya'an." Abu 'Ali al-Farisi refuted him in al-Idah and said: that is not permissible, because the matter is certain, so it is not permissible to command in it a thinking, and it is not valid to imply for it except the verb of thinking. So the reading of Ibn Abi 'Abla would require implying a verb other than "thinking," such as "i'taqidhum" (consider them) or "aj'alhum" (make them), and that is weak, since there is no indication in the speech of what is implied. End of Abu 'Ali's words. His statement "it is not permissible because the matter is certain, so it is not permissible to command in it a thinking" means that what is certain is not expressed by the verb of thinking, because it does not signify certainty. This is what he mentioned, and it is the more common usage, though "hasiba" may occur for certainty just as "zanna" does; but with "zanna" it is frequent, and with "hasiba" it is rare. Among such uses in "hasiba" is the poet's verse:

"I considered piety and praise the best trade, a profit, when a man becomes heavy (with debt)."

And another's verse:

"You witnessed and buried me, and I thought you (to be) in need of one who would witness, and of my absence."

So if "bal uhsibhum" were estimated to mean "bal i'lamhum" (know them), it would be valid, because the meaning indicates it, not because of the wording of "wa la tahsabanna," since the two meanings differ, and when the meaning differs, neither indicates the other. His statement "and it is not valid to imply for it except the verb of thinking" is not accepted, because if implying it is impossible by virtue of meaning, one implies something else, since the meaning indicates it, not the wording. His statement "or make them" is not valid at all, whether "aj'alhum" means "create them," or "make them into," or "name them," or "throw them." His statement "and that is weak," that is, the nasb, and his statement "since there is no indication in the speech of what is implied": if he means by wording, it is correct; if he means by meaning, it is not accepted from him, rather the meaning allows the nasb in the sense of "a'taqidhum" (I consider them), and this is on the assumption that "hasiba" is not taken in the sense of knowledge.

The meaning of "'inda rabbihim" is in rank and nearness, not in place. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it contains an omitted genitive, its estimate being: "'inda karamati rabbihim" (in the honour of their Lord), because "'inda" implies the utmost nearness, and therefore it is diminutive; so said Sibawayh. End of quote. "'Inda rabbihim" may be a second predicate, an adjective, or a circumstantial state. Likewise "yurzaquna" may be a third predicate or a second adjective. He placed the adjective of the adverbial phrase before the adjective of the clause, because this is the more eloquent arrangement: that the adverb or prepositional phrase precede the clause when both are descriptions; and because the meaning of being described with nearness to Allah and closeness to Him is more noble than being described with provision. It may also be a state from the pronoun concealed in the adverb, the operative in reality being the operative in the adverb.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Allah, exalted is He, informed about the martyrs that they are in Paradise being provided for; this is the place of the benefit. Without doubt they died, and their bodies are in the dust, while their spirits are alive like the spirits of all the believers. They were distinguished by being provided in Paradise from the time of their killing, as though the life of this world were perpetual for them. So His words "bal ahya'un" serve as an introduction to His words "yurzaquna," since none is provided except a living being. This is like one who says to someone who blames a man: "Rather, he is a virtuous man," so you bring the generic noun upon which the description of virtue is built. End of what Ibn 'Atiyya said. It does not follow from what he mentioned, that the word "ahya'" was brought in as an addition for the mention of provision, because life is shared by the martyr and the believers; for it is possible that this report about the life of the martyrs preceded the report that the spirits of the believers in general are alive, so the life of the martyrs' spirits was first conveyed, then after it came the report of the life of the believers' spirits. Also, in mentioning it there is an explicit text against what they supposed, namely that the martyrs are dead. And it is remote (p-114) that by His words "yurzaquna" be meant what the imperfect tense may bear of futurity; for when something preceding it indicates being characterized by the description at the time of the report, the ruling of what follows is its ruling, since the basic principle in a report is that the one of whom it is predicated is characterized by it in the present, unless a clear indication, lexical or semantic, points to past or future, in which case one turns to that.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 170:

﴿Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾: That is, glad at what Allah has bestowed upon them of His nearness, and of entering His Paradise, and of being provided for therein, along with all the other honours He has granted them. There is no contradiction between *farihin* (rejoicing) and ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love those who rejoice﴾ [al-Qasas: 76], concerning the story of Qarun, because that rejoicing was over worldly pleasures, while this is over otherworldly pleasures. For this reason it was said, ﴿Say: "In the bounty of Allah and His mercy, in that let them rejoice"﴾ [Yunus: 58], and it came in ﴿For this let the strivers strive﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 26].

It is possible that *min* (from) is causal, meaning: what Allah has given them is caused by His bounty, so that *bi* (with) in *bima atahum* is connected to *atahum*. It is also possible that *min* is partitive, in which case it occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the omitted pronoun referring back to *ma* (what), meaning: with what Allah has given them, being part of His bounty. It is also possible that *min* indicates the starting point (*ibtida' al-ghayah*), in which case it is connected to *atahum*. They also permitted *farihin* to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *yurzaqun* (they are provided for), or from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase, or from the pronoun in *ahya'* (alive), and that it be an attribute of *ahya'* when it is in the accusative.

﴿And they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them from behind them﴾: These are all the believers. That is, they obtain good tidings through the removal of fear and grief from their fellow believers who have not yet joined them in martyrdom. So they rejoice in what has come to them, and they are glad at what comes to their fellow believers. This is the view of al-Zajjaj, Ibn Furak and others. Qatadah, Ibn Juraij, al-Rabi' and others said: they are the martyrs who will be joined later by their fellow believers whom they left behind, striving and then being martyred. They rejoice for themselves and for those of the martyrs who will join them, since those will arrive at what they have arrived at of Allah's honour, the Exalted.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: *istaf'ala* (the form in *yastabshirun*, "they rejoice/receive good tidings") in this place does not mean "seeking good tidings." Rather, it means the same as *istaghna Allah* (Allah is self-sufficient) and *istamjada al-markh wal-'afar* (the markh and the 'afar plants were made glorious). End of his words. As for his saying that it does not mean seeking good tidings, that is correct. As for his saying that it means the same as *istaghna Allah* and *istamjada al-markh wal-'afar*, he means that it may be equivalent to the bare verb, as *istaghna* means *ghaniya* (to be rich), and *istamjada* means *majjada* (to glorify). It has also been reported that it is said *bushshira al-rajul* (the man was given good tidings) with a kasra on the shin, so that *istabshara* has the same meaning. This meaning is not required, however. It may be that it is *mutawi'an* (the reflexive/intransitive counterpart) to *af'ala*, and this is the more evident, meaning: Allah gave him good tidings and so he rejoiced. This is like their saying *akanahu fa-istakana* (he subdued him and he submitted), *ashlahu fa-istashla* (he incited him and he was incited), *arahahu fa-istarah* (he gave him rest and he rested), *ahkamahu fa-istahkam* (he firmed it and it became firm), *akannahu fa-istakann* (he concealed it and it was concealed), *amarahu fa-istamarra* (he ordered him and he continued), and this is common. The reason this is the more evident here is that, in terms of the reflexive form, it indicates being affected by another, so the good tidings were obtained through Allah's giving them good tidings of that. This meaning does not follow when it has the sense of the bare verb, because that does not indicate the reflexive. As for the meaning of *min khalfihim* (from behind them): they remained after them, while they had preceded them, if the meaning of "those who have not joined them" refers to the martyrs. If the intended ones are the believers, then the meaning of "not yet joined them" is that they have not attained their merit and rank.

﴿That there is no fear upon them, nor do they grieve﴾: They permitted in the *i'rab* (grammatical analysis) of *yastabshirun* that it be conjoined to *fariheen* and *mustabshirin* (rejoicing), as in His saying, ﴿ranks and seizing [their wings]﴾ [al-Mulk: 19], meaning *qabidat* (seizing). Or that it be on the basis of an implied subject. The *waw* is for the circumstantial, so it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *fariheen*, or from the object pronoun in *atahum*, or it is for conjunction, and it is an independent clause, by way of conjoining a nominal or verbal clause to its counterpart.

*In* here is the light (*mukhaffafah*) form of the heavy *inna*, its noun is an omitted pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), and its predicate is the negated clause with *la*. What follows it is in the sense of a verbal noun in the genitive, as an inclusive substitute (*badal ishtimal*) for *alladhina* (those who), so that it is in reality what is rejoiced over. Or it is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*), so that it is the cause of the rejoicing, and what is rejoiced over is something else. The estimate is: "because there is no fear upon them." Essences are not rejoiced over, so a suitable omitted noun must be estimated. The explanation of "there is no fear upon them, nor do they grieve" has already been given, so it is not repeated here.

In mentioning the state of the martyrs and their rejoicing over those behind them, there is an incitement for those who remain after them to increase in obedience, to exert themselves in jihad, to desire attaining the ranks of the martyrs and obtaining their merit, and a praise of the condition of one who sees himself in good, so that he wishes the same for his brothers in Allah, and good tidings to the believers of success in the return. This is what al-Zamakhshari said, and it is a fine statement.

It has been said: these verses include types of *badi'* (rhetorical embellishment): *tibaq* (antithesis) in His saying, ﴿Allah certainly conferred favour upon the believers﴾ and so on, since the estimate is: Allah conferred favour upon them by guidance, so that is in this implied element. And in His saying, ﴿in manifest error﴾, and in ﴿they say with their mouths﴾, where "say" is evident, and ﴿they conceal﴾. And in ﴿they said to their brothers while they sat [at home]﴾, since the estimate is: when they went out and they sat, themselves. And in ﴿dead? Nay, they are alive﴾, and in *fariheen* and *yahzanun* (rejoicing and grieving). And the repetition in ﴿and that He might know the believers﴾ and ﴿and that He might know those who are hypocrites﴾, the difference being in what the knowledge relates to. And in *fariheen* and *yastabshirun*, and *tajnis* (paronomasia) that is different in ﴿a misfortune has struck you﴾, and the similar kind in ﴿it has struck you, and you had struck [them] twice as much﴾. And the interrogation that is intended as denial in ﴿Why, when a misfortune has struck you﴾. And the rational argument in ﴿Say: "Avert from yourselves [death]"﴾. And emphasis in ﴿nor do they grieve﴾. And ellipsis in several places, where the meaning is not complete except by estimating it.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 3, verses 171–173 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿They rejoice in a blessing from Allah and bounty, and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾ ﴿those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after the wound had befallen them; for those among them who did good and were mindful of Allah there is a great reward﴾ ﴿those to whom people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them." But it increased them in faith and they said, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"﴾ ﴿So they returned with a blessing from Allah and bounty; no harm touched them, and they followed the pleasure of Allah. And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 174] ﴿That is only the Shaytan who frightens his allies, so do not fear them but fear Me, if you are believers﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 175] ﴿And do not let those who race to disbelief grieve you. Indeed, they will never harm Allah at all. Allah intends not to give them a share in the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 176] ﴿Indeed, those who exchange disbelief for faith will never harm Allah at all, and for them is a painful punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 177] ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that Our granting them respite is good for them. We only grant them respite so that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 178] ﴿Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good. And Allah would not inform you of the unseen, but Allah chooses from His messengers whom He wills. So believe in Allah and His messengers, and if you believe and are mindful of Allah, for you is a great reward﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 179] ﴿And let not those who withhold what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them. Rather, it is bad for them. They will be encircled by what they withheld on the Day of Resurrection. And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 180].

*al-ḥaẓẓ* (ḥaẓẓ, "portion"): the share. When it is not qualified, it is used only for good. *Māza* and *mayyaza* (to distinguish): to separate one thing from another. Ya'qub said: they are two forms with one meaning. End of quote. The doubling (in *mayyaza*) is not for causing the action to be transitive. It was said: the intensive form is closer to grandeur and more common in usage. Do you not see that they used the verbal noun in accordance with the intensive form, saying *al-tamyīz*, and did not say *al-mayz*? End of quote. He means: they did not say it as something heard; but by analogy it may be said. It was said: *māza* is used only of many from many, whereas one from one is distinguished in the sense of "separating." For this reason Abu Mu'adh said: one says *mayyaztu bayna shay'ayn* ("I distinguished between two things"), and *miztu bayna al-ashyā'* ("I distinguished between the things").

*ijtabā*: chose and selected. It is from *jabaytu al-māʾ wa-l-māl* and *jabawtuhumā*, and then *ijtabā* is its *iftaʿala* form derived from it. So the radical *lām* may be a *wāw* or a *yā'*.

﴿They rejoice in a blessing from Allah and bounty, and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾: He repeated the verb for emphasis, if the blessing and bounty are an explanation of the object of the first rejoicing. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. He said: He repeated "they rejoice" in order to attach to it what explains His saying: ﴿that no fear will be upon them nor will they grieve﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 170], namely the mention of the blessing and bounty, and that this is their reward for their faith, which in Allah's justice and wisdom must be granted to them and not wasted. End of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (the school holding that reward is obligatory upon Allah) in his mention of the obligation of reward and its attainment for their faith. Ibn 'Atiyya took the path of Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni majority), and said: He emphasized their rejoicing by His saying "they rejoice," then He explained by His saying "and bounty" that the admission into Paradise, which is bounty from Him and not by the deed of anyone. As for the blessing in Paradise and the ranks, He has informed that they are according to the measure of deeds. End of quote.

Others said: it is a substitute (*badal*) for the first, which is why the conjunctive *wāw* was not attached to it. As for the one who holds that the clause is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to the pronoun in *yaḥzanūn*, with *yaḥzanūn* being its governing verb, this is far from the correct view, because the apparent meaning is the difference between that from which grief is negated and the one who rejoices, and because a *ḥāl* is restricted while grief is not restricted. The apparent meaning is that His saying "they rejoice" is not an emphasis of the first, but a new independent clause (*istiʾnāf*) connected to the people themselves, not to those who had not yet joined them. The two verbs therefore differ in their objects, so there is no emphasis, because this thing they rejoice in is theirs: Allah's blessing upon them and His bounty. In the indefiniteness there is an indication of an unspecified part, and an allusion to the vagueness of the intended meaning, to magnify the matter and to draw attention to the difficulty of grasping it, as in the hadith: "In it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." The apparent meaning is that "blessing" and "bounty" are different by the conjunction, and it fits to explain them by His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best (reward) and an increase﴾ [Yunus: 26]. So "the best" is the blessing, and "the increase" is the bounty, by the indicator of His saying "who did good," and His saying: ﴿for those among them who did good and were mindful of Allah there is a great reward﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: the blessing is the reward, and the bounty is what exceeds it in the amount of the reward. It was said: the blessing is the sufficient provision, and the bounty is what is multiplied upon it together with the multiplication of joy and pleasure in it. It was said: bounty is included within blessing, indicating its vastness and that it is not like the blessings of this world.

Al-Kisa'i and a group read "wa-inna Allāh" with a *kasra* on the *hamza*, as a new independent clause, and the reading of 'Abd Allah and his codex supports it: "wa-Allāh lā yuḍī'u ajra" ("and Allah does not waste the reward of"). Al-Zamakhshari said: and it is also possible that the clause is a parenthetical insertion (*iʿtirāḍ*), and this is the reading of al-Kisa'i. End of quote. But the clause here is not a parenthetical insertion, because it did not come between two things one of which depends upon the other; it came only to begin a new statement. The remaining seven readers and the majority read it with a *fatḥa* on the *hamza*, as a conjunction to the object of the rejoicing, so it is included within it. Abu 'Ali said: they rejoice at the full provision of that to them and its reaching them, because if He does not waste it, it reaches them and they are not deprived of it. Rejoicing cannot be (in the sense) that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers, because rejoicing occurs only with what was not previously known, and they had known before their death that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers. So they rejoice that Allah did not waste their rewards, in that He singled them out with martyrdom, granted them the completion of blessing, and sealed for them with salvation and success. They had been fearful for their faith, and feared a bad ending that nullifies deeds. When they saw what the believers have with Allah of happiness, and what He singled them out with of a good ending in which rewards are valid and deeds are multiplied, they rejoiced, because they had been anxious about that. End of his words. In it there is a lengthiness resembling oratory. It was said: it is also possible that the rejoicing is for those they left behind of the believers, when they witnessed their station with Allah.

﴿those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after the wound had befallen them; for those among them who did good and were mindful of Allah there is a great reward﴾: It was said: the response was the aftermath of the withdrawal from Uhud. The Messenger called for pursuit of the disbelievers, and ninety responded to him. That was when it was mentioned to the Messenger that Abu Sufyan was with a large gathering. The Messenger refused except to pursue them, but Abu Sufyan outran him and entered Makkah, and then this was revealed. This was said by 'Amr ibn Dinar. There is disagreement about the mention of this occasion in several places. It was also said: the response was in the following year after the affair of Uhud, when Abu Sufyan and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agreed to meet at the season of Badr. When the following year came, Abu Sufyan went out and was frightened, and it seemed to him best to return. He said to Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud: "I promised Muhammad and his companions that we would meet at the season of Badr al-Sughra (the Lesser Badr). It is a year of drought that is not suitable for us, so discourage them from us and inform them that we are in a large host." He did so and frightened them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out with his companions, and they remained at Badr waiting for Abu Sufyan, and then this was revealed. Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said this in its meaning.

It was also said: when it was the second day after Uhud, which was Sunday, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out to the people to follow the polytheists, and said: "None shall go out with us except those who witnessed us yesterday." The people had injury and grave wounds, but they bore it with endurance. Two hundred men of the believers set out with him until he reached Hamra' al-Asad, which is eight miles from Madinah, and he remained there three days. The story of Ma'bad ibn Abi Ma'bad occurred, which has been mentioned, and the Quraysh passed by, and the Messenger returned to Madinah, and then this was revealed. It is narrated that two brothers went out, and both had severe wounds, and one of them became weak, so his brother carried him for a stretch and walked for a stretch. Since the response of the servant to Allah is not complete except by his response to the Messenger, He combined the two, because what the obligation cannot be fulfilled without is itself obligatory. It was said: the two responses are different, for they are, in relation to Allah, through monotheism and worship, and in relation to the Messenger, through receiving the message from him and giving him sincere counsel. The apparent meaning is that it is one response, namely their answering him when he called them to pursue the disbelievers, as narrated in the account of the revelation's occasion. The *iḥsān* (doing good) here is what is in addition to faith, by characterizing oneself with what is recommended (*mustaḥabb*) together with characterizing oneself with what is obligatory.

The apparent parsing (*i'rāb*, grammatical analysis) is that "alladhīna" is in the nominative as a subject (*mubtada'*), and the clause after it is the predicate (*khabar*). They allowed its following as an adjective (*na't*) or substitute (*badal*), or breaking off into the nominative or accusative. As for *min* in "minhum" (among them), al-Zamakhshari said: it is for specification (*tabyīn*), like it in His saying: ﴿Allah has promised those who believed and did righteous deeds, among them, forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Fath: 29], because those who responded to Allah and the Messenger all did good and were mindful of Allah, except for some of them. From 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr: 'A'ishah said to me: "Indeed your two parents (*abawaka*) are among those who responded to Allah and the Messenger." She meant Abu Bakr and al-Zubayr. End of quote. Abu al-Baqa' said: "minhum" is a circumstantial element (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in *aḥsanū*. On this view, *min* is for partitioning (*tab'īḍ*), and this is the view of one who does not hold that *min* can be for explaining the genus (*bayān al-jins*).

﴿those to whom people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them." But it increased them in faith and they said, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"﴾: It was said: the first "people" refers to Abu Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i. This is the view of Ibn Qutaybah, and Ibn 'Atiyya weakened it. The second "people" refers to Abu Sufyan. The account of Nu'aym has already been mentioned. The commentators narrated it at length, and in it: Abu Sufyan had granted him a reward for discouraging the Companions from Badr al-Sughra, which was ten camels, guaranteed to him by Suhayl ibn 'Amr. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), frightened the people, and made them fear the encounter. The Messenger (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, I will indeed go out, even if alone." As for the coward, he returned; as for the brave, he prepared for battle and said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." They reached Badr al-Sughra and began to meet the polytheists and ask them about the Quraysh. They would say: "They have gathered against you." It was the site of a market for them in the Jahiliyyah, where they gathered every year for eight days. He remained at Badr waiting for Abu Sufyan, who had returned from Majannah to Makkah. The people of Makkah called the expedition's retreat "the army of the sawīq (roasted grain drink)." They said: "You only went out to drink sawīq." The Companions had trade and provisions with them, so they sold, and gained two dirhams for each dirham, and returned to Madinah as booty-takers. The Messenger reckoned it for them as a raid (*ghazwah*). In the course of that, he captured Mu'awiyah ibn al-Mughirah ibn al-'As and Abu 'Izzah al-Jumahi and killed them. According to this view, the one who discouraged was Abu Nu'aym alone, and "the people" was applied to him figuratively, because he is of the same kind as people, as one says: "So-and-so rides horses and wears striped garments," while he has only one horse and one garment. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. He also said: because when he said that, there were people from the people of Madinah who joined him, supported his words, and were discouraged in the same way as his discouragement. End of quote. This does not fit under the supposition of the question, namely that Nu'aym alone was the discourager, because people had joined him, so he would not then be alone in the discouragement.

Some say: the first people were a group from Abd al-Qays who passed by Abu Sufyan, intending to go to Madinah for provisions. He offered them a reward, which was the load of their camels of raisins, on condition that they inform (the Muslims) that he had gathered (forces) to completely eradicate the remnant of the believers. They informed them of this, and the Messenger and his companions, who at that time were at Hamra' al-Asad, said: ﴿Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian.﴾ The second people are the Quraysh. This view is closer to the apparent meaning of the wording.

They allowed, in the parsing of "alladhina qala" (those who said), several possibilities: that "alladhina" refers to the people mentioned before it. The subject of "zada" (increased) is a concealed pronoun referring to the verbal noun understood from "qala" (said), meaning: that statement increased them in faith. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it refers to the statement, and that it refers to the people when "Nu'aym" alone is intended. Both are weak: the first, because the statement increases faith only by being uttered, not in itself; and the second, because when the singular is referred to by a plural word metaphorically, the pronouns follow that plural, not the singular. So one says "mafariquhu shabat" (its parting-places have turned grey), considering the report about the group, and one does not say "mafariquhu shab" (its parting-place has turned grey), considering "mafraquhu" (his parting) as singular.

The apparent meaning of the wording is that faith increases. Its meaning here is that that statement increased them in steadfastness and readiness, so the increase of faith in this sense is in deeds. The scholars differed on this. One group said: it increases and decreases with regard to acts of obedience, since they are fruits of faith, and it decreases through disobedience; this is the position of Malik, and it is attributed to al-Shafi'i. Another group said: it increases with regard to acts of the heart, such as intention, sincerity, fear and sincere counsel. Another group said: it increases through the evidences, their multiplicity and their convergence upon one belief. Another group said: it increases through the revelation of obligations and reports during the lifetime of the Messenger. Another group said: it does not accept increase or decrease; this is the position of Abu Hanifah, and al-Baqillani related it from al-Shafi'i. Abu al-Ma'ali said in "al-Irshad": its increase is in terms of its persistence and its constant recurrence, since it is an accident that does not endure for two moments; so for the righteous it is continuously successive, and for the wicked and the heedless it is not successive. This is the meaning of increase and decrease. Another group held what the text expresses, namely that it increases and does not decrease; this is the position of the Mu'tazilah. A similar view is related from Ibn al-Mubarak. What appears to be correct is that when faith is intended as affirmation (tasdiq) and is connected to a single object, increase and decrease are impossible in it; rather, that varies according to its objects, not its essence. The proofs for these views are mentioned in the books that contain this issue, and some scholars devoted a separate book to it.

Since there preceded from the discouragers a report that Quraysh had gathered against you, and a command from them to you to fear them because of this gathering they had assembled, two things followed from this statement. One is inward: the increase of faith, which corresponds to the command to fear. He informed that tranquillity was produced in the heart, which counters fear. Then he informed of what counters the gathering of people, namely that the one who suffices them against the evil of people is Allah, Exalted is He. Then they praised Him, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿and He is the best Guardian﴾, indicating that their saying "Allah is sufficient for us" is an expression of extreme reliance upon Him and of entrusting their affairs to Him, Exalted is He. Observe the excellence and eloquence of this speech, in that one statement is answered by another, and the object of one heart is matched by the object of another heart.

The discussion of "hasb" (sufficient) has already occurred in His saying: ﴿so Hell is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206], and from the saying of them: "ahsabahu al-shay'" (the thing sufficed him), meaning it satisfied him. "Hasb" in the sense of "muhsib," i.e., sufficing, is used and intended with the meaning of the active participle. Do you not see that it is used as a descriptive, so you say: "marartu bi-rajulin hasbuka min rajulin," meaning: one who suffices you? So you describe an indefinite noun with it, since its annexation is not definite, because it has the meaning of the active participle that is not past and not bare of "al". And he said:

"Wa-hasbuka min ghinan shibaʿin wa-riyyi"

meaning: sufficient for you. "Al-Wakil" is on the pattern "fa'il" in the sense of "maf'ul," i.e., one to whom affairs are entrusted. It is said: this hasbalah (saying "hasbuna Allah") was the statement of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when he was thrown into the fire. The object of praise is omitted because the meaning is understood; the estimate is: "and the best Guardian is Allah." Ibn al-Anbari said: "al-Wakil" is the Lord; this was said by a group. End of quote. The meaning is that it is among the names of His attributes, Exalted is He, just as you say: "al-Qahhar" is Allah. It is also said: it means the Protector and the Guardian, and this returns to the meaning of one to whom affairs are entrusted. Al-Farra' said: "al-Wakil" is the Guarantor.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 3, verses 171–173 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿They rejoice in a blessing from Allah and bounty, and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾ ﴿those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after the wound had befallen them; for those among them who did good and were mindful of Allah there is a great reward﴾ ﴿those to whom people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them." But it increased them in faith and they said, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"﴾ ﴿So they returned with a blessing from Allah and bounty; no harm touched them, and they followed the pleasure of Allah. And Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 174] ﴿That is only the Shaytan who frightens his allies, so do not fear them but fear Me, if you are believers﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 175] ﴿And do not let those who race to disbelief grieve you. Indeed, they will never harm Allah at all. Allah intends not to give them a share in the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 176] ﴿Indeed, those who exchange disbelief for faith will never harm Allah at all, and for them is a painful punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 177] ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that Our granting them respite is good for them. We only grant them respite so that they may increase in sin, and for them is a humiliating punishment﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 178] ﴿Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good. And Allah would not inform you of the unseen, but Allah chooses from His messengers whom He wills. So believe in Allah and His messengers, and if you believe and are mindful of Allah, for you is a great reward﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 179] ﴿And let not those who withhold what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them. Rather, it is bad for them. They will be encircled by what they withheld on the Day of Resurrection. And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 180].

*al-ḥaẓẓ* (ḥaẓẓ, "portion"): the share. When it is not qualified, it is used only for good. *Māza* and *mayyaza* (to distinguish): to separate one thing from another. Ya'qub said: they are two forms with one meaning. End of quote. The doubling (in *mayyaza*) is not for causing the action to be transitive. It was said: the intensive form is closer to grandeur and more common in usage. Do you not see that they used the verbal noun in accordance with the intensive form, saying *al-tamyīz*, and did not say *al-mayz*? End of quote. He means: they did not say it as something heard; but by analogy it may be said. It was said: *māza* is used only of many from many, whereas one from one is distinguished in the sense of "separating." For this reason Abu Mu'adh said: one says *mayyaztu bayna shay'ayn* ("I distinguished between two things"), and *miztu bayna al-ashyā'* ("I distinguished between the things").

*ijtabā*: chose and selected. It is from *jabaytu al-māʾ wa-l-māl* and *jabawtuhumā*, and then *ijtabā* is its *iftaʿala* form derived from it. So the radical *lām* may be a *wāw* or a *yā'*.

﴿They rejoice in a blessing from Allah and bounty, and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾: He repeated the verb for emphasis, if the blessing and bounty are an explanation of the object of the first rejoicing. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. He said: He repeated "they rejoice" in order to attach to it what explains His saying: ﴿that no fear will be upon them nor will they grieve﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 170], namely the mention of the blessing and bounty, and that this is their reward for their faith, which in Allah's justice and wisdom must be granted to them and not wasted. End of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (the school holding that reward is obligatory upon Allah) in his mention of the obligation of reward and its attainment for their faith. Ibn 'Atiyya took the path of Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni majority), and said: He emphasized their rejoicing by His saying "they rejoice," then He explained by His saying "and bounty" that the admission into Paradise, which is bounty from Him and not by the deed of anyone. As for the blessing in Paradise and the ranks, He has informed that they are according to the measure of deeds. End of quote.

Others said: it is a substitute (*badal*) for the first, which is why the conjunctive *wāw* was not attached to it. As for the one who holds that the clause is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to the pronoun in *yaḥzanūn*, with *yaḥzanūn* being its governing verb, this is far from the correct view, because the apparent meaning is the difference between that from which grief is negated and the one who rejoices, and because a *ḥāl* is restricted while grief is not restricted. The apparent meaning is that His saying "they rejoice" is not an emphasis of the first, but a new independent clause (*istiʾnāf*) connected to the people themselves, not to those who had not yet joined them. The two verbs therefore differ in their objects, so there is no emphasis, because this thing they rejoice in is theirs: Allah's blessing upon them and His bounty. In the indefiniteness there is an indication of an unspecified part, and an allusion to the vagueness of the intended meaning, to magnify the matter and to draw attention to the difficulty of grasping it, as in the hadith: "In it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." The apparent meaning is that "blessing" and "bounty" are different by the conjunction, and it fits to explain them by His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best (reward) and an increase﴾ [Yunus: 26]. So "the best" is the blessing, and "the increase" is the bounty, by the indicator of His saying "who did good," and His saying: ﴿for those among them who did good and were mindful of Allah there is a great reward﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: the blessing is the reward, and the bounty is what exceeds it in the amount of the reward. It was said: the blessing is the sufficient provision, and the bounty is what is multiplied upon it together with the multiplication of joy and pleasure in it. It was said: bounty is included within blessing, indicating its vastness and that it is not like the blessings of this world.

Al-Kisa'i and a group read "wa-inna Allāh" with a *kasra* on the *hamza*, as a new independent clause, and the reading of 'Abd Allah and his codex supports it: "wa-Allāh lā yuḍī'u ajra" ("and Allah does not waste the reward of"). Al-Zamakhshari said: and it is also possible that the clause is a parenthetical insertion (*iʿtirāḍ*), and this is the reading of al-Kisa'i. End of quote. But the clause here is not a parenthetical insertion, because it did not come between two things one of which depends upon the other; it came only to begin a new statement. The remaining seven readers and the majority read it with a *fatḥa* on the *hamza*, as a conjunction to the object of the rejoicing, so it is included within it. Abu 'Ali said: they rejoice at the full provision of that to them and its reaching them, because if He does not waste it, it reaches them and they are not deprived of it. Rejoicing cannot be (in the sense) that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers, because rejoicing occurs only with what was not previously known, and they had known before their death that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers. So they rejoice that Allah did not waste their rewards, in that He singled them out with martyrdom, granted them the completion of blessing, and sealed for them with salvation and success. They had been fearful for their faith, and feared a bad ending that nullifies deeds. When they saw what the believers have with Allah of happiness, and what He singled them out with of a good ending in which rewards are valid and deeds are multiplied, they rejoiced, because they had been anxious about that. End of his words. In it there is a lengthiness resembling oratory. It was said: it is also possible that the rejoicing is for those they left behind of the believers, when they witnessed their station with Allah.

﴿those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after the wound had befallen them; for those among them who did good and were mindful of Allah there is a great reward﴾: It was said: the response was the aftermath of the withdrawal from Uhud. The Messenger called for pursuit of the disbelievers, and ninety responded to him. That was when it was mentioned to the Messenger that Abu Sufyan was with a large gathering. The Messenger refused except to pursue them, but Abu Sufyan outran him and entered Makkah, and then this was revealed. This was said by 'Amr ibn Dinar. There is disagreement about the mention of this occasion in several places. It was also said: the response was in the following year after the affair of Uhud, when Abu Sufyan and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agreed to meet at the season of Badr. When the following year came, Abu Sufyan went out and was frightened, and it seemed to him best to return. He said to Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud: "I promised Muhammad and his companions that we would meet at the season of Badr al-Sughra (the Lesser Badr). It is a year of drought that is not suitable for us, so discourage them from us and inform them that we are in a large host." He did so and frightened them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out with his companions, and they remained at Badr waiting for Abu Sufyan, and then this was revealed. Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said this in its meaning.

It was also said: when it was the second day after Uhud, which was Sunday, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out to the people to follow the polytheists, and said: "None shall go out with us except those who witnessed us yesterday." The people had injury and grave wounds, but they bore it with endurance. Two hundred men of the believers set out with him until he reached Hamra' al-Asad, which is eight miles from Madinah, and he remained there three days. The story of Ma'bad ibn Abi Ma'bad occurred, which has been mentioned, and the Quraysh passed by, and the Messenger returned to Madinah, and then this was revealed. It is narrated that two brothers went out, and both had severe wounds, and one of them became weak, so his brother carried him for a stretch and walked for a stretch. The apparent meaning is that it is one response, namely their answering him when he called them to pursue the disbelievers, as narrated in the account of the revelation's occasion. They allowed its following as an adjective (*na't*) or substitute (*badal*), or breaking off into the nominative or accusative.
