﴿They rejoice in a blessing from Allah and bounty, and that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers﴾: He repeated the verb for emphasis, if the blessing and bounty are an explanation of the object of the first rejoicing. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. He said: He repeated "they rejoice" in order to attach to it what explains His saying: ﴿that no fear will be upon them nor will they grieve﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 170], namely the mention of the blessing and bounty, and that this is their reward for their faith, which in Allah's justice and wisdom must be granted to them and not wasted. End of quote. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilah (the school holding that reward is obligatory upon Allah) in his mention of the obligation of reward and its attainment for their faith. Ibn 'Atiyya took the path of Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni majority), and said: He emphasized their rejoicing by His saying "they rejoice," then He explained by His saying "and bounty" that the admission into Paradise, which is bounty from Him and not by the deed of anyone. As for the blessing in Paradise and the ranks, He has informed that they are according to the measure of deeds. End of quote.

Others said: it is a substitute (*badal*) for the first, which is why the conjunctive *wāw* was not attached to it. As for the one who holds that the clause is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to the pronoun in *yaḥzanūn*, with *yaḥzanūn* being its governing verb, this is far from the correct view, because the apparent meaning is the difference between that from which grief is negated and the one who rejoices, and because a *ḥāl* is restricted while grief is not restricted. The apparent meaning is that His saying "they rejoice" is not an emphasis of the first, but a new independent clause (*istiʾnāf*) connected to the people themselves, not to those who had not yet joined them. The two verbs therefore differ in their objects, so there is no emphasis, because this thing they rejoice in is theirs: Allah's blessing upon them and His bounty. In the indefiniteness there is an indication of an unspecified part, and an allusion to the vagueness of the intended meaning, to magnify the matter and to draw attention to the difficulty of grasping it, as in the hadith: "In it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived." The apparent meaning is that "blessing" and "bounty" are different by the conjunction, and it fits to explain them by His saying: ﴿For those who did good is the best (reward) and an increase﴾ [Yunus: 26]. So "the best" is the blessing, and "the increase" is the bounty, by the indicator of His saying "who did good," and His saying: ﴿for those among them who did good and were mindful of Allah there is a great reward﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: the blessing is the reward, and the bounty is what exceeds it in the amount of the reward. It was said: the blessing is the sufficient provision, and the bounty is what is multiplied upon it together with the multiplication of joy and pleasure in it. It was said: bounty is included within blessing, indicating its vastness and that it is not like the blessings of this world.

Al-Kisa'i and a group read "wa-inna Allāh" with a *kasra* on the *hamza*, as a new independent clause, and the reading of 'Abd Allah and his codex supports it: "wa-Allāh lā yuḍī'u ajra" ("and Allah does not waste the reward of"). Al-Zamakhshari said: and it is also possible that the clause is a parenthetical insertion (*iʿtirāḍ*), and this is the reading of al-Kisa'i. End of quote. But the clause here is not a parenthetical insertion, because it did not come between two things one of which depends upon the other; it came only to begin a new statement. The remaining seven readers and the majority read it with a *fatḥa* on the *hamza*, as a conjunction to the object of the rejoicing, so it is included within it. Abu 'Ali said: they rejoice at the full provision of that to them and its reaching them, because if He does not waste it, it reaches them and they are not deprived of it. Rejoicing cannot be (in the sense) that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers, because rejoicing occurs only with what was not previously known, and they had known before their death that Allah does not waste the reward of the believers. So they rejoice that Allah did not waste their rewards, in that He singled them out with martyrdom, granted them the completion of blessing, and sealed for them with salvation and success. They had been fearful for their faith, and feared a bad ending that nullifies deeds. When they saw what the believers have with Allah of happiness, and what He singled them out with of a good ending in which rewards are valid and deeds are multiplied, they rejoiced, because they had been anxious about that. End of his words. In it there is a lengthiness resembling oratory. It was said: it is also possible that the rejoicing is for those they left behind of the believers, when they witnessed their station with Allah.

﴿those who responded to Allah and the Messenger after the wound had befallen them; for those among them who did good and were mindful of Allah there is a great reward﴾: It was said: the response was the aftermath of the withdrawal from Uhud. The Messenger called for pursuit of the disbelievers, and ninety responded to him. That was when it was mentioned to the Messenger that Abu Sufyan was with a large gathering. The Messenger refused except to pursue them, but Abu Sufyan outran him and entered Makkah, and then this was revealed. This was said by 'Amr ibn Dinar. There is disagreement about the mention of this occasion in several places. It was also said: the response was in the following year after the affair of Uhud, when Abu Sufyan and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) agreed to meet at the season of Badr. When the following year came, Abu Sufyan went out and was frightened, and it seemed to him best to return. He said to Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud: "I promised Muhammad and his companions that we would meet at the season of Badr al-Sughra (the Lesser Badr). It is a year of drought that is not suitable for us, so discourage them from us and inform them that we are in a large host." He did so and frightened them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out with his companions, and they remained at Badr waiting for Abu Sufyan, and then this was revealed. Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said this in its meaning.

It was also said: when it was the second day after Uhud, which was Sunday, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called out to the people to follow the polytheists, and said: "None shall go out with us except those who witnessed us yesterday." The people had injury and grave wounds, but they bore it with endurance. Two hundred men of the believers set out with him until he reached Hamra' al-Asad, which is eight miles from Madinah, and he remained there three days. The story of Ma'bad ibn Abi Ma'bad occurred, which has been mentioned, and the Quraysh passed by, and the Messenger returned to Madinah, and then this was revealed. It is narrated that two brothers went out, and both had severe wounds, and one of them became weak, so his brother carried him for a stretch and walked for a stretch. Since the response of the servant to Allah is not complete except by his response to the Messenger, He combined the two, because what the obligation cannot be fulfilled without is itself obligatory. It was said: the two responses are different, for they are, in relation to Allah, through monotheism and worship, and in relation to the Messenger, through receiving the message from him and giving him sincere counsel. The apparent meaning is that it is one response, namely their answering him when he called them to pursue the disbelievers, as narrated in the account of the revelation's occasion. The *iḥsān* (doing good) here is what is in addition to faith, by characterizing oneself with what is recommended (*mustaḥabb*) together with characterizing oneself with what is obligatory.

The apparent parsing (*i'rāb*, grammatical analysis) is that "alladhīna" is in the nominative as a subject (*mubtada'*), and the clause after it is the predicate (*khabar*). They allowed its following as an adjective (*na't*) or substitute (*badal*), or breaking off into the nominative or accusative. As for *min* in "minhum" (among them), al-Zamakhshari said: it is for specification (*tabyīn*), like it in His saying: ﴿Allah has promised those who believed and did righteous deeds, among them, forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Fath: 29], because those who responded to Allah and the Messenger all did good and were mindful of Allah, except for some of them. From 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr: 'A'ishah said to me: "Indeed your two parents (*abawaka*) are among those who responded to Allah and the Messenger." She meant Abu Bakr and al-Zubayr. End of quote. Abu al-Baqa' said: "minhum" is a circumstantial element (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in *aḥsanū*. On this view, *min* is for partitioning (*tab'īḍ*), and this is the view of one who does not hold that *min* can be for explaining the genus (*bayān al-jins*).

﴿those to whom people said, "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them." But it increased them in faith and they said, "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs"﴾: It was said: the first "people" refers to Abu Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i. This is the view of Ibn Qutaybah, and Ibn 'Atiyya weakened it. The second "people" refers to Abu Sufyan. The account of Nu'aym has already been mentioned. The commentators narrated it at length, and in it: Abu Sufyan had granted him a reward for discouraging the Companions from Badr al-Sughra, which was ten camels, guaranteed to him by Suhayl ibn 'Amr. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), frightened the people, and made them fear the encounter. The Messenger (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, I will indeed go out, even if alone." As for the coward, he returned; as for the brave, he prepared for battle and said: "Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs." They reached Badr al-Sughra and began to meet the polytheists and ask them about the Quraysh. They would say: "They have gathered against you." It was the site of a market for them in the Jahiliyyah, where they gathered every year for eight days. He remained at Badr waiting for Abu Sufyan, who had returned from Majannah to Makkah. The people of Makkah called the expedition's retreat "the army of the sawīq (roasted grain drink)." They said: "You only went out to drink sawīq." The Companions had trade and provisions with them, so they sold, and gained two dirhams for each dirham, and returned to Madinah as booty-takers. The Messenger reckoned it for them as a raid (*ghazwah*). In the course of that, he captured Mu'awiyah ibn al-Mughirah ibn al-'As and Abu 'Izzah al-Jumahi and killed them. According to this view, the one who discouraged was Abu Nu'aym alone, and "the people" was applied to him figuratively, because he is of the same kind as people, as one says: "So-and-so rides horses and wears striped garments," while he has only one horse and one garment. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. He also said: because when he said that, there were people from the people of Madinah who joined him, supported his words, and were discouraged in the same way as his discouragement. End of quote. This does not fit under the supposition of the question, namely that Nu'aym alone was the discourager, because people had joined him, so he would not then be alone in the discouragement.

Some say: the first people were a group from Abd al-Qays who passed by Abu Sufyan, intending to go to Madinah for provisions. He offered them a reward, which was the load of their camels of raisins, on condition that they inform (the Muslims) that he had gathered (forces) to completely eradicate the remnant of the believers. They informed them of this, and the Messenger and his companions, who at that time were at Hamra' al-Asad, said: ﴿Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Guardian.﴾ The second people are the Quraysh. This view is closer to the apparent meaning of the wording.

They allowed, in the parsing of "alladhina qala" (those who said), several possibilities: that "alladhina" refers to the people mentioned before it. The subject of "zada" (increased) is a concealed pronoun referring to the verbal noun understood from "qala" (said), meaning: that statement increased them in faith. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it refers to the statement, and that it refers to the people when "Nu'aym" alone is intended. Both are weak: the first, because the statement increases faith only by being uttered, not in itself; and the second, because when the singular is referred to by a plural word metaphorically, the pronouns follow that plural, not the singular. So one says "mafariquhu shabat" (its parting-places have turned grey), considering the report about the group, and one does not say "mafariquhu shab" (its parting-place has turned grey), considering "mafraquhu" (his parting) as singular.

The apparent meaning of the wording is that faith increases. Its meaning here is that that statement increased them in steadfastness and readiness, so the increase of faith in this sense is in deeds. The scholars differed on this. One group said: it increases and decreases with regard to acts of obedience, since they are fruits of faith, and it decreases through disobedience; this is the position of Malik, and it is attributed to al-Shafi'i. Another group said: it increases with regard to acts of the heart, such as intention, sincerity, fear and sincere counsel. Another group said: it increases through the evidences, their multiplicity and their convergence upon one belief. Another group said: it increases through the revelation of obligations and reports during the lifetime of the Messenger. Another group said: it does not accept increase or decrease; this is the position of Abu Hanifah, and al-Baqillani related it from al-Shafi'i. Abu al-Ma'ali said in "al-Irshad": its increase is in terms of its persistence and its constant recurrence, since it is an accident that does not endure for two moments; so for the righteous it is continuously successive, and for the wicked and the heedless it is not successive. This is the meaning of increase and decrease. Another group held what the text expresses, namely that it increases and does not decrease; this is the position of the Mu'tazilah. A similar view is related from Ibn al-Mubarak. What appears to be correct is that when faith is intended as affirmation (tasdiq) and is connected to a single object, increase and decrease are impossible in it; rather, that varies according to its objects, not its essence. The proofs for these views are mentioned in the books that contain this issue, and some scholars devoted a separate book to it.

Since there preceded from the discouragers a report that Quraysh had gathered against you, and a command from them to you to fear them because of this gathering they had assembled, two things followed from this statement. One is inward: the increase of faith, which corresponds to the command to fear. He informed that tranquillity was produced in the heart, which counters fear. Then he informed of what counters the gathering of people, namely that the one who suffices them against the evil of people is Allah, Exalted is He. Then they praised Him, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿and He is the best Guardian﴾, indicating that their saying "Allah is sufficient for us" is an expression of extreme reliance upon Him and of entrusting their affairs to Him, Exalted is He. Observe the excellence and eloquence of this speech, in that one statement is answered by another, and the object of one heart is matched by the object of another heart.

The discussion of "hasb" (sufficient) has already occurred in His saying: ﴿so Hell is sufficient for him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206], and from the saying of them: "ahsabahu al-shay'" (the thing sufficed him), meaning it satisfied him. "Hasb" in the sense of "muhsib," i.e., sufficing, is used and intended with the meaning of the active participle. Do you not see that it is used as a descriptive, so you say: "marartu bi-rajulin hasbuka min rajulin," meaning: one who suffices you? So you describe an indefinite noun with it, since its annexation is not definite, because it has the meaning of the active participle that is not past and not bare of "al". And he said:

"Wa-hasbuka min ghinan shibaʿin wa-riyyi"

meaning: sufficient for you. "Al-Wakil" is on the pattern "fa'il" in the sense of "maf'ul," i.e., one to whom affairs are entrusted. It is said: this hasbalah (saying "hasbuna Allah") was the statement of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, when he was thrown into the fire. The object of praise is omitted because the meaning is understood; the estimate is: "and the best Guardian is Allah." Ibn al-Anbari said: "al-Wakil" is the Lord; this was said by a group. End of quote. The meaning is that it is among the names of His attributes, Exalted is He, just as you say: "al-Qahhar" is Allah. It is also said: it means the Protector and the Guardian, and this returns to the meaning of one to whom affairs are entrusted. Al-Farra' said: "al-Wakil" is the Guarantor.

So they returned with a blessing from Allah and bounty, no harm touching them, and they followed the pleasure of Allah; and Allah is the possessor of tremendous bounty. That is, they returned from Badr accompanied by a blessing from Allah, namely safety and the enemy's fear of them, and bounty, namely profit in trade, like His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198]. This is what al-Zamakhshari chose as the explanation of this "returning," and he mentioned no other. It is also the view of Mujahid. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The majority hold that the meaning of this verse, "they returned with a blessing," is: in safety and in gaining the upper hand, and in pursuing the enemy and protecting the territory, and "with bounty" is: in the reward they obtained and the honour they earned. They hold that it was revealed concerning the expedition of Uhud, at the going out to Hamra' al-Asad. Mujahid deviated and said: it was about the Prophet's ﷺ going out to Badr al-Sughra, and he mentioned the story of Nu'aym and Abu Sufyan. He said: The correct view is what the majority said, that this verse was revealed concerning the expedition of Hamra' al-Asad. End of his words.

The discussion of this verse is built on the disagreement over His saying: ﴿Those who responded to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [Al 'Imran: 172], which has already been mentioned when its exegesis was discussed. Some scholars distinguished between *inqilab* (turning over, transformation) and *ruju'* (returning), on the basis that *inqilab* is the thing becoming the opposite of what it was. He said: This is clarified by the fact that you say, "The wine turned into vinegar" (*inqalabat al-khamr khallan*), and you do not say, "The wine returned as vinegar" (*raja'at al-khamr khallan*). End of his words. There is room to examine this.

It was also said: the blessing is the reward. This was said by Mujahid. It was said: it is well-being and victory. This was said by al-Zajjaj. It was said: the bounty is the profit of trade. This was said by Mujahid, al-Suddi and al-Zuhri, and the report of this view from Mujahid has already been mentioned. It was said: they encountered a detachment at al-Safra' and were provided for from it. This was said by Muqatil. It was said: it is the reward. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The clause ﴿no harm touched them﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: safe. And "with a blessing" is also a circumstantial phrase, because the *ba'* in it is the *ba'* of accompaniment (*ba' al-musahaba*), meaning: they returned enjoying favour, safe. A circumstantial clause negated with *lam* and containing a pronoun referring back to the subject (*dhu al-hal*) may be introduced by *waw* or may be left without it. An example of the first is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or who says, "It has been revealed to me," while nothing has been revealed to him﴾ [al-An'am: 93], and the words of the poet:

Do not hold me to account for the words of slanderers, though I have committed no sin, even if many sayings are spread about me.

An example of the second is His saying: ﴿And Allah turned back those who disbelieved in their rage; they gained no good﴾ [al-Ahzab: 25], and the words of Qays ibn al-Aslat:

I strike the crown of the head on the day of battle with the sword, and my arm does not fall short with it.

Ustadh Abu al-Hasan ibn Kharuf erred in this matter. He claimed that when the clause is past in meaning but not in form, it requires *waw* if it contains a pronoun, and it did not contain one here. But the usage in the Arabic language is what we have mentioned.

Their following the pleasure of Allah consists of their going out to the enemy, their boldness, and their obedience to the Messenger ﷺ. He concluded it with His saying: ﴿and Allah is the possessor of tremendous bounty﴾, which corresponds to His saying: ﴿with a blessing from Allah and bounty﴾. He bestowed upon them His favour by facilitating and granting success in what they did. In this there is also a rebuke for those who stayed behind from going out, since they deprived themselves of what these people attained of reward in the Hereafter and of fine praise in this world. It is reported that they said: "Would this count as a military expedition?" So Allah, exalted is He, granted them the reward of a military expedition and was pleased with them. This is the outcome of entrusting their affair to Him, exalted is He: He recompensed them with His blessing, His bounty, their safety, and their following of His pleasure.

(p-120) "It is only Satan who frightens you of his allies, so do not fear them, but fear Me, if you are believers." (3:175)

"Ma" here is the one that prevents inna from governing (al-ma al-kaffa) from acting on the verb. Most of the scholars of usul al-fiqh claim that when it is not a relative (mawsulah), it confers restriction (al-hasr) together with inna. "Dhalikum" is a reference to the dismounted riders who discouraged the believers. It has been said that by "al-Shaytan" is meant Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, or Abu Sufyan. On these opinions the reference is to particular persons. It has also been said that "dhalikum" refers to everything that occurred of the news of the Abd al-Qays riders concerning the message of Abu Sufyan, and Abu Sufyan's conveying of that statement, and the anxiety of whoever among the believers or the wavering was anxious because of it. On this view the reference is to meanings, and it is necessary then to posit an omitted modifier (mudaf), whose estimate is: "It is only the deed of Satan that is that." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "the saying of Satan," i.e., the saying of Iblis. On this estimate the reference is to the preceding statement, namely that "the people have gathered against you, so fear them." On all these opinions, the predicate about the subject "dhalikum" being "al-Shaytan" is metaphorical (majaz), because the persons are not themselves Satan, nor is what passed as speech only, or speech alone. What was joined to it of the frightening that came from the enemy, and the anxiety that came forth, is not the very saying of Satan nor his deed; rather it was attributed and ascribed to him, because it arises from his whisperings, his seduction and his casting.

The doubling in "yukhawwif" is for transitivity (li-al-naql). Before it, it was transitive to one object; when it was doubled it became transitive to two. It is one of the verbs whose two objects may be omitted; and one of them is either an abbreviation (iqtisar) or an abridgement (ikhtisar), or here it is transitive to one and the other is omitted. It is permissible that the first is the one that is omitted, and the estimate would be: "he frightens you of his allies," i.e., the evil of his allies on this aspect, because the persons themselves do not fear; and the ones frightened would then be the believers. It is also permissible that the omitted one is the second object, i.e., "he frightens his allies of the evil of the disbelievers," and "his allies" on this aspect are the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease, who held back from going out with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), meaning that his frightening does not reach beyond the hypocrites, and his frightening does not reach you. On the first aspect, his allies are the disbelievers: Abu Sufyan and those with him. This aspect is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, "yukhawwifukum awliyahu," since in it appears that the omitted one is the first object. Ubayy and al-Nakha'i read "yukhawwifukum bi-awliya'ihi," so it is permissible that the ba' is extra, like it in "yaqra'na bi-al-suwar," and the second object would be "bi-awliya'ihi," i.e., "awliyahu," like the reading of the majority. It is also permissible that the ba' is for causation, and the second object of "yukhawwif" is omitted, i.e., "he frightens you the evil through his allies," so that they are instruments of the frightening. Some grammarians have taken the reading of the majority, "yukhawwif awliyahu," to mean that the estimate is "bi-awliyihi," so that the two objects of "yukhawwif" would then have been omitted, the meaning indicating the omission, and the estimate would be: "he frightens you the evil through his allies." This is distant. The best parsing is that "dhalikum" is the subject (mubtada'), and "al-Shaytan" its predicate. "Yukhawwif" is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), and the coming of a singular accusative in the place of this clause indicates that it is a circumstance, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So those are their houses, empty﴾ (27:52), and ﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾ (11:72). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "al-Shaytan" be a substitute (badal) or an explanatory apposition (atf bayan), and that "bi-khawf" be the predicate about "dhalikum." Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-Shaytan" is the predicate of "dhalikum," in the sense of: "It is only that discourager who is Satan," and "yukhawwif awliyahu" is a resumptive clause explaining his discouragement; or "al-Shaytan" is an adjective of the demonstrative, and "yukhawwif" is the predicate. The intended "al-Shaytan" is Nu'aym or Abu Sufyan. End of his words. On this view the clause has no place in the parsing. He only said "the intended al-Shaytan is Nu'aym or Abu Sufyan" because it cannot be an adjective; and the intended one is Iblis, because if Iblis is intended, it is then a proper noun by predominance, since its origin is an adjective, like al-Ayyuq, which then became predominant over the star by which it is named.

Ibn Atiyya said: "dhalikum" in parsing is a beginning (ibtida'), and "al-Shaytan" is another beginning, and "yukhawwif awliyahu" is a predicate about "al-Shaytan," and the clause is the predicate of the first beginning. This parsing is preferable in harmony of meaning, since it would come in meaning as a distant metaphor if "al-Shaytan" were the predicate of "dhalikum." End of his words. This parsing that he chose is not permissible if the pronoun in "awliyahu" refers to Satan, because the clause that falls as a predicate about "dhalikum" contains no resumptive pronoun linking it to "dhalikum," and it is not the very subject in meaning, like the saying of the people: "The habitual saying of Abu Bakr is: There is no god but God." But if it refers back to "dhalikum," and that is about Satan, it is permissible, and it becomes like: "It is only Hind, Zayd beats her servant." The meaning then: It is only that riding party, or Abu Sufyan, who is Satan, who frightens you of his allies, i.e., the allies of the riding party or of Abu Sufyan. The pronoun in "takhafuhum," in its apparent reference, returns to "awliyahu," if by His saying "awliyahu" is meant the disbelievers of Quraysh and others among the allies of Satan. If by it is meant the hypocrites, then it returns to "the people" in His saying: ﴿Indeed the people have gathered against you﴾ (3:173). He strengthened the souls of the Muslims, so He forbade them from fearing the allies of Satan, and commanded them to fear Him, exalted is He, and tied that to faith. That is, the quality of faith suits that the believer fear none but God, as in His saying: ﴿and they fear none but God﴾ (33:39). He expressed this condition in the form of possibility, though it is actual, since they are characterised by faith, as you say: "If you are a man, then do such-and-such." Abu 'Amr affirmed the ya' of "wakhafun," which is the object pronoun, and the original is affirmation. It is permissible to omit it for pausing on the nun of protection with sukun, so that the indication of the omitted one is lost.

It is one of the verbs whose two objects may be omitted; and one of them is either an abbreviation (iqtisar) or an abridgement (ikhtisar), or here it is transitive to one and the other is omitted. It is permissible that the first is the one that is omitted, and the estimate would be: "he frightens you of his allies," i.e., the evil of his allies on this aspect, because the persons themselves do not fear; and the ones frightened would then be the believers. It is also permissible that the omitted one is the second object, i.e., "he frightens his allies of the evil of the disbelievers," and "his allies" on this aspect are the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease, who held back from going out with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), meaning that his frightening does not reach beyond the hypocrites, and his frightening does not reach you. On the first aspect, his allies are the disbelievers: Abu Sufyan and those with him. This aspect is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas, "yukhawwifukum awliyahu," since in it appears that the omitted one is the first object. Ubayy and al-Nakha'i read "yukhawwifukum bi-awliya'ihi," so it is permissible that the ba' is extra, like it in "yaqra'na bi-al-suwar," and the second object would be "bi-awliya'ihi," i.e., "awliyahu," like the reading of the majority. It is also permissible that the ba' is for causation, and the second object of "yukhawwif" is omitted, i.e., "he frightens you the evil through his allies," so that they are instruments of the frightening. Some grammarians have taken the reading of the majority, "yukhawwif awliyahu," to mean that the estimate is "bi-awliyihi," so that the two objects of "yukhawwif" would then have been omitted, the meaning indicating the omission, and the estimate would be: "he frightens you the evil through his allies." This is distant. The best parsing is that "dhalikum" is the subject (mubtada'), and "al-Shaytan" its predicate. "Yukhawwif" is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), and the coming of a singular accusative in the place of this clause indicates that it is a circumstance, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So those are their houses, empty﴾ (27:52), and ﴿And this is my husband, an old man﴾ (11:72). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "al-Shaytan" be a substitute (badal) or an explanatory apposition (atf bayan), and that "bi-khawf" be the predicate about "dhalikum." Al-Zamakhshari said: "al-Shaytan" is the predicate of "dhalikum," in the sense of: "It is only that discourager who is Satan," and "yukhawwif awliyahu" is a resumptive clause explaining his discouragement; or "al-Shaytan" is an adjective of the demonstrative, and "yukhawwif" is the predicate. The intended "al-Shaytan" is Nu'aym or Abu Sufyan. End of his words. On this view the clause has no place in the parsing. He only said "the intended al-Shaytan is Nu'aym or Abu Sufyan" because it cannot be an adjective; and the intended one is Iblis, because if Iblis is intended, it is then a proper noun by predominance, since its origin is an adjective, like al-Ayyuq, which then became predominant over the star by which it is named.

Ibn Atiyya said: "dhalikum" in parsing is a beginning (ibtida'), and "al-Shaytan" is another beginning, and "yukhawwif awliyahu" is a predicate about "al-Shaytan," and the clause is the predicate of the first beginning. This parsing is preferable in harmony of meaning, since it would come in meaning as a distant metaphor if "al-Shaytan" were the predicate of "dhalikum." End of his words. This parsing that he chose is not permissible if the pronoun in "awliyahu" refers to Satan, because the clause that falls as a predicate about "dhalikum" contains no resumptive pronoun linking it to "dhalikum," and it is not the very subject in meaning, like the saying of the people: "The habitual saying of Abu Bakr is: There is no god but God." But if it refers back to "dhalikum," and that is about Satan, it is permissible, and it becomes like: "It is only Hind, Zayd beats her servant." The meaning then: It is only that riding party, or Abu Sufyan, who is Satan, who frightens you of his allies, i.e., the allies of the riding party or of Abu Sufyan. The pronoun in "takhafuhum," in its apparent reference, returns to "awliyahu," if by His saying "awliyahu" is meant the disbelievers of Quraysh and others among the allies of Satan. If by it is meant the hypocrites, then it returns to "the people" in His saying: ﴿Indeed the people have gathered against you﴾ (3:173). He strengthened the souls of the Muslims, so He forbade them from fearing the allies of Satan, and commanded them to fear Him, exalted is He, and tied that to faith. That is, the quality of faith suits that the believer fear none but God, as in His saying: ﴿and they fear none but God﴾ (33:39). He expressed this condition in the form of possibility, though it is actual, since they are characterised by faith, as you say: "If you are a man, then do such-and-such." Abu 'Amr affirmed the ya' of "wakhafun," which is the object pronoun, and the original is affirmation. It is permissible to omit it for pausing on the nun of protection with sukun, so that the indication of the omitted one is lost.

(p-120) "It is only Satan who frightens you of his allies, so do not fear them, but fear Me, if you are believers." (3:175)

"Ma" here is the one that prevents inna from governing (al-ma al-kaffa) from acting on the verb. Most of the scholars of usul al-fiqh claim that when it is not a relative (mawsulah), it confers restriction (al-hasr) together with inna. "Dhalikum" is a reference to the dismounted riders who discouraged the believers. It has been said that by "al-Shaytan" is meant Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud, or Abu Sufyan. On these opinions the reference is to particular persons. It has also been said that "dhalikum" refers to everything that occurred of the news of the Abd al-Qays riders concerning the message of Abu Sufyan, and Abu Sufyan's conveying of that statement, and the anxiety of whoever among the believers or the wavering was anxious because of it. On this view the reference is to meanings, and it is necessary then to posit an omitted modifier (mudaf), whose estimate is: "It is only the deed of Satan that is that." Al-Zamakhshari estimated it as: "the saying of Satan," i.e., the saying of Iblis. On this estimate the reference is to the preceding statement, namely that "the people have gathered against you, so fear them." **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 178 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And let not those who race to disbelief grieve you. Indeed, they will never harm Allah at all﴾ [Al-Imran: 176]: When He forbade the believers from fearing the allies of Satan, and commanded them to fear Him alone, the Exalted, He forbade His Messenger from grieving over the hastening of those who hasten into disbelief. The meaning: he should not anticipate grief or harm from them. Therefore He justified it by His saying: ﴿Indeed, they will never harm Allah at all﴾, that is, they will never harm the Prophet of Allah and the believers. The harm negated here is a specific harm, namely the annulment of Islam and its plotting until it vanishes; this will never happen. Rather, their affair will vanish, and your affair will prevail over them.

It was said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. It was said: it was revealed concerning a people who apostatized. It was said: the intended ones are the disbelievers of Quraysh. It was said: the leaders of the Jews. The better view is to take it in its generality, as in His saying: ﴿O Messenger, let not those who race to disbelief grieve you﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 41]. It was also said: what stirs the grief is his compassion and his preference for their Islam, so that he might rescue them from the Fire; so he was forbidden from excessiveness in that, as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿So let not your soul go out in regret over them﴾ [Fatir: 8], and His saying: "Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers." This is from the abundance of his mercy toward people and his tenderness toward them.

Nafi' read ﴿yuhzinka﴾ from the form ahzana (to cause grief), and likewise wherever the imperfect occurs, except in ﴿They will not be grieved by the greatest terror﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 103], which he read from the form hazina, like the reading of the majority throughout the Qur'an. It is said: hazina al-rajulu means the man was struck by grief; hazantuhu means I made grief enter him; and ahzantuhu means I made him grieved. An-Nahwi read ﴿yusri'una﴾ from asra'a throughout the Qur'an. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the reading of the majority is more eloquent, because one who hastens others is more diligent than one who hastens alone. Within His saying ﴿Indeed, they will never harm Allah at all﴾ is an indication that the consequence of that returns upon them, and they harm only themselves. The word shay'an is in the accusative as an infinitive (maf'ul mutlaq), meaning "any harm." It was said: its accusative is by the omission of the preposition, meaning "anything."

﴿Allah intends not to give them any share in the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment﴾ [Al-Imran: 176]: The Exalted explained that what they are upon of hastening into disbelief is by the will of Allah, the Exalted, that He will not guide them to faith, so that they would have a portion of the bliss of the Hereafter. This is a consolation from Him, the Exalted, to His Prophet ﷺ regarding abandoning war; for Allah's intention concerning them is what they are upon, and in place of bliss there is for them a great punishment. Az-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Was it said: Allah will not give them any share in the Hereafter, and what is the benefit of mentioning the will? (I say): Its benefit is to indicate that the motive for their deprivation and punishment has become so pure that no diverting factor remains with it at all, when they hasten into disbelief, alerting to their persistence in rebellion and their reaching its utmost limit, to the extent that the Most Merciful of the merciful wills not to show mercy to them. End of quote. In this there is a trace of Mu'tazilite doctrine, for he sensed that His, the Exalted's, will that He not give them a share in the Hereafter entails that the cause of that is something He wills, namely disbelief. According to his school, He, the Exalted, does not will disbelief nor desire it; so he interpreted the connection of His will to the negation of their share in the Hereafter as its connection to the negation of His mercy toward them because of the excess of their disbelief.

Al-Mawardi related three opinions regarding "yurid" (intends): First: that He decrees this. Second: He intends in the Hereafter to deprive them of their reward, because their deeds are nullified by their disbelief. Third: He intends to nullify their deeds for the sins they have deserved. This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

﴿Indeed, those who have purchased disbelief in exchange for faith will never harm Allah at all, and for them is a painful punishment﴾ [Al-Imran: 177]: This is general concerning all disbelievers. His saying ﴿And let not those who race to disbelief grieve you﴾ [Al-Imran: 176] was general, so this is repeated for the sake of emphasis; and even if it was specific to the hypocrites or the apostates or the disbelievers of Quraysh, this is not a repetition for emphasis, but rather a ruling upon the general category that they will never harm Allah at all. That specific category is also included within it, so the ruling regarding them is for emphasis, and it has combined for the specific group the punishment in both its kinds of greatness and pain, and this is more forceful against them regarding punishment. He made that a purchase from the standpoint of their capacity to accept good and evil, so they preferred disbelief over faith.

﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that Our giving them respite is good for themselves. Rather, We give them respite only that they may increase in sin﴾: The meaning of numli is: We grant respite and extend them in life. Al-mula'ah is a period of time, and al-malawan are the night and the day. It is said: mallaka Allah ni'matahu, meaning He granted it to him as a long life. Hamzah read ﴿la yahsabanna﴾ with the second-person address (ta' of address), so that ﴿alladhina kafaru﴾ is the first object. ﴿Anna ma numli lahum khayrun﴾ cannot be in the position of the second object, because the infinitive of the second object in this construction is, in meaning, the first, and an infinitive cannot be the essence; so it is taken as the omission of a modifier from the first, meaning: "Let not the affair of those who disbelieve..." or from the second, meaning: "Let not those who disbelieve consider that the respite is good for them" until it is correct for the second to be the first. Ibn al-Badhish and az-Zamakhshari construed it so that ﴿anna ma numli lahum khayrun li-anfusihim﴾ is a substitute (badal) for alladhina. Ibn al-Badhish said: the second object is omitted, being indicated by the context, and the estimate is: "Let not those who disbelieve [think] that the goodness of Our respite for them is existent or occurring." Az-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): How is the substitute valid when only one of the two objects was mentioned, and it is not permissible to limit the verb of thinking to one object? (I say): It is valid because the reliance is upon the substitute and the substituted-from, which are in the status of what is set aside; do you not see that you say: "I placed your goods, some of them upon others," together with the impossibility of your being silent on "your goods." End of his words. This construal which Ibn al-Badhish and az-Zamakhshari gave was preceded to it by al-Kisa'i and al-Farra', who said the basis of this reading is repetition and emphasis, the estimate being: "Let not those who disbelieve [think], and let them not think that We give them respite." Al-Farra' said: a parallel to it is ﴿Do they await only the Hour, that it come upon them suddenly?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 66], meaning: "They await only that it come upon them." End of his words. Some scholars explained the words of al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' and said: omitting the second object of these verbs is not permissible according to anyone, so it is an error from both of them. End of his words.

We have already elaborated at length on omitting one of the two objects of ẓanna, in what preceded from az-Zamakhshari's statement regarding His saying ﴿And do not think those who were killed in the way of Allah to be dead﴾ [Al-Imran: 169], that its estimate is: "and do not think them [to be dead]." We mentioned there that the view of Ibn Malkun is that this is not permissible, and that the view of the majority is permissibility; but it is extremely rare, so that it is not found in the Arabic language except infrequently, and that the Qur'an should be exalted above it. Abu Ishaq az-Zajjaj construed this reading as a substitute, but the apparent sense of his words is that it is with the accusative of khayrun. He said: a great many people have read with it, and he cited as an example the poet's verse:

*Qays's ruin was not the ruin of one man, but it was the building of a people that collapsed.*

with the accusative of the second hulk, the first being a substitute. On this basis, "anna ma numli" is a substitute, and "khayran" is the second object, i.e., "Our respite is good." Abu Bakr ibn Mujahid denied this reading which az-Zajjaj related, and claimed that no one had read with it. Ibn Mujahid is the authority referred to in the field of readings.

Abu Hatim said: I heard al-Akhfash mention the ugliness of using this reading as evidence for the Qadariyya, because he was one of them, and he made it by inversion and reordering, as if he said: "Let not those who disbelieve think that We give them respite only that they may increase in sin; that We give them respite is good for themselves." End of quote. According to al-Akhfash's view, ﴿anna ma numli lahum li-yazdadu ithman﴾ is in the position of the second object, and ﴿anna ma numli lahum khayrun﴾ is a subject and predicate, meaning "Our respite of them is good for themselves." Beginning with anna (with fatha) was permitted, because al-Akhfash's school allows that. Because of the difficulty of this reading, Abu Hatim and others claimed it was a solecism (lahn) and rejected it. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the alif of "inna ma" should be kasra in this reading, and "inna and what follows it" would be in the position of the second object. Makki said in his (Mushkil): I know of no one who read "la tahsabanna" with the ta' from above and the kasra of the alif of "inna ma." The remaining seven and the majority read "la yahsabanna" with the ya', and the grammatical analysis of this reading is clear, because the subject is "alladhina kafaru," and ﴿anna ma numli lahum khayrun﴾ fills the place of the two objects of yahsabanna, as you say: "I thought that Zayd is standing." "Ma" in this reading and in the one before it may be a relative pronoun meaning "alladhi," or a verbal-infinitive (masdariyya), meaning: "that which We respite," with the returning pronoun omitted, and in this there is the condition for permissibility of omission, namely that it be a connected object of a complete verb and necessarily linked; or "that Our respite is good." Some permitted that the verb be ascribed to the Prophet ﷺ, so that the subject of the absent form is like the subject of the address form, and the two readings would have one meaning.

Yahya ibn Wathhab read "wa la yahsabanna" with the ya', and "innama numli" with the kasra. If the verb is ascribed to the Prophet ﷺ, then the first object is alladhina kafaru, and "innama numli lahum" is a clause in the position of the second object. If it is ascribed to alladhina kafaru, then yahsabanna requires two objects. Had "anna ma" been with fatha, it would have filled the place of the two objects; but Yahya read with kasra, so it was construed as ta'liq (suspension), so the alif of inna was made kasra, even though the lam is not within its scope. The clause from which the verb is suspended is in the position of the two objects of yahsabanna, and this is far-fetched because of the omission of the lam, analogous to the suspension of the verb from action, together with the omission of the lam from the subject, as in the poet's verse:

*Indeed I have found the foundation of disposition to be good manners.*

meaning: "Surely the foundation of disposition is good manners," and had it not been for the belief in omitting the lam, it would have been in the accusative. Az-Zamakhshari related that Yahya ibn Wathhab read with the kasra of the first "innama" and the fatha of the second. The meaning of this is: "Let not those who disbelieve think that We respite them only that they may increase in sin, as they do; but it is only that they may repent and enter into faith." The clause "anna ma numli lahum khayrun li-anfusihim" is a parenthetical insertion between the verb and its complement, and its meaning is: "Our respite is good for them if they act upon it and recognize Allah's favor upon them by widening the term and refraining from hastening punishment." The apparent sense of "alladhina kafaru" is generality.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning the Jews, the Christians, and the hypocrites. 'Ata' said: concerning Qurayzah and an-Nadir. Muqatil said: concerning the polytheists of Makkah. Az-Zajjaj said: these are a people whom Allah informed His Prophet that they will never believe, and it is not about every disbeliever, since respite may be of that which brings him into faith, so it would be better for him. Makki said: this is the correct of the meanings. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the meaning of this verse is a refutation of the disbelievers in their saying: that our being dominant, wealthy, and healthy is evidence of Allah's pleasure with our state and the soundness of our way with Him. Allah, the Exalted, informed that this delay and neglect is only a respite and gradual leading on in order to increase their sins. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: there is no soul, pious or wicked, but death is better for it: as for the pious one, let it hasten toward the mercy of Allah, and he recited: ﴿And what is with Allah is better for the righteous﴾ [Al-Imran: 198]; and as for the wicked one, lest it increase in sin, and he recited this verse. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-imla' (the granting of respite) for them means leaving them alone, and the expression is borrowed from *amla li-faraslhi*, when one loosens the tether for his horse so that it may graze as it wishes. It was also said that it means giving them respite and prolonging their lives. The meaning is that the respite is better for them than withholding it from them or cutting short their terms. *Innama numli lahum* is a new clause (*jumla mustani'fa*) explaining the clause before it, as if it were said: 'Why do they reckon that the respite is good for them?' And it is answered: '*Innama numli lahum liyazdadu ithman*' (We grant them respite only so that they may increase in sin). (If you ask): How can the increase in sin be a purpose (*gharad*) for God, the Exalted, in His granting them respite? (I answer): It is the cause (*'illa*) of the respite, and not every cause is a purpose. Do you not see that you say: 'I stayed back from the raid because of incapacity and poverty, and I left the town for fear of harm,' and none of these is your purpose; rather they are causes and reasons. Likewise, the increase in sin has been made a cause of the respite and a reason for it. (If you ask): How can the increase in sin be a cause of the respite, as incapacity was a cause of staying back from war? (I answer): Since it was in the all-encompassing knowledge of God that they would increase in sin, the respite occurred for its sake and because of it, by way of metaphor (*majaz*). End of his words. All of it proceeds according to the method of the al-Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites, a rationalist theological school)."

"Al-Maturidi said: The Mu'tazilah took it in two ways. One of them is by inversion of order (*taqdim wa ta'khir*), i.e.: 'And let not those who disbelieve reckon that *innama numli lahum liyazdadu ithman*; *innama numli lahum* is better for their souls.' The second: this is a report from Him, glorified and exalted, about their reckoning concerning what their affair will end in, in the sense that they reckon that their being given respite in this world, and their being granted health, safety and wealth, is good for their souls in the end; rather, the outcome of that is evil. In the first interpretation there is a corruption of the wording (*ifsad al-nazm*), and in the second there is an alerting of one who should not be alerted, for reporting about the outcome occurs through heedlessness or negligence at the beginning, and the one who knows from the beginning does not alert himself." End of his words.

"They wrote *ma* joined to *anna* in both places. It was said: the more proper approach in the science of orthography would have been to write it separately, but it occurs in the Imam (the standard 'Uthmanic codex) joined, so it is not opposed, and we follow the practice of the Imam in the mushafs. As for the second *ma*, its correct form is to be written joined, because it is *kaffa* (a restraining particle) without governing action, and it cannot be a relative (*mawsula* bi-ma'na alladhi) nor a verbal-source particle (*masdariyya*), because the necessary consequence is that it cannot validly occur as the predicate of a subject or of its abrogating particles (*nawasikh*). It was also said: the *lam* in *liyazdadu* is for becoming (*lil-sayyura*)."

﴿And for them is a humiliating punishment﴾: "This *wa* in *wa lahum* is for conjunction (*lil-'atf*)." Al-Zamakhshari said: "(If you ask): What is the meaning of His saying '*wa lahum 'adhabun muhin*' according to this reading, meaning the reading of Yahya ibn Wathhab with *kasr* on the first *innama* and *fath* on the second? (I answer): Its meaning is: 'And do not reckon that our granting them respite is for an increase in sin and for punishment,' and the *wa* is for the circumstantial (*lil-hal*). As if it were said: 'That they may increase in sin, with a humiliating punishment prepared for them.'" End of his words.

"Those who transmitted the reading of Yahya did not mention that anyone read the second with *fath* except him; they only mention that he read the first with *kasr*. But al-Zamakhshari, in his eagerness to support his school, seeks to bring everything back to it. When he established in this reading that the meaning is a prohibition on the disbeliever from reckoning that God grants them respite for an increase in sin, and that He grants it only for the sake of good, then His saying '*wa lahum 'adhabun muhin*' contradicts this interpretation, so he construed it as the *wa* being circumstantial, to remove this contradiction between this reading and the apparent sense at the end of the verse."

"God, the Exalted, described His punishment at the endings of these three verses as: *'azim* (great), *alim* (painful), and *muhin* (humiliating). Each of these attributes has a fitting relation that calls for ending the verse with it. As for the first, hastening toward a thing, hurrying to obtain it and adorning oneself with it, requires the magnificence of what is hastened toward and that it is of such preciousness and greatness that people compete for it; so the verse is ended with the greatness of the reward, which is their recompense for hastening into disbelief, indicating the baseness of what they competed for. As for the second, He mentioned there the purchase of disbelief with faith, and it is customary for the buyer to rejoice in what he has bought, to be pleased with it and to be glad; so the verse is ended by the fact that his bargain has lost, with the pain of punishment, as the defrauded buyer finds in his trade. As for the third, He mentioned the granting of respite, which is the enjoyment of wealth, sons and health, and this enjoyment was a cause of prestige, pleasure and capability; so the verse is ended with the humiliation of punishment for them. And the respite that produces in this world prestige and arrogance has its end in the Hereafter in their humiliation through a punishment that humbles tyrants."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 179:

﴿Allah would not leave the believers in the condition you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good.﴾ The address in "you are" (anthum) is to the believers, and the meaning is: "in the condition you are in, O believers, of mixing with the hypocrites, the confusion of their affair, and treating the hypocrite as if he were a believer. But He has distinguished some of them from others by what appeared from these and those of statements and actions." This was said by Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Ishaq. It was also said that the address is to the disbelievers, and the meaning is: "in the condition you are in, O disbelievers, of mixing with the believers." This was said by Qatadah and al-Suddi. Al-Suddi and others said: In some of their disputation, the disbelievers said: "You, O Muhammad, claim about a man among us that he is among the people of the Fire, and that if he follows you he is among the people of Paradise. How can this be valid? But inform us of who among us will believe and who will remain upon his disbelief." So this was revealed. It was said to them: "There must be distinction." Ibn Abbas and most of the exegetes said: the address is to the disbelievers and the hypocrites. It was also said: the address is to the believers and the disbelievers, and this is close to what al-Zamakhshari said. The most that can be said of it is that he replaced the disbelievers with the hypocrites. He said: "If you ask: To whom is the address in 'you are'? I answer: To all who affirm (the faith), both the sincere and the hypocrites. It is as if it were said: Allah would not leave your sincere ones in the state you are in of mixing some of you with others, and your sincere one would not be known from your hypocrite, because you all agree in professing belief, until He distinguishes them from you through revelation to His Prophet, by informing him of your conditions." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that it means: He would not leave you mixed together until He distinguishes the wicked from the good, by imposing upon you the difficult obligations which none endures except the sincere whose hearts Allah has tested, such as giving up souls in jihad and spending wealth in the way of Allah. Thus He makes that a criterion for your beliefs and a witness to your inner hearts, so that some of you know what is in the heart of others by way of inference, not by way of knowing the secrets of the breasts and having knowledge of them, for that is among what Allah has reserved for Himself." End. The meaning of this statement is that of Ibn Kaysan. Ibn Kaysan said: The meaning is: He would not leave you upon acknowledgment until He tests you with the laws and obligations. Al-Zamakhshari took this and the statement before it, and adorned both with his eloquence and fine oratory.

It was also said: The meaning is: Allah would not leave your children, whom He has judged to be believers, upon what you are of polytheism until He separates them from you. It was also said: They used to mock the believers in secret, so He said: He would not leave you in what you are of defaming them and mocking them, but He tests you so that you are exposed and your hypocrisy becomes clear to them, not in one abode, but He will make for them another abode in which He distinguishes the wicked from the good, so He places the wicked in the Fire and the good in Paradise. The wicked is the disbeliever, the good is the believer, and the distinguishing is by emigration and jihad. Mujahid said: the good is the believer and the wicked is the hypocrite; (p-126) He distinguished between them on the day of Uhud. It was also said: the wicked is the disbeliever and the good is the believer, and the distinguishing is by bringing one of them out from the loins of the other. It was also said: the distinguishing of the wicked is the removing of sins from the living believers through afflictions and calamities. It was also said: the wicked is the disobedient, and the good is the obedient. The alif-lam in "the wicked" (al-khabith) and "the good" (al-tayyib) is for the genus or for a known reference, since what was known at that time was that the wicked is the disbeliever and the good is the believer, as He said: ﴿Wicked women are for wicked men﴾ [al-Nur: 26], and so on.

The lam in His saying "li-yadhara" (so that He would leave) is what is called lam al-juhud (the lam of denial). According to the Kufans, it is an extra particle for emphasizing the negation, and it itself governs the subjunctive in the imperfect verb. The predicate of kana is the verb after it, so you say: "ma kana Zayd yaqumu" and "ma kana Zayd liyaqum" when you emphasize the negation. The view of the Basrans is that the predicate of kana is omitted, that the subjunctive after this lam is by a concealed "an" which is obligatorily concealed, and that the lam strengthens the requirement of that omitted element for what follows it. The estimate is: "Allah was not intending to leave the believers in what you are in," that is, He was not intending to leave the believers. We have discussed this issue in our book called al-Takmil fi Sharh al-Tashil. "Hatta" is for the bare limit (al-ghayah al-mujarradah), and the estimate is: "until He distinguishes them." Thus they said, and it is problematic if it is taken as a limit according to the apparent wording, because the meaning would be: He does not leave them mixed until He distinguishes, so that He would have limited the negation of leaving to the existence of distinguishing; when the distinguishing exists, He would leave them in the mixing they are in. This becomes like the saying: "I strike Zayd until 'Amr comes," whose implication is: when 'Amr comes, I strike Zayd. That is not the meaning of the verse. Rather, it is a limit for what the preceding speech includes of meaning that can validly be a limit for it. The meaning of "Allah would not leave the believers in what you are in" is that He, exalted, purifies what is among you through trial and testing, until He distinguishes the wicked from the good. The two brothers (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i) read ”يُمَيِّزَ“ (yumayyiza) from mayyaza, and the rest of the seven read ”يَمِيزَ“ (yamiza) from maza. In a narration from Ibn Kathir: ”يُمَيِّزُ“ (yumayyizu) from amaza, and the hamza is not for causation, just as the doubling is not for causation; rather af'ala and fa'ila have the meaning of the bare triliteral, like hazina and ahzana, and qadara Allah and qaddara.

﴿Nor would Allah disclose to you the unseen.﴾ Since He, exalted, has previously stated that it is He who distinguishes the wicked from the good, and that this distinguishing is not for them, He informed that He does not make any of the addressees acquainted with the unseen.

﴿But Allah chooses﴾: that is, selects and chooses.

﴿from among His messengers whom He wills﴾: so He informs him of what He wills of the unseen matters. The occurrence of "but" (lakinna) here is because what follows it is opposite to what precedes it in meaning, since the choosing of whomever He wills from among His messengers includes His informing him of what He intends of the knowledge of the unseen. The messenger's knowledge of the unseen is through Allah's informing him by revelation, so he tells that in the unseen there is such-and-such of the hypocrisy of this one and the sincerity of that one. He therefore knows it by way of revelation, not by way of making himself aware of the unseen matters without an intermediary of revelation. Al-Suddi and others said: "so that He may acquaint you with the unseen concerning who will believe and who will remain a disbeliever. But this is a chosen messenger." Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and others said: it concerns a particular matter, namely that He may let you know that you will be defeated, or that you will refrain from fighting. It was also said: so that He may let you know the hypocrites explicitly, naming them individually, but through indications of their actions and statements. The unseen here is what is hidden from humans of the events in Allah's knowledge that will happen, and of the secrets in the hearts of the hypocrites, and of the statements they make when they are away from people. Al-Zajjaj and others said: It was reported that some of the disbelievers said: "Why should not all of us be prophets?" So this was revealed. It was said: they said: "Why was revelation not sent to us regarding Muhammad?" So this was revealed. It was said: they said: "We have more wealth and children, so why was revelation not sent to us?" So this was revealed. It was said: the devils used to ascend to the heaven and eavesdrop, then bring its news to the soothsayers before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent, so Allah revealed this after his mission. "But Allah chooses whom He wills," that is, He makes him a messenger and reveals to him. That is, revelation from the heaven is not for anyone other than the prophets. The apparent meaning of the verse is what we have mentioned earlier: that He, exalted, is the one who distinguishes between the wicked and the good, and He informed that you yourselves do not perceive that, because He, exalted, has not made you aware of what (p-127) the hearts conceal of faith and hypocrisy; but He, exalted, chooses from among His messengers whom He wills and makes him aware of that, so you are informed of it through the messenger by his telling you of it through Allah's revelation. This is the meaning of what was also related from al-Suddi, that he said: "It has been decreed that this distinction will become manifest." Then by this verse He explained that it is not permissible that this distinction be placed among common people by Him making them aware of His unseen, so that they would say: "So-and-so is a hypocrite, and so-and-so is a believer." Rather, the sunnah of Allah, exalted, is that He does not make the common people aware, and they have no way to know that except through testing. As for knowing it by way of awareness of the unseen, that is among the special attributes of the prophets; for this reason He, exalted, said: "But Allah chooses from among His messengers whom He wills," so He singles them out by informing them that this one is a believer and this one is a hypocrite. All these statements and exegeses imply that this unseen which Allah has denied people knowledge of relates to the conditions of the believers and the hypocrites, and it is possible that this is meant in a general sense: that is, Allah would not make all of you knowers of the unseen matters in the way the Messenger knows, so that you would become independent of him; rather Allah singles out whom He wills of His servants for that, and he is the Messenger, so the conditions of the hypocrite and the believer fall under this general statement.

﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers﴾: since He mentioned that He chooses from among His messengers whom He wills and makes him aware of the unseen matters, He commanded belief in the one chosen. The one chosen and "whom He wills" is Muhammad (ﷺ), since his prophethood was established through Allah's informing him of the unseen matters and his telling you of them on more than one occasion. In His saying "and His messengers" the plural is used to draw attention to the fact that the way of establishing the prophethood of all the prophets is one, namely the appearance of a miracle at their hands. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers﴾: by affirming Him as He truly deserves, and making Him known as the sole one who is aware of the hidden matters; and by placing them in their proper stations, by knowing them as servants who are chosen, who know only what Allah has taught them, and who report only what Allah has informed them of the unseen, and who have no part in the knowledge of the unseen whatsoever. End.

﴿And if you believe and fear Allah, then for you is a great reward﴾: He made the attainment of the great reward conditional upon faith, and the meaning is: the faith that precedes, namely belief in Allah and His messengers, and upon piety, which is additional to faith. It seems that it is intended within the previous clause, as if it were said: "So believe in Allah and His messengers and fear Allah."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 180–184:

﴿Let not those who withhold what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them. Rather, it is evil for them.﴾ Al-Suddi and a group said: it was revealed concerning the withholding of wealth and not spending in the way of Allah. Ibn Abbas, in the narration of Atiyya, and Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and a group said, and al-Zajjaj preferred this view: it was revealed concerning the People of the Book and their miserliness, and their concealing what Allah had taught them about the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said: it was revealed concerning those who withhold the obligatory zakat. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayra, and Ibn Abbas in the narration of Abu Salih, al-Sha'bi and Mujahid. It was also said: it concerns the provision for dependents and close relatives.

Its connection with what precedes it is that, when Allah (exalted is He) had emphasized in the preceding verses the encouragement to give up lives in jihad, He began here to encourage the giving of wealth in jihad and otherwise, and He explained the severe warning for the one who is miserly. Miserliness in the legal sense (al-bukhl al-shar'i, i.e., the withholding of what is obligatory) is the refusal to give what is required.

Hamza read ﴿تَحْسَبَنَّ﴾ with a ta' (taHsabanna), so that ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ is the first object of tahsabanna, and this is by omission of a modifier, i.e., "the miserliness of those who..." The rest of the seven readers read it with a ya' (yaHsabanna). If the verb is ascribed to a pronoun, then the first object is omitted, its estimated form being "their miserliness" (bukhluhum), and it was omitted because of the indication of yabkhalun upon it. Its omission, as we have said, is very rare according to the majority; therefore the better way to explain this reading is to take it on the reading with the ta', with alladhina being the first object by omission of a modifier, and huwa being a separator (fasl). Al-A'mash read without "huwa," and khayran is the object of yahsabanna. Ibn Atiyya said: his saying "yabkhalun" indicates this omitted miserliness, just as "al-safih" (the foolish one) indicates folly in the poet's saying:

"When the foolish one forbids, he goes toward it and opposes, while the foolish one is toward opposition."

The meaning: he went toward folly. End of quote. The indication in these two is not the same, for two reasons. The first: in the verse the indicator is the verb, while in the verse of poetry it is the active participle, and the indication of the verb on the verbal noun is stronger than the indication of the active participle; therefore the omission of the verbal noun because of the verb is frequent in the Qur'an and Arabic speech, whereas the indication of the active participle on the verbal noun is not frequent; it occurs only in this line or elsewhere if found. The second: in the verse there is omission of an apparent element, since they estimated the omitted element as "bukhluhum," while in the poem it is a concealed pronoun, not an omission.

A strange construction appears clear to me in the verse, required by the rules of Arabic grammar: that the matter is of the type of i'mal (the doctrine of two verbs governing one noun, i'mal al-fi'layn), if we make the verb ascribed to alladhina. That is because tahsabanna requires two objects, and yabkhalun requires an object with a preposition. So his saying "ma atahum" is governed by yahsabanna, as its first object, and huwa is a separator, and khayran is the second object, and yabkhalun governs it through the intermediary of the preposition. The second verb was made to operate, according to the most eloquent usage in the language of the Arabs and what came in the Qur'an, which is "yabkhalun." Thus the operand of the preposition was made single, and the first operand of tahsabanna was omitted, and its second operand remained, since it was not in dispute; the dispute is only regarding the first object. Omitting it alone is permissible, just as omitting both objects is permissible in Sibawayh's example: "Whenever I saw, or said: Zayd is departing" — because "ra'aytu" and "qultu" in this example compete over "Zayd is departing." In the verse, they compete only over the single object. The meaning, estimated, is: "Do not let those who are miserly with what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it (the miserliness or what is withheld) is good for them." According to this estimation and explanation, huwa is a separator for "ma atahum" which is omitted, not for their estimated miserliness.

A parallel to this structure is: "I thought the one who passed by Hind was she who is departing." The meaning: I thought Hind, the person who passed by her, was the one departing. Thus the one over which both verbs compete is the first noun; the second verb operates, and the first remains seeking an omitted element, while the second object remains affirmed, since no dispute occurred over it.

Since the prohibition includes the negation of the withholding, or of what is withheld, being good for them, and under this negation are two divisions — one that there is neither good nor evil, and the other the affirmation of evil — the verse brought the sentence that specifies one of the two divisions, which is the affirmation that it is evil for them.

﴿They will be made to wear, on the Day of Resurrection, what they withheld﴾: This is an explanation of His saying ﴿Rather, it is evil for them﴾. The apparent reading is that it is to be taken figuratively, i.e., they will be bound to its punishment as a necklace binds, and in the proverb for one who brings a shameful thing: "wear it like the collar of the dove." Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: a collar of fire will be made for them on the Day of Resurrection. Mujahid and others said: it is from ability (al-taqah), not from encircling (al-taTwiq), and the meaning is: they will bear the punishment of what they withheld, like His saying ﴿and upon those who are able to fast (yutiqunahu)﴾ [al-Baqara: 184]. Mujahid also said: they will be charged to bring the like of what they withheld. This explanation does not fit His saying that the miserliness is the knowledge which Allah bestowed upon them concerning the matter of the Messenger. Abu Wa'il said: it is the man whom Allah provides with wealth, but who withholds from his relatives the right which Allah has assigned to them in his wealth; so it becomes a serpent which encircles him, and he says: what is between me and you? It says: I am your wealth. It has come in a hadith: "There is no possessor of kinship who comes to a relative of his, asking him for some surplus he has, and he is miserly toward him with it, except that there will be brought out for him on the Day of Resurrection a serpent of fire, licking its lips, until it encircles him." The hadiths on this matter, concerning the withholding of zakat and the hoarding of wealth, are many and sound.

﴿And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth﴾: Regarding this there are two views. The first: that He (exalted is He) has ownership of everything that comes into inheritance in the heavens and the earth, and that He is the true owner of it; so whatever comes to His creatures which is attributed to their ownership is in truth His ownership. This is what He owned, so why do you withhold something you are merely enjoying, not truly owning, as He said: ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾ [al-Hadid: 7]. The second view: that He informs of the annihilation of the world, and that all that they create is His inheritance. This is an address according to what human beings understand, indicating the annihilation of all, and that no owner remains but Allah, although His ownership over everything has never ceased.

﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾: He concluded with this attribute, and its meaning is a threat and a warning regarding the ugly sin they commit of miserliness. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿ya'malun﴾ (they do) in the third person, following "yabkhalun" and "sa-yutawwaquna." The rest read it with the ta' (ta'malun) in the second person as an iltifat (shift of address), so that it is an address to the miserly. Ibn Atiyya said: this is a return from the third person to the second person, since it was previously mentioned: ﴿And if you believe and fear Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 179]. End of quote. So it is not, according to his statement, an iltifat, though the iltifat is the better view.

These verses contain varieties of eloquence and rhetorical ornament: the particularization (ikhtisas) in "ajr al-mu'minin" (the reward of the believers). Repetition (takrar) in "yastabshirun," in "lan yadurru Allah shay'an," in His name in several places, in "la yahsabanna alladhina kafaru," and in the mention of respite (imla'). Antithesis (tibaq) in "ishtaraw al-kufr bi'l-iman," and in "li-yut'ligakum 'ala'l-ghayb." Metaphor (isti'ara) in "yusari'un," in "ishtaraw," in "numli," in "li-yazdadu ithman," and in "al-khabith wa'l-tayyib." Paronomasia of similar form (tajnis mumathil) in "fa-amanu" and "in tu'minu." Iltifat in "antum," if it is an address to the believers, since if it had followed the wording of the believers it would have been about them as they are; and if it is an address to others, it is a variation of address (talwin al-khitab). And in "ta'malun khabir," according to him who reads with the ta' of address. And omission in several places.
