This is what He owned, so why do you withhold something you are merely enjoying, not truly owning, as He said: ﴿And spend of that in which He has made you successors﴾ [al-Hadid: 7]. The second view: that He informs of the annihilation of the world, and that all that they create is His inheritance. This is an address according to what human beings understand, indicating the annihilation of all, and that no owner remains but Allah, although His ownership over everything has never ceased.

﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾: He concluded with this attribute, and its meaning is a threat and a warning regarding the ugly sin they commit of miserliness. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read ﴿ya'malun﴾ (they do) in the third person, following "yabkhalun" and "sa-yutawwaquna." The rest read it with the ta' (ta'malun) in the second person as an iltifat (shift of address), so that it is an address to the miserly. Ibn Atiyya said: this is a return from the third person to the second person, since it was previously mentioned: ﴿And if you believe and fear Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 179]. End of quote. So it is not, according to his statement, an iltifat, though the iltifat is the better view.

These verses contain varieties of eloquence and rhetorical ornament: the particularization (ikhtisas) in "ajr al-mu'minin" (the reward of the believers). Repetition (takrar) in "yastabshirun," in "lan yadurru Allah shay'an," in His name in several places, in "la yahsabanna alladhina kafaru," and in the mention of respite (imla'). Antithesis (tibaq) in "ishtaraw al-kufr bi'l-iman," and in "li-yut'ligakum 'ala'l-ghayb." Metaphor (isti'ara) in "yusari'un," in "ishtaraw," in "numli," in "li-yazdadu ithman," and in "al-khabith wa'l-tayyib." Paronomasia of similar form (tajnis mumathil) in "fa-amanu" and "in tu'minu." Iltifat in "antum," if it is an address to the believers, since if it had followed the wording of the believers it would have been about them as they are; and if it is an address to others, it is a variation of address (talwin al-khitab). And in "ta'malun khabir," according to him who reads with the ta' of address. And omission in several places.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 3, Verse 185 (part 1 of 3)**

﴿Certainly Allah has heard the saying of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich." We will record what they have said and their killing of the prophets without right, and We will say, "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 181] ﴿That is for what your hands have put forward, and [because] Allah is not ever unjust to the servants.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 182] ﴿[They are] those who said, "Indeed, Allah has taken our covenant that we not believe in any messenger until he brings us an offering which fire consumes." Say, "There have certainly come to you messengers before me with clear proofs and with what you [now] say. So why did you kill them, if you should be truthful?"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 183] ﴿And if they deny you, [O Muhammad], [it is no new thing, for] messengers before you were denied who came with clear proofs, scriptures, and the illuminating Book.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 184] ﴿Every soul will taste death. And you will only be given your full compensation on the Day of Resurrection. So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has succeeded. And what is the worldly life except the enjoyment of delusion?﴾

Az-Zubur (الزُّبُرُ): the plural of zabur, which means a book. It is said: zabartu, meaning "I wrote," so the word is in the sense of a passive participle, i.e., mazbur (written), like ar-rukub (riding) in the sense of al-markub (the thing ridden). Imru' al-Qays said:

"For whom is this campsite? I saw it and it stirred my longing, like the writing of a zabur on a palm-frond of Yemen."

It is also said: zabarahu means "he read it," and zabbarahu means "he embellished it," and tazabbarahu means "he rebuked him." It has been said that the derivation of zabur is from az-zubrah, which is a piece of iron left in its own state.

Az-Zahzahah (الزَّحْزَحَةُ): removing and distancing. It is a repetition of az-zahh, which is pulling with haste. It is said: "makan zahzah," meaning a distant place.

Al-Fawz (الفَوْزُ): being saved from what is feared and attaining what is hoped for. A vast, desolate land in which there is a fear of destruction is called mafazah, by way of optimism, because whoever crosses it succeeds (faza). It has also been said that it is because it is a place where one is likely to perish. The Arabs say: "fawwaza al-rajul," meaning the man died.

﴿Certainly Allah has heard the saying of those who said, "Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 181]: It was revealed concerning Finhas ibn 'Azura'. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) debated with him about Islam and about [the verse] "Who will lend Allah a goodly loan?" Finhas made this statement, so Abu Bakr struck him and, because of their previous covenant, he (Finhas) complained to the Messenger (ﷺ) and denied what he had said. So [this verse] was revealed to refute Finhas and to confirm the truthfulness of as-Siddiq (Abu Bakr). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, as-Suddi, Muqatil, and Ibn Ishaq, may Allah be pleased with them, and they related the story at length.

Qatadah said: it was revealed concerning Huyayy ibn Akhtab. He, al-Hasan, Ma'mar, and others said: it was revealed concerning the Jews. Abu Sulayman ad-Dimashqi mentioned Ilyas ibn 'Umar.

When [the verse] "Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan?" [al-Baqarah: 245] was revealed, one of them said, or they said: "Indeed, the poor is borrowing from the rich." The apparent meaning is that the speaker was a group. It is possible that this statement first came from Finhas or Huyayy, and then the Jews repeated it, or that it came from one person only and was attributed to the group, following the habit of Arabic speech of attributing the act of one member to the tribe as a whole.

The meaning of "Certainly Allah has heard" is that their saying was not hidden from Him, the Exalted. Their saying was either by way of mockery at the command to lend [to Allah], or by way of disputation and argument, since whoever asks for a loan is poor, or it was based on belief. Such [a belief] is not improbable from their minds, since Allah has related of them: ﴿And the Jews say, "The hand of Allah is chained up." Their own hands are chained up﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64]. Whatever the reason, this indicates their persistence in disbelief and their exaggeration in it, for they attributed to the One who brought things into existence from pure non-existence, the One who is self-sufficient beyond what He brought into existence, a description that indicates need for something He created, and they attributed the reverse to themselves.

The sentence came emphasized with the lam, indicating His knowledge of their saying and confirming it. And since they attributed to Allah what they attributed, they emphasized the sentence with "inna" (indeed) by way of exaggeration. But since they attributed to themselves what they attributed, they did not emphasize it; rather they presented the sentence as if it needed no emphasis, as though richness were a quality of theirs about which there could be no dispute, and so it would need to be emphasized.

﴿We will record what they have said and their killing of the prophets without right, and We will say, "Taste the punishment of the burning."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 181]: The apparent meaning is that writing is to be taken literally. Many scholars have said so, namely that deeds are recorded in pages, and that those pages are what are weighed, and Allah, glorified and exalted be He, will create lightness and heaviness in them according to what is written in them of good and evil.

It has been said: "We will record what they have said" refers to [their statements] about the Qur'an, so that the people may know the extent of their obstinacy and envy in their criticism of him (ﷺ).

Some people held that writing is metaphorical, and its meaning is counting a thing, recording it, not neglecting it, and its existence in the knowledge of Allah as a preserved thing that is not forgotten, just as writing establishes what is written. Others held that the meaning of "We will record" is: We will make it obligatory upon them in the Hereafter to be recompensed for what they said in this world, like His saying: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183]. The word "sanaktub" was used in the future form rather than the past, because it includes the requital for what they said. In it there is a threat and warning which is not hidden.

Their killing of the prophets is attributed to them, although it was the act of their forefathers, because they were content with it. They also named the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and intended to kill him. This statement and this act point to all the ugly sayings and deeds that proceeded from them, for the saying in this verse is the most grievous of statements about Allah, the Exalted, and killing is the most grievous of the deeds they committed against the prophets of Allah, the Exalted. Coupling killing with this saying indicates that both cause the deserving of punishment. Since what proceeded from them was both speech and action, it was fitting that the requital be both speech and action. Thus His saying, "and We will say, 'Taste the punishment of the burning,'" [al-'Imran: 181] includes both speech and action. In combining speech with action there is the greatest retribution, and it is said to the one who is avenged against: "Feel it and taste it!"

Abu Sufyan said to Hamzah (may Allah be pleased with him), when Wahshi stabbed him: "Taste it, 'Uqquq!" The word "dhawq" (tasting) is borrowed for direct experience of punishment, because tasting is among the most emphatic forms of direct contact, and its sense is especially distinct.

Al-Harik (الحَرِيقُ): the burner, of the form fa'il in the sense of muf'il, like alim in the sense of mu'lim. It has been said: al-Harik is a level of the levels of Hell. It has also been said: al-Harik is the blazing part of the Fire, and the Fire includes both the blazing and the non-blazing, with the blazing being the most intense. The apparent meaning is that this statement will be made when they enter Hell. It has been said: it may be at the reckoning, or at death.

"Anna" and what follows it are quoted by "qalu" (they said). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be quoted by the verbal noun (masdar), so that it would be a case of i'mal (the second verb governing the object). He said: the governing of the first is a weak principle, and it becomes weaker because the second is a verb and the first is a verbal noun, and the governing of a verb is stronger. The apparent meaning is that "ma" in "ma qalu" is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," though it was permitted that it be a verbal (masdariyyah) particle.

The majority read "sanaktub" and "qatlahum" in the accusative. "Naqul" is with the first person plural of majesty, or it may refer to the angels. Al-Hasan and al-A'raj read "sayaktub" with the third person (ya'), in the absent form. Hamzah read "sayaktub" with ya', in the passive voice, and "qatluhum" in the nominative, as a conjunction with "ma," since it is in the nominative by virtue of "sayaktub." And "yaqulu" with ya', in the absent form. Talhah ibn Musarrif read "sanaktub ma yaqulun" (We will record what they say). Ad-Dani related from him: "satuktab ma qalu" with a dammed ta', in the sense of their saying. Ibn Mas'ud read "wa yuqalu dhuqu" (and it will be said, "Taste"). They related from Abu Mu'adh an-Nahwi that in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it reads: "sanaktub ma yaqulun wa naqulu lahum dhuqu" (We will record what they say, and We will say to them, "Taste").

﴿That is for what your hands have put forward﴾ [Al 'Imran: 182]: The reference is to the punishment mentioned earlier. What they put forward of disobedience, whether in speech, action, or belief, is attributed to the hands by way of taghlib (the dominance of one term over another), because hands carry out most actions, so every action is done through them. This sentence is included within what is said, and by it they were given the cause that necessitated their punishment. It is possible that it is addressed to the contemporaries of the Messenger (ﷺ) on the day this verse was revealed, and so it is not included under the governed object of His saying "and We will say."

﴿And [because] Allah is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Al 'Imran: 182]: This is conjoined to His saying "for what your hands have put forward," meaning: that punishment is due to your disobedience and to the justice of Allah the Exalted toward you. The word "zallam" (very unjust), which is intended for intensification, is used here, and this is intensification with regard to its object. Some scholars held that the form fa''al may be used without intending intensity, as in the saying of Tarafah:

"I am not one who halts at the high grounds out of fear, but whenever the people seek help, I give help."

He does not mean that he sometimes halts at the high grounds a little, because the second half of the verse rejects that, indicating the negation of stinginess in every state. Full praise is not achieved by intending multiplicity. It was also said: when He negates great injustice, He necessarily negates small injustice as well, because one who commits injustice does so for the benefit he derives from it. If he abandons great injustice despite its greater benefit toward someone who can benefit or be harmed, then he will be even more inclined to abandon small injustice whose benefit is slight.

Al-Qadi said: the punishment with which He threatened them, if He were unjust, would be great, so He negated it according to its greatness, were it established. "Al-'Abid" (the servants) is the plural of 'abd, like al-Kulayb. The collective noun has come in this pattern, like ad-Da/fan and other broken plurals, permitting its predicate to be stated in the singular as is the case with collective nouns. The word of this plural suited the verse rather than the word "'ibad," because of the harmony with the preceding rhyme-endings (fawasil), which came in this pattern, just as it suited that word in Surah Fussilat, and just as the word "'ibad" in Surah Ghafir suited what precedes and follows it.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "'Abid" was pluralized in this verse as "'abid" because it is a place of deliverance and rescue from injustice. End of his words. This reasoning which he gave for this plural is not clear to me.

Az-Zamakhshari said: (If you ask): Why did He conjoin His saying "and [because] Allah is not ever unjust to the servants" to "what your hands have put forward," and how did He make His not being unjust to the servants a partner to their committing evil deeds in the deserving of punishment? (I answer): The meaning of His not being unjust to the servants is that He is just toward them, and justice requires that He punish the wrongdoer among them and reward the doer of good. End of his words. In it there is a scent of Mu'tazilism.

﴿[They are] those who said, "Indeed, Allah has taken our covenant that we not believe in any messenger until he brings us an offering which fire consumes."﴾ [Al 'Imran: 183] Al-Ka'bi said: it was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Malik ibn as-Sayf, Wahb ibn Yahudha, Zayd ibn Manu, Finhas ibn 'Azura', and Huyayy ibn Akhtab, who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "You claim that Allah sent you to us as a messenger and revealed a Book to you, and that Allah has covenanted with us in the Torah that we not believe in any messenger who claims that he is from Allah until he brings us an offering which fire consumes. If you bring it to us, we will believe you."

The apparent meaning of this statement is that He covenanted with them in the Torah. It has been said: this was in the Torah, but the complete statement was: "until there comes to you the Messiah and Muhammad, and when they come to you, believe in them without an offering." It has also been said: the matter of offerings remained established until it was abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one) through the tongue of the Messiah. And it has been said: their mention of this covenant is part of their lying against Allah, the Exalted, and their fabrication against Him and against His prophets.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 185 (part 2 of 3):

The meaning of ʿahida (عَهِدَ) is "commanded" (waṣṣā), and the ʿahd (covenant) is more specific than the amr (command), since it is about what is long-lasting and remains through the ages past. Its explanation has preceded. The verb nu'mina (نُؤْمِنَ, "we believe") takes the preposition lām, as in His words ﴿So none believed in Moses, except...﴾ [Yunus: 83], meaning "believed in" (yu'minu li-Allah, "believes in God"). The qurbān (قُرْبان, "offering") is that by which one draws near to God, such as a sheep, a cow or other things. It is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar) that has been used for the object, like rahn (pledge). Its ruling was ancient among the prophets. Do you not see the story of the two sons of Adam? The fire's consuming of that offering was a sign of the acceptance of the deed, whether charity or some other action, or the sincerity of a statement. When the fire does not descend, it is not accepted. The fire also used to descend upon the spoils of war and burn them. The attribution of the consuming (akl) to the fire is a metaphor (majāz) and an figurative usage (istiʿāra) for the removal and annihilation of a thing, since the true meaning of eating is found only in a living, feeding animal. The offering and the fire's consuming were a miracle (muʿjiz) for the prophet, which makes belief in him obligatory, so it is equal to all other miracles. It is for God to designate of the signs whatever He wishes for His prophets, and this is the counterpart of what they propose of signs by way of rebuke and to challenge them. God has informed that even if what they proposed had descended, they would not have believed.

﴿Those who said...﴾: "alladhīna qālū" is an attribute (ṣifa) of "alladhīna qālū" [as in the previous clause]. Al-Zajjaj said: "alladhīna" is an attribute of "al-ʿabīd" (the servants). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This corrupts both the meaning and the description." He concluded, and it is as he said. They also permitted cutting it off for the nominative or accusative, and making it a substitute (badal). In "an lā nu'mina" (أنْ لا نُؤْمِنَ, "that we should not believe") there is an implied preposition (ḥarf jarr), which has been omitted, and it remains subject to the dispute over it: is it in the position of an accusative or a genitive? It may also be an object, with ʿahida taken to include the meaning of "to bind" (ilzam), as if He had obliged us that we should not believe. ʿĪsā ibn ʿUmar read "bi-qurbānin" with a ḍamma on the rāʾ. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This is by analogy with the ḍamma of the qāf, and it is not a dialect form, because there is no fuʿulān with a ḍamma on the fāʾ and the ʿayn in speech." Sībawayh cited "al-sulṭān" with a ḍamma on the lām, and said that this is by way of analogy (ittibāʿ). He concluded. But Sībawayh did not say that this is by analogy; rather he said: "We do not know of fuʿlān or fuʿulān in speech, nor anything of this kind that he has not mentioned. But fuʿulān has come, and it is rare: they said al-sulṭān, and it is a noun." He concluded. The commentator (al-shārih), the author of this dialect, said: it is not vocalized with sukūn nor followed (by ḍamma), and likewise the morphologists (taṣrīfiyyūn) mentioned that it is a pattern of the future. They said regarding what has two additional letters after the lām and is on the pattern fuʿlān and is not found except as a noun: it is rare, like sulṭān.

﴿Say: Messengers have certainly come to you before me with clear proofs and with what you have mentioned, so why did you kill them, if you are truthful?﴾ [Al ʿImran: 183] God refuted them and denied their proposal, and held them to account that messengers had come to them with what they said, namely bringing an offering that fire consumes, and other signs, yet they did not believe in them, but killed them. They did not content themselves with denying them until they inflicted upon them the worst act, which is the destruction of life by killing. The meaning is that this is, from you, O assembly of Jews, a pretext and obstinacy; and if he had brought them the offering, they would have pretended otherwise by proposing something else. Proposing has no limit, and its proposer is answered only if God wills his destruction, as in the story of the people of Ṣāliḥ and others. Likewise it was said to the Messenger of God ﷺ regarding the proposal of Quraysh, and he (peace be upon him) refused and said: "Rather I will call them and treat them." The meaning of ﴿if you are truthful﴾ [Al ʿImran: 183] is: in your claim that faith requires the bringing of clear proofs and the offering, or truthful in that God has bound a covenant with you.

﴿So if they deny you, [it is no new thing, for] messengers before you were denied, who came with clear proofs, and the scriptures and the illuminating Book﴾ [Al ʿImran: 184]: The address is to the Messenger ﷺ, and this is by way of consolation, since their lie against God had become apparent by mentioning the covenant they had fabricated; and within it was their denial of him, as they tied belief in him to a proposed condition on their part by way of obstinacy, and God did not answer them in that. So He consoled the Messenger ﷺ that this is their habit, (p-133) and there had preceded from them the denial of messengers who came with what makes belief obligatory: the manifest miracles clearly indicating their truthfulness, and the luminous divine heavenly books that remove the darkness of doubts.

al-Zubur (الزُّبُر) is the plural of zabūr, which means "book." It is so named, it is said, because it is written, since one says zabarahu, meaning "he wrote it." Or because it is restraining (zājir), from zabarahu, "he restrained him." By this the Book of Dawud was called Zabur because of the great number of restraints and admonitions in it, or because of its rulings. Al-zubur means the rulings. Al-Zajjaj said: the zabur is every book in which there is wisdom. It is said: al-kitāb is the zubur. Both words are combined for emphasis, or because their meanings differ, although the intended referent is one, but their meanings differ in respect of their attribute. It is said: al-kitāb here is a genus including the Torah, the Gospel and others. It is possible that by His words "and the zubur" is meant the admonitions, without meaning books. That is: they came with manifest miracles, threats, and illuminating books.

The answer of the condition is omitted, because the sentence indicates it; the estimate is: "and if they deny you, then console yourself with him." It is not possible that ﴿messengers were denied﴾ [Al ʿImran: 184] be the answer, because it is in the past, whereas the answer of the condition must be future, since it is consequent upon the future. What occurs in the speech of the grammarians, that such a past form is the answer of the condition, is by way of leniency and not literal truth. He made the verb passive, because he did not confine the denial of the messengers to the Jews alone denying their prophets; rather he drew attention to the fact that it is the custom of the Jews and others among the nations to deny the prophets. So the meaning is: nations among the Jews and others denied the messengers. It is said: rusul is indefinite because of their multitude and wide spread. "Min qablika" is connected to "kudhdhiba," and the clause "jā'ū" is in the position of an attribute of "rusul." He concluded. The bāʾ in "bi-l-bayyināt" may be circumstantial (ḥāl) or transitive: they came to their peoples accompanied by the clear proofs, or they brought the clear proofs. The majority read "wa-l-zubur." Ibn ʿĀmir read "wa-bi-l-zubur," and so it is in the codices of the people of Syria. Hishām, with a variant from him, read "wa-bi-l-kitāb." The majority read "wa-l-kitāb." Repeating the preposition in the conjunction is for emphasis. The mention of the kitāb in the singular, although it is plural in meaning, was for the sake of the harmony of the fāṣilas (verse endings), and it was not considered that it should be pluralized like the words conjoined with it.

﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾: this clause and what follows contain admonition and consolation for the Messenger of God ﷺ regarding the world and its people, and a promise of salvation in the Hereafter, by mentioning death and reflecting on it, which makes easier what proceeds from the disbelievers of denial and other things. Since the deniers who lie against God among the Jews and the hypocrites were mentioned earlier, as was their mention of the believers, all of them were alerted that they are mortal and their final destination is the Hereafter, where the saved and the lost will become manifest, and that what they clung to in the world of wealth, family and clan is only a deceptive enjoyment; all of it will dissolve and vanish, and nothing will remain but what a person has done, and he will be paid for it in the Hereafter, paid according to his obedience and disobedience.

Muhammad ibn ʿUmar al-Razi said: in this verse there is evidence that the soul does not die with the death of the body, and that the soul is other than the body. He concluded. This is an obstinacy in interpreting the evidence, for the apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the soul dies. He also said: the word nafs is specific to bodies. He concluded. Al-Yazidi read "dhā'iqatun" with tanwīn and "al-mawta" with a fatḥa, as Zamakhshari reported from him. Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmitted it from Abu Ḥaywa, and others transmitted it from al-Aʿmash, Yaḥyā, and Ibn Abi Ishaq. Al-Aʿmash read, as Zamakhshari reported, "dhā'iqatu" without tanwīn and "al-mawta" with a fatḥa, and similar to it:

"I found him not seeking to make amends, nor remembering God except a little."

He dropped the tanwīn because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters, like the reading of those who read ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1] ﴿God, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2], dropping the tanwīn from "aḥad." ﴿And you will only be paid your rewards on the Day of Resurrection﴾: the word tawfiyya indicates completion on the Day of Resurrection, so what precedes it, such as the grave being a garden among the gardens of Paradise or a pit among the pits of Hell, is only a part of the rewards. And what has not entered Paradise or Hell is not yet fully paid. What the context indicates is that the rewards are what is consequent upon obedience and disobedience, although in common usage ajr is generally what is consequent upon an act of obedience. For this reason Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: God specified the mention of the rewards because of their nobility, and as an indication of His forgiveness for Muhammad ﷺ and his community. There is no doubt that on the Day of Resurrection the rewards occur, and the completion of punishments. He concluded.

﴿Whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has indeed triumphed﴾: He made triumph (fawz), which is the attaining of a share of good and salvation from evil, conditional upon being removed from the Fire and entering Paradise. For whoever is not saved from the Fire but is admitted to it, even if he will eventually enter Paradise, has not triumphed, like one of the people of major sins who enters it. And whoever is removed from it but does not enter Paradise, like the companions of the Heights, has also not triumphed. It is related in a ḥadīth from the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Whoever would be pleased to be drawn away from the Fire and to enter Paradise, let his death come to him while he testifies that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and let him treat people as he would like to be treated." It is said: fāza means "was saved." It is said: "preceded." It is said: "gained booty."

﴿And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion﴾: al-matāʿ is what is enjoyed of implements, wealth and other things. ʿIkrima explained it as: the axe, the bowl, and the cooking-pot. Al-Ḥasan explained it, saying: it is like the greenness of plants and the play of girls; it has no substance, it gleams like a mirage and passes like a cloud. This from ʿIkrima and al-Ḥasan is by way of illustration (tamthīl). Al-Zamakhshari said: He likened the world to goods which are concealed from the buyer and deceive him until he buys them, then it becomes clear to him that they are defective and worthless, and the Devil is the concealer, the deceiver. He concluded. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: this applies only to the one who prefers it over the Hereafter; as for the one who seeks the Hereafter through it, it is a sufficient provision. ʿIkrima also said: "the enjoyment of delusion" is like glass vessels, which must break and be ruined, and so is the whole matter of the world. This is a simile (tashbīh) from ʿIkrima. Al-ghurūr means deceptions and false hopes. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Sābiṭ said: the enjoyment of delusion is like a shepherd's provision: he takes a handful of dates and some flour on which he drinks milk, meaning that the enjoyment of the world is little, not sufficient for the one who enjoys it and not enough to carry him through his journey. Among Arabic sayings: "Live, but do not be deceived," that is, do not be content with what does not suffice you. Ibn ʿArafa said: al-ghurūr is whatever you see as having a good appearance but which has a hidden inside that is disliked or unknown; and the Devil is a deceiver because he drives people to their hidden desires, and behind that is what will harm. He said: from this is the sale of ghurūr, which is a sale that has an apparent form but an unknown hidden side. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: "wa-mā al-ḥayāt al-dunyā" is with an omitted genitive; its estimate is: "the benefit of the life of this world is nothing but the benefit of delusion," that is, a benefit that diverts from the true benefit because of its impermanence, which is the benefit in the afterlife. The annexation of matāʿ to ghurūr: if ghurūr is taken as a plural, it is like your saying "the benefit of the heedless"; and if it is taken as a verbal noun, it is like your saying "the benefit of diversion (ighfāl)," that is, neglect, which results in heedlessness of preparation for the Hereafter. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar read "al-ghurūr" with a fatḥa on the ghayn, and it was explained as the devil, and it may be a faʿūl in the sense of a maf'ūl, that is, "the enjoyment of the one who is deceived," that is, the one who is misled.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 185 (part 3 of 3):

These verses contain paronomasia (tajnis) of the differing kind (al-tajnis al-mughayir) in His saying: "alladhina qalu" (those who said), and of the identical kind (al-tajnis al-mumathil) in: "qalu" (they said), and "wa-sanaktubu ma qalu" (and We shall record what they said), and in: "﴿kadhdhabuka fa-qad kudhdhiba﴾" (they denied you, so messengers before you were denied) [Al 'Imran: 184]. There is antithesis (tibaq) in: faqir (poor) and aghniya' (rich), and in: al-mawt (death) and al-hayah (life), and in: "﴿zuhziha 'ani al-nar wa-udkhila al-jannah﴾" (he is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to the Garden). There is iltifat (shift of grammatical person) in: sanaktubu and naqulu, and in: "ajurakum" (your rewards), since it was preceded by "kullu nafs" (every soul). There is repetition (takrar) in: the Divine Name (lafz al-jalalah), and in: al-bayyinat (the clear proofs). There is metaphor (isti'arah) in: sanaktubu according to the view of those who do not take writing literally, and in: "qaddamat aydikum" (your hands have sent forward), in: "ta'kuluhu al-nar" (the fire consumes it), and in: dhuqu (taste) and dha'iqah (one who tastes). There is the theological method (al-madhhab al-kalami) in: "﴿falima qataltumuhum﴾" (why did you kill them?) [Al 'Imran: 183]. There is specification (ikhtisas) in: aydikum. There is indication (ishara) in: dhalika, and the conditional used figuratively (al-sharṭ al-mutajawwaz fihi). There is an added particle for emphasis (ziyadah li-l-tawkid) in: "wa-bi-l-zuburi wa-bi-l-kitab" (and with the scriptures and the Book) according to the reading of those who read it thus. There is ellipsis (hadhf) in several places.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 186–189 (part 1 of 2):

﴿You will surely be tested in your possessions and your selves, and you will surely hear much hurt from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate partners with God. But if you are patient and mindful of God, that is indeed among the steadfast resolutions of affairs.﴾ ﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it." But they cast it behind their backs and bartered it for a small price. How evil is what they barter.﴾ ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done and love to be praised for what they did not do, do not think them safe from the punishment. For them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and God is over all things capable.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for people of understanding.﴾ [Al-Imran: 190] ﴿Those who remember God standing, sitting, and on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Glory be to You; protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ [Al-Imran: 191] ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have truly disgraced him, and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.﴾ [Al-Imran: 192] ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins, remove from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die with the righteous.﴾ [Al-Imran: 193] ﴿Our Lord, grant us what You promised us through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed You do not break the promise.﴾ [Al-Imran: 194] ﴿So their Lord answered them: "I do not waste the work of any worker among you, male or female, you are of one another. Those who emigrated, were driven from their homes, were harmed in My cause, fought, and were killed, I will surely remove their misdeeds from them and surely admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, as a reward from God. And with God is the best reward."﴾ [Al-Imran: 195] ﴿Do not let the movement of those who disbelieve through the land deceive you.﴾ [Al-Imran: 196] ﴿A brief enjoyment; then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place.﴾ [Al-Imran: 197] ﴿But those who are mindful of their Lord will have gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, as a provision from God. And what is with God is better for the righteous.﴾ [Al-Imran: 198] ﴿And indeed among the People of the Scripture are those who believe in God, and in what was revealed to you and what was revealed to them, humbling themselves before God. They do not trade the signs of God for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed God is swift in reckoning.﴾ [Al-Imran: 199] ﴿O you who believe, be patient, endure together, stand ready on the frontier, and be mindful of God, that you may prosper.﴾ [Al-Imran: 200]

Al-judub (الجنوب) is the plural of janb (جنب), which is well known (the sides of the body). Al-murabata (المرابطة) is remaining constantly at the frontier for jihad, and its origin is from tying horses (ربط الخيل).

﴿You will surely be tested in your possessions and your selves, and you will surely hear much hurt from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate partners with God﴾: It is said that it was revealed concerning the incident of Abdullah ibn Ubayy when he said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while the Messenger was reciting the Qur'an to them: "If what you say is true, then do not trouble us with it in our gatherings." Ibn Rawahah answered him, saying: "Come to us with it in our gatherings, O Messenger of God." The Muslims, the polytheists, and the Jews then reviled one another. It is also said that it concerned what occurred between Abu Bakr and Phinehas. It is also said that it concerned Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, who in his poetry incited the polytheists against the Messenger and his companions. God, exalted is He, informed them of this testing and hearing so that they would be better prepared to bear what came upon them from it, since when the news comes in advance, it differs from one to whom the matter comes suddenly, for the latter's pain is greater. The verse is directed at the censure of the People of the Scripture and others among the polytheists, and it fits with the preceding verses which came in censure of the People of the Scripture and other polytheists.

In His words "latublawunna" (لتبلون), the apparent meaning is that those addressed are the believers. Ata' said: they are the emigrants, whom the polytheists dispossessed of their dwellings, selling them, and plundering their wealth. It is also said that the testing in possessions is what they suffered of plunder of their wealth and the loss of their numbers on the day of Uhud. The apparent meaning is that this is address to the believers concerning the trial that will occur in possessions, through the calamities and losses that befall them, and through spending in the way of God and in the obligations of the Law. The testing in the self (النفس) is through desires, or bodily obligations, or illnesses, or the loss of relatives and kin, or through killing, wounds, captivity, and various kinds of fears; these are the views. He placed possessions before selves, either by way of ascending to what is more noble, or by way of quantity, because misfortunes in possessions are more numerous than misfortunes in selves. Al-adha (الأذى) is a comprehensive noun meaning harm. It includes their statements about the Messenger and his companions, about God, exalted is He, and His prophets, their attacks upon the religion, their denigration of those who believed, and the satire of Ka'b and his composing amorous verses about the women of the believers.

﴿And if you are patient﴾: over that testing and that hearing.

﴿and are mindful of God, then indeed that﴾: i.e., indeed patience and piety.

﴿is among the steadfast resolutions of affairs﴾: It is said: among the most firm and most excellent of them. Al-azm (العزم) is carrying out a matter after deliberation and refinement. Al-Naqqash said: al-azm is the same as al-hazm (الحزم, firmness of judgment), the ḥāʼ being substituted for the ʻayn. Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: this is an error. Al-hazm is the soundness of consideration of a matter, and its result is caution against error in it. Al-azm is the intent to carry it out. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And consult them in the matter; then when you have resolved﴾ [Al-Imran: 159], so consultation and what is in its meaning is al-hazm. The Arabs say: "I may exercise firm judgment, if I resolve." Al-Zamakhshari said: "min ʻazm al-umūr" means among the resolved matters, i.e., of what it is obligatory to resolve upon among affairs, or of what God has resolved to be; that is, that it is a resolution from the resolutions of God: you must be patient and mindful. It is also said: "min ʻazm al-umūr" means from its seriousness. Mujahid, in His words "fa-idha ʻazama al-amr," said: i.e., when the matter has come into being.

﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it"﴾: They are the Jews, upon whom the covenant was taken concerning the matter of the Messenger (ﷺ), but they concealed it and cast it away. This was said by Ibn ʻAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, and Ibn Jurayj. Some people said: they are the Jews and the Christians. The majority said: it is general to everyone whom God has taught knowledge, and the scholars of this community are included in this covenant. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, and Abu Bakr read the verbs with the ya' (الياء) in both places, in the third person (غيبة), since before it is "those who were given the Scripture" and after it is "fa-nabadhuhu." The rest of the seven read them with the ta' (التاء) for direct address, and it is like His saying: ﴿You worship none but God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]; it is read with both ta' and ya'. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun returns to the Scripture. It is also said it returns to the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also said it returns to the covenant. It is also said it returns to belief in the Messenger, due to His saying: ﴿You shall surely believe in him and surely support him﴾ [Al-Imran: 81]. The nominative of "wa-la taktumunahu" (ولا تكتمونه) is because it occurs as a circumstantial clause (حال), i.e., "without concealing it," and it is not included in the oath-subject (المقسم عليه). They said: it is the waw of circumstance, not of conjunction, like His saying: ﴿So continue straight and do not follow﴾ [Yunus: 89], and His saying "wa-la yasal" in the reading of the one who lightened the nun and raised the lam. It is also said that the waw is for conjunction, and it is part of what is sworn to. Since it was negated by "la," it was not emphasized; you say: "By God, Zayd will not stand," so the nun does not enter it. This latter view is, in my opinion, more correct in grammatical analysis (إعراب) and more eloquent, because the first view requires the omission of a subject before "la," so that the clause is a nominal clause in the position of a circumstantial clause, since a negated present verb with "la" does not take the waw of circumstance. Ibn Masʻud read: "layubayyinunahu," without the nun of emphasis. Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: this nun is not necessarily required with the lam of emphasis, as reported by Sibawayh. End. This is not known from the saying of the Basrans; rather, the alternation of the lam and the nun is, in their view, a necessity of poetry. The Kufans permit it in ordinary speech, so they permit: "By God, I will stand," and "By God, I will surely stand." The poet said:

"By your life, O Salma, I am certain that I would be permitted whatever you wished, even if it were death."

Another said:

"By oath, I shall surely hate every man who embellishes speech and does not act."

Ibn ʻAbbas read: "mithaqa al-nabiyyin li-tubayyinunnahu li-l-nas," so the pronoun in "fa-nabadhuhu" returns to the people, since it is impossible for it to return to the prophets; that is, "the people to whom the covenant was made clear cast it away." The meaning of His words "fa-nabadhuhu wara'a zuhurihim" has been explained previously in His saying: ﴿A party of those who were given the Scripture cast the Book of God behind their backs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 101].

﴿and bartered it for a small price. How evil is what they barter﴾: The explanation of this sentence has been given before, and the discussion of the grammatical analysis of what follows "bi'sa" was given, so there is no need to repeat it.

﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done and love to be praised for what they did not do, do not think them safe from the punishment. For them is a painful punishment﴾: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, who used to stay behind from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the expedition, and when he returned they offered excuses to him; he would accept their excuses and ask forgiveness for them, so God exposed them by this verse. This was said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Ibn Zayd, and a group. Many exegetes said: it was revealed concerning the rabbis of the Jews. "Ata" (أتى) comes with the meaning of "fa'ala" (did), as in His saying, exalted is He: (p-137) ﴿Indeed His promise was ever fulfilled﴾ [Maryam: 61], that is, done. So the meaning of "bima ataw" is "by what they did," and this is indicated by the reading of Ubayy: "bima fa'alu." Concerning what they did and rejoiced in, there are several views. The first: the concealment of what the Messenger had asked them about, and informing him of something else, and showing him that they had informed him of it, thereby seeking praise from him; this was said by Ibn ʻAbbas. The second: what they gained of the world and loved that it be said that they were scholars; this was also said by Ibn ʻAbbas. The third: their saying, "We are upon the religion of Abraham," and their concealment of the matter of the Messenger; this was said by Ibn Jubayr. The fourth: their letters to the Jews of the whole earth that Muhammad (ﷺ) is not a prophet, so hold fast to your religion; their word came together upon disbelief in him, and they said: "We are the people of fasting and prayer and the friends of God"; this was said by al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. The fifth: the statement of the Jews of Khaybar to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions: "We are upon your religion, and we are a support for you," while they were holding fast to their misguidance, and they wished that he would praise them for what they had not done; this was said by al-Suddi. The sixth: the Jews' equipping of an army against the Prophet (ﷺ) and their spending upon that army; this was said by al-Nakha'i. The seventh: the informing of a group of Jews to the Muslims when they left the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), he having informed them of things they knew, so the Muslims praised them for that, while they concealed the opposite of what they displayed; this was mentioned by al-Zajjaj. The eighth: the following of people in their distortion of the interpretation of the Torah, and they loved that they be praised for that, while they did nothing beneficial or sound; this was said by Mujahid. The ninth: the staying behind of the hypocrites from the expedition, and their swearing to the Muslims that they were pleased with their victory, and they loved that it be said that they were in the rank of the fighters; this was said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

The views preceding this last one are all based on the premise that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews. It has been said: it is possible that it includes everyone who performs a good deed and rejoices in it with the joy of self-admiration, and loves that people praise him and extol him for piety and asceticism, and for what is not in him. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʻAmr read: "la yahsabanna" and "la yahsabannahum" with the ya' in both, and with the raising of the ba' in "yahsabannahum," on the basis that "yahsabanna" is attributed to "alladhina" (those who). This reading has been explained in two ways. The first, which Abu ʻAli said: "la yahsabanna" did not govern any object, and "alladhina" is raised by it. These verbs may come as idle (لغوًا), not in the position of complete meaningful sentences, like His saying:

"And I did not think that among us there remained any affection, the lean necks of the stallions and the mares..."

Al-Khalil said: the Arabs say: "I did not see him say that except Zayd, and I did not think him to say that except Zayd." Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: the reading is then consistent with "fa-la yahsabannahum" being a substitute for the first, and it has transitively taken two objects, which are the pronoun and "bi-mafazah," and it has dispensed with the two objects thereby, as it dispensed in His saying:

"By what book or by what custom do you see their love as a shame upon me, and you reckon..."

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 186–189 (part 2 of 2):

That is: "and you think their love (for praise) to be a disgrace upon me." The second possibility is what al-Zamakhshari said: that the first object is omitted, with the meaning of "lā yaḥsabannahumu alladhīna yafrahūna bi-mafāzatin" as "lā yaḥsabanna anfusahumu alladhīna yafrahūna fā'izīn" (let not those who rejoice think themselves victorious). And "fa-lā yaḥsabannahum" is an emphasis. The refutation of al-Zamakhshari regarding his estimate of "lā yaḥsabannahumu" in His words, ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178], has already been presented to us, and that estimate is not valid, so it should be sought there. In this reading, the verb of reckoning (ḥusbān) is transitive to its two attached pronouns, the nominative and the accusative, and this is something specific to ẓanantu (I thought) and its sisters, and to others besides them: wajadtu (I found), faqadtu (I lost), and 'adimtu (I lacked), and this is established in the science of grammar (naḥw).

Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim read: lā taḥsabanna and fa-lā taḥsabannahum, with the tā' of address and the opening of the bā' in both, addressed to the Messenger. This reading has been given two interpretations. One of them, mentioned by Ibn 'Atiyyah, is that the first object is: alladhīna yafrahūn (those who rejoice), and the second is omitted, due to what follows it indicating it, as was said just above regarding the two objects. The repetition of the verb in fa-lā yaḥsabannahum is good because of the length of the speech, and this is the habit of the Arabs, and it brings the listener's mind closer. The second interpretation was mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, who said: one of the two objects is "alladhīna yafrahūn," and the second is "bi-mafāzatin." His saying "fa-lā yaḥsabannahum" is an emphasis, its estimate being "lā yaḥsabannahum, fa-lā yaḥsabannahum fā'izīn." It was also read: lā taḥsabunna and fa-lā taḥsabunnahum, with the tā' of address and the damma of the bā' in both, addressed to the believers. The disagreement about the second object comes in the same way as the disagreement about it in the reading of the Kufans.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read: lā yaḥsabanna with the yā' of the third person, and fa-lā taḥsabannahum with the tā' of address and the opening of the bā' in both. This reading has been explained as the omission of the two objects of yaḥsabanna, due to what follows them indicating them. The substitution (badal) that was permitted in the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr is not permitted in this reading, because the two verbs differ in their subject. When "fa-lā yaḥsabannahum" is an emphasis or a substitution, the entry of the fa' is only justified on the basis that it is extra (ziyadah), since it cannot be for coordination (ʿaṭf) nor the fa' of the answer of a condition. They cited as evidence for the extra fa' the words of the poet:

"Until I left the recurring ones (women) returning to him,
saying: 'fa-lā tab'ud' (so do not be far), and I said to him: 'ub'ud' (be far)."

And another said:

"When the one whose offence is great pressed with a hand,
so I left the upper part of his palm swinging."

That is: "lā tab'ud" and "tarakt" (I left). Al-Nakha'i and Marwan ibn al-Hakam read: bi-mā ātaw, meaning "they gave." Ibn Jubayr and al-Sulami read: bi-mā ūtū, in the passive. The views on "ātaw" have already been given, and some of them agree with these two readings.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: (bi-mā lam yaf'alū bi-mafāzatin), and "fa-lā yaḥsabannahum" is dropped. "Mafāzah" is a noun of place from fāza, meaning a place of winning, i.e. salvation. Al-Farra' said: that is, it keeps far from punishment, because fawz means distance from what is disliked. In this verse there is evidence that a person adorning himself with what is not in him, and loving to be praised for it, is forbidden and blameworthy in the Law. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2]. And in the authentic hadith: "The one who pretends to have what he does not have is like one who wears two garments of falsehood." Allah the Exalted has informed of their punishment in His words: ﴿And for them is a painful punishment.﴾ Describing it as painful is fitting because of their rejoicing and their love of being praised for what they did not do.

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is over all things competent.﴾ He, the Exalted, mentioned that they are among what He owns, and that He is capable over them. Thus they are owned, subdued, and subject to His power, so they are not safe from punishment.

﴿You will surely be tested in your possessions and your selves, and you will surely hear much hurt from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate partners with God. But if you are patient and mindful of God, that is indeed among the steadfast resolutions of affairs.﴾ ﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it." In His words "latublawunna" (لتبلون), the apparent meaning is that those addressed are the believers. Ata' said: they are the emigrants, whom the polytheists dispossessed of their dwellings, selling them, and plundering their wealth. It is also said that the testing in possessions is what they suffered of plunder of their wealth and the loss of their numbers on the day of Uhud. The apparent meaning is that this is address to the believers concerning the trial that will occur in possessions, through the calamities and losses that befall them, and through spending in the way of God and in the obligations of the Law. The testing in the self (النفس) is through desires, or bodily obligations, or illnesses, or the loss of relatives and kin, or through killing, wounds, captivity, and various kinds of fears; these are the views. He placed possessions before selves, either by way of ascending to what is more noble, or by way of quantity, because misfortunes in possessions are more numerous than misfortunes in selves. Al-adha (الأذى) is a comprehensive noun meaning harm. It includes their statements about the Messenger and his companions, about God, exalted is He, and His prophets, their attacks upon the religion, their denigration of those who believed, and the satire of Ka'b and his composing amorous verses about the women of the believers.

﴿And if you are patient﴾: over that testing and that hearing.

﴿and are mindful of God, then indeed that﴾: i.e., indeed patience and piety.

﴿is among the steadfast resolutions of affairs﴾: It is said: among the most firm and most excellent of them. Al-azm (العزم) is carrying out a matter after deliberation and refinement. Al-Naqqash said: al-azm is the same as al-hazm (الحزم, firmness of judgment), the ḥāʼ being substituted for the ʻayn. Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: this is an error. Al-hazm is the soundness of consideration of a matter, and its result is caution against error in it. Al-azm is the intent to carry it out. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And consult them in the matter; then when you have resolved﴾ [Al-Imran: 159], so consultation and what is in its meaning is al-hazm. The Arabs say: "I may exercise firm judgment, if I resolve." Al-Zamakhshari said: "min ʻazm al-umūr" means among the resolved matters, i.e., of what it is obligatory to resolve upon among affairs, or of what God has resolved to be; that is, that it is a resolution from the resolutions of God: you must be patient and mindful. It is also said: "min ʻazm al-umūr" means from its seriousness. Mujahid, in His words "fa-idha ʻazama al-amr," said: i.e., when the matter has come into being.

﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it"﴾: They are the Jews, upon whom the covenant was taken concerning the matter of the Messenger (ﷺ), but they concealed it and cast it away. This was said by Ibn ʻAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, and Ibn Jurayj. Some people said: they are the Jews and the Christians. The majority said: it is general to everyone whom God has taught knowledge, and the scholars of this community are included in this covenant. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, and Abu Bakr read the verbs with the ya' (الياء) in both places, in the third person (غيبة), since before it is "those who were given the Scripture" and after it is "fa-nabadhuhu." The rest of the seven read them with the ta' (التاء) for direct address, and it is like His saying: ﴿You worship none but God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]; it is read with both ta' and ya'. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun returns to the Scripture. It is also said it returns to the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also said it returns to the covenant. It is also said it returns to belief in the Messenger, due to His saying: ﴿You shall surely believe in him and surely support him﴾ [Al-Imran: 81]. The nominative of "wa-la taktumunahu" (ولا تكتمونه) is because it occurs as a circumstantial clause (حال), i.e., "without concealing it," and it is not included in the oath-subject (المقسم عليه). They said: it is the waw of circumstance, not of conjunction, like His saying: ﴿So continue straight and do not follow﴾ [Yunus: 89], and His saying "wa-la yasal" in the reading of the one who lightened the nun and raised the lam. It is also said that the waw is for conjunction, and it is part of what is sworn to. Since it was negated by "la," it was not emphasized; you say: "By God, Zayd will not stand," so the nun does not enter it. This latter view is, in my opinion, more correct in grammatical analysis (إعراب) and more eloquent, because the first view requires the omission of a subject before "la," so that the clause is a nominal clause in the position of a circumstantial clause, since a negated present verb with "la" does not take the waw of circumstance. Ibn Masʻud read: "layubayyinunahu," without the nun of emphasis. Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: this nun is not necessarily required with the lam of emphasis, as reported by Sibawayh. End. This is not known from the saying of the Basrans; rather, the alternation of the lam and the nun is, in their view, a necessity of poetry. The Kufans permit it in ordinary speech, so they permit: "By God, I will stand," and "By God, I will surely stand." The poet said:

"By your life, O Salma, I am certain that I would be permitted whatever you wished, even if it were death."

Another said:

"By oath, I shall surely hate every man who embellishes speech and does not act."

Ibn ʻAbbas read: "mithaqa al-nabiyyin li-tubayyinunnahu li-l-nas," so the pronoun in "fa-nabadhuhu" returns to the people, since it is impossible for it to return to the prophets; that is, "the people to whom the covenant was made clear cast it away." The meaning of His words "fa-nabadhuhu wara'a zuhurihim" has been explained previously in His saying: ﴿A party of those who were given the Scripture cast the Book of God behind their backs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 101].

﴿and bartered it for a small price. How evil is what they barter﴾: The explanation of this sentence has been given before, and the discussion of the grammatical analysis of what follows "bi'sa" was given, so there is no need to repeat it.

﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done and love to be praised for what they did not do, do not think them safe from the punishment. For them is a painful punishment﴾: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, who used to stay behind from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the expedition, and when he returned they offered excuses to him; he would accept their excuses and ask forgiveness for them, so God exposed them by this verse. This was said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Ibn Zayd, and a group. Many exegetes said: it was revealed concerning the rabbis of the Jews. "Ata" (أتى) comes with the meaning of "fa'ala" (did), as in His saying, exalted is He: (p-137) ﴿Indeed His promise was ever fulfilled﴾ [Maryam: 61], that is, done. So the meaning of "bima ataw" is "by what they did," and this is indicated by the reading of Ubayy: "bima fa'alu." Concerning what they did and rejoiced in, there are several views. The first: the concealment of what the Messenger had asked them about, and informing him of something else, and showing him that they had informed him of it, thereby seeking praise from him; this was said by Ibn ʻAbbas. The second: what they gained of the world and loved that it be said that they were scholars; this was also said by Ibn ʻAbbas. The third: their saying, "We are upon the religion of Abraham," and their concealment of the matter of the Messenger; this was said by Ibn Jubayr. The fourth: their letters to the Jews of the whole earth that Muhammad (ﷺ) is not a prophet, so hold fast to your religion; their word came together upon disbelief in him, and they said: "We are the people of fasting and prayer and the friends of God"; this was said by al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. The fifth: the statement of the Jews of Khaybar to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions: "We are upon your religion, and we are a support for you," while they were holding fast to their misguidance, and they wished that he would praise them for what they had not done; this was said by al-Suddi. The sixth: the Jews' equipping of an army against the Prophet (ﷺ) and their spending upon that army; this was said by al-Nakha'i. The seventh: the informing of a group of Jews to the Muslims when they left the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), he having informed them of things they knew, so the Muslims praised them for that, while they concealed the opposite of what they displayed; this was mentioned by al-Zajjaj. The eighth: the following of people in their distortion of the interpretation of the Torah, and they loved that they be praised for that, while they did nothing beneficial or sound; this was said by Mujahid. The ninth: the staying behind of the hypocrites from the expedition, and their swearing to the Muslims that they were pleased with their victory, and they loved that it be said that they were in the rank of the fighters; this was said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

The views preceding this last one are all based on the premise that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews. It has been said: it is possible that it includes everyone who performs a good deed and rejoices in it with the joy of self-admiration, and loves that people praise him and extol him for piety and asceticism, and for what is not in him. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʻAmr read: "la yahsabanna" and "la yahsabannahum" with the ya' in both, and with the raising of the ba' in "yahsabannahum," on the basis that "yahsabanna" is attributed to "alladhina" (those who). This reading has been explained in two ways. The first, which Abu ʻAli said: "la yahsabanna" did not govern any object, and "alladhina" is raised by it. These verbs may come as idle (لغوًا), not in the position of complete meaningful sentences, like His saying:

"And I did not think that among us there remained any affection, the lean necks of the stallions and the mares..."

Al-Khalil said: the Arabs say: "I did not see him say that except Zayd, and I did not think him to say that except Zayd." Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: the reading is then consistent with "fa-la yahsabannahum" being a substitute for the first, and it has transitively taken two objects, which are the pronoun and "bi-mafazah," and it has dispensed with the two objects thereby, as it dispensed in His saying:

"By what book or by what custom do you see their love as a shame upon me, and you reckon..."

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 186–189 (part 2 of 2):

That is: "and you think their love (for praise) to be a disgrace upon me." The second possibility is what al-Zamakhshari said: that the first object is omitted, with the meaning of "lā yaḥsabannahumu alladhīna yafrahūna bi-mafāzatin" as "lā yaḥsabanna anfusahumu alladhīna yafrahūna fā'izīn" (let not those who rejoice think themselves victorious). And "fa-lā yaḥsabannahum" is an emphasis. The refutation of al-Zamakhshari regarding his estimate of "lā yaḥsabannahumu" in His words, ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178], has already been presented to us, and that estimate is not valid, so it should be sought there. In this reading, the verb of reckoning (ḥusbān) is transitive to its two attached pronouns, the nominative and the accusative, and this is something specific to ẓanantu (I thought) and its sisters, and to others besides them: wajadtu (I found), faqadtu (I lost), and 'adimtu (I lacked), and this is established in the science of grammar (naḥw).

Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim read: lā taḥsabanna and fa-lā taḥsabannahum, with the tā' of address and the opening of the bā' in both, addressed to the Messenger. This reading has been given two interpretations. One of them, mentioned by Ibn 'Atiyyah, is that the first object is: alladhīna yafrahūn (those who rejoice), and the second is omitted, due to what follows it indicating it, as was said just above regarding the two objects. The repetition of the verb in fa-lā yaḥsabannahum is good because of the length of the speech, and this is the habit of the Arabs, and it brings the listener's mind closer. The second interpretation was mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, who said: one of the two objects is "alladhīna yafrahūn," and the second is "bi-mafāzatin." His saying "fa-lā yaḥsabannahum" is an emphasis, its estimate being "lā yaḥsabannahum, fa-lā yaḥsabannahum fā'izīn." It was also read: lā taḥsabunna and fa-lā taḥsabunnahum, with the tā' of address and the damma of the bā' in both, addressed to the believers. The disagreement about the second object comes in the same way as the disagreement about it in the reading of the Kufans.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read: lā yaḥsabanna with the yā' of the third person, and fa-lā taḥsabannahum with the tā' of address and the opening of the bā' in both. This reading has been explained as the omission of the two objects of yaḥsabanna, due to what follows them indicating them. The substitution (badal) that was permitted in the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr is not permitted in this reading, because the two verbs differ in their subject. When "fa-lā yaḥsabannahum" is an emphasis or a substitution, the entry of the fa' is only justified on the basis that it is extra (ziyadah), since it cannot be for coordination (ʿaṭf) nor the fa' of the answer of a condition. They cited as evidence for the extra fa' the words of the poet:

"Until I left the recurring ones (women) returning to him,
saying: 'fa-lā tab'ud' (so do not be far), and I said to him: 'ub'ud' (be far)."

And another said:

"When the one whose offence is great pressed with a hand,
so I left the upper part of his palm swinging."

That is: "lā tab'ud" and "tarakt" (I left). Al-Nakha'i and Marwan ibn al-Hakam read: bi-mā ātaw, meaning "they gave." Ibn Jubayr and al-Sulami read: bi-mā ūtū, in the passive. The views on "ātaw" have already been given, and some of them agree with these two readings.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: (bi-mā lam yaf'alū bi-mafāzatin), and "fa-lā yaḥsabannahum" is dropped. "Mafāzah" is a noun of place from fāza, meaning a place of winning, i.e. salvation. Al-Farra' said: that is, it keeps far from punishment, because fawz means distance from what is disliked. In this verse there is evidence that a person adorning himself with what is not in him, and loving to be praised for it, is forbidden and blameworthy in the Law. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2]. And in the authentic hadith: "The one who pretends to have what he does not have is like one who wears two garments of falsehood." Allah the Exalted has informed of their punishment in His words: ﴿And for them is a painful punishment.﴾ Describing it as painful is fitting because of their rejoicing and their love of being praised for what they did not do.

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is over all things competent.﴾ He, the Exalted, mentioned that they are among what He owns, and that He is capable over them. Thus they are owned, subdued, and subject to His power, so they are not safe from punishment.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 186–189 (part 1 of 2):

﴿You will surely be tested in your possessions and your selves, and you will surely hear much hurt from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate partners with God. But if you are patient and mindful of God, that is indeed among the steadfast resolutions of affairs.﴾ ﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it." But they cast it behind their backs and bartered it for a small price. How evil is what they barter.﴾ ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done and love to be praised for what they did not do, do not think them safe from the punishment. For them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and God is over all things capable.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for people of understanding.﴾ [Al-Imran: 190] ﴿Those who remember God standing, sitting, and on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Glory be to You; protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ [Al-Imran: 191] ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have truly disgraced him, and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.﴾ [Al-Imran: 192] ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins, remove from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die with the righteous.﴾ [Al-Imran: 193] ﴿Our Lord, grant us what You promised us through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed You do not break the promise.﴾ [Al-Imran: 194] ﴿So their Lord answered them: "I do not waste the work of any worker among you, male or female, you are of one another. Those who emigrated, were driven from their homes, were harmed in My cause, fought, and were killed, I will surely remove their misdeeds from them and surely admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, as a reward from God. And with God is the best reward."﴾ [Al-Imran: 195] ﴿Do not let the movement of those who disbelieve through the land deceive you.﴾ [Al-Imran: 196] ﴿A brief enjoyment; then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place.﴾ [Al-Imran: 197] ﴿But those who are mindful of their Lord will have gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, as a provision from God. And what is with God is better for the righteous.﴾ [Al-Imran: 198] ﴿And indeed among the People of the Scripture are those who believe in God, and in what was revealed to you and what was revealed to them, humbling themselves before God. They do not trade the signs of God for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed God is swift in reckoning.﴾ [Al-Imran: 199] ﴿O you who believe, be patient, endure together, stand ready on the frontier, and be mindful of God, that you may prosper.﴾ [Al-Imran: 200]

Al-judub (الجنوب) is the plural of janb (جنب), which is well known (the sides of the body). Al-murabata (المرابطة) is remaining constantly at the frontier for jihad, and its origin is from tying horses (ربط الخيل).
