The eighth: the following of people in their distortion of the interpretation of the Torah, and they loved that they be praised for that, while they did nothing beneficial or sound; this was said by Mujahid. The ninth: the staying behind of the hypocrites from the expedition, and their swearing to the Muslims that they were pleased with their victory, and they loved that it be said that they were in the rank of the fighters; this was said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

The views preceding this last one are all based on the premise that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews. It has been said: it is possible that it includes everyone who performs a good deed and rejoices in it with the joy of self-admiration, and loves that people praise him and extol him for piety and asceticism, and for what is not in him. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʻAmr read: "la yahsabanna" and "la yahsabannahum" with the ya' in both, and with the raising of the ba' in "yahsabannahum," on the basis that "yahsabanna" is attributed to "alladhina" (those who). This reading has been explained in two ways. The first, which Abu ʻAli said: "la yahsabanna" did not govern any object, and "alladhina" is raised by it. These verbs may come as idle (لغوًا), not in the position of complete meaningful sentences, like His saying:

"And I did not think that among us there remained any affection, the lean necks of the stallions and the mares..."

Al-Khalil said: the Arabs say: "I did not see him say that except Zayd, and I did not think him to say that except Zayd." Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: the reading is then consistent with "fa-la yahsabannahum" being a substitute for the first, and it has transitively taken two objects, which are the pronoun and "bi-mafazah," and it has dispensed with the two objects thereby, as it dispensed in His saying:

"By what book or by what custom do you see their love as a shame upon me, and you reckon..."

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 186–189 (part 2 of 2):

That is: "and you think their love (for praise) to be a disgrace upon me." The second possibility is what al-Zamakhshari said: that the first object is omitted, with the meaning of "lā yaḥsabannahumu alladhīna yafrahūna bi-mafāzatin" as "lā yaḥsabanna anfusahumu alladhīna yafrahūna fā'izīn" (let not those who rejoice think themselves victorious). And "fa-lā yaḥsabannahum" is an emphasis. The refutation of al-Zamakhshari regarding his estimate of "lā yaḥsabannahumu" in His words, ﴿And let not those who disbelieve think that...﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178], has already been presented to us, and that estimate is not valid, so it should be sought there. In this reading, the verb of reckoning (ḥusbān) is transitive to its two attached pronouns, the nominative and the accusative, and this is something specific to ẓanantu (I thought) and its sisters, and to others besides them: wajadtu (I found), faqadtu (I lost), and 'adimtu (I lacked), and this is established in the science of grammar (naḥw).

Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim read: lā taḥsabanna and fa-lā taḥsabannahum, with the tā' of address and the opening of the bā' in both, addressed to the Messenger. This reading has been given two interpretations. One of them, mentioned by Ibn 'Atiyyah, is that the first object is: alladhīna yafrahūn (those who rejoice), and the second is omitted, due to what follows it indicating it, as was said just above regarding the two objects. The repetition of the verb in fa-lā yaḥsabannahum is good because of the length of the speech, and this is the habit of the Arabs, and it brings the listener's mind closer. The second interpretation was mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, who said: one of the two objects is "alladhīna yafrahūn," and the second is "bi-mafāzatin." His saying "fa-lā yaḥsabannahum" is an emphasis, its estimate being "lā yaḥsabannahum, fa-lā yaḥsabannahum fā'izīn." It was also read: lā taḥsabunna and fa-lā taḥsabunnahum, with the tā' of address and the damma of the bā' in both, addressed to the believers. The disagreement about the second object comes in the same way as the disagreement about it in the reading of the Kufans.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read: lā yaḥsabanna with the yā' of the third person, and fa-lā taḥsabannahum with the tā' of address and the opening of the bā' in both. This reading has been explained as the omission of the two objects of yaḥsabanna, due to what follows them indicating them. The substitution (badal) that was permitted in the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr is not permitted in this reading, because the two verbs differ in their subject. When "fa-lā yaḥsabannahum" is an emphasis or a substitution, the entry of the fa' is only justified on the basis that it is extra (ziyadah), since it cannot be for coordination (ʿaṭf) nor the fa' of the answer of a condition. They cited as evidence for the extra fa' the words of the poet:

"Until I left the recurring ones (women) returning to him,
saying: 'fa-lā tab'ud' (so do not be far), and I said to him: 'ub'ud' (be far)."

And another said:

"When the one whose offence is great pressed with a hand,
so I left the upper part of his palm swinging."

That is: "lā tab'ud" and "tarakt" (I left). Al-Nakha'i and Marwan ibn al-Hakam read: bi-mā ātaw, meaning "they gave." Ibn Jubayr and al-Sulami read: bi-mā ūtū, in the passive. The views on "ātaw" have already been given, and some of them agree with these two readings.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: (bi-mā lam yaf'alū bi-mafāzatin), and "fa-lā yaḥsabannahum" is dropped. "Mafāzah" is a noun of place from fāza, meaning a place of winning, i.e. salvation. Al-Farra' said: that is, it keeps far from punishment, because fawz means distance from what is disliked. In this verse there is evidence that a person adorning himself with what is not in him, and loving to be praised for it, is forbidden and blameworthy in the Law. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2]. And in the authentic hadith: "The one who pretends to have what he does not have is like one who wears two garments of falsehood." Allah the Exalted has informed of their punishment in His words: ﴿And for them is a painful punishment.﴾ Describing it as painful is fitting because of their rejoicing and their love of being praised for what they did not do.

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is over all things competent.﴾ He, the Exalted, mentioned that they are among what He owns, and that He is capable over them. Thus they are owned, subdued, and subject to His power, so they are not safe from punishment.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 186–189 (part 1 of 2):

﴿You will surely be tested in your possessions and your selves, and you will surely hear much hurt from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate partners with God. But if you are patient and mindful of God, that is indeed among the steadfast resolutions of affairs.﴾ ﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it." But they cast it behind their backs and bartered it for a small price. How evil is what they barter.﴾ ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done and love to be praised for what they did not do, do not think them safe from the punishment. For them is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and God is over all things capable.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for people of understanding.﴾ [Al-Imran: 190] ﴿Those who remember God standing, sitting, and on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth: "Our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Glory be to You; protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ [Al-Imran: 191] ﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have truly disgraced him, and for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.﴾ [Al-Imran: 192] ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed. Our Lord, forgive us our sins, remove from us our misdeeds, and cause us to die with the righteous.﴾ [Al-Imran: 193] ﴿Our Lord, grant us what You promised us through Your messengers, and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed You do not break the promise.﴾ [Al-Imran: 194] ﴿So their Lord answered them: "I do not waste the work of any worker among you, male or female, you are of one another. Those who emigrated, were driven from their homes, were harmed in My cause, fought, and were killed, I will surely remove their misdeeds from them and surely admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow, as a reward from God. And with God is the best reward."﴾ [Al-Imran: 195] ﴿Do not let the movement of those who disbelieve through the land deceive you.﴾ [Al-Imran: 196] ﴿A brief enjoyment; then their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place.﴾ [Al-Imran: 197] ﴿But those who are mindful of their Lord will have gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, as a provision from God. And what is with God is better for the righteous.﴾ [Al-Imran: 198] ﴿And indeed among the People of the Scripture are those who believe in God, and in what was revealed to you and what was revealed to them, humbling themselves before God. They do not trade the signs of God for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed God is swift in reckoning.﴾ [Al-Imran: 199] ﴿O you who believe, be patient, endure together, stand ready on the frontier, and be mindful of God, that you may prosper.﴾ [Al-Imran: 200]

Al-judub (الجنوب) is the plural of janb (جنب), which is well known (the sides of the body). Al-murabata (المرابطة) is remaining constantly at the frontier for jihad, and its origin is from tying horses (ربط الخيل).

﴿You will surely be tested in your possessions and your selves, and you will surely hear much hurt from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate partners with God﴾: It is said that it was revealed concerning the incident of Abdullah ibn Ubayy when he said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while the Messenger was reciting the Qur'an to them: "If what you say is true, then do not trouble us with it in our gatherings." Ibn Rawahah answered him, saying: "Come to us with it in our gatherings, O Messenger of God." The Muslims, the polytheists, and the Jews then reviled one another. It is also said that it concerned what occurred between Abu Bakr and Phinehas. It is also said that it concerned Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, who in his poetry incited the polytheists against the Messenger and his companions. God, exalted is He, informed them of this testing and hearing so that they would be better prepared to bear what came upon them from it, since when the news comes in advance, it differs from one to whom the matter comes suddenly, for the latter's pain is greater. The verse is directed at the censure of the People of the Scripture and others among the polytheists, and it fits with the preceding verses which came in censure of the People of the Scripture and other polytheists.

In His words "latublawunna" (لتبلون), the apparent meaning is that those addressed are the believers. Ata' said: they are the emigrants, whom the polytheists dispossessed of their dwellings, selling them, and plundering their wealth. It is also said that the testing in possessions is what they suffered of plunder of their wealth and the loss of their numbers on the day of Uhud. The apparent meaning is that this is address to the believers concerning the trial that will occur in possessions, through the calamities and losses that befall them, and through spending in the way of God and in the obligations of the Law. The testing in the self (النفس) is through desires, or bodily obligations, or illnesses, or the loss of relatives and kin, or through killing, wounds, captivity, and various kinds of fears; these are the views. He placed possessions before selves, either by way of ascending to what is more noble, or by way of quantity, because misfortunes in possessions are more numerous than misfortunes in selves. Al-adha (الأذى) is a comprehensive noun meaning harm. It includes their statements about the Messenger and his companions, about God, exalted is He, and His prophets, their attacks upon the religion, their denigration of those who believed, and the satire of Ka'b and his composing amorous verses about the women of the believers.

﴿And if you are patient﴾: over that testing and that hearing.

﴿and are mindful of God, then indeed that﴾: i.e., indeed patience and piety.

﴿is among the steadfast resolutions of affairs﴾: It is said: among the most firm and most excellent of them. Al-azm (العزم) is carrying out a matter after deliberation and refinement. Al-Naqqash said: al-azm is the same as al-hazm (الحزم, firmness of judgment), the ḥāʼ being substituted for the ʻayn. Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: this is an error. Al-hazm is the soundness of consideration of a matter, and its result is caution against error in it. Al-azm is the intent to carry it out. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And consult them in the matter; then when you have resolved﴾ [Al-Imran: 159], so consultation and what is in its meaning is al-hazm. The Arabs say: "I may exercise firm judgment, if I resolve." Al-Zamakhshari said: "min ʻazm al-umūr" means among the resolved matters, i.e., of what it is obligatory to resolve upon among affairs, or of what God has resolved to be; that is, that it is a resolution from the resolutions of God: you must be patient and mindful. It is also said: "min ʻazm al-umūr" means from its seriousness. Mujahid, in His words "fa-idha ʻazama al-amr," said: i.e., when the matter has come into being.

﴿And when God took the covenant of those who were given the Scripture: "You must make it clear to the people and not conceal it"﴾: They are the Jews, upon whom the covenant was taken concerning the matter of the Messenger (ﷺ), but they concealed it and cast it away. This was said by Ibn ʻAbbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, and Ibn Jurayj. Some people said: they are the Jews and the Christians. The majority said: it is general to everyone whom God has taught knowledge, and the scholars of this community are included in this covenant. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, and Abu Bakr read the verbs with the ya' (الياء) in both places, in the third person (غيبة), since before it is "those who were given the Scripture" and after it is "fa-nabadhuhu." The rest of the seven read them with the ta' (التاء) for direct address, and it is like His saying: ﴿You worship none but God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]; it is read with both ta' and ya'. The apparent meaning is that the pronoun returns to the Scripture. It is also said it returns to the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also said it returns to the covenant. It is also said it returns to belief in the Messenger, due to His saying: ﴿You shall surely believe in him and surely support him﴾ [Al-Imran: 81]. The nominative of "wa-la taktumunahu" (ولا تكتمونه) is because it occurs as a circumstantial clause (حال), i.e., "without concealing it," and it is not included in the oath-subject (المقسم عليه). They said: it is the waw of circumstance, not of conjunction, like His saying: ﴿So continue straight and do not follow﴾ [Yunus: 89], and His saying "wa-la yasal" in the reading of the one who lightened the nun and raised the lam. It is also said that the waw is for conjunction, and it is part of what is sworn to. Since it was negated by "la," it was not emphasized; you say: "By God, Zayd will not stand," so the nun does not enter it. This latter view is, in my opinion, more correct in grammatical analysis (إعراب) and more eloquent, because the first view requires the omission of a subject before "la," so that the clause is a nominal clause in the position of a circumstantial clause, since a negated present verb with "la" does not take the waw of circumstance. Ibn Masʻud read: "layubayyinunahu," without the nun of emphasis. Ibn ʻAṭiyyah said: this nun is not necessarily required with the lam of emphasis, as reported by Sibawayh. End. This is not known from the saying of the Basrans; rather, the alternation of the lam and the nun is, in their view, a necessity of poetry. The Kufans permit it in ordinary speech, so they permit: "By God, I will stand," and "By God, I will surely stand." The poet said:

"By your life, O Salma, I am certain that I would be permitted whatever you wished, even if it were death."

Another said:

"By oath, I shall surely hate every man who embellishes speech and does not act."

Ibn ʻAbbas read: "mithaqa al-nabiyyin li-tubayyinunnahu li-l-nas," so the pronoun in "fa-nabadhuhu" returns to the people, since it is impossible for it to return to the prophets; that is, "the people to whom the covenant was made clear cast it away." The meaning of His words "fa-nabadhuhu wara'a zuhurihim" has been explained previously in His saying: ﴿A party of those who were given the Scripture cast the Book of God behind their backs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 101].

﴿and bartered it for a small price. How evil is what they barter﴾: The explanation of this sentence has been given before, and the discussion of the grammatical analysis of what follows "bi'sa" was given, so there is no need to repeat it.

﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done and love to be praised for what they did not do, do not think them safe from the punishment. For them is a painful punishment﴾: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, who used to stay behind from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in the expedition, and when he returned they offered excuses to him; he would accept their excuses and ask forgiveness for them, so God exposed them by this verse. This was said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Ibn Zayd, and a group. Many exegetes said: it was revealed concerning the rabbis of the Jews. "Ata" (أتى) comes with the meaning of "fa'ala" (did), as in His saying, exalted is He: (p-137) ﴿Indeed His promise was ever fulfilled﴾ [Maryam: 61], that is, done. So the meaning of "bima ataw" is "by what they did," and this is indicated by the reading of Ubayy: "bima fa'alu." Concerning what they did and rejoiced in, there are several views. The first: the concealment of what the Messenger had asked them about, and informing him of something else, and showing him that they had informed him of it, thereby seeking praise from him; this was said by Ibn ʻAbbas. The second: what they gained of the world and loved that it be said that they were scholars; this was also said by Ibn ʻAbbas. The third: their saying, "We are upon the religion of Abraham," and their concealment of the matter of the Messenger; this was said by Ibn Jubayr. The fourth: their letters to the Jews of the whole earth that Muhammad (ﷺ) is not a prophet, so hold fast to your religion; their word came together upon disbelief in him, and they said: "We are the people of fasting and prayer and the friends of God"; this was said by al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. The fifth: the statement of the Jews of Khaybar to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions: "We are upon your religion, and we are a support for you," while they were holding fast to their misguidance, and they wished that he would praise them for what they had not done; this was said by al-Suddi. The sixth: the Jews' equipping of an army against the Prophet (ﷺ) and their spending upon that army; this was said by al-Nakha'i. The seventh: the informing of a group of Jews to the Muslims when they left the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), he having informed them of things they knew, so the Muslims praised them for that, while they concealed the opposite of what they displayed; this was mentioned by al-Zajjaj. The eighth: the following of people in their distortion of the interpretation of the Torah, and they loved that they be praised for that, while they did nothing beneficial or sound; this was said by Mujahid. The ninth: the staying behind of the hypocrites from the expedition, and their swearing to the Muslims that they were pleased with their victory, and they loved that it be said that they were in the rank of the fighters; this was said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.

The views preceding this last one are all based on the premise that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews. It has been said: it is possible that it includes everyone who performs a good deed and rejoices in it with the joy of self-admiration, and loves that people praise him and extol him for piety and asceticism, and for what is not in him. And "fa-lā yaḥsabannahum" is an emphasis. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 190–191:

﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, there are signs for those of understanding.﴾ The explanation of the like of this sentence has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah. The meaning of ﴿signs﴾ is clear indications of the Creator and of His remarkable wisdom, and this is not apparent except to those endowed with intellects who contemplate it through the way of reflection and inference, not as cattle look.

Ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas that the Quraysh said to the Messenger ﷺ: "Ask your Lord to make Safa gold for us," when the Jews and Christians mentioned to them some of the miracles brought by Musa and Isa, peace be upon them both, so this verse was revealed. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is clear, for when He, exalted is He, mentioned that He is the Owner of the heavens and the earth and mentioned His power, He mentioned that in their creation there are clear proofs for those of intellect.

﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾ The apparent meaning is that remembrance is by the tongue together with the presence of the heart, and that it is glorification (tahmid), declaring Allah's oneness (tahlil), magnifying Him (takbir), and the like of such invocations. These three postures are the most common states in which a person is, so they were used, and what is meant by them is all states. As Aisha said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to remember Allah in all his times." The apparent meaning of this hadith and the verse indicates the permissibility of remembering Allah while relieving oneself. Abdullah ibn Umar, Ibn Sirin and al-Nakha'i held this permissible, while Ibn Abbas, Ata' and al-Sha'bi disliked it. It is narrated from Ibn Umar, Urwah ibn al-Zubayr and a group that they went out on the day of the Eid to the musalla and began to remember Allah, and some of them said: Did not Allah say: ﴿standing and sitting﴾? So they stood, remembering Allah on their feet.

It is related in a hadith: "Whoever wishes to frolic in the gardens of Paradise, let him increase remembrance of Allah." Ibn Jurayj and the majority went to the view that the meaning of remembrance is the apparent one we have mentioned, and remembrance is among the greatest acts of worship, and the hadiths on it are many. Ibn Abbas and a group said: What is meant by remembrance is the prayers, so in a state of excuse (p-139) they pray them sitting and on their sides, and He called them remembrance because they include remembrance. It was said: What is meant by remembrance is voluntary prayer, which one performs however one wishes. The exegetes brought in this verse many matters concerning how prayer is performed standing, sitting and lying down, and the disagreement of the jurists on that and their evidences. That is established in the science of fiqh. According to the apparent sense of the meaning of remembrance, standing is mentioned first because remembrance in it is lighter for a person; then he moves to the state of sitting, and remembrance in it is harder than in the state of standing, because a person does not usually sit except for a task he is occupied with, such as a craft or other things. Then he moves to the posture of lying down, and remembrance in it is harder than in the posture of sitting, because lying down is a posture of rest and freedom from preoccupations. It is possible in these postures that the ordering is according to what is shorter in duration, so it begins with standing, because that posture generally lasts less time than sitting, then with sitting, since its time is longer, and with lying down, since its time is longer than the time of sitting. Do you not see that the whole night is the time of lying down, and it corresponds to the time of sitting and standing, which is the day? As for when remembrance is meant as the obligatory prayer, the postures come by way of exception: whoever is able to stand does not pray sitting, and whoever is able to sit does not pray lying down. As for when it is meant as voluntary prayer, the postures are by way of preference, since the best is to perform voluntary prayer standing, then sitting, then lying down. Farther from the exegesis is the one who went to the view that the meaning is: they remember Allah standing by His commands, sitting by refraining from His prohibitions, and on their sides, meaning distancing themselves from opposing His command and His prohibition. This resembles the speech of the people of hearts and is close to the Batiniyya.

They permitted, regarding ﴿those who﴾, the description (naʿt), the cutting for nominative (raf'), and the accusative (nasb). ﴿And on their sides﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (hal) conjoined to a circumstantial phrase, and here the prepositional phrase is conjoined to the explicit noun. In His saying: ﴿He calls Us for his side, or sitting, or standing﴾ [Yunus: 12], the explicit noun is conjoined to the prepositional phrase.

﴿And they reflect upon the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ The apparent sense is that it is conjoined to the relative clause, so it has no place in terms of grammatical case (i'rab). It was said: the clause is in the position of accusative as a circumstantial phrase, conjoined to the circumstantial phrase before it. When He mentioned remembrance, whose locus is the tongue, He mentioned reflection, whose locus is the heart. ﴿Creation﴾ may be understood as the verbal noun, for reflection on the creation of these wondrous made things, of such strange form and of the power to bring these into being from pure non-existence, indicates complete power, knowledge, oneness and the rest of the exalted attributes. In reflection on that there is what dazzles the intellects and absorbs the thoughts. It may also be understood as the created thing, and he attributed it by meaning to the two places, not to the object. Reflection on what Allah placed in the heavens of shining stars and the spheres in which the victory is found, and what He placed in the earth of animals, plants and minerals, and the difference of their kinds, species and individuals as well, dazzles the intellect and multiplies lessons.

A poet said:
"And in every thing there is a sign that indicates that He is One."

The Prophet ﷺ passed by a people reflecting on Allah and said: "Reflect upon the creation and do not reflect upon the Creator, for you cannot measure His measure." Some scholars said: One who reflects on the essence of Allah is like one who looks at the sun's disc, because He, exalted is He, ﴿there is nothing like unto Him﴾. Reflection is only the extension of the mind upon the created things and upon the created things of the Hereafter. In a hadith: "There is no worship like reflection." The exegetes mentioned much of people's speech on reflection and of the notable reflectors, and we have judged it not to lengthen our book by transmitting them.

﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain; glory be to You, so protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾ This sentence is related by an omitted verb whose estimate is: they say. This verb is in the position of accusative as a circumstantial phrase, and the indication by ﴿this﴾ refers to the creation if what is meant is the created thing, or to the heavens and the earth, since they are in the meaning of created thing. That is: You did not create this wondrous creation in vain. It was said: the meaning is: a vain creation, that is, without purpose; rather You created it and created mankind so that they would look into it, and thus unify and worship. Whoever does that You will bless, and whoever goes astray from that You will punish. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is: You did not create it as a vain creation without wisdom (p-140), but You created it for a great wisdom, which is that You make them dwellings for the accountable and proofs for them of Your recognition, the obligation of obeying You, and avoiding Your disobedience. For this reason He connected to it His saying: ﴿so protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾, and because it is the recompense of one who disobeys and does not obey. End. In it are the indications of the Mu'tazilites, from his saying: "rather You created it for a great wisdom." On this basis, ﴿vain﴾ is in the accusative as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun. It was said: ﴿vain﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial phrase from the object. It was said: it is in the accusative by dropping the preposition, that is, with vanity, but You created it with Your power which is truth. It was said: by dropping the lam, and it is an object of purpose, and the agent is in the sense of the verbal noun, that is, vanity. It was said: it is a second object of "created," and it is in the sense of "made," which takes two objects; this is the reverse of what is transmitted in grammar, which is that "made" can mean "created" and take one object. As for "created" meaning "made" and taking two objects, I know of no one of knowledge who went to that. The vain (batil) is that which is perishing and departing, and from it:

"Surely everything other than Allah is vain."

The best of its grammatical analyses is that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial phrase from "this," and it is a circumstantial phrase that cannot be dispensed with, like His saying: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ [al-Dukhan: 38]. In this circumstantial phrase it is not permissible to omit it, lest the meaning become negation, and that is not permissible.

Since this sentence contained the acknowledgment that this wondrous creation was not vain, and the alerting that this is the speech of people of understanding who remember Allah in all their states and reflect on creation, it indicates that others, from among the heedless and ignorant, go to the opposite of this statement; so they declared Him exalted above what those falsifiers say, from what He pointed to in His saying "in play," and in His saying: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115]. And there was objection to this declaration of transcendence, which includes Allah's freedom from all deficiencies and the actions of created beings, between that acknowledgment and their desire toward their Lord that He protect them from the punishment of the Fire, while they had no concern for anything of the affairs of this world, nor any regard for it; they only humbly begged for the protection from punishment on the Day of Resurrection. This request is the outcome of remembrance, reflection, acknowledgment and declaration of transcendence. The "fa" in ﴿so protect us﴾ is for conjunction and for ordering the request upon the acknowledgment mentioned. It was said: it is for ordering the request upon what the word "glory be to You" includes of the verb, that is: We have declared You far above what the ignorant say, so protect us. The one who went to the view that it is for ordering upon what the call includes was far off.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verses 190–191:

The meaning of ﴿signs﴾ is clear indications of the Creator and of His remarkable wisdom, and this is not apparent except to those endowed with intellects who contemplate it through the way of reflection and inference, not as cattle look.

Ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas that the Quraysh said to the Messenger ﷺ: "Ask your Lord to make Safa gold for us," when the Jews and Christians mentioned to them some of the miracles brought by Musa and Isa, peace be upon them both, so this verse was revealed. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is clear, for when He, exalted is He, mentioned that He is the Owner of the heavens and the earth and mentioned His power, He mentioned that in their creation there are clear proofs for those of intellect.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 192–194 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Our Lord, indeed whoever You admit to the Fire, You have disgraced him.﴾ This is a plea for refuge and protection. That is, "Do not treat us that way, and do not make us among those who do its deeds." The meaning of *akhzaytahu* is *fadahtahu* (You exposed him). From *khazia al-rajulu yakhza khizyan*, it means he was exposed (disgraced), and *khizaya* means he felt shame. The verb is one, but the verbal noun differs: from exposure comes *khizy*, and from shame comes *khazaya*. From the same root is ﴿and do not disgrace me regarding my guests﴾ [Hud: 78], that is, "do not expose me." It is said that the meaning is "You humiliated him." Al-Mufaddal said: "You destroyed him." It is said *khazaytuhu* and *akhzaytuhu*, in triliteral and quadriliteral forms, and the quadriliteral is more common and more eloquent. Al-Zajjaj said: the *makhzi* in the language is the one who is humiliated and despised because of a matter that has befallen him. It is said *akhzaytuhu*, "I imposed on him an argument by which I humiliated him." Anas, Sa'id, al-Suddi, Muqatil, Ibn Jurayj and others said: this refers to whoever abides in the Fire forever, but whoever comes out of it through intercession and faith is not *makhzi*. Jabir ibn Abdullah and others said: everyone who enters the Fire is *makhzi*, even if he comes out of it, and that for anything below it there is disgrace. Ibn Jurayj and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi preferred this view.

﴿And there are no helpers for the wrongdoers.﴾ This is from the words of those who supplicate. Ibn Abbas said: "The wrongdoers here are the disbelievers," and this is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun). It has been stated explicitly in His words: ﴿And the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 254], and His words: ﴿Indeed, associating partners with God is a great injustice﴾ [Luqman: 13]. This interpretation fits best if what precedes it concerns those who abide in the Fire, because the negation of helpers is either by preventing (punishment) or by intercession, and this is specific to the disbelievers. As for the believer, God is his helper, the Messenger ﷺ is his intercessor, and some believers intercede for others, as is related in the hadith. Al-Zamakhshari said: the *lam* in ﴿for the wrongdoers﴾ indicates those who enter the Fire, and it informs that whoever enters the Fire has no helper, neither by intercession nor otherwise. End of quote. This is according to the Mu'tazili method (i'tizal, the rationalist theological school) that whoever enters the Fire never leaves it, whether he was a disbeliever or a sinner. The word *man* is the object of the conditional verb. Some grammarians (mu'rabun, those who analyze the i'rab, the grammatical case endings) reported the following text: Some people permitted that *man* be in the accusative governed by a verb implied by the answer of the conditional, which is ﴿then You have disgraced him﴾. Others permitted that *man* be the subject, with the conditional and its answer as the predicate. End of quote. As for the first view, it comes from one ignorant of the science of grammar. As for the second, parsing *man* as the subject is extremely weak. And placing the answer of the conditional in the predicate together with the conditional verb is ignorance. Who is greater in burden than one who speaks about the Book of God without knowledge?

﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we believed.﴾ (*Sami'a*, "heard") if it is followed by an object of hearing, is transitive to one object, like *sami'tu kalama Zayd* ("I heard the speech of Zayd"), like other verbs of the senses. If it is followed by a person and then by a verb or a noun with the meaning of a verb, like *sami'tu Zaydan yatakallamu* ("I heard Zayd speaking") and *sami'tu Zaydan yaqulu kadha* ("I heard Zayd say such-and-such"), there is a disagreement on this matter. Some held that this verb or noun, if preceded by an indefinite noun, is an adjective of it, or if preceded by a definite noun, is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of it. Others held that this verb or noun is in the position of the second object of *sami'a*, and they made *sami'a* transitive to one object if it is followed by an object of hearing, and to two if followed by a person. This is the view of Abu Ali al-Farisi. The correct view is the first, and this is established in the science of grammar. Accordingly, *yunadi* ("calling") is in the position of an adjective, because it is preceded by an indefinite noun. According to Abu Ali's view, it is in the position of the second object. Al-Zamakhshari adopted the first view and said: you say *sami'tu rajulan yaqulu kadha* and *sami'tu Zaydan yatakallamu*, so that the verb falls on the man, and you omit the object of hearing, because you described him with what he hears, or you made it a circumstantial qualifier of him, and so it suffices you from mentioning it. Without the description or the circumstantial qualifier there would be no alternative. And one can say *sami'tu kalama fulan* or *qawlahu* ("I heard the speech of so-and-so, or his saying"). End of his words. His statement, "Without the description or the circumstantial qualifier...," is not so. Rather, there is neither description nor qualifier, and *sami'a* enters upon a person, not upon an object of hearing. That is when the speech contains something that indicates the object of hearing, even if it is neither a description nor a qualifier. Among this is the words of God Most High: ﴿Do they hear you when you call?﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 72]; the mention of the time of the call suffices in place of mentioning the object of hearing.

The caller here is the Messenger ﷺ. God Most High said: ﴿and as one who calls to God by His permission﴾ [al-Ahzab: 46], ﴿Call to the way of your Lord﴾ [al-Nahl: 125]. This was said by Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd and others. Or the caller is the Qur'an, as said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: because not all the believers met the Messenger. According to the first view, describing him as a caller is literal; according to the second, it is figurative. The words ﴿a caller calling﴾ are combined: he mentioned the first without restriction and restricted the second to magnify the caller's station, because there is no caller greater than one who calls to faith. That is because when a caller is mentioned without qualification, the mind goes to a caller to war, or to extinguish a conflict, or to relieve the distressed, or to meet some calamity, or to bring some benefit. So when you say ﴿calling to faith﴾, you have raised the caller's rank and magnified him. The *lam* is connected to *yunadi*. *Nada*, *da'a* and *nadaba* are transitive with *li* and with *ila*, just as *hada* is transitive with both, because both meanings of specification and limit of the goal are present. For this reason some said that the *lam* is in the sense of *ila* ("to"), since *yunadi* means *yad'u* ("calls"), so its reaching by *lam* is good in the sense of *ila*. It is said the *lam* is the *lam* of cause, that is, for the sake of faith. It is said the *lam* is in the sense of *ba'* ("with"), that is, with faith. The hearing is taken in its literal meaning: that is, we heard the voice of a caller. It is said: whoever makes the caller the Qur'an, for him hearing is figurative for acceptance. The *an* is explanatory, the sense being *an amminu* ("namely, believe"). It is permitted that it be verbal, connected to an imperative verb, that is, *bi-an amminu* ("that you believe"). According to the first, it has no place in the grammar; according to the second, it has a place, which is the genitive or the accusative, by disagreement. The coordination of ﴿so we believed﴾ with *fa* indicates the hastening of acceptance and that faith follows from hearing without delay. The meaning: "So we believed in You" or "in our Lord."

﴿Our Lord, so forgive us our sins and remove from us our misdeeds.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: the *dhunub* ("sins") are the major sins, and the *sayyi'at* ("misdeeds") are the minor sins. This is supported by: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾ [al-Nisa': 31]. It is said: *dhunub* is abandoning acts of obedience, and *sayyi'at* is committing sins. It is said: the forgiveness of sins and the expiation of misdeeds are close to one another, but it was repeated for emphasis, and because both are ways of covering and of removing the judgment of sins after they have occurred. The forgiveness (*ghufran*) and the expiation (*takfir*) have the same meaning, and the sins and misdeeds have the same meaning, and they were joined for emphasis and intensification, and so that there would be insistence in supplication. It has been related: "Indeed God loves those who insist in supplication." It is said that *takfir* carries the meaning of covering, so that they would be safe from disgrace. The *kaffara* ("expiation") is the act of obedience that covers a misdeed, such as freeing a slave, fasting, or feeding (the poor). A man is *mukaffar* with weapons, that is, covered.

﴿And take us in death with the righteous.﴾ *Abrar* is the plural of *barr*, on the pattern *fa'al*, like *salaf*. Or it is the plural of *barr* (*bārr*), on the pattern *fa'il*, like *darib*, and the *r* was assimilated into the *r*. They are those who are obedient to God, and the meaning of righteousness has been discussed earlier. It is said: here they are those who were good to their fathers and sons. The word *ma'a* ("with") here is figurative, shifting from temporal companionship to companionship in attribute, that is: "Cause us to die as righteous ones counted among the righteous." The meaning is: make us among those whom You cause to die obedient to You. It is said the meaning is: gather us with them in Paradise.

﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers.﴾ The apparent meaning is that they asked their Lord to give them what He promised them through His messengers. The promised thing was interpreted as Paradise, as said by Ibn Abbas. It is said the promised thing is victory over enemies. It is said it is the prayers for forgiveness of the prophets, like the forgiveness-seeking of Nuh, Ibrahim and the Messenger of God ﷺ, and upon them all, and the forgiveness-seeking of the angels for them.

His words ﴿through Your messengers﴾ involve an omitted noun. Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya supplied: "through the tongues of Your messengers." Al-Zamakhshari supplied: "in the confirmation of Your messengers." He said: this *ala* is connected to the promise, as in your saying, "God promised Paradise in return for obedience." The meaning: "what You promised us in return for the confirmation of Your messengers." Do you not see how it followed the mention of the caller to faith, who is the Messenger, and their words "we believed," which is confirmation? It may also be connected to an omitted element, that is: "what You promised us, sent down upon Your messengers," or "carried through Your messengers," because the messengers carry it, and upon them is what they are charged with. End of quote. That is because when a caller is mentioned without qualification, the mind goes to a caller to war, or to extinguish a conflict, or to relieve the distressed, or to meet some calamity, or to bring some benefit. So when you say ﴿calling to faith﴾, you have raised the caller's rank and magnified him. The *lam* is connected to *yunadi*. *Nada*, *da'a* and *nadaba* are transitive with *li* and with *ila*, just as *hada* is transitive with both, because both meanings of specification and limit of the goal are present. For this reason some said that the *lam* is in the sense of *ila* ("to"), since *yunadi* means *yad'u* ("calls"), so its reaching by *lam* is good in the sense of *ila*. It is said the *lam* is the *lam* of cause, that is, for the sake of faith. It is said the *lam* is in the sense of *ba'* ("with"), that is, with faith. The hearing is taken in its literal meaning: that is, we heard the voice of a caller. It is said: whoever makes the caller the Qur'an, for him hearing is figurative for acceptance. The *an* is explanatory, the sense being *an amminu* ("namely, believe"). It is permitted that it be verbal, connected to an imperative verb, that is, *bi-an amminu* ("that you believe"). According to the first, it has no place in the grammar; according to the second, it has a place, which is the genitive or the accusative, by disagreement. The coordination of ﴿so we believed﴾ with *fa* indicates the hastening of acceptance and that faith follows from hearing without delay. The meaning: "So we believed in You" or "in our Lord."

﴿Our Lord, so forgive us our sins and remove from us our misdeeds.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: the *dhunub* ("sins") are the major sins, and the *sayyi'at* ("misdeeds") are the minor sins. This is supported by: ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds﴾ [al-Nisa': 31]. It is said: *dhunub* is abandoning acts of obedience, and *sayyi'at* is committing sins. It is said: the forgiveness of sins and the expiation of misdeeds are close to one another, but it was repeated for emphasis, and because both are ways of covering and of removing the judgment of sins after they have occurred. The forgiveness (*ghufran*) and the expiation (*takfir*) have the same meaning, and the sins and misdeeds have the same meaning, and they were joined for emphasis and intensification, and so that there would be insistence in supplication. It has been related: "Indeed God loves those who insist in supplication." It is said that *takfir* carries the meaning of covering, so that they would be safe from disgrace. The *kaffara* ("expiation") is the act of obedience that covers a misdeed, such as freeing a slave, fasting, or feeding (the poor). A man is *mukaffar* with weapons, that is, covered.

﴿And take us in death with the righteous.﴾ *Abrar* is the plural of *barr*, on the pattern *fa'al*, like *salaf*. Or it is the plural of *barr* (*bārr*), on the pattern *fa'il*, like *darib*, and the *r* was assimilated into the *r*. They are those who are obedient to God, and the meaning of righteousness has been discussed earlier. It is said: here they are those who were good to their fathers and sons. The word *ma'a* ("with") here is figurative, shifting from temporal companionship to companionship in attribute, that is: "Cause us to die as righteous ones counted among the righteous." The meaning is: make us among those whom You cause to die obedient to You. It is said the meaning is: gather us with them in Paradise.

﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers.﴾ The apparent meaning is that they asked their Lord to give them what He promised them through His messengers. The promised thing was interpreted as Paradise, as said by Ibn Abbas. It is said the promised thing is victory over enemies. It is said it is the prayers for forgiveness of the prophets, like the forgiveness-seeking of Nuh, Ibrahim and the Messenger of God ﷺ, and upon them all, and the forgiveness-seeking of the angels for them.

His words ﴿through Your messengers﴾ involve an omitted noun. Al-Tabari and Ibn Atiyya supplied: "through the tongues of Your messengers." Al-Zamakhshari supplied: "in the confirmation of Your messengers." He said: this *ala* is connected to the promise, as in your saying, "God promised Paradise in return for obedience." The meaning: "what You promised us in return for the confirmation of Your messengers." Do you not see how it followed the mention of the caller to faith, who is the Messenger, and their words "we believed," which is confirmation? It may also be connected to an omitted element, that is: "what You promised us, sent down upon Your messengers," or "carried through Your messengers," because the messengers carry it, and upon them is what they are charged with. End of quote. This last possibility that he mentioned is not permissible, because among the rules of the grammarians is that when the preposition-and-object or adverbial phrase's governing verb is restricted, it cannot be omitted, and a verb is omitted only when it is a general existential verb. An example: *Zayd dahik fi al-dar* ("Zayd is laughing in the house"): the word *dahik* cannot be omitted at all. But if you say *Zayd fi al-dar* ("Zayd is in the house"), the governing element is a general existential verb, which may be omitted. Similarly, *Zayd naji min Bani Tamim* ("Zayd is one who escaped from the Banu Tamim") does not permit omitting *naji*. If you say *Zayd min Bani Tamim*, it is permitted with the supposition *ka'in min Bani Tamim* ("being from the Banu Tamim"). The element omitted in what al-Zamakhshari permitted, which is his phrase "sent down or carried," cannot be omitted according to what is established in the science of grammar.

When the governing element of an adverbial phrase or preposition-and-object is restricted, that phrase becomes incomplete, so it cannot be a relative clause complement, nor a predicate, either in the case of the original, or as an adjective, or as a circumstantial qualifier. The meaning of their request that He give them what He promised them is: that He reward them for faith and obedience so that they would be among those to whom God gives what He promised the believers. It is known that He Most High fulfills what He promises, so they asked for the fulfillment of what is due upon faith. The meaning: steadfastness upon faith so that they would be among those who deserve, by God's mercy, the fulfillment of the promise. It is said this request came as a way of seeking refuge in God Most High and humbly imploring Him, just as the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, sought forgiveness, although they knew they were forgiven, intending by that humility, supplication, and seeking refuge with Him. It is said they found the victory they were promised slow, so they asked that He hasten His promise to them. According to this, if the promised thing is victory, the giving is in this world; and if it is Paradise, the giving is in the Hereafter. Al-A'mash recited *ala rusulika* with the *sin* sukun (*rusulika*).

﴿And do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ Disgracing here is interpreted with the same sense as in ﴿then You have disgraced him﴾. *Yawm al-qiyama* ("the Day of Resurrection") is the object of ﴿do not disgrace us﴾. It is permitted that it be a case of *i'mal* (the grammatical principle of two verbs competing for one object), since it can be in the accusative governed by ﴿disgrace us﴾ and by ﴿give us what You promised us﴾, if the promised thing is Paradise.

﴿Indeed, You do not break the promise.﴾ Its apparent meaning is that it is a reason for His words ﴿and give us what You promised us﴾. Ibn Atiyya said: it refers to His words, "On the Day when God will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him" [al-Tahrim: 8]. So this is His promise, and it indicates that disgrace comes only together with eternal abiding. End of quote.

Consider the excellence of the dialogue of these remembering and reflecting people. They addressed God Most High with the word "Our Lord," which indicates that He is their Lord who set them right and prepared them for worship. They first reported the result of their reflection, which is their words: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ [Al 'Imran: 191]. Then they asked Him to protect them from the Fire after glorifying Him above all deficiencies. They reported the condition of those who enter the Fire, who are the wrongdoers who do not remember God and do not reflect on His creation. Then they also mentioned what their reflection produced: the answer of the caller to faith, since that is dependent on the fact that He Most High did not create this wondrous creation in vain. Then they asked for the forgiveness of their sins and their death upon the faith they had reported in their words, "So we believed." Then they asked God for Paradise and that He not disgrace them on the Day of Resurrection, and that is the utmost of what they asked.

The phrase "رَبَّنا" was repeated five times, all of it in the manner of supplication and seeking the mercy of Allah the Exalted, by calling upon Him with this noble name which indicates nurturing (tarbiyah), dominion (milk) and reform (islah). Likewise this name was repeated in the stories of Adam and Noah and others. The repetition of "Rabbana... Rabbana" indicates the permissibility of persistence in asking and of relying on frequent request from Allah the Exalted. In a hadith: "Persist in saying, O Possessor of Majesty and Honour" (ألِظُّوا بِـ يا ذا الجَلالِ والإكْرامِ). Al-Hasan said: "They kept saying 'Rabbana, Rabbana' until He answered them."

This is a matter on which the scholars of the cities (ʿulamaʾ al-amsar) have agreed, unlike some of the Sufis, who permitted it only regarding the Hereafter and not regarding this world. Also some of the mutasawwifah said: Allah the Exalted takes charge of whoever follows the command, avoids the prohibition, and is relieved of the burden of making requests and supplications.

Abu Nasr al-Wa'ili al-Sijistani, the memorizer of hadith (al-Hafiz), narrated in his book al-Ibanah from Abu Hurayrah: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite ten verses from the end of Surat Al ʿImran every night," meaning: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Al ʿImran: 190].

The scholars said: It is recommended for one who wakes from his sleep to wipe his face, and to begin his night prayer by reciting these ten verses, following the example of the Prophet (ﷺ). This is established in the Two Sahihs and elsewhere. Then he should pray what has been written for him, combining reflection (tafakkur) with action.

﴿So their Lord answered them: "I do not waste the work of any worker among you, whether male or female; you are of one another."﴾ It is related that Umm Salamah said: "O Messenger of God, God has mentioned the men in emigration (hijrah) and has not mentioned the women in any of it." So this was revealed, and verses with this meaning were revealed, in which the women are mentioned. The meaning of *istajaba* is *ajaba* (answered), and it is transitive either directly or with *li* (to). The discussion of ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186] has already preceded. Taj al-Qurra' reported that *ajaba* is general, while *istajaba* is specific to the attainment of what is sought.

The majority read *anni* (أنِّي) with the *ba'* (بِ) omitted, meaning *bi-anni* (that I). Ubayy read *bi-anni* with the *ba'*. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read *inni* (إنِّي) with a *kasrah* on the *hamzah*, so that it is according to the view of the Basrans as an implied saying (*idmar al-qawl*), or as a quotation introduced by *fastajaba* (so He answered), because it contains the meaning of saying according to the method of the Kufans.

The majority read ﴿uḍīʿu﴾ (أُضِيعُ) from *aḍaʿa* (to waste). Some read *uḍayyiʿu* (أُضَيِّعُ) with *tashdid* from *ḍayyaʿa*, and the *hamzah* and the *tashdid* in it are for transitivity (*al-naql*), as the poet said:

*Like a wet-nurse who nurses the children of others, and neglects her own children; this is the error that strays from the right course.*

The meaning of that is: I do not withhold the reward of any worker among you. ﴿Among you﴾ (مِنكم) is in the position of a qualifier, meaning "being from among you." As for His saying ﴿male or female﴾ (مِن ذَكَرٍ أوْ أُنْثى), it has been said that *min* (مِن) is explanatory of the kind of worker, so the implied sense is "the one who is male or female." It has also been said that *min* is superfluous, because of the preceding negation in the speech. It has also been said that *min* is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in the agent of ﴿among you﴾, meaning: a worker who is among you, being male or female.

Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿male or female﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿among you﴾, a substitute of a thing for a thing, and both are for one referent. End of quotation. Thus he has repeated the governing element, which is the preposition, and it is a detailed substitute (*badal tafṣīlī*) from the addressee. What prevents it from being a detailed substitute is that it is joined by *aw* (or), whereas the detailed substitute is only with *wa* (and), as in the poet's saying:

*I was like one who has two legs: one healthy leg, and a leg which time has struck, so it is paralysed.*

What also prevents it from being from the addressee is that the position of the majority is that it is not permissible to substitute from the pronoun of the speaker or the pronoun of the addressee a substitute of a thing for a thing when both are for one referent, while al-Akhfash permitted that. Some of our companions stated the disagreement absolutely, while some restricted it to when the substitute is for comprehensiveness (*iḥāṭa*), in which case it is permissible. This restriction is correct, and from it is ﴿It will be a festival for the first of us and the last of us﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 114]: His saying ﴿for the first of us and the last of us﴾ is a substitute from the pronoun of the speaker in His saying "for us" (*lanā*). And the poet's saying:

*Our feet did not leave their place, the three of us, until the deaths were shown to us.*

So "the three of us" (*thalāthatinā*) is a substitute from the pronoun of the speaker. He permitted that because it is a substitute with the meaning of emphasis. What supports the position of al-Akhfash is the poet's saying:

*By you, O Quraysh, we were relieved of every difficulty, and whoever was astray was guided to the path of right guidance.*

And the other's saying:

*And a broad-faced she-camel carries me towards the crier of battle, with a warrior clad in armour, like a stallion groomed and combed.*

So "Quraysh" is a substitute from the pronoun of the addressee, and "with a warrior clad in armour" is a substitute from the pronoun of the speaker. *Aw* may also come with the meaning of *wa* when it conjoins what cannot be avoided, as in his saying:

*A people who, when they hear the cry for help, you see them between one who bridles his colt and one who bridles it and mounts.*

He means: "and one who mounts." Likewise it is permissible here that *aw* has the meaning of *wa*, because when He mentioned ﴿the work of a worker﴾, it indicated generality; then He substituted from it by way of emphasis, and conjoined with the limits of the two parts what cannot be avoided, because general meaning is emphasised only by a general meaning like it. So there was no alternative to conjunction, so that the collective of the two conjoined elements might convey emphasis of generality. It became like the verse: *between one who bridles his colt and one who mounts*, because *bayn* (between) does not enter upon a single thing, so it is necessary to conjoin the companion of its genitive.

The meaning of ﴿you are of one another﴾: that is, the gathering of your males and your females is a single origin, so each of you is from the other, meaning from his origin. Since you share in the origin, likewise you share in the reward and in the acceptance of the work. Thus *min* here conveys true partitive meaning, and by this shared origin it points to the sharing in reward on one and the same footing. It has been said: its meaning is "some of you are from others" in religion and support, and the meaning is that the attribute of faith gathers them, as has come: "The Muslims' blood is equal" (*al-muslimūna tatakāfa' dimā'uhum*). It has been said: its meaning is that males are from females and females from males, and so the reward is likewise. Just as they share in this partial relation, so they share in the reward and the recompense. The sum of the meaning of this sentence is that it has been brought to clarify the participation of women with men in what God has promised His worshippers who work, and the cause of its revelation has already been mentioned, namely the question of Umm Salamah, and al-Hakim related it in his *Ṣaḥīḥ*.

﴿So those who emigrated, and were expelled from their homes, and were harmed in My way﴾. When He, exalted is He, mentioned that He does not waste the work of any worker, He mentioned those who did the noble deeds by which they deserve that their work should not be wasted and that their reward should not be withheld. He first mentioned emigration, which is leaving the homeland in which it is not possible to establish one's religion, for a place where that is possible. This is among the hardest things for a human being, for it is leaving the place in which he was raised and grew up with his people and in their way of life. Were it not for the impulses of error that were nurtured over the restraint of upbringing, he would not have been able to do it. Do you not see the saying of the poet, namely Ibn al-Rumi:

*Love of their homelands was made dear to men by the aims that youth fulfilled there.*

*When they remember their homelands, the covenants of childhood there remind them, so they yearn for it.*

And Ibn al-Ṣafī, Rifa'ah ibn ʿĀṣim al-Faqʿasī, said:

*The most beloved of God's lands to me, between Manʿaj and Salmā, is that its clouds should pour rain.*

*A land in which my amulets were hung on me, and the first earth that touched my skin was its dust.*

*In it my robe long trailed behind me for a period, and Zaynab, whose anklet jingles, and whose girlhood is full-bodied.*

The name of emigration and its specific merit ended after the Conquest, but the meaning remains until the Day of Resurrection. The meaning of the *mufāʿalah* in *hājara* has already preceded. Then He mentioned expulsion from homes, which means that they were compelled and forced to it, and in it is the imputation of the sin to the unbelievers. The meaning is that the emigrants were driven out only by the evil conduct of the unbelievers towards them and their ugly deeds, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the expulsion of its people from it is greater in the sight of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217]. When the going out is by a person's own judgement and strength against the enemies, the speech attributes the going out to him, so it is said: "So-and-so went out." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said this meaning. He said: From this is the Prophet's ﷺ denial of Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith when he recited to him:

*And he who drove me away returned me to God, every driving away.*

The Messenger ﷺ said to him: "You drove me away every driving away," as a denial against him. And from it is the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

*In a band of Quraysh, one of them said, when they had embraced Islam in the valley of Makkah: "Depart!" They departed, and there was no retreat, nor any turning aside at the encounter, nor any leaning of those who had been dismissed.*

End of quotation. Then He mentioned being harmed in the way of God, and the meaning is: in the religion of God. He began first with the specific, which is emigration, and it was used to refer to emigration to Madinah to the Messenger of God ﷺ; then He followed it with what arises from it and is more general than emigration, which is expulsion from homes, for one may go out to emigrate to Madinah or to other than it, like those who went out to Abyssinia, and like the going out of Abu Jandal when he was not left to remain in Madinah. Thirdly He mentioned harm, which is more general than being expelled from homes or other kinds of harm. After these noble attributes, He rose to the rank of striving against the one who expelled them, resisting him, and being martyred in the religion of God. So He combined the ranks of these deeds: the diminishing of their conditions in life for the sake of the religion of God through emigration, the expulsion from their homes, the harm inflicted upon them for God's sake, and their end, which is finally their being annihilated by being killed in the way of God. The apparent reading is that the reference to the one who combined all these attributes is by the predicate that follows, and it is permissible that this be coordination of relative clauses (*ʿaṭf al-ṣilāt*). The meaning is the difference of the relative pronouns, not their unity; so it is as if it were said: "those who emigrated, and those who were expelled, and those who were harmed, and those who fought, and those who were killed," and the predicate would concern each of these. The majority of the Seven read ﴿and fought and were killed﴾, while Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "and were killed and fought," beginning with the passive and then the active, so this reading is explained on the basis that *wa* does not indicate order, so the second happened first. It may also be that this is by distribution, so the meaning is: some of them were killed and the rest of them fought. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz read "and killed and were killed" without an *alif*, beginning with the first built for the active and the second built for the passive, and this is a good reading in meaning, covering both states in the commonly known order. Muharib ibn Dithar read "and killed" with a *fatḥah* on the *qāf*, and "and fought." Talhah ibn Muṣarrif read "and were killed and fought" with a *ḍammah* on the *qāf* of the first, and *tashdīd* on the *tāʾ*, and in its explanation it is like the first reading. Abu Raja' and al-Hasan read "and fought and were slaughtered" with *tashdīd* on the *tāʾ* and the passive construction, meaning they were cut to pieces in the battle.

﴿I will surely remove from them their misdeeds, and I will surely admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. *La-ukaffiranna* is the answer to an omitted oath, and the oath with what it is attached to is the predicate of His saying ﴿So those who emigrated﴾. In this verse and its like, such as His saying ﴿And those who emigrated for God's sake after they had been wronged, We will surely settle them﴾ [al-Nahl: 41], and ﴿And those who strove in Us, We will surely guide them to Our ways﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 69], and the saying of the poet:

*She became distressed, so I said: "Surely what you fear will come to pass; and when it comes upon you, there is no escape."*

This is a refutation of Ahmad ibn Yahya Thaʿlab, who claimed that a clause occurring as the predicate of a subject cannot be an oath clause.

﴿As a reward from God; and with God is the finest reward﴾. *Thawāban* is in the accusative as an emphasising infinitive (*maṣdar mu'akkad*), although the reward is the thing by which one is rewarded, just as the gift is the thing given. It is used in some places with the meaning of the verbal noun which is giving, so *thawāban* is placed in the position of *ithābah* (rewarding), or of *tathwīban*, because what precedes it has the meaning of "I will surely reward them." Its parallel is: *ṣun'a Allāh* (the work of God) and *waʿd Allāh* (the promise of God). It is permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the gardens, meaning rewarded by them, or from the pronoun of the object in ﴿and I will surely admit them﴾, meaning rewarded. It is also permitted that it be a substitute from the gardens by implying in ﴿and I will surely admit them﴾ the meaning "and I will surely give them." It is also permitted that it be an object of an omitted verb indicated by the meaning, meaning: He gives them a reward. It has been said that it is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyīz*). Al-Kisa'i said: it is in the accusative as a cut-off (*qaṭʿ*), and the meaning of these two sayings does not become clear to me here.

The meaning of "from God" (*min ʿind Allāh*) is from the side of God's bounty, which is exclusive to Him: no one else rewards with it, and no one else has power over it. Just as you say: "With me is what you want," meaning your exclusive possession of it and your ownership of it, even if it is not in your presence. They parsed ﴿with Him is the finest reward﴾ as a subject, and a predicate in the position of the predicate of the first subject. The better view is that "the finest" (*ḥusn*) is raised as the agent, since the adverbial phrase has taken the place of a predicate, so the implied sense is: "And God is established; or the finest reward is established with Him." Al-Zamakhshari said: This is an instruction from God on how one should call upon Him, and how one should supplicate and humble oneself before Him. The repetition of "our Lord" is from the category of supplication, and an announcement of what necessitates the goodness of the answer and the goodness of the recompense: enduring hardships in the religion of God, patience over the difficulty of its obligations, cutting off the hopes of the lazy who wish for things from Him, and a record against him who does not see reward as connected to deeds, because of ignorance and dullness. End of quotation. The last of his words is an allusion to the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah and a criticism of the People of the Sunnah and the Community (*Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamaʿah*).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 3, verse 196–198:

﴿Let not the fluctuating fortunes of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you.﴾ It is said: it was revealed concerning the Jews, who would travel through the land and gain wealth; this is related from Ibn Abbas. He also said: they are the people of Makkah. It is also narrated that some of the believers used to see the abundance, ease and comfortable living in which they were, and would say: "The enemies of Allah are, as we see, in good, while we have perished from hunger and hardship." Muqatil said: it refers to the polytheists of the Arabs; the word "those who disbelieved" is general, and the kaf is for address. It was said: it is addressed to every listener. It was also said: it is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, and what is meant is his ummah. This is said by Ibn Atiyyah. He said: "Let not deceive you" in this verse is revealed in the sense of: "Do not think that the state of the disbelievers is good, so that you should be concerned about it." This is because the one who is deceived is joyful about the thing by which he is deceived. The disbelievers are deluded by their fluctuations, while the believers are concerned about them. But it may occur to the heart of a believer that this respite granted to the disbelievers is in fact good for them, and so this becomes an inclination towards their condition and a kind of being deceived. For this reason, "Let not deceive you" is apt. Its parallel is the saying of Umar to Hafsah: "Let not deceive you that your neighbour is more beautiful than you and dearer to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." The meaning: do not be deceived by the favour that accrues to that woman, lest you fall into it and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ divorce you. End. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Let not deceive you" is addressed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, or to everyone. That is: do not look at what they have of abundance of provision, the movement, the attainment of the immediate, and the acquisition of worldly portions, and do not be deceived by the outward appearance of their expansion in the land and their dealings in the lands. If you say: how was it permissible for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to be deceived by that, so that he was forbidden from it and from being deceived by it? I say: there are two aspects to this. One is that the leader and foremost of a people is addressed with something, and his address stands in place of addressing them all; it is as if it were said: "Let not deceive you." The second is that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was not deceived by their condition, but he was emphasised in what he already was and remained firm in his commitment, as in His saying: ﴿And do not be among the disbelievers﴾ [Hud: 42], ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 14], ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾ [al-Qalam: 8]. In prohibition this is the parallel of His saying in command: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6], ﴿O you who have believed, believe﴾ [al-Nisa: 136]. The prohibition is outwardly directed at the fluctuation, while in meaning it is directed at the one addressed. This is of the type of attributing the cause to the effect's place, because if the fluctuation were to deceive him, he would be deceived by it; so the cause is forbidden in order that the effect may be prevented. End of his words. The summary of the two aspects he mentioned: either the address is to him while the intended meaning is his ummah, or it is to him by way of emphasis and warning, even though he is protected from falling into it, as it is said:

Sharp sword is brandished though it is a sword, and the steed is hamstrung though it is a steed.

Ibn Abi Ishaq and Yaʿqub read: ﴿لا يَغُرَّنْكَ﴾ and (لا يَصُدَّنْكَ), (لا يَصُدَّنْكم), (لا يَغُرَّنْكم) and the like, with the light nun. He also said: they are the people of Makkah. Muqatil said: it refers to the polytheists of the Arabs; the word "those who disbelieved" is general, and the kaf is for address. It was said: it is addressed to every listener. It was also said: it is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, and what is meant is his ummah. This is said by Ibn Atiyyah. He said: "Let not deceive you" in this verse is revealed in the sense of: "Do not think that the state of the disbelievers is good, so that you should be concerned about it." This is because the one who is deceived is joyful about the thing by which he is deceived. The disbelievers are deluded by their fluctuations, while the believers are concerned about them. But it may occur to the heart of a believer that this respite granted to the disbelievers is in fact good for them, and so this becomes an inclination towards their condition and a kind of being deceived. For this reason, "Let not deceive you" is apt. Its parallel is the saying of Umar to Hafsah: "Let not deceive you that your neighbour is more beautiful than you and dearer to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." The meaning: do not be deceived by the favour that accrues to that woman, lest you fall into it and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ divorce you. End. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Let not deceive you" is addressed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, or to everyone.
