﴿Wa-inna min ahli al-kitabi la-man yu'minu billahi wa-ma unzila ilaykum wa-ma unzila ilayhim﴾ (And among the People of the Book are those who believe in God, and in what has been sent down to you and what has been sent down to them). This was revealed when Ashama al-Najashi, king of Abyssinia (al-Habasha), died. The meaning of Ashama in Arabic is "gift" (atiyya).

Sufyan ibn Uyayna and others said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed over him (the funeral prayer)." Someone said: "Is the Christian foreigner (ilj) prayed over, while he is in his own land?" So this was revealed. This is reported by Jabir ibn Abdullah, Ibn Abbas, and Anas.

Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning the Najashi and his companions.

Ibn Abbas, as transmitted from him by Abu Salih, said: it was revealed concerning the believers among the People of the Book, from the Jews and the Christians. Mujahid also said this.

Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd and Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions.

Ata said: it was revealed concerning forty men from Najran, thirty-two from Abyssinia, and eight from Byzantium (al-Rum), who were upon the religion of Jesus and then believed in the Prophet (ﷺ).

As for "man" (من) in "la-man" (لمن), the apparent view is that it is a relative pronoun (mawsula). It has also been permitted that it be an indefinite noun with a descriptive clause (nakira mawsufa), meaning: "la-qawman" (indeed, a people). "What has been sent down to us" is the Qur'an, and "what has been sent down to them" is their Book.

﴿Khashi'ina lillahi la yashtaruna bi-ayati Allahi thamanan qalila﴾ (humbly submissive before God, they do not barter the signs of God for a small price), as their rabbis bartered them, those who did not believe.

The accusative form of "khashi'in" (خاشعين) is a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "yu'minu" (يؤمن). Likewise, "la yashtaruna" (لا يشترون) is in the position of an accusative circumstantial state. It has been said that "khashi'in" is a state from the pronoun in "ilayhim" (إليهم), with the governing element being "unzila" (أنزل). It has also been said that it is a state from the pronoun in "la yashtaruna," but these two opinions are weak.

For the one who takes "man" as an indefinite noun with a descriptive clause, it is permissible that "khashi'in" and "la yashtaruna" are two descriptions of the indefinite noun. "Khashi'in" is put in the plural according to the meaning of "man," just as it is in "wa-ma unzila ilayhim" (وما أنزل إليهم). It was first treated according to the wording (lafz) in His saying "yu'minu," so it was made singular. When two kinds of agreement (hamlan) occur together, the preferable approach is to begin with agreement according to the wording.

In the verse, the expression "yu'minu" is used instead of "amana," even though the faith of those concerning whom it was revealed had already occurred, as an indication of continuity and persistence. He described them with humility (khushu'), which is submission and lowliness, incompatible with arrogance and pride, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿wa-annahum la yastakbirun﴾ (and that they are not arrogant) [al-Ma'ida: 82].

﴿Ula'ika lahum ajruhum 'inda rabbihim﴾ (Those will have their reward with their Lord). That is, the reward of their faith. This reward is doubled twice, according to the explicit text of the authentic hadith: "Indeed, whoever among the People of the Book believes, his reward will be given twice" (wa-anna man amana min ahli al-kitabi yu'ta ajrahu marratayn). The reward is multiplied for them in accordance with the multiple causes that were combined for them.

"'Inda" (عند) is an adverbial expression of place in the position of a circumstantial state, and the governing element in it is the same governing element in "lahum." The meaning of "'inda rabbihim" is: in Paradise.

﴿Inna Allaha sari'u al-hisab﴾ (Indeed, God is swift in reckoning). That is, He is swift in bringing the Day of Resurrection, which is the Day of Reckoning. The meaning is: their reward is near in coming, or its reckoning is swift because of the all-encompassing reach of His knowledge, for He knows what reward each doer deserves. The explanation of this sentence has already been given in full.

﴿Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu isbiru wa-sabiru wa-rabitu wa-ttaqu Allaha la'allakum tuflihun﴾ (O you who believe, be patient, outdo others in patience, be steadfast, and fear God, that you may succeed). God, may He be exalted, concluded this surah with this exhortation, which combines victory over the enemy in this world and success with the bliss of the Hereafter. So He commanded patience, perseverance in patience, and steadfastness (ribat).

It has been said: "isbiru" and "sabiru" have one meaning, for emphasis. Al-Hasan, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Jurayj said: be patient in obedience to God in His obligations, persevere in patience against the enemies of God in jihad, and be steadfast on the frontiers in the way of God. That is, tie down horses as your enemies tie them down.

Ubayy and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: it is the perseverance in waiting for God's promise of victory, that is, do not grow weary, and await relief.

It has been said: "rabitu" means prepare for jihad, as He said: ﴿wa-a'iddu lahum ma istata'tum min quwwatin wa-min ribati al-khayli turhibuna bihi 'aduwwa Allahi wa-'aduwwakum﴾ (and prepare against them whatever you can of power and of steeds of war, to strike terror into the enemy of God and your enemy) [al-Anfal: 60].

Abu Salama ibn Abd al-Rahman said: ribat is waiting for prayer after prayer, and there was no garrison-based warfare (ghazw murabit) during the time of the Messenger (ﷺ). He used as evidence the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Shall I not direct you to that by which God erases sins and raises ranks: performing ablution thoroughly in difficult conditions, walking many steps to the mosques, and waiting for prayer after prayer? That is ribat, that is ribat, that is ribat" (three times). According to this view, "rabitu" is not of the form of mufa'ala (reciprocal form).

Ibn Atiyya said: the correct view is that ribat is constant presence in the way of God. Its origin is from tying horses, then every person who remains constantly at one of the frontiers of Islam was called murabit, whether he was a horseman or on foot, and the picked-up item (luqata) is derived from ribt (tying). The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "That is ribat" is only a comparison to ribat in the way of God, since waiting for prayer is only one of the paths that save. The linguistic ribat is the first meaning.

According to the jurists, the murabit in the way of God is the one who travels to one of the frontiers to garrison there for a certain period. This was stated and transmitted by Ibn al-Mawwaz. As for those who live permanently on the frontiers with their families, who earn their living and make their livelihood there, they, although they are protectors, are not murabitun. The end of his words.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "wa-sabiru" (and outdo in patience) against the enemies of God in jihad means: surpass them in patience through the hardships of war, so that you are not less patient or steadfast than they are. Musabara is a kind of patience, mentioned after patience regarding what must be patiently endured, to confirm its intensity and difficulty. "Rabitu" means: stay on the frontiers, stationing your horses there, watching and prepared for raiding. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿wa-min ribati al-khayli turhibuna bihi 'aduwwa Allahi wa-'aduwwakum﴾ [al-Anfal: 60]. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever garrisons for one day and one night in the way of God, it is like the reward of fasting a month and standing in prayer during it, without breaking his fast and without turning from his prayer except for a necessity." The end of al-Zamakhshari's words.

In al-Bukhari, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A day of ribat in the way of God is better than the world and what is in it." In Muslim: "A day and night of ribat is better than a month of fasting and standing in prayer during it; and if he dies, his provision continues for him and he is safe from the tempter (fattan)." In the Sunan of Abu Dawud, he said: "Every dead person is sealed upon his deeds, except the murabit, for his deed continues to grow for him until the Day of Resurrection, and he is secured from the two tempters of the grave."

These verses include various kinds of eloquence and rhetorical ornament (badi'): 

Metaphor (istiara): He expressed the taking of the covenant as their commitment to the rulings of what was sent down to them of the Torah and the Gospel; the casting behind their backs as abandoning acting upon the requirements of those rulings; the purchase of a small price as what they accepted of worldly goods in exchange for concealing the signs of God; the hearing of the caller, if it is the Qur'an, as accepting what they received of command, prohibition, promise and warning, in responding to the acceptance of their petition; the absence of waste as not repaying them for their small deeds; turning about as striding through the land seeking gains; the cradle (mihad) as the settled place in which they dwell; the descent as what God hastens for them of honor in Paradise; the humility (khushu') which is the collapse of a place and the change of its landmarks, as their submission and humbling before Him; and the swiftness which is literally walking, as hastening His honor. It has been said: "al-hisab" may have been used metaphorically for recompense, as in ﴿wa-lam adri ma hisabiyah﴾ (and I did not know what my reckoning is) [al-Haqqa: 26], because the disbelievers are not given a reckoning, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿fa-habitat a'maluhum fa-la nuqimu lahum yawma al-qiyamati wazna﴾ (their deeds have come to nothing, and We shall not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection) [al-Kahf: 105].

Antithesis (tibaq): in ﴿la-tubayyinunnahu lil-nasi wa-la taktumunahu﴾ (you shall make it clear to the people and not conceal it) [Al 'Imran: 187]; in ﴿al-samawati wa-l-ard﴾ (the heavens and the earth) [Al 'Imran: 191]; and in ﴿ikhtilafi al-layli wa-l-nahar﴾ (the alternation of night and day) [Yunus: 6]. The sky is the direction of height, the earth is the direction of lowness, the night is an expression for darkness, and the day is an expression for light. Also in ﴿qiyaman wa-qu'udan﴾ (standing and sitting) [Al 'Imran: 191], and ﴿min dhakarin aw untha﴾ (male or female) [Al 'Imran: 195].

Repetition: in ﴿la tahsabanna﴾ (do not think) [Al 'Imran: 188] and ﴿fa-la tahsabannahum﴾ [Al 'Imran: 188]; in "Rabbana" (our Lord) in five places; and in ﴿fa-ghfir lana dhunubana wa-kaffir 'anna sayyi'atina﴾ (so forgive us our sins and remove from us our misdeeds) [Al 'Imran: 193], if the meaning is one; and in ﴿ma unzila ilaykum wa-ma unzila ilayhim﴾ (what has been sent down to you and what has been sent down to them), and in ﴿thawaban﴾ (reward) [Al 'Imran: 195] and ﴿husnu al-thawab﴾ (the best reward) [Al 'Imran: 195].

Restriction (ikhtisas): in ﴿li-ulil-albab﴾ (for people of understanding) [Al 'Imran: 190]; in ﴿wa-ma lil-zalimina min ansar﴾ (and the wrongdoers have no helpers) [Al 'Imran: 192]; in ﴿wa-tawaffana ma'a al-abrar﴾ (and let us die with the righteous) [Al 'Imran: 193]; in ﴿wa-la tukhzina yawma al-qiyamah﴾ (and do not disgrace us on the Day of Resurrection) [Al 'Imran: 194]; and in ﴿wa-ma 'inda Allahi khayrun lil-abrar﴾ (and what is with God is better for the righteous) [Al 'Imran: 198].

Paronomasia (tajnis): the identical kind in ﴿an amminu bi-rabbikum fa-amanna﴾ (believe in your Lord, so we believed) [Al 'Imran: 193], and in ﴿'amala 'amilin minkum﴾ (the work of any worker among you) [Al 'Imran: 195]; and the different kind (mughayir) in ﴿munadiyan yunadi﴾ (a caller calling) [Al 'Imran: 193].

Allusion (ishara): in ﴿ma khalaqta hadha batilan﴾ (You did not create this in vain) [Al 'Imran: 191]; and omission (hadhf) in several places.

﴿Wa-inna min ahli al-kitabi la-man yu'minu billahi wa-ma unzila ilaykum wa-ma unzila ilayhim﴾ (And among the People of the Book are those who believe in God, and in what has been sent down to you and what has been sent down to them). This was revealed when Ashama al-Najashi, king of Abyssinia (al-Habasha), died. The meaning of Ashama in Arabic is "gift" (atiyya).

Sufyan ibn Uyayna and others said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed over him (the funeral prayer)." Someone said: "Is the Christian foreigner (ilj) prayed over, while he is in his own land?" So this was revealed. This is reported by Jabir ibn Abdullah, Ibn Abbas, and Anas.

Al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning the Najashi and his companions.

Ibn Abbas, as transmitted from him by Abu Salih, said: it was revealed concerning the believers among the People of the Book, from the Jews and the Christians. Mujahid also said this.

Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd and Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions.

Ata said: it was revealed concerning forty men from Najran, thirty-two from Abyssinia, and eight from Byzantium (al-Rum), who were upon the religion of Jesus and then believed in the Prophet (ﷺ).

As for "man" (من) in "la-man" (لمن), the apparent view is that it is a relative pronoun (mawsula). It has also been permitted that it be an indefinite noun with a descriptive clause (nakira mawsufa), meaning: "la-qawman" (indeed, a people). "What has been sent down to us" is the Qur'an, and "what has been sent down to them" is their Book.

﴿Khashi'ina lillahi la yashtaruna bi-ayati Allahi thamanan qalila﴾ (humbly submissive before God, they do not barter the signs of God for a small price), as their rabbis bartered them, those who did not believe.

Likewise, "la yashtaruna" (لا يشترون) is in the position of an accusative circumstantial state. It has been said that "khashi'in" is a state from the pronoun in "ilayhim" (إليهم), with the governing element being "unzila" (أنزل). It has also been said that it is a state from the pronoun in "la yashtaruna," but these two opinions are weak.
